# INSTITUTIONS CONCERNING THE DECALOGUE OF THE LORD’S LAW (G)*

Its chapters are as follows:

**CHAPTER I.** On the three commandments of the first tablet.—**CHAPTER II.** On the seven commandments of the second tablet.—**CHAPTER III.** On the order of God’s commandments.—**CHAPTER IV.** On the substance of love and ordered charity.

## CHAPTER I.—On the three commandments of the first tablet

[Col. 0009A]

“Hear, O Israel: your God, God is one; you shall worship him, and serve him alone” (Deut. 6). Not all that is said here belongs to the commandment, because before the commandment the hearer’s mind is prepared for obedience by an exhortation. “Hear, O Israel.” Here note obedience. “Your God”: here note grace. “God is one”: here note doctrine; as if it were said: Offer obedience, understand grace, acknowledge truth.

What you hear is the obedience required of you. “Your God” is the grace that goes before. “God is one” is the truth by which you are enlightened and perfected. Hear your God, who has already shown you mercy and has not yet received service from you, so that you may know that both come from him: both the work of virtue which he requires of you, and the reward of recompense which he promises you.

[Col. 0009B] “Hear, O Israel,” that is, listen and assent. For every virtue begins with obedience, just as every vice proceeds from disobedience. Grace would be given in vain to one who disobeys; doctrine to one who is obstinate; a commandment to one who does not understand. Therefore first, “Hear, O Israel,” so that you may be obedient; “your God,” so that you may be devout; “God is one,” so that you may acknowledge truth.

Then follows the commandment: “You shall worship him”; this pertains to faith. “And serve him alone”; this pertains to action. For faith working through love makes a person perfect, since neither a work without faith nor faith, when there is opportunity for action, is acceptable without works. Therefore worship by right belief; serve by good action.

It may be asked whether the words “him alone” are to be referred to both clauses, so that one should say, “You shall worship him alone and serve him alone.” But how could this stand, since we read frequently in the Old Testament that holy men worshipped not only [Col. 0009C] angels [Col. 0010A] but also human beings, and yet nowhere find them reproved for this? And in the New Testament the Apostle strongly exhorts even the faithful to serve those above them and their prelates.

We must therefore know that people are worshipped in one way, while God is commanded to be worshipped in another. For in ancient usage all superiors were said to be worshipped by inferiors when reverence was shown them by bending the knees or inclining the head. But to worship God is to subject one’s whole mind to him in humility and devotion, and to believe him to be the beginning and end of every good. No one of sound mind can doubt that we owe this to him alone. Thus he himself also testifies concerning himself through the prophet, saying: “I will not give my glory to another, [Col. 0010B] nor my praise to graven images” (Isa. 42).

The same may fittingly be understood concerning service. Certainly, the person most rightly said to serve God alone is one who humbly subjects himself, in accordance with God, to a human superior, and who confidently resists wherever God’s cause is attacked; who carefully avoids doing anything against God in his service through fear of a human being, or preferring the gain of earthly recompense in his intention to the heavenly reward.

But the meaning is expressed more clearly in Greek. Greek speech distinguishes divine service from human service by its own proper term, which Latin does not possess: for there service to God is called *latria*, and human service *dulia*. Hence idolaters are so called because they rendered to idols the service they owed to God. But the Latin language [Col. 0010C] includes both kinds of service under the one name *servitus*, and therefore the meaning becomes more obscure when it says, “You shall serve him alone”; in Greek it is not ambiguous.

[Col. 0011A] But since this commandment pertains to the Father, why is it said, “You shall serve him alone,” as though the Son and the Holy Spirit were not also to be served? Yet the word “alone” does not exclude the fellowship of the Son and Holy Spirit, but excludes whatever is not God. For Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God; he alone is to be worshipped, and to him alone—and not to another—is due that service which is owed to him alone.

For in the Gospel, when it says, “No one knows the Father except the Son” (Matt. 15), etc., the Holy Spirit is certainly not excluded from knowledge of the Father, since, as the Apostle testifies, he searches even the depths of God (1 Cor. 2). But this is a manner of speaking: “no one except that one,” namely, one who is not other than he.

[Col. 0011B] Having treated these briefly, let us proceed to examine the following commandment, which is this: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Exod. 20). In its plain literal sense, this must be understood to mean that a person must not take God’s name in vain, that is, either to confirm a lie or to worship an idol: he must neither honor idols with the divine name nor associate God’s name with falsehood.

Mystically, however, to take God’s name in vain is to suppose that the Son of God, made visible through humanity, is a creature. For that person takes God’s name in vain who believes that the eternal Son of God began in time. The Son is called the name of the Father, because in the Son and through the Son the invisible Father is made manifest, not only when the world was made through him, but [Col. 0011C] also when humanity was redeemed through him.

Certainly, those who confess that the Son of God was made man by no means take God’s name in vain, because they acknowledge as true God, in respect of what he was from eternity, him whom they believe to be man in respect of what he assumed in time.

The saying, “You shall not take the name of your God in vain,” may still be understood in another way. For those take God’s name in vain who despise the Son of God sent to them and incarnate for their salvation. What, then, is the meaning of “You shall not take the name of your God in vain,” except: As you revere and worship him because you were made by him, so worship and revere him because you were redeemed by him, who conferred no less upon you in redeeming you than in creating you?

The same meaning is intended by what the Son himself says in the Gospel to the disciples, and through the disciples to all who believe in him: “You believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14). [Col. 0011D] With a restrained intimation—fitting for one who is loving—he warns us to understand that he is to be worshipped by us not only in his divinity, by which he created, but also in the humanity by which he redeemed.

The third commandment is: “Observe the Sabbath day” (Deut. 5). Scripture seems to mention four Sabbaths. The first is that on which God is said to have rested after perfecting his works. The second is that which the children of Israel are commanded to observe carnally. The third is that which the people of God are commanded to keep spiritually. The fourth is that which God promises his lovers in the promise: [Col. 0012A] “Sabbath for Sabbath, month for month.”

There are, then, two outward Sabbaths, one of God and one of humanity; and two inward Sabbaths, one of God and one of humanity. God’s Sabbath, on which he is said outwardly to have ceased from work, is the sacrament of that inward Sabbath of his in which his eternal immortality and immortal eternity, enjoying perpetual and unshaken blessedness, is never wearied by any labor. Humanity’s Sabbath, which it is commanded visibly to observe outwardly, is the sacrament of the inward Sabbath, where the holy mind, resting through a good conscience from the bondage of sin, rejoices in the joy of the Holy Spirit.

Whoever keeps this Sabbath in the present life in such a way as to consent to no evils will attain in the future life to that inward and eternal [Col. 0012B] Sabbath of God, where he will feel no evils, as it is said: “And there shall be Sabbath for Sabbath, month for month.” This commandment seems especially to refer to the person of the Holy Spirit when it says, “Observe the Sabbath”: namely, that in the present we may receive him and keep him within us in the joy of a good conscience, so that in the future we may deserve to receive and possess him in the joy of eternal life.

These, then, are the three commandments of the first tablet, in which love of God is chiefly commended, and the whole Trinity—one God—is commanded to be worshipped and honored equally.

## CHAPTER II.—On the seven commandments of the second tablet

The second tablet contained seven other commandments which instruct humanity in love of neighbor. They are accordingly divided by the number seven, because only in the present life, which revolves through seven days, is our charity exercised toward our neighbor in works of piety; afterward, when the works are accomplished and the labors ended, it is to be made blessed in God through contemplation together with the neighbor.

[Col. 0012C] Thus love of neighbor is temporal in regard to the performance of the work, and eternal in regard to the effect of love. The first commandment of the second tablet concerns the human father, as the first of the first tablet concerns God the Father. In both places fatherhood is put first; in both it is honored with the dignity of a principle. For, in a certain manner, we have from a human father, through generation, the principle of being born, just as we have received from God the Father, through creation, the principle of existing. And human fatherhood is the sacrament and image of divine fatherhood, so that the human heart may learn from the principle it sees what it owes to that principle from which it is and which it does not see.

Thus it is said: “Honor your father and your mother, that it may go well with you, and that you may be long-lived upon the earth” (Deut. 5). As was said above concerning the first commandment of the first tablet, so here too not everything set down belongs to the command. There what was outside the command was placed before it; here it is added after it. “Hear, O Israel: your God, God is one”: all this is placed before the commandment; the command itself is then introduced: “You shall worship him and serve him alone.” Here the command comes first: “Honor your father and your mother,” [Col. 0013A] and then is added, “that it may go well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth.”

Why, then, is the ground for the command added before the command there, but after it here, except because God is to be loved for his own sake, and humanity for God’s sake? For even love of parents, if it looks only to the flesh, does not obtain a spiritual reward. Thus, in God there is first within us that for which he is afterward to be loved by us, because our love is preceded by his grace, and follows after it, awakened through his grace.

But in the fathers of our flesh, if our love is directed only to the benefit by which our desert is carnally anticipated by them, then, because it advances no further than fleshly affection and the perspective of flesh, it does not reach the perfection of spiritual reward. Therefore the author of temporal life is to be loved for the sake of eternal life: that is, he should be loved not because we have received this life from him—or rather through him—but because through him we shall enter into life.

Rightly, then, when it had been said, “Honor your father,” the reason was added: “that it may go well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth,” namely, the earth of the living. For in the author of this life we ought to love this: that through him we have been initiated through this life into the life to come. And long life is beautifully promised to one who honors his principle, because clinging to God through love earns eternity.

Certainly, as regards the literal sense, we ought to honor our parents in two ways: by obeying them in all things except those in which love of God the Father is offended, and by helping them, insofar as our means allow. Nothing prevents the same from being understood concerning spiritual fathers, that is, our prelates, to whom we owe obedience insofar as we can, and help—indeed service—insofar as our resources allow.

[Col. 0013C] The second commandment is: “You shall not kill” (Deut. 5). It is fitting that one to whom long life is promised in the preceding command is here forbidden to extinguish another’s life: so that it belongs to love of God that, honoring his own principle, he should aspire to a life without end; and to love of neighbor that he should not surrender himself to any cruel hatred that brings another’s life to an end.

Then follows the third commandment: “You shall not commit adultery” [Col. 0013D] (ibid.); and the fourth: “You shall not steal” (ibid.). “You shall not commit adultery” pertains to one’s own life; “you shall not steal” pertains to another’s life. Above, one was commanded to preserve both one’s own life and another’s; here one is commanded not to harm either one’s own or another’s life.

For it is just that one who awaits incorruptible life in the homeland should avoid corruption on the way of life; and that one who does not oppress a neighbor’s life by open violence should not harm him by secret fraud in those things given for the use of life. Nor should he himself cause harm, nor presume to give, by his authority or testimony, confidence or support to persons who cause harm or wish to cause it. For this is forbidden in the following command [Col. 0014A] when it says: “You shall not give false testimony” (ibid.).

And because a person cannot long restrain himself from the act of injury if he does not restrain his mind from the intention and will to injure, it follows and says: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife; nor shall you covet your neighbor’s property” (ibid.). So that you may not commit adultery, do not covet your neighbor’s wife; so that you may not steal, do not covet your neighbor’s property.

These are the ten commandments, which lay open the path and track of the first perfection. The first perfection directs a person within himself through good action. The second expands him broadly through charity toward neighbor. The third raises him on high through charity toward God. For the number ten extends the line of the first perfection; a hundred expands the breadth of the second; a thousand [Col. 0014B] raises the summit of perfection on high.

## CHAPTER III.—On the order of God’s commandments

One ought not to pass over without consideration the order of God’s commandments themselves. For if there is an order of living, there is certainly also an order of commanding.

First, therefore, attend to what is said to you: that you should worship your God and serve him. This is the first commandment. In worship recognize faith; in service understand good action. After this follows the second commandment: that you should not take the name of your God in vain, so that the word of truth may be in your mouth for truth’s sake, and confession with the mouth may follow faith of the heart. First devotion for a good conscience; afterward the example of action for a good reputation; finally, the word of preaching for instruction.

Then [Col. 0014C] follows the third commandment, and you are told to observe the Sabbath: that is, preserve the tranquility of your mind, so that you are not disturbed, for the sake of truth, by adversities encountered from without. Rather, learn to be peaceable even among those who hate peace; preach truth, and do not neglect charity.

These are the three commandments of the first tablet, concerning matters that pertain to God. After these follows the second tablet, concerning matters that pertain to neighbor. The first commandment of the second tablet commands you to honor your principle, so that you may have long life, since one who does not honor him from whom he is deserves to be unable to retain that which he is.

The second, “You shall not kill,” follows in due order, because if, by keeping the first commandment of this tablet, [Col. 0014D] you wish to be long-lived upon the earth, it accords with reason and the dictate of nature that you should kill no one, and should do to no other person what you would not wish done to yourself. The third, fourth, and fifth also agree with this. For just as you wish not only to have your life preserved but also your spouse, property, and reputation inviolate, so it is fitting that you should not commit adultery, steal, or give false testimony, by which, finally, you can harm your neighbor in three things: life, property, and reputation.

Moreover, because for justification it is not enough to restrain the hand from unlawful acts through fear of punishment, but it is necessary that we restrain even the mind through love of God and virtue, the two remaining commandments are rightly added: that you should covet neither your neighbor’s wife nor his property.

[Note: [Col. 0015D] The manuscripts present this chapter, under the title “On the Substance of Love,” as a distinct little work. [Col. 0016D] It also appears among the works of Saint Augustine, vol. VI, col. 843, Migne edition.]

## CHAPTER IV.—On the substance of love and ordered charity

[Col. 0015A]

We sow daily discourse concerning love, lest perhaps, without our noticing, it should sparkle in our hearts and blaze up into flame, either consuming everything or purging everything. For from it comes everything that is good, and from it comes everything that is evil. One fountain of love, springing within, pours out two streams. One is love of the world, namely cupidity; the other is love of God, namely charity.

For the human heart is the middle place from which the fountain of love bursts forth; and when it is drawn outward by appetite, it is called cupidity; but when it directs its desire inward, it is called charity. Thus two streams flow from the fountain of love: cupidity and [Col. 0015B] charity. Cupidity is the root of all evils, and charity the root of all goods. Therefore from it comes everything good, and from it comes everything evil.

Whatever this thing is that is within us, then, it is great; and from it comes all that is in us. But this is love. What is love, and how great is it? What is love, or whence is love? And the word of God speaks of love. Is this subject not rather the business of those who are accustomed to prostitute love and chastity? See how many wish to receive its mysteries, and how few are not ashamed to bring its words into public.

What, then, are we doing? Perhaps we have a brow hardened by much shamelessness, since we are not ashamed to frame a discourse on love, which even the shameless sometimes cannot express in words without embarrassment. But it is one thing to investigate vice so that it may be uprooted; another to exhort people to vice, so that virtue and truth may not be loved.

We investigate and inquire in order to know, and, knowing, to beware. They investigate in order to know, but to know in order to do. We ask what it is in us that divides our desires in so many directions and draws our heart into diverse paths. We find it to be nothing other than love. Although by nature it is one single and unique motion of the heart, it is divided in its action: when it moves in a disordered manner, that is, toward things toward which it ought not to move, it is called cupidity; but when it is ordered, it is called charity.

By what definition, then, can we designate this motion of the heart which we call love? [Col. 0015D] It is expedient to look more closely at it, lest it be concealed and unknown, and thus neither avoided when evil nor sought and found when good. For when it is evil, such great evils arise from it; and when it is good, such great goods proceed from it. Let us therefore investigate and consider how we define it, since what we seek is hidden; and the more inwardly it is situated, the more it rules the heart in both directions.

Thus love appears to be, and is, the heart’s attachment of someone to something for the sake of something: desire in seeking, joy in enjoyment; running through desire and resting through joy.

[Col. 0016A] Here is your good and here is your evil, O human heart, because you are good from no other source if you are good, and evil from no other source if you are evil, except that you love that which is good either badly or well. For everything that exists is good; but when that which is good is loved badly, that thing is good, but the loving is evil. Therefore neither the one who loves is evil, nor what he loves is evil, nor the love by which he loves is evil; but he loves badly, and this is all evil. Therefore order charity, and there is no evil any longer.

We wish to commend a great matter, if indeed we can accomplish what we wish. Almighty God, who needs nothing because he himself is the highest and true good; who can receive nothing from another by which he may increase, since all things are from him; and can lose nothing of his own by which he may decline, since all things stand unchangeably in him: he created the rational spirit from charity alone, not from any necessity, in order to make it a participant in his blessedness.

Moreover, so that it might be fit to enjoy such great blessedness, he made love in it—a spiritual palate, signifying something for the tasting of inward sweetness—so that through this love it might taste the delight of his happiness and cling to it with tireless desire.

Thus through love God joined the rational creature to himself, so that by always adhering to him it might, from him, as it were, draw by affection the good by which it was to be made blessed; drink from him by desire; and possess him in joy.

[Col. 0016C] Draw, O little bee, draw! Draw and drink the ineffable sweetness of your sweetness. Immerse yourself and be filled, because he does not know how to fail, unless you begin to grow weary. Therefore cleave and adhere; take and enjoy. If the tasting is everlasting, the blessedness too will be everlasting.

Let us no longer be ashamed or repent that we have spoken of love. Let there be no repentance where there is such great usefulness; no shame where there is such honorableness. Thus the rational creature has been joined to its Maker through love; and love’s bond alone binds both into one and the same reality—the more happily, the more strongly.

For this reason, too, so that undivided fellowship and perfect concord might be maintained on both sides, this bond has grown into charity toward God and neighbor: so that through charity toward God all might adhere to the One, and through charity toward neighbor all might become one with one another. Thus what each person could not receive in himself from that One to whom all adhered, he might possess more fully and perfectly in another through love of neighbor; and the good of all might become wholly the good of each.

[Col. 0016D] Therefore order charity. What is it to order charity? If love is desire, let it run well; if it is joy, let it rest well. For love, as has been said, is the heart’s attachment of someone to something for the sake of something: desire in seeking, and joy in enjoyment; running through desire and resting through joy; running toward that thing and resting in it.

Toward what, or in what? Listen, if perhaps we can explain toward what our love ought to run, or in what it ought to rest. There are three things which may be loved well or badly: God, neighbor, and world. God is above us; neighbor is beside us; the world is beneath us. Therefore order charity. If it runs, let it run well; if it rests, let it rest well.

Desire runs; joy rests. Hence joy is uniform, because it is always in one thing and cannot be altered by change. Desire, however, admits changeability; therefore it does not keep itself to one thing but presents various forms. For every running is either from, with, or into that toward which it is directed.

[Col. 0017A] How, then, ought our desire to run? God, neighbor, and world are three. God should have three modes in the running of our desire; neighbor two; and world one. In this consists ordered charity in desire.

For through desire, love can run in an ordered way from God, with God, and into God. It runs from God when it receives from him that by which it loves him. It runs with God when it contradicts his will in nothing. It runs into God when it seeks to rest in him. These are the three things pertaining to God.

There are two concerning the neighbor. Desire can run from the neighbor, but it cannot run into the neighbor. It runs from the neighbor when it rejoices in the neighbor’s salvation and advancement. [Col. 0018A] It runs with the neighbor when it desires to have him as a companion on God’s way and a fellow participant in arrival. But it cannot run into the neighbor so as to place its hope and trust in a human being. These are the two things concerning the neighbor: from him and with him, but not into him.

There is one thing concerning the world: to run from it, not with it or into it. Desire runs from the world when, on seeing outwardly God’s work, it turns inward toward God himself more ardently through admiration and praise. It would run with the world if, through the changeability of temporal things, it conformed itself to this age, whether by being cast down in adversity or lifted up in prosperity. It would run into the world if it wished always to rest in its pleasures.

Therefore order charity: let desire run from God, with God, and into God; from the neighbor and with the neighbor, but not into the neighbor; from the world, but neither with the world nor into the world. And let it rest in joy in God alone. For if love is joy, let it rest well; if it is desire, let it run well. For love, as has been said, is the heart’s attachment of someone to something for the sake of something: desire in seeking and joy in enjoyment, running toward one thing and resting in it. This is ordered charity; apart from it, everything done is not ordered charity, but disordered cupidity.

[Col. 0017]

# DIALOGUE ON THE SACRAMENTS OF THE NATURAL AND WRITTEN LAW, THE TEACHER MARKED BY M. AND THE DISCIPLE MARKED BY D. The disciple speaks first.

[Col. 0017C] **D.** What existed before the world was made?  
**M.** God alone.

**D.** How long had he existed before it?  
**M.** From eternity.

**D.** Where was he when nothing existed besides himself?  
**M.** He was then where he is now.

**D.** Where is he now?  
**M.** He is in himself, and all things are in him, and he is in all things.

**D.** When did God make the world?  
**M.** “In the beginning” (Gen. 1).

**D.** Where was the world made?  
**M.** In God.

**D.** From what was the world made?  
**M.** From nothing.

**D.** How was the world made?  
**M.** First all things were made together in matter; afterward, all things were composed and ordered over six days into that form in which the world is now seen.

**D.** How could matter exist before form?  
**M.** That matter was not [Col. 0017D] altogether without form; yet it is said first to have been unformed, because in its first creation it did not yet have as seemly and suitable a form as it now has.

**D.** Why did God wish first [Col. 0018C] to create crude matter, as though he could not have created it together with form?  
**M.** He wished first to show what the creature was in itself, and what it afterward received through the Creator’s beneficence; and therefore he first created its essence and afterward gave it form.

**D.** To whom was he showing this, when there was as yet no one able to see it?  
**M.** The angels already existed then, to whom this might be shown, so that outwardly in created things they might see what they inwardly recognized in themselves, lest they too should think that the glory they had received was to be ascribed to themselves rather than to their Creator. This is shown also to us, who, although we did not see it when it was done, nevertheless have heard on the testimony of sacred speech that it was done.

**D.** Where, or of what kind, was that first matter before it was formed?  
**M.** It lay there confused where it now stands ordered. For the earth, set in the same place in which it now is—that is, in the middle place—was surrounded on every side by the three remaining [Col. 0018D] elements, water, air, and fire, still confused together in one darkness. This confusion, surrounding the earth on every side, occupied upward the same extent of space that the whole universe of creatures now encompasses.

The earth already had then some form, superior to that of the other elements; but being wrapped and covered over, what it was could not yet appear. The other three, as has been said, were altogether confused and unordered, suspended like a kind of cloud in the space now occupied by air and heaven. Scripture called that dark gloom “darkness”; at the beginning it hung over the face of the abyss—which had not yet been filled—being spread above it by the massing of waters.

D. What ordering was accomplished on the first day? M. Light was made on the first day [Col. 0019B] (Gen. 1). It had indeed previously been created materially among the other things; but now, for the first time, it was separated and distinguished from the others so that it might shine and give light. D. What kind of light is that to be thought to have been? M. Some maintain that it was a luminous cloud which, like the sun now, moved in a circuit around the earth. When, rising, it illumined the upper parts of the world, it made day; but when, setting, it descended to the lower regions, its withdrawn light made night. From this they hold that the first three days were distinguished and named at the beginning of creation, before the sun and the other lights were made. D. Where should that light now be said to be? M. They say that it is now scattered throughout the upper regions of the ether, and can still be seen if the greater brightness of the sun did not conceal it [Col. 0019C]; and that at night, to careful observers, traces of that light may still appear against the firmament, as it were certain very thin luminous clouds scattered about, which the greater brightness of day wholly hides from the eyes of those looking upon them.

D. What ordering was accomplished on the second day? M. The firmament was made on the second day (ibid.). It too had previously been created materially, but until then remained undistinguished and mingled in that universal confusion. Now, however—that is, on the second day—it was drawn out of the mixture, formed, and set in place, so as to divide the upper waters from the lower waters. Thus it came into the midst of that cloud-like confusion hanging around the earth [Col. 0019D] and, as it were, cut it in two; enclosing one portion beneath itself by embracing it on every side with its circuit, and separating the other outside itself. That is: the firmament, placed between the waters and the waters, was surrounded on every side by the waters which remained outside, or above, after the division; while the waters left inside, or below, were wholly enclosed on every side by the firmament. One part of the waters, therefore, remained above the firmament; the other part, enclosed below the circuit of the firmament, filled and occupied all the space of the air around it. D. Must we believe that waters still exist above the firmament? M. So it is thought, because Holy Scripture clearly confirms this in various places, as in the Psalmist’s testimony: [Col. 0020A] “Let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148).

D. How can waters remain above heaven? M. Either in a frozen state, or—what is more credible—there they hang firmly suspended, like the first chaos, in the manner of a light cloud; such, it is thought, was in the beginning the nature of all waters.

D. What was the ordering of the third day? M. Those waters which had remained hanging beneath the firmament were compacted together; and at last, pressed downward by their weight, they were gathered into one place (Gen. 1), namely, into that great abyss which they had previously covered from above. From it they are even now conducted to all parts of the earth through their channels and riverbeds. When the waters had been gathered [Col. 0020B], “the dry land appeared” (ibid.), that is, the earth, which had previously lain hidden, enveloped in that darkness and confusion. When it appeared, God clothed it with its plants; and thus the work of the third day was completed.

D. What ordering was accomplished on the fourth day? M. The lights were created in heaven—that is, the sun, moon, and stars—to shine upon the earth, illumine it, and distinguish the seasons by their course (ibid.).

D. What ordering was accomplished on the fifth day? M. Birds and fishes were made from the waters. The birds were then placed in the air; the fishes remained in their original abode (ibid.).

D. What ordering was accomplished on the sixth day? M. Beasts and the other living creatures which live upon the earth were created from the earth [Col. 0020C]. When all things had been completed and prepared, man was made last—though still on that same sixth day—to rule over the whole creation. D. Why were birds, which were placed in the air, not made from the air itself, as fishes were from water and both beasts and man from earth? M. Because air does not possess such corporeal substance that an animal can be made from it as from earth. D. Why was man made last? M. Because man was to be set over the whole creation, it was fitting that his dwelling should first be prepared and that he himself, after all things had been ordered, should then be introduced into the world as its possessor and ruler. These, then, are the works of creation which God made and completed in six days: creating before every day [Col. 0020D], arranging and ordering during the first three days, and adorning during the following three. On the first day he separated; on the second, distinguished; on the third, arranged; on the fourth, adorned the heavens; on the fifth, the air and water; and on the sixth, the earth. D. Why did God make his works in six days and rest on the seventh? M. Because the number six, being composed of its parts, is a sign of perfection. Therefore God chose to complete his works in six days, in order to show that in what he had made he had placed nothing superfluous and left nothing imperfect. When the six days had been completed, he finally rested on the seventh day (Gen. 2), that is, he ceased from work—not because he himself, as though weary, needed rest, but so that he might promise us rest to come if we strive, according to our own measure and capacity, to do good and perfect works. D. How is God said to have rested on the seventh day, when he himself says in the Gospel, “My Father is working still, and I am working” (John 5)? M. God is said to work in many ways. There is the work of creation, the work of ordering, the work of propagation, and the work of governance. He performed the work of creation before every day; he completed the work of ordering in six days; he does not abandon the work of propagation until the end of the age; and he will not cease from the work of governance unto eternity. D. If God first rested on the seventh day, what then did he do from the beginning of the first day, after making light, until the rising of the next day, when he was making the firmament? M. If you wish to consider the matter more closely, you will find that God did not, after the beginning of light on the first day, rest entirely from every work [Col. 0021B]. For not only did the making of the light belong to his work, but so also did its being directed until, having completed the circuit of its course, it finished its journey. Therefore, first, in order to begin his work with what was complete, he made the rising light; then, directing it onward, he completed first evening and then morning—that is, the first day. D. Must the works of the remaining days be understood in the same way? M. I would not rashly affirm anything in these matters. For although one might similarly say of the work of the second day that God first made the firmament between the waters and the waters, and then directed its course until the rising of the third day, nevertheless we have not yet found certain evidence concerning the motion of the firmament. Let us, if you please, untie the knot of this question in another way. For it may fittingly be said [Col. 0021C] that in those six days the Lord did not continue the sequence of his work in such a way as though he had interrupted it at no intervening interval of time; rather, he omitted no day in working. On the seventh day, however, he finally rested from every work, so that thereafter he neither created anything besides those things already made nor ordered, so far as pertains to the order of the universe, anything otherwise than it had already been ordered. For he afterwards added nothing to the number of the universe, nor changed the order of the universe in any respect. D. But what of the fact that even now new souls are created every day? M. Nevertheless, nothing new is said to be added, because those souls, although created from nothing and now beginning for the first time to exist, were nevertheless in some manner created then also in their likeness [Col. 0021D]. And, to state briefly what I think should be said on this point: all things were then made so that nothing might afterwards be made which had not previously been created either in matter or in likeness.

D. I see still further matters in these works worthy of inquiry, which I am compelled, though unwilling, to pass over, lest, if I detain you too long in such matters, I fail to reach the other matters which remain and are more necessary. Let us now, if you please, return to man, so that you may explain to me—the explanation being most earnestly desired—the cause of his creation. For surely it is fitting that we who already believe that all things were made for his sake should not be ignorant also why he himself was made. M. God, who is the highest, true, and perfect good, was from eternity so blessed in himself and through himself that his glory and blessedness, because eternal and unchangeable, could not be diminished, and because full and perfect, could not be increased [Col. 0022A]. Needing nothing, yet willing to share with others the good that he himself was and by which he was blessed, and to make others blessed in it and through it, he created rational creatures—not from any necessity, but from love alone—that is, rational spirits. He commanded that some should remain in their purity, while others, clothed with flesh, should animate a human body with life and sensation. For those spirits which were to be joined to bodies, he established a place and dwelling on earth; but for those which were to remain in their purity, he appointed a dwelling in heaven. The former he placed on high by condescension; the latter he ordered below by dispensation, so that he might at some time raise these from below to the heights through obedience, and confirm those in the heights through obedience. D. Why did God wish to join spirits to bodies, when they would have been of greater excellence had they remained in their purity? M. He wished to show in them through creation what he himself would afterwards accomplish in them through condescension. For since among created things nothing is more excellent than spirit and nothing lower or more corruptible than earth, when he gave to a body made from earth and possessing corruptible matter a rational spirit—that is, a rational soul—he joined, as it were, the lowest things with the highest in a single fellowship and society. He thereby showed that what the body was to the spirit, the spirit was in some manner to himself. And just as one creative act had joined the excellence of spirit to the weakness of bodily nature [Col. 0022B], so one merciful condescension ought to join the lowliness of the spiritual creature to the excellence of the Creator. Therefore, as has been said, he made the human body from the mud of the earth and breathed into it a rational soul, which he created from nothing (Gen. 2), so that, when it lived obediently in the body, he might at some time raise it, together with the body, to fellowship with those spirits who lived without bodies—that is, the angels—and likewise raise both alike to participation in his glory. Thus he would glorify spirit in himself and body in spirit; and as much as he had first lowered the highest things by dispensation in creating, so much would he now exalt the lowest things by condescension. D. Why did God not create human beings all at once, as he had created angels? M. Because he wished there to be one origin of the human race. D. Why did he wish this? M. To check the pride of the devil. Since the devil proudly sought to be an origin other than God, his exaltation would be more thoroughly confounded if man received this: namely, that even in this he should possess the dignity of God’s likeness, that as God was the principle of creation for all things, so man should be the principle of generation for all human beings. And all people, recognizing that they came from one and were one, should love one another as though they were one. D. Why was woman made? M. As a help for generation. D. Why was she made from man? M. Because, if she had been made from elsewhere, there would not be one origin. D. Why was she made from his side? M. To show that she was created for fellowship in love; lest, if she had been made from his head, she should seem to be set over the man in dominion [Col. 0023A], or, if from his feet, to be subjected to slavery. Therefore, because she was prepared for the man neither as mistress nor as handmaid but as companion, she was to be brought forth neither from his head nor from his feet, but from his side, so that he might recognize that she was to be placed beside him, having learned that she was taken from beside him. Therefore God cast a sleep upon Adam, took one of his ribs (Gen. 2), and fashioned a woman from it. D. Why did he wish to take the rib from him while he slept rather than while he was awake? M. Lest it be thought that he had taken it from him as a punishment. D. How could a woman be made from a rib alone? Did God add anything else externally to that rib for its increase, or create something new in addition, or did the rib itself begin to multiply within itself? M. If, for the completion of the woman’s body, God added external increase to that rib—when what was added was much greater than the rib itself to which it was added—Scripture ought rather to have said that the woman was made from that source from which she received the greater parts of her substance. Likewise, if what came to the rib as an increase is believed to have been made from nothing, why do we say that she was made from man rather than from nothing, when that part of her which was made from nothing is much greater than that which passed into her body from the man’s substance? It remains, therefore, that we should believe that the rib multiplied within itself and received no external addition. D. How can something grow when nothing is added to it from elsewhere? M. It is a greater thing to make something from nothing than to multiply a small substance within itself.

[Col. 0023C] D. That is certain; therefore continue with what remains. M. Thus, having been made outside paradise, they were placed in paradise, being instructed by precepts of life and discipline. D. Why was man, whose dwelling was to be in paradise, made outside paradise? M. So that he might attribute God’s benefit not to nature but to grace. D. By what precepts did God instruct man when he placed him in paradise? M. By two: the precept of nature and the precept of discipline. For God prepares two goods for man: one temporal and the other eternal, each full and perfect. He placed the first—that is, the temporal good—fully in man; and he set before him the other—that is, the eternal good—in its fullness. To that which he had given, he attached the safeguard of the precept of nature; to that which he had set before him, he opened the way by the precept of discipline [Col. 0023D]. The precept of nature contains command, prohibition, and permission. The natural command was the discernment by which he was inspired to know what was necessary to his nature; the natural prohibition was the discernment by which he was naturally instructed what was harmful; permission was the discernment of matters indifferent, that is, things which he could use or not use without harm. Therefore, if man, instructed by the natural precept, had guarded against negligence, divine providence would have permitted no violence to overwhelm him. For by the precept of nature man could preserve the good he possessed, but by it he could not attain the good he did not yet possess. For it could not be merit to a man either to avoid harmful things, seek wholesome things, or use indifferent things in either direction, since in all these he would attend not so much to the will of the one commanding as to the advantage of the one obeying. Therefore, in order that man might be able to merit something, it was necessary to add the precept of discipline. But this could be taken neither from command nor from prohibition, lest either, if God commanded or prohibited the same things, obedience should not be meritorious, as has been said, or, if he changed the command, he should become contrary to himself. It was necessary, therefore, that it be taken from permission; yet in such a way that permission was not changed by the precept itself—that is, so that the precept did not corrupt nature, but disobedience harmed the transgressor, not nature. Since, however, the precept of discipline had to be formed from natural permission, it was more fitting [Col. 0024B] that this be done in the form of a prohibition, lest the devil be able to malign obedience; and in one matter only, not several, lest disobedience be excused by man. Therefore, if man had persisted in this obedience, after a period appointed by God he ought to have been transferred, without the pain of death, to that highest good prepared for him in heaven, there to live eternally with all his offspring in the fellowship of blessed angels. D. Why did God will that there be need in man? M. So that he might take from it an occasion for exercise, and so that outward need might show him his inward need. D. Before sin, was man mortal or immortal? M. Both by power, neither by necessity; afterwards he would be both by necessity, neither by power—the one first through fault, the other afterwards through grace.

D. Where is paradise? M. Why do you ask for what you see? Your entrance is toward the east; that is the tree of life which you behold. D. Why was it called the tree of life? M. Because it possesses such power that its fruit can protect human life from the affliction of death and every infirmity. D. What is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil? M. That in which Adam transgressed. D. Why was it so called? M. Before Adam sinned, he knew good and evil: good both by knowledge and by experience, but evil by knowledge alone. But after he touched the forbidden tree, he began also to know evil by experience. Yet it was not the nature of the tree, but human disobedience, that gave this knowledge [Col. 0024D], since through the experience of evil he recognized also how strictly good ought to have been held. Therefore the name should be believed to have been given to the tree not from the nature which it possessed, but from the occasion which it supplied. D. How did man transgress? M. Seeing that man would ascend through obedience to the place from which he himself had fallen through pride, the devil envied him; and because he could not harm him by violence, he turned to deceit. But lest his deceit, if too hidden, could not be guarded against at all, he was not permitted to tempt through any animal other than the serpent, so that the serpent’s natural cunning might reveal the malice of the tempter; so that by the outward garment, as it were, man might know how greatly he ought to beware the craftiness of the one governed within it [Col. 0025A]. D. How was man tempted? M. By external temptation only. D. What is external temptation? M. The persuasion of someone, made by sign or word, so that the person to whom it is made may be inclined to consent to sin. D. What is internal temptation? M. The movement of the first delight by which the mind is impelled to sin. This is more difficult to overcome, because the assailant within is strengthened from what is ours against us. Therefore the devil did not obtain pardon, because he sinned under no temptation; whereas man, who fell when struck by external temptation, ought to have been punished all the more severely because he had been overthrown by a lighter impulse. Yet, because in falling he experienced some violence, so to speak, God’s grace eventually raised him to pardon. But we, the greater the violence of temptation that we suffer in sinning [Col. 0025B], are restored to lost grace by the lighter expiation. D. In what order was man tempted? M. Because the devil saw that the woman, as weaker and less strong in reason, could more easily be deceived by fraud, he first approached her with a question. He wished to draw out her mind, so that from her answer he might gather how thereafter he should address her. D. Why was the woman not alarmed by the serpent speaking to her? M. Because she thought that it had newly received from God the office of speaking. D. How did he address her? M. “Eat, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3). He tempted through three things: gluttony, vainglory, and avarice. Gluttony is an immoderate desire for eating; vainglory is love of one’s own praise; avarice [Col. 0025C] is an immoderate desire for possessing. He tempted through gluttony when he said, “Eat”; through vainglory when he said, “You shall be like gods”; through avarice when he said, “knowing good and evil.” D. I would like you to explain the very root of this sin; and as you have shown me in what order it was committed, so also show me what it is. M. In the first man God had placed two desires: namely, the desire for what is right and the desire for advantage. The one—the desire for what is right—was according to will; the other—the desire for advantage—was according to necessity. He made the former voluntary so that man might merit in it, either by retaining it well when he could abandon it, or by abandoning it badly when he could retain it. He willed the latter to be necessary so that man might be recompensed in it, either with punishment if he abandoned it, or with glory if he retained it. Therefore he inseparably attached its effect—justice—to the former; but he set before the latter its effect—advantage—as separable, so that man, having lost the former alone, might lose the inclination toward both the latter and the former; or, retaining the former alone, might retain the effect of both the latter and the former. But man did only what he could do. Since he voluntarily abandoned the desire for what is right, he justly lost both justice and advantage, while retaining only the desire for advantage, to increase his misery. For just as, for one persevering in justice, it would have been an increase of glory to be unable to grow cold in the love of the good he possessed, so now it is an accumulation of misery to be unable to restrain oneself from the desire for the good, even though one cannot attain it [Col. 0026A]. D. Did man abandon the desire for justice willingly or unwillingly? M. If he abandoned it unwillingly, it should be called violence rather than fault. But if a willing act is said to have preceded in him, then the abandonment of justice itself is denied to have been the first sin; nor will it be possible to find whence such a will came to him that he wished to abandon good, because he could not have willed anything from himself, nor did he receive from God the power to will anything except what was advantageous and right. D. Yet when he abandoned it, he must be believed to have willed what he did. M. You would say this rightly if ceasing to do something were doing something. But because he did not begin to be unwilling to do what he had previously been unwilling to do, but merely ceased to will what he had previously willed, it is not necessary to say that he did this either willingly or unwillingly. Yet he did will something which, because he could not will it together with this willing [Col. 0026B], caused him to cease to will this which he had willed. He did not will the former because he ceased to will the latter; rather, he ceased to will the latter because he willed the former. D. Why, then, is he said to have sinned more in ceasing to will this than in beginning to will that? M. Because if he had not ceased to will this, whether he willed that or something else, he could never have sinned. D. What, then, is justice? M. Measure in the desire for advantage. D. What is the desire for justice? M. Love of measure. D. What, then, did he will, that he ceased to will this? M. He willed something beyond measure. D. Was this willing not itself a sin? M. It was not sinful that he willed this; rather, by willing it, he lost the measure of willing—that is, the desire for justice. D. What did he will beyond measure? M. He desired the likeness of God. Therefore man sinned [Col. 0026C] in abandoning the desire for what is right, and was punished in retaining the desire for advantage. D. How? M. He was punished in the desire for advantage in two ways: either when he is restrained from the advantages which he seeks to order, or because he is released to desire disordered advantages. In the one is punishment; in the other, punishment and fault. D. Whence comes to man the desire for disordered things? M. From the punishment of sin. D. I ask for the manner of it. M. God made the first human body sound and whole: whole, indeed, because nothing was lacking to it for perfection; sound, because nothing was present in it for corruption. But in both respects he had imposed such a condition that neither its wholeness nor its soundness could be preserved without assistance. Therefore, among created things, he ordered certain external things which could avail to preserve and protect its well-being and wholeness [Col. 0026D]; and he assigned to the spirit which ruled the body the care and duty of providing these things. Yet, lest he should be oppressed by a servile condition in fulfilling this duty, if he fulfilled it from command alone and not also from love, God gave him an inclination by which he might love his body, so that as he loved its wholeness and soundness, he might also gladly provide all that could preserve them. Again, lest there be labor in seeking such things or danger in taking them, he tempered both need and carnal appetite by a fixed measure, so that little might suffice him for sustenance and modest amounts for satiety. Thus, if man had retained justice, prudence with regard to the flesh would have been labor, pleasure, and exercise alike. But because the spirit, lifted up in pride, refused to restrain its desire within measure, it deserved that it should now be worn down below by endless labors and be unable to keep measure in the desire of its flesh [Col. 0027A]. For by mortality God broke the wholeness of the human body; consequently it now needs more supports than before, both to restore as much well-being as has perished and to preserve as much as remains. From this arises that harsh necessity by which appetite extends beyond the order of nature, so that it may not only preserve nature but also drive out the defect of nature. For as it is naturally given to the spirit to love the advantage of its flesh, so it naturally has the inability to love its disadvantage. Yet it must be understood that this necessity of desiring is not free from fault merely because it is a necessity: for the cause of this necessity was not necessity, but will. Nevertheless, this may truly be said of all such desires: the soul desires nothing, however disordered it may seem, except for some advantage—either to preserve a good or to remove an evil. Thus, for example, when it desires intercourse, it wishes to extinguish the itching of the flesh; when it desires food or drink, the burning of gluttony. D. If every desire seeks an advantage, and the desire for one’s own advantage, both in preserving good and removing evil, is given by nature, why is this concupiscence imputed to man as fault? M. He sins not because he seeks his own advantage, but because he seeks it in a disordered way. D. Can he avoid desiring in a disordered way? M. He cannot. D. [Col. 0027C] Why can he not? M. Because of his weakness. D. Why was he weakened? M. Because God broke the wholeness of nature by the liability of mortality. D. Why did he do this? M. I see where you are leading. D. Yet what was the cause? M. Human fault. D. Therefore through his own fault he came to this necessity. M. So it is.

D. Therefore this necessity does not excuse him. M. It cannot excuse him. D. But what shall he do? M. Let him seek the help of grace and say, “Deliver me from my necessities, O Lord” (Ps. 24); as the Apostle says, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7). D. Therefore man cannot be delivered except through God’s grace? M. He cannot. For we say that man sinned willingly in abandoning the desire for what is right; and that he was punished in two ways in retaining the desire for advantage: either because he is restrained from ordered advantages, or because he is released to disordered advantages. In the one is punishment; in the other, punishment and fault [Col. 0027D]. Therefore, since man was punished with such a punishment that did not purge fault but increased it, unless he had been delivered through grace, through this punishment he would deservedly have descended to the punishments of eternal condemnation. Therefore his judgment was deferred, lest he be found fit for condemnation. And because God had predestined him for salvation, he granted him a place and time for correction and repentance, so that in the meantime, through his grace, he might make him such that he could finally judge him unto salvation not only mercifully but also justly. D. What is the place of repentance [Col. 0028A] which God granted to man? M. This world. D. And what is the time of repentance? M. The present life, that is, from the beginning of the world until the end of the age. D. These are very ample reprieves; but I should like you to say further why you call this world a place of repentance. M. There are four places: one in which there is only good, and the highest good; one in which there is only evil, and the greatest evil; one in which there is only good, yet not the highest good; and one in which there is good and evil, neither the highest good nor the greatest evil. D. I would like you to set forth examples of each. M. In heaven there is only good and the highest good; in hell there is only evil and the greatest evil; in paradise there is only good, but not the highest good; in the world there is good [Col. 0028B] and evil, neither the highest good nor the greatest evil. D. Why have you distinguished these places? M. Paradise is the place of those beginning and advancing toward better things. Therefore only good ought to have been there, because the creature was not to be initiated in evil; yet not the highest good, so that those who were beginning might have something in which they could advance. Heaven is the place of those confirmed in good and, through discipline, attaining the highest progress. Therefore only the highest good is established there. Hell is the place of those confirmed in evil and irrecoverably abandoning discipline; therefore only the greatest evil is established there. The world is the place of those who wander and are to be restored; therefore good and evil are ordered together in it, so that they may receive consolation through the good and correction through the evil [Col. 0028C]. Yet neither the highest good nor the greatest evil is there, so that those persisting in evil may have something by which they can decline, and those departing from evil something by which they can advance. Heaven, therefore, is at the highest point; hell is at the lowest; paradise is in the middle; the world lies between the lowest and the middle. Therefore man, who had fallen from the middle, since he was awaited for restoration, had to be placed between the lowest and the middle. D. Behold, man waits a long time; and what will he do? M. He will not be able to find a plan of escape. D. What benefit, then, is there in deferring judgment if man cannot be delivered? M. By himself he cannot. D. By whom, then? M. He who through his grace defers judgment must meanwhile, through that same grace, show the plan of escape.

D. Then will the judge give counsel to the accused?

M. For the time being he will lay aside the person of judge and assume that of counsellor.  

D. When will he come?

M. In the last times.

D. Why does he delay his coming so long?

M. So that he may first allow man to experience his own insufficiency. Patriarchs and prophets and lawgivers will come first; righteous men and wise men will come; they will seek and not find; they will labour and fail; many will promise, and none will show the way. But when all have failed, and, having uttered many promises and many words, have fallen silent, then he himself will utter one word and give counsel.

D. What counsel will he give?

M. Am I privy to the secrets of God? This counsel is secret and hidden from the ages.

D. Yet it is manifest in the last times. [Col. 0029A] Moreover, if we wish to belong to the lot of redemption, it is just and fitting that we should not be ignorant of the manner of that redemption of ours.

M. This counsel concerned how man might either justly be rescued from the devil’s power or be reconciled to God.

D. I very much desire to know how this could have happened.

M. First consider man’s case, and then you will easily be able to see by what justice he was delivered.

D. I also desire that case to be set before me.

M. Man’s case stands against two parties, namely against God and against the devil; therefore do not be displeased if I explain this very case as though under the arrangement of three persons.

D. You have made me wholly attentive.

M. Three come into the case: man, God, and the devil. The devil is convicted of having committed an injury against God, because [Col. 0029B] he both deceitfully led away and violently held God’s servant, that is, man. Man is convicted of having committed an injury against God, because he both despised God’s command and, placing himself under another’s hand, inflicted upon God the loss of his own servitude. Likewise, the devil is convicted of having committed an injury against man, because he first deceived him by promising good things and afterwards injured him by inflicting evil things.

Therefore, the devil holds man unjustly, but man is justly held. For the devil never deserved to oppress man as subject to himself; but man deserved by his own fault that he should be permitted to be oppressed by him. Although man did not know that what the devil promised was false, he nevertheless knew that he ought not to desire it against the Creator’s will, even if it had been true. Therefore man is subject to the devil justly [Col. 0029C] insofar as his own guilt is concerned, but unjustly insofar as the devil’s deception is concerned.

If, then, man had such an advocate that the devil could be brought to trial before him, man could justly contest the devil’s dominion; for the devil had no just cause why he ought to claim a right over man. But no such advocate could be found except God. Yet God was unwilling to undertake man’s case, because he was still angry with man on account of his guilt. It was therefore necessary first that man should appease God and then, with God’s advocacy, confidently bring his case against the devil.

But man could not reasonably appease God unless he restored the loss he had inflicted and made satisfaction for his contempt. Yet man possessed nothing by which he could worthily compensate God for the loss taken away, [Col. 0029D] because, if he offered something from irrational creation, it would be less than the rational creature that had been taken away. Nor could he render one man for another, because he had taken away a righteous and innocent man, while he found no one except a sinner. Therefore man found nothing by which he could appease God; for whether he gave what was his or gave himself, it would not be worthy compensation.

God, therefore, seeing that man could not escape by his own strength the yoke of just condemnation, had mercy on him; and first, by mercy alone, freely went before him, in order afterwards to deliver him through justice. That is: because man had from himself no justice by which to escape, God through mercy gave man justice. For man’s rescue would not be perfectly reasonable unless it occurred justly on both sides: that is, just as God had justice in demanding man, so man also should have justice in escaping. But man could never have possessed this justice unless God had bestowed it upon him through mercy.

Therefore, so that God might be appeased by man, God freely gave man what man would render to God as a debt. He gave man a man, whom man might render to God for man; and this man, so that a worthy recompense might be made, would be not only equal to the former man but greater than him. Therefore, in order that a man greater than man might be rendered for man, God was made man for man; and he gave himself, man to man, so that he might receive himself from man. God, the Son of God, was incarnate; and Christ, God and man, was given to human beings, as Isaiah says: “A child is born to us” (Isa. II), etc.

Therefore, that Christ was given to man [Col. 0030B] was God’s mercy; that Christ was rendered by man was man’s justice. For in Christ’s birth God was justly appeased toward man, because such a man was found for man as was not merely, as was said, equal, but greater than man. Hence, at Christ’s birth the angels announce peace to the world, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to persons of good will” (Luke II).

But it still remained for man that, just as by restoring the loss he had appeased wrath, so also by making satisfaction for contempt he might become worthy to escape punishment. But this could not fittingly occur unless he voluntarily and obediently underwent a punishment which he did not owe, so that he might become worthy to be rescued from the punishment which he had deserved through disobedience. A sinful man could not pay this punishment, [Col. 0030C] for whatever punishment he underwent, he would endure it only worthily and justly, on account of the guilt of his first contempt.

Therefore, in order that man might justly escape the punishment due to him, it was necessary that such a man should undergo punishment for man as owed no punishment at all. But none such could be found except Christ. Thus Christ, both by being born, paid to the Father man’s debt; and, by dying, expiated man’s guilt. Since he himself underwent death for man—a death which he did not owe—man could justly escape, for his sake, the death which he did owe; and the devil would no longer find room for accusation, because he himself ought not to have ruled over man, and man had become worthy to be liberated.

Thus he accomplished both our judgment and our cause. Hence the Psalmist: “For thou hast maintained my judgment and my cause” [Col. 0030D] (Ps. IX). He accomplished our cause because he paid the debt to the Father for us and, by dying, expiated guilt. He accomplished the judgment because, descending into hell and breaking the gates of death, he liberated the captivity that was held there.

Therefore the devil’s judgment against God took place at the very beginning of the age; man’s judgment against the devil, in Christ’s Passion. Man’s judgment against God is postponed until the end of the age. And therefore, if man first wishes to be reconciled to God through Christ, he can await his judgment without fear of condemnation.

D. Here you ought appropriately to have distinguished the modes of judgment, so that, by comparing them with the others, I may discern more clearly and approve more truly what has here been said about judgment.

M. [Col. 0031A] There are four judgments: according to foreknowledge, according to cause, according to operation, and according to recompense. According to foreknowledge we were judged before we existed; according to cause we are judged from the time we begin to exist, when we are good or evil; according to operation we are judged when by outward deeds we show what we are inwardly in ourselves; according to recompense we are judged when, in receiving the reward of our deeds, we shall know what we were foreseen to be from eternity before God.

Of these four judgments, two are hidden: judgment according to foreknowledge and judgment according to cause; therefore human judgment has no place in them. Two are manifest: namely, judgment according to operation and judgment according to recompense. In one of these, that is, judgment according to operation, God gives human beings in the present the power to judge; but the other, that is, judgment according to recompense, will be judged not by human beings but by God before human beings.

But judgment according to foreknowledge is hidden and immutable; judgment according to cause, hidden and mutable; judgment according to operation, manifest and mutable; judgment according to recompense, manifest and immutable. Judgment according to operation is in some fashion an image and sacrament of judgment according to recompense: for the former makes the cause manifest and intimates foreknowledge; the latter will make the cause manifest and confirm foreknowledge.

[Col. 0031C]

D. What does it matter to us that Christ conquered the devil?

M. Christ is called Son of Man for this reason: human nature, which in the first parent had grown old through sin, was renewed in Christ and flourished again as though in the strength of youth. It was just also according to the law that, for a father decrepit and weak as though through the decline of age, a son stronger in vigour should engage the tyrant; and that his victory should avail for freedom not principally for himself, but for him on whose behalf he had fought. For this reason too the Son of God wished to become Son of Man: that he might take from man that through which man might conquer the devil for man.

D. Had not the devil also been cast out by certain persons before Christ’s Passion?

M. He had, but not except through [Col. 0031D] the Passion.

D. How can this be?

M. Just as Christ’s Passion, now past, sanctifies those who believe in it, so, when it was still future, it sanctified those who believed in it.

D. By what reasoning can you establish this?

M. What shall I call the incarnate Word except a king who entered this world through assumed humanity, to wage war with the devil and thereafter expel him as a tyrant violently ruling over what belonged to another? And what shall I call all the earlier saints, chosen from the beginning before the Incarnation, except certain excellent soldiers going before the king who was to come in battle array, equipped and girded, as it were, with the very sacraments by which they were then sanctified, as with weapons? Likewise, what shall I call those chosen persons who follow after the Incarnation until the end, except other soldiers, yet following not another king but [Col. 0032A] their very king who goes before them, unanimously and eagerly? They too possess new weapons, though they are armed by the same king and are to fight against the devil.

Therefore those who go before and those who follow after bear the sacraments of one king, serve one king, and overcome one tyrant: the former go before him as one who is to come, the latter follow him as one who goes before. You see, therefore, how all the good from the beginning to the end belong to Christ. Nor does anyone conquer the devil except those alone who belong to Christ.

D. Then they were Christians from the beginning?

M. Nothing is truer.

D. But many think otherwise.

M. Do you wish this to be shown to you more plainly?

D. I do.

M. There are three times through which the course of the present age runs. The first is the time of natural law; the second, the time of written law; the third, the time [Col. 0032B] of grace. The first is from Adam to Moses; the second, from Moses to Christ; the third, from Christ to the end of the age.

Likewise there are three kinds of human beings: persons of natural law, persons of written law, and persons of grace. Those may be called persons of natural law who direct their lives by natural reason alone; or rather, persons of natural law are those who walk according to the desire in which they were born. Persons of written law are those instructed by outward precepts to live well. Persons of grace are those who, breathed upon and illuminated by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, are enabled to recognize the good that must be done, are inflamed to love it, and strengthened to accomplish it.

To express the same thing by a clearer distinction: persons of natural [Col. 0032C] law are openly evil; persons of written law are falsely good; persons of grace are truly good. Pagans are included in the first kind; Jews in the second; Christians in the third. These three kinds of persons have never been absent at any time from the beginning; nevertheless, the time of natural law belongs to those openly evil, because they were then both more numerous and more eminent in condition. The time of written law belongs to those falsely good, because people then served in fear and cleansed their outward work, not their mind. The time of grace belongs to those truly good, who now, even if they are not more numerous, are nevertheless more eminent in condition and by God’s grace are publicly preferred even by those whose conduct opposes it.

Know, therefore, that at whatever time, from the beginning of the world [Col. 0032D] to its end, no one has been or is truly good unless justified through grace; and that grace could never be obtained except through Christ. Thus recognize that all alike, whether preceding or following, have been saved by one remedy of justification. Look, then, upon the camp of our king and the battle-lines of his army glittering in spiritual arms, and see with what a multitude of preceding and following peoples he advances surrounded.

D. I should like you now to describe to me individually the army of so great a king: who and what kind of soldiers his have been from the beginning; what arms and what enemies they have had; where and when, and what kinds of wars they have waged; how they have conquered; and finally, once victory was complete, what rewards they received.

M. After the first parent of the human race, banished from paradise because of the guilt of disobedience, came into this world, [Col. 0033A] the devil, exercising tyrannical right over him, possessed him violently, just as he had first seduced him deceitfully. But God’s providence, which was ordering this man toward salvation, so tempered the rigour of justice with mercy that it allowed him indeed to be oppressed by the devil for a time; yet, lest he should be oppressed by him for eternity, it prepared for him from that very punishment a remedy.

Accordingly, from the very beginning of the world God set before man the sacraments of his salvation, by which he might seal him under the expectation of future sanctification, so that whoever received them with right faith and firm hope, because of obedience to the divine institution, might, though placed under the yoke, belong to the fellowship of freedom. Accordingly, he issued an ordinance instructing and teaching man, that whoever chose to await him as saviour and liberator should confirm the vow of that choice by receiving his sacraments:

> “The devil also set forth his sacraments, by which he might bind his own to himself, so that he might distinguish them more plainly from those who rejected his rule and hold them more securely. Thus the human race immediately began to be divided into opposing parties: some receiving the devil’s sacraments, others receiving Christ’s sacraments; and two households came into being, one of Christ and the other of the devil.”

The devil, therefore, seeing that the offspring of the human race, which he had corrupted in its root, although it all came forth in birth with corruption, did not nevertheless all persist in that same corruption, being renewed by rebirth, [Col. 0033C] determined through those whom he possessed to oppress by persecution those whom he was losing. He presumed all the more then to inflict violence because he remembered that he had formerly prevailed by deceit.

Yet this crafty contrivance of the evil one became an ordering of divine mercy: namely, so that man, strengthened by grace, might defend against him the justice which he had earlier abandoned when seduced by him. In this, indeed, the tyrant’s pride is fittingly confounded: he is now unable through torments to overcome mortal and weak man, whom he had formerly seduced by persuasion alone when he was surrounded by no weakness.

Thus, with wholly different intentions, one work is accomplished: the devil exhorts his soldiers to persecution [Col. 0033D] and violence, but Christ exhorts his to patience. Since the devil from the beginning, whether through himself or through his own, attacks the good for no other reason than to take justice from them; and since the good seek through this contest nothing other than not to lose their justice, it is plain that, because he cannot accomplish what he wishes, he is always conquered by the good, even if outwardly he seems to have prevailed. Therefore, when the devil’s soldiers inflict violence outwardly, Christ’s soldiers conquer inwardly through patience.

D. Then Christ’s sacraments are weapons?

M. Not only weapons, but medicines as well.

D. How?

M. They are medicines because they heal the sick; weapons because they protect the healthy.

D. What is a sacrament?

M. A sign of a sacred thing.

D. In how many ways are sacraments made?

M. [Col. 0034A] In three: by things, words, and deeds. By things, as in water, bread, wine, salt, ashes, oil, fire, and other such things; by words, such as the invocation of the Trinity and other words possessing divine power which are uttered in blessings, consecrations, or exorcisms; by deeds, such as the sign of the cross, bending of the knees, extending of the hands, and every other such thing.

D. Why is a sacrament called a sign of a sacred thing?
