M. Because through that which is visibly seen outwardly, something else invisible inwardly is signified. For example: through water, remission of sins; through fire, the ardour of charity; through oil, mercy; through salt, wisdom; and so forth.

D. Then will man, though rational and more worthy in his nature than senseless things, seek salvation in such things? How can these give salvation and heal the ailments of souls, when they are bodily things, possessing nothing beyond a visible appearance?

M. There is certainly something else there besides what is seen with bodily eyes; and it is this that invisibly cleanses the stains of sins and heals the ailments of souls.

D. From where, then, does that power come?

M. Not from the nature of what is visibly seen there, but from the operation of the Holy Spirit, who works invisibly in that visible thing.

D. Could not the Holy Spirit have bestowed this same power for man’s restoration without the presentation or assistance of bodily things?

M. Certainly he could, if he wished.

D. Why, then, were these things instituted, so that man should be commanded to seek salvation, as it were, in things lower and less worthy, when [Col. 0034C] God alone is he from whom man both ought to seek salvation and can hope for it?

M. Man is commanded to seek salvation in these things, not from these things; so that when he has obtained it, he may know that he has received it from him who commanded him to seek it in them.

D. Tell me, then, why God commanded man to seek salvation in things of this kind.

M. So that man might be humbled and instructed. He is humbled because he is now compelled, while fallen, to seek his good in what is lower, whereas formerly, while standing, he despised receiving it from his superior. Thus, a remedy of subsequent humility is fittingly applied to the disease of preceding pride, so that man, who formerly, ruinously exalted in himself, despised God, might afterwards, beneficially humbled, voluntarily subject himself even to sensible [Col. 0034D] things beneath God.

The sacraments were also set before man for instruction, so that through what is done outwardly he might recognize what is bestowed inwardly upon him.

D. Then in every sacrament must one believe that there is more than what can be seen and perceived by bodily sense alone?

M. There are two things there: one which we perceive outwardly by bodily sense, which is properly called the sacrament, that is, the sign of a sacred thing; the other, which we do not see but believe, which is rightly called the thing or power of the sacrament.

D. What is the difference between a sign and a sacrament?

M. A sign signifies only by institution; a sacrament also represents by resemblance. Again, a sign can signify a thing without conferring it. But in a sacrament there is not merely signification, but efficacy as well: it both signifies by institution, represents by resemblance, and confers by sanctification.

D. Can a sacrament ever be understood as a sign?

M. Improperly, a sacrament is called such for signification alone.

D. What if we said that those figures of the Old Law were merely signs of future things, not sacraments, and that the spiritual grace given in them was conferred through those sacraments which were to come?

M. If anyone denies that the earlier sacraments had an effect of sanctification, he does not seem to me to think rightly. Yet in this respect we unquestionably place the dignity of the later ones above them: the former were both visible and signs of visible things, whereas the latter, while visible, are themselves sacraments only of invisible grace. Therefore the sacraments of grace [Col. 0035B] first receive sanctification in themselves through the invocation of the Trinity, and then confer sanctification, so that, being sanctified, they sanctify, and by the sanctification divinely bestowed upon themselves confer what the former sacraments were accustomed to confer through these sacraments by their signification alone.

D. What are those things without which salvation could not from the beginning be possessed?

M. There are three: faith, sacraments of faith, and good works. These appear to have been set before man from the beginning for obtaining salvation. Christ’s soldiers have always used them: receiving strength in faith, weapons in the sacraments of faith, and missiles in good works, by which they fought against the devil. Certainly, just as neither strength in an unarmed person, nor weapons without strength, nor missiles, can benefit one fighting against a strong armed opponent, [Col. 0035C] so faith without works and the sanctification of the sacraments, and conversely sacraments or works without faith, do not have the effect of salvation.

D. What is faith?

M. Paul says that faith is “the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not appearing” (Heb. XI).

D. How do you think this should be understood?

M. Whatever things are either future and do not yet exist; or past and have already ceased to exist; or present but conceal the reality of themselves from our senses or knowledge—all these, insofar as we are concerned, are in a sense not. But because through faith a certain certainty concerning all these things arises in us as though they were existing and present, faith itself is not without reason called both the substance of things not existing and the evidence of things not appearing.

Moreover, it must be considered that by faith alone no one can please God unless charity is joined to it, so that faith may be operative through love. Nevertheless faith is, as it were, the foundation and beginning of good in man: from faith charity is born, and from charity hope is generated; because faith belongs to thought, charity to love, and hope is confidence.

D. I should like, briefly, that after their definitions have been set forth, these things themselves should be distinguished more clearly for me.

M. Faith is voluntary certainty about absent things, situated above opinion and below knowledge. Charity is love of God for God’s own sake, and love of one’s neighbour for God’s sake. Hope is confidence in future goods arising from God’s grace and a good conscience. Faith and hope also seem to differ in this: [Col. 0036A] faith can concern things present, past, and future alike; hope only future things. Faith concerns things belonging both to ourselves and to others; hope only our own things. Faith concerns good and evil things; hope only good things.

D. What is a sacrament of faith?

M. “Sacrament of faith” can be understood in two ways: either the sacrament itself which is faith; or the sacrament of faith, that is, of the faithful, which the faithful use and by which they are sanctified.

D. On what grounds is faith called a sacrament?

M. Just as when one says “the sacrament of baptism,” no sacrament other than baptism itself is signified, so we are accustomed sometimes to understand “sacrament of faith” as faith itself, which is a sacrament. All the other things, moreover, are called sacraments of faith because they were instituted only to sanctify those who have faith.

Faith itself, as was said, is a sacrament because, just as in baptism and the other sacraments one thing is outwardly displayed and another is the spiritual power inwardly bestowed, so faith—by which now, as the Apostle says, we behold God “as through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. XIII)—is one thing, while the manifest vision by which afterwards, contemplating him face to face (ibid.), we shall see him, is another. Faith, therefore, is the sacrament of the future vision; and that vision itself is the power of the sacrament which is faith.

D. I should now like to be taught what matters pertain to faith.

M. There are two: Creator and creature. Sound faith ought so to distinguish these that it attributes neither the divinity of the Creator to the creature nor the weakness of the creature to the Creator; that is, it neither confines God within time [Col. 0036C] nor extends the creature into eternity. For if either is done, faith necessarily suffers harm.

It follows that faith, after rightly distinguishing between Creator and creature, should also strive rightly to offer the Creator his honour, by granting him his due: namely, confessing that all things were made from him and through him, while he himself subsists not from another but from himself, without beginning or end. Then follows a third point: that one should believe and await as the saviour of humankind him whom one confesses as Creator of all things.

To state it briefly, these are the things without which faith could never be sound: that one God be believed—the maker of all things and the saviour of humankind. For those who worshipped a creature as God, deceived by a double error, believed either that the creature was eternal or that God was temporal. What else can they be said to have done than to attribute the excellence of the maker to the work and the weakness of the work to the Creator?

Again, the philosophers of the Gentiles, because they did not have faith concerning the Saviour, although they were by no means mistaken in distinguishing the Creator from his work, are nevertheless not to be called believers, because they did not possess faith in the Saviour.

D. What kind of faith did the ancients have concerning the Saviour to come, especially those who lived around the world’s beginnings and had not yet received the Scriptures in which his coming was promised?

M. We need not say that his coming in the flesh, crucifixion, and resurrection had been plainly revealed to all who were believers at that time, since even the apostles who saw him present in the flesh—whose faith and righteousness are commended by the Saviour himself—are recorded to have been ignorant of this. Nevertheless, they believed that they would be saved through him, in whatever way and at whatever time pleased him. But that they were to be redeemed by his death—except for the few to whom God had revealed this—is clearly shown by the fact that Peter tried to oppose the Lord when he foretold his death (Matt. XVI), and all the other apostles are recorded rather to have despaired at his death, so much so that, despairing already because of the cross, they said: “But we had hoped that he was the one who was to redeem Israel” (Luke XXIV). For those who had hoped for redemption while he lived, but afterwards despaired when he died, plainly show that they did not know that they were to be redeemed through his death.

D. Could it have sufficed for those earlier persons unto salvation that they should believe him the Creator of all things and await the Saviour’s coming?

M. This could then have sufficed them together with the other things without which, as was said, faith could not please God—at least in those who had time for doing good: that is, with reception of the sacraments and practice of good works, their faith strengthened through charity and hope.

D. Then did faith afterwards increase?

M. Faith grows in two ways: through constancy and through knowledge. Some have faith great in knowledge and small in constancy; others small in knowledge and great in constancy. But before God great constancy of faith is more precious than great knowledge. Therefore the ancient [Col. 0037C] saints for the most part had faith small in knowledge and great in constancy; whereas, conversely, many now have faith great in knowledge and small in constancy.

D. What sacraments existed under natural law?

M. Offerings, sacrifices, and tithes.

D. On what grounds are these called sacraments?

M. Because they are signs of a sacred thing.

D. Of what?

M. Of remission of sins.

D. How?

M. Man’s substance is twofold: one part inward, which is himself; the other outward, in the things he possesses. Therefore God willed that man should make from his outward substance an offering for himself, so that, by a just recompense, when he devoutly returned what he had outwardly received from God, he might, God granting it, recover what he had inwardly lost from himself.

Therefore through faith and offerings or sacrifices, all those then received remission of sins who, putting off the old man, that is Adam, became members of the new man, that is Christ. For offerings and sacrifices, through the mediation of faith, worked in them what circumcision later worked under written law, or baptism under grace: namely, that, justified from every sin, whether original or actual, they too might be counted among the members of him by whose faith and sacraments they were sanctified.

For the Passion of the Saviour bestowed upon the preceding sacraments—the offering under natural law and circumcision under written law—the same power and efficacy of sanctification as it bestows upon those that follow and succeed them. This alone is excepted: sacrifices and offerings were performed under natural [Col. 0038A] law not for the necessity of salvation in the way circumcision was under written law and baptism under grace, but for the worship of devotion; at that time faith alone justified and purified believers.

And in circumcision this too is excepted: however righteous and pleasing to God those earlier fathers were, before the victim was offered they could not enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom. They were kept only in Abraham’s bosom, that is, in peaceful rest, until he should come who, dying and rising for us, would ascend to heaven in assumed flesh and open the way to all who believe in him and follow him.

D. If the same power existed in those sacraments as exists in these, what was the reason that those should cease and these succeed?

M. A more manifest truth is declared in these. And it was fitting that, as knowledge of faith grew gradually with the passage of time, other sacraments should likewise be instituted which, even if they conferred no different sanctification of spiritual grace, nevertheless disclosed the same sanctification more plainly.

For the Saviour was the same, faith the same, grace the same: there, of the one to come; here, of the one presented. But since he through whom salvation was given was still far off, the signs of that salvation had to be obscure, so that, as his coming gradually drew nearer, faith might increase further and grace reveal itself more clearly. Therefore the sacrament of expiation and justification was instituted to be formed first through offering, afterwards through circumcision, and finally through baptism. For the form and likeness of the same cleansing is obscurely intimated in offering, expressed more plainly in circumcision, and openly declared through baptism.

Man first received justification, that, as remedies of salvation, he might offer one part of his outward substance to God and retain another part for his own use, in order that by this action he might learn to ascribe inward goods to God, but inward evils to himself. But this sign, taken from afar, taught man more what it was than what was done.

Therefore, when the time had come for truth to be declared, the remedy of circumcision was given him as a sacrament. There, when a part is cut away from man’s inward substance—not a part naturally superfluous, but a figure of that which is superfluous—the circumcision of sin which grace accomplishes in the inward man is now demonstrated more plainly. But because circumcision cuts away outward stains and deformities, while washing cleanses even inward stains, circumcision ought to cease when Christ came and manifest truth arrived, so that the sacrament might succeed which could declare man’s perfect cleansing and the inward brightness of the soul—which he obtains in and through that very sacrament.

Those first sacraments, then, seem like a certain shadow of spiritual grace; those which followed later possess, as it were, an image and, if one may say so, outlines of truth. But these are no longer shadow or image, but the body of truth; in them, because the effect of salvation is given fully and shown clearly, [Col. 0039A] just as the spirit in a living body reveals itself through outward movement, so the invisible life of grace is most clearly displayed in them.

D. It remains now, concerning works, that you explain what must be said.

M. There are three kinds of deeds. Some are altogether good and can never lawfully be omitted; some are altogether evil and can never lawfully be committed; some are intermediate, such that whether they are done or not done there is neither fault nor merit. Natural law therefore prohibited only those things which can never lawfully be done; it commanded only those things which can never lawfully be omitted, leaving all intermediate matters open either way. But among matters which were either to be commanded or left free, it placed only one commandment in the human heart: “What you wish for yourself, do for others; what you do not wish for yourself, do not do to others” (Matt. VII; Tobit IV), so that by considering himself a person might learn how he ought to conduct himself toward his neighbor. But afterwards, when the Law entered and proposed a stricter discipline of life, it began to select certain matters from those which were intermediate, assigning some of them to one side through command and others through prohibition. Thus, just as God had first set apart for the first man in Paradise one thing from natural permission as a test-command of discipline, so now, for his children—who did not stand in one truth but had been scattered through various errors—he fashioned not one command of discipline from natural permission, as for persons being tested, but many, as for persons being corrected and restored; so that the more they learned to restrain themselves in intermediate matters, the more easily they might avoid what was not permitted. [Col. 0039B–C]

D. What were those things which natural law proposed to be done or avoided?

M. They were the seven things which the written Law later commanded on the second tablet concerning love of neighbor. The first was: “Honor your father and your mother, that it may go well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth”; the second: “You shall not kill”; the third: “You shall not commit adultery”; the fourth: “You shall not steal”; the fifth: “You shall not bear false witness”; the sixth: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife”; the seventh: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Deut. V). The first was a positive command; the other six were prohibitions.

D. Why was only one commandment given concerning things to be done, and several concerning things not to be done? [Col. 0039D]

M. The first sin of the human being was disobedience; and therefore this life, granted to humanity for repentance, is wholly assigned to obedience. Since a person is drawn in different directions in doing evils by his own desire, whereas in doing good is governed by the rule of obedience alone, he had to be instructed individually in avoiding evils—which he has from himself and can do through himself—but, for doing good, recalled only to obedience, so that there, by another’s judgment, he might more beneficially learn what he himself ought to do. For when a person is commanded to render honor to father and mother, this is not to be referred only to carnal parents. Rather, he is commanded not to disdain, for God’s sake, to render obedience and honor to a human superior, because he once despised this in God’s commands. [Col. 0040A]

D. You have shown three things: faith, the sacraments of faith, and works. It remains now that you show what kind of restoration, or how great a restoration, was effected in those who possessed these things.

M. If the highest good of humanity were contemplation of the God who is present—and especially since the first human being is believed to have been created for enjoyment of this—then faith is rightly called the beginning of his good and the starting-point of his restoration: through faith he begins, in a certain manner, to see him who is absent. For because a person who lost the knowledge of God through sin is again enlightened through faith, so that he may see and know him, it is clear that that through which the first good he had lost is restored to him is rightly called the beginning of his restoration. [Col. 0040B]

This restoration, of course, grows in accordance with the growth of faith, while a person is increasingly enlightened through knowledge and inflamed through love. Faith itself, then, is that through which a person is restored and in which his lost good is returned to him, so that, gradually increasing through it alike in knowledge and love, he may deserve to attain that full blessedness of vision. For thus, as long as the righteous person lives in this body, while he is a pilgrim away from the Lord, he must live by faith; just as, once he has been led out of this prison-house and brought into the joy of his Lord, the blessed person will live by contemplation.

But by a marvelous dispensation of God, the malice of the ancient enemy is meanwhile allowed to attack and persecute the faithful, so that it may be reckoned to a person as merit if, now walking by faith, he does not abandon the way of truth even when attacked—he who earlier, strengthened by the vision of the God who was present, had been overthrown by persuasion alone. So that he may stand unconquered in this battle and keep his good unharmed, he is given, as has already been said, weapons in the sacraments with which to fortify himself, and missiles in good works with which to strike down the enemy; that is, joined to faith by love and hope, he may be inwardly strengthened and may conquer. By now, I think, it has been sufficiently shown to you what kind of faith, what sacraments, and what works were necessary for those first holy people to obtain salvation. [Col. 0040C]

D. How long did this earlier state last?

M. Until Abraham. For then God, wishing to gather his people into one body and separate them from the company of unbelievers, so that they might be not only in one faith but also in one fellowship, called Abraham in order to lead him out of his land; and through that one man, and in that one man, to lead out of their former way of life all who would be born from him or follow him, and gather them into one fellowship of new life. He also commanded him to circumcise the flesh of his foreskin, as a sign for himself and an example for his descendants. This was the only addition to the former condition: through this sign the people of God were to be distinguished from unbelievers until he should live who would gather believers not only from Abraham’s children but also from all nations, and who would separate them now not by a sign of flesh according to lineage, but by the sign of baptism in cleansing. [Col. 0040D–0041A]

D. Were believers not also distinguished from unbelievers long ago, before the Flood?

M. They were; but after the Flood, when the human race had again been reduced to one people, it began to be distinguished a second time in Abraham.

D. How was circumcision performed?

M. It was commanded that a male child should be circumcised on the eighth day after his birth, in the flesh of his foreskin, with a knife made from stone.

D. What was the reason for commanding it to be done in this way?

M. There are three circumcisions: one, merely outward, in the flesh, which is the sacrament; and two others, which are the reality and efficacy of the sacrament. One takes place in the present, when the mind is circumcised through putting away iniquity. The other will take place in the future, when the body is circumcised through putting away corruption. Thus the first is in the flesh; the second in the mind; the third in the body. [Col. 0041B]

Now the number eight in Sacred Scripture sometimes signifies the time of resurrection which follows this present life, which runs through seven days; sometimes the time of grace, in which eternal goods are promised to those who serve God. Therefore that first circumcision, which was the sacrament of the other two, was rightly commanded to be performed on the eighth day, in order to show that in the time of grace hearts were to be circumcised through cleansing from iniquity, and that in the time of resurrection bodies were to be circumcised through the putting away of corruption. [Col. 0042A]

Circumcision of the flesh was given only to males because Sacred Scripture is accustomed to signify the soul by the male sex and the flesh by the female sex. Thus it was shown that this outward circumcision conferred justification upon souls, but did not take away corruption from the flesh. The knife made from stone signifies Christ, concerning whom the Apostle says, “And the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X), who takes away the sins of the world (John I). It was commanded to be performed in the flesh of the foreskin because it was given as a remedy against original sin, which we contract from our parents through that member by which we are propagated.

D. What remedy, then, did women have, since they were not circumcised?

M. Faith, offerings or sacrifices, and circumcision itself—not by receiving it, however, but by believing.

D. What should be said of children dying before the eighth day, since they could not reach that remedy? Were they saved or condemned? [Col. 0042B]

M. This, it seems to me, must be left to the judgment of God.

[Col. 0041]

# SUMMARY OF SENTENCES, DIVIDED INTO SEVEN TREATISES. (G)*

**TREATISE I.** On the three theological virtues—faith, hope, and charity; on the most sacred Trinity; and on faith in the Incarnation of the Word.  
**TREATISE II.** On the creation and state of angelic nature.  
**TREATISE III.** On the creation and state of human nature.  
**TREATISE IV.** On sacraments in general and the divine commandments.  
**TREATISE V.** On the sacrament of baptism.  
**TREATISE VI.** On the sacrament of confirmation, the Eucharist, penance, and extreme unction.  
**TREATISE VII.** On the sacrament of marriage.

# PREFACE

As Peter says in his Epistle, we ought to be ready, with gentleness and fear, to give an account to everyone who asks concerning the faith and hope that are in us (I Pet. III). Therefore, so that gentleness in speech and caution in assertion may alike be preserved, let us avoid, as the Apostle commands, profane novelties of expression (I Tim. VI), and let us not incline in any direction through hasty assertion. For it is better not to utter great things, where one cannot err without danger, than to define their contraries. But wherever we can, let us follow the tracks of authorities; where certain authority is lacking, let us strive especially to agree with those who come closest to the authorities and who, without presuming upon their own judgment, interpret the Scriptures devoutly.

For Holy Scripture, as blessed Augustine says, mocks the proud by its loftiness, holds the attentive by its depth, satisfies the great by its truth, and nourishes the little by its gracious accessibility. Therefore, if anything obscure presents itself to us, let the first purpose of our inquiry be to have recourse to authorities; then to set forth what the learned persons of our own time think about it; and, insofar as we can, to bring to light why it is preferable to follow these rather than those, with reason and authority alike concurring.

# FIRST TREATISE

## CHAPTERS

**Chapter I.** On faith.  
**Chapter II.** On hope and charity.  
**Chapter III.** On the faith of the ancients.  
**Chapter IV.** Of what faith consists.  
**Chapter V.** Whether a created spirit is local.  
**Chapter VI.** On the distinction of the Trinity.  
**Chapter VII.** On the names that distinguish the persons of the Trinity.  
**Chapter VIII.** On the equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.  
**Chapter IX.** That nothing concerning the Holy Trinity is said according to accident.  
**Chapter X.** On the diverse meanings of names.  
**Chapter XI.** On what is appropriated to the persons.  
**Chapter XII.** On foreknowledge and predestination.  
**Chapter XIII.** On the will of God.  
**Chapter XIV.** On the whole power of God.  
**Chapter XV.** On faith in the Incarnation.  
**Chapter XVI.** That Christ assumed soul and flesh at the same time.  
**Chapter XVII.** That Christ assumed all our infirmities except sin.  
**Chapter XVIII.** Whether Christ is a creature.  
**Chapter XIX.** Whether in Christ’s death divinity was separated from humanity.

## CHAPTER I. On Faith

[Col. 0043A]

Since all things must be regulated by faith, as by a measure of rightness, lest anything overflow as superfluous—as the Apostle says, “God has distributed to each a measure of faith” (Rom. XII)—we must first consider what faith is and what parts it has. Faith, as the Apostle says, “is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. XI). It is the substance of things hoped for because the things hoped for subsist in us through faith. He calls those eternal goods which we desire “things hoped for,” such as immortality and the rest—things which now subsist in us through faith and will subsist in the future through experience. It is the evidence of things not seen, that is, proof, because if anyone doubts them, they cannot at any time be proved by human reasoning. For example, if someone asks, “How do you know of the Virgin’s childbirth, or of the future condition of the elect?” I have no other proof except that I believe without doubt what the prophets and others who spoke through the Holy Spirit said concerning these matters—persons whom God could in no way deceive when he spoke in them and performed miracles. And since I see that a great part of what they said has been fulfilled, I do not doubt that the remaining things will also be fulfilled.

Thus faith is the substance of things hoped for in relation to us; it is the evidence of things not seen in relation to others. Yet this definition shows more the effect of faith than what faith itself is; nor does it include all the parts of faith, since “things hoped for” contains not past things but future ones only. It may therefore be defined thus: faith is a voluntary certainty concerning absent things, standing above opinion and below knowledge. It is voluntary because it is not compelled; concerning absent things, that is, things not subject to bodily senses; above opinion, because believing is more than opining; below knowledge, because believing is less than knowing. For we believe in order that we may someday know. [Col. 0043B–C]

## CHAPTER II. On Hope and Charity

Hope arises from faith and may be defined thus: hope is confidence concerning future goods, arising from the grace of God and from a good conscience. From faith, as the foundation of all goods, arise hope and charity, because nothing can be hoped for or loved as hoped for unless it is first believed; though something may be believed which is neither hoped for nor loved. Although they exist simultaneously in time, and faith—which has merit—is not earlier than hope and charity, yet in causality faith precedes hope and charity, because we hope for and love what we believe; similarly, charity arises from hope, because we love future goods because we hope for them. For what we hope to obtain, we love.

But because, as authority says, hope is certainty arising from preceding merits; and likewise, “to hope without merits ought to be called not hope but presumption”; and because there is no merit without charity, some maintain that hope arises from faith and charity. For Augustine says in *On Faith and Works*: “Faith which works through love is the foundation”—not the faith of demons, by which they believe and tremble. And if hope arises from faith working through love, then it arises from faith and charity. But, they say, the reason authorities frequently put the order faith, hope, charity is that charity is greater.

Yet that opinion, as it seems to me, can be resolved in this way. “Hope is certainty arising from preceding merits” should not be understood of merits preceding hope itself, since no merit precedes hope, but of merits preceding that which is hoped for. This is the difference between faith and hope: faith concerns past matters, such as Christ’s birth and passion; present matters, such as that what is on the altar is the true body of Christ; and future matters, such as immortality. Hope, however, concerns future matters only. Likewise, faith concerns goods and evils; hope concerns only goods to be obtained. For hope for some misfortune ought rather to be called despair concerning a good than hope. [Col. 0043D–0044B]

It must also be known that faith concerns only things which are not seen. Gregory, Homily III: “Things apparent do not have faith, but recognition.” Likewise, in the *Dialogues*: “When Paul says, ‘Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen’ (Heb. II), what is not able to be seen is truly said to be believed. For what can be seen can no longer be believed.” Thomas saw one thing and believed another: he saw the human being and confessed God, saying, “My God and my Lord” (John XX). “We believe in order that we may know; we do not know in order that we may believe. For what is faith except to believe what you do not see? Faith, therefore, is to believe what you do not see; truth is to see what you believed.”

Nevertheless, certain authorities seem to intend that faith also concerns things which are seen, as in John: “Now I tell you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe” (John XIII). Hence Augustine: “What does this mean, ‘so that when it has happened you may believe’? For he also to whom it was said, ‘Because you have seen, you have believed’ (John XX), did not believe what he saw. He perceived flesh; he believed God hidden in the flesh.” But if we say that visible things are believed—as someone says that he believed his own eyes—this is not the faith itself which is built up in us; rather, through the things we see, we are led to believe things not seen. [Col. 0044B–D]

The same Augustine, in the book *Questions on the Gospels*: “There is also a faith of things, when one believes not through words but through the things themselves being present, when the very wisdom of God will offer itself to the saints to be contemplated in clear vision. Perhaps Paul speaks of this faith of things and of the presence of light itself when he says: ‘For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith unto faith’” (Rom. I). But it may be said that Augustine speaks here not of the sacrament of faith but of the reality of faith. For the faith by which we now see God “through a mirror, in an enigma” (I Cor. XIII) is the sacrament of that future vision by which we shall see God face to face (ibid.), as he is.

One may ask whether Peter had faith concerning Christ’s passion, which he saw with his eyes, since faith is not of apparent things. To this one may say that he had not faith but recognition of it—unless one uses the customary loose expression, “I believe my eyes.” In what he saw there was no merit if he believed; but there was merit in believing him to be God whom he saw hanging on the wood. Therefore faith that contributes to edification concerns things not seen. [Col. 0045A]

It is customary to ask whether faith is a virtue. Prosper, from Augustine’s statements, says: “There are three highest virtues: faith, hope, and charity.” And the Apostle says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gal. III). Likewise, faith has merit; but nothing has merit except a virtue. Yet some say that it is not a virtue, because of the Apostle’s words: “If I have all faith but do not have charity, I am nothing” (I Cor. XIII), where he indicates that faith can exist without charity, whereas no virtue can exist without charity.

Yet it may properly be said that faith working through love is a virtue; without love it is not a virtue. If it is objected that then there are two faiths, there are not two, but one and the same faith increased—hence, “Increase our faith” (Luke XVII). For, as Jerome says: “To the extent that we believe, to that extent we love,” and conversely. [Col. 0045B]

## CHAPTER III. On the Faith of the Ancients

[Col. 0045C]

It now seems necessary to speak concerning the knowledge of faith which the ancients possessed and how it was increased through the Law of Moses and the Gospel. For faith is sometimes small in knowledge yet great in constancy or devotion. It was great in devotion in the woman to whom it was said: “O woman, great is your faith!” (Matt. XV). Sometimes it is great in knowledge yet small in constancy or devotion, as in Peter when he denied, and also in us; and this does not please God so greatly.

Since faith cannot be entirely without knowledge, though that knowledge need not be perfect, God nevertheless tempered the knowledge of himself from the beginning in such a way that, just as he could never be wholly comprehended, so he could never be wholly unknown. He did not wish to reveal himself wholly so that faith might have merit; nor to conceal himself wholly, so that unbelief might not be excused through ignorance. There is a certain faith, or knowledge of faith, without which salvation could never exist at any time: namely, knowing that God exists and that he is the rewarder of those who hope in him, according to the Apostle: “One who approaches God must believe that he is and that he is the rewarder of those who hope in him” (Heb. XI).

But since God is invisible, according to the saying, “No one has ever seen God” (John I), how could he be known? Partly by human reason and partly by divine revelation. The Apostle shows both when he says: “What is known of God is manifest in them” (Rom. I). He does not say, “manifest to him.” In saying “manifest in them,” he plainly shows that there was in them that by which they could know God. But when he adds, “God revealed it to them” (ibid.), he shows that human reason by itself would be insufficient unless divine revelation were present to assist it. [Col. 0045D–0046A]

Divine revelation occurs in two ways: by inward inspiration and by instruction of discipline, which takes place outwardly through deeds or words. They could also know God by human reason. Since the human mind cannot be unaware of itself, it knows that it at some time began to exist; nor can it fail to know this, because, since it did not always exist, it could not give itself the subsistence by which it exists. Therefore it knows that it began to exist from another. And it is clear that this other did not begin to exist, because if it had begun from another, it could not be the first author of existence for all things. They could also discern divine wisdom and goodness in the governance and ordering of visible things. Thus it is evident that even before the Law “the invisible things of God” could be perceived from the creation of the world through the things that were made. [Col. 0046A–B]

Through the written Law the knowledge of faith began to grow. For then he through whom deliverance would occur, namely the Messiah, began to be promised; nevertheless, the manner of redemption was not yet fully known. Yet both before the Law and during the time of the Law there were always some to whom faith in the Incarnation was revealed, so that they might be like pillars of the Church.

It is asked concerning those simple persons to whom no revelation had been made, though they believed that God exists and is the rewarder of those who hope in him, whether they were saved. Some say that they were not saved, because of these authorities. Augustine, to Optatus: “Only that faith saves by which we believe that no human being is delivered from the contagion of death, contracted through the first birth, except through the one mediator; by faith in this mediator those also were saved who, before he came in the flesh, believed that he would come in the flesh.” “For their faith and ours are the same: what they believed would occur, we believe has occurred.” The same Augustine, in *On Correction and Grace*: “No one is delivered from the condemnation brought about through Adam except through faith in Jesus Christ.” Gregory on Ezekiel: “‘Those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying, Hosanna to the Son of David’” (Matt. XXI), and so forth. “For all the elect who could be in Judea, and those now in the Church, believed and believe in the mediator between God and human beings.” [Col. 0046B–C]

Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*: “The same faith in the mediator saved the ancient righteous, little and great alike; for as we believe Christ came in the flesh, so they believed he would come; as we believe he died, so they believed he would die; as we believe he rose again, so they believed he would rise; and both we and they believe that he will come for the judgment of the living and the dead.” Therefore these persons say that none of the ancients could be saved unless at least he believed these four things: that Christ would come, die, rise again, and come for judgment. But those to whom revelation had not been made entirely ignored these things. How, then, did they believe them?

Others, with whom we agree more, say that they possessed faith in Christ veiled in mystery; and that what those to whom revelation had been made knew and believed, these persons believed even if they did not know it, for they had entrusted their faith to those others. Hence in Job: “The oxen were ploughing and the asses were feeding beside them” (Job I). These were the asses feeding beside the oxen. Likewise, today in the Church, many simple people, although they do not know how to set forth the Trinity with such distinctions, nevertheless believe, because in faith and humility they adhere to those who know and believe these things. [Col. 0046D–0047A]

An objection is raised: to possess faith in Christ veiled in mystery was to believe that God exists and is the rewarder of those who hope in him; philosophers also believed this; therefore they possessed faith in Christ veiled in mystery. But authority says that they could not have had faith in the Incarnation by human reasoning; yet they believed nothing except what could be demonstrated by human reasoning. But, as we have said, to adhere in faith and humility to the oxen as they ploughed—that was to possess faith in Christ hidden in mystery. We think that certain Gentiles were such, for example the widow of Zarephath and Job. Thus we say that simple people of that time believed all that we believe, because they believed those who believed it.

But in the time of grace it no longer suffices, as it did then, to believe that God exists, because the manifestation of truth has now taken place. For the measure of faith has advanced according to the times. Cornelius had faith, but not faith sufficient for salvation. Hence Augustine says: “The alms of Cornelius were accepted before he believed in Christ; yet he did not give and pray without some faith. For how did he invoke one in whom he had not believed? But if salvation could exist without faith in Christ, Peter would not have been sent to him.” From this it is apparent that, although Cornelius believed the same thing as the simple people of old, this was no longer sufficient because of the character of the time. Let us proceed, after what has been said above, to the parts of faith. [Col. 0047B–C]

## CHAPTER IV. Of What Faith Consists

Faith consists chiefly in two things: the mystery of divinity and the sacrament of the Incarnation. First, let us consider that part of faith which pertains to the unity of the divine substance. Just as reason establishes that God exists, so it also affirms that he is one, so that the principle and end of all things may be one. For if there were two, either both would be deficient or one would be superfluous. If something were lacking to one which the other possessed, it would not be supremely perfect. But if nothing were lacking to one which the other possessed, since all things would be in one, the other would be superfluous.

Therefore there is one principle, one author of all things; and many authorities establish this in order to assist reason. Thus in the prophet Moses: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, God is one” (Deut. VI). And he is truly one because he is immutable and unchangeable. For with him there is no change or shadow of alteration (James I), because for him to be is not one thing and to be wise, immense, eternal, good, or just another thing. When he is called just, wise, and so forth, we do not indicate a diversity of properties—which in God does not exist—but diverse effects which God produces in creatures. For when he is called just, we understand that he judges justly; when wise, that he makes and governs all things wisely; when merciful, that he mercifully spares sinners. [Col. 0047D–0048A]

Augustine, *Against Arius*: “Let us understand God, insofar as we can, as good without quality, great without quantity, creator without need, present without position, wholly everywhere without place, eternal without time, making mutable things without change, and suffering nothing. If anyone thinks of God in this way and still cannot discover altogether what he is, let him nevertheless devoutly take care, insofar as he can, not to think anything about him which he is not.”

This divine substance is wholly everywhere, and all things are in it. John testifies that all things are in God, saying: “All things in him were life” (John I), that is, immutably, because their disposition and order were in him from eternity. For things which in actuality have origin and mutability did not begin to exist in God. God himself says through the prophet that he is everywhere and in every creature: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII). And elsewhere: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. CXXXVIII). Likewise Wisdom: “She reaches mightily from end to end” (Wis. VIII), that is, from the smallest creature to the greatest, or from one extremity to the other, “and disposes all things sweetly” (ibid.). [Col. 0048A–B]

But all things are in God in one way; God is in all things in another. All things are not in God by essence, for, as Augustine says, whatever is in God is God; rather, they are in him by disposition, as we have said. For, as the same author says, just as an ark exists in the mind of its maker before it is made, so all things have existed in God from eternity. Yet it does not follow that they therefore existed from eternity; they existed in God from eternity. For if they had begun to exist in God, there would already be change in him.

The following objection is customary: if creatures are in God because they are known by him before they are made, then evils are in God because they are known by him before they occur. But, as I said, creatures are in God because their disposition and cause are in him; God, however, is not the author of evils. As we have shown, creatures are not in God by essence; God, however, is in every creature by essence.

Some detractors of truth say that he is everywhere by power, not by essence, because the defilements of filth could touch him if he were essentially everywhere. This is so frivolous that it does not deserve an answer, since even a created spirit cannot be defiled by bodily filth, even if the body is leprous or polluted to any degree whatever. Finally, let them be asked which they are more prepared to grant concerning him: that he is nowhere by essence; that he is everywhere; or that he is somewhere but not everywhere. But who would dare to say that the divine essence is nowhere? Who, likewise, that it is somewhere and not everywhere? For if the divine essence or substance is somewhere in such a way that it is not everywhere, then it is local. Therefore let them grant that it is everywhere essentially. [Col. 0048B–D]

For the authority of Augustine which they are accustomed to introduce destroys rather than assists their error. By saying that God is everywhere not by places but by actions, they become thieves of truth in order to foster their error. For the authority runs thus: “God is everywhere; we approach him not by places but by actions.” Therefore it must be confessed that God is truly and essentially in every place, yet is not comprehended by any place, because he is incapable of spatial circumscription.

Augustine himself testifies to this elsewhere, in his letter to Dardanus: “Let us not imagine God to be spread throughout all things by a spatial magnitude, as earth or this light is spread out; but rather as wisdom is in two persons, neither of whom is wiser, though one is greater in body. The one wisdom in each is not greater in the greater person or less in the lesser; nor is it less in one than in two. So also God, governing without labor and containing the world without burden, is wholly in heaven, wholly on earth, and wholly in both; and is contained by no place, but is wholly everywhere in himself. He is called everywhere because he is absent from no part of things; wholly, because he does not present one part of himself to one part of things and another part to another, nor is he contained in those to which he is present as though he could not exist without them. Take away spatial extensions from bodies and bodies will not exist; take away bodies themselves from qualities, and there will be nowhere for them to be, and therefore they must cease to be.” [Col. 0049A–B]

An objection is raised: today some new creature comes into being, such as a soul. Before, it itself was nothing, because it was made from nothing; God was not in it when it was nothing, but now he is in it. Therefore he is where he was not before, and so he is mutable.

But just as, if a cloud comes before a ray of the sun, the ray is nevertheless not elsewhere than it was before—the cloud, however, is where it was not before, while the ray is not, because the cloud began to be where the ray already was—so, although God was everywhere before that creature existed, he was in the very place where it was made. Therefore he is not elsewhere now than before. We say the same of the world and of all creatures: although they did not always exist, since authority says that God is in each of them, he is nevertheless not where he was not before, because he is truly everywhere without place, just as he is eternal without time, as Augustine says. [Col. 0049B–C]

Although we are not sufficient fully to investigate these matters, we nevertheless believe without doubt that God is everywhere essentially. Nothing of all that he has made can subsist even for a moment without him, because he contains and penetrates all things and is contained by none. He cannot be comprehended because of his immensity, defiled because of his purity, or divided because of his simplicity.

Augustine, to Dardanus: “He is present wholly and equally not only to the whole creation but even to every part of it.” In the same work: “It must be confessed that God is everywhere through the presence of divinity, but not everywhere through the grace of indwelling. For because of this indwelling, where the grace of his love is without doubt recognized, we do not say, ‘Our Father who is everywhere,’ although this is true; but, ‘who art in heaven’” (Matt. VI).

Let us say, therefore, that God is in all creatures and equally in them through the presence of divinity, or through essence; but through indwelling grace he is not in all, but only in the good, and not equally in them. For the better they are, the more abundantly he dwells in them—that is, the more perfectly he is known and loved by them. As Augustine says to Jerome concerning the origin of the soul, the soul is wholly and simultaneously present through all the parts of the body, neither less in the smaller parts nor greater in the greater; but it nevertheless exercises its effects more intensely in some and more weakly in others, though it is essentially in every part of the body. [Col. 0049C–0050A]

God is not in the wicked through indwelling grace, for they are not enlightened by him. Hence: “The light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John I)—as the sunlight floods the eyes of a blind person but is not received by him. This light enlightens the good, but not equally. Augustine, to Dardanus: “Although God, who is everywhere, does not dwell in all, he does not dwell equally even in those in whom he dwells. Hence Elisha asked that the Spirit of God who was in Elijah might rest in him doubly” (IV Kings II). And whence are some saints holier than others, except that they have God dwelling in them more abundantly?

Those who have made themselves unlike him by sinning are also said to be far from him; and those who receive his likeness by living well are said to draw near to him. Therefore God is everywhere through presence, or through essence, and equally in every place; but he is not in a place—that is, he is not local. [Col. 0050A–B]

## Chapter V. On whether a created spirit is local

It is asked concerning a created spirit whether it is in a place, or is local. Some maintain and say that it is neither local nor in a place, adhering too closely to Augustine’s statement on Genesis: “A bodily creature is moved through times and places; a spiritual creature only through times.” To be moved through time is to be moved through affections—for example, from sorrow to joy—or by learning what it does not know, as occurs in angels; for in this there is a before and after. God is moved neither through times [Col. 0050C] nor through places.

But when Augustine says, “A spiritual creature is not moved through places,” he means that it does not have local circumscription. Things that have extension are circumscribed by place, since a beginning, middle, and end are assigned to them according to place. A created spirit, however, does not have extension; nevertheless, because it has a limit, being here in such a way as not to be elsewhere, it is local, although it does not create a spatial interval in a place. For even if many spirits were here, they would not crowd the place so that it contained fewer bodies. Therefore God alone, because he contains all things within himself, according to the saying, “In him we live, move, and are” (Acts 17), has neither limit nor is contained in a place. But whatever has a limit is, in some respect, local.

Ambrose, in the book *On the Faith*: “Thus Isaiah said: ‘One of the Seraphim was sent to me’ (Isa. 6). The Holy Spirit indeed is said to be sent; but a seraph is sent to one person, the Holy Spirit to all. A seraph is sent for ministry; the Holy Spirit works a mystery. A seraph passes from place to place, for it does not fill all things, but is itself filled by the Spirit.” Here Ambrose plainly says that angels are local.

## Chapter VI. On the distinction of the Trinity

Having considered these matters, it remains to examine those which concern the distinction of the persons of the Trinity; and first let us bring forward the testimonies of authority.

In Genesis it is said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 2). By the plural number he indicates the Trinity. And the Psalmist says: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son” (Ps. 2). And John: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1).

Reason also finds certain models for this investigation and consideration in created things. God, who cannot be seen in himself, is manifested in his work. For just as a person’s wisdom is not seen by that person except when it is manifested through speech, so God’s wisdom could not be known until it was manifested through his work. That work is, as it were, an external word, in some manner revealing God’s wisdom, just as the word of the heart—that is, the thought of the mind—is made known through the word of the mouth.

And because among all creatures the rational creature comes closer to God’s likeness [Col. 0051B]—for it alone was made in the image and likeness of God—the human mind could find within itself a trace of the Trinity more clearly than in other things. It saw that wisdom, which is within it, is born from itself; and that it loves its own wisdom. Thus wisdom proceeds from the mind, and love proceeds from mind and wisdom, by which the mind itself loves the wisdom generated from itself. These three are simultaneous, and yet there is one substance in which these three are found: mind, wisdom, and love. And these three are distinct from one another, since mind is neither wisdom nor love, nor wisdom mind or love; nevertheless, the unity of substance remains.

From these things the mind ascends to its Creator and considers that he possesses wisdom. And since he has never been without wisdom, it further considers that he has always loved his wisdom and has always had love toward it. For love is coeternal with the eternal One, because it is coeternal with his wisdom. Again, it considers that in God nothing can be different from him. Thus the wisdom of God is God, and his love is God; and therefore unity remains in the Trinity.

This Trinity is the Father, who is from no one; the wisdom of the Father, which is generated from the Father; and the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from both, and is very often called in Scripture the love of the Father and the Son. These three persons are distinct, yet there is one substance and one God.

Augustine, in *On the Trinity*: “We say three persons of the same essence, or three persons [who are] one essence; but we do not say three persons from the same essence,” as though essence were one thing and person another. [Col. 0051D]

Here it must be considered why that person in the Holy Trinity who is from no one is called Father. Namely, because from his own substance he generated the Son. The wisdom or Word of the Father is called Son because it is generated by the Father himself. Hence the Psalmist: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. 44).

He who proceeds from Father and Son is called the Holy Spirit because he is breathed forth by Father and Son for sanctification; and yet he does not come without Father and Son, because the Trinity is undivided. But to be breathed forth by the Father and Son is, for him, to be from the Father and Son. This is eternal for him who is given and received in time. Thus the Holy Spirit is the gift of Father and Son; and when he is given, he is given in time; yet to be given by Father and Son is not something different for him from being from Father and Son—which is eternal and not temporal for him who is given in time. Likewise, that he is the Spirit of Father and Son is eternal for him who is breathed forth in time by Father and Son.

Bede, in the first homily after the Ascension: “When the grace of the Spirit is given to human beings, the Spirit is certainly sent by the Father, sent by the Son, proceeds from the Father, and proceeds also from the Son; because his mission itself is that procession by which he proceeds from Father and Son.”

Augustine, book five of *On the Trinity*, says: “He proceeds, not as born, but as given. For what is given is referred both to him who gave it and to those to whom he gave it.” The same author: “If he does not proceed except when he is given, he certainly would not proceed unless there were first someone to whom he might be given. For a gift can exist before it is given, but it cannot in any way be called given unless it has been bestowed.” [Col. 0052B]

Here a great question arises: why are the three things which are in the soul not called three persons, whereas those things which, by the likeness of these, are found in the Godhead are called and are three persons? It may be said in reply that they are not persons because they are mutable affections of the soul. For sometimes the soul is without knowledge and love. Nor can it be said, “A human being’s knowledge is a human being,” or “A human being’s love is a human being.” But the wisdom of God is God, and the love of God is God, because in God there is nothing other than God himself.

Therefore: three persons, one God, one substance, one nature; three persons—Father, Son, Holy Spirit. But the Father is from no one. Hence Augustine: “The Father is the principle of the Trinity—that is, within the Trinity—because he is not the principle of himself; but the Son and Holy Spirit are from him, while he himself is from no one.”

We have many authorities for the Holy Spirit’s proceeding from the Son. The Apostle: “The Lord sent the Spirit of his Son, crying in your hearts: ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. 4). And in the Gospel: “Power went forth from him” (Luke 6). The Greeks, however, say that the Holy Spirit proceeds only from the Father and not from the Son. They say this because no mention of it occurs in the Apostles’ Creed—that is, in the shorter Creed—nor in the Creed given at the Synod of Nicaea. At its end is found: “Whoever says otherwise, let him be anathema.” We explain this as meaning: whoever says otherwise, that is, the contrary. But since this point is neither affirmed nor denied there, we do not say that it is contrary to that Creed. [Col. 0052D]

## Chapter VII. On names distinguishing the persons of the Trinity

After these preliminaries, it must be seen that in the Holy Trinity some names distinguish the persons, while others signify the unity of nature or substance: such as God, omnipotent, eternal, immense. These are said according to substance. For God’s being of a certain nature is not different from his being God, omnipotent, eternal, immense, just, wise, and the like. Therefore, just as there is one essence and not three, so there is one God and not three, one omnipotent, one eternal, one immense, and so forth.

Augustine, book seven of *On the Trinity*: “Because for him to be God is to be, it is not permissible to say either three essences or [Col. 0053A] three gods.”

There are also other names by which the Trinity is distinguished. Father, unbegotten, begetter: these belong to the Father alone. These others belong only to the Son: Son, begotten, born, Word, and similar names. To the Holy Spirit belong: Holy Spirit, gift, proceeding from Father and Son. These names signify the properties by which the persons are distinguished. For it belongs properly to the Father alone to be Father and to be unbegotten, because he is from no one. It belongs properly to the Son to be begotten from the Father. It belongs properly to the Holy Spirit to proceed from Father and Son.

But in being God, omnipotent, wise, and so forth, the Father is not distinguished from the Son and Holy Spirit, since the Son too is God, omnipotent, and the like, and likewise the Holy Spirit.

It is asked whether, since being begotten does not belong to the Holy Spirit, he may be called unbegotten. Augustine to Orosius: “The certain faith declares the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten. For if we call him unbegotten, we seem to affirm two fathers; but if begotten, we shall be blamed for believing in two sons.”

Again, Orosius to Augustine: “Did the Father generate the Son by will or by necessity?” Augustine: “Neither by will nor by necessity; for there is no necessity in God, and will cannot precede wisdom. For one of our own number, when a heretic asked him whether the Father generated the Son unwillingly or willingly, is reported to have answered commendably: ‘Tell me, heretic, is God the Father God by necessity or by will?’ If he had said, ‘By necessity,’ a great absurdity followed; if, ‘By will,’ the answer would have been made to him: ‘Then God is God by will, not by nature.’ Thus, just as the Father is God by nature, so by nature he generated the Son.”

This generation is eternal and ineffable. Hence the prophet: “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. 53).

Some are accustomed to object in this way: “For the Son to be generated by the Father is nothing other than for him to be from the Father.” We answer that although both Son and Holy Spirit are from the Father, the Son is from the Father in one manner and the Holy Spirit in another. Augustine: “The Spirit too is from the Father, but not as born—rather, as given.” The Son also proceeds from the Father, as he himself shows in John, saying: “I proceeded from God and came into the world” (John 8). Thus the Son is from the Father by proceeding and by being born; the Spirit, however, is from the Father not by being born but by proceeding. Both proceed from the Father, but in an ineffable and dissimilar manner.

The Holy Spirit, then, is not begotten; for, since he is from Father and Son, if he were begotten he would already have two fathers, and thus there would be confusion in the Trinity, in which there would be two fathers and two sons. What it is to beget, and what it is to proceed, cannot be known in this life.

Augustine, book two of *On the Trinity*, says concerning this generation: “For him, to be from the Father—that is, to be born from the Father—is nothing other than to see the Father; nor is seeing the Father at work something other than working equally with him. But who understands this?”

Ambrose, *On the Trinity*: “How the Son is begotten cannot be known: the mind fails, the voice is silent—not only that of human beings but of angels. It is above angels, above cherubim, above seraphim, above every understanding. We are commanded to believe; we are not permitted to investigate. Remove arguments where faith is sought.” The same author: “It is permitted to know that he was born, but not to investigate how he was born.”

Yet some, presuming upon their own intellect, say that they do not fail to know such matters, adhering to Jerome’s authority on Ecclesiastes: “Who in the sacred Scriptures is very often used not for the impossible but for the difficult,” as in: “Who shall recount his generation?” But Jerome understood this of the generation according to the flesh, which can in some fashion be recounted.

It is customary to ask, since the generation of the Son from the Father has neither beginning nor end, because it is eternal, whether one should say, “The Son is always being begotten,” or “The Son is always begotten.”

Gregory, on Job: “The Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he is the power and wisdom of God, was born from the Father before times; or rather, since he neither began to be born nor ceased, let us more truly say: always born. Yet we cannot always say ‘is being born,’ lest he seem imperfect. But so that he may be designated both eternal and perfect, let us say both ‘always’ and ‘born’: ‘born,’ so as to pertain to perfection; and ‘always,’ to eternity. Although, in saying ‘perfect’ itself, we depart far from expressing that truth; for what was not made cannot be called perfect. Yet the Lord, condescending to the words of our weakness, says: ‘Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect’ [Col. 0054C] (Matt. 5).”

And in the Psalm it is said: “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2). He said “today” because that generation does not pass away; “I have begotten,” because it lacks a beginning.

## Chapter VIII. On the equality of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit

To the foregoing must be added that although the Son is from the Father, he is not therefore to be thought later than or inferior to the Father. Rather, the Son is coeternal, co-omnipotent, consubstantial, and coequal with the Father; and the Holy Spirit is coequal with Father and Son.

Augustine, in *On the Trinity*: “The Son is coeternal with the Father just as brightness is coeval with fire; and it would be eternal if the fire were eternal.”

It should be noted that the Son is equal to the Father according to substance, not according to the property by which he is distinguished [Col. 0054D] from the Father. In that the Son is one God with the Father, one nature, one substance, he is equal to the Father. But insofar as he is begotten from the Father, he is not equal to him. Is he therefore unequal? This is not true, because insofar as the Father is unbegotten and the Son begotten, neither equality nor inequality is considered. The same applies to the Holy Spirit.

Augustine, book five of *On the Trinity*: “Since the Son is spoken of relatively to the Father, the Son is not equal to the Father according to that in which he is spoken of relatively to the Father; rather, the Son is equal to the Father according to that in which he is spoken of in relation to himself. But whatever is spoken of in relation to itself is spoken according to substance. It follows, therefore, that he is equal to the Father according to substance.” Therefore the substance of both is the same.

One person of the three must not be called a part of this Holy Trinity. For the whole Trinity is one substance, simple and indivisible. Nor are two persons something greater than one, nor three greater than two. Since each one is divine substance and these three are the same substance, three are not something greater than one.

Augustine: “In the Trinity, which is God, the Father is God, the Son God, the Holy Spirit God; and these three are one God. Nor is one God a third part of this Trinity; nor are two a greater part than one; nor are all the persons something greater than the individual persons, because its magnitude is spiritual, not bodily.” The same author: “God is not to be considered triple because God is Trinity; otherwise he would be less in each one than in all three together.”

## Chapter IX. That nothing is said of the Holy Trinity according to accident

[Col. 0055B]

This also must be considered: nothing is said of the Holy Trinity according to accident. For what is said according to accident is mutable; but in God there is nothing mutable. Yet not everything said of God is said according to substance, because some things are said according to relation or property, such as Father and Son.

Augustine, book five of *On the Trinity*: “An accident is not usually called an accident unless it can be lost through some change in the thing to which it happens. But nothing is said of God according to accident, because nothing happens to him. Yet not everything that is said is said according to substance.”

Those things are said according to substance which are said without any reference to a relation, or which express the unity of the divine substance: God, Omnipotent, and the like. And, as Augustine says, all these are said of the individual persons, and are said not plurally but singularly of all three together. For just as the Father is God, omnipotent, wise, eternal, and so forth, so the Son is God, omnipotent, and so forth, and likewise the Holy Spirit. And these three are one God, one omnipotent being; and so with all things said according to substance—except the name *person*.

For although the name *person* is said according to substance—since it can be predicated of each individual person: “The Father is a person, the Son a person, the Holy Spirit a person”—nevertheless one cannot say, “These three are one person.”

Augustine: “Person is said in relation to itself, just as God and similar terms are. But this is the only name which, although said of the individual persons in relation to themselves, is in the totality understood plurally rather than singly.” This name *person*, Augustine says, was devised so that, when the question was asked, “What three?” or “What are the three?”, one answer might be given in one word: namely, “three persons.”

Augustine: “We say three persons not so that any diversity of essence may be understood, but so that an answer may be possible with one term when it is asked, ‘What three?’ or ‘What are the three?’” The same author: “When it is asked who the three are, or what three things are meant by Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, it has been said: three persons. By this term he did not intend diversity to be understood, but neither did he wish singularity, lest only unity and not Trinity be understood there.”

For in the Trinity there is no diversity, because such as the Father is, such is the Son; but there is distinction. God is not to be called singular, because then there would be only one person.

Augustine, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*: “He is one indeed, but not singular; and in the mystery he has another who is with the other.” Ambrose, *On the Faith*, addressed to the Emperor Gratian: “What is of one substance cannot be separated, so that there is not singularity but unity. Singularity pertains to person; unity to nature.” [Col. 0056A]

From this a substantial question arises. Since the name *person*, according to Augustine’s testimony, is said according to substance, and since this is the definition of person—“a person is an individual nature of rational substance”—how should it be understood that “the Son is another person from the Father”? For this can certainly be said: “The Father is a person,” that is, a rational substance; “the Son is a person,” that is, a rational substance. Again, when we say, “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons,” we cannot say “three rational substances.”

The answer may be that when it is said simply, “The Father is a person; the Son is a person,” it is rightly expounded thus: “The Father is a person,” that is, a rational substance. But by an addition the meaning is restricted: “The Son is another person,” that is, distinct by another property; “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons,” that is, distinct by three properties.

For when it is said, “The Son is God,” he is not distinguished from the Father; but when there is added, “The Son is God from God,” distinction is thereby made. Thus, when it is said, “The Father is a person; the Son is a person,” no distinction has yet been made; but when “another person” is added, or when, through the plural, “three persons” is said, distinction is marked. If anyone can solve this question more fittingly, I do not prejudge anyone.

Moreover, there is one name, namely Trinity, which is not said separately of any person but of all together. It is not substantial, but designates the plurality of persons. Thus some names in the Holy Trinity are said separately and not jointly—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—which refer to property; some jointly and not separately, as Trinity; and some separately and jointly, as God, omnipotent, and the like.

## Chapter X. On the differing sense of names

[Col. 0056D]

It must now be considered that those names which pertain to the unity of the divine substance are sometimes, with qualifications and sometimes without qualification, taken also to distinguish the persons: wisdom and goodness, for instance. They refer to substance, because the three persons are one substance, one wisdom, one goodness. Yet when “wisdom of the Father” is said, it refers only to the Son; “goodness of the Father and Son,” to the Holy Spirit. Likewise with spirit and charity: the whole Trinity is one spirit and one charity. But when “holy” is added, or when “the charity of the Father and Son” is said, these refer only to the Holy Spirit. For the Father is spirit, and the Father is also holy, but he is not the Holy Spirit.

Even without added qualifications these names are accustomed to signify persons: through “wisdom” the Son may be understood, as very often in the Proverbs of Solomon; through “goodness,” the Holy Spirit.

Jerome also used the name *spirit* to signify persons, saying thus in the Psalm of confession: “David asks for three spirits, saying: ‘Confirm me with a sovereign spirit; renew a right spirit within my inward parts; do not take your Holy Spirit from me’ (Ps. 50). Who are these three spirits? The sovereign spirit is the Father; the right Spirit, the Son; the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit.” Thus Jerome says “three spirits,” that is, three persons.

Augustine likewise, in *On Christian Doctrine*, speaks of three things in reference to the plurality of persons. He says: “Some things are to be enjoyed, others are to be used. Those which are to be enjoyed make us blessed. By those which are to be used, we are helped as we tend toward blessedness. If we wish to return to our homeland, we must use the world, not enjoy it. Therefore the things which are to be enjoyed are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. And that same Trinity is one thing, common to all who enjoy it. To enjoy, moreover, is to cling in love to some thing for its own sake.”

It is therefore clear that the same names are used now to signify unity of substance, now plurality of persons. Likewise, power, wisdom, and goodness are names of substance and belong equally to the individual persons; nevertheless, in sacred Scripture the Father is very often understood through power, [Col. 0057C] the Son through wisdom, and the Holy Spirit through goodness.

It is well to satisfy one who asks why this is done. Since the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have been transferred from creatures to the Creator himself, power is attributed to the Father and wisdom to the Son, lest what they signify in us seem to signify the same thing in God. Among human beings a father is prior to a son, and a son later than his father; and from antiquity a defect is customarily noted in the father, from posterity an imperfection of understanding in the son. Therefore power is attributed to the Father, lest he appear prior to the Son and consequently less powerful; wisdom to the Son, lest he appear later and consequently less wise than, or inferior to, the Father.

Nor is the Son called wisdom because he alone is wise, since the whole Trinity is one wisdom; nor is the Father called power because he alone is powerful, since the whole Trinity is one omnipotence. But this was especially to be said where it could be more greatly doubted. Hence it is said: “I believe in God the Father almighty.”

Moreover, *spirit* is accustomed to be used in a sense signifying severity and to denote cruelty; therefore goodness or kindness is more frequently ascribed [Col. 0057D] to the Holy Spirit.

Here a difficult question arises. If three persons are said to be in God because he is powerful, wise, and kind, why are there not rather four, or five, or many more, since he is strong, just, merciful, pious, and so forth? It may be answered that whatever is said of God and truly believed to be in God is referred to these three. If he is called strong, incorruptible, immutable, and the like, all this belongs to power. If provident, watchful, understanding, all this belongs to wisdom. If pious, gentle, merciful, all this belongs to goodness. In these three is supreme perfection. For where these three concur—to be able, to know, and to will, which belongs to kindness—nothing is lacking. If one of these is removed, there is no supreme perfection. Therefore the Trinity is perfect: it can neither be diminished nor increased.

In creatures signs of this holy and indivisible Trinity appear. The sign of power is the immensity of things; of wisdom, beauty; of goodness, usefulness. Thus through these outward things the invisible things of God are known by the rational creature.

Just as the names of substance, of which we have spoken above, are said of the individual persons, so likewise are those names which belong to God in relation to a creature in time: Lord, Creator, [Col. 0058B] Merciful One. For, as Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, “He was not Lord before he had a servant.” Thus he began to be Lord in time, because a creature, made in time, began to serve him. Likewise God began to be Creator in time, from the time when he made the creature. For he did not create it from eternity, nor is the creature coeternal with the Creator.
