And although Father is Lord and Creator, and likewise Son and Holy Spirit, nevertheless there are not three Lords but one Lord, not three creators but one Creator.

That some things are said of God in time without any change in him, Augustine shows through the likeness of a thing that begins to be a price without changing itself, in book four of *On the Trinity*: “When a coin is called a price, it is spoken of relatively, yet it was not changed when it began to be a price; nor when it is called a pledge, or in other similar instances.” If, therefore, a coin can be spoken of relatively without any change in itself, how much more should this be understood of the immutable substance of God: although he begins to be called something in time, nothing is thereby said to have happened to the substance of God, but to the creature in relation to which he is so called.

Therefore, what begins to be said in time, though it was not said before, is plainly said relatively: not according to an accident which has happened to him, but according to an accident of that in relation to which he is spoken. Thus it is clear that God is Lord and Creator in time; yet it is true that he is Lord of all things from eternity and Creator from eternity—but he is not Lord from eternity, nor Creator from eternity. Nor should it seem strange that something is said to belong to him in time. For assuming flesh belongs to him in time, [Col. 0058D] and the name Christ belongs to the Son of God in time; nevertheless, Christ is from eternity.

## Chapter XI. On the properties of the persons

It must be asked whether those properties by which the persons are distinguished are the persons themselves. That persons are distinguished by properties is contained in the authority which says: “In the essence, unity; in the persons, property”; and in many other authorities.

Yet some wished to say that those properties were not the persons themselves, objecting: if persons are discerned through them, how are they themselves the persons? Authority and reason refute them. For Augustine says: “Whatever is in God is God.” Therefore the property of the Father is God, because the Father’s property is the Father himself. Yet one should not say simply, “Property is God,” or “Property is Father,” but “the property of the Father,” just as one does not say absolutely, “Will is God,” but “the will of God is God.”

For what are the property of the Father, the property of the Son, and the property of the Holy Spirit except these persons, mutually discrete and distinct? Jerome, to Pope Damasus, *On the Explanation of the Faith*: “Confounding Arius, we say that the Trinity is one and the same substance; avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons expressly under property.” Again: “For we confess not merely names, but also the properties of the names—that is, persons, or, as the Greeks express it, hypostases, that is, subsistences.” Thus Jerome says “properties,” that [Col. 0059B] is, “persons.”

God is called simple either because he does not lose what he has, or because he is not one thing and that which is in him another. Reason may also be brought against them in this way. If there are three properties or relations in God which are not the divine substance itself, it appears that the divine substance—which is the Trinity—was not alone from eternity. But the Trinity alone, which is one God, is from eternity. Therefore let us confess that the three persons, or the three properties of those persons, are one God, one essence, and one divine substance: whether we say that the three persons are these, or the properties.

Although this is far from our senses and human reason, it must nevertheless be believed without doubt. For, as Gregory says: “Faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof”—that is, in that respect in which human reason supplies proof. For faith is not contrary to reason, but above reason. Therefore one who wishes to believe nothing except what he comprehends by reason, as philosophers do, has no merit in his faith; but merit belongs to the one who believes what is not contrary to reason and yet is above reason. Hence the Apostle: “The word of faith is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Rom. 10): near, because it is not contrary to reason, but above reason.

What is proper to the Father has been stated above: namely, to be unbegotten, which is to be Father. Nor should it disturb us that Augustine says: “To say ‘unbegotten’ is not the same as to say ‘Father,’ because Father is said in relation to the Son, while unbegotten marks no relation.” Therefore, it is not the same to say that the Father is unbegotten and that he is Father; but in the Holy Trinity being unbegotten and being Father are the same, just as being the wisdom of the Father, being his Son, and being the Word of the Father are the same. Yet the name Son marks relation, while the name Word or Wisdom does not.

Augustine, in *On the Trinity*: “To say ‘unbegotten’ is not the same as to say ‘Father’; for even if he had not begotten a Son, nothing would prevent our calling him unbegotten. For no one is a father because he is unbegotten, nor unbegotten because he is a father. Therefore unbegotten is said not relatively but in relation to itself. But begotten cannot be said except relatively. For he is Son because begotten, and because Son, certainly begotten. And as Son is related to Father, so begotten is related to begetter; [Col. 0060A] and as Father to Son, so begetter to begotten.”

At this point it should be noted that, since the Son is wisdom generated from the Father and the Father is wise by his own wisdom, the question arises whether the Father is wise by wisdom generated from himself. Augustine says that this must not be conceded. For if he were wise by wisdom generated from himself—since for him being is the same as being wise—the Father would then have being from the Son, not the Son from the Father.

Therefore the Father is not wise by wisdom generated from himself, but by unbegotten wisdom, which he himself is. For the Father is unbegotten wisdom. If it is objected: “Since the Father is wise, he is wise either by wisdom generated from himself or by another wisdom,” this is not true. For the one wisdom is the whole Trinity, but is unbegotten in the Father and begotten in the Son.

Just as it is said, “The Son is God from God, light from light, principle from principle,” while the Father is not God from God or principle from principle, it does not follow that he is other and something else. For he is one God with the Son and one principle of all creatures. The Father is the principle of the Son, because the Son is from him; Father and Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit; the whole Trinity is one principle of all creatures.

Likewise, although the Father is not wise by wisdom generated from himself, he is not wise by some other wisdom. Augustine, *On the Trinity*: “If the Son alone understands for the Father, himself, and the Holy Spirit, the consequence is that the Father is not wise from himself but from the Son; nor has wisdom generated wisdom from itself, if the Father is said to be wise by the wisdom which he generated. For where there is no understanding, there can be no wisdom. From this it is clear that, if the Father does not understand for himself and the Son understands for the Father, the Son makes the Father wise. And if being God is the same as being wise, and essence is the same for him as wisdom, then the Father has essence not from the Father—which is true—but rather from the Son, which is false.” Therefore God the Father is wise by that which is wisdom itself, and the Son is the wisdom of the Father. [Col. 0060C]

Some customarily raise this question: God the Father generated God the Son; and thus “God generated God” may rightly be conceded. For concerning the Son it is read: “God from God, light from light.” But if it is asked, since God generated God, whether he generated himself or another, neither must be conceded. That he did not generate another God is plain, because there is only one God. That “God generated himself” must not be conceded is shown by Augustine in *On the Trinity*, saying: “Whoever thinks God has such power that he generated himself is all the more in error, because not only is God not so, but neither a spiritual creature nor a bodily creature is so. There is absolutely no thing which generates itself.” Therefore one must not say, “God generated himself.” For the divine substance did not generate itself, nor another divine substance; rather, the person of the Father generated the person of the Son.

Moreover, it should be known that, just as the Trinity is inseparable, so it works inseparably.

Whatever the Father does, the Son and the Holy Spirit do the same. An objection is raised: to the Son alone belongs the assumption of flesh; but this is an operation. Therefore the Son does something which neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit does. To this it is said [Col. 0061A] that although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit operate inseparably, something may nevertheless belong to one which does not belong to the others. The saints illustrate this by an analogy. In a ray of sunlight, brightness and heat are joined inseparably; yet brightness illuminates, heat dries out, heat does not illuminate, and brightness does not dry out. Likewise, in the Holy Trinity the whole Trinity effected the incarnation of the Son. For the whole Trinity effected both that that man should exist and that he should be united to the Word; but not that he should be united to the whole Trinity. Therefore that operation belongs no more to the Son than to the Father; but the union is of the Son and not of the Father, just as the voice from the cloud was heard from the Father alone: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3), and so forth. For if it were the voice of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, “This is my Son” would be false [Col. 0061B]. For he is not the Son of himself or of the Holy Spirit. And yet the whole Trinity effected that voice; but it belongs to the Father alone, because the Father alone was signified by it. So also the Holy Spirit alone appeared in the dove, although the whole Trinity effected it. But the Holy Spirit alone appeared in it, because he alone was signified by it. It is asked whether the Holy Spirit was otherwise in that dove than in other creatures. The answer is: not otherwise with respect to the presence or essence of the Godhead, as we have already said, which is in all creatures and equally so; but otherwise with respect to signification.

## Chapter XII. On Foreknowledge and Predestination

Since the foreknowledge [Col. 0061C], disposition, and will of the Trinity precede the act of everything which it performs, an inquiry arises concerning God’s foreknowledge and providence, predestination, will, and power. It must be known that, because of its various functions, the wisdom of God is called by several names: knowledge, foreknowledge, providence, knowledge, predestination, and disposition. Knowledge concerns things existing; foreknowledge, future things; providence, things to be governed; disposition, things to be made; predestination, those to be saved.

Regarding foreknowledge, it is commonly asked whether it is itself the cause of things, or whether things are the cause of foreknowledge. But, as Boethius shows in *The Consolation of Philosophy*, neither should be conceded. For if things came to be because they are foreknown by God—since evils too are foreknown—then foreknowledge would already be the cause of evils [Col. 0061D], which is wholly irrational. Again, if things are foreknown by God because they are future, then what is temporal is the cause of what is eternal.

Origen, however, says in his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans: “A thing will not be because God knows it will be; rather, because it will be, it is known by God before it comes to pass.” This may be explained as follows: “because it will be”—that is, because it is going to be—so that no causal relation is denoted there. For just as Isaiah foretold that the blindness of the Jews would occur, saying, “He gave them eyes, that they might not see” (Isa. 6), yet it did not occur because he foretold it, but he foretold what was going to occur; so God from eternity foreknew that blindness, but it did not occur because he foreknew it. Rather, because it was going to occur, he foreknew it—he from whom nothing can be hidden.

“Foreknowledge” is said improperly of God [Col. 0062A]. For with him nothing is future and nothing past; in him there is neither earlier nor later. But with respect to things which are future to us, we say that he foreknows future things; whereas, as regards him, he knows them as present. Authority says that his knowledge can neither increase nor decrease. One who knows all things cannot know more; nor can one who cannot forget know less.

An objection is raised from what Jerome says on Habakkuk: “It is absurd,” he says, “to reduce the majesty of God to this: that he knows, moment by moment, how many gnats are born and how many die, what is the number of fleas and flies, how many fish swim in the waters, and similar things. Let us not be such foolish flatterers of God that, while we drive down his power even to the lowest things, we do injury to ourselves by saying that his providence is the same over irrational creatures and rational beings” [Col. 0062B].

Some explain this thus: it is absurd to reduce God’s majesty to this, that he knows moment by moment how many gnats there are, and so forth. He indeed knows, since nothing can be hidden from him; but not moment by moment, as we do, who cannot know all things at once. Others explain it thus: it is absurd to reduce God’s majesty to this, that he should know how many gnats there are in such a way as to take care over this. For “God is not concerned with oxen” (1 Cor. 9), but he is concerned with human beings, because he assigns angels for their guardianship. Hence: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matt. 18).

Another difficult objection may be made here. There is someone who will never read, though it could be that he reads. It is asked whether God knows that this man will read [Col. 0062C], or does not know it. We cannot say that he knows he will read, because it is false that he will read. Augustine, in his book addressed to Renatus, says: “What if foreknowledge itself is emptied, if what is foreknown will not be? For how can what is not future rightly be said to be foreknown as future?”

If we say, “He does not know that he will read,” the objection is raised: it can be that this man reads; and if it were so, it would certainly be known by God; and this can be. Therefore it can be that it is known by God; therefore he can know more than he knows, which is wholly false. I leave the solution of this question to the judgment of others. Yet it seems to me that neither of those alternatives should be conceded. For if someone asks, “Does he know that this man will read?” I shall say neither, “He knows that he will read,” nor, “He does not know that he will read” [Col. 0062D], but, “He knows that he will not read.” For it should never be said that God does not know this, or is ignorant of this, since nothing is hidden from him.

This is the difference between foreknowledge and predestination: foreknowledge concerns both those to be saved and those to be damned; predestination concerns only those to be saved. None of the predestined can be damned; none of the reprobate can be saved. The reprobate are foreknown unto death; the predestined are foreseen unto life. Augustine, *On Correction and Grace*: In the Apocalypse it is said, “Hold fast what you have, lest another receive your crown” (Rev. 3). For if another will not receive it unless this man loses it, the number of the elect is fixed. The same author: “The predestined number of the elect can neither be increased nor decreased.”

An objection is raised that it can be decreased, because all can be damned. For everyone who is saved is saved by grace; and what is given freely could have not been given. Likewise, it is argued that it could be increased, because all can be saved; for unless they could be saved, they could not be blamed for being damned [Col. 0063A]. The solution: it is true that the number of the predestined cannot be increased, because it cannot be that someone is saved without being predestined. It cannot be decreased, because it cannot be that someone is predestined and damned. For, considered by itself, “this man can be damned” is true, because he could have not been predestined; but “this predestined man can be damned” is not true, because it cannot both be that he is predestined and that he is damned. Likewise, “this man can be saved” is true; but “this reprobate man can be saved” is not true, because it cannot be that he is reprobate and saved.

[Col. 0063B] An objection commonly made concerning foreknowledge is this: God foreknew that this man would read, or something of that kind; but it can be that he does not read; therefore what God foreknew can fail to be; therefore God’s foreknowledge can be mistaken. But as we said of some future thing: if this is future, namely, that this man will read, it cannot be otherwise than that it is so. For it cannot be that something is future and does not occur; yet what is future can fail to occur, because it is future in such a way that it can either not be or be future. Likewise, if it is foreknown, it cannot fail to occur, because it cannot be that it is foreknown and does not occur; yet what is foreknown can fail to occur. This is true because it could have not been foreknown. Nor does it follow that God’s foreknowledge can therefore be mistaken; for it would be mistaken only if both were the case: namely, that it was foreknown that something would occur and that it did not occur [Col. 0063C].

Since divine predestination is election, according to the Apostle’s statement, “Whom he chose before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1), it is commonly asked why God chose this person rather than that one, as in the case of Jacob and Esau. Some say: “He chose this one because he foreknew that he would be such a person as would believe in him and serve him.” But Augustine retracts this in the *Retractations*, clearly showing that if one were chosen on account of future works, election would no longer be by grace. For if it is by works, as the Apostle says, it is no longer grace (Rom. 11).

The same Augustine, in *On Predestination*, says: “He did not choose us because he foreknew that we would be such persons, but in order that we might be such through that election of his grace by which he made us gracious in his beloved Son.” Therefore, when he predestined, he foreknew his own work. The same Augustine, commenting on the prophet Malachi’s passage, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1), says: “‘He has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills’ (Rom. 9). [Col. 0063D] But this will of God cannot be unjust. For it arises from most hidden merits; because even if sinners themselves, on account of original sin, have formed one mass, there is nevertheless among them some diversity. Therefore something precedes in sinners whereby, though not yet justified, they are made worthy of justification; and likewise something precedes in other sinners whereby they are worthy of hardening.”

But we do not know what he meant, unless perhaps we say either that he understood then what we have said above, or that he later retracted it [Col. 0064A]. Some, however, attempt to explain this authority thus: “it arises from most hidden [merits],” that is, in order that their merits may become most hidden.

Gilbert says: “Unless man had sinned, none of those to be damned would have been born; but because he sinned, those to be damned are born together with those to be saved. The saved are born in the place of those who otherwise would then have been born; the damned are born in no one’s place, but for the exercise and crown of the good.”

It is further asked whether from eternity he loved those predestined. It is so. Therefore he loved Paul too. It is so—and equally, because from eternity he loved him no more than when Paul was persecuting the Church of God, since what was future concerning him was present to God. And this was not according to merits, but according to the rewards which he prepared for him from eternity; yet he hated Paul’s evil. Note that he loves all alike according to their nature, both [Col. 0064B] good and evil, because “he hates nothing that he has made” (Wis. 11); yet he does not love the good alike according to the preparation of rewards, nor does he hate the evil alike according to the foreknowledge of punishments.

But it is asked whether he loved Judas. Answer: yes, from eternity, as much as now according to nature; yet he hated him because he saw that he would be such a person. Note that Judas could have been saved, yet the reprobate person could not have been saved.

God disposes both good and evil things. Hence it is asked whether all things, both good and evil, are within his disposition. Some say yes, and they have the authority of Augustine saying: “God left nothing unordered.” And elsewhere: “God is the arranger of evil wills.” And again: “It is in the power of evil people to will evil; but whether they accomplish this or that evil by their wickedness is in the power of God, who divides and orders the darkness.”

But others object: if God disposes evils, then evils please him. But this is false, because evils do not please him; rather, their being done pleases him for the sake of the whole. Because of this objection, some say that he does not dispose evils, but disposes concerning evils by drawing from them something that benefits the good: as from Nero, what benefited Peter; from Decius, what benefited Lawrence. For he does not wish anyone to stand idle in his commonwealth without serving him. Yet, because this service is rendered with an evil intention, it is evil for those serving him in this way [Col. 0064C].

## Chapter XIII. On the Will of God

[Col. 0064D] It remains now to consider the will of God. God’s will is the first cause of all things and therefore is immutable. Other causes are mutable because they are not first, and therefore they often fail. But this will, because it has no cause prior to itself, can neither fail nor change. And because God’s will is the first cause of all things, when it is said, “This is so because God willed it,” one must not ask why he willed it. For a first cause has no cause.

Although God’s will is one—for it is God himself, who is one—nevertheless, on account of diverse effects, several wills of God are spoken of. Hence the Prophet says: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all his wills” (Ps. 110). Likewise, because of the diverse effects of God’s mercy and justice, the same Prophet speaks in the plural: “I will sing forever of the mercies of the Lord” (Ps. 88) [Col. 0065A]. And elsewhere: “The justices of the Lord, gladdening hearts” (Ps. 18). Yet, with respect to God himself, mercy is one and justice is one, and each is what he himself is. So also with will.

For in Sacred Scripture the will of God is sometimes understood as that which is identical with God and coeternal with him; and this will is always fulfilled. Of this the Apostle says: “Who resists his will?” (Rom. 9). And elsewhere: “That you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Rom. 12). This will may be called God’s good pleasure or disposition. Hence the Prophet says: “Whatever he willed, he did” (Ps. 113)—that is, whatever he disposed that he would do.

At other times God’s command or prohibition is called the will of God, because they are signs of the divine will. Just as signs of anger are called anger, so signs of love are called love. God is said to be angry though anger is not in him; rather, the outward sign by which God is shown to be angry is called anger, as in the drowning of the Egyptians. So command and prohibition, because they indicate to us what God wills to be done or not done, are called will. Of this the Lord says in the Gospel: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth” (Matt. 6). And elsewhere: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother and sister” (Matt. 12). Many things are done contrary to this will. Augustine, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, says: “Unbelievers indeed act contrary to God’s will when they do not believe his Gospel” [Col. 0065B].

As command and prohibition are signs of the divine will, so operation and permission are also signs; and therefore in Sacred Scripture they are often called the will of God. Hence the Apostle’s statement: “He wills all to be saved” (1 Tim. 2). Augustine explains it thus in *On Correction and Grace*: “He wills all to be saved,” that is, “he makes us will.” Behold: that which he works in us is called the will of God. The same applies to permission. Hence the Apostle’s statement: “He hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9). And Augustine in the *Enchiridion*: “Nothing happens unless the Almighty wills it to happen, either by permitting it to happen or by doing it himself. Nor should it be doubted that God acts beneficently even by permitting whatever evils happen to occur. For he permits these only by a just judgment; and certainly everything that is just is good.”

Thus we have four signs of the divine will: command, prohibition, operation, and permission; although God’s will itself remains one and immutable [Col. 0065D]. Therefore one must carefully observe where Scripture speaks of God’s own good pleasure, and where it speaks of a sign of that good pleasure.

When it is found that “God wills good” or “does not will evil,” this is understood of God’s good pleasure. He wills good, that is, he approves it and judges it consonant with himself; he does not will evils, that is, he does not approve them or judge them like himself. And although he does not will evils, nevertheless he wills evils to exist. To understand this, note that some things are good in themselves and for another end; some are good for another end but not in themselves; and some are good in themselves but not for another end.

Those things which are good in themselves and for another end God wills, that is, approves; and he wills them to exist because they are good for another end, as are all good things that come to pass. Things good in themselves but not for another end—such as good things which could occur but do not occur—God wills, because he wills every good, that is, approves it; but he does not will them to exist, that is, he does not approve their existing, because they are not good for another end [Col. 0066A]. Things which are evil in themselves but good for another end, such as evils which occur, God does not will—that is, he does not approve them—yet he wills them to exist because it is good that they exist. For unless he willed evils to exist, they could in no way exist. If he willed them not to exist and could not bring this about, he would be powerless, as we are, who sometimes cannot do what we will. Thus evils could not exist unless he willed them to exist. For how could anything happen against his will, when Scripture says: “Who resists his will?” (Rom. 9).

Therefore, since God from eternity, in his foreknowledge and wisdom, saw all things both good and evil, among all those things he saw certain things which, if they existed, would be good in themselves and also good for another end; and he not only willed them but also willed them to exist. He saw other things which, if they existed, would indeed be good in themselves, but not for another end; and therefore, although he approves them—since he wills nothing to exist without a reason—he did not will them to exist. Likewise, when he saw other things evil in themselves and good for another end, he willed them to exist. For which is better to exist: things good only in themselves, or things which, though not good in themselves, are nevertheless good for another end? Certainly those which are good for another end [Col. 0066B]. Yet we do not concede that, if he wills them to exist, he also wills them; nor, if they are good for another end, that they are thereby good.

Accordingly, when someone sins, he acts contrary to God’s will, because he acts contrary to God’s command and because God does not will what he does; yet he does what God wills to exist. For example, the Jews crucified Christ: in killing him, they acted contrary to God’s will; and yet God willed that evil to exist, because it was good for another end [Col. 0066C].

Some are accustomed to object thus: God the Father willed Christ to suffer and die; therefore he willed the Jews to scourge and kill him, and so they did what God willed. This should not be conceded. For since their act was evil, it did not please God, who wills no evil, although it pleased God that that act should exist. For these words are customarily understood thus: “This man does what God wills,” that is, what he does God rewards and holds pleasing. Thus it is clear that God wills evil to exist, though he does not will evil; nor does he will anyone to do evil, because he does not reward it but rather punishes it. But he wills good to exist and wills human beings to do it, because he finds it pleasing and rewards it.

This is what Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*: “God’s will is always fulfilled, either concerning us or by us.” It is fulfilled concerning us, but we do not thereby fulfill it when we sin. It is fulfilled by us when we do good. For we do what we know pleases God. Augustine: “These are the great works of the Lord, sought out in all his wills” (Ps. 110), and so wisely sought out that, when angelic and human creatures sinned—that is, when each did not what God willed but what it itself willed—even through the will of the creature itself, by which what the Creator did not will was done, that which he willed was fulfilled: he, supremely good, making good use even of evils, for the damnation of those whom he justly predestined to punishment and for the salvation of those whom he kindly [Col. 0067A] predestined to grace. For, so far as they themselves were concerned, they did what God did not will; but so far as the omnipotence of God was concerned, they could in no way bring this about. For by the very fact that they acted contrary to God’s will, his will was done concerning them. Thus the works of the Lord are sought out in all his wills, so that in a wonderful and ineffable manner nothing happens outside his will—not even what happens contrary to his will, since it would not happen if he did not permit it. And he permits it not unwillingly but willingly; nor would one who is good permit evil to occur unless one who is omnipotent could also make good from evil.”

Gregory: “Many carry out God’s will by the very means through which they strive to alter it, and in resisting his counsel they serve it, because what resists through human effort serves his disposition.”

[Col. 0067B] An objection can be raised in this way: It is good that evil exist; but God is the author of every good; therefore he makes evil exist. This should not be conceded, because then evils would be made with him as their author. But it may be said that he makes it good for evil to exist; for he works evil into good.

The following objection is commonly made concerning command and prohibition. God commands what he does not will to exist, because good things are commanded to many people which they do not do. Thus he very frequently commanded the Jews things which they did not do; yet it was not in God’s good pleasure that they should do them or that those things should exist, because, as we have already said, whatever God wills to exist—since he can do all things—exists wholly; otherwise he would be powerless if he willed something to exist and it did not exist. Likewise, he prohibits someone from doing evil—as he did the same Jews very frequently [Col. 0067C]—yet that evil comes to pass. For God willed that evil to exist, because nothing can exist unless God wills it to exist.

It is therefore apparent that he sometimes commands what he does not will to exist—for nothing can exist unless he wills it to exist—and prohibits what he wills to exist. But if he wills it to exist, why does he prohibit it? If he does not will it, why does he command it? To this it may be said that he commands it because it is good for that person; and it belongs to a lord to command his servant what is good in itself and good for the person to whom he commands it. If it pleases the Lord to help the servant to do it, that is mercy; if it does not please him to help, that is justice. Likewise, he prohibits evil to a servant because it is evil in itself and evil for the one to whom he prohibits it; and it belongs to a lord to prohibit evil to a servant so that the servant may have no excuse.

It must also be observed here that, although what is commanded is good for this person, it is not good for the whole; and although what is prohibited is evil for him, it is good for the whole [Col. 0067D]. Because the good of the whole is greater than that of a part, and the evil of one part is less than the evil of the whole, therefore he does not will to exist what is good for one person but not for the whole; and he wills to exist what is evil for one person but good for the whole, lest the good of the whole be hindered. For nothing happens that is not good for the whole, although God’s judgments are hidden from us. But as it is said in Job: “Nothing happens on earth without a cause” (Job 5); and so not even a leaf falls from a tree without a cause.

## Chapter XIV. On the Omnipotence of God

[Col. 0068A]

We must now speak of God’s power. Many authorities say that God can do all things. Augustine, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*: “God can indeed do all things, but he does only what accords with his truth and justice.” In the same work: “God could have made all things at once, but reason forbade it.” Therefore it must be said that God can do all things.

An objection is raised from Augustine’s statement in *On the Spirit and the Letter*: “God is not called omnipotent because he can do all things, but because he can accomplish whatever he wills, so that nothing can prevail against his will to prevent its fulfillment or impede it in any manner.” To this one may say that where Augustine says, “He is not called omnipotent because he can do all things,” he takes “all things” so broadly as to include [Col. 0068B] even evils, which God neither wills nor can do.

The same author, in the book *On the Creed*: “Almighty God cannot die, cannot be deceived, cannot become miserable, cannot be conquered. Far be it that the Almighty should be able to do these and similar things! Consequently, truth not only shows that he who cannot do these things is omnipotent; truth also compels us to say that he who can do these things is not omnipotent.”

It is therefore clear that God is omnipotent because he can do all that he wills. It may also be said absolutely that he can do all things; yet he cannot sin, because sinning is not one of “all things.” But if an objection is raised from our actions, such as walking and the like, one may say that these belong to his omnipotence, although he cannot have them in himself: for he cannot walk, yet he can cause walking to occur.

[Col. 0068C] I think we must consider whether God can do more things than he wills to do or does. Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*: “The omnipotent will can do many things which it neither wills nor does.” For he could have caused twelve legions of angels to fight against those who seized him. In the Gospel, Matthew says: “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will furnish me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26). Hence the same Augustine: “Then, in the clearest light of wisdom, what the faith of the devout now holds will be seen: how immutable and most effective God’s will is, how many things he can do and does not will, yet how he wills nothing which he cannot do.”

These authorities make it clear that God can do many things which he does not will; reason proves the same. God does not will all people to be justified; yet who doubts that he can do so? Augustine, in *On Nature and Grace*: “The Lord raised Lazarus in body; should we say that he could not raise Judas in mind? He could indeed, but he did not will to.”

Against our saying that God can do certain things which he does not will to do is raised Augustine’s statement in the book *On the Creed*: “This alone God cannot do: what he does not will.” Thus it appears that he cannot do something which he does not will. But that statement must be explained thus: “This alone God cannot do: what he does not will”—that is, he can do nothing unwillingly. For it cannot be that one who cannot be compelled does something unwillingly.

Again an objection is raised: whatever God can do, he can will; but he can do something that [Col. 0069A] he does not will; therefore he can will what he does not will. And if he can will what he does not will, his will is mutable and not eternal, but begins to will something which previously it did not will.

Augustine, speaking to God in the *Confessions*, says: “Nor are you compelled unwillingly to do anything, because your will is not greater than your power. Yet it would be greater if you were greater than yourself.” Hence it would appear that God cannot do something which he does not will to do, and can will nothing except what he wills.

To this it may be said that God’s will is understood in many ways, as explained above: sometimes as the effect of the divine will; sometimes as that which is in God, which is God himself. When Augustine says that God can do many things which he does not will, he has regard to the effect: “which he does not will,” that is, which he does not bring about, he is able to bring about. For he does not refrain from them through powerlessness. In this sense one may say, “God can will what he does not will.” But if we speak of God’s will itself, which is what he himself is, he can do nothing except what he wills and can will nothing except what he wills [Col. 0069B]. For willing is the same as being, and willing is likewise the same as being able. Therefore Augustine says: “The will is not greater than the power.” In this or another suitable way the foregoing contradiction may be resolved.

It should not go unmentioned here that some, puffed up by knowledge, say that God cannot do anything other than what he does, nor omit any of the things which he does. They attempt to establish this as follows. Whatever God does, it is good and just that it be done, for he can do only what is just; and what is good to be done ought not not to be done. Therefore [Col. 0069C] God ought not omit what he does; and what he ought not do, he cannot do; therefore he cannot fail to do what he does. Likewise they seek to prove that he cannot do anything other than what he does in this way: what he does not do ought not to be done, because if it ought to be done, he would do it; and what ought not to be done by God cannot be done by him. Therefore he cannot do the things which he leaves undone.

But, in my view, poison lies hidden under that word “ought.” For if we say, “God ought not to do those things,” they infer, “therefore he cannot do them.” If we say, “He ought to do those things,” they infer, “therefore he cannot refrain from doing them.” But neither proposition should be conceded concerning God. For, as Augustine says: “Another way was possible for God, but none more fitting for the healing of our misery.” Yet we shall not say that he ought to have redeemed the world in another way or ought not to have done so, because [Col. 0069D] he does nothing from obligation but from goodness alone. Human beings act from obligation because they become better by doing so, or worse if they do not.

Some are accustomed to say that God cannot make the things he makes better, because if he could make them better and did not, he would be envious. Augustine, in the book *Questions*, says: “The God whom he begot, since he could not beget one better than himself—for nothing is better than God—he ought to beget equal to himself; for if he could and would not, he would be envious.” From this they wish to conclude that if God could make things better and did not, he would be envious. But the analogy does not hold, because he begot the Son from his own substance. Therefore, since he begot the Son from his own substance, if he could have begotten him equal and did not, he would be envious. But other things [Col. 0070A], which he did not make from his own substance, he could have made better.

Augustine, commenting on Genesis: “God could have made a human being such that he could not and would not sin; and if he had made such a person, who would doubt that he had made a better one?” We must ask how they understand a thing not to be able to be better: either because it is supremely good, in which case a creature would be equal to its Creator; or because the greater good which it lacks cannot be received by it. But if this is so, it can be better if it is made capable of a greater good—which he who made it can do.

That expression, however, is ambiguous: “God can make better.” If it is objected that he can make something better—that is, make something with greater wisdom—the statement is false, because his wisdom cannot be increased. [Col. 0070B] But it is true in this sense: he can make better, that is, make a better thing.

## Chapter XV. On Faith in the Incarnation
Now we must treat that part of the faith which concerns the mystery of the Incarnation, as the Apostle says: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, that he might condemn sin through sin” (Rom. VIII). By these words he in part discloses the mystery of the Incarnation. For this purpose he came into the world: to condemn the devil and to free humankind. But since the Son of God, who is everywhere, was in the world, how did he come into the world? He came because he appeared visibly.

It is commonly asked why neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit assumed flesh, but the Son alone. It may be answered that this did not befit the Father, because it does not belong to him to be sent by another, since he is not from another. Nor did the Holy Spirit [Col. 0070C] assume flesh, lest one should be Son in humanity and another in divinity, and there should thus be two Sons in the Trinity. Therefore it is the person of the Son that is incarnate, so that he who was Son in divinity might be Son in humanity also. It was fitting, moreover, that as the Father made the world through his Wisdom, so he should redeem it through that same Wisdom. And because in man both natures were corrupted, namely soul and body, he assumed both, in order to free both.

Yet he did not assume a human person; he assumed nature, not person. Augustine, in *On Faith to Peter*: “For God the Word did not take the person of a human being, but nature.” For in Christ there are two natures, divine and human, and three substances: flesh, soul, and Word; but not two persons. For God is one nature and man another [Col. 0070D]; yet God is not one person and that man another. As Augustine says to Felicianus: “The Son of God is one thing, the son of man another; but he is not another.” Again: “The Son of God is one thing from the Father, another from the mother; but he is not another.”

Against the statement that he did not assume a person, the following objection is made: he assumed soul and body, but these are one person; therefore he assumed one person. Some answer it thus. Those two things, when joined together, are one person; but before they were assumed by the Word, since they were not joined together, they were not one person. For by assuming them he united them, and by uniting them he assumed them.

Yet it may still be objected that the soul is a rational substance of an individual nature—which is the definition of a person. Therefore, if he assumed a soul, [Col. 0071A] he also assumed a person. This would indeed follow if the soul existed before it was assumed. For a soul is a person, as an angel is. For what is a human being except a soul possessing a body? But he did not assume a person because that which he assumed was not a person. For in creating the soul he assumed it, and in assuming it he created it.

The same objection may be put thus: the Son of God assumed a human being, but no human being exists who is not a person. This we readily grant; but, as we have said, that man did not exist before he was assumed. For although the body existed previously, the soul did not. Therefore he did not assume a man who already existed, but created him by assuming him.

Still, it does not seem that one should grant, “He assumed some human being,” but simply, “He assumed humanity.” Yet the former seems capable of proof: “He assumed the [Col. 0071B] man who hung upon the cross, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit; therefore, he assumed some man.” This seems sophistical, like this other argument: “Last year I saw him who is bishop; therefore I saw some bishop.” But whatever may be granted in disputes of this kind concerning words, we must hold without doubt that he did not assume a person. For, as Augustine says: “When the matters are agreed, there should be no controversy over words.”

To the preceding question may further be added this objection. If no person was assumed because that man did not exist before he was assumed by the Word, then that man was a person from the time he was assumed. And if the man assumed by the Word is a person, since he is united to the Word, a person is united to the Word, and thus person is united to person—which must not be conceded [Col. 0071C]. For the man assumed by the Word is not another person, but one person with the Word. For it is written: “The man was assumed into unity of person, not of nature”; because he is not one nature with the Word, but one person.

For as soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ, although the union between God and man is far greater than that between soul and flesh. For the union possible between a spiritual nature and a spiritual nature is greater than that possible between a spiritual and a bodily nature. God, indeed, is a spiritual nature, and man is a spiritual nature. Hence the union between God and man is such that God is called man and man God; but the soul is not called flesh, nor flesh soul. Again: that person, Christ, is true God and true man; but it cannot be said, “A human being is flesh,” or “A human being is soul” [Col. 0071D].

“Man is God” is explained thus: that is, man is united to God; “God is man,” that is, God is united to man. I do not reject this explanation; nevertheless, it seems to me that more is contained in these words. For if “man is God” says nothing other than “man is united to God,” why cannot it be said, “flesh is soul,” since it is united to soul? Or, “soul is God,” since it is united to God? Therefore “man is God” and “God is man” are said because the same one who is man is God, and the same one who is God is man. Hence the Prophet says: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI). And in John: “No one has ascended into heaven except him who descended [Col. 0072A] from heaven” (John III). For, as Gregory says: “He himself is temporal from his mother, eternal from his Father; he himself who made, he himself who was made.”

Concerning this, it is commonly asked whether “the assumed man is God” should be conceded. But since Augustine says, “The assumed man is the only-begotten Son of God,” I do not see on what grounds it could be denied. Yet some concede its negative: “The assumed man is not God,” that is, human nature is not divine nature. They attempt to prove that it bears this sense by Jerome’s authority, who says: “The Word is God, not the assumed flesh.” This authority does nothing against us. For no one concedes the propositions, “The assumed flesh is God,” or “Human nature is God.” Although “the assumed man” and “human nature” are the same thing, they nonetheless distinguish the manner of speaking, [Col. 0072B] just as God is nothing other than divinity; and although “man is God” is said, “man is divinity” is not said. For that would be to say that man is the divine nature. As Ambrose says: “Not by changeability of nature, but by unity of person, is man God and God man.”

## CHAPTER XVI. That Christ assumed soul and flesh simultaneously

Moreover, this must be believed without doubt: he did not first assume flesh, as some have said, and then soul; rather, the Word of God united both flesh and soul to himself at the same time. The learned are not found to disagree on this point.

Some say that the flesh which he received from Mary was formed over forty days; and, when it had been formed and had the outlines [Col. 0072C] of a human being, the Word of God simultaneously united to himself both that flesh and that soul. They wish to draw this from Augustine’s authority in his commentary on John, where it is said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The Jews therefore said: “Forty-six years …” (John II), etc. On this passage Augustine says: “This number accords with the perfection of the Lord’s body; for, as physicians say, the form of the human body is completed in so many days.”

Others wish to say that, as soon as that flesh was separated out by the Holy Spirit, it had some differentiation of members, though so slight that it was not perceptible to the eyes; but over the forty days of which Augustine speaks, it became perfect and conspicuous. At the very moment of its separation, he assumed flesh and soul. The authorities more strongly favor this latter view. Gregory: “When the angel announced it and the Spirit came, immediately the Word was in the womb; immediately, within the womb, the Word was flesh.” Augustine, in *On the Trinity*: “He would not be the mediator of God and human beings unless the same one were both true God and true man, in both respects, and one. The whole Trinity, whose will and operation are one, made that servant-form which the Son alone assumed. Yet flesh was not first conceived in the Virgin’s womb, and divinity afterward came into the flesh; rather, as soon as the Word came, in the womb—while the truth of its own nature was preserved—it became flesh and a perfect human being; that is, he was born in the reality of flesh and soul.”

Concerning that flesh to which the Word was united, it is asked [Col. 0073A] whether it was previously in Mary, bound by sin.

> [Note: Here he speaks according to the common opinion of his time, when the Church had not yet defined that another view was to be held.]

Augustine says that this was so; but at the very separation it was cleansed by the Holy Spirit both from sin and from the tinder of sin (*fomes peccati*, the inclination to sin). Mary, however, he cleansed altogether from sin, but not from the tinder of sin; though he weakened this so greatly that she is believed not to have sinned thereafter.

Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*: “With the exception of the holy Virgin Mary, concerning whom, for the honor of God, I wish to entertain absolutely no question when sins are under discussion—for we know from this that more grace was bestowed on her to conquer sin entirely, since she merited to conceive and bear him whom we know had no sin—if, with this Virgin excepted, all the holy men and women could be gathered together, what would they answer except what John says: ‘If we say [Col. 0073B] that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us’” (1 John I).

But if Christ’s flesh in Mary and in the others from whom he descended was liable to sin, how is this to be resolved: “Levi was tithed in Abraham” (Heb. VII), whereas Christ was not tithed in Abraham? Augustine resolves it thus: Levi was tithed in Abraham because he descended from him through concupiscence; Christ was not tithed in him because Christ’s flesh did not descend from him through concupiscence. But did not that same flesh descend through concupiscence into David and Mary? Nevertheless, not Christ’s flesh; for that would be to say that it descended into Christ through concupiscence, which is altogether false.

Some wish to say that, as before the sin there was in Adam a certain particle [Col. 0073C] clean and holy, so after the sin it was preserved in him and in all his successors in a direct line down to Mary. They say that they have this from Gregory.

Many authorities testify that this man, from his very conception, was full of grace and truth, and possessed such wisdom that it could not be increased. Jeremiah: “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI), in the bosom of her womb. What does “a woman shall encompass a man” mean, except that from his very conception he was a perfect human being in wisdom, though not in bodily size—as some have held, namely, that he was as large in the womb as upon the cross? For from his very conception God anointed him with the oil of gladness above his fellows [Col. 0073D] (Heb. I).

But this seems opposed by the Gospel saying: “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom before God and before men” (Luke II). It may be said, however, that although he did not advance in wisdom in himself, he nevertheless advanced among human beings, who advanced through his wisdom and became better. Thus one commonly says, “This man advances in his bishopric,” not because he becomes wiser at some time, but because he instructs others well before God and before human beings—that is, for God’s honor and for human beings’ advancement. Bede on Luke: “He is rightly said to be full of wisdom, not advancing in wisdom through intervals of time, since he was always full from the hour of conception. For, as the Apostle says, ‘In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily’” [Col. 0074A] (Col. II).

Some commonly ask whether Christ’s soul possessed knowledge of all things. Some say that it did not possess all knowledge and did not know everything that God knows. They seek to prove this as follows: that soul is a creature, but no creature is equal to the Creator in any respect; therefore it does not know whatever God knows. Again, if that soul has wisdom equal to God’s, then it will be false that God has greater sufficiency than his creature in every good. Again, the Apostle says: “The Spirit of God alone searches all things, even the deep things of God” (1 Cor. II); therefore that soul cannot know all things.

It may be said in reply that although the soul united to the Word of God knows whatever the Word knows, it is not equal to him in knowledge, [Col. 0074B] because that knowledge belongs to the Word by nature and to the soul by grace. Again, concerning the objection that God has greater sufficiency in every good than his creature: let them know that this was said where a creature’s good is distinct from the Creator’s good; but since the wisdom of that soul is not other than divine wisdom, how can there be a comparison?

For it must be said without doubt that there was in Christ no wisdom other than divine wisdom. If the wisdom of Christ’s soul were other than divine wisdom, it would be lesser. If the wisdom of that soul were less than the wisdom of God, how could it comprehend the whole of it? Therefore that man would know less than God. Hence, in order firmly to hold the truth that that soul was ignorant of nothing but knew all things, it must be said that it was not by another wisdom that [Col. 0074C] that soul was wise, but by wisdom which is in God by nature and in that soul by grace.

What they say, “The Spirit of God alone searches all things,” serves rather against them; for the Apostle immediately adds: “But we have the Spirit of God” (ibid.). But that soul possessed the Spirit of God above all others. Against their perversity John the Evangelist says: “The Spirit is given to others by measure, but to Christ it was not given by measure” (John III). But since there are two natures in Christ, let us see to which the Spirit was given: to the divine or the human. It is not fitting for the divine nature to receive, but to give; therefore the Spirit was given without measure to the human nature. But where there is no measure, there is no limit; therefore that soul knew all things. For if it knew some things and did not know others, it knew by measure, because its knowledge had a limit.

Fulgentius [Col. 0074D] raises many objections against that error, maintaining by the Apostle’s authority that that soul had knowledge of all things, where he says: “In whom are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God” (Col. II). The same can also be proved by reason: no one knows anything that his soul does not know; but all grant that Christ knows all things; therefore his soul knows all things.

Yet although they do not know how to answer the foregoing, they still object: if that soul knows all things because it is united to the One who knows all things, then it ought to be called omnipotent because it is united to the Omnipotent One. To this it may be said that the soul is naturally capable of knowledge, and that which it is naturally capable of receiving was bestowed upon it without measure; but since to be God is the same as to be omnipotent, this could not be bestowed upon a creature [Col. 0075A].

## CHAPTER XVII. That Christ assumed all our infirmities except sin

After what has been said, we must consider Leo the Pope’s statement: “Our Lord assumed all the infirmities of our nature except sin.” In order that he might be proved to have a true body, he assumed bodily deficiencies—hunger, thirst, and so forth. In order that he might be proved to have a true soul, he assumed deficiencies of the soul—namely sadness, fear, and other such things.

Here it may be objected that he did not have ignorance, and yet ignorance is not sin; therefore he did not assume [Col. 0075B] all our infirmities. It may be answered that, just as concupiscence is sin and yet after the remedy of the sacrament is not imputed unless consent is given to that movement, so ignorance is sin, though it is not imputed unless negligence is present. Of this the Apostle says: “Whoever is ignorant shall be ignored” (1 Cor. XIV). But invincible ignorance is not imputed; nonetheless, as we have explained, it is sin. For everything that separates us from God is called sin; but by these things we are unlike God and depart from him, and therefore they are called sins.

If it is objected that he did not have repentance, this is not among all our infirmities. That he had sadness and fear is found in the Gospel: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV). And [Col. 0075C] elsewhere: “Jesus began to be afraid and distressed” (Matt. XIV [probably Mark XIV]). Augustine: “He assumed sadness as he assumed flesh. For if he was not sad when the Gospel says, ‘My soul is sorrowful unto death,’ then neither, when the Gospel says, ‘He slept,’ did he sleep. Therefore Jesus was sad; but he willingly assumed true sadness.” Ambrose: “He assumed, therefore, my sadness; he assumed my will. I confidently name sadness, since I proclaim the cross.”

Yet other authorities are found which seem to remove sadness and fear from the Savior. Jerome: “Lest passion should rule his mind through passion, he began to be sad.” For it is one thing to be sad, another to begin to be sad. Again: “Let those be ashamed who think that the Savior feared death and, from dread of suffering [Col. 0075D], said: ‘Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me’” (Matt. XXVI). Augustine: “Representing the weak in himself, he said: ‘Let this cup pass from me.’ For the Lord did not truly fear to suffer when he was to rise on the third day, whereas Paul longed to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I).

It must be said in reply that there is a kind of sadness and fear which so dominates the soul and overwhelms reason that it leads a person into sin, with God’s command despised, as Peter denied through fear. The authorities speak of fear of this sort when they say that Christ did not fear. But there is a moderate fear which belongs naturally to every human being and is without sin, like hunger and thirst; and this was in Christ, for he recoiled from death.

It should also be noted [Col. 0076A] that there were two wills in Christ. Augustine says: “The will of the Father is not other than that of the Son”; and according to that will Christ willed to suffer and die, as the Father willed it. But there was also another will, which may be called the natural appetite, whose function is to will not to die. According to this will it was said: “Not my will, but yours be done” (Luke XXII). Elsewhere: “I came not to do my own will, but that of the Father who sent me” (John VI). But in him the will of reason always prevailed, by which he willed the same thing as the Father.

That there were two wills in Christ is known from the metropolitan synod at which Macarius the archbishop was condemned, because he maintained that Christ did not have two wills. It is also commonly asked whether he prayed or desired anything which he did not obtain [Col. 0076B]. Some wish to say that the prayer in which he prayed, “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me,” was not heard, because he prayed this from human weakness. Likewise, they wish to say that according to human affection he willed the salvation of all. Hence: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII), that is, when I desired their faith. But since he says in John, “I do not pray for those who are of the world” (John XVII), it does not seem that he ever prayed except for those who were to be saved. For it does not seem fitting that his prayer should not have been heard, or that he should have prayed for something which he knew did not please the Father, since he knew all things.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Whether Christ is a creature

Some commonly ask whether this proposition should be conceded: [Col. 0076C] “Christ is a creature.” It does not seem that it should be conceded without qualification. For if he is a creature, he has a beginning. If he has a beginning, he has not existed always. But it may be conceded with a qualification: “Christ is a creature according as he is man,” because according as he is man he has a beginning. Yet the unqualified statement “Christ has a beginning” must not be conceded.

Ambrose likewise proves by many arguments against Arius that Christ is not a creature or an adopted son. For although he is not the Son of God by nature according as he is man, because according as he is man he is not of the same substance as the Father, he is nevertheless not adopted. For an adopted son is one who, having previously not been a son, is later adopted as a son. But that man was never prior to being the Son of God. Therefore, if I am asked, “Is Christ the Son [Col. 0076D] of God?” I shall grant it, but with a qualification: Christ, according as he is man, is the Son of God. If it is said, “By nature or by adoption?” I shall concede neither, but say: by union. Hence the Apostle: “Who was predestined Son of God in power” (Rom. I). For predestination belongs to him not according as he is God but according as he is man.

Ambrose says of this: “Whatever the Son of God has by nature, the Son of Man has by grace.” An objection is commonly made: God is eternal, immeasurable, and immortal; therefore that man is eternal, immeasurable, and immortal. But that man is mortal and passible in time. It may be answered that, just as God is said to have suffered, died, and been crucified—whence the Apostle says: “They crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. [Col. 0077A] II)—although God in his own nature cannot die or suffer, and these things are said of God through union with the man, so the things belonging to God are said of that man through union with the Word. Hence the Prophet: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI). In John: “No one has ascended into heaven except the Son of Man who descended from heaven” (John III).

But it is objected: if that man is eternal, then he lacks a beginning; but this is false, for he has a beginning in time. Yet it does not follow, from “that man is eternal,” that he lacks a beginning, because the proposition is figurative. Just as it would not follow: “God is crucified, dies; therefore he ceases to be or to live.” For, as Augustine says, we must consider what is said of what, and in what respect.

It is also commonly asked whether Christ had [Col. 0077B] faith, hope, and charity. Of charity there is no doubt, for out of charity he laid down his life for his brothers. That he had hope is found in the Psalm: “Keep me, O Lord, for I have hoped in you” (Ps. XV); and in another: “In you, O Lord, I have hoped” (Ps. XXX), which the authorities expound concerning Christ. But the Apostle says: “Hope which is seen is not hope; for what one sees, why does one hope for it?” (Rom. VIII). Yet Christ saw all things. But the Apostle says this of hope as it exists in us. That he had faith must not be conceded.

It is asked, moreover, whether he merited anything for himself; for it is certain that he merited for his members. The Apostle says that he also merited for himself, where he says: “Therefore God also exalted him” (Phil. II), etc. And in the Prophet: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he exalted [Col. 0077C] his head” (Ps. CIX). He merited for his body both immortality and impassibility. But since he was innocent, all this was due to him, and thus he did not have it by merit. Yet someone can merit what was due to him, as a son to whom his father’s inheritance is due can earn it by serving his father.

Many say that Christ merited nothing for his soul and that nothing accrued to his soul; for, as they say, it was perfectly blessed, because, as John says: “This is eternal life: to know you and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII). Gregory likewise says: “Christ’s soul had nothing in which it could advance.” Yet it can be proved that he merited even for his soul, and that something accrued to it after the Passion. For previously it had fear and sadness; but after the Passion it could neither be sad nor troubled. Therefore impassibility accrued to that soul, so that it could no longer suffer. Hence he merited glorification and impassibility not only for his body but also for his soul.

But Gregory’s statement, “Christ’s soul had nothing in which it could advance,” must be understood of knowledge and love. For his knowledge and love could not be increased.

It should also be known that God is not one part of that person who is Christ and man another. For if they were integral parts of that person, that person would have been increased by the assumed man. Augustine: “Christ is one person of twofold substance; yet God cannot be called a part [Col. 0078A] of this person. Otherwise the Son of God, before he assumed the form, was not whole, and grew when man was added to his divinity.”

It is commonly asked whether Christ could sin. Some wish to prove that he could by this authority: “He could transgress and did not transgress; he could do evil and did not do it” (Ecclus. XXXI). But we do not think this was said of Christ, but of holy men. Again they object: Christ had free choice; therefore he could be inclined in either direction. But this is invalid, since angels also have free choice, yet are so confirmed by grace that they cannot sin. Much more, then, we believe that that man, united to God by grace, was confirmed from his very conception.

Again they object: that man could [Col. 0078B] have not been united to the Word; and if he had not been united to the Word, he would sin like other human beings; therefore that man could sin. We do not deny that that man could sin if he were not united to the Word; but after he was united to the Word, he could not sin. For if he could sin, he could also be damned, since damnation follows sin. But what could be more absurd than that the Son of God—who was that man—could be damned?

Here it should be noted that there are three states of humankind, and we must see what the Son of God assumed from each. The first state was before sin, in which man was created. The second [Col. 0078C] state is that into which he fell through sin. The third is that into which he is to be brought after the resurrection. The first state had the possibility of dying, not the necessity. The second state has the necessity of dying, for man necessarily dies. The third state has neither the necessity of dying, as the second does, nor the possibility of dying or sinning, as the first does.

From the first state Christ had the ability to die and the ability not to die; for he died solely by his will. Hence some say: “He died by will; he was mortal by will, immortal by nature”; because, since he was without sin, which is the cause of death, he would never have died if he had willed otherwise. From the second state he had such deficiencies as hunger, thirst, and so forth. From the third state he had the inability to sin.

It may be asked, since Christ could have died a death not inflicted by others and thereby redeemed the human race, why he wished to die such a death as brought about [Col. 0078D] the condemnation of many, such as Judas and others. It was in order to draw us to love of himself. For the graver the death he endured for us, the more we ought to love him.

## CHAPTER XIX. Whether, in Christ’s death, divinity was separated from humanity

Moreover, it is commonly asked whether, in death, divinity was separated from humanity. Some wish to say that divinity was separated from the flesh but not from the soul. They are not to be believed, since Pope Leo says: “From the time he assumed man, he did not lay him aside.” All the orthodox hold that after that ineffable union divinity was separated neither from flesh nor from soul. For divinity was not incarnate twice, nor did it assume flesh twice. Therefore, beyond doubt, from the time the Son of God became [Col. 0079A] man, God is always man and man is God.

The soul was separated from the flesh, but divinity from neither. Hence Augustine explains thus the words: “I have power to lay down my soul and to take it again.” Divinity did not lay down the soul; rather, at death the flesh laid down the soul, and at the resurrection took it up again. Again, Augustine says in his book to Felicianus: “As he did not abandon his flesh in the tomb, so in the Virgin’s womb he formed it by being born. Thus, without life departing, he died; thus he suffered without the power of life perishing. For at one and the same time he was wholly in hell and wholly in heaven. Among the dead he was the resurrection of the dead; above the heavens he was the life of the living. Truly dead, truly alive: in him the assumption of mortality received death, and divinity, preserved, did not lose life” [Col. 0079B].

It is objected: if the Son of God was not separated from the man in death itself, then he has not now ceased to be man; but a dead man is not a man; therefore neither then was he man. How frivolous this is is evident. For one could likewise say: he is not now man, because he is not a rational and mortal animal—which is altogether false. For when even philosophers said, “A dead man is not a man,” or “is not a rational mortal animal,” they spoke of man according to this state.

Again it is objected: if he was then man [Col. 0080A], he was either mortal or immortal; but he was not mortal, because dead, nor yet immortal, because only after the resurrection. We readily concede that he is now neither mortal nor immortal. Yet they object by Anastasius’s authority, namely: “Cursed be whoever does not confess that this whole man—that is, the soul and body which he assumed—was assumed anew, or freed from the dead, and rose again after the third day: so be it, so be it.” We answer that Anastasius speaks against those who denied his resurrection and thought that he, who alone was free among the dead, was held in death. Therefore he said “assumed anew,” that is, freed from death.

Again [Col. 0080B] Ambrose, on the passage, “He cried with a loud voice, saying: ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’” (Matt. XXVII): “The man, about to die, cries out the separation of divinity. For since divinity is free from death, death could not exist unless life departed, because life is divinity.” But Ambrose understood divinity to be separated from that man insofar as God exposed that man to death, as in the Psalm: “Why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. XXI), that is, “Why have you exposed me to death?”—not because he was forsaken or divinity was separated from him. For he seemed to be forsaken by God, or divinity seemed to depart, when God did not show his power by defending him.

# SECOND TREATISE: ON THE CREATION AND CONDITION OF ANGELIC NATURE

[Col. 0079]

## CHAPTERS

CHAPTER I. On the creation of things, and especially of angels.—CHAPTER II. On the state of an angel at the beginning of its creation.—CHAPTER III. On the state of angels immediately after their creation.—CHAPTER IV. On Lucifer’s excellence before his fall and his punishment after it.—CHAPTER V. On the distinction of the orders.—CHAPTER VI. On the mission of angels.

## CHAPTER I. On the creation of things, and especially of angels

[Col. 0079C]

Having treated the parts of faith, it seems fitting to add something concerning the first creation of things. Plato said that there are three principles: matter, form, and maker. Catholic faith believes that there is one principle of all things, namely God, whose goodness was the cause of all things. For, being eternally supremely good and perfectly blessed, he willed that some should share in his blessedness. And because his blessedness cannot be shared except through understanding, and is possessed the more fully the more it is understood, he made a rational creature so that it might understand, by understanding love, by loving possess, and by possessing enjoy. He distinguished it in this way: one part remained in its own purity [Col. 0079D], namely the angels; another part was joined to a body, namely souls.

It is asked why this was done, since the soul would have been of greater dignity if it had remained in its purity and simplicity [Col. 0080C]. It may be answered that although the soul would be more dignified without a body, God nevertheless willed it to be united with a body in order, in the human condition, to show a new example of the eternal union which exists between spirit and God. For it seemed to the creature that it could not be united to its Creator. But when a spirit—which is the more excellent creature—is united in such love to so lowly a creature as the body that it cannot be compelled to will to abandon it, it is clear that a created spirit can in the same way be united to the supreme good. Souls are also joined to bodies so that they may serve the Lord in them and earn the true and supreme good.

Since, therefore, rational creation is divided into angels and human beings, we should first discuss angels [Col. 0080D]. Concerning them, we must consider when they were created, where they were made, and what they were made like. Some authorities seem to hold that angels were made before every other [Col. 0081A] creature. Hence the statement, “Wisdom was created before all things” (Ecclus. I), which was said of angels. This seems contrary to Genesis: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I). For if these were created in the beginning, nothing was made before heaven and earth. And in the Prophet: “In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth” (Ps. CI).

Therefore it seems that angelic and bodily creation were created together. Hence Solomon’s statement: “He who lives forever created all things at once” (Ecclus. XVIII), that is, spiritual and bodily nature. Thus the angels were not created earlier in time than that bodily matter of the four elements. Yet wisdom was created before all things, because, though it does not precede in time, it does in dignity.

Jerome, however, in his letter to Titus [Col. 0081B] seems to hold otherwise, saying: “Not yet have six thousand years of our time been completed; and how many prior eternities, how many times, how many beginnings of ages must be thought to have existed, in which angels, thrones, and dominions served God and stood at his command without vicissitudes and measures of time?” Some, adhering to this authority, say that time began with the world, because there was no changeability before the world; nevertheless, they maintain that angels existed immutably and outside time.

We, however, approve rather what was stated first. What Jerome says was drawn from Origen’s statements; it was not said as an assertion, but as a question, asking how many eternities and so forth ought to be thought to have existed beforehand.

Where they were made [Col. 0081C] is asked. The authorities seem to mean that they were made in heaven. Hence in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). Here we do not call “heaven” the firmament made on the second day, but the empyrean heaven—that is, the splendid heaven—which was immediately filled with angels: namely, that upper region as far as which the still undifferentiated mass of the elements extended. For, as we have said, the angels and that corporeal matter were created together. Thus Augustine expounds that passage: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”: heaven, that is, angels; earth, that is, the corporeal mass, in the upper part of which heaven—that is, the angels—were made. But if they were in heaven, how could Lucifer say, as is read in Isaiah: “I will ascend into heaven; [Col. 0081D] I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14)? But there he calls heaven the sublimity of the Godhead. “I will ascend into heaven,” that is, to equality with the Deity.

## CHAPTER II. On the state of the angel at the beginning of its creation

It remains, then, to consider what kind of beings they were made. In their first condition three things seem to have been attributed to them: an indivisible and immaterial essence, and therefore unfailing through the reason naturally implanted in them; spiritual intelligence; and also free choice, by which they could turn, without compulsion, in either direction according to their own will.

Some are accustomed to ask whether they were created good or evil, just or unjust, blessed or miserable. It must be granted that they were good at the first beginning of creation [Col. 0082A], that is, without vice. For the supremely good Creator could not be the author of evil. Yet at that time they were neither just nor unjust, nor did they then possess any virtue. For every virtue is merit, and all merit proceeds from free choice; but free choice always concerns the future, not the present or the past. What is cannot then not be, and what is not cannot then be; therefore it is not within the power of free choice. Thus it was not within their free choice that they should then be good—which they then were by creation—or evil—which they were not, but could be only in the future.
