A person sitting has it in his power to stand, but not at that very moment: he cannot stand at that very moment, but only in the future. Therefore we say that at the beginning of their creation they possessed no virtue or justice [Col. 0082B], unless we understand natural capacities as virtue, such as reason, intelligence, and the like. Nor can we say that they were unjust, for they were without vice. And since they were without vice, they were not miserable, since punishment does not precede fault; yet neither were they blessed, because they were not created in blessedness but for blessedness.

If, however, some authority says that they were just, unjust, or blessed in their very creation, it calls “justice” or “blessedness” that state of being without misery and without vice. Some object in this manner: if at the beginning of creation they did not possess virtues and blessedness, then God made them imperfect; but it was unfitting for him who is supremely powerful and perfectly blessed to make anything imperfect. But it may be said that they were perfect, because they had everything [Col. 0082C] that they ought to have. For “perfect” is said in three ways: perfect in respect of time, perfect in respect of nature, and universally perfect. A thing is perfect in respect of time when it has everything that time requires and that is fitting for it to possess at that time; and in this manner the angels were perfect. A thing is perfect in respect of nature when it has everything owed or conducive to its nature for glorification; and in this manner the angels were perfect after their confirmation, as the saints will be after the resurrection. Universally and supremely perfect is that to which nothing is lacking; and this belongs to God alone.

## CHAPTER III. On the state of the angels immediately after their creation

[Col. 0082D] We have already said what the angels were like in creation. Immediately after creation, however, some turned to their Creator, while others turned away. To turn to God was to love; to turn away was to hate. In those who turned, the wisdom of God began to shine as in a mirror, and by it they were enlightened. Those who turned away were blinded, and divine wisdom did not shine forth in them, because they turned away from the light, like a mirror turned away from the face of one looking into it. But while the former stood and the latter fell, God divided light from darkness: he made the light and divided it, because their goodness was a gift. He did not make the darkness, but divided the light from it. Thus the angels were first created, whence it was said: “In the beginning God created heaven” (Gen. 1), that is, the angels. Afterwards they were formed [Col. 0083A], namely, when they turned to the Creator. Hence it was said: “Let there be light” (ibid.).

But it must be asked whether something was bestowed upon these after creation through which they might love. It was: namely, cooperating grace, without which a rational creature cannot advance. For it can fall by itself, but cannot advance unless grace cooperates. It may therefore seem that those who fell ought not to be blamed, since without cooperating grace they could not advance; but that grace was not given to them, and it was not their fault that it was not given, since no fault had yet preceded in them. To this it may be said that the grace given to those to whom it was given was not given on account of merit, since as yet there was no merit; but that it was not given to the others was their fault—not [Col. 0083B] a fault preceding in time, but in causal order. For just as grace in the former is the cause of merit, yet does not precede that merit in time, so in the latter their fault was the reason why, by God’s just judgment, grace would not be given; yet this did not precede that in time. For since all things are present to God, he has no need of anyone’s testimony. As soon as anyone sins, God can justly judge him—not afterwards, but simultaneously; and if he chooses to defer this, it is mercy.

Their fault can be understood in this: although without cooperating grace, which they had not yet received, they could not advance, nevertheless by what had been bestowed on them through creating grace they could avoid falling. For nothing in them compelled them to do so. And if they had not turned aside [Col. 0083C] by their own will, what was given to the others would also have been given to them.

It is asked whether there was any interval between their creation and their fall. It may be said that there was no interval, yet the former was prior and the latter subsequent, but without a lapse of time. For they were not always evil, as some wish to say on account of the authority: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth” (John 8). But it does not say that he did this “in the beginning,” but “from the beginning,” that is, immediately after the beginning; and “he did not stand in the truth” means that he did not remain in it, if he was in it. He can be called the murderer of himself, since he too is called “man,” as in: “An enemy, a man, did this” (Matt. 13). Or, as Augustine explains it, “from the beginning” means from the time man existed: he was a murderer, because through envy he cast man into [Col. 0083D] death.

Again, Augustine says concerning Genesis: “It may not without reason be thought that the devil fell through pride from the beginning of time, and that there was no previous time in which he lived in peace and blessedness with the holy angels; but that he apostatized from the very beginning of creation. For, as the Lord says, he did not stand from the beginning—from the time when he himself was created—though he would have stood if he had wished to stand.” This authority can be expounded in the manner stated above.

## CHAPTER IV. On Lucifer’s excellence before his fall and his punishment after it

Among those who fell, one was more excellent than all the others [Col. 0084A]; and the authorities seem to mean that he was more excellent not only than those who fell, but than all the others as well. Thus Job said: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40). And in Ezekiel: “You are the seal of likeness, full of knowledge and perfect in beauty, in the delights of paradise” (Ezek. 28). Gregory expounds this thus: “The subtler his nature in him, the more closely does the image of God appear expressed in him.” Again, in Ezekiel: “Every precious stone was his covering” (ibid.), that is, every angel was his covering; because, as Gregory says, in comparison with the others he was brighter than the rest. Hence he was called Lucifer; for he is to be understood not as an order but as an individual spirit. For, as Isidore says, immediately after he was created, without any interval, considering the depth of his own knowledge, he grew proud against his Creator; and, as is said in Isaiah, he wished to be equal to God [Col. 0084B], saying: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). He wished to be like him, not by imitation but by equality; and the authority seems to mean that he wished not only to be equal but even superior: “He is exalted above everything that is called God or worshipped as God” (2 Thess. 2).

Because he was so proud against his Creator, he was cast down with all who consented to him into this darksome air, for our testing, so that they might serve as an aid to our exercise. They were not allowed to dwell in heaven, the bright homeland; nor on earth, lest they trouble human beings too greatly; but in the dark air, which is their prison until the day of judgment. Then indeed they shall be cast down [Col. 0084C] into the abyss of hell, according to: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). And as they possess greater or lesser knowledge, so they have greater or lesser dominions: for some preside over one province, some over one person, some over one vice. Hence there is said to be a spirit of pride and a spirit of lust.

But there is doubt whether all are now in this air until the day of judgment, or whether some of them are in the lower hell; we have no very certain authority on this. Yet some wish to say that Lucifer, who sinned more than the rest, was immediately plunged there, as were also some of the others. Origen also says that those who are conquered by saints living justly and chastely no longer have power to tempt others, but are immediately plunged there; and this seems quite plausible. Origen: “I indeed think that the saints, resisting those tempters and conquering them, diminish the army of demons, as though they kill very many of them; nor is it thereafter lawful for any spirit conquered by any saint through chaste and pure living again to attack another human being.”

It must also be known that the good angels are so confirmed through grace that they cannot sin, while the evil are so hardened through wickedness that they cannot do good.

It is objected that they have free choice; therefore they can turn in either direction. But [Col. 0085A] it is not for that reason called “free choice,” as we shall show in its proper place, but “free,” that is, voluntary. The good abstain from evil not under constraining necessity but by free will; and similarly the evil abstain from good. Again, an objection is drawn from Jerome’s statement: “God alone is one in whom sin cannot occur; all other things, since they have free choice, can bend their will in either direction.” But how this should be understood may be inferred from Isidore’s words: “The angels are mutable by nature, immutable by grace.” Hence it seems we must concede: good angels can sin according to their nature, that is, their nature does not oppose this; yet we must not concede simply that good angels can sin. Rather, they cannot sin, that is, the grace through which they are confirmed [Col. 0085B] opposes it.

And although the evil are hardened through wickedness, they have not lost keen perception. For, as Isidore says, “They are vigorous in knowledge with a threefold sharpness: subtlety of nature, experience of times, and revelation from higher powers.” Augustine: “Evil spirits are permitted to know certain true things concerning temporal matters, partly through subtlety of sense, partly through more skilful experience of times because of their very great length of life, and partly through holy angels, who learn them from almighty God and reveal them to the evil spirits at his command. At times these wicked spirits even foretell, as though by divination, things that belong to the Creator himself.”

It is asked whether they foreknew their fall. But if they did foreknow it, either they were unwilling to avoid it, and thus were foolish and wicked before the fall; or they wished to avoid it but could not, and thus were miserable before they fell. On account of these incongruities, Augustine says concerning Genesis that they did not foreknow their fall.

## CHAPTER V. On the distinction of orders

After the foregoing, it must be considered that Scripture bears witness in many places to nine orders of angels. In these orders there are found three groups of three, and three orders in each group, so that the likeness of the Trinity may seem impressed on them beyond other creatures. There are three higher orders, three lower, and three middle orders. The higher are seraphim, cherubim [Col. 0085D], and thrones; the middle, dominions, powers, and principalities; the lower, virtues, archangels, and angels.

It must therefore be considered what we call an order, and whether this distinction of orders existed from their very creation. An order of angels is called a multitude of heavenly spirits who, among themselves and above others, resemble one another in some gift: as the seraphim, who burn with charity above others—for *seraphim* means “burning”; and the cherubim, who excel above others in knowledge—for *cherubim* means “fullness of knowledge.” *Throne* means “seat.” Thus, as Gregory says, those are called thrones who are so filled with the grace of divinity that God sits in them and decrees his judgments through them. Dominions are those who transcend principalities in authority. Principalities are called those who, while arranging what is to be done for those subject to them [Col. 0086A], preside over them in carrying out divine mysteries. Powers are those who have received this more powerfully than others in their order: that adverse powers subject to them may be restrained by their authority, lest they be able to tempt human beings as much as they desire. Virtues are those through whom signs and miracles occur more frequently; archangels are those who announce greater matters; angels, those who announce lesser matters.

And because charity is a greater gift than knowledge, the highest order received its name from the more worthy gift. Again, it is greater to know than to judge, for knowledge informs judgment. The same may be inferred of the others individually; thus the excellence of the orders is assigned according to the excellence of their gifts. Yet, as Gregory says, those gifts are common to all. All [Col. 0086B] burn with charity and are full of knowledge; but the higher they are, the more excellently they possess these gifts above others. Gregory: “In that highest city, each order is designated by the name of that thing which it has received more fully as a gift.”

Here arises the following question. If each order possesses more fully the gift from which it is named, then the cherubim surpass all in knowledge; but the one who loves more knows more, for God is known only insofar as he is loved. Therefore the seraphim surpass not only in charity but also in knowledge. Some therefore explain that authority thus: “Each order is designated by the name of that thing which it has received more fully as a gift.” “More fully” is understood not in comparison with all, but with the lower orders. Or we may say [Col. 0086C] that the comparison is made not with angels, but with other gifts. Just as among human beings, one and the same person has several virtues but possesses one more fully than the others—Job patience, David humility—so too among angels. Thus that authority may be explained: each order is designated by the name of that thing which it has received more fully as a gift, not more fully than all other angels, but more fully than its other gifts.

It remains to ask whether these orders existed from their creation. It is clear that they did, since authority states that some fell from each order. But on the other hand, it cannot be said that they then burned with charity. Thus it does not seem that there was then a seraphic order. To this it may be said that, although at the beginning of creation they did not burn with charity, that order was nevertheless distinguished from the others in this: it was more capable than the rest of loving. For just as we see in bodies that, by their nature, some are more solid and firm than others, and also cleaner and brighter than others, so in those spiritual natures there could be, at the very beginning of their making [Col. 0086D], degrees of differences suited to their purity and excellence, both in essence and form, by which some were higher and others lower: higher, because they were created with a more subtle nature; lower, because they were created with a less subtle nature and a less penetrating wisdom. But he alone could weigh these invisible distinctions among invisible things who “made all things in number, weight, and measure” (Wis. 11).

It is asked whether all in the same order are alike and equal [Col. 0087A]. Some have thought so. But this cannot stand with Scripture’s statement that Lucifer was more excellent than all the others. He was certainly of the highest order, yet in that order he was more excellent than the rest. For just as all virgins belong to one order, yet one excels another in virginity, so it can be among angels.

We read that a tenth order is to be filled from human beings. For when evil angels fell from each of the orders, they made one order, because they are alike in wickedness, although “order” is said of them improperly. And that tenth order, as Scripture says, is restored from human beings. But since Gregory says that human beings are to be assumed into the orders of angels—some into the order of the higher angels, namely those who burn more with charity; others into the order of the lower [Col. 0087B], namely those less perfect—it does not seem that a tenth order is made from human beings, but that only nine remain. To this it may be said that, according to the correspondence of gifts which they have with angels, they are said to be assumed into angelic orders; but according to their nature, which differs from that of angels, they are said to constitute another order.

And although what fell among the angels is restored from human beings—on account of which the Apostle says: “God purposed to restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth” (Eph. 1)—it must not be understood that humanity was made solely on account of those who fell. Even if no angel had fallen, humanity would nonetheless have been made. Hence Gregory says that human beings are not chosen according to [Col. 0087C] the number of those who fell, but according to the number of those who remained. Gregory: “Because the heavenly city consists of angels and human beings, we believe that as many of the human race ascend there as the number of angels that remained there, as it is written: ‘He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.’”

## CHAPTER VI. On the sending of angels

Certain authorities appear to hold that not all angels are sent. Thus in Daniel: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7). Dionysius: “Those higher ranks never depart from the innermost realities, since those which excel never perform the function of an exterior office.” From these authorities, some say that only the lower orders are sent. But this is opposed by what Isaiah says: “One of the seraphim flew to me” (Isa. 6). Dionysius resolves this as follows: “Those spirits who are sent receive the names of those whose office they perform.” Hence they say that the angel sent to Isaiah to cleanse the prophet’s lips was of the lower order, but was called a seraph because he came to burn and consume the prophet’s sins.

Again, the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent for ministry?” (Heb. 1). Hence it seems to some that all are sent, and that the one sent to announce the Holy of Holies was of the highest order. If it is objected: why then [Col. 0088A] are not all called angels, but only the two lower orders? The answer is that these two orders have this task more often and almost as an office imposed on them. Nor should it seem unworthy if even the higher orders are sent, since he who is Creator of all descended to these lower things. Thus Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael seem to belong to the higher order. They are not names of orders, but of spirits. Michael means “Who is like God?” Gabriel, “strength of God”; Raphael, “medicine of God.”

Scripture says that angels are assigned to guard human beings, as in the Gospel: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matt. 18). Gregory also says that each person has one good angel assigned for protection and one evil angel for exercise. For although all good angels desire our good and commonly seek the salvation of all, the one assigned to guard someone urges that person more particularly toward good, as we read of Tobit’s angel and of Peter’s angel in the Acts of the Apostles. Likewise, although evil angels desire the evil of all, the evil angel permitted to tempt a person incites that person more especially.

[Col. 0088B] But it is doubtful, and we have no determination from Scripture, whether one angel is given for the guardianship of several people or whether individual angels are given to individual persons. Yet, since the elect are as numerous as the good angels, it is evident that there are more good and evil human beings than good angels. How, then, do individual good and evil human beings have individual angels sent as guardians?

Furthermore, it must be known that the knowledge of angels [Col. 0088C] can increase until the judgment. Hence, when the Lord ascends in Isaiah, the angels ask: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63); and in the Psalm: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 23). Thus it may be said that their knowledge does not diminish, because, being confirmed through grace, they forget nothing; but it can increase until the future consummation, when they shall be fixed and immovable in what they know, so that they can know neither more nor less.

[Col. 0088D] What Isidore says seems opposed to our statement that angelic knowledge can increase: “Angels know all things in the Word of God before they happen.” Gregory says in the *Dialogues*: “What can they not know there, where they know him who knows all things?” But it may be said that, although they see him—indeed, have him—in whom are all the treasures of wisdom (Col. 2), they nevertheless know in him only as much as he wishes to disclose to them. Yet they are said to know all things, that is, to be ignorant of nothing. For one is ignorant of nothing who knows whatever he ought to know and whatever God wills him to know. For in all things their will agrees with the divine will; nor do they desire to know anything other than what they know God wills them to know. The merit of angels is said to consist in this: that they desire our good and seek our advancement. Hence the Apostle: “And the angels are ours” (Heb. 1).

# THIRD TREATISE. ON THE CREATION AND CONDITION OF HUMAN NATURE

[Col. 0089]

## CHAPTERS

CHAPTER I. On the works of the six days.—CHAPTER II. On the creation of humanity.—CHAPTER III. On the formation of woman.—CHAPTER IV. On the condition of humanity before sin.—CHAPTER V. Why the woman was not terrified by the serpent.—CHAPTER VI. On the sin of the first human being.—CHAPTER VII. On the grace possessed before sin.—CHAPTER VIII. On human free choice.—CHAPTER IX. That free choice relates only to the future, and on its fourfold condition.—CHAPTER X. Why the sin of the first human being is imputed to descendants.—CHAPTER XI. What original sin is.—CHAPTER XII. On the rationale of original sin.—CHAPTER XIII. On actual sin.—CHAPTER XIV. On sin in general.—CHAPTER XV. In what nature sin exists.—CHAPTER XVI. What are the modes of sinning.—CHAPTER XVII. What is the difference between gifts and virtues, and what are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER I. On the works of the six days

[Col. 0089A]

As we have said: at the beginning of creatures God created heaven, that is, the angels, and earth (Gen. 1), namely that still confused matter of the four elements, which was called chaos; and this was before every day. It remains, therefore, to see how over six days he distinguished that matter. As is said in Genesis: light was made on the first day (ibid.). Some interpreters say that this light was a certain shining body, like a bright cloud, which, like the sun, moved around by its rising and setting, making day and night. Others say that the light made on the first day was the angelic creature turned toward the Creator, as we have already said. On the second day the firmament was made to divide waters from waters. Bede [Col. 0089B] says that the firmament consists of waters solidified like crystal stone; this seems quite plausible, since its color also indicates it. Some interpreters, however, seem to maintain that it is of fiery nature.

That waters are above the firmament is found in Genesis (ch. 1), and also in the Prophet: “Waters above the heavens, bless the Lord” (Ps. 148). What sort of waters these are is not certain to us. But, as interpreters say, they are either solidified like ice, or suspended like vapor, that is, smoke; which is plausible. On the third day waters were gathered into one place and dry land appeared (Gen. 1). On the fourth day the luminaries were made (ibid.), to serve as signs and seasons: that is, so that the divisions of time might be made through them. For since there has been creature, there has been time; because a creature could not exist without changeability, and wherever there is motion, there is before and after. Time is nothing other than the passage from what is before to what is after. But before the luminaries there was not that division of time which now exists through the sun, moon, and stars. On the fifth day water brought forth fish and birds. Hence: “In part you release them to the deep, in part you raise them into the air.” On the sixth day earth brought forth animals of different kinds; and on the same day, after all the rest, humanity was made in the image and likeness of God. Humanity was fittingly made after everything else, because it was to be set above all things [Col. 0090A].

According to the account we have followed, this sequence, and many interpreters, seem to maintain that that unformed matter was made before every day, as we have said, together with the angels; and that afterwards, over six days, the kinds of things were distinguished out of that matter. Some, however, think that those distinctions of things were not made through intervals of time, but simultaneously. But since Moses spoke to an uncultivated and carnal people, it was necessary for him to speak of God as though he were a human being who forms and completes works through temporal delays. Hence Augustine: “What could be made simultaneously by God could not be spoken simultaneously by man.” Nor do we deny that God could have done this if it had pleased him. Nor does Augustine assert it; he says only: “It could be made simultaneously.” Again, Augustine: “Because that from which something is made, even if not earlier in time [Col. 0090B], is nevertheless earlier in origin than that which is made from it, Scripture could divide into times of speaking what God did not divide into times of making.” Those who adhere to these authorities call the six days six distinctions of works: according to them they were made simultaneously, but had to be spoken of in order. Yet the first opinion is more probable.

“On the seventh day God rested from all the work which he had accomplished” (ibid.), because afterwards he made no new kinds of things. But this is opposed by the Gospel’s statement: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5). For he works daily by creating new souls and also by propagating one thing from another. But this is not to make new kinds of things. For although a new soul is now created, nothing new is added [Col. 0090C], since soul existed previously. Another reading in Genesis says: “God rested on the sixth day.” But both are true: that he rested on the sixth day, because he completed all things in six days; and that he rested on the seventh day, because, with the sixth day completed and the seventh begun, he ceased from distinguishing kinds of things.

Here one may ask: since he completed all works in six days and added nothing new after those six days, why do we continue counting days up to the seventh? If it is said that the seventh is different from those days, then so also are the eighth, ninth, and the rest. But these are not different in the distinction of things; likewise, the seventh was not different in the distinction of things, since no distinction of any work was made in it, as in the six days. For making the seventh day was not making another kind of thing, because day had already preceded it. [Col. 0091A] It may be said in answer that, although no work was made on the seventh day, there was nevertheless a state of things there—namely, the completion of all things—and therefore we proceed as far as it, and after it immediately begin again.

## CHAPTER II. On the creation of humanity

Having examined these matters, it remains to treat of the creation of humanity, its fall, and its restoration. Genesis says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” [Col. 0091B] (Gen. 1). Humanity was made in God’s image according to the soul. For just as the image of a thing is seen in a mirror, so the soul can know God in its reason. Hence: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us” (Ps. 4). Just as a human being is recognized in the face, so God is known in reason itself, as in his image. Humanity, therefore, is God’s image through reason. Hence the Apostle: “Man is the image and glory of God” (1 Cor. 11), that is, in his image, because humanity is not altogether like him. But the Son is the image of the Father, and not merely “in the image,” because everything the Father has the Son possesses wholly by nature. Humanity, however, is so the image of God as to be “in the image,” because it possesses the things of Deity not by nature but by participation or imitation. For God is wisdom itself, justice itself, goodness itself [Col. 0091C]; but humanity is not wisdom, justice, or goodness itself, but can be wise, just, good, and so forth. Augustine, in *On the Trinity*: “Humanity is God’s image in the image, because it is not equal to the Father but approaches him by a certain likeness. The Son is image and not in the image, because he is equal to the Father.”

It should be noted that humanity was made not only in the image of the Father but also of the whole Trinity, since it is written: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” “Our” means the whole Trinity’s. It should also be noted that “image” is called both the image itself impressed on some thing and the thing in which it is impressed. Thus reason itself is called an image, being like a seal impressed upon the soul; and humanity [Col. 0091D] is called an image. Augustine, in *On the Trinity*: “The Trinity itself is one thing, and the image of the Trinity in some thing another; yet because of the image, that in which the image is impressed is likewise called an image.” Thus both the tablet and what is painted upon it are called an image of God, on account of the painting that is on it. Humanity was made in God’s likeness because it was made innocent and without vice.

It is customary to ask whether angels were made in God’s image, since this is nowhere read. But although it is not written, it ought not therefore to be doubted. What Scripture says concerning humanity, it intended to be understood also concerning angels.

[Col. 0092A] Humanity is also said in another manner to be in God’s image: as all things are from God, so all human beings are from Adam. But being in God’s image in this way belongs only to the first human being. The soul can also be said to be in God’s likeness because it is immortal and indissoluble. Augustine, in *On the Quantity of the Soul*: “The soul was made like God, because God made it immortal, that is, indissoluble—but from nothing.” Augustine: “Whatever is from God must be of the same nature as he himself, and therefore immutable. But the soul is mutable; therefore it is not from him. If it was made from no other thing, then without doubt it was made from nothing, but by God himself.”

But he formed the body from the mud of the earth, into which he breathed a soul. Hence Genesis says: “He breathed into his face the breath of life,” that is, he breathed a soul into him. But whether the soul was created in the body or outside the body, we have no very certain authority [Col. 0092B]. Augustine, however, seems to say concerning Genesis that the soul of the first human being was made outside the body and entered it by its own will. But, as he himself said, he spoke concerning Genesis more by inquiry than by assertion. Whatever may be said about the first human being’s soul, it is more plausible that other souls are created in bodies. If it is asked at what age humanity was made, Augustine says: “Adam was immediately made, without any gradual development of limbs, at the age of a man, just as the rod in Moses’ hand was immediately changed into a serpent.”

## CHAPTER III. On the formation of woman

As Genesis relates: “God cast a deep sleep upon Adam, took one of his ribs, and formed a woman from it” [Col. 0092C] (Gen. 2).

Here one may ask why God did not create human beings all together, as he did angels. Because he willed that there should be one origin of the human race, in order to check the devil’s pride. For so that his exaltation might be confounded, humanity received what the devil sought through pride: namely, to be a beginning. Thus, as God is the beginning of creation for all things, so Adam might be the beginning of generation for all human beings. There is another reason why he willed all to come from one: that, recognizing themselves to be from one, they might love themselves as though they were one.

In this act the mystery of Christ and the Church was prefigured. For just as woman was made from the side of the sleeping man, so the Church came from the sacraments which flowed from the side of Christ sleeping in death upon the cross [Col. 0092D], namely blood and water. By blood he redeemed the faithful; by water he washes away sins in baptism.

It is commonly asked whether the woman was made from that rib with the addition of some material taken from outside, as some are accustomed to say. But if, in order to complete the woman’s body, God added external increase to that rib (and what was added was greater than the rib itself), Scripture ought rather to have said that the woman was made from that material—from which, namely, she received the greater number of the parts of her substance. It remains, therefore, that we say that the rib multiplied within itself, and that the woman was formed from it without any externally acquired addition. For it was a greater thing to make something from nothing than to multiply that small substance within itself [Col. 0093A]. We say the same concerning those five loaves of the Gospel (Matt. 14).

It is asked whether it was in the nature of that rib that a woman should be made from it. To consider this, one must recognize that the causes of all things that come to be existed eternally in God. For the manner in which a human being, a horse, and similar things should come to be was eternally present in God’s ordering. These are called in Scripture “primordial causes,” because no others precede them. And although there is one cause of all things—namely, the divine ordering, which is nothing other than God himself—nevertheless, because there are many effects, Augustine speaks in the plural of the primordial causes of all things as existing in God. Hence he also offers the comparison of an artisan, in whose design lies the determination whether a chest will be square or oblong. So too [Col. 0093B], in God, the cause and ordering of every individual thing eternally preceded it before it was made.

But not all causes precede in the natures of certain things. For God, as Augustine says, has assigned certain causes to things, according to which certain results proceed from them: from this seed, such grain; from this tree, such fruit; and so that one who is now young grows old at a particular time; and similarly in other cases. These too are called primordial causes, though not very properly. For they have causes before them which existed eternally in God, which are uncreated and universally first. Those causes which are in creatures, however, are not universally first; yet they are first in their own kind, since they are first in relation to what follows. These too are called primordial because, in the first formation [Col. 0093C] of things, which was made in six days, God implanted them in things; and, just as creatures are mutable, so these causes are mutable. For although it belongs to the nature of a young person eventually to grow old, this can nevertheless be changed. But those causes which are in God are both uncreated and immutable. For God’s ordering cannot be changed, because God is immutable.

It is evident, therefore, from these points that the causes of all things are in God. Some, however, are also in the natures of things, as we showed concerning seed and a tree; and these are said to occur according to nature—that is, according to the customary course of things. But the causes of other things exist in God alone and not in the natures of things: for example, when the dry rod blossomed (Num. 17), when the ass spoke (Num. 22), and similar events. These are said to occur by miracle [Col. 0093D], because they occur contrary to the nature of the things themselves—that is, not according to the causes implanted in those things by God. Augustine places among these cases the woman’s being made from the rib. For it was not causally present in the rib that a woman should be made from it, but it was in the power of God, who did not bind his power to the natures of things.

Augustine, *On Genesis*: “There is one manner in which one plant germinates thus and another does not; one age bears children thus and another does not; a human being speaks, but livestock cannot speak. The reasons for these and similar modes exist not only in God, but have also been placed by him in created things. But that dry wood should blossom and bear fruit; that a woman barren in youth should bear in old age; that an ass should speak; and similar things—God indeed gave to the natures which he created the capacity for these things also to occur from them [Col. 0094A], but not so that they should have them in their natural course. Therefore God has hidden within himself the causes of certain deeds, which he did not implant in created things; and he fulfills them not by that work of providence through which he establishes natures so that they may exist, but by that through which he administers them as he wills, since he created them as he willed. If among such things was this one—that the woman was thus made from the side of the sleeping man—the first condition of things did not contain the fact that a woman should altogether be made in this way; yet it did contain the possibility that she might be so made.”

Just as the woman’s body was derived from the man’s body, so some have wished that the soul of Eve herself was propagated from the man’s soul, and that all souls except the first were derived by propagation, just as bodies are. But Jerome forbids this under an anathema [Col. 0094B], adducing this authority of the Prophet: “He who fashioned their hearts individually” (Ps. 32). Here he sufficiently indicates that God does not create one soul from another soul, but made them individually from nothing. Augustine, however, asserts nothing on the matter, but reports differing opinions concerning the soul as questions. Some wished all souls to have been created simultaneously; some, not simultaneously but by propagation; others, neither simultaneously nor by propagation—an opinion which Jerome maintains.

## Chapter IV. On the state of humankind before sin

“God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight” (Gen. 2). By these words Moses plainly shows that he was created outside Paradise and afterward placed in Paradise. This is said to have been done because he was not to remain there permanently, or lest he attribute God’s gift to nature rather than to grace [Col. 0094C]. The saints report that Paradise is a most elevated place in the eastern region, such that even the waters of the flood could not reach it. In it were trees of various kinds: the tree of life, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and many others.

It was called the tree of life because its fruits were of such a nature that they protected against the onset of death and every distress of bodily infirmity. The other was the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. It received its name not from its nature, but from the occasion which it provided. For it did not possess by its own nature the power to confer knowledge; rather, this was to follow from the prohibition: as soon as the human being ate its fruit, he would immediately know by experience of evil the difference between the good he had left behind and the evil he had found. For beforehand he had knowledge of good and evil: of good, through knowledge and experience; of evil, through knowledge only, and not through experience [Col. 0094D].

Here we must consider the state of humankind before sin. As the Apostle says, “The first Adam became a living soul” (1 Cor. 15), that is, an animate body, which was still animal in character. For it required the nourishment of food. It also had a mortal body. For it could die, and it could also not die; it could sin, and it could also not sin. But once the measure of obedience had been fulfilled, it would be transferred to that state in which it could neither die nor sin. Therefore before sin the human being was immortal, namely, capable of not dying; not immortal in the sense that he could not die. And if he had not sinned, Augustine says, there would have been in Paradise an undefiled marriage-bed: conception without lust and childbirth without pain [Col. 0095A].

But what their children would have been like if they had not sinned—whether they could immediately walk, speak, and do the other things—we have no certainty from authority. Augustine nevertheless seems to hold that, as soon as they were born, they could perform the aforementioned acts. He says:

“It raises the question whether, if the first human beings had not sinned, they would have had children who used neither tongue nor hands. For perhaps, because of the necessity of the womb, it was necessary that infants be born. Yet although a rib is a small part of the body, God did not therefore make the man’s wife small. Hence the Creator’s omnipotence could have made her children large as soon as they were brought forth [Col. 0095B]. But, leaving this aside, he certainly could do so, since he has granted this to many animals: although their young are small, as soon as they are born they run and follow their mothers. By contrast, when a human being is born, neither are the feet suitable for walking nor the hands even fit for scratching; and, though the breasts lie beside them, they are more able to cry from hunger than to suck. Therefore this weakness of flesh corresponds to weakness of mind.”

But since Augustine says this without asserting anything definitively, some reasonably hold that then too an age of development would have been awaited in children before they could do these things and the like—not because they could not do them owing to a defect, but owing to the condition of nature; just as they could not altogether abstain from food, though this too would have arisen not from defect but from the condition of nature.

Here one may object as follows: if they had not sinned, they would never have died; and if they had not eaten, they would not have sinned. Therefore, if they had not eaten, they would never have died; consequently, they could live without nourishment. To this we reply that they would sin not only if they ate from the forbidden tree, but also if they did not use what was permitted when they naturally desired it. For in this they would act against the reason of nature, which was given so that they might use lawful things.

Again, it is objected: since hunger is a punishment for sin, they would not have suffered hunger if they had not sinned; but without hunger, eating seems superfluous. The reply is that, even if they had not sinned, they would have had an appetite for eating; and, having this appetite, they would have used what was permitted in order to forestall hunger. That appetite is natural and moderate; hunger, however, is an immoderate appetite for eating [Col. 0095C].

From the state which we have described, the human being, together with all his offspring, was to be transferred without the pain of death to that highest good which had been prepared for them in heaven. For just as there are two natures in the human being, bodily and spiritual, so God had prepared two goods for the human being, temporal and eternal. And because “first that which is animal, afterward that which is spiritual,” the temporal good was given first. The other—that is, the eternal—was not then given, but was set before them. God attached a precept of nature to preserve the good which he had given. The natural precept was discernment, through which it was instilled in him what was necessary and what harmful to his nature. To merit the good which he had set before him, he gave the precept of obedience, saying: “Do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen. 2).

Therefore the devil, seeing that through obedience the human being would ascend to the place from which he himself had fallen through pride [Col. 0096A], envied him. And he who had first become the devil through pride—that is, one “flowing downward”—became Satan through envy, that is, adversary. Therefore he tempted the woman, in whom he knew reason to be less vigorous than in the man. And lest that temptation be too hidden and thus incapable of being guarded against, he was permitted to tempt only through the serpent, so that through the outward covering she might notice the cunning of the tempter.

Augustine, *On Genesis*: “Since the devil could not approach in order to tempt except by permission, he could do so only through that by which he was permitted.”

## Chapter V. Why the woman did not recoil from the serpent

It is asked why the woman did not recoil from the serpent [Col. 0096B]. Because, having been newly created, she supposed that it had received from God the office of speech. The temptation took place in this manner. First, he approached by a question, so that from her answer he might gather how he should address her thereafter: “Why do you not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil?” (Gen. 3). To him the woman replied: “Lest perhaps we die” (*ibid.*). In this expression she gave the tempter an opening when she said, “perhaps.” Hence the devil immediately said: “Eat, and you will be like gods” (*ibid.*). He tempted through three things: through gluttony, when he said, “Eat”; through vain glory, when he said, “You will be like gods”; through avarice, when he said, “Knowing good and evil” (*ibid.*).

Gluttony is an immoderate appetite for eating; vain glory is love of one’s own praise; avarice is an immoderate appetite for possessing. Since one temptation is inward and another outward, the human being was tempted by outward temptation. Outward temptation takes place externally by sign or word, so that the person to whom it is directed may be inclined to consent to sin. Inward temptation is a movement of perverse delight through which the mind is impelled toward sin; and it is conquered much more difficultly. Therefore the human being, who fell when assailed by outward temptation, was to be punished all the more severely because he had been overthrown by a lighter impulse [Col. 0096C].

## Chapter VI. On the sin of the first human being

At this point it seems necessary to inquire into the origin and root of that sin. Augustine, *On Genesis*: “The tempter would not have cast down the human being unless an exaltation had first existed in his mind which needed to be checked.” Hence some maintain that, before he yielded to temptation, he had that exaltation. But since exaltation is a vice, it follows that he sinned before yielding to the temptation. Thus he would not first have sinned through suggestion, since authority says that the devil’s sin is incurable because he fell not through suggestion but through his own pride. But the human being, because he fell not by himself but through another, could rise through a mediator.

Therefore that authority may be explained thus: the tempter would not have cast down the human being—namely, into these miseries—unless exaltation had first existed in his mind. I do not say that it preceded the suggestion; rather, after the suggestion it preceded, in his mind, the end and completion of that sin itself [Col. 0096D]. Otherwise, even if the devil had suggested it, he would not have reached the effect of the suggestion. For if we said, “he would not have cast down the human being into sin where exaltation had preceded,” then he would have possessed exaltation before he sinned.

It may also be said that he would not have cast down the human being into the act of that sin—that is, into eating the forbidden fruit—unless exaltation had preceded. For pride is the root of every sin. On hearing, “You will be like gods,” the woman was raised up in pride; and that pride was to be checked by the punishments following that sin.

But since human nature was without defect, it is commonly asked from where that consent to evil proceeded. To understand this, one must recognize that God placed two appetites in the first human being: namely, an appetite for what is just and an appetite for what is advantageous. He placed the appetite for what is just according to the will, so that in it the human being might merit, whether by retaining the good when he could abandon it or by abandoning it wickedly when he could retain it. He placed the appetite for what is advantageous according to necessity; for the human being cannot fail to desire his own advantage. Therefore God placed this in the human being necessarily, so that through it the human being might be rewarded [Col. 0097A].

Hence in hell this was the greatest punishment of the wicked: that they would always desire what is advantageous and would never be able to attain it; just as an increase of glory belongs to the good, who will be unable to grow lukewarm in love for the good which they possess. And in this appetite for advantage God established a measure, so that the human being should desire what ought to be desired, and when and how. But because he desired advantage beyond measure—namely, to be like gods—he immediately abandoned the appetite for what is just. And in this he sinned, because he abandoned justice. For he did not sin because he desired his own advantage, but because, in desiring it, he abandoned justice; and this was to desire advantage beyond measure. For justice is the measure in the appetite for advantage. Therefore the sin of the first human being was the abandonment of justice, which the Apostle calls disobedience.

It is asked whether the will preceded that sin. But it does not seem that he willed or deliberated to abandon justice; nevertheless, he willed to desire that for the sake of which he abandoned justice. It may therefore be said that he abandoned justice willingly, because he willed that for the sake of which he abandoned it. Yet he did not will to abandon justice; rather, he willed that for the sake of which he was abandoning justice. Therefore he abandoned justice by will, not because the will preceded it in time. For it is not true that the will temporally precedes every sin, since the will itself may be sin; but it is said with reference to the act that every evil proceeds from the will [Col. 0097B]—for example, the act of eating the fruit, which some call the first sin in the human being, a claim which may readily be granted. For in one sin there are both guilt and act, yet they are not called two sins but one. Thus, one who has the will to commit homicide and afterward commits it does not then commit another sin, but performs in deed what he previously had in will.

It is asked which of them sinned more, the woman or Adam. But as the Apostle says, “Adam was not deceived, but the woman” (1 Tim. 2). When questioned, the woman says: “The serpent deceived me,” as in Genesis (ch. 3). But when questioned, the man does not say, “The woman deceived me,” but, “She gave to me, and I ate” (*ibid.*). The woman is said to have been deceived in this: having heard the words, “You will be like gods,” she became so puffed up that she believed what was said to be true. Adam, however, was not deceived because, as Augustine says, he did not believe it true, but thought that both things could be done: that he could comply with his wife and make satisfaction to God through repentance. Therefore he sinned less, because he contemplated forgiveness.

From this it is evident that the woman’s pride was greater than the man’s; therefore her sin too was greater. The woman also sinned against God and neighbor; the man against God alone. Again, the woman was punished more severely, to whom it was said: “In pain you shall bear children” (*ibid.*), etc.; from which it is evident that she sinned more [Col. 0098A].

An objection is raised from what Isidore says: “Sin is committed in three ways: through ignorance, weakness, and deliberation. Eve sinned through ignorance because, as the Apostle says, she was deceived” (1 Tim. 2). “Adam sinned through deliberation because he was not deceived” (*ibid.*), but sinned knowingly and prudently. Peter sinned through weakness. To sin through weakness is more grievous than to sin through ignorance; likewise, to sin through deliberation is more grievous than to sin through weakness. One sins through deliberation who commits evil by intent and deliberation; one sins through weakness who transgresses by chance or disturbance.

From these words it seems to be asserted that the man sinned more than the woman. To this it may be said that he sinned more in one respect: namely, in that greater deliberation seems to have been present in the man than in the woman, and that he had greater knowledge; and from one to whom more is entrusted, more is required. Yet we shall not say absolutely that he sinned more. It is as if we were to speak of a certain presbyter and a certain layman who commit homicide: the layman from long-standing hatred, the presbyter in sudden anger. One could not say absolutely that the ordained man sinned more, and yet in one respect he sinned more—namely, in acting against his own order [Col. 0098B].

It is commonly asked why God permitted the human being to be tempted, though he knew that he would yield to the tempter. Augustine resolves this question thus: “It does not seem to me that the human being would have had great praise if he could live well merely because no one urged him to live badly, since he had both the capacity by nature and the power to will not to consent to the persuader, with God’s help.”

This too is commonly asked: why did God create the human being whom he knew would fall, when he is supremely merciful? The same question applies to the angels who fell. Augustine, *On Genesis*: “Since the just profit through the unjust and the pious through the impious, it is said in vain that God ought not to have created those whom he foreknew would be evil. For why should he not create those who would benefit the good? Because, just as he foresaw that they would be evil, so too he foresaw what good he himself would bring about from their evil deeds” [Col. 0098C–D].

## Chapter VII. On the grace possessed before sin

It remains now to inquire what grace the human being had before sin, and whether through it he was able to stand or not. To understand this, one must recognize that he could not make progress without added grace, as we said also concerning the angels; but he could refrain from turning away from what he had received through grace bestowed upon him in creation. For it is one thing to do good and another to turn aside from evil. Through that assistance of grace which he had received in creation, he could turn aside from evil; but without superadded grace he could not himself do good.

Augustine, in *On Rebuke and Grace*: “If this assistance had been lacking to either angel or human being when they were first made—since their nature was not such that it could remain [in the good] without divine assistance, even if it willed to do so—then it certainly would not have fallen through its own fault. For the assistance without which it could not remain would have been lacking.” In the same work: “God had given the human being a good will; for in that will he made him upright. He gave assistance without which he could not remain in it if he willed, and through which he could; but he left it to his own choice whether he would will it.” In the same work: “He had received the ability, if he willed, but did not possess the willing of what he was able to do. For if he had possessed it, he certainly would have persevered” [Col. 0099A].

These authorities make clear that through what he received in creation the human being could refrain from yielding to temptation. For unless he had been made such that he could avoid falling and resist the tempter, as Augustine says, he would not have fallen through his own fault.

It is objected that the human being could make progress without cooperating grace, as follows: through the assistance of creative grace, he could refuse consent to the persuader; but this would be merit, and every merit is progress; therefore he could make progress through it. To this we say that the refusal to consent to evil is not itself merit; rather, merit lies in loving the good by refusing consent to evil. For merit does not consist in turning aside from evil, but in doing good through turning aside from evil. Yet the one cannot exist without the other [Col. 0099B].

Thus we say that, if a human being or angel had turned aside from evil, he would certainly have had merit and made progress; but not in the fact that he turned aside from evil, rather in the fact that, by turning aside from evil, he loved the good. For this he required cooperating grace. But for the first matter, the assistance of creative grace sufficed. Before sin, through free choice and through that assistance of grace, the human being had the ability not to sin—that is, to avoid evil; but, as we have said, he required cooperating grace to accomplish good. After the fall, however, he requires not only cooperating grace but also operating grace. Operating grace causes one to rise from sins; it also causes one to will the good. Cooperating grace cooperates with one who wills, so that he may do good.

But before the fall he required only cooperating grace; for he had not yet fallen, and therefore did not need grace through which he might rise, but only that through which he might make progress. After the fall, however, operating grace comes first, moving and awakening the heart. Of it the Prophet says: “His grace will go before me” (Ps. 58). It goes before by inspiring; it follows through by helping. For grace first acts without us, and there the human being merits nothing, because at that point he receives the will for good; but afterward he uses the will he has received, and grace cooperates, and in this lies human merit. For human merit does not lie in receiving a good will, since there one does nothing, but in using the will once received. Hence the Apostle says: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not empty” (1 Cor. 15) [Col. 0099C–D].

This may be seen by a comparison. First an instrument is made, so that a human being may do something with it; the instrument does not cut by itself, but through the guiding hand of the craftsman. So the will is first raised up by operating grace; and, once raised, it is aided and guided by cooperating grace to perform good. Hence the Apostle says: “To will is present with me, but I do not find the accomplishment of the good” (Rom. 7). But grace works both “to will and to accomplish” (Phil. 2). Its working “to will” pertains to operating grace; “to accomplish,” to cooperating grace.

It is commonly asked whether the human being possessed virtues before the fall. Some say that he did not, and attempt to show it thus. He did not have fortitude, because he yielded to a wicked suggestion; nor justice, because he despised God’s command; nor prudence, because he did not guard himself; nor temperance, because he desired what belonged to another. But we readily grant that he did not have them at the time when he sinned; yet it must not be granted that he had not possessed them previously, since Augustine says in a certain homily: “Adam, having lost charity, was found evil.” Again: “When the prince of vices saw Adam made from the clay of the earth in the image of God, armed with chastity, ordered by temperance, resplendent with charity, he stripped the first parents of those gifts and such great goods, and at the same time destroyed them.” Ambrose, *To Sabinus*: “When Adam was alone, he did not transgress, because his mind clung to God” [Col. 0100A–B].

Some, however, assert that from the moment someone possesses charity, that person cannot lose it. This is objected to what we have said. Augustine, *To Count Julian*: “Charity that can be abandoned was not true.” To this we say that “true” is used in two ways: with respect to permanence and with respect to substance. It was not true—that is, permanent and steadfast. Again: “Let your own spring be yours, not shared with a stranger.” But this does not mean one who will be a stranger—that is, evil—but one who is then a stranger. For while one is evil, one cannot have charity; nevertheless, someone who will be a stranger may now have it, or one who is now evil may have it at another time. For it seems foolish to say that someone in this life is so confirmed that he cannot become evil; this is promised only in the other life.

Therefore we acknowledge that he had charity and afterward lost it. Yet no one should suppose that we say that he possessed it at the very beginning of creation, as we said above concerning the angels; rather, it was after creation. For he did not fall immediately, like the angel, but remained in Paradise for some time, since Scripture says that he was put to sleep, and that the animals were led before him and he gave them names [Col. 0100C–D].

It is asked whether he foreknew his own fall. To this we say that he did not foreknow his fall, just as we said concerning the angel. This is proved by the same reasoning which we gave there. Augustine also says the same in *On Genesis*.

As punishment for this sin, the human being was cast out of Paradise into this place of miseries. As it says there: “God cast him out of Paradise lest perhaps he eat of the tree of life and live forever” (Gen. 3). These words seem to imply that if he had afterward eaten, he would never have died; but on the other hand, he was made mortal because of sin. How, then, would he not die while sin remained [Col. 0101A]? The reply is that, if he were not punished by this penalty—namely, death—he would be punished by a graver one, because the miseries which now end in death would never end, just as the devil’s miseries never end.

But because we have no certain authority for this, some wish to say that, if he had eaten, it would thereafter not have conferred immortality on him. They explain the words in this sense: “Lest he eat of the tree of life,” that is, he is unworthy to feed upon that tree which formerly conferred immortality. Therefore, lest he should be able to approach it, a certain fiery guard was placed before Paradise: namely, the flaming and turning sword, which was whirled before Paradise through the ministry of the cherubim.

This sword signifies the sufferings of the present life, which burn for a time but are transitory. *Cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of wisdom,” and signifies charity. Therefore, after sin, it was necessary to return to the eating of the tree of life through many tribulations and through charity, which is the fullness of knowledge. For since the cherubim with the flaming sword stands at Paradise’s gate, a human being cannot enter it without passing through the flaming sword [Col. 0101B].

It is commonly asked whether they had previously eaten from the tree of life. Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*: “They are quite rightly understood, before the devil’s malicious persuasion, to have abstained from the forbidden food and to have used what was permitted, especially the tree of life.” But this does not seem to be stated assertively.

## Chapter VIII. On free choice

Besides the other penalties incurred for that sin, the human being incurred the penalty of the impairment of free choice. For, as Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*: “By making bad use of free choice, the human being both lost himself and it.” Therefore we must consider what free choice is, what it was like before sin, and how it was impaired by sin. It may be defined thus: free choice is the capacity of the rational will by which good is chosen with grace cooperating, or evil when grace abandons it. It consists in two things: will and reason. For it is called “free” with respect to will; “choice” (*arbitrium*) with respect to reason. It belongs to reason to see what ought or ought not to be chosen; it belongs to will to desire. Thus reason, like an attendant, shows the way by advising what it sees ought to be done and dissuading from the contrary; will, like a mistress, leads reason with it toward whatever it inclines to [Col. 0101C–D].

For the will is not drawn by reason; reason only shows what the will ought to desire. But reason is drawn by the will even in matters contrary to reason. For reason naturally objects—that is, it judges that the thing ought not to be done—and yet it is overcome and consents. Since free choice consists in these two things, it is given only to the rational creature. For among creatures only the rational creature has both will and reason. Brute animals have sensation and appetite, namely sensual appetite; but they lack will and reason, and therefore do not possess free choice.

Although, therefore, we have sensation and appetite in common with beasts, free choice distinguishes us from them [Col. 0102A], and all merit consists in it. Since the human being is compelled by no force and no necessity, he not undeservedly merits either blessedness or misery. Sensation and appetite make neither blessed nor miserable; otherwise brute animals could participate in blessedness or misery. Natural ability, memory, and other such things likewise constitute neither the just nor the unjust. For neither slow intelligence nor a failing memory is imputed. Therefore will alone, which is always free and can never be compelled, is judged before God according to merit. It is always free from necessity. For where there is necessity, there is no freedom; where there is no freedom, there is no will; and consequently no merit.

## Chapter IX. That free choice concerns only the future, and concerning its fourfold state
[Col. 0102B] Furthermore, it should be known that free choice concerns only future things. What is present is not in our power, so that it may then be or not be; but whether it shall be so or not in the future is within the power of free choice. Nor does it concern all future things, but only those which can come to pass and can fail to come to pass.

We must now consider what it was like before sin. Four states of free choice may be observed in a human being. Before sin, nothing hindered the good and nothing compelled evil: then reason judged without error, and the will desired the good without difficulty. After sin, however—before it has been restored by grace—it is oppressed by concupiscence and overcome. After restoration—before the confirmation which will take place in the future—it is oppressed but not overcome. After confirmation, [Col. 0102C] it will be able neither to be overcome nor oppressed.

For there is a threefold freedom: from necessity, from sin, and from misery. It is equally free from necessity both before and after sin. For just as it could not then be compelled, neither can it now; this freedom is equal in all, no less in the wicked than in the good, and as complete after sin as before sin. There is another freedom, from sin, of which the Apostle says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3). And elsewhere: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness; but now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification” (Rom. 6).

Man lost this freedom by sinning; and this is what Augustine says: “By making bad use of free choice, man destroyed both himself and it.” [Col. 0102D] Freedom from necessity was not lost, but freedom from sin. “For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8). Only those who are restored through grace possess this freedom from sin—not because they are wholly without sin, but because sin does not rule over them; and this is properly called freedom.

In doing evil, choice is not properly called free, because reason disagrees with the will. For reason judges that what the will desires ought not to be done. In the good, reason agrees with the will and, without contradicting it, serves it. Hence Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*: “This is true freedom, because of the capacity for acting rightly; and devout servitude, because of obedience.” Thus it is apparent that in both good persons and evil persons the will is free from necessity; but only in the good is it free from sin.

Hence Augustine, in *On Grace and Free Choice*: “The will is always free in us, but it is not always good. Either it is free from righteousness when it serves sin, and then it is evil; or it is free from sin when it serves righteousness, and then it is good.” There is, again, freedom from misery, concerning which the Apostle Paul says to the Romans: “The creation itself also shall be delivered from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the Son of God” (Rom. 8). No one possesses this freedom in the present life. For a person can at present be free from sin, because, as we said above, although no one is without sin, yet once sin does not reign in a person, he is free from sin; but no one is at present delivered from the punishment of sin.

From what has been said it is clear in what respect free choice [Col. 0103B] has been diminished through sin. For then there was no difficulty in willing rightly, no hindrance from the law of the members to carrying out the good; but now, before it has been freed from sin by grace, it can neither will nor accomplish the good. We might say of someone in fetters: “This person cannot walk,” that is, he does not have it in his own power; yet we would concede, “It is possible for this person to walk,” because it may happen that he is released and walks.

The Apostle recalls this defect of ours when he says: “To will is present with me, but I do not find the accomplishing of the good” (Rom. 7). Unless it is freed by grace working inwardly and stirring the heart, choice itself cannot be raised to the good. Hence: “If the Son shall make you free, you shall indeed be free” (John 8). And after it has been freed, [Col. 0103C] unless it is aided by cooperating grace, it cannot accomplish the good.

Thus it now needs operative grace, by which it is freed, and cooperating grace, by which it is helped to merit; whereas before sin, as we said above, it needed cooperating grace alone. For before it fell, it did not need a liberator, but a co-worker.

An objection is customarily made here in this way. Before anyone has free choice restored—that is, while he remains in sins—he has free choice; therefore he can be bent in either direction. Accordingly, either choice is not free, or, if it is free while he is still in sins, he can will the good; and thus it appears that, before grace is given, he can will the good.

But the situation is like that of the fettered person who cannot walk before he is released, and yet it is true in itself that this person can walk, or that it is possible for him to walk. In the same sense, likewise, we do not deny concerning that sinner, pagan, or anyone else, that it is possible for him to will the good, or that he can will the good; but only in this way: namely, if grace is given by which he is freed and which cooperates with him.

To will simply is one thing; to will the good is another. Just as to fear simply is one thing, and to fear God another; to love simply is one thing, and to love God another. “To fear” and “to love,” stated simply, are affections; with an addition, they are virtues. To will belongs to us by nature; to will the good, by grace. For simple affections are naturally in us, as though from ourselves; [Col. 0104A] the additions are from grace.

Hence Augustine, in the *Retractations*: “Some goods are great, some intermediate, some least. The virtues by which one lives rightly are great goods. The forms of any bodies, without which one may nevertheless live rightly, are least goods. The powers of the mind, without which one cannot live rightly, are intermediate goods. No one uses virtues badly. But anyone can use the other goods, both intermediate and least, not only well but also badly. Therefore no one uses virtue badly, because the work of virtue is the good use of those things which we can also use badly. Free choice is found among intermediate goods, because we can use it badly; yet it is such that without it we cannot live rightly. But its good use is already virtue, which is found among the great goods, which no one can use badly.”

From this authority it is clear that the will belongs among intermediate goods, while a good will belongs among the great goods that are in us not by nature but by grace. Yet it may be said that even evil people naturally will the good; thus it appears that someone has willing the good before receiving grace. But naturally to will the good is nothing other than for reason to judge that thing to be good. Thus some tyrant says: “I would wish to be a good monk, to leave the world,” and similar things. Such a person naturally desires the good, but the good does not delight him. Therefore he cannot properly be said to will the good, nor does such willing have merit; rather, merit belongs to that willing which is accompanied by delight in the good—when, that is, the good pleases him and he has it as his intention.

Hence the Apostle: [Col. 0104C] “God is the one who works in us both to will and to accomplish, according to good will” (Phil. 2). A good will exists first by nature and has no merit; afterward it becomes good through grace, and then it has merit.

Furthermore, free choice is not so called because it stands equally toward both alternatives, namely good and evil. For a person can fall by himself, but cannot rise by himself unless aided by the grace of Christ. Free choice by itself is sufficient for evil, but is not by itself sufficient for good. The good angels also do not lack free choice, and yet they have been so confirmed that they cannot be evil. Likewise, the evil angels do not lack free choice, although they are so obstinate that they cannot [Col. 0104D] be good. Free choice is therefore so called because it is voluntary.

That good angels cannot be evil is not caused by necessity, but by a will confirmed through grace. That evil angels cannot be good is not caused by any compulsion, but by a will obstinate in evil. Yet both these and those are mutable by nature.

Hence Jerome: “God alone is one in whom sin cannot occur; all others, since they possess free choice, can be bent in either direction.” It is also written of God that he has free choice. Ambrose, to Gratian: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3). The Apostle likewise says that one Spirit works all things, “distributing to each individually as he wills” (1 Cor. 12). “As he wills,” he says—that is, according to the free choice [Col. 0105A] of the will, not according to the service of necessity. Nor is free choice in God anything other than the divine will, which does all things not from necessity but from goodness alone. For his nature is goodness.

## CHAPTER X. Why the sin of the first human being is imputed to his descendants

After the sin of the first human being, and the punishment which we have assigned as incurred from it, we must consider why it is imputed to his posterity. For all who descend from him through concupiscence are liable to that sin and are guilty of original sin on its account.

It may be said that it is imputed to all because all committed it, as the Apostle says: “In whom all sinned” (Rom. 5). This can be explained thus: “In him all sinned,” that is, they are held guilty [Col. 0105B] by sin. For, as the Apostle says: “Through the disobedience of one, many were made sinners” (ibid.). This is because they descend from him through the law of sin.

It is not imputed to them because they were then originally in him, since Christ too, according to the flesh, was then in him; but because they descended from him through concupiscence, which arose from that sin. Thus it may be said that it is imputed to the whole posterity because they are conceived in the effect of this sin—that is, in the law of sin arising from it—namely, in concupiscence. Theft, homicide, and the rest are not imputed to descendants, because generation itself does not take place according to the effects of those sins, that is, according to a movement arising from them.

Some customarily resolve the foregoing question in this way: that sin is imputed to all descendants, unlike other sins, because the sin committed in paradise was most grave. For ignorance did not lead him to sin, nor did frailty of the flesh, because before sin neither existed in him. Hence that sin was so great that it even changed nature. For the whole nature of man was corrupted through that sin.

Augustine, *City of God*: “That command was violated with so much the greater injustice as it could have been kept by an easier observance. Desire did not yet resist the will, as afterward followed from the punishment of transgression.” Yet it does not seem that one should grant without qualification that this sin was graver than all others, since it is written: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, either in this [Col. 0105D] age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12; Luke 12; Mark 3). But the authorities say that this sin was afterward forgiven to the first parents.

Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*: “Just as those first human beings, afterward living righteously, and therefore rightly believed to have been delivered from the final punishment through the Lord’s blood, nevertheless did not merit by that life to be recalled to paradise; so too, although sins have been forgiven and a person lives righteously in the flesh of sin, he does not immediately merit not to undergo the death which he derived from the propagation of sin.”

The following objection is customarily raised against what we said, that all were in Adam. All who descended from Cain were in Adam, since they existed there through the substance which Cain received in the first parents. Yet in that particle propagated in Cain [Col. 0106A] there were not as many atoms as the persons who descended from him; therefore it does not seem true that the substance of each individual was in the first parent.

It may be said in reply that, although that particle was at first very small, no external substance passed into it, but it grew and became large—namely, as large as it will be at the resurrection. For it receives nourishment from foods; but foods do not pass into human substance itself. This may be proved as follows: a child who dies on the day of birth will rise again in the nature which he would have possessed had he lived to full age, with no illness or bodily defect hindering him.
