Thus it is apparent that even if he had lived, the parts of that substance would not have been taken from elsewhere, but would have increased within themselves, like the rib from which the woman was made, and like the five Gospel loaves.

Nevertheless, we do not deny that foods pass into humors and flesh; hence some persons are more corpulent than they should be. But that excess will not exist at the resurrection, because it does not belong to the truth of human nature. The “truth of human substance” means that which was in the first parents, and that alone will be present at the resurrection. But those parts which arise from foods, and into which foods pass, will be cast off as superfluous.

## CHAPTER XI. What original sin is

Next we must inquire what is called original sin, and why it is called original. Some say that original sin is the debt by which all are bound on account of the sin of the first human being, because on account of it eternal punishment is owed to all unless they are freed by grace. These people say that original sin is not sin; but if Scripture sometimes calls it sin, they maintain that “sin” there is taken for the punishment of sin. And just as children are sometimes exiled for a parent’s sin under the justice of the world, so by God’s justice all are held guilty on account of that sin. Thus, according to them, there is no sin in a child’s soul. For they say: if a child’s soul has never sinned, there is no sin in it; yet they concede that original sin is in it, because it is bound by the debt of sin.

But these people plainly speak against the Apostle, when the Apostle says: “Through the disobedience of one, many were made sinners” [Col. 0106D] (Rom. 5). Behold: the Apostle calls them sinners before they are regenerated; but if there were in them only punishment and not guilt, as these people say, they would not be sinners. Again the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death” (ibid.). The sin which entered is one thing; the punishment itself, indicated in the Apostle’s words, is another.

Others say that original sin is disobedience, and that this disobedience is in all before they are reborn. But it does not seem that a child is disobedient, because nothing has ever been commanded of him. And how can one who cannot yet use reason be called either obedient or disobedient? For disobedience belongs to the will, as does obedience; but original sin is not voluntary.

Leaving these views aside, it may be said that [Col. 0107A] original sin is desire for evil and ignorance of good. Hence Augustine, in *On Rebuke and Grace*: “These two things are penal in every human being: ignorance and difficulty. From ignorance comes error, so that one approves false things as true; from difficulty comes torment, so that, through the resistance and anguish of the pain of the carnal bond, one cannot restrain oneself from desire.”

But an objection may be raised: since a child’s soul does not yet will or not will anything, how does it possess desire for evil? It possesses a defect, not an act; this is proved by the fact that, when it reaches the years of discernment, it then desires evil and abandons good.

Likewise one objects: since it does not yet have to know anything, how does it have ignorance? But just as in the eye of a blind person at night the defect of blindness exists but does not appear, [Col. 0107B] and one cannot distinguish the sighted from the blind unless light comes; so too there is a defect in a child, but it does not yet appear. When the time comes at which the child ought to desire good and be ignorant of evil, it is ignorant of good and desires evil.

Again, one objects: in baptism original sin is remitted, but after baptism desire for evil and the rest remain; therefore it does not seem that original sin is remitted in baptism. But, as Augustine says, although concupiscence remains after baptism, it does not remain as guilt; for it is not imputed to those who have been reborn. And this is the remission of original sin: that it is not imputed. For although the concupiscence of the flesh is in the baptized person, it is not imputed to him unless he follows his concupiscences. If that occurs, it is no longer original sin but actual sin.

Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*: “From this concupiscence of the flesh—which, although it is no longer reckoned as sin in the regenerate—whatever offspring is born is bound by original sin.” And a little later: “The concupiscence of the flesh is forgiven in baptism, not so that it does not exist, but so that sin is not imputed. For this is not to have sin: not to be guilty of sin.” Again: “Just as other sins pass away in act and remain in guilt, such as homicide and the like, so conversely concupiscence may pass away in guilt and remain in act.”

Behold, from these authorities it is clear that desire for evil is original sin, under which ignorance of good is included, because it arises from it. For unless desire for evil had preceded, ignorance of good would not have followed. This is why in Holy Scripture we sometimes find “original sins” in the plural, because ignorance of good and desire for evil are different; and sometimes “original sin” in the singular, because, as we have said, one of these arises from the other. Thus one is included under, or in, the other.

## CHAPTER XII. On the basis of original sin

After this we must consider why that sin is called original. It is so called because it is derived from origin; that is, when someone is generated, he derives that sin from his parents. Hence David: “My mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. 50).

An objection may be made in this way. When someone is generated, only flesh is propagated from the parents, because, as we said above, souls [Col. 0108A] are not propagated by descent. Moreover, philosophers say that even in the propagation of flesh the soul is not yet infused until the body is already formed. Moses shows this most clearly in Exodus, saying: “If anyone strikes a pregnant woman and causes a miscarriage, if it is still unformed, he shall be fined money; but if it has been formed, he shall render life for life” (Exod. 21). By “formed” he understands already ensouled.

If original sin is transmitted from the parents in propagation itself, it seems that original sin is in that which has been propagated. But it is still inanimate, and every sin belongs to the soul. How then can sin be in that seed? For as virtue is in the soul, so too is every sin.

It may be said in reply that not only the soul but also the flesh is liable to the bond of original sin—not because that sin is in the flesh, but because the soul contracts it from the corruption of the flesh. For unless flesh were propagated in concupiscence, the soul would not be held by that sin. Hence we find that Christ did not have sinful flesh, but flesh “like sinful flesh” (Rom. 8), because that flesh was not propagated from the mother through a man’s concupiscence, but by the operation of the Holy Spirit. Others have sinful flesh—not because sin is in the flesh, but because it is the cause of sin.

Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*: “While man and woman join with one another in order to generate children, the parents’ intercourse is not without lust; and for this reason the conception of their children born from the flesh cannot be without sin, where propagation does not transmit sin to little children, [Col. 0108C] but lust does.” Thus it is apparent that original sin is transmitted in conception itself, because unless conception occurred in the flesh in this manner, the soul would not contract concupiscence from union with the flesh.

If one asks what the corruption is which we have said exists in the flesh, whether it is sin or not, it may be called sin, that is, the punishment of sin—just as we customarily take “sin” to mean guilt; but it itself will not be called sin. Yet that there is corruption of sin in the flesh may be known from its effect, as a defect is known to be in a vessel from the fact that it makes wine sour.

Again, it is customarily asked: since someone’s parents have been cleansed of original sin by baptism, how can the child contract that sin? Augustine shows this in *On the Baptism of Infants* by these comparisons: “Just as the foreskin is removed by circumcision, yet remains in the one whom the circumcised beget; and just as chaff, carefully separated by human effort, yet remains in the grain which is born from purified wheat: so the sin cleansed by baptism remains in those whom the baptized beget.” Again, in the same work: “For a person begets from that by which he still bears the old nature, not from that by which renewal has advanced him among the children of God. Parents do not generate their children according to that generation by which they have been newly born, but rather according to that by which they themselves were first generated carnally.”

Furthermore, it is customarily asked by what justice [Col. 0109A] that innocent soul, created by God, is held by sin when it is not in its power to avoid it. For it is not in free choice’s power either to avoid it or not to avoid it, since it does not yet use free choice and is not in that body before it is liable to that sin.

Some resolve this thus: that soul, although not derived by propagation but newly created and clean by God, is guilty of that sin because, when it is infused into the body, it finds the body suited and fit for sinning, delights in this, and contracts that sin from such delight. But if this were so, it ought to be called actual rather than original sin. For if this sin arises from delight, it is not another’s but belongs to one’s own will, whereas Augustine and others call it another’s.

Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*: “It is clear that there are for each person particular sins, in which only those whose sins they are have sinned; and another one sin, in which all sinned.” We therefore think that the justice of God is hidden, by which the soul is held guilty of that sin which it is not in its power to avoid and which it did not commit through its own will. For, as the Apostle says, “The judgments of God are incomprehensible, and his ways unsearchable” (Rom. 10).

It is also customarily asked whether that sin is voluntary or necessary. That it is not voluntary is clear from what has been said above. Again, if it is called necessary, it ought not to be imputed. Therefore someone wished to say that it is neither necessary nor voluntary. Yet the prophet says: “Deliver me, O Lord, from my necessities” (Ps. 24). Therefore it does not seem absurd [Col. 0109C] for it to be called necessary.

If anyone asks again: since God, who makes that soul immaculate, knows that it will contract the stain of sin from the body, and that it will sometimes be separated from that body by death before baptism and thus condemned, why does he join it to the body? We give the same answer as above: namely, that the justice of God is hidden.

Some also object in this way: since the soul is created in the body and is not in the body before it is held by that sin, then it has the stain of sin when it first exists. Therefore it is never such as God creates it. For it is created innocent by God, but it is never innocent, since it is stained when first [Col. 0109D] created.

But it should be said that God creates it clean, that is, it has no stain from its creation; and thus, with respect to creation, it is such as God creates it. For it is always good and clean with respect to creation.

Accordingly it is customarily asked whether all souls are equal by creation, or whether some are more excellent than others, as was also the case among angels. It seems to many that, from creation itself, one soul is more capable than another of understanding and retaining in memory; this is quite probable.

An objection is raised: if they depart from the body before baptism, they have equal punishment; if immediately after baptism, equal crowns; and so it seems that they are undifferentiated in creation itself. But, as we have already said in the *Treatise on Free Choice*, those things which arise from creation itself, such as natural ability and memory, make a person neither more nor less blessed, nor deserving of punishment.

## CHAPTER XIII. On actual sin

Having spoken of original sin, it seems fitting to add something concerning actual sins. First, it must be observed that they are not imputed to descendants, according to Ezekiel: “This proverb shall no longer be in Israel: ‘Our fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge’” (Jer. 31; Ezek. 18). “The soul that sins shall itself die. The son shall not bear the father’s iniquity” (Ezek. 18).

It seems contrary to this that Exodus says: “I repay the iniquity of the father upon the children to the third and fourth [Col. 0110B] generation of those who hate me” (Exod. 20; Deut. 5). But, as Jerome says, this is said of children who imitate their fathers’ evils, as the conclusion of that authority indicates: “of those who hate me.” For if the son does not imitate the father’s sins, he will not be punished for them.

One objects: if this is to be understood of imitators, why did he say only to the third and fourth generation, since all who imitate the sins of their parents, in any generation whatever, are liable for them? The saints resolve this as follows: it was said “to the third and fourth” because children are usually more apt, up to the fourth generation, to imitate their parents’ deeds, while these are still known to them and, as it were, present.

Augustine explains this as a temporal punishment: in the punishment of parents, children are often punished temporally for their parents’ sins, so that they are born blind, become lame after birth, or suffer some other penalty. But in the future, as the Apostle says, “each shall bear his own burden” (Gal. 6).

Jerome, commenting on Ezekiel, says that within us the prompting of the flesh is like a father; the son is the first impulse of thought toward sin, and this is the first offspring. The grandson arises if one decides to act, or carries it out in deed. The great-grandson arises if one not only does what is evil but also glories in one’s crime; this is the fourth generation—not because three generations precede it, but because it is called the fourth from the first movement, which is posited as a kind of father.

Therefore God does not punish the first and second incitement, namely thoughts—without which no one can exist—with damnation; [Col. 0110D] but he punishes the third and fourth generations, which are sins unto death. In proof of this—that the first movement is not punished—when Ham sinned by mocking his father’s nakedness, the one who laughed did not himself receive the sentence, but his son did: “Cursed,” he said, “be Canaan; he shall be servant of his brothers” (Gen. 9). What justice would there be in the father’s sin and the pronouncement of sentence upon the son, unless this occurred for the sake of such a signification?

## CHAPTER XIV. On sin in general

We have set out the difference between original and actual sins. Now we must speak of sin without distinction. Four questions must be investigated: what is the cause of sin; what is called sin; why it is so called; and in what ways it is said to occur.

The cause of every sin is a will that falls away from God. Augustine: “The cause of all good things is God’s goodness; but the cause of evil things is a mutable will falling away from God—first the angel’s, then the human being’s.”

If one asks what sin or evil is, one may answer: nothing, according to the saying: “All things were made through him, and without him was made nothing” (John 1). For, as Augustine says, evil is nothing other than the privation of good. Thus evil is not a thing, but the privation of something. For whatever exists is either God’s work or the work of a human being imitating God. That sin is not God’s work is clear; nor is it the work of a human being imitating God, because by sinning one departs from God. That can be called the work of one imitating God which, in acting, [Col. 0111B] does not depart from God—for example, a house and similar things.

If we wish to weigh these matters more subtly, it may be said that whatever exists is God’s work. For God works in two ways: some things through himself, such as natural things; others through his servants, such as artificial things. Since he makes the latter through his servants, it is clear that he himself makes them too. Thus it may be said that whatever exists is God’s work; but evil is not God’s work, and therefore it is not anything.

But if evil is nothing, how can it corrupt good? Augustine: “Abstaining from food is not a substance; yet the substance of the body, if it abstains entirely from food, languishes and perishes. Thus sin is not a substance; but God is a substance, as the true food of rational creation.”

But since evil is said to be the privation of good, we must consider of what good it is the privation. To understand this, it should be noted that “good” is said in different ways. God is the highest good, whose essence is goodness. For him, to be good is the same as to be. Therefore, just as he cannot not exist, since he lacks both beginning and end, so he cannot not be good, since his essence is goodness; and therefore there can be no privation of this good.

Creatures are called good by participation; thus they can be deprived of their good. And just as there are two kinds of creature, spiritual and bodily, so there is a twofold good of the creature. The good of the spiritual creature is one thing; that of the bodily creature another. The good of the spiritual creature consists chiefly in two things: knowledge of truth and love of virtue. The good of bodily creation is either within it or outside it. The good within it is the soundness of the senses and affections according to the five senses; the good outside it is an ordered distribution among creatures. For the corruption or amendment of these is for the sake of human beings, and whatever is good or evil is good or evil for human beings.

There is therefore a threefold good of the human being: one outside the person, namely that which is in creatures; another within the person; and of what is within, one good is in the soul and another in the body. Thus there are three kinds of evil. Universally, the privation of any good is called evil, whether it is the privation of good in the soul, in the body, or in creatures. Yet, although each of these is evil, one is guilt, another is punishment and not guilt, and another is neither guilt nor punishment but leads to punishment.

For the corruption of that good which is in the soul is both sin and guilt. By the incorruption of a good of this kind we live toward God; by its corruption we are removed from God. As we said, the good of the soul consists especially in two things: knowledge of truth and love of virtue. The corruption of knowledge may be called ignorance, concerning which the Apostle says: “Whoever is ignorant shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14). The corruption of love is cupidity, which is “the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6). And the more this ignorance and cupidity increase, the more the good of the soul is corrupted; in this respect the soul is said to be corrupted.

For since the soul is an incorporeal substance, it cannot be corrupted in its substance, but only with respect to the good in which it participates.

Here one may ask how the soul can be corrupted further [Col. 0112B] after it lacks those two things, namely knowledge of truth and love of virtue. Since only the substance itself and the defect remain there, as in demons or evil persons, when they sin again, the corruption of what good will that sin be called? There is no other good there except nature itself, which has been deformed; but it cannot be corrupted in essence, because it is simple and incorporeal, nor is there virtue in it that could be corrupted. From what, then, can it be deprived? For once the eye has been deprived of sight, it cannot be deprived further.

It may be said in reply that the more it loves injustice, the more it is deprived of justice—not by losing a justice which it does not possess, but by losing its capacity to recover it, which is certainly a good. For the more unjust it is, the farther [Col. 0112C] it withdraws from justice; and so in other things. Just as a sick person, the more ill he becomes, is the more deprived of health—not by losing a health which he does not possess, but because he is removed farther from it—so too those natural goods which the soul still has, such as reason, natural ability, memory, and the rest, are increasingly impaired and darkened as the soul is more deformed by sins.

## CHAPTER XV. In what nature sin exists
It now seems necessary to say in what nature sin is said to exist: whether in the spiritual, the bodily, or both. But, as we have already said, not every corruption of a good is sin, but only the corruption of that good which is in spiritual nature. It is therefore apparent that fault or sin can exist only in spiritual nature [Col. 0112D]; nor do we deny that evil also exists in bodily nature. Hence in the prophet: “There is no evil in a city which the Lord does not do” (Amos 3). But he calls punishment, not fault, “evil,” such as illnesses and things of that kind. And since every nature, whether bodily or spiritual, is good, it is clear that evil exists only in a good. Hence Augustine: “Nothing called evil exists if nothing called good exists; nor can evil exist except where there is some good.” Again Augustine: “What is a bad man except a bad nature? For man is a nature; and if man is some good because he is a nature, what is a bad man except an evil good? Good because he is man, evil because he is unrighteous.” Therefore whoever says that it is evil to be a human being, or that it is good to be unrighteous [Col. 0113A], falls under this saying: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isa. 5).

Here it must be considered whether evil acts ought to be called sins or not. Some say that all acts are indifferent, so that in themselves they are called neither good nor evil; but an act is called good because it is done with a good intention, evil because with an evil intention. Thus, to kill a man out of zeal for justice is good; out of hatred, evil: in itself it is neither good nor evil. Hence Ambrose: “Your dispositions give your work its name.” This opinion is opposed as follows: If every act is indifferent, then committing adultery and perjuring oneself are indifferent acts; but these acts can only be evil; therefore not every act is indifferent. They answer thus: “To commit adultery” and “to commit perjury” denote not only the act [Col. 0113B] but also the vice; and therefore, although these are not indifferent, the act itself—namely, intercourse with a woman and swearing—is nevertheless indifferent. Accordingly, in respect of these acts they are not sins. Nor is killing a man called an evil act because it is a sin, but because it proceeds from an evil intention; and so in other cases.

Yet it may properly be said that an evil act is sin, in this sense: killing a man is sin, that is, an act of sin. For, as Augustine says, two things are considered in sin: the act and the guilt. The act lies in the deed; the guilt in the will. Thus, in the sin which is homicide, the guilt is the will itself, or the vice of the will. So long as this remains, a man is guilty whether the act exists or has not yet occurred, or has already passed; and both are called homicide by common usage [Col. 0113C] and by the usage of Scripture. They are not two sins or two homicides, but one and the same thing, though in different modes: namely, in will and in act.

For evil is spoken of in two ways: substantively and adjectivally. The corruption or deprivation of good that occurs in the soul is not merely evil, but is evil itself, that is, wickedness, as injustice and similar things are. An action is called evil not because it is evil itself, but because it is the manifestation of evil.

## Chapter XVI. The modes of sinning

Sin is committed in two ways, as Isidore says: by desire and by fear—when someone either wishes to attain what he desires, or fears that he may incur what he fears. Again, a human being sins against himself, against God, and against his neighbor. That which is done against God is called an offence: for example, perjury and unworthy participation in the sacraments. These sins are said to be committed against God because in them there is greater contempt of God. Other sins, those against ourselves and our neighbor, are called not offences but sins. An offence is also what occurs when we omit to do what is commanded; a sin, when we do what is forbidden—though either term is used indifferently for the other.

Again, as Gregory says, there are seven capital vices: pride, envy, anger, acedia or sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust. From these, as from seven fountains, flow all corruptions of souls. They are called capital not because they are greater than the others, since other vices are equally great or greater, but as capitals from which all the others arise [Col. 0114A]. For there is none which has not sprung from one of these.

Pride is love of one’s own excellence. It is not a vice that we love what is excellent, but that we strive to appropriate to ourselves by participation that which is good—namely, excellence—as though by exclusive possession. And there are four species of pride, as Gregory says. The first is when a man attributes to himself the good that he possesses; the second, when he believes it has been given by God, yet on account of his own merits; the third, when he boasts of possessing things he does not possess; the fourth, when, despising others, he wishes to appear singularly distinguished. This final species comes nearest to the devil, who wished to be above all the other angels.

From pride, in the first place, is born envy, which is hatred of another’s happiness. For when the proud person sees his neighbor equally exalted in the same position, or exalted above himself [Col. 0114B], he begins to envy him. Then, from a slight injury, he is stirred to anger against his neighbor. Anger is impatience with inward pain. These three strip a person of every interior good. For there are three things to be loved: God, one’s neighbor, and oneself. Pride removes God; envy, one’s neighbor; anger, oneself.

Then follows acedia, that is, confusion of mind or inward sadness. And because the human mind cannot live without some joy, when it has lost inward joy it wanders out toward external things. This is done by avarice, which is an immoderate love of possessing. And when it now takes delight in external things, it first takes delight in the vice nearest to nature, namely gluttony. Then comes lust, which is the appetite for libidinous pleasure. The other vices are subordinated to pride not because they are predicated of it [Col. 0114C], but because they are placed after it, which is the mother of the others. For “pride is the beginning and root of all evils” (Ecclus. 10). But again we read: “Desire is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6); therefore pride is not the root of all evils. Yet it can be said that avarice is contained in pride, since pride is love of one’s own excellence. For, as Augustine says: “What person is more avaricious than one for whom God is not enough?” Or it may be said that pride is the root of all evils, that is, of evil affections, while desire is the root of all evils, that is, of evil actions.

## Chapter XVII. The difference between gifts and virtues, and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit

Opposed to those seven vices are the virtues which the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit produce. The difference between gifts [Col. 0114D] and virtues is this: gifts are the first movements in the heart, like seeds of virtues cast upon the soil of our heart; virtues are like the crop which rises from them. For the effects of gifts are certain confirmed habits already good. And they are called the seven gifts of the Spirit. Hence in the Apocalypse: John saw seven spirits moving before the throne of God (Apoc. 1). They are called spirits, that is, breathings or inspirations which precede the virtues; and they are gifts only, not merits. Virtues are both gifts and merits. In the former God works without us; in the latter he works with us. From fear, which is “the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110), humility is born; from the spirit of piety, meekness is born [Col. 0115A]; and so with each of the things enumerated there: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5), etc.

But here it must be noted that there are four fears, as Augustine says: servile, worldly, initial, and filial. Servile fear is refraining from evil because of punishment threatened by a human being, while the will to evil is nevertheless retained. Worldly fear is refraining from good because of punishment feared from a human being, as occurred in Peter. There is besides divine fear: fearing God because of either present punishment or the punishment of Gehenna. If one fears God only for punishment, without love of the good, this is sickness and has the torment of punishment; that is, it belongs to the wicked, and this fear is servile. But if one fears with the joy of the good joined to it, it is initial; and this fear is the beginning of wisdom, since a person begins to know [Col. 0115B] and taste God where fear and hope accompany one another. Hence we read: “Fear is not without hope”; and the more good will grows, that is, charity, the more the fear of punishment decreases. But if love alone is present, fear becomes filial and chaste; it remains for ever and ever. It is therefore clear that initial fear is not without charity—not perfect charity, I mean, but incipient charity. Hence John says in his Epistle: “Perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4), namely initial fear. Here he indicates that, though charity is not yet perfect, it is nevertheless present in initial fear.

Christ prohibits servile and worldly fear, saying: “Do not fear those who kill only the body, but can do nothing to the soul” (Matt. 10). Then he adds concerning initial fear [Col. 0115C]: “But fear him who can cast soul and body into Gehenna” (ibid.). He would not command this unless charity, though not yet perfect, were in it. And it should be noted that this fear is sometimes called servile in divine Scripture because it is akin to servile fear; for in both cases one refrains from an evil work through fear of punishment. But servile fear causes one to refrain from the evil work and not from the will; this fear, however, causes one to refrain from both work and will.

Bede, commenting on Proverbs, says that both fears will cease in the future. This seems contrary to what the Psalmist says: “The holy fear of the Lord remains for ever and ever” (Ps. 18). But Bede’s statement may be explained thus: both fears will cease, that is, both effects of fear. The effect of initial fear is fear of being punished. The effect of filial fear is fear of being separated [Col. 0115D]. Hence Augustine: “Chaste fear loves gratuitously, fearing not punishment but separation.” For the perfect do not fear punishment by the penalty of Gehenna, but fear being separated in the present by some fault. In the future, however, they will fear neither punishment nor separation; yet there will be fear there, namely reverence. For they will behold two things in God himself: majesty and mercy; from majesty, reverence [Col. 0116A], and from mercy, love. Therefore they will fear majesty—that is, they will be subject to it with reverence.

It is customary to ask whether both fears were in Christ. That filial fear was in him is clear. For according to his humanity he rendered reverence to God. Initial fear, as some say, was not in him. For John says of it in his Epistle: “Perfect charity casts out fear.” But who doubts that Christ possessed charity in the highest perfection? Again, initial fear is fear of Gehenna, but Christ did not fear Gehenna, since he was free from every sin. Hence he was certain that those punishments would by no means lay hold of him.

But it is objected that Isaiah enumerates seven gifts as having been in Christ, saying: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11). But, they say, what belongs to the members is attributed to Christ. Christ did not have that gift in himself, but in his body. Again it is objected against them that in Christ was the fullness of all gifts; therefore that gift too was in Christ. They answer thus: Christ did not have every individual gift in himself, since he did not have repentance for sins, which is a certain gift of God; and he had the fullness of all gifts because nothing necessary to his perfection was lacking to him. But if he had possessed initial fear, repentance, or similar things—which, although gifts, belong to the imperfect—they would undoubtedly not have conferred perfection, but would merely have made a beginning of the perfect life [Col. 0116C].

Others hold that the gift which is initial fear was in Christ; yet it should not be conceded: “Initial fear was in Christ.” For the fear of the Lord is one gift among those seven, not two; but it has two effects. According to one effect it is called initial; according to the other, chaste and filial. According to this latter effect it was in Christ. Therefore the gift which is initial fear in others was in Christ, yet initial fear was not in Christ, because Christ did not have fear according to that effect. It is as when two persons have faith, one imperfect and the other perfect and steadfast: we say that they have only one faith, one virtue; yet it does not follow that, if they have the same faith and this one has it imperfectly, therefore the other has it imperfectly [Col. 0116D]. And this seems more probable than what we said first.

Some concede these words: “Christ had initial fear and feared Gehenna”; yet he was certain that it could not lay hold of him. It is as if someone stationed in a high tower feared the precipice from a certain horror, although he were certain that he would not fall.

# Fourth Treatise: On the Sacraments in General and the Divine Precepts

[Col. 0117]

## Chapters

Chapter I. On the sacraments in general.—Chapter II. On the sacraments of the Law.—Chapter III. On the precepts of the first tablet.—Chapter IV. On the first four precepts of the second tablet.—Chapter V. On the fifth precept of the second tablet.—Chapter VI. On the sixth and seventh precepts of the second tablet.—Chapter VII. On love of neighbor.—Chapter VIII. On love of God.

## Chapter I. On the sacraments in general

[Col. 0117A]

Against both original and actual sins, of which we have already spoken, remedies of the sacraments have been devised. Three matters concerning them must be considered: what a sacrament is, why it was instituted, and in what it consists. Augustine: “A sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing.” Again: “A sacrament is a visible form of invisible grace,” as in the sacrament of baptism, where inward cleansing is figured by the outward and visible cleansing. For every sacrament ought to have a likeness of that of which it is the sacrament. Hence Augustine: “For if sacraments did not possess some likeness of those things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all.”

It is objected that the foregoing definition does not belong to sacraments alone, since even before consecration it is fitting for water to be a visible form of invisible grace; for just as water removes the filth of the body, so grace removes the filth of the soul. But in order that it may apply to sacraments alone, it must be understood thus: A sacrament is a visible form of invisible grace conferred in it—grace, that is, which the sacrament itself confers. For it is not merely a sign of a sacred thing, but also efficacious. This is the difference between a sign and a sacrament: for a thing to be a sign requires nothing but that it signify that of which it is said to be a sign, not that it confer it. A sacrament, however, not only signifies but also confers that of which it is the sign or signification.

Again, there is this difference: a sign may exist for signification alone, even though it lacks likeness, as a wine-circle; but a sacrament not only signifies by institution, but also represents by likeness [Col. 0117C]. For, as we have already said, a sacrament must have some likeness to that thing of which it is called the sacrament. It should also be known that in sacred Scripture “sacrament” is sometimes called a sacred and mystical thing, such as the sacrament of the Incarnation.

Next, it must be considered why sacraments were instituted. They were instituted for three reasons: instruction, humiliation, and exercise. For instruction, because before sin man possessed knowledge of truth and could then see God without mediation; but he was blinded through pride. Thus, in order that he may return to knowledge, these visible things are necessary, through which the mind is instructed to understand invisible things. For humiliation, because the rational creature was of such dignity that its good was not itself, but only that which is the highest good—whereas for other things, what they are is their good, as for a stone or wood. Before sin, in order to obtain that good, it was necessary only to desire it; for if it desired it, it would know it to be its good; and if it knew it to be its good, it would know it to be better than itself, because whatever is anyone’s good outside that person is better than that person. And if it knew it to be better than itself, it would subject itself to it and possess it through that desire. For rational nature has such freedom that it can never possess that good except willingly; hence it alone comes into judgment. But because through pride it lost that good, it must recover it through humility. Yet it is not enough to be humbled merely in this respect, that it should be subject to God; for it ought to have done this before sin as well, but after sin it must do more. Therefore sacraments were instituted so that we may be subject not only to God but also to an inferior nature: so that in these things a human being may seek salvation, though not from these things. For it is a great display of humility to seek salvation in visible things much inferior to man.

They were instituted for exercise because a human being cannot be without exercise; therefore, in order that he might be removed from bad and superfluous exercise and exercise himself in good, God instituted sacraments and fixed places for them: so that Mass may be heard in church, confession made there to a priest, and the like. There are three kinds of exercises: one pertains to the building up of the soul, the second to sustaining the body, and the third to the destruction of the soul. He enjoined the first, permitted the middle one, and prohibited the last [Col. 0118C].

A sacrament consists in three things: things, acts, and words. Things, such as water, oil, and the like. Acts, such as immersion and breathing upon. Words, such as the invocation of the Trinity. Here one may ask: since human salvation principally consists in these sacraments, why were they not established from the beginning, so that from the beginning there might have been the sacrament of baptism, the sacrament of confirmation, and so on? It may be answered that just as the knowledge of faith gradually grew through intervals of time, so it was fitting that sacraments then be obscure; now, because truth has come into the light, they are manifest. For although circumcision and baptism are signs of the same grace that inwardly frees from sin, this is signified more clearly in baptism, which washes the whole body, than in circumcision, which removed only the skin of one part.

Therefore from the beginning of the world, both in the time of natural law and in the time of written law, there were sacramental remedies against both original and actual sins. At first there were sacrifices, such as the offering of Abel, Noah, and the other faithful. Later there were not only sacrifices, but circumcision also, which was commanded in the time of Abraham. Gregory, in the *Moralia*: “What baptismal water accomplishes among us, among the ancients either faith alone accomplished for infants, or the efficacy of sacrifice for adults, or the mystery of circumcision for those who came from Abraham’s stock.” But if sacrifices were offered for infants, how can Gregory’s statement, “faith alone for infants,” be true? It may be answered that by “alone” sacrifices are not excluded; rather, “faith alone” means bare faith, then veiled in mystery, in infants—that is, in those to whom no revelation had been made of the future Incarnation [Col. 0119B]. For adults there was the efficacy of sacrifice, because the perfect, to whom the mystery of the Incarnation had been revealed, understood the efficacy of sacrifices—namely, what those sacrifices signified.

Circumcision, commanded to Abraham, was performed on the eighth day and with stone knives. It was rightly performed in the flesh of the foreskin because it was instituted as a remedy against original sin, which we contract from our parents, having been begotten in concupiscence, which exercises greater dominion in that member. Circumcision of the flesh signified circumcision of the mind, because the soul is cleansed from vices. It was performed on the eighth day because resurrection is signified by the eighth day, which will occur after this life that turns through seven days; and there will be perfect circumcision when the flesh is freed from the bondage of corruption [Col. 0119C].

Therefore the thing signified by that sacrament was twofold: circumcision from sins in the soul, and circumcision from sin and every punishment of sin, which will occur in the resurrection, in both soul and body. It is thus clear that there are three circumcisions. The first is the sacrament, and the two others are the things signified by that sacrament. The stone knives signified Christ. Hence the Apostle: “The Rock was Christ” (John 1); namely, he who takes away the sins of the world (1 Cor. 10).

With regard to women, it is asked what remedy they had against original sin. The answer is: faith, offerings, and sacrifices. It is also customary to ask concerning infants who died before the eighth day: what remedy did they have, or were they damned? Bede seems to say that they were damned, saying: “He who now cries terribly and salutarily through the Gospel, ‘Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God’ (John 3), himself long ago cried through his Law: ‘The male whose foreskin has not been circumcised shall perish, that soul from among its people, because he has made my covenant void’” (Gen. 17). But it seems better to leave this to God’s judgment than rashly to determine anything.

It is asked what difference there is between baptism and circumcision as regards efficacy. Bede: “Circumcision under the Law rendered against the wound of original sin the same aid of saving remedy which baptism is now accustomed to render in the time of revealed grace, except that they could not yet enter through the gate of the heavenly kingdom; nevertheless, after death, comforted in blessed rest in Abraham’s bosom, they awaited with happy hope the entrance of heavenly peace” [Col. 0120A].

## Chapter II. On the sacraments of the Law

Having stated what remedies against sins existed before the Law, it remains to see what was added by the Law itself. The following matters concerning it must be considered: why it was given, to whom, when, and where. The written Law was given in order to restore the natural law and revive those things which had been abolished through sin, and in order to prepare an untrained people for future truth through the figures of the Law. It accomplishes the first through the natural Ten Commandments; the second through figurative matters, such as the Paschal lamb and similar things.

To whom was it given? To Abraham’s seed, that is, to the twelve tribes descended from the twelve sons of Israel. Here one may ask: Why to these alone [Col. 0120B]? It may be answered that it was given to one people rather than all because it was set forth as a figure. Hence the Apostle: “All things happened to them in a figure” (1 Cor. 10). And it was sufficient to show in one people that which was presented as a figure and example. But the new Law is commanded by God to all; it is not a figure, but the reality itself of the figure.

And since among that people there were some perfect, some middling, and some utterly wicked, it was given to the perfect as a sign, as circumcision was to Abraham; to the middling as a pedagogue, to teach what was to be done, forbid what was to be avoided, and correct faults by punishment; to the utterly wicked it was given by the angry judge as punishment, “that he who is filthy may be filthy still” (Apoc. 22). Conversely, it was provided for the good by the compassionate Father: “that he who is righteous may be made more righteous” (ibid.) [Col. 0120C].

When was the Law given? On the fiftieth day after the departure from Egypt and the immolation of the Paschal lamb. So too the new Law was given to the Apostles—that is, the Holy Spirit writing in their hearts—on the fiftieth day after the immolation of the true Lamb, Jesus Christ. Where? On Mount Sinai, just as this signifies the discourse containing perfection which Christ delivers on the mountain.

Both the Old and the New Testament contain three things: promises, sacraments, and precepts. The promises of the Old are temporal goods—whence it is called Old—in which, nevertheless, eternal goods were prefigured, though obscurely. The promises of the New are eternal blessedness. The sacraments of the former are circumcision, which was also before the Law, and the observance of the Sabbath. There were also many sacrifices, such as that of the Paschal lamb and the like, which were added in the Law though they had not existed before. Through them future truth was shown more clearly than previously, though still hidden. The sacraments of the New are baptism, etc. God wished brute animals to be sacrificed to him in order to exercise the people in his worship and to remove them from idolatry, lest they sacrifice such animals to demons [Col. 0120D].

## Chapter III. On the precepts of the first tablet

It remains now to speak of the precepts. The precepts include natural and figurative matters. The natural are called those ten which flow from natural law; they were not begun in the written Law but renewed, because they had been erased through sin. These are the Ten Commandments, also called moral commandments; they were not terminated in the new Law, but rather fulfilled more perfectly. Figurative precepts were given for a time to prefigure future truth; they were set forth beforehand by God and came to an end when truth fulfilled them [Col. 0121A].

In those Ten Commandments, love of God and neighbor is commanded. The three on the first tablet concern love of God; the other seven on the second tablet concern love of neighbor. The first commandment of the first tablet is this: “The Lord your God is one God; you shall worship him and serve him alone” (Deut. 6; Matt. 4). From this it must be understood that one sort of service is to be rendered to God alone, which in Greek is called *latria*; and another may be rendered also to human beings, which in Greek is called *dulia*. We ought also to render reverence to human beings, as the Apostle commands, but not as to God. Hence: “I will give my honor to no one” (Isa. 42).

This honor is that reverence which we render to God alone: to lay the whole mind beneath him through humility and devotion, and to believe him to be the beginning and end of every good. In this manner God alone is to be worshipped. And this service, as we said, is called *latria* among the Greeks. Hence idolaters are called those who attribute this worship to a creature, “serving the creature rather than the Creator”: namely, attributing to an idol what belongs to God. Of the idol the Apostle says that it is nothing: “An idol is nothing in the world” (1 Cor. 8). This was not said of its material, such as stone or wood, for these are creatures of God; rather, it seems to have been said of its form. For that is called a form, and that properly is called an idol, upon which some form is impressed so that it may be worshipped as God; this form is not God’s work but the work of a human being imitating God [Col. 0121C], and in this respect it is nothing.

For whatever exists is either God’s work or the work of a human being imitating God. Thus the idol is nothing—that is, that for which it is called an idol. Or it is said as though one were to say: “A corporeal angel is nothing.” It does not deny that an angel exists, nor a body; but it denies that one thing exists from those two. Thus whoever says, “An idol is nothing,” denies that there is such a thing as what they supposed the idol to be: namely, one person composed of that image and the spirit presiding over it, just as one human being is composed of body and soul. For they thought that the idol lived and could speak, as a person composed of the image and the spirit presiding over that image; and such a thing is nothing.

The second commandment is: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Exod. 20) [Col. 0121D]. And just as the first commandment pertains to the Father, so this one pertains to the Son. He takes the name of God in vain who believes the Son of God to be merely a human being. He takes it in vain who does not worship him, both because he himself was made by him and because he himself was redeemed by him. Hence he himself said: “Do you believe in God? Believe also in me” (John 14). Thus we understand that he is to be worshipped by us not only in the divinity by which he created, but also in the humanity by which he redeemed. Hence the Prophet: “Worship his footstool, because it is holy” (Ps. 98). For whoever thus worships the humanity of Christ Jesus—that is, him who redeemed in humanity—worships not a creature but the Creator.

The third pertains to the Holy Spirit: “Observe the Sabbath day” (Exod. 20), that is, await rest through God’s goodness, that is, through the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter IV. On the first four precepts of the second tablet

[Col. 0122A]

On the second tablet, the first commandment concerns the carnal father, just as the first of the first tablet concerns the heavenly Father. It is this: “Honor your father and your mother, that you may be long-lived upon the earth” (Exod. 20). Honor them in matters not contrary to the supreme God, by obeying them and helping them in their needs as far as you can. “That you may be long-lived upon the earth,” namely, the land of the living.

The second commandment is: “You shall not kill” (ibid.). Homicide is committed in these ways: by hand, by tongue, and by consent. For the Jews, although they did not kill Christ with their hands, nevertheless killed him with their tongues. Many are also murderers by the consent of their will. Hence: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” [Col. 0122B] (1 John 3). A judge may kill, and if he does so from zeal for justice he does not commit homicide.

The third commandment: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20). There is a twofold fornication: spiritual, concerning which it is said, “You have destroyed all who fornicate away from you” (Ps. 72); and bodily, which is under discussion here. In the Gospel Christ prohibits every unlawful desire, saying: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5). For these commandments were begun in the Law and brought to completion in the Gospel.

The fourth commandment is: “You shall not commit theft” (Exod. 20). Under theft is included sacrilege, which is to take either a sacred thing from a sacred place, a non-sacred thing from a sacred place, or a sacred thing from a non-sacred place. Sacred is called whatever is assigned to divine worship, whether it is a temple or a thing belonging to the temple [Col. 0122C]. Robbery also is included under theft. For he who prohibited theft did not permit robbery. Augustine says concerning it: “So long as the thing for which sin was committed is not restored, repentance is not performed but feigned.” Usury is included under robbery. Jerome: “There is no difference between seeking usury, defrauding, and robbing: lend to your brother and receive what you gave, and seek nothing beyond it.” Augustine: “Usury is to receive more than one gives.” What the children of Israel did to the Egyptians was not theft, because they did it by a familiar command. For if he who makes the law commands otherwise, the person who obeys him does not transgress the law.

## Chapter V. On the fifth precept of the second tablet

[Col. 0122D]

The fifth commandment is: “You shall not bear false witness” (Exod. 20). Here perjury is forbidden; but since every perjury is a lie, it must be said what a lie is, and that a lie is perjury. Augustine: “To lie is to speak contrary to what one feels in one’s mind.” An objection is raised concerning Jacob, who said to his father, “I am Esau” (Gen. 27), at his mother’s advice—something he said against his conscience, for he truly knew that he was not Esau. Augustine nevertheless says: “What Jacob did at his mother’s urging, so that he might seem to deceive his father, if carefully considered, is not a lie but a mystery.”

Likewise, an objection is raised concerning Joseph, who said to his brothers, “By the life of Pharaoh, you are spies” (Gen. 42), and said that he divined by means of the cup—something which was nevertheless not true [Col. 0123A]. Some say that this was a lie, but not the sort of lie that is sin. For they say that not every lie is sin, but only that which is spoken with the intention of deceiving. Jacob’s intention, however, was to obey his mother. Similarly, Joseph did not intend to deceive; rather, he did not wish to reveal himself so quickly. But Augustine does not seem to intend this when he says that one must not lie even for someone’s life. It therefore seems better to say that they did not lie, but said these things by a special command, just as the Hebrews are excused from theft by a special command. For since Jacob’s mother commanded this to him through the Holy Spirit, by obeying his mother he obeyed the Holy Spirit.

Likewise, an objection is raised: if whatever is said contrary to what is from the Holy Spirit is a lie [Col. 0123B], then when a Jew says against his conscience, “Christ is true God and true man,” it would be a lie; yet no one would dare say that this is a lie. To this it may be said that what he says is true, not a lie; and yet he himself lies—just as a righteous person who thinks he is speaking truth, while saying something false, does not lie. Augustine in the *Enchiridion*: “Certainly no one is to be judged to lie when he says what is false while thinking it true; for, so far as lies within him, he does not deceive, but is himself deceived. On the contrary, he rather lies who says what is true while thinking it false.”

Likewise Augustine: “A lie is a false signification by speech with the intention of deceiving.” This should be understood as “with an intention of deceiving” which is either present then or arises afterward [Col. 0123C]. For sometimes, when someone makes a promise, he does not then have the will to deceive.

Likewise Augustine: “When you lie on grounds of humility, if before lying you were not a sinner, you become guilty through the lie. For if you call yourself a sinner and do not believe it to be so, truth is not in you.”

Augustine also says that one must not lie for another’s safety. It is indeed permitted to conceal the truth, so as not to betray someone being sought for execution; but one ought not to deny the truth. An objection is raised against this: if the intention is good, the action is good; but someone who denies that he has seen a man, though he has seen him, acts with a good intention in order to free him from death. To this it may be said that an intention which is not according to knowledge must not be called good, even if it is pious. For a good intention must be both pious and right; since mercy without justice is not a virtue [Col. 0123D].

Some nevertheless say that this is not a sin, and that Augustine said this as a warning, in order to deter people from lying. An objection is raised from the midwives and Rahab, who were rewarded for such a lie. But, as Augustine says: “They were rewarded not for the lie but for their piety.” For two things are considered in lies of this sort: the disposition of piety for whose sake they are told, and the lie itself. The disposition is rewarded, not the lie. Jocular lies and ironies are not lies.

Now it must be considered what perjury is. Perjury is a lie confirmed by an oath. If someone happens to swear that he will do evil to another, it is better to break the oath than to fulfil it. Yet he ought to repent because he swore rashly [Col. 0124A].

Isidore: “An oath by which evil is carelessly promised is not to be kept. For example, if someone promises an adulteress his pledged faith that he will remain with her forever: it is more tolerable not to fulfil the oath than to remain in fornication.”

Bede: “Thus David swore by the Lord to kill the foolish man Nabal; but at the first intercession of the prudent woman Abigail, he withdrew his threats, recalled his sword to its sheath, and did not regret that he had incurred any guilt by such perjury” (1 Sam. 25).

Likewise Isidore says: “He who swears by an artifice of words—God, who is the examiner of thoughts, so regards it as the person to whom the oath is made understands it.” This should be explained thus: “by an artifice of words,” that is, one who swears in order to defraud another; God then truly regards it as the person who is unjustly deceived understands it [Col. 0124B]. But if, in order to avoid danger—not in order to injure his neighbor, but to free himself or another from necessity—someone tells the truth, and yet by that truth conceals something else which, if disclosed, would be dangerous, he does not sin. Thus Abraham, saying of Sarah, “She is my sister” (Gen. 20), did not lie, since she was his sister—that is, his kinswoman; and if he had sworn this, he would not have sinned.

## CHAPTER VI. On the sixth and seventh commandments of the second table

The sixth commandment: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Exod. 20). The seventh: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (ibid.).

Here an objection is raised from the fact that the Lord, in the Gospel, when he supplemented the commandment “You shall not commit adultery” (ibid.), says: “It was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you: Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her” (Matt. 5) [Col. 0124C]. But this was not an addition, since the same thing is forbidden in the Law, as in this commandment: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” For desire seems to be forbidden here as there.

To this it may be said that this commandment, truly understood, forbids both the deed and the will; and those who, by understanding it in this way, refrained from evil in deed and will were to be called not people of the Old Testament but of the New. The Law, so understood by them, was not old but new. Accordingly, no addition was made in the Gospel; rather, what had been hidden there was explained.

But although the Law, rightly understood—not according to the letter but according to the spirit—prohibited both, carnal people understood only one thing: namely, that the deed was forbidden, and this according to the letter of the Law. Hence: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3). In this respect, then, an addition was made.

Thus in this commandment, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property,” both the will and the act are forbidden. The act is forbidden according to the sound of the letter: namely, do not do outwardly that by which you may seem to covet. The will is forbidden when this commandment is understood spiritually. Hence Augustine also says: “This seems to distinguish the Old from the New Testament: there the act is forbidden; in the New, both the will and the act.” Augustine takes “Old Testament” to mean the letter, not the spirit, just as the Apostle does everywhere.

## CHAPTER VII. On love of neighbor

[Col. 0125A]

In these seven commandments love of neighbor is contained. Hence in Leviticus: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19): that is, in those things in which you love yourself, namely, in possessing eternal goods. Or thus: “as yourself,” that is, in those things in which you wish to be loved, namely, in supplying necessities. Nor should “as yourself” be understood as meaning “to the same degree as yourself,” as some explain it.

It is asked whether we ought to love all equally, or one more than another. Some say that an equal effect of charity ought to be bestowed upon all; but an order must be observed in works of charity. Hence Paul: “Let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” (Gal. 6) [Col. 0125B]. And Augustine appears to intend this when he says: “All are to be loved equally; but since you cannot benefit all, you must especially provide for those who, by opportunity of place and time or by any other circumstance, are more closely joined to us.”

Augustine’s statement, “All are to be loved equally,” may be explained thus: all—that is, nature in all persons—is to be loved equally; or we ought equally to love the salvation of all. For if anyone loves the salvation of his father or friend more than that of others, this is not from charity but from carnal affection, which is natural. Nor is it blameworthy, but this is not perfection.

Some object: whom God loves more, we too ought to love more. Therefore we ought to love a good and just person more than another. Thus it is also proved that we ought to love others more than ourselves [Col. 0125C], since we know them to be better than ourselves and more loved by God. To this it is said that two things are to be loved in a human being: nature and virtue. Nature is to be loved equally; virtue more or less, according as it is greater or lesser. And so we ought to love this person’s good more than that person’s, because it is greater; yet we ought not to love nature more or less, nor desire one person’s salvation more than another’s [Col. 0125C].

But it is objected that for the same reason I ought to love another’s good more than my own, because it is greater. This may readily be granted, but I do not thereby love it more than I love my own. Thus, if someone’s good garment pleases me more than my own less good one, nevertheless I would not wish his garment to belong to him more than I would wish mine to belong to me. And if one of us had to go without, I would rather that he lack his than that I lack mine.

So it is said here that, although his good is greater than mine, if one of us had to go without it, I would rather that he lack his good than that I be deprived of mine; nor would I in any respect act contrary to perfection, even if I were as perfect as Paul was [Col. 0126A]. In this, too, an order of charity may be considered: we ought to love God above all things, namely, with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind (Matt. 22); after him, ourselves; and in the third place, others. Hence: “You shall love your neighbor,” etc. For unless one first loves oneself, how can one love others as oneself?

## CHAPTER VIII. On the love of God

Charity is honorable love directed to the end to which it ought to be directed. Love is a good will toward another for that person’s own sake. Hence Cicero: “Friendship is a will toward someone for good things, for the sake of the one whom one loves.”

It is asked concerning the love which God has toward us whether he loves all equally. To answer this, we must see what it means to say, “God loves this person”: namely, God approves his works. In this sense it can be said that God loves one more than another [Col. 0126B]. It may also be said of the same person that God loves him more now than formerly; that is, God approves his works more than before. Or, “he loves him more” means that he pours his grace into him more abundantly than before. For God is said to love the person whom he makes to love and know himself, by pouring his grace into him.

The love of God is also called divine election itself; the hatred of God, reprobation itself: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1). And elsewhere: “He chose us before the foundation of the world in charity” (Eph. 1). And in another place: “Because of his exceeding charity with which God loved us, even when we were dead in our sins, he made us alive together in Christ” (Eph. 2) [Col. 0126C].

In this sense it may be said that he loves one more than another—that is, he has prepared a greater crown for him. But in this sense it cannot be said that he loves the same person now more and now less. For from eternity he loved each person as much as he loves him now. He loved Paul as much even when he was wicked as he loves him now, though he did not love Paul’s wickedness. For all things are present to him; what was future in time concerning Paul was present with God, and he loved him as he would be—which with God was not future—and as he had from eternity chosen him in the present.

Augustine, in *On the Trinity*: “Far be it that God should love anyone temporally, as though with a new love which was not previously in him; for with him past things have not passed away, and future things are already done. He loved all the saints before the foundation of the world, just as he predestined them. But when they are converted and come to him, then they are said to begin to be loved by him. And when he is said to be angry with the wicked and appeased toward the good, they are changed, not he” [Col. 0126D].

[Col. 0125] Here ends the fourth treatise, *On the Sacraments in General and the Divine Commandments*.

# FIFTH TREATISE. ON THE SACRAMENT OF BAPTISM

[Col. 0127]

## CHAPTERS

CHAPTER I. On baptism.—CHAPTER II. What is to be considered in baptism.—CHAPTER III. On the form of baptism.—CHAPTER IV. What the sacrament of baptism is.—CHAPTER V. On receiving baptism.—CHAPTER VI. Whether infants are saved without baptism.—CHAPTER VII. On the justification of adults before receiving baptism.—CHAPTER VIII. Who may baptize.—CHAPTER IX. Whether there is baptism when the words are pronounced incorrectly.—CHAPTER X. On the matter of baptism.—CHAPTER XI. On the response of godparents.—CHAPTER XII. Whether someone can be baptized in his mother’s womb.—CHAPTER XIII. On catechism and exorcism.

## CHAPTER I. On baptism

[Col. 0127A]

After the Law of Moses came the Law of the Gospel, whose sacraments must now be discussed; first, baptism, which is first among the sacraments of the New Testament.

John foretold Christ’s baptism by his own baptism, which was performed with water alone and not with the Spirit. Hence he himself says: “I baptize in water unto repentance” (Matt. 3). For he washed bodies only; he did not take away sins. What use, then, was it? It was to prepare for Christ’s baptism, just as catechism precedes baptism.

His statement that he baptizes “unto repentance” may be explained thus: that is, while teaching repentance. For he baptized penitents. And so, although that baptism bestowed no remission upon them, nevertheless through the repentance and circumcision which they possessed they could still immediately be saved [Col. 0127B].

Or it may be explained thus: he baptized “unto repentance,” that is, as a sign of repentance. For John’s baptism was a seal of repentance, because as water washes bodies, so souls are cleansed by repentance. Thus, by John’s baptism the sacrament of the New Testament began to be indicated. Hence: “The Law and the prophets were until John” (Matt. 11). This does not mean that the Law ended in John, since the legal observances still remained in force, but because their abolition there began to be shown. For if the legal observances had ended before the Passion, Christ would not then have celebrated the Passover lamb with his disciples.

If it is asked with what words John administered baptism, we have no certain authoritative account. Some nevertheless say that it was in the name of the One to come [Col. 0127C]. Again, if it is asked why it did not confer remission of sins: it is because it was not instituted for that purpose, but to prepare the way for Christ’s baptism. For sacraments have their power and efficacy from their institution.

While John was baptizing, Christ came to him to be baptized by him in the Jordan; not because he himself, being without sin, had need of it, but in order to sanctify the waters. For there the water received that efficacy: that whoever afterward was immersed in it with the name of the Trinity invoked would obtain remission. Then Christ’s baptism was instituted, in which the whole Trinity effects remission, whose presence was displayed there: the Spirit in the dove, the Son in the man, the Father in the voice [Col. 0128A].

Of those who had been baptized by John, some were baptized again with Christ’s baptism. Others were not baptized afterward; but, after hands had been laid upon them, they received the Holy Spirit. Yet it is usually asked why the former were baptized again and not the latter. Some say that the former presumed upon John’s baptism, whereas the latter did not. Jerome, in the letter *On the Husband of One Wife*, says: “Because those who had received John’s baptism did not know the Holy Spirit, they were baptized again, lest anyone should think that waters without the Holy Spirit could suffice either for Gentiles or for Jews.”

## CHAPTER II. What is to be considered in baptism

In the sacrament of baptism, the following are to be considered: its institution, the cause of its institution, the form of baptism, what is the sacrament, and what is the reality of the sacrament. The institution, as we have said, occurred when Christ came for baptism [Col. 0128B]. The cause of its institution was that in baptism a human being might rise again from sins. For it is a remedy against sins, both original and actual.

But since among the ancients circumcision and the other legal sacraments effected the same as baptism and the other sacraments among us, it may be asked why those ceased and these succeeded them. Hence the Apostle gives a general solution when he says: “All these things happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. 10). Therefore, once truth arrived, the figures ceased.

They also had to cease in order that two peoples might be joined into one. For the Gentiles recoiled from Jewish ceremonies; and therefore, in order that Jews and Gentiles might become one people, it was necessary to remove the cause of enmity. This the Apostle makes clear when he says: “Breaking down the middle wall, the enmities, abolishing by decrees the law of commandments” (Eph. 2) [Col. 0128C].

The sacrament of circumcision was also imperfect, because it suited men alone. But he who came to fulfil the Law wished for a perfect sacrament; and he who bore our pains wished to free us from such pain and to confer the very gentle sacrament of baptism, from which no one would recoil.

It is usually asked whether circumcision lost its standing from the time baptism was instituted. To this it may be said that it had lost its standing among those to whom this newness of the sacraments had been announced, believed, and received; among others it still retained its standing and conferred remission upon them until the time when Truth itself began through the Apostles to be preached and made manifest everywhere—namely, when it was said to them: “Preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16), which was after the Resurrection.

Thus an objection is raised that those two sacraments, circumcision and baptism, since they conferred the same thing, ought not to have held standing at the same time. It may be said that they did not hold standing at the same time with respect to the same persons [Col. 0129A].

## CHAPTER III. On the form of baptism

Christ handed down the form of this sacrament when he said: “Go, teach, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). And the sacrament must be administered in this form.

Nevertheless, it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that the Apostles baptized in the name of Christ (Acts 19) [Col. 0129B]; in which, as Ambrose says, the whole Trinity is understood. For in this name is understood he who was anointed, namely the Son; he by whom he was anointed, namely the Father; and he through whom he was anointed, namely the Holy Spirit.

Ambrose, in *On the Holy Spirit*: “For when it is said ‘in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,’ the mystery has been fulfilled through the unity of the name; nor is the Spirit separated from Christ’s baptism. For if you say Christ, you designate both God the Father, by whom the Son was anointed; the Son himself, who was anointed; and the Spirit, by whom he was anointed. For it is written: ‘God anointed this Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit’” (ibid.).

From this some wish to maintain that if someone is baptized in the name of the Father alone, or in the name of the Son alone—provided he does not intend to introduce error—he is baptized and should not be rebaptized. This is not certain to us by authority; but from Ambrose’s authority cited above, by analogy, they wish to affirm this also [Col. 0129C].

## CHAPTER IV. What the sacrament of baptism is

Now it must be considered what the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament are in the sacrament of baptism. For in every sacrament these two things must be considered. Here the sacrament may be called the consecrated water itself.

Augustine, *On Catechism*: “You ought to know why the power of that water benefits both soul and body. For not every water cleanses; this water is sanctified by the consecration of the word. Take away the word, and what is water but water? The word comes to the element, and it becomes a sacrament.”

The reality of this sacrament is inward washing. The threefold immersion itself is also called a sacrament, either of the Trinity or of the three-day burial. And many other sacramental signs occur in this sacrament, such as breathing upon the candidate and the invocation of the Trinity, which are parts of this sacrament. Each of these is not called the sacrament of baptism, but is contained within it.

Baptism is immersion performed with the invocation of the Trinity. The other things which precede serve for ornament and reverence, but the power of the sacrament itself is not in them. For *baptism* is interpreted as “anointing.” Baptism may also be called the consecrated element itself, but not so properly [Col. 0129D].

At this point it must be said that immersion ought to be performed three times. Augustine: “After you promised that you would believe, we immersed your heads three times in the sacred font; this order of baptism is celebrated with a twofold signification of mystery [Col. 0130A]. For you were rightly immersed three times, since you received baptism in the name of the Trinity. You were rightly immersed three times, since you received baptism in the name of Jesus Christ, who rose from the dead on the third day. For that threefold immersion expresses the type of the Lord’s burial, through which you were buried together with Christ in baptism.”

Likewise Gregory, to Bishop Leander, *On the Threefold Immersion in Baptism*: “Nothing truer can be answered than what you yourselves have perceived: where faith is one, a differing custom does not harm the Church. Since there is one substance in three subsistences, it cannot in any way be blameworthy to dip an infant in baptism either three times or once; for in three immersions the Trinity of persons may be signified, and in one the unity of divinity.”

Behold, from this authority it is permissible to immerse only once; nevertheless, it seems to us that the Church’s custom should be followed rather.

Haimo, on the Epistle to the Romans: “Cyprian was abundant in his own understanding, because he immersed infants only once in baptism. For what he understood, he diligently fulfilled by abounding in good works, although he sinned in this unknowingly. But because he abounded in good works, after being corrected by God he abounded in a higher understanding, immersing them three times” [Col. 0130B].

## CHAPTER V. On receiving baptism

Next it remains to see that some receive both the sacrament and its reality; others the sacrament but not its reality; others the reality but not the sacrament.

Infants, wherever and by whomever they are baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, receive both the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament [Col. 0130C]; in their case personal faith is not required. Adults likewise, if they approach with personal faith, have both the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament. In their case personal faith is required, without which they obtain no remission.

Those receive the sacrament but not its reality who approach insincerely, or without faith and with an unrepentant heart. Augustine: “Everyone who has now become the master of his own will, when he approaches the sacrament of the faithful, cannot begin a new life unless he repents of his old life. When infants are baptized, they alone are exempt from this repentance, since they cannot yet use free choice.”

Peter likewise speaks thus to the Jews in the Acts of the Apostles: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized” (Acts 2).

But against the foregoing is raised what Ambrose says on the passage: “The gifts and calling of God are without repentance” (Rom. 11) [Col. 0130D]. God’s grace in baptism does not require groaning or lamentation; it freely forgives all things. But this is said of outward groaning; for even if outward repentance is lacking, all things are nonetheless forgiven.

But Gregory’s statement that a penance of forty days should be imposed is done as a test, in order that it may be known with what disposition they seek baptism, since sometimes they seek baptism deceptively.

Again, an objection is raised from Augustine, book 5, *On the One Baptism*: “The grace of baptism is not prevented from forgiving all sins even if fraternal hatred persists in the mind of the person to whom they are forgiven. It is loosed the day before, and whatever was committed earlier is loosed; it is also loosed if committed in the momentary hour before baptism and in baptism itself [Col. 0131A]. But thereafter he immediately begins to be guilty not only of subsequent days, but also of former days, hours, and moments, as all the things that were forgiven return.”

But he did not say this according to its proper sense, since the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you do not forgive people their sins from your heart, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Mark 2).
