Augustine also says elsewhere: “Baptism then begins to avail for salvation when that pretense has departed through a truthful confession.”

An objection is raised from the Apostle: “All of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3). But we say that those are baptized in Christ who are baptized in conformity to Christ, in order that they may die to the oldness of sin, just as in Christ the oldness of sin was crucified through death [Col. 0131B].

Augustine resolves this differently, saying: “People put on Christ sometimes as far as receiving the sacrament, sometimes as far as the sanctification of life; and the former can be common to both good and evil persons.”

Those who have the reality but not the sacrament are martyrs; martyrdom itself is called baptism because it fulfils the place of baptism. An objection is raised from what is read in the Gospel: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3). But Scripture customarily determines preceding statements by subsequent ones. For elsewhere it says: “Whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it” (Matt. 10). Likewise: “Whoever confesses me before people, I too will confess before my Father” (ibid.).

Concerning those who have faith in Christ but, through an emergency, cannot receive the sacraments, it is asked whether they are saved or not. Authority and reason seem to establish that they are saved. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, shall live” (John 2) [Col. 0131C]. And elsewhere: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3).

But the objection is raised: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” Unless this were determined by what follows, it would be false that martyrs are saved without baptism.

Augustine, book 4 of *On the One Baptism*, says that suffering sometimes fulfils the place of baptism, as in that thief to whom, though unbaptized, it was said: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23). Blessed Cyprian advanced no slight evidence: “Considering this again and again, I find that not only sufferings for Christ’s name can supply what is lacking from baptism, but also faith and conversion of heart, if in the straits of time it is not possible to obtain help for the celebration of the mystery of baptism. For that thief was not crucified for Christ’s name but for his crimes. Nor did he suffer because he believed; rather, while suffering he believed. How greatly baptism without the visible sacrament avails is shown in that thief by the Apostle’s saying: ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation’” (Rom. 10).

But then the mystery of baptism is invisibly fulfilled when not contempt for religion but an emergency excludes it [Col. 0132A].

Some say that Augustine retracted this; but that is false. For he did not retract the proposition, but the example he had introduced concerning the thief. Augustine in the *Retractations*: “When I said that suffering can take the place of baptism, I gave an insufficiently suitable example in that thief; for it is uncertain whether he had not been baptized, and it is more credible that he had been baptized.”

Ambrose, *On Valentinian*: “My heart grieves, and I shall use a prophetic example, because I have lost one whom I was about to regenerate; yet he did not lose the grace which he requested.”

[Col. 0132B]

These authorities make clear that faith without the sacrament is sufficient for those who have no time, and reason also proves this. For just as baptism without personal faith avails infants who cannot have faith, so faith ought to avail those who cannot have the sacrament. Again, no one will deny that faith and charity can be possessed before baptism; for many approach baptism with faith and charity. Nor will anyone deny that they can then die; and if they died then, when they possess faith and charity, it is certain that they would not be damned. For no one is damned in charity.

But some say that it cannot happen that someone possesses faith and charity and dies without baptism. For, they say, God would not permit them to die without baptism. But, in my view, since they are not God’s advisers, it is foolish and rash for them to affirm this.

Again, those who say this—namely, that no one is saved without baptism or martyrdom—raise authorities against us [Col. 0132C]. Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*: “From the time when the Savior said, ‘Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God,’ no one can receive either the kingdom of heaven or eternal life without the sacrament of baptism, except those who in the Catholic Church shed their blood without baptism.”

Likewise, from the sayings of Bishop Anselm: “Although a catechumen dies in good works, we do not believe that he has life, unless the sacrament is completed by martyrdom alone.”

But these and similar statements are said concerning those who despise baptism. For if someone despises the sacrament of baptism, the other things do not suffice.

## CHAPTER VI. Whether infants are saved without baptism

[Col. 0132D]

It is asked concerning infants who die without baptism, not from contempt for religion but because in some emergency help cannot be brought to them: are they saved? It is said in reply that they are not saved, because they do not have faith, which in adults, as we have said, supplies the place of baptism when there is no contempt for religion. Augustine shows in many places that they are not saved. Yet, as he says in the *Enchiridion*, the mildest punishment of all will be theirs who have added no sin beyond original sin.

Here it is usually asked whether, if a city were captured by pagans and children were killed, they would be saved or not, since they would be killed for Christ, whose worshippers their parents are. We have no settled determination on this. It seems, nevertheless, that the mercy which delivered the little children killed by Herod would not despise these also, if they were killed for that reason: because they would be believed to be going to believe in Christ by those who killed them [Col. 0133A]. But since we have no authority concerning this, let us leave it to divine judgment.

## CHAPTER VII. On the justification of adults before receiving baptism

Concerning adults who approach baptism with faith, love, and a contrite heart, it is asked whether they are justified before baptism. This authority seems to affirm it: “In whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall live” (Ezek. 8). Likewise: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness” (Rom. 10). And elsewhere: “The righteous shall live by faith” (Rom. 1). From this, when a person has faith and love, he has the indwelling Spirit.

But it is written in the Book of Wisdom: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will not dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1) [Col. 0133B]. Hence it seems that he is already cleansed from sins. But if by faith and true contrition of heart he is already released from sins, what is afterward remitted to him in baptism? For it seems that nothing is remitted in baptism, since his sins were forgiven beforehand.

To this it may be said that, although the person of whom we speak is already righteous because he has no will to sin and grieves for past sins, nevertheless he is not yet justified, since he is still held by the debt of sin. For when the wound has already been shown to the physician by confession of heart, it remains to receive his medicine. But who does not know that sacraments are medicines? Hence: “He heals the broken in heart and binds up their wounds” (Ps. 146). Nor is it enough to confess the wound to the physician if his medicine is despised [Col. 0133C].

Therefore it is established that he must still receive the medicine of the sacrament for his sins. He has not yet been released from the debt of sin, and consequently has not been fully justified from sin while still held by its debt. But after receiving the sacrament he is fully cleansed; and if he then died, he would go to glory without delay.

If it is objected that no sin goes unpunished, we say that contrition of heart itself, death itself, and even the shame which he suffers while being baptized naked do not leave sin unpunished.

But if someone has faith with love, wishes to be baptized, and cannot because an emergency intervenes, we believe that through God’s ineffable mercy he is released from the aforementioned debt. For so long as he can make payment, he is bound unless he does so; but when he can no longer do so and yet wishes to, God does not impute it to him [Col. 0133D]. For God has not bound his power to the sacraments; and although he has decreed to give salvation through the sacraments, he can nevertheless both give salvation without them and does give it.

## CHAPTER VIII. Who may baptize
It must now be said to whom it has been granted or is lawful to administer baptism. It is established that baptism has been entrusted to priests alone, and that its ministry may not lawfully be performed even by deacons without a presbyter or bishop, unless, when these are far away, the final necessity of illness compels it; this is often permitted to lay believers, according to the statements of Bishop Isidore. The Roman pontiff says: “It is not the man who baptizes who judges, but the Spirit of God supplies the grace of baptism, [Col. 0134A] even if the one who baptizes is a pagan.”

Concerning those baptized by women, the question is asked whether they ought to be rebaptized. Some say that they must be rebaptized, on the authority of the Fourth Council of Carthage: “Let a woman not presume to baptize.” But it is not presumption when necessity compels it. Isidore likewise says: “Those who are baptized by women are not to be rebaptized.”

Concerning those baptized by heretics, likewise, the question is asked whether they should be rebaptized. Bede: “Whether a heretic, schismatic, or criminal person baptizes in the confession of the holy Trinity, one who has been baptized by good Catholics may not be rebaptized, lest the confession or invocation of so great a name appear to be annulled.” Augustine, in his response to Orosius’s question: “Although the baptism of heretics is one baptism—namely, of those [Col. 0134B] who baptize in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit in the Catholic Church—nevertheless those baptized outside the Church do not receive baptism unto salvation but unto destruction, having the form of the sacrament while denying its power. Therefore the Church does not rebaptize them, because they were baptized in the name of the holy Trinity, which is indeed the form of the sacrament itself.”

Augustine, in the book *On Faith to Peter*: “If anyone, in any heresy or schism, has received the sacrament of baptism in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, he has received the sacrament intact; but he will not have salvation, which is the power of the sacrament, if he had that sacrament outside the Catholic Church.” Again Augustine, on John: “Baptism is such as is he in whose power it is given, [Col. 0134C] not such as is he through whose ministry it is given.” The same author: “The power of baptism passes to no one; but its ministry passes to good and bad persons. Let not the dove recoil from the ministry of the wicked, but look to the will of the Lord. What can an evil minister do to you, where the Lord is good? Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3). “If the minister is proud, he is counted with the devil; but Christ’s gift is not contaminated. What flows through him is pure; what passes through him is clear.” Again: “Water passes through a stone channel to the garden-beds. In the stone channel it produces nothing, but the garden yields many fruits.”

Again we say: “The ministers of so great a Judge ought to be righteous. Let the ministers be righteous if they wish; but if those who sit in Moses’ seat are unwilling to be [Col. 0134D] righteous, my master has made me secure, concerning whom his Spirit says: ‘This is he who baptizes’” (John 1). In accordance with the authorities stated above, we say without hesitation that, through whomever baptism is given, provided that the form of the sacrament has been observed—that is, that it is administered in the name of the holy Trinity—such persons are not to be rebaptized, because they possess the sacrament of baptism. But they do not possess the reality of the sacrament if they assent to the heretics’ error. Therefore, when they come to the Church, they are instructed in the faith and receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. The laying on of hands is sometimes performed with an anointing of chrism, and sometimes without chrism, by a prayer pronounced over the person.

Of those baptized by heretics without knowing that they are [Col. 0135A] heretics, and not consenting in any respect to their error, it may be said that they receive both the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament. Nevertheless, when they come to the Church, hands are laid upon them, to show that the error is detested. But those baptized by heretics not in the name of the Trinity must be rebaptized when they come to the Church; nor is this called repetition, because they had not previously received Christ’s baptism.

Cyprian, however, and certain others say that heretics cannot administer Christ’s baptism and that those baptized among heretics must be rebaptized. Cyprian: “Water must first be sanctified by a priest, so that through its baptism it may be able to wash away sins. But how can one sanctify water who is himself unclean, and in whom the Holy Spirit is not, [Col. 0135B] when the Lord says in the book of Numbers: ‘Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean’” (Num. 19)? “Who can give what he himself does not possess? Or how can one perform spiritual acts who has himself lost the Holy Spirit? And therefore the baptized person must be baptized and renewed.”

But Cyprian and the others said this either of heretics baptizing outside the form of the Church, who truly do not administer Christ’s baptism; or they said it from ignorance. Augustine seems to mean this in *On the One Baptism*, saying: “The most glorious martyr Cyprian, who was unwilling to recognize Christ’s baptism when administered among heretics or schismatics because he detested them too greatly, had merits so great, extending even to the triumph of martyrdom, that both that shadow was dispelled by the light of the charity in which he excelled, [Col. 0135C] and whatever he had needing purification was removed by the final sickle of his suffering. Nor are we better than Cyprian because we recognize the truth of baptism in the wickedness of heretics, any more than we are better than Peter because we do not compel the Gentiles to become Jews.”

## CHAPTER IX. Whether there is baptism when the words are pronounced incorrectly

The question is asked whether baptism occurs or not if someone pronounces those words incorrectly. Pope Zacharias to Boniface: “Your messengers reported to me that there was a priest in the same province who was wholly ignorant of the Latin language and, while baptizing, not knowing how to speak Latin, mutilated the language and said: ‘I baptize you in the name of the *Patria* (“Fatherland”), and the *Filia* (“Daughter”), and the Holy *Spiritus sancta* (“Holy [feminine] Spirit”)’;” and that because of this you considered rebaptizing them. But if the one who baptized, [Col. 0135D] introducing neither error nor heresy, but solely because of ignorance of Latin speech, had said to those baptized, while mangling the language, what we stated above, we cannot consent that they be baptized again.”

It is customarily asked concerning one who is immersed in sport or mimicry, though with commemoration of the Trinity, whether he must be rebaptized. Augustine decides nothing about this, but speaks thus: “If the whole thing is done playfully, theatrically, or in jest, whether baptism administered in that manner ought to be approved, I should judge that a divine oracle must be sought.” Yet it does not seem to the wise that baptism ought to be said to exist where there is no intention to baptize. Thus women, when they immerse children in a bath, invoke the name of the Trinity; but because they do not intend to baptize, [Col. 0136A] there is no baptism. For in every sacrament these two things are necessary: that the form of the sacrament be preserved and that there be an intention of celebrating it.

## CHAPTER X. On the matter of baptism

Why baptism is performed only in water: Haimo, on the Epistle to the Romans: “Someone asks why baptism is consecrated only in water and not sometimes in wine. Blessed Ambrose answers that it is done uniformly in water in order that it may be understood that, just as water washes away the dirt of the body or garment, so baptism, by cleansing, removes the stains of the soul and the filth of vices.” Augustine gives this reason: that no one might be excused by poverty, as could happen if it were performed with wine or oil; and that the material of baptism might be common and accessible to all. Or it is in water because water flowed from Christ’s side.

If there is doubt whether someone has been baptized, he must be baptized. For, as the saints say, that which is not known to have been done is not judged to have been repeated. But it is asked whether baptism administered a second time confers remission upon him. This must not be conceded; for if it did, baptism would have to be administered often. If a son is baptized by his mother because of necessity, must she be separated from her husband? Pope Deusdedit of Rome says that she must be separated. The decrees of others deny this, and we give them greater credence. For, as Christ says in the Gospel, a wife ought to be dismissed only on account of fornication (Matt. 19).

## CHAPTER XI. On the response of godparents

The question is asked in whose person the godparents’ response is made. For when the priest asks, “Do you wish to be baptized?” and the godparent answers, “I do,” it is certain that he does not answer in his own person. Again, when he asks, “Do you believe in God?” and the godparent answers, “I believe,” if he answered in the child’s person, this does not seem true, since the child does not yet believe. But if it is said in this sense, “I believe,” that is, “he will believe,” the response seems rash, since he is not certain of this.

Augustine says that the sacrament of faith is called “faith”; and in this sense it is true that the child believes—that is, receives the sacrament of faith. Augustine to Bishop Boniface: “Thus, although the little child does not yet possess that faith which consists in the will of believers, nevertheless the sacrament of faith already makes him a believer. For just as ‘he believes’ is answered, so they are called believers, [Col. 0136D] not by mentally assenting to the thing itself, but by receiving the sacrament of that thing.”

Since a person is freed from every sin in baptism, it is customary to ask why he is not also freed from sin’s penalty. Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*: “If people were freed from present punishment through baptism, they would regard that as the reward of baptism, rather than the eternal reward. Therefore, once the guilt of sin has been discharged, a certain temporal punishment remains, so that the life which will be free from all punishments may be sought more eagerly.”

## CHAPTER XII. Whether someone can be baptized in the mother’s womb

It is customarily asked whether anyone can be baptized while still in the mother’s womb. Isidore: “Those who are in their mothers’ [Col. 0137A] wombs cannot be baptized together with their mothers, because one who has not yet been born according to Adam cannot be born according to Christ. Nor can regeneration be spoken of in one for whom generation has not preceded.” Augustine to Dardanus: “No one can be born again before he has been born.”

But an objection is raised concerning John and Jeremiah, who were sanctified from the womb. For it is written of John in Luke’s Gospel: “And he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” (Luke 1). Again: “The child leaped in the womb” (ibid.). But how could he be full of the Holy Spirit unless he had been cleansed from sin? Thus it seems that he was born again before he was born, and was born according to Christ before he was born according to Adam.

Augustine, in the book to Dardanus: “If in that child the use of will and reason was accelerated to such a degree that, within the maternal [Col. 0137B] womb, he could already know and believe—whereas in other little children age must be awaited for this capacity—this is to be regarded among the miracles of divine power, not drawn into an example for human nature. For when God willed, even a beast of burden spoke.”

The same is said of Jeremiah: “Before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jer. 1). Yet that sanctification by which we are made the temple of God belongs only to those who have been born again: “Unless someone is born again, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3). A person is not born again unless he has first been born. Therefore, Jeremiah’s sanctification may suitably be understood according to predestination, just as the Gospel calls those not yet regenerated “children.” See that Augustine speaks uncertainly about this [Col. 0138A] and asserts nothing concerning it. For it could be that they were cleansed of original sin from the womb; but no rule for others should be drawn from what was performed in these persons by miracle. And this is more plausible. Or, even if they were not cleansed of original sin from the womb, they were nevertheless sanctified because the judgment of sanctification—that is, that they were predestined—appeared in them from the womb.

For Augustine says in the same book: “It was not said, ‘The child believed in the womb,’ but ‘he leaped.’ Nor did Elizabeth herself say, ‘He leaped in faith,’ but ‘he leaped in generation.’ And this sign could have been of so great a matter to be known by adults, not a matter known by the little child.”

## CHAPTER XIII. On catechesis and exorcism

Concerning those things that precede baptism, it must be considered what they confer, such as exorcism and catechesis. To exorcize is to adjure: “Come out of him, unclean spirit”; and to catechize is to instruct, concerning the Creed and the other rudiments of faith. The *symbolum* is called a “sign” or a “contribution”: a sign, because by it believers are distinguished from unbelievers; a contribution, because in it the apostles brought together the whole completeness of faith. For when they were about to depart from one another, they issued the Creed—that is, the compilation of the whole faith.

These things that precede baptism do not confer remission. What then are they good for? They diminish the devil’s power, as we also see in someone over whom the devil has less power because of the sign of the cross. Some, however, maintain that remission begins from that point; this does not seem true.

# SIXTH TREATISE. ON THE SACRAMENTS OF CONFIRMATION, THE EUCHARIST, AND EXTREME UNCTION

[Col. 0137]

## CHAPTERS

CHAPTER I. On the sacrament of confirmation.—CHAPTER II. On the sacrament of the altar.—CHAPTER III. That there are three things in the sacrament of the altar.—CHAPTER IV. On the form of this sacrament.—CHAPTER V. On the error of certain persons concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist.—CHAPTER VI. Why it is received under two species.—CHAPTER VII. On the twofold reception.—CHAPTER VIII. On the apparent breaking.—CHAPTER IX. What the parts signify.—CHAPTER X. On penance.—CHAPTER XI. When a person is saved from sin.—CHAPTER XII. What penance is.—CHAPTER XIII. Whether sins return.—CHAPTER XIV. On the two keys.—CHAPTER XV. On the sacrament of oil, or extreme unction.

## CHAPTER I. On the sacrament of confirmation

[Col. 0137C]

It must now be considered concerning the sacrament of confirmation. The authorities say that this sacrament ought to be given only by high priests. Thus in the time of the apostles it was given only by them; and if it were administered by another, it would be held invalid. For whenever any sacrament is celebrated contrary to its institution, it is deemed invalid. Pope Eusebius: “The sacrament of the laying on of hands must be held in great reverence. It cannot be performed by anyone except high priests. Nor in the time of the apostles is it read to have been done by anyone other than the apostles themselves, nor can or ought it ever to be performed [Col. 0138C] by anyone other than those who hold their place. For if it is otherwise presumed, it shall be regarded as invalid and void, and shall not be counted among the ecclesiastical sacraments.”

The question is asked what the efficacy of this sacrament is: namely, since someone is wholly cleansed in baptism, what does this sacrament confer upon him? The answer is that in baptism the Spirit is given for remission; here it is given for strength. Rabanus: “Finally, by the laying on of the high priest’s hand, the Paraclete is imparted to the baptized person, so that he may be strengthened through the Holy Spirit to preach to others what he himself has received in baptism.” Pope Miltiades says that this sacrament must be held in greater veneration than baptism itself because it has been entrusted to greater persons, that is, to supreme pontiffs. It is not called greater because it has greater efficacy, since children can be saved without it. Of adults, the saints say that they cannot be saved without it if it is omitted through contempt or negligence.

## CHAPTER II. On the sacrament of the altar

After the sacrament of baptism follows the sacrament of the altar. Through baptism we are washed from vices; through the sacrament of the altar we are nourished. These are the two principal sacraments by which a person is both freed from evils and filled with goods. Since hearts cannot be nourished unless they have first been cleansed, baptism comes first, [Col. 0139B] and communion at the altar follows; it is the sacrament of sacraments. Hence it is preeminently called *eucharistia*, that is, “good grace.” For in this sacrament not only grace, but he from whom all grace comes, is received.

A figure of this sacrament preceded it in the Old Testament, namely manna, which was given to the Jewish people in the wilderness. And just as manna was not given until after the crossing of the Red Sea, where the Hebrews were delivered when the Egyptians had been submerged, so this spiritual manna of the Lord’s body ought to be given only to the baptized. And just as they reached the land of promise through that bodily bread, so we, journeying through the wilderness of this age, are brought by this heavenly bread to the land of the living. Hence it is also called *viaticum*, provision for the journey. Of this bread the prophet says: “You have prepared [Col. 0139C] before me a table against those who trouble me” (Ps. 22).

A figure of this sacrament also preceded it in the bread and wine offered by Melchizedek. Hence Ambrose says: “Understand that the mysteries of Christians are earlier than those of the Jews.” Our Lord Jesus Christ delivered this sacrament to his disciples at supper, when this sacrament was first instituted. The reason for its institution was that it might be a remedy against recurring sins. For if that manifest presence of Jesus Christ, in which he lived among men, was necessary to us, so that in it he might be scourged and die for our redemption, then his presence is likewise necessary throughout this present life, in that mode by which the living bread that came down from heaven might be eaten. Hence he himself says: “Unless you eat [Col. 0139D] my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6).

Thus he who, out of exceeding love, offered himself so as to be wounded by a lance, in order that he might cleanse us by his blood, now likewise, until the end of the age, offers himself in such a manner that he may be eaten in the sacrament, so that through participation in him his members may be united to their head and freed from daily sins. When we say “in such a manner,” we speak humanly because of our weakness. For while we confess without hesitation that the very body which hung on the cross and lay in the tomb is upon the altar, and is as great here as it was there and now is at the Father’s right hand, there is no doubt that Christ’s body does not lack its own form upon the altar, but [Col. 0140A] there it is visible, while at the altar it lies hidden invisibly beneath an alien form.

## CHAPTER III. That there are three things in the sacrament of the altar

It must now be considered in this sacrament what is sacrament and what is the reality of the sacrament. Three things must be considered here: one that is sacrament only; another that is sacrament and the reality of the sacrament; and a third that is reality only. The sacrament and not the reality are the visible species, namely bread and wine, and the things visibly performed there, such as breaking, placing down, and elevation. For a sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing. A sign is what, beyond the appearance it presents, causes something else to come to mind. These visible things cause death, burial, ascent to heaven, and the whole [Col. 0140B] sequence of the event of which they are sacraments, to come to mind.

Moreover, the species of bread and wine are called sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood because, just as the body is refreshed above all other foods and drinks by bread and wine, so the soul is nourished unto true life by that true food and true drink. The Church too is very frequently called Christ’s body in sacred Scripture; and bread and wine are read to be sacraments of this body, because just as one bread is made from many grains and wine flows together from many clusters into wine, so from very many members the Church, which is Christ’s body, is made one.

The sacrament and the reality are Christ’s own body and blood: reality in relation to those species by which it is signified. This reality is again the sacrament of another reality, namely the unity of head and members, which faith in the Lord’s body and blood produces; and this reality of the sacrament is called its power. It is also called Christ’s spiritual flesh. Jerome, on the Epistle to the Ephesians: “Christ’s flesh is understood in two ways: either that spiritual and divine flesh, of which he himself says, ‘My flesh is truly food’ [Col. 0140C] (John 6), or the flesh that was crucified and buried. Of this spiritual flesh Jesus says: ‘He who eats my flesh abides in me, and I in him’ (ibid.). He eats this flesh who is joined and conformed to Christ through faith.”

Augustine: “No one should in any way doubt that every one of the faithful is then a participant in the Lord’s body and blood when he is made a member of Christ in baptism. Nor is he excluded from fellowship in that bread and cup, even if he departs this world before eating that bread, provided that he is established in the unity of Christ’s body; nor is he deprived of participation in that sacrament when he is found to possess in himself that which the sacrament signifies.”

Thus three things must be considered in this sacrament: the visible species, which are sacrament and not reality; Christ’s true body, which is beneath the species of bread and wine; and thirdly the very efficacy of the sacrament, called Christ’s spiritual flesh and the power of the sacrament, as we have said.

## CHAPTER IV. On the form of the sacrament of the Eucharist

The form of this sacrament is the recitation of those words which Christ spoke at supper when he gave his disciples his body and blood, saying: “Take, [Col. 0141A] this is my body” (Matt. 26), etc. And just as he then changed that bread and cup into his true body and true blood by his word, so we believe without hesitation that those words, spoken by the priest in that order and with that intention, change bread and wine into Christ’s true body and true blood.

But these three things are necessary for this sacrament: order, action, and intention. Order: that there be a priest. Action: that he pronounce those words. Intention: that he pronounce them for this purpose. For sometimes a priest pronounces those words in order to teach another how he is to do this; but at that time they do not possess that efficacy, because they are not said for this purpose.

Although the substance of bread is converted into Christ’s body, Christ’s body is not thereby increased. If anyone asks how it can happen [Col. 0141B] that the substance of bread passes into another substance, namely into the body that lay in the tomb and ascended into heaven to the Father’s right hand, and how that into which it passes is not increased, this should be ascribed to the will and power of him who caused that same body to proceed from a virgin without a man’s seed. Ambrose: “A virgin gave birth outside the order of nature; and what we make is the body from the virgin.” Again: “Why do you seek here the order of nature in Christ’s body, when the Lord’s very birth from a virgin is outside nature?”

And although after consecration the bread and wine which previously were bread and wine no longer exist, the species nevertheless remains, and the taste also remains. For bread appears and wine appears. It also has the same taste as before, although it is not material bread [Col. 0141C] or material wine, but Christ’s true flesh and true blood. This occurs for three reasons: so that faith may be proved, because faith concerns things not seen; so that we may not recoil from consuming it; and so that unbelievers may not ridicule us if they saw us consume blood.

The question is asked in what that species and taste exist. For we cannot say that they exist in the substance of bread and wine, since there is no substance of bread and wine there, but Christ’s true body; nor do we dare say that they inhere in Christ’s body. For Christ’s body does not have in itself the round form, but the form in which we shall see it at the judgment. But to him for whom it was easy to create both the formed thing and its form from nothing, it will not be difficult to change the formed thing and preserve its form, [Col. 0141D] and to cause it to subsist apart from substance. Thus, for the rite of the mystery and for the aid of taste, these subsistent appearances remain so as in some manner to cover the Lord’s body, which truly persists beneath them in its own form and nature.

## CHAPTER V. On the error of certain persons concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist

Against the truth stated above, some have presumed to speak both in former times and now. Since light becomes clearer by comparison with darkness, we have thought it fitting not to pass their error over in silence. Taking occasion from Christ’s words, “You are not to eat this body [Note: [Col. 0141D] *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “Not This Body.”] which you see, nor drink that [Col. 0142A] blood which those who crucify me will shed; but I have commended to you a certain sacrament,” some have dared to say that the truth of Christ’s body is not on the altar, but only a sacrament and not the thing itself. And, as they say, it is called Christ’s body as the Apostle said, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10): not in reality but in signification.

But Truth itself sufficiently shows what we ought to believe, saying: “Take; this is my body” (Matt. 26). Again Ambrose, in the book *On the Sacraments*: “Before it is consecrated, it is bread; but when Christ’s words have been added, it is Christ’s body. And before Christ’s words, the cup contains wine and water; when Christ’s words have done their work, it becomes blood.” Again: “Can Christ’s word, which could make from nothing what did not exist, not change the things [Col. 0142B] which exist into what they were not?” Again Eusebius of Emesa: “The invisible priest, by his word and secret power, changes visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood.” Gregory, in Book Four of the *Dialogues*: “Christ’s true flesh and true blood are indeed present even in sinners and unworthy recipients; but there is the essence, not the saving efficacy.”

Even if there were no other authority, it would suffice that the universal Church holds this, to which Christ is always present, as he says: “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). In the *Life of Saint Basil* it is also read that, while Basil was performing the divine mysteries, a certain Hebrew mingled with the Christians, wishing to investigate the mystery of the offering; and he saw a child in [Col. 0142C] Basil’s hands. When the others received communion, he too came, and the host was given him, truly made flesh. Consequently, believing in the wondrous mystery of the Christians, he was baptized by Basil on the next day.

What leads them into that error is explained by the saints in many places as to how it should be understood: “You are not to eat this body which you see,” that is, not while seeing it in this species as you suppose, but in the sacrament. Others are willing to say that Christ’s true body is on the altar, but deny that the bread is changed into it. For they say that the substance of bread is annihilated and does not pass into another thing; and, when that substance has been annihilated while the species remains, Christ’s body is there beneath it. The authorities stated above refute them.

## CHAPTER VI. Why it is received under two species

[Col. 0142D] It now seems necessary to say that, although it is received under two species, nevertheless whole Christ is received in each. For body cannot exist without blood, nor blood without body; but it is received under two species so that the twofold effect of this sacrament may be signified. For, as Ambrose says, it avails for the protection of body and soul; and what is received in bread avails for both, as does likewise what is received in wine, because in the bread the whole and entire Christ is received, and likewise in the wine the whole and entire Christ is received.

But if it were received in bread alone, only one thing would be signified, namely, that it avails for the protection of the body; and again, if it were received in wine alone—although this would suffice [Col. 0143A] for the protection of body and soul—only this would be signified, that it is received for the salvation of the soul. For the soul is signified in the blood. Thus it is received under two species because redemption is of body and soul. It frees the soul from sins and prepares the body for the future resurrection. Hence in the Old Testament it is also read that the Hebrews smeared both doorposts with the blood of the lamb, because in Egypt they were delivered from the destroying angel (Exod. 12). By the two doorposts soul and body are signified. Gregory: “What the blood of the lamb is, you have learned now not by hearing but by drinking; that blood is placed upon both doorposts when it is drawn in not only by the mouth of the body but also by the mouth of the heart.”

Whole Christ is received under either species—namely, that person in whom are those natures, divinity, flesh, and soul. Yet that material bread passes into Christ’s body alone, just as whole Christ was on the cross, though the flesh alone was wounded. It should likewise be noted that a double reception ought not to be said to occur, although it is received under two species, because it is one sacrament and consecrated by one blessing. Therefore, one who receives under those two species is said to receive communion not twice but only once; nor should repetition of this sacrament be spoken of except according to the same species.

## CHAPTER VII. On the twofold reception: of the good and the wicked

After the foregoing it must be considered that both the good and the wicked receive the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood; but only the good receive the reality of the sacrament. In this place we call the sacrament Christ’s body and blood themselves; but the reality of the sacrament, its very efficacy, which, as we said above, Jerome calls Christ’s spiritual flesh. Judas received the same thing as Peter. I mean the same as to essence, namely Christ’s true body; but not the same as to effect. For Peter received unto life, Judas unto condemnation.

Augustine: “The sacrament is for some unto life, for others unto destruction; but the reality of the sacrament is unto life for every person, unto destruction for no one.” Again: “Why do you prepare tooth and stomach? Believe, and you have eaten.” Thus those who believe in heart have the power of the sacrament [Col. 0143D] whether they receive the sacrament or not. But those who approach without faith working through love, even if they receive Christ’s true body in the sacrament, nevertheless do not possess the reality of the sacrament. Unless they regarded the blood of the covenant as defiled, they would consider it fearful to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb. 10). For “he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11).

Unworthy is one who is in sin. Unworthy also is one who handles it irreverently. Yet God bears with such persons in the same patience with which he himself bore the Jews who mocked, spat upon, and crucified him. Therefore, just as Christ’s flesh is understood in two ways, as we have said, so too the reception of the Lord’s body and blood is called twofold: sacramental and spiritual. Sacramental reception, which is common [Col. 0144A] to good and wicked alike, does not profit without spiritual reception. Spiritual reception, received through faith, suffices without sacramental reception where there is no contempt for religion.

Augustine speaks thus of this sacrament in the book of Prosper’s *Sentences*: “This is what we strive in every way to establish: that the sacrifice of the Church consists of, and is made up of, two things—the visible species of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body—just as Christ’s person consists of, and is made up of, God and man, since Christ himself is true God and true man. For every thing contains in itself the nature and truth of those things from which it is made.”

“Therefore the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament are Christ’s same body. Again, his flesh, which we receive in the sacrament veiled by the form of bread, and his blood, which we drink beneath the species and taste of wine—flesh, namely, is the sacrament of flesh, and blood the sacrament of blood—are understood by flesh and blood, each invisible, intelligible, and spiritual; while Christ’s visible and tangible body, full of grace and divine majesty, is signified.”

How Augustine’s statement, “flesh is the sacrament of flesh,” is to be understood must be considered and known: that visible species is called “flesh” according to the Scriptural custom by which sacraments receive the names of the things of which they are sacraments. The flesh is called invisible and intelligible because, under that species, flesh is not seen but understood; and it is the sacrament of visible, tangible flesh [Col. 0144C] that is at the Father’s right hand. The meaning is: Christ’s flesh, according to that species in which flesh is not seen but bread, is the sacrament of itself according to the visible species which can be seen at the Father’s right hand.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the apparent breaking
The question is raised concerning that breaking which is seen there: whose breaking it is, or in what thing it exists. For since there is nothing else there in substance except Christ’s body, if that breaking exists in any thing, it will exist in that body. Yet, on the other hand, we do not dare say that Christ’s body is corruptible, since it is immortal and impassible. Christ also reproved the disciples’ carnal understanding in this matter, since they thought that it was to be divided into parts like another flesh [Col. 0144D].

Some say: “There is no breaking there; it merely appears so, and is not so.” Against them it is objected that, if this is the case, our sense is deceived—as Ambrose says that “nothing false is to be supposed in the sacrifice of truth”—or else it is as in the tricks of magicians, where the eyes are deceived by a certain illusion so that what does not exist at all seems to exist. But they say: “Sight neither deceives us nor is deceived.” It would deceive us if it were believed to be broken as it appears. Nor is that an illusion which is done for usefulness and not for deception, just as it was not an illusion when Christ showed himself to the two disciples in the form of a traveler.

Others say that, just as the species of bread is there and yet is not the species of any thing which is there, but is bread which was and is not; so the breaking is there, but is not the breaking of any thing which is there, but the breaking of bread, although bread is not there [Col. 0145A]. And this seems to be what the Apostle means when he says: “The bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of the Lord?” (1 Cor. 10).

For it must be believed without doubt that in each of those parts the whole and entire body of Christ is present. Augustine: “When Christ is eaten, he is so eaten that he is not destroyed by being eaten; nor, when he is eaten, do we make parts of him.” And again, in the sacrament this is so. Likewise: “The faithful know how they are to eat Christ’s flesh: each receives his own portion; it is eaten in portions and remains whole; wholly in heaven, wholly in your heart.”

Behold: according to the authorities of Holy Scripture, Christ’s body, remaining whole and incorrupt within itself, is eaten, and Christ’s body is divided in the sacrament. This is a great and inscrutable mystery [Col. 0145B]: we are commanded to believe, but forbidden to investigate. Augustine, in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*: “Therefore, when the host is broken, and the blood is poured from the chalice into the mouths of the faithful, what else is signified but the immolation of the Lord’s body on the cross and the pouring out of his blood from his side?”

## Chapter IX. What the Parts Signify

Pope Sergius: “The Lord’s body is threefold. The portion offered and put into the chalice shows Christ’s body which has already risen; the portion eaten, his body still walking upon the earth; the portion remaining on the altar until the end of Mass, his body lying in the tomb, because until the end of the age the bodies of the saints will be in their graves.”

Since we have been delivered by the Lord’s death, it is signified that we are mindful of this fact when we eat the flesh and drink the blood [Col. 0145C] which were offered for us. By the water put into the chalice the people are signified; it is therefore offered with wine, so that the people may be understood to have been redeemed by Christ’s passion.

It is customary to ask whether, if water were omitted through forgetfulness or some negligence, the sacrifice would become invalid. But because we possess no authority on this point, we do not dare assert anything from our own judgment. We can nevertheless say that a person responsible for such an act ought to be severely punished.

That the Eucharist ought not to be given by intinction is found in the decrees of Pope Julius; for, as he says, Christ gave dipped bread to Judas alone. But, as Augustine says on John, Judas did not then receive Christ’s body, but bread alone; he had received it earlier with the disciples [Col. 0145D].

We have briefly treated certain matters concerning this sacrament. Yet the authorities speak of it very obscurely and, as it seems, contradictorily in their wording. We shall therefore set down some of their authorities.

Augustine: “Until the age is ended, the Lord is above; yet the truth of the Lord is also here with us. For the Lord’s body in which he rose must be in one place; but his truth is spread everywhere.” This must be understood thus: the Lord’s body must be in one place according to its visible form, that is, in the form in which it can be seen; his truth is spread everywhere, that is, either his divinity or his very body is celebrated everywhere. For the phrase “his truth” may refer either to Christ [Col. 0146A] or to the body itself. We said “is celebrated everywhere” because Christ’s body must not be said to be everywhere: that belongs to divinity alone.

Augustine: “God and man are one person: everywhere by that whereby he is God; in heaven by that whereby he is God and man.”

In the same way the saying is explained: “You will always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me” (Matt. 26). The saints explain it with reference to that presence in which he had formerly lived among them, eating, drinking, and doing the other things. Elsewhere Augustine, speaking of the Lord’s body, uses these words: “the same, and not the same.” This is to be understood thus: the same in essence, not the same in visible form.

Jerome on Isaiah: “They eat the food of impiety while they are not holy in body and spirit; nor do they eat Jesus’ flesh or drink his blood” [Col. 0146B].

Augustine, *City of God*: “Those who are not counted among Christ’s members must not be said to eat Christ’s body.” Finally, he himself says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6). This is to be understood of that spiritual and divine eating of which we spoke above.

Concerning those outside the Church, such as the excommunicated and manifest heretics, the question is asked whether they consecrate Christ’s body. Some think that, although it is for their condemnation, they nevertheless consecrate it, because they have not lost the ordination in which the power to consecrate it is given. Others think that neither the excommunicated nor manifest heretics consecrate it. For no one says in the consecration itself, “I offer,” but “We offer,” in the person of the whole Church. Although the other sacraments can be performed outside the Church, this one can never be performed outside it; and this latter opinion seems the more deserving of assent [Col. 0146C].

## Chapter X. On Penance

The sacrament of penance is always necessary for those returning to God. For “penance is the second plank after shipwreck”: after baptism, if anyone loses the garment of innocence by sinning, he can recover it through penance.

John’s preaching began with penance. For he says: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 3). What the herald had said, Christ himself later taught at the beginning of his preaching, saying: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” [Col. 0146D]. And rightly did the former precede so that the latter might follow; for adults must be preceded by penance if they are to attain the kingdom of heaven. Penance begins from fear, which is the beginning of wisdom (Ps. 110). For a person is compelled to penance by fear of Gehenna’s punishment.

In penance these three things must be considered: compunction, confession, and satisfaction. Compunction consists in contrition of heart; it arises from remembrance of past evils and fear of the coming judgment. Confession is the detestation of one’s own act together with self-accusation. Hence: “The righteous person is the accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18). Satisfaction follows confession through fasts, prayers, and other good works [Col. 0147A].

Compunction is commanded in the prophet where he says: “Rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2). Confession is commanded in the Epistle of James when he says: “Confess your sins to one another” (James 5; the source’s “VIII” is evidently erroneous). Satisfaction is commanded where John says: “Produce fruits worthy of penance” (Matt. 3). In those who have time, these three are necessary, and one without the others is insufficient. For it does not suffice to confess in the heart unless one who has time also confesses with the mouth and produces fruits of penance.

An objection is made from what the supreme bishop says: “I find,” he says, “that Peter wept; I do not find what he said. I read his tears; I do not read his satisfaction. For a tear washes away the offense which shame prevents one from confessing aloud.” This may be explained thus: it is shameful to confess openly and publicly, but at times it suffices to confess secretly to a priest [Col. 0147B]. Or it may be said that this institution had not yet been established in the New Testament when Peter performed penance for his sin; therefore he could obtain pardon without oral confession.

## Chapter XI. When a Person Is Released from Sin

It is customary to ask whether a person is released from sin as soon as he has true contrition of heart. That authority seems to maintain it: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31). Likewise: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 18).

But if he is released from sin through contrition of heart, he is not released in oral confession. What use, then, is oral confession? And if before oral confession he is released from sin, from what does the priest release him? Some say that what the priest is said to release is nothing other than to show that one has been released; similarly, he is said to bind, that is, to show that one has been bound. And this seems to be proved by the following authorities.

The Lord says in the prophet: “I alone blot out the iniquities and sins of the people” (Isa. 43). Likewise Ambrose: “He alone forgives the sins of the people who alone died for our sins.” Likewise Jerome on Matthew: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matt. 16), etc. “Certain persons, not understanding this passage, assume something of the Pharisees’ arrogance for themselves [Col. 0147C], so that they think they can condemn the innocent or release the guilty, whereas with God it is not the sentence of priests but the life of the accused that is sought. Hence in Leviticus lepers are commanded to show themselves to priests (Lev. 13); the priests do not make them leprous, but distinguish who are clean and who unclean. Thus also here, when the priest, according to his office, has heard the varieties of sins, he knows who is to be bound and who is to be released.”

But we must interpret these authorities in such a way that we do not take away the power which God has granted to human beings. For Truth himself says: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20). Likewise, after Christ raised Lazarus, he said to the disciples, “Release him” (John 11). This was not merely to show him to be released, but to release him.

It must therefore be seen both that God releases from sin and that a human being also releases, but a human being in one manner and God in another; and that God forgives sins and that the human being—to whom God has given power—forgives sins, but God in one manner and the human being in another. For God forgives sins from himself and through himself, whenever he wills; human beings forgive sins not from themselves but through grace working in and through them [Col. 0148A].

Thus it is true that God alone forgives sins, just as it is true: “You alone do wonders” (Ps. 71). Yet it is not denied that human beings perform miracles, but not from themselves as God does from himself. Likewise: “No one is good except God” (Mark 10), because he is good from himself. Yet we do not deny that human beings are good, but not in the same manner as God.

But, in order that we may see more plainly how God releases without a human being and how he releases through a human being, let us first consider how the sinner himself is bound. The sinner is bound by two things: blindness of mind, namely, and the debt of future damnation corresponding to it; he is held by sin and by sin’s punishment.

Through true contrition of heart he is released from blindness of mind. For one who was dead now lives, and because he lives he is inwardly enlightened; yet he remains a debtor until he has made satisfaction to the Church. Behold: he has already come forth from the tomb, but is still bound, because he has not yet been released from the debt of future punishment. He comes to the priest not to show himself righteous, but a sinner. He confesses his sin to the priest, who imposes just satisfaction on him; for he ought to make satisfaction not at his own discretion, but according to the priest’s judgment [Col. 0148B]. Then the priest releases him from the debt of future damnation—that is, God releases him through the priest.

But if, as they say, before he comes to the priest he is fully cleansed and no longer held by that sin, he lies if he confesses himself unjust and a sinner. To say this is wholly contrary to the faith of the Church.

But it is objected that he had already been released from the aforesaid debt through contrition of heart: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50). Hence in another psalm: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin.” Likewise it is said elsewhere: “Whenever a person groans, I shall not remember any of his iniquities” (Ezek. 18). From these texts it may seem to follow that the debt is already released through contrition of heart [Col. 0148C]. Reason also confirms this, because one who is truly contrite is established on the path of salvation: if he died at that moment, he would be saved.

To this we say that the true invisible priest releases from this debt one who wishes to confess but cannot; but so long as he can do it, he is not absolved unless he confesses with his mouth. For it is certain that one who has a contrite heart wishes to confess; but he can abandon this good will. For while a person is in this life, he wills nothing which he cannot cease to will. If, having lost this will, he were unwilling to confess and then died, no one doubts that he would be damned for that sin which he refused to confess. No sin goes unpunished: either the human being punishes it, or God does.

It is therefore clear that he was not released from the debt of future punishment in contrition [Col. 0148D]. We say this because some are accustomed to say that he is punished not for that sin but for contempt. It is therefore apparent that God alone forgives sins by inwardly giving life through grace; the priest forgives, not by inwardly giving life, but by absolving from the debt of future punishment through the satisfaction which he imposes.

As for the saying, “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved,” it is thought to have been said of those who, at the moment of necessity, cannot have time for satisfaction—as if it said: “At whatever hour in this life he truly repents, he shall not perish in the future life.” Or it may be said of everyone: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved,” because the sinner’s salvation begins at that moment.

Likewise there is an objection from the psalm: “I said, ‘I will confess,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin” [Col. 0149A]. The “impiety of sin” is most rightly called the mind’s very excommunication, which is released in compunction; nevertheless, as we have said, he is not yet fully released. For just as iron is first drawn from a wound so that medicine may afterward be applied, so first the impiety of sin—that inward blindness—is removed from the heart, so that afterward the medicine of the sacrament may be added through priests. For sacraments are like plasters.

## Chapter XII. What Penance Is

Having spoken of the matters to be considered in penance, we must say what penance is. As Gregory says: “Penance is to lament evils committed and not commit again what must be lamented. For one who so laments some sins that he nevertheless commits others either does not know how to perform penance or pretends to do so. What benefit is it if someone weeps for sins of lust yet still pants with the heats of avarice?”

Some, attending more to Gregory’s words than to his meaning, say that one who repents once no longer sins mortally; and if it happens that he sins mortally again, the penance he formerly performed was not penance. They bring forward other authorities to establish the same point.

Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*: “The penitent who still does what he repents of is a mocker; he does not seem to ask God as a subject, but to ridicule him as one proud.” Isaiah says to sinners: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 1). He is washed and clean who both laments past acts and does not commit again deeds to be lamented. He is washed but not clean who laments what he has done but, after his tears, repeats what he had wept over [Col. 0149C]. Likewise: “Penance which a subsequent fault defiles is empty.”

Ambrose, *On the One Penance*: “There are those who think that penance should be performed repeatedly, who indulge in immorality in Christ. For if they truly performed penance in Christ, they would not think it must be repeated.” Likewise: “As there is one baptism, so there is one penance.”

But because “the letter kills, whereas the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3), let us consider the meaning of the authors in the passages above. Penance is to lament evils committed and not commit again what must be lamented; that is, to grieve for them and not then have the will to sin again. For God does not judge a person for future things which are not presently present in deed or will. Nor does it follow with any probability: “If penance is to lament evils committed and not commit again what must be lamented, and this person commits what must be lamented, therefore he was not penitent.” What follows is: “Therefore he is not penitent”—which we rightly grant, namely, that at that time he is not truly penitent. But Catholics must by no means say that he was not penitent formerly [Col. 0150A].

[Col. 0150B]

What Isidore says—“Penance which a subsequent fault defiles is empty”—must be understood thus: it is empty, that is, without fruit. For the fruit of penance is to avoid Gehenna’s punishment and attain glory. That penance is dead, just as other good works are dead on account of an evil which supervenes. Although those good works are dead, nevertheless no one dares say that they were not good. So we say of the earlier penance that it was true penance if it had a contrite heart; and although it is now dead, like other former goods, it can revive if he repents of what he afterward committed.

What Ambrose says again, “As there is one baptism, so there is one penance,” was said concerning solemn penance. In the same chapter Ambrose adds that it is carried out publicly only. Solemn penance is called that which is performed openly outside the Church, namely, that imposed only for grave sins and upon those who have openly injured the Church. Formerly this penance was not repeated, and even now this practice is preserved in some churches out of reverence for the sacrament. Nor is that solemn penance imposed again on one who sins criminally again; rather, some counsel is given.

Therefore, as followers not of the letter which kills [Col. 0150C] but of the spirit which gives life, we should not say that someone does not repent because he will sin again; but rather that he truly repents because he grieves for past sins and does not then have the will to commit others. For it is recorded of David that, after his penance had been completed and he had already been told, “The Lord has taken away your sin from you” (2 Sam. 12), he committed the sin for which so many thousands of people died: namely, because he numbered the people.

## Chapter XIII. Whether Sins Return

Some say that one who has contrition of heart and makes worthy satisfaction for past sins truly obtains remission, and if he died then would not incur damnation; but if afterward he sins mortally, all sins return, and if he died then he would be punished for all of them. They wish to prove this from the parable: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all the debt because you begged me. Therefore ought you not also to have had mercy upon your fellow servant?” And his master, angered, handed him over to the torturers until he paid the whole debt. “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, unless each one of you forgives his brother from your hearts” (Matt. 18).

Likewise Jerome: “If we do not forgive from the heart what is committed against us, that too which had been forgiven through penance is exacted from us.” Gregory says the same.

But against this is opposed what is read in the prophet: “A double affliction shall not arise” (Nah. 1). Or, according to another translation: “The Lord will not judge twice in the same matter” [Col. 0151A], which was said of those to be saved. Some say—and do not consider it unsuitable—that a double affliction may arise upon others; or, as has been said, that what was not sufficiently punished here, if punished afterward, is not a double but one affliction and one punishment.

But it is again objected that it is quite possible for someone to sin criminally after worthy penance. Nor can it be denied that the penance had been sufficiently performed; for if he had died after completing that penance, he would have suffered no punishment for it. To this they say that unless it is accompanied by perseverance, it is not sufficient.

Others, whose view seems more deserving of assent, say that he ought no longer to be punished for those sins for which he made satisfaction to God through penance, even if he afterward commits similar or graver sins. “For the Lord does not judge twice in the same matter.” But for ingratitude—namely, because he was ungrateful for the grace by which his earlier sins had been forgiven—it must truly be maintained that he is punished more severely [Col. 0151B].

For this reason too the Church imposes upon him a more difficult penance than she would have imposed at first. The saying in the parable, “He shall not go out from there until he pays the whole debt,” seems to be explained thus: “The whole debt” is called not that which had already been forgiven, but rather the mercy which he ought to have bestowed upon others because he had received mercy from the Lord. Hence it is said: “With the measure [Col. 0151C] with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. 7). For this parable concerns mercy, as though it said: if you are unwilling to show mercy to others, as the heavenly Father showed mercy to you by forgiving sins, this debt shall be exacted from you.

What the interpreters say—that what had been forgiven through penance shall be exacted from you—seems to have been said as a warning. Yet we do not deny that, if God wished to act with strict justice, he could justly punish again for the same sins which he had earlier forgiven, since the human being has proved ungrateful for the benefit received. Just as someone freed from servitude can offend his master so grievously that he may rightly be reduced to slavery again. But because in God there is no justice without mercy, it is more probable that he does not punish further for forgiven sins [Col. 0151D].

It is customary to ask concerning those who are guilty of two crimes whether they can make satisfaction through penance for one while they remain in the other. Gregory seems to hold this in his commentary on Ezekiel, saying: “The Lord rained upon one of the cities” (Amos 4), and so on: when one who hates his neighbor corrects himself of other vices, one and the same city is rained upon in part and remains dry in part. For there are people who, although they cut off certain vices, persist grievously in others.

To this it is said that, even if he becomes less evil—which is to be rained upon in part—such penance does not wholly erase the offense. For he cannot be living and dead at the same time. And if he does not yet live, he does not truly repent. Thus he is rained upon, but not irrigated.

## Chapter XIV. On the Two Keys

[Col. 0152A]

At this point it seems necessary to speak of the keys possessed by priests. It was said to Peter, and in Peter to the others: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16). We must consider what they are, when they are given, and who possesses them. These keys are discernment and power. First one must discern who are to be bound and who released; then power must be used.

At consecration, through the ministry of the bishop, these keys are given to priests alone. Yet it does not appear that either priests alone or all priests possess them: for many before ordination possess discernment concerning who are to be bound and who released, while many after consecration lack that discernment; thus not all priests possess those two keys. Some readily concede this [Col. 0152B]. But it seems better to say that only priests, and all of them, possess these keys.

Although someone may possess that discernment before consecration, it is not a key in him, because he does not have the office of acting thus and cannot close or open. Therefore a key is not in him. Again, although an undiscerning priest lacks that discernment, he nevertheless has the office of discerning in this way; and thus, although he does not have its use, he seems nevertheless to possess it. Accordingly, it may be said that at consecration those two keys are given to all: that is, the office of exercising discernment and the office of exercising power.

Yet in matters of this kind, where nothing is said against faith or authority, either opinion may reasonably be accepted. Gregory, however, says thus in his *Homilies on the Gospels*: “Those alone, while placed in the flesh, possess the power of binding and releasing, like the holy apostles, who hold their examples together with their teaching.” Again, from Origen’s writings: “This power was granted to Peter alone and to Peter’s imitators. For whoever imitates Peter’s footsteps rightly possesses the power of binding and releasing.”

But it is one thing not to be able to do this rightly and worthily, another not to be able to do it absolutely. These authorities do not establish that they cannot do it, but that they cannot do it rightly. What was said to Peter—“Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you release upon earth shall be released in heaven” (ibid.)—must be understood thus: whatever you release according to the keys entrusted to you, or whatever you bind according to those keys [Col. 0152C], shall be released in heaven or bound in heaven [Col. 0152D]; that is, it is approved by God as bound or released.

But if they bind or release someone unjustly, he is not bound or released before God unless he himself has been contemptuous. Nor do we say that a priest binds or releases someone unjustly if he applies as much discernment as he can. For although that person is unjustly bound in respect to himself, the Church nevertheless acts justly, and he ought in this matter to obey the Church.

For example, someone abandons his wife, goes into another province, and there takes another wife. Later he wishes to dismiss the second, acknowledging that he has another wife; but perhaps, after legal proceedings have been held, he cannot at all prove the matter by witnesses. The Church excommunicates him unless he returns to the second wife; and the Church acts justly in doing this, and he ought to obey her in this matter.

[Col. 0153A]

If it is objected that he cannot be saved with this woman since he has another lawful wife, we say that he is excused by the obedience which he renders to the Church; yet he should always render the marital debt as though unwilling. Some nevertheless say that he ought not obey the Church in this matter when he knows that the Church is mistaken; yet he should not treat the excommunication with contempt, but should fear and reverence it.

If the saying is objected: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven,” they say: he is bound in heaven, that is, God approves what the Church has done; nevertheless the man is not guilty before God. Or they say thus: “Whatever you bind,” etc., is to be understood as qualified by: “as their merits require.”

But concerning those who indiscreetly and not according to the keys entrusted to them release or bind, it is said in the prophet: “Woe to those who give life to souls which do not live, and put to death souls which do not die” (Ezek. 13) [Col. 0153B].

## Chapter XV. On the Sacrament of Oil, or Extreme Unction

Besides the sacraments mentioned above, there is another sacrament: the anointing of the sick, performed with oil consecrated by a bishop. This sacrament was instituted by the apostles themselves. Hence in the Epistle of James: “If anyone among you is sick, let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord” (James 5).

As in the other sacraments, so also in this one, the sacrament is one thing and the reality of the sacrament another. The sacrament is the anointing itself; the reality of the sacrament is the forgiveness bestowed by the inward anointing. For it says in the same canonical Epistle: “And if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven him” (ibid.) [Col. 0153C]. If this sacrament is [Col. 0154A] omitted out of contempt, it is truly dangerous and damnable.

In some churches this sacrament is customarily repeated, although Augustine says that a sacrament ought not to be repeated and that no injury ought to be done to any sacrament.

But the sacrament of the altar may be objected against this, since it is often repeated in the same person. Some say that this statement was made concerning the sacrament of baptism and the sacrament of ordination, which must never be repeated, but, they say, it is not to be understood of other sacraments. But it is better to say it generally of all sacraments.

When it is said that a sacrament is not to be repeated, it must not be understood of a part of it, but of the whole sacrament itself. For example, when someone is baptized, the water is blessed through invocation of the Trinity. If another person is baptized in the same water, the same blessing of the water—that is, the invocation of the Trinity by which the water is sanctified—is repeated; nevertheless baptism is not said to be repeated, because the sacrament itself is not repeated by the repetition of one part [Col. 0154B]. But if that sanctification of the water were repeated and this were done in the same person, then an injury would be done to the sacrament.

So also with the sacrament of the altar or of anointing: although there is repetition with respect to the person who receives the sacrament again, the sacrament is not repeated because the same host or the same oil is not blessed again. For if these sacraments are said to be repeated because one part is repeated, then baptism too is repeated, since, as we have said, one part is repeated there—namely, the sanctification received by the water through invocation of the Trinity [Col. 0154C].

# Seventh Treatise: On the Sacrament of Marriage

## Chapters

[Col. 0153]

1. On the origin of marriage.
2. That marriage is a good thing.
3. That marital intercourse is sometimes performed without sin.
4. What the goods of marriage are.
5. On the various customs of marriages according to the diversity of times.
6. What is sufficient for contracting marriage in the time of grace.
7. That an oath concerning the future does not create marriage in the present.
8. That marriage is not contracted between a believer and an unbeliever, but between two believers or two unbelievers.
9. That, while one spouse lives, another cannot be joined to either of faithful spouses.
10. That persons under a vow seem able to contract marriage, and which persons cannot.
11. That relatives ought not to be joined before the seventh degree.
12. That marriage cannot take place in spiritual kinship.
13. Whether persons who have previously known one another in adultery may validly marry one another.
14. Whether marriage can be contracted between a servile person and a free person.
15. At what age marriage can be contracted.
16. That marriage cannot be contracted by the insane.
17. That the frigid cannot contract marriage.
18. On the permanence of marriage.
19. On the causes of marital divorce.
20. On spiritual fornication.
21. On second marriages.

## Chapter I. On the Origin of Marriage

[Col. 0153D]

Marriage, also called matrimony, took its origin from the institution of the Creator before human beings had sinned. For we read in Genesis that, after the first woman had been made, the man, after an ecstasy, prophetically declared—while the Lord spoke through his mouth—“Therefore a man shall leave [Col. 0154D] father and mother and shall cleave to his wife” (Gen. 2).

Now, I think, it must be shown for what causes marriage is customarily contracted. The principal cause of marriage, therefore, is the hope of offspring; for this cause the first human beings were joined by the Lord, who said: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1) [Col. 0155A]. A second cause, after Adam’s sin, is the avoidance of fornication, according to the Apostle, who says: “Let each have his own [wife] because of fornication” (1 Cor. 7).

There are besides other honorable causes, concerning which little or nothing is found written, such as reconciliation of enemies and restoration of peace. There are also less honorable causes, such as a man’s or woman’s beauty, which frequently impels minds inflamed by love to enter marriage so that they may fulfill their desire. Gain and love of riches are also frequently a cause, as are certain other things which anyone willing to apply diligence can perceive for himself.

Nor should those be believed who say that a union contracted for the latter causes—that is, for beauty or other such reasons—is not marriage at all. For it is clear that all persons become spouses who mutually receive one another by common consent, even though, inflamed by love, they come together to fulfill desire. This is most plainly evident from the example of the patriarch Jacob, who wished to join Rachel to himself rather than Leah because of her beauty. Scripture says: “Leah had weak eyes, but Rachel was beautiful in face and lovely in appearance.” Loving her, Jacob said: “I will serve you seven years for Rachel your daughter” (Gen. 29) [Col. 0155B].

The same matter is declared in Deuteronomy in these words: “If among the number of captives you see a beautiful woman, and you love her and wish to have her as your wife, you shall bring her into your house” (Deut. 21).

## Chapter II. That Marriage Is a Good Thing
For there are certain heretics who detest [Col. 0155C] marriage and judge the marital union of man and woman to be damnable, we must now say whether marriage is a good thing or an evil. We therefore affirm that marriage is a good thing and in no way evil. This is apparent not only from the fact that the Lord is read to have first instituted marriage in Genesis, saying, “Increase and multiply” (Gen.
