I); but also because Christ, at Cana of Galilee, by changing water into wine, commended marriage by a miracle (John II), and afterwards forbade a separation between husband and wife, except on account of fornication. The Apostle likewise says: “A virgin does not sin if she marries” (I Cor. VII). It is therefore established that marriage is a good thing.

Its act—that is, the mingling of the sexes—would at all times have been performed among the first human beings [Col. 0155D] and their descendants without the prompting of the flesh and the ardour of lust, had human beings remained obedient to their Creator. And just as giving alms is a good and rewardable work, so intercourse between man and woman would have been good and rewardable when performed without any fault and solely with the intention of begetting children. But because human beings, by their transgression, incurred carnal concupiscence, without which man and woman cannot mingle, that act became evil and blameworthy unless excused by the goods of marriage. That it is excused through marriage Augustine testifies when, speaking of marriage in his *Literal Commentary on Genesis*, he says: “What might be a duty for the healthy is a remedy for the sick.”

## CHAPTER III. That marital intercourse is sometimes performed without sin.

[Col. 0156A]

It now seems necessary to ask whether man and woman sin as often as they have intercourse. It must therefore be known that intercourse with a woman other than one’s own is sin. Every act of intercourse contrary to nature, with whatever woman it is performed, is criminal and abominable. Intercourse also with one’s own wife, if it is performed solely for the satisfaction of pleasure, is blameworthy; but through marriage it is venial and excusable by a light satisfaction. Hence Augustine, in *On the Good of Marriage*: “That use which married persons, overcome by concupiscence, make of one another beyond the necessity of begetting children, I would place among those matters for which it is said daily: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we forgive [Col. 0156B] our debtors’” (Matt. VI).

But the intercourse of those who unite with their spouses in order to beget offspring and bring them up in the worship of God does not appear blameworthy; nor that of those who render the debt of the flesh when their spouses demand it. This seems approved by the authority of the Lord: after the Flood, when human beings could no longer unite without carnal concupiscence, he nevertheless commanded man and woman to unite for procreation, saying, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. VIII). Certainly the Lord would not have commanded this if marital intercourse could in no way occur without sin. For the Lord forbids sins, nor does he command evil to be done for the sake of good.

Augustine, considering this command of the Lord, affirmed that spouses who come together for the sake of offspring do not sin, [Col. 0156C] saying thus in *On the Good of Marriage*: “Marital intercourse for the sake of begetting has no fault; but intercourse for satisfying concupiscence—though with one’s spouse—has venial fault on account of fidelity to the marriage-bed.” But if someone objects that every pleasure of the flesh is evil and a sin, without which marital intercourse cannot occur, we answer indeed that such pleasure is evil because it is the penalty of sin; nevertheless, not every pleasure of the flesh is sin. For it is likely that the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, which was always free from sin, experienced pleasure in resting after weariness and in eating after hunger. Such pleasure is natural to every human being after the transgression [Col. 0156D] of the first human beings, and, unless it is excessive, it is not sin. Likewise, the pleasure naturally felt in intercourse, unless it is excessive, does not appear to be sin in spouses who come together for the sake of offspring or who render the marital debt.

For marriage is completely excused, and nowhere do we read that spouses suffer any punishment for it, although no sin remains unpunished. Blessed Gregory appears to dissent from this view and to testify that spouses cannot unite without sin. For he says: “From ancient times it has always been the custom among the Romans, after intercourse with one’s spouse, to seek purification by washing and to refrain for a little while from entering church. In saying this, we do not reckon marriage to be a fault; but because even lawful intercourse between spouses [Col. 0157A] cannot occur without pleasure of the flesh, one must abstain from entering a sacred place, because that pleasure can in no way exist without fault.”

But if we wish to follow the earlier authorities and arguments, we should determine that blessed Gregory said this concerning that pleasure—that is, excessive lust—for whose satisfaction spouses frequently have intercourse; not because they always do this, but because no spouses are able to avoid it altogether. Therefore, because spouses sometimes incurred such pleasure, they refrained from entering church after their intercourse.

## CHAPTER IV. What are the goods of marriage.

Let us now briefly inquire what the goods of marriage are. There are, therefore, three goods of marriage: fidelity, offspring, and sacrament. Augustine says of these: “The good [Col. 0157B] of marriage is threefold: fidelity, offspring, sacrament. In fidelity, it is observed that, after the marital bond, neither party lies with another; in offspring, that it be lovingly received and religiously instructed; in sacrament, that marriage not be separated, and that one who has been dismissed, whether man or woman, not be joined to another even for the sake of offspring.”

Observe that the third good is called sacrament because it is a sign of a sacred thing, namely, of the inseparable union between Christ and the Church. Besides these, other goods of marriage include the avoidance of fornication and the friendship of man and woman arising from marital fellowship; and sometimes peace between people previously hostile to one another. Yet it must be known that marriage is sometimes contracted between certain persons in which none of the aforesaid goods can be found. For it happens [Col. 0157C] that some are joined neither for the sake of offspring nor to avoid the evil of fornication, and from their union neither love nor concord arises either among themselves or among others.

## CHAPTER V. On the various customs of marriages.

Because we know that people of different times have had differing laws and customs concerning marriages, let us briefly review the different states of marriage according to the differences of the times. At the beginning of time marriage was instituted between two persons—that is, one man and one woman—through the mouth of Adam, when the Lord said: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II). It is likely that marriage would have been contracted between two persons and not more throughout all the succession [Col. 0157D] of time, had the first human beings remained obedient. For then, uniting without the prompting of the flesh, human beings would have begotten children subject to God; and no man would ever have needed to be joined simultaneously to two wives for the extension of God’s worship, since all would have known and loved the one God.

After the union of the first man and first woman, their sons and daughters were joined in marriage, but one man to one woman only. That at that time a brother was joined to his sister is known to have happened for this reason: no other women or men were found to whom the sons and daughters of Adam might be joined. But Lamech is read to have been the first of all men to join two women to himself at the same time; and this deed is reproved in Lamech, because it is established that he did this [Col. 0158A] to satisfy fleshly pleasure.

Later, when the human race had multiplied and almost all were worshipping false gods, while very few remained in the worship of the one God, it was permitted—indeed, specially commanded—that marriage be contracted with two or more women at one time. This was done lest, if those few and their children failed, the knowledge and worship of God should be destroyed by forgetfulness. Nor was this contrary to the Lord’s institution. For although the Lord instituted marriage between two, he did not forbid its being made among more if necessity pressed.

From the time of the Law, Moses forbade marriages with one’s own mother, stepmother, sister, niece, paternal aunt, maternal aunt, daughter-in-law, or one’s own wife’s daughter. Yet he permitted separation between lawfully joined spouses by the issuance of a bill of divorce. And I think that at that time, for contracting marriage, mutual provision by man and woman in necessary matters, and agreement to render the debt of the flesh, sufficed; provided that the woman promised to preserve fidelity to the marriage-bed for the man, while the man could take another wife and dismiss his wife by issuing a bill of divorce. But when the time of grace came, and the faithful people had grown to abundant numbers, the law of marriage was brought back to its earlier and more honourable institution: that one man be joined to one woman. This union more honourably signifies the union of one Christ and one Church. It was also forbidden that persons be joined in marriage within the seventh degree of kinship. This was done so that charity arising from marital fellowship might bind together those whom no affection of kinship joined as strangers. [Col. 0158C] Separation by a bill of divorce was also utterly forbidden.

## CHAPTER VI. What suffices for contracting marriage in the time of grace.

Let us now see what suffices for contracting marriage in the time of grace. We believe, therefore, that the lawful consent of two suitable persons to union suffices, according to the authority of Pope Nicholas, who says: “According to the laws, the consent alone of those whose union is at issue suffices. If this consent alone should perhaps be lacking in the marriage, all the rest—even intercourse itself—comes to nothing.” Hence John Chrysostom also says: “It is not intercourse that makes marriage, but will.” Blessed Ambrose likewise says concerning the same matter: “It is not the deflowering of virginity that makes marriage, but the marital compact.”

It remains to explain briefly the words included in the aforesaid definition of marriage. We said “of two persons,” because at this time marriage is not entered upon with one woman simultaneously with several others, the Apostle saying: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband” (I Cor. VII). By saying “his own wife,” not “wives,” he indicated that a Christian man may not have several at once. We said “suitable persons,” because there are many kinds of people who may not contract marriage either with one another or with certain other persons, of which we shall speak more fully below. We said “lawful consent to union,” because those who are joined ought to consent in such a way that they voluntarily receive one another, which is judged to occur if they do not object at the betrothal. For one who does not object is deemed to consent, according to the *Digest*: “A daughter is always understood to consent to her father unless she plainly dissents.” And elsewhere: “She who does not oppose her father’s will is understood to consent.”

When, by consenting, they receive one another, that consent contains the commitment that, so long as each lives, they will provide for one another in necessities; that they will not withhold the debt of the flesh except by mutual consent; and that they will keep faith. But they ought to consent to these things willingly, not under compulsion. For coerced consent—which ought not even to be called consent—does not make a marriage.

[Col. 0159B] Urban testifies to this in writing to Sancho, king of Aragon, in these words: “Concerning the marriage of your niece, whom, when an emergency arose, you promised under a pledge of faith to give to a certain knight, we determine this: if she wholly refuses that man, as is said, do not compel her, unwilling and resisting, to be joined in marriage to him. For those whose body is one ought also to have one mind.” From this authority it is understood that marriage is made between those who consent and act voluntarily, not between those who refuse and are unwilling.

Nevertheless, if it happens that persons joined unwillingly and under compulsion live together for some period in familiar and friendly relations, and remain long in one another’s company while they have an opportunity to depart, it certainly seems that subsequent consent supplies what the preceding coercion had diminished. We believe that consent defined in the aforesaid manner suffices to contract marriage, even if there is no dowry, priestly blessing, or other marriage solemnities, or even sexual union itself—without which persons may truly be called spouses, as is plainly shown by the marriage of the Virgin Mary and Joseph.

But what Pope Evaristus says—“Marriage is not otherwise lawful unless the wife is endowed, blessed by a priest, and solemnly received”—was not said because consent alone does not suffice to make marriage. Rather, it was said because persons are not joined so honourably and lawfully when they are secretly and furtively united, omitting those things which the laws command to be performed for the honour of the sacrament. Nor does Leo deny that marriage is made by consent alone, although he says: “Since the fellowship of marriage was so established from the beginning that, beyond the union of the sexes, it also had in itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that that woman does not belong to marriage in whom it is shown that there was no nuptial mystery,” etc. For he says this concerning concubines who are taken by men for a time, without consent to permanence, permission to maintain marital fidelity, and celebration of the nuptial mystery; they are not to be called spouses, not because the marriage celebration was lacking, but because marital consent was absent.

## CHAPTER VII. That an oath concerning the future does not make a present marriage.

[Col. 0160A]

One may ask whether, for contracting marriage in the present, an oath concerning the future suffices—namely, when a man of mature age swears to a woman that he will take her in the future, and the woman swears the same to the man; yet they do not receive one another in the present, nor do they yet promise to preserve fidelity to the marriage-bed. It is likely that an oath pertaining to the future does not make a marriage.

For what Augustine and Isidore say—that spouses are called such from the first pledge of espousal—and what the laws say—that she is a lawful wife, even if not endowed, to whom a man has sworn, touching the Holy Scriptures or in an oratory, that he will have her as wife—must be understood of that oath and betrothal [Col. 0160B] in which man and woman, receiving one another, swear that they will preserve marital fidelity and the other rights of marriage in the present and thereafter. Such an oath makes marriage, not an oath which simply pertains to the future.

For since only those who receive one another by present consent become spouses, how can those be called spouses who have not yet done this but promise under oath that they will do it in the future? Again, if by an oath pertaining to the future they receive one another in the present and become spouses, why do they swear that they will do in the future what they accomplish in the present? It is foolish, or even false, to swear that something will be done in the future when it has been accomplished in the present. Again, if from the moment they swear they become spouses so quickly and without delay, [Col. 0160C] then it is true that they cannot swear that they will do this thing before they perform it. But what thing is there that people cannot promise or swear before they perform it?

## CHAPTER VIII. That marriage is not contracted between a believer and an unbeliever.

Let us now continue concerning persons unsuitable for marriage. A Christian cannot contract marriage with a Jew or a gentile. For even in the Old Testament faithful men were forbidden to take unbelieving wives, the Lord saying: “You shall not take a wife from their daughters for your sons, lest they make your sons commit fornication with their gods” (Exod. XXXIV). In accordance with this command of the Lord, Ezra rightly separated Jewish marriages with gentiles. But as the Lord established in the Old Testament, so it is observed in the New. Hence Augustine, to Pollentius: “This concerns those spouses who are first joined to one another: a woman is not to marry except a man of her own religion, nor is a man to take such a wife. For the Lord commands the same thing, the Apostle teaches it, and each Testament prescribes it.”

It is commonly asked whether Jews among themselves, and other unbelievers, contract marriage at this time. Hence Augustine, in the first book *On Adulterous Marriages*: “When the Gospel began to be preached to the gentiles, I found gentiles who were already spouses joined to gentiles.” And shortly afterwards: “Both being gentiles, they had not been joined contrary to the command of the Lord.” The same author, in *On the Good of Marriage*: “The good of marriage among all nations and all [Col. 0161A] people consists in the matter of begetting and in the fidelity of chastity; but, as regards the people of God, it consists in the fidelity of sacrament.” Innocent says on the same point: “Only sins are remitted in baptism; the number of wives is not abolished. For if a wife is prepared by God for a husband, and ‘what God has joined let not man separate’ (Matt. XIX), how can we believe that such things can be remitted among sins?”

From these authorities it is apparent that marriages exist among unbelievers; this is also most strongly confirmed by the Apostle’s authority, since he permits a person coming to the faith to remain with an unbelieving spouse (I Cor. VII), which he certainly would not do unless he recognized a marital union between them. Yet it should be noted that the words of certain authors seem to weaken this position, such as authorities stating [Col. 0161B] that true chastity does not exist among unbelievers. But this does no harm, since the same can truly be said even of Christian spouses who act perversely, in whom no virtue is perfect. Nor was Ambrose’s statement—“Marriage outside God’s decree ought not to be reckoned as marriage, because marriage is made by God”—said because it is not marriage, but because it is not firm; indeed, it is dissoluble, as the Apostle shows.

## CHAPTER IX. That, while one faithful spouse lives, the other cannot be joined to another.

If a man has a faithful wife, neither of them can lawfully join himself or herself to another while the other lives. Hence Clement, from the sayings of Peter: “The first kind of adultery is that a man is not content with his own wife alone, and that a woman does not preserve herself for her own husband alone.”

But since it frequently happens that women whose husbands are believed to have died in war, captivity, or a distant journey are joined to other men, it may rightly be asked whether the second union is a marriage while the first husbands are still living, since there is no plain authority on the matter. Yet this is certain: they must be restored to their former husbands if those husbands return and wish to have them. Hence Leo, to Bishop Nicetas: “If husbands, returning after a long captivity, persist in love for their wives so as to desire them to return to their fellowship, what necessity brought about is to be passed over and judged blameless, and what fidelity requires is to be restored. But if any women are so captivated by love for their later [Col. 0161D] husbands that they prefer to cleave to them rather than return to their lawful fellowship, they are rightly to be censured, so that they are deprived of ecclesiastical communion.”

This authority seems to excuse such women on account of ignorance, yet to call the first union alone marital and lawful. Therefore it is likely that the second union is not lawful or marital, but is venial because of ignorance. For if unions with the second husbands became lawful in such circumstances, one woman would then have two lawful husbands at the same time: one whom she knew to be living and another whose survival she did not know. Something similar may be said of a man who, having left his wife, travels and remains some years [Col. 0162A] in a distant region and, while his wife is still living, takes another woman who does not know that he has another wife. For marriage does not appear to exist between them; but the fault is venial on the part of the ignorant woman and criminal on the part of the man who knows. For if there were a lawful union between them, one man would then have two lawful wives at the same time, which cannot occur in the time of grace.

## CHAPTER X. Which vowed persons appear able to contract marriage, and which do not.

Consecrated virgins, after they have been consecrated by a bishop, and veiled widows cannot in any way contract marriage. Paul, writing to Timothy, implies this to be true of veiled widows in these words: “Avoid younger widows. For when they have become wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, having condemnation because they have made void their first faith” (I Tim. V). In accordance with this authority, blessed Gregory, writing to Boniface concerning those same veiled widows, says: “I believe you know from Saint Paul that widows who depart from their purpose of widowhood are condemned unless they return; and we judge that, by apostolic authority, they must be condemned and excluded from the communion of the faithful and from the thresholds of the Church until they return, willingly or unwillingly, to the good which they began.” And shortly afterwards: “Widows who promised to veil themselves and afterwards apostatized and returned to their former vomit are to be removed from the thresholds of the Church and the assembly of the faithful until satisfaction is made, and handed over to prisons.”

[Col. 0162C] Blessed Innocent decreed concerning veiled virgins: “Therefore, those who marry spiritually and are veiled by a priest, if afterwards they either marry publicly or corrupt themselves secretly, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the man to whom they joined themselves has departed from the world. For if this rule is observed among human beings, that any woman who marries another while her husband lives is held to be an adulteress, and she is not permitted to undertake penance unless one of them has died, how much more must this be maintained concerning her who had first joined herself to an immortal bridegroom and afterwards passed over to human marriage?”

It seems, however, necessary to dwell somewhat on these words of Innocent. For they appear not merely to deny marriage to veiled virgins, but also to deny them a place for penance so long as their seducers [Col. 0162D] live. But it should rather be understood that penance is forbidden them only so long as they themselves and those who corrupted them live together in their union and in the will to sin. This is demonstrated by the following comparison of a woman who has her own husband and commits fornication with another: penance cannot be denied to her, although her seducer lives, if she has withdrawn from his companionship and from the crime.

But Innocent seems to permit un-veiled virgins—although they have bound themselves to continence by vow—to remain in a marriage entered after the vow. He decreed thus concerning such virgins: “Those who, although not yet under the sacred veil, have nevertheless steadfastly humbled themselves to remain in a virginal purpose: if perchance they marry, they must perform penance for some time, even if they have not been veiled, because their promise was held by the Lord.” Concerning un-veiled widows, however, we have no certain authority either forbidding or permitting them to remain in a marriage begun after the vow.

As for men who have vowed continence, it must be observed that if they have become hermits, monks, or clerics, they may in no way enter marriage after the vow. But concerning laymen who make a vow and do not assume the habit of religion, there is doubt whether they can contract marriage. Yet this authority of Jerome seems more than any other to deprive them, after a vow of continence, of the power to contract marriage: “For those who vow chastity, not only to marry but even to wish to marry is damnable.”

I do not think it should be passed over here that Bede, in his exposition on Luke, seems to affirm that the Blessed Virgin Mary, before entering marriage with Joseph, determined to lead a virginal life. This indeed appears to conflict with the truth, since the Blessed Virgin was most prudent and knew that whatever is devoutly promised to the Lord must be faithfully fulfilled. It is therefore likely that from adolescence she had committed herself wholly to God, ready either to marry or to remain continent according as she knew God to will. Augustine testifies to this in *On Marriage and Concupiscence*: “It must be believed that the Blessed Virgin was the wife of Joseph only in mind—that is, by consent of mind—and that she proposed to remain in virginity [Col. 0163C] if it pleased God, and to act otherwise if he wished.” From this authority and from the fact that she did not refuse betrothal, it is plainly apparent that she had not vowed continence before she was betrothed. Yet it is certain that she and her husband afterwards promised it, once the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation had become known to each of them through angelic revelation.

## CHAPTER XI. That relatives ought not to be joined before the seventh degree.

Blood relatives in the seventh degree or closer cannot be joined. Hence Gregory: “We have decreed that each person shall observe the seventh generation of his or her descendants; and so long as they recognize themselves as relatives by affinity, we deny them access to marital union; if they do so, they must be separated.” From the Council of Lyons: “Let no one take wives from among those related by his own blood up to the seventh degree.”

It should be known that the first degree of kinship is brother and sister, whom Isidore also calls the trunk; the second degree is grandson and granddaughter; the third, great-grandson and great-granddaughter; the fourth, great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter; the fifth, great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter; the sixth, great-great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-great-granddaughter; the seventh, the grandson and granddaughter of a great-great-great-great-grandchild. It should be noted that Isidore, who enumerates no more than six degrees of kinship, omits the first degree—that is, brother and sister—and calls grandson and granddaughter the first degree.

To the foregoing must be added that relatives who knowingly unite with one another do not contract marriage, but must be separated [Col. 0164A] and subjected to penance for incest. Those who unite unknowingly are excused from the crime by ignorance; nevertheless, it should not be asserted that marriage exists between them unless, by the Church’s permission for some benefit, it is dispensatorily confirmed—for example, blessed Gregory permitted the Angles, after their reception of the faith, to marry in the fourth degree.

Just as those related to one another may not unite up to the seventh degree, so, if one of two lawfully joined spouses dies, the other may not take as spouse anyone related to the former spouse up to the seventh generation. Here we should not pass over something which Gregory, writing to Bishop Venerius, seems to affirm. He says that when man and woman have become one flesh in intercourse, [Col. 0164B] the kinship of one pertains to the other. Therefore, if a husband dies and his wife takes another man, he forbids the children born from the second husband to take wives from the kinship of the former husband, maintaining that, through their mother, those children belong to the kinship of the former husband, with whom their mother had become one flesh.

But the Church does not observe this decree of Gregory. For it would follow that among two different kinship groups, no one could marry except two persons alone. Thus it would happen that scarcely anyone could find a suitable spouse.

## CHAPTER XII. That marriage cannot take place in spiritual kinship.

Just as marriage may not take place in carnal [Col. 0164C] kinship, so neither may it in spiritual kinship. Spiritual kinship exists between a godfather and godmother; and between those of whom one has raised the other from the sacred font, or held the other at catechization or confirmation. Spiritual kinship also exists between a man’s natural children and his spiritual children. Spiritual children are those raised from the sacred font, or held at catechization or confirmation.

That godfather and godmother cannot be joined to one another, nor a spiritual father to his goddaughter, nor a spiritual mother to her godson, is shown by the Council of Mainz in these words: “If anyone takes his goddaughter or spiritual godmother in marriage, we judge that they must be separated and punished by severe penance.” That a spiritual son or daughter may not be joined to any natural son or [Col. 0164D] daughter of that same person is shown by Pope Nicholas, writing to the Bulgarians: “There is a welcome and holy communion among spiritual brothers and children. It should not be called consanguinity, but rather regarded as spiritual proximity. We therefore judge that marital union cannot take place between them, since the venerable Roman laws do not permit marriage to be contracted either between those who are children by nature or those who are children by adoption.”

It should also be noted that the same pope, writing to Bishop Solomon, affirms that the same man may not have two godmothers, one after another—an institution which the Church does not observe very closely.

## CHAPTER XIII. Whether those who previously knew one another in adultery can be joined together.

[Col. 0165A]

Those who have first defiled themselves with one another by adultery are forbidden by the canons thereafter to unite with one another in marriage. Hence Leo: “There cannot be marriage with the woman with whom there was adultery.” Concerning the same matter, from the Council of Tribur: “It has been reported to the ears of the holy priests that a certain man violated another’s wife by illicit intercourse and, moreover, gave an oath that after the death of her lawful husband, should that occur, he would take her as wife; and this was done. We therefore forbid and anathematize such a union.”

By these authorities, persons who first polluted themselves with one another by adultery are forbidden to contract marriage with one another. Yet Augustine testifies that marriage may be contracted between such persons, saying in *On Marriage [Col. 0165B] and Concupiscence*: “Finally, when the husband has died, where there was a true marriage, a true marriage can be made with him with whom there was previously adultery.” Since this latter authority permits what the earlier ones prohibit, one may observe that in former times such persons could lawfully be joined, as is related of David and Bathsheba. But later this was forbidden as a deterrent. Therefore, if such persons are joined in these times, and the aforesaid institution has been received and confirmed in the churches, marriage is not made between them unless it has been permitted by a dispensation from the Church.

## CHAPTER XIV. Whether marriage can be contracted between a slave and a free woman.

Marriage between a slave and a free woman, or between a free man and a female slave, is forbidden under Roman laws. [Col. 0165C] Hence in the constitutions of the Novels: “If anyone, through error, has taken a woman who is a slave, believing her to be free, or conversely, if a free woman has through error been joined to a slave, it must altogether be said that no marriage has been constituted. Marriage cannot be contracted between a free man and a female slave, or a slave and a free woman.” The same appears to be affirmed by the council held at Tertineria, in which a decree of this sort was made: “If a freeborn man takes as wife another’s female slave, believing her to be freeborn, and that woman is afterwards reduced to slavery, let him redeem her from slavery if he can; if he cannot, let him take another if he wishes. But if he knew that she was a slave and had approved this, let him afterwards keep her as a lawful wife. A freeborn woman must do likewise with respect to another’s slave.” [Col. 0165D]

Accordingly, these authorities indicate that marriage is not made between a servile person and a free person in all churches where this has been forbidden and generally confirmed. But in those churches which have not yet received that ordinance, marriage between such persons is valid, as frequently occurs in many Gallican churches: the free person retaining freedom and the slave remaining in slavery. This appears to be affirmed by Augustine, who says: “If a freeborn woman takes a slave, knowing that he was a slave, let her keep him; for we all have one Father in heaven, and one law shall apply to man and woman.” The laws likewise seem to affirm a remarkable point: namely, that marriage cannot take place between a free person and a female slave, even if [Col. 0166A] their masters permit it and consent of their own will. But we believe that marriages are made between servile persons at least when their masters consent, following the example of the Hebrews, who, although slaves in Egypt, nevertheless lawfully celebrated marriages.

This is also confirmed by the Council of Mainz, in which the following was decreed concerning the marriage of a male and female slave: “If the master of both joins a male slave and a female slave in marriage, and afterwards, when the male slave has been freed, the female slave who remains in service cannot be redeemed, for that reason their marriage is not to be preserved.” Concerning this matter a decree was also made at the Council of Chalon: “It has been reported that some persons, by an arbitrary presumption, dissolve lawful marriages among us, without considering that Gospel saying: ‘What God has joined together, let no human being separate’” (Matt. 19). “Therefore it has seemed good to us that the marriages of slaves should not be dissolved, even if they have different masters; but, remaining in one marriage, let them serve their own masters. And this is to be observed where their union was lawful and took place by the will of their masters.”

Observe that at the end of this chapter it seems to be affirmed that a marital union cannot take place between a male and female slave without their masters’ permission. Yet it seems reasonable that marriage may take place between them if they are joined by mutual consent, even though their masters are unaware. For if a young man and a young woman, both Christians and free, happened to be captured by Saracens and reduced to slavery, what reason would forbid their being joined by mutual consent in order to avoid fornication?

## Chapter XV. At What Age Marriage May Take Place

[Col. 0166C]

Under the laws, young men under fourteen years of age and girls under twelve cannot enter marriage. If they have entered into a union before the stated ages, they may be separated, even though they were joined voluntarily and with their parents’ consent. But those joined in childhood who, after reaching the years of puberty, do not wish to leave one another but remain in their union thereby become spouses, and thereafter cannot be separated.

## Chapter XVI. That Marriage Cannot Be Contracted by the Insane

While they are in a state of madness, insane persons cannot make a marriage, according to this canonical decree: “Neither an insane man nor an insane woman can contract marriage; [Col. 0166D] but, if it has been contracted, they are not to be separated.”

## Chapter XVII. That the Sexually Incapable Cannot Make Marriage

If a man is of a frigid nature, or if a woman is naturally without an organ fit for intercourse, so that they can in no way have sexual relations, such persons can make no marriage either with one another or with others.

## Chapter XVIII. On the Stability of Marriage

Having shown which persons cannot contract marriage with one another or with others, we must next discuss the stability of marriage. When the Jews asked whether it was lawful to give a bill of divorce, the Lord, indicating that marriage is not to be dissolved rashly or indiscriminately, said: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19). Following this command of the Lord, the Apostle Paul likewise forbade a wife to dismiss her husband or a husband his wife. [Col. 0167A]

Therefore, once a man and woman have been lawfully joined, they must always preserve their marital fellowship as long as they live; neither may withhold the debt of the flesh from the other when requested. For the Apostle says: “The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the man does; likewise, the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman does” (2 Cor. 7). If both agree by mutual consent, however, they may abstain for a time; afterwards they must return to the marriage-bed. Hence the Apostle: “Do not defraud one another, except by mutual consent for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7). It is therefore clear that neither can make a vow of continence unless this pleases both alike and both make the same vow, since they are one flesh [Col. 0167B] and each has the other’s body in his or her power.

Thus Gregory, writing to the patrician Theotista, says: “When good spouses desire either to increase their merit or to wipe out the faults of their former life, it is lawful for them to bind themselves to continence and seek a better life. But if the woman refuses the continence which the husband desires, the marriage may not be divided.” On the same subject Nicholas, writing to King Charles, says: “Queen Theoberta wrote to us that she wished to be released from rank and from marriage, and desired to be content with a private life alone. We wrote to her that this could not be done otherwise unless her husband Lothair chose the same life.”

These authorities affirm that both may make the vow together, but that one may not do so without the other. Thus it is clear that if one, without the other’s consent, enters religious life [Col. 0167C] and the other objects, the convert must be compelled to return to the marriage-bed and to secular life, even if he has received monastic tonsure and clothing. But if both make the vow, they must remain in continence. Hence it is written in the *Register*, to Adrian the notary:

“Agothosalatrix, bearer of this letter, has complained that her husband, against her will, has become a convert in the monastery of Urbicius. There is no doubt that this pertains to the fault of the same abbot. Therefore we order your skill diligently to investigate whether he perhaps converted with her consent, or whether she herself promised to change her life; and, if you find this, arrange that he remain in the monastery and compel her to change her life as she promised. But if none of these things is so, and if you learn that the aforesaid woman has committed no crime of fornication [Col. 0167D] (on account of which a husband may leave his wife), we wish you to restore her husband to her, even if he has been tonsured, every pretext having ceased.”

Here it must be observed that when persons bind themselves by vow to God’s cause, or practise continence, they do not dissolve their marriage contrary to the Lord’s command. But since God, for whose love they practise continence, separates them from embrace, their carnal marriage becomes holy and spiritual. And although the man becomes an abbot and the woman an abbess, while they live they are always spouses. Yet no one ought therefore to suppose that marriage can be contracted between a monk and a nun, since they cannot make lawful consent concerning the rendering of the debt of the flesh.

## Chapter XIX. On the Causes of Marital Divorce

[Col. 0168A]

We must discuss those causes which bring about divorce between spouses. Our Lord indicated that a wife may be dismissed by her husband for the cause of fornication, when he said: “Whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery; and whoever marries the dismissed woman commits adultery” (Matt. 9). It is clear that for the same cause a wife is permitted to dismiss her husband. For since they are one flesh, and the body of one is in the power of the other, they have received the same law of remaining together or separating.

But although fornication causes divorce, it is not the person who dismisses the other, but the one who is dismissed on account of his or her own fault, who separates the marriage. Fornication is twofold: bodily and spiritual. Bodily fornication occurs when a man, while his wife lives, or a woman, while her husband lives, [Col. 0168B] knowingly joins himself or herself to another, secretly or openly. I have added “knowingly,” because if it happened that, without the husband’s knowledge, his wife put another woman in his bed and the deceived husband had intercourse with her, ignorance would excuse the husband from fornication.

When one spouse incurs fornication, the other may not dismiss the fornicator unless that other has remained free from fornication. Hence Augustine, commenting on the Sermon on the Mount, says: “Nothing is more unjust than to dismiss one’s wife for the cause of fornication if one is oneself convicted of fornication. Therefore, whoever wishes to cast away his wife for the cause of fornication must first be cleansed from fornication.” Augustine further says: “When marriage is separated because of such fornication, neither the person dismissing nor the person [Col. 0168C] dismissed may enter another union,” as the Apostle says: “To those joined in marriage I give command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband; but if she departs, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband” (1 Cor. 7).

From this authority it is understood not only that, after separation on account of fornication, spouses should remain apart from one another because they cannot enter another union, but also that they may be reconciled and dwell together as before if either wishes to call back the one dismissed. Solomon seems nevertheless to contradict this, saying: “He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and unwise” (Prov. 18). Jerome also seems to forbid the reconciliation of such persons. Writing to the presbyter [Col. 0168D] Amandus concerning a woman who had married another while her husband was alive, he says: “I speak of a new matter—indeed, not new, but old—confirmed by the authority of the Old Testament. If a woman leaves her second husband and wishes to be reconciled to the first, she cannot be.”

But we place greater trust in the Apostle, who, as stated above, permits a husband to be reconciled to a woman who, after leaving her fornicating husband, does not wish to remain unmarried. Accordingly Augustine, following the Apostle, says in the second book *On Adulterous Marriages*: “Even after adulteries have been committed and purged, reconciliation of spouses will not be shameful or difficult where remission of sins through the keys of the kingdom of heaven is not doubted.” On the same subject Hermes says in the book of the *Shepherd*:

“I said to the shepherd: [Col. 0169A] ‘Lord, if someone has a faithful wife in his house and finds her in adultery, does the husband sin if he continues to live with her?’ And he said to me: ‘So long as he does not know her sin, he lives with her without fault. But if the husband learns that his wife has sinned, and the woman does not repent but remains in her fornication, and the husband lives with her, he will be guilty of sin and a participant in her adultery.’ ‘What then if the woman persists in her vice?’ And he said: ‘Let him dismiss his wife, and let the husband remain by himself.’ ‘But if the dismissed woman repents and wishes to return to her husband, will she be received by her husband?’ And he said: ‘Certainly; and if her husband does not receive her, he sins and incurs a great sin. Therefore he ought to receive the sinner who has repented—but not repeatedly.’” [Col. 0169B]

Thus, from the foregoing authorities, it is clear that a husband should not cast away a woman who wishes to depart from fornication; rather, for God’s sake, he both ought and may receive a woman who repents of fornication and seeks reconciliation.

It must not be omitted here that, when someone has defiled by incest a blood-relative of his own wife, if this is secret and cannot be proved, the Church judges that he, as a sinner who has undertaken penance, should remain with his wife, and that he does not commit incest with his lawful wife. But if it is public, the Church usually judges that he must be separated from his wife’s society. Indulgence may nevertheless be granted if his wife and the woman whom he defiled are related in more remote degrees.

## Chapter XX. On Spiritual Fornication

Spiritual fornication is either general, concerning which it is said: “You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you” (Ps. 72); [Col. 0169C] or it is spiritual in the sense of idolatry and other unbelief contrary to the Christian faith, such as Judaism. On account of this spiritual fornication, a faithful person is permitted to dismiss an unbelieving spouse.

This is understood from the words of the Apostle. After forbidding, by the Lord’s authority, the separation of one faithful spouse from another, he then speaks of a faithful husband and an unbelieving wife: “To the rest I say, not the Lord: if any brother has an unbelieving wife and she agrees to live with him, let him not dismiss her; and if any woman has an unbelieving husband and he agrees to live with her, let her not leave him” (1 Cor. 7). These words show that a faithful person may leave an unbeliever, although it is perfect, for the purpose of winning the unbeliever to God, to remain with the unbeliever if the latter agrees. [Col. 0169D]

For unless it were lawful to dismiss an unbeliever, the Apostle would have forbidden divorce between such persons by the Lord’s authority just as he had forbidden it between two faithful persons. The Apostle also seems to permit the faithful person, after dismissing the unbeliever, to join himself or herself to another faithful person. For he says: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart; for a brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such cases” (ibid.). By saying this, and not adding that after the unbeliever’s departure the faithful person must remain unmarried—as he had commanded in the case of two faithful persons—he clearly indicates that, after an unbeliever has departed, the faithful person may join himself or herself to another faithful person.

Nor is this contrary to the Apostle’s statement: “I command—not I but the Lord—that a wife not depart from her husband; but if she departs, let her remain unmarried” (ibid.). [Col. 0170A] For this was said concerning those of whom both are faithful. But where one is an unbeliever, a faithful person may retain or dismiss the unbeliever, as Pope Eutychian shows when he says: “If a pagan has taken a pagan woman as wife before baptism, after baptism it shall be in his power to keep or dismiss her.”

It seems worthy of inquiry whether a husband may dismiss his wife for every kind of fornication—that is, for avarice or other crimes—to which a wicked wife, while believing and confessing the Catholic faith, tries to induce her husband. Here it must be noted that if the wife will not allow the husband to live with her unless he shares in her crimes, the husband ought sooner to separate from her company than defile himself by her crimes, [Col. 0170B] according to the Lord’s command: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you” (Matt. 5). But if a wife who confesses the Catholic faith permits her husband to live with her, however wicked she may be, the husband ought not to leave her.

If, after the lawful betrothal of a man and a woman, either should fall into leprosy or any other illness, however grievous, the healthy person may not dismiss the sick person for that reason, but must support him or her and render the debt of the flesh if the sick person requests it. Hence Augustine, in *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*: “If anyone has a wife who is barren, physically deformed, weak in her limbs, blind, lame, deaf, or otherwise afflicted, or worn down by diseases, pains, and labours, then—whatever exceedingly horrible condition may be imagined apart from the cause of fornication—he should endure her for the sake of fellowship and faith.” [Col. 0170C]

Concerning those who, though lawfully joined, afterwards cannot have sexual intercourse, if one of them—or both—complains because they cannot render one another the debt of the flesh, the Gallican Church judges, in accordance with the tenor of the laws and certain decrees, that, after an undertaking of faith and lawful proof, they should separate and, if they wish, join themselves to others. Hence in Book Six of the *Code*: “If a husband, from the beginning of marriage until two full years have elapsed, is altogether unable because of natural weakness to have intercourse with his wife, the woman, or her parents, may divorce the husband without danger of losing the dowry.” “If any woman declares that her husband has never had intercourse with her, let them go to the cross; and, if it is true, let them be separated, and let her do what she wishes.” [Col. 0170D]

Blessed Gregory, however, does not allow persons known to have had intercourse with others to separate after they have been joined, although they cannot consummate the work of marriage with one another. But if the husband is of a frigid nature, after proof of this he permits the man and woman to separate, saying:

“Having been consulted concerning those who, because of a frigid nature, are said to be unable to have intercourse with one another while rendering the works of the flesh, we permit separation. But he, if he cannot use her, should have her as a wife as though she were a sister. If the woman pleads, ‘I wish to be a mother,’ each is to state with seven hands that they had never become one flesh through sexual union; then the woman appears able to contract a second marriage. But if he too has entered another union, then, after penance has been completed, they are to be compelled to resume their former marriages.” [Col. 0171A]

This authority of Gregory the Great expressly forbids the separation of lawfully joined spouses who can have intercourse with others, although they cannot have intercourse with one another. In this he agrees with the Lord, who forbade a husband to dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication (Matt. 19).

But if, after lawful union, it happens for some reason that the husband lifts his wife’s son from the sacred font, or the woman lifts her husband’s son, or holds the child during catechization or confirmation, they ought not to be separated for that reason. Thus Nicholas, writing to Bishop Solomon, says: “You wish to know whether a woman who has lifted her husband’s son from the sacred font can be joined with the same husband. We decree that such persons may be joined, because, according to the sacred canons, a spouse ought not, under the pretext of any religious observance, to dismiss a spouse except with both parties’ consent. For the Apostle commands: ‘Do not,’ he says, ‘defraud one another except by consent, that you may devote yourselves to prayer’” (1 Cor. 7). [Col. 0171B]

On the same matter Pope John writes as follows to Anselm, bishop of the Church of Legunigina:

“A man named Stephen, coming in person to the thresholds of the Apostles, made known to our authority that, when his son was at the point of death and had not yet been washed with the water of baptism, necessity compelled him to baptize the child and receive him in his own hands. When this affair was revealed to your knowledge, your reverence, burning with zeal for God, judged that the said man should be separated from his wife. This must by no means be done, for Scripture says: ‘What God has joined together, let no human being separate’” (Matt. 19).

On the same matter, at the Council of Chalon: “It was said that certain women, fraudulently seeking to be separated from their husbands, had held their own children before bishops for confirmation. We therefore judged it fitting that, if any woman has held her own child before a bishop for confirmation, she should do penance as long as she lives; nevertheless, she is not to be separated from her husband.” [Col. 0171C]

These authorities establish that spouses ought not to be separated if, after they have been lawfully joined, one lifts the other’s child from the sacred font or holds the child for confirmation. But Pope Deusdedit seems to affirm the contrary when he says:

“A deacon of your holiness has brought us a letter reporting that, last Saturday, because of a great influx of people, certain men and women unknowingly received their own children from the holy washing. But the holy Fathers Innocent and Celestine, of blessed memory, with the consent of many fellow bishops, wrote and confirmed prohibitions against such acts in the church of the Prince of the Apostles: women and men who had received newborn children for whatever reason were in no way to take one another in marriage, but were to separate, lest, at the Devil’s persuasion, such a vice grow throughout the world.” [Col. 0171D]

This is Pope Deusdedit’s statement. But he is not to be followed in this, since the Lord forbids a husband to dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication (ibid.). Moreover, Innocent and the other authorities whom he adduces to strengthen his opinion seem to deal only with those who became godfathers and godmothers before becoming spouses; these they rightly forbade to marry one another.

[Col. 0172A]

As stated above, bodily or spiritual fornication suffices for the separation of marriage. So too it is true that all causes mentioned above which prevent certain persons from being able to marry undoubtedly suffice for the separation of the same persons if such persons have in fact been joined. For since a vow of continence made before the union prevents a monk and nun from contracting marriage, they ought likewise to be separated if they were joined after such a vow. The same judgment applies to kinship and other matters: whatever causes prevent persons from becoming spouses also avail for their separation if they have been joined. [Col. 0172B]

With regard to kinship, however, this must be observed: if it is found between a husband and his own wife in more remote degrees, indulgence may be granted to them; but if it is not granted, they must be separated. Separation of relatives should take place in this manner: two or three members of the family should swear to the kinship; or, if their entire family line has died out, the oath of proof should be made by the older and more truthful neighbours.

## Chapter XXI. On Second Marriages

To what has preceded must be added that, concerning a man and woman lawfully joined, if one dies and the other survives, the survivor may without offence enter a second marriage, according to the Apostle: “A woman is bound to her husband as long as her husband lives; [Col. 0172C] but if her husband sleeps, she is released from the law of her husband; let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Cor. 7).

Nor are only first or second marriages lawful, but third, fourth, and further marriages as well, according to Augustine, who says: “People are accustomed to raise a question about third, fourth, and very numerous further marriages. I answer briefly: I dare not condemn any marriages, nor remove the shame attached to their multiplicity.” Jerome testifies likewise: “I now cry out in a free voice that bigamy is not condemned in the Church—indeed, not even trigamy; and that marriage to a fifth or sixth husband is likewise lawful, since marriage to a second husband is lawful.”

It therefore appears from the foregoing authorities that, after a spouse’s death, marriages may be celebrated many times. Yet some may think that bigamy is sinful, since the Apostle, describing a person worthy of episcopal honour, says that he must be “the husband of one wife” (1 Tim. 3), excluding bigamists from that honour as though they were transgressors. But it must be understood that this is not done because bigamy is culpable, but for the propriety of the sacrament. For a bishop more fittingly represents Christ if he is joined to one woman alone, just as Christ is joined to one Church.

Nevertheless, the decree of the Council of Caesarea seems to affirm that bigamy is sinful: “It is not fitting for a presbyter to dine at the wedding of a bigamist; for, since a bigamist needs penance, what presbyter can give consent to such a wedding?” But we do not say that a bigamist needs penance because entering a second marriage is sinful; rather, because perhaps, being excessively incontinent—as often occurs—[Col. 0173A] he indulges lust toward his own wife beyond measure. Nor should a presbyter consent to such marriages, [Col. 0174A] because by attending them he encourages people to marry repeatedly.

[Col. 0173]

# On the Sacraments of the Christian Faith

## Short Preface

I have been compelled by the earnest request of certain people to write a book on the sacraments of the Christian faith. In it I have inserted certain matters which I had previously dictated separately, because it seemed burdensome or superfluous to set forth the same things anew in the same style. If, in these passages, a plainer manner of expression has perhaps failed to preserve the elegance of composition, I did not consider that of much importance, since the truth remains the same.

What moves me more is that, when I first set down these same matters more carelessly—as one who did not yet have the design of the future work in view—I wrote them out here and there, intending them to be copied piecemeal. At that time I considered it sufficient for such brief notes or annotations to become known. But afterwards, when I inserted them into the text of this work, reason required that some things in them be changed, while others be added or removed. Therefore I wish the reader to be warned: if he finds them outside the sequence of this work containing something different, or expressed differently, he should know that this is the reason for the variation; and if anything in them needs correction, he should bring it into conformity with the form of this work.

I have divided this work into two books, so that, amid so great a multitude and length of subjects, a break in the exposition might remove weariness for readers, and at the same time offer a more convenient form to those unable to write out both books together or wishing to possess them separately.

## Contents of This Work

[Col. 0173]

There is a prologue and two books. The first book carries the sequence of the narrative from the beginning of the world to the Incarnation of the Word. The second proceeds in order from the Incarnation of the Word to the end and consummation of all things.

The first book likewise comprises twelve divisions, or parts. The first part treats the creation and ordering of this sensible world. The second, the cause of human creation and the primordial causes of all things. The third, knowledge of God: how from the beginning he was made known as both one and three. The fourth, the will of God and the diverse ways in which sacred Scripture customarily speaks of the will of God. The fifth, the creation of angels, their confirmation and fall, and the other matters pertaining to them. The sixth, the creation of humanity and humanity’s state before sin. The seventh, the fall. The eighth, restoration. The ninth, the institution of sacraments. The tenth, faith. The eleventh, the sacraments of the natural law. The twelfth, the sacraments of the written law.

We have arranged below the chapters of this book under their respective parts, as follows.

## PROLOGUE TO THE FIRST BOOK ON THE SACRAMENTS: Why He Changed His Course of Reading

[Col. 0183]

Therefore, having previously composed a concise volume on the first instruction in sacred discourse, which consists in historical reading, I have now prepared this work for those to be introduced to the second instruction, which lies in allegory. Its purpose is that, if they establish their minds upon a certain foundation of the knowledge of faith, all else that they may subsequently build upon it, whether by reading or hearing, may remain unshaken.

For I have compressed this as a kind of brief summary of everything into a single sequence, so that the mind may possess something certain upon which it can fix and to which it can conform its attention, lest it be carried away without order or direction through the various volumes of Scripture and the divergent paths of reading.

## CHAPTER I. What Must Be Learned at the Beginning

[Col. 0183A]

Whoever approaches the reading of the divine Scriptures in order to be instructed must first consider what the subject matter is about which their treatment is occupied; for, if he possesses knowledge of those things concerning which Scripture has been written, he will afterward more easily perceive the truth or depth of its sayings.

## CHAPTER II. What Is the Subject Matter of the Divine Scriptures

The subject matter of all the divine Scriptures is the works of human restoration. For there are two works in which all things that have been made are contained. The first is the work of creation; the second is the work of restoration. The work of creation is that by which things that did not exist were brought into existence. The work of restoration is that by which things that had perished were made better.

[Col. 0183B] Therefore, the work of creation is the creation of the world with all its elements. The work of restoration is the incarnation of the Word with all its sacraments: both those which preceded it from the beginning of the age and those which follow it until the end of the world.

For the incarnate Word is our king, who came into this world to fight with the devil; and all the saints who existed before his coming are like soldiers going ahead before the face of their king; while those who came afterward and will come until the end of the world are soldiers following their king. And the king himself is in the midst of his army, advancing enclosed and attended on either side by his ranks.

Although in so great a multitude diverse kinds of arms appear in the sacraments and observances [Col. 0183C] of the peoples who preceded and those who followed, nevertheless all are shown to serve one king, follow one banner, pursue one enemy, and be crowned with one victory. In all these the works of restoration are considered, and the whole intention of the divine Scriptures is occupied with them.

Worldly or secular writings have as their subject matter the works of creation. Divine Scripture has as its subject matter the works of restoration. For this reason it is rightly believed to excel all writings by so much as the subject in which its consideration and treatment are occupied is worthier and more exalted.

For the works of restoration [Col. 0184A] are much worthier than the works of creation, because the latter were made for service, so that they might be subject to man while he stood; whereas the former were made for salvation, so that they might raise him when fallen. Thus the former, as though a small matter, were completed in six days; but the latter can be completed only in six ages. Yet six are set against six in correspondence, so that the same one may be shown to be both restorer and creator.

## CHAPTER III. How Divine Scripture Descends through the Works of Creation to Narrate the Works of Restoration

Although the principal subject matter of divine Scripture is the works of restoration, yet, in order to approach their treatment more suitably, it first narrates briefly, at the very beginning of its account, the origin and establishment of the works of creation according to the truth of what occurred.

For it could not fittingly show how man was restored unless it first demonstrated how he fell; nor could it fittingly show his fall unless it first explained how he had been established by God. To show man’s first establishment, it was necessary for the founding and creation of the whole world to be disclosed, because the world was made for man.

Spirit was made for God, body for spirit, and the world for the human body: so that the spirit might be subject to God, the body to the spirit, and the world to the body. In this order, therefore, sacred Scripture first describes the creation of the world, which was made for man; then it recounts how man, once made, [Col. 0184C] was disposed in the way of justice and discipline; afterward, how man fell; and lastly, how he was restored.

Thus it first describes his substance in that he was made and disposed; then his misery in fault and punishment; then restoration and mercy in the knowledge of truth and the love of virtue; and finally the homeland and joy of blessedness.

## CHAPTER IV. That Sacred Discourse Treats Its Subject Matter in Three Ways

Divine Scripture treats this subject matter according to a threefold understanding: namely, history, allegory, and tropology.

[Col. 0185A] History is the narration of events that occurred, contained in the first meaning of the letter. Allegory occurs when, through that which is said to have happened, something else that has happened—whether in the past, the present, or the future—is signified. Tropology occurs when, through that which is said to have happened, something that ought to be done is signified.

## CHAPTER V. That in Sacred Discourse Not Words Alone but Things Also Have the Function of Signifying

From this it is apparent how greatly divine Scripture surpasses all other writings, not only in its subject matter but also in its manner of treatment, subtlety, and depth. For in other writings words alone are found to signify, whereas in this writing not words alone, but things also, are signifying.

Just as, therefore, in that sense which concerns words and things, knowledge of words is necessary, so in that sense which consists in mystical things done or to be done, knowledge of things is necessary. Knowledge of words is considered in two respects: pronunciation and signification. Grammar pertains to pronunciation alone; dialectic to signification alone; rhetoric to both pronunciation and signification.

Knowledge of things concerns two matters, namely form and nature. Form consists in outward arrangement; nature, in inward quality. The form of things is considered either in number, to which arithmetic pertains; or in proportion, to which music pertains; or in dimension, to which geometry pertains; [Col. 0185C] or in motion, to which astronomy pertains. Physics, however, pertains to the inward nature of things.

## CHAPTER VI. How All the Arts Serve Divine Wisdom

From this it is established that all the natural arts serve divine knowledge, and that lower wisdom, rightly ordered, leads to higher wisdom.

Thus history is contained under that sense which lies in the signification of words in relation to things; and, as stated, the three disciplines—grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric—serve it. Allegory is contained under that sense which lies in the signification of things in relation to mystical events. Tropology is contained under that sense which lies in the signification of things in relation to mystical acts to be done; and arithmetic, [Col. 0185D] music, geometry, astronomy, and physics serve these two.

Above all these, before everything else, is that divine end to which divine Scripture leads, whether in allegory or tropology. The one of these, allegory, forms right faith; the other, tropology, forms good action. In these consist knowledge of truth and love of virtue; and this is the true restoration of man.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Number of Books of Sacred Discourse

Having shown what the subject matter of the divine Scriptures is and how they treat their subject matter in the three senses of history, allegory, and tropology, it is now appropriate to show in what books the writing which is rightly designated by the name of divinity consists.

There are two Testaments which encompass the whole body [Col. 0186A] of the divine Scriptures: the Old and the New. Each is distinguished into three orders. The Old Testament contains the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa, a name which when translated means “holy writers” or “those writing holy things.”

The Law contains five volumes: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. Genesis is named from generation; Exodus, from departure; Leviticus, from the Levites. The book of Numbers is so called because the children of Israel are numbered in it. Deuteronomy means “second law”; in Hebrew, however, [the names are] *bresith*, *hellesmoth*, *vagetra*, *vegedaber*, *adabarim*.

In the order of the Prophets there are eight volumes. The first book is Joshua, also called Jesus Nave and Joshua Bennun—that is, son of Nun. The second is the book of Judges, called *Sopthim*. The third is the book of Samuel, which is First and Second Kings. The fourth is *Malachim*, which translates as “of kings,” and is Third and Fourth Kings. The fifth is Isaiah; the sixth Jeremiah; the seventh Ezekiel; the eighth the book of the Twelve Prophets, called [in Hebrew] *thareasra*.

These are called prophetic because they belong to the prophets, even though not all are prophecies. A prophet, however, is so called in three ways: by office, by grace, and by mission. But in common usage those are more especially called prophets who are prophets either by office or by an open mission, as in this place. According to this usage David, Daniel, and many others are not called prophets, but hagiographers.

The order of the Hagiographa contains nine volumes. The first is Job; the second, the book of Psalms; the third, the Proverbs of Solomon, called in Greek *parabolae* (“parables”) and in Hebrew *masloth*; the fourth, Ecclesiastes, called in Hebrew *coeleth* and translated in Latin “preacher”; the fifth, *syra syrim*, that is, *Song of Songs*; the sixth, Daniel; the seventh, Paralipomenon, which in Latin means “words of the days” and is called in Hebrew *dabreniamin*; the eighth, Ezra; and the ninth, Esther.

All these—that is, five, eight, and nine—likewise make twenty-two, the same number as the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Thus the life of the just is instructed toward salvation by as many books as the language of learners is instructed toward eloquence by letters.

There are besides certain other books in the Old Testament which are indeed read, but are not written in the body [Col. 0186D] of the text or in the canon of authority: the book of Tobit, Judith, the Maccabees, the book entitled the Wisdom of Solomon, and Ecclesiasticus.

The New Testament contains Gospels, apostles, and Fathers. There are four Gospels: those of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Likewise there are four apostolic volumes: the Acts of the Apostles; the Epistles of Paul; the Catholic Epistles; and the Apocalypse. Joined with the aforementioned twenty-two books of the Old Testament, these make thirty, in which the body of the divine page is completed.

The writings of the Fathers are not counted in the body of the text, because they add nothing else, but enlarge what is contained in the writings mentioned above by explaining and treating it more fully and clearly.

# THE FIRST BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0187]

# PART ONE. THE HEXAEMERON IN THE WORKS OF CREATION

[Col. 0187A]

Moved by your frequent entreaties, I undertake a work surely arduous and laborious: not only to reduce the whole sequence of the divine Scriptures to a concise summary, but also, by exposition, to bring the hidden things of its depth into the light. I offer the beginning of this work in ready devotion; in hope I promise its completion.

## CHAPTER I. That There Is One Principle from Which All Things Were Made Out of Nothing

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). Whatever is created is made out of nothing. For what is made from something is indeed made, but is not created, since it is not made out of nothing. Therefore God made heaven and earth; and he not only made them but created them—that is, he made them out of nothing.

The philosophers of the Gentiles posited three principles of things without beginning: an artificer, matter, and form. They professed that all things which have been made were produced from matter into form by an artificer. But they professed God as maker only, not as creator.

True faith, however, confesses one sole first principle which always existed; and through that principle alone it came about that what once did not exist should exist. The power of its ineffable omnipotence, just as it could not have anything besides itself coeternal with it to assist it in making, so had all things subject to it when it willed, so that whatever it willed, and whenever and however much it willed, might be created out of nothing. Therefore God not only made all things that were made from matter, but he himself created the matter of all things out of nothing.

## CHAPTER II. Whether Matter Was Made Before Form

[Col. 0187C]

But there is no small question whether the things that were made came forth simultaneously in matter and form, or whether they were first established essentially in matter and afterward formed.

I know that certain holy Fathers, who before you searched excellently into the hidden things of the Word of God, left writings that appear to be opposed on this inquiry. Some indeed maintain that all things were created simultaneously in matter and form; others more strongly uphold the view that all bodily things which were made should be believed to have first been established together and at once materially, and afterward arranged into form at intervals over six days.

I think that men of wisdom, in matters so obscure, doubtful, and remote from our perception, neither rashly asserted what they did not know nor, especially in matters they set forth with such care, could have erred. I should rather believe that beneath the form of assertion there was at times an exercise of inquiry. Those who wish to interpret the sayings of the saints piously neither fall into error by believing falsehoods nor into pride by criticizing truths.

Therefore, declining toward neither side by a hasty assertion, we set forth that to which our understanding for the present more nearly inclines, insofar as we can grasp it. Those who contend that God made all things simultaneously in matter and form perhaps judge their assertion to be correct for this reason: that it appears unworthy of the Creator’s omnipotence, after the likeness of human weakness, to advance his work to perfection by intervals of time. Moreover, certain passages of Scripture are found which in some manner assert the same thing, such as: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18).

The very text of Genesis itself—from which the first knowledge of this matter flowed to us—speaks so ambiguously of the work of the six days [Col. 0188B] that it often seems rather to prove that all things were made at once. For these and similar reasons, therefore, they say that the mystical distribution of the six days in Genesis should be believed, but that in the actual truth of the matter every creature, from the very beginning of time when it began to exist, began to exist in the condition and form which it now appears to possess, insofar as this pertains to the arrangement of the universe.

## CHAPTER III. Why God Willed to Bring His Works to Completion through Intervals of Time, and to Make Them Exist Before Making Them Beautiful

It seems to us, however—except that we do not wish rashly to determine anything in this matter—that the Creator’s omnipotence is in no way diminished if he is said to have brought his work to completion through intervals of time; provided that it is nevertheless believed without doubt that he could also have acted otherwise, if the reason of his omnipotent will had required it.

For almighty God, whose will can never be deprived of his goodness, made all other things for the rational creature; and therefore, in making all of them, he especially had to preserve that mode which was more suitable to the advantage and purpose of that rational creature. This was the mode in which provision was made for the rational creature not only by service but also by example: that is, the mode in which it received not only what it needed for service, but through what it received also recognized what it had been.

For this reason, in other things unformed matter was first made and then formed, [Col. 0188D] so that it might thereby be shown that, having previously not existed, they had received essence from him, without whom, while confused, they could in no way have form and order. In the same manner, through what was done outwardly, the rational creature itself might recognize within itself that it had its being from him who is, and that from him it must seek what it was to become. Thus it might rise in thanksgiving for what it had received, and extend itself in the affection of love toward obtaining that which it was to receive.

For the rational creature itself was in its own way first made unformed and was afterward to be formed by conversion to its Creator. Therefore unformed matter was first shown to it outwardly and then formed, so that it might learn how great is the distance between existing and existing beautifully. And thus it was admonished not to be content with having received being from the Creator through creation, until it attained both beautiful being and blessed being, which it was to receive from the Creator through conversion in love.

If anyone asks what rational creature already existed at the very beginning of the world to whom this example ought to have been offered, the ready answer is that angels had already been created, who might be admonished by this deed to know themselves; and that human beings would exist until the end, who, although they did not see this when it occurred, nevertheless, instructed by the Scriptures, cannot now fail to know that it occurred.

If the argument we have proposed appears insufficient to anyone for proving our opinion concerning the creation of things, we grant, in peace, that he may either seek some other argument, better and more subtle, for proving the same point more clearly; or, if the assertion of this side does not please him, adopt the other as he wishes. We shall, however, according to the plan we have begun, pursue the subject in order.
