## CHAPTER IV. Whether Matter Could Ever Have Existed Without Form

[Col. 0189C]

It remains, if we assert that the matter of things was first created unformed, to show whether something could have existed without form, and what sort of essence it ought to be believed to have had before form was given to it.

To state briefly what I think on this matter, I certainly do not think that that first matter of all things was unformed in such a way that it had no form whatever. For I do not believe that anything can exist which has being of some sort and yet has no form at all. Nevertheless, it can not improperly be called unformed, because, subsisting in a certain confusion and mixture, [Col. 0189D] it had not yet received the beautiful and fitting arrangement and form in which it is now seen.

Therefore matter was made before form, yet in a form: in the form of confusion before the form of ordered arrangement. In the first form, that of confusion, all bodily things were first created materially, together and at once; in the second form, that of ordered arrangement, they were afterward ordered through the intervals of six days.

## CHAPTER V. That All Things, Visible and Invisible, Were Created Simultaneously

Nor, in my judgment, will it be absurd if we believe that there was one and the same instant of time in which, in the beginning, both the matter of visible and bodily things and the essence of invisible things in angelic nature were created simultaneously. This is what Scripture means when it reports that all things were created together, as we said above: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18). For in the same instant both the matter of visible things was created essentially and the nature of invisible things was created; and afterward nothing was made whose matter, as in bodies, or likeness, as in spirits, had not preceded in that first beginning.

For although new souls are still created daily, no new creature is made, because its likeness had already preceded in angelic spirits when they were created. Two matters now present themselves for our examination: first, what that unformed condition of the first creation was like; second, how it was brought from that formlessness into the form it now possesses.

## CHAPTER VI. What the First Formlessness of All Things Was Like, and How Long the World Remained in It

[Col. 0190B]

As far as I have been able to infer from those things which I find in the Scriptures, whether stated plainly or obscurely, concerning this matter according to the truth of what was done: when that first mass of all things was created, it came forth there and then in the place where it now subsists once formed. This earthly element lay settled in the middle and lowest place (the others being mingled together in a single confusion), endowed with a better form; yet it was so enveloped by those same elements massed about it like a kind of mist that what it was could not appear. But the other three, still mingled in one confusion—or rather confused in one mingling—as has been said, hung about it on every side and extended upward as far as the highest limit of corporeal creation now reaches. [Col. 0190C] And all the space extending from the surface of the earth, lying in the middle place, to the outermost and highest boundary of heaven’s circuit was filled with that mist and darkness.

And what are now channels or hollows for waters were already prepared, at the very beginning of the world’s birth, as future receptacles for waters in the body of the earth. In these also, that great abyss—from which all streams of waters were to issue or be derived—displayed, with its mouth still open and empty, a dreadful void plunging downward. Above it stretched the mist of that dark gloom by which the whole surface of the earth was then wrapped; and these, I suppose, are the darkness which Scripture testifies to have been upon the face of the abyss when heaven and earth were created.

Such was the appearance of the world in the beginning, before it received form or arrangement, as Scripture indicates when it says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth. But the earth was empty and void” (Gen. 1); or, as another translation has it, “unordered” (incomposita); “and darkness was upon the face of the abyss” (ibid.). By “heaven” and “earth,” I think that the matter of all heavenly and earthly things is signified here, from which, successively afterward, those things were made in form which had previously been created together in it in essence. For there “earth” was the very element of earth; and “heaven” was that mobile and light confusion of the remaining three elements, borne suspended around the earth lying in the middle. In these two was contained the matter for forming all heavenly and earthly bodies. [Col. 0191A]

Then Scripture continues and says: “And darkness was upon the face of the abyss.” Above it had set forth two things, namely heaven and earth. Now it adds two others: darkness and the abyss—signifying that one, the abyss, is to be understood in the earth, and the other, darkness, in that which it had called heaven. For darkness was upon the face of the abyss because the abyss was beneath and dark gloom was above. Nor was the abyss itself darkness, since light was not to come from it; rather, the place of darkness was above the face of the abyss, namely in that element from which light was afterward to come. For darkness could exist only in the place of light; therefore darkness was upon the face of the abyss.

“And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1). Suddenly it names waters, though earlier, in the creation of things, it had mentioned only earth and heaven. Yet one must not therefore believe the waters uncreated because the name of waters was not set down in the creation of things: for heaven itself is the darkness, and the darkness itself is also the waters. It is heaven by reason of lightness; darkness by reason of the absence of light; waters by reason of movement and fluctuation. For if the abyss was in the earth and darkness was upon the face of the abyss, then darkness was above the earth. But what was above the earth? At the beginning, two things were set forth: heaven and earth. Which of these, do you think, was below, and which shall we say was above? Was earth above and heaven below, or earth below and heaven above? [Col. 0191B]

But can it be believed that, in that first condition of things, heaven was created beneath and afterward, in its formation, placed above? Perhaps someone will say that heaven was created beneath as a foundation because Scripture named heaven before earth. I judge, rather, that this order was established not for order’s sake but for dignity’s sake; and because the following discourse had to concern the element of earth as the nearer subject—and for this reason the later-mentioned one—heaven had to be named first and earth afterward. Nor would the nature of the things created allow any other order of position or location than that heavy things should be set below and light things above.

Therefore earth was below and heaven above; and that which was above earth was heaven. Therefore heaven was above earth. And where were the waters? Beneath heaven or above heaven? The waters were neither beneath heaven nor above heaven; rather, the waters were in heaven, because heaven itself was the waters. All was waters and all was heaven, because waters and heaven were the same thing. On the second day the firmament was made and called heaven; and it was placed to divide between waters and waters. Thus what had previously been waters became waters and waters: waters beneath heaven and waters above heaven. And heaven came to be—heaven and heaven: heaven above heaven, and heaven beneath heaven. [Col. 0191C]

Even to this day there is heaven above heaven and heaven beneath heaven; and all is from one heaven and is one heaven. But before this heaven, called the firmament, was made from that heaven, that heaven was not heaven and heaven, but only heaven. Nor were those waters waters and waters, but only waters. And the waters and heaven were one heaven; and that heaven and those waters were neither above heaven nor beneath heaven, but above earth. Nothing was between heaven and earth, because there was nothing besides heaven and earth.

Yet there were waters, darkness, and an abyss. The abyss was in the earth; darkness and waters were in heaven. Darkness was upon the face of the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters. Therefore the Spirit of God was above all things, because all things were in God’s power, and the power of God was not confined within any of them.

Perhaps it is now enough, so far as our intended brevity allows, to have discussed these matters thus far, if we add only how long the world remained in this confusion before its ordering began. That the first matter of all things arose at the beginning of time—or rather, together with time itself—is clear from the words: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” But Scripture does not plainly show how long it remained in this formlessness or confusion. It seems to me, however, so far as I can infer, that between the creation and the ordering of things there was indeed an order of time, but no intervening delay. Thus it may truly be said that this was done after that, but that absolutely no interval occurred between this act and that. [Col. 0192A]

To state briefly all that seems to me to be thought on the matter: I believe that at the first beginning of time—or rather, with the beginning of time itself, that is, when time itself began—the matter of all visible things began at once, and at precisely the same moment the essence of invisible things in the angelic nature: each in some way formed and each in some way without form. For just as the matter of bodies to be formed, when first created, possessed a certain form in which it began to subsist, and yet was formless because it had not yet been arranged and ordered, so too that rational nature, when first created in angelic spirits, was indeed immediately formed through wisdom and discernment; but because it had not yet, by the turning of love, impressed itself upon that highest and true Good in which it was to be made blessed, it remained in some manner still formless.

Thus both natures—corporeal through matter, and incorporeal through essence—came into being together: the former in that from which it was made, the latter in that which was made. [Col. 0192B] For spiritual nature, since it is simple and its being is altogether identical with what it is, cannot come to be materially before it comes to be personally, as corporeal nature can. Therefore, while the corporeal nature was being created, it first came into being through the matter from which it was made; whereas the incorporeal nature immediately received being in the simple life in which it subsists, and in an immortal, indissoluble essence.

Nevertheless, both were made together: the corporeal, that is, in that from which it is; the incorporeal in that which it is. Both formed, and both formless, as has been said.

## CHAPTER VII. On the distinction of formation

[Col. 0193A]

Let what has been said concerning the state of that first condition, before nature came into form and arrangement, suffice. Next follows the task of setting forth in order how that arrangement itself was perfected.

In six days God disposed, ordered, and reduced to form everything that he had made: “And he finished his work on the sixth day. And then on the seventh day he rested” (Gen. 2), that is, he ceased from work. On the first day light was made; on the second, the firmament was made; on the third, the waters were gathered; on the fourth, the luminaries were made; on the fifth, fishes and birds; on the sixth, wild animals, domestic animals, and creeping things; and lastly, though on that same day, humankind.

First, in this place, we wish to warn the reader that whenever, in these works of the six days, he hears that something is made—for example, when it is said, “On the first day light was made; on the second day the firmament was made; on the third day the waters were gathered; on the fourth day the luminaries were made”—he should not suppose merely because they are said to have been made that they were created from nothing at that point. Rather, he should understand that they were formed from the matter which had previously been created from nothing. Even if he sometimes finds a verb of creation, as there: “God created the great sea-creatures, and every living and moving creature” (Gen. 1), he should know that this refers not to the matter by which they began to exist, but to the form by which they began to be what they are. [Col. 0193B]

## CHAPTER VIII. On the mystery of light; why it was made first

God, therefore, beginning his works in order to complete them, first made light, so that afterward he might make all other things in the light. For he signified to us that he does not love works done in darkness, because they are evil. “For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved, because they are evil. But whoever does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be made manifest, because they have been done in God” (John 3).

Therefore he who was to do truth was unwilling to work in darkness; rather, he came to the light and made light, that he might manifest himself through the light. He did not make light so that he himself might see by means of light, but so that he might make his works manifest through light, because they were done in God. And therefore “God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1). For the moment, this is what I had to say in accounting for why God first made light.

## CHAPTER IX. What sort of light it was, and where it was made

[Col. 0193C]

But now it remains to pursue more carefully the truth of what was done. The beginning of the divine works, therefore, was the making of light, when light itself was not materially created from nothing, but was formally made from that pre-existing matter of the universe, so as to be light and possess the power and property of shining. This work was done on the first day; but the matter of this work was created before the first day. And with the light itself, day immediately began, for before light there was neither night nor day, although there was time.

If, however, it is asked what sort of light this was—corporeal or incorporeal; and, if corporeal, what sort of body it had; whether confined in one place or spread everywhere; whether in motion or motionless—it seems to me that the most correct answer is that, since it was to illuminate corporeal and visible things, it could only fittingly have been corporeal light. But every body, however subtle and however nearly it approaches spiritual nature, must be confined to a place. Again, unless that light had been movable, it could not by alternating succession distinguish day and night, nor could it by any means complete the course of time without movement. [Col. 0194A]

Accordingly, I think it more fitting to believe that this light made in the beginning to illuminate corporeal things was undoubtedly corporeal, perhaps like some luminous body whose presence illumined all things, as may now be seen in the sun. I believe that it was made in the role and place of the sun, so that for the time being it might be carried round in its motion and distinguish night and day. Since the first day arose with it, I believe rather that, when it was made, it first appeared there where the sun, carried in its daily course, rises in the east. Traversing the same path, it first descended in the west to make evening, and then, brought back to the east, it illumined the dawn—that is, the morning before the rising of the following day.

And because the first day had no preceding dawn, since before light was created there was complete darkness, while immediately upon light’s appearance over the earth there was full day, and because God’s work ought to have begun from what was complete, Scripture therefore said: “And evening and morning came: one day” (Gen. 1). It did not say, “Morning and evening came,” but: “Evening and morning came: one day.” For, as we have said, the first day had no preceding morning because it began from full and perfect light. Thus every dawn belongs to the preceding day, and every day begins from the rising of the sun. [Col. 0194B]

A natural day is that period of time which passes from sunrise to sunrise and includes within itself both night and day. Since day naturally precedes night, we call evening the end of the day and dawn the end of the night; it is unquestionably evident that dawn must always be referred to the preceding day.

Therefore, at that first moment of time when the nature of all visible and invisible things was created, there was neither night nor day; nevertheless, there was time, because there was mutability. Afterward, immediately upon the making of light, darkness and light were divided, and time began to be distinguished by day and night.

## CHAPTER X. That visible and invisible light were made together and divided together from darkness

[Col. 0194C]

And it seems to me that at precisely the same moment at which light was visibly and corporeally divided from darkness, the good angels were invisibly separated from those evil angels falling into the darkness of sin; the former turned toward the light of righteousness and were illuminated by the light, so that they might be light and not darkness. For the patterns of God’s works had to correspond in such a way that visible works of wisdom should follow the outcomes of invisible ones, according to which the wisdom working in both exercised judgment there and formed an example here.

Thus light was divided from darkness; and there was visible light and visible darkness; likewise there was invisible light and invisible darkness; and a division of both was made, and the division of darkness and light was made at once. “And the light was called day, and the darkness night.” God divided both and named both, yet he did not make both. For God is not the author of darkness but of light, because sin is darkness and sin is nothing: “And without him nothing was made” (John 3). Light was made by him, because righteousness and truth are light; and concerning the light we have heard that God said: “Let there be light,” and immediately light was made (Gen. 1). Nowhere did God say: “Let darkness be made.” [Col. 0195A]

But concerning light he said: “Let there be light”; and he divided light from darkness; and he called light day and darkness night (ibid.). Therefore he did not make both, yet he divided both and named both. He divided by judgment and named according to merit; he judged and arranged. For even what was disordered among the sinners could not be disordered in the judgment of God: he called light day and darkness night.

## CHAPTER XI. That light illuminated for three days, and why it was made before the sun

Therefore let no one say, “How could there have been day before the sun was made?” For before the sun was made there was light: “And God saw the light, that it was good, and called the light day and the darkness night” (Gen. 1). That very light made those first three days before the sun was made and illuminated the world.

But what does it signify that the sun was not made immediately when light had to be made, but rather that light existed, as it were, before clear light? Perhaps the confusion was not worthy of full light; nonetheless, it received some light, so that it might see itself emerge into order and arrangement. [Col. 0195B]

## CHAPTER XII. The sacrament of the divine works

I think that some great mystery is commended here. For every soul, so long as it is in sin, is as though in a kind of darkness and confusion. Yet it cannot escape its confusion and be arranged into the order and form of righteousness unless it is first illuminated to see its evils and discern light from darkness—that is, virtues from vices—so that it may bring itself into order and conform itself to truth.

A soul lying in confusion cannot do this without light. Therefore light must first be made, so that it may see itself, recognize the horror and ugliness of its own confusion, unfold itself, and fit itself to that rational arrangement and order of truth. But when all its things have been ordered and set in accordance with the pattern of reason and the form of wisdom, then at once the sun of righteousness will begin to shine upon it, for thus it has been said in the promise: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5).

Therefore light is first created in the rational world of the human heart, and the confusion is illuminated in order that it may be reduced to order. After its inner parts have been purified, the clear light of the sun comes and illumines it. [Col. 0195C] For it is not worthy to contemplate the light of eternity until it has been cleansed and purified, possessing in some manner both a likeness through matter and an arrangement through righteousness.

Thus law preceded grace; word, Spirit; thus John the forerunner preceded Christ; light, light; the lamp, the sun. Christ himself first showed his humanity in order afterward to manifest his divinity; and everywhere light precedes light: the light that illuminates sinners toward righteousness precedes that light which illumines those made righteous toward blessedness.

Thus light was made before the brightness of the sun was revealed, and there was day; and there were three days when there was light and no sun. On the fourth day the sun shone forth, and that day was clear because it possessed the true light and there was no darkness at all. So no soul deserves to receive the light of the sun and contemplate the brightness of highest truth unless these three days have first preceded within it.

On the first day light is made, and light and darkness are divided; light is called and becomes day, and darkness night. On the second day the firmament is placed between the upper and lower waters, and the firmament is called heaven. On the third day the waters beneath heaven are gathered into one place, and the dry land is commanded to appear and to be clothed with its grasses. [Col. 0195D] All these things set forth spiritual teachings.

First light is created in the heart of the sinner when the person begins to know himself, so as to divide light from darkness and begin to call light day and darkness night; thus he is no longer among those of whom it is said: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness” (Isa. 5). Then, when he has begun to divide light from darkness and call light day and darkness night—that is, when he begins truthfully to condemn his evils by the judgment of reason and to choose what is good and praiseworthy, the works of light—it remains for a firmament to be made within him: that is, for him to be strengthened in a good purpose.

It must divide between the upper waters and the lower waters, that is, between the desires of flesh and spirit, so that, standing in the middle as mediator, it permits neither the mingling nor transposition of two opposing things: so that what ought to be divided may not be together, nor what ought to be below be above, nor what ought to be above be below. Finally, in the order of this arrangement, the work of the third day follows: the waters beneath heaven must be gathered into one place, lest fleshly desires remain fluid and extend beyond the boundary of necessity. Thus the whole person, restored to the condition of nature and ordered according to reason, gathers every desire into one place, so that flesh may be subject to spirit and spirit subject to the Creator. [Col. 0196A]

Whoever is thus ordered is worthy of the sunlight: with mind raised upward and desire fixed upon things above, the light of highest truth shines upon the contemplator, who no longer knows and tastes truth “through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13), but knows and tastes it in himself as it is.

Nor should this be passed over carelessly: “God saw the light, that it was good; and he divided the light from darkness; and he called the light day, and the darkness night” (Gen. 1). For he made and saw; then he divided and named. Why did he see? He was unwilling to divide before he had seen; he first saw whether it was good, and only then divided light from darkness and called light day and darkness night. For he will bring every work into judgment.

God not only saw that the other works which he made in the light were good; he also saw that light itself was good, and divided light and darkness. For the evil angel sometimes transforms himself into an angel of light and presents himself to deceive the mind as though he were true light. But this light must not be divided from darkness nor called day, but night; for it has the appearance of light but true darkness. [Col. 0196B]

For this reason God first saw whether the light was good, so that we may not immediately believe every spirit, but “test the spirits, whether they are from God” (John 4). When we have seen that the light is good, then at last let us divide light from darkness and call light day and darkness night.

Therefore we must strive not only that light may precede in our works and that our works may be done in light; the light itself must first be examined and considered diligently. Finally, once we have seen that the light is good, let us divide light from darkness and call light day and darkness night.

## CHAPTER XIII. Why Scripture says: “God saw the light”

But perhaps the question occurs: how did God see that the light was good, divide light from darkness, call light day, and darkness night (Gen. 1)? For if he saw that his other works were good in light, in what light did he see that light was good, divide light from darkness, and call light day and darkness night? Nothing can be seen without light; but darkness itself is not seen without light—how much more is light not seen without light?

What, then, was that light through which God saw that the light was good and divided light from darkness? Did he see that it was good through that very light, or through another light? But how could he have seen through it that it was good if he did not possess another light through which and in which he saw that light itself was good? [Col. 0196C]

For if he saw that this light was good and truly saw it, he saw it in something whose goodness could not be doubted. Therefore there is another, uncreated light in which this created light was seen to be good, because it imitated that light which is always good. For in that light, since it alone is good, both evil and good are seen; and not only are evil and good seen in it, but evil is seen to be evil and good to be good, because it itself is truly and supremely good. For what seems to disagree with it is seen to be evil, and what seems like it is seen to be good; and neither is seen except in it and through it.

Therefore he tested light through light, because in unchangeable light he saw that this changeable light was good in its own manner and order. He divided light from darkness and called light day and darkness night. And in the light in which he saw that light was good, he also saw that his other works were good; and he saw nothing, good or evil, without that light—whether among the good things he himself made or among the evil things that we made, all of which he saw not evilly but well. [Col. 0196D] And he saw there where he saw no evil.

This is the very light by which we too must see whether every light is good. We cannot judge truly whether a light is good until we have been illuminated by this light, which is truly good: “The spiritual person judges all things, and is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2). And if the Spirit of God truly dwells in us, spirits of error will not be able to deceive us, even if they come to us in light; for we shall have light within us, in which it will be manifest to us concerning every light whether it is good.

Thus we shall confidently divide light from darkness, and we shall judge not only between darkness and light, but also between light and light; not only between night and day, but also between day and day; and we shall judge every day. For it is too little, for perfection, to judge between day and night; it is too little to divide light and darkness—that is, to separate virtues from vices—unless we also know how to judge between day and day and to judge every day: so that we may understand which impulses come to us under the appearance of virtues, as though in borrowed light, and which are from above and display the true brightness of virtue; and so that among virtues themselves we may test not only which are good but which are greater. “The spiritual person judges all things, and is judged by no one,” because “the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (ibid.); and “his anointing teaches us about all things” (1 John 2). [Col. 0197A]

## CHAPTER XIV. What caution in good works is signified here

Here attend to how much caution must be applied to a good work. At the beginning of all your works, see that you have light within yourself, so that all your works may be works of light and not of darkness. Then carefully consider whether your light is pure and not darkened; and when you find that it is good, only then divide it from darkness and call light day and darkness night.

Then examine whether the rest of your works, which you have done in the light, are also good. Let no work whatever pass without judgment, until you recognize all that you have done. Thus the judgment is twofold. The first is that in which the light is judged and seen to be good, in order that it may be divided from darkness. The second is the judgment in which the works themselves done in light are summoned to judgment and seen also to be good; and only then does God rest.

For the moment, passing rapidly over the subject, we have touched upon certain mysteries of light. Let us now return to weave together the sequence of our undertaking.

## CHAPTER XV. What became of that primary light after the sun was created; and whether the sun was substantially made from it

[Col. 0197B]

God therefore wished first to make light to illuminate the world before creating the sun, as a temporary and substitute aid, until that which is perfect should come. Some ask what became of that light, since no trace of it can now be found after the brightness of the sun shone forth.

Some say that, scattered through the broad spaces of the air, it lost its power of shining and illuminating; but that certain thin remnants still remain, visible at night to careful observers, scattered here and there within the circuit of the firmament, while by day they are hidden by the greater brightness of the sun and cannot be seen. Thus people devise their opinions as best they can according to what seems possible.

But who knows whether that same light was afterward transferred into the substance of the sun and, with its brightness enlarged, received a better form? So Jesus at the wedding made wine from water, to signify the condition of reformation for the better and the mystery of restoration. For light existed before the sun was made, just as water existed before it was changed into wine, so that not something different might be made, but rather something might be produced from that very thing which before had been held in lower esteem. Thus, concerning doubtful things, no one can define anything with certainty. [Col. 0197C]

## CHAPTER XVI. Whether God worked through the six days without interval, or in some other way

One question alone remains concerning the work of the first day: whether God created light at the first rising of that same day—that is, of the first day. Since we read that he made nothing else on that day except light, should we believe that he ceased from work until the rising of the following day, when he made the firmament, although Scripture testifies that he rested only on the seventh day?

We shall meet this question with a twofold answer. Either we shall say that during those six days God continued his work with such unbroken persistence that he never ceased working for any interval of time; or that he worked during the six days in such a way that he omitted no day from working, though not without ceasing to work for some period of time.

For if we wish to establish the former assertion—that his work was continuous—we may say that on the first day he made light at the day’s rising, then directed it first from east to west and then from west to east, so that by its course it might distinguish day and night. Nor was his work only that light was made, but also that, governed and directed by him, it completed its course. [Col. 0197D] The same will be said of the second day, when the firmament was made and received at the same time the command and law of perpetual revolution. Anyone who chooses to maintain this view will investigate the same point concerning the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth days, as reason shall dictate.

But if this interpretation seems too obscure to anyone—especially because the assertion concerning the motion of the firmament is not yet established—let him have recourse to the other exposition we proposed, which is easier and lends itself more readily to understanding. He will say, then, that God worked for six days and afterward rested from work on the seventh day, because among the six days none is found on which God did not work, until the seventh day came, when he afterward rested from every work.

Let this suffice concerning the work of the first day.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the work of the second day, when the firmament was made

[Col. 0200A]

“And God saw that it was good; and he said: ‘Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters’” (Gen. 1). God, therefore, was unwilling to proceed to the next work until he had judged the first. When, then, he had seen that the light was good, he said: “Let there be a firmament.”

As regards the literal sense, the firmament was made on the second day: it had indeed first been created from nothing in that matter of the universe, and now was drawn forth from that same matter and made into such a firmament that, intervening somehow in the middle by its enclosing circuit, it might separate and divide from one another that great and immense mass of waters, and make waters into waters and waters—that is, waters which it enclosed within its circuit and held beneath itself, and waters which it left outside and above the circle of its boundary. [Col. 0200B]

## CHAPTER XVIII. From what matter the firmament was made, and what sort of thing it was made

There are indeed many questions concerning the nature of the firmament which might press upon the mind, if human inquiry did not see that they should rather be left alone than investigated. For it might properly be asked whether it was made of pure fire, or of air, or even of water, or finally of two or three of these mingled; whether it has a solid and tangible substance; how great its density should be believed to be; whether it is hot or cold; or what other quality it possesses—if anything certain could be known about it.

But now I do not think that we should labor much over questions of these matters, since neither reason comprehends them nor authority worthy of faith proves them. We must believe without doubt only what we read: that the firmament was made to divide waters from waters, that is, to enclose one part of the waters within its circuit and separate another part outside it. [Col. 0200C]

## CHAPTER XIX. The mystery of the things stated above

But why the firmament was made to divide the waters from itself, and why the nature of those same waters should remain partly above and partly below, let no one who believes that these things were made for his sake seek outside himself. For in that inner world which has been fashioned there is something possessing the form and pattern of this work. There, in the lower place, is a kind of earth: the sensual nature of the human being. Above is heaven: purity of understanding and reason, quickened as it were by a motion of immortal life.

But between these two natures, so unlike one another yet existing in one human being, wanders a great mass of desires, fluctuating on either side and often tending in contrary directions through alternating movements. For one thing is what the flesh, pressed down by weakness, desires below; another is what the spirit, raised upward by contemplation of truth, seeks above.

But contrary movements sometimes generate confusion unless reason intervenes between them to divide and distinguish their wills and judge their desires: namely, what draws downward from the flesh and what reaches upward from the spirit, seeking that highest and immortal Good. [Col. 0200D] For when reason itself places itself in the middle like a firmament, with the strong judicial authority of judgment, and separately orders the waters above heaven on the one hand and the waters beneath heaven on the other, the lower corruption cannot infect the lower purity of the soul; nor is the sincerity above permitted to incline itself toward the abject and low things beneath. [Col. 0201A]

## CHAPTER XX. Why God is not said to have seen that the work of the second day was good
But it is remarkable why God did not see the work of the second day to be good, as in all the other days it is written: “And God saw that it was good.” [Cols. 0201B–C] Either it was not his work, and it was not good; or, if it was his work, it was good. But if it was good and was his work, he surely saw that it was good—he who could not be ignorant of what existed, whether it was good or evil. Why, then, is it not said here, “God saw that it was good,” as everywhere else it is said, “God saw that it was good” (Gen. 1)? For if it is said elsewhere because it was made, why should it not also have been said here, if it was made?

Perhaps because the number two is a sign of division, being the first to depart from unity: some sacramental meaning is being commended here. The second works, then, were not praised, not because they were not good, but because they were a sign of evil things. For God made the first works, and they were all very good (ibid.); in them there was neither corruption nor lack of perfection. But afterward the devil and the human being came and made their own works; and these were works of the second order after the first, evil after good. God did not will to see those works because they were evil; rather, what he saw through wisdom, he rejected through judgment.

## CHAPTER XXI. How the waters were gathered into one place so that the dry land might appear [Cols. 0201C–D]

And God said: “Let the waters which are under heaven be gathered into one place” (Gen. 1). Taken literally, the one place into which the waters beneath heaven were gathered is believed to be the great abyss, which is thought to have been made from the very beginning of the world within the body of the earth with such capacity that it could contain all waters.

For the nature of water at the beginning was exceedingly thin and light, dispersed like a kind of mist. After, by divine power and command, it began to be compressed, as it were, and condensed into a single mass, it inclined downward by its own weight, sank to the depths, and was received by the earth. It left clear and pure the space which it had occupied above, up to the very firmament. The surface of the earth itself also began to appear, once all the waters had been enclosed within their channels. At first it was muddy, slippery, and bare, as one which had not yet put forth any shoots by which it might be clothed and covered.

## CHAPTER XXII. How the earth produced shoots [Col. 0202A]

God therefore said that the earth should bring forth green grass bearing seed, and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit according to their kind, whose seed should be in themselves upon the earth; and it was so (Gen. 1). Then, to irrigate the whole earth, waters were led from that great abyss as from a fountain: inwardly, indeed, through the bowels of the earth by hidden channels and concealed passages; and above, upon its surface, through their beds into every region—by a wonderful and unceasing going and returning, according to an everlasting law, to one place.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Why Scripture does not say that the waters above heaven were gathered into one place [Cols. 0202A–D]

Of those waters which are above heaven, Scripture does not say that they were gathered into one place, as it says of those which were beneath heaven. Great mysteries lie in all these matters, and they cannot be explained within the present brevity: that the waters beneath heaven are gathered into one place; that dry land appears and produces shoots; that at the same time the spaces of the air, at length freed from contracted darkness, grow clear; and that streams of water are scattered through its body in every direction for watering and soaking the earth. Nothing was made without a reason.

This seems remarkable: the waters beneath heaven are gathered into one place, whereas those above heaven are neither gathered nor assigned one place, but are left spread out and extended, as though waters did not wish to be confined or collected. What do you think this signifies, except that “the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5)? These are the supercelestial waters; for the Apostle says: “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12). “Though I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels; though I have all prophecy; though I know all mysteries”—what is it? It profits nothing if I do not have love (1 Cor. 13). “May the peace of God,” he says, “which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds” (Phil. 4).

We now see, in some measure, why those waters above heaven ought not to have been gathered and confined into one: because love must always be enlarged and extended; and the more widely it is spread abroad, the more loftily it is raised. But the waters beneath heaven must be gathered and confined in one place, so that from there they may be led everywhere through definite courses and ordered outlets. For unless the lower affection of the soul is restrained by a definite law, dry land cannot appear, nor can it produce shoots. Thus the Apostle disciplines his body and reduces it to servitude, lest, after preaching to others, he himself should perhaps become disqualified (1 Cor. 9).

## CHAPTER XXIV. That during those three days the arrangement of things was made [Col. 0202D]

Behold, these are the works of three days, before the sun or the other luminaries had been made. In these first three days the fabric of this universe was arranged and distributed among its parts, with the firmament expanded above. Then the earth was uncovered, settled in the depths, and balanced by its own weight; the masses of water were gathered into their receptacles; and the air was made clear. The four elements of the world were distinguished and ordered in their proper places.

## CHAPTER XXV. How the world was adorned during the following three days [Cols. 0203A–B]

Then followed the adornment of these things, and this likewise was accomplished in the next three days. On the fourth day, which was the first of the three, the firmament was adorned with sun, moon, and stars. On the fifth day, which was the second of the three, the air received its adornment in birds and the waters in fish. On the sixth day, which was the third of the three, the earth received beasts, cattle, creeping things, and the other living creatures that move upon the earth.

But on the final day the human being was made from the earth and upon the earth—yet not for the earth, nor on account of the earth, but for heaven and on account of him who made earth and heaven (Gen. 1). Therefore the human being was made not as an adornment of the earth, but as its lord and possessor, so that the condition of the one for whose sake the earth was made should not be referred to the earth.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Whether the things made for the adornment of the elements were made from the elements themselves [Cols. 0203B–C]

If someone asks about the adornments of the elements whether one ought to believe that the things made for the beauty or ornament of each element were created from those very elements, so that, for example, things made to adorn the earth could be taken only from the earth: even if we grant that this is true of the other elements, we cannot establish it in any way concerning the element of air. For we plainly read that birds received both their origin from the waters and their dwelling in the air.

Why this occurred—why they did not, like the other things created for the adornment of the elements of the world, take their material from that very element in which they were destined to have their place—someone might perhaps refer to the material nature of the element itself: air may not have possessed such bodily density that the bodies of living creatures, which require solid material, could be formed from it. The nature of water, however, is more akin to earth and possesses greater corporeality, and is therefore better suited for forming bodies. Yet a deeper force of sacramental meaning is presented in these matters.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The sacramental meaning of why fish and birds were made from one material, yet were not placed in one dwelling [Cols. 0203C–D]

There are two kinds of living creatures that proceed from one origin, yet they do not receive one dwelling-place. Fish remain in their original seat. Birds are lifted upward and become, as it were, above that from which they were made. Thus the entire offspring of the human race is drawn from one mass of corruptible nature, subject to dissolution through its own mutability; yet some are justly left below in the corruption in which they were born, while others are raised above by the gift of grace to the lot of the heavenly country. The equity of judgment is preserved.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Why the works of creation are first recalled, and then the works of restoration [Cols. 0204A–B]

Very many other mystical things could be said concerning these days. But we have touched on these matters swiftly, as though outside our subject, so that we might have a more fitting approach, as it were, from what preceded to the treatment of that same subject. For we intend, so far as the Lord grants in this work, to treat the sacrament of human redemption, which from the beginning was prefigured in the works of restoration.

But because the works of creation were earlier in time, we took the beginning of our discourse from them, so that from there we might make a path in due order to the matters that follow. We call the works of creation the creation of all things, when things that did not exist were made to exist; but the works of restoration are those by which the sacrament of redemption was fulfilled or figured, through which what had perished was restored.

Therefore the works of creation are those made in the beginning of the world during six days; whereas the works of restoration are those accomplished from the beginning of the world for the repair of humankind through six ages. To express this in a brief definition, we say that the works of restoration are the incarnation of the Word, and the things which the Word performed in the flesh and through the flesh, together with all its sacraments: both those which preceded from the beginning of the world in order to prefigure that incarnation, and those which follow until the end of the age in order to announce and proclaim it.

All divine Scripture speaks of these things, and all divine Scripture was made concerning them and for their sake. For just as the books of the Gentiles investigate and discuss the works of creation, so the divine utterances devote their principal effort to discussing and commending the works of restoration.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That the discussion is chiefly occupied with the works of restoration [Cols. 0204B–D]

Therefore, in the works of restoration the mystery of redemption must be investigated from its beginning. If we diligently seek this throughout all these matters according to the sequence of times, the succession of generations, and the ordering of commandments, we may confidently declare that we have attained the whole sum of the divine Scriptures.

This must begin with the creation of the first parent; and, as we advance, we must always look gradually toward those matters which follow in order. But we briefly gather together in this concluding statement what is needed for understanding what is to be said.

The works of creation—that is, this sensible world with all its elements—were made in matter, before every day, in time and together with time; afterward they were arranged into form during six days: ordered during the first three days and adorned during the following three. Finally, on the sixth day, Adam and Eve were made, for whose sake all the other things were made. He was placed in paradise, first to dwell and work there, so that, when the work had been completed and obedience fulfilled, he might then be carried from there to that place where he would remain forever.

But because we intend to derive the sequence of the following work from the creation of the first human being, it is right that at the very beginning of this book we should first investigate the cause of human creation, so that it may at the same time be shown that humanity was first created rationally by God and afterward mercifully restored. There, when it was created, a gratuitous rational work was made; here, when it was redeemed, a work of grace was rationally fulfilled.

## CHAPTER XXX. The four matters through which the following discourse proceeds [Cols. 0205A, 0206A]

There are, then, four matters through which the following discourse must proceed in order: first, why the human being was created; next, what kind of being the human was created; then, how the human fell; and finally, how the human was restored.

# PART TWO. ON THE CAUSE OF HUMAN CREATION, AND ON THE PRIMEVAL CAUSES OF ALL THINGS [Col. 0205]

## [CHAPTER I] [Cols. 0205B–0206C]

At the beginning of the work—which I undertook more at your urging than through any eagerness of my own—I explained, as briefly as I could and in the manner best suited to introducing the purpose before us, the origin and arrangement of this sensible world. It now follows that we should pursue in discourse the creation of the human being, for whose sake the world itself was made, proceeding in our argument according to the very order which the Creator of things himself displayed in his work.

For God the Craftsman first made the world; then he made the human being, possessor and lord of the world, so that the human might rule all other things by right of creation, being subject in free will only to him from whom he had been made. Hence it is clear that the creation of humankind, though later in time than the creation of all visible things, was prior in cause: for the one made after all things was the one for whose sake all things were made.

The cause of human creation, therefore, is before all things; and it must be sought above all things, before all things which arose in time and were ordered before times. For if God made all things for the human being, the human being is the cause of all things; and causally the human being is prior to all things. But that for which the human being was made is prior to the human being, and far prior to all things to which the human being is causally prior.

And what is that for which the human being was made, except the one by whom the human being was made? Therefore, if the human being is the cause of the world because the world was made for the human being, and God is the cause of the human being because the human being was made for God, then God existed while neither world nor human existed. The human being who did not exist was made for God, and the world was made for the human being who did not yet exist. It thus appeared that the same kind of causation obtained in the human being’s being made for God and the world’s being made for the human being.

For the human being was made to serve God, for whose sake the human was made; and the world was made to serve the human being, for whose sake the world was made. It was, as it were, the same, and yet not the same, because those for whose sake they existed were not the same. God was perfect and full of consummate good; he had no need to be helped from elsewhere, since the eternal could not be diminished nor the immeasurable increased.

The human being, however, was by nature in need of another’s aid, either to preserve what had been received as mutable or to increase what was not possessed in perfection. Thus the human being was placed in the middle, so that others might serve the human and the human might serve another; so that the human might receive from both sides and claim the whole for himself. Everything, both the service received and the service rendered, was to flow back to the good of the human being.

For God willed to be served by the human being, yet in such a way that by that service not God but the serving human being might be helped. He willed the world to serve the human being, and in this way likewise the human being might be helped. The whole good was to belong to the human being, because the whole was made for the human being.

Therefore every good belonged to the human being: both that which was made for the human being and that for which the human being was made. But one good was below and was received from beneath for necessity; the other was above and was received from above for happiness. The good placed in the creature was the good of necessity; the good in the Creator was the good of blessedness. Both were directed toward the human being because both were owed to the human being: the human was made for the one, in order to possess and enjoy it; the other was made for the human, in order that the human might receive it and be helped by it.

Thus the condition of the rational creature is shown to surpass all the other things made for its sake, inasmuch as it is itself the cause of them all. But it has no other cause except him from whom it exists. For just as it is from him that it exists at all, so it is for him that it may exist blessedly: receiving from him one thing, namely that it should exist; and receiving in him the other, namely that it should exist blessedly.

But someone will say: Why did God make a creature if he could not himself be helped by the creature? He made for another what he did not make for himself, when there was no other except himself who made it. For it seems as though it were made for nothing and lacked any cause for being made: the one who made it was not helped by it, since he was perfect and had no need; nor was another helped by it, since apart from him who made it there was no other who could be helped.

Perhaps this, more carefully considered, may trouble someone. Therefore the cause of rational creatures’ creation, which we have located in the sole Author of all things, must be investigated by a general consideration—not only on behalf of human beings, of whom our proposed discourse is concerned, but also on behalf of angels. For as they share the same nature, so too they derive their cause from the same fountain of origin. In this cause lies the beginning of all things that have been made.

## CHAPTER II. On primeval causes and their effects [Cols. 0206D–0207C]

The order and arrangement of all things, from highest to lowest, proceeds in the structure of this universe through certain causes and the productions of principles, so that nothing whatever among all things that exist is found by nature unconnected, separable, or externally alien.

For all things whatsoever are found either to be causes of subsequent effects or effects of preceding causes. Some things are causes only and not effects, such as the first cause of all things. Others are effects only and not causes, such as the last and final things in the universe. Others, however, are both causes with respect to the later things that they produce and effects with respect to the prior things by which they are produced.

Just as among the last things, which are only effects of earlier things, nothing later is seen, so among the first things, which are only causes of what follows, nothing earlier is found. Among intermediate things, those which are earlier are called causes more properly and effects less properly; those which are later are effects more properly and causes less properly. The first are most causal. Those which are first after the first are the first effects; those which are last before the last are the last causes. The last things are generated, and the first things generate.

Of first causes, some are created and are first in their own genus; others are uncreated and are universally first. Those which are first in their own genus are first in relation to something, but they are not universally first. For although they precede all that follows them, they themselves have something by which they are found to be later, since they do not precede everything.

For in this universe of all things, all cohering causally, something first is found such that nothing among all these can be earlier than it, because it is the first of all of them; yet something must be prior to it, because it belongs among all those things of which something is universally prior. But no cause is prior to those causes which are universally first, because they themselves are first of all things and have no other causes prior to them, since they are causes of all things.

## CHAPTER III. On the production of primeval causes [Cols. 0207C–D]

These produce without movement and generate without transmission, because eternity neither abandons its own state while ordering times nor supplies substance from itself while creating corruptible things. Remaining what it was, it made what did not exist, containing within itself the power of making but not taking from itself the material of what was made.

For in creating lower things it did not degenerate, as though its nature descended into the things to which it gave a beginning. For its omnipotent nature itself contained the power to create nature without nature, so that things which did not exist might receive a beginning; since the work and its maker could not be the same nature.

Therefore, just as eternity was not diminished in making things, so immensity was not increased in the things made. Before things were made, it stood full without deficiency; after they were made, it remained unfailing without movement. It assumed nothing new and lost nothing old, giving all things and rejecting nothing.

This first cause of all things worked its work according to itself and for itself: according to itself, because it did not receive the form of its work from without; for itself, because it had no cause of working from elsewhere. For it made, in its own likeness, that which it was ordaining for participation in itself, so that what was to possess the same good together with it might derive the same form from it.

## CHAPTER IV. What is the first cause of the creation of rational beings [Col. 0208A]

From this, then, the condition of rational creation took its first cause: God willed, by his eternal goodness, that creatures should become participants in his blessedness, which he saw could be communicated without being diminished in any way.

That good which he himself was, and by which he himself was blessed, was drawn to communicate itself by goodness alone, not by necessity. For it belongs to the best to will to benefit, and to the most powerful to be incapable of harm.

## CHAPTER V. That divine will possessed both goodness and power [Col. 0208B]

Divine will would not have been perfect by goodness alone unless power had also been present with it. For what it willed with goodness preceding, it fulfilled with power following. In the predestination of those to be created, goodness was at work; in the creation of those predestined, power was at work; but in the beatification of those created, power and goodness were at work together.

## CHAPTER VI. On the three things that are perfect and perfect all things [Cols. 0208B–D]

There were, indeed, three things, and these three were one; these three were eternal; nothing could be perfect without these three, and with them nothing was deficient. For it necessarily followed that, if these three were present, nothing necessary to perfection was lacking; but if one of these three were lacking, nothing could be complete.

These three were power, wisdom, and will. The three concur in every effect, and nothing is accomplished unless they are present. Will moves; knowledge orders; power works. If you distinguish them, to be able is not the same as to know, nor to know the same as to will; yet in God, being able, knowing, and willing are one. Reason distinguishes them, but nature does not divide them. The undivided Trinity comes to us, containing all things; without it, all is nothing.

Whatever is truly said of God, or can be devoutly believed concerning God, is contained in these three: power, wisdom, and goodness. All three are alike complete.

If you call God immense, incorruptible, eternal, immutable, or anything of that kind, all this belongs to power. If you call him knowing, foreknowing, observing, searching, considering, or discerning, all this belongs to wisdom. If you call him gentle, mild, compassionate, kind, or anything of this sort, all this belongs to goodness. There is nothing that is not in these three; and whatever is in them is wholly full and complete.

For this reason these three were specially distinguished, and the catholic faith received the Trinity. It did not wish to increase it in number, lest it appear to confess something outside the three; nor did it wish to confuse it in nature, lest it be convicted of denying something belonging to the three. It found that in God there are three, and that in God the three are one. The three were not thereby not three because they were one; nor was the one not one because it was three.

Admonished by the three, it said that the three are three persons, because they were God by nature and one substance, and therefore one God. It assigned power to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Holy Spirit; and it confessed the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER VII. That these three are said of God according to substance [Cols. 0209A–B]

The Son seemed, as it were, not powerful from himself, since power belonged to the Father; nor did the Father seem wise from himself, since wisdom belonged to the Son; nor did the Father or Son seem good from himself, since goodness belonged to the Holy Spirit. If this were said, truth would suffer scandal and unity division; nor could one be called perfect in the three if he lacked as his own something which another possessed singly.

Therefore the Father’s power was also the Son’s and the Holy Spirit’s, and it existed substantially and equally. The Son’s wisdom was also the Father’s and the Holy Spirit’s, existing substantially and equally. The Holy Spirit’s goodness was also the Father’s and the Son’s, existing substantially and equally. Yet there was cause for what was the same substantially to be distinguished personally.

## CHAPTER VIII. Why these three, though said according to substance, are found in certain passages as though attributed specially to the persons [Cols. 0209B–0210A]

Faith did not signify the persons through these three as properties, because they existed according to substance; rather, it assigned these three to the persons according to a necessary conception, in order to affirm that they existed by the communion of nature.

The Father and the Son had to be named in the Trinity, and the very terms were taken from human usage, to which they had first been given. What was similar only in one respect had to be spoken of as similar in every respect. The prudence of sacred speech guarded against a full likeness being believed between unequal things if, in the Godhead, the Father were called prior or the Son later.

For in human beings nature is such that no one can be a father who has not been earlier than his son, nor a son who is not later than his father. Therefore power was assigned to the Father and wisdom to the Son, not because one had it more, but because one was more liable to be believed to have it less.

Holy Scripture had said that God is Father. A human being heard this, having seen a human father but not seen God the Father; and began to think, according to the human being seen, of a long span of time, a multitude of years past, and the infirmity of old age. Scripture then intervened and called the Father powerful, lest you believe him powerless or less powerful; not merely powerful, but almighty. Thus he was not said to be the only one who was this because the Father alone was this, but because the Father alone was thought to be less so.

Again, when Scripture called the Son God, lest a human being who knew human things but not divine things should suppose some diminishment of sense and understanding in the Son, as though he were still below the perfection of completed age, it added “wise.” This was not because he alone possessed what was common to all, but because he alone was the one of whom it could more readily be doubted whether he possessed it.

The Spirit also was called God, and God was said to have Spirit. This seemed, as it were, a name denoting inflation and swelling; human consciousness was troubled concerning God by thoughts of harshness and cruelty. Scripture then followed and moderated its expression, calling the Spirit gracious, lest he who was gentle be thought cruel.

Things common substantially were thus personally distinguished so that the human mind might learn not to judge the truth of divine things by human things, when it heard certain things said of God contrary to human custom.

God the Trinity, therefore, brought all his works to completion by this threefold power, so that perfect things might follow and imitate their perfect Author. Whatever appeared in time had been arranged before times in eternity. That eternal arrangement had as its coeternal cause the will of the Creator of all things, by which it came to pass that whatever was made was made; and that will itself was not made.

## CHAPTER IX. That the wisdom of God, though one in itself, receives diverse names in relation to us [Col. 0210B]

Divine wisdom is called knowledge, foreknowledge, disposition, predestination, and providence: knowledge of things existing; foreknowledge of things future; disposition of things to be done; predestination of those to be saved; providence of things subjected to governance.

All this was one wisdom and one disposition, and it was eternal. The will coeternal with it was present with it; the disposition was according to the will, yet it was not later than the will.

## CHAPTER X. That the will of God concerning a temporal work was eternal [Cols. 0210C–D]

According to his will, he arranged what he would make by his will. The will was eternal, but the work of the will was not eternal. For he always willed to make it, but he did not will always to make it; rather, he willed at some time to make what he always willed at some time to make.

Thus the will concerning a temporal work was eternal, because time itself was in the eternal will, when that which would be future should come to be. These two, then, goodness and wisdom, were alike in the Creator, and they were eternal; coeternal power was likewise present. By goodness he willed, by wisdom he arranged, and by power he made.

There seems, as it were, to be a distinction and temporal succession. Goodness first presents itself to consideration, because through it God willed; then wisdom, because through it he arranged; and power last, because through it he made. For there appears to be an order: will first, disposition after it, and operation following last. Unless he had willed, he would not have arranged; and unless he had arranged, he would not have made. Weighty reasoning at once presents itself, because in human beings will always precedes deliberation, and deliberation is followed by action.

But what are we to do? Shall we dare to introduce times into eternity? For if these things are in God as they are in human beings, something in him was earlier and something later; and God is not wholly eternal God. But it is impious to confess this.

## CHAPTER XI. That the three in God were coeternal [Col. 0211A]

Therefore, by eternal goodness he always willed, and by eternal wisdom he always arranged, what by coeternal power he makes at some time. Goodness, wisdom, and power always existed together; and those which were substantially the same could not be divided or separated from one another in time. By these God the Craftsman gave form to his work: by these all things were brought to completion from the beginning of the age and ordered at the beginning of eternity.

## CHAPTER XII. That the three visible things of the world display the three invisible things of God [Col. 0211A]

In the three things there was found an ineffable Trinity: in the Creator these are one, but through the appearance of creation they pour themselves forth, divided for knowledge. The immensity of things received the form of power; beauty, that of wisdom; usefulness, that of goodness. These appeared outwardly and converged with another, more perfect image within.

## CHAPTER XIII. That the likeness of God is more perfect in the rational creature than outside it [Cols. 0211B–C]

For the rational creature came possessing within itself a more perfect likeness of these things in will, counsel, and power. It compared what it found outside with what it possessed within, and joined the two, so that through visible things it might see invisible things. Stimulated to recognition by what appeared outwardly, it perceived from itself the Creator’s power, wisdom, and goodness.

These were, as it were, the first reminder and recollection that God is threefold; but not yet the perfect completion of recognition, because they belonged to substance and those which were one could not be individually divided. For power did not belong individually to the person of the Father, since it also belonged to the Son and Holy Spirit; nor did wisdom belong individually to the person of the Son, since it also belonged to the Father and Holy Spirit; nor did goodness belong individually to the person of the Holy Spirit, since it also belonged to the Father and Son.

Thus the Trinity was proclaimed from these things, but not signified in them. Yet these three were eternal, were the cause of all things, and through them all things were made, whereas they themselves were not made. We assigned will to goodness, disposition to wisdom, and operation to power. Then there arises a grave inquiry and profound investigation concerning God’s will, his foreknowledge, providence, disposition, and power. For all these lie in the causes of things and present a question to the proposed inquiry.

## CHAPTER XIV. On God’s knowledge and foreknowledge; and that necessity seems to arise in things from it [Cols. 0211D–0212B]

For necessity seems to befall God with respect to things to be made, as though the Creator could not exist unless creation existed. Then, from God’s own foreknowledge and providence, another necessity seems to arise in things made or to be made: as though it could not happen that what God has foreseen or foreknown should not occur. Both possibilities trouble the mind and disturb reflection with equal incongruity.

First, then, we must consider by what reasoning a necessity of making things seems to befall God from his foreknowledge and providence, from the disposition and predestination of the things which were to be made by him. For every knowledge, foreknowledge, providence, disposition, or predestination seems to be directed toward something and to concern something.

Every knowledge, indeed, is “of something” because it is in someone; and it is “of something” because it concerns something. For everyone who knows knows something; one who knows something does not know nothing. Knowledge concerning nothing is no knowledge at all. Therefore all knowledge is of something, because if there were nothing of which there could be knowledge, there would be no knowledge.

Consequently, there would not be eternal knowledge or foreknowledge in God unless there were something future of which it could be knowledge. If nothing had been created or was to be created, nothing in the Creator would have been known or foreknown. Thus there would have been neither knowledge nor foreknowledge. But if there had been no knowledge in the Creator, it plainly follows that he himself would not have been Creator, since he certainly could not exist without knowledge—for in him, being and knowing are the same.

Therefore, in order that knowledge or foreknowledge could exist in the Creator, it was necessary that something should exist or be future, of which it could be knowledge; since, as has been said, if it were of nothing, it would be nothing. For every knowledge is knowledge of something and is about something. Therefore, if the Creator’s foreknowledge depends causally upon creatures, what is created will seem to be prior to the one who created it.

## CHAPTER XV. How all things were in God eternally before subsisting in themselves; and how there was not foreknowledge there of them, but knowledge
Can we say that all things which were created by the Creator in time existed in him uncreated from eternity, and were known there where they were possessed; and were known in the manner in which they were possessed; and that God, who possessed all things in himself, knew nothing outside himself? [Col. 0212C] Nor were they there because they were to be here; nor should their being there be believed to have been caused by these things here; nor did they come here because they were there, as though those things could not have existed without these. For those things would have existed even if these things were not to proceed from them; only they would not have been the cause of these things, if these were not to be.

## CHAPTER XVI. If future things had not existed, God’s wisdom would have been knowledge, but it would not have been called foreknowledge.

There would indeed have been knowledge of things which were; but there would have been no foreknowledge of things which were not going to be. Nor would anything have been less in the Creator if there had not been foreknowledge of things that were not going to be; because that which is foreknowledge would have been knowledge even if it had not been foreknowledge, since [Col. 0212D] there would have been nothing future.

## CHAPTER XVII. How both are eternal: being foreknown and being future.

But now, what has been foreknown from eternity has been future from eternity; yet the thing which is future is not itself eternal. For if it were eternal, it would not be future but present. And it was not foreknown before it was future; rather, it was foreknown before it came to be, and it was future before it came to be. And before it came to be, while it was still future, it could contingently have been that it would not happen; and this could always have been so, as long as it was future that it would not happen, just as it was always future that it would happen. What was future belonged to the fact that it was future; what could be belonged to the fact that it could be and was not future. [Col. 0213A] Thus, from eternity these two ran together: that which was future, and that which could be but was not future.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How, if the outcomes of things were changed, foreknowledge nevertheless would not be changed.

And if what could be had occurred, although it was not future, then that which was not future would have been future and foreknown; nor would the foreknowledge of this future have been changed, but it would never have been possessed, because it would not have been future. But what God predestined, he resolved that he himself would do; and he predestined only what he was going to do. Yet he foreknew certain things which he was not going to do, because he foreknew everything that was going to be; among these future things were some which he was going to do, and some which he was going to permit. Therefore predestination seems to contain something more than foreknowledge, [Col. 0213B] because foreknowledge extends even to what belongs to another, whereas predestination can exist only concerning what belongs to oneself.

## CHAPTER XIX. On God’s providence, and on the fact that God’s providence is twofold: toward what is his own and what is other.

If, however, you ask about God’s providence, we rightly say that providence is care for those things which must be supplied to subjects, and which it is fitting to bestow upon those entrusted to one. It is written: “For he himself has care for all things” (Wisdom 12). This, then, is that providence by which God cares for all that he has made; he abandons nothing among all things that belong to him and are subject to him, but provides for each that it may have what is owed and fitting to it. According to this universal providence over all, he dispenses what is due not only to his own things, which he made good, but also to things alien to him, [Col. 0213C] which he did not make evil but permitted; so that nothing in his kingdom escapes just ordering. For even iniquity itself receives its wages from this providence, and even malice could not fall into oblivion with the Provider of all things. Do you wish to know the wages of iniquity and sin? It is written: “For the wages of sin are death, but the grace of God is eternal life” (Rom. 6). The wages of sin are death; the wages of righteousness, life. Death is given to sin, life to righteousness; punishment to guilt, glory to virtue. Each receives what is its own. This is providence: it operates in both spheres, in what is its own and in what is alien. In what is its own, which it made; in what is alien, which it permitted. All things are subject to him, and he provides for all, presiding over all: the governance of creation, [Col. 0213D] the glorification of righteousness, the condemnation of malice.

## CHAPTER XX. On the divine ordering.

In like manner, divine ordering is considered in two ways. Good things have their ordering from above: both that they exist, because they are good, and that they exist as they do, because they are ordered. Evil things, however, do not have from the higher ordering that which they are, insofar as they are evil; yet they do have from it that they are as they are, because they are ordered. For God does not make evil; but when it has been made, he does not allow it to remain disordered. For he is not the author of evils, but their orderer.

## CHAPTER XXI. On divine predestination.

Predestination is the preparation of grace.
