The purpose [Col. 0214A] of God, therefore, in which he resolved to give grace to his elect, is predestination itself; and it is called predestination because in it what was to be done was arranged before it was done. Sometimes, however, predestination may be understood generally as the ordering itself of things to be done; so that God may be said to have predestined from eternity whatever he was thus going to do. But what he was not going to do, but was going to permit, he did not predestine, but only foreknew.

## CHAPTER XXII. On God’s power, and on the fact that power is considered in God in two ways; and that in both ways God is omnipotent.

As we have said certain things about God’s wisdom in relation to time, so too it is necessary to recall certain things about his power for the instruction of readers. Power [Col. 0214B] is twofold: one kind is power to do something; the other, power to suffer nothing. In both respects God is most truly affirmed to be omnipotent. For there is neither anything able to inflict upon him corruption to be suffered, nor anything able to bring an impediment to his acting. For he can do all things except only that which cannot be done without injury to him; yet in this he is no less omnipotent, because, if he could do it, he would not be omnipotent. I say, therefore, that God can do all things; and yet he cannot destroy himself. For to be able to do this would not be ability, but inability. Therefore God can do all things which ability is power to do. And therefore he is truly omnipotent, because he cannot be impotent.

Let those, then, who suppose that they investigate divine works by reason, [Col. 0214C] and confine his power within a measure, now go and glory in their own judgment. For when they say, “He can do thus far and no farther,” what is this except to enclose and restrict within a measure his power, which is infinite? They say: “God cannot do otherwise than he does, nor can he do better than he does.” For if he can do otherwise than he does, he can do what he did not foresee; and if he can do what he did not foresee, God can act without providence. For he does everything which he foresaw that he would do, and he does nothing which he did not foresee. If, therefore, his providence cannot either be changed, so that something other than what was foreseen may occur, or frustrated, so that what was provided may not occur, then everything that was provided must occur, and nothing that was not provided [Col. 0214D] can occur. Moreover, whatever happens is certainly foreseen, and whatever is foreseen will undoubtedly happen. If it is impossible for anything to occur apart from providence—and everything foreseen to be must necessarily occur—then it is in no respect possible for anything other than what happens to occur.

Further, whatever God does: if he can do it better than he does, then in this very point he does not do well, because he does not do in the best way what he does. For he would do better if he did what he does better. Indeed, to do something and not will to do it better is, even when one is doing good, to do badly. But a devout mind cannot endure this to be said of God; and hence it seems immediate and consequent that he cannot do better than he does, since he acts in such a way that he does not act badly in what he so does.

By causes and arguments of this sort some are led to say [Col. 0215A] that God is so constrained and bound by the measure and law of his works that, beyond what he does, he can do nothing either otherwise or better. And thereby they are plainly shown to bind that infinite and immeasurable power of divinity under a limit and measure, since they extend it only as far as something that truly has an end, and deny that it proceeds beyond. For it is certain that everything made “in number, weight, and measure” (Wisdom 11) has its own determinate limit and end. Therefore, if the Creator’s power is made commensurate with the measure and mode of his work, it is undoubtedly declared to be limited by end and measure.

Accordingly, lest we seem either without cause to refuse assent to arguments which appear plausible, or indiscriminately, without examination, to accept falsehood for truth, we must briefly answer the matters stated. First, it must be considered whether God can, for any reason, do otherwise than he does without either changing or frustrating his providence. For it is certain that everything which happens was foreseen from eternity as going to be, because from eternity it was going to be—though it was not itself eternal. And we say that what will be can possibly not happen. If what will happen did not happen, and its not happening is possible, it would never have been future or foreseen. Because it will happen, it has always been future and has been foreseen. Therefore no change or frustration of providence appears here; for, as it has been foreseen, so it will happen; just so, if it had not been foreseen, it would not happen.

“But,” they say, [Col. 0215C] “it has now been foreseen.” Certainly: it has been foreseen because it will be. And they say: “But providence cannot be changed or frustrated; whereas the event may be prevented, so that what is future does not occur. But if the event of a thing were prevented—which can happen—providence would be changed or frustrated, which absolutely cannot happen.” But we answer that, if the event, which can happen, were changed, providence would neither be changed nor frustrated, because this absolutely cannot happen. Rather, what had never been going to be would never have been foreseen; and providence would stand in this: that it should not occur, just as it now stands in this: that it should occur—not changed so as to become one thing after another, but so as never to be other than it is. Therefore God can do otherwise than he does, provided that he himself, in doing otherwise, does not become other. [Col. 0215D] Whether he does the same or something different, he nevertheless always remains the same.

It remains now to examine whether God can make something better than what he makes. Here those investigators of ours, who have exhausted themselves in investigating investigations, say that they bring forward something new—and truly new, though not so much true as new. They say that individual creatures, considered separately, fall short of perfection; [Col. 0216A] but that the whole universe of all things is expressed in such a consummation of goodness that it cannot be better than it is. Here I first demand an answer: when they say that the universe of things cannot be better than it is, how should their statement that it cannot be better be understood? Is it because it is supremely good, so that no perfection of goodness at all is lacking to it; or because it cannot receive the greater good which it lacks?

But if it is called supremely good in such a way that no perfection of goodness is lacking to it, then the work would plainly be made equal to its Creator; and either what is within the boundary is extended beyond it, or what is supreme is constricted below immensity—both of which are impossible with equal absurdity. But if it cannot be better because it cannot receive the greater good which it lacks, then this very inability is a defect, not a consummation; and it can be better if it is made capable of a greater good, since he who made it can do this also. Therefore it cannot be better in itself, but it can in God; because it cannot, but God can, and how much he can cannot be spoken. Therefore he himself cannot be better. But everything which he has made can be better, if he who can do so wills it. And he can make better what he has made—not by correcting something badly made, but by advancing something well made into better; not so that he, in respect to himself, may act better, but so that what he has made may become better while he himself repeatedly acts and remains the same. Therefore he is supremely [Col. 0216C] powerful, who can do everything possible; nor is he less powerful because he cannot do impossibilities, since to be able to do impossibilities would not be power but inability. Thus God can do all things which ability is power to do; and therefore he is truly omnipotent, because he cannot be impotent.

Since, then, there are three things in God—wisdom, power, and will—the primordial causes proceed, as it were, from the divine will; are directed through wisdom; and are brought forth through power. For will moves, wisdom orders, power unfolds. These are the eternal foundations of all causes and the first principle, ineffable and incomprehensible to every creature. For as time does not equal God’s eternity, nor place his immensity, so neither does understanding equal his wisdom, nor virtue his goodness, [Col. 0216D] nor a work his power. Many questions remain concerning God’s will and providence. First, whether God’s foreknowledge and providence compel things—a matter already much discussed. Afterwards, certain things must be said concerning God’s will. Yet first we must turn, with the eyes of faith, to contemplate him himself, as far as human frailty permits.

# PART THREE. ON THE KNOWLEDGE OF DIVINITY.

[Col. 0217]

## CHAPTER I. How God was known from the beginning, and that he is one and three.

[Col. 0217A]

Scripture says: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1); nevertheless faith believes what it does not see. And the merit of faith consists precisely in not having seen and yet believing. Hence that fine saying: “For if you see, it is not faith.” Faith therefore believes what it has not seen; and it has indeed not seen what it believes. Yet it has seen something by which it was admonished and stirred to believe what it did not see. For God so moderated humanity’s knowledge of himself from the beginning that, just as what he is could never be wholly comprehended, so too that he is could never be wholly unknown.

## CHAPTER II. Why God can neither be wholly known nor wholly unknown.

[Col. 0217B] Therefore God willed from the beginning neither to be wholly manifest to human consciousness nor wholly hidden, lest, if he were wholly manifest, faith should have no merit and unbelief no place. For unbelief would be convicted by what was manifest, and faith would not be exercised by what was hidden. But if he were wholly hidden, faith would receive no assistance toward knowledge, and unbelief would be excused on the ground of ignorance. Accordingly, it was necessary for God, though hidden, to disclose himself, lest he be wholly concealed and utterly unknown; and again, having disclosed and made himself known in some measure, to conceal himself, lest he be wholly manifest—so that there might be something known to nourish the human heart, and again something hidden to summon it onward.

## CHAPTER III. By what means the knowledge of God comes to humanity.

[Col. 0217C]

The first matter now to consider is how God, hidden, concealed, and latent, was first apprehended by the human heart, so that it could be known that God exists, or believed that he existed. There are two modes, two ways, and two manifestations by which God, though hidden, was from the beginning disclosed to the human heart and judged to be concealed: namely, partly through human reason and partly through divine revelation. Human reason itself apprehends God by a twofold inquiry: partly in itself and partly in things outside itself. Likewise, divine revelation by a twofold disclosure made known him who was unknown or only doubtfully believed, and confirmed what had been believed in part. For at one time, illuminating human ignorance within by inspiration, it instructed; at another time, outwardly, it either taught through doctrinal instruction or confirmed through the display of miracles.

The Apostle explains both modes of divine manifestation—by which God was known by humanity through human reason or made manifest to humanity through divine revelation—when he says: “What may be known of God is manifest in them; for God revealed it to them” (Rom. 1). He then adds: “For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are perceived by the things that have been made” (ibid.). For when he says, “What may be known of God,” that is, what is knowable concerning God, he shows that God is neither wholly hidden nor wholly manifest. But when he says, “It is manifest in them,” and does not say, “It is manifest to them,” he plainly shows that it had been made known to them not only by divine revelation, which had been made to them, but also by the human reason which was in them. And when he adds, “But God revealed it to them,” he shows that human reason would have been wholly weak and insufficient for investigating and understanding such lofty and sublime matters unless divine revelation had been joined to it as an aid and support for knowing the truth.

After showing the inward mode of inquiry or revelation, he immediately adds a statement concerning the outward mode of both, saying: “For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are perceived by the things that have been made.” For the invisible things of God, which were inward and hidden, were seen through the things outward and known: either by human reason in the creation of things, or made visible by divine revelation in their governance and administration. [Col. 0218B]

## CHAPTER IV. That God is three and one; and what belongs to unity and what to Trinity.

Thus from the beginning God was disclosed to human consciousness, and faith, aided by indications of truth, confessed that God exists and that he is one. Then it also confessed that he is three. In unity it confessed eternity and immensity; in eternity, immutability; [Col. 0218C] in immensity, simplicity—that is, eternity without time and immensity without quantity. But in the Trinity it confessed the communion of unity, the equality of immensity, and the coeternity of eternity: communion of unity without division; equality of immensity without diminution; coeternity of eternity without order or succession. This is what it means for each, in unity, to be whole; in immensity, full; and in eternity, perfect.

## CHAPTER V. Explanation of the distinctions proposed.

It is now necessary to consider in sequence each of the points proposed: how the human mind, which is so far from God, could have comprehended so much concerning God, whether guided by its own reason or assisted by divine revelation. First, it is worthy of consideration how far human reason itself has prevailed through the innate light of truth, lest, if everything is attributed to humanity, we should be convicted of denying grace, or, if everything is taken away, of excusing ignorance. Let us therefore pursue in order both modes of human inquiry, by which human reason, either guided through itself or prompted by the natural visible things outside itself, has striven to know the truth.

## CHAPTER VI. On that kind of knowledge by which the rational mind can see God in itself.

[Col. 0219A]

First let us examine that which was within it, since this too was its first and principal mirror for contemplating truth. Therefore the invisible God could first and principally be seen there—according to the manifestation already expounded—in that which had been made nearest and most akin to his image and likeness. This was reason itself and the mind using reason, which had been made according to the first likeness of God, so that it could discover through itself him by whom it had been made.

## CHAPTER VII. That the rational mind sees that it itself exists.

For, to speak of the first thing that occurs, even among those who know, the mind can scarcely fail to know that it itself is something, when, from all the things [Col. 0219B] it sees in itself—that is, in its own body—it sees that none is itself or can be itself. It therefore separates and distinguishes itself, through itself, from that whole which it sees visibly within itself; and it sees itself to be altogether invisible, in that it sees itself and yet sees that it cannot be seen. Therefore it sees that invisible things exist, though it does not see them visibly, because it sees itself to be invisible and yet does not see itself visibly.

## CHAPTER VIII. And that it understands that it has begun.

Since, therefore, it cannot doubt that it exists—because it cannot be ignorant of itself—it is compelled, from itself, also to believe this: that it remembers that it once began, since it cannot be always existent because it cannot fail to know itself while it exists. Since, therefore, it sees through and in itself that it began and had a beginning, it cannot be ignorant of this either. [Col. 0219C] For when it did not exist, it could in no way give itself a beginning and subsistence in order that it might exist.

## CHAPTER IX. That God exists and is without beginning.

Therefore, in order that what did not exist might begin, it was made by another who did exist. And this other necessarily did not himself begin to exist through another, since one who received existence from another could not be the first author of existence for all things. Therefore, he who gave existence to all things could not receive existence from another; and for this reason we must confess that he has always existed and never began, since everything which at some point began to exist had an author through whom it began. It is certain, therefore, and cannot in any way be doubted, that he through whom that began which did not always exist never began, but has always existed. In this way reason investigates that author of things and first principle; piety venerates him when found, and faith proclaims him to be worshipped as God. [Col. 0219D]

## CHAPTER X. An argument for the same matter drawn outwardly from creatures.

Reason confirms this discovery within itself also in the things which it sees outside itself. For all things having birth and passing away could have neither origin nor restoration without an author. That all these things at some time began cannot be doubtful, because in their parts, without ceasing and daily, that which does not exist is seen to arise, and that which exists to pass away. But everything mutable must once not have existed, because that which could not remain while present indicates that it once did not exist before it existed. Thus the things outside answer the things seen within, [Col. 0220A] to confirm the truth; and nature proclaims its author, showing that it was made by him.

## CHAPTER XI. That God is three and one.

Thus reason, through reason, discovers that God exists; and another line of reasoning comes, proving not only that God exists but that he is one and three: first through itself, then through those things outside itself which were made according to it. One piety, one devotion, one worship: one Lord and one God. Thus reason declared and proved within itself, lest there should be a schism of minds into many principles and no secure salvation. It declared that it is better, more consonant with truth, and more agreeable to nature that there be one principle and one end, toward which all things existing from it may have a return. Otherwise, the universe would be a dispersion without head, principle, [Col. 0220B] or governor. And nature cried out from without, bearing witness to the same truth, saying: one work and one author; one concord, one counsel; one administration, one providence. And God was shown to be one: one Creator, one governor, and one ruler, because the whole is one and the one is whole.

## CHAPTER XII. That God is truly and supremely one.

Reason approved and accepted these things, and said that he is one: not by an aggregation of different things, lest he make a crowd; nor by a composition of parts, lest he form a mass; nor by the likeness of many, lest a superfluous plurality or an imperfect singularity appear. For every unity consisting only in the likeness of many either shows imperfection in the part, if the individual members have less, or superfluous duplication in the whole, if all are perfect. In all such cases there is no true unity; they merely imitate unity, because in some fashion they approach it, but do not attain it. For they are not one; and those things which are said to be truly one are not one, but are merely joined and brought together. Their being together and converging into one is called being one. Yet they are not truly one, because they are not one essentially, nor is the whole which they are one. But God must be one, essentially one, immutably one, and supremely one. For what is essentially one is truly one; what is immutably one is supremely one. What is good in both respects is better in both than in either alone. To be essentially one is good; to be immutably one is good; and to be both is better. But God is the highest good, and a good which is better cannot be absent from the highest good. Reason urges that the better good be attributed to the best. Therefore it confesses that its God, its author, and its principle are one, because this is better; truly one, because he is substantial; and supremely one, because he is unchangeable. [Col. 0220D]

## CHAPTER XIII. That God is immutable.

Reason ascends, passes beyond, and proves that this is so: that God cannot at all vary or change. [Col. 0221A] For he who is immense cannot be increased; nor can he who is one be diminished. He cannot be changed in place, because he is everywhere; nor in time, because he is eternal; nor in knowledge, because he is supremely wise; nor in affection, because he is supremely good.

## CHAPTER XIV. That, when rightly considered, creation assists reason in knowing God.

Creation cries out from without, proves this reasoning, and commends it as true. The supreme beauty of the work shows the perfect wisdom of the Creator. The enduring permanence of its beauty reinforces this. What was first established as good is not diminished. Creation says that his wisdom is eternal and cannot at all be diminished; the fullness of his understanding never declines from perfection. Reason proceeds with this further testimony and sees that God’s will is eternal, and that to hold this is good. His work, which does not change, and the abiding order of the universe prove it. Reason itself adds that nothing is new to God, such that he should begin then or now to love what he formerly did not know; or, like a human being, forget an ancient affection, so that what had formerly been known should not come to mind; or mistake evil for good, so as to love what ought not to be loved, and afterwards, as though repenting, change heart and alter affection when he begins to recognize his error. Such things are not worthy of God, nor does reason approve our thinking thus of him who is wise, good, and perfect. No mutability is found in him, when every kind of mutability has been brought under consideration, [Col. 0221C] whether those found in bodies or those affecting the nature of spirits.

## CHAPTER XV. In what ways bodies change.

Every body changes either in place, form, or time. Things that change in form undergo either increase, diminution, or alteration. In things undergoing alteration, it does not appear that anything is added which was not there, nor is it shown that anything which was there departs; rather, what was there is merely altered and possessed otherwise. This does not occur without place, because the parts change place while the whole remains the same; yet it occurs only in respect of place. Nevertheless, it is not called change in respect of place because the whole does not change place, but because another form appears in the whole owing to the parts which have changed place. Therefore this is called change in form, because it is manifestly seen in the whole. It is not called change in place, although it occurs in the parts in respect of place, because this is not manifestly seen. Form is nothing other than the arrangement of the parts in the whole; when this changes—because the parts change place—the form of the whole changes, because the arrangement of parts, which is the form of the whole, changes. Thus change of form in the whole cannot occur without change of place in the parts. But change of place is said only when the whole changes place while its parts remain together in the whole.

Thus change of time follows change of place and form, and in a body never occurs without them. For only according to these is there order and succession, [Col. 0222A] which is called time. Again, it must be considered that, of these three changes, two occur externally, because they do not change the being of the thing, but something about the thing: namely, change of place and time. Again, the first change brings about the second and third, because it is their cause; the second brings about the third, because it is its cause; but the third is only brought about and brings about nothing, because it is only an effect. Change of form alone is called intrinsic, because it changes something not around the thing but in the thing itself; yet it too does not occur without change of place and time.

## CHAPTER XVI. In what ways spirits change.

After these changes of bodies—to which all things that change bodily are subject—we pass to spiritual creation, considering its mutability: which of these changes may apply to it, and whether any other change beyond the nature of bodies may occur in it. We see that a spirit cannot at all grow by increase of parts, because it is not a body; nor decline by diminution, because it is a simple nature. Yet spirit changes in affection and knowledge. It passes from this to that, varies, and undergoes the alternation of joy, sorrow, repentance, and will; knowledge increases, forgetfulness befalls it; it varies its thoughts and understands successively. This change of knowledge and affection in it is, as it were, a change of form. Temporal change follows this, and it is subject to time because of those things in it which vary. No one can doubt this of a created spirit, because it changes in time in respect of the things which do not remain the same in it. [Col. 0222C]

Concerning change of place, however, great uncertainty arises among investigators. For there are some who say that no spirit can change in place, because place, properly speaking, is the seat of a body and the capacity for a body, defined with respect to the body—at times what is in it, at times that in which it itself is. And a body is not place, since place is not a thing and does not posit a thing; rather, it is as it were an emptiness and void where a body is or can be, and it is not itself a body. Yet it is called place only when determined by a body: either by what is in it, according to the boundary of dimension where the body ends and is no further; or by the body which contains the place; or by the circumscription of the body itself, [Col. 0222D] because within that circumscription the body is not.

Thus nothing can be in place except what has bodily dimension and circumscription, because place is constituted according to bodily dimension and circumscription; and this can in no way belong to a spirit, which is devoid of bodily quantity. Therefore only a body can properly be in place, change place, and be in time. A created spirit, however, is not in place, because it is not a body; it does not change in place, but in time. The Creator Spirit is neither in place nor changed in place, because he is not a body; nor is he changed in time, because he is altogether unchangeable.

Therefore it is rightly ascribed to body alone both to be a certain thing, because it is defined; to be somewhere here, because it is circumscribed; and to be sometime now, [Col. 0223A] because it is variable. To a created spirit it belongs to be a certain thing, because it is defined, and to be sometime now, because it is variable; but not to be somewhere here, because it is not circumscribed and cannot receive dimension. But to the Creator Spirit it belongs neither to be a certain thing, because he is not defined; nor to be somewhere here, because he is not circumscribed; nor to be sometime now, because he is unchangeable. Yet he is truly and essentially present to everything which is a certain thing, to everything which is somewhere here, and to everything which is sometime now, because he is in all things, everywhere, and always: always without time, everywhere without place, in all things without limit or definition.

We by no means accuse this lofty consideration of falsehood; yet we judge its terms too elevated and forceful beyond the capacity and possibility of weaker and simpler understanding. [Col. 0223B]

## CHAPTER XVII. That God exists essentially and truly; and is in every creature, nature, or essence without being himself defined; in every place without circumscription; and in every time without vicissitude or change.

We judge, then, and altogether approve that it ought to be affirmed far more soundly, fittingly, and truly that God is substantially, or essentially, properly, and truly: in every thing, whether nature or essence, without being defined by it; in every place without circumscription; and in every time without changeability. For what certain foolish persons—indeed, persons who savour only of the flesh and consider only the things of the flesh—suppose, namely, that the defilements and contaminations of bodily filth could affect God if He is said to be essentially or substantially present in all things [Col. 0223C], is so frivolous that it does not deserve an answer, since even a created spirit cannot be contaminated by bodily filth.

For if bodily filth affects spirits, let them themselves say how the human soul, placed in flesh, can remain undefiled, when no greater contamination or pollution can be found than that of human flesh. Let them say, concerning the flesh of a leper—whose touch even a human being cannot endure without horror—how it does not defile a holy and righteous soul which lives in it so entirely without pollution that it is even cleansed from pollution through it. [Col. 0223D] Finally, let them answer whether they think it preferable to grant concerning God that God is nowhere, or that He is everywhere. But if it is altogether absurd to confess that God is nowhere, they must necessarily, by their own judgment, confess what is also more fitting and more beautiful to say: that He is somewhere.

For those who have chosen to serve words rather than truth, and think that only that is to be rejected from which popular ears recoil, ought rightly not to depart from their own opinion in this matter either. Let them therefore say, if they dare bring themselves to utter it, that God is nowhere; and let them not immediately infer from this that what is nowhere is altogether nothing. If, therefore, it cannot suitably be said that God is nowhere—He whom it is necessary to believe both to exist and to exist more truly than all things that exist [Col. 0224A]—let them say where He is. For if He is somewhere and is not everywhere, then there is where He is and where He is not; and God thereby becomes local and is bounded by a limit and an end—which is altogether impossible.

We must therefore admit and confess without doubt that the divine nature, which by reason of its immensity can be absent from nowhere, is truly and essentially in every place; yet it is comprehended by no place, because it is altogether incapable of circumscription. Thus it is wholly wherever it is: it contains all and penetrates all. Nothing of all the things made by it can exist without it; and it can neither be divided, because of its simplicity, nor defiled, because of its purity, nor in any way comprehended, because of its immensity.

## Chapter XVIII. How created spirits are local, and how bodies are.

[Col. 0224B]

Certainly, concerning a created spirit, we confess that it is more fitting to say, and more suited to understanding, not only that it is in a place but that it is local, without doubt. It is in a place because it is seen to be present here or somewhere; it is local because, although it is somewhere, it is not found everywhere. For everything that is defined is in some respect local, because, in the very fact that it has an end and limit, it has place and determines a place, just as it is determined in a place.

But a body, because it possesses extension, is circumscribed by place, since with respect to place a beginning, middle, and end are assigned to it. A spirit, however, because it does not admit extension but is bounded by definition alone, does not indeed receive the circumscription of place [Col. 0224C]; yet it is in some manner enclosed by place, because, though wholly present here or somewhere, it is not found elsewhere. Thus a body is local because it is circumscribed by place; a spirit likewise is rightly called local because it is enclosed in a place through the presence of its nature and operation.

But the uncreated Spirit, because He is present in every place and yet can be enclosed or circumscribed in no place, is truly said to be in every place; yet He is never, on any ground, called local. I do not, however, fail to know that some have wished universally to remove place from every spirit, because they have proved that place consists only in extension and bodily circumscription. But their consideration, as we said above, has departed too far from common usage and ordinary intelligibility [Col. 0224D]. Rather, those expressions should be adopted for use in speech which naturally accommodate themselves to the matter and introduce nothing extraneous to the truth.

## Chapter XIX. The reasoning by which God is not only one but also three.

We have now said how true reason proves that God is one, and judges to be true the things pertaining to the unity of the Godhead. It further argues and establishes that God is not only one but also three. This inquiry and reflection, too, has good and true exemplars from God. For God, who could not be seen in Himself, was manifested in His work; and human reason saw Him not in Himself, because He was invisible, but in His likeness [Col. 0225A], because it was made for this purpose: that God might be seen in it.

## Chapter XX. On the external and internal word.

For just as a human being’s wisdom is not seen except by that person himself until it goes forth and is manifested through speech, so God’s wisdom was invisible and could be known only by Him whose it was, until it was manifested through His work. And that wisdom itself was the Word.

But it was, as it were, an inward and hidden word, which could not be known at all unless it were manifested through an outward word; just as a person’s thought is, as it were, that person’s inward word, hidden and concealed until it is revealed by the utterance of the mouth. The very utterance of the voice is a word, just as the thought of the heart is a word. But the manifest word [Col. 0225B] comes forth and reveals the hidden word.

So too in God, the inward, hidden, and invisible Word was the word of His heart; and this invisible Word was wisdom, until it was manifested through the outward word which became visible—namely, His work. As the word of the heart is manifested through the word of the mouth, so every nature speaks to its Author and indicates its Maker to those who possess understanding.

## Chapter XXI. That the image of God is more express in the rational creature, and that a trace of the Trinity is found in it.

In these things there are certain likenesses, as though signifying from afar and possessing resemblance in part. [Col. 0225C] Others, marked by an express image and perfect imitation, produce a clear demonstration. Therefore, the invisible things of God are more readily recognized in those things in which they are displayed by a more evident manifestation. For those things reveal their Author more perfectly which approach more closely to His likeness.

Such is the rational creature itself, which was made excellently and properly in His likeness. It recognizes its Creator, whom it does not see, more readily when it understands itself to have been made in His image. Thus the first trace of the Trinity was found in it when it began to recognize what was within itself and, from that, to consider what was above itself.

For it saw that wisdom is born from itself and is within itself; that it loves its own wisdom; and that love proceeds from itself [Col. 0225D] and its wisdom, by which it loves that wisdom begotten from itself and abiding within itself, does not divide it from itself. Three things appear in one: mind, wisdom, and love. Mind and wisdom are from mind; and from mind and wisdom comes love. Thus a certain trinity arises, while unity does not depart; and trinity and unity coexist according to the power and efficacy of the image.

Illuminated by these things, the mind ascends through them and considers that its Creator is wise and possesses wisdom; that His wisdom is from Himself; that He was never without wisdom, because He was always wise; and that He always loved His own wisdom and always had love for His wisdom—love coeternal with His eternal and coeternal wisdom.

## Chapter XXII. How the three persons are one essence or substance.

[Col. 0226A]

Again it considers that in God there can be nothing different from Himself, and that all that He is is one; and therefore the Trinity is true while unity remains. For because there is there One who is from none, One who is from Him, and, together with both, One who is from both, there is a Trinity. For He who is from none cannot be He who is from another; nor can He who is from both be either He who is from none or He who is from Him alone.

Thus the Trinity is true and unity remains perfect, because in God nothing can be which is not God. For an undivided nature and true unity exclude division, while distinction and propriety teach the Trinity.

## Chapter XXIII. On the distinction of names in the Trinity.

[Col. 0226B]

Faith supplied names by which what is believed might be signified. He was called Father in the Trinity because the Son was from Him and was from His substance. For one who begets begets from one’s own substance; one begets what one is. Therefore He from whom was He who was with Him and was the same as He was, was called Father, because the Son was from Him.

But He who was from both was not the Son of both, lest two should be fathers of one Son, and the Father be called Son, and the distinction of the Trinity be confused. Rather, He is the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeding from the Father and the Son. And the Catholic faith professed the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

There is the Father, who has the Son; the Son, who has the Father; and the Holy Spirit, who is from the Father [Col. 0226C] and the Son. Indeed, the Father is spirit, because He is God. Likewise, the Father is holy, because He is God. But faith wished to distinguish one person in the Trinity when it called Him the Holy Spirit. For He is the one given for sanctification when He is breathed into those to be sanctified. Nor does He come without the Father and the Son, because the Trinity is undivided.

## Chapter XXIV. How the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son: by eternal procession from them and by temporal coming to us.

But to be breathed forth by the Father and the Son means that He comes from the Father and the Son. This is eternal to Him, lest it be merely the name of a temporal bestowal: He who is given in time and received. For His being from the Father and the Son is not temporal but eternal.

Accordingly, He is said to be given [Col. 0226D] when He comes from the Father and the Son, because His being from the Father and the Son is eternal, not temporal. Just as the Holy Spirit is the gift of God because He is the gift of the Father and the Son, so, when He is given in time, He is given by the Father and the Son; and for Him, being given by the Father and the Son is nothing other than being, when He is given, from the Father and the Son, on account of that which is eternal to Him from the Father and the Son.

And in the Trinity are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: the Father from Himself; the Son from the Father alone; the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. Since there is one nature and one substance, there is one Trinity in one nature and one substance. When the mind considers what is distinct and proper in the Trinity, it finds three and confesses three. But when it begins to attend to what is the same in the three, one is shown.

## Chapter XXV. Why those three ineffable realities in the Godhead are called three persons, whereas the three in humanity are not so called.

[Col. 0227A]

Again, from the opposite side, another doubt arises and presses upon the mind from the deep obscurity of things. A question comes forth, and reason asks itself why the three things found in the Godhead are called persons, whereas in that trinity which the mind first finds within itself, three things are likewise found, yet rational reflection does not permit us to say that the rational mind contains three persons in itself or that the soul consists of three persons.

Reason diligently inquires why this is so, since it cannot doubt that it is so, yet cannot easily know how it is so. Nevertheless, it sees something of that which it does not see wholly, and it is not permitted to be ignorant of what it is not allowed to grasp [Col. 0227B]. For it sees that the things in the mind are not truly the same as the mind itself. They are at times separated from the mind: when present they depart, and when gone they return again; they vary about it. They are not truly identical with it, but are, as it were, certain affections and forms of it. It is not their own being to be a concrete thing; they merely belong to the being which is a concrete thing.

Thus, since the human being is a person, while these are found to be merely certain affections adhering to the person and existing about it, it does not properly belong to them to be persons, but merely to inhere in a person. But since the things that are in God cannot be other than God Himself—nor, as it were, accidents or affections mutable in time or separable from the unchangeable nature of the essence, for which the whole of its being is identical with what it is [Col. 0227C]—three are truly predicated of Him and one is predicated of the three; and their eternal and perfect identity is affirmed as proper to them.

They are called three persons, not three essences, because the nature is perfect in each of the three and undivided among the three. Therefore they are individually called persons, because they are God; and the three are one God, because there is one Godhead in the three.

## Chapter XXVI. Why power is attributed to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness or benevolence to the Holy Spirit.

Power is attributed to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness or benevolence to the Holy Spirit. Things that are common are distinguished. In these attributions, what is not the case is not said; yet what is the case is left unstated, lest it be believed not to be the case [Col. 0227D].

For the Father is called powerful, and the Father is powerful; but the Father alone is not powerful, for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are powerful. Nor are there three powerful beings, but one powerful being, because there is one power in one nature and one substance. The Son is wise, but not alone, for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are wise. Nor are there three wise beings, but one wise being, because there is one wisdom in one nature and one substance.

The Holy Spirit is called kind and good, and the Holy Spirit is indeed kind and good; but the Spirit alone is not kind and good. Rather, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are kind and good. Yet there are not three kind beings and three good beings, but one kind and one good being, because there is one benevolence [Col. 0228A] and one goodness in one nature and one substance.

But Scripture guarded the human conscience against error: lest, in thinking about its God, it should suppose that things resembling human beings were in Him when they were not. For certain terms were taken from all things, not so as to imply complete likeness, but to signify what belonged to God above human beings. There was something similar, lest the resemblance be wholly alien; but not the whole, lest that which differed so greatly be believed identical.

Thus in the Godhead He was called Father because there was One from whom was One who was from His substance. Just as one who begets begets from one’s own substance, and the one who begets is not the same as the one begotten, but one is distinct from the other—yet the nature of begetter and begotten is not different—so in this there was a likeness between divine and human things. Therefore Father and Son are named from this: the one begot and the other was begotten.

The one who begot is not the Father who was begotten—the latter is the Son. Yet because the nature of the begetter and begotten is one, and the substance one, the begetter is not another than the begotten in the sense of a different God, because He is God; and the begetter and begotten are one God, because the Godhead of begetter and begotten is one. Therefore they are found to be one in that they are God, because the whole of what they are is one; but not one person in one person: for there is the Father, who is from none; the Son, who is from the Father; and the Holy Spirit, who is from both, and is not a Son, because He is from both and equally from both. These three are therefore called three persons, because each of the three is wholly this and is a person; yet they are not one person, although this whole is one. They are three persons because there are three in this one, and this one is wholly one. These three are three persons [Col. 0228C], and this one is one God; these three are this one, and the three persons are one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The Father, then, was called Father because He begot the Son from His substance, and in this there was a likeness. But lest the Father should be thought earlier than the Son—as among human beings the father is always prior, and can never be otherwise than antecedent to the son—the Father was called powerful, not because He alone was powerful, since the Son and Holy Spirit also were powerful, but because power was to be said especially of Him alone: for concerning Him there could more readily arise doubt that He was prior, ancient, and weakened by a multitude of years.

The Son was called wise, not because He alone was wise, but because concerning Him alone there could more readily arise doubt that He was later, still immature in age, and imperfect in understanding. Therefore the Father was called powerful, lest He be thought prior to the Son; the Son wise, lest He be believed later than the Father; and the Holy Spirit good or kind, lest God be thought cruel and the human conscience be terrified at Him, if God were said to have a spirit and “holy” or “kind” had not been added. For “spirit,” by itself, seems to signify a certain severity and to denote cruelty.

## Chapter XXVII. Another reason why things said according to substance and common to all are distinguished personally.

Moreover, on account of its own likeness—by which the supreme Trinity was discovered—the rational mind likewise displayed a trinity, as though a trace and image of the ineffable Trinity. And this was so in it: for in the rational mind there was, as it were, a certain power and force from which there could come to be what was not yet [Col. 0229A]. From it was born understanding, which alone was its wisdom; and without it the mind was not wisdom. Finally, love or joy of the mind for its wisdom proceeded; and this alone was love, because without it there was no love in mind and wisdom.

These names were assigned according to propriety, because each was by itself; and these three were distinguished: first, power, from which wisdom came; then wisdom itself, born from power; finally, love, proceeding simultaneously from power and wisdom. They were distinguished because they were by no means the same things, since they were mutually separable and did not subsist in one.

Therefore, in the rational mind power was one thing, because it was prior, without wisdom, and wisdom was not yet present. Wisdom came later and began to exist with power, as though one thing in another. There were now two, power and wisdom; and a third was added. Thus there began to be three: power, wisdom, and love. Power was not from anything, but wisdom was from it; love, however, was from power and wisdom, which preceded it.

Nor was power wisdom, because power existed before wisdom and wisdom came forth from it. Again, love could not be called power or wisdom, because it proceeded only from them and they had at some time existed without it. These three were distinct in the soul, and in these three the trinity of the soul was found.

The soul ascended from these to the supreme Trinity and found there [Col. 0229C] the Father, who was from none, as power was within itself; the Son, who was from the Father, as wisdom was within itself; and the Holy Spirit, who was from the Father and the Son, as love had proceeded within itself from power and wisdom. Therefore it attributed power to the Father, because it had found in itself a likeness of Him; wisdom to the Son, because this was the image of Him in itself, arising from power; and love to the Holy Spirit, because within itself love had proceeded from power and wisdom, just as the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and is the love of the Father and the Son.

Thus it distinguished the truth according to the image through which it had discovered the truth: what was found here as proper merely for signification, it called there, as it were, singular according to propriety. Yet because for God all that He is is one being [Col. 0229D], and nothing can be found different where, in a simple nature, all is identical, nor can what belongs to one fail to belong to the other where one is what the other is, it necessarily follows that where there is one essence there are one power, one wisdom, and one love: common, whole, proper, and equal.

Thus the Father’s power is also the Son’s and the Holy Spirit’s, and it is proper and equal. The Son’s wisdom is also the Father’s and the Holy Spirit’s, and it is proper and equal. The Holy Spirit’s love or goodness is also the Father’s and the Son’s, and it is proper and equal.

And because for God to possess is identical with to be, and nothing in God can be other than God, the Father is power, the Son is power, and the Holy Spirit is power; and there is one power because there is one essence. Similarly, the Father is wisdom, the Son wisdom, and the Holy Spirit wisdom; and there is one wisdom because the essence is one. The Father is love, the Son love, and the Holy Spirit love; and there is one love because the essence is one.

But the Father is power, and is the power of no one, because He is from none. Likewise the Father is wisdom, and is the wisdom of no one, because He is from none. The Father is love, and is the love of no one, because He is from none. The Son, however, is power and is the Father’s power, because He is from the Father. The Son is wisdom and is the Father’s wisdom, because He is from the Father. The Holy Spirit [Col. 0230B] is the love of the Father and the Son, because He is from the Father and the Son.

Here one must carefully guard against confusing, through commonality, what ought to be distinguished, or distinguishing, through singularity, what is proper. That is: when we wish to distinguish the persons in the Trinity, we should not attribute to one what is common to another; nor, when we demonstrate the unity of substance, should we assign to another what is proper to one.

## Chapter XXVIII. That a trace of the Trinity is found not only in the rational creature but also in the bodily creature.

Behold, we have shown a certain trace of the supreme Trinity, so far as human reason can from that small portion which is its own, which has been given to it and is in it, and which is slight in comparison with perfect totality. For it found three things in itself and, from them, apprehended the Trinity above itself [Col. 0230C].

And outward nature bore witness to it, as it did to the unity of the Godhead. Three external signs of the Trinity appeared, though not an image such as those interior things were; and these signs had but an imperfect likeness. Within there were power, wisdom, and love. These three were an image of the Creator’s power, wisdom, and love, because they existed here and existed there. Here, however, they existed as image; there, as truth. Yet they existed in both places and were the same, because what was here was what was there. But what was here was image, whereas what was there was truth.

Outside, however, there was not power but only a sign; not wisdom but only a sign; not love or goodness but only a sign. Nor were the signs themselves power, wisdom, or love as the things within were; they were only signs [Col. 0230D] of power, wisdom, and love. For the sign of power was the immensity of things; of wisdom, their beauty; of goodness, their usefulness. The signs themselves were not power, wisdom, or goodness, but only signs bearing witness to these things, which properly belonged to what was within.

The true Trinity was demonstrated in its works. Reason could add nothing to these things, because they were perfect, nor remove anything, because they stood distinct. For these are the three things which perfect every rational being, and without them nothing is perfect. Likewise, these three concur in every effect: if anything of them is lacking, nothing is completed; if all are present together, all is brought to completion. These are power, knowledge, and will. If you remove any one of them, you diminish perfection; if you establish all together, you acknowledge that nothing is lacking [Col. 0231A].

By these, therefore, the Creator of things Himself perfected His works, and He is Himself manifestly perfect, because the things in Him are perfect: they can neither be increased in part, because they are full; nor completed in totality, because they are perfect; nor divided in unity, because they are one.

## Chapter XXIX. That all things are contained in these three.

Whatever is said of God and truly believed to be in God is referred to these three and consists in these three. As has been said, if you remove anything from them, what remains is not perfect; if you try to add anything, what is set forth is not greater. For if you call Him strong, incorruptible, unchangeable, invincible, and the like, all this belongs to power. If you call Him provident, watchful, searching hidden things, and understanding, all this belongs to wisdom [Col. 0231B]. If you call Him devout, gentle, merciful, patient, all this belongs to goodness.

Truth can add nothing to these, because everything perfect and true is contained in them. Therefore these three displayed truth in a perfect likeness and demonstrated that nothing should be added to the three, because this is perfect; and nothing should be removed, because thus it stands complete. These three were one in God and were one to God; but they were found distinct here, where they were not one, and therefore became an image of the Trinity.

Reflection followed the propriety found here up to the ineffable Trinity, and distinguished there as proper what was here only proper and found to differ; whereas there all was in one, and one was the whole.

## Chapter XXX. Recapitulation of what has been said above.

We have now said how human reason first discovered God to exist within itself, confirmed this outside itself, and judged that God is one and a simple nature: immense and eternal; great not by quantity, simple not by smallness. We have said that He is three without division of unity, and one without confusion of Trinity; how the supreme Trinity was discovered through that which was its image in us; how it argues that the three things in us are not persons, whereas the three in God are persons because they are God; how nothing can be added to the three because they are perfect, and nothing removed because they are distinct; and how the things in God were distinguished according to things distinct in us, because they are an image of those things and demonstrated the Trinity.

These matters we have gathered together according to the judgment of reason, because reason thus approved the truth. For something was added from those things which surpass reason, to which reason did not attain sufficiently, because they are formed according to reason. For some things are from reason, some according to reason, some above reason, and besides these there are things contrary to reason. Things from reason are necessary; things according to reason are probable; things above reason are wonderful; things contrary to reason are unbelievable.

The two extremes admit no faith at all. Things that are from reason are altogether known and cannot be believed, because they are known. Things contrary to reason likewise cannot be believed on any ground [Col. 0232A], because they admit no reason and reason never assents to them. Therefore only things according to reason and things above reason admit faith.

In the first category faith is assisted by reason, and reason is perfected by faith, because the things believed are according to reason. Although reason does not comprehend their truth, nevertheless it does not contradict faith in them. In matters above reason, faith is assisted by no reason, because reason does not grasp what faith believes; nevertheless, there is something by which reason is admonished to venerate the faith it does not comprehend.

Therefore the things that have been said, being according to reason, were probable to reason, and it assented to them of itself. But the things above reason were disclosed by divine revelation [Col. 0232B]; reason did not operate in them, but was nevertheless restrained lest it contend against them. It now remains to show how much divine revelation has added to the matters proposed and plausibly developed in reasoning: what has been made manifest by inspiration, what established through teaching, and what confirmed by miracles, insofar as may seem fitting and possible.

## Chapter XXXI. A brief summary of the matters stated above, with the addition of certain points.

Before every creature, the Creator was alone indeed, but not solitary, because His wisdom was with Him. In that wisdom all things existed eternally by providence which were made by Him in time by essence. He was alone when nothing existed besides Him [Col. 0232C]; yet He was not solitary, because He who was sufficient to Himself had no need of an external companionship. Nothing was lacking to Him because, as has been said, everything which was to be made by Him in essence was already in Him by providence.

These two things, then, must be carefully distinguished from one another and considered in themselves: namely, Creator and creature—lest either the creature be believed eternal or the Creator temporal. For all knowledge of truth consists in these two. First, therefore, we must consider what is to be said or believed concerning the Creator.

We therefore confess that the Creator of all things is one and three: one in essence, three in persons; for the essence of deity is one, and in the one essence are three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Father is from no one; the Son is from the Father alone; the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son. Just as in one soul there are mind, understanding, and joy: the mind is from itself; understanding is from the mind alone; and joy is from mind and understanding. Yet these three are, as regards substance, one soul. So also in one body there are figure, form, and beauty—these three. Figure seems first in relation to substance, then form, and beauty from both; and these three are in one body and are one body, so that in each nature the image of the Creator may shine forth: in the first according to likeness; in the second as an imitation of likeness.

If, therefore, we confess God there to be one in essence and three in persons, then in unity we acknowledge eternity and immensity; in eternity, immutability; and in immensity, simplicity—that is, eternity without time and immensity without quantity. In the Trinity we confess the communion of unity, equality of immensity, and coeternity of eternity: communion of unity without division, equality of immensity without diminution, and coeternity of eternity without order or succession. Thus each person is whole by unity, full by immensity, and perfect by eternity.

The three persons are nothing other than the one essence, because for the three to be one is for there to be one essence. Accordingly, the three are one, but the three are not one person: for if the three were not one, there would not be one essence of the three; and if the three were one person, they would not be three. Therefore the three are not one person, lest the substance be divided; and the three are not one, lest the persons be confused.

What the Father is, the Son is, because the nature of Father and Son is one. But he who is the Father is not the Son, because the person of the Father differs from that of the Son. Likewise, whatever is said of God according to substance is said equally of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For the substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, and exists equally. “God” is the name of the substance, and for God to be is for the substance to be. Therefore the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God: not three gods, but one God, because there is one substance.

Likewise, the other things said of God according to substance are said equally. They are said of each person singly and equally, and of all together—not plurally, but singly and equally. When they are said singly of each, nothing less is said; and when they are said commonly of all, nothing more is asserted. For when it is said, “The Father is God,” nothing less is said than when it is said, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are God.” For the whole deity is in the Father, the whole in the Son, and the whole in the Holy Spirit; nor is it less in the Father alone than it is jointly in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The same is to be understood of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

There is only one name which is said singly of each person, yet when taken collectively is uttered not in the singular but in the plural, though it is said with respect to substance. For one says: “The Father is a person,” “the Son is a person,” and “the Holy Spirit is a person”; yet one cannot say jointly, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is a person,” but rather, “three persons.” This alone, among the things said with respect to substance, is said singly of each but collectively not in the singular, rather in the plural.

Things said according to relation are said with reference to themselves; they are said singly of each person, but collectively are uttered neither singly nor plurally, because they are said relatively and therefore cannot be said reciprocally. Again: to be the Father is to be from oneself; to be the Son is to be from the Father; to be the Holy Spirit is to be from both. The Son has being born; the Holy Spirit has proceeding; and being born belongs to the Son alone, not to the Holy Spirit. For to be born is to be from another, though not into another. But to proceed is to be from someone and sometimes into someone. For what is breathed is breathed from someone and is breathed into someone. Terms, therefore, have been adopted to signify what had to be said concerning God, so that something might be understood of what could not be comprehended.

Likewise, from the beginning God so moderated his knowledge of himself before humanity that he was neither wholly manifest nor wholly hidden. For if he were wholly manifest, faith would not be exercised and unbelief would be refuted; but if he were wholly hidden, faith would not be aided and unbelief would be excused. Again, the invisible God comes forth into human knowledge in four ways: by two inwardly and by two outwardly. Inwardly, through reason and inspiration; outwardly, through creation and teaching. Of these, two belong to nature and two to grace: reason and creation belong to nature; inspiration and teaching to grace. Therefore, after these, those things must be considered in teaching which authority confirms, because human reason cannot see the way of truth unless it is enlightened by the word of God.

## PART FOUR. ON THE WILL OF GOD, WHICH IS ETERNAL AND ONE, AND ON THE SIGNS OF HIS WILL

These, indeed, are temporal and are called “will” figuratively, because they are signs of will.

[Col. 0233]

## CHAPTER I. That the will of God is just.

[Col. 0233D]

The first cause of all things is the will of the Creator, which no preceding cause moved, because it is eternal; nor does any subsequent cause confirm it, because it is just from itself. For he did not will justly because what he willed was going to be just; rather, what he willed was just because he himself willed it. For it belongs to his will itself and properly to be just as it is; and because what is just in it is the source from which what proceeds from it is just. For what is just is just according to it, and certainly would not be just if it were not according to it.

Therefore, when one asks why that which is just is just, the most fitting answer is: because it is according to the will of God, which is just. But when one asks why the will of God is just, the sounder answer is: because the first cause has no cause, and has from itself the being that it is. This alone is the source from which whatever exists has arisen; and it has not arisen, but is eternal.

## CHAPTER II. In how many ways Scripture understands the will of God.

Here we must not pass over the fact that sacred Scripture customarily speaks of the will of God in various ways. The will is not diverse; rather, the manner of speaking about the will—which is not diverse—is diverse. For in sacred discourse the will of God is sometimes understood as that which truly exists in him, is identical with him, and is coeternal with him. At other times, however, by a figure of speech, that is called his will which, properly speaking, is not his will but a sign of his will. The sign of the will itself is called “will,” although it is not will but only a sign.

Thus signs of wrath are called wrath, and signs of love are called love. God is said to be angry, though there is no anger in him. Rather, only the external signs by which he is shown to be angry are called his wrath. This is a figure of speech by which what is said is not false, but what is said is shaded by reference to resemblance. According to these figurative modes, therefore, wills as though diverse are attributed to God, because the things figuratively called his will are diverse, although the will spoken of properly is one.

## CHAPTER III. The first will of God is called good pleasure.

[Col. 0235C]

Thus, that which is called the will of God first and principally is that which truly is his will. It is one and admits neither multiplicity nor change.

## CHAPTER IV. The second is operation; the third, permission.

There follow two wills, and two things called wills. These two are predicated of God and are called God’s wills because they are signs of his will. Of these wills, one is called permitting, the other effecting—that is, permission and operation. For his permission is called his will, and his operation is called his will, because they occur according to his will and are signs of his will. These two are, as it were, consequences of the supreme will, its unfolding and its effect, and corresponding to it, though not coeternal with it.

For whatever is always in that will is at some time in these; and whatever is at some time absent from these is never absent from that will. Everything in that will is always present, while everything in these is present at some time; for nothing exists outside his will, nor can anything occur outside his operation or permission. The two follow the one, and the one is found in both, because he neither acts unwillingly nor permits anything except willingly. When something occurs, this too is called the will of God, because it was done or permitted to occur by God’s will. By will he made what he made; he made well, and he made good what he made. He also permitted voluntarily, even if what he permitted was not good.

## CHAPTER V. That God made good things and permitted evil things.

For he made good things and did good; he permitted evil things and did not make them. He did well, because both were good. Therefore he willed both, because it was good that both should exist. Good things were good, and evil things evil; good things were not evil, nor evil things good. Yet it was good that both good and evil things should exist. God willed both to exist, because it was good that both should exist; but both were not good, because evil was not good.

Therefore God did not will evil, although he willed that evil too should exist. He did not make it among the things that he made good, but permitted it to exist, because what he willed was good. Nor was that good itself evil; rather, good came from evil. He did not make evil good, but made good from evil—he who knows how to use evils and goods for good.

## CHAPTER VI. Why God permitted evils.

It was a greater good that good should arise from both good and evil than from good alone. Accordingly, the supreme good willed this good to exist, and what he willed was good. Just as nothing that was to happen could be unknown to his eternal wisdom, so nothing that existed could displease his coeternal will. He saw all that was to come, and saw that it was good for this whole to exist as a whole; and he willed it to exist as a whole, because it was good that the whole should exist.

Before they existed, he saw the evils that would be far in the future together with the goods, and considered that, with these evils joined to them, the goods would be commended [Col. 0236C], rendered more beautiful by comparison with evils, and that evils would be good among goods although they were not good. For by them goods would be adorned and commended, and would receive a further good for the beauty and adornment of the universe.

He looked upon all things in their order; he saw goods there, and the things that were good for those goods; and he willed all things so to be, as was good, because it was good in the manner in which he saw and willed what would come to pass. With an equal judgment he weighed all that he saw in one good pleasure, in which it was good and just for the whole to be, and for nothing else to be; and he willed the whole to be and nothing else to be. By this will he afterward brought it about that the goods should exist whose existence was good, as he had seen and willed. And he permitted those evils to exist whose existence was good [Col. 0236D], which he had foreseen would come with goods, and which he had willed to exist with goods because it was good.

His will concerning the goods and evils which he willed to exist was eternal; but it was not known to human beings until they were fulfilled and came to pass—the goods and evils concerning which his will was that they should exist.

## CHAPTER VII. Why God’s operation and permission are called his will.

When he made a good thing and permitted an evil thing, his will concerning it became apparent to us, because he wills what he makes or permits to be. His eternal will does not begin then with the thing that occurs; rather, the hidden will is shown by that which occurs. Therefore the thing itself which occurs is called his will, because it is a sign of his will. Thus there appears to be one will and another [Col. 0237A], because they are different signs of the one will.

## CHAPTER VIII. That there is a twofold distinction of God’s will: in his good pleasure and in the sign of his good pleasure.

From this arises a distinction necessary for our knowledge of the divine will: between his good pleasure and the sign of that good pleasure. We say that his good pleasure is his will, and we call the sign of his good pleasure his will. Both are true, and both are truly said. But his good pleasure is eternal: whatever is in it cannot fail to be, and whatever is not in it cannot be. Nothing exists against it, outside it, or without it, in all that exists. It is fixed and settled; what is in it can never be annulled.

“He has done all that he willed” (Ps. 113) proves that his will is not annulled. “Who has resisted his will?” (Rom. 9) proves that his good pleasure is not hindered. His good pleasure thus accords with the effects of things, and the effects of things do not conflict with it. For everything that he wills comes to be, and everything that he does not will does not come to be. Whatever he wills to occur, he always wills to occur, although what he wills is not always present at some particular time.

This universal good pleasure, which is eternal and by one simple motion of his justice together approves all things that come to be in their times, so that they may advance to their effect and come to be, is fulfilled, consummated, and manifested through the two things which follow in time: divine permission and operation. These themselves embrace the whole totality of all things that receive effect or subsistence [Col. 0237C], and correspond to the Creator’s good pleasure—which is one in both and alike toward all unlike things. Therefore these two are also called wills. God’s will is his good pleasure; his will is his operation; and his will is his permission.

## CHAPTER IX. The fourth is in command; the fifth in prohibition.

His command and his prohibition follow, and each is called his will. For when he commands that something be done, he shows that he wills it to be done; and when he forbids that something be done, he shows that he wills it not to be done. Therefore these likewise are called his will, because they are signs of his will in some respect, just as are his operation and permission. Yet they signify his will differently, in another manner, and only in part.

## CHAPTER X. That command and prohibition are not signs of eternal good pleasure like operation and permission.

Command and prohibition do not extend to everything as his operation and permission do, since nothing occurs without those. The former two are directed only toward rational creatures, which alone are capable of command and prohibition, being equipped by their implanted reason for each. Therefore these are partial signs: they do not concern all things, nor do they universally bring into manifestation the supreme will and all that is in it, as operation and permission do. Rather, they signify only the things concerning those to whom command and prohibition are addressed, because these things are in the supreme will and eternal good pleasure.

Neither are these signs alike. God’s operation and permission are certain and true signs of eternal good pleasure; command and prohibition, however, do not make wholly certain what is in the eternal good pleasure until it is proved by operation or permission after the event has occurred. For it is certain, when God has done something or permitted it to be done and it has been done, that it was so in the eternal good pleasure—that it should be as it occurred—according as he voluntarily did or permitted that which was done to occur; for it is good for it to be as it is.

But when something has been commanded or forbidden, it is not yet clear what has been determined about it in the eternal good pleasure, until the effect of things brings it into evidence by operation or permission: as it is good for it to be, and as the good pleasure concerning what will be is before it is. Command and prohibition merely indicate that the will of the one who commands is that something should or should not occur. They demonstrate that it is just and devout for the person addressed to believe nothing else, even though there is something else in the one by whom the command is given.

Often something is commanded to occur which will not occur and will not be done. Something is forbidden not to occur which will occur and will be done; and in the good pleasure there is only this, that what will occur should occur, because it is good that it should be so and not otherwise than it will be—whether by God’s operation, which is good, or by permission, where it is evil [Col. 0238C]. It is good that this whole should exist. Thus his command and prohibition do not correspond to his good pleasure as his operation and permission do; rather, they proceed contrariwise, are differently ordered, and sometimes do not agree as to what will occur and be done.

## CHAPTER XI. How God seems to deceive by command or prohibition, indicating something other than what is in his good pleasure.

The commands of God appear liable to the charge of deception and to speak falsely concerning truth, when they signify something else concerning his will, affirming to us things that are alien and external, which are not settled and do not stand according to his good pleasure—that fixed determination concerning all things that will occur [Col. 0238D].

Human conscience struggles severely between two opposing things that do not agree: either why God commanded what he did not will, or why what he willed did not happen. For if there is truth in the command, he seems altogether to have willed what he commanded; and if there is omnipotence in the good pleasure, what he willed seems to have been done. Yet what he commanded was not done, and what he forbade was done. What follows from this except either that he did not will what he commanded, or that he was unable to do what he willed?

For what was done was done by him; and if it was not done, it was nevertheless permitted. If it was done, it was done voluntarily; and if permitted, it was permitted voluntarily. For he could neither be compelled to act against his will [Col. 0239A] nor forced to permit without willing. Therefore what was done was done by his will, even if it was not done because of his will; for it was done by another will, which is not friendly to his will. Yet he wholly willed what was done, because it is good that it was done as it was done and that it should be as it is.

Why, then, did he command that it should be otherwise and forbid it to be thus, when it is good that it be thus, and it was to be thus before it was, and this was his good pleasure because it was good that it should be so and not otherwise?

## CHAPTER XII. That each alternative sounds difficult: either that God commands what he does not will to be done, or that he permits what he does not will to be done.

[Col. 0239B]

This question constrains us and leads us into doubt, so that we scarcely dare readily to affirm either: that God commanded what he did not will to occur, or that he permitted to occur things which he did not will. Yet of these two we more easily admit that he willed the good which he commanded than that he willed the evil which he permitted, although the good which he commanded did not occur, while the evil which he permitted did occur.
