For it is easy and without scruple of conscience to say, “God wills good,” and when it is said, it sounds right: “God wills good.” But if one says, “God wills evil,” it is hard to hear, and a devout mind does not easily receive of the good God that he wills evil. For when it is said that God wills evil, it seems to mean only this: that the good God loves evil, approves what is wicked, reckons iniquity his friend, rejoices in it as in something like himself, and judges evil to be good. Therefore the devout mind rejects this—not because what is said is not correctly said, but because what is correctly said is not correctly understood.

## CHAPTER XIII. That God does not will evils, although he wills that evils exist, because this is good.

For more is understood in the statement than is explicitly said: he wills evil to exist, and he does not will evil. If only this is to be understood when it is said, “God wills evil,” then it ought not to be said at all; for he does not approve it in any way, nor judge it good. Rather, he judges evil contrary to his own good and alien to himself; he does not desire it as fitting, harmonious with what he is, with what is from him, or with what is like him. Instead, he judges it foreign, distant, and established in every dissimilarity.

Yet he wills evil to exist, and in this he wills nothing but good, because it is good that evil should exist; but he does not will evil itself, because evil itself is not good. He wills good alone; he loves and delights in it as in one akin, friendly, and near to himself. Therefore it sounds right and is gladly received when one says, “God wills good,” because he loves that alone and not evil, with which he has no fellowship or likeness—unlike the things that are from him and possess likeness to him.

Thus God wills good and does not will evil; he wills every good and wills no evil. We accept, approve, and say all this: all this is true, because he loves wholly what is his own. He loves only what is his own, and hates only what is not his own; he loves all that is his and hates all that is not his. Therefore he willed the good that he commanded and did not will the evil that he permitted, because the good was his own, from himself, friendly to himself, and of himself. He loved, approved, desired for himself, and loved in himself with eternal desire what was his own.

But evil, which was not his own, he did not love in itself or desire for himself. Rather, he rejected and refused it in the disposition of love; he did not receive it into himself by the consent of charity, to give it a place among his good pleasures.

## CHAPTER XIV. That the will of God is always fulfilled.

[Col. 0240B]

But you say to me: “Therefore, if he willed—or rather, because he willed—the good that he commanded, and did not will the evil that he permitted, then what he did not will happened, and what he willed did not happen. For what he commanded did not happen, but what he forbade happened, which he permitted. Therefore what he willed did not happen, while what he did not will did happen.”

On the contrary: what he willed did happen, and nothing happened except what he willed, because he willed it to happen so and to be as it happened, since it was good for it to happen and be as it happened, and not otherwise. It was good that it should be so even in that which was not good. He did not will that very thing which was not good, but he willed its existence because that was good. When it occurred, therefore, what he willed occurred, because it was good, and this he willed.

“But,” you say, “his will obtained less, attained less, and was fulfilled less; it remained imperfect, because the good which he willed did not happen, and the evil which he did not will did happen.” You fail to consider that, just as evil does not possess the fact that what he did not will occurred, so good does not lack the fact that what he willed did not occur. What he wills and loves, he possesses; and what he does not will and hates, he does not possess. What he wills to exist, he obtains because it occurs; and likewise what he wills not to exist, because it does not occur. His will is never frustrated, so that what he wills does not happen; nor is it ever weak, so that what he does not will happens.

## CHAPTER XV. How the wicked are not excusable although through them God’s will is fulfilled.

But perhaps the wicked may again seem excusable when they do evil, because God’s will is fulfilled even in the evils which they perform. Yet the wicked are judged by their own will, because they are opposed to God’s will. They do not oppose his will so that what he does not will may occur—for they cannot do this—but they resist by willing, because they are wicked. Their evil will, by which they will something else, is itself their fault; their inability to do otherwise is just.

When they will what God wills, they are not thereby good, because they do not will it for the reason that God wills it. God himself does not will the thing that they will, because they will evil and God does not will evil. They approve and love what God hates; therefore they are opposed to God, wicked, sinners, and guilty—not by bringing about what God justly did not will to occur, but by loving and approving [Col. 0241A] what God does not love.

They do not, therefore, hinder God’s will in the fact that what occurs does occur; but in the very thing that occurs, they depart from the love of God. They are wicked not by producing what is contrary to his will, but by loving what is contrary to his love. Thus God’s will is always fulfilled, and the wicked are not excused because his will is fulfilled in them and through them. They are not guided by their own will toward fulfilling God’s will; rather, by his hidden dispensation, through which they cannot do otherwise, they are brought to fulfil his will.

But you say again: “If God willed the whole to be as it happened, because it is good for the whole to be thus, and not otherwise than it happened, why did he command what did not happen and forbid what did happen, when both are good: both that what did not happen should not happen and that what did happen should happen? Why did he not instead command only that which was good to occur, and forbid only that which it was likewise good not to occur?”

## CHAPTER XVI. Why God commands everything that he commands.

But here it is necessary to consider more deeply the character and reason of command and, in the same way, of prohibition. Every command or prohibition is made either for the sake of the person to whom it is given, for the sake of the person by whom it is given, or for the sake of another person for whom it is given. The whole usefulness and good of a command—whether in what is enjoined to be done or in what is ordered to be avoided—is referred only to the person for whom it is made, whether that person is identical with, or other than, the one to whom it is given or the one by whom it is given.

The end of the command is the benefit, usefulness, cause, and good which follows upon the completion of the command. This good pertains only to the one for whom the command is made; the fulfilment of the command ought to be that person’s good.

## CHAPTER XVII. That everything called good is good either in itself or in relation to something.

Again, it must be considered that everything called good is called good either in itself or in relation to something. What is called good in itself is called substantially good, because it is good itself. But what is called good in relation to something and not in itself is not called substantially good, because it is not good itself; rather, it is good accidentally and by denomination, because good comes from it.

Thus one good is good because it is good itself. Another is good because it is good for someone, although it is not itself good. What is good, good for itself, and good for another is good in its entirety. But what is good and good for itself, yet not good for another, is good only in part—as is that which is good and good for another, but not good for itself.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That what is called good in itself and universally is truly and supremely good.

There is another good, higher than other goods, which is truly good because it is good in itself, universally good because it is good in relation to all things, and the good of all things. For what is good in itself is truly good, and what is the good of all is universal good. It is every good, because it is the good of all things, and there is no good outside it [Col. 0242A].

But what is not good in relation to itself is not truly good or genuine good; it is called good only because good comes from it and it is beneficial, not because it is good itself.

## CHAPTER XIX. On three kinds of good.

The highest good, therefore, is that which is good itself and is good in relation to every good. The middle good is that which is good itself and is good in relation to something. The lowest good, however, is, as it were, extrinsic, merely denominative, derivative rather than proper good: it is good in relation to something, but is not good itself. For it is not good itself; rather, what comes from it is good.

Accordingly, in a certain sense it too is good, because good comes from it and it is beneficial. It is good that even that which is not itself good should exist, because unless that which is not good itself existed, that which is good through it would not exist. Evils do not therefore excel because good comes from them; rather, they serve the one who excels and bestows, because through them that which comes from them exists.

## CHAPTER XX. That that from which greater good arises is a greater good.

When two things compete in relation to one outcome—one which is good but not good for someone, and another which is not good but is good for someone—and both cannot exist, so that of the two only one must exist, it is a greater good for that to exist which is good for someone even though it is not itself good, than for that to exist which is good only in itself and not good for anyone [Col. 0242C].

For from that which is not good but is good for someone, it necessarily follows that there is also that which is good and good for someone; and this is altogether a greater good than that which is good only and not good for someone. For what is not good but is good for someone would not be good unless from it there came that which is good and good for someone. Thus what is good because it is good itself is not good for someone because no good comes from it; and what is not good because it is not good itself is good for someone because good comes from it.

This sometimes occurs, and at their end all things are judged as good or evil. For Scripture plainly shows that the one good, and the good itself, is “an aroma of life leading to life” for some and “an aroma of death leading to death” for others (2 Cor. 2). Thus from good comes evil and from evil good; good is for the wicked unto evil, and evil for the good unto good. What is good in the whole is greater than what is good only in part. This is proved as follows: every universal good is greater than that which consists only in part, and what contributes and benefits more is rightly called greater.

Now let us bring together and gather what has been said: the fulfilment of every command is good for the person for whom the command itself is made. Every good is either good in itself or good in relation to something. What is not good in itself but is good for someone is a greater good than what is good only in itself and is not good for anyone [Col. 0243A]. What contributes and benefits more is always rightly judged a greater good, since every good is in its fruit and is good only to the extent that it is good.

## CHAPTER XXI. That God commands nothing for his own sake—that is, for his own advantage or benefit.

Let us now see whether everything God commands he commands for his own sake or for the sake of the one to whom he gives the command. If he commands for his own sake, then what he commands is for his good, and the fulfilment of his command is good for him. But how could he command for his own sake, who has no need of improvement in himself and cannot be aided by another’s good, being incapable of becoming better?

Scripture, and the fulfiller of the command in Scripture, cries out: “You are my God, because you have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15). Therefore God does not command what he commands for his own sake, but for the sake of the one to whom he commands, because what is enjoined is good for the one to whom a good command is given.

## CHAPTER XXII. That God must command each person what is good for that person, even if it is not the good of all.

Since, therefore, the command is made for the one for whom it is made, the command itself must be the good of the person to whom it is given. Nothing should be commanded except what is good for the person to whom the command is given. For a command would be pointless if it were not good for the one for whose sake it was made—especially when it comes from the Good One, who ought to command nothing except good.

God must not be the author of evil to his creature, nor take upon himself its causation, as though by teaching he had corrupted what he had created incorrupt. Therefore he must command that person nothing except what is good for that person—the person who has from God everything good that he has, and no evil. Since the Creator can be the author of evil to none of his creatures, he must command each only what is good for that one, so that his instruction may be sincere, just as the created condition was incorrupt.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That God must not prevent the good of the universe, even if it is not good for someone.

Then it happens that what is good for some one person is good for that person and is not good in every respect; and again, that what is evil for someone is evil for that person and yet is the good of all, because from it comes the good of all. And that which is good, and good for someone, is less good than that which is evil and evil for someone, because from that very thing a greater good comes, from which comes the good of all. And it is a greater good that there should be that from which a greater good comes, even when it is not good for someone, because it is good in the whole. But that which is the greater good ought not to be hindered, in compensation for the lesser good, by him who is supremely good. And we have said that it is a greater good for good to arise from evil and good than from good alone. Therefore evils ought to have been permitted to exist, because their existence was good in view of the good that was to arise from them. God therefore commanded what was good for each individual and permitted what was good for the universe. For the good of the universe, which he ought not to hinder, was greater; while that which was evil for someone was not good, and he could not be its author. And therefore he commanded to each person what was good, and what was good for that person; and by commanding it he signified that he willed it. His commands are signs of his will, and are called his will because they are signs of his will. For he wills, approves, loves, and judges as friendly to himself the goods which he commands; and he hates and detests the evils which he forbids, finding neither harmony nor friendship in them. Yet he wills those evils to exist which he does not will, for the sake of the greater good that comes from them, which he wills more. But nothing belongs to us or is required of us except what is ours and what is our good: namely, that we should do, approve, and love the good in ourselves, just as God loves and approves our good in us, so that we may be like him in loving and doing good things, just as he himself loves and does good things alone. And when what is our good is commanded to us, it is signified to us that God wills this; and it concerns us to think and believe thus: that God wills what he commands us to do. Yet nothing happens except what he himself wills to happen, whether we do or do not do what he commanded us. And if we do good, God willed this; he willed it because it has come about here, and he approves what has come about; he wills what has come about, and it is good. And if we do evil, he wills that we do not do good, and approves that because it is good; yet he does not approve the evil that we do, because it is evil. Nevertheless, he wills what has come about because it has come about, since what has come about is good, and he himself wills what is good. And his omnipotent will stands sure and firm in its good pleasure, approving goods and permitting evils for the sake of goods; it can neither be hindered so that what is in it does not happen, nor ever weakened so that what is not in it happens.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That God’s action and permission are signs of what is good to exist, even if the thing itself is not good; command and prohibition are signs of what is good, even if it is not good for it to exist.

After it follow his signs: his permission and his action; and they show what is in it, because the same thing is in them. Commands and prohibitions are added, and they too are signs and demonstrations of the supreme will and eternal good pleasure, through approval and love. Yet they are not signs like the former, but only demonstrations and indications of approval and good pleasure in regard to a thing’s being good, and not in regard to whether it is good for that thing to exist, whether the thing itself be good or evil. Therefore they indicate not that this is in the supreme will so as to happen, but what is in approval and good pleasure if it happens; and yet both belong to the will, and this is good even if it does not happen, whereas that is good in such a way that it happens.

## CHAPTER XXV. God’s good pleasure sometimes concerns a thing, sometimes the occurrence of a thing.

Whoever, then, wishes to make a distinction when speaking of God’s will may say this: it must be carefully considered how God, in one case, wills the thing itself which exists; while in another case he wills something only because it exists. In the case in which he wills the thing itself which exists, he approves the thing; but in the case in which he wills it because it exists, he approves the occurrence of the thing. In the case in which he approves the thing and not its occurrence, he wills something, yet does not will that what he wills should as yet exist. In the case in which he approves the occurrence of the thing and not the thing itself, he wills something to exist, and yet does not will the very thing whose existence he wills. For not everything which is itself good is good to exist; just as, sometimes, that which is evil is not evil in its very existence. And God wills only what is good, even when its existence is not good; and he wills to exist only what is good to exist, even when the thing itself is not good. And when he wills something because it is good, but does not will its existence because it is not good for it to exist, his will is fulfilled and does not remain without effect, even though the thing is not brought about, because he wills it thus and what he wills is good. And when he does not will something because it is evil, yet wills it to exist because its existence is good, his will is fulfilled when the thing comes about, because he wills it thus and what he wills is good. His will is always fulfilled, and his good pleasure is never in vain, because what he wills is always good and things are always as he wills.

And these are five terms: good pleasure, permission, action, command, and prohibition. Good pleasure is distinguished according as the thing is approved or the occurrence of the thing is approved. Action is distinguished according as God acts or cooperates: for some things he does by acting, which he does alone; other things he does by cooperating, which he does not do alone. Command is distinguished into that which is given outwardly through speech and that which is given inwardly through inspiration. And in all these matters what had to be said concerning God’s will is established: namely, his good pleasure and the sign of his good pleasure. Hence many wills of his are spoken of, though his will is one, because there are many signs of his will. As it is written: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. CX [110]); because of the many things that proceed from it and are in accordance with it. We have spoken here of God’s will because it is the first cause of all things, as was our purpose, and we have pursued the matter according to our understanding. Perhaps there are many lofty matters which cannot be comprehended and escape our understanding and speech.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the order of things: first, second, and third.

Thus the order of things is established: later things follow after first things. The first of all things is the will of the Creator, because all things are from it. After it follow those things which are from it. First things are those which are in it; second things are those which are from it. Those which are in it are eternal and have neither rank nor succession, because they subsist in unity and do not pass away in eternity. Those which are from it are created through it: they receive their cause from it, not their substance in it. For the divine nature did not substantially generate from itself what it causally created, since that which made and that which was made cannot naturally be the same.

Therefore the things that have been made are not one, and among them some are first and some second—not first in relation to the first things, but first in relation to the second. For those which, in relation to the first things before them, are second, are first in relation to the second things proceeding from them; and the latter are third in relation to the first. Those which are eternal and invisible in God’s will are first of all. Those which are temporal and invisible from God’s will are second after the first; those which are temporal and visible are third after the second. Among visible things, those that are rational are nearer to invisible things, because rational things are invisible in themselves. Thus in the first place are set the primordial, invisible, and uncreated causes of all things to be created, in the divine mind. In the second place is angelic nature: invisible indeed, but created. In the third place is human nature: visible and created, invisible in one respect and visible in another. In the fourth place is bodily creation, wholly visible and wholly temporal.

After the first, uncreated and invisible causes, therefore, our consideration will proceed to angelic nature, rational and invisible; then to human nature, visible and rational, with which our initial purpose was concerned, so that it may be completed. For we made our first proposal concerning visible things, which are last, in order that from what lies open to view we might lead the human mind more conveniently to the knowledge of what is hidden.

# PART FIVE. ON THE CREATION AND NATURE OF ANGELS, THEIR CONFIRMATION AND FALL, AND OTHER MATTERS PERTAINING TO THEM.

[Col. 0245]

## CHAPTER I. What is to be investigated concerning angels.

[Col. 0245C]

After the other matters spoken of concerning the beginning of the world—and prefaced for this reason, that we may ascend from visible things to invisible—you raise the question of angelic nature: when angels were created; what they were like when first made; then what they became when they were divided by turning away and turning back; and how they were disposed when they were judged, by condemnation and glorification. You also ask about their number and orders, their excellence, their relation to human beings, the diversity of gifts, their offices, governance, and God’s direction and rule in them; and many other matters which follow from these and are contained within them. Therefore we must form instruction, according to our ability, concerning the multitude of hidden matters, and not promise what we cannot attain.

## CHAPTER II. That angels were created in the beginning.

Scripture says that wisdom was created first of all (Ecclus. I); and we understand “created wisdom” to mean rational creaturehood. For it too is wisdom, as a shining light from light, not light that gives illumination. But that Wisdom which is wise is not this created wisdom; it is neither created nor a creature, nor does it have being from another, just as it does not have wisdom from another. But this wisdom, which does not have wisdom from itself and does not have being from itself, was itself created and has a beginning. And Scripture says when this wisdom was made: it was made first of all.

Again, another Scripture says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I). These assertions seem to give rise to some contradiction. For if wisdom was created first of all, everything was made after it. Heaven and earth were made after it; thus wisdom itself was made before heaven and earth. But if in the beginning God created heaven and earth, nothing was made before heaven and earth, nor was wisdom itself made before heaven and earth. These positions cannot both stand. Therefore, lest the testimonies of the divine Scriptures seem to be contradictory—which it is altogether unlawful to think—we seek the understanding of truth, since in truth that which is true does not conflict with itself.

## CHAPTER III. That the rational creature was made first of all in dignity, because the condition of the rest is referred to it, just as its own condition is referred to God, because it alone was made in the likeness of God.

We say that the rational creature was made first, and bodily creature after it; yet not in time, but only in causality, relation, and dignity. For the constitution of bodily creation is referred to rational creaturehood and was perfected according to it, just as its own constitution is referred to the Creator alone, because it alone was made according to him. For rational creaturehood alone is said to have been made in the likeness of God; no creature besides the rational creature alone is said to have been made in the likeness of God, although every creature had, in the divine reason and his eternal providence, the cause and likeness from and according to which it was perfected in its own subsistence.

But there is a great difference, and a great distance, between having a likeness in God and having God himself as one’s likeness. For although nothing can be in God as though less than, different from, or other than God, it is nevertheless very different for something to be made according to the likeness of that which is in God—within his reason and providence—and to be made according to the likeness of God and to be like God. For all things were in God before they existed in themselves, according to the reason, cause, and providence by which they were to be; but each was there, as it were, less than perfect, each a particular thing and not the whole, according to the reason and distinction of each thing, although that reason contained all things and was greater in the whole, as though overflowing beyond individual things. Therefore individual things were not that whole; rather, individual things were in the whole, because the whole corresponded to the whole and individual things to individual things. Yet in God there was nothing less in the part than in the whole, because part and whole were one; but by the one reason and providence, distinct things which were to be in part and in whole were distinguished, and were to be less in the part than in the whole. Thus they themselves had less in the reason, because they were to be less from the reason. Yet God had nothing less, since he was wholly present in the whole, perfect and one.

Therefore, for rational creaturehood, not one thing or another in the divine reason could suffice as an exemplar according to whose likeness it might be formed; rather, it received God, as it were, as a whole, that it might become his very image, fashioned wholly in emulation of perfection. Thus, just as God was spirit and one, and all things were in him according to reason, providence, foreknowledge, and cause, so it too might be spiritual, capable in unity of the foreknowledge, providence, reason, and providence of all things. A perfect image shone forth, imitating its author; it appeared as though the very same being were in another, and as though the two were one. In the second, too, were found—in emulation, imitation, image, and likeness—those things which were in the first: reasons and causes, likenesses and forms, dispositions and providences of future things that were to be made. And when those things were made which were made according to the likeness of these things, the things present in the second were made; just as they were made according to the likeness of those things which were in the first, unmade.

According to this reasoning and consideration, bodily creation comes third, after rational creaturehood as the second, because it was made for that creature, just as rational creaturehood itself was made for the first, uncreated nature.

## CHAPTER IV. That at the first beginning all bodily things were made together in matter, and all incorporeal things in angelic nature.

So far as moments, intervals, and spans of time are concerned, we confess for the present, more conveniently and more nearly in accordance with truth, that at one and the same time, and at the beginning of time when time itself began, the matter of all visible things and the invisible things in angelic and spiritual creaturely nature were made or created together. Neither existed in time, nor began, without the other; neither one was prior to the other. Both were together in time and with time. Yet that for which the other was made was prior: in it were the exemplars of wisdom, of which the visible creatures are effects and expressions. In this sense wisdom was created first of all.

But those who say that angels were created before heaven and earth, and existed before all changeable things were made, and who calculate spans, years, and ages during which they served God before the constitution of the world, maintain that time began with the world and that there was no time before the world because there was no changeability. Yet they also maintain that angels existed immutably and timelessly before the world was made, and that when the world began, time began for the first time because changeability began, and that the world was made at the beginning of time. But for the present, according to the measure of our understanding and with reverence for mysteries—about which we judge that nothing ought rashly to be asserted—we approve more readily what has been said. And for the present we have determined in this way: that all visible and invisible things were made together (Gen. II), as Scripture says: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclus. XVIII).

## CHAPTER V. That bodily and incorporeal nature were each made, in one respect, formless, and in another respect formed.

For all things were created together, because we believe that the matter of all visible things and the nature of invisible things both began equally at one and the same time—each formless in one respect and each formed in another. For just as the matter of all visible and bodily things, in that beginning of primary creation, had the form of confusion and did not have the form of ordered arrangement until it was subsequently formed and received order and disposition, so spiritual and angelic nature, in its creation, was formed through wisdom and discernment according to the habit of nature. Yet it did not possess the form which it was afterward to receive through love and conversion to its Creator; it was formless in relation to that form, to be formed by it.

## CHAPTER VI. What angels were like when first made.

We shall further set forth a more carefully examined account of what angels were like when they were made. For we have said when they were made: they were made in the beginning, the first creature before which nothing had been made, according to which things were made, and that which was made along with it. Thus, in one respect, it was made before all things: it is the form and cause of all things. Next it is necessary to show what angels were like in that first origin, first subsistence, and beginning of their creation: when they first began to exist, what that first existence was like, and what it was in them to have been created in the first instance.

## CHAPTER VII. That they were not made from pre-existing matter as bodily things were.

Spiritual nature was not created from pre-existing matter, as we have said bodily nature was created. For it is not so; nor can it be, since in a simple substance what it is cannot be distinct from that from which it is. Everything that it is is one, simple, indivisible, and immaterial. But it was made in its own nature, perfect in being so far as spiritual substance is concerned—not as a mass or confused matter, as a rough heap, pile, accumulated assemblage, or anything of this kind, which does not apply to it. Rather, it was a rational and intelligible multitude, personally distinct, formed, and marked by the number of spiritual and intelligible differentiation: intelligible spirits subsisting, possessing innate reason, a connatural form of wisdom, and the spiritual quality of an intelligence capable, according to the mode and measure of their creation, of higher advancement and illumination to come upon them. They also possessed, immediately from the beginning, free choice implanted and inborn alike, by which they could, without compulsion, incline by their own will toward either alternative: in one they were aided without coercion; in the other abandoned without oppression.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the four properties of angelic nature.

If, then, anyone asks what spiritual nature was like when it was made or created in its beginning, there are four things which we have proposed and said were attributed to angels in their creation. First, simple and immaterial substance; second, personal distinction; third, the rational form of wisdom and intelligence; fourth, the power of a will and choice free to incline either toward good or toward evil. There follows upon this a great consideration necessary for understanding the truth: whether, in their spiritual substance, their wisdom, their freedom of choice, and the other matters related to these, the things which belonged equally to all were equal in degree. For those things common to all, of which nothing was excepted that was not in all, belonged equally to all. But it is not yet established whether what belonged equally to all belonged to all equally in degree. Here one must inquire first concerning substance, afterward concerning form, and then concerning power. For substance belongs to persons, form to wisdom, and power to choice. To substance belongs the subtlety of nature; to form, the brightness of intelligence; to power, the capacity for intelligible motion, appetite, and rational will.

## CHAPTER IX. On the difference of spiritual substance.

Therefore the question is whether those rational essences, which were spirits, simple by nature and immortal in life, were created with one and the same subtlety, purity, and vigour—or whatever other name may be used to signify any good essence—or whether one is rightly called better or more fitting in form than another. For bodily nature displays this: some bodies are more solid and firm; others appear purer, more cleansed, cleaner, brighter, and as though possessing a better and worthier substance, essence, or form; others are lighter, better fitted, more ready, more sound, and more incorruptible; while others are fragile, near to corruption, weak, dreggy, base, heavy, and unsuitable. Yet this diversity is beautiful in the structure and order of the universe, in which a lesser good is not evil and a differing good is a greater good. In this way it is reasonable that those spiritual natures also, universally created good and suited to their purity and excellence, received in the very beginning of their creation distinctions and ranks, not unworthy in essence and form, by which some might be constituted higher and others lower according to the ordering wisdom of God, who creates all good things and orders them well.

## CHAPTER X. On the difference of knowledge.

For those created more subtle by nature and more penetrating in wisdom were fittingly established higher in dignity. Those created less subtle by nature and less penetrating in wisdom were fittingly ordered lower in dignity—yet so that those established more excellent might be set above without pride, and those set lower might be subject without misery.

## CHAPTER XI. On the difference of free choice.

Nor is there anyone who, if he wishes to assign a difference even in freedom of choice according to the differing strength of nature and force of wisdom, knowledge, and intelligence, can object on rational grounds. For just as a difference in the vigour and subtlety of nature does not bring weakness, and lesser knowledge of wisdom does not introduce ignorance, so an inferior freedom imposes no necessity upon the choice of the will.

## CHAPTER XII. In what respects they were created alike and in what unlike.

Therefore, that they were spirits, that they were life, that they were indissoluble or immortal: in these respects all were equal. But that they were powerful by nature, subtle in essence, wise in intelligence, and by freedom of will ready and capable for either alternative: this was not equal in all, though it was sufficient in all. God alone could weigh these invisible distinctions among invisible and intelligible beings, and comprehend in his wisdom each one’s measure, mode, and limit—he by whose power the whole was created and by whose providence it was ordered. We, however, with understanding darkened, approach them timidly and grope with the sense of weak knowledge after what we cannot comprehend by power. Therefore what force and how great a power belonged to the invisible essences; what wisdom, what freedom; how much in these things was common to all; and what was given to each individually as proper, singular, and distinct—all this is exceedingly ineffable and remote from human perception.

For divine power and divine wisdom alone are bounded by neither limit nor measure, and the good pleasure of the free choice of eternal and unchangeable will is never constrained by any diminution or strait of necessity. It is absolute, ruling, surpassing, effective, uniquely perfect in the freedom of its own nod, and full of its own power. But everything created is partial: partial in power, wisdom, and freedom. For not every effect is subject to a creature’s power, not every hidden thing is manifest to its wisdom, and not every outcome follows its choice or serves its will. Rather, creatures can act and know only in certain respects, and are free only in certain respects. Therefore their power, wisdom, and freedom must be bounded. Power pertains to action, wisdom to knowledge, and freedom to will.

## CHAPTER XIII. On their threefold power.

There was at first a threefold distinction of their power. One part was the power they had received over themselves; another, that which they had received in relation to one another; and a third, that which they had received over things ordered beneath them in creation. The first power was that of strength; the second, of dominion; the third, of administration. In the power they had received in themselves, all differed; in that which they had received in relation to one another, some excelled; and in that which they had received over things beneath them, they both differed and excelled. In the power which each received within himself, his own nature served him for effect. In the power which they had in relation to one another, the obedience of others was subject to some. In the power which they possessed over inferior things, subject creation rendered service to each according to the strength of his nature and the dignity of his office. These remarks on the primary power of rational nature set forth the first occasion for future inquiry.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the threefold knowledge of angels.

In the first consideration of their wisdom, a threefold distinction also presents itself. For they were enlightened threefoldly, or simply in relation to three things; and there was in them a threefold knowledge, so that they might know what they had been made, likewise by whom they had been made, and with whom they had been made. In knowing what they had been made, they received the knowledge of evil and good, so that they might understand what they ought to seek or reject, according to the power of strength within themselves and the freedom of their will. They also received knowledge of him by whom they had been made, so that they might understand and know their beginning and end—the one from whom they had proceeded in creation and toward whom they ought to turn in intention. They received knowledge of those with whom they had been made, so that they might know what they owed one another according to divine dispensation and ordering, and how far they could, without presumption, avail in those things which had been divinely subjected to them in creation. In this way those spiritual substances were created wise, discerning, and intelligent: wise in all these things as much as was fitting for a nature at its beginning, or necessary for acquiring, according to the merit of their strength.

## CHAPTER XV. Whether angels were made perfect or imperfect.

Many, through lack of knowledge and understanding, suppose that angels possessed a superabundant knowledge not relevant to the matter: cognition, providence, and foreknowledge of future events and of things that were to happen to them. Otherwise, they suppose angels to have been imperfect, ignorant, and not brought to completion and fullness as they ought to have been—such beings as it did not befit the omnipotent, perfect, and good God to make. But they do not distinguish between making something perfect for the purpose that what is imperfect may be perfected—and thus imperfect at first, then perfect, so that it may be perfected by him by whom it was made imperfect to be perfected—and an imperfection in the maker or a defect in the thing made. For the one who made it could have made it otherwise, and the thing made ought not to have been made otherwise. Here it must also be said that a thing is perfect in one respect when it possesses all that it ought to possess, even if it does not possess all that it will possess.

## CHAPTER XVI. That “perfect” is spoken of in three ways: according to time, according to nature, and universally.

For perfection is understood in three ways, and “perfect” is appropriately named in these three senses. There is perfection according to time, perfection according to nature, and universal perfection. The first perfection is, as it were, the beginning producing perfection according to time; next comes the greater perfection according to nature; and the third is the greatest and surpassing perfection universally. That is perfect according to time which possesses whatever time requires and whatever it is fitting to possess according to time. That is perfect according to nature which possesses all that has been given to, or is owed to, its nature. That is universally perfect to which nothing is lacking. The first perfection belongs to created nature; the second perfection belongs to glorified nature; the third and true perfection belongs to uncreated nature.

## CHAPTER XVII. That angels are perfect according to the first perfection.

In this way it is neither surprising nor a matter for questioning why angels were not created perfect: they were created in the first perfection and were to come to the second under the third. For just as they cannot attain the third, so they ought not to have begun from the second. Otherwise, those making progress could not have found room or access to go on to better things, unless something had remained after the first gifts of nature by which they could either grow or decline.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Whether angels foreknew their future outcome.

Here the question arises whether angels foreknew their future outcome and knew, in the wisdom given them, what was going to happen to them. For an incongruity seems to arise in either case. If those who were to become evil foresaw their fall and knew the punishment which had to follow their ruin and would have no end, then, seeing such great evils threatening them, either they wished to avoid them but could not, and so were miserable; or they could but would not, and so were foolish and malicious. But if they did not know, they were blind and did not know where they were going; they set foot into the contingent and accidental, proceeding further where they did not know. It seems as though some absurdity follows if this is said; it seems better and more fitting to say that they knew what was to happen.

But the other argument which we have set against this likewise resists; and a stumbling-block can easily arise for weak minds in either direction unless the positions are reconciled. Therefore we say that they did not foreknow their future outcome, nor was knowledge given to them of the things that were to happen to them. For it was not fitting that they should have such free choice of their will with fear and hope in either alternative. Therefore they were shown what had to be done, not what would happen, so that they might not seem to be driven by any necessity of foreknowledge, but guided by reason and turned in either direction by their own will. And this was good and fitting; God’s work is not deserving of blame because he made it as was good.

## CHAPTER XIX. What angels were like when created: good or evil, just or unjust, blessed or miserable.

But many other questions are also asked concerning that spiritual nature, upon which the curiosity of the human mind is not allowed to rest. They ask whether the angels were created good or evil, just or unjust, blessed or miserable; and perhaps certain other similar questions. And, since many other matters are amassed in the inquiry, we cannot meet them all with a lengthy answer; but we briefly determine that, at that first beginning and initial origin—which human reflection must understand as a point so brief and momentary, a simple instant without delay or interval, when the first subsistence appears from nothing into something, so that it may grasp what was first of all for them—this alone is found in created beings: what the nature of their creation bestowed. For whatever they received, they received wholly. And nothing in them could be from themselves, since everything that is from them is later than they are. Therefore, everything that they were, they did not make themselves; they were merely made, and, in all that they were, they were made good. For if they had been made evil in what they were made, the fault would lie with the maker, not with the thing made; because, when they were made, they could neither be otherwise nor themselves make themselves other than they were made.

Thus from their Maker, when they first existed, they had all that they were and had received all that they were; and they had nothing from themselves, since they had received even what they were—from nothing—and had received from the Creator what they were. But the supremely good Creator could not be the author of evil; and therefore all that they had from Him was wholly good, and it was wholly good because it was wholly from Him. In this way we prove that the angels were good when they were first made, and that all were made good, because they were made by the Good One, who cannot make evil. Thus they were good and not evil; and, just as they were good, so they were also just and blessed. Yet this was the goodness, justice, and blessedness which their beginning nature had received, not what it had itself made or earned by acting.

For if they are called good, they were good in the manner in which all that the Good One made was good. And if they were better—as indeed they were—they were better by reason of what they had been made, not by reason of what they themselves had done or were doing. Likewise, that they are called just meant only that they had not been unjust; and that they are called blessed, that they had not existed in misery. Nevertheless, they are not most properly said to have been just with a justice unto merit, nor unjust with an injustice unto guilt; just as neither blessed unto glorification or consummation, nor miserable unto torment or punishment. And perhaps it would be more exact and clearer to the understanding to maintain that they were created neither good nor evil, neither just nor unjust, neither turned toward nor turned away, neither blessed nor miserable. For one who calls them good signifies virtue; one who calls them just, merit; one who calls them converted, love; one who calls them blessed, glorification.

## Chapter XX. On their free choice at the first beginning of their creation, when they began to subsist

In them, however, the first thing—that is, to begin—was not to will or to act; for they were made for willing and acting, but not yet willing or acting. For willing or acting involves motion, a passage from this to that, succession and duration; and this cannot belong to the initial beginning, which merely begins and is not yet anything further, but is first and not subsequent.

But to will is to will by the will, when the will is moved and already does something; and there are then this and that, and a movement from this to that. The will by which there was willing had preceded, when as yet there was no willing; rather, there was only will, so that willing might arise from it—which, in the initial state, was neither willing nor acting. Therefore the simple beginning and first origin of a nature coming into being must not be understood in this way. Rather, it was one and this alone and nothing more, without space, motion, or duration—all of which follow afterwards, in which willing and acting consist, along with the progression of movements and actions after the first beginning.

But once the will was moved, there was willing; and it came from the will, which moved freely because it moved of itself and not by another’s impulse. This very thing was merit, and was called good or evil, because it was free and from itself. From the moment when they began to be moved by will, they began to merit. This was after the first beginning, and was from the first beginning, but not in it, because it was only from it. From the moment there was will, there was freedom, because freedom belongs to the will; for it was able to move of itself, to go further in this direction or that without compulsion, whether aided or abandoned. For freedom belongs to the will from the moment the will itself exists in that first beginning. Therefore free choice existed in them, because in them there was a will capable of moving and being carried by its own desire in either direction.

## Chapter XXI. What free choice is

For spontaneous movement or voluntary desire is free choice: “free,” indeed, in that it is voluntary; “choice” in that it is desire. But the very power and capacity of the will by which it is moved in either direction is freedom, and is called the free choice of the will. To be moved voluntarily and carried by spontaneous desire is to choose by power and judge by freedom; and free choice consists in this. They were therefore made with free choice, so that they might be moved by voluntary desire, according to the choice of their will and the inclination of their desire, without compulsion.

Yet what was first in them was not a beginning to be moved, nor to choose, nor to desire, because it was simple and the first beginning. Nevertheless, free choice already existed then, because there was a will in which this resided and from which it followed; for it was immediately moved from it and led by spontaneous desire to its own choice.

## Chapter XXII. That free choice always concerns not the present, but the future; and not everything, but only contingent things

[Col. 0256A]

This too must be known: the free choice which we have said existed at the first beginning on account of the will that existed in the first beginning did not itself concern that first beginning. For free choice does not refer to present time, but to things that are later to occur contingently. Everything which is determined cannot be otherwise than it is while it is itself. If it can be otherwise, it can be otherwise afterwards; not otherwise at the time when it is what it is, but afterwards, when it ceases to be what it is and begins to be something else which it is not.

For what can be in the present can indeed be, but cannot be otherwise than the present; and if it can be otherwise than the present, it can nevertheless do so only in relation to the future. Therefore, what they themselves were first made, they could not fail to be, because they were wholly made that; nor did they make themselves, nor could they, when first they existed, fail to be that, because they then were precisely that and merely began to exist. And if they had the power to be otherwise, because they had free choice, they nevertheless did not have the power to be otherwise then, because they were that; rather, they had the power to cease to be what they then were and begin to be what they were not.

For they could not be what they were not unless they first ceased to be what they were, and then afterwards began to be what they were not. Since free choice cannot concern present being, even though it itself exists in the present; rather, it always concerns future events, and only those which are contingent. For future things which are to occur necessarily do not follow free choice, but stand immovably toward one outcome only and admit no alternative contingency. Thus free choice then existed in them, not so that they might then be otherwise than they were, but in the power they had, while being what they were, to cease to be that and begin to be what they were not.

Thus, for those who inquire more carefully, an account is offered concerning the angels’ first state, the beginning of their existence: what they were first made to be by nature, and concerning wisdom and the freedom of choice proposed.

## Chapter XXIII. On the turning away and fall of the evil; and the turning toward and confirmation of the good

[Col. 0256D]

After this, reflection leads us to inquire what they became when they were divided by turning away and turning toward. For in one respect they were at first one, because all were good; and they were good not by doing good, but by being made good. Thus they were one in this: that they had been made good and had not yet become anything other than what they were made, because they had then first been made and had done nothing before.

But they began to be divided from what they had been made, so that they might now become something else: either advancing beyond it and becoming good, or falling beneath it and becoming evil. This is the turning toward and turning away by which those who had been one and good by nature were divided: some became good above that state through justice; others evil below it through guilt. For turning toward made them just, and turning away made them unjust. Both were acts of the will, and in both cases the will was free. Therefore both are reckoned according to merit and judged according to merit: whether it is judged for good merit unto glory, or for evil merit unto punishment.

## Chapter XXIV. How, in those who fell, guilt turned grace away; and, in those who stood, grace aided merit

Those who turned toward the good were voluntarily moved, with grace cooperating and without compulsion. Those who turned away from the good voluntarily plunged downward, grace abandoning them but without oppression. Those who turned toward were moved rightly because they possessed cooperating grace. But those who turned away did not plunge downward because they lacked cooperating grace; rather, grace abandoned them because they turned away and plunged downward.

Those who turned away were not first turned away and afterwards abandoned, because they did not fall while grace was with them. And those who turned toward were not first turned toward and afterwards received, because they did not advance without grace. Rather, those who turned away were abandoned in that very turning away; and those who turned toward were received in that very turning toward: abandoned for turning away and received in turning toward.

## Chapter XXV. That both justice and injustice are in the will alone

Since both justice and guilt are found in the movement of the rational will—because through movement of will they became evil by turning away from the good in which they were, and likewise through movement of will they became good by turning from the good in which they were toward the good in which they had not yet been—therefore all merit by which they were good or evil consisted in the movement of the rational will.

Therefore good and evil must be sought there where justice and guilt are, since justice is good and guilt is evil. Guilt itself was not the will, because the will was not evil, having been given by God. Nor was the movement of the will evil, because it came from the will and belonged to the will, and the will had received from God the capacity to be moved. Nor was that toward which the will moved evil, because it was something, and everything that was something was from God and was good.

## Chapter XXVI. That sin is neither a substance nor from substance, but a deprivation of good

[Col. 0257D]

What then was evil there, except that the movement of the will was not directed toward what it ought to have been directed toward? And it was therefore not so directed because it was directed toward something else toward which it ought not to have been directed. Yet sin consisted not in being directed toward this, but in not being directed toward that; for if that absence had not existed, even if this direction had existed, there would have been no sin.

Thus the rational mind, just as it had received a will and had received the capacity to be moved by will, had also received the objects toward which it might lawfully be moved by will. To be moved toward those things according to measure was to be moved according to justice. And if it had been moved only toward those things, it would have been moved according to justice, and the will would have been just because it had been moved according to justice. But when it was moved toward things which had not been granted, it was moved beyond measure; and in that respect it was not moved according to measure. There its evil lay: in not being moved according to measure.

Its evil was not that it moved toward what it did move toward, but that it did not move according to measure toward what it did not move toward; for if it had been moved according to measure, even while moving toward this, there would have been no sin. To move by will beyond measure was to desire what had not been granted; in this lay not being moved according to measure, and that was evil. The thing itself was the occasion of evil. Because the will was moved beyond measure, it was not moved according to measure. Yet its evil was not in moving toward what it moved toward, but in not being moved according to measure in the respect in which it was not moved. If this had not existed, there would have been no evil at all.

This, then, was the evil which befell the will that turned away and transgressed the measure: it became ugly, warped, and disordered, flowing out and not maintaining the measure and law of its own beauty. But the will which moved rightly and conformed itself to the Creator’s will turned toward Him by whom it was governed; and its good lay in not being moved outside the will of Him from whom it came.

## Chapter XXVII. How God bends every will and power of the angels to the order and disposition of His will

It must also be considered how God governs those invisible and spiritual natures. For if they possess free choice, they do what they will; and if they do what they will, how does what they do depend upon God’s decree? For if we say that they do this because God wills it, because they neither will nor can will anything other than what God wills—He who grants willing itself as He grants power—although this may sometimes be conceded concerning the good, it is in no way approved concerning the evil.

For God grants the evil only power, not will. Although their power to do evil is by His permission, their willing evil is not by His inspiration. For God is the orderer, not the creator, of evil wills. How, then, do they do only what God wills, when they never will except what God does not will, since they always will evil, which God never wills? For if they do what they will, and will what God does not will, how do they do what God wills? Again, if God does not will what they do, why does He permit them to do what He does not will, when it cannot be done unless He permits it, nor permitted unless He wills it?

Here we are compelled to investigate more carefully how the just governance of God rules rational nature, especially that rational nature which, by an unjust will, disagrees with the divine will. Here we consider four general modes of divine governance by which they are disposed and ordered in all that they do, so that even those evils which are contrary to God’s will, while they are what they are—for God does not approve them insofar as they are evil—do not flow beyond His ordering; and it is good and pleasing that they are ordered. Thus God governs and rules according to His will those who, by a warped and unjust will, strive against His will, so that those who rise against it may be led and disposed in accordance with it, to accomplish what pleases Him to be done by a will which displeases Him.

## Chapter XXVIII. That God restrains the will and power of evil angels in four ways

This governance, as we have said, is accomplished in four ways: by the limit of naturally bestowed power; by the miracle of a temporally imposed inability; by the obstacle of externally applied difficulty; or by the judgment of an inwardly operating disposition.

The limit of naturally bestowed power is the extent to which power is naturally granted. The miracle of temporally imposed inability occurs when this natural power itself is restrained, without outward impediment, by a sudden and hidden power of the divine presence. The obstacle of externally applied difficulty occurs when, by divine command, the wills of some are hindered from attaining their effect by other powers externally opposing them. The judgment of an inwardly operating disposition occurs when the divine power itself, which inwardly presides over every creature, bends even those wills which have arisen against its will to accomplish its own will.

By these four modes, therefore, God disposes the warped wills of angels and human beings under the rule of His will, so that even in that in which what exists displeases because it is evil, it may please because it is ordered.

## Chapter XXIX. On God’s hidden disposition, by which He bends even evil wills to His will and orders them according to His will

[Col. 0259C]

Concerning that mode of divine governance by which He who presides tempers and inclines even evil wills toward His purpose by hidden and invisible operation, this must be maintained: God gives evil wills not corruption, but order. For every will exists before willing; and willing is always directed toward something, because everyone who wills wills something. But a will is not always directed toward something before there is willing, because not everyone who has a will has it directed toward something until that person begins, by that will itself, to will and to will something; just as not everyone who possesses sight immediately has it directed toward something, until that person begins, by sight itself, to see and to see something.

A person can possess sight even in darkness, when he does not see; but he cannot see except in light, when he sees something. So too someone can possess a will which is not yet directed toward anything; but one cannot will except something. Every will, therefore, belongs to someone, but is not always directed toward something until it begins to will. But every act of willing belongs to someone, because it is in someone, and is directed toward something, because it concerns something.

Every will is either good, if it is from nature or according to justice; or evil, if it is outside nature or contrary to justice. In an evil will, therefore, its defect comes from itself, by which it is evil; but its order comes from God, by which its willing is toward this or that. Thus in the will is defect, and this itself is evil, and by it the will is evil. But in willing there is both defect, insofar as willing comes from an evil will, and order, insofar as it is directed toward this or that by the One who orders it.

Although this willing itself is directed toward some particular thing, it is evil in being directed toward that thing, because it is from an evil will. But that it is directed rather toward this than toward that is good, because this is order and comes from One who disposes well. An evil will, therefore, can be corrupted and dissolved in itself through its own defect, which is not given to it from elsewhere; but it cannot be hurled outward through willing except by a path opened to it.

And one who opens for it the road by which it hastens as it wills toward ruin somehow inclines it—not by driving it, but by permitting it and not restraining it. He is not the author of its falling, but the orderer of its course. “The Lord,” David says, “commanded him to curse” (2 Kings 16); and, “I have called my servant Nebuchadnezzar to destroy the land” (Jeremiah 25); and, “On that day the Lord will whistle for the fly that is at the end of the river of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria; and they shall come and all rest in the ravines of the valleys and the clefts of the rocks” (Isaiah 7).

In all these passages it is plainly shown that, for the fulfillment of His just judgments, God, by whatever means and occasions He wills, whether inward or outward, both stirs evil wills of men or demons to will, directs them to accomplish, and orders them to subsist. Their being evil is not from God; their being ordered is. This inward disposition of the invisible One who presides is so hidden that it escapes even the evil wills in which it exists, for they think that they are guided solely by their own choice because they feel themselves moved, without compulsion, by their own desire. Because they are not driven, they do not at all perceive that they are directed; and they do not know that they have One going before them so that they may be ordered, because they do not feel one driving them from behind so that they may be hurled downward. We do not wish here to discuss at length the other modes of divine governance, because they are more evident in themselves and raise no such great question.

## Chapter XXX. On the orders of angels: how many were created by God in the beginning

Authority has declared concerning the orders of angels that nine orders of angels were created by God in the beginning: namely angels, archangels, principalities, powers, virtues, dominions, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim; so that, with humanity added, the number ten might complete the perfection of heaven.

For the human condition was not, as some think, so provided for the restoration of the angels that humanity would not have been made unless an angel had fallen. Rather, humanity is said to have been made in order to restore and fill up the number of fallen angels because, when humankind, created afterwards, was led to the place from which they had fallen, the number of that fellowship, diminished by those falling, is repaired through humanity.

For nine orders of angels were created from the beginning; and those among them who fell—because all alike consented in wickedness—formed from themselves, as it were, one order of a perverse fellowship. Tradition, however, holds that some fell from each order. Thus the Apostle Paul, when mentioning the tyranny of malignant spirits, named “principalities and powers of darkness” (Ephesians 6), evidently to show that each now performs in evil, through perversity, the same ministry which by creation it received for accomplishing good. Yet nowhere in Scripture do I find wicked spirits called seraphim, because, although after their fall they still possess their other gifts in evil, they could by no means retain charity in the love of God.

## Chapter XXXI. Whether more remained than fell

No certain authority is found concerning the number of those who fell. Yet it seems altogether probable that more remained than fell. For the prophet, when he showed fiery chariots, said by way of consolation: “Those who are with us are more than those who are with them” (4 Kings 6). From this we infer that the elect angels are more numerous than the reprobate.

Some say that as many elect persons will be raised from humanity as there are elect angels who remained there, because of the Scripture which says: “He set the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God.”

> **Note: [Col. 0261]** Taken from the Song of Moses, Deuteronomy 32, where it reads: “He established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel.”

If this is true, since among human beings the reprobate are far more numerous than the elect, more human beings will be found reprobate than there are elect angels. But if reprobate human beings are more numerous than elect angels—and elect angels are more numerous than reprobate angels—then reprobate human beings will be more numerous than reprobate angels.

How, then, can it be true that each human being is said to have two angels assigned to him, one evil for assault and one good for defense, when the number of human beings exceeds the number of angels? For if among human beings the evil are more numerous than the good, while among angels the good are more numerous than the evil; and if as many elect human beings are to exist as there are good angels, it is beyond all doubt that there are more good human beings than evil angels, and far more evil human beings than evil angels, because evil human beings are more numerous than good human beings, while good human beings are more numerous than evil angels.

Unless perhaps it is said that this is because the human race does not exist all at once, but through the succession of times some follow after others; thus those human beings who exist at one time can be compared in number with angels, although the totality of humankind exceeds them. Yet since this cannot be certain, it is better reckoned among hidden things, where ignorance is not blamed but presumption is reproved.

## Chapter XXXII. On the distinct names of angels

Concerning the names of spirits, we think it especially necessary to recall here that their names were given not for their own sake but for ours. Those who are known to themselves by contemplation become known to us by designation. Thus the gifts of grace which are marked in each name are not those given uniquely, but those given preeminently in participation. For in that heavenly country, where there is fullness of good, although certain things are given preeminently, nothing is possessed uniquely. All things are in all, though not equally—for some possess some things more sublimely than others—but communally, because all possess everything.

Likewise, it must be known that the higher orders received all gifts of grace more sublimely and perfectly; yet, receiving their names only from their chief gifts, they leave the remaining gifts to the orders following them as grounds for their names. Thus, for example, the Seraphim—considered the most excellent order of all—receive both love and knowledge of divinity, and all other gifts of virtues, more sublimely than all the rest; nevertheless, taking their name from the more excellent gift, namely charity, they leave the other gifts to the orders after them for naming.

The order next after this one is called Cherubim from the next gift, namely knowledge of truth; *cherubim* is likewise interpreted “fullness of knowledge,” just as *seraphim*, because of the fire of love, is said to mean “burning” or “kindling.” The same understanding is to be applied to the remaining orders.

## Chapter XXXIII. Whether all heavenly spirits are sent

This too is asked: whether all those heavenly spirits are sent out to announce external matters. Some think that in that multitude some go forth outside for the office of announcing external matters, while others stand within, as it is written: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times one hundred thousand stood before him” (Daniel 7).

But the Apostle, commending the excellence of the Son, affirms that all angels are ministering spirits sent for service on behalf of those who inherit salvation (Hebrews 1). From this arises the question: how are all sent if some always stand by? And if all are messengers, how are some said always to stand by? If all are messengers, all are angels; and if all are angels, why is only one order among the nine designated by this name?

Some think that in that heavenly court all indeed are sent: some by office, those properly called angels or archangels; others temporarily and because of a circumstance arising outside the ordinary dispensation. These too, when they temporarily undertake the ministry of angels, assume the name in the ministry. As it is written: “He makes his angels spirits” (Psalm 103). That is, those who are always spirits by nature sometimes become angels—that is, messengers—by temporary office.

Others say that the three highest orders—Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones—are turned toward divine and inward matters alone and always stand before the Creator. The three lower orders, however, are sent for outward actions and announcements. The three middle orders stand between the two groups not only in rank or place, but also in office: they receive the Lord’s command from the higher orders and convey it to the lower. Therefore, since the highest announce the divine command to the middle, the middle to the lowest, and these to us, all are rightly called angels.

## Chapter XXXIV. On angelic ministries

[Col. 0263A]

Some interpret the ministry and offices of angels so that they believe that the whole world—that is, not only human life but everything pertaining to human life—is administered by angels according to God’s dispensation, under God and in accordance with God. Evil angels, however, do not possess power by office; rather, they sometimes receive power by permission.

# Part Six. On the Creation of Humanity and Its State before Sin

[Col. 0263]

## Chapter I. Why God made the human being from soul and body

[Col. 0263B]

We now undertake to explain in order what we distinguished in the first part of this work as requiring treatment concerning the human condition. For four matters were proposed from the beginning: first, why the human being was created; second, what sort of being the human was created and how established; third, how the human fell; fourth, how the human was restored.

We have already, to the extent of our ability, treated the first of these, namely the cause of human creation. It remains, therefore, that we proceed to examine the second part, in which it was proposed to ask what sort of being the human was created and how ordered. Almighty God, whose blessedness can in no way be increased because it is perfect, nor diminished because it is eternal, created the rational spirit solely out of charity and from no necessity of His own, in order to make it a participant in that good which He Himself was and by which He Himself was blessed.

But because it contributed to that spirit’s felicity that it should recognize the grace of its Creator, through whom it was to be glorified, the Creator wished first to show it in its creation what He would afterwards bring about in it by gracious condescension. Therefore He commanded part of the rational creation which He had made to remain in its purity; but, joining another part to bodily garments and earthly dwellings, He made clayly matter quicken with the sensation of life.

This was proposed as an image of the future fellowship to be accomplished in the glorification of rational spirit with God Himself: namely, that it might be shown that, as body then was to spirit in creation, so the spirit taken up by grace would in some respect afterwards be to God. Thus God demonstrated His power and showed His grace: first by fashioning the human being, as He would afterwards display it in glorifying the human being. Thus humanity might know that if God could join the so dissimilar natures of body and soul in one covenant and fellowship, it would by no means be impossible for Him to raise the humility of rational creation—though far inferior—to participation in His glory.

Again, if this mortal life, consisting in the presence of spirit in a corruptible body, possesses such joy and delight, how great would be the delight and joy of that immortal life which consists in the presence of Divinity in rational spirit? Therefore, because rational spirit was in part humbled, as an image of the whole, even to fellowship with an earthly body, lest this itself seem to tend toward its debasement, God’s providence added that it would afterwards, together with the same glorified body, be raised to fellowship with those who had remained in their purity. Thus what, when created, it had received as lesser through the dispensation of its Creator, it would afterwards receive through the grace of that same Creator when glorified.

Thus God the Creator arranged the rational spirits whom He had made in different ways, perhaps according to the choice of His omnipotent will: establishing a dwelling above in heaven for those whom He had left in their purity, and placing below in an earthly habitation those whom He had joined to earthly bodies. He set before both groups the rule of obedience, so that the former might not fall from where they were, and the latter might rise from where they were to where they were not; so that, when the latter had arrived and the former had not fallen, they might pass beyond what they had been made to be to that for which they had been made, so as to be with Him by whom they had been made.

Therefore God made the human being from a twofold substance: taking the body, in its material aspect, from the earth; but fashioning the soul without matter from nothing.

## Chapter II. How the human being was made in the image and likeness of God

The human being was made in the image and likeness of God because in the soul—which is the better part of the human being, or rather was the human being itself—there was the image and likeness of God.
