Image according to reason; likeness according to love. Image according to knowledge of truth; likeness according to love of virtue. Or image according to knowledge; likeness according to substance. Image, because all things in it are according to wisdom; likeness, because it is one and simple according to essence. Image, because it is rational; likeness, because it is spiritual. Image pertains to form; likeness to nature.

These things were made in the soul alone, because bodily nature could not receive the likeness of Divinity, from whose excellence and likeness it was far removed precisely in being bodily.

## Chapter III. On the creation and origin of the soul
Many questions are raised concerning the origin of the soul: when it was created, from what it was created, and what kind of thing it was created. But in the present abridgment we judge it superfluous and unprofitable to pursue so many opinions [Col. 0265A]; and we think it enough to set forth only those things which ought to be held and affirmed. On these matters, therefore, the Catholic faith has chosen, and judged more consonant with truth, that we should believe that the soul of the first human being, when it was made, was not made from any pre-existing material, but was created from nothing; and that it was not made at the beginning, when the angels were made, but later—when the very body into which it was to be infused had been formed—and was at once made by the Creator himself and joined to the body.

Whether it was created in the body or outside the body: the more difficult this is to know, the less dangerous it is not to know. Nor should human ingenuity be considered praiseworthy when it stubbornly persists in matters that are difficult; rather, when it prudently distinguishes those matters that ought to be known. For it is equally foolish to presume concerning matters that cannot be known and to fail in matters that ought not to be unknown. Therefore, let us seek to know as much as sound faith requires, and cease to investigate those things which curiosity alone urges us to probe.

God created the soul of the first human being from nothing and breathed it into the body, which had been taken from the earth as its material and formed; giving it perception and discernment of good and evil, so that it might enliven through perception the body joined to it, govern it through reason, and so that, in the human being himself, perception might be subject to reason, and reason to the Creator: so that the body might be moved through perception according to reason, while reason itself might be moved according to God by free choice.

## CHAPTER IV. On Free Choice

[Col. 0265C]

There are, moreover, three movements in the human being: the movement of the mind, the movement of the body, and the movement of sensuality. The movement of the mind lies in willing; that of the body, in action; that of sensuality, being intermediate, in pleasure. Free choice is found in the movement of the mind alone; the movements of body and sensuality are what follow free choice. For this was the original ordering of nature: the movement of the mind is a voluntary desire; in what is voluntary lies freedom, and in desire lies choice.

The mind, therefore, moves of itself and is the first movement of the will. The movement of the will is followed by the movement of the body. Thus the mind, as I have said, has the capacity to move itself; but it ought not to move according to itself, but according to the will of its Creator [Col. 0265D], which is for it a form, exemplar, and prescribed rule to follow. Therefore, if it moves according to God, this is justice; if it moves apart from God, or against God, this is injustice.

Thus the movement of the mind is always either justice or injustice; but the movement of the body is always obedience. For when the mind moves, it moves by freedom, because it moves voluntarily and of itself; and what is moved belongs to it, whether toward merit if it moves well, or toward guilt if badly. But when the body moves, it moves by necessity, because it is moved by another—namely, by the mind. What is moved does not belong to itself, but to that by which it is moved, whether toward merit if well, or toward guilt if badly.

Thus the movement of the mind rules the movement of the body, which is subject to it by the law of nature; and when it misuses that movement, the fault is the ruler’s, while the obligation belongs to the obedient one [Col. 0266A]. The one who is led is not blamed, because he is led by necessity; rather, the one who leads is blamed, because he misuses his freedom over that which is subject to him.

Moreover, if the will had retained justice, it would have had not only the obedient movement of the body but also the consenting movement of sensuality. But now, because it did not retain its own rectitude, it still has, through the Creator’s indulgence, the obedient movement of the body; but, through punishment, the resisting movement of sensuality. When weakened, it sometimes follows sensuality’s violence; when strengthened, it restrains and governs it.

But if the movement of sensuality rules the movement of the mind, it also rules the movement of the body, which is subject to it; and then sin begins to reign in our mortal body. But if sensuality does not rule, the mind uses the service of its body [Col. 0266B], presents its members as weapons of justice, and there are together the movement of the mind and the movement of the body, while the movement of sensuality remains apart; justice is accomplished and iniquity restrained.

## CHAPTER V. On the Soul’s Twofold Perception

The rational soul was furnished with twofold perception so that it might grasp visible things outwardly through the flesh and invisible things inwardly through reason, in order that both visible and invisible things might stir it to praise the Creator. For God would not be praised by the rational creature in all his works unless all God’s works were known by the rational creature. Therefore, so that the praise of God might be complete, the works of God were shown to the rational creature, that it might marvel at him inwardly and outwardly, and through wonder advance to love.

One creature was made whose perception was wholly inward, and another creature was made whose perception was wholly outward [Col. 0266C]. The perception of angels was inward; that of brute animals was outward. Angels, whose perception was inward, contemplated things inwardly and through the things that were outward. Brute animals, whose perception was outward, encountered visible things that were outward, but not likewise invisible things inwardly through them. For those who see invisible things see visible things in them, since visible things are known through invisible things; but those who see visible things do not equally see invisible things in them. For the perception by which invisible things are apprehended comprehends lower things in higher things; but the perception by which visible things are encountered does not grasp higher things in lower things.

Thus there was one creature whose perception was wholly inward, and another whose perception was wholly outward. And the human being was placed in the middle, so as to have perception inwardly and outwardly: inwardly for invisible things, outwardly for visible things; inwardly through the perception of reason, outwardly through the perception of the flesh. Thus he might enter and contemplate, and go out and contemplate: inwardly, wisdom; outwardly, the works of wisdom [Col. 0266D]. He might contemplate both, and be refreshed from both sides; might see and rejoice, love and praise.

Wisdom was pasture within; the work of wisdom was pasture without. Human perception was admitted so that it might go to both and find refreshment in both: it might go through knowledge and be refreshed through love. Wisdom was a book written within; the work of wisdom was a book written without.

Afterward Wisdom willed also to be written outwardly in another manner [Col. 0267A], so that it might be seen more clearly and known more perfectly, so that the human eye might be illumined for the second writing, since it had grown dim toward the first. Therefore he made a second work after the first; and it was more evident, because it not only showed but illumined.

He assumed flesh without losing divinity, and he was made a book written within and without: outwardly in humanity, inwardly in divinity; that he might be read outwardly through imitation, inwardly through contemplation; outwardly for healing, inwardly for blessedness; outwardly for merit, inwardly for joy. Within: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1); without: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.). Thus there was one book, written once within and twice without: outwardly first through the creation of visible things, and outwardly a second time through the assumption of flesh [Col. 0267B]. The first was for delight, the second for healing; the first for nature, the second against fault; the first so that nature might be cherished, the second so that vice might be healed and nature made blessed.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Human Being’s Two Goods

Since the human being had been composed of a twofold nature, the Creator prepared two goods for him from the beginning so that he might be made wholly blessed: one visible, the other invisible; one bodily, the other spiritual; one transitory, the other eternal. Both were full, and both perfect in their own kind. One was for the flesh, the other for the spirit: in the one, the perception of the flesh might be cherished unto delight; in the other, the perception of the mind might be filled unto blessedness. Visible things were for the flesh; invisible things for the spirit; the former for consolation, the latter for joy.

Of these goods, he gave one and promised the other [Col. 0267C]. He gave one to be possessed freely; he set forth the other to be sought through merit. He gave the visible good freely; he proposed the invisible good as something to be sought through merit, so that both the excellence of the promise and the faithfulness of the promiser might be demonstrated by the free gift. For if that which he gave freely is such and so great, what kind and greatness must we suppose that to be for which he seeks service? Again, if such goodness was in him that he gave so much to those with no merits, how could there be such malice in him that he would not reward those who serve him?

This was the purpose of all visible things being freely given to the human being: immediately upon being created, he was made lord of things. But afterward obedience was imposed upon him and a commandment given, so that he might first merit and then be rewarded [Col. 0267D]. He was not to be rewarded with those things already given as a gift, but with those things set forth as a gift, but with those things set forth as a reward. Nor was service required from the human being because the omnipotent Creator needed the service of the human being whom he had made, but so that the human being himself might possess more gloriously the true goods acquired through merit.

And because it belonged more to supreme goodness both to give merit and to give reward than, without merit, to give reward alone: the human being ought not to serve in exchange for temporal and transitory things, lest the dignity of the human condition be reduced to utility if he were compelled to serve for things already subject to him. Therefore invisible things, as true goods, are promised to one who serves well after merit; whereas these visible things, as slight and transitory, are added freely during the period of meriting. These are meanwhile for consolation [Col. 0268A]; those later for joy. These are for sustenance; those for glorification. Without the latter, the human being cannot be made blessed in the homeland; without the former, he cannot be sustained on the way.

Accordingly, the human being was made such that for the present and for a time he needed these things, so that through them he might recognize his need for those others, and understand that the good sufficient for him was not sufficient unless he also merited to possess that good from which he himself came. This was a good for him: that he was not sufficient for himself. For it is a great dignity of the human condition that it was made such that no good except the highest good sufficed for it.

And again, it is a great freedom that, meanwhile, it was left to its own choice, so that it could not be compelled to the supreme good, but might go to it by will alone—since it ought to possess it by love alone [Col. 0268B]. Therefore, so that it might learn to seek the good of inward life, its outward life was made such that, unable for a time to stand by itself, it needed support from a good other than and external to itself.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Two Commandments of Nature and Discipline

The good given or promised to the human being by God would have profited him nothing unless a safeguard had been added to preserve what had been given, and a path opened toward what had been promised so that it might be sought and found. Therefore a safeguard was set over the given good: the commandment of nature; and a path was opened toward the promised good: the commandment of discipline.

These two commandments were given to the human being: the commandment of nature and the commandment of discipline. The commandment of nature was what was breathed inwardly through nature; but the commandment of discipline was what was placed outwardly for instruction: inwardly through perception, outwardly through word [Col. 0268C]. In these two commands is contained everything good that is commanded either to be done or to be avoided.

In the commandment of nature there are three things: command, prohibition, and permission. By the commandment of nature we understand nothing other than the natural discernment itself, breathed inwardly, by which the human being was taught what he ought to seek and what he ought to flee. For to breathe into the human heart discernment and understanding of action was, as it were, to give a certain command. What, then, was knowledge of things to be done except a kind of command addressed to the human heart? And what, again, was knowledge of things to be avoided except a kind of prohibition? What was knowledge of things that were intermediate [Col. 0268D] except a kind of permission, so that the human being might be left to free choice where, whichever side he chose, he would not be harmed?

Therefore, for God to command was to teach the human being what was necessary to him; to prohibit was to point out harmful things; and to permit was to indicate things that may be taken either way.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Three Kinds of Things

Among visible things, which were created for the lower life, three kinds of things are found to have been created. Some are necessary for the use of life itself, so much so that a person is harmed if he does not use them. Some are harmful, and a person is harmed if he uses them. Others are intermediate: one may use them or not use them without harm.

For since this lower life is an image of the higher life [Col. 0269A], it was fitting that, in things made for this life, a lesson concerning matters that belong to the higher life should be set before the human being. There are, accordingly, certain things inwardly harmful to spiritual life, which it likewise cannot use without harm: namely, all vices that bring corruption to the soul. There are also certain inward things that are salutary and necessary, without which it cannot be without harm: such as knowledge of God and knowledge of oneself, and all virtues that work for the soul’s health and provide nourishment. There are also other things that may be present or absent without harm. These may be taken either way, since they do not impede salvation as harmful things do, nor produce it as necessary things do; such is knowledge of external things [Col. 0269B] and certain other things of this kind.

Command, therefore, applies to necessary and salutary things; prohibition, to harmful things; permission, to intermediate things.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Twofold Safeguard of the Lower Life

The human being was given reason and foresight through which to preserve this lower life of his: by natural foresight fleeing harmful things, seeking salutary ones, and using intermediate things either way. Fortified by this safeguard, he could avoid negligence, but he could not repel violence. For it was within human foresight to avoid every negligence, but it was not equally within human power to repel every violence.

Therefore divine providence was joined to human reason, so that human reason might keep watch in one respect against negligence, and divine providence might stand in the other [Col. 0269C] against violence. Thus the city of human life, protected by this twofold safeguard, would suffer harm from no adversities: for if human reason had not grown slack against negligence, divine providence would never have allowed violence any place in the human being.

But because reason first abandoned its post through negligence, divine providence afterward justly withdrew itself from protection, so that violence may now sometimes prevail in human life, and reason itself may now, even unwillingly, be compelled to endure what it formerly neglected voluntarily to avoid.

## CHAPTER X. On the Three States of the Human Being

But perhaps someone may think it should be asked how the human being before sin could have suffered any violence, since, if he had not sinned, he would apparently have been unable to suffer anything at all [Col. 0269D]. If, therefore, he could suffer nothing at all, violence could not harm him; nor did he need a safeguard against suffering violence, since whatever might be inflicted on him, he would suffer nothing at all. But if he could suffer violence, how could he also be unable to die? And if he could die, how was he immortal?

To resolve such arguments as are advanced by those accustomed to investigate hidden matters more carefully, we distinguish, as a first consideration, three states of human life. In these, we think it necessary to determine what the human being was like, in body and soul alike; how far he was changed from what he was when first made, and in what he remained the same.

The first state of the human being was before sin, in the condition in which he was created. The second state is after sin—if indeed it should be called a state rather than a ruin [Col. 0270A]—into which he fell through sin and through the punishment of sin that followed sin. The third state of the human being will be after the resurrection from the dead, when he will be fully and perfectly freed both from sin and from sin’s punishment; and he will be restored not only to that in which he was created, but also above it, even unto that for which he was created.

In the first state God and the human being divided things between them; in the second state the devil and the human being divided them; in the third state God receives all. In the first state there was praise of God and something besides praise, yet nothing against the praise of God. In the second state there was nothing for praise, but everything against the praise of God. In the third state everything will be for praise: nothing besides, nor against, the praise of God [Col. 0270B]. Love is for the praise of God; necessity is besides the praise of God; iniquity is against the praise of God. In the first state were love and necessity; in the second, necessity and iniquity; in the third, love alone.

## CHAPTER XI. On the First State of the Human Being before Sin

Many questions are raised concerning the first state of the human being before sin: what the human being was like before he sinned, and what he would have been like had he not sinned, in body and soul; whether mortal or immortal; passible or impassible; concerning the end of the lower life and the passage to the higher; concerning the character and manner of life; concerning the propagation of children; concerning the life and merits of those born from him and following after him; and many other matters which, though sometimes sought out of curiosity, are nevertheless usefully known if examined with discernment.

But among so many matters, especially those remote from our understanding and capacity, we ought to moderate our reply and distinguish what is merely probable from what is not doubtful [Col. 0270C]. Thus there will be no danger in careful inquiry if there is no presumption in rash assertion.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Human Being’s Knowledge before Sin

If, then, it is asked what the first human being was like before sin: with respect to the soul, he was rational, possessing discernment of good and evil, and also knowledge of things perfect insofar as the beginning of his created condition required. For just as, regarding the perfection of the stature and age of the human body, we believe the first human being to have been created perfect [Col. 0270D], so also, regarding the soul, we judge that immediately upon being created he received perfect knowledge of truth and learning—only such as befitted his initial perfection. He did not advance to this through study or some instruction over intervals of time, but perceived it all at once, from the very beginning of his creation, by one simple illumination of divine inspiration.

It is established that the first human being was instructed by a threefold knowledge: namely, knowledge of his Creator, that he might know by whom he was made; knowledge of himself, that he might know what he was made, and what he ought to do; and then also knowledge of that which had been made with him, and what he ought to do concerning it and within it.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Knowledge of Visible Things

[Col. 0271A]

No one should doubt that the human being received perfect knowledge of all visible things that had been made with him and for him, insofar as this appeared relevant either to the instruction of the soul or to the needs of bodily use.

For this reason the Creator himself willed that names for each individual animal should be formed not by himself or by any angel, but by the human being: so that he might plainly show that the human being recognized from the reason implanted in him the nature, use, and functions of each. For the things created for him were to be governed and arranged by him; and therefore God bestowed upon him knowledge of all these things and left their oversight to him.

For the Apostle says: “Is God concerned for oxen?” (1 Cor. 9) [Col. 0271B]. God entrusted to the human being care and foresight concerning the other animals, that they might be subjected to his dominion and governed by his reason, so that the one who ought to receive their service might know also how to provide what they needed.

Because the human being did not lose this knowledge—just as he did not lose that by which he ought to provide the advantages and necessities of his own flesh—by sinning, God afterward did not take care to instruct him through his Scriptures in such matters. But when the human being was restored, he had to be instructed only in the knowledge of the soul, because he had formerly lost that alone by sinning.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Knowledge of the Creator

[Col. 0271C]

There is no doubt that the first human being possessed knowledge of his Creator. For if he received so great a knowledge concerning transient things for the preservation of temporal life, much more ought he to have possessed superior and more abundant knowledge of heavenly things for the attainment of eternal life.

Therefore the human being knew his Creator, not by that knowledge received outwardly from hearing alone, but by that which is imparted more inwardly through inspiration. It was not the knowledge by which God, now absent, is sought by believers through faith; but that by which he was then more clearly perceived, by the presence of contemplation, by one who knew.

Yet it must be understood that we rightly call that first human knowledge of his Creator greater and more certain than the knowledge which now consists in faith alone [Col. 0271D]; so too we must confess that it was necessarily less than the knowledge which will later be openly revealed in the excellence of divine contemplation. Therefore the human being knew his Creator, but not as excellently as he ought afterward to have known him, had he persevered. For just as human disobedience, through the ignorance that followed, took much away from his first knowledge, so, had the human being persevered in obedience, much would have been added to that same knowledge through subsequent revelation.

It is difficult to explain the manner of divine knowledge that the first human being is believed to have possessed, except what we have said: that, taught visibly by inward inspiration, he could in no way doubt his Creator himself.

## CHAPTER XV. On Knowledge of Oneself—Whether the Human Being from the Beginning Foreknew His Own Fall and Ruin, and All Other Evils That Came upon Him and through Him upon His Descendants; and Whether He Likewise Foreknew the Goods He Would Have Possessed Had He Persevered in Obedience

[Col. 0272A]

We believe that this same human being received, from his first knowledge, such knowledge of himself that he recognized the obligation of his obedience toward what was above him and did not fail to recognize the obligation of his oversight toward what was below him. For this was to know himself: not to be ignorant of his condition, order, and duty above himself, within himself, and below himself; to understand what kind of being he had been made and how he ought to proceed; likewise, what he ought to do and what to avoid. All this was to know himself.

If the human being had not possessed knowledge and discernment of these things, he would not have known himself; nor would he afterward have been guilty of transgressing them, if he had not first been illumined to know them [Col. 0272B].

But if it is asked whether from the beginning the human being possessed knowledge of those things that would happen to him—that is, whether he foreknew his own fall and ruin, and all the other evils that first came upon him and afterward passed through him to all who came from him—and likewise whether he foreknew the goods he would have possessed had he persevered in obedience: it appears altogether probable and fitting that, for the establishment and pattern of right living, deeds to be done should have been indicated to him rather than future events foretold.

For it would appear altogether to diminish both freedom of choice and purity of obedience if the human being himself were said to have foreknown future events before earning them [Col. 0272C]. For he could not have hoped for good things while foreknowing evil things, nor have feared evils to come while foreknowing good things. Therefore it is judged more fitting that the first human being received knowledge and command concerning things to be done, but did not possess foreknowledge of things to come, so that free choice might stand open in either direction.

And let this be enough said concerning the human being’s knowledge insofar as it relates to the first state.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Quality of Free Choice through Three States

Concerning freedom of choice insofar as it relates to the same state, we add the following. There can be no doubt that the human being possessed free choice before sin: namely, that freedom by which he could incline the desire of his will either toward good [Col. 0272D] or toward evil. Toward good, with grace assisting; toward evil, with God merely permitting and not compelling.

The first freedom of choice, therefore, was the ability to sin and the ability not to sin, just as the final freedom will be the ability not to sin and the inability to sin. The first freedom had assistance toward good, but weakness toward evil; yet in such a way that it was neither compelled toward good nor held back against evil.

Final freedom will have grace in the good and no weakness in evil; and it will possess not only grace assisting in the good, but also grace strengthening against evil: assisting, so that there is the ability not to sin; strengthening, so that there is the inability to sin.

The intermediate freedom after sin but before restoration does not have grace in the good, but has weakness in evil [Col. 0273A]; and therefore in it there is the ability to sin and the inability not to sin. There is the ability to sin because it has freedom without strengthening grace; the inability not to sin because it has weakness without assisting grace.

Intermediate freedom after restoration but before confirmation has grace in the good and weakness in evil: grace assisting in the good on account of freedom, and grace assisting against evil on account of weakness. Thus in it there is the ability to sin on account of freedom and weakness, and the ability not to sin on account of freedom and assisting grace; but not yet the inability to sin, because weakness has not yet been completely removed and strengthening grace has not yet been fully brought to completion [Col. 0273B].

But when weakness has been entirely removed from the midst and strengthening grace has been completed, there will be the inability to sin. This is not because either freedom of choice or the humility of nature is then destroyed, but because strengthening grace—whose presence makes the presence of sin altogether impossible—is no longer removed.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Human Being’s Virtue before Sin

But if it is asked whether there were any virtues in the first human being before sin, and, if there were virtues in him, whether he merited anything through them, since virtues certainly seem unable to exist without merit: we answer that virtues are possessed in two ways, according to nature and according to grace.

For virtue is nothing other than an affection of the mind ordered according to reason. According to the various applications of that same mind, these affections are said to be many, although they have one root and origin: the will. For one will, according as it inclines itself toward various things by seeking or fleeing them, forms various affections and takes diverse names according to those affections, though all these are in one will, and are one will [Col. 0273C].

The will sometimes flees by nature and sometimes is stirred by grace. Nature itself is indeed by grace, but one grace is creative and another saving. By creative grace, things that did not exist were made; by saving grace, things that had perished are restored. Creative grace first implanted certain goods in created nature; saving grace both restores the goods that corrupted nature first lost and breathes in those goods which it had not yet received in its imperfection.

By the first goods, free choice is restored; by the second goods, free choice acts. In the first goods, God acts in the human being; in the second goods, God works together with the human being. The first goods are God’s gift, not human merit; the second goods belong both to God by gift and to the human being by merit. The first gifts are grace; the second gifts are grace for grace.

Therefore, when the human will moves according to nature alone, it does not merit beyond nature; but when it moves according to God, it merits above nature, because it merits him through whom and for whom it moves. For everyone who wills, wills something, and wills what he wills for some purpose. Whoever therefore wills something [Col. 0274A] and wills it solely because nature wills it, has that willing from nature. But whoever wills something and wills it because God wills it, has that willing from grace; and this is the human being’s merit: that he wills what he wills for God’s sake and does what he does for God’s sake.

For God is bound to repay what is done for his sake, whether by will alone in willing, or by will and deed in acting. Therefore the goods of nature and affections ordered according to nature are natural virtues. Although praiseworthy because they are good and belong to nature, they are nevertheless not worthy of the merit that is above nature, because they contain nothing beyond nature.

Yet I do not think it can properly be said that virtues of this kind merit nothing at all [Col. 0274B], although, being from nature alone, they merit nothing beyond those goods which were created for nature’s sake. But the virtues produced by grace that restores and is added to nature, because in merit they receive something above nature, are worthy also to be rewarded above nature: so that those for whom love of God is the cause of their action may have the presence of God as the reward in recompense.

But in those virtues which arise through restoring grace, the Holy Spirit first works good will; then he cooperates with good will as it moves and acts. First he breathes good will into being; then he inspires good will so that it may move and act rather than remain idle. First he works it; then he works through it. For good will is an instrument; the Holy Spirit is the craftsman [Col. 0274C].

Just as a craftsman first makes the instrument and then works through the instrument, what he first works in the instrument, he alone works; but what he afterward works through the instrument, he does not work alone, but the instrument itself through which he works also works it. So, what the Holy Spirit first works in the human being as good will, he alone works; but what he afterward works through good will, he does not work alone, but the will through which he works does so as well.

Nevertheless, the good work is from the Spirit who works, not from the human will through which he works. The good is indeed in that will, but is not from it. It is not from it because it received it from elsewhere; yet it is in it because it possesses what it received. The very same thing is both its own, insofar as it possesses it, and not its own, insofar as it does not have it from itself [Col. 0274D].

With this distinction established—that some virtues arise from nature alone and some from grace—if it is asked whether the first human being had any virtues in that first state of his created condition, we think without any doubt that good affections, ordered according to justice, were implanted in that nature from its first origin, through which he was drawn by natural desire to perform goodness and justice. In these good affections consisted the natural virtues with which human nature was formed and equipped from the beginning.

But concerning those virtues which are perfected by a good will moved by divine love, we do not wish rashly to define anything concerning him, insofar as that first state is concerned [Col. 0275A], especially since we have no certain argument, either from authority or from reason, regarding any work of his love. Even if he did begin to love his Creator, this was not altogether praiseworthy, because he did not persevere; for the movement of incipient virtue was extinguished and abolished by the slackness of the fault that followed.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What the First Human Being Was Like When Created according to the Body
Now it remains for us to consider what sort of being the first man was made to be in respect of his body: that is, whether mortal or immortal, passible or impassible, and the other questions which seem to require investigation concerning the condition of the human body. Thus the first man, with regard to the nature of his earthly body [Col. 0275B], was in one respect made immortal, because he was able not to die; and in another respect mortal, because he was able to die. For just as in that first state he had the ability to sin and the ability not to sin—for this was the first freedom of the will—so also in the same state he had the ability not to die, and also the ability to die, for this was the first immortality of the human body.

In the second state he has the ability to die and the inability not to die, just as he also has the ability to sin and the inability not to sin; for in this state there is necessity both of dying and of sinning: necessity of dying so long as life is present; necessity of sinning so long as grace is absent. In the third state he will have the ability not to die and the inability to die, just as also the ability not to sin and the inability to sin; for to this state belong the impossibility both of dying and of sinning [Col. 0275C]. Yet both are from grace, not from nature; for if grace were absent, in the one case the natural possibility of dying, and in the other the natural possibility of sinning, would not be absent. Therefore, if the final immortality will be from grace, where the possibility of dying will not exist, how much more was the first immortality not from nature, where the possibility of dying did exist?

Therefore the first man before sin was immortal, since there was in his body no corruption or infirmity; and, besides the other nourishment of foods by which he was to feed and sustain bodily life, he had received from the Creator a special remedy in the tree of life, by which he could preserve that same life sound and incorrupt against the failure of death [Col. 0275D], until he should be transferred to true immortality, where he could no longer die, and, once transferred, should be confirmed.

Therefore, just as we do not say that the first man before sin was immortal in such a way that he could not die at all, so neither ought we to believe that he was in no way passible, as though he could suffer absolutely nothing; for he possessed in himself a passible nature. Nevertheless, if he had not sinned, just as he would not have died, so neither would he have suffered anything at all, whether distress of the will in the mind or impairment of integrity in the body.

For Scripture plainly shows that that first man was able not to die not by the quality of his earthly body but by the benefit of the life-giving food, when it testifies that he was cast out from that tree lest he should be able to preserve life itself perpetually [Col. 0276A], saying: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil. Now therefore, lest perhaps he put forth his hand and take also of the tree of life, and live for ever”: the Lord God cast Adam out of the place of delight (Gen. III). Therefore, he who is said to have been expelled from the tree of life lest he live forever is plainly shown to have been destined to possess this through the benefit of that tree, if he had continued to live.

Thus the first man before sin was mortal and passible by nature; yet, through the prior benefit of the Creator and his own subsequent diligence, he could have brought it about that he neither died nor suffered corruption in life. Since, therefore, man possessed a passible nature, a safeguard against suffering was necessary for him: namely, that through his own reason he might be roused to guard against negligence, and through divine providence might be kept unharmed against every violence [Col. 0276B]; and thus, fortified on both sides, he would neither die nor suffer.

## CHAPTER XIX. How long man, if he had not sinned, ought to have remained in this lower life

As to how long man ought to have remained in this earthly life, no other argument can be had except that it is wholly probable that, after completing obedience, if he had persisted in that obedience, he ought immediately to have been transferred to the reward of that obedience, so that without the intervention of death he might pass from the first state, in which he had the ability not to die, to another state in which he could thereafter not die at all.

## CHAPTER XX. On his nourishment

[Col. 0276C]

Meanwhile, he would nourish earthly life by earthly fruits until he was transferred to that life in which he would need no nourishment whatever. As it is written: “The first man was made into a living soul; the second into a life-giving spirit” (I Cor. XV). For what lives has life, whereas what gives life bestows life; and to give life is altogether greater than to live. Therefore, because the first life could not stand by itself, while the final life will have no need to be sustained from elsewhere, the first man is said to have been made into a living soul: it had life in itself, indeed, but could not by itself give life to the body. The second, however, was made into a life-giving spirit, which will both have life in itself and give it to the body by itself.

## CHAPTER XXI. On his occupation

[Col. 0276D]

If, however, it is asked by what occupation human life, had man not sinned, ought to have been cultivated and exercised, it may fittingly be said that, besides inward and spiritual occupations of wisdom and divine contemplation, the first human beings were also to be exercised outside, upon the earth, in cultivation—whether ploughing, sowing, planting, and other such works by which good nature, when cultivated, advances toward what is better—not for labor but for delight: so that the work might be a delight and an example for instruction.

For the outward man was to be exercised by the very practice of outward work, so that he might take from it a pattern for inward occupation; and, in what he did outside, recognize what he must do within. For inwardly there was likewise a certain soil [Col. 0277A], which was indeed created good, yet could become still better if well cultivated; when cultivated it would yield good fruits, but when neglected it would produce evil and harmful shoots.

## CHAPTER XXII. What children man would have begotten if he had not sinned

After the matters already discussed, this too seems to require inquiry: how man could have procreated children if he had not sinned, and what those born from him would have been like. In matters of this sort, therefore, as we have often said, one must carefully distinguish things which are not doubtful from things asserted only as probable. For matters which neither authority proves nor clear reasoning demonstrates are left among doubtful things. Yet such questions are sometimes admitted not uselessly, so that either what is true may be found [Col. 0277B], or at least what is false may not be granted.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Whether they would be born righteous or unrighteous

Since we read that marriage between male and female was instituted by God before sin, and that they were granted and commanded, by the gift of blessing, to increase and multiply, we must in no way doubt that the union of flesh in the generation of offspring would have occurred without shame and concupiscence. Therefore, those begotten without sin would consequently also have been born without sin, just as those who are now begotten with concupiscence, drawing corruption as it were from the very defect of their root, are born with guilt.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Whether they would be heirs of paternal righteousness

[Col. 0277C]

It also seems worthy of inquiry whether the merit of paternal obedience ought, through an incorrupt origin, to have passed to all descendants, just as now the guilt of that disobedience, through the same origin when corrupted, spreads itself abroad by pouring itself out upon all. If this is true, then original righteousness would then have existed in those being born through the merit of their parents, just as original guilt is now found in them from the guilt of paternal transgression alone.

Yet this should not be asserted rashly, because it does not seem that, just as nature is now seen to have been changed into corruption through disobedience, so also then, through obedience observed, it would have been changed into incorruption—unless it had been preserved until a time predetermined by God [Col. 0277D]. For to transgress once was complete disobedience; but obedience would not likewise have been perfect if man had not persevered in that obedience unto the end.

Therefore, just as disobedience completed at one time changed nature into corruption, so obedience would not have changed nature into incorruption until it had at its proper time been kept unto the end and made perfect. Those who in the meantime were begotten would be conceived from a nature not yet transformed into true incorruption, nor would they receive, by being born, the merit of original righteousness; because those from whom they were born would not yet possess the righteousness of perfect obedience. Nature could not give to those being born what it did not yet possess in those who begot them, just as those who are now begotten in sin [Col. 0278A] draw in birth nothing other than the defect which they receive from the nature from which they are conceived.

Thus, during the time of his obedience, the first man, serving the divine institution by chaste marriage for the propagation of descendants, would have begotten children without sin indeed, because they would arise from a nature free from every defect; but they would not likewise have been heirs of paternal righteousness, because nature itself would not yet have been transformed to the reward of incorruption—which was not to be given except after obedience had been completed. But after he had been transformed from eternal life into a heavenly and spiritual state, he ought no longer to have begotten children, just as he now, though subjected to mortality through disobedience, does not cease from bodily propagation.

Therefore the condition does not seem to be the same in both cases, because the same reasoning does not appear on both sides [Col. 0278B]. Yet there are those who believe it should truthfully be maintained that, if the first man had not sinned, he would have begotten only good children, and that none of all who were born from his flesh would be condemned.

Still, one properly asks whether the obedience of the first man alone, once tested, ought to have sufficed for the merit of all descendants to be born from him; or whether each one after him, in his own time—just as the first man himself was tested—ought to have been tested by observing either the same command or some other command. Perhaps it may not unreasonably be believed that the same command given to the first parent ought also to have been observed by his descendants, so that each might be tested by his own obedience, and each glorified with a fitting reward according to his own merits [Col. 0278C]. Yet the first obedience, if observed, would be the cause of assisting grace for all who followed and imitated that obedience by obeying.

## CHAPTER XXV. Whether they would have been transferred together, or successively

Concerning the end of this lower life, in which man was to remain until the appointed time, until he was clothed over with heavenly and truly immortal life, and after completing obedience was transferred to the reward of obedience without the intervention of death: this seems more consistent with reason and more worthy of belief. Just as in this mortal life, while some depart through death, others who are to live succeed them through birth, so then also, when those before them had been transferred after the end [Col. 0278D] of this temporal life to eternal life, those born from them would succeed the departing; and they likewise would fulfill their own times and keep obedience, until at last the number of those predestined for life should be fulfilled and the time assigned to the human race for this lower life should be completed.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Whether they would be born perfect in stature and knowledge

But if it is asked what kind of children man ought to have begotten had he not sinned—whether, namely, just as the first man himself, immediately upon being created, was perfect in bodily stature and in mental understanding, so those who would have been born from him ought likewise to have been perfect both in body and understanding from the very beginning of their birth—we approve more strongly the following opinion [Col. 0279A]. The first man, as we have said, should be believed to have been made immediately perfect both in body and understanding; but those born from him would be born small, according to the same law by which we now see human birth ordered, and afterward would receive growth, through intervals of time, both in mental understanding and bodily stature.

For in every kind of thing we see that the first creation has one law, and subsequent propagation another. All first things were made perfect; but all others which arise from them and follow after them cannot reach perfection except by growing through intervals of time. We see this in trees, plants, and every kind of shoot; we see it in animals [Col. 0279B] and all living things. Everything begins from something small and afterward gradually reaches perfection through ordered stages of growth.

Accordingly, it must by no means be imputed as a defect of human nature if, after beginning in its first origin from perfection, it advances by subsequent propagation from small things to greater and better. With respect to the human body, perhaps it will not be difficult, nor will it seem inappropriate, to accept this opinion. But with respect to understanding and knowledge of truth it may perhaps seem less probable: namely, that those born without sin would be born imperfect in mental perception and understanding, because all ignorance in a rational creature seems to arise only from the punishment of sin.

But those who say this do not sufficiently carefully consider that not everyone who does not know something, or knows something less perfectly, must immediately be said to possess ignorance or to be in ignorance. For ignorance is spoken of only when that which ought not to have been unknown is unknown [Col. 0279C]. Such ignorance is known to exist only from the punishment of sin, when the mind, blinded from the light of truth so that it cannot know the things it ought to know, is darkened through its own fault.

But the imperfection of perception or knowledge which appears to exist from the beginning in all who are born now, and which is believed also to have had to exist then, belongs to nature, not guilt. This is plainly evident from the fact that the Lord in the Gospel, when under the figure of the soul he confronted the Samaritan woman concerning her hidden matters, testified that she had first had five husbands and that the man she then had was not her husband, saying: “For you have had five husbands, and he whom you now have is not your husband” (John IV).

Who are the five husbands to whom the rational soul is first said to have been lawfully joined, except the five bodily senses, according to which the first age of human life is governed without the discernment of reason? If proceeding according to the impulses of those senses belonged to that age through defect rather than nature, those senses would surely have been called not husbands but adulterers [Col. 0279D]. Moreover, when it is afterward added that the man she had was not her husband, it is plainly shown that the five whom she had previously had were hers—that is, lawful and not alien.

For it is natural to human nature in its first age to be moved and to proceed according to the impulses of the senses alone [Col. 0280A]. But when it reaches the years of discretion, if, having abandoned truth, it follows error, then that error is called not a husband but an adulterer. What it does earlier, while proceeding according to the movement of the senses alone, is reckoned neither as evil unto guilt nor as good unto merit.

Therefore it is not a defect, even for infants born in sin, to be born without knowledge. Rather, their defect consists in being born with such a defect that afterward, when they have reached the years of discretion, it may happen that, unless they possess assisting grace, they are hindered from knowledge of truth—especially that knowledge which pertains to salvation. If this is true, neither would it have been a defect for those born without sin also to be born without knowledge [Col. 0280B], because in being born they would have had nothing in themselves by which they might afterward, when they reached the time for knowing, be hindered from knowledge of truth.

We, indeed, choose in this manner, in hidden matters, what appears to us more probable; yet we do so without presuming to assert doubtful matters as certain in any respect. But as for our purpose, which was to discuss what sort of being the first man was created to be, we intend this present abridgment to suffice. It now remains to explain, insofar as occurs to the mind and seems suitable to our purpose, what follows: namely, how he was instructed by God.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the instruction of the first man

In order that we may more fully understand how the first man was instructed by God and formed for right living [Col. 0280C], we must return to the middle of what was said above. For above we said that two goods were prepared by God for man from the beginning: one bodily, the other spiritual; one visible, the other invisible; one transitory, the other eternal; one for the body, the other for the spirit; one for the lower life, the other for the higher, so that each life might have its own delight. Some were for support, others for joy; some for necessity, others for happiness; some for the use of time, others for the fruit of eternity.

The care of these goods, which belonged to each life, was entrusted to the spirit—which in man presided over the flesh—so that it might arrange the one, that is, bodily good, for the use of the lower life through prudence; and seek the other, that is, spiritual good, for the fruit of the higher life through obedience [Col. 0280D].

Both, therefore, pertained to the rational spirit: both that it might provide for its flesh and that it might provide for itself. It provided for its flesh in the good subjected to it for the use of that flesh; but it provided for itself in that good which was set before not only the flesh, but also the spirit itself, which was superior in dignity while in the flesh.

Therefore prudence was concerned with preserving the lower good, but obedience was necessary for obtaining the higher good. Prudence arose from reason; obedience from command. Prudence belonged to the command of nature; obedience to the command of discipline. Thus the first man was instructed so as to preserve the good of the lower life through prudence and seek the good of the higher life through obedience [Col. 0281A]. If he had proceeded according to this instruction, he would have maintained perfect righteousness; and, just as he would have been free from guilt, so he would have remained free and exempt from punishment.

But in order that we may understand more perfectly in both respects the manner of this instruction, it is necessary to consider more carefully the nature and pattern of each life, the goods which seem to belong to each life, and their use.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the instruction of man with respect to the lower life

Therefore God had prepared for man from the beginning the two goods which we distinguished above: one temporal and the other eternal, each full and perfect [Col. 0281B]. The one, namely temporal good, he supplied in full immediately upon man’s creation; the other, namely eternal good, he proposed to give in full after merit. To the good which he had given he added, together with his providence, the command of nature as its safeguard; toward the other good which he had proposed he opened a way, together with his grace, through the command of discipline.

The command of nature contains three things: prescription, prohibition, and permission. Natural prescription is natural discernment, through which man is taught what is necessary to his nature. Prohibition is that through which he is informed what is harmful. Permission is the discernment of intermediate things: things which he may use or not use without danger or disadvantage. Therefore, if man, instructed through the natural command, had been willing to avoid negligence [Col. 0281C], divine providence would have allowed no violence to oppress or injure him.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the instruction of man with respect to the higher life

Man, then, could by the command of nature preserve the natural good which he possessed; but by it he could not attain the eternal good, which he did not yet possess. For no merit toward the attainment of the higher life would accrue to him if he either avoided things harmful to this life, sought things beneficial, or used intermediate things for either purpose; because in all these things he would attend not so much to the intention of the one commanding as to the advantage of the one obeying.

Therefore, for man to merit something beyond this life, it was necessary to add the command of discipline to the command of nature, and that in carrying out this command man might be tested as embracing not so much the benefit commanded as love for the one commanding [Col. 0281D]. But what further thing could be commanded to him for testing human obedience, when everything belonging to human life is contained in the command of nature? For all things made for man are either necessary to human life and belong to prescription; or harmful and belong to prohibition; or intermediate and belong to permission.

The command of discipline, however, could be taken neither from natural prescription nor from natural prohibition. For if God either commanded or prohibited the same things which he had earlier commanded and prohibited, there would, as has been said, be no merit toward life for the one obeying [Col. 0282A]. But if he altered the command in either case, so as either to prohibit necessary things or command harmful things, he would unjustly injure the nature he had made. And in the conflict of his commands, whichever part was carried out would cast man into the necessity of transgression, since he could not fulfill one of two contrary commands without violating the other.

It was necessary, therefore, that the command of discipline be taken from natural permission, since merit could exist only where free choice existed, and where man could incline himself according to his wish toward either alternative. Yet the command of discipline had to be taken from permission itself in such a way that permission itself was not changed by the command: that is, the command should not corrupt the nature of the thing concerning which it was to be made [Col. 0282B], nor make it harmful contrary to the first ordering of human life, so that disobedience alone might harm the transgressor, and not the nature of the thing in which he transgressed.

And when the command of discipline was to be formed from natural permission, it was more fitting that this be done by way of prohibition rather than prescription, lest the devil be able to impugn human obedience; and it was fitting that it concern only one thing, not many, lest disobedience itself be capable of excuse by man. For if God had told man to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, the devil would have had something to say against man: namely, that in carrying out the command he had looked more to his own advantage than to the command of his Creator, and that he had been led to do what was commanded not by love of God but by delight in food [Col. 0282C].

Again, if God had prohibited many of those things naturally permitted to man and allowed few, man would seem to have an excuse before God for his transgression, since he could be shown to have been driven to transgression more by necessity than by will. Therefore, when God formed man by a command in order to test his obedience, he allowed many things and prohibited few, so that obedience itself might be free. And he prohibited what he prohibited rather than commanding it, so that obedience itself might be pure. “Of every tree of paradise eat,” he says; “but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat” (Gen. II): so that he might first console the weakness of human understanding by permission [Col. 0282D], lest it perhaps afterward be frightened by prohibition.

Therefore, if man had persisted in this obedience, after a time determined by God he ought to have been transferred, without the pain of death, to the good prepared for him in heaven, together with all his offspring following after him, to live without end in heavenly life in the fellowship of the blessed angels.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the place in which the first man was placed

As Scripture says, “The Lord God had planted from the beginning a paradise of delight, in which he placed the man whom he had formed” (Gen. II). What sort of paradise it was in which man was placed to be tested and exercised, Scripture goes on to say: “And the Lord brought forth from the ground every tree beautiful to behold [Col. 0283A] and pleasant for eating; also the tree of life in the midst of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. And a river went out from the place of delight to water paradise; and from there it was divided into four heads” (Gen. II).

It is clear, therefore, how delightful was that place in which human nature, still free from corruption, was to be cherished and nourished: it is described as watered by springs and streams, leafy and wooded with trees of every kind, and filled with fruit both beautiful to behold and pleasant to eat.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the tree of life

There, among the other gifts of God prepared for the delight of human life, is also mentioned that marvelous thing—that there was a tree of life whose power is reported to have been so wonderful that, when eaten at fixed times, it could preserve bodily life in man, so long as man used it, unharmed not only from death but also from every failing [Col. 0283B].

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the tree of the knowledge of good and evil

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is also said to have been there. It could not, in the same way, by its own nature give man knowledge of good and evil, as the tree of life by its own nature and the power implanted in it by God could preserve bodily life in man. It is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil only because it was prepared for testing man’s obedience or proving his disobedience.

For there were certain goods which man had not yet known by experience, and likewise certain evils which he had not yet known by experience. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil was set as though in the middle, so that through it man might, by obeying, pass on to taste and know goods; or, by not obeying, come to feel and perceive evils [Col. 0283C]. Thus in that place he was to receive an occasion for knowing either good or evil—not from the nature of the tree, which could not give this to man from itself, but because by obeying he received an occasion for good, or by not obeying an occasion for evil, as his due recompense.

If, however, we wish to interpret the force of this name differently, we may say that Adam before sin knew good and evil: good both by knowledge and experience, evil by knowledge alone. But after he touched the forbidden tree, he began to know evil also by experience; and through experience of evil itself he recognized how strictly the good ought to have been held. Thus that tree could benefit or harm man through the power of obedience or the guilt of disobedience. So far as its own nature was concerned, it is believed to have been such that, whether man ate its fruit or did not eat it, he would not be harmed [Col. 0283D].

It was fitting that the tree of life should bestow power from its own nature, whereas the tree of the knowledge of good and evil should furnish only an occasion for virtue: because the goods of the lower life are from nature, but the goods of the higher life are from grace.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. That man was placed in paradise, not created there

[Col. 0284A]

Thus man was placed, not created, in such a place, filled with such delights, so that he might attribute God’s benefit not to nature but to grace. As it is written: “The Lord God took the man whom he had made and placed him in the paradise of delight” (Gen. II). For in saying that he took him and afterward placed him in paradise, Scripture plainly shows that he was created elsewhere and brought from another place to be set here.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Why one man was created first

Therefore God first created one man, so that there might be one beginning of the human race; so that by this the pride of the devil might be confounded, and the humility of human nature glorified by likeness to the divine image [Col. 0284B]. For the devil had desired to be a principle other than God; and, in order that his pride might be more fully confounded, man received as a gift what the devil perversely wished to seize and could not obtain. Thus the image of God appeared in man: just as God was the principle of creation for all things, so this man would be the principle of generation for all human beings; and, while all human beings knew themselves to be from one man and to be one, they might all love themselves as though they were one.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Why woman was made from man, and why from his side

Afterward, woman was made from the man himself as an aid to generation. For if she had been made from elsewhere, there would certainly not have been one origin for all human beings [Col. 0284C]. She was made from the man’s side in order to show that she was created for partnership in love: lest, if she had been made from his head, she might seem to be preferred to the man unto his condemnation; or, if from his feet, to be subjected to servitude. Therefore, since she was being prepared neither as mistress nor slave for the man, but as his companion, she had to be brought forth neither from his head nor from his feet, but from his side, so that he might recognize that she was to be set beside him, whom he learned had been taken from beside him.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Why the rib was removed while the man slept

And the rib from which the woman’s body was to be fashioned was removed while the man slept rather than while he was awake, lest he be thought to have felt some punishment in it, and so that the wonderful work of divine power might at the same time be demonstrated: it opened the side of the sleeping man and yet did not rouse him from the rest of sleep [Col. 0284D].

With respect to the spiritual sense, however, the first Adam by sleeping supplied from his side the material from which that bride might be created, because the second Adam later, having been put to sleep by the sleep of death upon the cross, ministered the sacraments by pouring forth blood together with water from his side, so that his bride, the Church, might be formed.

Moreover, that the woman’s body is said to have been made from the man’s rib must be understood in this way: that from the substance of the rib alone, without any extraneous addition, that same body was made by divine power multiplying it in itself. This was the same kind of miracle by which, later, five thousand men were fed from five loaves multiplied in Jesus’ hands through heavenly blessing.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the six modes of working

[Col. 0285A]

Certainly there are six operations by which all things that come to be are brought into effect. The first operation is to make something from nothing. The second is to make some things from one thing, in substance and quantity, by increase. The third is to make one thing from some things, in substance and quantity, by decrease. The fourth is to make some things from one thing, yet not in substance and quantity by increase. The fifth is to make one thing from some things, yet not in substance and quantity by decrease. The sixth is to make nothing from something.

Of these six operations, four are possible to God alone; the remaining two belong only to the capacity of creatures. For God alone can make something from nothing; make some things from one thing [Col. 0285B] by increase; make one thing from some things by decrease; or make nothing from something. The remaining two—namely, making some things from one thing without increase, as when a whole is divided into parts; or making one thing from some things without decrease, as when parts are united in a whole—can be performed by a creature. Its work is rightly called nothing for this reason: through its work nothing is removed from or added to the essences of things, whether what was divided is joined or what was joined is divided.

But where something is made from nothing, something is made; for the very something, in order that it may be, is made in that act, and unless it were made, that very thing which is would not be something. Again, when more is made from something, something is made; for unless something were made in that which is already something, that which is subsequently more there would not be. Again, when one thing is made from some things [Col. 0285C], unless that which was formerly more were made into that which is now less, it would not exist at all.

Something is made from nothing when that which previously was nothing is made so as to be something. But when afterwards that which had first been made small is made greater, something is made from something by increase. And when that which has been made great is at some time made less, something is made from something by decrease. The first is the work of creation; the second, the work of multiplication; the third, the work of union or collection.

In the first operation something is made, and it is made from nothing. In the second operation something is made, and it is made from something. In the third operation something indeed is made, but not from nothing, because what is made has matter; nor yet from something, because, when it is made, it itself has in matter the form. But when two become one, the one becomes other and passes into that other so as to be that other; it indeed ceases to be what it is, and yet does not cease to be, because it begins to be what it is not. And when that which begins to be is made, something is made, because what begins to be, and what is made, is something. Yet what is made is not made from nothing, because before this was made something existed; nor again is what is made made from something, because what existed before ceases to be when that begins to be which did not exist before. [Col. 0285D]

Let us set forth what we say by an example. Everything which is one, and everything which ceases to be one, in ceasing to be one thereby also ceases to be. Thus nothing can subsist without unity. Yet among things which are and are one, some derive their unity from many things: such are composites and things consisting of parts. They possess being one, yet do not possess it from one thing, because they consist of many. [Col. 0286A] Others derive their unity from one and possess it in one, because that from which they are and that which they are are one and the same: such are all simple things, which do not consist of parts.

For composites, therefore, to be one is nothing other than to be united; and consequently this is not truly to be one, because it is from many and in many. But for those whose being is simple, truly to be one is to be one, because the whole is one—both that which is and that from which it is. Yet among those which are one by simplicity, some do not gather their unity from many, because they are not composite; nor do they diffuse their unity into many things, because they cannot be multiplied or become matter. [Col. 0286B] Such are incorporeal spirits, which are not from matter because they are simple, and cannot become matter because they are not bodies.

Other things indeed do not gather their unity from many things at once, because they are simple; nevertheless, they diffuse their unity into many things, because they are multiplied and become matter. Such are the simple bodies called atoms. They are not made from matter, because they are simple; yet they become matter, because they multiply in themselves and grow into increase. Therefore, when simple matter or a simple atom is made, something is made from nothing. But when that same simple body multiplies in itself and grows into a multitude, something is made from something by increase.

Although this may appear wonderful, it is nevertheless greater to make something from nothing than to make more from something. It was by this mode of operation that the woman’s body was made from the substance of the rib, multiplied in itself through divine power without any external addition. For it is not fitting to say that that rib received an addition from outside, so that it might grow to the quantity sufficient for forming a woman’s body. If this were true, it would be more appropriate to say that the woman’s body was made not from the rib but from that which was added besides the rib—which was certainly much greater. For that would have been greater and more primary in the matter, and should have been called the principal matter. [Col. 0286C]

Therefore nothing was added externally to that rib; rather, it was itself multiplied from itself, with divine power cooperating, just as we see human nature, sown from the first parents into succeeding generations, multiplied from a little into such abundance that we see many thousands of human beings already grown from it. And all this belongs to the second operation, when some things are made from one thing by increase.

But when, through gathering and union, many things return into a simple essence—as previously, through multiplication by growth, very many things went forth from a simple essence—the third operation occurs. Whether divine power performs this operation in the hidden bosom of nature with respect to certain essences—namely, by reducing some things from multiplicity to simplicity which it had previously brought forth from simplicity into multiplicity—we cannot know; yet neither ought we obstinately to deny it. [Col. 0287A] We need only observe that it is one operation when a simple essence is multiplied, and another when what is multiple is reduced to simplicity.

After these three operations, which are possible to God alone, follow the fourth and fifth operations, which also belong to creatures. In these, to make is nothing other than either to separate things that are joined or to join things that are separated. The sixth operation is to reduce something to nothing. It is possible to God alone. Whether God ever does this, this at any rate is wholly certain: He who was able to create all things from nothing could, if He willed, reduce created things to nothing. [Col. 0288A]

After the number six, assigned to works, follows the number seven, to which not work but rest belongs. We have distinguished these operations for the sake of those who are accustomed to wonder—or rather to doubt—how a woman can be made from a man’s rib, and how so numerous an offspring can grow from a small paternal seed.

## PART SEVEN. ON THE FALL OF THE FIRST HUMAN BEING

[Col. 0287]

## CHAPTER I. How he fell through the devil’s envy

[Col. 0287B]

When, therefore, the human being, lord of the world, had been placed by divine providence in the place of delights, as it were in its more excellent part; fortified by that same providence of God, joined to human reason, for preserving the goods he possessed; and instructed, through the commandment of obedience working with grace, to seek and obtain the goods he would possess: the devil saw and envied that the human being would ascend by obedience to that place from which he himself had fallen through pride.

## CHAPTER II. Why the devil came in an alien form

Since he could not harm by violence, he turned to fraud, so that he might overthrow by deceit the human being whom he could not overcome by strength. Yet lest his fraud be wholly ineffective if it were too plainly disclosed, he ought not to come in his own form, lest he be openly recognized and wholly rejected. Again, lest his fraud be too violent if it were completely hidden, and the human being should seem to suffer an injury if God permitted him to be deceived by a fraud against which he could not guard, he was permitted indeed to come in an alien form, but in one in which his malice was not entirely concealed. [Col. 0287C]

Thus, that he did not come in his own form came about by his own will; but that he could not assume another form except one suitable to his malice was arranged by divine ordinance. The cunning enemy therefore came to the human being in a serpent. Perhaps, if he had been permitted, he would have preferred to come in the form of a dove. But the Holy Spirit reserved that vessel for himself, because it was certainly not fitting that an evil spirit should make hateful to humankind the form in which the Holy Spirit himself was afterward to appear to them. [Col. 0287D]

## CHAPTER III. Why he came first to the woman

It is pleasing to consider how much the malice of this enemy was to be feared at the beginning, in his attempt to test human strength. As though trusting too little in his own powers, he attacked human nature in that part where it seemed weaker, so that, if perhaps he could prevail there to any extent, he might afterward approach with greater confidence to assail, or eventually overthrow, the other part which was stronger. Knowing therefore the truth—although it had not yet been spoken—“Woe to one who is alone, for when he falls he has no one to raise him up” (Eccles. 4); and, “If someone prevails against one, two resist him,” he carefully watched the woman when she was alone, and, finding her so, resolved first to test upon her the whole force of his temptation. [Col. 0288B]

## CHAPTER IV. Why he began with a question

Consider how great is the confusion and timidity of wickedness in the presence of virtue. Standing face to face with the woman, the proud enemy is confounded merely by the malice he has conceived but not yet uttered; and, fearing as though he had already been detected before he even spoke, he does not dare to proceed to words of persuasion until he has first sounded out the mind of the one to be tempted by a question.

“Why,” he says, “[Col. 0288C] has God commanded you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” The woman answered him: “We eat from the fruit of the trees that are in paradise; but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the midst of paradise, God has commanded us neither to eat it nor touch it, lest perhaps we die.” But the serpent said to the woman: “You shall by no means die by death” (Gen. 3).

Consider the stages of ruin. First God had said: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2). Then the woman said: “Lest perhaps we die” (Gen. 3). Finally the serpent said: “You shall by no means die by death” (ibid.). God affirmed; the woman doubted; the devil denied. But the devil would never have dared, in the woman’s presence, to deny God’s words if he had not first found the woman herself doubting. She therefore who doubted departed from the one affirming and approached the one denying. Thus she herself, in a certain respect, began the wickedness which gave boldness to the tempter’s evil persuasion. [Col. 0288D]

## CHAPTER V. That the commandment was not given to the man alone

Here it should indeed be observed that the commandment was not given, as appeared above, to the man alone. For the woman herself testifies here that the command was also given to her, that she should not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
