Scripture evidently wished to show that the woman, who was subject to the man, ought to receive the divine command only through the man: the word of God came first, as it were immediately, to the man, and then through the man to the woman also, who was subject to the man and was to be instructed by the man’s counsel. [Col. 0289A]

## CHAPTER VI. On the manner of temptation

This, moreover, must be carefully considered: how cunningly the enemy first removed, by denying it, the evil which the woman feared; then freely persuaded the evil which he himself intended. Finally, to support the persuasion itself, he added a promise; and, so that the same persuasion might be received more quickly, he made the promise twofold. For though he urged only one eating, he set forth two things as its reward: likeness to God and knowledge of good and evil.

Thus, in urging the food, he tempted the human being through gluttony; in the promise of divinity and knowledge, through vainglory and avarice. For an immoderate desire to eat is gluttony; an inordinate desire for excellence is vainglory; and an excessive appetite to have or possess is avarice. [Col. 0289B]

## CHAPTER VII. What evils were present in original sin

There were, therefore, in original sin three vices, two disobediences, and one sin. The three vices were pride, avarice, and gluttony; the two disobediences, one against the command of nature and the other against the command of discipline. Since all these were accomplished in one act, they are called one sin.

Among the vices, pride was first, avarice second, and gluttony third. In pride and avarice there was disobedience against the command of nature; in gluttony alone there was disobedience against the command of discipline. For nowhere do we read that God forbade the human being to desire likeness to divinity or knowledge of good and evil. Yet, because in desiring these inordinately the human being acted against his own reason, he became in some measure a transgressor of the natural command. We read that God forbade the human being only to touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; and therefore, when the woman touched it by desiring it, she incurred the guilt of disobedience against the command of discipline. [Col. 0289C]

## CHAPTER VIII. That the woman assented to persuasion through delight in the promise

We say that pride and avarice seized the deceived human mind in original sin before the vice of gluttony, because unless the woman had first desired what was promised, she would never afterward have assented to what was urged. But because she first took perverse delight in the promise, she afterward gave foolish assent to the persuasion. First she sought the promised excellence through pride; then she coveted through avarice the promised abundance—such abundance as befitted such excellence. Finally, so that she might deserve to attain these two according to her wish, corrupted by the vice of gluttony, she consented to taste the forbidden food.

At first, indeed, she consented on account of other things which she loved; afterward, looking again and seeing it desirable, she burned so intensely with desire that, even if there had been no reward at all, what she saw would nevertheless have pleased her for its own sake. Thus at first she was, as it were, hired by a price to consent; afterward, drawn by her own delight, she descended to the act. [Col. 0290A] Enticed by desire for the price in pride and avarice, she sold herself; but afterward, taking delight in gluttony, she willingly began to serve even without payment.

For when the foolish mind had first been bent by love of the promise, “the woman,” Scripture says, “saw the tree, that it was beautiful to behold and sweet for eating; and she took of its fruit and ate” (Gen. 3).

First she consented to see through pride and avarice; afterward she recognized beauty in the sight; then she apprehended sweetness in the beauty. Through sweetness she burned with the desire of gluttony; finally, overcome by desire, she took and ate. Thus she first sold herself to serve sin for a price; afterwards, overcome by her own delight, she willingly began to serve even freely. So too, sometimes a righteous mind in its perfection is first stirred by a proposed reward to serve God; but, when it has begun to grow into love of goodness, it is then held in God’s service by voluntary delight alone. [Col. 0290B]

## CHAPTER IX. On the two kinds of temptations

It should further be known that there are two kinds of temptation, one external and the other internal. External temptation occurs when evil to be done is suggested to us from outside, either visibly or invisibly. Internal temptation occurs when the mind is urged to sin inwardly by the movement of perverse delight. This temptation is more difficult to overcome, because the attacker within is strengthened from what is ours against us.

For this reason the devil did not deserve pardon, because he sinned without any temptation. But the human being, because he fell when assailed only by external temptation, was to be punished the more severely in proportion as he had been overthrown by a lighter impulse. Yet, because he had some occasion—though slight—for falling, God’s grace ultimately raised him to pardon. But the greater the violence of temptation that we suffer in sinning, the lighter the expiation by which we are restored to lost grace. [Col. 0290C]

## CHAPTER X. Whether Adam or Eve sinned more

They also ask which sinned more, Adam or Eve. But, as the Apostle says, “The woman was deceived, not the man” (1 Tim. 2). Eve was deceived because she believed the devil’s words to be true. And therefore she not only desired, inordinately, likeness to God together with the knowledge of good and evil, but is plausibly thought to have fallen into such perversity that she believed God had forbidden the tree of the knowledge of good and evil out of envy, lest the human being, by tasting it, might advance to equality with God.

For this is the perverse likeness not appropriate to a creature: it is sought not by imitation but by comparison. The woman, raised up in pride, therefore desired this; and, because she might not possess it, she supposed that the Creator himself, touched by envy, had forbidden this tree. Thus by voluntary malice she set herself against her Creator, perversely willing against him and holding an impious opinion concerning him.

But Adam was not deceived, because he knew that what the devil had promised was false. [Col. 0291A] Nor did he eat the forbidden fruit because he believed, or even wished, that by that eating he could be made equal to God. Rather, he acted only so as not to sadden the mind of the woman who had been joined to him through an affection of love, by resisting her request and will. Above all, he thought that he could both comply with the woman and afterward please the Creator through repentance and a request for pardon.

It was therefore truly said that the one who thought of repentance and mercy sinned less. Yet he sinned, because he consented to one sinning and did not correct the sinner. Consequently the guilt which is in original sin, though in a different manner, nevertheless falls in its entirety upon both: upon her because she sinned; upon him because he consented to her sin and, by consenting, made her sin his own. [Col. 0291B]

This, then, is the manner in which the human being was first deceived by the devil so as to sin. But if we wish to consider inwardly how sin entered into him, or indeed what sin itself is, which corrupts good nature and takes away its beauty and integrity, it is necessary to set forth certain matters concerning the condition of the inner human being which seem necessary for this inquiry.

## CHAPTER XI. On the desire for what is just and the desire for what is advantageous

God had placed in the human being from the beginning two things by which his whole nature was to be governed and led to the completion of its end. These were two desires: the desire for what is just, and the desire for what is advantageous. He gave the one, that is, the desire for what is just, so that it might exist in the will. He gave the other, that is, the desire for what is advantageous, so that it might exist according to necessity. One was voluntary, the other necessary.

God willed the desire for what is just to be voluntary so that by it the human being might merit either good, if he retained it when able to abandon it, or evil, if he abandoned it when able to retain it. But God willed the desire for what is advantageous to be necessary so that by it the human being might be recompensed either with punishment, if he abandoned the other—that is, the desire for what is just—or with glory, if he retained that same desire, namely the desire for what is just. God placed human merit in the desire for what is just, but reward in the desire for what is advantageous. [Col. 0291C]

Therefore he subjected the desire for what is just to the human will alone, because merit could not exist except in will and free choice. These two desires were followed by two effects, the just and the advantageous, though differently and in the reverse order. The desire or affection for what is just is separable, because it exists according to the will; but its effect—that is, what is just or justice—is inseparable from it, because the desire for what is just cannot exist without justice. For to desire justice is, in a certain respect, to possess justice.

Thus the affection for what is just can be separated from the will, but its effect, justice, cannot be separated from that affection. Conversely, the desire for what is advantageous is inseparable, because it exists according to necessity and can never be separated from the rational will. But its effect, namely advantage, is separable from it, because advantage can be desired when it is not possessed. In this consists the highest punishment: when a creature given over to punishment can neither reject its own advantage because of its immutable nature, nor possess it because of its unforgivable guilt. [Col. 0292A]

God therefore gave the human being a separable affection for justice, and established that, while this affection existed, its effect—justice—should be inseparably present with it. He bestowed an inseparable desire for advantage, but did not ordain that its effect, advantage, should be equally inseparably present. Thus, by losing that one desire alone, namely the desire for what is just, the human being would lose the effect of both; or, by retaining that one desire, would retain the effect of each.

But the human being did only what he was able to do. Because he voluntarily abandoned the desire for what is just, he deservedly lost both justice and advantage, retaining only the desire for advantage, to increase his misery. For just as it would have been an increase of glory for one persevering in justice to be unable to grow cold in love and desire for the good possessed, so it is an accumulation of misery to be unable to restrain oneself from desiring the good, even though one cannot attain it. [Col. 0292B]

## CHAPTER XII. Whether the human being lost the desire for what is just willingly or unwillingly

But it seems remarkable: if the human being first had the desire for justice, how did he afterward lose it? That is, did he abandon it unwillingly or willingly? If he abandoned it unwillingly—or rather, if he lost it unwillingly through suffering necessity—he did not commit iniquity. The fault should not be attributed to the one suffering violence, but to the one inflicting it.

But if a will is said to have preceded in him, because by some spontaneous deliberation he cast off the affection for justice, then the abandonment of justice itself is denied to have been the first sin, because an evil will preceded it, through which it was done. Nor can it be discovered how such a will came to the human being, by which he would will to abandon the good he possessed; for he could not have received the capacity to will it from himself, nor did he receive from God the capacity to will anything besides what is advantageous and what is just.

But we should consider that, since desiring what is just is nothing other than willing justice, abandoning the desire for what is just is the same as ceasing to will justice. Now one who ceases to will does not cease to will by willing not to will, but by ceasing from willing—just as one who ceases to do something ceases not by doing, but by stopping and resting from what he does. [Col. 0292D]

Therefore, when the human being abandoned the desire for what is just, he did not begin to will what he had previously not willed; he merely ceased to will what he had previously willed. It is not necessary, then, to say that he did this either willingly or unwillingly. Yet he did will something which, because he could not will it together with this willing, caused him to cease to will that which he had willed. Nor indeed did he will that thing because he ceased to will this; rather, he ceased to will this because he willed that thing.

Yet his sin and iniquity depend not on his willing that thing, but on his ceasing to will this, because if he had not ceased to will this, he could never have sinned by willing either that thing or anything else. What, then, shall that thing be said to have been, by willing which he ceased to will what is just, except that he willed something beyond the measure within which alone justice existed? For whatever is beyond measure cannot be just. But what was this measure within which the human will ought to have remained in order that it might be good and contain no evil? This must be carefully considered. [Col. 0293A]

## CHAPTER XIII. That justice is measure

God had prepared two goods for the human being, one temporal and the other eternal, so that he might use the temporal good and enjoy the eternal. But since it is not praiseworthy to use or enjoy goods unless one uses and enjoys them well, a measure was defined for the human being according to which he might use his temporal goods well and enjoy eternal goods well.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the measure of the lower good

The mode of measure in using the lower good consisted of four aspects: first, that he should use only those things which he ought to use; second, that he should use them in the manner in which he ought; third, to the extent that he ought; fourth, at the time when he ought. In transgressing any one of these, the human being would lose the measure. [Col. 0293B]

## CHAPTER XV. On the measure of the higher good

The mode of measure in enjoying the higher good was found to have only two aspects. First, the human being should know in what manner he ought to enjoy that good. Second, he should recognize also when it was fitting for him to enjoy that good. For there was no need to ask what good was to be enjoyed there, since there was only one good there. Likewise there was no need at all to ask how much that good should be enjoyed, since it was beyond doubt that the more anyone enjoyed it, the happier that person would be.

A measure of quantity is required only where there can be too little or too much. But the enjoyment of this good is such that it is full in one who possesses less, and not superfluous in one who possesses more. Thus the measure consisted only in recognizing how one should enjoy that good: so that one might not desire to possess it inordinately—not by imitation, as is fitting for a creature, but by equality, which exceeds a creature’s capacity. Likewise, one must take care not to hasten greedily to seize it before its time, since one ought not to receive it before completing obedience. [Col. 0293C]

Therefore, just as the human being’s advantage was established in these goods, so his justice ought to consist in the measure of using or enjoying these goods. And just as the will was given to him by which he might desire his goods and, in his goods, his own advantage, so there was implanted in his will the disposition that the very measure according to which he ought to use or enjoy those goods should not displease him.

Thus, in loving his goods, we discern the desire for advantage; but in loving the measure of advantage in his goods, we understand the desire for what is just. If, therefore, the human being had always loved the measure, he would not have lost the desire for what is just. He would always have loved the measure if he had willed nothing beyond measure. But once he began to will something beyond measure, he ceased to will the measure. Once he ceased to will the measure, he ceased to love justice. And he lost justice in the very act in which he lost love for justice. For just as justice cannot be absent from one who loves it, so it cannot in any way be present with one by whom it is not loved. [Col. 0294A]

The human being’s injustice, then, lay in extending his desire beyond measure both in quality, when he wished to be made equal to his Creator, and in time, when he hastened to snatch the reward before merit. Therefore, when he desired the highest good, he desired a good; but he did not desire it rightly, because he desired to grasp it both immoderately and untimely.

## CHAPTER XVI. What evil was in the human being

See, then, what the evil was there. The good which was desired was not evil; nor was the will by which it was desired evil insofar as it was will, or insofar as it was directed toward good. But the sole evil was that it was desired without measure. Therefore, in the human will, neither the fact that it is will is evil, because it is something and everything that is something is good; nor is that toward which it is directed evil, because it too is something and everything that is something is good. But that it is without measure—this is evil. [Col. 0294B]

For this is not to be something, but for something to be absent which ought to be present. And therefore evil is nothing, when that which ought to be is not. This evil, that is, this non-being, when elsewhere it is either punishment or ordered toward punishment, is guilt in the rational will; for whenever it is in that will, it is from the will, through the will, and in the will: from it, because it is brought about by its freedom; through it, because it is brought about by its choice.

In this the rational will withdraws from likeness to God by a certain perverse imitation: from whom, through whom, and in whom is all that is. For when it becomes perverse, from itself, through itself, and in itself there is only that which is nothing. This is its sin, injustice, and guilt, through which it appears ugly, blameworthy, and deserving of rejection, because it does not possess its form, adornment, or beauty, for which it should have been loved and led to glory. [Col. 0294C]

## CHAPTER XVII. That the human being, having sinned in the desire for what is just, was punished in the desire for what is advantageous

Because, then, the human being sinned by abandoning the desire for what is just, he was punished in retaining the desire for what is advantageous. For that desire was given in this way: it was to be inseparably present with the rational will, so that by it the human being might either be punished if he departed from justice or rewarded if he remained in justice. For he could not suffer punishment at all if he desired no advantage.

For disadvantage is plainly nothing other than that which is found contrary to one’s will or desire. Since, therefore, the human being abandoned the desire for justice, the desire for advantage alone remained to him for punishment. In it he is punished in two ways: either when he is restrained from things which he desires in an ordered way, or when he is released to desire other advantages which cannot be desired in an ordered way. In the one there is punishment; in the other, punishment and guilt. [Col. 0294D]

The measure of the higher desire had been placed in free choice; but the measure of the lower desire had been granted as a gift. Accordingly, to will to preserve the former would have belonged to virtue; but to be able to preserve the latter, to blessedness. Hence, just as it was guilt not to have preserved the former, so losing the latter became punishment. Yet even in this punishment there was guilt, because here too failing to preserve the measure was contrary to justice. But this guilt was the punishment of the preceding guilt: for unless the spirit had abandoned measure in its own desire, the flesh, subject to the spirit, would not have exceeded the limit of measure in its desire against the spirit itself. [Col. 0295A]

## CHAPTER XVIII. Why the lower desire does not keep measure

God had created the first human being’s body sound and whole. It was sound because it contained nothing tending toward corruption; whole because it lacked nothing required for perfection. But in both respects he had imposed such a condition that neither wholeness nor soundness could be preserved without assistance. Therefore, among created things he arranged certain external means capable of preserving and protecting its soundness and wholeness. [Col. 0295B]

## CHAPTER XIX. That care of the flesh was imposed upon the spirit

God imposed upon the spirit, which presided over the body, the care and office of providing these things. For just as God presided over the spirit, so the spirit presided over the flesh, and the flesh itself was the spirit’s beast of burden. Therefore it belonged to the rider to provide fodder for its beast, lest it fail; and perhaps this alone could then have been sufficient.

But now, beyond fodder, it needs both bridle and spurs: the bridle, indeed, to restrain it from evil when hot-blooded and headlong; the spurs, to stir it, when sluggish, toward doing good. Then, therefore, if it received fodder alone, without bridle and spurs, it would bear its rider gently; and if perhaps there were a bridle there by which it might be guided, though unable to proceed rightly on its own, it would nevertheless need no goad because it would not be sluggish, nor restraint because it would not be impetuous. [Col. 0295C]

Since the spirit was the rider, then, it was assigned the duty of providing fodder for its beast. But lest, in performing this duty, it should be oppressed by a servile condition if it fulfilled it merely from command and not also from love, God gave it an affection by which it might love its body, so that, as it loved its soundness and wholeness, it would gladly provide everything that could preserve them.

Again, lest there be labor in seeking such things or danger in taking them, God tempered both bodily need and bodily appetite by a fixed measure, so that few things might suffice it for sustenance and modest things for satiety. Thus care for the flesh would have been not so much labor as pleasure and exercise, had the human being retained justice.

But because the spirit, lifted above itself, refused to restrain its desire within measure, it consequently became its labor and misery that it could no longer keep measure in the desire of its flesh. To punish the spirit’s sin, God broke the integrity of the human body by mortality; and therefore it now needs more supports than before, both to repair the soundness that has been lost and to preserve what remains. [Col. 0295D]

From this arises that harsh necessity by which it must extend its desire beyond the order of the first arrangement, so that it may preserve not only nature but also expel [Col. 0296A] nature’s own defect and corruption. For just as it is naturally given to the spirit to love the advantage of its flesh, so it naturally cannot love its flesh’s disadvantage.

## CHAPTER XX. That the necessity of desiring does not excuse, because it comes from the will
It must be understood that this necessity of concupiscence is not thereby no fault because it is a necessity; for the cause why this necessity came to be was not necessity, but will. But what shall we say? If a human being has it naturally that he cannot love what harms him or disdain what benefits him, then whatever he desires is beneficial to him, and he never desires anything except his own benefit. If this is true, why is he sometimes [Col. 0296B] rebuked or accused for what he desires, since he never desires anything except his own benefit, and since it has been naturally granted to him to desire this, so fully that, while nature itself remains immovably fixed in what it was made to be, he cannot desire anything whatever other than his own benefit?

## Chapter XXI. That what is beneficial and ordered ought to be desired

But it is one thing to desire what is in some way beneficial in a manner in which it is not beneficial, and another thing to desire what is beneficial in the manner in which it is beneficial. For everything beneficial is beneficial in some respect; and likewise everything harmful is harmful in some respect, [Col. 0296C] and not universally. Therefore, one who desires what is in some way beneficial, but does not desire it in the manner in which it is beneficial—while nevertheless thinking that it is beneficial in the manner in which he desires it—desires nothing except benefit, although what he desires is not beneficial. For he desires what he desires on account of benefit, and thinks that his benefit lies in what he desires.

He is not, therefore, deceived in desiring his own benefit, because he knows that what he desires is his benefit; but he is deceived in thinking his benefit to be where it is not—namely, in that thing which he desires for the sake of his own benefit. But one who desires what is beneficial, and desires it in the manner in which it is beneficial, although it is not ordered, is at fault not because he desires [Col. 0296D] what is beneficial, but because it is not ordered. For just as it has been granted to him to desire what is beneficial, so he has also been forbidden to desire what is disordered.

Therefore, when that which is in some way beneficial and that which is not ordered coincide in one thing, if the desire is directed toward benefit in affection—for this is implanted in nature—it must nevertheless be restrained from effect, on account of the obligation of reason, to which it is not permitted to proceed toward disordered things. For herein the beauty and dignity of reason appears: that it restrains its affection from disordered things. For this is why there had to be many benefits: so that, when ruling reason restrained affection, which so far as it lay in itself would overflow, the greatness of reason’s dignity and excellence might appear.

## Chapter XXII. That nothing is desired except what is beneficial

[Col. 0297A]

Therefore, if we say that nature can desire absolutely nothing except what is beneficial, it should not consequently be judged false that it desires certain things in which its benefit does not lie when it is deceived; or that it desires certain things in which there is some benefit, but which are not ordered, when it transgresses.

We see that a sick person sometimes desires a potion or an incision; yet he does not desire bitterness or pain, but health. And there are certain sweet things that are desired and badly desired, because they are disordered; yet they are not bad because they are sweet, but because they are disordered. Again, there are certain bitter things that are desired and well desired, because they are ordered; yet they are not good because [Col. 0297B] they are bitter, but because they are ordered.

And it sometimes happens that things which are sweet have some good in themselves, yet produce much evil from themselves; and thus the good in them is small, while the evil arising from them is great. Again, it happens that things which are bitter have some evil in themselves, yet produce much good from themselves; and thus the evil in them is small, while the good arising from them is great. Therefore the imprudent, who see present things but do not foresee future ones, flee small evils and incur great ones; and likewise choose small goods and lose great ones.

Yet in all things only benefit is desired: when it is desired in an ordered way, rightly; but when in a disordered way, wrongly. Yet it is not wrong because it is beneficial, but because it is disordered.

## Chapter XXIII. How necessity comes from the will

[Col. 0297C]

If, however, a human being seems excusable because nature, corrupted by the weakness of mortality, can no longer by itself restrain its affection, which of necessity overflows beyond measure, it must be considered that the necessity brought about by a preceding will cannot excuse. For voluntary fault deserved punishment; punishment produced weakness; and weakness introduced necessity. Therefore, because the will brought about necessity, necessity cannot excuse the will itself.

Thus the transgression of the higher desire, which was fault alone, was followed by the transgression of the lower desire, which is both punishment and fault. In the spirit, fault alone; in the flesh, both punishment and fault. The disordered concupiscence of the spirit is fault; the concupiscence of the flesh is punishment and fault: punishment [Col. 0297D] for the preceding fault, and fault following upon punishment.

## Chapter XXIV. What we inherit by generation, and what we lose by regeneration

Therefore, when mortal flesh is sown through sexual intercourse for the generation of offspring in concupiscence, punishment and fault pass through concupiscence in the flesh to the offspring that is to be born. But when those who have been generated in punishment and fault are regenerated through the sacrament of redemption, in those cleansed through the spirit of regeneration, not the punishment but the fault is removed in that very original defect. The fault, indeed, is removed so that they may be justified; but the punishment remains so that they may be exercised.

## Chapter XXV. On original sin

Many difficult questions arise concerning original sin [Col. 0298A]; and I do not know whether they should be treated better by belief than by discussion—if indeed they admit any discussion, since they cannot have a full solution.

First, it is asked what original sin is; then, how it is transmitted from parents to children, especially from those in whom it has been removed through the sacrament of regeneration: whether through the soul alone, through the flesh alone, or through soul and flesh together. And if through the soul alone, whether by creation or by propagation. But if through the flesh alone, why does that which is not from the soul redound upon the soul?

## Chapter XXVI. In how many senses “original sin” is spoken of

Original sin may be understood in two ways: either as that first disobedience of the human being, which was the first [Col. 0298B] of all sins and became the origin of all that followed; or as that defect with which all who are descended from him are born, being descended from him through propagation of the flesh.

This defect of human origin infects nature with a double corruption: ignorance in the mind, and concupiscence in the flesh. In the first parent these two evils were punishment for the preceding fault and actual fault; but in us they are fault following punishment, and at once both fault and punishment that are original.

Therefore, when we speak of original sin in relation to the first human being, we mean that first fault of his disobedience. It is called original in him not because his nature received its origin from or with it, but because from it, as from the first of all things, all his [Col. 0298C] subsequent evils afterward arose and proceeded. But because no sin descended into him from a prior origin, even that sin called original in him was actual sin. For surely one who did not draw sin by being born had no sin except what he committed by acting.

## Chapter XXVII. What was actual for the first human being is original for us

But we, who drew our origin from him by being born, possess as original what was actual for him, because what existed in him through action descends to us through birth alone. For our nature transmitted to us solely through our birth the corruption which it conceived in him through his own action. Therefore, [Col. 0298D] by being born we conceive the sin which he had not by being born but by acting, from whom we come by birth.

For in him the spirit, swollen with pride against its Creator, did not retain obedience; and therefore God, in order to avenge His injury, condemned the spirit to ignorance and the flesh to concupiscence, so that the spirit might not see the good it ought to do within itself, while in its flesh it might desire to do evil. These two defects were justly established in him in order to punish human pride: ignorance, when the light of truth was withdrawn from the mind; concupiscence, when the flesh was struck by the punishment of mortality.

Thus nature, first corrupted, transmitted this original corruption to posterity: [Col. 0299A] ignorance to the soul, and concupiscence to the flesh, serving its corruption.

## Chapter XXVIII. What original sin is

Therefore, if it is asked what original sin is in us, it is understood as the corruption or defect which we draw by being born: through ignorance in the mind, through concupiscence in the flesh.

## Chapter XXIX. How original sin passes from parents to children

After it has been shown what original sin is, it follows that we should investigate how it is transmitted from parents to children: that is, whether according to the soul alone, the flesh alone, or both together.

Some thought that original sin descends from parents to children not only through the flesh but also [Col. 0299B] through the soul, because they believed that not only the flesh but the soul too comes from material propagation. For just as, in the generation of offspring, flesh is substantially drawn from the father’s flesh, so these persons suppose that the soul of the child is essentially derived from the soul of the begetter. Consequently, just as corrupt flesh is sown from corrupt flesh, so too a sinful soul, infected by original corruption, is drawn from a sinful soul.

## Chapter XXX. That the soul is not derived by propagation

Here, however, certain doctors are found to have brought forward many arguments and authorities from various directions, by which they endeavoured to establish that not the soul but the flesh alone is derived by propagation. The first argument is this: it does not belong to a spiritual nature either to be from matter, because it is essentially simple, [Col. 0299C] or to be matter, because, always remaining undivided in the simplicity of its unity, it cannot at all be increased or multiplied.

For a simple nature does not produce by propagation, where a part cannot be taken from that from which something is to be propagated for the thing to be propagated, unless the whole passes over. But if that which is one passes wholly between two, nothing of it remains in that from which it comes. If, however, the whole remains, nothing is conveyed to that to which it comes. Therefore, if soul is begotten from soul as flesh from flesh, let them say how that simple substance either remains whole in the begetter if it has passed into the offspring, or passes whole into the offspring if it remains in the begetter.

Unless perhaps they wish to say that all souls are consubstantial, and that this simple nature [Col. 0299D] in the propagation of children is multiplied personally, but not divided essentially—without noticing how many absurdities follow from this assertion, if one and the same essence is believed to be simultaneously assigned to blessedness and condemnation, glory and punishment.

Finally, when Scripture says, “Let the dust return to the earth from which it was taken, and let the spirit return to the Lord who made it” (Eccles. XII), it is plainly shown that not spirit from spirit but flesh from flesh is materially propagated. Although our bodies were not, in the first instance, materially taken from earth, they are nevertheless not improperly said to have been taken from earth, because the body of the first human being, from whom our bodies materially [Col. 0300A] descend from matter, was taken from earth through matter.

Although, under the same understanding, this might also be said of our spirits if they were believed to be propagated—namely, that they were given by God, because the first spirit from whom they descend through matter was given by the Lord—yet it is established more probably that souls are not propagated: because, just as in the first human being the body is read to have been taken from earth, while the spirit was given by God, so reason also requires us to believe that in subsequent human beings flesh descends from flesh, while spirit comes from the Lord.

Nevertheless, when we read that the rational spirit is given or breathed in by the Lord, we must by no means believe that it is taken, as it were materially, from the divine essence or substance. Rather, the body comes from earth through matter, whereas the spirit receives being without pre-existing matter, solely through the power of the Creator. As the body is from him from whom it drew its matter, so the spirit is from him through whom and from whom it began to be: through him when He made it, and from him when He gave it.

Again the Psalmist says: [Col. 0300B] “He who fashioned their hearts one by one” (Ps. XXXII). Hearts—that is, rational spirits or souls—are said to be fashioned one by one by God because He is declared to create them, not one from another as appears in bodily nature, but each separately, from nothing.

Therefore, when it is written in the Law, “If anyone strikes a pregnant woman and she miscarries, if it has not been formed, he shall render life for life” (Exod. XXI), it is openly declared that, when flesh is sown from flesh, [Col. 0300C] soul is not likewise drawn from soul. For if a soul is sown together with the flesh, why, in a miscarriage that is not yet formed, should life not be rendered for life? Since, then, life for life is commanded only in a miscarriage that has been formed, what is shown except that, in what has not yet been formed, there is not yet a soul?

Thus, just as we read that in the first human being the body was first formed and then the soul infused, so also in all subsequent human beings we should believe that the human body is first formed in the womb and then the soul infused. If anyone perhaps finds it strange how paternal seed in the womb can, before ensoulment, grow, possess life, or even advance to the very shape of the human body, let him consider how shrubs, plants, and all shoots [Col. 0300D] of this kind, having no such soul, live and grow by vegetation alone, and by their own motion are brought forth into a form appropriate to their species.

By these and similar arguments it has been made probable that souls are not derived by propagation, but are newly created from nothing and, when new bodies from paternal seed have daily been formed in the womb, are infused into them for their animation. Yet in all these matters no reasoning or authority has ever prevailed so greatly as to remove the uncertainty of the question, except that the Catholic faith chose it as more credible that souls are made from nothing daily to be joined to bodies needing animation, rather than propagated by descent according to the nature of the body and the property of human flesh.

[Col. 0301A] If souls were held to be derived by propagation, the question would not be so great, because the justice of saying that original sin passes from parents to children would be more evident. But if we cannot comprehend the hidden judgments of God by reason, we ought not, for the sake of resolving doubtful matters, to assert other doubtful things.

Yet it is asked: if souls are not propagated, how are children made liable by the sin of their parents? [Col. 0301B] For that nature alone in which sin exists in the parent descends into the child, which alone passes from parent to child through generation. Therefore, if flesh alone is sown, original sin is surely transmitted through flesh alone. But if this is true, two questions confront us. One is how sin passes from parent to child through flesh alone without soul; the other, how the soul becomes a participant in the sin which descends through flesh alone and in flesh alone. For how can flesh without a soul have sin, when without a soul it cannot sin at all? Therefore, if sin was not in the flesh without a soul, how could sin pass through flesh or in flesh to the soul? What was not at some time in the flesh, the soul did not afterward receive from the flesh.

## Chapter XXXI. How sin passes through the flesh to the soul

Human nature conceived two defects from its first corruption, from which the offspring of all subsequent evils afterward sprang. These were ignorance of good and concupiscence for evil. One of them, ignorance, infected the mind; the other, concupiscence, stained the flesh. Ignorance was the punishment of pride; concupiscence the effect of mortality.

Thus four evils appear in the human being: pride, ignorance, mortality, and concupiscence. Pride of mind is fault only; mortality of flesh is punishment only; ignorance is fault and punishment in the mind; concupiscence is punishment and fault in the flesh. Because of pride, the mind was darkened through ignorance; because of mortality, the flesh was softened through concupiscence. For because the mind swelled against God through pride, struck by ignorance it lost the light of truth. But because the flesh was struck by mortality, dissolved by the weakness of its own languor, it extended its desires beyond the measure of its first disposition.

This is precisely what is called the concupiscence of the flesh: that is, a natural appetite or affection transgressing order and exceeding measure. It transgresses order when it moves toward things it ought not; it exceeds measure when it moves otherwise than it ought. For the appetite transgresses order when we desire things which we ought not to desire. It does not retain measure when we desire even things that ought to be desired otherwise than we ought.

Thus, from the first fault and the final punishment two intermediate things arose, both fault and punishment: ignorance of good, fault and punishment in the mind; concupiscence for evil, fault and punishment in the flesh. In these lies the root of original sin.

Therefore, because human flesh [Col. 0302A] is sown from parents together with mortality, by the very fact that it is sown it is subject to mortality; and, when afterward animated, it is found subject to the necessity of fleshly concupiscence, because the weakness of mortality itself is the cause which the necessity of concupiscence follows. Thus flesh which is sown in concupiscence is conceived with mortality and born with the necessity of concupiscence.

In that from which it is sown, it has fault and the act of fault. In that it is sown, it has neither fault nor the act of fault, but the cause. In that it is born, it has the cause of fault and fault, but not the act. The cause of fault is the corruption of mortality; fault is concupiscence; the act of fault is to desire. The cause of fault is the root; fault itself is the tree; the act of fault is the fruit.

Therefore, in that which is sown is the corruption of mortality; [Col. 0302B] in that which is born is the defect of concupiscence; and in that which is moved by concupiscence is the act which begins from the movement of the will and is completed by the movement of deed. Therefore newborn children are not to be thought free from defect because they do not engage in concupiscence, since the defect of concupiscence is rooted in them, through which they afterward engage in concupiscence when they act.

## Chapter XXXII. How ignorance is a defect

Ignorance is not a defect in them because, when they are born, they do not know truth at a time when they ought not to know it; but because, when they are born, there is in them a defect by which they are afterward prevented from knowing truth when they ought. For to be born without knowledge is nature, not fault. But to be born in that defect [Col. 0302C] by which they are afterward hindered from the knowledge of truth is fault, not nature.

This defect is in the corruption of the flesh and in the corruption of the carnal sense. If that carnal sense had retained its integrity, once developed and trained, it would grasp the judgment of truth without labour, being instructed by things outwardly seen. But because it has been deprived of its integrity from corrupt flesh, it cannot draw pure truth without the confusion of error.

## Chapter XXXIII. That angels were made to be instructed inwardly, human beings outwardly

For angels, because they were made perfect, were instructed inwardly. Human beings, however—except only that first one, who, as he was made perfect in his own manner, was likewise instructed inwardly—because they were to advance to knowledge through intervals [Col. 0302D] of time, had to be awakened and instructed outwardly toward the knowledge of truth through the forms of temporal and visible things.

Yet this awakening and instruction would naturally have been present to the human being without labour if human sense in mortal flesh had not been corrupted through sin, so that the saying of the Apostle would then have held fully and perfectly: “His invisible things are perceived and seen through the things that have been made, from the creation of the world” (Rom. I).

## Chapter XXXIV. Whence concupiscence and ignorance arise

Therefore, from corrupted sensuality in mortal flesh arises the defect of concupiscence; from corrupted sense, the defect of ignorance. There, because the appetite of a need that must be sought [Col. 0303A] extends itself beyond measure; here, because the instrument for conceiving truth falls short of the strength of integrity.

But this introduces the greatest difficulty into the question: original sin appears to be assigned only to the defect of fleshly corruption, though we must acknowledge that it extends even to participation by the rational soul.

## Chapter XXXV. How the soul becomes a participant in original sin

How a soul created pure and without defect becomes a participant in the defect brought in through flesh alone would be worthy of inquiry, if it could be investigated with any diligence. But now, because it has not been exposed to human knowledge, it must be believed by faith, not investigated out of curiosity. [Col. 0303B]

For if we say that, when mixed with the body, the soul by some act of will inclines toward the delight of sin, we show it liable not only to original but also to actual sin. But if we confess that it has been driven by some necessity into companionship with the body and contagion by bodily defect, we show that it is absolved from guilt by that very necessity. For what is wholly a matter of necessity is not imputable; but what is a matter of will is not original, but one’s own.

It is therefore clear that the rational soul [Col. 0303C] infused into a human body is not corrupted by will, lest the sin be actual; nor is it corrupted by necessity, lest the defect be non-imputable. Therefore its evil is neither an evil will, because it has not yet received the capacity to will, nor an evil deed, because it has not yet been able to act either well or badly. But its evil is that it is such that, unless aided by grace, it can neither receive knowledge of truth nor resist the concupiscence of its flesh.

This belongs to it not from the integrity of its creation, but from fellowship with corruptible flesh. And because that corruption is transmitted from the first parent to all posterity through propagation of the flesh, the stain of original sin is extended to all in the defects of ignorance and concupiscence.

But if it is asked by what justice these things are imputed to the soul, which it received neither from creation nor committed by will, but contracted from fellowship with flesh alone—a fellowship which it did not claim by its own choice, but received by the command and ordinance of its Creator—we must finally confess what is true: [Col. 0303D] divine justice in this matter is indeed beyond reproach, but not comprehensible.

## Chapter XXXVI. The reasoning of some concerning the embodiment of souls

For those who say that God from the beginning proposed to join souls to bodies needing animation, and assigned to human beings the task of generating bodies while retaining for Himself the power of creating souls, say that a righteous human being would generate pure bodies, while righteous God would create pure souls and join them to bodies. And if the human being corrupted his work, God ought not to change His purpose. Therefore, in accordance with His good purpose, God would create pure souls [Col. 0304A] and join them to bodies; and, when they find corruption in those bodies and draw corruption from them, this is not from God, who makes them without corruption, but from the human being who corrupted the nature of bodies.

Those who say this do not explain the ground of divine justice. For just as it did not belong to divine goodness to make souls evil, so neither did it seem fitting that He should propose to place them where they must become evil. Therefore one should not insist greatly on investigating by reason what ought to be examined more by faith than by reason.

## Chapter XXXVII. How sinful children are born from righteous parents

Yet it is asked how those generated from persons who have received remission of original sin, [Col. 0304B] whether through the sacraments of faith or through faith alone, contract original sin. For how can that pass from parents to children which is not in the parents themselves?

But it must be understood that original sin, which is transmitted from parents to children through generation of the flesh, although remitted in those who generate with respect to fault, nevertheless remains with respect to punishment. It is remitted with respect to fault because it is not imputed; it is retained with respect to punishment because it is not removed. This is what the Apostle says: “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. VIII). He thereby shows that, although the weakness of original corruption is not removed in those reborn in Christ Jesus, nevertheless, through the intervention of the sacrament of regeneration, it is not imputed to condemnation. [Col. 0304C]

The tinder of sin may indeed be present in them, but sin cannot rule so long as they preserve their freedom and do not lose the spirit of adoption by voluntarily sinning. For, freed from the slavery of sin, we are indeed held under the corruption of mortality by necessity, but we are subjected to the dominion of sin only by will. Therefore the same Apostle says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI).

Our body, mortal by necessity, bears in the very root of its corruption the tinder of sin. But where the spirit of freedom is, sin itself cannot rise to rule. Thus original sin, which has been removed from parents by regeneration with respect to fault but remains with respect to punishment, when it passes to those who are generated, [Col. 0304D] is found not only as punishment but is also imputed as fault, until, after the laver of regeneration has been received, fault is removed in them also, even though punishment remains.

## Chapter XXXVIII. Whether all the sins of preceding parents pass to children

But it is asked whether all the sins of preceding parents pass to their children, just as we see that the transgression of the first parent overflowed into all born from him. If this is true, the later people are, of course, the more miserable. Nor does it seem an equitable condition that time should prejudice truth, unless perhaps nature, the more it is corrupted, is sown the worse.

For when Scripture says, “I will repay the sin of the fathers in the children unto the third and [Col. 0305A] fourth generation” (Exod. XX), it plainly shows that the sins of fathers are required from children. But why only to the third and fourth generation, and not without limit, is not easy to demonstrate, unless perhaps those sins which justice might pursue through all generations are, through mercy, terminated in the third and fourth generation, lest judgment become unbearable if divine vengeance punished in later generations all the sins of those before them.

But where it is said elsewhere, “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son” (Ezek. XVIII), it is rightly understood of that iniquity which father and son, personally distinct and essentially [Col. 0305B] separate from one another, commit. For once the son has become another person from the father, and the father another person from the son, just as each has the capacity to act by his own choice, so what one does ought not thereafter be imputed to the other.

But the saying, “I will repay the sins of the fathers in the children,” must be understood of sins which the fathers committed before those from whom the children were to be born had been born from them. Why, then, unto the fourth generation? Unless it is because the rigour of justice is tempered by mercy; or because every generation is understood through the third and fourth generation; or—what seems more probable—because the sins of fathers are said to be punished in their children only so long as the children themselves, seeing the sins of those same fathers, imitate them. [Col. 0306A]

Thus we should understand that children never become participants in their parents’ sins unless they have first become imitators by sinning, so that each is condemned for his own sin rather than another’s, when he makes another’s sin his own by lovingly following and imitating it. Thus the general saying is more fittingly understood: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son,” so that another’s sins never harm anyone except those who imitate them by sinning.

For, in opposition to the saying, “The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” (Ezek. XVIII), there is set the contrary: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son. The soul that sins, it shall die” (ibid.). Therefore, if in the former statement we understand the sins of previous fathers to be signified as passing to subsequent children, it is necessary in the later assertion to understand that each person is bound by his own sin, and that the preceding sins of fathers do not redound upon subsequent children.

If this is true, it is clear that the actual sins of parents [Col. 0306B] do not pass to children, but original sin alone: that sin which was greater than all others insofar as it was more capable than all others of changing nature itself. It is sown in the same corruption and passes into posterity by which, in its first root, it infected corrupted human nature.

# Part Eight: On the Restoration of the Human Being

[Col. 0305]

## Chapter I. That three things must be considered concerning the restoration of the human being

[Col. 0305C]

The first fault of the human being was pride, followed by a threefold punishment. One is punishment only: the mortality of the body. The remaining two are both punishments and faults: one is concupiscence of the flesh; the other, ignorance of the mind.

Therefore, because the human being was struck by such punishment that, unless afterward freed by grace, fault would not be purged but increased through it, he would descend from temporal punishment to eternal punishment. But lest he be found condemned if judged at once, his judgment was deferred. And because divine mercy predestined him for salvation, in this time of waiting and delay it assigned him a place for repentance and correction, so that through grace it might meanwhile make him such that it could finally judge him worthy of salvation not only mercifully but also justly.

Thus three things first present themselves here for consideration in the restoration of the human being: time, place, and remedy. Time is the present life, from the beginning of the world to the end of the age. Place is this world. The remedy consists in three things: faith, sacraments, and good works. [Col. 0306C] The time is long, lest one be overtaken unprepared. The place is harsh, that the transgressor may be chastised. The remedy is effective, that the weak may be healed.

## Chapter II. On the five places

There are five places. One in which there is good only, and supreme good. One in which there is evil only, and supreme evil. After these, two others: one beneath the highest, in which there is good only, but not supreme good; another above the lowest, in which there is evil only, but not supreme evil. One is in the middle, in which there are both good and evil, neither supreme.

In heaven there is good only, and supreme good; in hell evil only, and supreme evil; in paradise good only, but not supreme good; in purgatorial fire evil only, but not supreme evil; in the world there are good and evil, neither supreme.

Paradise is the place [Col. 0306D] of those beginning and advancing toward better things; and therefore only good ought to have been there, because the creature was not to begin from evil. Yet it ought not to have had supreme good, because if supreme good were there, those placed there would have no further progress. Heaven is the place of those confirmed in good and, through discipline, reaching the highest advance. One good only, and supreme good, has been placed [Col. 0307A] in it.

Hell is the place of those confirmed in evil and irrecoverably abandoning discipline; and therefore evil only, and supreme evil, has been placed there. Purgatorial fire is the place of those insufficiently corrected in the first correction and to be perfected in the second; and therefore it ought to have evil only, so that it might be worse than the former place where both evil and good coexist.

The world is the place of those who err and are to be restored; and therefore good and evil have together been ordained in it, so that through good they may receive consolation, and through evil correction. Yet neither supreme good nor supreme evil is there, so that those persisting in evil may have somewhere to decline, and those withdrawing from evil somewhere to advance.

Thus heaven is at the highest point; after heaven, paradise; after paradise, the world; after the world, [Col. 0307B] purgatorial fire; after purgatory, hell. Therefore the devil, who had fallen from the highest, was cast down to the lowest because he was not to be restored. But the human being, because he did not fall from the highest, was not placed in the lowest, but set in the middle, so that there might be a place for him to ascend through the merit of righteousness or descend through the guilt of fault.

## Chapter III. How the human being was disposed toward repentance
Man, therefore, was placed in this world, in a place of penitence, with a period for repentance granted to him, so that he might correct evils and restore goods, and so that, finally corrected, when he came to judgment, he might receive not punishment for guilt but the glory prepared for righteousness. It remains, therefore, that while there is time he should seek counsel and ask for the help necessary for his correction and deliverance. But because [Col. 0307C] he is found sufficient of himself for neither, it is necessary that he who by his grace postpones judgment should meanwhile, through that same grace, show the counsel by which escape is possible, and, after counsel, bestow help.

Thus it was fitting that meanwhile he should lay aside the role of judge, assume first the role of counsellor, and afterward that of helper—yet in such a way that first he should leave the whole man to himself, so that man himself might experience his ignorance and understand that he needs counsel; then also feel his deficiency and acknowledge that he needs help. Accordingly, in the time of the natural law the whole man was left to himself; afterward, in the time of the written law, counsel was given to one recognizing his ignorance; finally, in the time of grace, help was [Col. 0307D] granted to one confessing his deficiency. Counsel consisted in the principle of satisfaction; help consisted in the accomplishment of redemption.

Therefore, in order that we may more clearly understand the principle of satisfaction which man ought to render to the Creator for his sin, we must first consider somewhat more attentively the case of man. This case is constituted for litigation among three persons, namely God, man, and the devil.

## CHAPTER IV. On the case of man against God and the devil

These three, then, appear in the case: man, God, and the devil. The devil is convicted of having wronged God, because he both fraudulently led away God’s servant, man, and held him by force. Likewise man is convicted of having wronged God, [Col. 0308A] because he both despised his command and, placing himself under another’s hand, inflicted upon God the loss of his service. Again, the devil is convicted of having wronged man, because he first deceived him by promising good things and afterward harmed him by bringing evils upon him.

Therefore, the devil holds man unjustly, but man is justly held; for the devil never deserved to oppress man as subject to himself, whereas man deserved through his own fault to be permitted to be oppressed by him. For although man did not know that what the devil promised was false, nevertheless he did know that, even if it were true, he ought not to desire it contrary to the Creator’s will. Man, therefore, is justly subjected to the devil insofar as his own guilt is concerned, but unjustly insofar as the devil’s deceit is concerned.

If, therefore, man had such an advocate [Col. 0308B] that by his power the devil could be brought into court, man would rightly contest the devil’s dominion; for the devil had no just cause by which he ought to claim a right over man. But no such advocate could be found except God alone; and God was unwilling to undertake man’s case because he was still angry with man on account of his guilt. It was necessary, therefore, that man should first appease God, and then, with God acting as advocate, enter into litigation with the devil.

But man could not reasonably appease God unless he both restored the loss he had inflicted and made satisfaction for his contempt. Yet man had nothing with which he could worthily recompense God for the loss inflicted. For if he rendered something from irrational creation in return for what had been taken from rational creation, it would be less. Nor could he render man for man, [Col. 0308C] because he had taken away one who was just and innocent and found no one except a sinner. Therefore man found nothing by which he could appease God, because whether he gave what was his own or gave himself, it would not be a worthy recompense.

God, therefore, seeing that man could not by his own power escape the yoke of condemnation, had mercy on him; and first freely anticipated him by mercy alone, in order afterward to deliver him through justice. That is: because man did not possess in himself the justice by which to escape, God gave man justice through mercy. For man’s deliverance would not be perfectly reasonable unless it were made just from both sides: that is, just as God had the justice to demand man, so man also should have the justice to escape. But man could never have had this justice unless God had bestowed it upon him through his mercy.

Therefore, in order that [Col. 0308D] God might be appeased by man, God freely gave man what man should render to God as a debt. He gave man a man whom man might render for man, who, in order to be a worthy recompense, should be not only equal to the former man but greater. Therefore, in order that a man greater than man might be rendered for man, God was made man for man; and, as man, he gave himself to man, so that he might assume himself from man. God the Son was incarnate, and Christ, God and man, was given to human beings. As Isaiah says: “A child has been given to us” (Isa. 9), etc.

[Col. 0309A] That Christ was given to man was God’s mercy; that Christ was rendered by man was man’s justice. For at Christ’s birth God was justly appeased by man, because such a man was found for man as was not merely, as has been said, equal, but even greater than man. Therefore, at Christ’s birth the angels announced peace to the world, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2).

But man still had this remaining: just as by restoring the loss he had appeased wrath, so too, by making satisfaction for contempt, he should become worthy to escape punishment. Yet this could not fittingly be done unless he voluntarily and obediently underwent the punishment which he did not owe, so that he might become worthy to be rescued from the punishment which he had deserved through disobedience. But a sinful man could not pay this punishment, since whatever punishment he underwent he would endure only worthily and justly on account of the liability incurred by his original contempt.

[Col. 0309B] Therefore, in order that man might justly escape the punishment due to him, it was necessary that such a man should undergo punishment for man as owed no punishment. But no such man could be found except Christ. Therefore Christ, by being born, paid to the Father man’s debt, and, by dying, expiated man’s guilt; so that, since he underwent for man the death which he did not owe, man might justly escape through him the death which he did owe, and the devil might no longer find any ground for accusation. For the devil himself ought not to have ruled over man, and man was worthy to be set free.

Thus he accomplished both our judgment and our case, as it is written: “For you have accomplished my judgment and my cause” (Ps. 9). He accomplished our case because he paid the debt to the Father for us and, by dying, expiated guilt. He accomplished the judgment because, descending into hell and breaking the gates of death, he set free the captivity that was held there.

[Col. 0309C] The judgment of the devil against God, therefore, took place immediately from the beginning of the age. The judgment of man against the devil took place in Christ’s passion. The judgment of man against God is deferred until the consummation of the age. Therefore, if man first wishes to be reconciled to God through Christ, after his own judgment he will await [the outcome] without fear of condemnation.

## CHAPTER V. On the distinction of judgments

[Col. 0309D] There are four judgments: according to foreknowledge, according to cause, according to operation, and according to recompense. According to foreknowledge, we were judged before we existed. According to cause, we are judged from the time we begin to exist, when we are good or evil. According to operation, we are judged when by outward works we show what we are inwardly in ourselves. According to recompense, we shall be judged when, in receiving the reward of our works, we shall know what we were foreseen to be from eternity before God.

Of these four judgments, two are hidden: namely, judgment according to foreknowledge and judgment according to cause; and therefore human judgment is not admitted in them. Two are manifest: namely, judgment according to operation and judgment according to recompense. In one of these, that is, in judgment according to operation, God in the present gives human beings the power of judging. The other, that is, judgment according to recompense, will be judged not by human beings but by God before human beings.

[Col. 0310A] But judgment according to foreknowledge is hidden and immutable; judgment according to cause is hidden and mutable; judgment according to operation is manifest and mutable; judgment according to recompense is manifest and immutable. Judgment according to operation is in a certain way an image and sacrament of judgment according to recompense. For the former makes manifest the cause and intimates foreknowledge; the latter will make manifest the cause and confirm foreknowledge.

Again, it must be considered that judgment is performed differently where a sentence is formulated and differently where it is pronounced. In formulating the sentence of every judgment, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit judge together. But in pronouncing it, the Son alone judges, because in his divinity he possessed, together with the Father and the [Col. 0310B] Holy Spirit, the power to formulate the sentence of every judgment; in his humanity he alone received the power to pronounce the sentence of every judgment. Therefore humanity—which does not formulate the sentence—said, with regard to the formulation of the sentence: “I judge no one” (John 8). Yet, because it has the power to pronounce it as formulated, it adds: “As I hear, I judge” (John 5). For what he hears inwardly, where the sentence is formulated, he judges outwardly, where it is pronounced.

Having thus briefly set forth the distinction of judgments, let us now return to the course of our narrative itself.

## CHAPTER VI. Why God became man

God, therefore, was made man in order to free the man whom he had made, so that he might be both man’s creator and redeemer. [Col. 0310C] The Son, therefore, was sent in order to demonstrate his assent in the Father’s adoption. Wisdom came in order to conquer malice, so that the enemy who had conquered by cunning might be conquered by prudence.

## CHAPTER VII. How Christ’s passion concerned us

He took from nature a victim for nature, so that our own might be the holocaust offered for us, and so that redemption might in this very respect concern us, because the sacrifice was taken from what was ours. We are indeed made participants in this redemption if we are united by faith to the Redeemer himself, who has been joined to us through flesh.

[Col. 0310D] The whole of human nature had been corrupted through sin and the whole of it was liable to condemnation because of sin; and therefore, if all had been condemned, there would have been no injustice. But grace came and chose some from the mass of the whole human race for salvation through mercy; others it abandoned to condemnation through justice. Those whom it saved through mercy it did not save without justice, because it was in its power to do this justly; yet if it had not saved them, it would have acted justly, because it was in their merit that, if it did so, it would not be unjust.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the justice of power and equity

For one kind of justice is according to the obligation of the agent, another according to the merit of the recipient. Justice according to the obligation of the agent is that of power; justice according to the merit of the recipient is that of equity. Justice of power is that by which, without injustice, the agent may, if he wills, do what belongs to his power. Justice of equity is that by which what is due to the recipient according to his merit is rendered to him, even if he does not wish it.

[Col. 0311A] When, therefore, God punishes the sinner, he acts justly, because it belongs to his power that he may do this if he wills; and the one who suffers is justly punished, because according to his merit there is rendered to him what is due to his merit. There is there a just power by which God acts justly and is himself just. And there is an equitable recompense by which the sinner suffers justly, though he himself is not just, but his punishment is just.

But when God justifies the sinner, he acts justly and is just by the justice of power, by which it is lawful for him to do this. [Col. 0311B] The one who is justified is just by the justice which he receives, but not inasmuch as he receives it contrary to his merit. Yet he is not unjust, because he does not himself do what he receives; for he does not receive it through himself, but merely undergoes what he receives. There is one who acts because he acts, and there is the justice by which he acts; and the one who receives the justice which he receives is just, yet not because he receives it, because without justice of his own he receives justice by grace alone.

## CHAPTER IX. On justice that permits and justice that compels

Again, it should be known that one kind of justice permits and another compels. Permitting justice is that by which, if something is done, it is just; if it is not done, it is not unjust. Compelling justice is that by which something is done so justly that, if it were not done, it would be unjust. Therefore permitting justice allows dispensation; compelling justice entails necessity.

Thus, in taking some from the mass of the human race for salvation, God employs the justice of due power; but in abandoning some to perdition, he employs the justice of permitted equity. There, he acts from what is due to himself; here, from our merit. If he abandoned those whom he now takes for salvation, it would not be injustice, since according to their merits they would receive the justice of equity. [Col. 0311C] But if he took those whom he now abandons, likewise it would not be injustice, because in their salvation he would employ the justice of power.

Therefore, whether in those who are saved or in those who are damned, there is permitting justice, by which what is done is so just that, even if it were done otherwise, it would not be unjust. For those who are justly damned according to their merits could have been justly saved by God’s grace if God had willed it. And conversely, those who are justly saved through God’s grace could have been justly damned according to their merits if God had not willed to save them. [Col. 0311D] Thus whatever he willed was just, so that even if he had willed otherwise it would not have been unjust, because power lies in his will, since he may do without injustice whatever he wills.

## CHAPTER X. That God could have redeemed man otherwise, if he had willed

Therefore we truly profess that God could have accomplished the redemption of the human race in another way also, had he willed. But this way was more suited to our weakness: that God should become man and, taking human mortality for man, restore man to hope of his own immortality. Thus man may no longer despair of being able to ascend to God’s goods when he sees God descend to endure man’s evils; and so that humanity glorified in God might be an example of glorification for human beings. So that in what he suffered they may see what they ought to render to him, and in what he was glorified they may consider what they ought to expect from him. [Col. 0312A] Thus he himself may be the way in example, the truth in promise, and the life in reward.

## CHAPTER XI. By what rationale the sacraments were instituted

After the first parent of the human race, because of the guilt of disobedience, had been exiled from paradise and entered this world, the devil, exercising tyrannical right over him, possessed him by force, just as he had first seduced him fraudulently. But God’s providence, which was ordering this man toward salvation, so tempered the rigor of justice by mercy that it permitted him indeed to be oppressed by the devil for a time, yet prepared from the punishment itself a remedy, lest he should be oppressed by him eternally.

Thus, from the very beginning of the world, God set before man the sacraments of his salvation, by which he might mark him with the expectation of future sanctification, so that whoever received them with right faith and firm hope, [Col. 0312B] on account of obedience to the divine institution, might, even while placed beneath the yoke, belong to the fellowship of freedom. He therefore set forth his ordinance, forming and instructing man, so that whoever chose to await him as savior ought to approve the vow of that choice by receiving his sacraments.

The devil also set forth his own sacraments, by which he might bind his own people to himself, so that he might distinguish them more openly from those who rejected his rule and therefore possess them more securely. Thus the human race at once began to be divided into opposing parties: some receiving the devil’s sacraments, others receiving Christ’s sacraments. And two households were made: one of Christ, the other of the devil.

[Col. 0312C] For what else should I call the incarnate Word except a king who entered this world through assumed humanity, intending to wage war with the devil and afterward to expel him as a tyrant ruling violently over another’s domain? And what should I call all the earlier saints, chosen from the beginning before the incarnation of the Word, except certain excellent soldiers preceding their coming king in battle array, equipped and girded with the very sacraments by which they were then sanctified, as with weapons? Likewise, what should I call those chosen people who follow after the incarnation until the end, except other soldiers, following not another king but their own king himself, who goes before them, unanimously and eagerly, having themselves new weapons—yet armed by the same king and destined to fight against the same enemy?

[Col. 0312D] Whether, therefore, preceding or following, they bear the sacraments of one king, serve one king, and overcome one tyrant: the former precede the one who was to come; the latter follow the one who goes before. Hence it is clear that from the beginning they were Christians in reality, although not in name.

For there are three periods through which the course of the present age runs. The first is the time of the natural law; the second, the time of the written law; the third, the time of grace. The first extends from Adam to Moses; the second from Moses to Christ; the third from Christ to the end of the age.

Likewise there are three kinds of human beings: those of the natural law, those of the written law, and those of grace. Those of the natural law may be called those who direct their lives by natural reason alone. [Col. 0313A] Or rather, those are called people of the natural law who walk according to the concupiscence in which they were born. Those of the written law are those who are formed for good living by external precepts. Those of grace are those who, inspired and illuminated by the Holy Spirit, recognize the good that must be done, are inflamed so that they love it, and are strengthened so that they accomplish it.

And, to mark the same matter by a clearer distinction: people of the natural law are openly evil; people of the written law are falsely good; people of grace are truly good. The falsely good are covered; the openly evil are uncovered; these are signified by Gog and Magog, which is interpreted “covered” and “uncovered.” They are foretold as coming for the persecution of God’s people, because these two kinds of people always persecute the truly good.

[Col. 0313B] The pagans are contained in the first kind; the Jews in the second; the Christians in the third. These three kinds of people have never been absent at any time from the beginning. Yet the time of the natural law belongs to the openly evil, because they were then both more numerous and more eminent in status. The time of the written law belongs to the falsely good, because people then served in fear and cleansed their outward work, not their mind.
