The time of grace belongs to the truly good, who now, even if they are not more numerous, are nevertheless more eminent in status, and are publicly preferred through God’s grace, even by those who oppose them in conduct.

[Col. 0313C] Know, therefore, that at whatever time from the beginning of the world to its end, no one has been or is truly good except one justified by grace; and that no one could ever attain grace except through Christ. Thus recognize that all alike, whether preceding or following, are saved by the one remedy of sanctification. Behold, then, the camp of our king and the battle lines of his army shining in spiritual arms, with what a multitude of peoples preceding and following he advances surrounded.

## CHAPTER XII. On the time of the institution of the sacraments

The time of the institution of the sacraments is believed to have begun when the first parent, deservedly expelled from the joys of paradise because of disobedience, was held in the exile of this mortal life with all his posterity, subject to original corruption until the end. For from the time when man, falling from the state of original incorruption, began to be sick in body through mortality and in soul through iniquity, God immediately prepared in his sacraments medicine for his restoration.

[Col. 0313D] According to what reason and the case required, he provided these at different times and places for man’s healing: some before the law, some under the law, others under grace—different indeed in kind, but possessing one effect and accomplishing one healing. Therefore, if anyone asks about the time of the institution of the sacraments, let him know that as long as the disease exists, the time for medicine exists. The present life, therefore, running from the beginning of the age to its end through mortality, is a time of disease and a time of remedy.

The sacraments were instituted in it and for its sake; and some were instituted from its very beginning, which ran their course in their own time and were able to restore health, insofar as it was granted to them and was to be granted through them. These sacraments ceased when their time was completed, and others succeeded them to accomplish the same healing. And again, after those, others were added, as it were, last of all, to which others ought not to succeed: namely, perfect medicines which should consume the disease itself and fully restore perfect health.

[Col. 0314A] All these things were done according to the judgment and dispensation of the physician, who saw the disease itself and recognized what remedies should be applied to it at each time. Moreover, one sacrament is found to have been instituted even before human sin. Marriage, indeed, is read to have been established before man sinned, where, according to the witness of Scripture, the woman is said to have been made as a helper and joined to the man (Gen. 2).

[Col. 0314B] Yet the purpose of this institution was then not a remedy but an office, because there was no disease in man to be healed, but a virtue to be exercised. Therefore, of the three purposes for which the sacraments were instituted, we find here only two: instruction and exercise. Humiliation was not necessary there where there was no pride, but there was reason to be instructed toward greater knowledge and virtue to be advanced toward greater perfection.

Thus this sacrament is found to possess a singular law, just as it possesses a singular institution. And the order seems to require that before we approach, by discussion, what is to be said concerning the other sacraments, we should set forth separately certain matters concerning this one which appear to belong to its first institution, reserving for the following discussion those matters which belong to its second institution. [Col. 0314C] For this sacrament has a twofold institution: one before sin, for an office; the other after sin, for a remedy. According to that in which it was singularly instituted, it ought to be treated singularly; afterward, according to that in which it is joined with the others in time, it should not be separated from them in the discussion.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the institution of marriage before sin

The sacrament of marriage alone among all the sacraments instituted for the remedy of man is read to have been instituted before human sin—not, however, because of sin, but solely for sacrament and office. It was for sacrament on account of instruction and for office on account of exercise.

[Col. 0314D] For there were two things in marriage itself: marriage itself and the office of marriage, and both were sacraments. Marriage consisted in the consent of a social covenant; the office of marriage consisted in bodily union. Marriage was the sacrament of a certain spiritual fellowship which existed through love between God and the soul, in which fellowship the soul was bride and God bridegroom. The office of marriage was the sacrament of a fellowship which was to exist through assumed flesh between Christ and the Church, in which fellowship Christ was to be bridegroom and the Church bride.

In both cases the bridegroom was superior, and his love was drawn in mercy toward the inferior. But the bride was in both cases inferior, because she was not self-sufficient and could not stand through herself. Therefore her love was directed rather by necessity toward the superior. By loving, the superior bestowed a benefit; by loving, the inferior received a benefit.

[Col. 0315A] Thus, when marriage was instituted, the sacrament was formed of that fellowship which consisted on both sides in mutual love: the sacrament of one fellowship in marriage, the sacrament of the other fellowship in the office of marriage. Therefore human nature was distinguished by a twofold quality, so that in the man it might appear stronger, but in the woman weaker and needing another’s help. And the two were joined into one, by one love and one fellowship, so that they might be in one love and remain through one love in one fellowship.

The man, indeed, in order to become the image of God in this sacrament, was to be inclined to love through mercy. The woman, in order to express the form of the rational soul, was to be persuaded to love more through necessity and, as it were, consideration of a certain benefit. Yet love was voluntary on both sides, because if it had not been voluntary, it could have been neither true love nor a sacrament of true love.

[Col. 0315B] Again, in order that another sacrament might be formed in this fellowship, God commanded that male and female should be joined in one flesh, so that, just as they were formerly one in the sacrament of marriage through love, so afterward they might become one in the office of marriage through the union of one flesh. Thus it was shown that he who was formerly joined in divinity to the soul through love was afterward joined, through assumed flesh, to his Church.

Again, lest the fellowship of marriage between male and female should be idle, after the sacrament of marriage there was added the office which had to be fulfilled in the union of flesh, so that those joined in it might exercise themselves in virtue through obedience and be fruitful through the generation of offspring. In this office, the male, who was superior, was given the task of sowing from his own seed that which was to be propagated; but the female was given the task of conceiving and bearing, so that in the same likeness it might be shown that in that invisible fellowship the rational soul could in no way be fruitful unless it first conceived from God the seed of virtue.

[Col. 0315C] There was yet another feature in human nature which had to be shown through the fellowship of marriage. For man was so created that something in him should be highest, and that nothing should be higher in man; after this, something else should be beneath and subject to it; then a final thing should be placed lowest and subject to the other two. [Col. 0315D] For in man reason was established in the highest place, attending only to divine and invisible things and conforming itself to the divine will. After this was another reason, looking to bodily and visible things, which was subject to the higher reason and, being formed by it, ruled the sensual faculty subject to itself, which had been established in the third and lowest place.

Thus three things were found in man: wisdom, prudence, and sensuality. Wisdom, that is, reason directed toward divine things; prudence, that is, reason directed toward human things; sensuality, that is, affection or appetite directed toward earthly things. Of these, the first, namely reason, ruled only and was not ruled. Sensuality, the last, was ruled only and did not rule. The middle reason was both ruled by the superior and ruled what was beneath.

[Col. 0316A] In accordance with this likeness, three living creatures were made outwardly. One rational creature ruled; a second irrational creature was subject; a third rational creature was ruled by the superior and, together with the superior, ruled the inferior. Thus the man was an image of wisdom, the woman a form of prudence, and the beast a likeness of sensuality and concupiscence.

Therefore the serpent deceived the woman by suggesting sin, and the woman deceived the man. She who had been deceived inclined him to consent, because the concupiscence of the flesh first suggests to prudence the pleasure of sin; then prudence of the flesh, deceived through the pleasure of sin, draws reason to consent to iniquity.

[Col. 0316B] For these and similar reasons human nature was distinguished so that in one part it might be shown stronger and in the other weaker, so that there might be found in it one thing that rules and a whole that is ruled. There was then added outwardly in the flesh a distinction of sexes, which was not necessary for the virtue of the sacrament in marriage, but was necessary because without it the service of generation could not be fulfilled in the office of marriage.

Thus marriage and the office of marriage were instituted before sin, both for sacrament: marriage, indeed, so that it might be sanctified by pure love of mind; and the office of marriage, so that it might be fulfilled without pollution of the flesh. But now, because human flesh has been corrupted through man’s sin, after sin the union of flesh cannot occur without carnal concupiscence.

[Col. 0316C] Perhaps, however, someone may be troubled as to why, after sin, man cannot perform this particular work without sin. But to one who considers carefully, the reason is evident. For as long as the rational spirit was subject to its Creator, it found no resistance in its flesh; and the members of the body were subject to the command of the soul, so that they neither moved at any time apart from it nor toward anything against it.

[Col. 0316D] But after the spirit swelled in pride against its Creator, it deservedly lost, in what was beneath it, the right of its former dominion, so that the members of the body, which ought not to have been subject to it except through its Creator, should now resist its command in order to avenge the injury done to the Creator. But because human life could in no way continue if the rational spirit had no power at all over the members of its body, God exercised his vengeance partly through justice and partly tempered it mercifully, so that both guilt might be punished and nature preserved.

Therefore, in order that disobedience might be made manifest, he withdrew from the soul’s power one member of the human body—the member through which posterity was to be sown in the flesh—so that all who are generated through it might understand themselves to be children of disobedience and might recognize from their origin what they are and from what sort of persons they are generated. Therefore, because a sign of disobedience has been placed in this member through which human propagation was to pass, it is plainly shown to all who pass through it that they are generated with the guilt of disobedience. As though in the very inscription written upon the gate through which they pass, they recognize whence they come and whither they go.

[Col. 0317A] For this reason the other members of the body, which follow the command of reason, can act without guilt; but this member, in which concupiscence especially rules, because it does not follow the motion of the will, does not act without guilt. For this bodily member follows the soul’s command so little that, just as it is sometimes not moved when the soul wills, it is often moved even when the soul does not will.

[Col. 0318A] Therefore, from the point at which carnal intercourse could not be exercised without shameful concupiscence and the lust of the flesh, it ought not to have been exercised by man. For man made it unlawful to himself when he made himself such that he could not lawfully fulfill it. But because the weakness of human flesh would flow more shamefully into every kind of concupiscence if it were not lawfully admitted in some respect, what had formerly been instituted only for office was afterward granted as a remedy. Thus, while it is practiced by indulgence to avoid a greater evil, the evil of weakness present within it may be excused through conjugal chastity.

And these things concerning the first institution of marriage may suffice in the present place.

# PART NINE. ON THE INSTITUTION OF THE SACRAMENTS

[Col. 0317]

## CHAPTER ONE. Four matters to be considered in the institution of the sacraments

[Col. 0317B]

For those wishing to treat of the sacraments, four matters must first be considered. First, what a sacrament is. Second, why the sacraments were instituted. Third, what is the matter of each sacrament in which it is performed and sanctified. Fourth, how many kinds of sacraments there are. That is: definition, cause, matter, division. For if these four matters are examined through careful treatment, they can produce understanding of the matters proposed. We therefore undertake first to treat the first matter.

## CHAPTER II. What a sacrament is
What a sacrament is, the doctors have indicated by a brief description: “A sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing.” [Col. 0317C] For just as in a human being there are two things, body and soul, and likewise in a single Scripture two things, letter and meaning, so also in every sacrament one thing is visibly handled and seen outwardly, another is invisibly believed and prescribed inwardly. What is outwardly visible and material is the sacrament; what is inwardly invisible and spiritual is the thing, or power, of the sacrament. Yet the sacrament which is outwardly handled and sanctified is always a sign of the spiritual grace which is the thing of the sacrament and is received invisibly.

But because not every sign of a sacred thing can suitably be called a sacrament of that thing—for letters are signs of sacred meanings, and forms or pictures are signs of sacred things, though they cannot reasonably be called their sacraments—the description mentioned above seems to concern the interpretation or expression of the word rather than its definition. If anyone wishes to define more fully and perfectly what a sacrament is, he may define it thus: “A sacrament is a bodily or material element set forth outwardly to the senses, which by resemblance represents, by institution signifies, and by sanctification contains some invisible and spiritual grace.” This definition is recognized as so proper and [Col. 0318B] perfect that it is found to apply to every sacrament and to that alone. For everything having these three things is a sacrament, and everything lacking these three cannot properly be called a sacrament.

Every sacrament must have some likeness to the very thing of which it is the sacrament, by which it is suited to represent that same thing. It must also have an institution by which it is ordered to signify it. Finally, it must have a sanctification by which it contains that thing and is efficacious in conferring it upon those who are sanctified. This, however, seems to be the distinction: every sacrament has its likeness from its original formation, its institution from an added dispensation, and its sanctification from the application of the blessing of word or sign.

Thus, that in one sacrament we may recognize how these three things said of all are present, let us take baptismal water as an example. There is the visible element of water, which is the sacrament; and these three are found together in it: representation from likeness, signification from institution, and power from sanctification. The likeness itself comes from creation; the institution itself, from dispensation; the sanctification itself, from blessing. The first was imparted by the Creator; the second added by the Savior; the third administered by the dispenser. Visible water, therefore, is the sacrament, and invisible grace the thing or power of the sacrament.

Every water has, by its natural quality, a certain likeness to the grace of the Holy Spirit; for as this washes bodily filth away, so that cleanses [Col. 0318D] the defilements of souls. By this innate quality, every water was able to represent spiritual grace even before, by an added institution, it also signified it. But the Savior came and instituted visible water, through the washing of bodies, to signify through spiritual grace the cleansing of souls. Therefore water now represents not merely by natural likeness, but signifies spiritual grace by added institution.

[Col. 0319A] Yet since, as we have said, these two still do not suffice for perfection, the word of sanctification is joined to the element and it becomes a sacrament: visible water, representing by likeness, signifying by institution, and containing spiritual grace by sanctification. In the same manner these three things must also be considered in the other sacraments.

## CHAPTER III. Why sacraments were instituted

The first part of the proposition having been expounded, let us proceed to the second. Sacraments are known to have been instituted for a threefold reason: for humiliation, instruction, and exercise.

For humiliation: so that when the human being, a rational creature, is subjected by the command of his Creator to insensible elements—which by nature were created beneath [Col. 0319B] him—he may deserve through this very humiliation to be reconciled to his Creator. For humanity was so made that the One from whom it was made was its sole good; all other things were made beneath it, not so that its good might be in them, but so that they might render it service.

For every good is greater than the one whose good it is, since nothing is truly good unless it makes good the one whose good it is. Everyone, therefore, who is good is good by his good and is inferior to the good by which he is good, because without that good he is not good. If, then, the good of humanity was above humanity, its sole good was He who was above humanity. So long as humanity remained in the order of its creation, it was immediately joined to this good and freely enjoyed it, [Col. 0319C] since by its will it went toward it and by freedom stood in it.

But after it was drawn away from the higher through desire, it was turned toward lower things and cast down, and subjected itself to that which it made its good. Thus, by a just recompense, one who refused through obedience to be subject to his superior subjected himself through desire to his inferior, so that God Himself now stands between them as the means of division, not as the mediator of reconciliation. By this intervening division the human mind is both darkened, so that it cannot recognize its Creator, and chilled, so that it does not seek Him in love.

It is therefore just that the person who formerly abandoned God in pride and subjected himself through desire to earthly things should now seek God in humility and, in order more fully to show the affection of his devotion, bow himself in obedience to those same things for God’s command. For as the pride of refusing to be subject to a superior was ruinous, so the devotion of bowing even to inferiors for the sake of a superior is praiseworthy and fruitful. And as it was blameworthy pride to despise one who is present, so it is praiseworthy humility to seek one who is absent and, in persevering love, not to cease from seeking until finding—so that devotion may be in humility and humility in devotion.

No one, indeed, fails to know that a rational human being is superior by nature to mute and insensible elements. Yet when this same person is commanded to seek salvation in them, so that the power of obedience may be tested, what is this except that one who is superior is made subject to his inferior? [Col. 0320A] For this reason the eyes of unbelievers, who see only visible things, disdain to venerate the sacraments of salvation: seeing only what is outwardly contemptible in visible appearance, they do not recognize the invisible power within and the fruit of obedience.

They do not know that the faithful do not seek salvation from these elements, even though they seek it in them; rather, they seek it from Him and through Him in those elements, from whom they are commanded to seek it and whom they believe they receive in them. These things do not bestow what is bestowed through them; rather, He who commands salvation to be sought in them bestows salvation through them. This, then, is how it must be understood when we say that invisible sacraments were instituted for human humiliation.

Sacraments were also instituted for instruction, so that through what is outwardly seen in the visible appearance of the sacrament the human mind may be instructed to recognize the invisible power which inwardly belongs to the thing of the sacrament. A person knew visible things but did not know invisible things; he could not recognize divine things at all unless stirred by human things. Therefore, when the invisible good he had lost is restored to him, its signification is outwardly supplied through visible appearances, so that he may be stirred outwardly and restored inwardly; that, in what he handles and sees, he may recognize the nature of what he receives and does not see.

The spiritual gifts of grace are like invisible antidotes; when they are offered to a person in visible sacraments as though in vessels, what else occurs but that hidden power is displayed through an open appearance? [Col. 0320C] A sick person cannot see the medicine, but can see the vessel in which it is given. Therefore the power of the remedy is expressed in the very appearance of the vessel, so that he may recognize what he receives and, through that recognition, advance to love. This, then, is how we must understand the statement that sacraments were instituted for instruction.

Likewise, sacraments were instituted for exercise, so that, while the human mind is cultivated by being outwardly exercised through various kinds of works, it may inwardly become fruitful in the manifold fruit of virtue. The human good was one; and so long as humanity clung to it in love, it did not need this multiplicity. But after it allowed its mind to be divided by desire among these many transient things, it could not remain stable. For as one loving many things is divided among them in affection, so one pursuing mutable things is changed.

Whatever repose and consolation a person seeks in all these things, the very condition of mutability turns into labor and pain. Thus, as he is compelled to go to them lest he fail, so later he is compelled to leave them that he may rest, and there appears another Cain, “a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth” (Gen. III): a wanderer, seeking consolation in various things; a fugitive, everywhere avoiding the affliction he has found.

A human being walks, but if he walks continuously, he fails. He therefore sits or stands lest he fail; and yet, if he sits continuously, he fails. We hunger and fail; we eat lest we fail; but if we ate continuously, we would fail, and what was sought for consolation is turned to pain. So every human mutability has failure, not progress; and we fail because we change, though we never cease changing lest we fail.

[Col. 0321A] Since, therefore, human life here cannot exist without mutability, another mutability which produces progress is set against that mutability which produces failure. Thus, because a person cannot stand so as always to remain the same, he should move and continually advance so as to become better. The first good was to stand at the summit; the second good is to ascend to higher things. Therefore mutable life, lest through its own motion it be dissolved and continually decline to worse things, had to be nourished by such pursuits that, outwardly stirred by the variety of things and inwardly inflamed by emulation of virtues, it might find an opportunity for progress.

Times were divided and places distinguished; bodily forms were set forth; pursuits and works to be practiced were prescribed, so that the outward person might prepare the medicine of the inward person and learn to be subject and useful to it. For since human life had previously run through two kinds of exercise—one toward necessity, the other toward pleasure; one toward use, the other toward vice; one for nature, the other for guilt; one for sustenance, the other for ruin—it was fitting that a third kind of exercise should be added. By it, one of the first two was to be abolished because it was harmful, and the other perfected because it was insufficient.

Works of virtue were therefore set before humanity outwardly for the exercise of inward edification, so that, occupied by them, it might neither ever have leisure for works of wickedness nor always be occupied with works of necessity. [Col. 0321C] In these pursuits of virtue, moreover, God in marvelous dispensation provided multiplicity, variety, and interruption, so that the human mind might find exercise in multiplicity, delight in variety, and restoration in interruption.

Certain places were consecrated, basilicas built, and fixed times determined for the faithful people to gather in one, that unity might be commended, in order to give thanks, offer prayers, and fulfill vows. There God is now simply implored in silence, now devoutly praised in harmonious voices, so that in turn the hearts of the faithful may now be composed for rest, now stirred to devotion.

Nor is the same form of praise always offered in the divine proclamations themselves. At one time psalmody kindles devotion; at another, hymns and songs stir divine joy; at another, readings are recited for the formation of character and instruction in a good life. Our very actions in divine services do not always proceed according to the same institutional form. Now standing upright, now prostrate, now by bowing, now by turning, we express through bodily gesture the state of the mind.

The things in which the devotion of the faithful exercises itself by action and adorns divine worship are likewise many and variously provided according to the same principle, so that there may be very many sacred things and sacraments, in order that faith may find in them both material for exercise and a perfect cause of restoration. Thus, while the faithful mind is outwardly led to various pursuits of holy exercise, it is inwardly renewed ever more and more toward holiness by its own devotion. This, then, is how we think the statement that sacraments were instituted for exercise should be understood.

## CHAPTER IV. On the distinction of three works and three agents

There is, then, this threefold cause for the institution of all sacraments: the humiliation, instruction, and exercise of humanity. If these causes did not exist, sacraments—that is, signs or instruments of sacred things—could not be elements in themselves. For elements are not made sacraments by their original nature, but by an added institution through dispensation and grace infused through blessing. Unless elements received these two things after their original nature, they could not properly be sacraments.

Nature first gave them the capacity to be this; a second institution added the authority for them to become this; a third blessing added the holiness for them to be this. The first was accomplished by the Creator; the second set forth by the Savior; the third administered by the dispenser. The Creator first formed the vessels by majesty; afterward the Savior set the same things forth by institution; finally the dispenser cleansed these very things by blessing and filled them with grace.

It seems marvelous that the greater made what was lesser, and the lesser made what was greater. For sanctification conferred more than creation: in creation they received a nature, that they might exist; in sanctification, grace, that they might be good and holy. If, then, God creates and the priest sanctifies, it seems that a human being does more than God—which would be wholly absurd and improper, unless what the human being does were also done by God.

For God creates without a human being, but a human being does not sanctify without God. Thus grace begins, as it were, from the highest and is consummated in the lowest; and in this very fact the descent of grace is signified to us, because unless grace descended, it would not raise those lying fallen. God first created through Himself and in what is His—that is, alone and in majesty. The Savior afterward instituted through Himself indeed, but in what is ours—that is, alone and in humanity. Finally, the priest sanctifies neither through himself nor in what is his, since he is neither the sole agent nor the source of the power bestowed for sanctification.

For the One whose power sanctifies through the ministry of the minister cooperates with the minister. Thus there is one power, through one work, toward one effect; and this power is distinguished in two agents working together, because through one it is given, through the other it is administered. One is He from whom it is given; another is he through whom it is sent. And when grace itself comes to us, it comes through Him from whom it comes, because the author of the gift cooperates with the minister; but it does not come in the same way through the one through whom it comes, because one who is merely the minister of the dispensation cannot be the author of the gift.

Let no one, therefore, ask how a human being sanctifies when God sanctifies through a human being; for in this matter the human being more truly does what God does through him. What a human being does through himself and in what is his, however, he does not truly do, because he does not do truth; for through himself and in what is his he does nothing but evil.

Thus God alone performs wonders, because Scripture says of Him: “Who alone performs great wonders” (Ps. LXXI); for without Him no one acts, and everyone who acts acts through Him, and He Himself acts through every person who acts. Therefore He alone acts, because whatever every agent does belongs to Him alone. Yet it is written of God’s servant: “For he performed wonders in his life” (Ecclus. XXXI), because he acted from God, and God acted through him. No contradiction follows from this. Thus God alone sanctifies and blesses, because every sanctification and blessing is from Him; yet the priest, God’s minister, sanctifies and blesses, because a certain sanctification and blessing occurs through him—and this too is from God, who is author in the gift and, through God, who is coworker in the ministry.

By such consideration one may reasonably distinguish, in every sacrament separately, what creation accomplishes with respect to the nature of the element, and what institution and sanctification accomplish with respect to the power of the sacrament; and, in sanctification itself, how much comes from Him who is the giver of the gift, and how much from—or rather through—him who is only the minister of the dispensation.

Finally, five things, distinct and separate from one another, are set forth for understanding: God the physician; the human being the sick person; the priest, minister or messenger; grace, the antidote; and the vessel, the sacrament. The physician gives; the minister administers; the vessel preserves the spiritual grace which heals the sick recipient. Therefore, if sacraments are vessels of spiritual grace, they do not heal by what belongs to themselves, since vessels do not cure the sick person, but medicine does.

Sacraments, then, were not instituted so that what is in them might come from them, but so that the physician might display his skill by preparing a remedy in that from which the sick person had taken the occasion of sickness. Since a person was corrupted through desiring visible things, it was fitting that, in those same visible things, he should receive an occasion of salvation, so that he might rise again through the same things through which he had fallen.

## CHAPTER V. That the institution of sacraments is, in relation to God, a matter of dispensation; in relation to humanity, of necessity

The institution of sacraments is, in relation to God their author, a matter of dispensation; but in relation to the obedient human being, a matter of necessity. For it is in God’s power to save a person apart from these things; but it is not in a person’s power to attain salvation without them. God could save a person even if He had not instituted these things; but a person could by no means be saved if he despised them.

For Scripture says: “One who has not been baptized cannot be saved” (John III); one who has not done this or that cannot be saved. We confess this to be true: a person lacking those things without which salvation cannot be obtained by a human being cannot be saved. A person cannot be saved without them, but God can save without them.

A person could be saved without them if salvation without them lay within human power—if a person could, by his own choice, abandon the things prescribed for obtaining salvation and arrive at salvation by another way of his own choosing. Since this is altogether impossible for a human being, it is most rightly said that a human being cannot at all be saved without them.

But God can save a human being without them, since He can bestow His power, sanctification, and salvation upon a human being in whatever manner He Himself wills. By that Spirit by which He teaches a human being without a word, He is also able, if He wills, to justify without a sacrament. God’s power is not subjected to elements by necessity, even though God’s grace is given through sacraments by dispensation.

Hence we read and believe that some have been justified and saved even without sacraments of this kind. Thus Jeremiah is read to have been sanctified in the womb; John the Baptist is prophesied to be filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb; and we do not read that those righteous persons who pleased God under the natural law possessed these sacraments. Yet we do not at all doubt their salvation. Those among them who received these sacraments after justification had in them signs of their righteousness rather than the cause of it.

Those who, through the Spirit of God, received without these things whatever is conferred in them, were not damnably without them, because their failure to receive them was caused either by the order of the time, which did not require it, or by necessity, which did not permit it—never by contempt for religion. Therefore let no one establish the law of divine justice in elements in such a way as to say that a person cannot be justified without them even if he possesses justifying grace, or cannot be saved without them even if he is righteous, when he is excluded from receiving them by an urgent necessity or, as we have said, is not bound by the order of time to receive them.

Just as those righteous persons who lived under the natural law were not initiated into sacraments of this kind, so they were not bound by precepts of this kind. Whoever possessed the thing of the sacrament in right faith and true love was not damnably without these sacraments, because either they ought not to receive them at that time or, because of impending necessity, could not receive them.

What, then, do you think—you who venerate God’s sacraments and, while thinking that you honor God’s sacraments, dishonor God? You assign necessity to the sacraments, while taking power and denying mercy to the Author of the sacraments. You tell me that one who lacks God’s sacraments cannot be saved; and I tell you that one possessing the power of God’s sacraments cannot perish. Either deny that power can exist where the sacrament is absent, or, if you concede power, deny condemnation.

Which is greater: the sacrament or the power of the sacrament? Which is greater: water or faith? If you wish to speak truth, say faith. If, then, the sacrament of water, which is lesser, saves some who lack faith—and their lack of faith is not imputed to them because they cannot have it—how can faith, which is greater, not deliver those who have faith but lack the sacrament of water? And should they not much more be spared because they lack the sacrament of water, which they wished to possess but could not?

“But,” you say, “how then are we to understand what is written: ‘Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven’?” (John III). And I ask you how you think we should understand what is written: “Who believes in me shall not see death for ever” (John XI). You say that one who does not do this is not saved; I say that one who does this is not condemned. What middle place, then, will receive such people—neither to be saved because they lack water, nor to be condemned because they possess faith?

There is a person who has faith and, together with faith, love; he lacks water, yet does not despise water, but wishes to have it and cannot. Shall absent water then condemn him, rather than present faith and devotion save him?

“What then,” you say, “have I to do with sacraments? I will have faith, love, and other virtues; I shall be good, and that will suffice for me.” See, then, whether you can have the love of God and despise His commandments. If, therefore, you have the love of God, strive, labor, endeavor, insofar as you can, to fulfill His commands; and if you fall into necessity, seek mercy. For if no necessity is alleged, contempt is not excused.

Observe, then, that God’s sacraments are spiritual medicines: outwardly applied to bodies in visible form, but inwardly healing souls through invisible power. Their institution, in relation to the One commanding, is a matter of dispensation; their reception, in relation to the obedient person, is a matter of necessity.

Do you wish to know that, in these visible forms, God does not employ a remedy for curing spiritual diseases, but only establishes a sacrament? Learn sacrament from sacrament. Hezekiah became ill, and Isaiah the prophet was sent to him to foretell his imminent death. Stricken with terror and sorrow when he heard this, he poured out tears with prayer and obtained mercy. Isaiah was immediately sent back to announce that fifteen years would be added to his life and, further to commend the power of the sacrament, to prepare a new remedy in a new manner for healing his wound.

Medicine was applied outwardly so that hidden power might work inwardly; and health did not come from the medicine, since in itself the medicine was contrary to health. Thus it was plainly shown that what occurred through it did not come from it. A great sacrament concerning sacraments was commended.

The human race is sick: it languishes inwardly through iniquity and outwardly through mortality. The prophetic word is sent to it, that imminent death, not only present but future, may be announced. Those who are frightened confess, weep, pray, and obtain mercy. The prophetic word is sent back, making us certain that a longer span of life has been granted. For the same Scripture that consoles the repentant with the promise of eternal life terrifies those persisting in sin with condemnation to perpetual death.

Medicine is applied for healing our wounds; and since, by its own character, it appears contrary to the disease, the cure of the sick person most evidently displays not the power of the medicine but that of the healer. The medicine itself is the sacraments. When they are outwardly applied to us bodily by the ministers of the sacred dispensation, the wounds of our souls are invisibly healed, so that, cured and made whole, we may attain the promise of everlasting life.

This life is signified by the number of fifteen years: in the present it begins through the sevenfold rest of the mind, and in the future it is completed through the eightfold mortality of the flesh. Yet, with respect to its own nature, this medicine was fitted to increase disease rather than cure it, because all earthly things—so far as their own quality and our weakness are concerned—ordinarily produce corruption of souls rather than healing.

Yet when God accomplishes our healing through these things, what does He do but clearly show the might of His power, when He provides our remedy in the very thing from which we contracted the disease of weakness and corruption? Therefore what is administered to us through these things must not be ascribed to them; nor should we so venerate the visible form in them as to be compelled to subject the invisible truth to them.

By carefully considering this, it becomes clear how much is owed both to what is outwardly seen in the visible appearance of the sacrament and to what inwardly works invisibly in the power of the sacrament. All these things concern the question proposed for investigation: namely, why sacraments were instituted.

## CHAPTER VI. On the matter of sacraments

There remains to be discussed the third of the four parts proposed. All divine sacraments are performed in a threefold matter: in things, in deeds, or in words. Since the whole human being was corrupted, everything belonging outwardly to the human being was to be taken up for a sacrament, so that the whole might be sanctified outwardly in the sacrament and the power of the sacrament might inwardly work a remedy in the whole.

Thus sacraments were to be sanctified in things, that humanity’s material might be sanctified; in deeds, that its works might be sanctified; and in words, that its words might be sanctified—so that all may be holy: both what a human being is and what belongs to a human being.

Sacraments are performed in things: for example, the sacrament of baptism in water; the sacrament of anointing in oil; the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood in bread and wine; and whatever other bodily forms there are in which divine sacraments are performed. Sacraments are also found in deeds: for example, when we make the sign of the cross, either setting it against hostile powers as a defense or impressing it for sanctification upon whatever things are to be sanctified; or when, with hands outspread or raised in prayer, by bowing or standing erect, turning, or any other gesture, movement, or action, we express something sacred and a sign of a sacred thing.

A sacrament is found in words, such as the invocation of the Trinity and other things of this kind, whenever through the utterance of words we express and signify something sacred and sacramental. It should further be known that, although sacraments are performed in these three ways, those are called sacraments more properly and principally in which there is power through sanctification and an effect of salvation through operation. Having briefly prefaced these matters concerning the matter of sacraments, let us proceed to what follows.

## CHAPTER VII. That there are three kinds of sacraments

In the first consideration, three kinds of sacraments must be distinguished. There are certain sacraments in which salvation principally consists and is received, such as baptismal water and receiving the body and blood of Christ. There are others which, although not necessary for salvation—for salvation can be had without them—nevertheless advance sanctification, because through them power may be exercised and fuller grace acquired: such as water of sprinkling, receiving ashes, and similar things.

There are again other sacraments which seem to have been instituted only in order that, through them, the things necessary for sanctifying and instituting the other sacraments may in some manner be prepared and sanctified—whether concerning persons to be perfected in sacred orders, or things to be initiated that pertain to the habit of sacred orders, and other matters of this kind. The first, therefore, are established for salvation; the second for exercise; the third for preparation. Having treated these matters as reason appeared to require, we proceed to explain what remains.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the three things necessary for salvation

[Col. 0328A]

There are certainly three things which, from the beginning—whether before Christ’s coming or after—have been necessary to obtain salvation: faith, sacraments of faith, and good works. These three are so connected that they cannot have the effect of salvation unless they are present together. For faith without works, Scripture testifies, is dead (James II). Again, where faith is absent, a work cannot be good. Likewise, those who have faith working cannot be saved if they refuse to receive God’s sacraments, because they do not have the love of God, whose commandments they despise in His sacraments.

Nevertheless, where faith is joined with love, just as merit is not diminished if a work present in the good purpose of devotion is not outwardly completed, so the effect of salvation is not hindered if a sacrament present in true will and desire is prevented by an urgent necessity. But where the three can be possessed together, they can by no means be absent without danger to salvation. Faith has no merit if, though able to act, it neglects to do so; nor is any work good if done without faith. Again, working faith does not suffice to sanctify a person if he despises receiving the sanctification which belongs to God’s sacraments.

The three, therefore, are together: faith, sacrament, and work. In faith, strength is granted to the Christian; in sacraments, weapons; in good works, missiles for one who is to fight against the devil.

# PART TEN. ON FAITH

## CHAPTER I. That seven questions are to be examined concerning faith

[Col. 0327C]

For those wishing to treat faith, we set forth seven questions for examination: what faith is; wherein faith consists; the growth of faith; the things pertaining to faith; whether from the beginning faith among believers has changed according to changes of time; what is that without which true faith could never possess anything less; and the sacrament of faith and its power. Let us treat each in its proper order.

## CHAPTER II. What faith is
Faith is, as the Apostle says, “the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. XII). If by “faith” we understand the things believed through faith, signified by the term—as by “vision” we sometimes understand not the faculty by which we see, but that which we see—then faith is suitably called the substance of things hoped for, because through faith those good things which truly subsist are believed by those hoping and awaiting them as things to come. [Col. 0327D] According to this understanding it is not unreasonably called also the proof of things not seen, because we persuade ourselves that those things which we do not comprehend by human reason are credible and true for us through faith alone.

But if we explain this definition differently, we may say that faith is defined not by what it is but by what it does, so that the sense is: Faith is the substance—that is, the subsistence—of things hoped for, that is, of future goods, which [Col. 0328C] are hoped for by us as things to come, and which alone are worthy of our hope and expectation, because our good consists in them. Therefore faith is the substance of things hoped for, because the invisible goods which are not yet present in actuality nevertheless already subsist in our hearts through faith; and faith itself is their subsistence in us.

For when any thing subsists with us, it does so either in actuality, namely when things present are apprehended by the senses; or by understanding, when absent things—or even things not existing—are apprehended by the understanding in their likeness and image; or by experience, when we feel within ourselves such things as joy, sorrow, fear, and love, which subsist in us and are felt by us. Yet by none of these modes [Col. 0328D] are the invisible things of God apprehended by us: they can only be believed; they cannot at all be comprehended. For they are not present in actuality so as to be apprehended by sense, since they are neither bodies nor subsist in bodily things. Nor can they be apprehended imaginatively by the mind in any likeness, because by the excellence of their divinity and purity they transcend every likeness both of bodies and of bodily things. Nor are they like those things which are within us and are felt by us, since they are neither of the substance of the mind [Col. 0329A] nor among those things which subsist in the mind.

Therefore they subsist in us by faith alone; and their subsistence is the faith by which they are believed to exist, though they are not comprehended as to what they are like. Thus God can be believed, but cannot at all be comprehended.

“You ask me,” he says, “What am I to say? What is God?” I answer you that what God is is wholly inexpressible.

“At least,” you say, “what shall I think when I wish to think what God is?” I say further that God is unthinkable. Whatever is spoken or thought is spoken or thought in some respect. But what cannot be spoken or thought in some respect cannot be spoken or thought at all. What, then, will you say or think when you wish to say or think what God is? If [Col. 0329B] you think of earth, if you think of heaven, if you think of all things that are in heaven and on earth, none of these is God. Finally, if you think of spirit, if you think of soul, this is not God.

“I know,” you say, “that this is not God; yet it is like God, and God can be shown by a likeness of it.” Consider what kind of likeness it would be if you wished to show a spirit and displayed a body; and yet the difference between God and spirit is far greater than that between spirit and body. For everything created is less distant from another created thing than he who made it is from that which he made. God cannot be thought as to what he is, though he can be believed to be; nor can he be comprehended as to what he is like. “What,” says the Apostle, “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. II)—this is what we wish to say, [Col. 0329C] if indeed we can say what we cannot think. What eye has not seen nor ear heard is not perceived by sense; nor has it entered into the heart of man, because it is not comprehended by thought.

There were, indeed, three things: body, spirit, and God. The body was the world; the spirit was the soul. The soul itself stood, as it were, in a middle position, having the world outside itself and God within itself. It had received an eye by which it saw outside itself the world and the things in the world: this was the eye of the flesh. It had received another eye by which it saw itself and the things within itself: this is the eye of reason. Again, it had received another eye by which it saw within itself God and the things in God: this is the eye of contemplation.

So long as the soul possessed these eyes open and unveiled, [Col. 0329D] it saw clearly and discerned rightly. But after the darkness of sin entered it, the eye of contemplation was extinguished, so that it saw nothing; the eye of reason became bleared, so that it saw uncertainly. Only the eye which was not extinguished remained in its brightness; and so long as it has clear light, its judgment is not uncertain. But so long as the light of the eye of reason is clouded, it cannot have certain judgment, because it discerns ambiguously what it does not see clearly. Hence human hearts agree with one another more readily concerning things perceived by the eye of the flesh than concerning things reached by the sharpness of mind and the sense of reason; for where they are not dimmed in seeing, they do not differ in judging.

Therefore man, [Col. 0330A] because he has the eye of the flesh, can see the world and the things in the world. Likewise, because he possesses the eye of reason in part, he likewise sees the mind in part and the things in the mind. But because he does not possess the eye of contemplation, he cannot see God and the things which are in God. Faith, therefore, is necessary, by which things not seen may be believed and may subsist in us through faith, though they are not yet present to us by sight. Thus faith is their substance, because through faith alone they now subsist in us; and faith is likewise their proof, because through faith alone they are established for us.

For we can produce no greater proof for those who doubt these things than that the things believed by faith are not comprehended by reason. What other proof [Col. 0330B] can there be for things to which nothing can be like or comparable? Indeed, no proof could exist unless it also possessed some likeness to that for which it was a proof. By what likeness, then, can things which transcend every likeness and comparison be demonstrated and confirmed? Only because from the faith and devotion of the saints who went before we infer that we ought not to disbelieve the good things proclaimed as future. For this is a great reason, and wholly worthy of belief: all the saints and righteous would never have despised this present life with such constancy out of desire for eternal life, unless they had perceived something further, beyond our understanding, concerning the truth of that life.

Thus faith is the substance of things hoped for, because through it things future already [Col. 0330C] in some fashion subsist in us; and the proof of things not seen, because through it hidden things are approved by us. But because this description shows not what faith is but what faith does, and does not define the faith held concerning past or present things, anyone wishing to give a full and general definition of faith may say: “Faith is a certain assurance of the mind concerning absent things, established above opinion and below knowledge.”

For some immediately reject in their minds what they hear and contradict what is said: these are deniers. Others, in matters which they hear, choose one side or another for their judgment, but do not approve it for assertion. [Col. 0330D] Although they understand one of two alternatives to be more probable, they do not yet venture to assert that it is true: these are those who hold opinions. Others approve one side in such a way that they also adopt their approval as an assertion: these are believers. After these kinds of cognition comes the more perfect state in which the matter is made known not from hearing alone but through its own presence. Those who apprehend the thing itself as it is in its presence know more perfectly: these are knowers. Thus the first are deniers, the second doubters, the third holders of opinion, the fourth believers, and the fifth knowers.

From these points one may infer why we call faith assurance: where doubt still remains, faith does not exist. It is also clear why we say that the assurance called faith is established above opinion or estimation [Col. 0331A] and below knowledge. To believe something is less than to know it, but more than to opine or estimate it. I say “less” not with respect to merit, but with respect to cognition. For unless believing were sometimes greater in merit than seeing the truth, vision would never have been withheld so that faith might earn merit. Nor would it have been said: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John XX).

Therefore I said that believing is sometimes greater than seeing, with respect to merit but not with respect to joy. Otherwise, with respect to the fullness of blessedness and the perfection of truth, it is greater to see what is present than to believe what is absent, just as it is greater to stand firm in faith than to waver in opinion. Therefore it was rightly said: “Faith is assurance concerning [Col. 0331B] absent things, established above opinion and below knowledge.” Although sometimes the assurance itself which arises from present contemplation is improperly called faith. But concerning that which is properly called faith it has been said: “For if you see, it is not faith.”

## Chapter III. What Those Things Are in Which Faith Consists

There are two things in which faith consists: cognition and affection, that is, steadfastness or firmness in believing. In one it consists because it itself is that thing; in the other it consists because it is in that thing. For the substance of faith is found in affection; its matter is found in cognition. Faith by which one believes is one thing; that which is believed by faith is another. Faith is found in affection; that which [Col. 0331C] is believed by faith is found in cognition. Therefore faith has its substance in affection, because affection itself is faith; it has its matter in cognition, because faith concerns and is directed toward that which is in cognition. Thus believing belongs to affection, but that which is believed belongs to cognition.

Here by cognition we understand knowledge of things—not the knowledge which is apprehended from their presence, but that which is perceived through hearing alone and made manifest from the meaning of words. When what is said is understood by the hearer, even though the hearer does not know whether it is or is not as it is said to be, there is still knowledge insofar as the hearer understands and knows what is being said. This knowledge is cognition. Just as it can exist without that knowledge by which one knows whether a thing exists or does not exist, so it can exist without faith by which a thing [Col. 0331D] is believed to exist or not exist.

If faith is added to this cognition, so that what was heard and understood is believed, there is belief in cognition; and the substance of faith is found in belief, its matter in cognition. Cognition of this kind can exist without any faith; but faith cannot exist without any cognition. For one who hears and understands something does not always believe; but one who understands nothing believes nothing, although one may sometimes believe what one does not understand. For there is also faith concerning faith: one believes what one does not know because one believes a person who knows and believes. One who believes a believer is not improperly said to believe what that believer believes; and although he does not know the thing which the other knows and believes, he knows whom he believes.

Such are the simple members [Col. 0332A] of the holy Church, who believe those more perfect persons who believe and know. They are saved in their simplicity and are not excluded from those persons’ merit, even though they do not attain their knowledge. It is written: “The oxen were ploughing and the asses feeding beside them” (Job I). For although the simple in the holy Church cannot investigate the hidden mysteries of God together with the perfect, nevertheless, because they do not separate themselves from their fellowship, they feed themselves by good works in the same faith and hope, as though placed beside them.

Thus faith is sometimes with cognition, when one knows what one believes; sometimes without cognition, when one merely believes one who knows and believes. Yet some cognition must always accompany faith, directing faith itself through intention; for [Col. 0332B] if none of the things to be believed were known, faith would have nothing by which to direct itself in a good work, nor anything toward which to raise its hope by good works. But it is one thing for cognition to surpass faith in some matters; another thing not to know the things which must never be unknown to believers. In the former case faith has merit even where it does not distinguish by cognition; in the latter, because it is wholly deprived of cognition, faith itself fails and ceases.

## Chapter IV. On the Increase of Faith

There are two respects in which faith is said to grow: cognition and affection, that is, steadfastness or firmness in believing. Faith grows in cognition when it is instructed unto knowledge. It grows in affection [Col. 0332C] when it is stirred [Col. 0332D] to devotion and strengthened for constancy. Some persons’ faith is great in cognition but small in affection. Others’ is great in affection but small in cognition. Some have faith great both in cognition and in affection; others have it small in both cognition and affection.

Nevertheless, the Lord plainly shows that great affection in faith is more praiseworthy than great cognition, when he compared faith to a grain of mustard seed, which is small in size but not in ardour. Hence it was said to the Canaanite woman, who still knew little but trusted greatly: “Woman, great is your faith” (Matt. XV). For that faith is accounted great before God which, though it may be less vigorous in knowledge, is nevertheless outwardly displayed through constancy. Therefore, when faith grows in cognition, it is aided; when it grows in affection, it earns merit.

Likewise, according to the growth of faith, three kinds of believers are found. Some faithful people choose to believe through piety alone, although they do not comprehend by reason whether what they believe ought or ought not to be believed. Others approve by reason what they believe through faith. Others, by purity of heart and clean conscience, already begin inwardly to taste what they believe through faith. In the first, piety alone makes the choice; in the second, reason adds approval; in the third, purity of understanding apprehends certainty.

There is a fourth kind of people for whom believing consists merely in not contradicting faith. They are called faithful more by habit of life than by the power of believing. [Col. 0333A] Fixed only upon passing things, they never raise their minds to think of future things. Although they receive with other believers, by customary practice, the sacraments of the Christian faith, they do not consider why a human being is Christian or what hope a Christian has in expectation of future goods. Though such persons are called faithful by name, they are far from faith in reality and truth.

Nevertheless, persons of this kind are sometimes visited by divine grace and awakened to reflect upon themselves. They begin to ask why man was born; whether something else follows after this life; whether rewards are reserved for the righteous and punishments for sinners; and whether, after the end of one’s work, the reward of just recompense follows. When such reflection arises in the heart, the conscience itself is immediately shaken by a great movement of fear amid uncertainty about this mortal life; and the more it sees danger threatening itself in its error, [Col. 0333B] the more eagerly it strives to attain knowledge of the truth.

It considers how diverse human judgments are in this world concerning those matters on which human salvation depends. Pagans divide the unity of divinity among many gods. Jews confess the Creator but do not acknowledge the Saviour. Amid all these things the mind fluctuates; and unless it were held fast by piety to its own position, it might perhaps abandon truth and follow falsehood. To this is added—at the prompting of the Holy Spirit—the reasoning that, in many doubts, if one thing is rejected in order that another may be chosen, doubt is not removed but altered. A further and greater reason is added: it is better to confess one principle than many, because where there is multitude, either plurality is superfluous or unity is imperfect.

Further still, [Col. 0333C] it is better to confess both Creator and Saviour than Creator alone. One who speaks of the Creator confesses majesty; one who understands the Saviour venerates mercy. And the greatest good for man is to find in his God both the majesty which he contemplates with the eye of the heart and the humanity which he beholds with the eye of the flesh, so that the whole human being may be made blessed in God.

Strengthened by these reasons, the mind is stirred toward a fuller devotion to divine religion. By devotion it is cleansed and purified, so that with a clean heart it now begins in some manner to taste beforehand that which it hastens to know through faith and devotion. Thus a clean conscience is daily instructed and made certain concerning its God through invisible teachings and a secret, familiar visitation, until it begins in some fashion [Col. 0333D] to possess him as present through contemplation; and it can then be torn from his faith and love by no reasoning, even if the whole world should be transformed into miracles.

These, then, are the three stages by which advancing faith rises to perfection: first, to choose through piety; second, to approve through reason; third, to apprehend through truth.

## Chapter V. On Those Things Which Pertain to Faith

It is also asked what matters pertain to faith, which a person rightly called faithful ought to believe. For faith by which something is believed in such a way that the person believing by that faith is not called faithful is not the subject of the present discussion. For it is evident that even unbelievers cannot live without faith, since every human being living in [Col. 0334A] this life, just as he has certain things which he feels through experience, also has certain things which he believes by faith alone, neither having seen nor experienced them.

Yet no one is said to have the faith which is in God unless he believes those things by believing and loving which a human being merits God. Therefore those things are said to pertain to faith through believing which a person is called faithful. If we carefully inquire what those things are, we find that they consist principally in two. There are two things, and these two are in one; these two are one. Creator and Saviour are two names but one reality; nevertheless, “Creator” signifies one thing and “Saviour” another. He is Creator because he made us; Saviour because he redeemed us. At first we did not exist and were made; afterwards we had perished and were redeemed. [Col. 0334B] Both were done by one, so that all our good might be from one, wholly in one, and one.

We owe the Creator that we exist; we owe the Saviour that we have been restored. These, then, are the two things proposed to faith for belief: Creator and Saviour, together with those things which pertain to the Creator and those which likewise pertain to the Saviour. Creator and what pertains to the Creator: this is one part of faith. Saviour and what pertains to the Saviour: this is the other. In the first part faith distinguishes between the Creator and his works; in the second, between the Saviour and his sacraments. The works of creation made in six days pertain to the Creator. The works of restoration, completed in six ages, pertain to the Saviour.

In the first part, it pertains to faith to confess one Creator [Col. 0334C] and that all things which have being were made by him. In the second part, it pertains to faith to venerate one Saviour and to believe that the lost have been restored by him—those to whom blessedness has been given or will be given. In the first part, right faith ought to distinguish Creator and creature in such a way that it assigns to each what belongs to it and does not transfer the property of one to the other: that is, it neither attributes the majesty of the Creator to the creature nor ascribes the weakness of the creature to the Creator; it neither confines God within time nor extends the creature into eternity.

Thus, if faith assigns to each what is its own, it rightly renders what is due; if it distinguishes well between the two, it rightly divides and does not sin. But if it errs in either of these respects, faith must surely suffer loss. For those [Col. 0334D] who worshipped a creature as God, deceived by a double error, believed either that the creature was eternal or that God was temporal. What else can they be said to have done but assigned the excellence of the maker to the work, and the weakness of the made thing to the Creator?

Again, although the philosophers of the Gentiles rightly distinguished between the Creator and his work, they are by no means to be called faithful, because they did not have faith concerning the Saviour. What follows are the matters which we placed in the second part, where we first recognize redemption in the Saviour and preparation for that redemption in his sacraments. The first part of faith concerns the obligation of nature; the second part concerns the obligation of grace. We ought to believe the former because we were created by nature; we ought to believe the latter because we were restored by grace.

## Chapter VI. Whether Faith Has Changed According to Changes of Times

There [Col. 0335A] now follow for treatment the two matters which, in the first division of this discussion, we proposed in the fifth and sixth places after the four matters treated thus far. One is whether, according to changes of times, the faith of believers has changed from the beginning; or whether one and the same form of faith exists among the saints who were from the beginning and those who will be believers until the end. The other is what there is which right faith could never have had less of from the beginning: that is, what is that from which nothing could ever be taken away while right faith remained intact, even though something could be added so that it might grow. [Col. 0335B]

These two matters are connected in reasoning and therefore demand to be discussed together. Nor should we think slight consideration sufficient for such work, where there are so many human judgments and opinions and such diverse disputation concerning right faith; nor should this danger be thought small. For how can we think rightly concerning the things which ought to be believed through faith if we think wrongly concerning faith itself? Therefore every assertion must be carefully considered, so that in seeking to affirm right faith we may not be proved to oppose sound faith in the very things we say and think.

There are people who become impious toward God by a kind of apparent piety, and who, in thinking beyond what is true, stumble against truth itself. This [Col. 0335C] ignorance produces many errors concerning both goodness and truth. Some say that it is not fitting for divine goodness that God should be called cruel toward his works, or that he should permit anything he made to perish, when he made nothing for the purpose of perishing. Thus, while they think that they honour goodness, they offend truth. For he who was pious in creating things that did not exist is just in judging those who go astray and sin.

Others say that human righteousness requires a person to live in this life without struggle, though one cannot be righteous unless one struggles. For it does not belong to the righteousness of this life not to be tempted, but not to be overcome by temptation; nor does it consist in a good person’s never falling, but in rising again when he has fallen.

Likewise, there are those [Col. 0335D] who say that a person is not faithful if he believes some matters differently because, through weakness, he cannot comprehend them as they are in truth itself; or if he does not believe everything because, through ignorance, he cannot grasp all that there is. Such people think true faith should be made blessed by abundance of knowledge rather than greatness of devotion, although divine mercy does not attend to the extent of knowledge with which something is believed, but rather to the extent of devotion with which what is believed is loved.

We mention this because we have recognized that some people are insufficiently discerning and do not know the measure of human capacity. They do not consider their own capacity for suffering; or, if they do consider it, with still greater folly they suppose that all ought to be what they see themselves, above others, to have received in greater measure. They assert [Col. 0336A] that no one ought for any reason to be called faithful unless he has recognized many great and sublime mysteries of faith and has retained in memory some discussion of the Creator’s majesty and the Saviour’s humility, their profundity, and the sequence of events. They further maintain that the nature of divinity itself ought to be explained to untrained minds, scarcely adequate even for the things they see, and that by some subtle consideration it should be distinguished from bodily nature as incorporeal.

They also maintain that the things concerning the mystery of our redemption which have now been made manifest to the world in the birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension of our Saviour were, from the beginning of the world, known as future with the same knowledge by all righteous and faithful persons, both greater and lesser alike, as they are now known by us [Col. 0336B] as past. Otherwise, they say, those who did not recognize these things could not truly be said to have had faith.

They believe that they prove that all these things completed in the mystery of our redemption were both believed and known by those persons not only by this reasoning: just as we would not now belong to that redemption unless we recognized all these things as already done and believed them once recognized, so those persons would not have been saved through them unless they had known that all these things were to be done and had believed them once known. They also appeal to the fact that Scripture repeatedly testifies that no one has been saved from the beginning without faith in Christ; and blessed Augustine, speaking on this very subject, says:

> The same faith in the Mediator made the righteous of old, both small and great, saved: not the Old Testament which begets unto bondage; not the law, which was not given in such a way that it could give life; but the grace of God through Jesus Christ. For just as we believe that Christ came in the flesh, so they believed that he would come; just as we believe that he died, so they believed that he would die; just as we believe that he rose again, so they believed that he would rise again; and both we and they believe that he will come for the judgment of the living and the dead.

If these things are true (as they are thought to be by those persons, and as the authorities cited seem to affirm), then either salvation was exceedingly rare in ancient times, or perfection was excessively numerous—either of which views exceeds the bounds of sound judgment. But if it seems more tolerable, indeed more worthy of God, to judge that he filled and enriched those ages with a multitude of the perfect rather than that he was content with so great a scarcity of the saved, [Col. 0336D] so that not merely a few were then saved, but that all, filled with the prophetic Spirit, already penetrated mysteries not yet revealed—if, I say, this is accepted, we do indeed bless God in his gifts; but we do not see what has been reserved for the age of grace, unless rather that age should, according to this understanding, be called the age of knowledge: in which such and so great riches of the Spirit flowed to the people of God that what Moses desired when he said, “Would that all might prophesy!” (Num. II) would be seen to have been fulfilled in a wholly incredible felicity. What comparable thing, I ask, did the Gospel bring? Paul boasts in vain of the firstfruits of the Spirit, which he thinks he received with his fellow apostles, [Col. 0337A] when he could experience nothing of the kind in his own days. For he said: “Are all prophets?” (1 Cor. XII). In vain, I say, does he boast of his Gospel, because he received it neither from a human being nor through a human being, but, as though by some special prerogative, through the revelation of Jesus Christ, when it had been revealed even to peoples before him by the Spirit. Nor would the apostle Peter apply to his own times that prophetic saying: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon your sons and daughters, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy” (Joel II; Acts II), if a more abundant outpouring of the Spirit had already preceded it in ages past. Or certainly the prophet—or rather God speaking in the prophet—if he was truly contemplating those apostolic times when he said this, ought not plainly to have said, “I will pour out,” but rather, “I will withdraw from my Spirit.” [Col. 0337B]

For what follows? If we make all the righteous of old equal to the children of the Gospel in knowledge, must we not consequently admit that they were all superior in grace as well? For they were all taught about all things, not by reading, as we are, or by preaching, but by the anointing itself. Yet let us endure the wrong done to ourselves, and the apostles likewise the wrong done to them: let them also be reckoned inferior in knowledge to the least of the ancient righteous and found lesser in grace. But there is certainly something which we cannot endure on any terms: namely, that the Lord of glory should be thought either ever able to be deceived or willing to deceive—he who himself declared: “Among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. II). Consider whether we are not compelled truly to confess this testimony of Truth false if we ascribe so much [Col. 0337C] to the ancients as we cannot claim even for John. Certainly no injury is done to John if he is believed, or said, to have been ignorant—something which he himself does not deny. But if we give to another, contrary to the proclamation of truth, what we deny to the herald of truth, it is not merely an injury but blasphemy; and it is plainly to contradict, not John, but Truth.

What then? The Bridegroom’s friend doubts and asks, “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to await another?” (ibid.); while we, by our falsehood, assure thousands of people of certainty concerning everything. We may readily observe, from a few examples, that the ancients themselves did not think so highly of themselves. Moses writes that God, speaking to him, said: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; and I did not make known to them my name Adonai” [Lord] [Col. 0337D] (Exod. VI)—understand: “as I did to you.” He thus shows that he had received something additional concerning the knowledge of God beyond the preceding fathers. David too boldly claims for himself a gift of understanding above his teachers and elders, saying: “I have understood more than all who teach me, because your testimonies are my meditation” (Ps. CXVIII). And again: “I have understood beyond the aged” (ibid.). The prophet Daniel also says: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. XII), promising, that is, a more ample knowledge to those after him.
