But, as Saint Gregory also says, “According to the growth of the times, the knowledge of the spiritual Fathers also grew; and the nearer they were to the coming of the Savior, the more fully they perceived the mystery of salvation.” There is no doubt that the actual fulfillment of the things themselves, and the presence of the one fulfilling them, bestowed much more even upon those who were present. [Col. 0338A] Thus they hear: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke X). Likewise: “I have called you friends, because I have made known to you all that I have heard from my Father” (John XV). “Many kings and prophets,” he says, “desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke X). Why? So that they might perceive more clearly and abundantly what they had scarcely foreseen, faintly and obscurely.

Otherwise, what need was there to see outwardly the flesh and hear the words of the flesh, if they had already been perfectly instructed inwardly by the Spirit concerning all things—especially since the Lord says: “The flesh profits nothing; it is the Spirit who gives life” (John VI)? But if the prophets and those who seemed more illustrious among that people were not all equally able at any time to know all things, [Col. 0338B] but some more and others less, as the Spirit gave, distributing to each as he willed—and this without prejudice to their holiness and perfection—how much more could the simpler righteous, without loss of salvation, fail to know the time, manner, and order of salvation, while nevertheless holding most firmly, in sure hope and faith, that which had been promised. How many even today among the Christian people, concerning eternal life and the age to come, believe and hope without doubt and desire ardently, yet do not know even faintly how to conceive its form and condition. So likewise many before the Savior’s coming, holding and loving almighty God as the gratuitous promiser of their salvation, believing him faithful in his promise, hoping for him as the most certain fulfiller, [Col. 0338C] were saved in this faith and expectation, although they did not know when, how, and in what order the promised salvation would come about.

For even of the apostles themselves, whose righteousness no one doubts, it is recorded that, although the Savior was present and already preaching the kingdom of heaven in manifest light, the mystery of the Passion remained so unknown and hidden that, even when the Lord himself openly proclaimed and foretold it, they could not understand what was being said. Likewise, the two disciples to whom Jesus appeared as they were walking and doubting on the road, when questioned by him, are reported to have said among other things: “We had hoped that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel” (Luke XXIV). In this they plainly show that they had not believed that Israel’s redemption would come [Col. 0338D] through Christ’s Passion, since in the very Passion they despaired of redemption. Therefore they are told there: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe! Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer and rise from the dead, and thus enter into his glory?” (ibid.). Finally, it is “the mystery hidden from the ages”; and lest someone suppose that it had been hidden only from the wicked, it is added that it was revealed to the saints in the last times. If all the good knew this from the beginning, how could even the wicked have been ignorant of it—especially since the good themselves, who had perceived it, could not have discerned who were truly good or wicked, and to whom it should be revealed or concealed? Thus we plainly recognize the consequence: if we confess that these things were revealed to all the good, we cannot doubt that they were not unknown to the wicked as well. [Col. 0339A]

Moreover, if this must stand, who does not see how ineffably those former times are to be preferred to later ages? For faith, which here is received outwardly by the hearing of words alone, was there read inwardly by all in the full and manifest light of truth through contemplation inspired by prophecy. What is our faith in comparison with theirs but, so to speak, not faith but a kind of opinion? We know that they were so much more certain concerning the future than we are concerning the past: because they recognized by the Spirit what they did not see in actuality, whereas we receive by hearing alone, through the word, what we have not seen. If this is true, who does not see that Christ’s advent not only brought no illumination to believers, but took away a more certain and better knowledge? Therefore, consulting sound faith, let us confess what is more advantageous to salvation and nearer to truth: and let us not doubt that knowledge of those things which pertain to faith, just as we recognize it as differing at one and the same time according to the differing capacity of individuals, was likewise increased among believers from the beginning through the succession of times by certain stages of growth. [Col. 0339B]

Nevertheless, we confess without doubt that the faith of those who went before and those who came after was one and the same, though their knowledge was not the same; just as among those whom we see as believers in our own time we find the same faith, yet not the same knowledge of faith. Faith therefore grew through the ages in all, so that it might be greater; but it was not changed, so that it might become another faith. Before the Law, God the Creator was believed in, and salvation and redemption were expected [Col. 0339C] from him; but through whom and how that salvation was to be accomplished and perfected was not known even to the rest of the faithful, except for the few to whom knowledge of this had been singularly granted. Under the Law, however, the person of the Redeemer who was to be sent was foretold and awaited. Yet whether this person was a human being, an angel, or God himself was not yet disclosed. Only those knew this who had been singularly enlightened for that purpose by the Spirit. Under grace, however, both the manner of redemption and the nature of the Redeemer’s person are now openly preached and believed by all. Yet we believe that faith and knowledge of Christ’s incarnation and Passion have always existed in God’s Church from the beginning, because from the beginning there were never lacking [Col. 0339D] persons who knew these things. Others were saved because they joined themselves by simple faith to the perfection of these persons and followed them by doing good works.

## Chapter VII. What true faith could never have possessed less than this

These are the things of which sound faith could never from the beginning possess less: namely, to believe that there is one God, creator of all things, Lord and ruler of the universe; that he is not the author of evil, but is to be the future redeemer of those who, in their evils, sought or awaited his mercy. We believe these things sufficed at the beginning for the faith of the simple; and although nothing further was added to their knowledge, much was nevertheless bestowed upon their devotion. They did not openly know that the Redeemer would come in the flesh, [Col. 0340A] die in that same flesh, rise again, and ascend—or other things which were hidden in those times. Yet we most truly say that they possessed faith in his birth and Passion, and in his resurrection and ascension, because, under the hope and expectation of that same redemption, they adhered in faith and devotion to those who believed and knew these things, although they likewise did not know the manner of their redemption.

Thus, we think, Saint Augustine’s statement is to be understood: “The same faith in the Mediator made the righteous of old, small together with great, saved,” because the small righteous of old possessed the same faith in the Mediator together with the great. Some believed and knew the things to come precisely as things to come; others, however, [Col. 0340B] did not know them, but by believing and desiring adhered to those who knew and believed. As for what he adds—“as we believe that Christ came in the flesh, so they believed that he would come; as we believe him dead, so they believed that he would die,” and so on—this must either be referred not to all, but only to those to whom it was singularly granted to foreknow these future things, so that all are said to have had the same faith but not the same knowledge of faith; or, if this saying is understood of all, it may fittingly be affirmed that all who believed in the future redemption also believed the things of which redemption consisted. For insofar as they believed that redemption, which contained all these things, would come, they believed these things, although not all had the same knowledge of them in believing. [Col. 0340C]

Thus in a sound sense it may be said that all the righteous from the beginning possessed faith in the Savior, and that all were justified in faith in the redemption to come: because they either believed that redemption would come, or believed along with those who believed and knew; because they received in faith the sacraments of that redemption, instituted from the beginning, for sanctification; and because in them they bore that same redemption as it were in shadow and figure. This was aptly signified by the two men who carried, suspended on a pole, a cluster of grapes from the land of promise to the children of Israel in the wilderness. The cluster on the pole is Christ on the cross, whose mystery two peoples bear in sacrament. Those who went before did indeed bear it, but did not see it, because [Col. 0340D] before his coming all bore the sacraments of his Passion through faith, but not all merited through knowledge to understand what they bore. Those who follow both bear and see, because the faithful who follow after his coming in the flesh receive the sacrament of his Passion through faith and recognize it through knowledge now revealed. Hence Bede, on the same question, says: “The prophets and Moses knew and preached the one and same trophy of the Lord’s cross before the apostles did; but the prophets did so at times in figurative and veiled speech, whereas the apostles and the successors of the apostles always preached it openly in the unveiled light of the Gospel; so that now the whole Christian people [Col. 0341A] ought to know and confess the faith which at that time only very few, and the more perfect among them, knew—although even then all God’s people bore typologically the mysteries of the same faith in the legal ceremonies.”

## Chapter VIII. Recapitulation of the foregoing

There are, therefore, two things in which true faith consists: Creator and Redeemer. One does not suffice without the other. Know both; confess both. If you believe and acknowledge the Creator, you acknowledge that you were made; if you confess the Redeemer, you acknowledge that you were restored. The Creator and Redeemer are one. He made you in what is his; he remade you in what is yours; and one and the same person did both. If one had made you and another remade you, you would owe the first your existence and the other your restoration. Thus your intention, love, and obedience would be divided, [Col. 0341B] and you would not belong wholly to one. And of the two you would love more the one from whom you had more. He who created you gave you being; he who redeemed you gave you blessed being. Therefore, lest you should love some other redeemer more than the Creator himself, the Creator himself willed to be Redeemer, and endured your suffering in order to purchase your love. The natural Son was sent for the adoption of others, because without him strangers could not be admitted to the inheritance. Wisdom came, so that the enemy might be conquered not by power but by reason. In all these things your faith rests in one, is directed toward one, and is one; for when two are named, one is signified, because Creator and Redeemer are one. Creator pertains to nature; Savior, to grace. [Col. 0341C]

In these two the whole is one: this is that in which the faith of believers has been one from the beginning, although within that same faith knowledge of these matters was greater in some and less in others according to the diversity of times, just as at one and the same time knowledge of these same things is found greater in some and less in others according to individual capacity. Therefore, although faith grew, so that at times and in certain persons it was greater, it was not changed so as to become another faith. All believed one in one faith, and all who merited to be justified were justified by one faith. For, as the Apostle says, “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. II). And, as Saint Augustine says: “Where faith was not, there was no good work.”

## Chapter IX. On the sacrament and power of faith

[Col. 0341D]

“The sacrament of faith” may be understood in two ways. For either faith itself, which is a sacrament, is meant by “sacrament of faith”; or the sacraments of faith are meant, which are to be received with faith and have been prepared for the sanctification of the faithful. Certain military oaths are also called *sacramenta*, by which soldiers in their station bind themselves to their commander in order to keep faith; and unbelievers likewise possess certain *sacramenta*, which are called sacraments although they are neither sacred nor signs of a sacred thing. Rather, they are curses and abominations, by which persons are not consecrated but defiled. Yet, in distinction from these, the sacraments of faith may be understood as those handled by the faithful and received with faith for sanctification.

Let us first consider why faith itself is called a sacrament, or of what thing it is understood to be the sacrament. [Col. 0342A] The Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. XIII). That is, now, when we see through faith, we see through a mirror in an enigma; then, when we see through contemplation, we shall see face to face. What is it to see through a mirror? To see an image. What is it to see face to face? To see the thing itself. Suppose that someone is behind you or above you. You are turned away from him and do not see him face to face—your face directed toward his face. For your face is turned away from him; and perhaps he looks at you, but you do not likewise look toward him. So long as you remain thus, you cannot see him face to face. Bring forward a mirror and place it before you; [Col. 0342B] at once you will see in it the image of the one who is behind you or above your head, and you will say, “I see you.” What do you see? You now see something, but only an image. You see him, but in his image, not yet in his own face. You do not yet know as you are known; you do not yet see as you are seen. You are seen in yourself; you see in an image. The one who sees you looks upon you; but you are turned away from him. Turn yourself toward him and place face before face, and you will now see not an image but the thing itself. Earlier you saw him, but in his image; now you see him in his own face. Yet when you begin to see the thing itself, you recognize that what was seen in the image possessed some likeness to what is seen in the thing itself. What is seen in the image is the sacrament; what is seen in the thing itself is the reality of the sacrament. [Col. 0342C]

Therefore, what we now see through a mirror in an enigma is a sacrament of that which we shall see face to face in manifest contemplation. But what is the enigma, and what is the mirror in which the image is seen until the thing itself can be seen? Sacred Scripture is the enigma. Why? Because it has an obscure signification. Your heart is the mirror, provided that it is clean, polished, and made bright. The image in the mirror is faith in your heart. For faith itself is an image and a sacrament. Future contemplation, however, is the reality and power of the sacrament. Those who do not have faith see nothing; those who have faith have already begun to see something, but only the image. For if the faithful saw nothing, faith would not be illumination, nor would believers be called enlightened. But if they already saw the thing itself [Col. 0342D] and awaited nothing further to be seen, they would see not through a mirror in an enigma but face to face. Therefore those who see through faith see the image; those who see through contemplation see the reality. Those who have faith have the sacrament; those who have contemplation have the reality. Faith, therefore, is the sacrament of future contemplation; contemplation itself is the reality and power of the sacrament. For now, meanwhile, we receive the sacrament in order to be sanctified, so that, perfectly sanctified, we may be able to receive the thing itself. If, then, contemplation of one’s Creator is rightly believed to be the highest good of the human being, faith—through which one somehow begins to see him who is absent—is fittingly called the beginning of good and the principle of restoration. [Col. 0343A] This restoration grows in accordance with the increase of faith, as a person is more fully illumined through knowledge so as to know more completely, and is inflamed through love so as to love more ardently.

Thus the righteous person, so long as he dwells in this body, is away from the Lord and must live by faith; just as, when he has been led out of this prison and brought into the joy of his Lord, he will live by contemplation. Yet by God’s wondrous ordering the malice of the ancient enemy is meanwhile permitted to persecute and attack the faithful, so that [Col. 0344A] it may be counted to a person as merit if, now walking by faith, he does not abandon the way of truth even when attacked—he who previously, strengthened by the vision of God present, had been overthrown by persuasion alone. In order that he may stand unconquered in this battle and preserve his good unharmed, he is given, as has been said, weapons in the sacraments with which to fortify himself, and missiles in good works with which to strike down the enemy, so that faith, joined with love and hope, may at once be strengthened inwardly and live.

# Part Eleven: On the Natural Law

[Col. 0343]

## Chapter I. On the sacraments of the natural law

[Col. 0343B]

After faith we must treat of the sacraments of faith. Sacraments were instituted from the beginning for humanity’s restoration and healing: some under the natural law, some under the written Law, and some under grace. And among these, those which were later in time are always found more worthy in the effect of spiritual grace. For all the sacraments of the earlier period, whether under the natural law or under the written Law, were certain signs and figures of the sacraments now bestowed under grace. Therefore, the spiritual effect which they produced in their own time, standing in place of these sacraments, they produced by that power and sanctification which they received from these. If anyone denied that the earlier sacraments possessed an effect of sanctification, he would not, it seems to me, be thinking rightly. [Col. 0343C]

## Chapter II. On the first difference between the preceding and subsequent sacraments

Yet in this respect we undoubtedly judge the dignity of the latter to be superior: the former were visible and signs of visible things, whereas the latter, although themselves visible, are only signs and sacraments of invisible grace. Therefore the sacraments of grace first receive within themselves, through blessing, the power of sanctification; and then they bestow the sanctification which they contain, so that, sanctifying by virtue of the sanctification they possess, they confer by the sanctification divinely implanted in them what the former sacraments were accustomed to confer through these, solely through the latter’s signification. For the Passion of the Savior, which in the first place sanctifies the sacraments of grace for the effect of salvation, also sanctified through these the sacraments of the earlier period, so that the same salvation might belong both to those who in right faith venerated in them signs of things to come and to those who receive in these the effect of salvation. [Col. 0343D]

## Chapter III. Another difference

We also perceive this difference between the sacraments of the first period under the natural law and those instituted either under the written Law or under grace: [Col. 0344B] the former seem to belong more to voluntary choice, the latter to necessity. The former were observed by vow; the latter by command. For one must not think that those first sacraments of the natural law—tithes, sacrifices, and offerings—were imposed upon a person as a necessity, so that one who had not performed them incurred the guilt of transgression, just as one who faithfully observed them found the merit of devotion. Nowhere do we read that, before the written Law, God said to a person, “Whoever does not give tithes, whoever does not offer sacrifices,” as later he said through the Law: “The soul of the male whose foreskin has not been circumcised shall perish from his people” (Gen. XVII). And as under grace he thundered terribly: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III). Therefore we infer that those first sacraments were proposed more for the exercise of devotion than imposed for the obtaining of salvation. For one who possessed nothing—how was he to offer tithes? One who had nothing—what sacrifices and offerings could he make? Jacob made a vow to God, saying: “If the Lord my God shall be with me” (Gen. XVIII), and so forth. Then he adds: “Of all that you give me, I shall offer you tithes and peace-offerings” (ibid.). Thus the fact that he promised by vow to do this plainly shows that he was not bound to do it by the necessity of a command. [Col. 0344C]

## Chapter IV. That man was instructed by God to offer tithes

[Col. 0344D]

Nevertheless, it is altogether probable that from the beginning a person was instructed and taught by God to perform these acts, so that by the zeal of subsequent devotion he might erase the guilt of the first act of contempt, and that one who had proved rebellious in himself might later become accustomed to obey in what was his. How could a person have known that he should offer the tenth rather than the ninth, eighth, or any other [Col. 0345A] portion of his possessions, unless he had been taught by God? From this we infer that God indeed instructed a person by counsel from the beginning to perform these acts, but did not bind him by command until later, when he found matters in which a person, capable of command, might render obedience and learn to avoid transgression. Therefore, before the Law, he first nourished children by counsel; afterward, under the Law, he tested those who had been trained by command; finally, under grace, he permits the perfect to walk in the liberty of the Spirit. To recall briefly, then, what has been said above, let us consider what difference must be observed between the sacraments of the New Testament and those that were sacraments under either the natural law or the written Law.

## Chapter V. First difference, second difference, third difference

[Col. 0345B]

The first difference, then, is that the sacraments of the New Testament are in the first place signs of spiritual grace, instituted principally, by blessing infused into them, to impart that grace itself for the sanctification of recipients. The earlier sacraments, however, were only signs of these; and, through the mediation of those of which they were signs, they conferred grace as sustenance upon those who preceded the time of redemption, lest they be without salvation. The second difference is that the righteous of old, who were initiated by those sacraments, were not yet able to enter the gate of the kingdom of heaven until the Savior, having assumed flesh, ascended into heaven and opened a way for all who believe in him and follow him. The third difference is that the sacraments of the natural law do not appear to have been imposed by command, but proposed by counsel for a vow; whereas the sacraments of the written Law and of grace entail a certain necessity of performance because they are known to have been instituted not merely by counsel but by command. [Col. 0345C]

## Chapter VI. Why the first were changed by the second

But a question of no small importance arises: why, if grace conferred the same effect of salvation through both the earlier and the later sacraments, did the divine command abolish the rite of the ancients by instituting those that followed? For if the same power existed in those sacraments, why was it necessary that they should cease and these succeed them? But it must be known that the order and rationale of divine dispensation required this: as from the beginning, with time proceeding, the Savior’s advent drew nearer and nearer, [Col. 0345D] so the effect of salvation and knowledge of truth should always grow more and more. For this reason the signs of salvation themselves had to change one after another through the succession of times, so that, as the effect of divine grace for salvation increased, sanctification itself might at the same time appear more clearly in those visible signs. The Savior was indeed the same, grace the same, faith the same: there, faith in the one to come; here, faith in the one presented. But because he through whom salvation was given was distant, the signs of that salvation had to be obscure. Later, as his advent gradually approached, it was fitting that in the same order faith should grow in knowledge and grace in salvation, and that the same grace should manifest itself more clearly outwardly in the sacraments and their signs. [Col. 0346A]

Therefore the sacrament of expiation and justification was instituted to take form first through offering, afterward through circumcision, and finally through baptism, because the form and likeness of the same cleansing is found secretly in offering, expressed more clearly in circumcision, and openly declared through baptism. For a person first received the institution that, as a remedy of salvation, he should offer to God a portion of his outward substance and keep a portion for his own use, so that by this action he might learn to attribute to God the things that were good within, and to impute to himself those that were evil. The number ten, since it is a perfect number, is a sign of goodness and virtue, attributed to God and acknowledged in a human being as from God. But the number nine, because it falls short [Col. 0346B] of the perfect number, signifies defect and corruption, which are rightly ascribed to a person. Therefore a person is instructed to give the tenth to God and retain the ninth for himself, so that he may confess that what is good in him is from God, while what is evil is from himself. But this sign, being as it were drawn from the Law, taught a person more what ought to be than what came to pass.

Accordingly, when the time came in which truth itself ought to be disclosed, a remedy was given through the sacrament of circumcision. There a part of a person’s outward substance—not naturally superfluous, but a figure of what is superfluous—was prescribed, and the circumcision of sin, which grace accomplishes in the inward person, was now shown more clearly. But because circumcision cuts away outward uncleannesses and deformities, whereas washing cleanses inward stains, circumcision fittingly ought to cease once truth had been manifested in Christ’s advent, so that the sacrament might succeed which could declare the perfect cleansing of the person and the inward brightness of the soul that he obtains in and through the sacrament itself. Moreover, because circumcision removes uncleanness but inflicts pain, while washing cleanses the defiled without pain, circumcision was given for cleansing to the former people, serving in fear and laboring under the Law; but washing was given to the new people, walking in grace through love. [Col. 0346C]

Thus those first sacraments which preceded under the natural law seem to have been a kind of shadow of truth; those which later followed under the written Law [Col. 0346D], a kind of image or figure of truth; while those which finally follow under grace are no longer a shadow or image, but the body of truth. In them the effect of salvation, because it is both perfectly effected and plainly shown, is brought forth—as the spirit in a living body is displayed by outward movement; so in them the life of invisible grace is most clearly manifested. Therefore the first sacraments were shadow; the second, image; the third, body; after which, in fourth place, follows the truth of the Spirit. Let what has been said here concerning the sacraments of the natural law suffice. We believe, as was already mentioned above, that they were joined at that time to justifying faith in such a way that in them there was an exercise of devotion, not a necessity for obtaining [Col. 0347A] salvation. For at that time they were justified by faith alone working through love, who were preserved through grace for participation in the future redemption. But because we have already said something appropriate to the subject concerning those first sacraments by which the devotion of the faithful was then exercised, we think that something must also be said about works.

## Chapter VII. On the three kinds of works
There are three kinds of acts. Some are so good that they can never lawfully be omitted; some are so evil that they can never lawfully be committed; and some are intermediate, which may be done or omitted according to time and place. Therefore the natural law prohibited only those things which are such that they can never lawfully be done; it commanded only those which can never lawfully be omitted, leaving all intermediate matters open to either course [Col. 0347B]. Concerning things to be prohibited, it wrote one commandment upon the human heart: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. IV). Likewise, concerning things to be commanded, one commandment: “Whatever you wish men to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. VII); so that a person might learn, by considering himself, how he ought to comport himself toward his neighbor.

But later, when the Law entered in and proposed a stricter discipline of life, it selected certain matters out of those that had been intermediate: some it directed toward one side by commandment, others by prohibition. Thus, just as God had, for the first man in Paradise, taken one prohibition from natural permission as a commandment of discipline, so now, for his children—who did not stand in the one truth but had been scattered through various errors—he established, not one commandment of discipline drawn from natural permission, as though for persons being tested, but many, as though for persons being corrected and restored [Col. 0347C]. The more they learned to restrain themselves in intermediate matters, the more easily they would be able to avoid what was not permitted. There many things were allowed and few prohibited; here many things were prohibited and few allowed.

There man was told not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil—not because the tree was evil, but because obedience was to be tested [Col. 0348A]. Here they were told not to eat flesh with blood, so that they might learn to abhor cruelty; not to eat pork, so that they might detest uncleanness; not to plough with an ox and an ass, so that they might recognize sloth and stupidity as harmful to preaching; and other such things, all of which were intermediate matters.

Those things, however, which under the natural law had been contained in two commandments were later unfolded and distinguished by the written Law into those seven commandments set forth on the second tablet. The first of these was: “Honor your father and your mother, that it may go well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth” (Exod. XX). The second: “You shall not kill”; the third: “You shall not commit adultery”; the fourth: “You shall not steal”; the fifth: “You shall not bear false testimony” [Col. 0348B]; the sixth: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife”; the seventh: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.”

In these it must not be carelessly passed over that, of the seven, only one was given in the form of a positive commandment; the other six were given as prohibitions. For the first sin of humankind was disobedience, and therefore this life, granted to humanity for repentance, is entirely reckoned as obedience. Since, then, in doing evil a person is drawn in different directions by his own desire, whereas in doing good he is governed by the rule of obedience alone, he had to be instructed individually concerning the evils he possesses from himself and can perform through himself; but for doing good he was simply to be recalled to obedience, so that through the judgment of another he might more beneficially learn what he ought to do in himself [Col. 0348C].

For when a person is commanded to render honor to father and mother, this must not be referred only to bodily parents. Rather, he is commanded that he who at one time despised God in his commandments should now, for God’s sake, not disdain to show obedience and honor to a human superior.

## PART TWELVE: ON THE WRITTEN LAW

[Col. 0347]

### CHAPTER I. On the union of the faithful people

[Col. 0347C]

The first state, from Adam to Abraham, is more properly delimited. For although the written Law was given through Moses, legal observance nevertheless took its beginning before Moses in circumcision. That first age under the natural law had passed, as it were, in a certain confusion; and those who had been faithful in it were like a few grains scattered and separated from one another among the human race, united inwardly by faith alone.

Therefore, so that an outward unity might be established to commend the inward unity, and so that there might openly be a form of faith to which those who were to be called from their dispersion might be invited, one man was set forth, to whom all those who were later to be received might be gathered in being made one [Col. 0348C]. Abraham, one out of many, was called: unity, the beginning of union, so that all who after him were joined to him in faith and devotion might be gathered to his bosom.

He was called, then, to go out from his land and depart from those to whom he had been joined, and not to join himself to those to whom he was going. And a form was given to him which he should transmit to all who would be born from him; and all would become one in that one form, so that, while the number of the faithful increased, the unity of faith might not be multiplied. Thus first those who were born from him might be one in his form [Col. 0349A], and afterward those also who joined themselves to them in the same faith might become one.

From that point the unity of God’s people began, and the unity of faithful conduct, first marked by the sacrament of circumcision and afterward to be marked by the sacrament of baptism. The first seal was in the flesh, under which those who were one in flesh were to be united. Therefore circumcision was given only to Abraham’s seed, so that those who would be united in flesh might be marked in flesh. But after those who were not from him by bodily generation entered into this unity, the seal of union was placed outside the substance of the flesh, because those who had not been one in flesh were made one in spirit and faith.

### CHAPTER II. On circumcision

God accordingly commanded Abraham to circumcise [Col. 0349B] the skin of his foreskin: for Abraham himself as a sign, and for his descendants as an example. This added only so much to the earlier state: that by this seal the people of God might be distinguished from unbelievers, until he should come who would gather faithful persons not only from Abraham’s children but from all nations; and through him, as has been said, they would be set apart in sanctification no longer by a seal of flesh within a lineage, but by the seal of baptism.

Certainly, any who in the meantime became believers but were not of Abraham’s seed were not subject to this command. Nor were they bound by an obligation to receive circumcision, which had been imposed upon Abraham’s seed alone. Rather, by faith working through love—as formerly, under the natural law before circumcision had been instituted—those who were righteous were saved without circumcision.

The manner of circumcision was as follows. It was commanded that a male child should be circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day after his birth (Gen. XVII) [Col. 0349C]. Some think that one should add that it was done with a knife made from stone; but they establish this on no other authority than that Zipporah, Moses’ wife, frightened by the angel, is read to have taken a sharp stone and circumcised the foreskin of her son with it (Exod. IV). Joshua also, when about to enter the promised land, is recalled to have renewed the sacrament of circumcision a second time among the people of Israel with stone knives (Josh. V).

But it is not unfittingly thought that the former case occurred because of haste and fear, and the latter because of the type and signification of the true Jesus, rather than through customary practice [Col. 0349D]. Thus, to show that the sacrament of circumcision was to be performed not, like the earlier sacraments, according to the intention of the will, but from necessity, the commandment is reinforced by a threat: “The male whose foreskin has not been circumcised—that soul shall perish from his people” (Gen. XVII). A reason is also added when it says: “Because he has made my covenant void” (ibid.).

If, therefore, by the making void of God’s covenant we understand the transgression of the first parents, then, when the uncircumcised person is said to perish because of transgression of the covenant, it is plainly made clear that the sacrament of circumcision was instituted in order that through it a person might be freed from the debt of the first transgression. For circumcision under the Law supplied the same assistance of saving healing [Col. 0350A] against original sin that baptism now supplies—except that the first fathers could not enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom, for which reason Christ’s death was necessary, in order to open the entrance to life.

There are, moreover, three circumcisions. One is outwardly in the flesh alone, and is the sacrament. The other two are the reality and power of the sacrament. One occurs in the present, when the soul is circumcised through the putting away of iniquity; the other will occur in the future, when the body is circumcised through the putting away of corruption. The first, therefore, is in the flesh; the second in the mind; the third in the body.

In sacred Scripture, the number eight sometimes signifies the time of resurrection, which follows the present life that runs through seven days; sometimes it signifies the time of grace, in which, as it were after the Sabbath of the Law, eternal goods are promised to those who serve God [Col. 0350B]. Rightly, then, that first circumcision, which was the sacrament of these two, was commanded to be performed on the eighth day, so that it might be shown that in the time of grace hearts were to be circumcised through cleansing from iniquity, and in the time of resurrection bodies through the putting away of corruption.

Circumcision of the flesh was given only to males because sacred Scripture customarily signifies the soul by the male sex and the flesh by the female, so that it might be shown that this outward circumcision conferred sanctification upon souls but did not take corruption away from the flesh. The knife made from stone signifies Christ. Of him the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. X); and of the one it is written [Col. 0350C]: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John I).

It was commanded to be performed in the flesh of the foreskin because it was given as a remedy against original sin, which we contracted from our parents, having been propagated through that member. Women among the people of circumcision, however, were saved by faith alone, being purified by sacrifices and offerings and the other ceremonies of the Law; they also received circumcision itself by faith, reverently participating in those who received that fleshly circumcision.

Males prevented by death from reaching the eighth day, and therefore departing this life without the sacrament of circumcision, are not implausibly thought to have been saved by the faith of their parents, with offerings and sacrifices intervening. For the commandment of circumcision seems to have been imposed only upon males who reached the eighth day; and thus they were not guilty of transgression, because they had not been despisers of a commandment which was given only to those reaching the eighth day [Col. 0350D]. This is especially so lest this sex appear more wretched and be prejudged even in that matter from which the other sex is proved to have been wholly absolved.

Yet it is rightly asked whether those who, through their parents’ negligence or contempt, passed the eighth day without the sacrament of circumcision afterward obtained the effect of salvation by receiving the same sacrament, although the divine command had ordained that this sacrament be celebrated only on the eighth day. Perhaps it may not unreasonably be believed that, just as those coming from the Gentiles to the rite of the Law received this sacrament unto salvation at any age, so also those who under the Law had not received it at its proper time nevertheless received salvation and remedy through it if, by receiving it later, they corrected their earlier negligence [Col. 0351A].

Thus the sacrament of circumcision was given to Abraham’s seed both to sanctify and to mark it: to sanctify, that it might be justified; to mark it, that it might be distinguished from the other nations, so that there might remain a distinct and singular lineage from which Christ would be born. Hence it follows that it is probable that circumcision was enjoined by command upon that seed of Abraham from which Christ was to be born: namely, after Abraham, Isaac; after Isaac, Jacob; and then the twelve tribes that arose from Jacob himself [Col. 0351B]. For Job too is believed by some to have been of Esau’s line, yet he is not read to have been circumcised.

### CHAPTER III. On preparation for the Law

The sacrament of circumcision was given before the giving of the Law, and through it a certain preparation was made for receiving the Law. For just as now in the New Testament, a person is first washed in the water of baptism, receives the sign and name of his profession, and then, joined to the number of the faithful and instructed in the divine commandments, proceeds to fulfill his profession, so that ancient people were first marked by circumcision and afterward formed by the Law.

### CHAPTER IV. On the sacraments of the written Law

[Col. 0351C]

The written Law contains three things: commandments, sacraments, and promises. In the commandments is merit; in the promises, reward; in the sacraments, assistance. One had to proceed through the commandments to the promises. But because humanity was weak in itself, sacraments came between the commandments and the promises, to help it both fulfill the commandments and obtain the promises.

Under the natural law the sacraments were few; under the written Law both were multiplied—both commandments and sacraments. For when God the physician first came to cure sick humanity, disease had occupied all that health had abandoned. At first he applied a few antidotes to the body of the human race, and to a few members [Col. 0351D], that is, a few persons, so that disease might gradually decline and health increase. Later, under the written Law, he supplied more remedies and restored more persons.

Under the natural law there were two commandments and three sacraments. The two commandments: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. IV); and “Whatever you wish men to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. VII). The three sacraments: tithes, offerings, and sacrifices. Tithes concerned portions; offerings, things; sacrifices, animals. Under the written Law there were many commandments and many sacraments. The commandments of the written Law were of two kinds: movable and immovable. Movable commandments are those established temporarily by dispensation. Immovable commandments are those which come from nature and are either so evil that they cannot at any time be done without sin [Col. 0352A], or so good that they cannot at any time be omitted without sin.

### CHAPTER V. On immutable commandments

The natural law, therefore, had only the immutable commandments, contained in two precepts: in one commanding good, in the other prohibiting evil. These two commandments of the natural law were more fully unfolded and distinguished by the written Law through the seven commandments contained on the second tablet. They show how a person ought to comport himself toward his neighbor, just as the preceding three show how a person ought to comport himself toward God.

Hence it is called the first tablet because it contains the more excellent commandments, which concern the love of God; the second, because it contains the lower commandments following these [Col. 0352B], which concern love of neighbor. Or the first tablet is so called because it contains commandments that set forth faith; the second, because it contains commandments that instruct toward good action.

There are three commandments on the first tablet because the Trinity believed by faith is God. There are seven commandments on the second tablet because in the present life, which revolves only through the circuit of seven days, duties of humanity are performed toward one’s neighbor. But three and seven complete the number ten, because right faith and good action make a person perfect.

The first commandment of the first tablet pertains to God the Father, just as the first commandment of the second tablet pertains to one’s human father, so that fatherhood may be honored on both sides by the authority proper to a principle [Col. 0352C]. On the first tablet there is both commandment and prohibition, and likewise on the second, so that you may strive both to do what you ought and to avoid what you ought not. For if you offend in the latter, there is sin; but if you offend in the former, there is a fault. For to do what ought not to be done is sin; but not to do what ought to be done is a fault.

### CHAPTER VI. On the three commandments of the first tablet

“Hear, Israel: your God is one God; you shall worship him and serve him alone” (Deut. VI). Not all of this statement is commandment, because before the command the hearer’s mind is prepared for obedience by an admonition. “Hear, Israel”: here observe obedience. “Your God”: here observe grace. “God is one”: here observe doctrine; as if it said: render obedience, understand grace, acknowledge truth.

What you hear is the obedience required of you; “your God” is the grace through which you arrive; “God is one” is the truth by which you are enlightened and perfected [Col. 0352D]. Hear your God, who has already shown you mercy and has not yet received service from you, so that you may know that both things are from him: both the work of virtue which he requires from you and the reward of recompense which he promises you.

“Hear, Israel,” that is, listen and assent. For every virtue begins from obedience, just as every vice proceeds from disobedience. Grace would be given in vain to the disobedient, doctrine to the obstinate, and commandment to one who does not understand. Therefore he first says, “Hear, Israel,” that you may be obedient; “your God,” that you may be devout; “God is one,” that you may acknowledge truth. Then follows the commandment: “You shall worship him”: this pertains to faith; “and serve him alone”: this pertains to action [Col. 0353A]. For faith working through love makes one perfect, since neither a work without faith nor faith, when opportunity is available, without work is accepted. Therefore worship by believing rightly; serve by acting well.

It may be asked whether the phrase “him alone” applies to both clauses, so that the statement is: “You shall worship him alone and serve him alone.” But how can this stand, since in the Old Testament we often read that holy men worshiped not only angels but human beings also, and yet nowhere find them reproved for this? And in the New Testament the Apostle strongly exhorts the faithful to serve their superiors and prelates.

It must therefore be understood that human beings are commanded to be worshiped in one way, God in another [Col. 0353B]. For according to ancient usage, persons of higher rank were said to be worshiped by inferiors when reverence was rendered to them through bending the knees or bowing the head. But to worship God is to subject one’s whole mind to him in humility and devotion, and to believe that he is the beginning and end of every good. No one of sound mind doubts that we owe this to him alone. Hence he himself bears witness of himself through the prophet, saying: “My honor [my glory] I will not give to another, nor my glory [my praise] to graven images” (Isa. XLII).

With respect to service, however, the expression may appropriately be understood of God himself. For certainly everyone is most rightly said to serve God alone who both humbly submits himself to a human superior according to God [Col. 0353C], and faithfully resists where the cause of God is attacked; who carefully guards against doing anything against God in his service through fear of man, or preferring in his intention the gain of earthly reward to the heavenly reward.

But the meaning is expressed more plainly in Greek. For Greek usage distinguishes divine service from human service by a special term which Latin does not possess. There divine service is called *latria*, and human service *dulia*. For this reason idolaters were called those who rendered to idols the service they owed to God. But the Latin language includes both kinds of service under the same name, and thus the meaning becomes more obscure when it says, “You shall serve him alone,” whereas in Greek it is unambiguous [Col. 0353D].

But since the commandment pertains to the Father, why is it said, “You shall serve him alone,” as though the Son and the Holy Spirit were not also to be served? Yet the word “alone” does not exclude the communion of the Son and Holy Spirit, but excludes whatever is not God. For Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God: he alone is to be worshiped, and he—and no other—is to be served with that service owed to him alone.

Likewise, in the Gospel, when it is said, “No one knows the Father except the Son” (Matt. XI), the Holy Spirit is certainly not excluded from knowledge of the Father, since he searches even the depths of God, as the Apostle testifies (I Cor. II). But this is a manner of speaking in which “no one” is said, except one who is not what that one is. Having passed briefly over these things, let us proceed to examine the following commandment, which is this: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Exod. XX; Deut. V) [Col. 0354A].

According to the simple literal sense, this must be understood to mean that a person should not take God’s name in vain, either to affirm a falsehood or to venerate an idol: that is, he should neither honor idols with the divine name nor associate the divine name with falsehood. Mystically, however, to take God’s name in vain is to judge the Son of God, made visible through humanity, to be a creature. He takes God’s name in vain who believes that the eternal Son of God began in time. For the Son is called the name of the Father, because in the Son and through the Son the invisible Father is made manifest—not only when the world was made through him, but also when humanity was redeemed through him.

Certainly [Col. 0354B], those who confess that the Son of God became human do not take God’s name in vain, because they acknowledge as true God the one whom they believe to be human with respect to that which he assumed in time, by virtue of that which he was from eternity. It may also be understood otherwise that it was said: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain.” For those take God’s name in vain who despise the Son of God sent to them and incarnate for their salvation.

What, then, does it mean to say, “Do not take the name of your God in vain,” unless this: just as you venerate and worship him because you were made by him, so worship and venerate him because you were redeemed by him; for he conferred no less upon you when he redeemed you than when he created you. The same sense is intended by what the Son himself says in the Gospel to his disciples, and through his disciples to all who believe in him: “You believe in God; believe also in me” (John XIV) [Col. 0354C]. With the gentle exhortation fitting for the merciful one, he indicates that we should understand him to be worshiped by us not only in his divinity, by which he created, but also in his humanity, by which he redeemed.

The third commandment is: “Keep the Sabbath” (Exod. XX). Scripture seems to mention four Sabbaths. The first is that in which God is said to have rested after completing his works. The second is that which the children of Israel are commanded to observe carnally. The third is that which God’s people are commanded to observe. The fourth is that which God promises in the promise as Sabbath for Sabbath to those who love him.

Thus there are two outward Sabbaths: one of God and one of humanity; and two inward Sabbaths [Col. 0354D]: one of God and one of humanity. God’s Sabbath, in which he is said outwardly to cease from work, is the sacrament of that inward Sabbath of his in which his eternal and immortal eternity, enjoying unshaken blessedness, is never wearied by any labor. Humanity’s Sabbath, commanded to be observed outwardly and visibly, is the sacrament of the inward Sabbath in which the holy mind, resting from slavery to sin through a good conscience, rejoices in the joy of the Holy Spirit.

Whoever keeps this Sabbath in the present life, so as to consent to no evils, will attain in the future life to that eternal Sabbath of God, where he will experience no evils. As it is said: “There shall be Sabbath for Sabbath, month for month” (Isa. LXVI). Therefore that commandment seems especially to be referred to the person of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0355A], when it says, “Keep the Sabbath,” so that we may receive him in the present and keep him within ourselves for the joy of a good conscience, in order that we may deserve to receive and possess him in the future for the joy of life.

These, then, are the three commandments of the first tablet, in which love of God is especially commended, and the whole Trinity—one God—is commanded to be worshiped and honored equally.

### CHAPTER VII. On the other seven commandments of the second tablet

The second tablet contained seven other commandments, which instruct a person in love of neighbor. They are distinguished by the number seven because only in the present life, which revolves through seven days, is our charity exercised toward our neighbor in works of mercy [Col. 0355B]; afterward, when works are completed and labors ended, it is to be made blessed in God through contemplation together with the neighbor.

Love of neighbor, therefore, is temporal insofar as it concerns the rendering of service, and eternal insofar as it concerns the effect of love. The first commandment of the second tablet pertains to a human father, just as the first of the first tablet pertains to God the Father. In both places fatherhood comes first; in both it is honored by the dignity of a principle. For in one manner we have from a human father the principle of being born through generation, just as we have received from God the Father the principle of existing through creation. And human fatherhood is a sacrament and image of divine fatherhood, so that the human heart may learn from the principle it sees what it owes to that principle from which it exists [Col. 0355C] and which it does not see.

Thus it is said: “Honor your father and your mother, that it may go well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth” (Exod. XX). As was said above concerning the first commandment of the first tablet, not all that is set forth here pertains to the commandment. There, what was additional to the commandment was prefixed; here it is appended. “Hear, Israel: your God is one” (Deut. VI): all this is placed before the commandment; the commandment itself follows afterward when it says, “You shall worship him and serve him alone” (ibid.). Here the commandment comes first: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. XX); then is appended: “that it may go well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth.”

Why, then, is the reason for the commandment placed before the commandment there but added after it here [Col. 0355D], unless because God is to be loved for his own sake, and a human being for God’s sake? For parental love, if it regards flesh alone, does not obtain a spiritual reward. Therefore, in God there is first in us that for which he is afterward to be loved by us: for our love is anticipated by his grace, and our love, awakened by his grace, follows afterward.

But if in the fathers of our flesh our love tends only toward that benefit by which, in the flesh, they have anticipated any merit of ours, it makes no progress beyond affection for flesh and consideration of flesh, and does not attain the perfection of spiritual reward. Therefore, for the sake of eternal life, the author of temporal life must be loved: that is, he must not be loved because we receive this life from him—indeed, through him [Col. 0356A]—but because through this life we shall enter into that life.

Rightly, then, when it had been said, “Honor father and mother,” the reason was added: “that it may go well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth,” namely, the land of the living. For in the author of this life we ought to love this: that through him, by means of this life, we have been initiated into the life to come. And long life is beautifully promised to one who honors his source, because those who cleave to God through love obtain eternity.

Certainly, as regards the literal sense, we ought to honor our parents in two ways: by obeying them in all things, except those in which love for God the Father is offended; and by helping them insofar as our means permit. Nothing prevents the same understanding concerning spiritual fathers, that is, our prelates: we owe them obedience insofar as we are able, and help—indeed, service—insofar as our resources allow [Col. 0356B].

The second commandment of the second tablet: “You shall not kill” (ibid.). Homicide occurs in many ways: by hand, by tongue, and by consent. It is committed by hand when someone actually deprives another of life, or throws him into a place where life may be lost, such as a prison or any other such place. It is committed by tongue in two ways: by commanding or by urging. For the Jews killed Christ when they urged the judge that he be killed. Homicide is likewise committed by consent in two ways: when we desire and wish another’s death, or when, though we can free him from death, we neglect his life—that is, do not provide assistance.

[Col. 0356C]

The third commandment of the second tablet is: “You shall not commit adultery” (ibid.), that is, you shall not commit fornication. Fornication is every unlawful sexual union, and there are two kinds of fornication: that of the soul, of which the Prophet says, “You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you” (Ps. LXXII); and that of the body, which is under discussion here.

This commandment and certain others under the old Law were only begun—that is, given not fully but in part—because of the weakness of the hearers; afterward, with the coming of grace, they were brought to completion. For the Law says, “You shall not commit adultery,” prohibiting only bodily adultery. Christ says, “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V), opposing every unlawful desire of both soul and body.

[Col. 0356D]

The fourth commandment is: “You shall not steal” (Exod. XX). In this place theft is understood as any unlawful appropriation of another’s property, whether secret or open. For he who prohibited theft did not permit robbery, since it is a greater sin—as the saints testify—to seize openly and violently than to take away secretly, because it provokes greater hatred and anger. Usury too is included under theft.

The fifth commandment of the second table: “You shall not bear false witness” (ibid.). In order, therefore, that what false witness is may become clearer, we must begin further back—that is, with lying. For one kind of lie occurs in false testimony, another in perjury, another in a vow, when someone vows what he does not fulfil. Of all these matters [Col. 0357A] we must speak. First, however, concerning the simple lie. For this reason a definition of lying must be set down. Some think that a lie should be defined thus: a lie is a false signification accompanied by the will to deceive, whether that will is present at the time or comes afterward. For if someone, promising another that he will give him something, has the intention of giving it when he promises, but afterward, having changed his intention, refuses to give it, this would be a lie—not because his heart was double in making the promise, but because he who promised afterward made his heart double. Thus, then, the statement may be understood: a lie is false signification, that is, a speech or utterance through which the speaker intends and believes that he is signifying what is false to the hearer. For even if matters are as he says, the person who speaks with the opinion and intention of deceiving nevertheless lies.

[Col. 0357B] Jesting lies, irony, and parables are not lies; otherwise the saints would be found blameworthy, because they spoke many things in parables and ironies. But Christ himself spoke in parables to the crowds; and certainly he would not have employed them in his discourse if any falsehood were contained in them. The sole difference is that jesting lies, although they do not incur the guilt of falsehood, nevertheless do not escape the fault of frivolity. There is yet another kind of lie, when someone seems to lie, as though for the sake of humility—for example, when he calls himself a sinner, yet does not think as he says. Of this it has been most truly said that, when someone lies under the pretext of humility, if he was not a sinner before he lied, by lying he becomes what he was not; because in one who calls himself a sinner and does not believe it to be so, truth is not [Col. 0357C].

There is another kind of lie when someone lies in order to preserve another’s health or life; and this too is in no way to be approved. For he preserves life badly in another’s body by lying, who through a lie extinguishes truth in his own heart. Yet in such a case truth may sometimes be concealed without guilt, when reason requires it for the sake either of our own safety or of another’s benefit. For it is very different to keep silent about what is true and to assert what is false. Truth itself says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16); and certainly it would not have said this if it were always blameworthy to withhold the truth.

False witness occurs when someone, by another’s lie, gives testimony concerning truth [Col. 0357D]. Such a person becomes guilty not only by lying, but also because he attempts to support the lie itself against truth. If he does this knowingly, it is altogether condemnable malice; if ignorantly, blameworthy negligence. Not every oath is evil, and yet every oath, according to Truth’s witness, is “from evil.” For one who swears truthfully because of a neighbour’s necessity or benefit—namely, when the one to whom the oath is sworn either cannot believe because of ignorance or refuses to believe because of malice—such an oath is indeed not evil for the swearer, because out of necessity he calls truth to witness; yet it is from the evil of the person to whom he swears: either from weakness, if he cannot otherwise believe, or from perversity, if he scorns to believe. But one who swears without cause, even if he swears what is true, is not without fault: either he is reproved for frivolity or condemned for obstinacy.

Whoever swears that he will do evil sins. In this case it would nevertheless be better to break the oath than to fulfil it: so that he both avoids the evil which he swore and nonetheless acknowledges his fault in having sworn wrongly. Perjury is a lie confirmed by the introduction of a most sacred attestation. For whoever swears falsely commits perjury; in this the first evil is the guilt of lying, when what is false is said. The second is that, in order to defend falsehood, the testimony of truth is irreverently appropriated. Whoever sees another intending to swear falsely becomes a participant in the sin if he consents, and if, so far as he can without compromising truth, he does not prevent the evil from being accomplished by opposing and warning him [Col. 0358B].

Here it must be considered that, when we cannot prove a brother’s sin, we ought not to publicize it, lest we appear not to wish to correct our neighbour but rather to defame him. Therefore admonition must be applied to sinners where no convincing testimony can be produced against those who deny the charge.

A vow is a voluntary promise of the mind. Whoever vows a vow to God must render what he vows, according to the saying of the Prophet: “Vow and render to the Lord” (Ps. 75). Scripture, however, says: “The vows of fools must be broken” (Eccl. 5). Hence we understand foolish vows to include all that are either evil or, if good, nevertheless disordered, and in which the evil arising from them is greater than the good contained in them. For example, if a woman, against her husband’s will, or a man, against his wife’s will, vowed continence; or if a subject, without the counsel and permission of his superior, proposed an inordinate abstinence—such vows, because they would manifestly be foolish, ought not at all to be kept [Col. 0358C]. Whoever vows any good thing, if afterward he either cannot fulfil it or does not wish to fulfil it in order to accomplish a greater good, may, by permission of those to whom authority to dispense for him has been entrusted, have his vow relaxed or changed. Yet it must not remain at his own discretion either to abandon what he vowed to do or to do something else in its place, even if what he did not vow is greater.

The sixth commandment, which is also the ninth: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife” (Exod. 20). The seventh commandment, which is also the tenth: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s property” (ibid.).

Here an objection seems to arise against what was said above concerning the commandment previously given about avoiding fornication: “You shall not commit adultery,” where it was said that only bodily adultery was forbidden; whereas afterward, through what Christ says in the Gospel, “Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery in his heart,” every adultery, both bodily and spiritual, is forbidden. For how did the Gospel complete what the written law had possessed less fully, if the very thing believed to have been added by the Gospel is found previously written in the Law? He who said, “You shall not commit adultery,” thereby forbidding bodily adultery, afterward said, “You shall not covet,” thereby showing that spiritual adultery [Col. 0359A] must altogether be avoided. What, then, did the new law complete which the old had possessed less fully? The Law forbade bodily adultery; it forbade coveting. What more remained for the Gospel to do?

But it must be understood that the old law, although it restrained a person’s desire for another’s possession, by no means moderated it in regard to his own. For he who said, “You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife or property,” did not forbid one to desire a woman or property altogether; rather, he showed that desire must be restrained only from what belonged to another. The new law, however, taught that one ought to be moderate even with regard to one’s own possessions, so as to exclude every unlawful desire.

It may also suitably be said in another sense that the old law, when it spoke of coveting another’s wife or property, did not mean that desire which exists in the will alone, but ambition and scheming which, by a certain effort and striving to fulfil desire and obtain the object of desire, is exercised outwardly in action. The new law, however, not only condemned unlawful desire outwardly in the endeavour of action, but also showed it to be condemnable inwardly in the desire of the will [Col. 0359B].

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Order of God’s Commandments

The order of God’s commandments ought not to be passed over without consideration. For if there is an order of living, there is surely also an order of commanding. First, therefore, attend to what is said to you: that you are to worship your God and serve him (Deut. 6). This is the first commandment. In worship recognize faith; in service understand good action. After this follows the second commandment [Col. 0359C], that you are not to take the name of your God in vain (Exod. 20), so that the word of truth may be in your mouth for truth’s sake, and after faith in the heart there may follow confession by the mouth. First comes devotion toward a good conscience; afterward the example of action toward a good reputation; finally, the word of preaching for instruction.

Then follows the third commandment, and you are told to observe the Sabbath; that is, preserve the tranquillity of your mind, so that you are not disturbed by adversities encountered outwardly on account of truth, but learn to be peaceable even among those who hate peace. Preach truth, and do not omit charity. These are the three commandments of the first table, concerning matters that pertain to God.

Afterward follows the second table, concerning matters that concern one’s neighbour [Col. 0359D]. The first commandment of the second table commands you to honour your source or origin, so that you may have a long life (Exod. 20); for one who does not honour him from whom he has his being deserves to be unable to retain the being that he has. The second commandment is: “You shall not kill” (ibid.). Fittingly indeed, one to whom long life is promised in the preceding commandment is here forbidden to extinguish another’s life: so that, by the love of God, he who honours his own source may aspire to the life that knows no end; and, by the love of neighbour, may not give himself over through any cruel hatred to bring another’s life to its end.

Then follows the third commandment: “You shall not commit adultery”; and the fourth: “You shall not steal” (ibid.). “You shall not commit adultery” pertains to one’s own life. “You shall not steal” pertains to another’s life [Col. 0360A]. Above, a person was commanded to preserve both his own life and another’s; here he is commanded to injure neither his own nor another’s life. For it is just that one who awaits incorruptible life in the homeland should avoid corruption on the way of life; and that one who no longer oppresses his neighbour’s life through open violence should not harm him even through hidden fraud in those things given for the use of living. Nor should he merely refrain from harm himself; he should not presume to provide confidence or support, by his authority or testimony, either to those who do harm or to those wishing to do harm. This is forbidden in the following commandment, when it is said: “You shall not bear false witness” (ibid.).

And because one cannot long restrain oneself from an act of injury if one does not restrain one’s mind from the intention and will to injure, it follows and says: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife; nor shall you covet your neighbour’s property” (ibid.) [Col. 0360B]. These are the ten commandments, which open the way of first perfection and the path of rectitude. For the first perfection directs a person within himself through good action. The second expands him outward in the breadth of love for neighbour. The third raises him upward through love for God; for the number ten extends the line of first perfection; one hundred expands the breadth of the second; one thousand raises the summit of perfection on high. Let what has been said thus far concerning the exposition of the ten commandments of the Law suffice for the present.

## CHAPTER IX. On Mutable and Added Commandments

There follows another kind of commandments, called mutable [Col. 0360C], because they were added for a time to natural commandments by way of dispensation, either for exercise or for signification. They were for exercise, indeed, so that there might be many matters in which the obedience of those being trained could be tested and their devotion cultivated. They were for signification, so that signs of future truth might be prepared in them, and so that, through the things commanded to be done bodily, those things to be done or believed spiritually might be shown.

All these, however, were taken from intermediate matters; that is, from matters which in their own nature were neither so good that they had inevitably to be done, nor so evil that they had necessarily to be avoided altogether. For all things proposed in commandments of this kind were, as regards their own nature, such that they might be done without fault at the agent’s discretion and likewise omitted without fault. But when the commandment was added, it turned things which were in themselves intermediate and open in either direction toward one side or the other, either by commanding or by forbidding; so that those things now forbidden cannot be done without fault, nor again can those things commanded be omitted altogether without fault [Col. 0360D]. Yet this is not caused by the nature of the matter, but by the force and obedience of the command.

The Law forbade eating flesh with blood, not because this was evil in itself, as regards the nature of the thing, but because what ought to be signified by it was evil. For flesh is, as it were, eaten with blood when someone delights in deeds of fury and cruelty. The same Law also commanded abstinence from pork, signifying that works of uncleanness must be avoided [Col. 0361A]. In this manner it also excluded from human food certain other animals, birds, fish, and creatures that move upon the earth. And many other things which the first condition had not made harmful, the second institution, by dispensation, commanded to be avoided as though harmful.

There were, moreover, certain other intermediate matters which the written Law proposed more by concession than by command or prohibition, and which perhaps would have been evil in themselves had they not been permitted. For example, the Law says that if someone found some shameful matter in his wife and therefore hated her, he should write her a bill of divorce and thus dismiss her (Deut. 24); because it was plainly better that one hated should be dismissed in accordance with the will than, retained against the will, be killed [Col. 0361B]. It was also said in the Law: “You shall offer your oath to God and swear by God” (Deut. 6, 10). This was not, of course, because swearing by God is good, but because an oath is allowed to imperfect people so that perjury may more easily be avoided. At the same time, they were to learn to venerate God’s name, when they more frequently used it to affirm and bear witness to their statements and were not compelled to invoke the names of false gods to confirm their oaths. For they had been permitted—and commanded—to invoke the Lord’s name as witness, provided only that the need to confirm truth required it.

Similar was the permission granted to exact retaliation for an injury inflicted, lest perhaps, inflamed by more vehement fury, they should attempt to return evils greater than those done to them [Col. 0361C]. There are many other kinds of commandments contained in the written Law, suitable indeed to outward conduct and at the same time fitting for spiritual signification.

In all these, therefore, we observe the distinction which the Apostle set forth as signified in the elements, beginnings, and word of God’s discourse. For there are these three: elements, beginnings, and discourse. In the elements there is sound but no meaning; hence they are not called beginnings, because meaning does not begin in them. Words are beginnings of meanings; hence they are called *dictiones*, as though already saying something, and the first parts of speech, because the beginning of understanding arises from them. Thus in elements there is sound but no meaning; in a beginning there is meaning but it is incomplete; in discourse there is meaning and it is complete.

See these three corresponding realities in the Scripture of God. Scripture said: “You shall not eat flesh with blood” (Lev. 7; Deut. 12): this is an element. It afterward added: “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20): this is a beginning. Later it completed the teaching by forbidding anger also: this is discourse (Matt. 5) [Col. 0361D]. Again, it said that pork must not be eaten (Deut. 14): in this there was an element. Afterward it added: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20): in this there was a beginning. Finally it added: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery in his heart” (Matt. 5), and so forth: in this was the completion of discourse.

The commandments added for a time, therefore, were elements; the commandments of the Decalogue, beginnings; the commandments of the New Testament, discourse. The first belong to the institution [Col. 0362A] of discipline; the second to the truth of nature; the third to the perfection of grace. Immutable commandments are naturally prior. Mutable commandments, as has been said, precede in signification, because in them goodness is first given form, which afterward is begun in the former commandments and finally completed through grace.

Some of the added and mutable commandments are retained even now in the time of grace for exercise, such as the observance of fasts. Certain others, though instituted in earlier times, are nevertheless preserved for the instruction of the present. Above all, those which concern the exercise of spiritual striving are retained in the time of grace, while those pertaining to carnal observances have been abolished.

## CHAPTER X. That There Are Three Kinds of Sacraments in the Law

[Col. 0362B]
