Three kinds of sacraments are found to have existed under the written Law: some especially for remedy, others for service, others for divine worship. The first pertain to the remission of sins; the second to the exercise of devotion; the third to the cultivation of piety.

The first were instituted as though for necessity, so that in them a person might be sanctified: such as circumcision, sacrifices for sin and for trespass, and other things instituted especially for cleansing and remission.

The second were established, as it were, for exercise, so that the devotion of the faithful might be exercised in them and merit increased: such were peace-offerings [Col. 0362C], which the faithful offered in order to reconcile divine favour to themselves.

The third were instituted as a kind of preparation, so that they might be as it were instruments for handling and sanctifying the other sacraments: such were the court and the tabernacle, and all the utensils contained in them; likewise the sacred garments of the ministers, and all other things instituted to adorn the divine element.

Again, some sacraments were sanctified for cleansing; others were handled for devotion; the third were performed for veneration. The first were for necessity; the second for virtue; the third for praise. The first were received for sanctification; the second were handled for devotion; the third were performed for praise. Again, some sacraments consisted in certain sanctified things, others in sacrifices and offerings, others in divine ministries. Thus the same matter may be distinguished in many ways for clarity.

A sacrifice was so called when an immolation was made from animals. An offering, however, was the name for any other sort of thing. There are three kinds of sacrifices: some are whole burnt offerings, others simple sacrifices, others peace-offerings. A whole burnt offering was called that which, offered either by obligation or voluntarily, was entirely burned. A sacrifice was called that which, offered by the obligation of an ordinance, was partly burned and partly reserved [Col. 0362D]. Peace-offerings were those voluntarily offered either in thanksgiving, in fulfilment of a prior vow, or from voluntary and spontaneous devotion.

A whole burnt offering was sometimes made from cattle, sometimes from sheep or goats, sometimes from birds. An offering was sometimes made of fine flour, and was called an uncooked sacrifice; sometimes from an oven, sometimes from a frying pan, sometimes from a griddle, and was called a cooked sacrifice. Some sacrifices were for sin; others for trespass: for sin, that sin might be expiated; for trespass, that trespass might be expiated. Sin is when what ought not to be done is done; trespass is when what ought to be done is not done. In all these matters sacraments consisted.

It must be understood, however, that we ought not to regard all these as sacraments of the kind which, above, we defined the sacraments properly so called ought to be [Col. 0364A]. Rather, these and similar things were called sacraments solely because they were signs of sacred things. Thus one sacrament signifies sanctification and sanctifies by sanctification; another does not sanctify but only signifies. Let what has been said thus far concerning the sacraments of the written Law suffice. It was not the purpose of the present discussion to treat the promises which we placed in the third part of the first distinction. Therefore there were three things contained in the written Law: commandments, sacraments, and promises.

[Col. 0363] Here ends the first book.

# THE PROLOGUE OF THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

Great are the depths of spiritual meanings in the Holy Scriptures; but because the same grace of understanding has not been given to all, sacred discourse contains within itself certain things by which it nourishes the faith of the simple. These, joined to higher matters, complete one rule of truth. Therefore, in expounding sacred discourse, one must not everywhere preserve the same mode of treatment, because the higher mysteries must reverently be treated in more elevated language worthy of sacred things; while the lesser instruments of the divine mysteries must be explained, according to the capacity of the simple, in a humbler style of speech. Thus it may be evident that what is written is true: “Clothed around with variety in golden fringes” (Ps. 44).

For just as the holy Church of the elect is beautifully adorned with the variety of good practices and virtues, so sacred Scripture—from which that holy Church receives its pattern of life—is woven with beautiful variety in its language. Yet this variety is fitting, so that it does not generate schism; and its diversity is harmonious, so that it does not produce opposition. For in it greater things do not despise lesser things; nor again have lesser things disdained to be joined to greater things. Rather, they adorn one another in the one truth, because all things please on account of truth. Let no one, therefore, wonder if, after and among the great mysteries of faith, mention is made of things that seem lower in their order, because things that are one in truth do not shrink from being together. For God himself deigned to humble himself, descending to human things, that he might afterward raise humanity to divine things.

# THE SECOND BOOK HAS EIGHTEEN PARTS

The first part treats of the Incarnation of the Word. The second, of the unity of the Church, which is Christ’s body. The third, of ecclesiastical orders. The fourth, of sacred vestments. The fifth, of the dedication of a church. The sixth, of baptism. The seventh, of confirmation. The eighth, of the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood. The ninth, of lesser sacraments and sacred things. The tenth, of simony. The eleventh, of marriage. The twelfth, of vows. The thirteenth, of vices and virtues. The fourteenth, of confession, penance, and the remission of sins. The fifteenth, of the anointing of the sick. The sixteenth, of the end of humanity. The seventeenth, of the end of the age. The eighteenth, of the state of the future age.

# TABLE OF THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0365]

## Here Begins the Second Book, on the Incarnation of the Word and the Time of Grace

[Col. 0371]

### First Part

### Chapter One, or Prologue

[Col. 0371C]

In the preceding part of this work I have given, in summary, an account of the condition of all things from their first beginning, together with the fall of man and those things that were subsequently prepared for his restoration up to the coming of the Word. Now I wish to proceed in order through those things which follow, unto the end and consummation of all things.

The time of grace took its beginning from the coming of the Son of God in the flesh, as it is written: “Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). For the grace of God is the redemption of the human race; and while this is accomplished through Christ’s coming, the truth of God’s promise is fulfilled in the manifestation of his grace.

### CHAP. II. Why the Son was sent rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit

[Col. 0371D]

The Son, rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit, was sent because it was not fitting that the Father, who was not from another, should be sent by another. For if he were sent by another, he would have his coming from another—the one by whom he was sent—and that one by whom he was sent would stand to him, as it were, as a certain principle. Therefore the Father has no being sent by another, because he has no being from another.

The Son was first sent, who is from the Father alone; afterwards the Holy Spirit also, who is from the Father and the Son. First the Son came so that human beings might be freed; afterwards the Holy Spirit came so that they might be made blessed. [Col. 0372C] The former delivered them from evil; the latter recalled them to good. The former took away what we endured; the latter restored what we had lost.

The natural Son, sent by the Father, came in order to summon to the inheritance those who were to be adopted, and to demonstrate his own consent in the grace of adoption. For those alien to the inheritance could not be led into it without the Son’s consent. Thus the Father sent on behalf of sons; the Son came on behalf of brothers. For in the Father and the Son the names of fatherhood and sonship subsist, so that those to be adopted might receive the name of sons, both through him whose it was and from him from whom it was.

Wisdom came so that the enemy might be conquered by reason, and so that Wisdom itself might reclaim its dwelling-place, which malice possessed. For it was just that he who had conquered by cunning should be overcome not by strength but by wisdom, so that in that very thing in which he had raised himself up as victor, he might be cast down as defeated. [Col. 0372D]

The Son of God became the Son of Man, so that he might make the sons of men sons of God; and so that the name of Son might not pass to another person, with the result that there would be two Sons in the Trinity and the distinction of the Trinity would be confused. For if the Father had assumed flesh, he himself would be both Father and Son: Father of the Son whom he begot from eternity, and Son of the mother from whom he would have been begotten in time. If, however, the Holy Spirit had assumed flesh, there would be two sons in the Trinity: one, the Son of the Father without a mother; the other, the son of a mother without a father.

Therefore, lest the incommunicable name be divided, the Son alone received flesh, so that one and the same might be both Son [Col. 0373A] of God and Son of Man: Son of God according to divinity, begotten of the Father; son of man according to humanity, born of a mother.

### CHAP. III. How the Son alone assumed flesh

But perhaps there will be some who say: “If the works of the Trinity are inseparable, then whatever the Son does, the Father does. But if the Father does everything that the Son does, then, if the Son assumed flesh, the Father also assumed flesh. For the Son could not assume flesh without the Father, if he could do nothing without the Father.”

But here one must first consider that, when it is said that the Son does everything which the Father does, this is plainly to be understood of that operation by which God, Creator and Maker, creates, governs, and orders his creature. In that operation Father, Son, and Holy Spirit [Col. 0373B] cannot be separated at all, because in the one divinity in which and through which they work, they are one.

We distinguish these matters concerning divine operation so that no one may think that, against the statement, “Whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does” (John 5), one ought to object that the Father begets—which the Son does not do—and that the Son is begotten—which the Father does not do. For if the Son begot as the Father does, he would be the Father; and if the Father were begotten as the Son is, he would be the Son.

Thus, lest anyone suppose, because the Son does not beget, that the Son does not do whatever the Father does, we say that this is understood of that operation by which he either works upon a creature, so that what did not exist begins to exist, or works in a creature, so that what has been made may subsist in that which has been made. For there [Col. 0373C] the whole Trinity works inseparably, where neither Father is separated from Son, nor Son from Father, nor Holy Spirit from both in operation.

For operation is properly designated in a work. In that which is not made—namely, God—he does not act, but simply is. But in that which is made, everything that has been made was certainly made by him through whom it was made. Therefore here everything that the Father has made, the Son likewise makes.

Accordingly, in this operation in which the assumption of flesh is found, it is reasonably asked how it belongs to the Son alone and not to the Father. For when it is said that the Son assumed flesh, a work which the Son performed is certainly signified. If the Father is excluded from that work, then the Father does not do or perform everything which the Son does.

Or perhaps, because it was not said, “Everything [Col. 0373D] which the Son does, the Father does,” but rather, “Whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does,” one should suppose that the Son indeed does all that the Father does, but that the Son does some things which the Father does not do? Far be it! Rather, everything the Father does the Son does, and everything the Son does the Father does; for in that in which they are one in deity, they cannot be separated in operation.

Therefore everything which the Son does, the Father does, because in the divinity by which the Son is of the Father—because he is one with the Father—he does nothing without the Father’s operation. Yet he did certain things in the humanity according to which he was not the Father’s Son, because he did not receive that humanity from the Father by being born. These things are therefore referred to the person of the Son alone, because he did them in and according to that nature which he did not hold in common with the Father, but which he alone, in time, received as his own uniquely. [Col. 0374A]

Nevertheless, he did not do alone everything that he did in divinity, because he was not alone in divinity; but he who was the same with him did the same with him. If, then, the Son assumed humanity in divinity, how did the Father not do the same with him in that same divinity, he who was the same with him?

Perhaps when it is said, “The Son assumed flesh,” it is understood through the force of an implicit relation that he united it to himself; the same is not said of the Father, because if it were said, the meaning would not be the same but different. For if it were said, “The Father assumed flesh,” it would likewise be understood that the Father united flesh to himself; but this would no longer be the same thing, but another. [Col. 0374B] For it would be another thing if flesh were said to be united to the Father than when it is said to be united to the Son. Since the Father is one person and the Son another, something different is said when the Son is said to be incarnate from what would be said if the Father were said to be incarnate.

It does not therefore follow that, because the Son assumed flesh, the Father also assumed flesh; just as it does not follow that, because the Son united flesh to himself, the Father also united flesh to himself. But it does follow that, if the Son united flesh to himself, the Father also united that same flesh to the Son himself, because, while the operation of both is shown to be one, neither the Son without the Father nor the Father without the Son is shown to have acted.

But if the Father had clothed himself with flesh and the Son had clothed himself with flesh, that would not be the same thing but another thing, since in that very matter the same operation would not be shown, because the relation would not be proved to have been made to the same person on both sides. But now the Father wrought the assumption or union of flesh, because he clothed the Son with flesh; and the Son wrought it, because he clothed himself with flesh. There was one union and one operation.

The union was one because that which was united was united to one. The operation was one because that which was done was done in one. Three worked, and they did not work three things but one; and what was being done belonged to one, insofar as it was done to him alone, and belonged to three, insofar as it was done by them. [Col. 0374C]

It is read in the book of Judges (ch. 14) that Manoah obtained a wife for his son Samson; yet he who obtained a wife for his son did not obtain a wife for himself. And the Son asks the Father to obtain a wife for him, as though he could not do it by himself [Col. 0374D] alone; and no one argues, saying: “If the Father obtained a wife for the Son, then the Father obtained a wife,” or contends that the Father was married because he obtained one for the Son.

Why then should the Father be called incarnate because he united flesh to his Son, just as the Son himself is called incarnate because he joined flesh to himself? For the flesh is the bride of the Word. The Word assumed it to himself, and the Father of the Word likewise united it to his Word; two performed one thing, and in the one there was one operation of the two.

Therefore he says: “Whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does likewise.” “These things,” he says, “the Son likewise does.” What are “these things”? Not other things. What is “likewise”? Not differently. The unity of operation could not have been demonstrated more perfectly: not other things, not differently—both the same things [Col. 0375A] and in the same manner.

If they performed the same things but not in the same manner, the operation would not be one, because it would be otherwise. If they performed them in the same manner but did not perform the same things, the operation would not be one, because it would be another. But now he performs both the same things and in the same manner, so that there is nothing either different or otherwise in that operation.

Show me something which the Father does—if indeed one must ask what he does who does everything. Yet, for the sake of example, set forward one thing among all that the Father does: I say that the Son does that very thing. And I do not say “that very thing” as though it were similar to it, but as the identical thing.

For when I say, “I do the same thing that you do,” perhaps because I build a house as you build a house, although your house which you build is one house and my house which I build is another, I nevertheless say that I do the same thing [Col. 0375B] you do, because what I do is, in some respect, similar to what you do. This is not how I mean it when I say that the Son does that very thing which the Father does.

But if I built a house and you built the same house with me, I would say that you did the same thing I do—indeed, more truly, one thing, because it is the same thing and not another. Yet it would still not be truly one, because you would do one part and I another; you with your tools and I with mine; you with your hands and arms and I with mine; finally, you with your strength and I with mine. Thus it would no longer be truly one, but be done in another and through other things.

Do I mean this, then, when I say that the Son does that very thing which the Father does? Is the Son’s hand different from the Father’s hand, the Son’s arm different from the Father’s arm, the Son’s power different from the Father’s power, when the Son himself is the Father’s hand, arm, and power? [Col. 0375C]

Just as what a human being does with his hand is the same as what the person’s hand does, and what a human being does with his arm is the same as what the person’s arm does, and what a human being does by strength is the same as what the person’s strength does, so what the Father does is the same as what the Son does, because the Father does everything through the Son.

If the essence is one, the nature one, the power one, and the will one, how is the operation not one? You say that the Father does this, and I say that the Son does this very thing. The Father does this very thing; the Son does this very thing. The Father wholly does it, and the Son wholly does it. The Father’s doing is the Son’s doing.

Do not conceive of two actions, one greater and one lesser; or perhaps as two equal actions of similar weight. [Col. 0375D] There is unity there, nothing multiple. There is one action of two—indeed, one action of three—just as there is one deity; and in the one action, the three are not three agents but one agent, just as in the one deity the three are not three gods but one God.

Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons, but they are not three gods, nor three creators, nor three makers, because they cannot be divided in that in which they are one. Therefore, whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise. What can be more alike than unity? How can that which cannot be multiplied be divided? Or how can that which is one depart from itself?

Therefore do not wonder that the assumption of flesh, which is referred to the Son alone, was wrought not by the Son alone but also by the Father and Holy Spirit with the Son. Nor should you therefore call three incarnate, because three wrought the incarnation of one: the unity of nature made the operation inseparable, and the property of person made the assumption singular. [Col. 0376A]

### CHAP. IV. On the distinction of the three persons in the one deity

Since the weakness of human understanding is insufficient to comprehend the things it is commanded to believe, it must meanwhile be sustained by the authority of sacred discourse, not examined by human reasoning. Accordingly, I wish to set forth what the holy Fathers have already said concerning the distinction of the three persons in the one deity, according to the firmness of catholic truth, adding nothing of my own, since I am not found sufficient even for what has been said by them.

Augustine, *Against the Impiety of Arius*: The Fathers coined the new name [Col. 0376B] *homoousion*, but they did not designate a new reality by such a name. For that is called *homoousion* which is expressed in: “I and the Father are one” (John 10), namely, of one and the same substance.

The same author: All Catholics who wrote about the Trinity before me intended, according to the Scriptures, to teach that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, of one and the same substance and in inseparable equality, manifest the divine unity. [Col. 0376C] Therefore they are not three gods, but one God, although the Father begot the Son, and thus the Son is not the one who is Father; the Son was begotten by the Father, and thus the Father is not the one who is Son.

Likewise, the Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son, but only the Spirit of Father and Son, coeternal and coequal with the Father and Son, and belonging to the unity of the Trinity. Yet it was not that Trinity which was born of the Virgin Mary, but the Son alone; nor did that Trinity descend in the form of a dove, but the Holy Spirit alone; nor did that Trinity say from heaven, “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3), but it was the Father’s voice addressed to the Son. Yet Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as they are inseparable, so they work inseparably.

For by what understanding does a human being grasp God, when he has not yet grasped the very understanding by which he wishes to grasp him? Let us, however, understand God—if we can, and as much as we can—as good without quality, great without quantity, creator without need, present without place, containing all things without circumference, wholly everywhere without location, eternal without time, making mutable things without change in himself, and suffering nothing.

Whoever thinks of God in this way and cannot yet discover fully what he is, nevertheless piously takes care, as far as possible, not to think something of him which he is not. Yet he is without doubt substance—or, if that is a better term, essence—which the Greeks call *ousia* (οὐσία). [Col. 0376D]

The same, in the book *Against Maximinus*: Let there be no division into parts in the unity of the Deity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God; that is, the Trinity itself is one God. For Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons; and these three, because they are of one substance, are one and supremely one, where there is no diversity of natures and no diversity of wills.

For if they were one in nature but not in agreement, they would not be [Col. 0377A] supremely one. But if they were unequal in nature, they would not be one. Therefore these three, because they are one, are one God by reason of the ineffable union of deity through which they are ineffably joined.

But Christ is one person of twofold substance; yet God cannot be called a part of this person. Otherwise the Son, before he received the form of a servant, was not whole, and he increased when man was added to his divinity. But if it is absurdly said concerning one person that God cannot be part of that reality, how much more can anyone who is one among three not be a part of the Trinity?

Therefore in the Trinity which is God, the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; and together these three are one God. Nor is one a third part of this Trinity, nor are two a greater part there than one [Col. 0377B] is there, nor are all together something greater than each individually, because the greatness is spiritual, not bodily. Let whoever can receive it receive it (Matt. 19); whoever cannot, let that person believe and pray that what is believed may be understood.

Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God on account of indivisible deity; they are three persons on account of the proper character of each; and, on account of the perfection of each, they are not parts of the one God. The Father is power; the Son is power; the Holy Spirit is power.

The same, in the book *On the Trinity*: If the Son alone understands for himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit, it follows that the Father is not wise through himself but through the Son; that wisdom did not beget wisdom; and that the Father is said to be wise through the wisdom which he begot. For where there is no understanding, there cannot be wisdom. Consequently, if the Father does not understand for himself but the Son understands for the Father, then certainly the Son makes the Father wise. And if God’s being is his being wise, and that essence is wisdom, then it would follow not that the Son has essence from the Father—which is true—but rather that the Father has essence from the Son—which is false.

Therefore God the Father is wise by the wisdom which he himself is; and the Son is the Father’s wisdom, begotten from the wisdom which is the Father, from whom the Son was begotten. Hence the Father understands by the understanding which he himself is; but the Son is the Father’s understanding, begotten from the understanding which is the Father. [Col. 0377C]

The same: God is not to be thought threefold because he is Trinity; otherwise he would be less in each one than in all three together. [Col. 0377D] Likewise, when in this Trinity we speak of the person of the Father, we mean nothing other than the substance of the Father, because the person of the Father is nothing other than the Father himself. For “person” is said with reference to himself, not with reference to the Son or the Holy Spirit, just as “God” and similar terms are.

This is the only name which, while it is predicated of each severally in relation to himself, is received in the highest reality in the plural rather than the singular. For we say that the Father is a person, the Son a person, and the Holy Spirit a person; nevertheless, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not one person but three persons.

But when we say three persons and one essence, we do not predicate one essence as a genus of species or as a species of individuals. It seems possible to say that three humans are one nature, but two humans are more than one; whereas the essence of Father and Son [Col. 0378A] is not greater than the Father alone or the Son alone. And those three persons, if they are rightly so called, are equal in each individually—something the merely natural human being does not perceive (cf. 1 Cor. 2:14; the printed citation reads “I Cor. XXI”).

Why, then, did Latin usage employ this unfamiliar expression, unless because it wished one name to serve the signification by which the Trinity is understood, lest we say nothing at all when we confess that there are three? By this term it wished diversity not to be understood, but singularity.

Thus those three appear both to be defined in relation to one another and to be infinite in themselves; and each is in each, all are in all each, each is in all, and all are one. The same: Finally, if God has any community with other things in the use of some name, a different signification must beyond doubt be understood. But this must be shown by a more powerful argument.

If [Col. 0378B] the divine nature is incapable of receiving any accident, how is it called just or wise or anything of that kind? But it is certain that the supreme nature truly is because it is through itself whatever it is; and nothing is just except through justice. Therefore, if it is not just except through justice, and can be just through nothing other than itself, what follows more directly than that it is itself the justice through which it is just?

Accordingly, if one asks what that supreme nature itself is, what answer is more fitting than “justice”? And whereas a creature is called just with respect to what sort of thing it is, because it has justice, divine justice itself is not properly said to have justice, but to be justice. Therefore it is spoken of not in respect of what kind of thing it is, but in respect of what it is; and in it there is no difference whether it is called just or justice. [Col. 0378C]

What is recognized as established in the example of justice constrains the understanding, by reason, to perceive the same concerning all things which are similarly said of the supreme nature. Therefore, whatever among these things may be said of it, does not show what sort of thing it is or how great it is, but rather what it is. For whatever is of a certain quality or quantity also has in it something other than what it is; therefore it is not simple but composite.

For when a human being is called body, rational, and human, these three are not said in one manner or under one consideration. A person is body in one respect and rational in another; and neither of these individually is the whole of what a human being is. But that supreme essence, supreme life, supreme justice, supreme wisdom, supreme greatness, supreme eternity, and all other similarly [Col. 0378D] multiple terms, do not signify many things but one.

The same: Neither the person of the Father nor that of the Holy Spirit, but the person of the Son alone, assumed flesh. To help you understand this, I shall use comparisons, so that from the creature you may understand the Creator. In the soul there is reason; and though they are one, the soul does one thing and reason another: by the soul we live, by reason we are wise. Thus Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, although there is one substance: the whole Trinity made the human being whom it assumed, but the whole Trinity did not assume him; the person of the Son alone did so.

The same, in Book Five of *On the Trinity*: Nothing can happen to God as an accident. Something is said relatively, as Father in relation to Son and Son in relation to Father; this is not an accident, because the one is always Father and the other always Son. [Col. 0379A] But if Father were said with reference to himself, it would be said according to substance.

Likewise, although being Father and being Son are different, their substance is not different, because these terms are not said according to substance but according to relation. Yet relation is not an accident, because it is not mutable. Likewise, the Son is not equal to the Father according to that by which he is called relative to the Father; it follows, then, that he is equal according to that which is said of himself. But whatever is said of himself is said according to substance. It follows, therefore, that he is equal according to substance. The substance of both is thus the same.

When the Father is called unbegotten, this says not what he is but what he is not. When a relation is denied, it is not denied according to substance, because relation itself is not said according to substance. [Col. 0379B]

The same: “What are the three?” Human speech suffers a profound poverty. “Three persons” has been said, not in order that the matter might be expressed, but in order that it might not be left unspoken.

The same: The Trinity can in no way be called Son.

The same: It must be confessed that the Father and the Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit.

The same: The Son has being not only as Son, which is said relatively, but also absolutely: he has the very substance by being begotten.

The same: When human poverty sought, through speech, to utter what it holds concerning the Lord God, it feared to say “three essences,” lest some diversity be understood in that supreme equality.

The same: Therefore we speak of three persons, not so that any diversity of essence may be understood, but so that a single term may answer when it is asked, “What three?” or “What three things?”

Jerome: We confess one God in three persons; we distinguish three persons, made manifest under their proper characteristics—not merely names, but also the properties of the names, that is, persons. Or, as the Greeks express it, we confess *hypostases* (ὑποστάσεις), that is, subsistences. Neither does the Father ever lay aside the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, nor does the Son or the Holy Spirit receive the Father’s name and person. Rather, the Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always Holy Spirit. Thus they are one in substance and distinguished in persons and names. [Col. 0379C]

Ambrose, *On the Trinity*: This is the assertion of our faith: that we say there is one God, not two or three. One who says that there are three gods separates the divinity [Col. 0379D] of the Trinity. But we confess that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, so that in the perfect Trinity there are both the fullness of divinity and unity of power. For God is one. “God” is a name of majesty, not of power. If, then, God is one, the name is one, the power is one, and the Trinity is one.

Accordingly, he says: “Go, baptizing in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). Thus he says “in the name,” not “in the names.” The name is one where the substance, divinity, and majesty are one. This is the name in which all must be saved (Acts 4).

The same: “I and the Father are one.” He said “one” lest a distinction of power be made; he added “are” so that we may recognize the persons. For the Father is not himself the Son; rather, the Son is begotten of the Father: God from God, full from the Full One. [Col. 0380A] These, then, are not bare names but indications of power. The fullness of divinity is in the Father, and fullness is in the Son; yet what is one is neither discordant nor confused, and what is undifferentiated is not multiple.

How the Son is begotten of the Father cannot be known: the mind fails, the tongue is silent—not only the minds and tongues of human beings, but of angels also. It is above angels, above cherubim, above seraphim, above every understanding. We are commanded to believe, not permitted to investigate. Remove arguments where faith is sought.

We believe in one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Father, because he has the Son; the Son, because he has the Father; and the Holy Spirit, because he is from the Father and the Son. The Father, then, is the principle of divinity, who, just as he was never not God, was never not Father. The Son was born from the Father; and the Holy Spirit proceeds from him and from the Son. The Father is eternal because he has an eternal Son, of whom he is the eternal Father. The Son is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father and the Son.

The Trinity is not confused in one person, as Sabellius says; nor is it separated or divided in the nature of divinity, as Arius blasphemes. Rather, the Father is one in person, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; but in nature, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God in Trinity. [Col. 0380B]

The same: Neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit assumed flesh, but the Son alone, so that he who in the deity of God the Father was God’s Son might himself become, in humanity, the son of man—lest the name of son pass to another who was not Son by birth. Therefore, the Son of God by birth [Col. 0380C] became the son of man: according to the truth of nature, God’s Son born from God; and according to the truth of nature, the son of man born from a human being. Thus the truth of the one begotten might possess the name of Son in both births by being born, not by adoption or appellation; and one Son might be true God and true man.

The same: Therefore we do not speak of two Christs or two sons, but of God and man as one Son. For this reason we call him the Only-begotten, remaining in two substances, as the truth of his natures granted him, without confusion or intermixture of natures. Thus the Son assumed humanity so that he who assumed and that which he assumed might be one person in the Trinity.

For when humanity was assumed, a quaternity was not made; rather, the Trinity remained, [Col. 0380D] that assumption ineffably effecting the reality of one person in God and man. For we do not call Christ God only, nor man only, but true God, born from God the Father, and true man, born from a human mother. Nor does his humanity, by which he is less than the Father, diminish anything of his divinity, by which he is equal to the Father.

Therefore both are the one Christ: he who according to God said, “I and the Father are one,” and according to man, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14). From the time he began to be human, he did not begin to be anything other than the Son of God; he is the Only-begotten. And because of God the Word, who, when that humanity had been assumed, became flesh, Christ is one person—Word and human being—just as any human being is one person, namely rational soul and flesh. [Col. 0381A]

The same: Christ Jesus, the Son of God, is both God and man: God, because he is the Word of God; man, because a rational soul and flesh were added to the Word of God in unity of person. And he who is the only Son of God is also the Son of Man, the very same. Both, from both, are one Christ, one Son of God: not two sons, God and man, but one Son.

The same: God assumed humanity; humanity passed into God—not by a changeability of nature, but by God’s condescension. Thus neither was God changed into human substance by assuming humanity, nor was humanity, when glorified, changed into God; for change or mutability of nature produces either diminution or abolition. The Trinity is believed by us to be joined without confusion and distinguished without separation.

The same: Nothing created or servile is to be believed in the Trinity; nothing unequal; nothing equal by grace; nothing earlier or later; nothing greater or less; nothing alien or ministerial to another; nothing invisible to itself or visible to creatures; nothing diverse in character or will; nothing drawn down from the essence of the Trinity to the nature of creatures; nothing singular in office and incommunicable to another; nothing confused, but all wholly perfect, because all is from one and one, yet not solitary. [Col. 0381B]

The same: Therefore the Son is *homoousion*—of the same substance—in the deity of the Father; the Holy Spirit is *homoousion* with the Father and the Son; the one Son is *homoousion* with God and man, remaining God in his humanity, desirable to be seen in the Father’s glory by angels. Just as the Father and the Holy Spirit are worshipped by angels and every creature, so worship is offered not to the man on account of [Col. 0381C] God, nor to Christ alongside God, but to the man in God, and to God in the man.

### CHAP. V. That the Word assumed flesh with punishment but without fault; with mortality but without iniquity.

Many ask concerning that flesh which the Word assumed: how it was clean from sin, and how, being without sin, it bore sin’s penalty. As to how it was either clean from sin or cleansed from it, we must not pass over the opinion of certain persons in silence, lest, if it is not set out, it not be seen; and lest, if what is so is not seen, what is not so be believed.

Some think that the flesh assumed by the Word was, from the beginning—even in the first parent, when the whole mass of human nature was corrupted by sin—preserved immune from the contagion and [Col. 0381D] corruption of sin; that from the first parent until its assumption by the Word it was free from every sin and brought down undefiled, so that it was never under sin and therefore was not liberated from sin, but was free. For they say that that portion of human nature ought not to have been under sin through which human nature itself, when it had become liable to sin, was to be liberated from sin.

To establish this opinion, they adduce the Apostle’s statement when, in asserting that the new priesthood is to be preferred to the old, he shows that Melchizedek—who bore the type of Christ himself and of the new priesthood—received tithes from Abraham (Heb. 7). In that payment of tithes he proves that Levi also, from whom the ministers of the old priesthood undoubtedly descended, was tithed [Col. 0382A]; and thereby the old priesthood, which paid tithes in Levi, is to be considered inferior, while the new, which received tithes in Melchizedek, the figure of Christ, is superior and worthier.

Yet we do not say that Christ, who then according to the flesh was likewise in Abraham’s loins as Levi was, was tithed, lest by a similar argument we be compelled to conclude that the new priesthood also, which is in Christ, there paid tithes. They think that no other explanation can be found for why Levi, who was then in his father’s loins according to the flesh, was tithed, while Christ, who according to the flesh was there, was not tithed, except that Levi’s flesh was there with guilt, but Christ’s flesh was not. Therefore, they say, what was liable to sin required expiation, while what was [Col. 0382B] clean and free from sin did not require it.

By such reasoning they think they prove that the flesh assumed by the Word was never liable to sin, but was preserved clean from sin from the beginning—whether in him from whom it descended or in those through whom it descended—so that it might at some time become an offering for sin.

But the definition of Catholic truth declares that the Son of God, who was born for sinners and from sinners, assumed flesh liable to sin, though free from sin; and free precisely because it had been liberated. It was free, not because it had never been under sin, but because it at some time ceased to be under it. When it was assumed, it was cleansed. For human nature was cleansed by the same grace through which it was united, free from sin, to the Word of God, as the Christian is liberated from sin so as to be joined to that same nature in Christ, his head [Col. 0382C].

Therefore, as blessed Augustine says, let grace appear to us in Christ our head, whence, according to each person’s measure, it is diffused through all his members. By that grace every Christian is made a Christian from the beginning of his faith, by which grace that man was made Christ from his own beginning; this person is reborn from the same Spirit from whom that one was born. By the same Spirit remission of sins is effected in us by whom it was brought about that he should have no sin.

Thus it was brought about by grace that that flesh, which from its origin was under sin, should be cleansed from sin; and, cleansed from sin in him who was to be free from every sin in it, should be assumed free from sin—so that grace might not prejudice the corruption of nature, nor the corruption of nature impede grace [Col. 0382D].

“But,” they ask, “how was Christ not tithed in Abraham’s loins, if his flesh there was liable to sin?” It must be understood that although Christ’s flesh, like Levi’s flesh, was still under sin in Abraham’s loins, the sin under which his flesh was did not belong to him. For there belonged to him there only that which was thereafter to become his. Hence Levi there had both nature and guilt, because by propagation of origin he was to derive both nature and guilt from there. But because Christ had in Abraham’s loins nature alone, since that alone was what he was to receive from there, he undoubtedly did not need an offering, which was unnecessary for what alone belonged to him there. For an offering is made not for nature but for guilt: if there were no guilt, nature would have no need of an offering [Col. 0383A].

Thus Levi was tithed in Abraham’s loins because he had there both nature and guilt, both of which he was to receive from there. But Christ was not tithed, because, since he was to receive from there nature alone, he did not then have there the guilt, even though that nature which was to become his, being without guilt itself, was in its origin liable to guilt.

## Chapter VI. That the Word assumed, together with flesh, a rational soul; and what that soul was in wisdom, power, righteousness, goodness, and merit

There were certain heretics who thought that the Word did not assume a rational soul in Christ together with the flesh [Col. 0383B], but that flesh alone was united to the Word; that the divinity of the Word itself gave life to the flesh in place of a soul; that the same divinity withdrew from that flesh when it died upon the cross; and that, when it was raised, it returned to it in order to give it life and raise it again.

But the Catholic faith holds that God assumed everything belonging to humanity except guilt; for he could not otherwise have been truly human unless he had assumed everything pertaining to the reality of human nature. Therefore, together with and in the flesh itself he took a rational soul, which both animated that flesh and endowed it with sensation for life, and which, according to free will, rejected sin and pursued righteousness. By union with the divinity, it was also granted this: that it should indeed do good by spontaneous freedom, but should be wholly unable to turn aside through any necessity or weakness to doing evil.

For blessed Augustine says: “The only Son of God was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, not by the lust of the flesh but solely by God’s gift. In him there was free will, and so much the freer because it could not serve sin.”

Many questions are asked concerning that rational soul, of which this is one: whether it possessed knowledge equal to the divinity. I have discussed that question more fully in another little work entitled *On the Soul of Christ*. Here it is enough to recall only this: just as that soul had united to itself the full and perfect wisdom of God, so through and by that wisdom it was fully and perfectly wise; yet it was not equal to that wisdom in nature [Col. 0383D], because it is very different to be wise by wisdom from being wisdom itself.

For from the moment divinity was joined to humanity, humanity received from divinity by grace everything that divinity possessed by nature, so that according to that ineffable union, everything belonging to humanity was God’s in his humanity, and everything belonging to divinity was man’s in his divinity. Thus we believe that from its first conception the humanity of the Word, in its rational soul, received through the ineffable union of divinity full and perfect wisdom, power, strength, and goodness. We confess that it remained unchangeably in that fullness of power which came from union with divinity, just as it remained inseparably in the union of divinity itself [Col. 0384A].

For God did not will to live among human beings as man in order gradually, through intervals of time, to advance in wisdom or power, acquire merit, and become better than himself. Rather, he willed, by the wisdom and goodness which he always possessed fully and perfectly in his divinity and received fully and perfectly in his humanity once and all at once, to accomplish the dispensation of human salvation according to his ineffable ordering.

Accordingly, what the Evangelist says—that Jesus advanced in age, wisdom, and grace (Luke 3)—is not to be understood as though he became better in himself. Rather, he increasingly revealed to human beings, as the order of time required, the wisdom and grace which he possessed but which had remained hidden. Thus he advanced among human beings when they themselves advanced in their knowledge of him [Col. 0384B]. Before God, however, he advanced in that, by showing himself full of the wisdom and grace of God, he increasingly moved them to praise God the Father, from whom he testified that he possessed this.

Nor should we pass over what some are wont to say, with insufficient reflection, concerning Christ’s merit: namely, that Christ as man could not otherwise have attained the glory of immortality unless he had first merited it by enduring death through his passion. For such people do not observe that God’s being mortal as man was not a matter of necessity but of will. If the first human being could have attained immortality without death, had he wished to preserve himself from the guilt of disobedience, how much more could Christ as man—who was not merely a righteous man without sin but God above humanity—have given his flesh, which he had exalted at conception into fellowship with deity, the glory of incorruption, even had he not willed to humble it to endure passion and death [Col. 0384C]?

For if Christ could not attain the glory of resurrection except by dying, then Christ died for himself and needed to die in order to live. But what does he say? “I go,” he says, “to be sacrificed for you.” Attend to this: “I go to be sacrificed for you.” Why does Christ not say: “I go to be sacrificed for you and for myself”? If he died only for us, where is what you say, that he died for himself? Hear, then: Christ says that he died for us; and if we say that he died for himself, we deny the benefit, because we refuse to give thanks. If he died for himself, what do we owe him? Let him then congratulate himself. He endured it for himself; he received it for himself. Or perhaps for himself and for us? Why, then, was he silent about himself and said “for you”? Perhaps he was ashamed of necessity and gloried in compassion? Then he was ashamed to disclose it, while you are not ashamed to cast it as a reproach.

But they say: “If Christ did not merit the glory of resurrection through enduring his passion, what does the Apostle mean when he says: ‘Christ became obedient to the Father for us unto death, even death on a cross; therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name’ (Phil. 2)?” Clearly, they say, the Apostle states that Christ merited exaltation through the glory of resurrection because he had first not refused to be humbled through obedience in suffering even unto death [Col. 0385A]. If, therefore, he was exalted because he was humbled, then humiliation was the cause of exaltation. Therefore, he merited in humiliation, since in exaltation he received the reward of humiliation. But if he came to glory by merit, how could he have come to it if he had not merited it?

Thus, arguing in this way, they proceed from the premise of error to the conclusion of falsehood. They are deceived because they do not distinguish the meaning of “merit.” And therefore, because they do not dare say that Christ merited nothing—lest they seem to say that the things he did before God had no power or value—they throw themselves headlong into the opposite assertion: that Christ merited glory through suffering, so that, if he had not suffered, he could neither have possessed it nor ought to have possessed it [Col. 0385B].

For if we say that he merited nothing, they think it follows that he did no works of virtue or righteousness. But if we say that he merited, they immediately infer that by acting he obtained something not previously due to him. This is to say either that Christ did no good works or that, by acting, he earned something not previously due to him. But see how foolish this assertion is. What then? Is God unable to do a good work because he cannot earn anything not due to him? Or does he fail to merit by acting because what is due to him is due even if he does not act?

When God bestows benefits upon us and grants gifts of generosity, does he not, in doing these very things, merit from us love and praise for his benefits? Or because he merits, was he not previously worthy, or was he previously less worthy, and did a temporal work increase God’s merit and make God better than himself? Is it not better—indeed, much better—to say that by the eternal goodness which never increased in him, because it was always full and perfect in him, he was always fully and perfectly good and worthy to be praised and loved? And when he performs a temporal work and does good to us, he merits our love and praise; and the merit of the work in him is eternal, although it is displayed to us in time [Col. 0385C].

Nor does he therefore not merit now because he was previously worthy, nor was he previously unworthy because he merits now. There is merit in the work because what is done is a work of goodness; yet the merit itself does not begin with the work or in the worker, since goodness existed in the worker before the work was displayed [Col. 0385D].

Similarly, God as man, who just as in his divinity he had perfect goodness from eternity—indeed, was himself perfect goodness—so in his humanity received full and perfect goodness from his first conception, did not first begin to possess the obedience of suffering and dying when he began to suffer and die. We grant that Christ was exalted by the Father because he became obedient to the Father. We grant that obedience is merit and exaltation a reward. What then? If obedience is merit, did not merit begin when obedience began?

“He became,” it says, “obedient.” Who became so? Christ. In respect of what did he become so? In respect of his humanity. In respect of his humanity he became obedient; in respect of his divinity he could not be subject, in which he was equal. Another Scripture says: “He learned obedience from the things which he suffered” (Heb. 5) [Col. 0386A]. He learned what he did not know. What did he not know? Obedience. He did not know subjection; in that in which he was equal, he could not be inferior. Therefore he learned what he did not know, because through his inferior nature he took into use what he had not experienced in the excellence of deity.

He became obedient. From the moment he became man, he became obedient. From the moment he began to be man, he began to be subject: as man, in dignity; as good, in will. This is merit. If his will was always perfect, his merit too was always perfect—from the moment God began to be man and man began to be God. God began to be man subject, and man began to be God perfect [Col. 0386B]. If God was humbled as much as he could be in man, was man not exalted as much as he could be in God? If God, in becoming man, began to be passible and mortal, then man, in becoming God, began to be righteous, good, and perfect. For as God, when he began to be man, received what was human, so man, when he began to be God, received what was God’s. Therefore, as God is perfect wisdom, power, and goodness, so man, from the moment he was made God, was made perfectly powerful, wise, and good in God.

Or do you suppose that Christ as man first received the full and perfect power of divinity when he says, “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28)? How then had he previously commanded demons, had angels as ministers, and made the elements yield to the nod of his command? Or perhaps, because you read him praying, do you suppose that he obtained by prayers what he had previously been unable to do? “Father,” he says, “glorify your Son [your name].” And behold, a voice came from heaven saying: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (John 12; 17) [Col. 0386C]. You have heard the Son asking and the Father assenting. Do you suppose that he obtained by prayer what he would not have obtained if he had not poured out prayers? Hear what follows: “This voice,” he says, “did not come for my sake, but for yours” (John 12). If the answer was not made for my sake, neither was the request made for my sake. Therefore, as I do not take the Father’s answer as meaning that I was heard, so neither do I pour out prayers to the Father in order to obtain what I cannot obtain. For I can do all things. All that the Father can do, I can do, for I am the Father’s Son. “For whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5). For from the moment I received that I should be man as the Son of God the Father, I received the ability to do all that God the Father can do [Col. 0386D].

You see, therefore, how Christ as man had divine wisdom, power, and goodness because he was, and from the moment he was, the Son of God; and he had them fully and perfectly because he was fully and perfectly so. Or was this not so from the beginning because he did not say this from the beginning? “I did not tell you these things from the beginning” (John 16). Therefore Christ as man was not God from the moment he began to be man, because he did not say this from the moment he began to be man?

Christ was long among human beings as man before he called or proved himself God; and when he began to say this, he said it with great restraint and reverence, lest those who marveled should be scandalized and those who could not comprehend should not receive it. Therefore he presented himself reverently, not precipitately. “Who do men say that the Son of Man is?” he asks (Matt. 16) [Col. 0387A]. He did not proclaim; he questioned. He wished it to be said, but did not wish to say it, lest he appear not to teach truth but seek glory. “Believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14). Consider how modestly he joins himself to God, because he knew that believing a man to be God lay beyond human understanding. Therefore, as man he was still beneath human understanding and had not yet ascended in human faith to be believed as God.

Therefore he said to the doubting and loving woman: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20) [Col. 0387B]. Since he knew himself to be beneath human consciousness and knew that belief in him as equal was distant and foreign to that consciousness, he gradually cherished it, in order to accustom it to truth: that truth might enlighten it and novelty not scandalize it. Thus, as Christ the man lived among human beings, he revealed, according to the dispensation suited to human salvation, over intervals of time what existed in him all at once; and what he possessed fully and perfectly from the beginning, he increasingly showed to human understanding, through certain advances of revelation, that he possessed, as was fitting.

But they say: “If from the beginning merit existed in Christ as man through obedience in accepting the passion, it is thereby already established that, if he had not been going to suffer from the beginning, he could not have had the merit of obedience in suffering. For if the future passion had not existed, no obedience in suffering would have existed. If obedience had not existed, no merit of obedience would have existed.” Thus they try to introduce the necessity of passion in order to obtain the glory of incorruption.

But they insufficiently consider that by the same goodness through which he offered himself freely to obey in suffering—because he willed to suffer—he would have been righteous, good, and worthy of glory even had he not willed to suffer. For if he had not willed to suffer, he would not have been obedient in suffering; yet he would not have been disobedient, because in not willing this he would not have opposed the Father’s will, since the Father himself would likewise not have willed it [Col. 0387D]. For as he was obedient because, being willing, he consented to one who willed, so he undoubtedly would have been obedient if, not willing it, he had consented together with the Father who did not will it. Thus he would always have been obedient even if he had not suffered, and his merit would in no respect have been diminished even if he had not humbled himself to the passion—which he undertook not as a debt but by gracious condescension.

“Yet,” they say, “there is one thing Christ obtained through passion which he certainly could not have had if he had not suffered. By suffering he became for all believers an example of suffering, just as by rising again he became for all who suffer the pattern of glorification. Therefore he gained this by suffering: all who suffer well follow him as master and teacher.” He gained a great thing! What advantage does this bring to him? He goes before, and all follow. Whose good is this? “I found those who were wandering; I went before in order to show the way, and all followed. What does it profit me? I knew the way and could walk by it myself; but there would have been no reason to go forward unless compassion moved me to bring help” [Col. 0388A].

“Foolish and slow of heart to believe: was it not necessary for Christ to suffer and thus enter into his glory?” (Luke 24). Attend: “It was necessary,” he says, “for Christ to suffer and thus enter into his glory.” What is “thus”? By means of suffering: after suffering, glorification. What then? Could Christ not enter glory except by passing through punishment? For what is “it was necessary” except that he could not otherwise? How then was it his glory if it was necessary? And how was it necessary if it was his? If the glory was his, how was it necessary for him to suffer in order to enter it? But it was his for his own sake; it was necessary for our sake.

Christ could indeed, if he had willed, have entered his glory by another way and received it in whatever way he wished, just as, if he wished, he would never have lacked it but would always have possessed it. But for our sake he willed to go through punishment into his glory: by dying, to remove fear of suffering; by rising, to restore hope of glorification. He willed to go by this way because we had to go by this way and could not go by another. We will, but cannot. He could, but did not will it; for had he gone otherwise, he would have arrived, but would not have brought help [Col. 0388B].

Therefore whoever asserts that Christ gained something in his passion in such a way as to maintain that by that passion he obtained some good for his own advantage, benefit, or glory which he could not justly have possessed had he not suffered, plainly subjects Christ to the necessity of suffering. Such a person is also shown to diminish, or rather nullify, the grace of redemption displayed in Christ’s death, since he attempts to prove that the cause of Christ’s passion was not our need but Christ’s own necessity.

Therefore Christ did not merit as though acquiring something not due to him; yet he did merit by accomplishing a work of virtue worthy of recompense. The fact that he himself was already worthy does not mean that the work of virtue afterward performed was not recompensable; nor, conversely, does the statement that he is rewarded for a work of virtue deny that he was worthy even before he acted. Therefore he merited with respect to the virtue of the work, because he was worthy of recompense for the work; yet he did not merit as though he would not have been worthy even had he not acted [Col. 0388D].

The master of a household works in his own vineyard and afterward, when he comes to refresh himself, asks for food; he says that he has well deserved what he is about to receive. But a hired laborer merits differently from a master. The hired laborer merits because payment would not be due to him if he had not worked. Yet even if the master does not work, he eats his own bread because it is his; and he need not work for it, if he wishes, because it is his even without work.

Many things could have been said on these matters, but let these suffice for the present abridgment.

Finally, they ask concerning that rational soul which the Word assumed with flesh into unity of person, whether, as we say that it received from the ineffable union with divinity perfect wisdom, power, and goodness, we should also say that from the beginning, before it put on through the flesh’s immortality the glory of resurrection [Col. 0389A], it possessed from that same union with divinity full blessedness as well. If we grant this, they object that that soul endured passions and pains before the resurrection; and therefore, they say, full blessedness could not exist where punishment and pain existed.

But they do not observe that that soul was united to flesh in one respect and to divinity in another. Insofar as it was united to flesh, it was the life of the flesh. But insofar as it was united to divinity, divinity was its life. Insofar as it was joined to flesh, the flesh itself died when the soul departed. But insofar as it was joined to divinity, even when it departed from flesh it was not separated from divinity. Therefore, while it endured pain for a time in the sensation of the flesh, it always possessed full and perfect joy in fellowship with deity [Col. 0389B]. For where it was perfectly united, it was fully and perfectly made blessed. Where, however, it had less for a time by dispensation, this was afterward supplied in glorification—yet in such a way that the true good it possessed in its higher part was neither restored, because it had never been lost, nor supplied, because from the moment it was given it always remained perfect.

## Chapter VII. Concerning the flesh assumed by the Word: what it was according to passibility, sensation, and affection

Concerning the flesh of the Word, we must first observe that we believe it was so cleansed from conception itself by the operation of the Holy Spirit that the Word himself assumed it wholly free and immune from every sin. Yet the penalty of sin remained, by the will and not the necessity of him who assumed it [Col. 0389C], so that while the Savior suffered these things without guilt, that penalty which in those being saved had been liable to punishment because of guilt might be liberated.

Some inquire how this penalty of passibility or mortality existed in the Savior’s flesh. But it is easy to understand how that flesh, so long as it was in the mass of the human race under the original debt, necessarily bore also the penalty of transgression by which the whole mass was bound. But after it was singularly divided from that whole, so that it was neither in it nor participated with it in its cause, it owed no penalty, because it had no guilt. Therefore, as far as it itself was concerned, it ought not to have endured penalty once it no longer possessed guilt.

Thus the Savior could justly have chosen not to assume in his sinless flesh the penalty of mortality and the weakness of passibility. He could have clothed it from its first conception with the glory of immortality, not only above what we are as mortals, because he was not a sinner, but even above what the first human being was before sin, because he was not to be tested [Col. 0389D].

For the first human being, because he was to be tested, had to be such that he could both sin and not sin, so that both should depend upon will and not necessity. Neither merit for the obedient nor guilt for the disobedient could have existed unless both obedience and transgression had been voluntary. Therefore, because his will was awaiting testing in either direction, possibility in either direction was granted to him. And because he had the possibility of sinning and not sinning, he had to have also the possibility of dying and not dying.

For if immortality had been necessary, even a transgressor and sinner could not have died; and thus disobedience would not have had its due penalty, nor would the sinner ever have recognized himself if, dead within, he always lived outwardly. Again, if he had been mortal by necessity, even while persisting in obedience he would have had to die and would unjustly have been punished without guilt if he died while not sinning. Therefore, because he was to be tested and it awaited determination whether he would persist in obedience, his flesh too was in one respect mortal, since it could die; and in another respect immortal, because it could avoid dying. Thus, because it could die, it would die if he sinned; and likewise, because it could avoid death, it would not die if he persevered in obedience [Col. 0390B].

But Christ as man, because he was perfect from the beginning and was found tested, was not held in expectation of perfection or testing. Therefore, just as he had free choice but not such that he could sin, so also, so far as he himself was concerned, he ought to have possessed immortality such that he could not die at all. Hence it is evident that from the beginning Christ as man was owed not only the immortality which the first human being possessed before transgression, but also that which the second now possesses after the resurrection: namely, that just as through fellowship with deity his spirit was confirmed in truth so that he could not sin, so too through the merit of virtue his flesh should have been confirmed in incorruption so that it could not die [Col. 0390C].

But because sinful flesh could not be liberated from sin’s penalty unless his sinless flesh suffered, he retained in the flesh he assumed the weakness of passibility and mortality by power, endured it by will, and did not suffer it by necessity.

Some have been found to hold erroneous views concerning the experience of passion in Christ’s flesh. They assert that in all the kinds of suffering exhibited in and around that flesh, it underwent indeed an appearance of suffering and pain, but endured no pain or suffering whatever. Yet they do not observe the great absurdity that follows from such an assertion. How could there be true compassion in Christ if there was no true passion? How can the prophet’s saying stand: “Truly he bore our infirmities and carried our pains” (Isa. 53) [Col. 0390D]? If Christ suffered no pain on the cross, why did he so earnestly ask that the cup of suffering might be removed from him? What was the meaning of the blood he sweated, testifying to the anguish of impending death? What was the meaning of Christ himself, explaining both the weakness by which the flesh feared suffering and the will by which the spirit was ready, saying: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26; Mark 14)?

Those, therefore, who deny that there was true suffering in the Savior according to the weakness of the flesh are, so far as they are concerned, shown to deny the redemption accomplished through Christ’s passion.

Others have not feared to utter certain things, not merely false but even dreadful blasphemies, concerning the human affections in Christ [Col. 0391A]—affections which, according to the truth of nature, he assumed with and in humanity. Since the Apostle says, “We do not have a high priest unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one tested in all things” (Heb. 4), they maintain that Christ experienced human affection and even the motions of vices, though without the consent of reason, according to that weakness of concupiscence by which we, who are sinners, because of the original corruption we bear, are accustomed—even against our will—to experience unlawful desires, movements of rising concupiscence, and the pleasurable enticement of tempting vice.

They say that Christ voluntarily endured these motions in his flesh in order that, by resisting them when they tempted him, he might emerge as victor; so that both by overcoming temptations of vice he might acquire for himself the reward of righteousness and might furnish us, placed amid temptation, in himself an example of resistance and victory [Col. 0391B].

But far be it from the Christian mind either to say or to believe that there was in any way in that most holy flesh of the spotless Lamb any provocation of disordered pleasure or unlawful concupiscence. For if we said that there was in it even some root of perverse pleasure or disordered movement of concupiscence, we would surely deny that it was free from every vice. How could it cleanse vice if it bore vice?

For a disordered motion arising from the weakness of concupiscence, arising together with the very corruption from which it originates, is not only a penalty but also a fault. Yet in the baptized it is not imputed unto condemnation, because it is excused through the grace of new regeneration. As the Apostle says: “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8) [Col. 0391C]. Yet this corruption does not receive from sacramental grace the status of being no fault at all, but of not being condemnable. For if it were no fault whatever, it would have no need to be excused, since it ought not to be imputed.

Therefore we truly say that Christ assumed, with the assumption of flesh, only that weakness of human nature which is a penalty; but we firmly affirm that he admitted in no way that weakness which is a penalty in such a manner that it is also guilt. For we do not wish to call him conqueror of vices in such a way as to say that he at any time bore and experienced the very things by which he conquered vices. Therefore he consented to be weakened by penalty alone, so that those who were sick in both guilt and penalty might first be justified from guilt and afterward liberated from penalty [Col. 0391D].

## Chapter VIII. How the statement “He was conceived of the Holy Spirit” is to be understood
Since, as was said above, the Father and the Holy Spirit together with the Son himself effected the incarnation of the Son, it is rightly asked why Sacred Scripture mentions him as conceived specifically by the Holy Spirit. These matters, indeed, like the other things said of him, are approached with hesitation by human understanding; but the devotion of faith, venturing further in accordance with a pure conscience, inquires confidently. First, therefore, we must ask how it ought to be understood that the blessed Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit.

For we know—and all have now learned through the most common experience of nature—that when a woman is said to have conceived by a man, this means nothing other than that she has received, through the union of flesh, the substance of flesh for generating flesh. This substance of flesh, conveyed from the man’s flesh through that bodily union, becomes one flesh with the woman’s flesh, so that what is to be born, truly taking its origin from the substance of both, may be generated from him through her, and also from her. Therefore a woman conceives by a man when, through bodily union, she receives from the man’s flesh seed for generating flesh. Nor does she conceive anything other than what he is from whom she conceives; and she who conceives herself gives birth to what she conceives.

What, then, shall we say? Did the Holy Spirit pour into the virgin’s womb from his own substance the seed of offspring? How could a spiritual substance provide the seed of flesh? Or perhaps what was conceived was not seed of flesh, although what was born was flesh? What shall we say? How did Mary conceive by the Holy Spirit? And if she conceived by the Holy Spirit, how was the Holy Spirit not Christ’s Father?

All these things require serious consideration, lest in a difficult and very obscure matter human understanding presume something beyond its capacity. We ought not to doubt these matters because they are obscure, nor rashly define anything because they are to be believed. Let us ask, therefore, what Mary conceived. Either she did not conceive flesh and did not give birth to flesh; or, if she gave birth to flesh, she conceived flesh. For what she conceived, that she gave birth to. But how could that which is not flesh provide flesh? Or how could flesh give birth to that which is not flesh? Let us consider how this perplexing inquiry, or method of inquiry, may be understood soundly and fittingly.

First, in the conception carried out according to the usual and customary operation of nature, let us observe how the work of that same nature is completed. In parents who generate carnally and, through the union of flesh, fashion from flesh the flesh that is to be born, nature on both sides supplies substance for the offspring being formed, so that from the flesh of both may proceed that flesh which is to be fashioned in the flesh of one alone. Yet this contribution which nature pays, as though it were a certain debt established by the Creator for completing the formation of the human body, is required of it without any necessity or compulsion whatever: unless nature is inclined to give it by love alone—by what I may call spontaneous charity—it does not give it.

For nothing other than love alone can draw this debt from nature. But when nature has been persuaded by spontaneous charity, then, certainly, from each side it willingly and gladly comes to the aid of the other in completing the work. Whatever is violently seized from one unwilling is shown to be altogether unsuitable and ineffective for producing such an effect. Love alone, therefore, can persuade nature and, as it were, compel it willingly to sow offspring. In the woman, the love of the man, and in the man, the love of the woman, customarily accomplish the same thing: because in either one alone nature is not sufficient for itself, each comes to the aid of the other through love, so that what neither could accomplish independently may be accomplished by each together with the other.

Thus the seed of human offspring, to be formed by the woman alone, is conceived although it is sown jointly by man and woman. As has already been said, nature works this in the woman through love for the man, and in the man through love for the woman. Accordingly, a woman is said to conceive only by a man, although she receives from both herself and the man that by which she is made fruitful. And rightly she conceives by the man alone, because what she conceives is, in one respect, received from the man’s flesh, and in another, supplied from herself through love for the man. Therefore she conceives by the man not merely what she receives from the man, but also what she receives from herself through love for the man.

[Col. 0393B] We have wished to state this beforehand because it is said that Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit. Mary therefore conceived by the Holy Spirit, not because she received from the substance of the Holy Spirit the seed of offspring, but because, through the love and operation of the Holy Spirit, nature supplied from the virgin’s flesh the substance for the divine offspring. For because love for the Holy Spirit burned uniquely in her heart, the power of the Holy Spirit worked wonders in her flesh. His love admitted no companion into her heart; his operation in her flesh had no example.

The virgin therefore conceived only that which she received from her own flesh through the love and operation of the Holy Spirit; and from that flesh alone, without the admixture of male seed, she gave birth to a son. Thus fleshly desire did not effect conception in the virgin: she neither received seed from a man’s flesh nor conceived from her own flesh through love for a man, but through the love and operation of the Holy Spirit. Nor should the Holy Spirit for this reason be called Christ’s Father, because his love effected the virgin’s conception.
