For he did not bestow on the virgin from his own essence the seed of offspring; rather, through his love and power, he supplied to the virgin from her own flesh the substance required.

Christ, therefore, was born of a virgin because he received the substance of his flesh from the virgin’s flesh; and he was conceived by the Holy Spirit because the virgin herself conceived him from her own flesh alone, without the admixture of male seed, through the operation and love of the Holy Spirit. Hence the angel says to the virgin who was to give birth: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1). For the Holy Spirit came upon the virgin so that, through his operation, Christ’s flesh might be formed from the virgin’s flesh; and the power of the Most High overshadowed her so that, while supplying the substance of flesh, she might not employ fleshly concupiscence.

## Chapter IX. On the union of the Word, soul, and flesh

It is also asked whether the Word assumed flesh and soul simultaneously, or flesh before soul, or soul before flesh. But it is most truly and beyond every doubt believed that, from the moment God assumed man, he assumed the whole man. For from the moment he assumed man, just as man was God, so God was true man. He would not have been true man in flesh alone or in soul alone, for man is both flesh and soul. Therefore, when he assumed man, he assumed both at once.

He assumed flesh and soul—that is, man—nature, not person. For he did not assume a man who was a person; rather, he assumed man into a person. He assumed man because he assumed human flesh and a human soul. But he did not assume a person because that flesh and that soul, before being united to the Word in a person, were not united as a person. There was one union, and it was union into one: of Word, flesh, and soul. Neither Word and flesh first, nor Word and soul first, nor soul and flesh first; but Word, soul, and flesh simultaneously.

Yet the Word was a person before this union, because the Son existed and was a person, just as the Father was a person and the Holy Spirit was a person. The Word was an eternal person, just as the Word was eternal and the Son was eternal. Nor did the Word begin to be a person when he began to be man; rather, he assumed man so that man might begin to be a person, and no person other than that which assumed him. Therefore the personal Word assumed man—not a person, but a nature—so that he who assumed and that which was assumed might be one person in the Trinity.

For the assumption of man did not make a quaternity; the Trinity remained, because the assumed man, from the moment he began to be God, did not begin to be a person other than the person who assumed him. Whoever therefore denies that the assumed man is a person denies that man was assumed into a person. For if he were never to become this, he would have been assumed to it in vain.

[Col. 0394C] Now, therefore, the assumed man is a person, and not another person, but that very person by whom he was assumed; for the one assuming and the one assumed are one person. God is man: this is true because of his humanity. Man is God: this is true because of his divinity. God assumed humanity; man received divinity. God is man because of the humanity which he assumed and possesses; and man is God because of divinity. This is not said of two beings but of one, because God and man are not two but the one Jesus Christ.

But you say, “How is he one?” Tell me what kind of union it is, and I shall tell you how he is one. If the union of God and man is truly ineffable, then God and man are ineffably not two, but one. Yet God and man are by no means two, but one Jesus Christ. He who is God is himself man, and he who is man is himself God: not one and another, but one and the same.

What does “man” signify? Nature. Whom does “man” signify? A person. If you ask what “man” signifies, it signifies something different from “God.” For “man” signifies humanity, and “God” signifies divinity. If you ask whom “man” signifies, it signifies the same one whom “God” signifies, because he is both man and God. What is man? If you ask about nature: body and soul. I speak correctly, because this is man; this is what it is to be human, because this makes a human being. What is man? If you ask about person: God. Why is man God? Because humanity is personally united to divinity.

The nature of God is divinity; the nature of man is humanity. Divinity is not humanity; nevertheless God is man. The natures are different; the person is one. Because the nature is united, the person is one; and because the person of God and man is one, God and man are one. Therefore what God does, man does; and what man does, God does, because God and man are not two but one.

“No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven” (John 3). He spoke on earth and testified that he was in heaven. For he was in both places: on earth through humanity, in heaven through divinity. He who was in heaven was the same one who was on earth: through humanity on earth, and only on earth; through divinity in heaven and on earth. “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2). It is wonderful: man ruled in heaven, and God died on the cross. If man, situated on earth through humanity, could be in heaven through divinity, then God, reigning in heaven through divinity, could also die on earth through humanity.

But you say, “How could God die? How did God, who is immortal, die?” I knew that there would be persons who would say this: “God could not die; man died; God did not die.” Why, then, do you deny that God died? “Because,” they say, “divinity cannot die.” If God did not die because he did not die according to divinity, then neither was God born of the virgin, because according to divinity he was not born of the virgin; nor did God live among human beings, because according to divinity he did not live among human beings; and likewise all the other things which the Savior did in the flesh.

If, therefore, God did not do these things, who was it that did them? We thought that God did all these things. You say that God did not do them. Say, then: who was it that did them? “Christ,” they say, “did all these things.” Therefore Christ did them and God did not. Take care lest it be said to you: if Christ did these things and God did not, then Christ was not God. “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not deal wickedly with my prophets” (Ps. 104). You touch Christ and deal wickedly with the prophet. You do not say that Christ is not God; yet you say something from which it would follow that Christ is not God. Therefore you touch Christ. You do not deny him openly, but secretly kill him.

“We do not,” they say, “deny or kill him. But we say that God was not dead because Christ did not die according to divinity.” Then say that when Christ walked on earth, the Son of Man was not in heaven, because according to humanity he was not in heaven. But if man was not thereby absent from heaven when Christ walked on earth—because according to humanity he was not in heaven—neither was God thereby not dead when Christ hung upon the cross, because according to divinity he was not dead. What then? If something is not according to this respect or that respect, does it therefore not exist? If it is not according to one respect, nevertheless it is according to another.

Do you want authority? Hear the lamp, if you do not believe the light. Augustine says: “If God died on account of man, will not man live with God? Will not the mortal one, on whose account he who lives eternally died, live eternally?” But how did God die? From what did he die? Can God die? He received from you that by which he might die for you.

Again he says: “The Word was crucified, but was not changed into man.” And again: “Therefore through that whereby he was man God died; and through that whereby he was God man was raised.” And: “Whatever man suffered cannot be said not to have been suffered by God, because God assumed man; but he was not changed into man.”

Consider further. Who was it who said, “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8)? Was it not man? Who was it who said, “Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John 17)? Was it not man? Therefore man truly said, “Before Abraham came to be, I am.” Therefore man truly said, “Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world existed, with you.”

What? Does this scandalize you? Does this move you as it moved those who said, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” (John 8). Why not? Did not those who said this also speak truly? A little earlier the Evangelist had said that Jesus, when he began, was “about thirty years old” (Luke 3). Only a short time had elapsed from then to this point. Forty complete years had not yet passed; much less had fifty. Or perhaps was the one who said that he was thirty years old speaking truly because that was his age, while those who said that he was not yet fifty spoke untruly because that was greater? Whoever named thirty years did not deny what was greater; but those who did not believe that he had fifty years allowed much less what was greater.

What, then? When the Evangelist named thirty years, did he intend to determine for us nothing certain about the extent of Jesus’ age—that is, of Christ the man—beyond which our thought might proceed? If he was more advanced in age than this, why did the Evangelist not say more? But he was not more advanced in respect to that in which he had this age. Jesus was thirty years old; man was thirty years old, because his human age was thirty years. Thirty years, and no more, had elapsed since he began to be man. Therefore man was thirty years old and no more.

And what then? If man was only thirty years old, was not God likewise only thirty years old, he who was man only thirty years old? How recent was God! How small an age God had! Truly small, because he was made small. A small age in the little one; great eternity in the great one. Yet he had no more time where he was temporal. For where he was eternal, he was neither thirty years old, nor twenty, nor ten, nor five, nor one. There he was not yearly but eternal. Where, however, he was temporal, he was no more than this.

Where he was eternal, what shall I say? Was he more? That says too little. For time cannot in any way approach comparison with eternity. Therefore he was eternal, and he was only thirty years old; he began in time, and he was before times. In respect to that in which he began in time, he was made man; and in respect to that in which he was before times, he was God the Maker. And though he began to be man in time, he did not begin as though he had not existed before. Likewise, though he was made man, he was not made as though he had not existed before.

For this reason the Catholic faith condemned those who said that Christ was a creature: although Christ began to exist in time, he did not begin altogether to exist, because above times and before times he, the same one, was always God. To be a creature is to be something from nothing; that is, to be something and previously to have been nothing. But not everyone who begins to be something thereby begins to exist, because he begins to be something; just as one who ceases to be something does not thereby cease to exist because he ceases to be something. For something does not cease to exist in such a way as to become nothing, but only so that what it ceases to be no longer is.

Thus not everyone who begins to be something begins to be something as though beginning to exist in order to be something; rather, he begins to be something which he was not before, so that now he is. Thus Christ, when he began to be man, began to be something; nevertheless, he did not begin to be something as though he had previously not been something. For before he was what he at some point began to be, he was something which always was and never began to be.

Accordingly, God was made man, and yet God is not a creature. For what he was made, he was made in respect to that which he assumed temporally and had not always possessed; but he did not receive in time that which he had always possessed. Yet after God was made man and man God, God and man were one and not two. And because of that ineffable union by which God and man were one, just as God truly showed himself temporal through his humanity, so man truthfully proclaimed himself to have existed before times through his divinity.

If eternal God was at one time only thirty years old by reason of humanity, why was temporal man not likewise eternal by reason of divinity? “Then,” they say, “man existed from eternity; man created the world; and man was before man existed.” You are children and have not yet been able to free yourselves from the swaddling-clothes of infancy. The senses within you have not yet grown through exercise, so that you no longer need milk but solid food. For what are the wrappings of words except certain coverings of understanding? So long as human understanding is wrapped in them, the eye of the heart is never perfectly opened to the light of truth.

You ask whether man existed before times, and I ask you whether God began in time. If the eternal became temporal, did the temporal not become eternal? Or perhaps God was in time by reason of humanity because he was man when man was in time; but man was not before times by reason of divinity because, when God was before times, man was not yet God? Perhaps there is some rational basis for avoiding such expressions; provided, nevertheless, that the integrity of Christian faith is preserved, so that you believe him to be one and the same: man in time by reason of his humanity, and God before times by reason of his divinity.

Accordingly, he himself truly said that he came in time as man and that he existed before times as God. But when he said both this and that, it was not one person saying one thing and another saying the other; rather, he spoke according to one respect and another. What God said, man said; and what man said, God said, because man and God, God and man, were one.

When I say “man,” I signify human nature, that is, soul and flesh. When I say “God,” I signify divine nature, that is, the divinity of the Word. Again, when I say “man,” I signify the person composed of soul and flesh. Again, when I say “God,” I signify the person in divinity. “Man,” with reference to nature, denotes no more than soul and flesh; nor, with reference to person, more than one from soul and flesh. “God,” with reference to nature, denotes no more than divinity; nor, with reference to person, more than one in divinity. Yet in Christ the person from soul and flesh and the person in divinity are not two persons, but one person.

What is the nature of man? Humanity. What is the nature of God? Divinity. From humanity comes man; from divinity comes God. That he is man comes from soul and flesh; this is his being, because this is his nature. That he is man comes from what belongs to man. That he is God comes from what belongs to God. Indeed, that he is God comes from divinity: this is his being, because this is his nature. Therefore that he is God comes from what is his own; and that he is man from what belongs to man.

Accordingly, because God is man from what belongs to man, and man is God from what belongs to God, certainly God is man and man is God. Again, because man is God from no one other than the God who is man, and God is man from no one other than the man who is God, God and man are not another and another, but the same. Yet man is in his own condition, while God is in the same man by condescension; and God is in his own nature, while man is in the same God by grace.

Thus in Christ we say that human nature is one thing and divine nature another; but we do not say that man is one person and God another. Rather, God and man are the one Jesus Christ. What is Jesus? Savior. What is Christ? Anointed. Jesus denotes one thing and Christ another; yet Jesus does not signify someone other than Christ, because Jesus Christ is one.

Augustine says: “Jesus has one signification and Christ another, although Jesus Christ our Savior is one. Jesus, however, is his proper name, just as Moses is called by his proper name, and Elijah, and Abraham. Thus ‘Jesus’ is, as it were, our Lord’s proper name. But ‘Christ’ is the name of a mystery, as when he is called prophet or priest. Read Augustine’s sermon on the Epistle of John; there you will find this.”

The same author, in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, says: “He who made us believe in Christ made for us the Christ in whom we believe.” Augustine therefore says this: “Would you then hear still more fully how, or in what respect, the Lord Jesus Christ was made or unmade?”

Ambrose, in the book which he wrote *On the Trinity*, says: “We say, therefore, that he was made man, and that this must be referred to his humanity. For elsewhere you have: ‘Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh’ (Rom. 1). Certainly, according to the flesh, he was made from the seed of David. But as God he was born from God before the ages. Yet ‘was made’ is not always referred to creation. For it is written: ‘Lord, you have become a refuge for us’ (Ps. 90).” And shortly afterward: “Therefore, if ‘was made’ is frequently referred to something relative and not to nature, then ‘created’ also is referred to a purpose.”

From this we understand that the passage written concerning the Lord’s incarnation—“The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works” (Prov. 8)—signifies that the Lord Jesus was created from a virgin for the redemption of the Father’s works.

The same author, in the same work, says: “Paul forbids me to serve a creature, and exhorts me to serve Christ. Therefore Christ is not a creature. Paul says, ‘A servant of Christ Jesus’ (Rom. 1), and he is a good servant who recognizes his Lord. He forbids us to serve a creature. How, then, would he himself serve Christ if he thought Christ a creature?”

See, then, how he affirms that Christ was both made and created in a certain respect, while nevertheless denying that Christ is a creature. The same author also testifies in the same book that Christ is not an adoptive Son but the natural Son, saying: “We are called sons by adoption; he is so by the truth of nature. How, then, could he who made all things from nothing be from nothing?” Thus we must shape the course of faith according to the testimonies of Scripture, so that we may join to right belief the purity of sincere confession.

## Chapter X. On the separation of soul and flesh in Christ

[Col. 0399C]

Some have thought that, in death, divinity withdrew from Christ the man, and that the death of the man was nothing other than the separation of divinity from his flesh. For they find certain words in which this seems to be said; and, having found them, they cling to the letter of this kind of writing without attaining to the spirit.

The blessed Ambrose also seems to say something of the kind in his exposition of that psalm which the Lord himself, in his Passion, showed to have been written concerning himself, saying: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27; Ps. 22; Mark 15). On this passage Ambrose says: “The man cries out, being about to die through separation from divinity”; and other arguments are advanced as though to prove this: namely, that God is life, and where life was, death could not be. Therefore, unless life had first departed, death could not have come.

For it is written that Jesus, crying out with a loud voice, said: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” The man cries out that he has been forsaken by God and complains that God has departed from him, as though he is therefore about to die because God has withdrawn from him. Therefore Ambrose said: “The man cries out, being about to die through separation from divinity.”

But observe what is being said. If the matter concerns that separation of divinity for which Christ the man cried out on the cross, that separation had already taken place. For he declared himself not as about to be forsaken, but as already forsaken, saying, “My God, why have you forsaken me?” If, therefore, the matter concerns that separation of divinity, God had already departed when the man, hanging on the cross, cried aloud that he had been forsaken by God. Yet Christ was still alive in the flesh when God had thus departed from him.

Let them answer, then. If death could not exist unless life had first departed, how could life remain after life had departed? For God had already thus departed, and Christ still hung alive on the cross when he complained that he had been forsaken. If, therefore, they say that in this withdrawal of God and this separation of divinity the union of person which existed between divinity and humanity was dissolved, then there was a time when Christ was still a living man and was not God.

But who would say this? Who, in agreement with sound faith, would not recoil from attributing to God the claim that he accompanied the assumed man as far as death, but abandoned him at death, when the greater danger was at hand and greater help was needed? Why, then, does he so strongly reproach hired servants because, when the wolf comes, they flee and abandon the sheep whom they ought to guard, when he himself abandoned at the wolf’s coming that one sheep and that lamb—the son of the virgin ewe—whom he had assumed not only to guard but also to glorify?

The sheep, secure in the shepherd before the wolf’s coming, did not fear, saying: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14). But now, abandoned by the shepherd, he cries out in complaint and lamentation, “Why have you forsaken me?” He was man alone and not God; and God was no longer man, because God had now withdrawn from man; nor was man God, because while he still hung alive upon the cross he had been forsaken by God. Thus divinity had already withdrawn from man not merely in death but before death, when man, still mourning that God had withdrawn from him and therefore—so these people say—that he himself was not God, was still alive.

Who would say this? “How,” they ask, “is it to be understood that Christ cries out that he has been forsaken by God, and that Scripture affirms that man cried out, being about to die through separation from divinity, if God had not withdrawn from man?”

What then? Could divinity not have forsaken humanity in one respect—namely, insofar as it did not defend it for a time but exposed it to the power of its enemies—and not have forsaken it in another respect, insofar as it did not then depart from it in the presence of majesty? He gave it over to them, but did not forsake it. He gave it over to them, but did not forsake it to itself. He forsook it because he did not provide help; but he did not forsake it because he did not withdraw his presence. He withdrew protection, but did not sever the union. He separated himself outwardly, so as not to be present for defense against enemies; but he did not separate himself inwardly, so as to fail it in the union of person. Thus he forsook it so as not to help, but did not forsake it by withdrawing.

I travel along a road; you go with me; we walk together. I am secure, as though I have a friend with me. My enemy comes and, rushing upon one who is unarmed and unable to resist, wounds me with blows. Seeing me struck, you are unmoved; you endure it patiently and stand beside me as though unconcerned about my wounds. And I say, “Why have you forsaken me?” You still stand beside me, and yet I complain that you have departed from me. You are near in place but far in help. You were near when you showed yourself present in love; you became far when, as I stood amid dangers, you withheld compassion from me.

Thus humanity cried out in the Passion that it had been forsaken by divinity, because divinity had granted it over to the power of enemies to be crucified, as it is written: “You would have no authority over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19). Yet, because he endured that death hanging on the cross not for his own sin but for our redemption, he asks why he has been forsaken—not murmuring against God on account of punishment, but, being one who knew no sin, seeking the reason in order to show us his innocence amid punishment.

## Chapter XI. That Christ, when the soul was separated from the flesh, was both a person and God and man
[Col. 0401B] It is written: “And Jesus, crying with a loud voice, gave up the spirit” (Matt. 27). Who gave it up? Jesus. What did he give up? His spirit. To whom did he give it up? To the Father. Neither did the Jew cast it out, nor did the Father draw it forth; but he himself gave it up willingly. It was not taken from him by force, but given freely: “I have power,” he says, “to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again” (John 10). That soul itself is the spirit itself. Therefore the soul was sent forth by the power of the one dying, not by the violence of the one killing. The soul was sent forth. He sent it forth whose it was. From where did he send it? From the flesh. Where did he send it? To the Father. The soul departed, and the flesh died. Christ died because Christ’s flesh died. Just as God died because the humanity of God died, so man died because the flesh of man died. The flesh alone died, and by the flesh [Col. 0401C] the man whose flesh it was died; God also died, because God was man.

The separation of the soul was the death of the flesh. The flesh alone died, from which the soul—its life—was separated. The soul did not die, nor did the divinity die, but the flesh alone died, because the soul was separated from it. The soul descended into hell; the flesh lay in the tomb; the divinity remained with both. For flesh and soul, when separated, could not destroy the person which, even when united, they had not made. The Word was an eternal person. Nor did he begin to be a person when he took soul and flesh into his person. He took soul and flesh so that they might be a person in him, not so that they might make him a person. Therefore, because soul and flesh received being a person in him when they began to be united to the person of the Word, they always [Col. 0401D] remained one and the same person with the Word, because afterward they never withdrew from the Word or from one another in division.

Therefore the Word was an eternal person on account of the eternal divinity; and that very person was God on account of the divinity, and man on account of the humanity united to the Word. Thus Christ the person descended into hell, but according to the soul alone, because the soul alone descended into hell. And Christ the person lay in the tomb according to the flesh alone, because the flesh alone lay in the tomb. And Christ’s person was everywhere according to the divinity alone, because the divinity alone was everywhere. Neither did the soul lie in the tomb, nor did the flesh descend into hell, nor was either flesh or soul everywhere. The body alone lay in the [Col. 0402A] tomb, and because of this part of the man, Christ the man lay in the tomb.

Certain writings say this: when Christ is said to have lain in the tomb, the whole is put for the part; for not the whole man lay in the tomb, but only one part of the man, the body. Attend carefully here. Not the whole man, but a part of the man. Which man? Christ. The whole man: the whole Christ. A part of the man: a part of Christ. Christ lay in the tomb: the whole is put for the part. Therefore the whole did not lie there, but a part. What is the whole? Christ. What is the part? The body. Therefore either Christ did not lie in the tomb—or, if Christ is said to have lain in the tomb, then this is a figure of speech in which the whole is put for the part and the part is understood under the whole. Therefore neither did Christ truly descend into hell, but only a part of Christ, the soul alone.

This incurs a certain difficulty. Such statements are indeed suspect to Catholic truth, which neither accepts nor approves the assertion that Christ did not truly lie in the tomb or did not truly descend into hell. For what follows? If he did not truly lie in the tomb because only the body lay in the tomb, and did not truly descend into hell because only the soul descended into hell, then neither did he truly die, because the flesh alone died, not the soul or the divinity. What, then, does it mean that, when Christ is said to have lain in the tomb, the whole is put for the part? Or is it one thing for the whole to be put for the part, and another for the whole to act in the part?

For when the whole is put for the part, the whole itself is named but is not understood; rather, only its part is understood, for which it is put. [Col. 0402C] But when the whole is said to act in the part, the very thing spoken of is understood; nor is something else understood in place of what is spoken of, although it is understood to act according to something else—that is, according to a part. For when the whole acts in the part, the whole truly acts precisely because the whole is with the part and the part is in the whole, when both whole and part act. When they are together, they can act together. Thus the action of the part is rightly called the action of the whole when the part that acts belongs to the whole and is within the whole. But when the whole has been destroyed and is no longer whole, what the part alone does outside the whole is not properly called the action of the whole.

What then? Shall we say that, when Christ’s flesh died, Christ truly died because the man endured the passion in his part; but, when Christ’s body lay in the tomb, Christ did not truly lie there because the very part that lay there was by then separated from the whole? Thus Christ truly died, but was not truly buried. Far be it! Rather, he truly died and was truly buried; he truly descended into hell and truly ascended into heaven. How then is the whole put for the part when Scripture says that Christ lay in the tomb? What is the whole, and what is the part? For the whole is spoken of in relation to parts, and parts are referred to the whole.

Perhaps, then, you suppose that three things—divinity, soul, and flesh—composed Christ, and that Christ is some whole composed of three parts: divinity, flesh, and soul. Is the Word, then, a third part of Christ? Far be it! For the Word is not a part of Christ; the Word himself is Christ. He is wholly Word, just as he is wholly God—not one half of Christ Word and the other half man, but wholly Word and wholly man, because he is himself both God and man. Do you understand what I say? If you do not understand, nevertheless believe. It can be believed if it cannot be understood.

Yet this is so: Christ himself was both God and man. Nor was the Word a third part of Christ, nor was Christ some whole composed, as it were, of flesh, soul, and Word as parts, because the whole himself was the Word. Where, then, was there a whole composed of parts? Where parts were in the whole and the whole consisted of parts. But divinity was not a part, so that the whole composed from it might be greater than it; nor was a part in it, so that something in it might be less than it. [Col. 0403B] In humanity alone we find parts, and the whole consists of parts. Man is a certain whole consisting of two parts, soul and flesh. These are the two parts of man, and in these two parts the whole man consists. Divine nature is simple; human nature is twofold. Therefore the parts of man are two, because in human nature there are two things: soul and flesh. Where these two are, there is the whole man. Where one of them is, there is a part of man.

For this reason the Word assumed the whole man: because he assumed all that belonged to man, soul and flesh. But in the tomb the whole man did not lie, but only a part of man, namely the flesh. Likewise, the whole man did not descend into hell, but only a part of man, namely the soul. For if the whole man were said to have lain in the tomb, it would certainly be denied that the soul had departed from the dead flesh. Likewise, if the whole man were said to have descended into hell, it would necessarily be affirmed that the flesh descended there together with the soul.

Accordingly, only a part of man lay in the tomb, and not the whole man. Yet when Christ is said to have lain in the tomb, this is proved true because of the flesh alone that lay there. For when Christ is said to have been in the tomb, the whole man is said to have been in the tomb, because when Christ is named, the whole man is named; for the whole man is Christ. And it is true that Christ lay in the tomb, although the whole man did not lie in the tomb, even though Christ was the whole man. For Christ was the whole man because soul and flesh [Col. 0403D] were united to the Word in one person. Christ, however, truly lay in the tomb because his flesh lay there. And therefore the Word as person could not be absent where the flesh was, since it was personally united to that Word.

Thus Christ was in the tomb when his flesh was there, and yet the whole man was not there, because soul and flesh were not there together, but the flesh alone was there. Now when “man” is called man, and when the person is called man, this is said on account of the whole man and on account of everything that belongs to man. I am not now speaking of the fact that *homo* (“man”) is named from the earth (*humus*) from which a part was taken; rather, when “man” is said and the person is understood as all that man is, what belongs to man is spoken of from the whole.

But it is one thing when man is said to be what man is, and another when he is said to be what is in man. [Col. 0404A] When he is said to be man, this is said on account of the whole of man—that is, soul and flesh. But when he is said to be what is in man, this is said on account of a part of man, namely the soul alone or the flesh alone. When man is called man, the person is named; when he is called what is in man, that which is in the person is named.

Thus man is called wise, though this is not said on account of all that man is, but on account of the part that is in man; for wisdom is not in soul and flesh but in the soul alone. Likewise, when man is called white or black, this is not said on account of all that man is, but on account of the part that is in man; for whiteness and blackness are not in soul and flesh but in the flesh alone. And even if the whole man is perhaps called this, he is not so called as though this were all that belongs to man, but because all that ought to be this in man is so. For the whole man is called white when his entire body is white: not because everything that belongs to man is white, but because everything in man that can be white is white.

Thus also, when Christ is called man, he is so called on account of all that man is, namely soul and flesh. But when he is called mortal, dead, or buried, he is so called on account of a part of man, namely the flesh alone; for the flesh alone was mortal, when it bore the corruption of passibility, and the flesh alone was dead, when on the cross it hung without its soul, its life.

And it alone was buried when the soul was not with it in the tomb as it lay dead. Yet Christ [Col. 0404C] himself truly did all that the flesh alone did, because through his divinity he was personally present in the flesh and with the flesh that did this. Likewise, when Christ is said to have rejoiced in spirit, or to have had an emotion, desire, or fear, he is understood to have had this according to the soul alone; for the soul alone had it, and he truly had it through the soul which was personally united to his divinity. For that soul possessed, according to the natural affections with which it was assumed, desire and joy, sorrow and fear of the passion for its flesh. All these were reasonably admitted for a time, by the power of the one acting and the will of the one suffering.

And when he feared the punishment of his flesh and recoiled from its pains, he acted according to natural affection, by which no one hates his own flesh—though he can sometimes endure its suffering for a rational cause, he can never love its evil. Thus in Christ, according to the natural affection which the soul had in and for the flesh, there was a will by which he is truly said to have dreaded and refused death, pain, and passion. Yet the higher will of the spirit, ready to obey the Father’s command, directed this will. For the will of the spirit in Christ, situated as though in a middle place, governed by reason the subject will of the flesh and subjected itself through obedience to the higher will of the Father, saying: “Not my will, but yours be done” (Luke 22).

Thus what is said of Christ [Col. 0405A] is sometimes said according to the person, sometimes according to that which was in the person. Likewise, what is said according to man is sometimes said according to man himself, sometimes according to that which was in man. But in the nature of divinity, where there is no multiplicity or diversity, the person and that which is in the person cannot be different. In humanity alone, where multiplicity is found, one thing is shown to be the whole and another the part. The whole is the person; the part is in the person. The whole is soul and flesh; the part is the soul alone or the flesh alone.

Scripture says: “As the rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ.” Consider the comparison. It is correct to say, “Soul and flesh are man”; and again it is correct to say, “Man is a person.” And again, it is correct to say, “Soul and flesh are one person.” But I cannot likewise say, “The soul alone is man,” or “The flesh alone is man.” Consequently I cannot say, “The soul alone is a person,” or “The flesh alone is a person.”

In Christ, however, I can say, “God and man are Christ”; and similarly, “God is Christ,” and again, “Man is Christ.” Again I can say, “God and man are one person”; likewise, “God is a person,” and “Man is a person.” What sort of comparison, then, is this when it is said: “As rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ”? For if the likeness is complete, why is it said of Christ, “God is Christ” and “man is Christ,” but not likewise said of man that, as flesh and soul together are man, so the flesh alone by itself is man or the soul alone by itself is man? Or why, as in man soul and flesh together are called man, while neither the soul alone nor the flesh alone is called man, should God and man together be called Christ, in such a way that neither man alone nor God alone is called Christ?

There is great entanglement of speech in these matters. A person labours over what belongs to himself, who can scarcely understand anything except what, and according to what, he knows how to say. Such people inquire every day what ought to be said, and rarely what ought to be believed. They ask whether this expression is good, whether that expression should be received, whether that expression should be approved. They are occupied with the coinage of words; a great multitude [Col. 0405D] of expressions rushes together, and there is endless perplexity, because they wish to derive the judgment of the spirit from the letter, rather than the judgment of the letter from the spirit. For they do not know that the spirit ought to judge the letter, not the letter the spirit. As it is written: “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2).

Therefore they labour in judging speech because they do not possess the spirit for understanding. They wish to possess judgment and refuse to possess the spirit, without which they cannot judge rightly. Therefore they labour in speaking and produce one thing after another to be said about that which ought to be understood as one. They ask what a person is and then bring forward a definition of person, such as has been made and approved by some: “A person is an individual substance of rational nature.” Let us say, then, according to our level, that this is what a person is. According to our level, the definition of person is good. Let us speak thus according to our level. For what is above us cannot be spoken at all. It is unspeakable because it is incomprehensible.

Let us therefore say according to our level: a person is an individual substance of rational nature. What is rational substance except rational spirit? For rational substance properly is spiritual substance, which alone is capable of reason, because reason can exist in it alone. For if man is called a rational substance, he is not so called on account of all that he is, but on account of the soul alone, which is properly called rational substance. Man is rational only according to the soul, because he possesses a rational soul. But the soul is rational in itself because it possesses in itself reason or rationality, that is, the capacity for reason.

Thus rational substance properly and in itself is nothing but rational spirit, which is truly individual both because it is simple in nature, having no composition of parts, and because it is of a simple nature containing no plurality of the same property. This rational spirit, then, is properly called person: distinct in number and discerning by reason. Thus some have wished *persona* to be so called as though it meant “sounding through itself” (*per se sonans*) and “discerning singly,” so that, insofar as it is distinct in number, we understand it as existing through itself; and insofar as it discerns by reason, as sounding, pronouncing, or judging.

Accordingly, by this definition we properly say that rational spirit is a person, discerning itself through itself. There is no great question or ambiguity of understanding here, where that which is whole is one. But in man the same account does not apply, where there are indeed two things, yet not two persons, but one person: flesh and soul. Here certain people are found to have raved in manifold ways, clinging to words alone, so that the entanglements of their language could scarcely be judged unless their error finally showed itself openly.

They say that man is a certain whole composed of soul and body, something altogether other and different from soul and body, such that this whole is neither soul, nor body, nor likewise soul and body. For they say that the whole is not these things, but is from these things. They suppose this whole to be man, and that man himself, who is this whole, is rational by a rationality that is in the whole and differs from the reason or rationality [Col. 0406D] of the part, namely the soul, just as the whole itself differs from the part. Finally, they say that all things which are in the whole are altogether different from those which subsist in the parts, just as the whole itself differs from its parts.

Thus, as the rationality of man is different from the rationality of the soul, because one belongs to the whole and is in the whole, while the other belongs to the part and is in the part, so they say that the goodness of the whole, which is in the whole, is different, and the goodness of the part is different because it belongs to the part and is only in the part. Likewise, they say that the wickedness of man is different because it is in the whole, and the wickedness of the soul different because it is in the part. Finally, whenever the whole acts and the part acts, although they act together, they say that the action of the part, which is in the part, is different, and the action of the whole, which [Col. 0407A] is in the whole, is different, just as the whole itself is one thing and its part another.

Accordingly, whenever man sins or does well, they maintain that there is sin or righteousness in man, accruing to the whole as its property, and again sin or righteousness in the soul, accruing to the part as its property. Therefore, when man dies and the soul is separated from the flesh, the parts having been divided, they say that the whole itself which had been composed of them is now nothing, and hence that man himself, who was this whole, likewise is nothing and is nowhere. Meanwhile neither his sin is punished nor his righteousness rewarded; only the soul is in judgment, so that according to his merit man may receive either punishment or glory, until at last, when the soul returns to the body at the end, man begins again to exist, and then he too receives recompense according to his merit.

People devise such modes of speech and, through false verbal fictions, are led into true deceptions of error. For what is more foolish than to say that man then ceases to exist when he truly begins to exist, and indeed is so much the more truly existent as that in which he begins to exist is more truly existent? “No,” they say, “it is a figure when the saints are said to be with Christ.” Very well. When they are with you, it is truth; when they are with Christ, it is a figure. Believe this among yourselves; we do not believe it. For we know that Christ is truth. Those who go to Christ do not go to a figure but to truth, and escape the figure.

Why did holy people so greatly desire to die, if after [Col. 0407C] death they were to be nothing? “I desire,” says the Apostle, “to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1). What do you desire? To die and be with Christ. No: to die and be nothing. This is what these people say, because after death you will be nothing. If you believe them, you do not desire death—unless perhaps you desire not to exist. If good people are to be nothing after death, how has it been truly said of wicked and perverse people that they desire to be nothing, yet cannot be? Let both the good therefore cease to hope and the evil to fear, because when they depart from here they will not be anything that can experience either evils or goods.

“But,” they say, “let them rightly hope and fear, though not for themselves, yet for their souls; for when they themselves no longer exist, their souls will exist, and will either glory for righteousness or be tormented for guilt.” Therefore, they say, let them hope and fear for their souls. Would that you spoke as rightly as what you say is right! For you speak well when you say that a man ought to hope and fear for his soul, if only you understood that a man never fears more truly or more properly for himself than when he fears for his soul. For what is more truly man than the soul?

You do not think this, whoever you are who have fortified yourself with figures of speech. Something new has been brought to your ears when it has been said that what most truly belongs to man is more truly man. Hear, then. You, a Christian, do not know what that pagan testified: “The mind of each person—that is the person himself.” Therefore that pagan was more religious than you, a Christian, since he confessed the truth which you deny. “Then,” you say, “is man the soul?” Why not? Do you not say that man is body, yet fear to say that man is soul?

A little earlier you objected by argument that every man is body. Every man is an animal, and every animal is body; therefore every man is body. You think there is no contradiction here. For authority says this. You produce pagan authorities to prove that every man is body, but you refuse to believe pagan authorities that every man is soul. Perhaps because you prefer this to be man rather than that, because this pleases you more than that.

“But,” you say, “when I say that every man is body, I am speaking of the whole, not of the part of the whole that is body, nor of the part that is soul; for this whole is man, not any one of its parts. It is of this whole [Col. 0408B] that I say it is body.” Tell me, then: why do you call this whole body rather than soul, since it consists alike of soul and body? If on account of the one part, because it is body, the whole itself is called body, should it not much more be called soul on account of the other part which is soul? For if the whole is said to derive its nature and name from a part, it should beyond doubt more rightly derive both its nature and its name from the part that is better and more worthy.

“But,” you say, “ordinary speech does not call man a soul.” I grant this according to ordinary speech. Say whatever you please, provided that according to the rule of faith you understand what cannot be denied. Ordinary speech was invented by human beings and for human beings; therefore, in speaking, it ought rather to conform to the manner in which human perception apprehends and knows things.

For we know that truly one is nothing except that alone which is one by unity; reason alone truly discerns as one that in which it finds all that exists to be one. Whatever things are numerically many, even if they are sometimes joined, cannot truly be one. Yet things joined together in one composite somehow approach and draw near to one another, so as to imitate unity as far as they can; therefore, in a certain respect, even things joined together are called one. For just as reason does not divide in apprehension what is truly one, so sense does not distinguish in apprehension what is joined and united. [Col. 0408D] And just as there reason does not divide the essence of that which is wholly one, so here sense does not divide the form of that which is wholly united. There reason apprehends at once what is one, because there is not one thing and another in it; here sense apprehends at once what is united, because there is not one thing in one place and another elsewhere.

Nevertheless, things which are many though united are not truly one, even though they come together and in some way approach unity; but they do not do so truly or properly. For what can be more proper to unity than unity itself? Therefore, when many things are called one because they are united, they are not called so properly, because they are not truly what they are called, but only in some manner similar to it.

Yet it must be understood that things which together meet in order to make a union are united in one way, so that from beginning to exist together they begin in some respect to be one; but those are united in another way where unity precedes the union, and what is thereafter added approaches that unity through union. For it is one thing for certain things to be composed together into unity through union, and another for certain things to be attached through union to something already possessing unity.

For when things are composed into unity through union, the parts cannot share the name of the whole, because individually and separately they do not possess in themselves the unity which they together make from themselves. But when certain things are attached through union to something that possesses its own unity, they enter into participation in the thing to which they are attached, so that they begin to share its name as they begin, through their union, to share its unity.

For example, wall, roof, and foundation are three things, and none of them by itself is a house. Therefore, when they come together so that a house begins to exist, the three are composed together; two are not attached to a third. But body and soul are not joined in this way. For insofar as the soul is rational spirit, it possesses of itself and through itself personhood; and when the body is joined to it, it is not so much composed into a person as attached to a person. Thus, in that it is in some respect one with the soul through union, it begins to be the same person as the soul, together with it.

Therefore, insofar as the body is united with the soul, it is one person with the soul; but the soul possesses being a person of itself insofar as it is rational spirit. The body, however, possesses this from the soul insofar as it [Col. 0409C] is united to rational spirit. But because human perception apprehends body and soul together in the living human being—not the soul by itself or the body by itself, but soul and body together—human speech is accustomed to call the soul and body a person.

This person, which is properly one in the soul through unity, but one between body and soul through union, is called by different names according to ordinary speech. Some of these names are taken from a part, while others are taken from things which subsist in a part. Thus, the terms by which the rational person is called man, soul, or body are names taken from a part alone, because in man only the human body is found to be body, to have been taken from earth, and to have been made sentient through union with the soul. These terms, therefore, are taken from a part of man.

But when man is called white, black, large, or small, the names are taken from things that subsist in a part, because such properties are found in the body of man alone and not in his soul. But when man is called rational, wise, or just, names taken from things existing only in a part are applied to the whole, because not the human body but the rational soul alone is found rational, wise, and just.

Thus the name “man” is sometimes taken from the body; sometimes from things that are in the body; sometimes from things that are in the soul; but it is never taken from the soul itself. For from that part of man human speech formed the chiefest names for man which human perception first and principally recognized in man. [Col. 0410A] And man ought indeed to have taken his name rather from his better part, had language not been unable to serve human understanding except by first preserving in speech the mode which human perception follows in apprehending.

Accordingly, because what was from the earth was seen more plainly in man, he was called man from that rather. Thus, from the weakness of perception arose confusion in speech. We must preserve the customary manner of speaking for the sake of usage; yet we must not, because of the custom of speech, depart from the truth of faith. Therefore sacred Scripture, lest human words make us err regarding God’s truth, testifies that the person itself is properly the rational spirit itself. Although this person is called man on account of what was taken from the earth, it nonetheless, both when joined to that body, acts well or badly by itself, and when separated from it, receives recompense by itself in punishment or glory.

And just as, while situated in the body, it does some things by thought and will alone without the body, and other things after and according to the will through bodily action, so also it first receives its reward, separated from the body and without the body, according to its merits; afterward, united to the body, it receives it in the body.

Let us therefore say: man is an animal. This is true on account of that in man which has been made sentient by the soul. Man is a body. This is true because that which has been made sentient in man and taken from earth is body. Man is a person. This is true because that which was taken from earth is united to the soul in one person. Ordinary speech includes all this, and, insofar as it is truly said in this manner, it may be received for the truth without impropriety.

Let us say again: man is an animal. Ordinary speech does not accept this, having been formed according to the mode of perception. For only the body is seen in man, and man is seen only in the body; and therefore man receives his name from the body, because he is called man on account of the body. Again, because in what is seen something else is perceived which is not seen, two things are discovered in man—body and soul. Since these are found joined and united together, body and soul are called parts of man because of their common union. Let us therefore concede what ordinary speech supplies: man is body, and man is not spirit; [Col. 0410D] man is animal, and man is not soul.

Shall we likewise concede that a dead man is not a man, since a living man is a man? But if a dead man is not a man, then when man ceases to live, he ceases to be man. But what ceases to live except what dies? And what dies except the body alone, abandoned by the soul? For the soul does not die or cease to live, even when it ceases to give life. Therefore the body alone dies.

“But,” you say, “man—that is, the person himself—dies.” What is a person? Is it not an individual substance of rational nature? If, then, an individual substance of rational nature is a person, surely rational spirit, which is one by simplicity and by nature capable of reason, properly possesses personhood—of itself insofar as it is rational spirit, and through itself when it is without the body. But when the body is united to it, insofar as it is united with the body, it is one person together with the body. When it is separated from the body, it nevertheless does not cease to be a person; and it is the same person that it was before. For the body, departing from fellowship with the spirit, does not take personhood away from that spirit, just as formerly, when it was joined to the spirit, it did not give personhood to it.

Therefore the soul, separated from the flesh, remains the same person, a rational spirit. Although perhaps according to ordinary usage it can no longer be called man because it no longer has united with itself that which was taken from earth, it is not thereby any less a person; it is the same person it was before, when it also had that united to itself and, by reason of that union, was one person together with it.

Just as the body joined to rational spirit does not give it personhood, but, when joined to it, receives from it that it may itself be one person with it, so humanity joined to the Word did not give him personhood, but, united to him, received from him that it might be one person with him.

It should further be considered that, although Word and man are one person in Christ, we nevertheless rightly say separately, “The Word is a person,” and again rightly say separately, “Man is a person.”

And we rightly say that man and Word together are not two persons but one person. For because the Word was a person even before he assumed man, and did not cease to be a person after assuming man, we rightly say separately that the Word is a person. And because, moreover, there was a union greater and more excellent between assumed man and Word than between soul and body, we likewise rightly say separately that man is a person. For man—that is, body and soul joined together—is a person, yet not a person other than the Word, because man and Word are one person. Union makes one. Flesh and soul, joined together, would have been a person if they had not been a person together with the Word.

Therefore we rightly say both that the Word is a person and that man is a person; and likewise we rightly say that Word and man are not two but one person. [Col. 0411D] Again, we rightly say that the Word, from the time he became man, never afterward ceased to be man, because even in the death of his flesh he never separated himself from the humanity he had assumed. Therefore Christ, even in the death of his flesh, did not cease to be God, because he remained immortal in true deity; nor did he cease to be a person, because he was the Word; nor did he cease to be man, because his divinity did not depart from his humanity. The soul alone was divided from the flesh for a time, but the divinity was separated neither from soul nor from flesh. Thus Christ both truly died because of his dead flesh and truly remained living because of his immortal divinity; and he was at once true God and true man because of the inseparable union of divinity and humanity.

## Chapter XII. That through the man united to the Word all who are his members are united to God.

[Col. 0412A]

The Apostle says: “A mediator is not mediator of one; but God is one” (Gal. III). For God and man were two: different and opposed. God was just; man unjust: in this respect mark their opposition. Man was wretched, God blessed: in this respect mark their difference. Thus man was opposed to God through injustice, and different from God through misery. Therefore man first needed to be justified from guilt, so that he might be reconciled; and afterwards to be freed from misery, so that he might be restored.

Man therefore needed this mediator in relation to God, so as to be reconciled to him and brought back to him. But one who was not bound and akin to each of the two parties by some fellowship and friendship of peace could not fittingly undertake the cause of those at variance. [Col. 0412B] Therefore the Son of God became man, that he might be the mediator of reconciliation and peace between man and God. He assumed humanity, through which he might draw near to human beings. He retained divinity, through which he might not withdraw from God. Having become man, he endured punishment, in order to show his affection; he preserved justice, in order to bestow the remedy. For the Word, which was one with God the Father through an ineffable unity, became one with the assumed man through a wondrous union. Unity is in nature; union is in person. With God the Father, he is one in nature, not in person; with the assumed man, he is one in person, not in nature. What is more one than unity? That which is one by unity [Col. 0412C] is supremely one.

The Word and the Father were one by unity, because they were one in nature; and the Word himself willed to become one with us, so that he might make us one in himself and through himself, and one with him with whom he himself was one.

Therefore he assumed from us our nature, in order to join it to himself by union in person, since it was not joined to him by unity in nature; so that, through that which he had made one with himself from what was ours, he might unite us to himself, that we might be one with him; through that which was ours and was united to him; and through him might be one with the Father, with whom he himself was one. “Holy Father,” he says, “keep in thy name those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we also are. And I pray not for these only, [Col. 0412D] but for those also who shall believe in me through their word: that they too may be one in us, and that the world may believe that thou hast sent me. But I have given them the glory which thou gavest me, that they may be one, as we are one. I in them and thou in me, that they may be perfected into one, and that the world may know that thou hast sent me” (John XVII). Unity prays for union. The Word is one with the Father in nature; the man is one with the Word in person. The members are one with the head: first in justice, afterwards in glory. For, that they may be one in justice, “let the world know that thou hast sent me” (ibid.); but that they may be one in glory: “I will that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory which thou gavest me, because thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world” (ibid.).

## Chapter XIII. That Christ, according to his humanity, is in heaven; according to his divinity, everywhere.

[Col. 0413A]

You ask how the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (I Tim. II), is now believed to be in heaven; or, because God is everywhere, you wish it to be understood from this that that man also, who is in God, is diffused everywhere, and consequently could also have been in paradise because he is everywhere. Do not therefore doubt that the man Jesus Christ is now there whence he will come. Recall by heart also, and hold faithfully, the Christian confession: that “he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father.” Nor will he come from anywhere but thence to judge the living and the dead; and he will come in the manner testified by that angelic utterance: “As he was seen going into heaven” (Acts I), that is, in the same form and substance of flesh. To this, certainly, he gave immortality; he did not remove its nature. According to this form, he must not be thought to be diffused everywhere. For care must be taken lest, in affirming the divinity of the man, we take away the reality of his body. It does not follow that what is in God is everywhere in the same way as God is. For the most truthful Scripture says of us that “in him we live and move and are” (Acts XVII); yet we are not everywhere as he is. But that man is in God in one way, since God is in his man in another, proper and singular way. For God and man are one person, and both are the one Jesus Christ: everywhere according to that by which he is God, but in heaven according to that by which he is man.

[Col. 0413B] God, therefore, is diffused throughout all things. For he himself says through the Prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII). And, as I cited shortly before concerning his wisdom: “She reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII). Again it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wis. I); and in a certain psalm it is said to him: “Where shall I go from thy Spirit, or where shall I flee from thy face? If I ascend into heaven, thou art there; if I descend into hell, thou art present” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

[Col. 0413C] Yet God is so diffused everywhere through all things that he is not a quality of the world, but the substance that creates the world: governing the world without labour and sustaining it without burden. He is not, however, diffused through spatial extension as though by bodily mass, so that he is half in one half of the world and half in the other half; but is wholly throughout all, wholly in heaven alone, wholly on earth alone, and wholly in heaven and on earth; contained in no place, but everywhere whole in himself. Thus the Father, thus the Son, thus the Holy Spirit; thus the Trinity, one God.

But this is far more wondrous: although God is wholly everywhere, he nevertheless does not dwell in all. For not to all can there be said what the Apostle said, or what I have already said, or indeed this: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (I Cor. III). Conversely, the same Apostle says of some: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person is not his” (Rom. VIII). Who, moreover, would dare suppose—unless utterly ignorant of the inseparability of the Trinity—that the Father or the Son could dwell in anyone in whom the Holy Spirit does not dwell, or that the Holy Spirit could dwell in anyone in whom [Col. 0414A] the Father and the Son do not also dwell? We must therefore confess that God is everywhere by the presence of his divinity, but not everywhere by the grace of his divinity and indwelling.

Because of this indwelling, where the grace of his love is undoubtedly known, we do not say, “Our Father who art everywhere,” although that too is true, but “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. VI), so that in prayer we may rather call to mind his temple, which we ourselves also ought to be; and, insofar as we are such, we belong to his fellowship and household of adoption. Therefore, though he who is everywhere does not dwell in all, neither does he dwell equally in those in whom he does dwell. For whence comes the request of Elisha that the Spirit of God who was in Elijah might be doubled in him? (II Kings II). And whence are some saints holier than others, except by possessing the indwelling God more abundantly?

[Col. 0414B] How then is what we said above true—that God is wholly everywhere—when he is more in some and less in others? But the phrase we used must be carefully considered: “He is everywhere whole in himself.” He is not, then, whole in them, because some receive more of him and others less. He is said to be everywhere because he is absent from no part of things. He is whole because he does not offer one part of himself as present to one part of things and another part to another part: a part equal to equal things, a lesser part to lesser things, and a greater part to greater things. He is equally and wholly present not only to the creation as a whole, but also to every part of it.

Further, what we thought could be understood without much distinction when we said that God is everywhere whole, unless we added “in himself,” must be explained more carefully. [Col. 0414C] How, then, is he everywhere in himself? Everywhere, certainly, because he is absent nowhere; but in himself because he is not contained by those to whom he is present, as though he could not exist without them. Just as he is not absent from one in whom he does not dwell, and is wholly present though that person does not possess him, so he is wholly present in one in whom he dwells, though that person does not receive him wholly.

For in dwelling he does not divide himself among human hearts or bodies, giving one part of himself to this person and another to that, as this light enters through the openings and windows of houses. Rather, if any sound—though it is a bodily and passing thing—is not apprehended by a deaf person, while a partially deaf person does not apprehend it wholly, then among those who hear, when all are equally near to it, one receives it more than another insofar as his hearing is sharper, and less insofar as his hearing is duller, although the sound itself does not vary by being louder for one and quieter for another, but is equally at hand in the place where all are. [Col. 0414D] How much more excellently is this so of God, whose nature is incorporeal, immutable, and living: he cannot, like sound, be extended and divided through intervals of time; nor does he require airy space as though it were his place, in which he may be at hand to those present. Rather, abiding in himself in eternal stability, he can be wholly present to all things, and wholly present to each individually, although those in whom he dwells possess him according to the differing measure of their capacity, some more and some less—more, those whom by the grace of his goodness he builds up as a temple most dear to himself.

God is said to dwell even in human beings who are still natural and not yet spiritual, because he works secretly in them [Col. 0415A] so that they may become his temple; and he brings this about in those who make progress and persevere in progressing. Therefore God, who is present everywhere and wholly everywhere, does not dwell in all, but only in those whom he makes his most blessed temple, or his most blessed temples, rescuing them from the power of darkness and transferring them into the kingdom of his light, which begins with regeneration.

When, therefore, you think of his indwelling, think of unity and of the assembly of the saints, especially in heaven, where he is for that reason said particularly to dwell: [Col. 0416A] because there his will is perfectly done through the obedience of those in whom he dwells; then think of the earth, where, by building his house, he dwells in it, to dedicate it at the end of the age. But do not doubt that Christ our Lord, the only-begotten Son of God, equal to the Father, and also Son of man, by whom the Father is greater, is wholly present everywhere as God; wholly present in that same temple of God as the indwelling God; and, because of the measure of his true body, in some place in heaven.

# Part Two. On the Unity of the Church.

[Col. 0415]

## Chapter I. On the grace given through Christ, and the Spirit diffused from the head into the members.

[Col. 0415B]

It is written that “the law brought no one to perfection” (Heb. VII). For the law could teach ignorance; it could not aid weakness. There were two evils here in humanity, and from these all the other human evils proceeded. One was ignorance, the other concupiscence: ignorance of the good, concupiscence for evil. From ignorance comes transgression; from concupiscence, sin. These two, therefore, were in humanity from the beginning. But, in order that man might know his disease, he was left entirely to himself, lest perhaps he should judge grace superfluous if he did not first acknowledge the failure caused by his weakness.

Thus a period of natural law was established, so that nature might act by itself—not because it could achieve anything by itself, but so that it might recognize [Col. 0415C] that it could not do so. Left to itself, therefore, it began to stray from truth through ignorance, and was convicted of blindness; afterwards it was also to be convicted of weakness. The written law was given to illuminate ignorance, but not to strengthen weakness, so that man might be helped in that respect in which he recognized his deficiency. But where he thought that he could stand by himself, he was left to himself. Having received knowledge of the truth through the law, he began to strive to accomplish it; but, weighed down by concupiscence because he did not have assisting grace, he failed in the work of virtue. Thus he was convicted in both respects: namely, that by himself he can neither know the truth nor accomplish the good.

After this, grace was fittingly given: to enlighten the blind and heal the weak; to enlighten [Col. 0415D] ignorance and cool concupiscence; to enlighten for the knowledge of truth and kindle love for virtue. Therefore the Spirit was given in fire, that there might be light and flame: light for knowledge, flame for love. Moreover, just as the human spirit descends through the head to give life to the members, so the Holy Spirit comes through Christ to Christians. For Christ is the head and the Christian is a member. One head, many members; and one body consists of head and members, and in the one body there is one Spirit. Its fullness is indeed in the head; participation is in the members. Therefore, if the body is one and the Spirit is one, whoever is not in that body cannot be given life by the Spirit, as it is written: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person is not his” (Rom. VIII). For one who does not have the Spirit of Christ is not a member of Christ. In one body there is one Spirit. Nothing in the body is dead; nothing outside the body is alive. We become members through faith; we are given life through love. Through faith we receive union; through charity we receive vivification. In the sacrament we are united through baptism; through Christ’s body and blood we are given life. Through baptism we become members of the body; through Christ’s body we become participants in vivification.

## Chapter II. On the Church: what the Church is.

The holy Church is the body of Christ, given life by one Spirit, united by one faith, and sanctified. The individual faithful are members of this body; all are one body because of the one Spirit and the one faith. [Col. 0416C] Just as every member of a human body has its own distinct function, yet does not perform solely for itself what it alone performs, so in the body of the holy Church the gifts of grace are distributed; and yet no one possesses solely for himself even what he alone possesses. The eyes alone see, but they do not see solely for themselves: they see for the whole body. The ears alone hear, but they do not hear solely for themselves: they hear for the whole body. The feet alone walk, yet do not walk solely for themselves: they walk for the whole body. And in this manner, whatever each one has solely in himself, he does not have solely [Col. 0416D] for himself, so that, according to the ordering of the best giver and wisest distributor, the individual things may belong to all, and all things to each individual.

Whoever, therefore, has merited to receive a gift of God’s grace should know that what he possesses does not pertain to himself alone, even if he alone possesses it. By this likeness the holy Church—that is, the whole body of the faithful—is called the body of Christ because of the Spirit of Christ which it has received; participation in this Spirit is signified in a person when he is called a Christian from Christ.

This name, therefore, denotes the members of Christ who partake of Christ’s Spirit: the anointed person is from the Anointed One, because “Christian” is derived from Christ. For Christ is interpreted as “Anointed”; [Col. 0417A] with that oil of gladness which he received in fullness above all his fellow participants, and which, as head, he poured out by participation upon all his fellow participants, his members: “Like ointment upon the head, which descends from the head upon the beard and then even to the hem” (Ps. CXXXII)—that is, it flowed down to the extremity of the garment so as to flow through the whole and give life to the whole. When, therefore, you become a Christian, you become a member of Christ: a member of Christ’s body, partaking of Christ’s Spirit. What, then, is the Church but the multitude of the faithful, the whole body of Christians?

## Chapter III. On the two sides of the Church, clergy and laity.

This whole body comprises two orders, [Col. 0417B] laypeople and clergy, as though the two sides of one body. Laypeople are, as it were, on the left, because they attend to the necessities of the present life.

I do not say “on the left” in the manner of those who will be set at the left, to whom it will be said: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). Far be it from me to presume to place good laypeople there! For those who are good, whether lay or clerical, will not be there; and those who are evil, whether lay or clerical, will be there.

Therefore I do not place Christian laypeople who are true Christians at that left hand, but at the left hand of which it is said: “In her right hand is length of life, but in her left are riches and glory” (Prov. III). For what is at the left in the body belongs to the body and is good, although it is not the best.

[Col. 0417C] Christian laypeople, then, who deal with earthly matters and the necessities of earthly life, are the left side of Christ’s body. But clergy, because they administer matters pertaining to the spiritual life, are as it were the right side of Christ’s body.

Yet the whole body of Christ, which is the universal Church, consists of these two parts. *Laicus* means “of the people”; for Greek λαός (*laos*) is “people” in Latin. Hence also βασιλεύς (*basileus*), “king,” is thought to be so called, as though from βάσις λαοῦ (*basis laou*), “foundation of the people,” that is, “support of the people.” *Clericus* is called from the Greek κλῆρος (*klēros*), which translated into Latin signifies a “lot,” either because he has been chosen by lot by God for God’s service, or because God himself is his lot; and because he ought to have no other portion [Col. 0417D] on earth except God and those things which pertain to God’s portion. The cleric is appointed to be supported by tithes and offerings made to God. Thus faithful Christian laypeople are permitted to possess earthly things; but only spiritual things are entrusted to clerics. So formerly, in that earlier people, the other tribes, which bore the type of laypeople, received portions in the inheritance. The tribe of Levi alone, which represented ecclesiastics, was fed by tithes, offerings, and sacrificial victims.

## Chapter IV. That there are two lives, and according to the two lives two peoples; and within the two peoples two powers, with distinct degrees and ranks of dignities in each; one lower and the other higher.
