There are indeed two lives: one earthly, the other heavenly; [Col. 0418A] one bodily, the other spiritual. One by which the body lives from the soul, the other by which the soul lives from God. Each has its own good by which it is sustained and nourished, so that it may subsist. Earthly life is nourished by earthly goods; spiritual life by spiritual goods. Everything earthly pertains to earthly life; all spiritual goods to spiritual life. But, that justice may be preserved and benefit may result in each life, first persons were appointed in each who, through diligence and labour, might acquire according to need or reason the goods of each.

Then others were appointed who, by the authority of the office entrusted to them, might distribute those goods equitably, so that no one might overreach his brother in any transaction, but justice might be kept inviolate. Therefore, in each people, distributed according to each life, powers were established. Among laypeople, whose care and concern include the things necessary for earthly life, there is earthly power. Among clergy, whose office concerns the goods of spiritual life, there is divine power. The former is therefore called secular power; the latter is named spiritual power. In each power there are different degrees and orders of authority, [Col. 0418B] yet each is distributed under one head, as though derived from one beginning and directed to one end. Earthly power has the king as its head. Spiritual power has the supreme pontiff. Matters earthly and all things done for earthly life belong to the king’s authority. Matters spiritual and everything assigned to spiritual life belong to the authority of the supreme pontiff.

And as spiritual life is more worthy than earthly life, and spirit than body, so spiritual power precedes earthly or secular power in honour and dignity. For spiritual power has the authority both to establish earthly power, that it may exist, and to judge it if it is not good. Spiritual power itself was first established by God, and when it departs from the right way it can be judged by God alone, as it is written: “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (I Cor. II).

That spiritual power, insofar as divine institution is concerned, is both earlier in time and greater in dignity, is plainly shown in that ancient people of the Old Testament, in which the priesthood was first established by God, [Col. 0418C] and royal power was afterwards ordered through the priesthood at God’s command.

Hence in the Church priestly dignity still consecrates royal power, sanctifying it through blessing and giving it form through institution. Therefore, if, as the Apostle says, the one who blesses is greater and the one blessed is lesser (Heb. VII), it is evident beyond all doubt that earthly power, which receives blessing from spiritual power, is rightly considered inferior.

## Chapter V. That all ecclesiastical administration consists of three things: orders, sacraments, and precepts.

All ecclesiastical administration consists of three things: orders, sacraments, and precepts. [Col. 0419A] We consider orders in the persons of prelates; sacraments in their ministry; precepts in the conduct of subjects. Each requires its own consideration. Concerning orders, the first point to observe is that some differ according to rank, as deacon and priest do; while others are in the same rank but differ in the eminence of their authority, as deacon and archdeacon do. There is one rank in the sacrament, yet not one authority in ministry. For the deacon ministers to the priest in the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood. But the archdeacon has this further authority: in addition to ministry at the altar, under the bishop and in the bishop’s stead he has the care of churches, examines ecclesiastical cases, and administers ministries.

Likewise, priest and pontiff, or high priest, have one rank in the sacrament, but distinct authority in ministry. For although both have, in a certain manner, one dignity in consecrating Christ’s body and blood, baptizing, catechizing, preaching, binding, and loosing, pontiffs alone have been granted the authority to dedicate churches, ordain clergy, lay on hands, consecrate holy chrism, and pronounce the common blessing over the people. [Col. 0419B] Thus there is one sort of difference of ranks in holy orders and another sort of difference of dignities within the same rank. But the order in earthly or secular authority is different from that in spiritual authority.

## Chapter VI. On earthly power.

Earthly power pertains to earthly life, and [Col. 0419C] all things relating to earthly life are subject to earthly power. All these things pertain in two ways to the right of earthly power: namely, that earthly power itself both distributes them justly to those who possess them and defends them against the injustice of aggressors. Just as it is the duty of prelates to administer possessions justly to their subjects and to defend them against injustice, so it is the duty of subjects, according to the enactments of laws and reasonable customs, to render service to their prelates, both in their own persons and in what belongs to them.

One kind of service is fixed, such as rent and tribute paid annually. Another is contingent: that exacted for faults occurring by chance. Although this too is determined by laws according to the measure of the sin, it is in a certain manner not fixed because its occurrence is uncertain and it cannot rightly be exacted unless the fault for which it must be paid has occurred. [Col. 0419D] This, therefore, is the distinction of earthly power: that it may be known what prelates ought to render to subjects and what subjects ought to render to prelates in regard to the land itself or earthly property, concerning which the obligation of both is assessed.

## Chapter VII. How the Church possesses earthly things.

Of these earthly goods pertaining to earthly life—whether prelates possess them in their subjects or subjects possess them from prelates—some have been granted to the churches of Christ for possession through the devotion of the faithful, while the right of earthly power remains intact. [Col. 0420A] For this is reasonable and good, because our God is a lover of peace and true justice cannot approve anything disorderly. Spiritual power does not preside in order to prejudice earthly power in its own right, just as earthly power never, without fault, usurps what is owed to spiritual power.

Thus, when things of this kind that belong to earthly power are granted to the churches of Christ, those who make the grant can give only what they themselves possess in them. Subjects cannot transfer to another authority what is owed to their superiors; nor can prelates introduce outside possessors into things rightly possessed by subjects. That is: prelates must not give to others what belongs to subjects, nor may subjects presume to alter what belongs to prelates.

It should nevertheless be noted that earthly rulers sometimes grant to the Church, in earthly possessions which they possess either with subjects or without subjects, only the usufruct; at other times, both usufruct and authority. They grant usufruct without authority when they decree that the revenue of the possession be transferred for the Church’s use, but do not permit the authority to exercise justice in that possession to pass into the Church’s jurisdiction. At other times they grant both authority and usufruct together. [Col. 0420B] Yet here it must be carefully observed that, although the Church receives the revenue of an earthly possession for its use, it cannot exercise the authority of administering justice through ecclesiastical persons or secular courts. It may, however, have lay persons as ministers through whom it administers rights and judgments belonging to earthly power according to the tenor of the laws and the due requirements of earthly law.

But this must be done so that it recognizes that it has this authority from the earthly ruler; and understands that such possessions can never be so removed from royal power that, if reason and necessity require it, that power should not owe them protection and they should not owe it service in time of necessity. For just as royal power cannot grant to another the protection it owes, so a possession, even one held by ecclesiastical persons, cannot lawfully refuse the service owed to royal power in return for protection. As it is written: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII).

## Chapter VIII. In how many ways justice must be determined in secular power.

[Col. 0420D]

It should be known that the justice bestowed upon earthly power in relation to its subjects is determined in five ways: according to person, cause, manner, place, and time. For what is permitted in some manner is not immediately permitted in every manner; and justice itself, unless administered justly, loses the name of justice. Therefore one must carefully discern how what is permitted is permitted, and consider the ways by which the form of justice is determined.

Something is permitted according to the person, and something is not: for example, a secular judge may lay hands on a layperson if he has sinned, [Col. 0421A] but may not lay hands on a cleric. Justice is determined according to the cause, so that secular matters are examined by earthly power, while spiritual and ecclesiastical matters are examined by spiritual power. Justice is determined according to manner or measure when every fault is punished with a fitting and appropriate penalty, so that neither private affection subtracts anything from equitable punishment nor private hatred adds anything to due severity. Justice is determined according to place and time if judgment is exercised where and when fitting, and a sentence of truth is pronounced.

Thus justice would be violated according to person if a secular judge laid hands upon an ecclesiastical person; according to cause, if he undertook to examine ecclesiastical matters; according to measure, if he punished a lie or insult by hanging; according to place, if he presumed to violate sacred places and to inflict violence disorderly even upon those guilty persons who had fled to them and were to be condemned for their crimes; and according to time, [Col. 0421B] if he did not show reverence on sacred and solemn days, when even those to whom penalties are due for their offenses must be spared. Therefore secular power ought to exercise justice in these ways, following the enactments of laws and approving nothing in judgment beyond justice and truth.

Secular power has as its head a king or emperor, from whom it descends through subordinate powers—dukes, counts, prefects, and other magistrates—yet all of these derive their authority, insofar as they are set over subjects, from the first power.

## Chapter IX. On royal insignia.

Secular power has certain insignia of its dignity, by which both the excellence of its order is displayed and the sacramental meaning of its ministry is figured. [Col. 0422B] The ring signifies faith; the bracelet, good works; the sceptre, justice; the sword, punishment; purple, reverence; the diadem, glory. Let what has now been said concerning secular power suffice.

# Part Three. On Ecclesiastical Orders.

[Col. 0421]

## Chapter I. On spiritual power and its crown.

[Col. 0421B]

Spiritual power is ordered in the clergy, having distinct degrees [Col. 0421C] and ranks of dignities. The first sign of a cleric is the crown, by which he is marked as belonging to the allotted portion of divine ministry; to serve which is to reign. For the crown signifies royal honour. Thus the blessed Apostle Peter says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II). For this reason the hair of the cleric’s head is cut in the manner of a crown, and the very top of the head is bared and uncovered, so that it may be understood thereby that he is assumed into royal power in Christ, and that henceforth there ought to be no veil between him and God, so that with unveiled face and a pure mind he may contemplate the glory of his Lord. The highest part of the head is the highest part of the mind. The uncovering of the head signifies illumination of the mind.

## Chapter II. On clerics.

[Col. 0421D]

For a cleric ought not to be ignorant of God’s mysteries, since he is God’s messenger to the people. The hair of the head is also cut away as far as the opening and uncovering of the senses—that is, of the eyes and ears—so that earthly occupation, signified by the hair, may not hinder him from hearing and understanding God’s words. Once he has become a cleric, he ought henceforth to be supported from the Church’s stipends, and, under the protection and guardianship of spiritual teachers, instructed in divine knowledge and ecclesiastical discipline, so that when reason requires he may worthily approach the holy orders of divine ministry. No one is to be admitted to the clergy except under a definite title. Those who have no head are *acephali*, not clerics.

## Chapter III. On ecclesiastical tonsure.

[Col. 0422B]

The practice of ecclesiastical tonsure is thought to have arisen from the Nazirites, [Col. 0422C] who first kept their hair, then at last, because of continence of life, shaved their heads and placed their hair in the fire of sacrifice. From this the practice was introduced by the Apostles: those consecrated to God and devoted to divine worship should be found, like Nazirites—that is, holy persons—with their hair laid aside, as it is said to Ezekiel: “You, son of man, take a sharp sword and draw it over your head and beard” (Ezek. V; Acts XVIII). We read that in the New Testament those Nazirites, Priscilla and Aquila, first did this in the Acts of the Apostles. We read also of the Apostle Paul and certain disciples of Christ who proved imitators in this kind of observance: namely, that by this sign they might be taught to cut off vices springing up in heart and deed.

## Chapter IV. How sacred orders may be in monks.

[Col. 0422D]

Some hold that the crown should sometimes be understood as a sign of penitence, as in the order of monks, to whom the other sacred orders proper to the clergy are granted by dispensation. For they cannot preside over the people or undertake the care of spiritual dignity in the Church until they are admitted to the clergy. Therefore, whatever sacred sign they have is by dispensation, not for the authority of prelacy over God’s people, but so that even in that habit of penitence, in which they have voluntarily set themselves apart for God, they may not be unable either to have the most holy communion of Christ’s body and blood or to be compelled to seek it outside, to the disturbance of their quiet. [Col. 0423A] Therefore, that they may live more quietly within, the orders of divine ministry are granted to them by dispensation: not in order to exercise prelacy over God’s people, but to celebrate inwardly the communion of God’s sacrament. They say, however, that this was not so at the beginning. For monks and those dwelling in the desert are recorded in former times to have had priests.

## Chapter V. On the seven sacred degrees.

First, therefore, the cleric’s distinguishing mark is the tonsure, by which he is sealed for a share in the sacred ministry. There follow the promotions through seven grades, in which, by spiritual authority, he continually ascends higher to handle sacred things. The first grade is that of doorkeepers; the second, readers; the third, exorcists; the fourth, [Col. 0423B] acolytes; the fifth, subdeacons; the sixth, deacons; the seventh, priests. This grade contains unequal dignities within the same order. For above priests are the higher chiefs of priests, that is, bishops. Above them again are archbishops; and above these are those called primates, above whom some wish to establish patriarchs, while others call these same persons both primates and patriarchs. Yet from the ancient practice of the Church we find only four called patriarchs: first, the Alexandrian; second, the Jerusalemite; third, the Antiochene; fourth, the Aquileian, who was afterwards called the Gradensian—unless perhaps, according to the particular usage of languages, these same men are elsewhere called patriarchs and elsewhere primates.

After all these follows the supreme pontiff, whom ecclesiastical custom has established to call pope, [Col. 0423C] that is, “Father of fathers.” He is the chief and greatest successor of the apostolic see in the Roman Church; hence holy Church has also customarily called him, in a special sense, “apostolic.” To him, presiding in the place of Peter, prince of the apostles, every ecclesiastical order ought to submit; for he alone, by prerogative of dignity, possesses the keys for binding all things and loosing them upon earth. These sacred orders, therefore, are arranged in various places throughout the world, wherever the body of holy Church is spread: not merely by the voluntary ordination of spiritual fathers, but also by a fitting principle adopted from the very practice of the Gentiles. For in those cities where the Gentiles had formerly been accustomed to appoint their flamines, [Col. 0423D] bishops are now ordained; and where archflamines had been appointed, archbishops succeeded them. Read the book of Clement: there you will find how blessed Peter established that leaders of churches should be appointed throughout the various regions of the world.

Accordingly, the seven grades of spiritual offices have been distributed in holy Church according to the sevenfold grace, which the Lord Jesus Christ, possessing the fullness of that same Spirit, displayed wholly in himself and left for imitation to his body—that is, the Church—to which he granted participation in his own Spirit.

## CHAPTER VI. On Doorkeepers

Among these seven grades of spiritual office, the first is that of those called doorkeepers, who in the Old Testament [Col. 0424A] were formerly called gatekeepers. The keys of the church belong to the doorkeeper’s office, so that at appropriate hours he may close and open the temple of God; guard everything within and without; receive the faithful; and expel the excommunicated and unbelievers. When the doorkeeper is ordained, after being instructed by the archdeacon how he ought to conduct himself in the house of God, the bishop, at the archdeacon’s prompting, gives him the keys of the church from the altar, saying to him: “Act in such a way as one who must render an account to God for those things which are opened by these keys.”

The Lord undertook this office in his own person when, having made a whip of cords, he drove buyers and sellers from the temple. For he himself, the doorkeeper, says: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved; and he shall go in, and go in, and find pasture” [probably an OCR repetition for “go in and go out”] (John 10).

## CHAPTER VII. On Readers

The second grade is that of readers, which received its model and beginning from the prophets. For readers are those who proclaim the Word of God, to whom it is said: “Cry aloud; do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58). When they are ordained, the bishop first addresses the people concerning their life, faith, and ability; then, before the people’s eyes, a codex of the divine readings is given to them by the bishop, and they are told: “Receive it, and be bearers of the Word of God, having—if you faithfully and profitably fulfill your office—a share with those who have ministered the word of God.” Hence they have authority in the Church to recite before the people the prophetic and apostolic readings.

Those promoted [Col. 0424C] to this grade ought to be trained in literary learning, so that they may understand the meaning of what they read; recognize the force of accents in pronunciation; and read distinctly, lest by confused pronunciation they deprive their hearers of understanding. They must consider what should be read indicatively, what pronounced as a question, and where a full pause or a half-pause should be made in the sentence; for these matters too, when poorly observed, disturb understanding and, while presenting the appearance of grammarians, expose them to ridicule. A reader’s voice ought to serve the ears and heart, not the eyes, lest by undisciplined movement or gesture he make spectators of people rather than hearers. He should avoid a broken or effeminate sound no less than a coarse and rustic one. For readers were formerly called heralds or proclaimers, [Col. 0424D] because they raise their voice among the people.

The Lord displayed this office in his own person when, in the midst of the elders, opening the book of the prophet Isaiah, he read distinctly for understanding: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; he has sent me to proclaim good news to the poor” (Luke 4; Isa. 61). From this readers are given to understand that those who proclaim God’s word to the people ought to shine with spiritual grace.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Exorcists

In the third place follows the order of exorcists, who perform the sacrament of opening over catechumens and possess spiritual authority over unclean spirits, so as to drive them from possessed bodies. But one who commands unclean spirits ought to have a clean spirit, [Col. 0425A] so that life may not be at variance with office; and so that the evil one whom he expels from another’s body by the office he has received, he may expel from his own heart by purity of life. When they are ordained, they receive from the bishop’s hand the book of exorcisms, and are told: “Receive it, commit it to memory, and have authority to lay hands upon the possessed or catechumens.”

Exorcists were established in the order and ministry of the Church according to the offices arranged in the temple of Solomon, which were later apportioned by Ezra. For under Ezra there are said to have been temple workers, sons of Solomon’s servants, who had under their care the operation of the whole temple or served the sacred offerings. Although they were in the order of the temple’s ministry, [Col. 0425B] they nevertheless remained far from the office of God’s altar. For neither psalmists—that is, singers—nor doorkeepers, nor servants of sacred things, were permitted to approach the altar’s offerings; only Levites were.

Thus exorcists are, as it were, spiritual workers of God’s temple among God’s people: from the substance of their Lord, entrusted to them in spiritual gifts, they restore what has fallen into ruin in spiritual buildings and repair what has been scattered. The Apostle signifies exorcists when he says: “Do all have gifts of healing?” (1 Cor. 12). God exercised this office when he touched the ears and tongue of the deaf and mute man with his saliva, saying: “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened” (Mark 7). By this example he teaches us that we ought spiritually to open the ears of human hearts [Col. 0425C] for understanding and their mouths for confession, so that, once the demon has been expelled, the Holy Spirit may receive his vessel. Likewise he performed this office when he cast seven demons from Mary Magdalene (Mark 16; Luke 8).

## CHAPTER IX. On Acolytes

In the fourth place succeed acolytes, who in Latin are called *ceroferarii*, candle-bearers, because they carry lighted candles while the Gospel is read or while the sacrifice is offered. This is not to illuminate the darkness of the air, but so that, just as they carry visible light in their hands, so they may show works of light to their neighbors and, in the manner of light, offer guidance on the way to those wandering and feeling their way in darkness. When they are ordained, after they have been instructed by the bishop concerning how they ought to act in their office, [Col. 0425D] they receive from the archdeacon a candleholder, that is, a candlestick with a candle, so that they may know themselves assigned to tend the lights. They also receive an empty cruet for pouring wine into the chalice in which Christ’s blood is to be consecrated, so that there may be remembrance of the blood flowing from Christ’s side and of the water proceeding from it. These two are mixed in the chalice because we have been redeemed by Christ’s blood and washed from sins by the water of baptism.

The Lord testifies in the Gospel that he holds this office, saying: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John 8).

## CHAPTER X. On Subdeacons

In the fifth place is the order of subdeacons, who among the Greeks are called ὑποδιάκονοι, “subdeacons.” These are called in Ezra *Nathanaei*, that is, those serving the Lord in humility; from their order came that Nathanael who deserved both to confess the Savior in the Gospel and to be praised by him, when the Lord said: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no guile” (John 1). They serve the Levites and carry to them at the altar, and carry back again, the vessels of Christ’s body and blood.

Concerning these, indeed, the Fathers decreed that those who handle the sacred mysteries should observe the law of continence, as it is written: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52). In the Lord’s temple they receive offerings from the peoples. It belongs to their oversight to place upon the altar from the offerings only as much as may suffice for God’s people. Likewise, they themselves ought to wash the corporal cloths and altar coverings, and pour water into the baptistery; [Col. 0426B] they should also hold the pitcher and water, the hand-cloth or towel, and the hand-towel, supplying water before the altar to bishop, priest, and Levites for washing their hands. When they are ordained, they do not receive the laying on of hands as priests and Levites do, but only an empty chalice and an empty paten from the bishop’s hand.

From the archdeacon’s hand, however, they receive a cruet with water, a hand-cloth or towel, and a hand-towel, by which the priest and Levite who are to handle the divine sacraments must cleanse their hands. The Lord exercised this office when, after supper with his disciples, he girded himself with a linen cloth, poured water into a basin, washed his disciples’ feet, and wiped them with the linen cloth (John 13).

## CHAPTER XI. On Deacons

[Col. 0426C]

The order of deacons follows in the sixth place, not without some mystery of the number six, in which, because of its perfection, perfection of works is signified. This order had its origin in the Old Testament from the tribe of Levi. For God commanded Moses that, after the ordination of Aaron and his sons, the tribe of Levi should in turn be ordained to the ministries of divine worship and consecrated to the Lord; that they should serve on behalf of Israel before Aaron and his sons in God’s tabernacle; that they themselves should carry the ark and the tabernacle and all its vessels; that they should establish their camp around the tabernacle; and that in transporting the tabernacle they should take it down and again set it up. They were commanded to serve in the tabernacle from twenty years of age and upward. The holy Fathers also established this rule in the [Col. 0426D] New Testament, since that age is strong enough for carrying burdens, as Moses ordained for that order.

This is also represented in the New Testament when a stole is placed over the deacon’s left shoulder, and on fast days the chasuble is folded over that same shoulder: because whatever toil and endurance we bear in this life, we bear, as it were, on the left, until on the right—that is, in eternity—we have rest. This order took its beginning in the New Testament from the apostles, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles. The apostles chose seven men of good repute, full of the Holy Spirit, for this office (Acts 6), and, after prayer, laid hands upon them (ibid.). From that time the apostles and their successors decreed that in [Col. 0427A] every mother church seven deacons should stand in a higher grade around Christ’s altar, like pillars of the altar, again not without some mystery of the number seven. By this it is signified that, shining with the Spirit of sevenfold grace, they should be holy in body and spirit.

These are the seven angels sounding trumpets in the Apocalypse (Rev. 8); these are the seven golden lampstands (Rev. 1); these are the voices of thunder (Rev. 4). For they loudly, in the manner of a herald, admonish all alike—to pray, to bend the knee, to sing psalms, to read, and to hear the word. They proclaim the Gospel; they dispense God’s sacraments. Without them, the priest has the name but does not have the office. For as consecration belongs to the priest, so the dispensing of the sacrament belongs to the minister. Even priests themselves, because of presumption, [Col. 0427B] may not lift the Lord’s chalice from the table unless it has been handed to them by the deacon. Levites place the offerings upon the altar; they arrange the Lord’s table. Levites cover the ark of the covenant, because not all ought, or are able, to see the lofty mysteries which are covered by the Levites.

They stand by the altar clothed in white vestments, so that the whiteness of the garment may signify purity of life, and that they may approach the offerings clean and unstained. For it is fitting that the Lord should have such ministers as are corrupted by no contagion of the flesh but shine with perfect chastity of mind and body. The Apostle teaches most fully what sort of deacons ought to be ordained, writing to Timothy (1 Tim. 3). For after setting forth the selection of priests, he immediately adds: “Deacons likewise irreproachable,” [Col. 0427C] that is, without accusation; “chaste,” like bishops, that is, restrained from lust; “not double-tongued,” lest they disturb those who have peace; “not given to much wine,” because where drunkenness is, there lust and frenzy hold sway; “not pursuing shameful gain,” lest they pursue earthly profit from heavenly service. After this he adds: “But let these first be tested, and then let them serve, having no accusation.” Therefore they too, like bishops, ought to be tested before ordination; and if they are found worthy, only then are they to be admitted to sacred ministry.

When they are ordained, the bishop alone lays hands on them, because they are appointed to ministry, not priesthood. The bishop places upon them the *orarium*, that is, the stole, over the left shoulder, so that they may recognize that they have received the Lord’s yoke, [Col. 0427D] by which they must bravely endure all adversities belonging to the left—that is, to the present life—and subject them to the fear of God. They also receive the text of the Gospels from the bishop’s hand, by which they may understand themselves to be heralds of Christ’s Gospel. For just as readers are commanded to proclaim the Old Testament, so deacons are commanded to proclaim the New, especially the Gospel, which in the Church only they are permitted to pronounce.

It belongs to them to assist priests and minister in everything done in Christ’s sacraments: namely, in baptism, in chrism, in the paten and chalice; to bring and arrange offerings upon the altar; to prepare and clothe the Lord’s table; to carry the cross; and to proclaim the Gospel and the Apostle [the Epistle]. To them also belongs the office of prayers and the recitation of names. They bid [Col. 0428A] ears attend to the Lord; they exhort people to pray. They cry aloud and announce peace. The Lord exercised this office when, after supper, he dispensed with his own mouth and hands the sacraments he had consecrated, and when he urged the sleeping apostles to prayer, saying: “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Matt. 26).

## CHAPTER XII. On Presbyters

In the seventh place follows the order of presbyters, which in the Old Testament took its beginning from Aaron’s sons. For those then called priests are those now called presbyters, and those then called chiefs of priests are now called bishops. Presbyters are interpreted as “elders,” because the Greeks call elders *presbyteroi*. For [Col. 0428B] presbyters ought to be elders among God’s people, not so much in bodily age as in prudence of character and maturity of good conduct, as it is written: “Venerable old age is not that which is long-lasting, nor is it measured by the number of years. For a person’s gray hairs are understanding, and an unblemished life is the age of old age” (Wis. 4).

There is only this difference between pontiffs and priests of the present time: to pontiffs alone have been assigned the ordination of clerics, the dedication of basilicas, the consecration of sacred chrism, the laying on of hands, and the common blessing over the people. But in the other sacraments—namely, catechizing, baptizing, celebrating Mass, consecrating the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, and addressing the Church—the administration is common to both. The things mentioned above have therefore been reserved uniquely for high priests, lest precisely the same authority of power, claimed indiscriminately by all, make those beneath insolent toward their superiors and, once the bond of obedience has been loosened, produce scandal.

Presbyters are successors and vicars of the seventy disciples who went before the Lord Jesus into every city and place where he himself was about to come (Luke 10). Thus presbyters, who are assistants of bishops, initiate the untrained people by catechizing, incorporate them into the unity of the Church by baptizing, and minister to God’s people in the sacraments up to the laying on of hands. Bishops, however, are successors of the apostles; because of the need for assistance and support [Col. 0428D] in their office, amid so great a multitude of peoples to govern, they seek for themselves the ministry of priests. So Moses in the wilderness chose seventy prudent men, by whose counsel and assistance he might govern so great a multitude more easily.

Priests, whether of lower or higher order—that is, whether presbyters or bishops—act in the place of the supreme pontiff when they call sinful peoples to repentance and heal them by the remedy of their prayers. Hence the Apostle says: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, and placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we entreat you on Christ’s behalf: be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5). In this, then, priests perform the office of mediator: they entreat God for the people’s sins and reconcile penitents by absolving them. Therefore it is fitting [Col. 0429A] that, as good mediators between human beings and God, they bring God’s commands to the people by preaching the truth and offer the people’s prayers to God by interceding for sinners.

“But a mediator,” as the Apostle says, “is not of one” (Gal. 3), because one cannot reconcile persons at odds who is not himself in harmony with both sides through the peace of fellowship and the bond of friendship. Priests, therefore, ought to have peace with God through an outstanding holiness and preserve concord with their neighbors through an affection of compassion. The Apostle indicates what kind of presbyters they ought to be when he writes to Titus: “For this reason I left you in Crete: that you might appoint presbyters in the cities, as I directed you. If anyone is without accusation, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not under accusation of debauchery or insubordination. For a bishop must be without accusation” (Titus 1). By this statement he shows that presbyters too are designated under the name of bishops. Thus, writing to Timothy concerning the ordination of bishop and deacon, he says nothing of presbyters, leaving them to be understood under the name of bishops. Therefore both the Apostle affirms, and canons following apostolic authority testify, that such men as bishops ought to be established as presbyters in the Church.

When presbyters are ordained, as the bishop blesses them and holds his hand over their heads, all the presbyters present raise their hands beside the bishop’s hand over their heads and invoke the Holy Spirit upon those being ordained. The hands of presbyters are anointed as are those of bishops, so that [Col. 0429C] they may know that by this sacrament they receive the grace of consecrating and ought to exercise works of mercy toward all, according to their ability. The anointing of the head belongs particularly to the bishop, so that he may understand himself to be the vicar of him of whom it is written: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Ps. 44).

After the invocation of the Holy Spirit, they receive a stole over both shoulders; in the manner of supporting straps it protects their right side and their left, so that they may understand thereby that they are armed with weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, so that neither adversities may break them nor prosperity exalt them. They also receive from the bishop’s hand a chalice with wine and a paten with hosts, so that through these instruments they may recognize that they have received authority to offer sacrifices pleasing to God. It belongs to them [Col. 0429D] to consecrate the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood upon God’s altar, say prayers, and bless God’s gifts.

Our Lord Jesus Christ exercised this office when, after supper, he changed bread and wine into his body and blood and, when dying, instituted that his disciples should do the same in remembrance of his passion. He also displayed the fulfillment of this office in an eminent way when he himself, priest and victim, offered himself in the ark of the cross for the sins of the human race and, entering the holy eternal places with his own blood, made peace between heavenly and earthly things. In this is evident how great is the excellence of the priestly office, through which Christ’s passion is celebrated daily on the altar and every guilty person who turns from sins is reconciled to God.

[Col. 0430A] Having briefly discussed all these matters concerning the priestly office, Christ’s priests must be admonished that, just as they surpass others in the dignity of their order, so they may surpass them in holiness of life, so that the people entrusted to them and instructed by their disciplines may gladly obey them and, by imitating them, advance from day to day.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Bishops

The sacred canons determine that no one is to be chosen bishop unless he has first conducted himself religiously in sacred orders. They judge that only the diaconate and presbyterate should be called sacred orders, because the primitive Church is read to have possessed these alone, and we have an apostolic command concerning these alone. Yet, because subdeacons too minister at the sacred altars, they permit them, when need requires, to be chosen as bishops [Col. 0430B]—but very rarely, and even then not without permission from the Roman pontiff or metropolitan, provided they are of proven religious character and approved learning.

The consecration of basilicas, the anointing of the altar, the preparation of chrism, the laying on of hands, and the common blessing over the people belong especially to the bishop. He distributes the aforementioned offices and ecclesiastical orders; he blesses sacred virgins. While each person goes before others in particular matters, the bishop is the pre-ordinator in all matters. No bishop ought to consecrate another as bishop without the metropolitan’s consent; nor may a metropolitan ordain a bishop unless at least three bishops are present and all other bishops of the same province give their assent.

When he is ordained, two bishops place and hold [Col. 0430C] the codex of the Gospels over his head and crown, and, while one pours out the blessing over him, all the other bishops present touch his head with their hands. His head is anointed with sacred anointing because all sanctification consists in the Holy Spirit, whose invisible power is both signified and bestowed in the very anointing of holy chrism. The pontiff lays his hand upon the one being ordained; the deacon reads the Gospel reading, and the notary writes the letter of confirmation. Finally, both ordainer and ordained ought each to celebrate Mass in that ordination itself. This, indeed, is the form handed down by the holy Fathers for consecrating pontiffs.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Archbishops

[Col. 0430D]

But when an elected archbishop is to be ordained, all the bishops of the same province ought to assemble at the metropolitan see so that he may be ordained by all of them. For it is fitting that he who ought to preside over all of them be chosen and ordained by all of them; otherwise the consecration is judged void. It has also been established that, within three months of his consecration, the archbishop should send to the apostolic see in order to set forth his faith and receive the pallium, which he is known to possess beyond a bishop. For the archbishop presides over bishops and wears the pallium.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Supreme Pontiff

Because the apostolic see is set before all the Churches throughout the world [Col. 0431A] and cannot have a metropolitan above itself, the cardinal bishops undoubtedly perform the role of metropolitans, namely by raising the elected prelate to the summit of the apostolic dignity. But if, after the election, some accident or violence should prevent the elected man from being enthroned in the apostolic see according to custom, the elected man nevertheless ought, as has been established, to possess the authority of a pope to govern the holy Roman Church and administer its resources.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Other Offices Which Are among the Clergy

These are the orders and ministries of clerics. They are divided, however, among pontifical authority, the archdeacon’s care, and the solicitude of the *primicerius* and treasurer. [Col. 0431B]

## CHAPTER XVII. On Archdeacons

The archdeacon commands subdeacons and Levites; these ministries belong to him. The care and organization of parishes, and disputes, belong to his oversight. For repairing diocesan basilicas, he makes recommendation to the priest; by order of the bishop, he investigates parishes and the ornaments and property of basilicas or parishes; he reports to the bishop the records of ecclesiastical liberties; he receives the money collected from the communion and brings it to the bishop; and, as one called into a share of pastoral care under the bishop, he administers certain other duties of episcopal oversight in the examination of ecclesiastical cases.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the *Primicerius*

[Col. 0431C]

Acolytes, exorcists, readers, and psalmists—that is, singers—belong to the *primicerius*. It also belongs to him diligently to give the signal for clerics’ duties, for uprightness of life, and for carrying out the duty of singing: readings, blessings, psalms, praises, the offertory, and responsories; and to determine which cleric ought to say them. To him also belongs the order and manner of singing psalms in choir according to solemnity and season; the arrangement for carrying lights; and, if anything is needed for the repair of basilicas in the city, he reports what and of what sort these are to the priest. He sends the bishop’s letters concerning fast days to parishioners through the doorkeepers. Clerics whom he knows to be at fault he disciplines; but concerning those whom he cannot correct, he reports their offense [Col. 0431D] to the bishop’s notice. He appoints basilica officers and arranges the lists of recipients of church support. When the *primicerius* is absent, the person who is nearest to him either by law or by training proven for the fulfillment of these duties carries out the matters mentioned above.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Treasurer

Doorkeepers, the arrangement of basilicas, preparation of incense, care for preparing chrism, care for arranging the baptistery, and preparation of lights at the sacrifice and sacrifices belong to the treasurer.

## CHAPTER XX. When and How Ordinations Are to Be Performed

The holy Fathers decreed that sacred ordinations, namely of presbyters [Col. 0432A] and deacons, should be performed only at fixed times: in the fast of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months, and at the beginning of Lent and the middle of Lent, on Saturday toward evening, after the fast has been observed. When a bishop intends to perform ordinations, all who wish to approach sacred order must be summoned to the city on the Wednesday before the ordination itself, together with the presbyters who ought to present them. Then the bishop ought to select from his own side priests and other prudent men, knowledgeable in divine law and trained in ecclesiastical enactments, who may diligently investigate, without favor or desire for a gift, the life and learning of those to be ordained according to the truth; so that, after being carefully examined for three [Col. 0432B] consecutive days, those found approved may at last be presented to the bishop for consecration on Saturday. The sacred canons decreed that the blessings of pontiffs should be celebrated only on Sundays.

## CHAPTER XXI. At What Age Those Being Ordained Are to Be Ordained

[Note: [Col. 0431] See the Council of Trent, session 23, in the decree on reform, chapters 12, 13, and 14.]

Concerning the age of candidates for ordination, the ordinance of sacred Scripture has left us the following distinction: a subdeacon is not to be ordained before fourteen years of age, nor a deacon before twenty-five, nor a presbyter before thirty, so that afterwards, if he is found worthy, he may be chosen bishop.

## CHAPTER XXII. That Priests Are Not to Be Ordained Without a Definite Title

What need is there to say that a presbyter or deacon should not [Col. 0432C] be ordained without a definite title, since, even if we followed the perfection of ecclesiastical discipline, no one ought otherwise to be admitted into the clergy?

## CHAPTER XXIII. What Sort of Persons Are to Be Chosen for Sacred Orders, and What Sort Are Not

The Fathers have left us many instructions concerning the life and condition of those chosen for sacred orders.

For they decided to define what does not prevent from sacred orders those whose manner of life has been approved. Those who are perhaps made lame by a surgeon’s incision, or are mutilated because of illness or through violence; and those who have lost some member not voluntarily but by accident—provided this is such as does not prevent the performance of their ministry; likewise laymen who have known neither concubine [Col. 0432D] nor harlot, have not been bigamists, and have otherwise lived without accusation; and free persons who have been manumitted by their masters in such a way that no right or power of service remains over them, and who have lived without accusation—all these, they decreed, may be admitted to the clergy without objection.

But public penitents, criminals, the unlettered, bigamists, husbands of repudiated women, persons born from adultery, persons baptized by heretics, and those who have mutilated themselves are to be excluded from sacred orders; and the possessed are not to be received into the clergy. Nor are sons of presbyters to be admitted to sacred orders, except those commended by either religious habit [Col. 0433A] or the integrity of a spiritual life. Penitents, if necessity requires, may be assigned among doorkeepers or readers, provided that they do not read the Gospel or Epistle. But if they have been ordained, they permit them to be ranked among subdeacons, provided that they do not lay hands on anyone or touch sacred things.

By penitents we mean those who, after baptism, have been reconciled to the divine altar while performing public penance in haircloth for homicide, various crimes, or very grave sins. Likewise, they permit neither transmarine and unknown persons nor clerics of other churches to be ordained or, if already ordained, received, without letters of recommendation from their own bishops.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Grounds upon Which Transfer of Those Ordained May Be Made

[Col. 0433B]

The transfer of bishops from their own places to other places ought by no means to be made except under compelling great advantage [Col. 0434A] or necessity. This should not be done by the bishops themselves, but by the counsel and invitation of fellow bishops and by authority of the Roman pontiff. Likewise, the transfer of clerics or presbyters should not be made without great discernment and without the counsel and authority of their own bishops. The sacred canons also forbid a cleric to be enrolled in the Churches of two cities.

They further testify that presbyters ought not, having abandoned the care of their own Churches, undertake a journey, whether for prayer or for any other purpose, without consulting their bishop. They also determine what presbyters must necessarily know: namely, the sacramentary, lectionary, baptismal rite, computus, canon, penitential, psalter, homilies appropriate throughout the year for Sundays and each [Col. 0434B] feast, and many other things that have either been reasonably said or must necessarily be done concerning the life and conduct of sacred orders.

# PART FOUR. ON SACRED VESTMENTS

[Col. 0433]

## CHAPTER I. How Many Sacred Vestments There Are, and What They Are

[Col. 0433B]

Priests and ministers of Christ ought to know that a distinctive dress is assigned to them in sacred ministry so that, through what appears outwardly, the sort of persons they ought to be inwardly may be shown. The rite of sacred vestments has been derived partly from the Old Testament and partly added by later Fathers. We read (Lev. 8) that Moses brought his brother Aaron with his sons to the entrance of the tabernacle of witness for consecration, [Col. 0433C] washed him with water, clothed him in a linen tunic, then girded him with a belt, clothed him in an inner tunic, placed the shoulder-piece upon him, girded him according to the workmanship of the shoulder-piece, and placed upon him the *logion*, that is, the breastpiece, in which were manifestation and truth. He placed a mitre upon his head, and upon the mitre, on his forehead, a golden plate on which was written the name of God.

If you count the seven aforementioned articles of pontifical adornment, you will find: the linen tunic, belt, inner tunic, shoulder-piece, breastpiece, mitre, and golden plate. If you add the linen breeches, which by sacred rite were fastened around the pontiff’s loins, there are eight priestly vestments.

## CHAPTER II. On the Linen Tunic

[Col. 0433D]

The linen tunic is what is called in Greek ποδήρης (*podērēs*), that is, “reaching to the feet,” because it extends from the neck down to the ankles. In the new priesthood it is woven not only of fine linen but also of flax. Being fitted and adapted to the limbs of the body, it shows that nothing superfluous or disorderly ought to be present in the priest’s life. On account of its white appearance it bears the name *alba* (“white garment”), by which the purity of God’s ministers is signified. As it is written: “Fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints” [Col. 0434B] (Rev. XIX). For human flesh acquires through grace, by the effort of good striving, the purity which it does not possess by nature, so that, according to the Apostle, the minister of Christ may chastise his body and bring it into servitude (I Cor. IX), just as fine linen or flax acquires, through labor and industry—being worn down by many beatings and, as it were, by a certain affliction—the whiteness which it did not possess by nature.

## CHAPTER III. On the Girdle

[Col. 0434C] This garment, that is, the linen tunic, is firmly bound about the loins, so that the priest’s chastity may not be loosened by any heat of incitements, as it is written: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke V). The white garment signifies purity, while the girdle signifies self-restraint, so that the spiritual life may neither be defiled there nor flow away here. In the Old Testament this girdle is found distinguished by four colors: fine linen, purple, hyacinth-blue, and scarlet. By various interpretations these are thought to refer either to the four elements, from whose combination human nature consists—so that all that belongs to a human being may be bound and restrained from the flow of vices—or to the four principal virtues of the soul, with which a person ought to be girded and fortified on every side.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Linen Breeches

[Col. 0434D] As a sign of the same chastity and continence denoted by the tunic and the girdle, linen breeches are also commanded, among the other sacred vestments, to be applied around the loins of those entering upon the sacred ministry. This is required not so much from the necessity of covering nakedness—which was covered by the ordinary garments of daily use—as for signifying the preservation of chastity and purity. Nor should it be supposed that, among that earlier people, men were accustomed to go about with their flesh exposed or uncovered through lack of shame, and that only when entering [Col. 0435A] the holy place were they commanded to cover what ought to be concealed. Rather, the word of God willed that, in their sacred office, God’s ministers should have a special and distinctive covering for concealing the weaker parts of the body, in order to show thereby that their modesty and chastity ought especially, when they handled holy things, to be unique and distinctive.

Therefore, ministers of the new priesthood do not put on this distinctive covering in the sacred office, because they are charged with the daily necessity of preserving chastity, just as they have been granted the daily power of offering. But ministers of the old figure put on the breeches at the time of offering sacrifice and, when the ministry has been completed, loosen them again; because the old law prohibited from contact with flesh those who were about to handle sacred things, whom it afterwards released, once their turn of service had been fulfilled, to the activity of carnal intercourse. The remaining two garments, [Col. 0435B] namely, the linen tunic and the girdle, are known to be common to the priests of the Old and New Testaments, although our priesthood does not require a girdle woven with four colors—perhaps this was introduced to avoid superstition, or because of a lack of craftsmanship—being content with pure and simple continence.

## CHAPTER V. On the Inner Tunic

The fourth vestment follows: the inner, or hyacinth-blue, tunic, which only high priests use in both the Old and the New Testament. And fittingly the high priest is clothed with two tunics, for he ought to bring forth from his treasury things new and old. For this reason the second tunic itself is called the inner tunic, or hyacinth-blue, whose color imitates the appearance of a clear sky, so that it may be understood [Col. 0435C] thereby that the high priest ought to think more of heavenly than of earthly things. The proper order is this: first, purity of the flesh is expressed by the linen tunic, the girdle, and the breeches; then purity of heart is signified by the inner or hyacinth-blue tunic.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Shoulder-Garment

The fifth garment is the shoulder-garment, called in Hebrew *Ephot* [ephod]. In the Old Testament only high priests used it, and it was distinguished by the same colors as the girdle. Under grace, however, this garment is common to priests as well as high priests. What we said was signified by the four colors in the girdle is found signified by the same four colors in the shoulder-garment. The shoulder-garment [Col. 0435D] signifies strength in works and endurance in labors, because the shoulders are placed beneath burdens in order to carry them. Accordingly, on the shoulder-garment itself were set two precious stones, one upon the right shoulder and the other upon the left; on them the names of the twelve patriarchs were inscribed, six on one and six on the other. For by the names of the patriarchs is understood the remembrance of the saints, which the priest ought always to have impressed upon his heart and to bear on his right and on his left—that is, in prosperity and adversity. Our priesthood, however, does not possess a similarly woven shoulder-garment like that of old, because the Christian religion ought to devote itself more to simple truth than to superstition.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Breastpiece, Called *Logion* in Greek

[Col. 0436A]

Next follows the breastpiece, or *logion*, which is placed upon the high priest’s breast, to show that wisdom and discernment ought to dwell in his heart. In the breastpiece itself were placed “manifestation and truth,” so that in his teaching the high priest may not presume to propose or effect anything other than truth, nor cease to approve and make manifest through reason and deed that which he has inwardly drawn from truth.

It should be noted that the breastpiece and the shoulder-garment are joined to one another, because reason and works ought to adhere together and agree, so that we may fulfill in works what we apprehend by the understanding of the mind. Moreover, the breastpiece is not named before the shoulder-garment, because in the school of virtues works come first, so that you may attain wisdom, [Col. 0436B] as it is written: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Ps. CXVIII). And again: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I). Manifestation follows only after the breastpiece, lest you presume to teach what you have not first learned. This also accords with the fact that twelve stones were set into the breastpiece, containing upon themselves the inscribed names of the twelve patriarchs, because the high priest ought to keep the examples of the holy Fathers impressed upon his memory and regulate his deeds in accordance with them.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Mitre Called *Cydaris* or Tiara, and on the Golden Plate

After the other ornaments, the mitre is placed upon the high priest’s head; it is also called *cydaris* or tiara. By it is signified the governance of the five senses, which have their seat [Col. 0436C] in the head. Thus the minister who governs his life well adorns his head, Christ. But because, as the Apostle says, “the head of Christ is God” (I Cor. XI), fittingly, as the head’s final ornament, a golden plate is placed upon it, on which is inscribed the name of God, called ineffable in Hebrew. By this is signified that God, as he is the creator of all things, is likewise the ruler of all things; and that whatever has been well administered by priests and sacred ministers must be referred to his honor and glory.

Moses established in Exodus (ch. XXVIII) that these vestments ought to number eight. But, when discussing the same vestments in Leviticus (ch. VIII), he was silent concerning the eighth, namely the breeches—perhaps because the law does not lay its hand upon our genitals and shameful parts, since we ought to offer God a voluntary sacrifice of chastity, as it is written: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord” (I Cor. VII). And God himself, speaking of voluntary eunuchs, added: “Let him who can receive it receive it” (Matt. XIX). It is as though he said: “I do not clothe with breeches, nor do I impose necessity upon anyone. Whoever wishes to be a priest, let him clothe himself; and let those who enter into holy things voluntarily assume, for covering the parts that ought to be concealed, the defense of chastity.” It should also be noted that priests of the lower order are given neither the hyacinth-blue tunic, nor the shoulder-garment, nor the breastpiece, nor the golden plate. These are used only by high priests—that is, chief priests. They have only the *poderis*, the mitre, and the girdle with which the *poderis* [Col. 0437A] itself, that is, the linen tunic, is bound; for they do indeed exercise the priesthood, but not in the dignity in which those exercise it who are adorned with eight vestments.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Vestments of the New Priesthood

These are the vestments which the new priesthood adopted from the Old Dispensation: the linen tunic, girdle, shoulder-garment, inner tunic, breastpiece, and mitre. Yet only high priests use the inner tunic and the breastpiece. The new priesthood does not have the golden plate; in its place the sign of the cross is now impressed upon the foreheads of the faithful, because the blood of the Gospel is more precious than the gold of the law.

## CHAPTER X. On the Stole or Orarium

These are the things which the new institution added to the old. [Col. 0437B] The stole, also called the *orarium*, is placed upon the priest’s neck, to signify that he has taken up the Lord’s yoke. Descending from the neck over the front, it adorns the right and the left side, in order to teach him that through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left—that is, in prosperity and adversity—he must be fortified, as it is written: “You have need of patience, that you may receive the promises” (Heb. X). And again: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. X, XXIV). Hence the stole is joined to the girdle of the *poderis* by certain fastenings, because virtues are joined to virtues, lest they be moved by some onset of temptation.

## CHAPTER XI. On the *Planeta* or Chasuble

Thus, when the priest of the Lord has been adorned—by the tunic with purity, by the girdle with continence, by the shoulder-garment with justice, and by the stole with patience—the chasuble is finally placed over all these. It signifies charity, as it is written: “I show you a still more excellent way” (I Cor. XII). “Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I am nothing,” etc. (I Cor. XIII).

## CHAPTER XII. On the Cloth or Maniple

Because negligence sometimes steals even into minds that are well ordered and devoted to divine worship, continual diligence must be applied to cleanse it away, so that it may often be wiped away like a certain rheum that dims the eyes. For this reason a small cloth is placed in the left hand, to touch the frequently flowing rheum of the eyes and wipe away their bleared condition [Col. 0437D].

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Dalmatic

Moreover, levites use another garment called the dalmatic, deriving its name from the region where its use is thought first to have been instituted. In form it resembles the *colobium* [a sleeveless tunic] which the apostles and certain successors of the apostles are recorded to have used, but with sleeves added. [Col. 0438A] Because of its breadth, the dalmatic signifies care for neighbors, extending itself through love so as to benefit many people. The dalmatic’s significance for levites and the chasuble’s significance for presbyters thus tend to one end, because both are charged with care and concern for their neighbors, to be fulfilled through love.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Sandals and Fine-Linen or Linen Stockings

Bishops and cardinal presbyters use sandals, which are the footwear of preachers. Underneath, they have a whole sole, lest the foot touch the ground; above, however, they consist of leather perforated in places. This means that the preachers’ steps ought to be protected beneath, lest they be defiled by earthly things, and open above, so that they may be unveiled for knowing heavenly things. [Col. 0438B] Their being open in certain places means that evangelical preaching should neither be disclosed to everyone nor hidden from everyone, as it is written: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Luke VIII). For there the sandals are opened where the mysteries of the kingdom of God are known.

Before they put sandals on their feet, they are clothed in fine-linen or linen stockings extending to the knees and bound there. This signifies that they ought to make straight steps with their feet, strengthen weak knees—that is, knees made slack by neglect—and thus hasten to preach the Gospel.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Bishop’s Staff and Ring

High priests use staffs and rings. By its straightness, the staff signifies the justice of prelates, by which they ought to govern those subject to them. It has a point beneath in order to prick rebels by rebuke; it is curved above in order to draw the meek by consolation. The ring signifies the sacrament of faith, by which the Church, Christ’s bride, has been pledged. Bishops and prelates are her guardians and instructors, and bear this as a sign in testimony to her.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Archbishop’s Pallium

Archbishops use the pallium, which signifies the golden neck-chain that those lawfully competing were accustomed to receive. By the circle with which the shoulders are bound is understood the fear and discipline of the Lord, by which they ought to govern themselves and those subject to them. By the two bands hanging from the top downward on each side—that is, before and behind—[Col. 0438D] are figured the preaching of both Testaments, or love of God and neighbor.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Sacred Vessels

These are the points which we have briefly touched upon concerning sacred vessels in the divine ministry. The altar signifies the cross; the chalice, the tomb; the paten, the stone; the corporal cloth, the winding sheet in which Christ’s body was wrapped.

# PART FIVE. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[Col. 0439]

## CHAPTER I. On the Dedication of a Church

[Col. 0439A]

After the orders which we set forth in the first part of ecclesiastical administration, we pass to consideration of the sacraments. First, it seems proper to speak of the sacrament of the dedication of a church, in which all the other sacraments are celebrated. In the discussion of sacraments which we set forth above in general terms, we distinguished certain sacraments as being of salvation, others of administration, and others of exercise: the first for remedy, the second for office, the third for exercise. Those which belong to administration or preparation are connected with orders, because orders themselves are sacraments, as are the things considered in connection with orders, such as sacred vestments, vessels, and other things of this kind. Since all these things, as has been said, are considered in relation to the orders themselves, they ought not to have been treated separately.

All the other sacraments, however, for whose making and sanctifying all these things have been set forth beforehand as certain instruments, call for subsequent treatment. And first, as has been said, the dedication of the church: as it were a first baptism, by which the Church herself is in some fashion first baptized, so that afterwards people may be baptized in her and regenerated for salvation. For baptism is recognized as, in a sense, the first sacrament, by which all the faithful are numbered among the members of Christ’s body through the grace of new regeneration. Therefore this is the first matter that presents itself for treatment: first prefigured in the dedication of a church, and then displayed in the sanctification of the faithful soul. For everything visibly expressed symbolically in this house of prayer is displayed in the faithful soul by invisible truth. The faithful soul itself is the true temple of God, built through the harmony of virtues as by a certain structure of spiritual stones: faith makes the foundation, hope raises the building, charity sets on its completion. The Church itself too, gathered into one from a multitude of faithful persons, is God’s house constructed of living stones, where Christ has been placed as the cornerstone, joining the two walls, of Jews and Gentiles, in one faith. Therefore we first set forth the form of this sacrament displayed in the dedication of a church, so that we may then investigate the mystical understanding of faith which is formed in it.

## CHAPTER II. On What Is Done Visibly in It

[Col. 0439D]

First the high priest blesses water, mixing in symbolic salt; then he sprinkles the church itself externally, going around it three times, with clergy and people following. Meanwhile, within the circuit of the church to be dedicated, twelve lights are kindled. Each time he comes to the door of the basilica—which, for the figure of the sacrament, must be closed—[Col. 0440A] he strikes its lintel with the pastoral staff, saying: “Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter in” (Ps. XXIII). To him the deacon stationed inside replies: “Who is this King of glory?” (ibid.). The high priest answers: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (ibid.).

Finally, on the third occasion, when the door has been opened, the high priest enters with clergy and people, saying three times: “Peace to this house” (Luke X). Then he prostrates himself in prayer with the priests, levites, and clergy, for the sanctification of the house to be dedicated. Afterwards, rising from prayer, he does not yet greet the people by saying, “The Lord be with you” (Ruth II), but only urges everyone to pray. When these things have been completed, he begins at the left eastern corner of the basilica and writes the alphabet upon the pavement as far as the right western corner; then again from the right eastern corner as far as the left western corner. He then ascends to a higher place and, standing before the altar, calls upon God for help, saying: “O God, attend to my aid; O Lord, make haste to help me” (Ps. LXIX). “Glory be to the Father. As it was in the beginning, and now, and always,” etc., without Alleluia.

After this he blesses water, mixing in salt and ashes and making the sign of the cross over it three times; wine is also added to this mixture. Afterwards he dips his finger in the water and makes a cross over the four corners of the altar. Then he comes before the altar and, circling it, sprinkles it seven times with an aspergillum made of hyssop. He then goes around the whole church, sprinkling its interior walls with the same water, doing this a third time. [Col. 0440C] Meanwhile the psalm “Let God arise” (Ps. LXVII) is sung with an antiphon. The antiphon “He who dwells in the help of the Most High” (Ps. XC) is also sung. Meanwhile the high priest goes around, passing through the middle of the church and singing: “My house, a house,” etc. (Isa. LVI; Matt. XXI); and again: “I will declare your name to my brethren; in the midst of the church I will praise you” (Ps. XXI).

When these things have been done, the high priest gives himself to prayer, asking that all who enter that same house to pray may rejoice that they have been heard. When the expiation has been completed, he turns to the altar, beginning the antiphon “I will enter unto the altar of God” (Ps. XLII), with the psalm itself; and he pours what remains of the water of purification at the base of the altar [Col. 0440D]. Then the altar itself is wiped with a linen cloth, and the high priest places incense upon it. Afterwards he makes a cross in the middle of the altar and at its four corners with consecrated oil. Then, around the church, twelve crosses are anointed with chrism on the walls, three on each side being traced by the high priest himself. Returning once more to the altar, he offers burning incense upon it in the form of a cross; and thus, finally, when the consecration has been completed, the altar itself is covered with white veils.

## CHAPTER III. What Is the Mystery of the Things Mentioned Above?

[Col. 0441A]

Many profound mysteries lie hidden in all these things; of these we touch upon a few, to stir the memory. The house to be dedicated is the soul to be sanctified. Water is penitence, washing away the filth of sins. Salt is the divine word, biting in rebuke and seasoning tasteless hearts. The threefold sprinkling is the threefold immersion for purification through water. The twelve lights are the apostles, illuminating the Church through the four parts of the world and bearing throughout the world the mystery of the cross. The high priest is Christ; the staff is power. The threefold striking of the lintel is the condemnation of heaven, earth, and hell. The question asked from within is the ignorance of the people; the opening of the door, the removal of sin.

As the high priest enters the church he invokes peace upon the house, because Christ, entering the world, made peace between God and humankind. He prays prostrate for the sanctification of the house, and Christ, humbled, prayed to the Father for his disciples and for all who would believe, saying: “Father, sanctify them in your name” (John XVII). Rising from prayer, he does not greet the people, because those who have not yet been sanctified are not to be congratulated, but prayed for. The writing of the alphabet is the simple teaching of faith. The pavement is the human heart. The alphabet is written on the pavement when a carnal and unlearned people is initiated into the first and simple teaching of faith.

The line drawn from the left eastern corner to the right western corner, and again from the right eastern corner to the left western corner, expresses the form of the cross, which is impressed upon human minds through faith in evangelical preaching. And because faith was first among the Jews and afterwards passed to the Gentiles, and because again, in the end, the fullness of the Gentiles will have entered, then all Israel will be saved (Rom. XI). These two lines, joined in the figure of the cross, therefore signify the gathering of both peoples. This is what Jacob did when, blessing Joseph’s sons, he expressed the form of the cross by crossing his hands: he placed his right hand upon Ephraim’s head and his left upon Manasseh’s head, because the earlier people was rejected and the younger set on the right hand (Gen. XLVIII).

The crozier or pastoral staff, by which Scripture is symbolized, signifies the ministry of teachers, through whose effort and preaching the conversion of the Gentiles has occurred and that of the Jews must be brought to completion. [Col. 0441D] That, standing before the altar, he calls [Col. 0442A] upon God for help signifies those who, having received knowledge of the faith, prepare themselves for good works and for conflict against invisible enemies; and because they do not at all presume upon their own powers, they pray that divine help may be present to them. Since this expresses the labor of those who are fighting, Alleluia is not yet named, as though amid sighs and groans.

After these things water is blessed with salt and ashes, with wine added and mixed with the water. The water is the people; the salt, doctrine; the ash, remembrance of Christ’s passion; the wine mixed with water, Christ as God and man. The wine is divinity; the water, mortality. Thus the people are sanctified by the doctrine of faith and remembrance of Christ’s passion, united to their head, God and man. Afterwards the Church is sprinkled inside with sanctified water, to show that the soul to be sanctified must be sanctified inwardly as well as outwardly. The hyssop aspergillum signifies Christ’s humility, by which sprinkling the holy Church is cleansed. The high priest goes around the altar and the whole church, sprinkling as though purifying all, and, by word and example, making himself available to all in a common care for everyone. For this reason he also completes the work with prayer, praying that those asking just things there may be heard, since a human work may exist without divine help, but cannot be fruitful.

Finally, when the expiation has been completed, the high priest turns to the altar and pours at its base what remains of the water of purification, as though entrusting to God what remains—what exceeds his powers—in the perfection of the sacred ministry. Then the altar is wiped with a linen cloth. The altar is Christ, upon whom we offer to the Father the gift of our devotion. The linen cloth is his flesh, brought through the beatings of the Passion to the whiteness of incorruption. Incense signifies the prayers of the saints. Oil, however, denotes the grace of the Holy Spirit, whose fullness first went before in the head and then flowed down in participation to the members. Therefore twelve crosses are anointed with chrism on the walls from the consecrated altar, because spiritual grace descended from Christ to the apostles, so that they might preach the mystery of the cross through the four parts of the world together with faith in the Trinity. The white veil with which the altar is covered after consecration signifies the glory of incorruption, with which, after the Passion had destroyed mortality, the humanity of Jesus was clothed, as it is written: “You have torn my sackcloth and surrounded me with gladness” (Ps. [Col. 0442D] XXIX).

# PART SIX. ON THE SACRAMENT OF BAPTISM

[Col. 0441]

## CHAPTER I. Why It Is First, and What Must Be Investigated Concerning It

[Col. 0441D]

The sacrament of baptism is the first among all sacraments in which salvation is shown to consist. For the Lord says of it: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven [of God]” (John III). And again: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark XVI). These, therefore, are the principal matters which we propose to investigate concerning the sacrament of baptism.

First, what baptism is; second, why baptism was instituted, or why circumcision and certain other sacraments of the Old Law were changed; third, when baptism was instituted, and concerning the three periods. First, when circumcision had its standing before baptism. Finally, when baptism had its standing after circumcision. In the middle period, when circumcision and [Col. 0443A] baptism ran together: the one so that it might come to an end, the other so that it might be confirmed. Likewise, when people began to be bound by the command to receive baptism; likewise, what difference there is between the baptism of John and that of Christ; likewise, what the form of John’s baptism was; likewise, what the form of Christ’s baptism is; likewise, whether no one can be saved unless he has actually received the sacrament of baptism. Many matters remain to be investigated concerning all these things; but for the present, according to our ability, let us set forth a few.

## CHAPTER II. What Baptism Is, and on the Name of God in Which Baptism Is Performed, and on Faith and the Sanctifying Word
If, then, it is asked what baptism is, we say that baptism is water sanctified by the word of God for the washing away of sins. For water by itself can be an element, but it cannot be a sacrament until the word is added to the element and it becomes a sacrament. By the word the element is sanctified, so that it may receive the power of a sacrament. Thus, just as the element represents by a certain natural quality, signifies by an added institution, so by sanctification it contains the spiritual grace—which is to be bestowed through it upon those who are sanctified. The word by which the element is sanctified in order that it may be a sacrament, we understand to be that of which it was said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). Therefore the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit is itself the word of God by which the element is sanctified so that it may be a sacrament.
