And rightly are things sanctified by the word of God which subsist as created by the word of God: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 148). Could he create by the word and not sanctify by the word? Do you suppose that he who gave them existence through the word cannot also add grace through that same word? Therefore do not wonder that the sacrament instituted as a remedy of salvation is sanctified by the word of God.

But perhaps your thought asks: What is this word of God? What is this name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in which we are commanded to be baptized? Must one understand some utterance or a sound brought forth to human ears? If the name of the Trinity must be understood as some utterance, what utterance, or of what kind, must be understood? If we say that the utterance *God* is to be understood in this name, it follows that wherever that sound has not been uttered over the water to be sanctified, there can be no sacrament of baptism.

What then? You immersed a man and said: “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” And you tell me: “This man is a Christian. He was baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. I immersed him three times in the water. As I immersed him, I said: ‘I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’ Therefore I stand as witness that he was baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. He was baptized in the name of the Trinity.”

In what name? You told me that the name of the Trinity is *God*. I did not hear that name here when you spoke: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” What name, then, did you intend to say? You said that you baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; but you did not say the name of which you spoke. How, then, was the water sanctified in the name that was not spoken?

But if you suppose that in saying “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” you have said the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and that “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” is to be understood in this sense, that the Father’s name is said insofar as “Father” is said, the Son’s name insofar as “Son” is said, and the Holy Spirit’s name insofar as “Holy Spirit” is said—then there are many names, not one name. I received the Lord’s command to baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; but you baptized in many names. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three names, and the names of three, not one name or the name of one. For the three are not one person, although the three are one.

But he did not say “in the names,” but, “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” because there is one name where there is one nature, one substance, one divinity, one majesty. This is the name in which all must be saved (Acts 4). I should therefore like you to show me where you uttered this one name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit when, immersing the man, you said: “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

If, then, you conceive something of this kind in your mind and seek instruction as to what the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is in which we are baptized and obtain remission of sins, I consider your zeal for faith by no means to be despised. For how can we baptize in that very name if we do not know the name itself? Every day we cry: “Hallowed be thy name” (Matt. 6). But how is it hallowed in us if it is unknown to us? And if we ask that an utterance be hallowed, let one who can tell us how we ask to be saved in an utterance: “Save me, O God, in thy name” (Ps. 53). If salvation, therefore, is in an utterance, then those who are silent—or rather, who are unable to speak—cannot be saved because they cannot speak. Who would say this?

Therefore the name of God, in which we must be sanctified and saved, must be sought beyond the utterance, lest perhaps, by placing it in utterance alone, we create an obstacle to truth. “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75). Therefore where knowledge is, there is the name, because that knowledge itself is the name.

Someone says: “That man is of great name,” and “that man has a great name among the people.” Perhaps his name is great because it has many syllables. Therefore God’s name is small, because it comprises only two syllables and is formed from two syllables. You now see where the greatness of God’s name lies. For where the greatness of the name is, there also the name itself must be understood. If, therefore, we fittingly understand the greatness of the name as greatness of reputation and greatness of knowledge, we ought to understand the name itself as that reputation and knowledge rather than as some utterance or sound of a voice reaching the ears.

Therefore his reputation and his knowledge are his name. And again, his knowledge is nothing other than faith in him; for at present God is known only through faith, though afterwards he is also to be known by sight. Therefore faith in God is itself the name of God, through which his knowledge is now possessed in names, where his presence is not yet seen by human beings. I think it is now neither obscure nor ambiguous how one is saved in God’s name: one is justified by what one has been able to think concerning him and, in thinking, believe; and, being justified, is set free.

Likewise, how God’s name is hallowed when God is honored by those who know him is not doubtful, if we render reverence of chaste fear and love to him whom we have already merited to know through faith. What do you think? If God’s name is his knowledge, and faith in him is within us, are not those baptized in his name who are baptized in faith in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? For this is the one name and the name of the one, by which the Trinity is proclaimed and unity is not denied.

Therefore, when you baptize in faith in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, you baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. And you confess this name—that is, this faith—when you say: “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Thus is fulfilled what is written: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10).

But perhaps, since the Lord Jesus Christ said, “Baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” if the name is to be understood as knowledge and faith in the Trinity, it would suffice, for completing the form of the sacrament and accomplishing sanctification, to immerse the person to be baptized with faith alone and without uttering words. For he who said that people should be baptized in faith in the Trinity did not teach what should be said, but showed what should be believed.

Therefore, lest the profession of faith seem superfluous in the sanctification of the sacrament, we must understand something more in the words “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” than if it had been said, “in the faith of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” For a name seems to contain something more than faith. Faith is within and lies hidden, until it begins to be named and brought into manifestation. For then it begins to be a name, when it begins to be named and made known so as to be recognized.

Accordingly, we baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit when we baptize in the confession of faith in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For he himself said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Teach and baptize: if you immerse and remain silent, you immerse but do not teach. You have “baptize,” but you do not have “teach.” Therefore believe and confess; speak and immerse, so that those things which must be cleansed may be washed in confession.

But perhaps you ask what form of profession of faith ought to be understood in completing the sacrament of baptism. I think the brief answer is that the form of baptism is the one which the Lord Jesus Christ delivered when he sent his disciples to baptize all nations, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

Therefore you will rightly act if you confess what he commanded. He commanded that you baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. You immerse a person and say: “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” You rightly follow the form of the divine institution: you do what he commanded and profess what he instituted.

But you ask: What if someone, perhaps through ignorance and without conscious error, did not preserve the form of these words, but nevertheless baptized a person with full faith, saying: “I baptize you in the name of God the almighty Father,” or “in the name of the Son of God,” or “in the name of the Holy Spirit,” or even—as we read in the Acts of the Apostles—“in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 2), or something else similar, which would differ from the aforesaid form of expression in the wording of the utterance, but would not be contrary to it in the profession of truth? Would the true sacrament of baptism then subsist in that case?

Perhaps many arguments from both sides could be brought forward to resolve your question and to show that, where the same faith is present, a diversity of wording that does not depart from the sincerity and unity of that faith causes no harm. But on this point it seemed to me better to answer your question by authority rather than by my own reasoning.

Blessed Ambrose, in the book which he wrote on the Trinity, says:

> Those who denied that they knew the Holy Spirit, although they said that they had been baptized with John’s baptism, were baptized afterwards; because John baptized for remission of sins in the name of the coming Jesus, not in his own name. Therefore they did not know the Spirit, because they had not received baptism in Christ’s name, as John used to baptize. For although John did not baptize in the Spirit, nevertheless he preached both Christ and the Spirit. Finally, when he was asked whether perhaps he himself was the Christ, he answered: “I baptize you with water; but one stronger than I is coming, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3).
>
> Therefore those who were baptized neither in Christ’s name nor with faith in the Holy Spirit could not receive the sacrament of baptism. Accordingly, they were baptized in the name of Jesus Christ; and baptism was not repeated in their case, but renewed. For there is one baptism. But where the full sacrament of baptism is not present, not even a beginning or any appearance of baptism is deemed to exist.
>
> But it is complete to confess Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. If you deny one, you overthrow the whole. And just as, if you include in speech one—either Father, Son, or Holy Spirit—but in faith deny neither Father, Son, nor Holy Spirit, the sacrament of faith is complete; so also, although you say Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, if you diminish the power of either Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, the mystery is altogether empty.
>
> Finally, those very persons who said, “We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit” (Acts 19), were afterwards baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ; and this was sufficient for grace, because, with Paul preaching, they had already come to know the Holy Spirit. Nor should this appear contradictory, because, although the Spirit was afterwards unmentioned, he was nevertheless believed in. What was unspoken in word was expressed in faith. For when it is said, “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” the mystery is fulfilled through the unity of the name. Nor is the Spirit separated from Christ’s baptism, because John baptized in repentance, Christ in the Spirit.
>
> Let us now consider whether, just as we read that the sacrament of baptism is complete in Christ’s name, so also, when the Holy Spirit is named, nothing is lacking for the fullness of the mystery. Let us follow the reasoning, because whoever has named one has signified the Trinity. If you say “Christ,” you have indicated God the Father, by whom the Son was anointed; the Son himself, who was anointed; and the Holy Spirit, with whom he was anointed. For it is written: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 10).
>
> And if you say “Father,” you have likewise indicated his Son and the Spirit of his mouth, provided that you comprehend this also in your heart. And if you say “Spirit,” you have named both God the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds, and the Son, because the Spirit is also the Son’s Spirit. Therefore, that authority may be joined to reasoning, Scripture indicates that we can rightly be baptized in the Spirit also, the Lord saying: “But you shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1; Matt. 3). And he says to the apostles: “For we were all baptized in one Spirit into one body” (1 Cor. 12). One work, because one mystery; one baptism, because one death for the world. Therefore there is unity of operation and unity of proclamation, which cannot be separated.

Thus far the words of blessed Ambrose clearly explain how one ought to think concerning the proper form of baptism. You see, therefore, how the sacrament of baptism is complete in faith in the Trinity when the Father alone, or the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone is named; and how, without faith in the Trinity, it is imperfect even though all three are named together. For as complete faith is required everywhere, so, while that completeness of faith remains, the wording may vary without detriment to salvation.

Nevertheless, ecclesiastical custom has chosen especially to retain in baptism the form which it received, from the first institution, as one to be observed from the very author of sanctification. If someone perhaps asks whether, in an emergency, the full sacrament of baptism can be sufficient if someone has been baptized in faith in the Trinity without an utterance of words—because the baptizer could not speak, or because, through haste or the stupefaction of imminent danger, or for some other reason, he was overtaken while baptizing and did not remember to speak—if someone asks this, I do not wish to judge concerning things that are hidden, especially because I have not heard the name of the Trinity in this case. Even if true faith was present, there was nevertheless no confession of faith.

And these remarks for the present on what the sacrament of baptism is and on the sanctifying word are sufficient.

## CHAPTER III. Why the sacrament of baptism was instituted

It remains to show why the sacrament of baptism was instituted, and why circumcision, which is thought formerly to have stood in its place, was removed or changed when baptism succeeded it. For if sins were formerly forgiven through circumcision in the same way as they are now through baptism, what necessity was there for circumcision itself to be changed when the sacrament of baptism succeeded? Why, moreover, should that which is believed to have been of less benefit when received be declared no less harmful when neglected?

For just as it is now said through the Gospel: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of God” (John 3), so it was formerly said through the Law: “The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised—that soul shall perish from his people” (Gen. 17). Unless perhaps someone wishes to understand from the fact that the unbaptized person is said to be excluded from the kingdom of God, whereas the uncircumcised person is described as perishing, that baptism confers something more than circumcision: circumcision, when received, could only deliver from perdition, while baptism can lead the reborn even to glory.

For those ancient fathers who had received the justification of the sacrament of circumcision were indeed preserved from perdition, but they were not led to the glory of the kingdom until he came who, by shedding his blood, extinguished the fiery sword, reopened the entrance to paradise, and, himself going before as the first, opened the gate of the heavenly kingdom to all who believe in him. In this, therefore, baptism confers more: it sends those reborn who depart hence immediately into the kingdom. Yet this is granted by the power of the shed blood which sanctifies the water itself.

If, therefore, anyone wishes to say that circumcision was changed into baptism so that baptism might accomplish what circumcision could not fulfill, perhaps he may fittingly be answered that what baptism now possesses in addition does not come from baptism, but is accomplished by Christ’s passion sanctifying baptism. Circumcision could have done the same if Christ’s passion had been joined to it as cooperating in its sanctification. For in baptism, insofar as the power of baptism itself is concerned, only forgiveness of sins is received, just as in circumcision; for, as has been said, the later opening of access to the heavenly homeland for those who have been justified is granted by Christ’s cross.

For such a reason, we think another cause for the change of circumcision, more fitting and more evident, should perhaps be proposed. In an earlier passage, when we were treating of the sacraments, we said that all sacraments are certain signs of that spiritual grace which is bestowed through them. But, in accordance with the progression of times, the signs of spiritual graces ought always to be formed more and more evident and expressive, so that together with the effect of salvation knowledge of truth might grow.

Thus under the law of nature there were first given sacraments: tithings, sacrifices, and offerings. In tithing, indeed, forgiveness of sins was signified; in sacrifices, mortification of the flesh; and in offerings, the performance of a good work. But this signification was obscure in the sacrament of tithing, where a person offered a portion of what he possessed and retained a portion, in order that, in this manner, he might ascribe to himself what belonged to imperfection and defect, while attributing to God what pertained to goodness. The nine parts retained signified this for themselves, because nine is a sign of imperfection, falling short of the perfect number ten.

Therefore, because the sign of cleansing in tithing was obscure, circumcision was given in order that it might demonstrate the power of justification more plainly. A person was commanded to remove a portion of his flesh—not, indeed, something superfluous, but a sign of that which was superfluous in the human being—so that by this he might recognize that the fault which nature drew through that part of the body was cleansed by grace through the sacrament of circumcision.

But because circumcision can cut away only external deformities and cannot cleanse the inward filth of defilements, after circumcision came the washing of water, which cleanses the whole person, so that perfect righteousness might be signified. Again, because the cleansing of the former people, who served under fear, was burdensome, the sacrament of circumcision was given them in flesh, which feels pain. But to the new people, who serve by free will and love, the sacrament of justification was presented in the washing of water, which has a gentle purification. This, then, we think is the account to be given for the alteration of the sacrament of circumcision and the institution of the sacrament of baptism.

## CHAPTER IV. When the sacrament of baptism was instituted

It is also asked when the sacrament of baptism was instituted, from which time onward it was unlawful to neglect it and obligatory to receive it. There are, indeed, several differing opinions on this question.

Some say that baptism was instituted when Christ, setting forth to Nicodemus, who came to him by night, the manner of new regeneration, said: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3). Others say that the institution of baptism began when, after his resurrection, as he was about to ascend into heaven, Christ sent his disciples to preach, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). Some think that the institution of baptism began when John began to baptize in water, preaching that another would baptize in the Spirit. Others think that, in Christ’s passion, when he said, “It is finished” (John 19), all the sacraments of the Old Testament came to an end and those of the New began.

It seems more fitting, however, to say that baptism was first introduced into use, through John and afterwards through Christ or Christ’s disciples, for a time merely so that it might not be unfamiliar through lack of custom; but that it was instituted universally only at the end, when preachers were sent to baptize the whole world.

Here three periods seem to be distinguished. First, before baptism, circumcision alone held its standing and was received for justification without baptism. Last of all, now after circumcision, baptism alone holds its standing and is celebrated for salvation without circumcision. But there was a middle period in which circumcision and baptism ran together: the former, that is circumcision, so that it might be ended; the latter, that is baptism, so that it might be confirmed.

For things that were to be ended ought not to have been discarded suddenly or precipitately, but gradually and, as it were, with a certain reverence, so that they might be shown to have been good in their own time. Likewise, things that were to begin ought not to have been immediately invested with authority, but begun with delay and gravity, lest they be thought to have been introduced from elsewhere as something alien and irrelevant. Therefore the former were dismissed, not cast away; and the latter were instituted, not usurped, so that the authority of the divine plan might be preserved everywhere and human disputation might be warned not to dare criticize divine works.

Therefore, although in Christ’s passion, through which all things were completed, the order of the old figure received its end and the establishment of the new sacrament its beginning, nevertheless the new things had begun at an earlier time for the sake of custom, and the old things were subsequently tolerated for a while by dispensation. Thus both existed together during that period, whether before or after the passion: from the time the new things began until the old things were afterwards forbidden. Accordingly, in that middle period, baptism stood with circumcision from its beginning until Christ’s passion; and circumcision stood with baptism after Christ’s passion until the time when circumcision itself began to be prohibited.

For just as before the passion circumcision itself was received in its standing as a remedy, and yet baptism was not then despised without danger to salvation by those to whom it was preached, so after the passion baptism was received, as it were, in its standing for salvation, and yet circumcision was not then despised without danger to salvation by those to whom its end had not yet been made known. But after it was said, “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5), circumcision could no longer be received for salvation, just as previously, after it had been said, “The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised—that soul shall perish from his people” (Gen. 17), circumcision could not, especially by those on whom it had been imposed, be despised without danger to salvation.

Again, just as in the beginning baptism was administered by John according to the sacrament alone, in order that those unfamiliar with the practice of baptism might be instructed, so at the end circumcision was received by certain believers, by way of dispensation and according to the sacrament alone, lest those accustomed to circumcision should be scandalized.

## CHAPTER V. When people began to be bound by the command to receive baptism

If, then, it is asked when people began to be bound by the obligation of receiving baptism, this is shown to accord with truth and reason: each person began to be bound by the obligation to receive baptism from the time when, after its institution, he received the command to be baptized, or, before its institution, the counsel to be baptized. For one who was neither formerly blameworthy as a despiser of counsel nor afterwards as a transgressor of command was not blameworthy—unless perhaps someone is said to have been ignorant, before or afterwards, though knowledge of the divine institution would have reached him had his own fault not obstructed it.

Therefore, when Christ said to Nicodemus, who came to him by night, “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3), counsel was revealed to a friend. But when he later said, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28), the command was set forth for the instruction of all. There a general institution was made, which made each person liable from the time when the command of the institution came to that person through the apostles, the heralds preaching the word.

But concerning those who in the meantime were far away, or were near but situated in concealment, and perhaps were taken from this life before they had learned of the divine institution, I think the same should be held as concerning those who lived before the institution itself, whether uncircumcised or under the Law: absence accomplished for these what the times accomplished for them.

But if anyone wishes to be obstinate and maintains that even now certain people dwell in unknown regions and remote parts of the earth who perhaps have not received the divine command concerning the reception of the sacrament of baptism, I affirm without hesitation either that no such persons exist, or that, if perhaps someone does exist, he could and ought to have heard and known, had his own fault not obstructed it—especially since Scripture plainly cries: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18).

If, therefore, their sound has gone out into all the earth, then in every land persons either have heard and are condemned as despisers, or have not heard through their own fault, and, ignorant, are disregarded and are not saved. These things have been said concerning the time of the institution of baptism and the obligation to receive baptism.

## CHAPTER VI. The difference between John’s baptism and Christ’s; and the form of John’s and Christ’s baptism

The difference between John’s baptism and Christ’s baptism is this: in John’s baptism, only the sacrament was given through the dipping in water; whereas in Christ’s baptism, together with the sacrament, the reality of the sacrament is received. For John dipped sinners in water and imposed penance upon those confessing their sins; Christ baptizes and forgives sins. The former, in baptizing, preached one who was to come and baptize in the Spirit; the latter, in baptizing, bestows the Spirit for the remission of sins. There people were baptized in the name of the one who was to come; here people are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matt. 28).

Thus the sacrament was the same in both cases as regards its outward form, but it was not the same in effect, because there there was the sacrament alone, for there was no remission of sins; here, however, both the sacramental form is presented and the power of the sacrament is simultaneously granted in remission of sins.

## CHAPTER VII. Whether, after the command concerning baptism was given, anyone can be saved without actually receiving the sacrament of baptism

[Col. 0452A]

Some inquire—whether from curiosity or earnest study—whether, after the sacrament of baptism has been prescribed and publicly set forth, anyone can be saved unless he actually receives that sacrament of baptism itself. For the arguments seem manifest, and they have many authorities—if indeed those who do not understand can be said to possess them. First, because it has been said: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3). And elsewhere again: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16). There are many other such passages, by which it seems to be established, as it were, that he who has not had this sacrament can in no way be saved [Col. 0452B], whatever else he may have besides this sacrament. Though he have perfect faith; though he have hope and charity; even though he have a contrite and humbled heart which God does not despise; true repentance for past deeds and a firm purpose for the future—whatever he may have, he cannot be saved if he does not have this.

And this seems wholly so to them because it is written: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of God.” Yet, if someone asks what has become of those who departed this life for Christ’s sake through the shedding of blood, without the sacrament of water, they do not dare to say that such persons are not saved. And although they cannot show this in what was written above, nevertheless they do not dare to say [Col. 0452C] that it must be denied because it is not written there. For he who said, “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit,” did not add, “or by blood shed in place of water”; and yet it is true, though it is not written here. For if he who received water for God’s sake is saved, why should not he who shed his blood for God’s sake be saved all the more? For to give blood is greater than to receive water.

What some say—that those who shed their blood are saved because they also shed water with their blood, and receive baptism in the water which they shed—is plainly frivolous. For if those who are killed are called baptized because the moisture of water flows with bloody discharge from their wounds, [Col. 0452D] then those who are suffocated, drowned, or killed by any other kind of death in which no blood is shed are not baptized in their own blood; and they have died for Christ in vain, because they did not pour out the moisture of water which they had within their bodies. Who would say this? Therefore he who dies for Christ is baptized in blood; and even if he does not shed blood from a wound, he gives the life which is more precious than blood. For he might shed blood and yet not give his life; and it would be less to shed blood than to give life.

Therefore he rightly sheds his blood who lays down his life for Christ, and he has his baptism in the power of the sacrament—that power without which receiving the sacrament itself does not profit, while, when it is possessed, the inability to receive the sacrament does no harm. It is therefore true [Col. 0453A]—although it was not said there—that he who dies for Christ is baptized in Christ.

“So,” they say, “it is true although it was not said there; and it is true because it was said elsewhere, even though it was not said there.” For he who said, “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God,” himself elsewhere said: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father” (Matthew 10). Therefore, what was not said there must nevertheless be understood, although it was not said, because it was said elsewhere. See, then, what they say: “What was not said must be understood where it was not said, because it was said elsewhere.”

If, then, this must be understood in this place where it was not said because it was said elsewhere, why likewise should not faith be understood, because elsewhere it was said: “He who believes in me shall not see death for ever” (John 11)? [Col. 0453B] Again, he who said, “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God,” himself said: “He who believes in me shall not die for ever” (ibid.). Either, therefore, deny faith or grant salvation. What seems right to you? Where there is faith, where there is hope, where there is charity—indeed, where there is the full and perfect power of the sacrament—is there no salvation because the sacrament alone is absent, and absent because it cannot be had?

“He who believes,” he says, “and is baptized shall be saved.” Behold, then, there is no doubt that where faith and baptism are, there is salvation. And what follows? “But he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16). [Col. 0453C] Why did he choose to say it thus? Why did he not say: “He who does not believe and is not baptized shall be condemned,” as he had said: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved”? Why, except because believing belongs to the will, and faith cannot be lacking to one willing to believe? Thus, in one who does not believe, a perverse will is always charged, where there can be no necessity pleaded as an excuse.

But baptism may be within one’s will even when it is not within one’s power; and therefore a good will, together with the devotion of its faith, is rightly not despised, though an emergency prevents it from receiving the outward sacrament of water. Do you wish to know more fully whether this reasoning establishes itself anywhere by clearer authority, although the authorities mentioned above seem so evident that their truth cannot be doubted? [Col. 0453D] Hear, then, something further, if perhaps what you ought not doubt can be shown to you more clearly.

Blessed Augustine says in the book *On the One Baptism*: “Considering the matter again and again, I find that not only suffering for the name of Christ can supply what baptism lacked, but also faith and conversion of heart, if in the straits of time one cannot come to the celebration of the mystery of baptism.” You see that he plainly testifies that faith and conversion of heart, that is, a good will, can suffice for salvation where the visible sacrament of water cannot be received through necessity.

But lest some contradiction seem to you to arise from the fact that later, in the book of *Retractions*, he rejected the example of the thief which he had brought forward to support this judgment—in which he had said that the shedding of blood, or faith and conversion of heart, can fulfill the place of baptism—saying: “In the fourth book, when I said that suffering can take the place of baptism, I did not provide a sufficiently suitable example in that thief, of whom it is uncertain whether he was baptized”: [Col. 0454A] you should observe that here he corrected only the example which he had adduced for proving his judgment; he did not reject the judgment itself.

But if you think that the judgment must for this reason be rejected because the example was corrected, then it is false that he said the shedding of blood can take the place of baptism, since that very example was supplied to prove it. For he did not say, “When I said that faith can take the place of baptism,” but, “When I said,” he says, “that suffering can take the place of baptism,” although he had stated both in that one judgment. If, then, the example was supplied for what he said, that suffering can take the place of baptism, and this itself is certainly true without any ambiguity, it is clear that the example was afterward corrected, but the judgment was not rejected.

You must therefore either confess that, in a case of necessity, true faith and confession of heart can fulfill the place of baptism, or show how true faith and unfeigned charity can exist where salvation is absent. Unless perhaps you wish to say that no one who will not receive the visible sacrament of water [Col. 0454B] can possess true faith and true charity. By what reasoning or authority you would prove this, however, I do not know. Yet we do not now contend about whether someone who is not going to receive the sacrament of baptism can possess these things. Only this is certain: if there were anyone who possessed them, he could not perish even without the visible sacrament of water.

Many other arguments might have been adduced to prove this; but we do not think that those which we set forth above in the treatise on the sacraments to prove the same point should be repeated again.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Sacraments of Neophytes

*Neophyte* means “novice.” A neophyte is one recently converted to the faith, or inexperienced in the discipline of religious life. Those newly converted to the faith [Col. 0454D] must be instructed by visible sacraments, so that through the things which they see they may understand those which they do not see.

Such persons must be reminded to consider that the faith in which they themselves are new is not new. For, just as from the beginning of the world faithful and righteous members of Christ have never been absent at any time, so likewise from the beginning the sacraments of salvation have never been absent: sacraments which went before as preparation and sign of the redemption accomplished in Christ’s death.

For in the first age Abel offered a lamb in sacrifice, a figure of Christ’s death. In the second age Noah guided the ark amid the flood, just as Christ, governing the Church amid the waves of temptations, does not allow it to sink. In the third age Abraham slew a ram in place of his offered son, just as God the Father offered his Word for the salvation of the world. In him, while the inviolable divinity [Col. 0455A] remained, human nature alone endured the pain of death.

Afterward the people of Israel were led out of Egypt through the Red Sea in a pillar of fire and cloud, just as God’s faithful are delivered from the darkness of sin, renewed through the sacrament of baptism consecrated by Christ’s blood, following him in faith—in whom are both the cloud of humanity and the fire of divinity.

In the fourth age, the temporal kingdom of God’s people was raised up in Jerusalem, prefiguring the eternal kingdom. In it the Prince of Peace, the Father of the Age to Come (Isaiah 9), will lead his faithful into the vision of eternal peace. David was the beginning of this kingdom. Tested and glorified through many tribulations, he left his son, the successor of peace, in order to show that those who have not been strong in overcoming temptations and tribulations in this present life cannot arrive at the rest of future peace. Therefore those who are to be baptized on the holy Saturday of the Paschal solemnity are brought to church for catechesis on the Wednesday of the fourth week of Lenten observance, [Col. 0455B] which supplies us with weapons of self-restraint. There they are to hear and be instructed how they must fight against spiritual wickedness.

Yet their baptism is deferred until the Saturday of the Paschal solemnity, the Church observing that those who are summoned to knowledge in the present life are baptized in hope of the rest to come. In the fifth age the people, because of their sins, were led captive to Babylon; and again, when God had mercy, after seventy years, freed from the yoke of captivity, they were recalled to their own land. For God’s people, subject to vanity and confusion in this life [Col. 0455C] which revolves in the sevenfold course of days, bear the yoke of mortality; after its end they are freed from corruption.

Thus, from the beginning, God’s sacraments have never been absent at any time: through them the faithful people were nourished toward the reception of invisible things and trained for knowledge. Finally, in the sixth age Christ was born of a virgin, just as on the sixth day the first man was formed from virgin earth. Therefore he, as though about to bring all things to completion, when he had reached manhood, was baptized by John in the thirtieth year of his age—not from necessity, but by dispensation, in order to sanctify the washing for those to be cleansed.

Then, summoning the apostles as ministers of the Gospel, he began to preach that the kingdom of heaven was coming. Finally, for the completion of all things, offering himself as a victim to the Father upon the altar of the cross for the redemption of the world, [Col. 0455D] he endured death in order to take away the fear of death from those who believe in him; and he rose from death in order to give those dying for him the hope of life and resurrection. Thereafter, about to ascend into heaven, he sent his disciples into the whole world to teach and baptize all nations, so that those who were called might follow the one who had gone before them into life.

These are the sacraments of the Christian faith: established from the beginning, to be believed at the end, and profitable without end. With these we imbue catechumens, and we require from those to be regenerated by the sacrament of newness the faith to be obtained by a saving confession.

## CHAPTER IX. On Catechesis

*Catechumen* means “instructed” or “one who hears”; [Col. 0456A] for to catechize is to instruct. Those who are to be baptized are first instructed and taught what is the form of the Christian faith, in which they must be saved and receive the sacrament of salvation, as it is written: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28).

Teach first; baptize afterward. Teach for instruction; baptize for cleansing. Teach for faith; baptize for the remission of sins. Therefore teach, because “he who believes”; therefore baptize, because “he who is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16). This form of catechesis was accordingly instituted from the earliest times of the Christian faith. It was then necessarily observed when the rule of Christian faith was proclaimed to adults and persons possessing understanding before they approached the sacrament of baptism, [Col. 0456B] so that either, freely assenting to faith, they might be judged worthy of spiritual regeneration, or, refusing to believe, they might deservedly be rejected from receiving God’s sacrament as unworthy.

For the human will must be consulted in attaining salvation, because the work of salvation must be voluntary. This, indeed, was done in this way from the beginning. But after the multitude of the nations entered the faith, the same form is now observed also for little children born to believers. Mother Church, by provident dispensation, does not wish them meanwhile to lack the sacrament of salvation, lest by that very delay they should be cut off from salvation if, without receiving the sacrament of salvation, they should suddenly depart this life.

Therefore a remedy of salvation was fittingly provided for them: that they should be baptized in the sacrament of faith and reconciled to God through another’s faith—those who are known to have been alienated from God through another’s sin. Accordingly, for this purpose a new rite was instituted: little children are catechized, exorcized, initiated, and then baptized. [Col. 0456C] In their case the Church hears on behalf of the children, answers the questions, and makes promises, until they themselves reach years of understanding and can understand and keep for themselves the sacraments of faith, charity, and hope.

## CHAPTER X. On Exorcism

*Exorcism* is called *adjuration* when translated from Greek into Latin. Exorcists are those who, over catechumens or over the possessed—that is, those who have an unclean spirit—invoke the name of the Lord Jesus, setting divine power against it and adjuring it to depart [Col. 0456D] from them.

Therefore exorcism rightly follows catechesis, so that the hostile power may be driven from one already instructed in faith. Three things must indeed be performed before the reception of newness, by which the person to be baptized is, as it were, conceived and nourished, and advanced to the fullness of new life. These are catechisms, exorcisms, and prayers. First, therefore, the candidate for baptism is catechized, so that he may be moved toward faith by the choice of his own will. Then he is exorcized, so that the wicked power of the devil may be driven from him. Prayer is also added, so that grace may go before and follow after, giving strength to free will and putting far away every deception of the evil spirit.

The form of exorcism is thus performed. First the candidate for baptism is marked with the sign [Col. 0457A] of the cross on the forehead, breast, eyes, nostrils, ears, and mouth, so that the senses of the whole body may be defended by this sign, by whose power all our sacraments are accomplished and all the devil’s fabrications are frustrated. Then blessed salt is given into his mouth, so that, seasoned with wisdom, he may be free of the stench of wickedness and no longer rot from the worms of vices. Then the wicked strong one is breathed upon, so that spirit may drive out spirit. Afterward his ears and nostrils are touched with saliva, so that, by the touch of heavenly wisdom, his ears may be opened to hear the word of God, and likewise his nostrils to discern the odor of life and death. This is the sacrament of opening which the Lord signified in the Gospel when he touched the ears and mouth of the deaf and mute man, saying: “Ephpheta,” that is, “Open up” (Mark 7).

## CHAPTER XI. On What Follows Exorcism in Baptism

[Col. 0457B]

When these things have been completed, the priest comes to the font. The font is consecrated in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that it may be known that the holiness of the sacrament rests not on the one who ministers, but on the one who sanctifies, as it is written: “This is he who baptizes” (John 1). Thus it is neither given better by a good minister nor received worse from an evil one, because the holiness of the sacrament is accomplished not in the merit of those who minister but in the power of God who sanctifies.

The creed of faith, in which consists the form of apostolic teaching, is also handed down to those who are learning the new life. Finally, a little child presented for baptism and asked by the priest whether he renounces Satan, [Col. 0457C] all his works, and all his pomps, answers through the mouths of those carrying him, so that one bound by another’s wrongdoing may be saved by another’s faith and confession.

After the renunciation has been made, he is anointed with holy oil on the breast, as though to fortify him against the enemy, lest the enemy thereafter be able to persuade him of unclean and harmful things. He is also anointed between the shoulders, where the strength for carrying a burden lies, so that he may receive strength to bear the Lord’s burden. Then he is asked whether he believes in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; that there is one Catholic Church; the remission of sins; and eternal life. Under this confession of faith, he is washed by three immersions from the stains of oldness; clothed with the new man, he is buried together with Christ in his three-day death, as the Apostle says: “All of us who were baptized into Christ were baptized into his death. For we were buried with Christ through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6). [Col. 0457D]

For the threefold immersion is a threefold cleansing of thought, speech, and action. When the sacraments of baptism have been completed and the baptized person comes up from the font, he is anointed with holy chrism upon the crown of his head, so that, by sharing in the Spirit of Christ, he may thereafter rightly be called a Christian, made by sacred anointing a co-heir of the kingdom and glory.

Thereafter a white garment is given to the Christian, so that he who had obscured the beauty of his first birth with the rags of oldness may, in the clothing of regeneration, display the garment of glory. After the sacred anointing his head is also covered with a holy veil, so that he may understand [Col. 0458A] that he possesses the diadem of the kingdom and priestly dignity. Finally, a lighted candle is placed in his hand, in order that he may be taught to fulfill the Gospel saying: “So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5). If he preserves this lamp unextinguished, he shall enter the wedding-feast with the heavenly bridegroom among the wise virgins.

## CHAPTER XII. On Godparents

Those who present little children for baptism are called *patrini* [godparents], and by making promises for them become, as it were, sureties before God. They are called *patrini* because they offer those to be regenerated into new life and in some manner become the agents of that new regeneration.

Concerning them, the Fathers decreed that one godparent only should be admitted for each person to be baptized: one person alone, whether man or woman. [Col. 0458B] Perhaps this was in order that spiritual kinship, to which reverence ought to be shown, might not be spread abroad indiscriminately and so become an impediment to marriage. Yet some churches do not observe this custom, admitting several persons to receive little children.

Likewise it was enacted that one who has not been baptized or confirmed may not receive another as a godchild in baptism or in chrism—that is, confirmation. Nor may monks become co-godfathers or co-godmothers, since such ties of familiarity are forbidden to them. Godparents are sureties for those whom they have received at baptism, that they may admonish them, when they reach lawful age, to preserve the right faith and good conduct. Above all, they themselves should know the creed and the Lord’s Prayer, and should teach them to those for whose faith they made their pledge.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Rebaptism

The Apostle says: “One God, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4). Therefore what is one cannot be doubled. Hence, by a most reasonable definition, the holy Fathers established that one known to have received the sacrament of baptism once must never receive it again, whether in the Church or outside the Church—that is, whether he received it from a Catholic or a heretic, [Col. 0458C] indeed whether from a believer or an unbeliever, whatever the condition, age, or sex of the person from whom he received it—provided only that he received it according to the correct form of Catholic baptism. It must be held valid and can never be repeated.

For why should what he received as good not be judged good, even if he did not receive it from a good person? It did not belong to the one from whom—or rather through whom—he received it, who was not good; it belonged to him in whose name he received it, who is always good and could not give evil. Therefore the ancient tradition of the Fathers established that those baptized by heretics in the name of the Trinity, when they return to the unity of the Church, are not rebaptized but reconciled to the Catholic Church either by anointing with chrism or by the laying on of hands. Thus formerly the West restored Arians by the laying on of hands, while the East restored them upon entry into the Catholic Church by anointing with sacred chrism. [Col. 0458D]

For those who received the sacrament outside receive the Spirit within by the laying on of hands. Nevertheless, it was decided that those who do not know whether they were baptized and have no witnesses of their baptism should be baptized without hesitation, because what is not known to have been done ought not to be called repeated.

A question is also raised concerning those who are baptized *mimice*, that is, playfully: do they receive the true and full sacrament of baptism? But it should be understood that it is one thing to give or receive something jokingly or in sport and yet to will to give or receive it, wholly intending that what is jokingly given or received should indeed be given and received. It is another thing to perform something which has the outward form of that act, while neither willing nor intending to perform that act, but rather some entirely different thing. Where, therefore, there is an intention to baptize, even if due reverence is absent in the performance, there is indeed a sacrament, because the act is actually done and intended; yet the performer is not free from fault, because what is done and intended is not done worthily. [Col. 0459A]

But it is wholly ridiculous for there to be said to be an act where it is certain that no intention of performing the act exists, merely because of some appearance resembling the act—not assumed for this purpose, but perhaps arising from some other cause whatever.

Of this sort is the opinion of certain unlearned persons: that the words instituted for consecrating the Eucharist, if uttered over bread and wine by any person, in any place, and with any intention whatsoever, have the effect of consecration and sanctification—as though God’s sacraments had been instituted in such a way that they admit no rational manner of operation, but proceeded to their effect through some tumultuous, violent, and irrational obstinacy, without all intention or will on the part of those acting.

Perhaps I had taken my son to the baths. I came to the water not to baptize but to bathe; not to confer a sacrament but to wash away dirt [Col. 0460A] or to warm the body. I put my little child in the water; but because I wished him to grow well and thrive, I perhaps said—as I might have said while eating and drinking, ploughing and sowing, or doing anything else whatever—“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” You come and tell me that my son has been baptized. I know that he has been bathed; I do not know that he has been baptized. But if you think him baptized because, as I immersed him, I said, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” then even the morsel was baptized because, when I immersed it, I said, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

See, then, and consider that the work of God’s ministries must be rational, and that where there is no intention to act, no judgment should be made merely from the form alone.

## CHAPTER XIV. Why Baptism Is Celebrated in Water Alone

[Col. 0460B]

It should also be understood that the sacrament of baptism was instituted to be consecrated in the element of water alone, because this alone possesses full and perfect cleansing power. All other liquids, however, are purified by water. If anything has been touched by any other liquid, it is washed with water to cleanse it. Therefore the sacrament of cleansing consists in water alone, as it is written: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3).

## CHAPTER XV. On the Form of Baptism

The form of baptism was prefigured long ago in the flood, where, as a figure of those to be saved, eight souls were saved through wood. Likewise in the Red Sea, where the water represented [Col. 0460C] baptism and the redness represented blood. Likewise in the water of sprinkling, with which the ashes of the red heifer were mixed; she signified Christ’s flesh—denoted by the female sex because of weakness, and red because of blood.

# PART SEVEN. ON CONFIRMATION

[Col. 0459]

## CHAPTER I. On Chrism and Its Use

[Col. 0459C]

We read that anointing with chrism was instituted long ago in the Old Testament, when only kings and priests were anointed. By their anointing that unique Anointed One was prefigured, who was anointed above all his companions (Hebrews 1), so that those who shared his name might deserve to be participants in his anointing. For Christ is so called from *chrism*, and a Christian is named from Christ. Therefore, once all began to share the name, all had to receive anointing, because in Christ we are all “a chosen race” and “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2). Chrism is made from oil and balsam, because the infusion of grace is signified through oil, and the fragrance of good repute through balsam.

## CHAPTER II. That the Laying on of Hands Is Performed Only by Bishops

The laying on of hands, customarily called confirmation, by which a Christian is marked on the forehead with anointing by chrism through the laying on of hands, [Col. 0460C] belongs only to bishops, the vicars of the apostles, that they may seal the Christian and confer the Paraclete Spirit. Thus, in the primitive Church, the apostles alone are read to have possessed the power of giving the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. [Col. 0460D]

## CHAPTER III. That Pope Sylvester Instituted the Practice That a Priest Should Anoint the Baptized Person with Chrism on the Crown of the Head

In the pontifical acts it is read that Pope Sylvester decreed that the priest should anoint the baptized person on the crown of the head with chrism, on account of the possibility of death: lest perhaps, through the absence of a bishop and difficulty in reaching him, the baptized person might depart this life without the laying on of hands. This would indeed be altogether dangerous. For as remission of sins is received in baptism, so the Paraclete Spirit is given through the laying on of hands. There grace is bestowed [Col. 0461A] for the remission of sins; here grace is given for confirmation. What good is it if you are raised from a fall unless you are also strengthened to stand?

Therefore those who through negligence lose the bishop’s presence and do not receive the laying on of hands must fear lest for this reason they be condemned, because they ought to have hastened while they could. For the sake of those overtaken by the emergency of time, the anointing with sacred chrism was instituted, by which the priest immediately anoints the baptized person upon the crown of the head, so that by this very fact it may be shown how necessary this sacrament is for salvation, since such careful provision is made for everyone lest they be taken from this life without it.

It is evident, however, that in the earliest times every anointing with chrism was performed only by bishops. [Col. 0461B] But after it was instituted that the priest should anoint the baptized person on the crown of the head, the sealing of the forehead was nevertheless reserved to bishops alone. For only the bishop can seal and anoint the forehead and confer the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER IV. Whether the Laying on of Hands or Baptism Is the Greater Sacrament

It is also asked concerning the sacrament of confirmation, that is, the laying on of hands, whether it is a greater sacrament than baptism. But as the sacred canons determine, each is altogether a great sacrament and must be regarded with the highest devotion. Although the latter—the laying on of hands—seems to deserve greater reverence insofar as it is performed only by bishops, these two are so joined [Col. 0461C] in the work of salvation that, unless death intervenes, they cannot be separated at all.

## CHAPTER V. That the Laying on of Hands Must Not Be Repeated, Like Baptism; and That It Must Be Performed by Those Fasting

It has been determined concerning the sacrament of the laying on of hands [Col. 0462A] that it must never be repeated for any reason, just as baptism must not be repeated; and if it should perhaps be done, it is to be punished by severe penance. It has likewise been decreed that the sacrament of the laying on of hands must be given and received only by those fasting, if the children receiving it are of mature age, so that they may receive the gift of the Holy Spirit in purity.

For just as baptism—which is generally to be celebrated only at the two seasons of Easter and Pentecost—must be celebrated by those fasting, so also the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands ought to be celebrated only by bishops who are fasting and received by those fasting, except in the case of the sick and those in danger of death.

## CHAPTER VI. How Long Those Who Have Received the Laying on of Hands Should Remain under the Discipline of Chrism

[Col. 0462B]

Some commonly ask for how long they should observe the anointing of chrism upon the head—that is, for how long those receiving the laying on of hands should not wash their heads—apart from the period of the baptismal font. They may be answered that it is fitting for the coming of the Holy Spirit to be celebrated in each one who has received him for as long as the Church generally celebrates the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles: namely, seven days.

And rightly so, because there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit comes to his host with seven companions. It is fitting that each person should have his own day, and that a banquet should be prepared for each on his own day. Wisdom has one day, understanding another, counsel another, [Col. 0462C] fortitude another, knowledge another, piety another, and fear another. Such banquets Christ holds among his guests; such also does the Holy Spirit.

# PART EIGHT. ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE BODY AND BLOOD OF CHRIST

[Col. 0461]

## CHAPTER I. On Its Excellence

[Col. 0461C]

[Col. 0461D] The sacrament of Christ’s body and blood is one of those in which salvation principally consists, and it is unique among all, because all sanctification comes from it. For this victim, offered once for the salvation of the world, gave power to all sacraments preceding and following it, so that through it they might sanctify all whom it would deliver.

## CHAPTER II. When the Sacrament of Christ’s Body and Blood Was Instituted

The Lord Jesus Christ himself instituted the sacrament of his body and blood when, after the supper of the old Passover, by divine power transforming bread and wine into his body and blood, he gave them to the apostles to receive and commanded that thereafter they should do the same in remembrance of him.

## CHAPTER III. Whether Christ Gave His Disciples a Mortal or an Immortal Body at Supper

[Col. 0462D]

Some are accustomed to ask what kind of body the Lord Christ gave to his disciples: whether passible or impassible, mortal or immortal, and the other matters pertaining to this question. In such matters, as I have professed also in others, I judge the divine mysteries to be more worthy of reverence than of investigation. I think this sufficient for the simplicity of faith: that we say he gave such as he willed, and again, that he himself knows what he gave. For he gave such as he willed because he was almighty and could do whatever he willed. But he himself knows what he gave because he was Wisdom and could not be ignorant of what was. Therefore one frees oneself more easily from the question, and perhaps rests more safely within oneself, who does not say that he gave a mortal body, lest he seem to speak against the dignity of the [Col. 0463A] sacrament, nor says that he gave an immortal body, lest he be thought to believe against the reality of the mortal body which was in Christ before the resurrection. For this reason perhaps it is better that we should presume to define neither, although we nevertheless believe one of the two to have been the case. Thus let it not be said, “this or that it was,” although it be believed that one of the two it was. But if one must be affirmed, then, without prejudice to the truth, I incline in judgment rather to say that he gave it impassible and immortal, insofar, that is, as pertains to the sanctification of the sacrament.

But if anyone thinks it should be objected that before the resurrection the Lord Jesus Christ bore a mortal body, we also unhesitatingly profess that the Lord Jesus was mortal according to the humanity he assumed; [Col. 0463B] for if we did not believe him mortal, we would deny that he died. Human nature in Christ, therefore, was mortal, but by will, not by necessity. For from the time when, through grace, it was clean from every sin and was joined to the Word of God in the unity of person, it was made free from every necessity and debt of death, so that it owed nothing to death because it had no sin. Yet he willingly endured mortality because he willed to endure death; and if he had not endured mortality, he could not have died at all. Thus he willingly bore mortality until he tasted death, and so laid mortality aside.

Because, then, he was mortal by will and not by necessity, he sometimes [Col. 0463C] laid aside in part, when he willed, the property of that mortality before he wholly put it off through death, as the reason and order of time required; and when he willed he received it again. By this he proved that, insofar as he endured it, it was not by necessity: for one could not altogether endure something by power insofar as he willed not to have it. It is read in the Gospel that, when the Lord Jesus Christ preached the word of life and invited mortals, destined to die, to life, his jealous enemies—whom they could not refute by reason—wished to destroy in rage. Therefore, as though upon one who no longer had anything mortal, “they laid hands upon him and led him to the brow of the hill, that they might cast him down from it” (Luke 4). But he, in order to show that he was indeed mortal, endured being held; and in order again to show that he bore mortality and [Col. 0463D] passibility by will and not necessity, he did not endure being cast down.

When he was being led away, he patiently allowed himself to be held. But when he was to be cast down, he passed mightily through their midst. When he willed, he was held; and when he willed, he was not held. To the extent and at the time he willed, he admitted the nature of mortality. But to the extent he did not will to endure it, and at the time he did not will, he removed it from himself by power. “Passing,” it says, “through their midst, he went” (ibid.). Do you suppose that Christ struggled to pull himself out of the hands of his enemies when he was held by them, in order that, passing freely through their midst, he might go? Is bodily strength alone, then, to be praised in him and not the power of his divinity? That is not fitting. Rather, he showed himself such as he willed, admitting [Col. 0464A] to himself, from what he bore willingly, as much as he willed.

If, then, Christ, according to the plan of the divine dispensation, sometimes laid aside in part for a time the nature of mortality before he cast it off in order to conquer it forever, and again assumed it when the time required, what is surprising if it is said that at some time, for the cause and reason of the time, he laid it aside wholly in a certain respect, although he was still to suffer in it when the time required? If, then, this could be so—that he himself bore himself in his hands and distributed himself to his disciples to be eaten without corruption of himself; and yet he who gave and he who was given, he who bore and he who was borne, were the same—what is surprising if it is said that he was mortal in that which he gave and immortal in that which was given, and yet that he who gave as mortal and was given as immortal was not two, but one and the same?

How was he not given as mortal when he was received invisibly and eaten incorruptibly? “Invisibly,” I mean with respect to the proper form of his body, not with respect to the appearance of his sacrament. [Col. 0464B] For he was received invisibly because, in that which was received, that which he himself was was not seen. Christ was received, and only the appearance of bread and wine was seen. Therefore I say that he was received invisibly and that what he was was not seen. If, then, in that which he gave, that which he was was seen, and in that which was given, that which he was was not seen; and if in that which he gave he was held and crucified, while in that which was given he was broken and not divided, eaten and not corrupted: why do you wonder if, in that which he gave, [Col. 0464C] he is said to have been mortal, and in that which was given, he is proclaimed to have been immortal and impassible? Yet let these things be said in such a way that no prejudice be done to anyone in what remains hidden.

## CHAPTER IV. Whether that which Judas received by the dipped morsel was Christ’s body.

They also ask whether it ought to be believed that that was Christ’s body which he offered to his betrayer in a dipped morsel. “When Jesus had dipped the bread,” it says, “he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot” (John 13). But, as blessed Augustine says, Judas did not then receive Christ’s body, as some careless readers suppose. For it must be understood that he had already distributed to them all the sacrament of his body and blood, Judas himself being present, as Saint Luke relates with the greatest clarity. [Col. 0464D] Then they came to the point at which, according to John’s narrative, he most plainly identifies his betrayer by the dipped and offered morsel—perhaps signifying the latter’s deceit by the dipping of the bread. For not everything that is dipped is washed; some things are dipped in order to be stained. But if this dipping signifies some good thing, condemnation rightly followed upon one ungrateful for that good.

These are indeed the words of blessed Augustine upon the question whether Judas received Christ’s body in the morsel. Yet from the fact that the Lord gave his betrayer a dipped morsel in order to mark him out, the custom holds that the faithful do not receive Christ’s body dipped.

## CHAPTER V. That the paschal lamb was a figure of Christ’s body.

[Col. 0465A]

Just as circumcision of old served in effect in place of baptism for the remission of sins, while the Red Sea presented its likeness and figure, so the paschal lamb, whose flesh was eaten by the people and with whose blood the doorposts of houses were marked, came beforehand as a figure of the sacrament of Christ’s body. But after the reality came, the sign was removed from the midst, since there was no longer a thing to be signified as future, but one to be received as present. Yet the figure remained as long as the reality had not yet come; and that which was later to be fulfilled in reality was first displayed in likeness.

Egypt is the world; the destroyer, God; the lamb, Christ; the lamb’s blood, [Col. 0465B] Christ’s Passion; the houses of souls, bodies; the houses of thoughts, hearts. We stain the former with blood through faith in the Passion; the latter we stain with blood through imitation of the Passion, setting the sign of the cross both within and without against hostile powers. Finally, we eat the lamb’s flesh when, by receiving his true body in the sacrament, we are incorporated into Christ through faith and love. Elsewhere, what is eaten is incorporated. But when Christ’s flesh is eaten, it is not what is eaten, but the one who eats who is incorporated into him whom he eats. Therefore Christ willed to be eaten by us in order to incorporate us into himself. This is the sacrament of Christ’s body, and the reality of the sacrament of Christ’s body. Whoever eats and is incorporated has the sacrament and has the reality of the sacrament. Whoever eats and [Col. 0465C] is not incorporated has the sacrament but does not have the reality of the sacrament. Just as one who is incorporated, even if it does not happen that he eats, has the reality of the sacrament although he does not have the sacrament. Whoever receives has the sacrament; whoever believes and loves has the reality of the sacrament. Therefore it is better for one who believes and loves, even if he cannot receive and eat, than for one who receives and eats but neither believes nor loves, or who believes but does not love.

## CHAPTER VI. That the sacrament of the altar is both a figure, with respect to the appearance of bread and wine, and a reality, with respect to the truth of Christ’s body.

There are some who have thought to derive a defense for error from certain passages of Scripture, saying that in the sacrament [Col. 0465D] of the altar the reality of Christ’s body and blood is not present, but only its image, appearance, and figure. They do so because Scripture sometimes says that what is received in the Eucharist of the altar is its image or appearance—of that which is received in participation in Jesus Christ. These persons certainly would not fall into this snare of error if they either received the sacraments of God with right and humble faith or handled the Scriptures with fitting understanding. But now, because in the sacraments of God they prefer their own judgment to faith, they disdain to keep a sound method of interpretation in the sacred Scriptures. Thus the word of truth makes them more blind, while, when wrongly understood, it supplies error in place of truth. Yet this is no fault of Scripture, but the blindness of those who read and do not understand; [Col. 0466A] not confusion in God’s sacraments, but the perversity of the presumptuous.

Here, however, they have erred dangerously, preferring certain ambiguous passages to so many manifest statements and unquestionable affirmations, and choosing falsehood rather than truth even in those passages—not because that was more said there, but because that was more believed by them. For what? Is the sacrament of the altar not reality because it is a figure? Then neither is Christ’s death reality because it is a figure, nor Christ’s resurrection reality because it is a figure. For the Apostle plainly declares that both Christ’s death and resurrection are figure, image, likeness, sacrament, and example, saying: “Christ died for our offenses and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4), so that, dead to sins, we may live to righteousness. And the apostle Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2). Therefore Christ’s death was an example, that we might die to sin, and his resurrection was an example, that we might live to righteousness. Was it therefore not reality? Then Christ did not truly die and did not truly rise, if his death or resurrection was not real. Far be it! For it is written of him: “Truly he bore our infirmities, and carried our sorrows” (Isa. 53). Therefore Christ’s death was real, and yet it was an example; and his resurrection was real, and it was an example. Why, then, cannot the sacrament of the altar be both likeness and reality? It is likeness in one respect, reality in another.

## CHAPTER VII. That there are three things in the sacrament of the altar: the appearance of bread and wine, the reality of Christ’s body, and spiritual grace.

[Col. 0466C]

For although the sacrament is one, three distinct things are set forth in it: namely, the visible appearance, the reality of the body, and the power of spiritual grace. For the visible appearance which is visibly seen is one thing; the reality of body and blood, believed invisibly beneath the visible appearance, is another; and the spiritual grace, received invisibly and spiritually together with the body and blood, is another. What we see is the appearance of bread and wine; but what we believe beneath that appearance is the true body of Christ and the true blood of Jesus Christ, which hung upon the cross and flowed from his side. Nor do we believe that body and blood are merely [Col. 0466D] signified through bread and wine; rather, beneath the appearance of bread and wine, the true body and true blood are consecrated. The visible appearance is the sacrament of the true body and true blood; but the body and blood are the sacrament of spiritual grace.

And just as an appearance is seen there whose reality or substance is not believed to be there, so a reality is believed to be there truly and substantially present whose appearance is not seen. For the appearance of bread and wine is seen, while the substance of bread and wine is not believed to be present; but the substance of Christ’s body and blood is believed, though its appearance is not seen. Therefore what is seen according to appearance is a sacrament and image of that which is believed according to the reality of the body; and what is believed [Col. 0467A] according to the reality of the body is a sacrament of that which is received according to spiritual grace.

Thus the sacrament of the altar, the divine Eucharist, is an image in the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, according to the appearance of bread and wine in which it is seen; and it is a reality according to the truth of its substance, in which it is believed and received there. And again, what we now receive visibly according to the sacramental appearance, and bodily according to the reality of Christ’s flesh and blood—Christ upon the altar—is a sacrament and image of the way in which we ought to receive that same Christ invisibly and spiritually in the heart, according to the infusion of grace and participation in the Holy Spirit. Therefore the most divine Eucharist, which on the altar is handled visibly and bodily both according to the appearance of bread and wine and according to [Col. 0467B] the reality of Christ’s body and blood, is a sacrament, sign, and image of the invisible and spiritual participation in Jesus that is accomplished inwardly in the heart through faith and love.

## CHAPTER VIII. Why Christ instituted the sacrament of his body and blood under the appearance of bread and wine.

For the Wisdom of God, which manifests itself through visible things, willed to show that it is itself refreshment and food for souls; and therefore it set forth the flesh it had assumed as food, so that [Col. 0467C] through the food of flesh it might invite us to taste divinity. But lest again human weakness should recoil in horror from contact with flesh in receiving it, it veiled that flesh beneath the appearance of customary and chief food; and so set it forth to be received, so that the senses might be comforted in one respect and faith built up in another. For the senses are comforted in one respect when they perceive only what is familiar and customary. But faith is built up in another when, from what it sees, it recognizes the nature of what it does not see.

The appearance of bread and wine is therefore set forth in order to teach that complete and perfect refreshment lies in receiving Christ’s body and blood, from Christ’s divinity. Complete refreshment, moreover, is food and drink; and bread and wine are the principal substance of food and drink. The appearance is set forth from the principal substance of refreshment, in order that it may be received therein and that through it the reality of Christ’s body and blood may be signified. As he himself testifies, saying: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6). Yet because this reception of body and blood [Col. 0467D] alone, without spiritual effect, does not confer salvation, the same Savior declares: “The flesh profits nothing; the Spirit is the one who gives life” (ibid.).

Therefore the power and fullness of spiritual refreshment which is in Christ’s body and blood is signified by the appearance of bread and wine; but it is accomplished in the reception of grace, the infusion of inward and eternal refreshment. And thus, since three things are there in one thing: in the first is found the sign of the second; in the second, the cause of the third; and the third is the power of the second and the reality of the first. These three are in one, and are one sacrament.
