It is therefore clear that reception of the most divine Eucharist is a sacrament and image of participation in Jesus, because what we visibly receive as his sacrament is a sign that [Col. 0468A] we ought to be united to him spiritually.

The Eucharist itself—that is, “good grace”—namely this most divine sacred offering, is so called because it makes divine and makes participants in divinity those who worthily partake of it. And because it is both sign and reality, in which Christ’s true flesh is received beneath the appearance of bread, and in the worthy reception of his flesh the reception, participation, and fellowship of his divinity are also granted, it is therefore most divine, most holy, and sanctifying—the sanctifier of all things and all holy persons.

## CHAPTER IX. How the change of bread and wine into Christ’s body is to be understood.

Through the words of sanctification, the true substance of bread and the true substance of wine are converted into the true body and blood of Christ, with the appearance of bread and wine alone remaining, substance [Col. 0468B] passing into substance. This conversion, however, is to be believed not according to union but according to transition: since it does not happen by an addition to essence, such that through what is added, that to which it is added becomes greater; but by transition, such that what is added becomes one with that to which it is added. Nor do we say that Christ’s body is consecrated in bread in such a way as to receive its being as body from bread, nor as though a new body were suddenly made from a changed essence; rather, the changed essence becomes the true body itself. Nor is the substance of bread and wine reduced to nothing because it ceases to be what it was; rather, it is changed, because it begins to be something else which it was not. And that which it begins to be does not receive its being from the fact that it was bread; [Col. 0468C] rather, it receives its being when it ceases to be what it was.

We have distinguished this more explicitly because of those who, from their own reasoning, cast prejudice upon faith and, following their own judgment, strive to maintain either that only what is seen exists, or that what is believed is of such a kind—that is, because only the appearance of bread and wine is seen, that only the substance of bread and wine is there; or, because the substance of Christ’s body and blood is believed, that the visible appearance and quality of bread and wine can possibly inhere in it—as though an appearance could not appear without its substance being present, or a substance lie hidden whose form does not appear.

## CHAPTER X. What the three portions made from Christ’s body in the sacrament of the altar signify.

The three portions made from Christ’s body [Col. 0468D] upon the altar have a mystical meaning. For the entire Church is Christ’s body, namely the head together with the members; and in this body there are, as it were, three parts of which the whole body consists. One part is the head itself. For the head is both head and likewise a part of the body. Thus the head itself is one part of the body. Another part of the body consists in those members who have already followed the head and are with the head itself where the head is. As it is written: “Wherever the body shall be, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. 24; Luke 17). Those, therefore, who have already departed this life, whose bodies rest in tombs and whose souls are with Christ, are the second part of the body. Thus these are, as it were, two parts together: the head, namely, and this other part of the body. Therefore [Col. 0469A] two portions are reserved separately upon the altar outside the chalice, as though outside the Passion. For the head itself, having risen from death, is now immortal and impassible, to die no more and suffer no more.

Likewise, those who have departed this life in holiness and now glory and rejoice with their head, while awaiting the resurrection and immortality of their own flesh, feel neither pain nor any suffering any longer. These two portions together are outside the chalice and outside the Passion, because those former things have passed away. The third portion is placed in the chalice, signifying those who still live in suffering, until they too depart from this life and pass to their head, where they shall neither die nor suffer any more.

## CHAPTER XI. That when Christ’s body appears to be divided, it is divided only according to appearance; but in itself it remains whole, being wholly in each portion just as it is one and the same in different places.

[Col. 0469B]

Do not suppose, when you see portions in the sacrament of the altar, that Christ’s body is divided or separated from itself, or as though torn limb from limb. It remains whole in itself and is neither divided nor partitioned. But it was necessary that it be displayed to you according to appearance, as pertained to the mystical signification. Thus he shows you outwardly the appearance by which your sense may be instructed, and preserves inwardly the incorruption of his body, in which its unity is not divided. One portion is seen, and seems to be a portion, yet the whole is there; another portion is seen, and seems to be another, yet it is the same and the whole [Col. 0469C] itself. If a third portion is likewise seen, it too is the same and the whole itself. The whole is here and the whole there. It is no less in a portion than in the whole, nor greater in the whole than in a portion. However many portions you make, the whole is in each one.

Do not wonder: this is God’s work. If one person can be in different places, why can he not also be whole in every portion? Both are wonderful, but not false because wonderful. Indeed, it is true because it is wonderful; yet it should not be wondered at, because it is God’s work. It is no wonder if the Wonderful One works wonders. “How,” you ask, “can one body be in different places at the same time? It is here; it is there; and wholly in both places, and likewise in many places.” Do not wonder. He who made place made body, and made place in [Col. 0469D] body and body in place. He who made it so that one body should be in one place made it as he willed; and if he had willed, he could have made it otherwise. For when he wills, he makes it otherwise, and it is always as he wills.

But because he has made it so that one body should be in one place, you have seen what was made and know nothing other than what has been made and what you have seen. Therefore you wonder when you see or hear something other than what you are accustomed to see and hear. But he does not wonder when he does something other than what he is accustomed to do, because when he made the former thing, he knew already that he could make it otherwise if he willed. Therefore, when you begin to wonder at something and perhaps your thought asks you how this can be, think of the one who knows, and whatever it is will cease to be wonderful. Even if it does not cease to be wonderful, it will nevertheless not be incredible. If the almighty Maker is considered, whatever may be will not be impossible.

## CHAPTER XII. That things which appear unworthy in Christ’s body occur only according to appearance.

[Col. 0470A] If it sometimes happens, as it commonly can happen, that you see certain things done in this sacrament which seem less worthy, do not be horrified. This belongs only to the appearance which is manifest. He shows you the appearance and preserves for himself the reality. He presents to your sense the likeness of bodily food, so that your sense may in every respect be instructed by what is proper to it. He preserves for his body the reality of an inviolable and immortal nature, lest it be corrupted in what is its own. If it departed in any respect from the likeness, it would not be a true sacrament; it would disclose itself there and take away the place of faith, and would no longer be believed [Col. 0470B] but seen—which ought not to happen.

Therefore, with respect to us, it preserves in every way the likeness of corruptible food; and yet, with respect to itself, it does not lose the reality of an inviolable body. It appears to be gnawed, and remains incorrupt. It appears to be affected or stained, and persists inviolate. It allows these things to happen around itself, lest our sense perceive anything alien; but it does not receive them into itself, lest its incorruptible nature lose its purity. Such is the dignity and purity of Christ’s body that it can neither be affected by any corruption nor stained by defilements. Therefore, if you ever see these things happen, do not fear for it; rather, be solicitous for yourself. It cannot be harmed; you can be harmed, since you can believe wrongly.

## CHAPTER XIII. What becomes of Christ’s body and his bodily presence after the sacrament has been received.

[Col. 0470C]

But perhaps your thought says to you again: What becomes of Christ’s body after it has been received and eaten? Such are human thoughts that they scarcely wish to rest, especially in matters which ought not to be investigated. Your heart therefore says to you: What has become of Christ’s body after I received and ate it? Listen, then. Do you seek Christ’s bodily presence? Seek it in heaven. There Christ sits at the right hand of God the Father. He willed to be with you temporarily, when and for as long as it was necessary. He showed you his bodily presence for a time in order to stir you toward the spiritual presence. Therefore he came bodily to you and displayed to you for a time his bodily presence [Col. 0470D] so that the spiritual presence—which is not taken away—might be found through it.

Thus, through the flesh he assumed, he came into the world long ago and, according to bodily presence, lived with human beings for a time, in order to stir them to seek and find spiritual presence. Afterwards, when the dispensation was completed, he departed according to bodily presence and remained according to spiritual presence. For, to show that he did not depart according to spiritual presence when he intended to go away according to bodily presence, he said: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

Thus in his sacrament he now comes to you temporarily and is bodily with you, so that through bodily presence you may be stirred to seek spiritual presence [Col. 0471A] and helped to find it. When you hold his sacrament in your hands, he is bodily with you. When you receive it with your mouth, he is bodily with you. When you eat and when you taste, he is bodily with you. Finally, in sight, touch, and taste, he is bodily with you. As long as bodily sense is affected, his bodily presence is not taken away. But after bodily sense fails in receiving it, bodily presence is no longer to be sought; spiritual presence is to be retained. The dispensation is complete; the perfect sacrament remains in power; Christ passes from the mouth to the heart. It is better for you that he should enter your mind than your belly. This food is for the soul, not the body. Do not seek in it the customary condition of bodily food. He comes to you to be eaten, not to be consumed; to be tasted, not to be incorporated.

[Col. 0471B]

Augustine heard a voice from heaven, because this could not be said or answered to him by earthly things: “I am the food of the mature; grow, and you shall eat me—not that you may change me into yourself, as you do the food of your flesh, but you shall be changed into me.” Therefore wisely discern what in God’s sacrament has been presented to the senses and what has been adapted to the spirit, so that even if after reception has been completed you should again perceive something, in this too the appearance may serve the proper function of the senses, so that the truth of the likeness may be preserved everywhere. For if, in anything that ought to be presented to the senses, the likeness failed, there undoubtedly would not be a sacrament there. Rather, the thing itself would disclose and manifest itself by an evident miracle, which is not fitting while faith has a place.

[Col. 0471C]

After these things, therefore, if you seek Christ’s bodily presence, seek it in heaven. Seek it there where it was even before it began to be bodily with you through its sacrament, and from which it did not depart when it came to you.

## CHAPTER XIV. That the celebration of the consecration of Christ’s body is called the Mass; when the Mass was first instituted, by whom, and why it is called “Mass.”

[Col. 0472A]

The celebration of the Mass is performed in commemoration of Christ’s Passion, as he himself commanded the apostles when he gave them his body and blood, saying: “Do this in commemoration of me” (Luke 22). Blessed Peter the Apostle is said to have been the first of all to celebrate this Mass at Antioch. In the beginning of the faith, only three prayers were said in it, beginning at the place where it says, “Therefore, this offering.” The rest was added later by holy Fathers at different times.

It is called *missa*, as though *transmissa* (“sent across”) or *transmissio* (“a sending across”), because the faithful people send their prayers, vows, and offerings to God through the ministry of the priest, who performs the office of mediator [Col. 0472B] between God and human beings. The sacred offering itself may also be called *missa*, because it was first sent by the Father to us, that it might be with us; and afterward by us to the Father, that it might intercede for us with the Father. First it was sent by the Father to us through the Incarnation; afterward, by us to the Father through the Passion. So now in the sacrament: first by the Father to us through the sanctification by which it begins to be with us; afterward by us to the Father through the offering by which it intercedes for us.

Or, as some think, it is called *missa* from *emittendo*, “sending out,” because at the time when the priest begins to consecrate the Lord’s body, the catechumens are sent outside. For when the Gospel has been read, the deacon cries out: “If any catechumen is present, let him go outside.” [Col. 0472C] Catechumens ought not to be present at the sacred mysteries, which are entrusted only to the baptized and Christians; as it is written of certain people who bore the type of catechumens and of those not yet reborn: “But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them” (John 2).

# PART NINE. ON THE LESSER SACRAMENTS AND SACRED RITES.

[Col. 0471]

## CHAPTER I. On the sacraments instituted for spiritual exercise, and that all things are sanctified through the word of God.

[Col. 0471D]

There are certain sacraments in the Church in which, although salvation does not principally consist, salvation is nevertheless increased by them insofar as devotion is exercised. Although all of these cannot now be enumerated, some should not be omitted as examples of the whole. Of these sacraments, some consist in things, such as the water of sprinkling, the reception of ashes, the blessing of branches and candles, and other such things. Others consist in actions, such as the sign of the cross, exsufflation in exorcism, the extending of hands, the bending of knees, and other things of this kind. Others consist in spoken words, such as the invocation of the Trinity and whatever is of this sort.

[Col. 0472D]

All these are sanctified through the word of God: whether they are sanctified through utterance of words, with divine power invoked, or receive the effect of sanctification through faith alone being exercised, by that same divine power. For where true faith is, the word of God cannot be absent, because the word itself is conceived by faith and works through faith. “Whatever you do,” says the Apostle, “do all in the name of the Lord” (Col. 3). We should not, however, infer that the Apostle commanded us to utter words in all our works, but that we should maintain right faith in all our works. For that person does all that he does in the name of the Lord who, through right faith, recognizes that he cannot do any good without him and that, if he does anything praiseworthy, he ought not to glory apart from him. Such a person faithfully seeks help from him before every work, and after the work turns back to his praise and glory all the good that he has accomplished.

Therefore, just as all that we do is rightly said to be done in the name of the Lord through faith alone, even without the utterance [Col. 0473A] of words, so certain sacraments are sanctified through faith alone without utterance of words. For spoken words themselves are sometimes sacraments, though they do not receive sanctification from other words. Yet no sacrament is sanctified without that Word which, whether invoked through faith alone or through faith and utterance of words, accomplishes every sanctification.

## CHAPTER II. On water for sprinkling, which is blessed with salt.

Pope Alexander, the fifth from blessed Peter, established that salt and water should be blessed for sprinkling the people and their dwellings, following, of course, the example in which the prophet Elisha [Col. 0473B] is read to have put salt into water so that, by this seasoning, bitter springs might be changed into sweetness. With this consecrated water, therefore, the faithful are sprinkled, and the dwellings of the faithful are cleansed from the delusion and harassment of evil spirits.

This is the signification of this sacrament: water signifies repentance for past sins; salt, discernment and caution concerning the future. If these two are mixed together, a bitter conscience is changed into sweetness, and the assaults and harassment of demons no longer rule over it. We therefore, following the aforesaid institution, bless salt and water mixed together every Sunday, so that by this sprinkling we may fortify the faithful and the dwellings of the faithful against spiritual wickednesses.

## CHAPTER III. On the reception of ashes.

[Col. 0473C]

The ecclesiastical institution provides that every year at the beginning of Lent, called the head of the fast, on Wednesday, when the voluntary fast is undertaken, consecrated ashes are placed on the heads of the faithful, namely in remembrance of our mortality. Thus the mortal person who, through the garb of penitence and remembrance of his sins, is stirred to devout compunction may also be humbled through remembrance of his condition. For this reason he is told: “Remember that you are ashes, and to ashes you shall return” (Gen. 3).

## CHAPTER IV. On blessing palm branches and leafy boughs.

The ecclesiastical custom also provides that on the Sunday immediately preceding the Paschal solemnity, [Col. 0473D] branches of palms and foliage of trees are blessed and distributed to the people to carry, as a figure of those who, on that same day, went to meet the Lord Jesus as he ascended to Jerusalem, singing and praising with branches of palms and green foliage of trees (Matt. 21). In this, we are not merely instructed to perform bodily what they then performed bodily; rather, we are shown what is to be imitated spiritually in that bodily action, whether theirs or ours. For the palm is a sign of victory, while green branches signify good works. Therefore we meet Christ with branches of palms and foliage, praising him, when we praise with good works and worthy thanksgiving him who triumphed over death.

## Chapter V. On the candle blessed on Holy Saturday, and the lambs blessed at Easter

[Col. 0474A]

Pope Zosimus decreed that a great candle should be blessed on the holy Saturday of Easter; the deacon, having received a blessing from the priest, blesses it. This candle signifies Christ: in the wax, his humanity; in the fire, his divinity. It goes before the catechumens approaching baptism, giving light, just as of old the pillar of fire went before the children of Israel as they crossed the Red Sea, giving light by the fire and casting shade by the cloud (Exod. 14). Under the same figure, according to ancient custom, wax lambs are blessed in the Roman Church on Easter Day and distributed to the people.

## Chapter VI. On the bells whose sound summons the faithful together

[Col. 0474B]

The use of bells was adopted from the Old Testament, where the Lord commanded that silver trumpets, made of beaten metal, should be fashioned to summon the multitude of the people. In likeness of these trumpets, bells of bronze were made in the Church to stir the hearts of the faithful, so that by them a signal might be given when they ought to assemble together (Num. 10). These metal vessels signify the mouths of preachers. The iron clappers by which they are struck within so as to emit a sound are their tongues. The rope is the measure of life and the rule of conduct set forth in Scripture. The rope is held in the hand when Scripture is fulfilled in action. One follows the rope upward who is raised to good things under the guidance of Holy Scripture. One draws the rope downward who, taught by that same Scripture, recognizes how deeply oppressed he lies [Col. 0474C] in evils. He is fit to summon the people of God together who, exalted in conduct, displays examples of goodness, and, bowed down in humility, truthfully acknowledges his own weakness. Evangelical bells, therefore, are more enduring and are heard farther than the trumpets of the Law, because the voice of the Old Testament sounded only for a time, and only to the Jews. But the sound of evangelical preaching has gone out among all nations to the ends of the earth and will not cease until the end of the age.

## Chapter VII. On curtains

The curtain that hangs before the holy things—that is, between the people and the clergy—signifies the veil of the letter, through which the truth of the Gospel was still concealed from those who were under the Law. That curtain which is suspended between the holy things and the Holy of Holies, [Col. 0474D] that is, between the clergy and the sanctuary, signifies the veil of mortal nature, through which heavenly mysteries are still hidden from us even though we are established under grace. The first veil is that which, at Christ’s death, is read to have been torn (Matt. 27; Mark 15). The second veil will not be removed until the time of the resurrection. Therefore, during the season of Lent, which signifies the present life, only one veil is spread between us and the Holy of Holies; it will not be removed until the day of resurrection. For now the letter has indeed been unveiled, but mortality has not yet been removed; yet it will wholly be taken away in the future, when this mortal thing has put on immortality and this corruptible thing incorruption. Then indeed, with unveiled face, we shall enter—or rather, [Col. 0475A] go forth—to contemplate the glory of the Lord, so that, seeing face to face as he is, we may know him whom we now know through faith alone.

## Chapter VIII. On other sacraments consisting in actions

There are many other sacraments of the Church expressed in things or actions; all of them cannot be enumerated here. For they are many, and the brevity of the present discourse does not contain them. Breathing upon someone in exorcism signifies the power of the Holy Spirit, at whose coming the evil spirit is put to flight and overthrown. As it is written: “Your breath blew, and the sea covered them; they sank like lead in mighty waters” (Exod. 15). The sign of the cross displays the power of Christ’s Passion. Thus, when it is impressed upon the forehead, [Col. 0475B] the Christian is fortified; when it is set against an impending danger, the opposing power is driven away. The former is for arms; the latter, for missiles. The former is for defence; the latter, for attack. Striking the breast signifies compunction of heart. The breast is struck so that vain thoughts and wicked desires may be driven from the heart. Bowing the head, bending the knees, and prostration signify humility and reverence, or also the petition for pardon. Extending the hands shows charity and the breadth of good affections.

## Chapter IX. On those sacraments consisting in words

There are likewise other sacraments expressed in the utterance of words alone, and these too display varied significance. Pope Celestine instituted that antiphons from the psalms [Col. 0475C] of David should be sung before the sacrifice; this we call the Introit. Various persons composed the collects, especially Gelasius and Gregory. “The Lord be with you” (Ruth 2) derives from ancient usage: Boaz, greeting his reapers, used this salutation; and the prophet in Chronicles greets King Asa and those who were with him, saying, “The Lord be with you” (2 Chron. 15). In the earliest times the service began with a reading from an epistle of Paul, after which the Gospel followed; just as the angelic hymn now recited in the Mass office on solemn days is first read to have been sung by angels (Luke 2). The words added to it are believed to have been added by blessed Hilary of Poitiers, through whom it was enlarged and brought to completion in the form in which it is now sung. [Col. 0475D] Pope Symmachus, fifty-third in order, instituted that this hymn should be sung in church at the Mass office on Sundays and on the feasts of martyrs. The Italians handed down the responsory, which, through the harshness of its chant, signifies operation and the active life. *Alleluia* signifies joy. By the jubilation in which it ends, it expresses the ineffable joy that is to come at the end. The Tract sometimes signifies tribulation, as “Out of the depths” and “You have shaken”; at other times joy, as “Make a joyful noise” and “Praise.” “I believe in one God” was composed by the one hundred and fifty Fathers at the Council of Constantinople against the heresy of Macedonius, bishop of that city, who asserted that the Holy Spirit was a creature. Pope Sixtus instituted that before the consecration the hymn “Holy, holy, holy” should be sung; [Col. 0476A] its threefold repetition is a confession of the Trinity. It is called the *Secret* because it is said quietly, lest it become cheapened. Formerly it was said aloud; but it is reported that shepherds, having learned it through hearing it daily, sang it in the fields and were struck by divine power. Hence the custom is thought to have been changed.

Pope Pelagius teaches that those are separated from communion with the whole world who, in any dissension, customarily make commemoration of the apostolic pontiff during the sacred mysteries of the Mass. Pope Saint Gelasius composed, for the most part, this supplication and consecration beginning, “Therefore, first of all.” Blessed Gregory added, “Order our days in your peace,” and judged that the Lord’s Prayer should be recited over Christ’s body, as is read in his Life. “Who, the day before he suffered” [Col. 0476B] through “do this in remembrance of me”: the Apostles used these words and celebrated the sacrament of Christ’s body in them. Others report that Pope Alexander added them. Pope Leo decreed that within the Canon one should say, “a holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim.” Pope Felix decreed that Masses should be celebrated above the memorials of martyrs. Pope Gregory decreed that the following should be said in the Canon: “Whose solemnities are celebrated today before the sight of your majesty: O Lord our God, throughout the whole world, into whose fellowship [admit] us.” Pope Sergius decreed that “Lamb of God” should be sung at the breaking of the Lord’s body.

Pope Innocent, to Decentius: “You maintain that before the mysteries are completed peace is given by some to the people, or that priests give it among themselves, whereas—apart from all that [Col. 0476C] I ought not to disclose—peace must necessarily be announced, by which it may be evident that the people have given their assent to all that is done in the mysteries and celebrated in the Church, and that, when these are concluded, they are shown to be finished by the sealing of peace.”

“Glory and honour to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, unto ages of ages. Amen.” Three hundred and eighteen bishops composed this at the Synod of Nicaea against the heresy of Arius, who maintained that the Son was less than the Father and that the Holy Spirit was less than both. Jerome afterwards translated this hymn from Greek into Latin for Pope Damasus and added: “As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be.” “Our Father” (Matt. 6) Christ himself delivered to his disciples. It is therefore especially called the Lord’s Prayer, [Col. 0476D] in which the seven distinct petitions are a sacrament of sevenfold grace. The twelve Apostles composed the Creed of faith, namely “I believe in God,” comprised in the same number of clauses; this number is acknowledged to be a sacrament of the apostolic faith. Blessed Athanasius composed “Whoever wishes.” And many other holy Fathers added various other things to the celebration of the divine office, for the adornment of the Church and the instruction and devotion of the faithful.

## Chapter X. On sacred things and non-sacraments

There are certain other sacred things in the Church which nevertheless are not sacraments. Although they do not have the effect of spiritual grace or confer sanctification, they are sacred in this respect: they pertain to holy things and adhere to those things which possess holiness [Col. 0477A] and confer sanctification. Of this kind are all things belonging to the adornment of churches and whatever is contained in their possessions. In a certain respect they are sacred, in that they have been delivered and assigned to the service of holy things. These, then, are holy in a simple sense, as it were; but those by which these things are consecrated are the Holy of Holies. Whoever removes a holy thing from a holy thing commits sacrilege. But whoever dares to profane these holy things themselves commits an abomination.

Such, therefore, are the things called sacred, or sanctified by sacred things: whatever the Church possesses in earthly substance, whether money or land, especially tithes. From the beginning these were so instituted that they could never, without sin, be alienated from the divine ministry or from the use of those who serve God and are assigned to divine ministry. [Col. 0477B] At first they seem to have been instituted chiefly as a figure of a sacrament. Afterwards, under the written Law and under the law of grace, they were reserved for the support of God’s ministers, so that in them the devotion of those offering might earn merit and the need of those receiving might be relieved. Therefore they can in no way be alienated from the Church’s use, nor pass into lay possession either by exchange or by gift. The remaining corporeal things that the Church possesses, whether in lands or money, cannot be taken away without fault as long as they are lawfully possessed by it; but, if cause and reason require it, they may pass by exchange or gift into another’s possession. [Col. 0478A] Just as it is robbery and violence to take such goods from a person who justly possesses them, so it is sacrilege—and more than robbery—to take them from the Church, which justly possesses them. But no one may appropriate or retain tithes in any manner without the guilt of sacrilege, except those alone for whose support they were ordained by divine institution.

This, therefore, is the difference between tithes and the Church’s other possessions: tithes pertain to sacred things both by institution and by possession; the other ecclesiastical possessions pertain to sacred things by possession alone. Thus the Church’s other possessions cannot be transferred to other possessors without a reasonable exchange. Tithes, however, cannot at all be possessed by others. The former, therefore, cannot be taken away; [Col. 0478B] the latter cannot be transferred. In the former, there is sacrilege if they are taken away; in the latter, if they are transferred. Bishops ought to be stewards of tithes and of the Church’s other possessions, distributing them reasonably to those who serve the Church. If anything from them is at times granted for the support of those who do not serve in ecclesiastical offices but are nevertheless devoted in secret to divine service, it is an indulgence, not a right—provided that this itself comes from the share of the poor, not from the support of the clergy. For regarding what is owed to a minister: “the labourer is worthy of his wages”; nor does one properly support the needy who defrauds the servant.

# Part Ten: On Simony

[Col. 0477]

## Chapter I. Why it is called this, and what simony is

[Col. 0477C]

Simony takes its name from Simon Magus, who left to posterity a deadly example of this evil. Simony is the desire to purchase spiritual grace with money. When this occurs, both the seller and the buyer are surely struck by the same sentence, because they are proved liable to the guilt of the same offence.

## Chapter II. On the originators of simony

The contagion of the simoniacal heresy long ago sprang up in Balaam, who, when the reward for divination was offered, went to curse the people of God (Num. 22). Thereafter, two pestilent originators of this heresy are read to have arisen: one under prophetic teaching, the other under apostolic teaching. First Gehazi appears as the master of sellers (4 Kings 5); then Simon as the originator of buyers [Col. 0477D] (Acts 8). Their followers, as has been said, are no more distinct in their error than they are separate in their condemnation.

## Chapter III. On those who sell or buy spiritual things

Those convicted of buying or selling holy orders are deposed without mercy, since they are plainly unworthy of holy orders who are proved to have sinned in those very holy orders [Col. 0478C]. We sometimes read that heretics coming to the unity of the Church were received in their orders. For certain heretics did not err in receiving orders; rather, another cause and doctrine impeded their faith. But the heresy and sin of simoniacs is their ordination itself. They are therefore rightly not received in their orders, since they sinned in those very orders. It should, however, be understood that those who are unknowingly ordained by simoniacs, because they consider them Catholics and not simoniacs, receive spiritual grace through their ministry, provided that they do not become participants in their error, of which they were unaware. But those who offer money to purchase spiritual grace are simoniacs even when ordained by Catholics.

But [Col. 0478D] you say to me: How can one ordained by a simoniac receive the gift of the Holy Spirit through his laying on of hands? How can a simoniac give what he does not possess, even if he is regarded as a Catholic? Hear how. Just as an adulterer, a fornicator, a drunkard, or a miser can give what he does not possess, so a simoniac can give what he does not possess; and he can truly give it to those worthy to receive it. For it is given through his ministry [Col. 0479A], not through his merit. Hence grace is given through him, but not by him, to those who do not share his error and are not conscious of the guilt. He is an evil minister, yet a minister who dispenses. Just as a heretic or any other evil minister is evil and yet is a minister: evil in having error or wickedness, a minister in having office. So too the simoniac: for he too is a heretic, if not in faith, then in deed; he is an evil minister, yet a minister. He is evil in being a simoniac; a minister in having been ordained to an office; evil in having paid a price; a minister in having received order and office.

But you say to me: How could one who paid a price receive order or office? [Col. 0479B] Hear how: to ruin, to destruction. He could buy office; he could not receive grace. Yet because he has received and possesses office, through his ministry grace and office are given to the good. But the evil receive not grace but office alone; nonetheless they receive it, although it is to the destruction of him who receives wrongly, just as it is to the destruction of him who gave wrongly.

## Chapter IV. On those who, by purchasing corporeal things in the Church, buy spiritual things with and in them

There are certain things in the Church which, when purchased for a price, convey, together with the receipt of a bodily benefit, participation also in a spiritual dignity. In such a case, whoever is known to sell or buy one of the two is proved to have left neither unsold nor unbought [Col. 0479C]. But you say to me: How can this be? I bought food and clothing in the Church; I did not buy the Church. I bought an allowance, I bought a prebend; I bought bodily things only, and bought—or wished to buy—nothing spiritual. Then tell me: Who entered your name among the names of the brethren? Who assigned you a place in choir or chapter? If you did not buy these things, from where do you have them? Who gave them to you? But, you say, I received these freely; I bought the rest. These were given freely. Well do you say it. You bought the sheep and did not buy the wool, but received it freely. Yet if you had not bought the sheep, you would not have had the wool. You paid a price for the tree in order to eat its fruit freely. You thought you had escaped cleverly by a ridiculous contrivance. See, then, how you bought what you would not have had if [Col. 0479D] you had not paid the price. Either confess that you bought this as well, or, if you did not buy it, do not take what is not yours.

But you say to me again: What then? [Col. 0480A] May I not buy an allowance from the Church and purchase, for a price and without the guilt of simony, the expense of bodily support? Behold, I have my own estates or my own money, by which I could be supported and live; but perhaps I fear the violence of princes, the deceit of retainers, or some other thing whatever. Perhaps, too, I consider the decline of my age or the weakness of my strength. I see that I cannot myself properly administer my affairs and attend to my own interests. I come to the Church, entrust my possessions to it, and commit the care of my life to it, asking it to feed and support me, to provide me aid from what is mine; and, lest I perhaps be defrauded in something, I request that a fixed and determined allowance be established for me—namely, as much as any one of those who serve the Church [Col. 0480B] and are enrolled on the Church’s roll receives. I ask for a prebend for my daily sustenance, as another who is in the Church, lives from the Church, and serves the Church has it. The Church gives and grants this to me, receiving what is mine and returning its own—indeed, administering to me what is mine, not what is its own. What judgment, then, do you ask me to give concerning this? I answer you briefly: if in your lifetime you make the Church your steward, or after death leave it as your heir, I neither wish nor can forbid it. And if it feeds you from what is yours or on account of what is yours, it is prudence, not fault; necessity, not wickedness. Provided, however, that you neither seek nor receive anything else, bodily necessity is granted to you; commerce in iniquity is denied.

## Chapter V. On the case in which bodily things alone are sold

[Col. 0480C]

It sometimes happens that possessions of the Church, or any other corporeal ecclesiastical goods, are given or sold by wicked prelates and alienated from the Church’s use. In this kind of case the crime of simony does not seem to be present, although serious fault is not absent. For how great an iniquity it is is plain: those appointed to build and preserve churches labour for their destruction and for the dispersal of what belongs to them—especially if the things alienated are such that they can never lawfully pass to the use of outsiders, as are tithes, instituted from the beginning for the support only of those who serve the tabernacle. To transfer these, therefore, to laypeople—what else is it than to remove a sacred thing from what is sacred? [Col. 0480D] Thus, if each sin is given the name appropriate to its fault, no harm is done to equity in judgment.

# Part Eleven: On the Sacrament of Marriage

[Col. 0479]

## Chapter I. On the excellence of this sacrament, and what must be considered in it

[Col. 0479D]

Although all the sacraments took their beginning after sin and because of sin, the sacrament of marriage alone is read to have been instituted [Col. 0480D] even before sin—not, however, as a remedy, but as an office. In marriage, the matters first to be considered and distinguished are its origin and institution, with their manner and causes, [Col. 0481A] and its variation according to time, place, and rites.

## Chapter II. On the origin of marriage

God is the author of marriage. For he decreed that marriage should exist when he made woman as a help to man for the propagation of the human race. Adam too, recognizing in the Spirit for what purpose the woman had been made, said when she had been brought to him: “This now is bone from my bones, and flesh from my flesh. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother, cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2). Christ also, at Cana of Galilee (John 2), consecrated the wedding not only by his bodily presence but also by the performance of a miracle. In all these things it is shown that marriage is from God and is good.

## Chapter III. On the twofold institution of marriage, and the twofold cause of its institution

[Col. 0481B]

The institution of marriage is twofold: one before sin, for an office; the other after sin, as a remedy. The first was so that nature might multiply; the second, so that nature might be received and vice restrained. The first institution set marriage within a covenant of love, so that in it there might be a sacrament of the fellowship that exists in spirit between God and the soul. It set forth the office of marriage in the union of flesh, so that in it there might be a sacrament of the fellowship that was to exist in flesh between Christ and the Church. The second institution sanctioned marriage in a covenant of love, so that, through its goods, what was weakness and fault in the union of flesh might be excused. It permitted the office of marriage in the union of flesh so that, besides the multiplication [Col. 0481C] of offspring, the weakness of those begetting might be received.

Why the sacrament of marriage was instituted, the Apostle indicates (1 Cor. 11), where he shows that man is the image of God and that woman thereby bears, in a certain manner, the type of the rational soul. Why, again, the office of marriage was first instituted, God himself, its institutor and ordainer, shows when he says: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. 1). That the office of marriage—that is, the union of flesh—was instituted before sin not as a remedy for weakness but for multiplying offspring, and was after sin permitted for that same weakness as a remedy, blessed Augustine testifies in these words: “The weakness of both sexes, tending toward the downfall of shamefulness [Col. 0481D], is rightly received by the honourableness of marriage, so that what was an office for the healthy may be a remedy for the sick.”

Likewise, the same author testifies in *On the Good of Marriage* that marriage itself is one thing and is a sacrament of one reality, while the office of marriage is another thing and is a sacrament of another reality, saying: “In marriage there appears to be some good, not only on account of the propagation of children, but also on account of the natural fellowship of the different sexes. Otherwise marriage would no longer be spoken of among the elderly, even if they had lost children or had not begotten them; for in them, although the ardour of the flesh has withered, the order of charity still flourishes.” Again: “In marriage the holiness of the sacrament is of greater worth than the fruitfulness of the womb.”

Consequently, some people, failing to understand the statement that a woman with whom there is known to have been no carnal intercourse cannot belong to the sacrament of Christ and the Church [Col. 0482A], suppose that the sacrament of marriage cannot exist where no union of flesh has taken place. They do not know that the office of marriage, in the union of flesh, figures the union brought about between Christ and the Church through the assumption of flesh; and for that reason it cannot be the sacrament of Christ and the Church where there has been no carnal intercourse. Nevertheless, marriage is true, and is a true sacrament of marriage, even if carnal intercourse has not followed—indeed, it is so much the truer and holier insofar as it has in itself nothing for which chastity need blush, but something in which charity may glory.

For marriage itself is a sacrament, just as the office of marriage itself is known to be a sacrament. But [Col. 0482B] marriage, as is fitting, is the sacrament of that fellowship which is in spirit between God and the soul. The office of marriage, however, is the sacrament of that fellowship which is in flesh between Christ and the Church. For it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2); but if two are one flesh, they are no longer two, but one flesh. This is the sacrament which the Apostle calls great in Christ and the Church (Eph. 5), and a woman with whom there is known to have been no carnal intercourse cannot belong to this sacrament. Yet she can belong to the other sacrament: not the great sacrament in Christ and the Church, but the greater one in God and the soul. For what? If that which is in flesh is great, is not that which is in spirit great? Indeed, it is far greater. “The flesh,” he says, [Col. 0482C] “profits nothing; it is the Spirit who gives life” (John 6). Therefore, if what is in flesh is great, what is in spirit is surely greater.

If God is rightly called bridegroom in Holy Scripture and the rational soul is called bride, then there is certainly something between God and the soul of which that which exists in marriage between male and female is sacrament and image. And perhaps, to state it more explicitly, the fellowship itself which is outwardly preserved in marriage by the agreement of a covenant is a sacrament, while the reality of that sacrament is the mutual love of souls which is kept toward one another in the bond of marital fellowship and covenant. This love itself, again, by which male and female are united in their souls in the holiness of marriage, is a sacrament and sign of that love by which God is united inwardly to the rational soul through the infusion of his grace and participation in his Spirit [Col. 0482D].

The union of flesh, therefore, which before sin was an office in marriage and after sin was permitted in it as a remedy, is so joined to marriage in both cases that it belongs with marriage itself, but marriage is not derived from it. For marriage is true even before it, and can be holy without it: then, if it were absent, it would be less fruitful; but now, if it is absent, it would be more unalloyed. For the admission of the union of flesh into marriage after sin is more a matter of indulgence and compassion, lest the vice of concupiscence, which took root in human flesh after sin, should flow more shamefully into every excess if it could nowhere be lawfully received.

## Chapter IV. What marriage is; who may lawfully contract it; and what consent is lawful

[Col. 0483A]

Some have thought that marriage should be defined thus: “Marriage is the consent of a man and a woman maintaining an undivided manner of life.” To this definition one must add “lawful”; for if the consent of man and woman is not lawful—that is, made lawfully and between lawful persons—marriage cannot be consecrated therein. We call those persons lawful in whom no reasonable cause can be shown why they may not mutually confirm the covenant of marriage.

I say, “in whom no reasonable cause can be shown,” because even if such a cause perhaps exists, but is hidden and concealed and has not yet been established by the judgment of the Church, then, so far as the judgment of the Church is concerned, the marital covenant can neither be prevented from being made nor, once made, invalidated so that it does not stand. For what is wholly hidden must, as regards the judgment of the Church, be said not to exist, since for bringing about or preventing anything it differs in no respect from that which does not exist.

The first institution excluded only two persons from contracting marriage, namely father and mother, when it declared that a man, in order that he might cleave to his wife, would leave father and mother, saying: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and shall cleave to his wife” (Gen. 2). It is clear that those who are left for this purpose are not required for this purpose. Thus the first institution excluded those two persons alone. In all other cases it prohibited no one from entering into the sacrament of the marital covenant. [Col. 0483B]

Later came the second institution, made through the Law; and it excluded certain other persons, whether for the seemliness of nature or as a token of chastity. From that time onward, what had been permitted by nature began to be unlawful by prohibition. Yet where the prohibition is ignorantly transgressed without culpability, ignorance excuses the transgression. Nor is the force of the sacrament prevented so long as the transgression is not apparent. But when it becomes established that what was forbidden has occurred, it can no longer thereafter stand or be ratified; for what is manifestly done against a command is not judged lawful or valid.

Perhaps there will be those who think that ignorance cannot have such force that, on its account, a union should be called marriage between persons whose marital union would rightly be forbidden if the hidden cause were known. I ask them what they think concerning children begotten from such a union: whether they are to be judged legitimate or illegitimate. If it seems harsh that the children should therefore be called illegitimate because their parents, according to some hidden cause, were united unlawfully, but according to the judgment and permission of the Church lawfully, they must concede that the union from which they were begotten was lawful so long as the cause remained hidden, even if they maintain that it was rightly unlawful.

For not everything done unlawfully is therefore not done because it is done unlawfully. What is done must certainly be said to be done, although it is rightly said to be done wrongly when done in that manner. But if it is known that something is done, and that it is done unlawfully is not known, ignorance may indeed mitigate or excuse guilt, so that the act may be held lawful in what is done, although it cannot make it occur irreproachably in the manner in which it is done. Therefore, if the children are legitimate in some respect, the union from which they arise is legitimate in some respect as well. And if the union itself is rightly called legitimate in some respect, I do not see why marriage should not deservedly be named by that very fact. There is no great dispute about a name where the same judgment is held concerning the reality. [Col. 0484A]

Except, therefore, in such cases in which chastity seems to require protection because of horror or disgrace, I think that in all other cases, if an offence is perhaps committed through ignorance, so long as it remains hidden, it cannot prevent a marriage lawfully contracted according to the judgment of the Church from being called lawful. Let no one, then, set before me brother and sister or other such cases, in which the reasoning of ignorance admits no excuse. Persons are not permitted to offend in such matters in a way for which ignorance ought to excuse them. Such acts belong to horror, not to rational consideration; even if ignorance is present, modesty and chastity do not escape shame.

It is otherwise with those matters of which the Apostle says: “Let no temptation overtake you except what is human” (1 Cor. 10). In matters in which it is human to err, ignorance can excuse the guilt of error. Thus we consider those persons to be lawful according to the judgment of the Church in whom no cause exists for which what is to be done can rightly be forbidden, or, once done, invalidated. But so long as this is the case, what exists is called lawful.

If anyone asks how something can be lawful according to the judgment of the Church when it is not lawful according to the divine judgment, I for my part think it lawful according to both judgments. It is, however, called lawful specifically according to the judgment of the Church because, according to the Church’s judgment, there is nothing in it that ought prevent it from being called lawful; whereas according to the divine judgment there is something in it which, if it were manifest to the Church’s judgment, the marriage would not be lawful. That is: something in it is hidden from the Church but known to God. If it were likewise manifest to the Church, the marriage would not be lawful. [Col. 0484B]

But now it is excused through ignorance, so that by that very fact it is lawful both before God and before human beings so long as it remains unknown: before human beings, indeed, nothing in it is censured; before God, what is blameworthy, even if it entails guilt, is nevertheless not imputed to the shame of condemnation. Such persons, then, we consider lawful in the Church according to the judgment of the Church.

We consider lawful consent to be that which is made for the purpose for which it ought to be made. For those who consent merely to sexual intercourse cannot yet be called spouses on account of such consent. For fornicators and adulterers do this as well, though the name of marital chastity is known to be far from them. Therefore the consent by which marriage is made sacred between man and woman is something else. “What else can this be called but that fellowship which God the Creator established from the beginning between man and woman, when he joined to the man the woman formed from his side?”

Because she was given as a companion, not as a slave or mistress, she was to be brought forth neither from below but from the middle. If she had been made from the head, she would have been made from the highest part and would seem to have been created for dominion. If from the feet, she would have been made from the lowest part and would seem to be subject to servitude. Therefore she was made from the middle, to show that she was made for equality in companionship. Yet in one respect she was inferior: in that she was made from him, so that she might always look to him as to her source and, cleaving to him indivisibly, might not separate herself from that fellowship which ought to endure between them. [Col. 0485A]

This fellowship, then, is marriage, consecrated by the covenant of mutual promise, when each by a voluntary promise makes himself or herself debtor to the other: so that thereafter neither may enter another union while the other lives, nor sever himself or herself from the fellowship that exists between them. If consent to sexual intercourse is joined to consent to this fellowship at the initial making of the covenant, the married persons are afterward mutually bound by the obligation of that intercourse. But if, in making the marital covenant, consent to sexual relations is mutually waived by equal resolve, then thereafter the married persons are not held mutually indebted in this respect.

For what has been relinquished by the equal consent of both and confirmed by their resolve cannot afterward justly be demanded by one from the other. Yet even so the sacrament of marriage remains firm: just as the union of the flesh does not create its force when it is present, so its absence cannot remove that force. Such consent is believed to maintain an undivided manner of life when it is made so that the mutual fellowship initiated between them by it may suffer no further separation while both live.

Therefore, whoever wishes to define marriage may say: “Marriage is the lawful consent—that is, consent between lawful persons and lawfully made—of a man and a woman to preserve an undivided manner of life.” In this consent, by equal resolve, sexual intercourse is either not excluded from the future or is commendably not to occur.

## CHAPTER V. When marriage begins to exist

If anyone asks when marriage begins to exist, we say that from the moment such consent as we have defined above has been made between man and woman, marriage exists at once. Even if sexual union follows afterward, nothing further is added to marriage in respect of the force of the sacrament. Hence it is evident that, if after such consent a man or woman enters another union, even if sexual intercourse follows there, that person must nevertheless return to the earlier union in which the sacrament of marriage was ratified; and the second union is thereafter judged wholly unlawful. [Col. 0486A]

But you say to me: someone promised, or perhaps swore, to another that he would marry her at an appointed time; and she likewise promised or swore that she would marry him. Meanwhile, having changed their intention, one or both enter another union: he takes another wife and she marries another husband. What, then, is to be done? Must the covenant of the second union be broken because of the earlier promise?

But consider that promising is very different from doing. One who promises does not yet do; one who does already does what he does. In the case of one who promises, if he does not do what he promised, there is falsehood. But in the case of one who acts, even if he repents afterward, what has been done has nevertheless wholly been done. Thus the man who promised to take a wife had not yet taken a wife, and the woman who promised to marry had not yet married; marriage did not yet exist, but ought to have existed in the future. But when afterward he took a wife and she married a husband, marriage then existed in both cases; and what has been done cannot be dissolved, even though what was promised was not fulfilled. The prior falsehood, therefore, must be corrected by repentance, but the subsequent marriage must not be dissolved. [Col. 0486B]

It is otherwise when the sacrament of marriage is not merely promised, as stated above, to be future by a mutual promise, but is confirmed by the attestation of present consent. For after such consent, whatever may follow in another union—even sexual intercourse or procreation of children—must be wholly void.

But some think that the later act ought to stand because it seems to contain more, inasmuch as after consent sexual intercourse followed as well. But why should that in which more has occurred stand merely for that reason, if all that has occurred has not been done justly? If the later union is judged a marriage because it involved sexual union, which the earlier one did not, then if a third union follows this, someone will say that it should be judged better than the second because perhaps sexual intercourse occurred in it more often than in the second. Reason does not permit this.

Accordingly, whatever after the marital consent which makes marriage sacred is admitted with another man or woman, whether in consent or in intercourse, belongs to the stain of incest and adultery, not to the sacrament of marriage. [Col. 0486C]

But you say: If marriage exists immediately after the first consent of the marital covenant, what then does the authority mean when it says that a lawful marriage is not otherwise made except by those who appear to have authority over the woman; that she must be sought from those who guard her; that she must be betrothed by her nearer relatives, endowed according to the laws, and at the proper time blessed by a priest, as is customary, with prayers and offerings; together with certain other requirements which it adds in this manner, saying: “Unions presumed otherwise are to be called not marriages but adulterous cohabitations, or rather illicit sexual acts or fornications, than lawful marriages.”

But here “not lawful” must be understood to mean not made according to the institution of the laws which prescribe that spouses are to be betrothed in this way. For what it adds afterward—that unions presumed otherwise are rather adulterous cohabitations or illicit sexual acts than lawful marriages—it immediately qualifies in the following words, saying: “Unless perhaps their own will has supported it and lawful vows have come to its aid.” Therefore, where personal will and a lawful vow come to aid, there may be a lawful marriage even without all these things. [Col. 0486D]

For if marriage cannot exist where these things are absent, baptism likewise cannot exist where consecration of the font and exorcism of the candidate do not precede, and where anointing with oil and chrism does not follow. But just as baptism can exist without these things, although these ought to be present with baptism, so marriage can exist without those things, even where they ought to be in marriage and with marriage.

That marriage does not consist in intercourse but in consent—and not in consent to intercourse—is attested by blessed Ambrose, because, just as consent can exist without intercourse, so intercourse can exist without consent, if perhaps both have chosen a purpose of chastity and continence. He says: “It is not the loss of virginity but the marital compact that makes marriage.” Again: “Intercourse does not make marriage, but consent; if it is absent, all things, even intercourse itself, come to nothing.”

Isidore also says that spouses are more truly called such from the first pledge of betrothal, even though marital intercourse is not yet known between them. [Col. 0487A]

But perhaps this seems contrary to what we said above: that marriage is ratified in marital consent. For if marriage begins from the first pledge of betrothal, and the pledge of betrothal seems to precede in a promise of future consent, then, when marriage is said to be initiated from this pledge, the pledge itself is undoubtedly shown to precede even the consent to marriage.

But if we must understand betrothal itself as the agreement and promise of a future marriage, then by “the pledge of betrothal” we rightly understand the fulfillment of the promise and the performance of the agreement. Since this fulfillment is found in the aforesaid consent, marriage rightly takes its beginning from it; for when the faith of the agreement and promise mutually made concerning future marriage is fulfilled, the sacrament of marriage is completed in marital consent.

Moreover, we infer from the expression of the word itself that the term *desponsatio* (“betrothal”) signifies not the consent to marriage itself by which matrimony is established, but an agreement and promise of future consent, because *spondere* means not to give or do, but to promise. Thus the Apostle says: “For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (1 Cor. 11). [Col. 0487B]

But if the term “betrothal” is to be understood of the marriage contract itself, then by “the pledge of betrothal” we rightly understand the consent to the mutual fellowship called marriage. Thus Augustine says of the mother of the Lord that she was called Joseph’s wife from the first pledge of betrothal, though he had not known her by intercourse and was not going to know her. Ambrose likewise says: “Having been betrothed to a man, she received the name of wife.”

For when marriage is initiated, then the name of marriage is assumed. In these words, as stated above, if we understand betrothal as occurring when marriage is ratified by marital consent, then marriage itself is rightly said to begin then and the name of wife to be assumed. But if we understand betrothal as the promise of a consent to be given in the future for making a marriage, then marriage is said to begin in those things which precede marriage; and from that point even she who is to be a wife is designated by the name of wife because of those things by which marriage has already been initiated. [Col. 0487C]

But however one may think concerning these and similar matters, provided only that marriage is believed neither to be true before the attestation of lawful consent, in which each gives himself or herself to the other for fellowship in the marital covenant, nor incomplete afterward.

Do you wish to know what I mean? When he says: “I take you as mine, so that henceforth you may be my wife and I your husband,” and she likewise says: “I take you as mine, so that henceforth I may be your wife and you my husband”; or when they say this, plainly, or anything whatever like it—such that, though they do not say these exact words, they nevertheless mean this. Or, if they do not say it because perhaps in some places words are not ceremonially spoken but the thing itself is done, they nevertheless do this: he leads her away; he receives her, according to the lawful custom of taking wives.

When, therefore, they say or do this as custom requires and consent to it between themselves, this is what I mean: from that point they are spouses, whether they have said this and consented to it before lawful witnesses, as they ought, or perhaps alone, apart and in secret, with no one attesting or present, as they ought not. They are nevertheless wholly spouses and thereafter cannot lawfully be separated from one another unless some other cause of separation arises, even though, because of their clandestine consent, they cannot be convicted if they deny that it occurred. [Col. 0488A–C]

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning those who marry secretly, or who, after marrying, do certain shameful things contrary to marriage
But you ask: What, then, is to be done about persons of this kind who have come together secretly, if afterward either one or both, by denying what was done, enter into another union? Someone secretly took a wife, with no witnesses present, their mutual marital consent alone having been confirmed, avoiding, as sometimes happens for some reason, the knowledge of others. Then, after a short time had passed, before he had established by public action the secret consent [Col. 0488D], he repented of what he had done and dismissed the woman whom he had taken as wife in this manner. He took another woman with public ceremony; perhaps openly before the Church, with the giving away by her parents, with a priest’s blessing, he celebrated the marriage and fathered children. The first woman comes before the Church, invokes judgment, and demands justice, publicly setting forth the injury done to her. He denies it, and there are no witnesses able to prove what was secret. Here you ask what the Church ought to do, since it seems that some impropriety follows whichever course it takes.

For if that woman, who indeed speaks the truth, but whose allegation is nevertheless secret and unproved, is believed merely on her own assertion without lawful testimony, and if for the sake of what is uncertain and hidden that which is certain and manifest [Col. 0489A] is dissolved, thereafter any man or woman will be able to invent against another man or woman whatever they wish, in order to be believed by similar reasoning. If this is allowed, great confusion will result, and nothing stable will thereafter stand in the Church. But if, in order to preserve the marriage established by the Church’s authority, the first union is broken and the adultery rashly undertaken in the second is confirmed, that too is a great evil, since a person is not only given freedom but even compelled to remain in sin.

Here, then, you seek counsel. Perhaps I shall not tell you anything better; yet in such great evils we ought not to be altogether without understanding. If someone thinks that, in order to avoid evils of this kind, a consent which is established by no testimony and confirmed by no mutual confession of the parties [Col. 0489B] ought to be considered void, and that marriage can in no way subsist in it, he avoids the difficulty more easily. For the preceding statement—that secret consents are not marriages but adulterous cohabitations or fornications unless personal will supports them and lawful vows come to their aid—may be understood to mean that consents made in secret do not establish marriage unless those very persons who have consented to one another secretly voluntarily profess their mutual consent openly.

For then personal will supports it and lawful vows come to its aid, when both parties freely profess openly what they did secretly. Therefore, if someone says in this manner that marriage may indeed be initiated by secret consent [Col. 0489C] but is not confirmed except by the public confession of both parties, he avoids many evils by a shorter route. Yet the approval of the majority accepts this: whether such consent is made openly or secretly between lawful persons, it is to be judged a perfect sacrament of marriage.

If this must be held to be true, it must be considered how the question mentioned above ought to be answered. There is no doubt that the Church itself cannot judge what cannot be proved to the Church. And again, there is no doubt that what has been done by the lawful and manifest judgment of the Church cannot be annulled without a lawful, reasonable, and manifest cause. Reason compels us. This woman says that she contracted marriage with that man by mutual consent [Col. 0489D]. But what she says she cannot prove; nor can the Church approve what has not been proved. Therefore what is manifest cannot be invalidated because of what is hidden. Accordingly, the Church must judge that the second union, lawfully made under its judgment, ought to stand as valid.

But you ask: What, then, is to be done for this woman who demands her husband from the Church but cannot have him because she cannot prove what was secret? Perhaps, when she sees that she cannot have her husband, she will wish to marry another and will come to the Church demanding either that her husband be restored to her or that she be permitted to marry another. You ask, then, what the Church should do: because it cannot restore the first husband, will it permit the second [Col. 0490A]? But see how the Church can grant her another husband when she acknowledges that her own husband is still alive. She herself says, “My husband lives,” and yet ventures to request marriage to another. Therefore, you say, this woman must be compelled to continence. Certainly so: since she was unwilling to guard against negligence, it is just that she bear the penalty. Why did she not marry openly? If she formerly scorned to obtain the Church’s testimony when marrying, on what grounds does she now invoke the Church’s judgment? She has therefore bound herself. Let her now bear the penalty of her negligence, so that she may become an example of correction and warning to other women, lest they venture upon the same thing. Continence is not a sin, nor is it impossible, even though it is difficult. Therefore, if women are unwilling to remain continent, let them beware of marrying secretly. Let them marry where they can have witnesses [Col. 0490B], if they cannot have consenting husbands. If they are unwilling to avoid fault, let them bear the penalty.

Therefore, whoever wishes to undertake marriage should first consider that, once he has undertaken it, he must bear its law. Whoever seeks what delights must necessarily bear also, if it comes about in it or because of it, what burdens. Thus the Church does not permit that woman, who acknowledges that she married another man while her husband was living, to pass to other marriages. Even if it should later happen that the same man, after the celebration of the second marriage, returns to her, repents of what he has done, confesses that he sinned, wishes to return to his first wife, and testifies to her concerning the truth of the first agreement, the Church does not receive his testimony, because he has changed his statement. He has borne witness against himself and deprived himself of credibility in both matters [Col. 0490C]. Nevertheless, the Church cannot annul without lawful cause what it itself has done, but judges that it ought to remain valid, lest hidden matters prejudice manifest ones. Accordingly, it adjudges the woman to be that man’s lawful wife whom he is known to have taken lawfully according to the judgment of the Church.

But you ask: If he must thus abide by the judgment of the Church, because hidden matters cannot prejudice manifest ones, what is that man to do for his soul, who is compelled to remain joined to another woman while his wife is alive—a woman whom he can neither dismiss, lest he seem to oppose the Church’s command and judgment, nor retain without scruple of conscience, since he knows that, while the first wife still lived, he unlawfully associated her with himself contrary to divine justice and ordinance? If such a man therefore [Col. 0490D] flees to the Church seeking counsel for salvation, what will the Church say to him?

Hear and understand what the Church can say to him. If the Church tells him to dismiss the second woman whom he publicly married and return to the first—whom he now admits he took as wife contrary to his earlier testimony—and accepts his testimony in this matter, all who thereafter hate their wives will invent and falsely claim that they had previously taken other women as wives, in order to be separated from those whom they hate. Thus the law of marriage will have no stability in itself, but will everywhere be dissolved at each person’s pleasure. Therefore the Church can say nothing else to him than that he keep faith with the marriage confirmed by its attestation.

But you say: His soul is at issue; he seeks counsel for salvation. For he sees danger on both sides [Col. 0491A] and cannot determine which course he should choose. If he remains, he acts against conscience; if he departs, he acts against obedience. He therefore no longer asks whether departure is permitted, but whether, if he does not depart, it is expedient to remain. He lays bare his conscience and seeks counsel for salvation. What will the Church say to a man confessing sin and seeking counsel? If it tells him to remain after he has disclosed his sin, this seems to be telling him to remain in sin. But if it can say neither this nor that, then it seems that the way of salvation cannot be shown to such a person.

Yet it is greatly contrary to Christian faith to say that anyone is such that, if he truly repents, he cannot be saved in whatever danger he may be. Many things might occur in this way [Col. 0491B]. One man says that he has had intercourse with his sister or with his wife’s mother. Another confesses that he had previously taken another wife; and there are many other horrors which human misery either falsely invents or truly commits. It is indeed true that people do many horrible things in their evil desires, so blinded that they do what they ought not; and these evils are so great that they scarcely admit of counsel, unless God, who gave the law, grants grace and mercy. “For by the law no flesh shall be justified in his sight.”

Just as formerly the curse of the law weighed upon all who were under the law, and there was no one able to escape the curse because there was no one able to avoid transgression, until the Lawgiver himself came and removed the curse by grace; and, lest curse and transgression should reign forever, by that same grace he even changed the law itself [Col. 0491C]: so now also a man never comes, with his sin and wickedness pressing upon him, into a necessity of sinning such that he cannot bear the law without incurring the curse of transgression. God changes the law for him through mercy and grants the penitent person the possibility of salvation—one who certainly would not be saved if judged without mercy by the justice and strictness of the law.

Perhaps I am not answering according to your opinion or judgment. What I say is mine, not yours. I can say nothing else. I profess what my mind suggests to me. If I said otherwise, I would speak against my conscience and my judgment. Let each person judge for himself; I speak to you from my heart [Col. 0491D].

A sinner comes to me, lays bare his conscience, and seeks counsel for salvation. What shall I say to him? If I tell him, “Depart,” I make him disobedient to the Church, his mother; and by his example I strengthen others to dismiss their lawful wives. When they hate them, they will invent whatever they please and lie to the Church in order to gain freedom to depart from them because they do not love them. If the Church receives and tolerates this, a great evil will come: all will dismiss at will either their wives or their husbands, and because of one man many will be condemned—which ought not to happen.

Some thought that they had considered the matter acutely, without taking counsel for their neighbor’s good. They said that whenever something of this kind happened, the Church [Col. 0492A] should do both things: secretly counsel the penitent person to withdraw from such a union, and publicly compel the departing person to remain. But this would not be seeking the neighbor’s salvation; it would be as though one wished to free oneself from danger. My conscience does not persuade me to say this to him.

He asks me what he ought to do, shows me his danger, demonstrates his necessity, and testifies that he is ready for either course, whatever he may be commanded. Having little confidence in myself, I tell him to turn to God:

“Lord, through your servants, such as you willed and through whom you willed, you gave the law; and behold, we your servants are under the law, while you, the Lord and giver of the law, are not under the law. What you established when you willed and for as long as you willed, you can, when you will and for whom you will, dispense without the guilt of transgression [Col. 0492B]. For what is remission by one who grants indulgence will no longer be fault, not presumptuous action by the one who receives it.

“You commanded, Lord, through the servants through whom you spoke, and ordered your Church, that a man should not join himself to another woman while his wife lives. I had a wife, and while she lived I joined myself to another. Behold, I cannot now make it not to have been done; but you can make it not to have been done in a condemnable way. Likewise, Lord, you commanded that we obey your Church, which exercises your office on earth, as we obey you; that we not scandalize one of your little ones; and you said that whoever despised the command of your Church would not be obedient to you.

“Behold, wretched as I am, because of my sins I have come into contradiction and fallen into the snare of necessity, so that I cannot escape without sin [Col. 0492C]. If I remain, my conscience accuses me before you concerning my hidden acts, by which I act against your ordinance. If I depart, I shall be disobedient to your Church and shall scandalize not only little ones but also your great servants, who in this matter do not know what is hidden, yet will what is just; and my conscience accuses me concerning my public acts, by which I act against your command.

“Therefore, hemmed in and surrounded on every side by dangers, I implore your mercy, ready for whatever you command, if you grant me to know it. If you say, ‘Depart,’ I shall not remain.
