If you say, ‘Remain,’ I shall not depart. For I know that, at your command, whatever it may be cannot be evil. Yours is the power from which comes every good that pleases you [Col. 0492D]. The one to whom you grant indulgence is not charged; the one whom you charge is not granted indulgence.

“If, therefore, Lord, you command that, setting aside the scandal to the Church and disregarding the command of my teachers whom you gave me and whom you commanded me to obey, I should listen to you rather than to a man whom I ought not to hear except for your sake and whom I do not wish to oppose against you—if you command, Lord, I do not heed man. But if you wish to spare your little ones or preserve the authority of your Church for the salvation of many, then indeed I stand in your judgment because of my sins. Yet I know that you are gracious and merciful, and that, if you will, you can refrain from imputing necessity if you accept the will.

“Therefore I would rather fall into your hands than into human hands, because with you power is present [Col. 0493A] and compassion is not absent. A human being cannot change the law. The law does not rule you, because you are the maker and lord of the law. A human being judges acts, not intention; you spare acts because of intention. Therefore, trusting in your mercy, I commit to you the hidden things of my necessity, not presuming, because of fear of you, to cause scandal to the Church; for I hope that you will mercifully endure to forgive my offense against you. For this reason I do not presume to offend my neighbor, lest in my neighbor I offend my God.”

This seems to me appropriate whenever hidden matters oppress the conscience in a situation of necessity, especially if they are such matters in which dispensation from an ordinance admits pardon. For acts contrary to nature, which could never occur without sin, do not receive remission unless they receive correction [Col. 0493B]. Therefore, in hidden matters of this kind, in which the transgression is of a temporal ordinance and not of a natural command, it seems to me that what is hidden should never prejudice what is manifest—especially matters that cannot be changed without grave scandal. Rather, it is more expedient that scandal be avoided in public matters and that recourse be had to grace and mercy concerning hidden matters. It may happen that an act performed from necessity against an ordinance, in order to avoid scandal, because it is hidden and cannot be proved and therefore cannot be avoided, may not be imputed through mercy to one who repents and grieves.

“The husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife; likewise the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband” (1 Cor. 7). Therefore, by sinning, a husband or wife may cause himself or herself to lose authority over the other’s body; but cannot cause the other to lose authority over his or her own body, so far as lies within that person. One may lose what is under one’s own right; one cannot take away what is not one’s own. Thus, even if someone at some point acts so that he or she cannot lawfully demand his or her due in the other’s body, that person nevertheless does not thereby become able lawfully to deny the other’s due in his or her own body [Col. 0493C].

The question is also raised concerning those who say that, after the marital agreement—or before it—they have had carnal intercourse with sisters, mothers, or any other relatives near in the line of kinship: what should be done if this deed can be established by lawful testimony? So far as could reasonably be done to preserve the peace of the marital bed, I would avoid testimonies and proofs of this kind. But if the matter became wholly manifest, then, because of the horror of the deed and in order to avoid scandal, I would advise separation—yet so that both parties were compelled to remain continent, since the sacrament of marriage would not be severed from one another even though the act of carnal intercourse were prohibited.

If anyone asks how a woman who has not sinned can be compelled against her will to continence, let that person consider also that this belongs to the misery of the flesh: whoever does not restrain himself from its pleasure in prosperity deserves also to bear its pains in adversity. What would this woman, who now says that she cannot be continent, do if her husband were oppressed by a long and continuous, or even perpetual, illness? Therefore, let her not abandon now a husband who repents of wrongdoing, whom she would not abandon lying ill from bodily weakness [Col. 0494A]. Or, if perhaps she is unwilling to bear the condition of the flesh, let her not subject herself to the law of the flesh, nor undertake for pleasure what she is unwilling to suffer in affliction.

These, then, are the things that had to be said concerning the secret consent of marriage and the other matters in it which are hidden, ought to be concealed, or may be shameful. We confess, therefore, as has been said, that marriage is established in marital consent; and that, once it has been lawfully made, whatever else is done against it cannot stand, if this consent alone can be proved by lawful testimony. Having therefore shown what marriage is, and on what basis marriage must be called valid, we must now proceed to discuss the goods of marriage.

## CHAPTER VII. That three goods accompany marriage: fidelity, the hope of offspring, and sacrament.

[Col. 0494B]

There are principally three goods of marriage which accompany marriage: fidelity, the hope of offspring, and sacrament. In fidelity, care is taken that one does not have intercourse outside the marital bond with another woman or another man. In the hope of offspring, care is taken that offspring be devoutly awaited, lovingly received, and religiously reared. In sacrament, care is taken that marriage not be separated, and that a dismissed husband or wife not be joined to another, not even for the sake of offspring.

These are the goods that marriage sets against the concupiscence of the flesh which still remains in the flesh of sin, and without which the mingling of flesh cannot occur. For, as blessed Augustine says, the good of marriage in some measure limits and regulates the evil of disobedient members, so that carnal concupiscence becomes at least marital chastity [Col. 0494C]. This good supplies a remedy against that evil in two ways: by limiting the heat of immoderate lust under the fixed rule of a single covenant, it regulates it away from wandering intercourse; and by goods attached to it, it excuses what would in itself be evil.

Yet it does not make it altogether not evil, but makes it not condemnable. For that good does not become culpable because of this evil; rather, because of that good, this evil becomes pardonable. For unless it were evil, it would not need to be excused; and again, unless it had a remedy, it ought to be imputed. But if marriage contained no good in itself, it could not be a remedy against evil. Now, however, the goods that are inherent in it excuse the evil which is not sought from marriage but endured within it, so that what necessity imposes, rather than will demands, is not imputed for condemnation [Col. 0494D].

Again, Augustine, writing to Valerius: “Not only fruitfulness, whose fruit lies in offspring, nor only chastity, whose bond is fidelity, but also the sacrament of marriage is commended to married believers. The reality of this sacrament is that persons lawfully joined are not separated while they live.”

## CHAPTER VIII. Whether these goods are inseparable from marriage.

If the fidelity of marriage consists in knowing no other union besides the marital one, and the violation of this fidelity in committing adultery, it is clear that this good adheres to marriage in such a way that, if it is present [Col. 0495A], marriage is thereby further commended; but if it is absent, the sacrament of marriage is nevertheless not annihilated. For an adulteress is not therefore not a wife because she is an adulteress; indeed, if she were not a wife, she could not be an adulteress. For adultery does not exist except when fidelity to a lawful marriage-bed is violated. When this happens, guilt is committed, but the sacrament is not nullified.

Likewise, if the hope of offspring consists in offspring being devoutly awaited, lovingly received, and religiously reared, there is no doubt that this good also cannot always be present in every marriage or among all married persons. How can offspring be hoped for by those who preserve continence by a mutual vow, or who can no longer beget because of the defect of age? Therefore these two—fidelity and the hope of offspring—accompany marriage in such a way that, where they are present [Col. 0495B], marriage appears purer in the one respect and more fruitful in the other; but where they are absent, marriage is shown either more blameworthy or more unfruitful, and yet does not cease to be marriage.

Sacrament, however, seems so inseparable that marriage cannot exist at all without it. Hence Augustine: “To such an extent is the nuptial covenant the reality of a certain sacrament that it is not rendered void even by separation; for, while the husband from whom she has departed lives, she commits adultery if she marries another.” Such great firmness belongs to the marital bond that it would not have such force unless some sacrament of a greater thing were employed, which remains unshaken because the nuptial covenant is not abolished by divorce, so that the parties remain spouses even when separated.

For there are two distinct things: marriage, which consists in lawful partnership; and the office of marriage, which consists in the mingling of flesh. In the former—that is, marriage—there is sacrament; but fidelity and the hope of offspring seem to pertain to the latter—that is, the office of marriage [Col. 0495C]. The one, fidelity, serves to guard against unlawful mingling of flesh; the other, hope of offspring, serves to exercise lawful mingling of flesh for its sake. Just as the very office of carnal intercourse can be absent from marriage, so marriage itself can exist without those things that pertain to the office of carnal intercourse, although, as has been said, if it lacks fidelity it is found less pure, and if it lacks hope of offspring it is found less fruitful.

Fidelity has its fruit in the chastity of marital purity. The hope of offspring has its fruit in the exercise of fruitfulness. Marriage itself is a sacrament in the marital partnership; and therefore, just as the partnership itself is not divided while both live, so the sacrament of marital partnership is not separated from marriage itself as long as the marriage endures. In this marriage, then, the sacrament outwardly is the undivided partnership; the reality of the sacrament inwardly is the steadfastly burning love of the spouses’ hearts toward one another. The outward sacrament pertains to Christ and the Church; the inward reality of the sacrament, to God and the soul. Thus, just as we have called the union of flesh a sacrament of Christ and the Church, so we also show that the covenant of their partnership is a sacrament [Col. 0495D].

This has been said to show that marriage sometimes exists without fidelity and without the hope of offspring, but can never exist without sacrament [Col. 0496A]—although sacrament itself is sometimes found where the holiness of sacrament is shown not to exist. For blessed Augustine says that the sacrament of marriage can be common to all peoples, but the holiness of the sacrament exists only in the city of our God and on his holy mountain. Anyone who considers what has been said above can easily see how this is true.

For we said above that there are two sacraments in marriage: one in the mingling of flesh, a sacrament of the partnership between Christ and the Church; the other in marital partnership, a sacrament of the partnership between God and the soul. Or again, the sacrament of Christ and the Church is in the partnership of marriage, while the sacrament of God and the soul is in marital love [Col. 0496B]. Thus, if the sacrament of marriage is understood in this way, it is rightly said that the sacrament of marriage is common to all peoples; but the holiness or power of the sacrament exists only in the city of our God and on his holy mountain—that is, it is said to exist in faith and love, namely in the holy Church and among believers.

Those possess the sacrament of marriage who, by mutual consent, enter into the partnership established by God between male and female, to be preserved undivided between them. But only those possess the holiness of this sacrament who have become members of Christ through faith and are inwardly united to God in mind and devotion through love.

## CHAPTER IX. On those who live incontinently in marriage and serve the satisfaction of lust more than the generation of offspring.

[Col. 0496C]

Blessed Augustine says this concerning those who, conquered by such incontinence, weakness, or pleasure, give themselves to it:

“Marriage does not compel intercourse that is not undertaken for the sake of offspring; but obtains pardon for it, provided it is not so excessive as to hinder the times owed to prayer, nor changed into a use contrary to nature. For intercourse necessary for the sake of offspring is blameless, provided only that it is marital. But whoever goes beyond just necessity obeys not reason but lust; and it belongs to the spouse not to demand this, but to render it, lest the other commit fornication. But if both are subjected to such concupiscence [Col. 0496D], they do something that does not belong to marriage, a fault for which marriage is not an encourager but an intercessor.

“The honor of marriage is indeed the chastity of procreation and the fidelity of rendering the carnal debt. This is the work of marriage which the Apostle defends from every crime, saying: ‘If you have taken a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she does not sin’ [1 Cor. 7]. But immoderate excess is allowed by way of pardon. Not even an unbelieving spouse can harm the holiness of marriage; rather, the believing spouse benefits the unbelieving one. Hence the Apostle: ‘The unbelieving husband has been sanctified through the believing wife’ [ibid.], etc.”

## CHAPTER X. Why the ancients at one time had several wives.

Blessed Augustine likewise says concerning this:

“In ancient times, when the mystery of our salvation was still veiled, the righteous contracted marriages for the duty of propagation, not conquered by lust but guided by piety, though they could more easily have remained continent and would have wished to do so. Nevertheless they made use of wives, and it was permitted for one man to have several—wives whom they possessed more chastely than any one of those men whom we now see possesses one wife in the manner for which the Apostle grants pardon. For they had them for the work of generation, not for the disease of desire” [Col. 0497A].

Again, in the book *On Virgins*: “It was not sin for the righteous of old to make use of several women, nor did they act against nature, since they did this not for wantonness but for begetting; nor against custom, because such things were done at that time; nor against command, because no law forbade it.”

Nevertheless, as he testifies elsewhere [Col. 0497B], union of one man with one woman pertains more to the good of marriage than union with many. This is indicated by the divinely made union of the first married couple, so that marriages might take their beginning from the point at which the more honorable example was to be observed.

Again he says: “Just as the merit of patience is not unequal in Peter, who suffered, and John, who did not suffer, so the merit of continence is not unequal in John, who experienced no marriage, and Abraham, who begot children. For both John’s celibacy and Abraham’s marriage served Christ according to the differing allotment of times. But John possessed continence in practice; Abraham possessed it in disposition alone. The chastity of the unmarried is better than the chastity of marriage; Abraham possessed one in use, both in disposition. For he lived chastely in marriage; he could have been chaste without marriage, but at that time it was not fitting.”

Again: “Just as a righteous man, although he desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1), “nevertheless takes food not from a desire to live but from the duty of providing, so that he may remain because he is necessary for others: so intercourse with women by right of marriage was dutiful, not lustful, for holy men [Col. 0497C]. For what food is for the preservation of a human being, intercourse is for the preservation of the race; and neither is without carnal pleasure, which nevertheless, moderated and restrained by temperance and reduced to natural use, cannot be lust.

“But what unlawful food is in sustaining life, that is fornication or adulterous intercourse in seeking offspring; and what an excessively immoderate appetite is in lawful food, that is that pardonable intercourse among married persons” [Col. 0497D].

## CHAPTER XI. Whether that which can at some time be dissolved ought to be called marriage.

Some deny that a union is marriage at all if it can at some time admit separation. For they find certain authorities and words of the divine Scriptures set forth by the holy Fathers which seem, as it were, to establish this very point. Blessed Augustine says in the book *On the Good of Marriage*: “To such a degree is the nuptial bond a matter of a certain sacrament, that it is not made void even by separation; for, while the husband by whom she was left is alive, she commits adultery if she marries another.” And again: “Because the nuptial covenant is not abolished by the intervention of divorce, the spouses remain spouses even when separated.” Because of assertions of this kind [Col. 0498A], it seems to them that what at some time admits dissension and separation in such a way that those divided from one another are no longer called spouses ought not to be called marriage, even when it exists.

But for the present I do not see on what ground they can prove that this belongs to the efficacy of the sacrament of marriage: that an undivided fellowship must be preserved by both parties as long as each lives; and that therefore what could at some time be dissolved was not a marriage. For if they say that this is not a marriage because it does not possess in its entirety the things pertaining to marriage, let them observe that, when it is said that an undivided fellowship pertains to marriage, this is said truly: marriage ought to possess it—namely, when it exists where it ought to exist. For this belongs to marriage, and marriage demands—or rather bestows—it [Col. 0498B], so far as lies in itself.

Just as it belongs to baptism to confer remission of sins, and it is truly said that baptism confers remission of all sins; and just as the efficacy of the sacrament of Christ’s body is to confer fellowship and participation in Christ, and it is truly said that receiving Christ’s body confers spiritual participation in Christ; yet one who receives the sacrament of baptism deceitfully does not obtain remission of sins, and one who eats Christ’s body unworthily does not thereby merit spiritual participation in Christ. Therefore, if we truly say that these things pertain to those sacraments, and yet sometimes find those sacraments without these effects, nor do these effects therefore pertain to them any less when the sacraments exist without them—namely, when they are found where they ought not to be, and among persons among whom they ought not to be [Col. 0498C]—it is strange if we say that undivided fellowship pertains to marriage, although we find marriage without it, namely when it exists where it ought not to exist.

But if they say that it is not the sacrament of marriage because it lacks what it ought to have when it exists where it ought not to exist, let them likewise say that the sacrament of baptism is not genuine in a deceitful recipient, and that such a person is not truly baptized, because there it does not effect remission of sins; and that Christ’s true body is not what is received unworthily, because there spiritual participation in Christ is not conferred. Let them understand, therefore, that whenever spiritual effects of this kind are attributed to divine sacraments, the efficacy of those sacraments is expressed. This does not show what will occur, through the fault of those abusing God’s sacraments [Col. 0498D]; rather, it shows what may be accomplished by the sacraments themselves, according to the efficacy of the spiritual grace contained in them, if those who misuse them do not remain in perversity.

Accordingly, whoever said that this marriage has this quality intended, of course, to say that this marriage, so far as lies in itself, ought to have it if it exists where it ought to exist. But if perhaps it does not exist where it ought to exist, it is not surprising if it lacks what it ought to possess. Yet the sacrament is no less genuine while it exists, even though it is less beneficial to the person in whom it exists. In this manner we think that certain marriages can truly be called valid as long as they are held valid according to the judgment of the Church, but are afterwards rightly dissolved when lawful grounds emerge; and, if subsequently maintained in stubborn presumption against the Church’s prohibition, they are judged unlawful and illegitimate unions [Col. 0499A].

Nevertheless, as I noted above, we do not think this should be held concerning all such cases. For once the excuse of error has been set aside, they will be unable to retain the name of legitimate unions. The case is different where sin is venial: for example, if someone, in ignorance, rashly entered a union within the seventh, sixth, or perhaps even fifth degree of kinship. This would be contrary not so much to natural or ancient legal institution as to a later command of the Church. We read that blessed Gregory, to the English newly converted to the faith, lest they perhaps recoil from the Christian religion, dispensationally allowed marriages to be contracted from the fifth degree of consanguinity. From this it appears that things which sometimes admit dispensation, so that they may openly occur lawfully, have an excuse even if they occur ignorantly without that concession [Col. 0499B]. Therefore, perhaps such cases, so long as they remain wholly hidden, are more suitably regarded as excusable on account of ignorance; but once made public, because they are contrary to the command, they ought not to be tolerated. These things have been said against those who think that what can at some time be dissolved cannot be called marriage at all.

## CHAPTER XII. On Those Who Think That Mutual Consent Makes Marriage Even Between Any Illegitimate Persons

Others are borne by no less rash an opinion into the contrary assertion, so far as to say that persons however illegitimate, of whatever profession or rank, become spouses if they give equal consent to one another [Col. 0499C]. They think that priests who have professed continence, high priests, monks, and sacred virgins are not to be excepted from this rule. These likewise have certain words of Scripture with which they believe they can fortify and confirm their opinion. And there are indeed certain sayings of such a kind in which this may suitably be understood, if the action itself can suitably occur.

But those entrusted with the doctrine of God’s Word should not judge in such a way that, in order to establish one particular point, they depart from the meaning of the whole. Nor should the whole follow the part; rather, the part should follow the whole. But if a part is found discordant with the whole, it must either be fitted into it, if possible, or, if that is impossible, rejected. For it is better to depart from the part [Col. 0499D] than from the whole. Yet best of all is to retain both the part and the whole.

These, then, are the things they adduce in support of their assertion. Blessed Augustine says in the book *On the Profession of Holy Widowhood*:

> “If chastity is preserved in the marital bond, condemnation is not feared. But in widowhood and virginal continence the excellence of a greater gift is sought. Once this has been sought and chosen and offered under the obligation of a vow, not merely contracting marriage, but even wishing to marry, if one does not marry, is condemnable. For to show this, the Apostle did not say, ‘When they have behaved wantonly, they marry in Christ,’ but ‘they wish to marry.’ ‘Having condemnation,’ he says, ‘because they have made void their first faith’ [1 Tim. 5], even if not by marrying, nevertheless by wishing to marry. [Col. 0500A] It is not because marriages themselves, or such women’s marriages, are judged condemnable; rather, the fraud against their resolve is condemned; the faith of the broken vow is condemned; not the taking up of a lesser good, but the fall from a higher good. Finally, such women are condemned not because they subsequently entered into marital fidelity, but because they made void the first faith of continence.”

And shortly afterwards:

> [Col. 0500B] “Therefore those who say that such marriages are not marriages but rather adulteries do not seem to me to consider sufficiently sharply and carefully what they are saying; for a likeness to truth deceives them. Because women who do not marry through Christian holiness are said to choose marriage with Christ, some reason from this and say: ‘If a woman who marries another while her husband lives is an adulteress, as the Lord himself defined in the Gospel, then, since Christ lives and death no longer has dominion over him, she who had chosen marriage with him is an adulteress if she marries a man.’ Those who say this are indeed moved by a subtle argument; but they pay too little attention to the great absurdity which follows from it. For when, with her husband still living and with his consent, a woman commendably vows continence to Christ, according to their reasoning no woman should do this, lest she make Christ himself—an impious thought—an adulterer, by marrying him while her husband lives.”

And shortly afterwards:

> [Col. 0500C] “Through this insufficiently considered opinion—that women fallen from a holy resolution, if they marry, do not have marriages—there arises no small evil: wives are separated from their husbands as though they were adulteresses and not wives. And when people refuse to restore them, once separated, to continence, they make their husbands true adulterers, since they have taken other women while their own wives are alive. Therefore I cannot say that women who have fallen from a better resolution, if they marry, are adulteries rather than marriages. But I would certainly not hesitate to say that falls and collapses from the holier chastity vowed to God are worse than adulteries.”

Thus blessed Augustine speaks; and the authority seems clear, the reasoning evident, and incapable of doubt. But let us say and think that women fallen from the purpose and profession of continence, if they marry, contract true marriages which absolutely cannot be dissolved. What then? Should we not likewise, and for the same reason, think concerning the other sex that, if men fallen from the purpose and profession of continence take wives, their marriages are true and ought to be valid, to such a degree that they absolutely cannot be dissolved, although they cannot be defended from guilt? [Col. 0500D] Let us say, therefore, that this is so, and that we ought to think and maintain it. We have no reason by which we can overthrow or weaken so evident an argument and authority. Necessity compels us to think and maintain it thus.

See what follows. If this were promulgated and people heard that the Church holds that those fallen from the purpose and profession of continence, if they enter marriages, cannot be separated, and that the Church cannot compel them to return to observance of their purpose of continence, nothing thereafter could remain stable or valid. No order or religious habit, indeed no vow or profession whatever, could restrain people from loosening the reins of impurity and rushing into their desires, either when, beginning to tire of the good in which they are, they seek freedom, or when perhaps tempted by an evil in which they are not yet engaged, they hurry to fulfill their pleasure [Col. 0501A]. Thus every order would be dissipated, the beauty of the Christian religion reduced to nothing, and great shame would follow.

I speak according to the weakness of our time. Who henceforth, established in a religious habit or profession, would stand firm if the goads of the flesh began to press him—as mortal nature, subject to corruption, commonly suffers—and his own thought said to him: “You will not be able to resist so violent a passion, such fires and heats of your desires. They have not declared war upon you for today, tomorrow, three days, four days, eight days, one month, or one year; but as long as you live upon the earth [Col. 0501B], as long as you bear mortal flesh, as long as you can feel, they will not leave you, spare you, grant you peace, or give you rest. They will always oppress your attention and turn aside your thought, so that you can never raise a free mind or a pure will to God.

“See, then, that you lose this world also and do not gain the future one. It would at least be better for you to escape these torments than to perish altogether and experience no good. God sees that you suffer unwillingly, are drawn unwillingly, and assent under compulsion. Perhaps he will look upon the violence of your passion and, in mercy, grant pardon to your excess—especially since the Apostle says, ‘It is better to marry than to burn’ [1 Cor. 7], and ‘Let each have his own wife because of fornication.’ For the Apostle well knows human weakness [Col. 0501C]. Therefore he did not say, ‘Let those have wives, because it is permitted to them, and let these not have them, because it is not permitted to them’; but, ‘Let each have’: whoever cannot contain himself, it is better that he marry than burn. It is better to meet weakness lawfully than continually to burn through vice into passion. For the Lord himself says, ‘Let him who can receive this receive it’ [Matt. 19].

“He knows that I cannot receive this saying so as to remain continent. When I thought that I could, I willingly made the resolution; and I would gladly persevere in the same will even now, if I could endure it. But I cannot bear the heat of my boiling nature; I cannot withstand the ardour of burning concupiscence. Therefore I do what I can. I go and take a wife; I make allowance for my weakness, grieving indeed that I am compelled to descend from the higher good [Col. 0501D], yet not utterly despairing, because I descend to things permitted. I would rather be saved in a lower good than be endangered in the highest. And if there is perhaps some guilt, because I descend and do not keep my purpose, I shall do penance and appease God by satisfaction. Nothing will be harsh or difficult, provided only that I can escape this passion and avoid this death in which I am held while living.”

Who, do you think, would not spur and exhort himself with arguments of this sort when he began to be afflicted and inflamed by the goads of his flesh, if he knew that it was permitted and possible, that salvation belonged to those who did this, and that the Church did not compel those who thus looked back, but allowed them to live so and judged their marriages lawful? Who would not prefer, when in grave temptation, to do penance for many years and pay whatever satisfaction might be required, provided that he could enjoy his own choice and option and lawfully fulfill his desires [Col. 0502A]?

What, then, shall we say? We certainly dare affirm that, even if perhaps it cannot be denied that this was said thus and ought to be understood thus, nevertheless it is in no way advantageous, especially in these times when people are inclined toward vices, to hold and act in this manner. Perhaps someone might wish to say in this way that these things were said concerning those times when people were more ashamed to sin, when shame alone at violating their commitment could restrain those wavering and placed in temptation from falling away from their purpose and vow of holiness, and when they were more frightened because they knew that, after their fall, a return to the purity of their former excellence was no longer open to them [Col. 0502B]. The Church, therefore, in accordance with the condition of that time, then ought to have held—and did hold—that those who descended to marital union after a vow and profession of continence should remain so; that such contracts should not be dissolved; and that such marriages were then valid according to the judgment and permission of the Church.

But afterwards, when people began to abuse such a declaration and permission, the Church changed its practice because of the dangers threatening; it redirected its judgment to another end. Therefore such unions are now not marriages because of the Church’s prohibition and institution, according to which all things are judged lawful or unlawful, valid or to be dissolved. If someone says this, perhaps he will seem to have said something. We object to nothing among all things which allow the truth to remain undisturbed.

But if anyone understands these statements to concern persons who made a hidden vow of continence and offered their vow to God alone without human attestation, and holds that, if they later wish, after breaking their vow, to enter marital fellowship, they cannot on that account be prohibited by the Church because it did not receive their profession or prescribe the observance of continence to them—if, therefore, he thinks that such widows or virgins who descend to marital union after a vow of continence incur condemnation, that is, do a condemnable thing, not because they marry but because they break their vow, not on account of the lower good they seek but the higher good they abandon; that they incur condemnation because they violated their pledged faith, yet nevertheless are entirely spouses and ought not to be separated [Col. 0502D]—then it is certain, as we said above, that matters which cannot be proved to the Church cannot at all be judged by the Church.

Therefore, if we understand the matters which are known to be true as suitably spoken in the opinion mentioned above, no further question remains why we should approve them as truthfully said and profitably maintained. For it is certain that those who return to sexual experience after a hidden vow of chastity and a purpose of continence not yet confirmed by public profession cannot in any way be prohibited by the Church; nor does the Church itself, when such a union occurs, declare it invalid, but confirms it as valid and confirms that hidden things ought not prejudice manifest ones.

But if someone wishes to say against this that women spiritually married to Christ cannot thereafter, while he lives, have human husbands, his assertion is rightly refuted by the reasoning given above [Col. 0503A]. In this manner each person may think according to his own measure concerning matters that are manifestly false or secretly true.

For my part, this seems more probable if it can be found to preserve the truth without discrediting authority, especially the authority of so great a man, of whom we ought to think well even when we cannot ourselves think what he thought. Let us therefore say as much as we can say in accordance with truth: either this was said with reference to a time when it ought to be so done, or it was said only of those who return to sexual experience after a hidden vow of continence and become spouses. The Church cannot separate them because, while the act here is manifest, what was hidden there cannot be proved. In their case, however, the guilt of violated faith is said in one respect to be worse than adultery, because by adultery one sins against a human being, whereas by this one sins against Christ [Col. 0503B].

The case is otherwise for those who, after a vow, have bound themselves to God by public profession under the Church’s witness, and perhaps, what is more, have been consecrated to the holy state of continence. Of these we truly say that, after such a purpose and such a vow confirmed by public profession, they cannot descend to the marital covenant; and if they perhaps attempt this at any time, they are not spouses but fornicators and violators of spiritual chastity. They must be strictly recalled to restore and preserve the former integrity of their purpose [Col. 0503C].

But if, in rash audacity, they wish to persist in what they have begun and scorn to abandon the illicit union which they contracted contrary to the obligation of their first profession, they are to be cut off from communion with the Church by a sentence of just severity, as disobedient persons and as persons defiled by the incest of abominable fornication; nor are they to be admitted to penance in any way unless they withdraw from life in this shameful association.

And this is perhaps the meaning of those words, now almost universally known because of their ambiguity. For Pope Innocent, whose authority is celebrated in the Church of Christ, says:

> [Col. 0503D] “Women who spiritually marry Christ and are veiled by a priest, if they marry publicly or are secretly corrupted, are not to be admitted to do penance unless he to whom they joined themselves has departed from this life. For if this rule is observed among human beings, so that she who has left her husband and gone over to another is deemed an adulteress, and no place is granted her for doing penance unless the other has died, how much more so she who has joined herself to an immortal bridegroom!”

There is no doubt, therefore, that this concerns women who, in a purpose of continence, have been consecrated to preserve chastity under a manifest public profession. It is said of them that, if after such a purpose they pass to carnal marriage, they are not to be admitted to penance unless he to whom they joined themselves—that is, the fornicator or adulterer—has departed from this life, that is, from such a mode of life [Col. 0504A]. For they cannot do penance in the state in which, so long as they remain, they cannot be saved.

Some wish to interpret “him to whom they joined themselves” as Christ, to whom they had first vowed themselves by their purpose of continence; and to take the statement as conditional: the second person to whom they go over is not judged legitimate unless the first to whom they had formerly joined themselves dies. For if this rule is observed among human beings, that the second cannot be legitimate as long as the first lives, then plainly where the first cannot die at all, the second can by no reasoning be legitimate. In this way, by whatever force of reasoning, it is proved that women consecrated as brides of Christ together with a profession of continence cannot thereafter pass to carnal marriages [Col. 0504B].

There is indeed in this argument not reasoning compelling in every respect, but a suitable analogy in one respect, by which brides of Christ are taught that, if such fidelity is demanded in the carnal bed, much greater devotion and more sincere love are owed spiritually. Some think these words were spoken to inspire fear; others refer them to public penance, which on account of its severity sometimes seems to be denied in order to instill fear, so that, while the sinner is outwardly rejected according to dispensation, fear of falling may increase in those who stand and humility in rising again may increase in those who have fallen. I reject nothing that is not contrary to truth. Let anything be said, provided that only what is permissible is believed.

This is the sum of the matter. If anyone who has made a vow of continence passes to carnal marriage [Col. 0504C], and if the person’s vow was hidden, the Church cannot prevent that person from marrying. And if afterwards the person repents of the deed, the Church can neither repel a penitent person from the counsel of salvation because of hidden matters, nor dissolve manifest things because of hidden ones. But if persons who established their purpose by public profession and vow later wish to pass to the rights of a carnal covenant, the Church permits them in no way; and if they perhaps presume to contract such unions contrary to the purity of their purpose and profession, it dissolves them with due strictness as illegitimate and alien to the sanctity of marriage.

Thus the Church holds; thus we ought to hold, we who follow the Church’s institutions and believe wholesome whatever it establishes at the prompting of God’s Spirit and judges worthy of reverence [Col. 0504D]. And even if it is shown that at other times things were sometimes otherwise, and now are otherwise than they were, we ought not think that it happened through any fickleness that things are now held and instituted differently from what they once were; rather, what was then necessary and salutary required that they be held and commanded thus, whereas now the times are different and another course is fitting or necessary for human salvation.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Marriage of Unbelievers

Some think that the union of pagans or any unbelievers is not marriage, even if it has been lawfully made according to the manner of divine institution. For they say that what has been made without faith ought not to be called legitimate [Col. 0505A]. But I do not presently see any ground on which they can prove that a union of unbelievers made according to divine institution is not marriage—unless perhaps they also wish to say that the sacrament of baptism is not baptism when a heretic gives or receives it, because neither the giver nor the recipient is a believer.

Let them accordingly maintain that God’s sacraments cannot come into the participation of unbelievers if unbelievers cannot possess the sacrament of marriage; or let them say that the sacrament of marriage alone is more excellent than all the rest, if it alone cannot be shared outside faith. An unbeliever can possess the sacrament of baptism; an unbeliever cannot possess the sacrament of marriage. Therefore an unbeliever can possess the sacrament of baptism, in which the seal of faith is especially present, but neither believer nor unbeliever alike can possess the sacrament of marriage, which is not so much a sign of faith as of nature, not so much a judgment of virtue as an instrument of propagation [Col. 0505B].

“But,” they say, “when an unbeliever receives the sacrament of baptism, he receives it because, even if he was an unbeliever in another respect, he nevertheless received the sacrament itself according to the right form of faith. Otherwise, unless he had received it according to the right form of faith, he would not have received it, whether he was a believer or an unbeliever. Thus, because in receiving it he was not opposed to the faith, he could receive it, though he was not a believer in another respect.”

[Col. 0505C] And I say that when an unbeliever takes a wife for the procreation of children, preserves faithfulness to the marriage bed, loves and protects his companion, and does not pass, while she lives, into a union with another, then although in another respect he is an unbeliever—that is, because he does not believe—yet in this matter he acts neither against faith nor against divine institution.

“But authority,” they say, “declares that marriages of this kind are not true.” It says so because all things outside faith, though true in outward appearance, are not true unto salvation; and though true as to the form of the sacrament, they are not true as to the effect of spiritual efficacy and grace. Thus it has been said also of certain other sacraments that they are not true when they are shared by unbelievers. Nor only by unbelievers, but also when they are unworthily handled by depraved believers and those acting perversely. Authority says even of the sacrament of Christ’s body that what a schismatic consecrates is not Christ’s true body [Col. 0505D]. Again, another authority says that those are mistaken who think that a priest’s words, and not also his life, make Christ’s body; and many sayings of this kind are found.

It is fitting that we should reverence in every respect, as far as we can, the sayings of the saints, and believe true what has been said to us by those in whom and through whom the Spirit of truth spoke. Therefore we say that the truth of God’s sacraments is twofold: one truth in the sanctification of the sacrament, the other in its spiritual effect. For the efficacy and spiritual grace received in and through the sacraments is called the truth of the sacraments. Those who receive God’s sacraments unworthily cannot receive that truth. Thus [Col. 0506A] Holy Scripture sometimes says that God’s sacraments are not true for those who receive them unworthily, because, in handling the sacraments externally alone, they do not attain their truth, which consists in spiritual grace.

Accordingly, God’s sacraments are always true in themselves with respect to the sanctification accomplished through God’s word; but for those who handle and receive them unworthily they are not true with respect to participation in the spiritual grace received in them. Thus what a schismatic consecrates is not Christ’s true body, because, since Christ’s body is a sacrament of unity, the schismatic does not thereby bring unity about for himself when he divides himself from unity itself.

[Col. 0506B] Likewise, those who think that the priest’s words alone suffice for the consecration of Christ’s body, and that the priest’s good life and conduct are not also necessary in order that it may be effected for him and beneficially effected for the person through whom God’s sacrament is administered—those who think this are mistaken. For neither God’s sacraments nor the flesh of the Lamb sanctify those who remain in sin, although sacraments are effected through their ministry for the sanctification of others. Thus we say also concerning the sacrament of marriage: that in one respect it is rightly said not to be true, valid, or holy among those who possess only the sacrament but, whether through false belief or wicked life, do not deserve to receive its truth—that is, its efficacy and spiritual effect.

Blessed Augustine says that the sacrament of marriage [Col. 0506C] is common to all peoples; but the holiness of the sacrament exists only in the city of our God and on his holy mountain. Likewise: When the Gospel began to be preached, it first found Gentile spouses joined to Gentile spouses. Likewise: If the Lord admits fornication alone as a ground for dismissing a wife, and forbids the dissolution of a pagan marriage (Matt. V), it follows that paganism is not subject to fornication. What then, they ask, is meant by what blessed Ambrose says: “A marriage apart from God is not valid; and therefore dismissal for God’s sake is not a sin if she is joined to another”? Likewise blessed Gregory says: “Dismissal for God’s sake is not a sin if she is joined to another. For an injury done to the Creator dissolves the right of marriage.” But observe how they try to prove that such a union [Col. 0506D] is not a marriage: because, they say, it was said, “A marriage apart from God is not valid”; and again, “An injury done to the Creator dissolves the right of marriage.” Therefore, they say, he denied that it was a marriage because he calls it not valid. And because he said that an injury to the Creator dissolves the right of marriage.

But consider that in this very point he rather said that it was a marriage, since he affirmed that this marriage existed, though not as a valid one. In the same way, he who said that an injury to the Creator dissolves the right of marriage asserted that marriage existed there and possessed a right. This right would certainly stand firm and could not be denied without sin, unless it were dissolved by the intervention of a greater cause. For if there had previously been no right there, what need was there so earnestly to excuse those who withdrew themselves from paying that obligation [Col. 0507A]? If even the one who was dismissed seemed blameworthy unless excused by a greater cause, how could the one who dismissed without cause not rightly be accused? But now, because the obligation of the sacrament of marriage was real, it could by no means be denied without cause. For husband owes wife and wife husband, so that neither should depart from the other; and if one should perhaps depart, the one deserted should nevertheless preserve inviolate the right and obligation of marriage.

But the cause of God is greater, against which no cause ought to stand. When it is harmed, nothing is owed contrary to it. In every cause, the person who opposes this cause loses his own right; under it and according to it we owe certain things, but against it we owe nothing. Your wife says to you: “You have become a Christian; I shall not follow you, because [Col. 0507B] you do not worship idols, because you have rejected the rite and custom of your parents. I go to another man; or, even if I do not go to another, I no longer go with you. I do not acknowledge you as husband unless you deny Christ.” Give attention here. An injury to the Creator dissolves the right of marriage. You owe her nothing further. She who has injured her Creator has lost her right. You were not permitted to leave her if she had not lost her right in you. She possessed authority over your body, and you were not allowed to take from her what was hers until she herself wished to take from her Creator what was his. But after she chose to injure her Creator, she rightly lost her own right.

You must act in this way with father, mother, brother and sister, children and relatives, and finally with your own soul. For you owe something to all these, but for God’s sake, not against God. [Col. 0507C] Behold, your father or mother or brother or sister—or even your own soul—stands on one side, and someone says to you: “I love this; I seek this; I aim at this. I am going to obtain it, acquire it, accomplish it. Come after me, agree with me, cooperate with my will, favor my desire.” Your God stands on the other side and says to you: “I reject this; I detest that wickedness; that sin is not pleasing to me. Do not give assent; it is evil; do not do it. Attend rather to me, submit to me, come after me, pursue what I urge, follow where I lead.” On the other hand your father cries to you: “Son, how can you leave me? I begot you, I brought you into this life, I fed and nourished you, and trained you in morals [Col. 0507D] and discipline.” Your God says in reply: “He indeed begot you; but when he begot you, he received from what was mine. In producing substance for you from what was mine, he supplied to you what he gave. But he could not give life to the one begotten. I alone, without him, gave life to you through what from myself was supplied to you through him. I gave you your life; I also gave you my death. Your father did not die for you as I died for you, that you might live in me. He ought not to precede me in a cause when he could not surpass me in grace and benefit. Therefore do not listen to him against me; do not follow him in what displeases me. You owe him nothing except for my sake, from whom you could have received nothing unless it had been given by me.”

This I say: attend here. If anything of this sort should occur—whether father, mother, brother, sister, [Col. 0508A] wife, or children; indeed, I say more, even if our own soul should wish to turn us away from our God—we must neither listen to it nor heed it, nor follow its desires. The Gospel cries to us: “Whoever does not leave father or mother, brothers or sisters, wife and children, and even his own soul for my sake, is not worthy of me” (Luke XIV; Matt. X). Every piety there is impiety where one is pious in order to become impious. See therefore that no cause can stand against God’s cause; indeed, that which opposes it is not even a cause, since his is supreme and sole. In this manner dismissal for God’s sake is not a sin if the person is joined to another. For an injury to the Creator dissolves the right of marriage.

“If the unbeliever departs, let him depart. A brother is not subject to bondage in such cases” (1 Cor. VII), [Col. 0508B] he would be subject to bondage if he were either dragged away unwillingly or held against his will. He owes the unbeliever nothing, whether the unbeliever departs or remains; one who has injured the Creator has lost his right. Therefore, if the unbeliever departs, let him depart; it is no concern of ours. The believer is not compelled, as though bound by some obligation, either to follow one who departs or to endure one who despises him. He is not subject to bondage: he is free to do what he wishes, only in the Lord. If he is a man, let him take a wife; if a woman, let her marry. Let each choose whatever union he or she wishes; no longer is one held by the obligation of the former union, whose right has been dissolved because of injury to the Creator.

This injury to the Creator not only excuses the believer when one is dismissed by an unbeliever for God’s sake and without fault joins another; it also excuses the believer when he, choosing a faithful union, detests with Christian devotion an unbeliever who is willing indeed to cohabit [Col. 0508C] but refuses to receive the faith. For whether the unbeliever chooses to depart or to remain, the one who has become a believer owes that person nothing. No one can compel the believer not to do what he wishes. An injury to the Creator dissolves the right of marriage. The unbeliever can now demand nothing from the believer, because he has lost his obligation toward him after scorning to render to the Creator what he owes. The believer now has a cause by which he may justly refuse even that which he formerly owed, and which he would still owe had he not possessed an intervening cause that dissolved the obligation itself.

Therefore the believer is free if he wishes to choose a faithful partner; no one can forbid him. Yet if he tolerates an unbeliever willing to cohabit [Col. 0508D], he performs a work of perfection, in order to gain his neighbor. Thus the Apostle says: “The unbelieving husband is sanctified through the faithful wife; and likewise the faithful wife through the faithful husband” (1 Cor. VII). Therefore, if the believer tolerates an unbeliever consenting to cohabit in order to make that unbeliever a believer, whether he succeeds or does not succeed, so far as lies within him he gains the soul of his brother and fulfils a work of piety. But if he does not wish to tolerate the person, detesting that person’s unbelief, “a brother is not subject to bondage in such cases.” No one can compel him, if he wishes, not to leave the unbeliever, nor forbid him, even if he wishes, to join himself to an unbeliever.

There is sin in the unbeliever who rejects faith; that person’s fault dissolves the right of marriage, so that he can no longer lawfully demand what, if demanded by a believer, could not [Col. 0509A] be refused without injury. For the unbeliever’s fault frees the believer from obligation, just as, conversely, the believer’s righteousness binds the unbeliever by obligation. Thus the believer does not sin if joined to another, because he has been released from the right of marriage against the unbeliever; but even if abandoned without fault, the unbeliever may not seek another union, because the right of marriage and the obligation of the marital covenant toward the faith still bind him. Therefore the believer cannot be called adulterous if joined to another. But even when abandoned, the unbeliever incurs the crime of adultery if joined to another. Hence, if the believer even abstains from what is permitted in order to avoid danger to the neighbor, he performs a more perfect work. Yet he can in no way be compelled to do this, since it is not the work of obligation but the effect of charity, as blessed Augustine says in the book *On Adulterous Marriages*. [Col. 0509B] The Lord does not forbid the believer’s departure from the unbeliever, because it is not unjust in his sight. But the Apostle, by the counsel of charity, provides not only that those dismissed should not be scandalized, but also because, when they fall into other marriages, bound in adulterous ties, they are very difficult to free from unbelief. Thus an unbeliever commits adultery if joined to another, because he has not been released from the obligation of the former pact. But you say:

“Behold, an unbeliever—whether pagan or Jew—becomes a Christian. He leaves the wife whom he formerly had, because she does not wish to follow him into the faith, in the liberty of faith; he takes another faithful wife. The first, seeing herself rejected, marries another, binding herself in an adulterous tie. Later it happens that, pierced with compunction, she begins to abhor her unbelief, comes to faith, and becomes a Christian. [Col. 0509C] What is to be done with this woman? She cannot remain continent. She asks the Church either to restore her husband to her or to permit her to marry another. What will the Church say to her? If it restores her husband to her, it dissolves the marriage which has been confirmed by Christian holiness and makes him an adulterer, since, while his wife is alive—the wife whom, as a believer, he lawfully took as a believer—he is joined to another. This is altogether impermissible. Therefore the Church does not restore her husband to her.

“What then will it say to her? If it tells her to marry another, it seems to make her an adulteress, since it permits her, not yet released from the law of her living husband, to enter marriage with another. Therefore nothing else seems to remain except that the Church compel this woman to preserve continence, since she seems bound by her sin, so that she can have neither her own husband nor [Col. 0509D] another. But if the Church does this, it may happen that the woman is scandalized and, abhorring the Christian faith, returns to unbelief. Other women and men likewise, remaining in unbelief, whose husbands or wives have already come to faith and, having left them, entered marriages with other believers, may, upon learning this, fear to come to the Christian faith. Thus the destruction of many would follow while they flee faith because they either do not wish, or cannot, remain continent.

“Finally, if this woman is condemned after receiving the grace of baptism for her former sin, the grace seems incomplete, and not all that formerly stood in guilt has been washed away by the laver of regeneration; nor is it now true that ‘the old things have passed away [Col. 0510A] and all things have become new’” (2 Cor. V). For these reasons this woman seems freed after receiving the faith and putting on the sacrament of liberty and newness, so that henceforth she is not held by the obligation of the former union. For it is just that she whom injury to the Creator bound should now be released by reverence and faith in him. For this reason the Church does not forbid such persons, if they are unwilling to preserve continence, to be joined in marriage with others.

But it may be asked: if the one who first comes to faith has not entered a marital union until the other, who remained in unbelief, follows that person, what ought the Church to do in such a case? But there is no doubt that, after such persons have become one in faith, if they are unwilling to remain continent they ought to return to one another and again come together in Christian devotion, to discharge the obligation of their former marriage—which [Col. 0510B] they had entered not without the Creator’s institution. This too may be asked: if, after the one who first came to faith has been bound in a faithful marriage, the one who remained in unbelief likewise comes to the faith together with the person to whom he or she had been joined in an adulterous bond, ought the Church to tolerate their remaining together after receiving faith, though while in unbelief they had been wrongly joined? But since the same grace intervenes and washes away all former things, nothing prevents those who were wrongly united outside Christ’s faith from remaining rightly together in Christ.

It may also be asked concerning those who, while in unbelief, take their female relatives in marriage, or any others with whom they could not have been joined under Christian law, if both should perhaps come to faith together: may the Church tolerate such a union? But the reasoning here differs, because the grace of baptism removes guilt, not nature. In baptism what belongs to one’s kindred by nature is sanctified; what belongs to crime by fault is excused. Therefore, when such people come under its judgment, the Christian religion ought not to permit what could indeed have begun outside it but ought not be tolerated within it. These matters mentioned above are to be assessed in the same manner for both sexes: whether, that is, a man precedes his wife in the Christian faith or a woman her husband. [Col. 0510C]

## CHAPTER XIV. On consanguinity and the degrees of consanguinity

In the first degree, in the ascending line, are contained father and mother; in the descending line, son and daughter. No other persons are joined to these. In the second degree are contained [Col. 0510D], in the ascending line, grandfather and grandmother; in the descending line, grandson and granddaughter; and in the collateral line, brother and sister. These persons are doubled: grandfather and grandmother are reckoned both on the father’s and on the mother’s side. In subsequent degrees likewise, persons are doubled in the same order according to the nature of those found in each degree.

These persons are called double in the second degree because there are two grandfathers, paternal and maternal. Likewise there are two kinds of grandchildren, those born from a son and those born from a daughter. Brother and sister arise collaterally—that is, the father’s brother or the mother’s brother, who are called respectively paternal uncle (*patruus*) and maternal uncle (*avunculus*); they too are doubled in this order.

In the third degree above are great-grandfather and great-grandmother; below, great-grandson and [Col. 0511A] great-granddaughter; collaterally, the son or daughter of a brother or sister; paternal uncle and paternal aunt (*amita*), that is, the father’s brother and sister; maternal uncle and maternal aunt (*matertera*), that is, the mother’s brother and sister.

In the fourth degree above are great-great-grandfather and great-great-grandmother; below, great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter; collaterally, the grandson and granddaughter of a brother and sister; paternal first cousin and paternal first cousin female (*frater patruelis*, *soror patruelis*), that is, the son or daughter of a paternal uncle; *consobrinus*, *consobrina*, that is, the son or daughter of a maternal uncle and maternal aunt; *amitinus*, *amitina*, that is, the son or daughter of a paternal aunt. Likewise, those born of two sisters are *consobrini*. To these are added great paternal uncle and great paternal aunt, that is, the brother and sister of the paternal grandfather; great maternal uncle and great maternal aunt, that is, the brother and sister of the grandmother, whether paternal or maternal.

In the fifth degree above are great-great-great-grandfather and great-great-great-grandmother; below, great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter; collaterally, the great-grandson and great-granddaughter of a brother or sister; and the son or daughter of a paternal first cousin, [Col. 0511B] paternal first cousin female, *amitinus* and *amitina*, *consobrinus* and *consobrina*. A *proconsobrinus* or *proconsobrina* is the son or daughter of a great paternal uncle, great paternal aunt, great maternal uncle, or great maternal aunt. To these are added the great-great paternal uncle (*propatruus*) and great-great paternal aunt (*proamita*), namely the brother and sister of the paternal great-grandfather; the great-great maternal uncle (*proavunculus*) and great-great maternal aunt (*promatertera*), namely the brother and sister of the paternal and maternal great-grandmother; and the maternal great-grandfathers. This category can be explained neither in degrees other than those written nor by other terms.

In the sixth degree above are third great-grandfather and third great-grandmother; below, third great-grandson and third great-granddaughter; collaterally, the great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter of a brother and sister; the grandson and granddaughter of a paternal first cousin, paternal first cousin female, *amitinus* and *amitina*, *consobrinus* and *consobrina*; the grandson and granddaughter of a great paternal uncle, great paternal aunt, great maternal uncle, [Col. 0511C] and great maternal aunt; and the son or daughter of the nearer *consobrinus*, who are called *consobrini*. Added collaterally are the son or daughter of a great-great paternal uncle, great-great paternal aunt, great-great maternal uncle, or great-great maternal aunt; the great-great-great paternal uncle (*abpatruus*) and great-great-great paternal aunt (*abamita*), namely the brother and sister of a great-great-grandfather; the great-great-great maternal uncle (*abavunculus*) and great-great-great maternal aunt (*abmatertera*), namely the brother and sister of a paternal or maternal great-great-grandmother; and the maternal great-great-grandfathers. This likewise cannot be explained more fully than the author himself has set it forth.

In the seventh degree, kindred in the direct ascending and descending line are not called by their own names; but in the collateral line are included the fourth great-grandson and fourth great-granddaughter of a brother or sister, and the sons and daughters of *consobrini*. Seven degrees of succession have therefore been established because, beyond them, neither names can be found by the nature of things nor life be extended to successors. In these seven degrees [Col. 0511D] are contained all names of kinship; beyond them neither affinity can be found nor succession further propagated.

### Why consanguinity is observed to the sixth degree

When consanguinity, gradually separating itself through the orders of descendants, has withdrawn to the final degree and has ceased to be kinship, the law of marriage takes it up again through the bond of marriage and in some way calls it back as it flees. Consanguinity has been fixed to the sixth degree of lineage so that, just as the generation and condition of humankind end with the six ages of the world, so the kinship of a family may end with the same number of degrees.

Let the son and daughter—that is, brother and [Col. 0512A] sister—be the trunk itself. When these are separately divided, the following branches issue from the root of that trunk: grandson and granddaughter, the first; great-grandson and great-granddaughter, the second; great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter, the third; great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter, the fourth; third great-grandson and third great-granddaughter, the fifth; the grandson of a third great-grandson and the granddaughter of a third great-granddaughter, the sixth.

### How the degrees of consanguinity are to be counted

Pope Gregory VI: “We have decreed that each person is to observe his or her own offspring to the seventh generation; and so long as they recognize themselves as related by affinity, we forbid them to enter into marital union. If they do so, they are to be separated.”

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops and clerics, and also judges established throughout Italy: greeting and apostolic blessing.

A newly arisen question concerning degrees of consanguinity has been brought to the Apostolic See. Certain persons ignorant of laws and canons endeavor, contrary to the sacred canons and ecclesiastical custom, to count the same degrees of kinship in another way. In a novel and unheard-of error, they affirm that full brothers or sisters are among themselves in the second generation, their sons or daughters in the fourth, and their grandsons or granddaughters in the sixth; and they thus calculate descent, ending it in the sixth degree. They say thereafter that men and women may contract marital rights with one another. To confirm this profane error, they adduce as argument the secular laws promulgated by Emperor Justinian concerning the succession of blood-relations. Trusting in these, [Col. 0512C] they attempt to show that brothers are counted in the second degree, their children in the fourth, and grandchildren in the sixth. Thus, by ending the sequence of genealogy, they endeavor with a perverse subtlety to disturb the enumeration of the holy Fathers and the ancient computation of the Church handed down to us.

But we, with God’s assent, took care to investigate this question in a synod held in the Lateran consistory, bishops, clerics, and judges from different provinces having been summoned for this work. Finally, after the laws and sacred canons had long been examined, we found clearly that one computation belongs to laws and another to canons for distinct reasons. In the laws, indeed, the degrees themselves are mentioned for no other purpose than that inheritance or succession may pass among blood-relatives from one person to another. Therefore, since inheritances cannot pass except from one person to another, the secular emperor took care to assign an individual degree to each individual person. But because marriages cannot occur without two persons, the sacred canons place two persons in one degree.

Yet, if both computations are attentively and subtly considered, it will be clear that they intend the same thing, are identical in meaning, and converge upon the same limit. Justinian did not define in his laws the degree to which consanguinity itself lasts. But the canons count no generation beyond seven. For after determining the sixth [Col. 0513A] degree, the emperor added in those laws: “Let it suffice to have shown thus far how the degrees of kinship are counted; for from these it is plainly understood how we ought to count the further degrees. For each person born adds a degree.” Behold, in these few words it is openly shown that degrees such as these persons calculate must be counted not merely to the sixth but even beyond it, since he decrees that further degrees beyond six are to be counted. For when he says “further degrees,” he plainly indicates that there are not only six degrees, but that after six are completed there remain others to be counted.

Therefore, if the laws are to be true and the canons truthful, let us say what truth contains: namely, that consanguinity does not end at such a sixth degree, and that, according to the canons, it ends [Col. 0513B] in the seventh degree. For both computations, as we have said above, are concluded by one limit. Two legal degrees make one canonical degree. Thus brothers, who according to secular laws are said to be in the second degree, are counted according to the canons in the first; the children of brothers, counted there in the fourth, are counted here in the second. Grandchildren, who there are counted in the sixth, are counted here in the third. Likewise thereafter, those written in the laws as in the eighth and tenth degrees are assigned in the canons to the fourth and fifth. In the same way, the rest are to be understood: those called sixth or seventh according to the canons are reckoned twelfth or fourteenth according to the laws. For if they are canonically and customarily counted in seven degrees, all names of kinship are contained in them; beyond them neither consanguinity is found, nor names discovered, nor succession can be further extended, nor can it be remembered from any generation.

So that no ambiguity may henceforth remain in this computation of consanguinity, we have judged that another enumeration, used by some persons, must also be ended in this discussion. For there are some who begin to count genealogy not from brothers but from their children—that is, paternal cousins or *consobrini*—saying that the children of brothers ought to be counted in the first generation, because brothers are, as it were, a trunk from which the other branches arise. But even this computation of degrees, if correctly understood, cannot differ in meaning [Col. 0513D] from that which we explained above.

### From Book III of the *Institutes*, chapter 6, “On the degrees of kinship”

At this point it is necessary to explain how degrees of kinship are counted. We must first be warned that kinship is counted in one way upward, another downward, and another collaterally, which is also called sideways. Ascending kinship is that of parents; descending kinship, that of children; collateral kinship, that of brothers, sisters, and those begotten from them, and consequently paternal uncles, paternal aunts, maternal uncles, and maternal aunts. Both ascending and descending kinship begin at the first degree; but collateral kinship is counted from the second.

In the first degree above are father and mother; below, [Col. 0514A] son and daughter. In the second, above are grandfather and grandmother; below, grandson and granddaughter; collaterally, brother and sister. In the third, above are great-grandfather and great-grandmother; below, great-grandson and great-granddaughter; collaterally, the son and daughter of a brother and sister; and consequently paternal uncle and paternal aunt, maternal uncle and maternal aunt. A paternal uncle is the father’s brother, whom the Greeks call *patrōion* (πατρῷον) or *patradelphon* (πατράδελφον). A maternal uncle is the mother’s brother, who among them is properly called *mētrōios* (μητρῷος), and generically *theios* (θεῖος). A paternal aunt is the father’s sister; a maternal aunt is the mother’s sister, who, as is clear above, is called *theia* (θεία).

In the fourth degree above are great-great-grandfather and great-great-grandmother; below, great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter; collaterally, the grandson and granddaughter of a brother and sister, and consequently great paternal uncle and great paternal aunt—that is, the grandfather’s brother and sister. Likewise great maternal uncle and great maternal aunt—that is, the grandmother’s brother and sister. A *consobrinus* or *consobrina* is anyone begotten from brothers or sisters. But some rightly think that *consobrini* properly are those born of two sisters, as though *consororini*; while those born of two brothers are properly called paternal cousins (*fratres patrueles*). If daughters are born from two brothers, they are called paternal cousin-sisters (*sorores patrueles*). Those born from a brother and a sister, however, are properly called *amitini*. The children of your paternal aunt call you *consobrinus*, if she is your paternal aunt; and you likewise call your paternal aunt’s children *amitini*.

In the fifth degree above are great-great-great-grandfather and great-great-great-grandmother; below, great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter; collaterally, the great-grandson and great-granddaughter of a brother and sister; and consequently the great-great paternal uncle and great-great paternal aunt, that is, the brother and sister of a great-grandfather; the great-great maternal uncle and great-great maternal aunt, that is [Col. 0514C], the brother and sister of a great-grandmother. Likewise, the son or daughter of a paternal cousin, paternal cousin-sister, *consobrinus*, *consobrina*, *amitinus*, or *amitina* is a nearer cousin (*propior sobrinus*, *sobrina*). These are the son and daughter of a great paternal uncle, great paternal aunt, great maternal uncle, or great maternal aunt.

In the sixth degree above are third great-grandfather and third great-grandmother; below, third great-grandson and third great-granddaughter; collaterally, the great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter of a brother and sister. Consequently there are the great-great-great paternal uncle and great-great-great paternal aunt—that is, the brother and sister of a great-great-grandfather. Likewise, the sons and daughters born from paternal cousins, *consobrini*, or *amitini* are called *sobrini* and *sobrinae*. Let it suffice to have shown thus far how the degrees of kinship are counted. From these it is plainly understood how we ought also to count the further degrees. For every person born adds a degree [Col. 0514D], so that it is far easier to answer in which degree each person stands than to identify each by his or her proper kinship designation. The degrees of agnation are also counted in that manner. But because truth is more strongly impressed upon human minds through faith seen by the eyes than through the ears, we have thought it necessary, after the description of the degrees, to inscribe them also in the present book, so that young persons may attain the most complete knowledge of the degrees both by hearing and by sight.

### From the letter of John, bishop of Constantinople

When Pope Gregory was asked by Augustine, bishop of the English people, in what degree believers ought to marry, he replied by way of dispensation as follows: [Col. 0515A] “A certain Roman law permits in the commonwealth either a brother and sister, or the son and daughter of two full brothers or of two sisters, to have sexual relations. As we have learned by experience, offspring cannot increase from such a marriage. Therefore believers ought now to be permitted lawfully to join one another in the fourth or fifth generation.”

Likewise John says: “But long afterward, when he was asked by Felix, bishop of Messana in Sicily, whether he had written to Augustine that marriages contracted in the fourth generation among the English should by no means be dissolved, the most humble father Gregory among other things gave this explanation: ‘What I wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English people, your pupil, as you remember, concerning unions of consanguinity—to him and to the English people who had recently come to the faith—know that I wrote certainly in a special, not a general, sense, lest they withdraw through fear of stricter requirements from the good [Col. 0515B] they had begun. The entire Roman city is witness to me of this. I did not issue these commands to them with the intention that, once they had been established with a firm root in the faith, if they were found within their own consanguinity they should not be separated, or that they should be joined within the line of affinity, that is, to the seventh generation. Rather, while they were still neophytes, it was necessary first to permit them what was unlawful there, instruct them by words and examples, and afterward reasonably and faithfully prohibit what they should do in such cases.

“For, according to the Apostle who says, ‘I gave you milk to drink, not solid food’ (1 Cor.
