III), we allowed these matters to them [Col. 0515C] for the present time, not to their descendants, as was laid down above, lest the good which had been planted with a still weak root should be uprooted, but rather be strengthened somewhat and preserved until perfection.’”

Therefore I, John, have taken care to set these points forth briefly so that those who, on the occasion of a new dispensation, argue for unlawful marriages against this most learned man may know that he did not establish the union of the fourth generation generally, but permitted it pardoningly and temporarily.

### Pope Zacharias, chapter 1

I have learned from persons in the regions of Germany that Pope Gregory of blessed memory, while divine grace was enlightening them in the religion of Christianity, had granted them permission to join themselves in the fourth [Col. 0515D] generation. Although we find nothing written on this point, we do not doubt that this is not lawful for Christians once they recognize one another, but that, while they were inexperienced, they were to be invited to the faith.

### Likewise, chapter 5

Let no one dare to join in marriage a female cousin, granddaughter, stepmother, brother’s wife, a woman from his own kindred, or one whom a kinsman has had. Whoever enters into and remains in such a wicked marriage should know that he is bound by the bonds of anathema of apostolic authority, and no priest is to grant him communion. But if he has repented and separated himself from such a union, he is to undergo fitting penance, as the priest of the place shall judge.

[Col. 0516A]

### Decree of Gregory the Younger

If anyone takes his brother’s wife in marriage, let him be anathema. If anyone takes his stepmother or daughter-in-law, let him be anathema. If anyone takes in marriage a woman from his own kindred or one whom a kinsman has had, let him be anathema.

### Bede, *History of the English*

When Augustine asked whether two full brothers ought to take as wives individual sisters who are descended from them by a distant lineage, Gregory answered: “This is lawful in every way. For nowhere in the sacred writings is anything found that seems to contradict this union.”

### Gregory’s response to Augustine (chapter 37)

To have sexual relations with one’s stepmother is a grave crime, because it is written in the law: “You shall not uncover your father’s nakedness” (Lev. XVIII). For a son cannot uncover his father’s nakedness. But because it is written, “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II), whoever presumes to uncover the nakedness of his stepmother, who was one flesh with his father, undoubtedly uncovers his father’s nakedness. Sexual relations with a brother’s wife are likewise forbidden, because through the prior union she has become the brother’s flesh; for this reason John the Baptist also was beheaded and completed in holy martyrdom.

## CHAPTER XV. On affinity
Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to Venerius of Cartala.

To the diligent discernment of your brotherhood, beloved brother, I render the thanks I owe, because by asking what you ought to ask you have made me glad. Therefore I answer your inquiries calmly. You have resolved to consult the Apostolic See [Col. 0516C] whether a woman united in matrimonial intercourse to a man outside her own family becomes related to his kindred; whether, when he has died, the relationship remains the same; whether, under another husband, the terms of kinship are dissolved; or whether children subsequently born may lawfully enter into union with the kindred of the former husband.

For the word of the Lord is mighty and strong, enduring, abiding, unchangeable—not momentary, not passing away. Truth itself says, who is the Word of God: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Luke 21; Matthew 24). Before God appeared among humankind in the flesh, Adam, inspired by Him, said: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother, and [Col. 0516D] shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2; Matthew 1). God did not contradict this.

Finally, when Truth sprang from the earth into the earth and appeared visibly in humanity, He was asked whether it was lawful for a man to leave his wife. Forbidding this, He declared that it must not be done, except where fornication alone dissolved the marital union. He therefore at once brought forward that very statement which, remaining with the Father before the ages, He the Word had inspired in Adam, Himself confirming what He Himself as man had uttered: “Therefore a man shall leave,” etc.

If they become one flesh, how can a relative of either belong to one and not belong to the other? This must certainly be believed impossible. For when one has died, [Col. 0517A] affinity is not erased in the survivor; nor can another marital union dissolve the affinity of the earlier union. Nor is it fitting that the offspring of a second union should pass into participation in the affinity of the former, because the word of the Lord is mighty and strong; and, as the Prophet has said: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. He established them for ever and for age upon age; he set a commandment, and it shall not pass away” (Psalm 148).

Can He not, by His word and command, make male and female two into one flesh—He who has not ceased to make with Himself one an innumerable multitude of both sexes, as Truth Himself says: “I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may be one, as thou, Father, art in me and I in thee; [Col. 0517B] that they also may be one in us” (John 17).

Whoever, with rash and sacrilegious presumption, seeks relationship in one who has died, or seeks under another spouse to dissipate the terms of affinity, or believes that offspring born of another union may lawfully be joined to the kinship of the former union—such a person denies that the word of God is mighty or strong. And whoever so readily or swiftly seeks to dissolve it does not believe that the word of the Lord abides for ever.

Look upon the earth, separated by great intervals in its four regions, yet made and joined together; imagine a body of whatever shape or vastness you please.

### From the Council of Mâcon

[Col. 0517C]

Certainly, the consanguinity to be observed with respect to one’s own husband must likewise, under the law of marriage, be observed in the wife’s family; for it is established that the two were one flesh. Both families must be regarded as common to them, as it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2).

### From the Council of Chalon

We also forbid anyone any longer to be joined in marriage in the fourth, fifth, or sixth generation. Where such a union is found to have been contracted after the prohibition, let it be separated.

## Chapter XVI. On spiritual kinship. Concerning which Nicholas wrote to Solomon, bishop of Constance

Your Holiness asks us whether a man may have one [Col. 0517D] spiritual co-mother after another. In this matter your brotherhood ought to remember that it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2). Therefore, since it is established that husband and wife become one flesh through marriage, it follows that the husband is made spiritual co-father to that woman to whom the wife taken in marriage appeared to be spiritual co-mother. Thus it is clear that a man cannot be joined in marriage to a woman who was the spiritual co-mother of the woman with whom he had himself become one flesh.

### The same, to Charles, archbishop

If anyone has committed fornication with a spiritual co-mother, he is struck, as you know, by the penalties of anathema. Likewise, we decree that the same penalty be inflicted upon one who has perpetrated the crime of fornication with a woman whom he received from the sacred font of baptism, or with one whom he held before the bishop while she was anointed with sacred [Col. 0518A] chrism; nevertheless, if he has a lawful wife, he is not to be compelled to leave her.

### From the Council of Chalon

It has been reported to us that certain women, some through negligence and others deceitfully, have held their own children before bishops for confirmation in order to separate from their husbands. We have therefore judged it proper that, if any woman has held her own child before a bishop for confirmation through negligence or fraud, she should do penance for her deception or fraud as long as she lives; nevertheless, she is not to be separated from her husband.

### From the Council of Mainz

Concerning your question about a man who married his goddaughter, one who had intercourse with his spiritual co-mother, and one who baptized his own son and whose wife received him from the font, with the purpose that a marital separation might result—whether afterward they might remain in such unions: concerning such persons the answer must be as follows.

If anyone has taken his goddaughter or his spiritual co-mother in marriage, we judge that they are to be separated and subjected to severe penance. But if lawful spouses, one or both, have deliberately arranged to receive their own child from the font in order to bring about a separation, we give this counsel: if they wish to remain unmarried, that is good; but if not, severe penance is to be imposed upon the plotter, they are to remain together, and, if the violator of the marriage bond outlives the other, he is to be punished with the harshest penance and remain without hope of marriage.

### From the Council of Tribur

[Col. 0518C]

He who has a spiritual co-father whose son or daughter he received from the washing of the sacred font, while that man’s wife is not his spiritual co-mother, may, after his co-father has died, take the widow as his wife if they have no consanguineous relationship. For why should persons be unable to marry whom no carnal proximity or spiritual generation separates?

Likewise, for the same reason, one who has a spiritual co-father is not forbidden to become his son-in-law, provided it is not with the daughter whom he himself received from the sacred font. The sons or daughters of spiritual parents—that is, of co-parents—born before or after the establishment of co-parenthood may also lawfully marry. Except for those persons in relation to whom they are co-parents: for no one may take as wife the spiritual daughter of his father, although he is not forbidden to take as wife the daughter [Latin printed *filium*, evidently corrupt] of the man who is his father’s co-father, if she was not his father’s spiritual daughter.

## Chapter XVII. The difference between kinship or consanguinity, affinity, and spiritual kinship

There are three things—consanguinity, affinity, and spiritual kinship—in which the law lays down restrictions upon Christian marriage.

[Col. 0519A]

Consanguinity exists among those joined according to a line of descent. Affinity exists among those who are not indeed joined by birth, yet are connected through birth. For example: my brother’s son is my blood-relative; his wife, who is not of my family, has through him—who is of my family—become related to me by affinity, and I to her. Thus, whoever takes a wife from another family makes his own relatives related to her by affinity. Between the woman and the husband’s relatives, or between the man and the wife’s relatives, there is not consanguinity but affinity; and in affinity, as in consanguinity, the contracting of marriage is prohibited.

In consanguinity marriages are forbidden as far as the seventh degree. Some writings, however, seem to set the boundary of the prohibition at the sixth degree, and others at the seventh. For the wording is ambiguous when it is said that marriages may not be contracted “up to the seventh degree.” It can be understood either that they are prohibited as far as the seventh degree but permitted in the seventh, or that the seventh is the final degree in which they are prohibited and that they are permitted thereafter.

[Col. 0519B]

Some have placed children in the first degree, grandchildren in the second, great-grandchildren in the third, great-great-grandchildren in the fourth, great-great-great-grandchildren in the fifth, great-great-great-great-grandchildren in the sixth, and the grandchildren of great-great-great-great-grandchildren in the seventh. In this way seven degrees are included in the prohibition.

But those who say that father and mother are the root of the line of descent, while son and daughter form, as it were, its trunk, judge that the first degree should be counted among grandchildren. Under this reckoning, the degree which was seventh in the former arrangement is shown to be sixth in this one.

Consanguinity, however far it extends upward or downward, admits no marital union: thus from son to mother and to all above her—that is, grandmother, great-grandmother, and so forth—and from mother to son and all below her, that is, grandson, great-grandson, and so forth. Likewise, from father to daughter, or from daughter to father, it is considered upward and downward. Therefore the degrees of consanguinity for marriage are counted among those who descend collaterally.

[Col. 0519C]

Some have wished to limit affinity at the fifth degree. Others have judged that it should be observed through the seventh, like consanguinity.

[Col. 0520A]

Spiritual kinship or proximity is observed in this manner. No one may take his spiritual co-mother or spiritual daughter as wife. Likewise, a woman may not be wife to her spiritual co-father or spiritual son. A son is also forbidden to have as wife his father’s spiritual co-mother or spiritual daughter. Likewise, a daughter may not be wife to her mother’s spiritual co-father or spiritual son.

The Council of Tribur permits a man, after his co-father has died, to take that man’s wife if she is not his spiritual co-mother. If this is correct, then likewise a woman, after her spiritual co-mother has died, may marry her husband if he is not her spiritual co-father. Yet this is found forbidden in some places.

## Chapter XVIII. Whether deceit called substitution dissolves a marriage

We have heard that, when certain persons were betrothed [Col. 0520B] to wives whose appearance they did not know, other women of inferior station were deceitfully substituted. In such a case, if those deceived refuse afterward to give their assent to an act which they did not intend when it was done, we judge that the marriage ought by no means to be valid. For it is clear that the act was not done intentionally; nor can they be bound to carry out what they neither intended when they did it nor wished when they learned of it.

## Chapter XIX. Whether an unknown servile condition later dissolves a marriage

It is also asked whether, if a woman marries a slave believing him free, or a free man marries a female slave believing her free, the marriage should be dissolved once the deception has been discovered. Some think this deception ought to be judged differently from the preceding one. For here the error concerns not the person but only the person’s status; hence they judge that it ought to prejudice the sanctity of marriage. But perhaps this better accords with the truth and with the peace to which God has called us: where one party’s ignorance is not shown to be culpable, the other party’s deceit, in what it wrongfully appropriated by fraud to the injury of the innocent, ought not to be allowed to stand.

# Part Twelve. On Vows

[Col. 0519]

## Chapter I. On vows: whether they are diverse

[Col. 0519D]

Concerning vows, I do not discharge a vow; you have asked, and I am indeed compelled to fulfil what I promised. Stealing a little leisure amid frequent occupations, I have touched on the matter briefly, but have not fully pursued what you asked.

You ask whether vows bind their makers by an equal obligation and the same necessity. If I wished to give an answer merely to your question and not also for edification, I could have replied briefly that plainly not every vow involves the same obligation. But because I do not doubt that you raised not a question but rather sought edification, I have attempted, so far as opportunity and reason have presently allowed, to satisfy your devotion.

## Chapter II. On the five ways by which the mind considers matters to be done

[Col. 0520D]

There are five ways by which the human mind is accustomed to consider matters to be done: thought, will, deliberation, promise, and vow. It is one thing to think something and another to will what one has thought. For you can think what you do not will; but you cannot will unless what you have thought pleases you.

Yet it sometimes happens that what pleases according to inclination does not please according to reason, and that reason itself has not yet assented to performing what delights. In the delight itself there is, as it were, a certain will to do the act; but in reason itself there is not yet a resolve to do it.

But if, after the will, a resolve follows, so that the mind [Col. 0521A] confirms its assent to that which delights it, it is already bound—toward guilt if the matter is evil, toward merit if it is good. All this belonging to thought, will, and resolve remains within the person and binds that person alone, whether for good or evil; and the person is bound only in himself or herself, and only to the extent that it lies within that person.

But when a promise follows the resolve, the promisor begins to be bound toward another and becomes debtor for the truth of the promise that must be kept for one’s neighbor. If what was promised is good, the promisor is obligated because it is good and because it was promised. But if what was promised is evil, the promisor is not obligated in respect of the evil promised. Yet the promisor is guilty because he or she presumed to promise what could not be fulfilled without sin.

Lastly comes a vow, [Col. 0521B] in which something more seems to be contained than in a promise.

## Chapter III. What a vow is, and what it is to vow

A vow is a kind of attestation of a voluntary promise, more properly directed to God alone and to things belonging to God. To vow is, indeed, by the attestation of a voluntary promise, to bind oneself to God and establish oneself as His debtor.

For one who simply promises pledges to do something; but one who vows calls witnesses to the promise and confirms that promise itself. Insofar as it is a promise, one is bound; insofar as it is an attestation, one is obligated.

One kind of vow is hidden, made to God and before God; another is manifest, made to God before human beings. A hidden vow broken is sin. A manifest vow broken is both sin and scandal. In the former God is offended; in the latter one also sins against one’s neighbor.

[Col. 0521C]

If you ask which vows must altogether be kept, and which may without sin be omitted or even commuted, I begin with this first distinction.

## Chapter IV. Which vows need not be kept

Scripture says: “The vows of fools must be broken” (Ecclesiastes 5). By vows of fools we understand those made either concerning evil things or concerning good things in a bad manner.

For example, if someone vowed to kill another person, or vowed to commit any other act in which guilt plainly lay, the vow would concern evil, would itself be evil, and therefore ought not to be performed. In this case the first fault was making the vow; the second would be completing it if it were fulfilled.

Likewise, a [Col. 0521D] vow made concerning something good, if it is not made well, is counted among the foolish vows that must be broken. Even if a vow concerns something good, it is not well made if it vows either what is not permitted or what is not expedient.

It is not permitted, for example, if a woman vows continence without her husband’s consent—or rather, against his objection. It is not expedient if someone proposes to undertake a fast or any other work beyond his or her strength and capacity.

Therefore all these are counted among foolish vows: those which are perverse, unlawful, or undiscerning. But where something good is vowed and vowed well, some vows of this sort admit commutation by dispensation, whereas others admit substitution altogether.

## Chapter V. Which vow admits no commutation

[Col. 0522A]

Do you wish to know what things admit no commutation whatsoever? Perhaps you do not believe me, since you seek authority, if I were to produce just one item from all the rest. Yet there is one thing which admits no commutation.

For there can be no dispensation where there can be no substitution. “Dispensation,” as far as the word itself goes, is a term of loss; it denotes detriment. It is foolish voluntarily to suffer loss where no gain follows. But when one voluntarily bears a small loss in order that a greater gain may result, this is called dispensation, and it is a good dispensation.

See, then, how can one rightly bear loss voluntarily in that matter beyond which nothing greater can be acquired? There is one thing, if you seek authority, which admits no commutation. I do not say it, but Truth says it; and if I say it, I say it after Truth and according to Truth: “A man shall not give [Col. 0522B] an exchange for his soul” (Matthew 16).

But perhaps you will answer and say that Truth did not say, “He shall not give,” but, “What shall a man give in exchange for his soul?” Therefore He did not make an assertion but asked a question. You answer, if you can: what shall a man give in exchange for his soul? You plainly see that there is one thing which receives no commutation and admits no dispensation.

If you vow this—indeed, because you do vow it, for you cannot be good unless you vow it—render what you have vowed, and render the very thing you vowed. For if you wish to render something else, whatever it may be is not accepted in place of this.

[Col. 0522C]

“Vow and render to the Lord your God, all you who bring gifts round about Him,” says the Psalmist (Psalm 75). What gifts? “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord sons of rams” (Psalm 28). Perhaps these—the rams and sons of rams—are the gifts which the Psalmist commands us to vow and render when he says, “Vow,” etc.

To whom are gifts to be brought? Hear what follows: “To the Awesome One, and to Him who takes away the spirit of princes, awesome among the kings of the earth” (Psalm 75). Why, after saying, “Render gifts to the Lord your God,” did he immediately add, “Who takes away the spirit of princes,” unless he wished the gifts themselves to signify the spirit itself?

But if He takes away the spirit of princes, will He be unable to take away your spirit? Render it willingly, [Col. 0522D] therefore, lest you lose it unwillingly.

“Vow and render to the Lord your God, all you who bring gifts round about Him—to the Awesome One, and to Him who takes away the spirit of princes, awesome among the kings of the earth.”

See, then, brother, what we ought to vow and render to the Lord our God. If after vowing, or after making a vow, we refuse to render it, we still cannot retain it. If we render it, He will receive it; if we do not render it, He will take it. If we render it, He will reward what was given; if we do not render it, He will condemn what was not given.

For if we render it, we give what is ours and it is reckoned as righteousness; but if we do not render it, we retain what belongs to another and it is imputed as guilt. “He who loves his soul,” He says, “shall lose it” (John 12), and “he who loses his soul for [Col. 0523A] my sake shall find it” (Matthew 10). Whoever gives it to me keeps it for himself; whoever keeps it for himself loses it.

Vow, therefore, and render. If you vow your soul, render your soul. Do not think that you can render your money in place of your soul. That would be to vow more and render less; it would not be an equal substitution. If you give what is yours to God and yourself to the devil, it is not an equal division.

“If you offer rightly but divide not rightly, have you not sinned?” For the soul is worth more and money less. “Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?” (Matthew 6; Luke 12). If the soul is more than food, it is certainly more than money, since food too is more than money. Money is given for food; and if there were no food, what would money be? For what contributes and profits more must necessarily be more.

[Col. 0523B]

If, therefore, you vow your soul, do not give money in place of your soul; for if you do so, you commit fraud, vowing more and rendering less. You may give your money together with your soul; you may not give it in place of your soul—unless you wish to give your money for your soul in such a way that your soul, having been given, becomes more acceptable.

It is accepted for the soul when it is loved together with the soul; apart from the soul, it is not accepted for it. Do not therefore think that you can give your money in exchange for your soul—that is, as a commutation for your soul. For money given in this way would not be accepted, and you would not be able to save your soul by retaining it in this way. Thus both the money would be lost and the soul would not be saved. This, then, is the one thing that accepts no substitution.

## Chapter VI. Which vows admit commutation

[Col. 0523C]

All other things admit commutation according to place, time, and cause. You vowed gold; you may render silver, because what is less in price may be greater in weight. You vowed a pilgrimage to the Lord; it admits commutation if, as may happen, it is more expedient for you to remain in your own country and house.

For if there you can render something of equal value—whether in the labor of a work, in the devotion of virtue, or in the usefulness of administration—you may make a substitution. You vowed a fast; here too commutation may occur, if, as may happen, that course is not expedient.

I say something further. You vowed to serve God in a particular place, habit, or community: I say that all this may also admit commutation, because a place [Col. 0523D] may be destroyed, people may die, and a religious habit may be changed.

Do you suppose that you therefore lose your soul if a place is devastated or people die? Only let not what happens to them occur through you, nor let what ought to have been done by you remain undone in you. Your danger does not lie where your fault does not lie. Do what you can and as much as you can, and that suffices for you. No more is required from a good will than it is able to do.

But if you have vowed any of these things, or anything similar—things which may be taken away even from the unwilling or commuted by the willing—and you are indeed able to fulfil what you vowed, the commutation of your vow is not in your own discretion, even if you see something greater or better to do.

[Col. 0524A]

Dispensation may be made concerning you, but it ought not to be made by you. For, as far as you are concerned, you owe the very thing you vowed and not something else. You may not exchange one thing for another; but your steward and master may, if he wishes and knows it to be expedient, accept something else.

If the same thing is given by you, it is a debt; if something else is accepted by him, it is an indulgence. For this is why he is called a steward: he may, for the benefit and profitable result of substitution, impose upon those subject to him things different from the first things and other than those proposed, through a wholesome and reasonable commutation.

Thus, as your vow rests in your own will, so the commutation of your vow rests in his authority. There you may do through yourself the good which pleases you; here, however, you must consult him concerning what is more expedient.

There is yet something further that seems to need adding to what has been said.

[Col. 0524B]

Suppose you vowed to the Lord your God the virginity of your body. I say that you must render what you vowed. You may not look back, so as thereafter to descend to the experience of the flesh. I say, therefore, render what you owe. You may not render something else in place of this if you can render this.

But what shall we do? Suppose you vowed and did not keep the vow because you lost your virginity. You can no longer render virginity; you cannot give what you do not possess. Once virginity has been lost, it cannot afterward be repaired or recovered.

What then will you do? What will you render to the Lord your God for the virginity which you vowed and, after the vow, lost? Is there something else which can be rendered in place of it, so that the debt may be paid and so great a vow fulfilled?

[Col. 0524C]

If there is nothing else to render in its place, there is no salvation for those who vowed it and can no longer render what has been lost. Shall we then dare to cut off the bridge of mercy from such persons? Let him say this who dares. I neither presume nor wish to do so. Let anyone wishing to say it take heed lest perhaps he construct danger for himself.

Therefore there is something else which you can render for your virginity if you have lost it. What is that? Render your repentance; render your contrition; render your humility. For bodily virginity, render humility of heart; for broken flesh, break your heart. You owed humility in itself even if you had retained virginity; and yet, if you cannot render virginity, render humility in place of it, and it will make satisfaction both for itself and for virginity.

[Col. 0524D]

See how great the power of humility is. Virginity is the companion of humility, and humility the companion of virginity; and if humility is absent, virginity cannot satisfy God. But humility, if present, can satisfy God even if virginity is also present.

There is therefore something which you may render for your virginity if you cannot render it itself. And if you can make satisfaction to God even without offering that, do I say the same concerning your soul? Lose your soul so that you can no longer render it; then see whether anything remains which you can render in place of it.

For this reason I told you that this is the one thing for which no commutation can be given. If this alone is not given, then unless you render it, whatever else you give does not satisfy. If you render this, then whatever you do not give does not offend.

# Part Thirteen. On Vices and Virtues

[Col. 0525]

## Chapter I. On vices, virtues, and evil works

[Col. 0525A]

Sacred Scripture enumerates seven capital, principal, or original vices. They are called capital, principal, or original because they are the head, beginning, and origin of all the rest. For all other evils arise from these seven vices.

The difference between sins and vices appears to be this: vices are corruptions of the soul, from which, unless restrained by reason, sins—that is, acts of injustice—arise. But when consent is given to a tempting vice, the result is an act of injustice, called sin. Thus vice is a weakness arising from spiritual corruption; sin is an act of iniquity arising from corruption through consent.

Therefore vice without consent is a weakness, to which, insofar as it is weakness, mercy is due; and, insofar as it is [Col. 0525B] restrained from an act of iniquity, reward and a crown are due. But with consent vice becomes guilt: insofar as it is vice it is evil, and insofar as it is voluntary it deserves punishment.

Vice, then, lies in corruption; sin in action. The act of sin is completed by consent alone, even if no outward deed has occurred. For what belongs to iniquity is completed through perverse consent in the will alone, even when the will is involuntarily prevented from outwardly completing what it desires.

For it does all that is its own; and what more it does not do is not its own doing, but happens against it. Thus the deed is judged by consent alone; the outward deed merely adds to [Col. 0525C] malice insofar as it inflames toward malice the movement of the will which works inwardly.

Thus vices are the origin of sins, from which works of iniquity are born. As was said, without consent they entail punishment because they are corruptions; with consent they entail guilt because they are voluntary. Insofar as they are original, punishment is exercised in them; insofar as they are voluntary, punishment is owed to them.

They are these: first, pride; second, envy; third, anger; fourth, *acedia*; fifth, avarice; sixth, gluttony; seventh, lust.

Of these, three strip a person; the fourth scourges the stripped person; the fifth casts out the scourged person; the sixth deceives the expelled person; the seventh subjects the deceived person to slavery. Pride takes God away from a person; envy takes away the neighbor; anger takes away the self; *acedia* scourges the stripped person; avarice casts out the scourged person; gluttony deceives the expelled person; lust subjects the deceived person to slavery.

The rational soul in health is a firm [Col. 0525D] and sound vessel, having no corruption. Vices entering it impair and corrupt it in this way: by pride it is puffed up; by envy it dries out; by anger it bursts; by *acedia* it is broken; by avarice it is scattered; by gluttony it is infected; by lust it is trampled underfoot (*conculcatur*, apparently misread in the source as *concuicatur*) and reduced to mud.

[Col. 0526A]

Pride is love of one’s own excellence. Envy is hatred of another’s good fortune. Anger is an irrational disturbance of the mind. *Acedia* is sadness arising from confusion of mind, or excessive weariness and bitterness of spirit, by which spiritual joy is extinguished and the mind is overturned within itself by a kind of beginning of despair.

Avarice is an immoderate desire to possess. Gluttony is an immoderate desire to eat. Lust is excessive desire to satisfy pleasure, or desire for sexual intercourse boiling over beyond measure or contrary to reason.

[Col. 0526B]

Pride has two forms: one inward, the other outward. Inwardly it is pride; outwardly it is boastfulness. Pride lies in the exaltation of the heart; boastfulness in the display of a deed.

Pride, because it is pleased with itself, despises another’s testimony. Boastfulness, so as to please itself the more, seeks another’s testimony. Therefore boastfulness, through frivolity, feigns itself bland; true pride displays itself as cruel in swelling. Pride wishes to be feared; boastfulness to be loved.

Yet each, perversely pleasing itself in what it seeks, is proved to glory inordinately, though in different ways.

If, then, anyone counts pride and boastfulness under one heading, there are found seven capital vices, from which all sins, acts of iniquity, and works of injustice arise.

Some sins are called venial and others criminal.

Venial sins are those which cannot easily be avoided so as never to occur, and which, if they occur, involve neither great disgrace nor serious injury.

[Col. 0526C]

Criminal sins are those which either inflict great injury or entail disgrace, in which either God or one’s neighbor is greatly offended, or the doer is stained. Such are murders, adulteries, perjuries, thefts, and things joined to or contained in these, such as robberies, sacrileges, incest, and other such acts.

Venial sins include slight and passing anger, laughter, and the like, which happen without the agents’ deliberation, either heedlessly through negligence or precipitately through weakness.

## Chapter II. On virtues and good works

As we said above that vice is one thing and the sin proceeding from vice another, so we understand that virtues are one thing and works of righteousness arising from them another.

Virtue is, as it were, a certain [Col. 0526D] health and soundness of the rational soul, whose corruption is called vice. A work of righteousness consists in the movement of the rational mind proceeding according to God, arising from the conception of the heart and advancing outward as far as the completion of bodily action.

[Col. 0527A]

Many virtues are numbered in the Scriptures, but especially those which in the Gospel are arranged under the same number as certain antidotes or healings against the corruption of the seven vices.

First is humility; second, meekness; third, compunction of mind; fourth, desire for righteousness; fifth, mercy; sixth, purity of heart; seventh, inward peace of mind.

Therefore the person lying in sins is sick; vices are wounds; God is the physician; the gifts of the Holy Spirit are antidotes; virtues are states of health; beatitudes are joys. Through the gifts of the Holy Spirit vices are healed. Health from vices is the soundness of virtues. The healthy person acts; the one who acts is rewarded.

Thus good works follow virtues, and the works themselves arise from virtues.

Six works of mercy are specifically enumerated by the Lord in the Gospel (Matthew 25), in which the perfection of good works is signified. The first is to feed the hungry; [Col. 0527B] the second, to give drink to the thirsty; the third, to receive the stranger; the fourth, to clothe the naked; the fifth, to visit the sick; the sixth, to come to the imprisoned and confined.

In these needs every affliction of human life is either contained or bound together; and whoever for God’s sake has compassion upon a neighbor deserves mercy from God in his or her own necessity.

## Chapter III. On fear and love

There are, indeed, two movements of the heart by which the rational soul is impelled toward everything it does: one is fear, the other love. When these two are good, they accomplish every good. Through fear evils are avoided; through love goods are performed.

But when they are evil, they become the beginning and cause of all evils. [Col. 0527C] Through evil fear one withdraws from good; through evil love one perpetrates evils.

These two are therefore like two gates through which death and life enter: death when they are opened toward evil, life when they are directed toward good.

## Chapter IV. What fear is
Fear is a disposition of the mind by which it is moved to yield to what is superior; for by love one approaches, by fear one withdraws. Had man remained in righteousness, he would have been subject to what was better by his will. But now he is subject to what is stronger by necessity. This is that punishment of fear from which it is called servile. For he who formerly refused willingly to submit himself to what was better is now subjected by necessity to what is stronger. Charity indeed casts out this punishment when it makes subjection voluntary. The more charity increases, [Col. 0527D] the more the will increases; and the more the will increases, the more necessity diminishes. And when charity is perfect, a person willingly loves what is better out of reverence; he does not unwillingly fear what is stronger because of punishment.

They ask concerning Christ as man how he possessed the fear of the Lord. But it is easy to show how, voluntarily, inasmuch as he was man, he subjected himself to the Father as to one superior to himself, and yielded in spontaneous reverence to him whom he acknowledged as superior, saying: “The Father is greater than I” (John XI). Thus, just as love, though naturally one motion of the mind, receives different names according to different qualities, and is sometimes called desire—when it is directed toward the world—and charity when it is directed toward God: so fear also, though naturally one motion of the mind, [Col. 0528A] is denoted by different names according to the various ways in which it is possessed or operates.

## CHAPTER V. On the Four Fears

Holy Scripture distinguishes four kinds of fear: servile, worldly, initial, and filial. Servile fear is abstaining from evil in order to avoid punishment, while retaining an evil will. Worldly fear is abstaining from good in order to avoid punishment, while retaining a good will. Initial fear is, in order to avoid punishment, cutting off not only perverse actions but also wicked thoughts. Filial fear is clinging firmly to the good because one does not wish to lose it.

Of these four fears, two are evil—namely, servile and worldly—and two are good—namely, initial and filial. Servile fear fears punishment inflicted by human beings; and therefore it is content [Col. 0528B] merely to cease from an evil deed, since it serves only what is visible and does not fear the guilt of conscience, desiring to please men. Worldly fear, however, does not seek to please men, yet fears to displease them; it too pretends to be what it is not: as deceitful in denying truth as the other is deceptive in concealing falsehood. Both offend against truth: one because he timidly denies what is; the other because he perversely feigns what is not.

Initial fear, because it strives to escape the punishment threatened by God, sees that it is by no means enough merely to restrain itself from unlawful action. For to him who looks upon the heart, it is not sufficient proof that an action has been innocent unless the very thought of the heart also appears sincere and undefiled before his eyes. Therefore, because it fears displeasing him who sees everything, [Col. 0528C] it recognizes that, in order to attain complete innocence before him, it must correct everything. And so this is called initial fear, because under it, through a good will, virtue begins and vice comes to an end. Yet it is not perfection, since, while one thing is done and another intended, the good itself is not yet loved for its own sake.

Then charity comes and enters through that fear: while it shows what we ought to flee, it in some manner makes us seek and desire protection from the danger. It therefore turns the heart toward God, so that in some sense it flees from him to him: that is, while it fears having him angry, it strives to have him gracious. Filial fear follows this, born from charity as it succeeds, so that to fear him is nothing other than to be unwilling now to lose the good tasted in charity. This fear, indeed, [Col. 0528D] still has something of punishment joined to it while we walk in uncertainty, and the condition of mutable life can still turn in either direction. But when there is no mutability, then no penalty of suspicion arising from uncertainty will remain. Then fear will in a sense be without fear, when we shall be certain of stability and yet shall not cease to render reverence to the Creator.

## CHAPTER VI. On Charity

Holy Scripture commends to us a twofold charity: namely, love of God and love of neighbor. Love of God means loving him so that we rejoice in him. Love of neighbor means loving him so that we rejoice, not in him, but with him in God. That is, we are to love God for his own sake, but our neighbor [Col. 0529A] for God’s sake. God is to be loved for his own sake because he himself is our good. Our neighbor is to be loved for God’s sake because our good is, together with him, in God.

We love the one in order that we may come to him and rejoice in him; the other, that we may run with him and arrive with him. The one as joy; the other as a companion in joy. The one as rest; the other as a partner in rest. What is it to love God? To wish to possess him. What is it to love God for his own sake? To love him in order that you may possess him. What is it to love one’s neighbor for God’s sake? To love him because he has God.

Just as we love a person for righteousness—that is, because he has righteousness—and just as we love a person for wisdom—that is, because he has wisdom—so we love [Col. 0529B] a person for God’s sake, that is, because he has God; or, perhaps, because he does not yet have him but will have him; or in order that he may have him. Thus we love a person for God’s sake, whom indeed we would not love for God’s sake if we did not love God. In the same way, when I love a person for wisdom’s sake, I love him because I love wisdom itself; certainly I would not love him if I did not love the wisdom for which I love him. So, when I love my neighbor for God’s sake, I love him because I love God, for whose sake I love that neighbor; and I certainly would not love him if I did not love God, for whose sake I love him.

Thus, if I love rightly, I love what is good. For I do not love rightly unless I love what is good, and unless I love the good which I love for no other reason than goodness. Therefore, if I love rightly, I love in this way. How? A friend in God, and an enemy for God’s sake. What is it to love a friend in God? To love him because he has God—not in his riches, not in his strength, not in his beauty, but in his righteousness, holiness, and goodness. Although those things too are from God, they can be loved apart from God; and often, when they are loved, they turn away and corrupt the minds of those who love them, so that they do not love God. Therefore God is to be praised for them, because when they are given, they are given by him and are his gifts; but one’s neighbor is not to be loved in them, because they are not his virtue, nor do they make a person good, even if they abound; nor, if they are lacking, do they make him evil.

But goodness makes one good, righteousness one righteous, [Col. 0529D] and truth one true. And where these are present, God is present, because God is goodness, righteousness, and truth. Therefore a person is to be loved in goodness, righteousness, and truth. And when he is loved in these, he is loved in God, because God is goodness, righteousness, and truth. If, then, we love what is good and love rightly, we are good. For nothing makes us good except good love and love of the good.

But if we are good, we have no friends except good persons and no enemies except evil persons. For if we are good, we love nothing but good and hate nothing but evil. If, however, we have good friends and evil enemies, we ought to love our friends in their goodness—that is, because they are good. But since we cannot love enemies in goodness, because they are not good, we ought nevertheless [Col. 0530A] to love them in order that they may possess goodness and become good. In all these cases, only goodness is loved, whenever nothing is loved except for goodness’ sake.

In the same way, when God is loved, he is loved for his own sake, because he is not from another, nor is there anything other than himself which is loved in him. But when one’s neighbor is loved, he is not loved for his own sake, but for God’s sake: one—that is, the friend—because he has God; the other—that is, the enemy—in order that he may have God. In all these cases only God is loved, because there is nothing other than God which is loved in the former because it is there, and in the latter in order that it may be there.

Therefore, when God and neighbor are loved—if, when God is loved, why has Scripture said that both God and neighbor are to be loved? If in God you love God, and in your neighbor you love God, and love in your neighbor nothing other than what you love in God, why are there [Col. 0530B] two commandments of charity? For if God is loved in both, one thing is fulfilled in each, and there was no need to double the command concerning a single act. It would have been enough had it said: “Love the Lord your God” (Deut. VI; Matt. XXII). For everything is contained in this. Whoever truly loves God loves everywhere. If he is truly loved, he is loved wherever he is found: in oneself, in one’s neighbor, within and without, above and below, far and near.

If honey is sweet, the honeycomb too is sweet. If you love honey, you love also the honeycomb, the receptacle of honey. But honey is loved because it is itself sweet; whereas the honeycomb is loved because sweetness is in it. Honey is loved for its own sake; the honeycomb, however, for the honey’s sake. And if perhaps you see a honeycomb without honey, you see the receptacles where honey ought to have been, and you see [Col. 0530C] the cells empty; it does not please you because they are dry, and you desire the honey which you love to be there; and if it comes, you love more fully.

Thus love the Lord your God, because he himself is sweetness, goodness, and truth. Love your neighbor (Matt. XIX, XXII), however, because he is a receptacle of sweetness, goodness, and truth. If you find in him what he ought to possess—sweetness, goodness, and truth—love those things in him, and love him because of them. But if you find him empty of his goods, grieve because you see an empty receptacle; and desire his own goods to come to him and enter into him, so that he may become good, possessing his own goods, without which he cannot be good.

Love God, therefore, because he is goodness. Love your neighbor because from goodness he is good; or, if he is not good, in order that he may become good, since he can become good. Those who can no longer become good are not to be loved, nor are they neighbors; they are strangers, distant, and alien. “Do not give your honor to strangers,” he says, “nor your years to the cruel, lest strangers be filled with your strength and your labors be in an alien house” (Prov. V).

These, therefore, are strangers and aliens, exceedingly distant and far removed, to whom a return to goodness is no longer open: namely, demons and wicked persons condemned with demons. For this reason they are no longer to be loved by us: because they have irrecoverably fallen away from that good for whose sake everyone who is rightly loved is loved. Scripture nowhere tells us to love demons, nor those persons who are already condemned with demons. For they are not neighbors, but have become distant [Col. 0531A] and alien to us. We, however, ought to love neighbors, not aliens: that is, human beings, not demons; and those human beings who either have not departed from goodness or can return through freedom of choice. They are not wholly far away; though they have gone away, they can still return.

These are the neighbors whom we ought to love: in God, if they have not departed; or for God’s sake, if they can return. When we love them, we either love God in them because they are good, or love God in them and desire that they may become what they are not—good. For this reason there are two commandments of charity: love of God and love of neighbor. Through the charity of God, you love goodness itself; through charity toward your neighbor, you do not begrudge your neighbor the good which you love.

You could love something yet not love it for your neighbor; you could wish to possess something and nevertheless not wish your neighbor to possess it. But you could not do this in respect of God. For you could not love God unless you loved your neighbor, because God cannot be loved with envy and hatred. Yet because in other matters you could do this—wish something for yourself but not for your neighbor—it is distinguished, so that you may understand that you must do both, although you cannot do one without the other. Though they are together, love of God and love of neighbor are nevertheless two things; and therefore they ought not to have been confused in the commandment, although they cannot be separated in practice. There are, then, two commandments of charity: one by which we are commanded to love God, the other by which we are ordered to love our neighbor.

## CHAPTER VII. Why There Are Not Three Commandments of Charity

[Col. 0531C]

But you say: Why were not three commandments of charity given, so that a person might likewise love himself, just as he is commanded to love God and neighbor? Consider, however, that it would have been superfluous to command what a person was so inclined by himself to do that he either could not or would not cease doing it even if forbidden. Therefore a person did not need to be commanded to love himself; rather, he needed to fear or beware lest he love himself too much. For it was implanted in nature that he could not hate himself, according to which “no one has ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. V). The appetite implanted by nature for its benefit loves it inseparably, and always detests and flees what is contrary to it.

Nevertheless, since there seems to be some question [Col. 0531D] why a person is not commanded to love himself, as he is commanded to love God and his neighbor, we must consider whether perhaps in these two commands, which concern love of God and neighbor, there is also contained what a person ought either to be commanded or to do concerning love of himself. There are two things in a human being: soul and body, spirit and flesh. God made both, and man received both from God. Whatever is from God is wholly good, and whatever is good is wholly to be loved. Therefore a person ought to love everything good which he has received from God, because he would be ungrateful to goodness if he did not love what is good from it.

Therefore he does well when he loves his body, provided that he loves it rightly, that is, loves in it what ought to be loved. Likewise, when he loves his soul, he does well. And he does better when he loves his soul than when he loves his flesh, and so much the better as the soul is better than the flesh. Thus he does well in both cases when he loves each rightly. The body is to be loved for necessity; the soul is to be loved for goodness. The flesh is to be loved so that it may be sustained against corruption; the soul is to be loved so that it may be preserved against injustice. Yet if the necessity of one should arise and one of them must suffer, it is better that the flesh endure corruption than that the soul commit injustice.

Both, then, are to be loved, but that which is better more than the other. Yet although both were to be loved, it was not necessary that both be commanded to be loved. For since through natural affection love for his own flesh was sufficiently present in man, he did not need to be urged by a command to possess it, but rather to be restrained by warning lest he possess it excessively: “Make not provision for the flesh,” says the Apostle, “in its desires” (Rom. XIII). Before sin, a person loved his flesh through natural affection for necessity; but after sin, through the vice of concupiscence, he has now become accustomed to love it for superfluity. Thus in this respect he does not need a command, since he is voluntary of himself even if not admonished, but rather prohibition and warning, lest he rush headlong if not restrained. Therefore love of the flesh was not to be included in the command, since it was clear that it would be sufficiently present even without a command.

But concerning the love of the soul, [Col. 0532C] one may ask whether it has been established in the command; and, if it is commanded that a person love his own soul, whether this command is to be understood as another command besides the two commands above distinguished concerning love of God and neighbor, or as identical with them. What is it to love the soul but to love its good? Just as a person is said to love his flesh when he loves its good and seeks its advantage, and to hate it when he either deliberately does or willingly endures things adverse and harmful to it, so likewise he is said to love his soul when he loves what is good and wholesome for it, and what cooperates with its good and advances its salvation. But whoever loves what harms it does not love it. “He who loves iniquity,” it says, “hates his own soul” (Ps. X).

You love bruises, blows, and wounds, and say, “I love my flesh”—what kind of love is that? You do not cease to injure and afflict it, and yet say that you love it. If you love it, love its good. If you love it, do it good if you can; if you cannot, desire it. This is what it is to love: to do good and to will good. Whoever persecutes hates; whoever cherishes loves. If you wish to love me, love me thus; otherwise, if you persecute friends and cherish enemies, I would rather have you as an enemy than as an intimate.

We call it love when good is loved, advantage desired, and well-being sought. Whoever does this loves. But if this is loving, then surely that person loves his soul who loves its good, and loves what is good for it. What else is the good of the rational soul [Col. 0533A] but God? If, therefore, God is the true good of the soul, then surely the person who loves God loves his own soul, because he loves the good of his soul.

For what did you think was said to you when you were told to love God? Perhaps you imagined that you were told to love your God as you love your neighbor, kinsman, friend, or fellow human being. For how do you love him except by wishing good to him, desiring it and doing it if you can—and doing as much as you can if you love as much as you can? For you do as much as you love. If you can do as much as you love, you do as much as you love. If you can do less, nevertheless you do as much as you can. But if you can do more and love less, you do as much as you love.

What then? Do you suppose that you are commanded to love your God so as to do or desire good for him, rather than to desire him as your good? You do not love him for his good, but love him for your good; and you love him as your good. Nor do you love him for your good merely so that your good may come from him, rather than that he himself may be your good. Therefore you love him for your good, so that he whom you love may himself be your good.

For if you wish to love him for his good, what good can you give him which you have and he does not, when everything you have is from him? Have you forgotten to say to him: “You are my God, for you have no need of my goods” (Ps. XV)? What, then, will you give him who possesses everything that you possess, and possesses more than you possess? You are poor; he is rich. In this world the poor give to the rich, and those who have more can receive from those who have less what they do not have; for those who are richer have more, yet, because they do not possess everything, can receive what they lack. Your God possesses other riches. What you possess less fully, he possesses more fully; and whatever you possess in some measure, he possesses wholly. How, then, do you love him? What will you give him?

But you say: “Although I cannot give, still I can desire. I desire that good may come to him. My capacity in relation to him is indeed small and slight, but my affection and love toward him are rich. What I cannot do, I can will. I would do it if I could; but because I cannot, I do what I can.” What do you do? “I love my God.” How do you love? “I desire,” you say, “good for him.” What good can you desire for him when you cannot find good outside him? God is the highest good; in him is every good, and he is every good. What do you desire for one who has everything, who possesses everything? Do you wish good to Goodness, rightness to Justice, understanding to Wisdom, increase to Perfection? You are moved by a superfluous piety. Have pity rather on yourself. He has enough. Do you wish to make him who is best better?

Therefore, when you love God, you love for yourself: what you love is your good, and you love for your good because he whom you love is your good. When you love righteousness, for whom do you love it—for it, or for yourself? When you love wisdom, truth, and goodness, for whom do you love them—for them, or for yourself? When you love light itself, pleasant and delightful to the eyes, for whom do you love it—for it, or for yourself? So it is with your God. When you love him, understand [Col. 0534A] that he himself is your good.

What is loving except desiring, wishing to have, possess, and enjoy? If it is not possessed, it is wishing to have it; if it is possessed, it is wishing to retain it. Yet true good can never be loved unless it is possessed, nor possessed unless it is loved. Those goods which are outside are often loved when they are not possessed, and, when possessed, are sometimes despised. The good which God is is not such. If he is loved, he is possessed; if he is loved, he is tasted: he is present to love. If you can love, you can possess. If you give this, you receive this. Nothing else is sought in exchange for him, nor is one thing given for another.

## CHAPTER VIII. That One Who Loves God for His Own Sake Loves Purely and Freely

But perhaps you will be a hireling if you love God and serve him in order to receive a reward from him. Some foolish people say this—so foolish that they do not understand themselves. “We love God and serve him,” they say, “but we do not seek a reward, lest we be hirelings; we do not even seek him himself. He will give, if he wishes, but we do not seek. We shake our hands free from every gift so completely that we do not even seek him whom we love. For we love with pure, free, and filial love; we seek nothing. Let him consider whether he wishes to give anything; we seek nothing. We love him, but seek nothing—not even him whom we love.”

Listen, wise people. “We love him,” they say, “but do not seek him.” This is to say: “We love him, but do not care about him.” I, a human being, would not wish to be loved by you in this way. If you loved me in such a way that you did not care about me, I would not care about your love. Consider whether it is fitting to offer God what a human being would rightly reject.

“How,” they say, “are we not hirelings if we love God in order to receive a reward from him? This is not loving freely, nor is this love filial; it is the love of hirelings and slaves, who seek payment for their service.” Those who say this do not understand the power of love. For what is loving except wishing to possess him himself? To seek not something else from him, but himself—that is loving freely. If you sought something else from him, you would not love freely. But now you seek nothing other than that which you love, and yet you seek and desire something in him himself whom you love. Otherwise you would not love if you did not desire.

But it is one thing to love something in exchange for him, another to love something in him. If you love something in exchange for him, you are a hireling; if you love in him and love him himself, you are a son. Even if you were to think that eternal life is something else, distinct from the good which God is, and served only in order to obtain it in exchange for him, your service would not be pure, nor your love free. Those sons of Zebedee who asked to sit at his right and left in his kingdom conceived something else, foreign and different from this good; and for the sake of obtaining it they adhered to him for a time, until, rebuked and changed, they came to know the truth and corrected their intention. For they thought that God was to be served for something which he himself was not, because they did not understand that he himself is the good which alone is to be loved for its own sake, and that whatever is to be loved besides him is to be loved for his sake. This is loved more happily in proportion as it is loved more ardently.

He who loves this loves himself, because he loves his own good; and he loves truly, because he loves the true good. Therefore Scripture did not tell you to love yourself, lest perhaps you err and think you ought to indulge yourself and pursue outward conveniences and pleasures agreeable to your flesh, and imagine that you ought to love yourself in that way; lest you take occasion from Scripture to cherish your flesh alone and neglect your soul. For this reason it did not tell you to love yourself, lest you understand it in the sphere in which you would love more and neglect it in the sphere in which you would perish more dangerously.

Therefore it did not tell you to love yourself, yet neither was it altogether silent when it told you to love your God. For when you love your God, you love your good—the better good and the good of what is better. And when you love your good, you love yourself, since you love its good and love what is good for it.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Measure of Loving God

How greatly we ought to love our good, which is God, Scripture makes known to us when it says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your mind, and with all your soul” (Matt. XXII). It is as though it said: “I do not command you to love only so much, but to love your God at least so much: love as much as you can.” Your capacity will be your measure. The more you love, the more you possess; and the more you possess, the happier you are.

Stretch out and enlarge yourself as much as you can, so that all that is in you may be filled, even though not all that is in him may be contained. Do not fear, as though he must fail you if you become too capable. However much you are able, you will never be able as much as he is. If you could be as much, you would be as great. But now you can grow in him; you cannot equal him. Grow, therefore, and advance. The greater you are in the good, the better you are. If you were highest, you would be best. But because you cannot be highest, you can be in the Highest. This is great for you, and through it you are great, if you are in the Highest; and certainly you are greater in proportion as you are higher.

You ascend when you love. In charity you go upward, because charity leads upward, as the Apostle says: “I show you a still more excellent way” (I Cor. XI). Ascend, then, while you can. Now is the time for growing and being made perfect. Afterwards, when all things are consummated, you will stand in that to which you have come; and this will be your highest point in him, beyond which you will proceed no further. But his highest point will not be one at which you stop as though you could find no further place in which to grow. Therefore ascend while you can, as much as you can: you can never do too much where you can never attain the whole.

Love your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind, so that all of you may be filled from him, even though all of him cannot be contained by all that is yours. He fills all in you and abounds in himself. If the vessel does not fail, the oil is sufficient. Your heart is the vessel; his love is the oil. As long as you have a vessel, he does not cease pouring in oil; and afterwards, when you no longer have a larger vessel, he still has more oil. Therefore do not spare him: receive as much as you can; love as much as you are able, because he does not fail.

Love with all your heart, with all your soul, [Col. 0536A] and with all your mind—that is, with all your understanding, all your affection, and all your memory. Love as much as you understand, as much as you perceive, as much as you are able. Let all be filled with knowledge, all be moved by love, all be held in memory. In proportion as you are enlightened, be so affected, so that whatever comes into knowledge and memory concerning him may all be sweet. If all is rightly approved, why should all not be loved? Therefore let all that he deigns to make known to us be loved by us. Let us love all that we can comprehend, and as much as we can.

## CHAPTER X. On the Measure of Loving One’s Neighbor
Scripture says to us concerning love of neighbor: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22; Lev. 19). We certainly fulfill this command [Col. 0536B] when we genuinely wish our neighbor the same good that we wish for ourselves. In those respects in which we rightly love ourselves, we ought, without pretense, to love our neighbor both with regard to bodily need and the salvation of the soul, and to help him as far as we reasonably can.

But some ask whether the phrase “as yourself” is to be understood merely according to likeness, or also according to equality. For if we are commanded to love our neighbors only as much as ourselves, a difficulty seems to arise which we cannot easily resolve. Behold, there are two persons, one of whom must perish. One is given the choice to choose whichever he wishes of the two, since one of them cannot possibly be spared. If he chooses his own salvation more, he loves his neighbor less. If he chooses his neighbor’s salvation more, he loves God less than his neighbor, since for the neighbor’s sake he wishes to be separated from God.

But perhaps someone will say that equal love makes no choice possible: one wills both equally and refuses both equally, and cannot prefer one to the other in a choice when they are altogether equal in love. Thus someone may perhaps strive to avoid this objection. But what shall we say? If I ought to love one person only as much as myself, ought I not to love two, three, or four persons more than myself? Such are the questions men pursue, and they trouble themselves with their own thoughts. For they say: “That which is better ought to be loved more. Let us suppose three persons: one on this side, two on that. I say that either this one [Col. 0536D] or those two must perish. Tell me, then, what do you choose, you who love your neighbor as yourself? It is better that one should perish than two, because it is better that two should be saved than one. Therefore,” you say, “I choose rather that one perish and two be saved.” Therefore you wish those two to be saved more than this one; do you not then love more what you choose in preference? “Certainly,” you say, “I love them more.” See, then, what follows.

Above you confessed that you love—or, if you do not love, that you ought to love—your neighbor as much as yourself. Therefore, if you love this one as much as yourself, and again love those two more than this one, surely you love those two more than yourself. And if you love them more [Col. 0537A] than yourself, it seems that you love them more than God, since for their sake you wish to be separated from God, so that you may not possess God, nor love God, and may perish, in order that they may be saved.

And perhaps someone will think that Moses had such love: opposing the angry God for the salvation of his neighbors, he said, “If you do not forgive them this sin, blot me out of the book which you have written” (Exod. 32). And the Apostle wishes himself to be anathema, separated from Christ, for his brethren (Rom. 9), so that they may be saved in Christ. Perhaps someone will also believe that this belongs to the love of God: that we should love him so much that we wish his glory to be enlarged in others rather than diminished in ourselves. Accordingly, for the salvation of many, we ought to wish destruction upon ourselves, so that many may rather be saved while we perish, [Col. 0537B] than many perish while we are saved.

But consider that the order of love is not such that a person loves his neighbor before himself, although he is commanded to derive and shape the love of neighbor from his own love when it is said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” For if he loves his neighbor as himself, how does he love his neighbor when he does not love himself? If he loves his neighbor as himself, surely he wishes and desires for him what he wishes for himself. But if he desires for his neighbor what he desires for himself, how can he desire his neighbor’s salvation when he wishes his own destruction?

Therefore one must first love oneself rightly, so that afterward one may rightly love one’s neighbor according to oneself. But if one wishes to destroy oneself in order to save one’s neighbor, love is not ordered, because a person can give no exchange [Col. 0537C] for his soul. For this is what God first requires of you: that you give him your soul, and then add everything else. If you wish to give something for another, it is not accepted unless you give this also. First this; everything else together with this.

Therefore I do not say merely two, three, or four people: one must not love even the whole world against one’s own soul. For if you love anything more than your soul, you will certainly be shown to love that thing more than God; for you love your soul only in that you love its good, which is God. Therefore first love your soul by loving the good of your soul. Then love your neighbor also as yourself, by loving for him the good that you love for yourself. For this is to love him: to love good for him.

For you could love his good even if you did not love him. You could love it for yourself or for any other person, and not for him; and thus you would not love him, although you loved the good, because you did not love it for him. You could love his horse, clothing, house, field, money, strength, beauty, or wisdom, without loving him, because you loved these for yourself rather than for him. Thus you could love his good for yourself and nevertheless not love him, because you loved it for yourself, not for him. Yet you could not love true good for yourself unless you loved it and desired it for your neighbor.

Scripture therefore distinguished this love from the love that concerns and is directed toward others. It first commands a person to love God, intending certainly that in this very act he should love himself; for to love oneself [Col. 0538A] is nothing other than to love one’s own good, and to love one’s own good is nothing other than to love it for oneself—that is, to will and desire it. For since everyone who loves his own good loves it for himself, and likewise everyone who loves God loves his own good, it plainly follows that no one loves God who does not love him for himself. And everyone who loves loves for himself, because he desires and wishes to possess the one whom he loves.

Again, not everyone who loves another’s good loves the person whose good he loves, because he does not love the good for that person. Scripture distinguished for the human mind, according to things which are sometimes found divided among human beings, what in divine matters is inseparable. It tells a person that, after loving God, he should also love his neighbor—not because he could do the former without the latter, but lest [Col. 0538B] he suppose that he could.

Therefore it first said that he should love God; and in this very command it said that he should love God for himself, because everyone who loves his own good loves it for himself. But because not everyone who loves another’s good loves it for the person whose good it is, Scripture immediately added love of neighbor after love of God, so that a person, loving his neighbor, might desire for his neighbor what he desires for himself by loving God.

Therefore let no one think that, because it is said, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” one ought to love any single person as much as oneself, and two, three, or four people more than oneself. For if one loves oneself as much as one loves one’s own good, and loves one’s own good as much as one loves God, it would follow that one loved one’s neighbor as much as God if one loved him as much as [Col. 0538C] oneself. Therefore one is not told to love one’s neighbor merely as much as oneself, but to love him in that wherein one loves oneself, and to desire for him what one desires for oneself.

For this is to love as oneself: to wish and desire for another what one wishes and desires for oneself—good, first indeed for oneself and then for the other. One does not love another as oneself unless one first loves oneself.

With respect to bodily goods, however, which are sometimes restricted to such an extent that what is possessed by one person cannot pass to another’s use unless it wholly departs from the possessor: if a person is not, through gratuitous charity and for the sake of a fuller recompense or love of spiritual good, raised above what is due, he is not obliged to bestow upon his neighbor anything that is due to himself by necessity. For he owes his neighbor nothing except [Col. 0538D] after, and according to, what he owes himself. Therefore, when he cannot provide for both, let him first do what must be done first. For regarding what remains, if the effect is lacking, the disposition suffices.

And perhaps in order to show this disposition Moses asked to be blotted out of the written book, and Paul desired to be made anathema from Christ for his brethren—not because they wished to lose God for a human being’s sake, but because, if it were possible, they wished to possess God without losing the neighbor whom they loved. For affection was speaking, and, as though secure in love, in the sweetness of love it threatened the beloved and lover with separation—not because it loved that separation, but because it desired the other’s union.

Moreover, in loving his neighbor’s good and loving good for his neighbor, one loves one’s own good and loves it for oneself, [Col. 0539A] because the good of one’s neighbor is good to oneself, if one loves it and desires it for him, insofar as it is good for him. For true good is not possessed with envy, and is possessed more happily with charity.

But you say: “What is a greater good ought to be loved more; but it is a greater good for two to be saved than one. Therefore, if a choice were offered as to what I prefer, I ought to choose that many be saved rather than I alone.” Here you fail to notice that it is a greater good for me that I alone be saved and many perish than that I alone perish and many be saved. What is a greater good for me ought to be loved more by me, because I am first endowed to love my own good—above all, that which is truly good—and after and according to it, to love my neighbor’s good. I owe something to him after and according to [Col. 0539B] myself; before myself or against myself I owe him nothing. Otherwise, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” would not stand if I loved him while hating myself.

Accordingly, in this sense there are only two commandments of charity. The first concerns love of God, in which a person truly loves himself; the second concerns love of neighbor, in which he loves his neighbor as himself.

## CHAPTER XI. Whether charity, once possessed, can be lost

Some wish to say so much about charity that they begin to praise charity against truth; yet charity is not praised where truth is wronged. They say that charity has such and so great a power that, although all the other virtues may in some manner be present through nature’s inclination toward good, they nevertheless cannot possess before God the merit of eternal recompense without charity. For what is done without charity is not done for God; and what is not done for God, God has no recompense to grant, even if what is done is in some respect good. It is a good of nature, not of grace: in nature, not above nature. Therefore what is good from nature alone has, in nature alone, both its merit and its reward.

Thus what is done in nature alone without charity does not attain the reward that is in God above nature. It is clear, then, that in doing good no one merits the highest good except the person who performs what he does well for the sake of the highest good. Do you wish to merit God? Do what you do for God’s sake.

This, therefore, they say concerning charity: that it is the virtue of all virtues, and that the virtues please God on account of it; for without it, although they might be good in some respect, they could not be good for attaining the highest good. We gladly accept all this which has been said concerning charity as the good beginning of a true judgment. But there follows something else which indeed joins itself to truth, though it is false itself, so that it may enter together with truth and be received in truth’s place.

But we distinguish light from darkness, and we ridicule the darkness that thrusts itself into the light and imagines that it stands with the light. For if charity is light, error and folly are darkness. Where charity is, there is brightness; and no one gropes about in it.
