For whoever is in charity either walks, sees, or stands, and does not presume [Col. 0540A] beyond what he sees. So long as he remains in the light, whether standing or walking, he cannot err, because he sees where he is. But whoever casts himself down through presumption where he cannot see loses brightness, because he does not have charity; and wherever he goes farther, all is error.

Thus these people lie concerning charity because they do not know charity; for they ought not to presume concerning what they could not see. They say that charity, once possessed, can never afterward be lost. I therefore ask them whether they themselves have never lost charity; and would that they had not lost charity because they had retained it once possessed. But I fear that they have rather not lost it because they never possessed it. If they never possessed or tasted it, how do they dare assert what they do not know?

But if they ever had charity, they still possess the charity which they had, because according to their view they could not lose it once possessed. If they have charity, they walk according to charity and do not commit iniquity. But if they commit iniquity, they do not have charity. For if one who loves the world and the things that are in the world does not love God, how much more does one who loves iniquity not love God? “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10). Whoever hates his own soul does not love himself, or, if he loves himself, loves himself badly, because he loves himself only according to the flesh. Whoever does not love himself does not love his neighbor as himself. And whoever does not love the neighbor [Col. 0540C] whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? (1 John 4).

Let those, then, who sometimes commit iniquity say how they have charity. Or perhaps they will say that it is not they who commit iniquity, but sin that dwells in them. For there have been some foolish people, not understanding what the human person is, who thought that certain sins, even those committed deliberately, were such that a person could truly say of them: “It is no longer I who do it, but sin which dwells in me.” They did not observe that a person does not himself perform the fact that he feels concupiscence, because this arises from the necessity of corruptible life; but that he himself alone performs his consent to concupiscence, because this arises from his will.

Therefore, if through their own will they commit iniquity, surely they do not have charity. And what will they say? Let them consult their conscience and moderate their knowledge. Let conscience be humbled, lest knowledge puff itself up. Therefore let them not presume upon righteousness, lest perhaps through that presumption of false righteousness they lose the knowledge of truth.

They say that one who once has charity cannot thereafter lose it. This is to say that one who is good cannot become bad. Why, then, should we not likewise say that one who is bad cannot become good, if we say that one who is now good cannot become bad? Whoever has charity is good, and whoever does not have charity is not good. Therefore, if the good person who has it cannot lose it, neither can the bad person who does not have it acquire it. [Col. 0541A] If this were true, neither would one standing need fear, nor one fallen need hope.

We are in time, where all things are subject to change; and do you make eternity for me out of time? Scripture says that a human being never remains in the same state (Job 14). And do you contend—I do not know from where—that one who stands never falls? Why then was it said: “Let him who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10)? Would that it were true—provided it were just—that in this life everyone who is good could not become bad. But this present life ought not to have that condition, in which evil people are expected to become good, and good people are tested to see whether they turn aside to iniquity.

Outside this life there are certain evil persons who cannot become good, and certain good persons who likewise cannot become evil: the former are bound by wickedness, the latter strengthened by grace. Yet even in these cases, nature—which is mutable of itself—does not produce necessity. For in some, as has been said, it is not nature but wickedness that restricts nature’s mutability toward worse things; in others, it is not nature but grace that confirms the same mutability of nature toward better things. Thus those who are evil there cannot become good; likewise those who are good cannot become evil. For this belongs to eternity and immutability: there no transition from one state to another can occur.

But here, so long as life is mutable, both a good person can become bad and a bad person can become good. And even if someone is found so good that he is always good, that very person who is good can nevertheless become bad, so long as the person who is bad can become good. For both truly live under time, and their condition under time is one and the same.

But you say: “What, then, is the meaning of the authority which says, ‘Charity never fails’?” (1 Cor. 13). Hear this: perhaps you understood it to mean that, once it had been possessed, it could no longer be lost. Scripture did not intend to say this, but something else, which you did not understand correctly because you did not inspect Scripture carefully. What, then? What does that Scripture say? “Do not these three remain: faith, hope, and charity?” (ibid.). What does “now” mean? It means in this life, so long as what is not seen is believed, what is awaited is hoped for, and what is loved is desired.

But when this life has come to an end and all things have been made manifest, what will remain hidden to be believed [Col. 0541D] when there will be nothing that is not plainly seen? What could then be hoped for as future, when all things will be present and there will be nothing future? It is said that, if you see, there is no faith (Rom. 8); and again, “What a man sees, why does he hope for?” (ibid.). Therefore there you will not believe. I do not say that you will be unbelieving, but that you will not believe because you will know. Likewise I say that there you will not hope; yet I do not say that you will despair. I say that you will not hope because, possessing all that you hoped for, you will await nothing future.

Do I likewise say that there you will not love? Therefore, when you had not yet possessed, you loved; and when you possess, you will not love? Far be it! Rather, then you will love much more, when you see the one whom you love and possess the one whom you see. For this love is not such that one loves when the beloved is absent and is disgusted when he is present. [Col. 0542A] Therefore then too you will love, and you will love much more; and charity will remain when faith and hope are no more.

This, then, is the meaning of the statement, “Charity never fails”: it is possessed here and retained there. “Whether prophecies shall be done away, whether tongues shall cease, whether knowledge shall be destroyed.” For all these belong only to this life; even our present knowledge will not then be. Not because there will then be no knowledge, but because there will be another kind. Thus all these things fail together with this life, because they do not remain afterward, when the one believed will be seen and the one hoped for will be possessed.

But charity never fails, insofar as it is here and will be there; and love will never end, just as vision will never end. As we shall never be separated from contemplation, so we shall never be emptied of love; but we shall always see and always love. Thus charity never fails because it always remains. It did not say that it fails in no persons, but that it never fails: for although it does not remain in everyone, it always remains in those in whom it remains.

For if it does not always remain because it does not remain in everyone, then neither faith nor hope remains here, because it does not remain in everyone. Many have departed from faith and hope in God, and have abandoned the very faith and hope which they had begun to possess; faith and hope have failed in them even in this life. Yet this does not make the saying less true: “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity.” Therefore, if faith and hope, which sometimes fail in some persons here, nevertheless remain here because they do not utterly fail—[Col. 0542C] since they remain in others—then similarly charity, which sometimes fails here in some persons, nevertheless always remains. Although it fails in someone, it never utterly fails, because it always remains in others. For it does not perish merely because it perishes in me and for me. Nor is it destroyed merely because it is emptied from me and destroyed in me, since what does not remain for me remains for another.

But you say again: “If those who will become evil and perish can at some time have charity, how is charity called a proper fountain from which a stranger does not partake? For those who perish are strangers and do not belong to us or to what is ours. If, then, they are strangers, how can they partake of that which is properly ours?”

It is remarkable. For if those who were formerly strangers became neighbors by drawing near, why cannot those who are neighbors likewise become strangers by withdrawing? If those who are far off can draw near, those who are near can also withdraw. Those who draw near are reconciled; those who withdraw are alienated. If those who are reconciled are neighbors, then those who are alienated are strangers. Yet while they were neighbors they were not strangers, just as those who were strangers before they were reconciled were not neighbors.

Those who were neighbors, while they were neighbors, partook of the proper fountain. Likewise, those who were strangers, while they were strangers, did not partake of the proper fountain. But when those who [Col. 0543A] were strangers began to be neighbors, they began to partake of the proper fountain; and likewise, when those who were neighbors began to be alienated, they ceased to partake of the proper fountain. Yet the proper fountain always remains, from which a stranger does not partake. For a stranger cannot partake; and yet one who is a stranger can become a neighbor.

An evil person cannot have charity, but one who is evil can become good. When he begins to be good, he begins to have charity; and when he ceases to be good, he ceases to have charity. No one can ever have charity except one who is good, because no one can have charity and at the same time be evil.

You say again: “If charity once possessed is sometimes lost, what is the meaning of Scripture’s saying, ‘He who is a friend always loves’?” (Prov. 17). For if one who loves is a friend, and one who is a friend always loves, surely one who loves always loves; and one who always loves never loses charity. Therefore, if Scripture is true and one who loves always loves, one who once has charity never loses it.

This is how it appears to you. Many such arguments can be turned in any direction; but it is not a great thing to say something, but to understand whether what one says ought to be said in that way. “He who is a friend always loves.” This is true: a friend always loves and an enemy always hates; yet one who is a friend can become an enemy and hate, and one who is an enemy can become a friend and love. So long as he is a friend, he loves; and so long as he is an enemy, he hates.

But there are some who are not true friends, who pretend to love in prosperity and are tested in adversity as to what they are. It is because of such people that it was said that a true friend always loves—that is, not only in prosperity but also in adversity: that is, always. For one who wavers with circumstances and is moved in either direction by fortune is not a true friend, even when he appears to be a friend.

The person who always loves is not like that: he loves the person, not the money; the friend, not gain. Whoever loves only for money’s sake loves while money abounds; when money fails, love fails, and the person who seemed a friend is no longer a friend. Indeed, it is then plainly proved that he who was previously not a friend, though thought to be one, neither is nor was a friend.

Therefore it is rightly said to the one who is a friend: “He always loves.” If you were a friend in prosperity, love in adversity. For what you loved in prosperity you show in adversity. If you loved your friend, he is still himself: love him. Why should love cease when what is loved has not been taken away? But if you loved fortune, you no longer have what to love, because fortune has departed and the person remains alone. This is the meaning of the saying, “He who is a friend always loves.”

You persist, as though about to bring forward something greater to prove that charity once possessed does not depart. You point to Christ’s seamless garment, which could not be torn even when Christ could suffer. Christ’s body was wounded, yet Christ’s garment [Col. 0544A] was not torn. What you bring forward is great, if you understand it rightly.

For what is Christ’s garment but Christ’s Church? And what is the garment’s integrity but the Church’s unity? “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132). What unity? “Remain in my love” (John 15). Therefore charity is the unity of the Church. And Scripture says: “Those who are in the unity of the Church cannot perish.” This is what you wished to say: “Those who are in charity cannot perish.” Whether you call it charity or unity, it is the same, because unity is charity and charity is unity.

Therefore those who are in the unity of the Church are always in charity; and those who are in charity cannot perish at all. The truth is clear. No believer contradicts it. No one can perish in charity. He cannot perish there; but he can depart from there and perish. Whoever remains there does not fear destruction. Let him beware lest he go out. There is no destruction for those within, just as there is no salvation for those outside. Whoever begins to go out begins to perish. But when one who is outside returns to charity, he is restored to salvation.

What more do you seek? Perhaps you will wish to interpret another unity of the Church, of which you can truly say that no one will perish in it because no one will go out from it. There is indeed the unity of predestination, of which it is said: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2). And it is true that all who are in this unity will be saved, because none of those foreseen for life will perish.

For as Scripture says: “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8). These, then, are those who love God, for whom all things work together for good, who are called saints according to purpose (ibid.). For those who are not called according to purpose, and who are not predestined to life, even if they love God for a time, do not persevere in God’s love to the end. They perish because, after losing charity and falling into iniquity, they do not rise again to charity.

But after the predestined begin to love God, they either love perseveringly, so as not to fall from love, or, if they fall from love, rise again to it [Col. 0544D] so that they may not perish. What do you think? Do you believe that it is as I say?

Perhaps the Apostle who says this will not suffice for you, because you suppose that what he says ought not to be understood in such a way that he intended to include among those for whom all things work together for good not all who love God, but only those who are called saints according to purpose. The truth is plain, unless you wish shamelessly to deny it.

But perhaps you will say that the Apostle’s statement ought not to be understood thus: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called saints according to purpose.” You say, then, that it should not be understood as though, by adding “for those who are called saints according to purpose,” he intended to define for which persons who love God all things work together for good; rather, you will think that all those same persons who love God are called saints according to purpose.

Thus perhaps you will think that the Apostle’s words ought to be understood, and will not believe me if I say that this shows you that not all who at some time love God are predestined, because they do not remain in what they love.

These are Augustine’s words: “If you do not believe me, believe him, in order that you may believe me. Or rather, believe not me but truth. Hear, then, what the Apostle says. After he had said, ‘We know that all things work together for good for those who love God,’ knowing that some love God and do not remain in that good until the end, he immediately added, ‘for those who are called saints according to purpose.’ For these remain in what they love, namely God, [Col. 0545B] until the end. And those who depart from it for a time return, and bring to the end what they began to be in good.”

See: you have plainly that certain persons, possessing charity for a time, fall and perish because they do not persevere in it to the end; and again, that certain persons who fall from it for a time are preserved and saved because they rise again. Others, because they never fail from it, persevere to the end and carry through their devotion in the fervor of charity once received. What clearer thing do you seek? If you do not see this, what do you see?

But you say: “How could those who were not going to persevere in charity ever have true charity?” Remarkable! Then faith was not faith if it at some time ceased to be faith. Why do you not likewise say that one was never white who at some time ceased to be white? Do you not understand that one is said at some time to have been a thing precisely because one is remembered to have ceased at some time to be that thing? For what someone never was, he never ceased to be.

Accordingly, it is certain that one who at some time ceased to love loved before he ceased to love. But, you say, love was not true if it existed only for a time. Then neither was hatred true if it existed for a time; nor was one truly white who was white only for a time. Who would say this? Therefore love was true, and truly existed while it existed, even if in some respect it was not true in that it ceased, when it truly no longer existed.

Therefore, if you say that the love was not true which at some time ceased to be love, understand it thus: when it ceased to be love, it was not true love, because in the very fact that it wavered and failed so as not to be love, it began to be, and became such that what it had formerly been was no longer true love.

## CHAPTER XII. Whether every love of God should be called charity

Perhaps you will say that some people make this claim: those who love God but will not persevere have love of God indeed, but do not have charity, because they think that not every love of God should be called charity, but only that which perseveres to the end. But if anyone wishes to say this, I do not find by what reasoning or authority he can prove it.

Unless perhaps he thinks that “love” (*dilectio*) and “charity” (*charitas*) mean different things because he thinks one is a Latin and the other a Greek word. Holy Scripture tells us that love is charity, and that love of God is always good. It does not tell us that this man loves and does well, whereas that man loves and does badly.

Augustine says that the Apostle knew that some love God and do not remain in that good to the end; and he calls love of God good even in those who will not remain in it. Yet these people have discovered I know not how many kinds of charity, like spice-sellers at a fair of foolish declamations. They say that the statement “charity once possessed is not lost” is not to be understood of every charity, but only of perfect charity.

And if I ask them [Col. 0546B] what that perfect charity is, they answer me only: “That which is not lost.” For they do not dare to speak of it; rather, they speak of the perfection of charity which will be possessed in the future, lest they be convicted of speaking needlessly of that which does not belong to this life. Therefore they find no charity here that they can call perfect except that which is not lost. Again, when they wish to identify the charity that is not lost, they find nothing to say except that it is perfect charity. Thus they make a circle, entangling themselves because they have no way out.

Finally they are enveloped in such a darkness of error that, while stubbornly maintaining that charity once possessed cannot be lost, they begin to assert that some persons retain it even while deliberately committing not only lesser sins but also grave and damnable crimes. They say that David, adulterer and murderer, possessed the charity of God when, serving lust, he gave free rein to shamefulness in violating his neighbor’s wife; and when, in order to conceal that same shamefulness, he destroyed by cruel treachery the innocent and righteous man whose bed he had foully violated.

Let them tell me where charity then was—charity which “does not act shamefully”—when an innocent man is oppressed; charity which “does not seek its own,” when another’s possessions are seized. Let them show me here, if they can, the love which is the fulfillment of the law, where both the commandments of the law are violated and the law of nature is corrupted. The law says: “You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Rom. 13; Exod. 20; Deut. 5). If charity is here, the fulfillment of the law is here. If the fulfillment [Col. 0546D] of the law is here, how can transgression be present?

If they say that one acting in such a way possessed charity, why do they not also say that in acting thus he committed no sin, because Scripture says: “He who is born of God does not sin” (1 John 5), and because elsewhere it is said: “Have charity, and do whatever you wish”? For if it is true that those who do such things can retain charity, then persons who have charity are permitted to do whatever they please; and it is fully proved that whatever they do is not sin. Let them go, then, with their charity and do whatever they wish, because they have great defenders: some defending their claim that they do not lose charity, and others granting them permission to do whatever they wish with charity.

[Col. 0547A] But they say: “If David lost charity by sinning, how then is it true what is written of him, that the Spirit of the Lord did not depart from David from that day onward?” (1 Sam. 16). For if charity departed, how did the Spirit of the Lord remain? As though the Spirit of the Lord could not remain in many other respects, even if He had departed with respect to the gift of charity. Does He not remain also in those—or with those—whom, when falling, He preserves lest they perish, though He does not preserve them while standing so that they do not fall? “Though the righteous man falls, he shall not be dashed down, because the Lord upholds his hand” (Ps. 36 [37]). What then? If the Lord was present to him while he stood, why did he fall? And if He was not present to him when he fell, why was he not dashed down? For if he were held, he would not have fallen. Likewise, if the hand were not placed beneath him, he would be dashed down.

[Col. 0547B] Therefore he was not dashed down because he fell upon the hand. If the hand had fallen upon him, he would have been dashed down: “Whoever falls upon this stone,” he says, “shall be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it shall crush him” (Matt. 21). Therefore the Lord did not lay His hand upon the man lying down, in order to press him down; but put it beneath him, in order to raise him. He put it beneath him in order to restore him by helping, not laid it upon him in order to condemn him by judgment. Thus the Spirit of the Lord did not depart from David, because He was with him in order to bring him back when he had gone astray, and to justify him when repentant; and perhaps He was with him, but was not in him. He was with him for preservation, but was not in him for righteousness. For David was not then righteous when he lay prostrate in so grievous a sin, nor did that which is written apply to him then: “The righteous man falls seven times in a day, and yet does not lose the name of righteous” (Prov. 24).

[Col. 0547C] Therefore, although the Spirit of God was then with David, so that he should not perish by sinning, He was by no means with him in such a way that David did not sin damnably. Similar is the claim which they try to maintain regarding Peter: that he had not then lost the charity of God, when, being questioned, he denied that he knew Christ. For they do not attend to what is written: “No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Jesus be accursed’; and no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12). But if perhaps they wish to say that Peter indeed had the Spirit of God inwardly in his heart at that time, but did not say in the Spirit of God what he spoke outwardly, let them hear what is written: “Out of the abundance

[Col. 0547D] of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. 1 [probably 12]; Luke 6). Therefore that spirit spoke outwardly in the mouth which ruled inwardly in the heart. He who governed the heart moved the tongue. But perhaps they will say: “The Spirit of God indeed departed, but charity remained.” Consider whether truth can bear this assertion. The Apostle says: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). We do not possess charity except insofar as we possess the Holy Spirit; and do you say that charity remains when the Holy Spirit has departed and is absent? And they say: “What then? Did no spark of piety, no affection of love, remain in David and Peter, when the one, overcome by the affliction of fleshly desire, and the other, broken by fear of impending death, each somehow sinned unwillingly?”

[Col. 0548A] On the contrary, each sinned voluntarily; for if they had wished otherwise, neither would have sinned. But because they loved themselves more than God, they fulfilled their own will rather than God’s. The flesh urged one thing, and God commanded another; and they chose to obey the flesh rather than the Creator. Had they wished, they would have despised the will of the flesh and set the will of the Creator before it. But they did not yet imitate the good Master saying, “Father, not my will, but yours be done” (Luke 22). It may be that they wished the very will of the flesh, whose violence they felt, either not to exist or not to be so violent. Yet, in consenting to it as it tempted and wearied them, they acted only willingly, since they preferred to offend the Creator rather than endure that very affliction and weariness.

[Col. 0548B] Had they not willed it, they would not have done it at all. Therefore, in this they willingly did what the flesh willed; they did not will what the Creator willed. For had they willed that, they would not voluntarily have consented to do this. For when one of two things which cannot happen together is chosen by the will, the other is shown beyond doubt not to be in the will. Therefore, in that will by which they chose to consent to the flesh against God, they had no charity of God whatsoever. Yet, because they suffered great violence in temptation itself, they may have some excuse in their sin.

But concerning the affection of piety which persons sinning in this manner sometimes seem to have, when at once they consent to sin and nevertheless do not cease somehow to be affected by a certain grief over the sin which they do not abandon,

[Col. 0548C] one must take every care that they not be judged worthy of the name of charity or love of God. For if in those who turn from iniquity to righteousness there remain certain affections and attachments to former evils, which are not imputed as iniquity to those established in a good resolve, why should it not likewise be said that in those who have turned aside to iniquity certain affections of lost or corrupted good sometimes survive, out of the habit of former virtue, even while their purpose is evil? Such affections can indeed be present without a good purpose of the will, whether from habit or from nature; but without that purpose they cannot possess the merit of righteousness.

For this one thing is the purpose—namely, the will or consent of the mind arising from the will—which alone is subject to judgment with God. If this alone is good, whatever is in a person, whether good or evil, is not turned toward evil; likewise, if it is evil, whatever remains, whether good or evil, is not turned toward good.

[Col. 0548D] Therefore those who establish a person’s merit in certain undefined affections, which we see sometimes present in unbelievers and the wicked either by nature or habit, ought to have looked to this eye alone, from which alone the whole body is illuminated. These excessively superstitious questions might have come to an end—if indeed they could come to an end. But now they ask and always ask, and never find. They ask whether David and Peter ought to have been condemned had they died in their sins before repentance. Would that they could see what answer that question deserves!

[Col. 0549A] For why ought they not to have perished if they had died in their sins? “But,” they say, “they could not perish, because they were predestined to life.” Why then, likewise, could they not fail to sin, because they were foreknown as about to sin? For if predestination cannot be impeded, neither can foreknowledge be deceived. But if foreknowledge of sinning does not impose necessity, neither does predestination to damnation remove possibility.

Do you still wish to hear what Augustine says? Since you do not believe me, hear who those are who love, who those are who will persevere, what is the unity of love, and what is the unity of predestination:

“We know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to the purpose” (Rom. 8)—a purpose not their own but God’s—“who also are predestined and foreknown.”

[Col. 0549B] So utterly are all things so ordered that even if any of them stray and go out of their course, this very thing serves their good, because they return more humble and more instructed. If any one of these perishes, God is mistaken and overcome by human fault. But none of them perishes, because God is conquered or deceived by nothing. These are those marked out in the passage to Timothy where, after it had been said that Hymenaeus and Philetus overthrow the faith of some, there immediately follows: “But the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his’” (2 Tim. 2).

Their faith, which works through love, either does not fail at all; or, if there are any whose faith fails,

[Col. 0549C] it is restored before this life ends, and, once the intervening iniquity has been erased, perseverance is reckoned to them until the end. But those who will not persevere, and who will thus fall away from Christian faith and manner of life, so that the end of this life finds them such as they are, are beyond doubt not to be counted among these even during the time when they lived well and piously. For they are not separated from that mass of perdition by God’s foreknowledge and predestination; and therefore they are not called according to the purpose, and consequently are not elect. Rather, they are among those called of whom it was said, “Many are called,” not among those of whom it was said, “But few are chosen” (Matt. 20).

Yet who would deny that they are called elect when they believe and are baptized,

[Col. 0550A] and live according to God? Certainly they are called elect by those who do not know what they will become; not by Him who knows that they do not possess that perseverance which leads the elect to the blessed life. And He knows them to stand in such a way as He foreknew that they would fall.

If it is asked of me here why God did not give them perseverance, though He gave them the love by which they lived as Christians, I answer that I do not know. Let them also answer, if they can, why God, while they were living faithfully and piously, did not then snatch them away from the dangers of this life, lest wickedness should change their understanding and deceit should deceive their souls. Did He lack the power to do this, or did He not know their future evils? Surely any such assertion is utterly perverse and insane.

John says concerning such persons: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.

[Col. 0550B] For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2). And what else does he say except that they were not children, even when they bore the profession and name of children? This was not because they feigned righteousness, but because they did not remain in it. For he does not say: “For if they had been of us, they would certainly have held a true, not a feigned, righteousness with us.” But he says: “If they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.” They were indeed in the good; but because they did not remain in it—that is, did not persevere to the end—he says that they were not of us, even when they were with us. That is: they were not among the number of the children, even when they were in the faith of the children, because those who are truly children are foreknown, predestined, and called according to the purpose, so that they may be elect.

[Col. 0550C] For no son of promise perished, but only a son of perdition. Consequently none of the predestined ends this life changed from good to evil, since he is so ordained, and therefore given to Christ, that he does not perish but has eternal life. Of these John says: “We know that everyone who is born of God does not sin.” David sinned gravely; but because, born of God, he belonged to the fellowship of the children of God, he did not sin unto death, but by repenting deserved pardon. Indeed, concerning this sin unto death John had earlier spoken in these words: “There is sin unto death” (1 John 5). And immediately he added: “We know that everyone who is born of God does not sin.”

## Part Fourteen. On Confession, Repentance, and the Forgiveness of Sins

[Col. 0549]

### Chapter I. On confession and its command

[Col. 0549D]

Great is human wickedness. No one seeks authority when he wishes to act wickedly; but when we tell people to do good and to confess the evils they have done, they say to us: “Give us authority. What Scripture commands that we confess our sins?” Therefore, if Scripture does not command the confession of sins, answer now whether you have a Scripture which commands sins to be kept silent. If, then, you do not wish to confess because you have no authority for confession, why do you wish to be silent when you have no authority for silence?

Yet because you seek authority, receive authority. The ancient Law commands sins to be confessed and sends people to priests to confess their sins so that they may receive pardon. Thus transgression of the Law is abolished there by confession and offering, when it was still a shadow, and when confession of guilt

[Col. 0551A] ought still to fear punishment rather than expect mercy. If this authority is not sufficient, hear Scripture elsewhere plainly saying: “He who conceals his crimes shall not be justified” (Prov. 28). For what is concealment but silence and unwillingness to confess? Those who make their crimes known through the shamelessness of wicked conduct do not deserve justification but condemnation. Evils, therefore, must be concealed insofar as concerns the shamelessness of wicked action, and disclosed through the humility of confession.

Do you still wish to know the danger of silence and the benefit of confession? “Because I kept silent,” says the Psalmist, “my bones grew old, while I cried out all day” (Ps. 31 [32]). And again: “I made my sin known to you, and did not hide my unrighteousness. I said: ‘I will confess my unrighteousness against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (ibid.). See, therefore, and consider: if you are silent about your sins, they grow old; if you confess them, they are forgiven.

[Col. 0551B] If you say: “Behold, I confess my sin, but to God rather than to a human being; I follow Scripture. It tells me to confess my sin to God, does not send me to a human being in whom there is no salvation, but directs confession to the One from whom it promises remission. ‘I said: I will confess,’ etc.” What does the human being do? Hear what he does. Was he not a man who said: “Son, your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 19 [probably 9]; Mark 2)? And it is true that he who said this was a man. Therefore those who saw him to be a man but did not recognize God murmured among themselves, saying: “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” (Luke 7). For they knew that forgiving sins belonged to God, but did not know that what belonged to God had been received by a man from God. As man, he possessed what he possessed because he had received it; but as God, he possessed this same thing and had not received it.

[Col. 0551C] Therefore he chose at a certain time, in his humanity, to receive what he had always possessed in his divinity, so that he might draw near to the neighboring human being in what was human, and in that very humanity offer to human beings what was God’s. For in what was human he was joined more intimately to humanity; but in what was God’s he worked more powerfully in the human being. Therefore, “That you may know,” he says, “that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins,” he then said to the paralytic, “Rise and walk” (Matt. 19 [probably 9]). He showed what they could see, that through it they might believe what they could not see.

[Col. 0551D] Therefore God became man, in order to present himself to humankind as near and familiar for conversation, so that in one and the same person humanity might find one of its own kind to whom it could confidently disclose its weakness, while believing that above humanity he was God, and thus might not despair of receiving from him forgiveness of sins. Then, so that the grace of this dispensation might be multiplied more abundantly, God made human beings, who were mere human beings, participants in his power, so that they might fulfill his office by receiving the confession of penitents and exercise his power by forgiving the sins of penitents who confess. “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he says. “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20). Therefore Christ the man gave his disciples, acting in his place on earth, the power to forgive sins.

[Col. 0552A] But perhaps you say: “Why did Christ not likewise give people a command to confess their sins, as he gave his disciples authority to forgive the sins of those who confess?” Hear why Christ wished it to arise from yourself, lest your confession seem as though extorted or compelled. Therefore, as far as concerned himself, he entrusted his office to his disciples to perform, so that, after the manner of physicians, they might receive and heal the sick who came to them. Thus he told the physicians to cure; but he did not tell the sick to come to physicians for treatment. He wished it to be regarded as certain that the sick would willingly seek health and offer themselves to be cured, if they found physicians.

[Col. 0552B] Therefore he admonished the physicians alone; for a sick person is sufficiently admonished by his own sickness, and needs no command if he feels pain. Yet these physicians afterward, because they found the sick negligent in their treatment, themselves stirred them by admonition to seek health and drew them by command. “Confess your sins to one another,” says the Apostle James, “and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. 5). What does “to one another” mean? One person to another, a human being to a human being. Not only a human being to God, as that true confessor said, “I said: I will confess,” etc., but to a human being for God’s sake. For the person who humbles himself to a servant for the Lord’s sake does more than one who humbles himself to the Lord himself. Therefore: “Confess your sins to one another.” What does “to one another” mean? Not merely each person to every person,

[Col. 0552C] but reciprocally—that is, among yourselves: people to people, sheep to pastors, subjects to prelates; those who have sins to those who possess authority to forgive sins. It was indeed proper that those intending to confess should go to him who is over them; but now, for the administration of pardon, it is allowed that you confess your sins mutually among yourselves. He alone who would receive confession would not make confession, because he would have no sins. But those who receive the confession of sins and forgive sins to those confessing must themselves also confess their sins, so that their own sins may be forgiven them as penitents and confessors. Therefore: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another.”

[Col. 0552D] For what purpose? “That you may be saved.” Confess, that you may be saved. What does “confess, that you may be saved” mean? It means: you are not saved unless you confess. Perhaps you did not wish to hear this, because you seek hiding places and conceal your crimes so as not to be justified. It does not please you to be told that those who refuse to confess their sins cannot be saved; therefore perhaps you try to twist the Apostle’s saying to another sense, so that he is understood to have promised salvation to those who confess, while not denying justification to those who do not confess. Hear, then. Augustine says: “No one can be justified from sin unless he has confessed before the sin.” Likewise Bede, on the same Epistle of James from which we took the above testimony: “Without confession sins cannot be forgiven. But this distinction should be observed: daily and lighter sins should be confessed reciprocally to equals, so that we may be saved by praying for one another.

[Col. 0553A] But the uncleanness of a more serious leprosy should be disclosed to the priest, and we should seek to be justified according to his judgment.” See how the testimonies of truth agree. There is a certain common repentance in the Church, which we perform daily toward one another; in it, through prayer poured out for one another, we obtain pardon and remission for daily and lighter sins. But the liability of a more serious fault we disclose to a priest in individual confession; and, according to his counsel, having offered the service of satisfaction, we obtain pardon for sin.

But you say: “If a person cannot be saved unless he confesses his sins, what is this which is found written: ‘Tears wash away the offense which it is shameful to confess with the mouth’?” Certain sayings of this kind are found, and people eagerly seize upon them—not because they seek truth in them, but because they wish to defend their wickedness by them. For they say: “Why do you break us down? Why do you press us hard?

[Col. 0553B] Our deeds are shameful; modesty does not allow us to speak; we are ashamed to confess what we have done. Yet we do what we can: we offer a contrite and humbled heart, grieve over what we have done wickedly, shed tears, and punish our guilt by mortifying the flesh. Why do you demand words where good works exist? We have Scripture consoling us and saying: ‘Tears wash away the offense which it is shameful to confess with the mouth.’ We do not excuse wickedness, but spare modesty. Therefore what we are ashamed to say to a human being, we say to God, who does not reproach us.”

By such pretexts people seek an excuse for their sluggishness, and try to pervert the Scriptures because they themselves are perverse. For what follows? If Scripture says, “Tears wash away the offense which it is shameful to confess with the mouth,” did it therefore say: “If you are ashamed to confess, it is enough for your sin if you merely weep, even if you do not confess”?

[Col. 0553C] Is it not much better to understand that Scripture wished rather to say this: tears drawn from the innermost contrition of the heart can wash away even those sins which cannot be spoken without shame and embarrassment? What then? If tears wash away shameful sins, must one keep silent precisely where divine help is more necessary? On the contrary, one must confess there all the more, so that the humility of confession may aid the tears of contrition.

Likewise, when you are told, “If you are ashamed to tell your sin to a human being, tell it to God, who does not reproach,” you are not told: “If you are ashamed to tell it to a human being, do not tell it to a human being, but tell God.” Rather, you are shown the gentleness of God, who is so mild and gracious to all who flee to him that you need not fear any reproach from him, even if your sins are such that you cannot reveal them to a human being without shame.

[Col. 0553D] For in the matter about which you are ashamed when speaking to a person, you need not be ashamed when speaking to God, because he does not reproach the speaker but forgives the confessor. Therefore tell a human being, so that for a time you may be beneficially put to shame before him, and that shame may afterward bring you glory and give you confidence, so that you need not fear reproach when you begin to be made manifest before God. Yet lest perhaps your thought should say to you: “If it is so grave to reveal sins to a human being, and if we are so ashamed before a human being, what shall we do before God, whose majesty we cannot evade and whose judgment we cannot escape?”—lest, then, you should despair of yourself by thinking thus about God—you are shown God’s gentleness toward penitents and confessors: he forgives all sins to the penitent and does not reproach those who confess.

Thus understand what was said: “Tell God, who does not reproach,” as if it said: even if you are ashamed before a human being, do not be ashamed before God, because God is gentler than a human being,

[Col. 0554A] more mild, and more compassionate to the wretched, so that he does not reproach. In this sense, therefore, you are not told not to tell your sins to a human being; rather, you are told to trust in God’s mercy even in matters shameful before human beings.

You still object with those tears of Peter, which you read of but whose confession you do not read: “Tears wash away the offense which it is shameful to confess with the mouth.” You therefore object with those tears not because you love compunction, but because you flee confession. You say that you read of Peter’s tears but do not read of his satisfaction. You have heard that he wept, but have not heard what he said. Therefore, “Tears wash away the offense which it is shameful to confess with the mouth.” What then? Do you suppose this is said to you so that, because Peter is read to have wept and not read to have confessed, you may weep and not confess?

[Col. 0554B] Is it not much better to understand that this is rather being shown here: if tears had such force then, where there was no oral confession, how much more do they have force now, if genuine, where together with contrition of heart they also have oral confession? For this is shown to you when it is added: “First one must weep, afterward confess.” For true confession requires that you first be pierced with compunction, then confess.

For there are some who, as they are shameless in acting, are likewise unashamed in speaking. Since they do not perceive their own foulness in acting, they feel no shame in speaking. To them, indeed, it is said through the prophet: “You have acquired the brow of a prostitute; you did not know how to be ashamed” (Jer. 3). These people sometimes, without any movement of compunction, without any attraction of fear or love of God, put themselves forward to speak their sins merely to fulfill a custom,

[Col. 0554C] supposing that they are absolved from the debt of their sins through the mere utterance of words. To them it is rightly said: “First one must weep, afterward confess.” For in the confession of sins a person ought to be ashamed, so as humbly to acknowledge what he has done, but not so ashamed as to remain silent. That sinful woman knew this well: she came to show that she did not wish to hide her sins, yet stood not in front but behind, to show that she recognized the shamefulness of her disgrace. Therefore it is rightly said: first one must weep, afterward confess.

### Chapter II. On repentance and the fruit of repentance

Repentance is one thing inwardly and another outwardly. Outward repentance consists in affliction of the flesh; inward repentance consists

[Col. 0555A] in contrition of heart. Through outward repentance the fault of a minor deed is chastised; through inward repentance the fault of a perverse will is corrected. The measure of correction must be weighed according to the magnitude of the offense. “Produce fruits worthy of repentance,” he says (Matt. 3; Luke 3). For the fruits of repentance are one thing, and repentance itself another. As a tree is one thing and its fruit another, so repentance is one thing and its fruit another.

Repentance is sorrow for a past act that has been committed, when you grieve that you have done what is evil. Therefore, when you disapprove and condemn your evils, you have repentance; but when, with satisfaction following, you both punish and correct your evils, you have the fruit of repentance. If what you have done displeases you, you repent. If you pursue and punish what you have done,

[Col. 0555B] you produce the fruit of repentance. Repentance is disapproval of the deed; the fruit of repentance is correction of the offense. But because the measure of correction must be weighed according to the measure of the offense, one must therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance. If the affliction in correction is less than the pleasure was in fault, the fruit is not worthy of your repentance.

But you say to me: “How can I know when my repentance is proportionate?” Because you cannot know this, you must always repent. You can make satisfaction; you cannot do too much. It is better to do more than less. Therefore be diligent, exert yourself, take pains, devote effort, so that fault may have an end but devotion no end. Yet, so that the sinful conscience may at some point find comfort, a limit and measure of outward repentance has been established, so that when it has been completed or fulfilled you may begin to have confidence and, with a certain holy assurance in hope of the divine mercy, trust in pardon and remission of sins—more truly in proportion as you have sincerely fulfilled the repentance imposed upon you.

### Chapter III. On those who do not complete repentance in this life

But perhaps you answer in a silent thought: “How,” you ask,

[Col. 0555C] “can I be certain of pardon because of repentance and satisfaction imposed by a human being, even if I fulfill it diligently, when the very person to whom I confess my sins often either does not know through ignorance, or does not consider through negligence, what satisfaction he ought to impose on me according to the degree and measure of the offense?” To this I answer you briefly: if the human being does not know, God knows. Yet do what is commanded of you. Be obedient in what you are ordered. May God see your devotion, even if the human being does not properly regulate your affliction. You cannot perish if you are found devout.

“But,” you say, “I am deceived, thinking that I have made satisfaction when I have not made enough. He imposed on me only so much and did not command more. Behold, I have done everything and have not made satisfaction. I go to God as though secure, thinking I have made satisfaction to him, while I am still held bound because I have not made enough.

[Col. 0555D] Why then,” you ask, “has it happened that I do not have such a priest as tells me what is required?” Hear why: it has happened because of your sins, by which you deserved to have an evil one—though, if you were judged strictly, by them you had deserved to have none at all. “He will cause a hypocritical man to reign,” Scripture says, “because of the sins of the people” (Job 34). And: “I will cause your tongue to cleave to the roof of your mouth, and you shall not be like a reproving man, because they are a provoking house” (Ezek. 3).

For, that you may know that your wickedness caused this, see where your devotion was. If you had possessed perfect devotion, you could nevertheless have ceased even with no one urging you. But now your sloth and negligence sought an opportunity for delay, not correction. God saw this and gave you according to your heart, so that you did not find what you were not seeking to receive.

[Col. 0556A] Yet I do not say that you should despair, even if it happens that the person who applies outward medicine to heal the wounds of sins gives something less than sufficient. Often what is done less outwardly works more effectively inwardly. Great devotion can exist in a small work. “Man sees the face, but God looks upon the heart” (1 Sam. 16).

And, to say less, it is a great thing if in this life you can begin, even if you cannot complete it. For after death a certain purgatorial fire is also said to exist, where those are purified and cleansed who began to be corrected here but did not complete it. But those who were unwilling even to begin in this life cannot complete it there. For those to whom it is granted to begin their correction here, even if it is not granted them to complete it, the completion of correction is reserved there.

Nevertheless it is altogether safer to strive both to begin and to complete it here, so that nothing may remain for you there either to suffer or to do. It is hard to feel those torments, even briefly.

[Col. 0556B] Therefore it is altogether safer for you to begin and complete here what you ought to do. If you cannot complete it here, yet if you have begun, do not despair: you will be saved, but so as through fire (1 Cor. 3). You will indeed burn until what combustible material you carry has been consumed. But you will be saved, because the foundation of the charity of God remains in you.

### Chapter IV. Whether repentance can be repeated

There are those who say that for persons who relapse into their former sins there is no longer room for pardon, because certain testimonies of Scripture seem to deny the way of salvation to those who, after receiving penance, return to previous sins. There are indeed some sayings of this sort

[Col. 0556C] in which this is not actually said, but it seems to be said to those who do not understand them properly.

The Apostle Paul says in the Epistle which he wrote to the Hebrews: “It is impossible for those who were once enlightened, who have also tasted the heavenly gift and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, who have nevertheless tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to be renewed again unto repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt” (Heb. 10 [probably 6]). And again: “For if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins” (Heb. 10). And elsewhere it is again found written: “There is no place for a second repentance.”

But whether these or other such writings or sayings of Catholic men are found concerning this matter,

[Col. 0556D] it must by no reasoning be supposed that those who held right views wished to maintain that persons fallen into sins of whatever kind either could not repent, if they were regarded by divine mercy, or could not obtain pardon, if they were moved to compunction by true repentance. For Catholic faith absolutely does not admit this. He who said, “I do not say to you seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matt. 18), showed that he rejects neither a sinner’s second, nor third, nor any-numbered repentance, provided only that it is true.

Therefore, the statement that it is impossible for those who, after illumination by grace, tasting the heavenly gift, and partaking of the Holy Spirit, have fallen away to be renewed again unto repentance, must be understood in this way: they could fall by themselves, but cannot rise by themselves; and thus what is impossible to them is not impossible to God. As it is written: “A spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. 77 [78]). This is said of the way of perdition: all who enter by it shall not return again, because a human being can indeed go to evil by himself,

[Col. 0557A] but cannot return by himself unless aided by grace; and, when aided, is thus renewed unto repentance.

Or the written statement that those who have fallen away cannot be renewed unto repentance, or that prophetic saying, “The virgin Israel has fallen; the virgin Israel shall not rise again” (Amos 5)—in which likewise some have erred from the right understanding—may fittingly be explained in these terms.

Because Saint Jerome expounded certain ambiguous words on this passage [Col. 0557C], some who prefer to derive from the Scriptures material for error rather than for edification try to establish that the fallen cannot be restored. For he says: “Although God can do all things, he cannot make a virgin out of one who has been defiled.” Let him himself see what he intended to say; I do not depart from the purity of the Christian faith. Truth is one. I hear the Apostle saying: “If an angel should preach another gospel, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1). Yet I think that he intended to say something, even if I do not know what he intended to say. Still, it is devout for me to think that he said what is true, even if perhaps he might have said more aptly or more plainly what he said. I shall try to interpret the statement of a Catholic man in accordance with Catholic truth.

Yet if this is understood of corruption of the flesh, it is foolish [Col. 0557D] to think that a human being can defile his own flesh but God cannot heal it. If it is understood of corruption of the heart, it is likewise foolish to say that a human being can sin but God cannot justify—indeed, cannot justify as fully as that person can sin. But if God is said not to be able to do this because it has occurred, and what has occurred cannot be made not to have occurred—because what is true cannot be false, and therefore he cannot do it because he cannot act against truth; for if he could act against truth, he could act against himself, who is Truth—what force does this statement have beyond what might be said of any other thing: that what has happened can no longer be unhappened, even if what has happened can be corrected, so that its having happened does no harm [Col. 0558A]?

It is certain that one who falls can rise again, and not only rise again, but rise better than he was when he fell. Many have fallen and risen better than they were before they fell; indeed, better than they would have been had they not fallen, because they were permitted to fall precisely so that they might be instructed by their own fall and ruin and be made better. Yet no one rose, or could rise, better after falling than he would have been if he had not fallen and had performed, while standing firm, all the good deeds which he now performs in rising again. In this respect one may say that everyone who falls cannot thereafter wholly recover what he loses by falling, because whatever he later adds for correction [Col. 0558B] or recovery cannot be done without his having been better had he possessed all these things and nevertheless not fallen.

Therefore no one ought to sin in hope of correction, because what is once lost is not recovered as the very same thing; for whatever is afterward added to repair what was lost is not that thing itself, but something else in its place—and it would certainly be greater if both existed together. This cannot occur because, just as past times do not return, so things once perpetrated cannot afterward be made not to have been done.

Therefore, if you are a virgin, carefully preserve what you have. Do not sin in hope; do not fall as though you would rise better. Whatever you may afterward do, you cannot do it without having been better if you did this and remained a virgin. Thus perhaps in this manner it may fittingly be understood that “the virgin Israel has fallen and shall not again rise as the virgin Israel” (Amos 5), and that where there were a thousand there shall be a hundred, and where a hundred, ten in the house of Israel [Col. 0558C]. If we say in this sense that the fallen cannot be renewed unto repentance, perhaps we say nothing improper; nor do we close the way of pardon to penitents, but we show the danger of falling. For if it is a great thing to rise at some time, it is surely greater never to have fallen. If it is good to have been healed, it is better never to have been corrupted.

There is still another sense in which we can understand the foregoing statement with the same truth; whether with equal appropriateness, I do not know. “It is impossible,” he says, “for those who have once been enlightened,” and the rest which he added, [Col. 0558D] “when they have fallen away, to be renewed again unto repentance”; and he seems to have added the reason why such persons cannot be renewed unto repentance: “crucifying again,” he says, “and exposing the Son of God to public shame.” Therefore, they cannot be renewed anew in this respect because they cannot have another cross and another death of the Son of God; not because pardon is denied to penitents, but because Christ will not die again for sinners.

Guard, therefore, your salvation: Christ died once for it. If you lose it, you cannot have another Christ to die for you, nor another death of the same Christ. Christ says to you: “Preserve your salvation; I died once for it. If you lose it, I cannot die again; nevertheless, by that same death [Col. 0559A] I can restore what was lost.” But I do not want you to wrong me; for if, by voluntary sin, you again lose the salvation acquired by my death, then, so far as lies in you, you compel me to be crucified again and to die again.

I offered my flesh as a sacrificial victim, so that those repenting of sin might obtain pardon, not so that those voluntarily sinning and persisting in sin might be justified. Those, therefore, who repent of sin have in that sacrifice an offering of expiation. But those who voluntarily remain in their sins have in it no ground of salvation. This sacrifice was given to them so that, repenting of sin, they might be expiated through it; but now that sacrifice is not left to them so that, while voluntarily persisting in sin, they might be justified through it. Therefore let those who sin voluntarily not think that this sacrifice pertains to them, because for those who sin voluntarily there is no longer left a sacrifice for sin. They cannot appropriate to themselves that offering which was made so as to benefit those who repent of sins, not those who remain in sins.

Thus, when one truth is made manifest, another likewise comes to light. As for the statement that “there is no place for a second repentance,” some wish to understand it thus: this whole life is a place of repentance for the sinful human being. Those who wish to repent here have a place, because this place has been given to human beings for repentance. But those who do not wish to repent here, even if in the other life they should wish to repent, will be unable to repent in such a way that their repentance bears fruit, because it has no place. The first repentance, therefore, has place in this life. A second repentance after this life [Col. 0559C] has no place; nor does it bear fruit, even if they have sorrow.

Others understand this saying of public repentance, which they say cannot be repeated because of strictness and discipline, lest people despise the sacraments of God. But let each person think according to truth as best he can. I think that the person who says that there is no place for a second repentance because a human being ought to have one repentance as long as he lives—so that he may always grieve over past sins, guard himself against future ones, and never return to the sins he has once abandoned—has found an easier way out and avoided, without the scruple of a question, the difficulty involved. Whoever does this does what he ought to do. Whoever does otherwise—that is, whoever returns to past sins, so that after sinning he may return again to repentance as often as he wishes, and, as it were, make a second repentance after the first—does what he ought not to do. Yet he does not do wrong in repenting, but does wrong in not persevering in repentance [Col. 0559D].

## CHAPTER V. On those who repent at the end.

Some ask what should be thought of those who persist in their sins until the end of life, yet at the last, terrified by approaching death, are pierced with compunction and repent, and seek mercy and pardon with their whole heart, even if, overtaken by the moment of death, they cannot render the satisfaction due. Briefly, I shall state what seems to me right. I think that, so long as a person lives in this life, just as he can do evil [Col. 0560A], so he can also amend it if he has done it; and that a person’s repentance is never fruitless, at whatever time, even at the last extremity and in the crisis of necessity, provided it is genuine.

I hear Scripture saying: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 18, 33). It does not say, “If he groans two days or two years before death,” but “At whatever hour he groans, he shall be saved.” Therefore do not set a time limit to God’s mercy, lest perhaps your judgment turn against yourself. Do not lay down a law that is not to your advantage. Sinner, love mercy, because unless you love it, you do not deserve it. Yet you must not sin securely under this hope. Salvation is promised to you if you are converted at the end; for although pardon is promised to you even then, if you truly [Col. 0560B] repent, it is not promised to you so that you ought to repent truly only then.

It is very difficult for repentance to be genuine when it comes so late, when suffering binds the limbs and pain overwhelms the senses, and a person can scarcely think of anything else. Therefore, if you wish to be secure, repent while you are well. While your mind can attend to itself, exercise it in its proper work. Repentance that seems compelled ought to be very suspect. It is easy for a person to think he does not will what he is not permitted to do. Opportunity most clearly tests the will. If you plainly do not act while you can, you show that you do not will it. Although repentance in time of health is safer, late repentance is still better than none. Before the end, fear lest you delay repentance; at the end, take thought, so that you may at least then come to your senses. And if at that time you perhaps see that no time remains to you for a good work, nevertheless depart in firm hope, with the earnest of good devotion.

The thief’s repentance was very late, but pardon was not late. Though he delayed so long in asking, see how quickly he received! “A contrite and humbled heart our God will never despise” (Ps. 50); for he does not will the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live (Ezek. 33) [Col. 0560C].

## CHAPTER VI. That good will alone suffices if the ability to act is not granted.

If, therefore, you have good will, do not despair. The angels cry from heaven: “Peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2). They did not say, “Peace to rich, noble, powerful people, or to those able to do many things.” Had they said this, you would have reason to fear [Col. 0560D]. For all these things may be absent even from those unwilling to lack them, and may likewise be present to those who do not love them. Will can be absent from no one except one who wills it absent. Will is such a thing that it can neither be given nor taken away against one’s will.

Therefore a human being’s will is the power of God. And it is a human being’s will because willing lies within human power; no violence coming from without, no sickness, no adversity, and no poverty can take will away from a person unless that person himself wills it. Work can be taken away even when the person does not wish it; will cannot. Therefore it does not lie within him when he is able, but it does lie within him when he wills, even though the will itself, when he wills, is not from himself; for even the willing of good is from God [Col. 0561A]. Nevertheless, it is said to lie within the person when he wills, because nothing from without can hinder a person’s willing.

In order that he may will, nothing external is required; everything needed for this act is within him. He does not seek anything outside himself in order to have will within himself. Therefore willing is within him; being able is not within him unless something else from without is added to carry out the will—something whose presence or absence is not within human power. Therefore, when he does not will the good, he is blameworthy only himself. But when he cannot act, if indeed he wills, the impossibility is not imputed to him because of his will; but if he does not will because of the impossibility, his will is not excused. Thus all merit lies in the will. As much as you will, so much you merit.

But you say [Col. 0561B]: “If willing alone is merit, and if a person’s merit consists in will alone, what then does work accomplish? I have will, and it suffices for me. What need is there to act, if the work accomplishes nothing?” But you cannot have will without work when you are able to act. There is no will if it does not do what it can. But if it cannot act, it suffices for itself and has its merit in itself, in that it alone pleases because it is good.

But you say again: “If all merit lies in the will, nothing further comes from the work, even when the work itself accompanies the will. Why, then, is work required, if nothing is added to or taken from a person’s merit through the work?” Hear why. Work is required after will so that the will may be increased by the work itself. Such is the human heart that it grows more fervent through its work, whether toward loving goodness, if it is upright, or toward wickedness, if it is perverse. Thus in either direction affection is nourished by work so that it may grow and become greater [Col. 0561C]; and it can scarcely happen that will is not increased by its work. Therefore, as much as the will grows, so much does merit grow; and the work itself benefits the will toward good, or harms it toward evil, inasmuch as it trains and kindles the will itself toward an affection for goodness or wickedness. And if perhaps it should happen that the will in one who does not act is as great as in one who performs the work, where the will is the same, the merit cannot be different.

But you say again: “If all merit lies in the will [Col. 0561D], then a good work is not rewarded, but will alone.” Consider how you wish to understand this. For in one sense it is truly said that a person’s will, whether toward good or evil, alone is rewarded. Again, it is fittingly said that the work, the will, and the very person who wills and works are rewarded for will and work. Will is said to be rewarded because merit consists in it. Work too is said to be rewarded because in it lies the cause or occasion of reward. Will is rewarded for the work; work is rewarded for the will. Will is rewarded for the work because in it the will merited to be pleasing. Work is rewarded for the will because it received from the will the capacity to be pleasing.

Will is pleasing because it itself is good, and the justice in it is pleasing. Work [Col. 0562A] is pleasing because it is good from the will, and the sign of the justice and goodness that are in the will is pleasing. Will is pleasing on account of what is in itself; work is pleasing on account of that from which it comes. Therefore, just as there is one justice alone on account of which both will and the work of will are pleasing, so there are not two but one recompense by which both will and the work of will are rewarded. Thus there is one recompense by which the human being is said to be rewarded because it is given to him, and will is said to be rewarded because it is given for it. And work is said to be rewarded, in which the will itself merits to be pleasing.

Even when it does not act, will is pleasing in that it willed to act; and it is pleasing with regard to the work itself even when it cannot perform it. Therefore will is always pleasing for the work, and work never pleases except for the will [Col. 0562B]. Yet when work pleases for the will, it pleases because the will itself pleases. But when will pleases on account of work, it does not please as though work pleased on its own account and will on account of work; rather, will pleases on its own account and work on account of will. But will is said to please on account of work because it is a will of work, and it is from the work that it is pleasing. For to will is always to will something; and a person is pleasing because he wills something through a just will that concerns something, and it is just because it concerns what it ought to concern, and is such as it ought to be. Thus all merit lies in will, even if it is with respect to a work; whether that work exists or does not exist, nothing is diminished in the will, unless perhaps the will itself would have become greater if the work had been done.

Therefore, if you wish to have great merit, have a great will. Great confidence: as much as you will, so much you merit. People may be equal in will while unequal in means. Zacchaeus, who was rich, gave much and had much. That widow who put in two small coins had little and gave little, yet gave as much as Zacchaeus [Col. 0562C]. She had lesser means, but an equal will. If you consider what they gave, you will find differences; if you consider from what they gave, you will find equality. God does not weigh how much is given, but from how much it is given.

Therefore, if where more is given and where less is given merit is not different when will is equal on both sides, then where something is given and where nothing is given merit cannot be different if will is equal on both sides [Col. 0562D]. This is why I told you not to despair if you lack means: let good will be present; as much as you will, so much you merit. Make your will great, therefore, if you wish to have great merit.

That sinful woman understood this well. Because she had much to be forgiven, she did not bring great wealth but great love: much against much. If great iniquity were redeemed more by much money than by much charity, the rich would be more fortunate than the poor, and they could sin securely as much and as long as they wished. For redemption from their sins would lie within themselves: whenever they wished, they could give money and possess righteousness. But God acts well in placing our redemption in that which no one, unless he himself wills, can lack [Col. 0563A]. Rich and poor alike can love, even if they cannot give money equally.

Love greatly if you wish much to be forgiven you. “Many sins are forgiven her,” he says, “because she loved much” (Luke 7). The one to whom more is forgiven loves more. Here there seems to be some contradiction. For if many sins are forgiven her by God because she loved much, love seems prior to forgiveness; and again, if the person to whom more is forgiven loves more, forgiveness seems prior to love. For it was said thus: “Two debtors owed one moneylender: one owed much, the other little; one more, the other less. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both. Which, therefore, loves him more?” And he answered: “I suppose the one to whom he forgave more” (ibid.). Here forgiveness seems prior [Col. 0563B], and love subsequent. For he is loved because much is forgiven.

Afterward he adds, showing why he made this comparison. “Do you see this woman?” he says. “I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet. But she, from the time I entered, has washed my feet with tears and dried them with her hair” (ibid.). And afterward: “Therefore,” he says, “I tell you: many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much. To whom less is forgiven loves less” (ibid.); and the one to whom more is forgiven loves more. These statements do not seem to cohere, because he said that the one to whom more is forgiven loves more, and that much was forgiven this woman because she loved much. Thus the comparison does not appear fitting unless perhaps he means this: it is apparent that much is forgiven her because she loved much, since the one to whom more is forgiven loves more.

“Many sins are forgiven her because she loved much.” Many sins are forgiven her. And from what do I prove, or how do I show, that many sins are forgiven her? “In this,” he says, “because she loved much.” Great love is an indication of great forgiveness. For the one to whom more is forgiven loves more [Col. 0563C]. The person to whom more is forgiven is obliged to love more; and if he loves more, he does what he owes and shows that he has received much in rendering much. Thus this woman, most attentive, most diligent, and most devoted, loves much because she recognizes that she has received much. “Many sins are forgiven her because she loved much.” If anyone wishes to understand the saying in this way, there will be nothing improper in it.

But perhaps it will seem to someone more consonant with truth that we understand here the love by which the sinful woman, inflamed with desire for healing, began to love the Savior from whom she believed that she would receive salvation. And because she recognized how much she hoped would be forgiven her by him, she loved greatly. She had not yet heard: “Your sins are forgiven you.” The woman was still asking for what she desired to obtain; yet, as though she had already received it, she loved her giver, from whom she did not doubt she would receive what she requested. Therefore he says: “Your faith has made you whole” (ibid.). Because you believed, you loved; and because you loved, you merited; therefore: “Your faith has made you whole.” From the moment faith began, salvation began. But [Col. 0564A] you did not know that by faith and love I was drawing you to myself, in order to forgive many sins to one believing and loving. Yet perhaps you did not think this. Therefore, so that you may know and be comforted, I now say: “Your sins are forgiven you.” The one to whom more is forgiven loves more. Others love after they receive; you loved before you received, because you believed that you would receive. Therefore: “Your faith has made you whole. Go in peace” (ibid.).

See now how much charity accomplishes, how much good will accomplishes. Therefore do not fear. If good will is not sluggish, pardon will not be slow.

## CHAPTER VII. That man judges the work; God weighs the will.

There are two things: will and the work of will. God weighs the will [Col. 0564B]; man judges the work.
