But again, some works are hidden and unknown, others doubtful and not distinguishable, others manifest—either so evil that they cannot be concealed, or so good that they cannot be doubted. Hidden and doubtful matters are reserved for divine judgment. But manifest matters, if good, are judged by approval, but not by recompense, because their prize and reward are reserved for the future.

God willed evil deeds to be judged and punished here, lest, if their judgment were reserved for the future, every judgment should be exercised not for correction but for condemnation. Therefore human beings were appointed judges in God’s stead, so that by examining the faults of those subject to them they may punish and correct them, in order that, when God the Judge comes at the end [Col. 0564C], he may save those corrected persons whom he subjected to human judgment in order to be corrected. Judgments were therefore established; and against diverse faults requiring expiation, a mode and measure of corrections and satisfactions is prescribed by reasonable definition. There is a written penitential book in which, as it were, antidotes of spiritual medicine are set forth, so that physicians of souls may take from it what they should apply to sick minds for healing against the diseases of sins.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the forgiveness of sins, and whether priests, who are human beings, can forgive sins.

Some attempt to ascribe the power of forgiving sins to God alone, allowing in no way that a human being can share in it. In confirmation of this assertion [Col. 0564D] they adduce the cleansing of that leper whom the Lord first restored to health by himself and then sent to the priests—not that his cleansing might be accomplished by their power, but only confirmed by their testimony. In the same way, they say that the ministries of priests in the present Church possess no further efficacy than that they are merely signs: namely, that one who has first been absolved inwardly by the Lord through contrition of heart may afterwards be shown, through them, to have been absolved in oral confession.

They wish to prove by that prophetic testimony which says, “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. XVIII, XXXIII), that sins are forgiven in contrition of heart alone, even before oral confession. And elsewhere: “While you are still speaking, I shall say: Behold, I am here” (Isa. LVIII). And the Psalmist says: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. XXXI).

Yet they hold that oral confession is necessary after contrition of heart, because if anyone, even after obtaining forgiveness of sins, neglects to confess those same sins, he will be guilty as a despiser of the divine ordinance. Although he is not held guilty for the sins already forgiven, he will nevertheless be guilty of contempt. Or perhaps those very sins return to the person who is obstinate, which had previously been forgiven when he was humbled by compunction.

By this reasoning they prove that human beings have no power whatever to forgive sins, but that this belongs to God alone; just as, in the Gospel, the Jews murmured against [Col. 0565B] the Lord because he had said to the paralytic, “Your sins are forgiven you” (Mark II; Luke V), and declared that God alone could forgive sins.

But perhaps those who say these things concerning the absolution of sins do not attend carefully enough to the manner in which a person is bound by sin. For a sinner is bound in two ways: he is bound by hardness of mind, and he is bound by the debt of future condemnation. For as long as the grace of God is with a person, that person is free and unhindered in doing good. But when, through sin, God’s grace is withdrawn, the mind is immediately bound inwardly by its own hardness.

This hardness or blindness of mind is the inner darkness in which a person is held bound in the present because of sin; and unless he is released from it in this life, he will afterwards be cast, with hands and feet bound, into outer darkness [Col. 0565C]. But since no one could rise after the fall of sin by his own strength unless divine mercy, freely preceding him, raised him up, it is necessary that, when we are to be restored to life through repentance, God restore by mercy alone—without any preceding merits of ours—that grace which he had justly withdrawn while we were sinning. Thus, when grace comes, it awakens our heart from the torpor of unbelief and the death of sin, so that, first, when by its operation alone we are moved to repentance, we are released from the bonds of torpor; and then, by its co-operation, we who repent may deserve to be released from the debt of condemnation.

This is well signified in the raising of Lazarus [Col. 0565D]. The Lord himself first released him inwardly from the bond of death; but, once restored to life, he commanded that he be loosed outwardly through the ministry of the apostles. Thus now, in the holy Church, by his grace alone he gives inward life to those dead in sins and kindles them to compunction; he commands those restored to life to come forth through confession; and then, through the ministry of priests, he absolves those who confess from the outward bond—that is, from the debt of condemnation.

The debt of condemnation is rightly called an outward bond, because it belongs to the outer darkness which no one is worthy to escape unless he first deserves to be released in this life from inner darkness.

“But,” they say, “you make a god out of the priest when you attribute to him the power of forgiving sins, which belongs to God alone.” I do not make priests gods. The divine word, which cannot lie, calls priests gods: “You shall not speak evil of the gods, and you shall not curse the ruler of your people” (Exod. XXII). These people, however, speak evil of gods contrary to the commandment of the Law, because they wish to take away from priests the power divinely conferred upon them.

Nor indeed did I confer upon priests the power to forgive sins. He who made gods out of human beings conferred divine power upon human beings. Yet, just as he is God of himself, so also he can, whenever he wills, forgive sins through himself without human co-operation. But those who are not gods of themselves cannot forgive sins unless he from whom they have what they are works in them and through them, and co-operates with them.

Therefore, just as God alone is good, yet it does not follow from this that even those who serve God are not good; and just as God alone works wonders, yet it is said of a righteous man, “For he worked wonders in his life” (Ezek. XXXI); so too God alone forgives sins, even when a priest forgives them from him and through him [Col. 0566B]. For he himself does in a human being what the human being does through him. Nor should one say that the human being does nothing there because God acts through him. Rather, he acts all the better and all the more truly precisely because God acts through him.

Hence he says to Peter, prince of the apostles: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. XVI). He did not say, “Whatever you loose”—that is, as they say, “whatever you show to have been loosed”—“was loosed”; but “shall be loosed,” because the judgment of heaven does not precede but follows Peter’s judgment.

But lest you suppose that this was granted to Peter alone, hear what he says to all the apostles, and through them to all successors of the apostles and to those who discharge the office of the apostles: “Receive,” he says, “the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John XX). Where did he say, “If you show it, it was”? He said this nowhere; rather, he said, “If you do it, it shall be.” Let them therefore hear and understand: “Whose sins you forgive,” and so forth.

To those to whom this was said, it had first been said, “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive,” and so forth, lest either what was given should be thought contemptible, or what those who receive it accomplish should be supposed to proceed from human power [Col. 0566D]. It is therefore no wonder that human beings can forgive sins, because they receive the ability to do so not from their own power but from divine power. And for God to give this to human beings is nothing other than for God to do it through human beings.

What they object concerning the cleansing of the leper gives no support at all to their opinion. For if a sinner is to be believed absolved before confession because the leper was cleansed before his presentation, then by the same reasoning, after contrition the sinner ought not to go to the priest to lament his sin, but to display his righteousness. For the leper too was sent to the priests not to receive health but to display health. Yet Christian faith utterly recoils from this.

Therefore, if the miracle which [Col. 0567A] the Lord performed is presented to priests not in honour of their office but to reproach them, what else is produced but contempt also for the new priesthood in spiritual healing?

And concerning their saying, “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved,” I think it is said especially of those who, having spent their whole life in sin, repent at the end and abandon their sins, when they can no longer have time in this life to make satisfaction. They are told nevertheless not to despair in any way of forgiveness, because even then, if they truly repent, they can obtain mercy.

For this is the meaning of “at whatever hour”: namely, even at the last extremity, even at the moment of necessity, if the sinner groans—that is, if he is converted through complete contrition of heart—he shall be saved from eternal condemnation. It is as though it were said in other words: “At whatever hour during the present life the sinner truly repents, he shall not perish in the life to come.”

But if anyone argues that the words “he shall be saved” do not refer to the salvation granted in the future, but rather to that forgiveness of sins bestowed in present absolution, we need not therefore say that the sinner is absolved from every debt as soon as he begins to groan, before he has received the whole remedy which God instituted for obtaining forgiveness. This remedy is that he should repent in heart and confess the offence with his mouth. Once he has done this, he will no longer be a debtor to condemnation, even though satisfaction remains to be rendered for the sin (ibid.).

But if perhaps a sinner truly repents, yet because of an intervening emergency cannot come to confession, I confidently declare that in him the supreme priest accomplishes what a mortal could not; and it is established that before God what the person truly willed, but was unable to fulfil, has already been done. For it was not contempt that excluded confession, but necessity that prevented it.

Accordingly, if the words “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” are understood of present salvation, they should be understood as though they said: the sinner’s salvation begins when he truly groans over his offences; but that salvation is fully completed when he also confesses with his mouth what caused him to groan [Col. 0567C].

Likewise, the saying, “While you are still speaking, I shall say: Behold, I am here,” can fittingly be understood in this way: God is first present by grace in order to move the heart to repentance, and is then present in order to grant forgiveness of sins to the one who confesses.

Finally, concerning what they object from the Psalmist—“I said, ‘I will confess,’” and so forth—Saint Gregory maintains that it was said only of the sin of thought, in these words:

> Often the merciful God washes away sins of the heart all the more quickly because he does not permit them to proceed into actions. Hence it is rightly said through the Psalmist: “I said, ‘I will confess,’” and so forth. And shortly afterwards he shows how easy forgiveness is in this matter: while the Psalmist still promised himself that he would seek what he promised to seek, he obtained it; so that, because the fault had not gone as far as an act, repentance might not go as far as torment, but mental affliction might cleanse the mind which iniquity conceived only in thought had defiled.

But if anyone wishes to understand this of any offence whatever, let him nevertheless know that sin is one thing and the impiety of sin another. For the impiety of sin is most properly understood as hardness of heart itself, which is first released in compunction, so that afterwards the sin itself—that is, the debt of condemnation—may be absolved in confession [Col. 0568A].

But whether these authorities are explained in this manner or in any other, we confess as probable that God’s priests in the Church possess the power of binding and loosing, not signified merely in some cursory and unusual mode of speech, but truly granted by God to those to whom it was said: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained.”

[Col. 0568B] But perhaps someone will object that priests bind many persons in the Church who are not bound before God; likewise they loose many who remain bound before God, because they often bind the innocent and absolve those who remain guilty. Thus “Whose sins you forgive,” and so forth, would not be true.

But it must be known that Sacred Scripture often speaks of something in such a way that it appears to predict what will result from it, while it expresses its power rather than its outcome; for it shows not what must happen, but what can happen. For example, Scripture says in one place: “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark XVI); and yet we know that many believers receive baptism who are later rejected because of their sins and do not attain eternal salvation.

Again, elsewhere: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and shall not come into judgment, but shall pass from death to life” (John VI). Yet Paul says: “Whoever has presumed to eat the body of the Lord and drink the cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Cor. II).

Therefore, everywhere the power of the sacraments is expressed more than their outcome. It is not signified that all who participate in them will be saved, but that they can be saved. It is as though one said: “Such is the power of baptism that whoever receives it faithfully and devoutly can attain eternal salvation through it.” Likewise, such is the power in receiving Christ’s body and blood that through it whoever receives worthily can obtain eternal life.

I think this saying should be understood in the same way: “Whose sins you forgive,” and so forth [Col. 0568D]. As though he had said more openly: “I grant you such power in loosing and binding sins that whoever deserves to be bound by you cannot be loose before me, and whoever deserves to be loosed by you is no longer bound before me.”

Let people hear; let sinners understand that assistance is granted them by God, and that judgment is again prepared. Perhaps they do not yet presume to appeal to God; they have human priests acting in God’s stead, with whom meanwhile they can plead their case without danger. Let them love their intercessors and fear their judges.

But perhaps someone again asks why God should seek human beings as co-workers in loosing human sins, as though he could not accomplish by himself what he wills [Col. 0569A]. But we must know with certainty that human co-operation contributes nothing to God in the blotting out of sins. Yet a human being becomes a co-worker because the sinner’s salvation is accomplished more fittingly in this manner.

For what are sins except certain wounds? And what is repentance except medicine? We know that in healing wounds of the flesh, unless a remedy suited to the pain is applied, the effect of healing does not follow. Since every sin is committed through pride, every repentance must necessarily be seasoned with humility, so that obedience may break disobedience and the devotion of humility may suppress the swelling of exaltation.

It is therefore most fitting that we who, by sinning, were defiant toward God should, by repenting, be suppliants even to human beings who are servants of God; and that the person who needed no human mediator in order to preserve God’s grace may now be unable to recover it except through a human mediator [Col. 0569B].

For it is also most beneficial for the sinner to learn how far, by sinning, he has departed from God, when he returns to God through repentance only with difficulty. Thus he becomes more cautious in the future, because access to forgiveness is opened only through the hard labour of repentance.

Let the sinner therefore groan and sigh; let him be anxious, fearful, and trembling over his sin; let him run about with concern, seek helpers and intercessors, and humbly prostrate himself before a human being, because he was unwilling humbly to stand before his Creator. Thus even in this act he may in some manner cry out to God and say:

> See, O Lord; consider and observe what I do. I know indeed, Lord, and confess that it was damnable pride not to be willing to submit to you. But now, I pray, let it not be contemptible devotion that I prostrate myself before a human being for your sake. Great is what I took away, and not small is what I restore.

Oh, how sweet and delightful is the mercy of our God! He himself works all our good within us; and, like a father playing with his children, he does everything in such a way as to seem almost to do nothing. Behold, the sinner pierced with compunction groans, sighs, weeps, confesses his guilt, seeks pardon, begs for mercy; and all this is believed to arise, as it were, from the human being. But who, I ask, does this except him who presides inwardly and moves the human heart to do it?

I ask that it not be burdensome if I offer a brief example of this matter. A certain father drove out his defiant son as though in great anger, so that, afflicted in this way, he might learn humility [Col. 0569D]. But while the son persisted in his defiance, by a certain hidden ordering of counsel the mother was sent by the father, so that she might come not as one sent by the father but as one led by her own maternal affection. With feminine gentleness she was to soothe the obstinate son, bend the defiant one to humility, report that the father was vehemently angry, yet promise that she would intervene, promise forgiveness, suggest a plan of salvation, advise him to seek intercessors, say that the father could not be appeased except by great prayers, nevertheless declare that she herself would undertake the cause of the matter, and promise to bring the whole affair to a good end.

See, I ask, whether our case is not handled in this manner. God the Father, as though angry, drove out the sinning son; yet perhaps in the purpose of his good will he was never angry with him. But because human weakness cannot rise by itself from its fall, mother grace is sent to the sinner’s heart, and a priest is sought as intercessor, so that God, who had not been angry, may be pleased [Col. 0570A].

What shall I say? “Who is wise and will keep these things, and understand the mercies of the Lord?” (Ps. CVI). Was what was done therefore done superfluously because God was not changed from angry to merciful—he who is never not merciful to his own? Far be it! Rather, it must happen in this way because the guilt of our wicked deed cannot otherwise be expiated. It must happen in this way because God commanded that even what he desires to give should be sought from him. It must happen in this way because, even if in God, according to his purpose toward us, there was no wrath, yet in us, according to our guilt, wrath remained; and when this is removed by the satisfaction due, then, so to speak, not God is reconciled to the human being, but the human being to God.

As to whether sins return or do not return once they have been forgiven, I judge for the present that this matter is not to be asserted but feared. Whether it is so or not, and by what justice it happens or does not happen, awaits the labour of another treatise—especially because some testimonies of the divine Scriptures concerning this matter are expressed ambiguously, so that from them a certain degree of absurdity seems capable of arising. These matters certainly must not be examined with light or passing consideration.

## CHAPTER IX. On whether sins return after they have once been forgiven

There are many human questions; as long as one lives, one always inquires. For whoever inquires has not yet found what he seeks; and yet he seeks because he has lost what he seeks. And if he has not lost it because perhaps he never had it, still, as long as he seeks, he signifies that he does not yet possess what he seeks [Col. 0570C]. Therefore, as long as we live, we must always seek, because we do not yet possess all that we ought to possess.

But what is it that we ought to seek except truth and goodness? If we possessed these perfectly, we ought to seek nothing further, because if anything further existed, it would be added even if it were not sought. “Seek first,” he says, “the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. VI; Luke XII). The kingdom of God is truth; his righteousness is goodness. If you seek these two as you ought, all the rest is added freely.

Why, then, do you labour to seek those things which you can possess freely? If you seek these without those, either you do not have them, or, if you have them, you do not have them beneficially. If you seek those without these, you have those for salvation and these for usefulness. “All these things,” he says, “shall be added to you.” These things are many; those are few. There are two there; here very many are found. Yet those two are worth more than all these things. Do not look to what is greater, but to what is better. Do not attend to the heap, but weigh the price. Seek few things in order to find many.

Thus truth and goodness are the only things that human beings ought to seek. And would that they were as zealous in seeking goodness as they are found curious in seeking truth! I do not know how it happens, but it is common to everyone to seek truth, even to those who do not love goodness. For all wish to know truth so greatly that no one is found who wishes to be deceived.

Many seek truth without goodness, but goodness is truth’s companion. Truth does not willingly come without goodness; or if it comes, it does not come from those regions or from that country where salvation is [Col. 0571A].

People ask whether their sins return to them after they have once been forgiven. They wish to know this and do not wish to guard against it. Why then do they wish to know what they do not wish to avoid, unless curiosity draws them while goodness does not delight them? They inquire in case they may be told that it is not so; they hang upon a message that would leave their torpor undisturbed, in hope that someone may come who tells them what they wish to hear.

They inquire as though after truth, not because they love truth itself—for they do not love goodness—but because they want what they themselves desire to be true. Therefore they inquire in hopes that they may receive the answer that they would rather hear. And if a witness of truth comes and speaks truth against their will, they are not stirred up but dismayed; they collapse in spirit because they have not heard what they wanted to hear.

Therefore truth answers them according to their wickedness: either as they wish, so that they may err further; or as they do not wish, so that they may not despair further. Yet because this too must be investigated for the sake of those who are stirred up and make progress, it is not absurd to inquire of truth what, even in this matter, the human conscience ought to answer itself if it is disturbed, as usual, by some thought.

Thus the question is whether sins once forgiven to a penitent person are afterwards imputed. Perhaps one who says that this is not to be asserted but feared will judge more safely [Col. 0571C]. For in matters of this kind, hidden things which may be unknown without danger to salvation, it is sometimes better to fear than to define anything. Let someone therefore say that it is to be feared, not asserted. I think this sufficient for the person who can discipline his thought so that this suffices for him; indeed, perhaps it is better that he inquire no further.

But one who is pressed and troubled in mind, and cannot stop here without proceeding further in inquiry, ought, I think, to be answered as far as possible without violating reverence for hidden matters. Therefore, whoever you are who wish to be certain whether those sins which have once been forgiven return again, let us examine and discuss what troubles you.

“My sins,” you say, “were forgiven. I wish to know whether they ought to be imputed again.” What then do you think?

“It does not seem to me,” you say, “that sins which have been forgiven ought to be imputed anew. Otherwise God would seem changeable, because he would not maintain his own judgment and would alter his decision so readily.”

How does he alter it?

“He alters it,” you say, “in this: when he first forgave my sins, he said that he would no longer require them from me. He would not have forgiven them unless he had said this. But now he requires them again and exacts from me as punishment what he had previously forgiven. Therefore I say that if God is said to impute again sins which he once forgave, he is proclaimed changeable and one who alters his word, which ought always to remain firm.”

Therefore, since this cannot be so, it seems to me [Col. 0572A] that sins once forgiven by God ought in no way to be imputed again.

Perhaps this seems correct to you, and you will strengthen yourself by this reasoning so that you need not fear your danger. But tell me now how you understand what you say: that your sins are forgiven. For if you do not understand how they depart, you do not understand how they return; indeed, if you do not understand how they are present, you do not understand how they depart or how they return.

What, then, is meant when God is said to impute sins? If this is said because, when he imputes them, he is angry with the sinner, then, when he forgives sins to the penitent, he is appeased. If, therefore, we say that God is at one time angry and afterwards appeased, how can you deny that in this very respect he changes?

Thus, when he imputes and when he forgives, he imputes and forgives not by a change in himself but by a change in you. He imputes sins when he judges the sinner worthy of punishment. He forgives sins when he judges the penitent worthy of pardon. In both cases he is the same.

You change from one thing into another: now a sinner through fault, now righteous through repentance. He does not change, but always remains the same; and, standing immutably in what he himself is, he sees and discerns what you have become changeably—whether evil from good or good from evil. When he sees you as a sinner, he imputes your sins to you because he discerns you to be such a person as he may worthily punish. But when he sees you as penitent, he forgives your sins because he discerns you to be such a person as he may justly spare [Col. 0572B].

He performs all these things immutably. For even when by repentance you cease to be a sinner, he nevertheless does not cease to know what you were; and when you begin to be righteous, he nevertheless does not begin to know what you begin to be. Before you began, he knew what you would be; and when you cease to be what you were, he nevertheless does not fail to know what you were.

Do not, therefore, understand it as though God changes when you change. Rather, he is said to impute sins to you because he discerns you as deserving his wrath and indignation; and afterwards to forgive those same sins when he recognizes you as worthy of pardon and mercy.

If, then, to have sins imputed is to be guilty through fault, and to have sins forgiven is to become righteous through repentance, why should sins not be said to return to a person when the person himself returns to sins?

But you say to me: “When I return to sins, I return in such a way that I do something similar to what I did before, but not the very thing I previously did. Even if I do the same thing, it is the same in resemblance, not in actuality: the same because like that former act, but not the same because it is that act. There is one likeness of acting, but not one action.

“If, therefore, I am said to deserve punishment for past offences because, after they were forgiven, I return to committing similar deeds, I confess that this is just if I am said to be punished for those offences in the same manner in which I am said to commit them. But if I am said to commit the first evils anew solely because I commit other deeds similar to them, then likewise, when I am said to be punished for them, reason urges that nothing else should be understood except that I am to be punished for those things which I afterwards committed and which resemble the former acts.”

But this was not the question. The question was whether, after forgiveness for an earlier offence, if that offence itself is repeated, the guilt of the sin which had been forgiven returns with the subsequent offence and is doubled [Col. 0573A].

For example: someone did penance with his whole heart for a murder he had committed, and obtained forgiveness. It later happened that he committed murder again. Behold, this person committed two murders—or rather, committed murder twice. For this is the more fitting and precise expression according to the proper usage of speech. Murder is one kind of evil, just as adultery, theft, and fornication are each individual evils, in the same way that charity, patience, and chastity are each individual virtues. And one who loves two people does not love with two loves, but with one charity and one love.

Thus this person committed murder twice: after the first, by repenting, he obtained forgiveness; after the second, when, after receiving forgiveness, he again committed murder. This person afterwards died without repentance and was condemned for his sins. The question, then, is whether he ought to be punished for that murder for which he repented and received forgiveness. And if this is asserted, it is not apparent by what justice it happens. For if he is punished for what he sinned and did not amend, the justice is evident.

If, however, what had been forgiven is demanded again, then either the injustice is real or the justice is hidden. It must therefore be shown by what justice a man is punished again for what had already been forgiven. Perhaps you think that this objection may be raised on this point. [Col. 0573C] Tell me then: does it seem just to you that, because of subsequent repentance, a preceding fault which was imputed should be forgiven, yet that, likewise because of a subsequent fault, the preceding fault which had been forgiven should not again be imputed? If a subsequent virtue closes the gaping wound of sin, does a subsequent fault not reopen what was closed? If living good works die through fault, and through righteousness things once dead are restored to life, why likewise are evil works, which are excused through virtue, not again imputed through fault? You wish repentance to have such power that sins which were imputed are forgiven; and do you not wish fault to have such power that sins which were forgiven are imputed? Subsequent repentance could excuse preceding fault, so that [Col. 0573D] what was once imputed might not harm; and can subsequent fault not nullify preceding repentance, so that what was once praised might not benefit? If your judgment can stand, you seek what is advantageous rather than what is just. “Cursed is the man who makes his own side the worse.” Therefore you make your own side good, and judge well for your own side. Perhaps it would go well with you if the judgment of truth followed your judgment. With you as judge, you would never be condemned. But I fear that, while you will something other than truth, truth may do something other than you will. For truth must be fulfilled rather than your will.

You say that what has been forgiven ought not to be imputed again. Then likewise what has been imputed ought not to be forgiven, if what has been forgiven ought not to be imputed again. [Col. 0574A] If repentance, because it pleases God, causes imputed wickedness to be forgiven, does contempt, because it displeases Him, not likewise cause forgiven sins to be imputed? If the humility of repentance makes you worthy not to be punished even for things formerly imputed, do contempt and the transgression of sin not make you worthy to be called to account, as blameworthy, even for things that had been forgiven? Do you not observe that the more often grace is given, the more wicked ingratitude is judged to be?

Behold, there are two persons: one offends repeatedly, and repeatedly, when praying and entreating, is granted pardon; the other lives innocently and always humbly obeys the will and command of his ruling Lord, and has nothing for which to entreat. It may afterwards happen—as it can happen—that both offend in a similar fault. Tell me, then, which of these [Col. 0574B] is judged more guilty, unless it be the one shown to be ungrateful after such great grace? Laws punish second crimes more severely, repeated wounds are restored to health with greater difficulty, and yet you say that it makes no difference to the guilt incurred subsequently what the preceding acts were, or how great they were?

If earlier evils, which had been excused through later goods, are not restored to life for guilt through subsequent evils, then are earlier goods, which had been killed through later evils, not restored to life for merit through subsequent goods? “Judge rightly, sons of men” (Ps. 57). If you judge one way in your own favor and another way against yourself, you are not a just judge. You ought to love justice so greatly that you do not even love yourself against it. There are scribes who [Col. 0574C] transform cases and alter truth for advantage. Justice does not approve such persons: “Lord,” he says, “I have not known scholarship; I will enter into the powers of the Lord; Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone” (Ps. 70). This is just judgment: that in it justice alone is so regarded that nothing is preferred to justice.

Therefore judge judgments justly: if you wish your good deeds, long since dead through fault, to be restored to life again through righteousness, do not be angry or think an injury is done to you if your evil deeds, long since excused through repentance, are again imputed to you on account of your wickedness. But, you say, God said concerning my evils, when I repented, that He would no longer impute them to me. Likewise God said concerning your good deeds, when you sinned, that He would no longer reward them. [Col. 0574D] If, therefore, because of God’s word it must stand that those former things are no longer imputed, why likewise ought God’s word not stand, that these latter things are no longer rewarded? For your own advantage you wish God to lie. But where you feel yourself injured, you labor to preserve His truth. Why do you do this, except because you love yourself perversely and do not love God? He, however, rightly loves His truth and justly condemns your perversity.

Yet because you think you derive an argument from God’s saying, and invoke His promise to defend your injustice, let Him Himself answer you how far you ought to presume when you act wrongly, since He previously promised pardon to the penitent; and likewise whether, when you act well, you ought for that reason to despair because He threatened death and destruction to one previously acting badly. The Lord speaks through the [Col. 0575A] prophet, saying:

“You, son of man, say to the children of your people: The righteousness of the righteous man shall not deliver him on whatever day he sins; and the impiety of the impious man shall not harm him on whatever day he turns from his impiety. Nor shall the righteous man be able to live by his righteousness on whatever day he sins. Even if I say to the righteous man that he shall surely live, and, trusting in his righteousness, he commits iniquity, all his righteousnesses shall be given over to oblivion, and in his iniquity which he has committed, in it he shall die. But if I say to the impious man, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he repents of his sin and performs judgment and justice—if that impious man restores a pledge and returns what he has taken by robbery, walks in the commandments of life, and does nothing unjust—he shall surely live and shall not die. None of the sins which he has sinned shall be imputed to him; he has performed judgment [Col. 0575B] and justice; he shall surely live. Yet the children of your people have said, ‘The way of the Lord is not of equal weight,’ while the way of the impious is unjust” (Ezek. 33).

See, therefore, that you ought not to presume, if you sin, because pardon was previously promised to the penitent; nor ought you to despair if you do well because death and condemnation were threatened to the sinner. God answers you concerning what is yours, not concerning what is His. He indicates your merit to you; He does not reveal His counsel. To the evildoer He says, “You shall die”; to the one doing good He says, “You shall live.” What is it to say, “You shall die,” except “You shall be condemned”? And what is it to say, “You shall live,” except “You shall be saved”? What is it to say, “You shall be condemned,” except to judge you worthy of condemnation? And what is it to say, “You shall be saved,” except to determine you worthy of salvation? Therefore He tells you what is yours, what is due to you, what will happen as regards your [Col. 0575C] merit, not as regards His counsel. For it is just that He answer you concerning what is yours and set before you what appears to belong to you.

Thus He declared to the Ninevites according to their merit, not according to His counsel, saying: “Yet forty days and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 3). Their merit required this, and thus it would have happened according to their merit. The same applies also to what was said to Hezekiah: “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live” (Isa. 38). For so far as Hezekiah himself was concerned, this would happen; and what was in him required that it should happen so. His illness was such that he could not live longer unless he were aided from elsewhere [Col. 0575D] and received from elsewhere the means to do so. Therefore, so far as they were concerned, what was said would happen, although it was delayed and otherwise ordered by Him who said it.

Thus, when it is said to you while sinning, “You shall die,” your merit is expressed; just as, when it is said to you while doing good, “You shall live,” what is due to you is announced. Even when the saying seems to change, it is not changed because of the speaker, but because of you for whom it is said: for you change and do not remain the same, nor do you deserve that the same thing should always be said to you. Therefore do not become confident because of God’s saying if you have acted badly, because when you change in relation to Him, His saying changes in relation to you. “Even if I say to the righteous man that he shall surely live, and, trusting in his righteousness, he commits iniquity, all his righteousnesses shall be given over to oblivion.” If all [Col. 0576A] his righteousnesses are given over to oblivion, then also his repentance, his humility, and the other good things he has performed are given over to oblivion. But if repentance is given over to oblivion, by what is fault excused? Therefore, if repentance is erased, the fault which had been forgiven because of repentance must necessarily be reborn. And deservedly: grace itself did not remain with one who, after receiving grace, proved ungrateful; rather, it changed away from him because he was unwilling to remain the same toward it.

See what the Gospel (Matt. 18) says to you concerning the wicked and ungrateful servant, to whom, when he entreated his lord, the whole debt had been forgiven; but because he was unwilling to show mercy to his fellow-servant, whatever had been forgiven through the gentleness of grace was again exacted from him through the strictness of justice. [Col. 0576B] Therefore it was rightly said that, when we refuse to forgive those who sin against us their debts, it is justly exacted again even from us what we rejoiced had been forgiven us. And deservedly so. That fault was forgiven the sinner was grace, not a debt. If he voluntarily rejects the grace bestowed, it is surely just that having received grace should not profit him.

But you say to me: If, after repentance has been made, earlier sins are once more imputed to the sinner, where is what is said, that no good can go unrewarded? Here is a certain good: namely, this man’s repentance, which was good so long as it was true. Yet that good has no reward, because this man’s sins are imputed to him as though he had never repented. Or [Col. 0576C] that repentance was not good; or, if it was good, show its reward. What then? Does remission of sin not seem to you a great reward? When this man repented, his sin was forgiven him. So long as he repented, his sin was not imputed to him. So long as the merit endured, the reward remained.

Did you wish to grant people this liberty: that after they had given merit and received reward, they could again, whenever it pleased them, take away the merit and retain the reward? This would not be an equitable exchange. You would act unjustly toward God if you gave what was yours and received what was His in such a way that you afterwards took back what was yours while retaining what was His. If you gave what was yours and received what was His, then, if you take back what is yours, He wishes to have what is His. Does it not seem so to you? Perhaps you say that the Lord’s way is not equitable, and you will think against truth.

[Col. 0576D] How, you ask, will what is written stand: “God will not judge twice in the same matter” (Nah. 1), if things that had been forgiven are again demanded for punishment? Hear how God does not judge twice in the same matter: a sin shown to have been erased by worthy satisfaction is in no way imputed by Him for punishment. But, you say, what was erased by satisfaction is again demanded for punishment. It is demanded because there is no longer any satisfaction to be set against it as its excuse. So long as satisfaction remained, remission remained, and what had once been forgiven was not punished. But satisfaction ceased when wickedness was repeated, [Col. 0577A] because it also belonged to satisfaction that the deeds should be corrected and, once corrected, not repeated.

Therefore, after fault returned, it was in some sense no longer the same matter, because one sin began to be liable twice over. Because fault returned, punishment also returned; and punishment would certainly not have been repeated if fault had not returned. When fault came, punishment followed. When fault was corrected, [Col. 0578A] punishment was removed; when fault returned, punishment too returned. One against one, and two against two—not one against two, nor two against one. This is justice. As much as is put in, so much is set back. What do you think? Answer, if you can. But if you cannot answer, do not contend; instead, entreat. It is not to your advantage to enter into judgment with God. Seek mercy, so that you may be able to bear justice.

## Fifteenth Part. On the Anointing of the Sick

[Col. 0577]

### Chapter I. On the three kinds of holy oil and the excellence of chrism

[Col. 0577B]

There are three kinds of holy oil. The first is the oil of anointing. The second is the oil of principal chrism. The third is the oil called the oil of the sick. In Greek, *chrisma* means “anointing”; in Latin, *unctio*. Yet although every oil is consecrated for performing an anointing, not every oil is called the oil of principal chrism, but only that by which the principal anointing is performed, which is also singularly called *chrism*. Chrism is oil mixed with balsam, with which the heads of kings and bishops are anointed; with it the priest also anoints baptized persons on the crown of the head, just as the bishop, by the laying on of hands, anoints on the forehead those to be confirmed. This oil mixed with balsam [Col. 0577C] is therefore called chrism, or the oil of principal anointing. For the anointing performed with chrism is called the principal anointing because in it the Paraclete is principally given. Therefore, on account of the abundance of grace, it contains two mingled liquids: oil and balsam. Oil is for conscience; balsam for reputation: oil, by which the conscience is anointed inwardly; balsam, by whose fragrance one’s neighbors outwardly are perfumed. Oil inwardly, for peace with God; balsam outwardly, for an example to one’s neighbor.

There is another oil, called the oil of anointing, with which catechumens and neophytes are anointed on the breast and between the shoulders for receiving the sacrament of baptism. The third kind of oil is called the oil of the sick, and belongs to the present sacrament.

### Chapter II. When, and by whom, the anointing of the sick was instituted

[Col. 0577D]

The sacrament of the anointing of the sick is said to have been instituted by the apostles.

> [Note: [Col. 0577] The most holy Council of Trent teaches that the sacrament of extreme unction was instituted by Christ.]

For the apostle James, writing in his Epistle, says: “Is any among you sick? Let him bring in the priests of the Church, that they may pray over him, anointing him with holy oil; and if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven him, and prayer shall save the sick person” (James 5). In this passage it is shown that this sacrament was instituted for a twofold reason: namely, for the remission of sins and for the relief of bodily infirmity. Hence [Col. 0578B] it is clear that whoever receives this anointing faithfully and devoutly deserves through it, without doubt, to receive relief and consolation both in body and soul—provided, however, that it is beneficial for him to be relieved in both. But if it is perhaps not beneficial for him to have bodily health and soundness, he undoubtedly obtains, by receiving this anointing, that health and relief which belong to the soul.

### Chapter III. Whether this sacrament may be repeated

Some ask whether the anointing of the sick may be repeated, since baptism, confirmation, and certain other sacraments, once received, are not repeated again. But for the present no reason occurs to me why this sacrament cannot suitably be repeated. For one who has been baptized has been baptized in order to be a Christian. [Col. 0578C] But one who has once become a Christian cannot here become more of a Christian, even if he becomes evil; for a Christian can be evil and yet does not cease to be a Christian, even if he ceases to be good. Moreover, one who has once been baptized is not baptized again, even if he is converted from evil to good.

But one who is anointed with oil is anointed so that his sins may be forgiven and his infirmity relieved. Yet one who is justified can sin again, and one who is healed can become sick again. But one who becomes a Christian, because he cannot lose the sacrament of the name which he possesses, cannot receive it again. The sacrament of anointing is not so: it is a kind of spiritual medicine for body and soul, relieving and healing weaknesses. For oil heals aching limbs. Thus oil is useful for healing both. If the illness does not return, the medicine need not be repeated. But if the illness cannot be restrained, why should the medicine be prohibited? [Col. 0578D] If anointing cannot be repeated, neither can prayer be repeated. For both are mentioned there: “Let them pray over him, anointing him with holy oil; and if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven him, and prayer shall save the sick person” (James 5).

But perhaps you will say that anointing pertains only to the remission of sins, while prayer pertains only to the relief of the body, because it is said, “prayer shall save the sick person.” Take it either way. But you say that anointing [Col. 0579A] grants remission of sins and prayer relief of infirmity. I confess this is true, provided you do not deny the converse: for anointing grants bodily relief, and prayer remission of sins. Each applies to each. Both work so that each works upon both sides, and both cooperate with the other; both have one effect. What is not divided in the sacrament is not separated in the power of the sacrament. Yet because the anointing heals the pain of the limbs and appears to benefit bodily weakness more directly, perhaps he therefore said, “prayer shall save the sick person,” so that you may understand both in each and not suppose that anointing pertains more to bodily health than to remission of sins.

The soul is healed first; the body is healed afterwards. [Col. 0579B] The body became infirm for the correction of the soul. Therefore, in order to obtain bodily health, the soul must first be healed. And if the body does not perhaps recover its former soundness, there is no danger if only the soul has recovered its health. Why, then, should it be denied that the sacrament of anointing [Col. 0580A] may be repeated over the sick person, for often restoring health and often obtaining remission of sins, when it cannot be denied that prayer must be repeated often for the same bodily health and likewise for remission of sins? And, to demonstrate the same from the sacraments, who would say that a person once cleansed by the water of sprinkling cannot thereafter be sprinkled again, or—what is greater—that after receiving once the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, he ought not receive it again?

But perhaps you think it should be answered to this that a body once consecrated is not blessed again in the same sacrament, nor is the blessing of sprinkling repeated often in the same water. Observe that, similarly, the same oil after one consecration is not sanctified by another blessing or [Col. 0580B] consecration; and yet, just as one who has already received the sacrament of Christ’s body is not thereby forbidden to receive it again, so one who has received the sacrament of anointing is not reasonably prevented from receiving it again, should necessity arise and either need or devotion require it.

## Sixteenth Part. On Those Dying, or on the End of Man

[Col. 0579]

### Chapter I. That those who die in the Lord will be blessed even with small merit

[Col. 0579C]

Scripture says: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14). They die in the Lord who, though dying in the flesh, are nevertheless found living in the Lord. What does “in the Lord” mean? In faith, hope, and charity. For by these one lives in that life by which one lives in the Lord. There is one life by which the body lives from the soul, and another life by which the soul lives in God: now indeed through faith, hope, and love; afterwards, in place of faith and hope, through contemplation, while love remains. Therefore it cannot harm the soul if the body loses its life, when the soul itself, persevering in faith, hope, and charity, does not lose its own life.

Therefore let no one tell me: those who have little faith, little hope, and little [Col. 0579D] charity are not saved. I will not measure them. Let them grow as much as they wish; the greater they are, the better. Yet I do not dare condemn them, however small they are. Since they have been born of God, they are children of God. Do you think that God will save His great children and condemn His small ones? Scripture tells me: “Your eyes saw my imperfection, and all shall be written in your book” (Ps. 128). If all, then both small and great. What means, “your eyes saw”? They approved. What means, “they shall be written in the book”? They shall be saved. Therefore even the imperfect shall be saved. For those who are imperfect are something; they are some persons, are numbered, and are written. Those who are nothing are no persons; nor can those who have nothing be written or numbered. Therefore, “To everyone who has shall be given, and he shall abound” [Col. 0580C] (Matt. 25): to everyone who has merit, reward shall be given. He did not say, “To one who has great merit, reward shall be given, and to one who has little merit it shall not be given”; rather, He says, “To everyone who has shall be given, and he shall abound.” Therefore even one who has little merit, when he receives reward, will have enough, though he will not have as much as one who has great merit. The only person excluded from receiving reward is the one who has nothing of merit. Therefore all who die in the Lord are blessed, because after the merit of virtue they attain the reward of blessedness.

### Chapter II. On the departure of souls

Many things can be asked, if indeed everything that can be asked ought to be asked. People ask concerning the departure [Col. 0580D] of souls from bodies: how they leave; where they go upon leaving; or, when they arrive where they go, what they find, receive, or endure. But all these things are more to be feared than investigated. They are hidden precisely so that they may not be sought or found, but feared. For who can be secure when journeying into uncertainty? This alone should not be uncertain: that an evil death cannot follow a good life. For the only evil death is that which evil things follow. Therefore, whoever wishes to die well should live well, since the things which come after death are disposed contrary to—or correspondingly to—and are repaid according to those which precede death in life.

Up to death there is merit; after death, reward. Death is the middle point, in which the day of the Lord begins [Col. 0581A] and the day of man comes to an end. In his own day, man is left to himself, to do what he wills. But on the day of the Lord, man is no longer in his own power, but in the power of Him to whom he has come in order to be rewarded. Therefore it belongs to man to strive only to order well what has been entrusted to him; but what has not been entrusted to him, though promised to him, he should leave to the judgment of Him by whom it must be fulfilled.

Many ask about the departure of souls: how souls leave their bodies—whether that is, in such a way that they go out essentially and locally, beginning to be outside as though expelled; or whether their going out consists only in withdrawing themselves from giving life to bodies and, as if gathering themselves into themselves, ceasing from the animation of the body, so that they subsist in themselves. For example: [Col. 0581B] when this bodily breath is exhaled, it goes out from the body and begins to exist essentially and locally outside the body, whereas it had previously been contained essentially and locally within the body. But when bark begins to dry upon a tree, its moisture leaves it and contracts inward, nor does it go outwards so as to be outside; rather, it remains inwardly in that which is within, whether in the wood or the pith, so that it is not in the bark itself. Nevertheless, it wholly leaves the bark, so that it is no longer in the bark; nor does it leave as though poured forth outwardly, but as though gathered inwardly. And if the moisture perhaps comes out again from its interior so as to pour itself once more into the bark, that bark becomes green again, because the moisture is in it as its life.

Thus they ask, when the soul leaves the body, whether its going out consists only in withdrawing itself [Col. 0581C] into itself from the animation of the body; and, in this very respect, it is no longer in the body, because it ceases to animate the body. For in this respect, it seems already somehow to be outside every body, since, subsisting in itself alone, it is not poured out to animate the body. But when it is not in a body, it is not in a place, because place exists only in a body. And when it is outside a body, it is outside place, because there is no place between it and the body; and it is equally distant from every body, because there is no body between it and every body. But if there is no body between it and every body, it is surely clear that there is no place between it and every body, because place does not exist where body does not exist. Therefore, when it is outside every body, it is equally near to every body with respect to place, [Col. 0581D] because if, placed outside a body, it were nearer to one body and farther from another, there would surely be space between it and the body. If there were space, there would be place; if there were place, there would be body. But if there were body between it and every body, a body would be outside every body—which cannot be.

Thus they say that the soul neither withdraws from a body through a body nor approaches a body through a body; and therefore it is not moved in place so as to withdraw from a body which is in a place, nor is it moved in place so as to approach a body which is in a place. For between every place and that which is in no place there is no place. For this reason they think it is said that a created spirit is indeed moved in time, because it is changeable, but is not moved in place, [Col. 0582A] because it is not moved in place when withdrawing from a body which is in a place, nor moved in place when approaching a body which is in a place.

For it is not moved in place when it withdraws from a place, nor again moved in place when it approaches a place; even when the soul, placed in a body, moves the body locally, it is itself nevertheless not moved locally. For if it is thought to be moved locally for the reason that it is in a body which is moved locally, why should wisdom not likewise be said to be moved locally because it is in a heart which is moved locally? If it is said that wisdom is in the heart through the soul itself, then, when the soul itself is said to be moved locally through a body moved locally, why should not wisdom which is in the soul likewise be said to be moved locally through the soul itself moved locally? But if reason does not establish that wisdom is moved locally, though it is nevertheless in the soul, why should the soul be said to be moved locally, although it is in a body which is seen to be moved locally?

[Col. 0582B] By such reasoning they maintain that spirit is not moved locally, although it is in a body which is moved locally; yet it is moved temporally, because, subject to change, it is transformed from one state into another. But we ought not be excessively curious concerning hidden things, lest perhaps we presume beyond our power. What the way of the spirit is, God knows, who made it. We neither know how it comes nor comprehend how it goes away. When this bodily breath is drawn in, it enters bodily and locally; when it is breathed out, it departs bodily and locally. But the nature of spirit is one thing, that of body another. [Col. 0582C]

When the soul was given to the first man, “God breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. 2). And who can say how God breathed the soul into the body to give it life—whether He created it outside and sent it in to animate the body, or made it there where He placed it and commanded animation, created inwardly, to proceed; nor was the breathing anything other than the very act of giving life? Therefore, if it is not known how it is breathed in, how can it be known how it is breathed out? God breathes in; man breathes out. God sends; man sends back. By the same way by which it is sent when it approaches, it is sent back when it withdraws.

This one thing we know: when the soul departs, the body dies, and that very separation of the soul is the death of the body. It is enough for us to know that it departs. To investigate how it departs is superfluous. Yet from many examples we have learned that, at the departure of souls, the presence of evil or good angels is at hand, to drag them according to their merits either to torments or to lead them to rest. We have also learned that souls still placed in bodies have sometimes known beforehand, before their departure, many things which were to happen to them, whether through the answer of their inward conscience or through revelations made outwardly. [Col. 0582D] We have also known some to be carried away and then restored again to their bodies, and to relate certain visions and revelations made to them, whether concerning the torments of the impious or the joys of the righteous; and in all these accounts they related nothing except what was bodily or like bodily things: rivers, flames, bridges, ships, houses, groves, meadows, flowers, black and white people, and so forth—such things as are commonly seen and possessed in this [Col. 0583A] world, loved for joy or feared for torment.

They also relate themselves, when released from bodies, being drawn by hands, led by feet, suspended by the neck, scourged, cast down, and other such things which can altogether suit only bodily nature. If we believe that all these things exist there visibly and bodily, then, apart from the other absurdities that arise, we must certainly confess that the souls themselves, even separated from bodies, are bodies, compounded and distinguished in limbs after the likeness of bodies.

[Col. 0583B] For my part, I ought not to keep silent about what I heard concerning this matter. A brother of proven testimony told me that he had heard his abbot affirming truthfully the following. Once, when that abbot was traveling to visit certain brethren dwelling at a distance, he took lodging on the road, as is customary, in a certain place. There he learned that an event, which had happened a few days before and had become widely known among all the inhabitants of that place, had occurred. A certain pilgrim, traveling to Saint James for the sake of prayer, had lodged in that same place. At night, as travelers customarily do, he rose before dawn, left the village, and came into a wood nearby. There, separated by chance from his traveling companions at a division of the road, as often happens, he began to wander astray. When he had gone farther on, he encountered a man of venerable bearing and appearance, who asked him who and whence he was and where he was going. He explained his name, country, and likewise the purpose of his journey. [Col. 0583C] The other declared himself to be Saint James, toward whom he was making his way. He said that he had long known all these things; now, as though coming to meet him in approval and gratitude, he praised his devotion, commended his good purpose, and said that a great reward was being prepared for him there and that recompense was not far off.

After many words passing back and forth, he finally expounded what and how great are the miseries and pains of this life; how quickly everything loved here flees away; and likewise how everything feared or suffered passes without delay. By these and similar arguments, under the appearance of rational persuasion, he gradually instilled into the mind of the man, who suspected nothing sinister, contempt for life and removed the fear of death. At last he asserted that nothing was more advantageous for true virtue than that he should hasten to depart hence and, if no other way were available, bravely provoke death by his own hand; nor allow himself to be held long amid these pains, since he did not doubt that joy was prepared for him. In short, deceived, [Col. 0583D] he assented to the fraudulent persuasion and, driving in a sword, cut his own throat.

After seeking him for a long time through the byways, his companions finally found him dead and carried his lifeless corpse back to the village from which he had departed. Because the host with whom he had stayed that night seemed plausibly to have known of this crime, they demanded that he be given over for punishment on a false accusation. But when he saw his innocence endangered without cause and invoked divine help to be with him in the inward devotion of his heart, behold, the man who had died suddenly arose; explaining the occurrence to all who stood by in amazement, he cleared the innocent man.

He reported that he had been led to torments by the same evil angel who had persuaded him to kill himself. But [Col. 0584A] while he was being led away, a man of radiant countenance—whom he said was Saint James himself—had met them on the way, snatched him away, and led him up to heaven to the throne of the Judge; there, after prayers had been offered for him, he had obtained that he be restored again to life. He affirmed that he had seen there many thousands of angels. When questioned concerning their state and appearance, however, he said that nothing in this world resembled them by which he could express the quality he had seen in them, except perhaps fire or light—yet very remotely and very dissimilarly. He said that he remembered, but could in no way express what he had seen.

We have wished to mention this so that it may not seem strange if certain signs resembling bodily things are presented to souls that have departed from bodies, for the manifestation [Col. 0584B] of spiritual realities. Unless souls stripped of the body saw such things and through such things, souls returning to bodies could in no way speak of them to those living in bodies and knowing only bodily things. For although, stripped of bodies, they might see those things there in another manner, they could not here tell them to us in another manner; those things would always remain hidden, and there would be nothing reported to us by those who returned unless, when departing and seeing, they were shown according to such images.

But whether souls which leave and will not return hither any more see or experience those things in this way is wholly uncertain. It seems more probable only that souls which, while living in bodies, are affected through delight in visible things by bodily images, suffer torments there [Col. 0584C] in those same images when they depart from bodies. For they do not altogether strip off bodily passibility when they depart wrapped and entangled in images of bodily things impressed upon them by the practice of perverse delight. But souls which, while remaining here, have striven to cleanse and strip themselves of the same delights and phantasms of thought do not afterwards, when they have departed from bodies, experience punishment and torments in them; because in that very respect they are somehow impassible, namely, that they carry with them nothing deserving punishment.

### Chapter III. On the punishments of souls
Some believe that souls cannot be tortured by bodily punishments except through bodies and while remaining in bodies. Therefore they believe that souls stripped of bodies undergo no other punishments [Col. 0584D] than those inflicted inwardly by an accusing conscience alone. But it is most truly demonstrated by the authority of sacred discourse and attested by catholic truth that souls are tortured even now, before they receive bodies again, by corporeal and material fire. For if corporeal fire is said to have been prepared for demons, who are spirits, what wonder is it if souls stripped from their bodies are tortured by corporeal fire? “But how,” they ask, “can souls without bodies suffer from corporeal things?” Let us answer: We do not know how this can happen. Does that mean that what we do not know how it happens is not true? Yet what is strange if souls suffer outside bodies? If, when clothed, they are harmed when struck, why should they not be harmed when struck while unclothed? If they can be affected [Col. 0585A] when between them and that by which they are affected there is an intervening medium through which they are affected, is it not altogether probable that they ought much more to be affected when they are immediately joined to that by which they are affected?

Yet one must not investigate this matter everywhere, so as always to attempt to examine by our own reason what we are commanded to believe. Sacred Scripture, the teacher of our faith, tells us this. What more do we seek? Let us accept it, not contradict it. Blessed Gregory says that they burn in that in which they see themselves burning. What, do you think, does he mean when he says that souls burn in the very thing in which they see their own burning? With other bodily things it is not so: whoever sees fire does not therefore feel its heat. What then is that vision of the soul by which it feels everything that it sees—or, if not [Col. 0585B] everything, certainly what it sees as punishment? Is it because the soul’s sense, when it leaves through the body, perceives in different ways because it perceives through different instruments, and for that reason does not perceive certain things placed at a distance by bodily sense, because the instrument of bodily sense is insufficient for perceiving them? For sense fails where its instrument is no longer sufficient. Hence those senses that have more adequate instruments have greater power in perception. The eye sees things far off; touch, however, cannot feel except what is immediately joined to it. If the instrument of touching were as penetrating as that of seeing, touch would perceive distant objects as sight does.

What then? Where there will be no diversity of instruments, why should not every sense be equal, so that [Col. 0585C] there seeing may be the same as touching, and touching the same as suffering pain? This, however, must be understood only of those who can be affected by torments because, when leaving this world, they carry with them susceptibility to suffering amid the corruption of vices. Yet when we say that the soul’s sense is affected at a distance, we do not thereby place, as it were, some spaces of location between bodily punishments and the soul itself. For the soul, which by its own nature is extended by no dimension, is shown to be present by itself in sensation wherever it is present. Since there is no place within it, there is no place between it and a place.

But because all these matters cannot be investigated by human reasoning, let us establish our minds firmly upon those things which undoubting faith proves: namely, [Col. 0585D] that sinful souls which have not corrected their fault in this life undergo punishment after this life. Although we do not understand how that punishment is felt by them, what does it matter, since it is not any less felt by them because it is not understood by us? For it makes no difference from what things they suffer, but how much they suffer; for the force of pain consists not in the instrument of torment but in the sufferer’s perception. What good would it do if the material of outwardly tormenting elements were absent, while the sufferers’ inward pain were nevertheless no less? Why do you fear fire and flame except because you fear being burned? But if wounds and blows did not hurt, who would fear weapons or missiles? Observe, then, that none of these things from which pain may arise are feared except because of pain itself. Remove [Col. 0586A] the sense of pain, and there is nothing to fear.

God could therefore have given souls the sensation of pain for their torment even without material elements. But it is fitting that they should be punished in those things in which they previously sinned: first without bodies, just as in those things they wickedly delighted; afterwards with bodies, just as through them they acted unjustly by means of their bodies.

## Chapter IV. On the places of punishments

Just as God prepared bodily punishments for the torture of sinners, so he also assigned bodily places for those bodily punishments. For external things, which are his works, ought to be not only instruments but also signs of those things which he works invisibly. Therefore he distinguished both the torments of the wicked and the joys of the righteous also in bodily places. [Col. 0586B] Hell is the place of torments. Heaven is the place of joys. Appropriately, the place of torments is below and the place of joys above, because guilt presses downward and righteousness raises upward. The greatest torments have their place in the lowest region; the greatest joys in the highest. Intermediate goods and evils are mingled in the middle—that is, in this world.

Hell is said to be a lower place, prepared in the depths of the earth for the punishments of the condemned. Yet it is not at all certain in what part of it it is situated—that is, whether within its hollow interior or outside, in some region of its circumference—although it seems more probable that it is placed beneath the earth as a kind of prison and dungeon of darkness. In this hell, they say, there is unquenchable fire, which, in order [Col. 0586C] always to burn, needs no fuel, having been prepared from the beginning of the world for the eternal torture of demons. In that fire wicked human beings also will suffer eternal punishment together with demons, because, while placed in this life, they consented to guilt with them.

Souls of criminals, when they have departed from their bodies, are thought to be immediately confined in this hell; conversely, the souls of perfectly righteous persons, and of those who leave this life purified, are believed to be led without delay into heaven—where Jesus Christ, according to his humanity, sits in glory at the right hand of the Father—as it is written: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. 24; Luke 17).

There is another punishment after death called purgatorial punishment. [Col. 0586D] In it those who depart this life with certain faults, yet righteous and predestined to life, are tortured for a time so that they may be purified. Its place is not at all determined, except that many examples and revelations of souls placed in such punishment have often shown that it is exercised in this world; and perhaps it will be more probable to believe that individual souls undergo punishment especially in those places in which they committed their fault, as has often been demonstrated by many proofs. Other places of such punishments, if any exist, cannot easily be specified.

Blessed Augustine, from the Epistle of Peter, shows how apostate angels, falling into the lower regions of this world, were cast down until their final condemnation on the day of judgment. For what Peter calls [Col. 0587A] “the prison of hell’s darkness” (2 Pet. 2), Paul is shown to have called “darkness,” saying: “the rulers of this darkness, the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6). We understand this prison, or this darkness, to be this air. Hence they are also called aerial powers. In it the evil spirits are, in one respect, bound before the day of final judgment, insofar as they are constrained by consciousness of their future condemnation; and in another respect free, insofar as they are meanwhile permitted, according to the ordering of divine providence, to devote themselves to tempting human beings, having been released from those greatest torments of Gehenna.

But concerning hell, where that eternal fire is prepared for torture, Blessed Gregory testifies in the *Dialogues* that it is judged more probable that, [Col. 0587B] as we have said, it is believed to be beneath the earth, because of the Scripture which says: “Neither in heaven nor on earth nor under the earth was anyone found able to open the sealed book” (Rev. 5).

It may reasonably be asked whether the souls of the damned—namely, those who were less evil in their manner of life than the impious and most wicked—are seized immediately upon leaving their bodies and carried to the places of hell; or whether, by God’s hidden dispensation, they are meanwhile deferred in certain other penal places from the more severe torments of Gehenna, so that, just as the good who are held back with certain faults in temporary abodes do not immediately ascend to the joys of heaven, likewise the less evil, when they depart from here, though destined for condemnation, may nevertheless not immediately descend to the torments of hell, but undergo certain lighter punishments apportioned to the measure or degree of their faults.

For concerning the perfectly good there is no doubt that, upon departure, they immediately pass to joys. Likewise, concerning the very evil there is no doubt that, when they leave here, they descend without delay to the torments of hell. Concerning imperfectly good persons it is also certain that they are for the time being delayed from the coming joys by certain punishments, until full purification. But concerning the imperfect or less evil it is not certain where they are now, until, at the time of the universal resurrection, having received their bodies, they descend to those torments where they will remain forever. For they are said to be deferred from those torments because they are less evil; by the same reasoning they may be believed not to be deferred because they are destined for condemnation. [Col. 0587D] For what purpose does delay serve where amendment or purification cannot occur? Yet since this is altogether hidden, it must by no means be rashly defined.

## Chapter V. On the nature of the torments of Gehenna

This appears very worthy of inquiry: whether fire alone has been prepared for the tortures of the damned, because Truth alone mentions it, saying: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). Since in this life punishments and tortures arise not only from fire but also from other elements, why should the punishments of the damned not likewise consist there in other elements as well as in fire? For it is written concerning the torments of the wicked: “They pass from snowy cold to fiery heat” (Job [Col. 0588A] 24). And elsewhere: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66).

Now if someone wishes to refer the worm solely to the compunction of a sinful conscience and therefore thinks that fire should be understood as corporeal but the worm not corporeal, rather spiritual, what then is meant by the words written elsewhere: “The vengeance upon the flesh of the wicked is fire and worm” (Ecclus. 7)? For if fire is believed corporeal because it is vengeance upon the flesh, why is the worm not likewise said to be corporeal, since it is mentioned as prepared for the vengeance of the flesh? On grounds of this kind, no single conclusion can lightly be defined.

Yet one who says that vengeance upon the flesh of the wicked will be in worm and fire because the wicked person, having also lived wickedly in the flesh, will be tortured in the flesh by fire and in the spirit by the worm of conscience, will rightly understand the worm that does not die as the eternal torture of conscience, and the unquenchable fire as fire in the flesh. But how shall we interpret that snowy cold and fiery heat, through which the wicked who are to be tortured are said to pass alternately?
