Perhaps this should be understood only of that punishment in which they are now tortured in spirit before the final judgment, so that through a variety of torments they pass to that one supreme punishment, in which, just as they remain without end, so also they remain without variation.

For the final punishment of the damned, just as it is rightly believed to exceed all punishments, is likewise not unreasonably thought to be the torment sharper and more violently excruciating than all others. Perhaps it will be the sole and highest punishment forever for this reason: whatever should be changed in it would diminish it. [Col. 0588C]

Some, however, as has been said, thought that the torments of Gehenna should be understood as spiritual only and not corporeal, because certain words of Scripture are found which seem to assert the same. For certain Scriptures say that the substance of the infernal regions is spiritual, not corporeal; that the gnashing of teeth and the weeping of souls must be understood spiritually; and that flames and torments too are to be thought not corporeal but spiritual. Those who are not rooted in faith fluctuate amid ambiguities of words. For why was it necessary to believe the torments of Gehenna spiritual only because the substance of the infernal regions was said to be spiritual and not corporeal?

For what are the infernal regions except evil spirits, who fell from the heights to the depths through guilt and were pressed down through punishment? Their substance, indeed, is said to be not corporeal but spiritual even after guilt, because although their will has been changed to another state through wickedness, their nature nevertheless remained the same even after it. The substance of souls now damned in hell is likewise rightly declared to be not corporeal but spiritual, because, now released from bodies, they are held there in torments in their spiritual nature alone. Therefore whatever is said of them in Holy Scripture according to the nature of corporeal things is rightly believed to be understood not corporeally but spiritually. For if what they themselves are [Col. 0589A] is not body but spirit, what is in them must be understood not corporeally but spiritually. In this way, then, the substance of the infernal regions is truly reckoned spiritual and not corporeal.

Likewise, the statement that, if we take the weeping of souls and gnashing of teeth spiritually, we must believe the flames of their torments likewise to be not corporeal but spiritual, may indeed be understood in this way: the torments of souls thought to arise from corporeal flames are not produced in them corporeally—that is, by the mediation of bodies. There are many other things that have either been said ambiguously or can be said ambiguously. But the truth of things is one matter; the variety of words another. We ought not, because of a multiplicity of ways of speaking, depart from simplicity in believing.

Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*: “The time which lies between a person’s death and the final resurrection holds souls in hidden receptacles, according as each is worthy either of rest or of misery.” Therefore the receptacles of souls are hidden, and a human being cannot determine what a human being cannot know. Likewise, what kind of fire that fire of Gehenna is to be understood to be, and how incorporeal spirits or souls released from their bodies can be tortured by corporeal fire, is not explained either by the authority of the Christian faith or by that of sacred discourse.

### That the corporeal fire of Gehenna will torture not bodies only, but spirits also. Augustine, *City of God*, on the same matter

Gehenna, which is also called the lake of fire and sulphur [Col. 0589C], will be corporeal fire, and it will torture the bodies of the damned, both human and demonic: the solid bodies of humans, the aerial bodies of demons; or perhaps only human bodies together with spirits, while demons, spirits clinging without bodies, undergo punishment—not by receiving life—from corporeal fires. For why should we not say that, by modes wonderful indeed but true, even incorporeal spirits can be afflicted by the punishment of corporeal fire, if the spirits of human beings, themselves certainly incorporeal, could be enclosed in bodily members then and will be able then to be bound inseparably by the chains of their own bodies?

If the incorporeal spirit of a living human being is held in a body, why should not the spirit, though incorporeal, after death also be held by corporeal fire? For we say that the spirit is held by fire in this way: it is in the torment of fire by seeing and feeling. For it suffers fire in the very act by which it sees it; and because it sees itself being burned, it burns. Thus a corporeal thing burns an incorporeal one, when from visible fire invisible heat and pain are drawn, so that an incorporeal mind is tortured even by corporeal flame through corporeal fire. And a little later: Since Truth declares that the rich sinner was condemned to fire, what wise person would deny that the souls of the reprobate are held in flames? [Col. 0589D]

### That the fire of Gehenna will in one respect give light and in another not give light. Gregory, *Morals*, on the same matter

That avenging flame has the burning of vices, but does not have light. There fire does not shine for consolation, [Col. 0590A] yet, in order to torment more, it does in one respect shine. For, with the flame giving light, the reprobate will see in torment those who followed them, with whom, while alive, they sinned through love, so that the sight of those whose life they had carnally loved contrary to the Creator’s commands may also afflict them by increasing their damnation. Just as fire knows how to burn for the consolation of the elect, yet does not know how to burn for punishment, so conversely the flame of Gehenna neither shines for the reprobate unto the grace of consolation, nor yet fails to shine for punishment: so that the fire of punishment may gleam before the eyes of the damned with no brightness, and, for the increase of their pain, show the elect how the damned are being tortured.

### That the fire of Gehenna was created from the beginning so as to need no fuel. The same author, in the same work

The justice of the Almighty, foreknowing future things, created from the very origin of the world the fire of Gehenna, which would begin to exist once in the punishment of the reprobate but would never end its burning, even without wood. For corporeal fire, in order to be fire, needs corporeal fuel; and since it must be preserved by piled-up wood, it is doubtless nourished thereby, and can exist only if kindled and continue only if replenished. In contrast, the fire of Gehenna, though corporeal and physically burning all the reprobate, is neither kindled by human effort nor nourished by wood; having been created once, it endures unquenchably, needs no kindling, and lacks no heat. Therefore it is rightly said of the wicked: “A fire that is not kindled shall devour him” (Job 20). [Col. 0590B]

### What purgatorial punishments are in this life, and what are after it. Augustine, *City of God*

[Col. 0590C]

We confess that in this mortal life there are certain purgatorial punishments—not those by which persons are afflicted whose life is not thereby made better, or rather is made worse; but they are purgatorial for those who, restrained by them, are corrected. All other punishments, whether temporal or everlasting, are imposed, as each person is to be dealt with by divine providence, either for sins in the past or sins in which the person punished still lives, or for the exercise and manifestation of virtues, through human beings and angels, whether good or evil.

Some suffer temporal punishments only in this life, others after death, others both now and then—yet before that most severe and final judgment. But not all who suffer temporal punishments after death will enter the everlasting punishments which will exist after that judgment. For we confess that for some, what is not remitted in this age is remitted in the age to come—that is, lest they be punished by the eternal punishment of the age to come. Very few, however, pay no punishments in this life but only after it. Yet we ourselves have known and heard of some who, however they lived, did not feel even the slightest fever until decrepit old age, although the whole life of mortals is itself a punishment.

For ignorance or lack of skill is no slight punishment, and it is rightly judged so necessary to flee that children are compelled through punishments full of pain to learn skills of every kind or letters; and learning itself, to which they are driven by punishments, is so painful to them that they sometimes prefer to endure the very punishments by which they are compelled to learn rather than to learn. Who would not shudder and choose death if offered the choice of death through punishment or infancy again? Infancy, indeed, because it begins not with laughter but with weeping, somehow prophesies, though ignorant of what evils it has entered, what evils it has entered upon in this light. Zoroaster alone, they report, laughed when he was born. Yet that monstrous laughter foretold nothing good for him. For he is said to have been the inventor of magical arts. Defeated in war by Ninus, king of the Assyrians, he died.

But so great is God’s mercy toward the vessels of mercy that he prepared for glory, that even the first age of a human being—infancy, which lies subject to the flesh without any resistance—and the second, called childhood, in which reason has not yet undertaken battle against vices and lies almost under every vicious delight: if, though it can already speak and therefore appears to have passed infancy, the weakness of its mind is not yet capable of command, and it has received the sacraments of the Mediator, even if it ends its life in those years, having been transferred from the power of darkness into the kingdom of God, it is prepared not merely for no eternal punishments but does not suffer even those purgatorial torments after death. [Col. 0591B] Spiritual rebirth alone is sufficient to prevent after death the harm caused by carnal generation together with death.

But once one has come to the age capable of receiving a command and of being subjected to the rule of law, one must undertake battle against vices and wage it keenly, lest it lead to damnable sins. If vices have not yet been strengthened by the habit of victories, they are more easily conquered and yield. But if they have become accustomed to conquering and ruling, they are conquered only with laborious difficulty. This battle would never exist if human nature had remained, through free will, in the uprightness in which it was made. But now, unhappy because it did not will to possess peace in happiness, it fights against itself unhappily.

Very few are so fortunate that from the first onset of adolescence they commit no damnable sins, whether in disgraceful acts, crimes, or the error of some impious wickedness, but by a great bounty of spirit crush whatever in them might be condemned through carnal delight. Most, however, after receiving the command of the law and first being overcome by prevailing vices, become transgressors of it; from that point they flee to the grace that helps them, so that, having first submitted to God by more bitter repentance and more vigorous battle, they may become conquerors by placing the mind over the flesh. [Col. 0591D]

Whoever therefore desires to escape everlasting punishments must not only be baptized but also justified in Christ, and thus truly pass from the devil to Christ. Nothing in a building is placed before its foundation. Therefore we shall find a person who can be saved through fire only if we first find what it is to have Christ as foundation. If a Christian loves a prostitute and, joining himself to her, becomes one body with her, Christ is no longer his foundation. But if someone loves his wife according to Christ, who can doubt that Christ is in his foundation? But if he loves according to this world, carnally, in the sickness of concupiscence, like the Gentiles who do not know God, even this the Apostle allows by concession—indeed, Christ through the Apostle. Thus such a person can also have Christ in his foundation. For if he sets nothing before such affection and pleasure, although he builds upon it wood, hay, and straw, Christ is the foundation. Therefore he will be saved through fire, because the fire of tribulation burns up the delights of this world and earthly loves which, for the sake of marital union, are indeed not condemnable.

“He who loves father or mother or son or daughter more than me,” says the Lord, “is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10). Yet a person who loves these family ties carnally, but does not set them before Christ the Lord and would rather lack them than Christ, should he be brought to such a point of trial, will be saved through fire; for the pain of their loss must burn him as greatly as love had adhered to them. Thus that building will be ruinous to its builder, because he will not retain what he built upon it and will be tortured by the loss of things whose enjoyment had certainly made him glad. [Col. 0592B]

See in the Apostle’s words one person building upon the foundation precious stones, gold, and silver (1 Cor. 3): “He who is without a wife,” he says, “thinks of the things of God, how he may please God” (1 Cor. 7). See another building wood, hay, and straw (1 Cor. 3): “But he who is joined in marriage,” he says, “thinks of the things of the world, how he may please his wife” (1 Cor. 6). “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous persons” (Ecclus. 27); and “the fire will test what sort of work each person’s work is” (1 Cor. 3). “If anyone’s work remains” (1 Cor. 3)—for what remains is that one thinks of the things of God, how one may please God (1 Cor. 7)—“he will receive a reward” (1 Cor. 3), that is, from what he thought upon, that he will receive. “If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss” (ibid.), because he will not possess what he loved; “but he himself will be saved” (ibid.), because no tribulation has moved him from the firm stability of that foundation—yet “as through fire” (ibid.). For what he did not possess without alluring love, he does not lose without burning pain.

Behold, so far as it seems to me, the fire has been found which damns none of them, enriches one, causes the other loss, and tests both. He held that there would be no punishments after death except purgatorial ones, since air, water, and fire are elements above the earth. By one of these, that which has been contracted through earthly thought is cleansed through expiatory punishments. Hence the Gentile poet:

> [lacuna]  
> Others are spread out, empty,  
> suspended to the winds; others beneath the vast flood  
> have their foul guilt washed away, or are burned by fire.  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid*, VI.740 ff.

For they think it unjust that a person should be damned to eternal punishment for sins, however great, committed in a brief period, as though any justice anywhere took account that anyone should be punished for as long a period as that in which he committed what merited punishment. Must someone be judged worthy to remain in chains for as long as he did what deserved that he be bound, when a slave may most justly suffer punishments of many years in fetters because, in a word or blow that passed with utmost speed, he either provoked his master or struck him? [Col. 0593A]

Therefore what the Lord said through his prophet concerning the everlasting punishment of the damned will indeed happen: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66). Some wish both fire and worm to belong to the punishments of the soul rather than the body, because it is written: “As moth to a garment and worm to wood, so grief torments a man’s heart” (Prov. 25). But those who do not doubt that in that punishment there will be penalties both of soul and body affirm that the body is burned by fire, while the soul is, as it were, gnawed by the worm of grief. This is said more plausibly, since it is certainly absurd that there should be no pain there either of body or soul. Yet I think it easier to say that both belong to the body than that neither does.

For in the Old Scriptures one reads: “The vengeance upon the flesh of the wicked is worm and fire” (Ecclus. 7). It could have been said more briefly, “the vengeance of the wicked.” Why then is it said, “upon the flesh of the wicked,” unless both—that is, worm and fire—will be punishment of the flesh? “How then,” they ask, “is what our Christ said true: ‘In whatever measure you have measured, it shall be measured to you again’” (Mark 4), “if a temporal sin is punished by everlasting punishment?” They do not observe that “the same measure” was spoken not because of an equal span of time but because of reciprocity of evil: that one who has done evil should suffer evil. For the Lord was speaking about judgments and condemnations. Therefore one who judges and condemns unjustly, if judged and condemned justly, receives in the same measure, although not the very thing he gave. For he acted by judgment and suffers by judgment; though by condemnation he did what was unjust, he suffers what is just. [Col. 0593C] Nor is there anyone who thinks that the torments of wrongdoers ought to end as quickly as murder, adultery, sacrilege, or any other crime was committed; they are to be measured not by the length of time but by the magnitude of injustice and impiety.

## Chapter VI. On the care to be given for the dead, from Augustine’s *Enchiridion*

It must not be denied that the souls of the departed are relieved by the piety of their living relatives, when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them or alms are given in the Church. But these things benefit those who, while living, merited that they could benefit them. There is a certain manner of life neither so good that it does not require these things after death, nor so bad that these things do not benefit it after death. There is one kind of person so good that he does not require them; and another so bad that, once he has passed from this life, he cannot be helped even if he has them. Accordingly, every merit is acquired by which someone may be relieved or burdened after this life. Let no one hope, once dead, to merit from God what he neglected here.

Therefore those rites which the Church regularly performs in commending the departed are not contrary to that apostolic statement which says: [Col. 0594A] “For we must all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5). For each person acquired, while living in the body, even this merit: that these things might be able to benefit him. For they do not benefit everyone. And why not everyone, except because of the difference in the life each person lived in the body? Therefore, when sacrifices, whether of the altar or of any alms, are offered for all baptized dead, they are thanksgivings for the very good; propitiations for those not very bad; and, for the very bad, even if they are no help to the dead, they are consolations of some kind to the living. But for those whom they benefit, they benefit either so that there may be true remission, or at least so that the condemnation itself may become more tolerable.

## Chapter VII. Whom it benefits after death, or how that which is done for them benefits them. Augustine, *City of God*

[Col. 0594B]

There is, then, a certain manner of life not so bad that the generosity of almsgiving does nothing for those who live in it toward attaining the kingdom of heaven—almsgiving by which even the poverty of the righteous is sustained. Such persons make friends who may receive them into eternal dwellings. Nor is it so good that almsgiving itself suffices them for attaining such blessedness, unless through the merits of those whom they made friends they obtain mercy.

I am accustomed to wonder that this saying is found even in Virgil, where the Lord says: “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of unrighteousness, that they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). For when that poet described the Elysian fields, where they think the souls of the blessed dwell, he placed there not only those who could reach those abodes by their own merits, but added and said:

> And those who, mindful of themselves, made others mindful by deserving them.  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid*, VI.664.

That is, those who gained others’ favor and, by gaining it, made them mindful of themselves. It is exactly as though those words were spoken to them which are often on Christian lips when a humble person commends himself to one of the saints and says, “Remember me,” and makes this possible by gaining such remembrance. But what that manner of life is, and what those sins are which so impede entry into the kingdom of God that sinners nevertheless obtain pardon through the merits of saintly friends, is exceedingly difficult to discover and most dangerous to define. Certainly, up to this time, though I have labored to trace them out, I have been unable to reach their discovery. But while the measure of venial iniquity, even if it persists, remains unknown, surely greater diligence is applied—by prayer, persistence, and watchfulness—to progress toward better things, and the care of making holy friends from the mammon of unrighteousness is not despised. Yet this liberation, whether through one’s own prayers or through the intercession of saints, accomplishes this: that one is not sent into eternal fire, not that, once sent there, one may be extracted after however long a time. [Col. 0594D]

### On the same subject, the same author in Book II

Let us not think that anything reaches the dead for whom we care except what we solemnly request for them by sacrifices of the altar, prayers, or alms. Even these do not benefit all for whom they are made, but only those for whom it was acquired while they lived that they might benefit. But because we do not discern who they are, these things ought to be done for all the baptized, so that none of those to whom these benefits can and ought to reach may be omitted. For it is better that these things be superfluous for those whom they neither harm nor help than that they be lacking for those whom they help. Yet everyone performs this more carefully for his own close relations, so that it may likewise be done for him by his own.

Whatever is bestowed upon the human body is not an aid to salvation but an office of humanity, according to that affection by which no one ever hates his own flesh. Therefore one who can ought to care for the body of a neighbor when the one who used to care for it has departed from it. [Col. 0595B]

## Chapter VIII. On funerals. The same author, in the same work, Book I

The care of the funeral, the condition of burial, and the pomp of obsequies are consolations for the living rather than assistance for the dead. If an expensive burial benefits the wicked, a cheap burial, or none at all, will harm the godly. A splendid funeral in the sight of human beings was provided for that rich man clothed in purple by a crowd of servants; but a far more glorious service was supplied in the sight of the Lord for that ulcer-covered poor man by the ministry of angels, who carried him not to a marble tomb but to Abraham’s bosom.

## Chapter IX. On sacrifice for the departed. Gregory, *Dialogues*

If faults are not beyond release after death, the sacred offering of the saving victim is accustomed to help many souls even after death. [Col. 0595C]

## Chapter X. Whom it benefits. The same author, in the same work
Sacred offerings for the dead, however, must be understood to benefit those who, by living well here, obtained that the good things done here for them by others might aid them even after death. For this sacrifice alone saves the soul from eternal destruction, since it represents to us the death of the Only-begotten. Although, having risen from the dead, he now dies no more and death no longer has dominion over him (Rom. 6), yet, living in himself immortally and incorruptibly, he is again sacrificed for us in this mystery of the sacred offering. For there his body is received; his flesh is distributed for the salvation of the people; his blood is poured out not into the hands of unbelievers but into the mouths of the faithful. [Col. 0595D] Let us therefore consider what kind of sacrifice this is for us: one which, as our offering, continually imitates the passion of the Only-begotten Son. For what believer can doubt that, at the very hour of immolation, at the priest’s voice, heaven is opened [Note: [Col. 0595] He speaks of communion from the chalice according to the custom of that period.]; that choirs of angels are present in that mystery of Jesus; that the lowest things are joined to the highest, earthly things to heavenly, and visible things to invisible, all becoming one?

### CHAPTER XI. Whether souls know what takes place in this world

Some ask concerning souls released from the flesh whether they know what occurs in this life, especially those who already rejoice in the joy of their Lord and in the hidden place of his countenance, illumined by the true light. They also add the question concerning the souls of the saints which many raise: whether they hear the prayers of suppliants, and, when invoked to intercede, whether the petitions of those who ask reach [Col. 0596B] their knowledge.

It is difficult to judge such matters. For how can our knowledge be certain about those whose knowledge of us we can neither grasp nor investigate? This one thing is certain: souls of the saints, established in the secret place of divine contemplation, know of outward events only as much as is evidently useful either for their joy or for our help.

We seek intercessors with God. What more do you want? Are you afraid that perhaps those who always pray do not pray? How will they not pray for you when you pray, since, even when you do not pray, they nevertheless do not cease from praying? “But,” you say, “they do not hear, and I pour words into the wind, speaking to those who neither hear nor understand.” Very well, let us say it: the saints do not hear the words of petitioners, nor does it belong to their blessedness to know what occurs outside. Very well, let us say it: they do not hear. Does God not hear? Why then do you labor to investigate what the saints whom you pray to hear, and how much they hear, when God himself hears for whose sake you pray? He sees your humility, and he will reward your devotion.

Yet, if they hear, and to whatever extent they hear, what is hearing but knowing? For there is one light in which they hear so as to perceive, and see so as to know. If perhaps something occurring outside is for the time being neither heard nor seen by them, that is a mystery of divine dispensation, not a defect of blessedness. Yet some of the holy Fathers are found to have said certain things as though there were nothing in creation which those who see him who sees all things do not see. I do not presume to judge further [Col. 0596D] than this alone: they see as much as pleases him whom they see, and in whom they see.

## SEVENTEENTH PART. ON THE END OF THE WORLD

[Col. 0597]

### CHAPTER I. On the time of Christ’s coming at the end, Augustine to Hesychius

[Col. 0597A]

Concerning the Savior’s coming, awaited at the end, I do not dare to calculate times; nor do I think that any prophet fixed a number of years in this matter. Rather, the saying of the Lord himself prevails: “No one can know the times which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1). Therefore to calculate times—that is, *chronous*, χρόνους—so that we may know when the end of this age or the coming of the Lord will be, seems to me nothing other than wishing to know what he himself said no one can know.

The occasion of that time certainly will not come before the Gospel has been preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations. For the Savior’s very clear declaration on this subject is read: “This Gospel of the kingdom shall be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations. Then the end shall come” (Matt. 24). What does “then the end shall come” mean except “it shall not come before then”? How long afterward it will come is uncertain to us. Yet we certainly ought not to doubt that it will not come before then. If, therefore, it is hidden when, as the Church bears fruit and grows, the whole world from sea to sea will be filled, then without doubt it is hidden when the end will be. For it will not be before that. Then that lawless one, that is, Antichrist, will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus Christ will slay with the breath of his mouth (2 Thess. 2).

### CHAPTER II. On the final tribulation, Augustine, *The City of God*

Then Satan shall be released from his prison and shall go out [Col. 0597C] to deceive the nations which are in the four corners of the earth: Gog and Magog. We have learned that the interpretation of their names is: Gog, “a roof”; Magog, “from a roof,” as though the one were a house and the other proceeded from the house. Thus they are the nations in which we previously understood the devil as enclosed, as it were, in an abyss; and he himself, in a manner, rises and proceeds from them, so that they are the roof and he is from the roof.

### CHAPTER III. Why the devil is bound now

The binding of the devil consists in his not being permitted to employ the whole temptation that he can: either by force, coercing people violently into his own party, or by deceit, fraudulently misleading them. If this were permitted over so long a period and amid the great weakness of so many, he would cast down many such persons as God does not wish to be subjected to this, even among the faithful, and would prevent them from believing. He is bound lest he do this.

For he will be released when the time is also short. For it is read that for three years and six months he will rage with all his own strength and that of his followers; and those with whom he must wage war will be such that they cannot be overcome by so great an onslaught and snares of his. Satan will be released at the end of the age so that the city of God, with immense glory to its Redeemer, Helper, and Deliverer, may behold how mighty an adversary it has overcome. [Col. 0598A]

### CHAPTER IV. Why he will be released at the end

As has been said, Satan will go out into open persecution; he will burst forth from the hiding places of hatreds. For this will be the final persecution, with the final judgment imminent, which the holy Church will suffer throughout the whole world: namely, the whole city of Christ from the whole city of the devil, however great each may be, both upon the earth. Hence the Apostle says: “The love of many shall grow cold, and iniquity shall abound” (Matt. 24). Hence Daniel says: “There shall be a time of tribulation such as has not been since a nation was born upon the earth, until that time” (Dan. 12).

### CHAPTER V. How long the final tribulation will last

[Col. 0598B]

This final persecution, to be brought by Antichrist, will last three years and six months. For Christ will not come to judge the living and the dead unless his adversary Antichrist has first come to deceive those dead in soul, whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth [the printed text reads *cris sui*, evidently for *oris sui*] (2 Thess. 2).

### CHAPTER VI. On the coming of Elijah and Enoch

Then Elijah the Tishbite will come before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes; he will turn the heart of the father toward the son and the heart of a person toward his neighbor, lest, when I come, I strike the earth utterly (Mal. 4). It is a very widely held belief in the utterances and hearts of the faithful that through this great and marvelous prophet Elijah, and with the Law set before them, the Jews will believe in the true Christ, that is, in our Christ, in the last time before judgment.

For he is rightly expected to come before the coming of the Savior as Judge, since he is also rightly believed still to be alive. For he was taken away from human affairs in a fiery chariot, as Holy Scripture most plainly testifies (4 Kings [2 Kings] 2). When he comes, by expounding spiritually the Law which the Jews now understand carnally, he will turn the heart of the father toward the son—that is, the hearts of the fathers toward their sons. Thus the hearts of the fathers will be turned toward their sons when the understanding of the fathers is brought to the understanding of the sons; and the hearts of the sons toward their fathers when these also assent to what those understood.

### CHAPTER VII. On the character of the Judge’s person, Augustine, *On the Trinity*

[Col. 0598D]

“When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all his angels with him, then all nations shall be gathered before him” (Matt. 25). Indeed, the Jews who persist in wickedness and are to be punished in that judgment shall, as is written elsewhere, “look upon him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12; John 19; Rev. 1). Since both good and evil persons will see the Judge of the living and the dead, the evil undoubtedly will be able to see him only [Col. 0599A] according to the form in which he is the Son of Man. Yet they will see him in the splendor in which he will judge, not in the humility in which he was judged. For Christ will not again be seen upon the cross.

Moreover, the ungodly certainly shall not see that form of God in which he is equal to the Father, for they are not pure in heart: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). Otherwise, if the Son of God as Judge appears even to the ungodly in the form in which he is equal to the Father, what is the meaning of his great promise to the one who loves him: “I will love him and will manifest myself to him” (John 14 [the citation is printed “IV”])?

Accordingly, the Son of Man will judge, yet not by human power, but by that power by which he is the Son of God. Again, the Son of God will judge, yet not appearing in that form in which he is God [Col. 0599B] equal to the Father, but in that in which he is the Son of Man. Therefore both statements may be made: the Son of Man will judge, and the Son of Man will not judge. The Son of Man will judge, so that what he said is true: “When the Son of Man comes, then all nations shall be gathered before him.” And the Son of Man will not judge, so that what he said is true: “I do not judge, and I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges” (John 8).

For, insofar as at the judgment not the form of God but the form of the Son of Man will appear, the Father himself will not judge. In this sense it was said: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). But in the sense in which it is said, “The Father gave the Son to have life in himself” (ibid.), it certainly is not said that the Father judges no one. For insofar as the Father begot the Son as his equal, he judges with him.

Thus it was said because at the judgment not the form of God but the form of the Son of Man will appear—not because he who gave all judgment to the Son will not judge, though the Son says of him, “There is one who seeks and judges”; but it was said, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,” as though it were said: no one will see the Father in the judgment of the living and the dead, but all will see the Son, because he is also the Son of Man and can be seen by the ungodly, since they too shall see him whom they pierced.

Therefore he gave all judgment to the Son because the Judge will appear in the form of the Son of Man—a form that is not the Father’s but the Son’s; nor that form of the Son in which he is equal to the Father, but that in which he is less than the Father—so that he may be visible in the judgment to both good and evil. [Col. 0599D] When the evil see the Judge, he will not seem good to them, because they will not rejoice in heart toward him; rather, then all tribes of the earth shall mourn (Matt. 24). This vision of the Son of Man will be neither a good for all the evil and unbelieving, who will be sent into eternal fire, nor the highest good for the righteous. For he still calls the righteous to the kingdom prepared for them from the beginning of the world.

For just as he will say to the former, “Depart into eternal fire” (Matt. 25), so he will say to the latter, “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you” (ibid.). And as those will go into eternal burning, so the righteous into eternal life. But what is eternal life except, as he says, “that they may know you, the one living God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17)? Yet this will be in that glory of which he says to the Father: “which I had with you before the world was made” (ibid.). Then he will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father, so that the good servant may enter into the joy of his Lord. [Col. 0600A]

### CHAPTER VIII. On the swiftness of judgment, Augustine to Consentius

The Apostle says, “in an atom,” that is, in a point of time which cannot be divided, “in the twinkling of an eye”; that is, with the utmost swiftness, and “at the last trumpet,” that is, at the final sign which will be given in order that these things may be completed. “For,” he says, “the trumpet will sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Cor. 15).

This change must undoubtedly be understood as a change for the better, because all, both righteous and unrighteous, will rise. But, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Those who have done good [shall rise] to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5), calling judgment eternal punishment, as he says elsewhere: “He who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3).

Accordingly, those who rise for judgment will not be changed into that incorruptibility which can suffer neither the punishment of pain nor corruption. That belongs to the faithful and the saints. But these persons will be tortured by everlasting condemnation, because “their fire shall not be quenched and their worm shall not die” (Isa. 66). Thus they shall indeed rise incorruptible in the completeness of their limbs, yet subject to corruption through the pain of punishments when they hear: “Depart into eternal fire, prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). From hearing this evil report the righteous person shall not fear.

### CHAPTER IX. On the same subject

[Col. 0600C]

Just as the ray of our eye does not reach nearer things more swiftly and farther things more slowly, but reaches both distances with equal speed, so, since the resurrection of the dead takes place in the twinkling of an eye, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 15), it is equally easy for the omnipotence and ineffable command of God to raise bodies recently dead and bodies dissolved over a long period of time.

### CHAPTER X. On the same subject

The judgment, at the Lord’s unexpected coming itself, will be exceedingly swift, though it was thought most prolonged, because he will convict consciences themselves without a lengthy discourse. For “the questioning of the ungodly shall be in their thoughts,” as it is written (Wis. 1). And the Apostle says: “Their thoughts accusing or else excusing them on the day when God will judge the secrets of human beings according to my Gospel, through Jesus Christ” (Rom. 2). Thus the Lord must also be understood to be a swift witness, since without delay he will call back to memory the things by which he convicts and punishes the conscience. [Col. 0600D]

### CHAPTER XI. On the order of rising

The prophet Isaiah says: “The dead shall rise, and those who were in the tombs shall rise” (Isa. 26). Hence the Apostle says: “The Lord himself, at the command, at the voice of the archangel, and at the trumpet of God, shall descend from heaven; and the dead who are in Christ shall rise first. Then we who are alive and remain shall together be caught up with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air. And so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4).

These apostolic words very plainly show that the resurrection [Col. 0601A] of the dead will occur when Christ comes to judge the living and the dead. But it is commonly asked whether those whom Christ will find alive here—whose persons the Apostle represented in himself and in those then living with him—will never die at all, or whether, in the very instant of time in which they are caught up with the risen in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, they will pass through death to immortality with marvelous swiftness.

Therefore, if we believe that the saints who will be found alive at Christ’s coming and caught up to meet him will depart from mortal bodies in that same rapture and immediately return to the same bodies now immortal, we shall suffer no difficulty in the Apostle’s words—whether where he says, “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies” (1 Cor. 15), or where he says, “We shall all rise,” or “we shall all sleep” (ibid.). For neither will they be made alive through immortality unless, however briefly, they first die; and thus they will not be excluded from resurrection, which is preceded by sleep, however very brief, yet not nonexistent. [Col. 0601B]

### CHAPTER XII. How the statement “He will judge the living and the dead” is to be understood

That he will judge the living and the dead is understood in two ways. Either by “the living” we mean those whom his coming will find not yet dead but still living in this flesh, and by “the dead” those who departed, or will depart, from the body before he comes. Or else by “the living” we mean the righteous and by “the dead” the unrighteous, since the righteous will judge and the unrighteous will be judged.

### CHAPTER XIII. On the resurrection of bodies: how and of what kind they will rise

[Col. 0601C]

There are some who, considering that the spirit is separated from the flesh, that flesh turns to decay, decay is reduced to dust, and dust dissolves into the elements so as no longer to be seen by human eyes, despair that resurrection can occur. When they look upon dry bones, they distrust that these can again be clothed with flesh and flourish back into life. Since they do not hold the faith of resurrection through obedience, they should at least hold it through reason.

For what does the world daily imitate in the elements except our resurrection? At every daily moment even this temporal light seems to die, when, with the coming darkness of night, what was seen is withdrawn; and it seems daily to rise again when, night having been put down, the light removed from our eyes is restored. In the course of the seasons we see trees lose the greenness of their leaves and cease producing fruit. Yet behold: as if a resurrection were suddenly arriving from a withered tree, we see leaves burst forth, fruit grow large, and the whole tree clothed in renewed beauty.

But behold, I hear of resurrection; yet I seek the manner of that resurrection. I believe that I shall rise, but I wish to hear in what condition. I need to know whether I shall rise in some other body, perhaps subtle or aerial, or in the body in which I now remain. But if I rise in an aerial body, I shall no longer be the one who rises. For how [Col. 0602A] can there be a true resurrection if true flesh cannot exist? Clear reasoning therefore shows that, if there is not true flesh, there will undoubtedly not be a true resurrection. A resurrection cannot rightly be called such where that which fell does not rise.

Thus also our Redeemer, to disciples doubting his resurrection, showed them his hands and side, and offered them bones and flesh to touch, saying: “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24). Now, concerning the resurrection of the flesh—not such as that of certain persons who rose and then died again, but unto eternal life, like Christ’s own resurrection—I do not find how I may argue briefly and satisfy every question commonly raised concerning it.

Yet a Christian ought by no means to doubt that the flesh of all who have been born, are born, have died, and will die, shall rise. The first question that occurs concerns aborted fetuses, which have indeed been born in their mothers’ wombs, but not yet so born that they can be born again. If we say that those already formed in some fashion will rise, what is said can be tolerated. But who would not more readily suppose that unformed abortions perish, like seeds which have not been conceived? Yet who would dare to deny—or, though not daring to affirm, deny—that the resurrection will accomplish this: whatever was lacking in form will be supplied, and thus just as defects which came with time will not remain, so nature will not be deprived of what fitting and appropriate days would have brought, nor disfigured by what hostile and contrary days have brought; rather, what was not yet present will be completed, and what had not yet been damaged will be restored whole. [Col. 0602C]

### CHAPTER XIV. Whether aborted fetuses and monsters will rise, and in what condition

Concerning this matter, it is commonly asked with the greatest scrupulousness among the most learned, and it can be debated; but whether it can be discovered by a human being, I do not know. When does a human being begin to live in the womb? Is there some hidden life which has not yet shown itself in the movements of a living being?

For it seems the height of impudence to deny life to fetuses which, for that reason, are cut up limb by limb and expelled from the wombs of pregnant women, lest, if they remain dead there, they also kill the mother. [Col. 0602D] From the moment a human being begins to live, from that moment he can also die. But I cannot find how anyone who has died, wherever death may have overtaken him, should not belong to the resurrection of the dead.

Nor will the so-called monsters who are born and live, even if they die very quickly, be denied resurrection; nor should they be believed to rise deformed, but rather with nature corrected and amended. Far be it from us to suppose that the double-limbed person recently born in the East—concerning whom beloved brothers who saw him have reported, and concerning whom the blessed presbyter Jerome left a written account—will rise as one doubled human being rather than as two human beings, as would have happened had twins been born!

So too all other births which are called monstrous because each individual birth possesses something more or less than usual in excessive deformity will, in the resurrection, be recalled to the form of human nature. Each will possess its own body; none of those born joined together will remain joined, but each will bear separately its own limbs, through which the completeness of the human body is achieved. [Col. 0603A]

Earthly matter, from which the flesh of mortals is created, is not lost to God. Whether it is dissolved into whatever dust or ashes, escapes into whatever vapors or breezes, is changed into whatever other substance or even into the elements themselves, passes into the food of whatever animals or human beings and is changed into flesh, it will return in an instant of time to that human soul which first animated it so that it might become and grow as a human being. [Col. 0603B]

### CHAPTER XV. On the manner of resurrection

The restoration of all limbs is promised, to be returned and made whole again in an instant of time not only from the earth but also from the most hidden bosom of the other elements into which the dissolved bodies have receded. Therefore that earthly material which becomes a corpse when the soul departs will not be restored at the resurrection in such a way that the parts which dissolve and are changed into the various species and forms of other things must, even though they return to the body from which they dissolved, necessarily return also to the same parts of the body where they once were.

Otherwise, if hair returns to hair—the hair removed by such frequent cutting—and if nails return to nails—the nails removed by the excessive cutting away of the whole nail—there arises an unsightliness in the thoughts of those who do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh. But just as, if a statue of any fusible metal were melted by fire, ground into powder, or fused into a mass, and an artist wished to restore it from that mass to the measure of its former size, it would make no difference to its completeness which particle of the material was returned to each limb of the statue, so long as the whole from which the object had been made was restored; so God, the wonderful and ineffable Craftsman, will restore our flesh from the whole of which it consisted with wonderful and ineffable swiftness.

Nor will it matter for the completeness of the thing whether hairs return to hairs, nails to nails, or whether whatever of these had perished is changed into flesh and assigned to other parts of the body, as the providence of the Craftsman takes care that nothing unbecoming occurs. [Col. 0603D] Nor does it follow that the stature of individual persons rising again will therefore be different because it was different while they lived, or that thin persons will rise with the same thinness and fat persons with the same fatness.

But if it belongs to the Creator’s plan that, in each person’s appearance, individual character and recognizable likeness be preserved, while in the other bodily goods all things are restored equal, then that material will be apportioned in each person so that nothing of it is lost; and he who could make from nothing what he willed will supply what anyone lacked. But if there will be a reasonable inequality among the bodies of those who rise, as there is among the voices that fill out a song, then this will be done for each from the material of his own body in such a way as both to render the human being fit for angelic companies and to introduce nothing unsuitable to their senses. For nothing unbecoming will be there; whatever will be, will be fitting, because it would not be if it were not fitting. [Col. 0604A]

### CHAPTER XVI. An example of the foregoing

For if a human craftsman can melt down a statue which, for some reason, he had made deformed, and render it most beautiful, so that none of its substance but only its deformity perishes; and if something in its former shape stood out unbecomingly and did not agree with the proportionality of its parts, he need not cut it off and separate it from the whole material from which he made it, but can blend and mix all of it so that it produces neither ugliness nor a diminution in size—what should be thought concerning the Almighty?

### CHAPTER XVII. That the bodies of the saints will rise without defect and incorruptible

[Col. 0604B]

Therefore the bodies of the saints shall rise without any defect, without any deformity, just as without any corruption, burden, or difficulty. Their blessedness will be so great that they are called spiritual, although they will undoubtedly be bodies, not spirits. But just as what is now called an animal body is a body and not a soul, so then there will be a spiritual body, though it will still be a body and not a spirit.

Accordingly, in respect of the corruption which now weighs down the soul (Wis. 15), and the vices by which the flesh desires against the spirit (Gal. 5), there will then be not flesh but body, because even heavenly bodies are so called. Hence it is said: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15). And, as though explaining what he had said: “Neither,” he says, “shall corruption possess incorruption” (ibid.). What he first called “flesh and blood,” he afterward called “corruption”; and what he first called “the kingdom of God,” he afterward called “incorruption.”

But in respect of substance there will even then be flesh. Hence after the resurrection Christ’s body was called flesh. Therefore the Apostle says: “An animal body is sown; a spiritual body shall rise” (ibid.), because there will be so great a harmony of flesh and spirit—flesh subject to the life-giving spirit without the support of any need—that nothing in us will resist us. As we shall suffer no one outside us as an enemy, so neither shall we suffer ourselves as enemies within. [Col. 0604C]

### CHAPTER XVIII. That infants will not rise at the stature at which they died

[Col. 0604D]

What, then, shall we say about infants, except that they will not rise in the small bodily stature in which they died? Rather, what would have come to them more slowly in time, they will receive through that marvelous and most swift work of God. For in the Lord’s saying, “Not a hair of your head shall perish” (Luke 21; Acts 27), it is said that what existed will not be lacking; it is not denied that what was lacking will be present.

But the infant who dies lacks the completed size of his body. For an infant lacks perfection—namely, the perfection of bodily magnitude—which, once attained, cannot be increased by further growth in stature. All possess this measure of perfection such that they are conceived and born with it; but they possess it in principle, not in bulk, just as all the limbs already lie hidden in the seed, although even those already born still lack certain things, such as teeth or anything similar.

In this principle, implanted in the bodily matter of each person, what does not yet exist—or rather, what lies hidden—seems already, so to speak, outlined; yet in the passage of time it will be, or rather it will appear. Thus the infant is already either short or tall, who will be short or tall. It remains, then, that each person receive his own measure, such as he had in youth even if he died old, or would have had if he died earlier; so that the bodies of the dead rise neither beyond nor short of youthful form, but at that age of full strength to which we know Christ attained.

For even the most learned persons of this age have determined youth to extend to about thirty years; once its proper span has ended, a person then begins to decline toward the losses of a heavier and more sensuous age. Therefore it was not said “to the measure of the body” or “to the measure of stature,” but “to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4). [Col. 0605B]

### CHAPTER XIX. That all will rise in the same stature which they had, or would have had, at mature—that is, youthful—age

The Apostle’s statement, “predestined to be made conformed to the image of the Son of God” (Rom. 8), can be understood thus: as he was made conformable to us in mortality, so we are made conformable to him in immortality. But if by these words we are warned what form the bodies will have in the resurrection, then, as with that measure, so with this conformity, the point is to be understood not of size but of age.

Therefore all will rise as large in body as they were, or would have been, in youthful age. But if anyone maintains that each person will rise in the bodily condition in which he died, there is no need to contend with him in laborious contradiction. [Col. 0605C]

### CHAPTER XX. Whether the reprobate will rise with defects

But all who are not delivered from that mass of perdition brought about through the first human being by the one mediator between God and human beings will also rise, each with his own flesh, in order to be punished with the devil and his angels. Whether they will rise with the defects and deformities of their bodies—the limbs they bore in a deformed and defective condition—why need we labor to investigate? For we should not be troubled by the uncertain bodily condition or beauty of those whose condemnation will be certain and everlasting.

Nor should it trouble us how their body will be incorruptible if it can suffer pain, or corruptible if it cannot. For there is no true life except where one lives happily, nor true incorruption except where health is not ruined by any pain. But where the unhappy person is not permitted to die and, so to speak, death itself does not die; where perpetual pain does not kill but afflicts, corruption itself does not end: this is called in Holy Scripture the second death (Rev. 20, 21).

Yet neither the first death, by which the soul is compelled to leave its body, nor the second, by which the soul is not permitted to leave its penal body, would have befallen humanity if no one had sinned. Certainly the mildest punishment of all will be that of those who have added no sin beyond the original sin which they inherited; and among those who have added other sins, each person there will endure a more tolerable condemnation insofar as here he has had less iniquity. [Col. 0606A]

### CHAPTER XXI. How earthly bodies will remain in heaven

Some say: earthly bodies must be held on the earth or driven toward the earth by their natural weight, and therefore cannot be in heaven. The first human beings, indeed, were in an earth covered with woods and fruits, which received the name Paradise; and from the weights of the elements they argue as follows. They say that they learned from their teacher Plato that the two greatest and extreme bodies of the world are connected and joined by the two intermediate bodies—namely, air and water.

Therefore, they say, because from here upward earth is first, water second above earth, air third above water, and heaven fourth above air, an earthly body cannot be in heaven. For the elements are balanced by their own weights so as to keep their proper order. Behold the arguments by which human weakness, possessed by vanity, contradicts the omnipotence of God.

What then do so many earthly bodies do in the air, when air is third above earth, unless perhaps he who by the lightness of plumage and wings granted to the earthly bodies of birds that they should be borne through the air will be unable to grant to the immortalized [Col. 0606C] bodies of human beings the power by which they may dwell even in heaven? For although we are accustomed to feel earthly bodies as burdens when carrying them, so that the greater their bulk, the greater their weight, nevertheless the soul bears the members of its flesh more lightly when they are robust in health than when they are emaciated in sickness. And although, to those who carry them, a sound and vigorous person is more burdensome than one thin and diseased, that person himself is more agile in moving and bearing his own body when in good health and possessing greater bulk than when, through plague or famine, he possesses the least strength. So much force, even in possessing earthly bodies, though still corruptible and mortal, belongs not to the weight of bulk but to the measure of their proportion. And who can explain in words [Col. 0606D] how great is the difference between the health which we now name and the future immortality? Philosophers, therefore, do not refute our faith by arguments concerning the weights of bodies. For earth is first from here upward, water second, air third, heaven fourth, in such a way that the nature of the soul is above all. Aristotle indeed called it a fourth body, while Plato called it no body at all. If it were fifth, it would surely be higher than the rest. But if it is no body, it surpasses all the more greatly. What, then, does it do in an earthly body? What does that which is subtler than all things do in this mass? What does that which is lighter than all things do in this weight? What does that which is swifter than all things do in this slowness? Is it then impossible, by virtue of the excellence of this nature, for its body [Col. 0607A] to be raised into heaven? And while the nature of earthly bodies can now at times press souls downward, will souls not be able to raise earthly bodies upward?

Finally, if the order of the elements is so arranged that, according to Plato, the two extremes—that is, fire and earth—are joined by the two middle elements, air and water, and that the former occupy the highest place of heaven, while the latter holds the lowest place as the foundation of the world, and therefore earth cannot be in heaven: why is fire in the earth? For according to this reasoning, these two elements, earth and fire, ought to be in their proper places, the lowest and the highest, so that, just as they are unwilling for that which belongs below to be able to exist above, so that which belongs above could not exist below. Therefore, just as they think that no particle of earth either is or will be in heaven, [Col. 0607B] so we ought to see no particle of fire in the earth. Yet now it is so not only upon the earth but even beneath it, that mountain summits belch it forth; besides the fact that, in human use, we see both that fire exists in the earth and that it is produced from earth, since it is produced from wood and stones, which are unquestionably earthly bodies. Why, then, are they unwilling for us to believe that the nature of earthly bodies, once made incorruptible, will be suited to heaven, just as corruptible fire is now suited to these earthly regions? Therefore, from the weights and order of the elements they establish nothing by which they can prescribe limits to almighty God, preventing him from making our bodies such that they may dwell even in heaven.

## CHAPTER XXII. What the future judgment will be like.

[Col. 0607C] A certain divine power must be understood, by which it will come about that all the works, whether good or evil, of each person are recalled to memory and beheld with marvellous swiftness by the gaze of the mind, so that knowledge may accuse or excuse conscience, and thus all and each may be judged at once. This divine power, undoubtedly, has received the name of a book. For in it, in some manner, whatever is recollected by its doer is read.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That God will use our conscience as a witness in judging us.

When the Judge comes, the conscience of each person will be brought forward for testimony. Then every fault is brought before the eyes, and the mind is tortured over the fires of Gehenna by a fire heavier than its own.

[Col. 0607D] We must often consider what we shall be like on the day of judgment, when we are to be presented before the most pure gaze of the angels and render an account to the eternal Judge from the books of conscience. For once every external proof has been removed, it is certain that on that day the human being himself will be set before himself, his own soul shown to him in the mirror of his heart, and witnesses against it produced not from outside or elsewhere but inwardly, from itself. Not foreign evidence but testimony all too familiar will be added: namely, its own deeds.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How God judges in the present time.

God judges at this time not only universally concerning the race of human beings and demons, so that they are miserable on account of the guilt of the first sins, but also concerning the particular deeds which individuals perform [Col. 0608A] by the choice of their will. For we do not know by what judgment of God that man is a good poor person and this man a wicked rich person. One may rejoice whom his ruined character persuades us ought to have been tormented for his own conduct; another may leave court not only unavenged but even condemned, though innocent, either oppressed by the injustice of the judge or overwhelmed by false testimony. Conversely, his criminal adversary may not only go unpunished but may even exult after being vindicated. The impious person may flourish in excellent health, while the pious wastes away with illness; very healthy young men may commit robbery, while those who could injure no one even by a word are afflicted by the terrible severity of various diseases. Infants useful to human affairs may be snatched away by untimely death; and one who seems not even to have deserved birth may, moreover, live very long, full of crimes, be raised to honors, while the darkness of obscurity conceals a blameless person [Col. 0608B]—and other things of this sort.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the same subject.

Now, when not only are good people in adversity and bad people in prosperity—which appears unjust—but often evils also happen to the wicked and good things come to the good, the judgments of God are more inscrutable and his ways unsearchable (Rom. 11). But when we come to that judgment of God which is now called, as the time approaches, the day of judgment and at some point the day of the Lord, not only whatever will then be judged, but also whatever has been judged from the beginning and whatever is to be judged up to that time, will appear altogether just. There it will also become manifest by how just a judgment of God it comes about that now so many, [Col. 0608C] indeed almost all, of God’s just judgments are hidden from the senses and minds of mortals, although in this matter the faith of the pious is not ignorant that what is hidden is just.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the same subject.

Since the divine judgments explaining why in this life things sometimes go badly for good people and well for bad people are exceedingly hidden, they are more hidden still when things go well here for good people and badly for bad people. For when things go badly for the good and well for the evil, perhaps this is discerned: good people, if they have committed any fault, receive their recompense here, so that they may be more fully freed from eternal condemnation; and evil people receive here the good things which they do for this life, so that afterward they may be drawn away to punishments alone. Hence the rich man burning [Col. 0608D] in hell is told: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke 16). But when things go well here for good people and badly for evil people, it is very uncertain whether good people receive their blessings for this reason: that, stimulated by them, they may grow toward something better; or whether they receive here, by a just and hidden judgment, the recompense of their deeds, so that they may be emptied of the rewards of the life to come. Likewise, it is uncertain whether adversities strike evil people so as to preserve them from eternal punishments, or whether their punishment begins here, in order that it may at last be completed in the final torments of Gehenna.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the same subject.

God judges a human being in this life in two ways: either by present evils he begins already to inflict the torments to come, [Col. 0609A] or by present chastisements he extinguishes the torments to come.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Where the saints will be bodily when the world burns.

Someone may perhaps ask: if, after judgment has taken place, this world will burn before a new heaven and a new earth are restored in its place, where will the saints be during the very time of its conflagration, since, having bodies, they must necessarily be in some bodily place? [Col. 0610A] We may answer that they will be in the higher regions, to which the flame of that fire will not rise, just as the waters of the Flood did not rise there. For they will possess bodies such that they will be wherever they wish to be. Yet, having been made immortal and incorruptible, they will not fear the fire of that conflagration, just as the corruptible and mortal bodies of those three men could live unharmed in the burning furnace (Dan. 3).

# EIGHTEENTH PART: ON THE STATE OF THE FUTURE AGE.

[Col. 0609]

## CHAPTER I. On the renewal of the world.

[Col. 0609B]

After those not written in the book of life have been judged and cast into eternal fire—a fire of what kind it will be, and in what part of the world or earth, I suppose no human being knows, unless perhaps the divine Spirit has revealed it—the form of this world will pass away in the conflagration of worldly fires, just as it passed away in the flood of worldly waters. Accordingly, in that worldly conflagration, as he said, the qualities of the corruptible elements, which suited our corruptible bodies, will wholly perish by burning; and the substance itself will possess qualities suited, through a marvellous transformation, to immortal bodies, so that the world, renewed for the better, may plainly be fitted to human beings also renewed for the better in the flesh [Col. 0609C].

## CHAPTER II. What benefit the eternal punishment of the wicked will bring to the good.

The wicked will burn for this purpose: that all the righteous may see in the Lord the joys which they receive and behold in them the punishments which they have escaped, so that they may recognize themselves as all the more enriched forever by divine grace, the more openly they see forever that the evils which they overcame by his help are punished.

## CHAPTER III. That the good will see the wicked, but the wicked not the good; and on the second death.

Those who are in punishments do not know what takes place within, in the joy of the Lord; but those who are in that joy know what takes place outside, in the outer darkness. For death will not be nonexistent but everlasting, when the soul can neither live because it does not possess God nor escape bodily pains by dying. The first death drives the unwilling soul from the body; the second death holds the unwilling soul in the body. Both deaths have this in common: that the soul suffers in its own body what it does not wish.

## CHAPTER IV. That the wicked will live forever in order to die forever.

There the soul, having lost blessedness, has not lost existence. For this reason it is compelled always to suffer death without death, failure without failure, and an end [Col. 0610B] without end, so that for it death may be immortal, failure unfailing, and the end infinite.

## CHAPTER V. That eternal fire will not torment everyone equally.

The dissimilarity of those suffering remains even amid similarity of sufferings; and although under the same torment, strength and vice are not the same. For just as under one fire gold glows while straw smokes; and under the same threshing-sledge stalks are crushed while grain is cleansed; nor is olive dregs mixed with oil because it is pressed by the weight of the same press: so one and the same force, rushing upon them, tests, purges, and refines the good; it condemns, devastates, and destroys the wicked. The difference lies wholly not in the kinds of things suffered, but in the kind of person who suffers.

## CHAPTER VI. On the same subject.

[Col. 0610C] It must by no means be denied that even eternal fire itself, according to the diversity of merits—though all are evil—will be lighter for some and heavier for others, whether its own force and heat vary according to each person’s deserving punishment, or whether it burns equally but is not felt with equal distress.

## CHAPTER VII. On the same subject.

There is indeed one fire of Gehenna, but it does not torment all sinners in one manner. For there each person will feel punishment to the extent that guilt requires. Just as in this world many are placed under one sun, yet they do not all feel the heat of the same sun equally, because one swelters more and another less, so there is not one degree of burning there in one fire; for what diversity of bodies accomplishes here, [Col. 0610D] diversity of sins accomplishes there: they have a fire not unlike, yet it burns each individual differently.

## CHAPTER VIII. How it is just for eternal punishment to be rendered for temporal guilt.

“How then,” they ask, “is what your Christ says true: ‘With the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you’ (Mark 4; Matthew 7), if a temporal sin is punished by eternal punishment?” They fail to observe that “the same measure” was spoken not on account of an equal span of time but on account of reciprocity in evil: that one who has done evil should suffer evil. For the Lord was speaking about judgments and condemnations [Col. 0611A]. Therefore, one who judges and condemns unjustly, if he is judged and condemned justly, receives in the same measure, though not the very thing he gave. For he acted by judgment and suffers by judgment. Though he inflicted condemnation, which is unjust, he undergoes condemnation, which is just. Nor does anyone hold that the torments of offenders ought to end as swiftly as murder, adultery, sacrilege, or any other crime was committed; they are to be measured not by duration of time but by the greatness of wickedness and impiety.

## CHAPTER IX. On the same subject.

Christ says: “With the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you” (Mark 4; Matt. 7)—that is, what you have done, you will suffer. Not that if someone has committed sexual violation, he will suffer sexual violation, [Col. 0611B] but that what he does to the law by this sin, the law will do to him: that is, because he has removed from his own life the law prohibiting such things, the law itself will remove him from the human life which it governs. Likewise: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged. For with the judgment with which you have judged, you shall be judged” (Matt. 7). Will they be judged unjustly if they judge by an unjust judgment? Far from it! For there is no injustice with God. Rather, “With the judgment with which you have judged, you shall be judged” is said as if it were: “By the will with which you have done good, by that same will you are freed; or by the will with which you have done evil, by that same will you are punished.” For right actions and sins are measured by the qualities of wills, not by spans of time. Otherwise it would be considered a greater sin to fell a tree than to kill a human being. The former [Col. 0611C] is done after a long delay, with many blows; the latter with a single blow in a very brief time. In this saying, the same measure applies only to this: what he bestowed is not bestowed upon him. Thus what he is judged for will be eternal, although what he judged could not be eternal. Therefore, eternal punishments will be measured back in the same measure to perpetrators of non-eternal evils, because one who wished to have everlasting enjoyment of sin finds everlasting severity of retribution.

## CHAPTER X. On the same subject.

“I would like to know how it is just for a fault committed with an end to be punished without end.” Gregory: This would be rightly said if the strict Judge weighed human deeds rather than human hearts. For the wicked sinned with an end because they lived with an end. Indeed, had they been able, they would have wished to live without end so that they might be able to sin without end. For those who never cease to sin while they live show that they desire always to live in sin. Therefore, it belongs to the great justice of the Judge that those who were unwilling in this life to be without sin should never be without punishment.

## CHAPTER XI. How the devil is tormented now, and how he will be tormented in the future.

The ancient enemy, bound by the chains of his wickedness, suffers one thing now and will suffer another at the end. For because he fell from the order of inward light, he now confounds himself inwardly in the darkness of horror. But afterward he will be enveloped in bitterness, because punishments not only complete but also infinite are prepared for his pride [Col. 0612A]. This punishment of his plainly begins when the strict Judge comes at the end.

## CHAPTER XII. On the same subject.

For the devil, being exempt from the death of the flesh—a fact by which he proceeds in excessive pride—has a death of another kind prepared for him: in the eternal fire of Tartarus, where spirits may be tormented not only along with earthly bodies but also with aerial bodies.

## CHAPTER XIII. That, after the condemnation of the reprobate, the saints will know God’s grace more fully.

Therefore, once the reprobate angels and human beings remain in eternal punishment, the saints will then know more fully what good grace has conferred upon them.

## CHAPTER XIV. That, when the wicked have been condemned, the saints will enter eternal life.

[Col. 0612B]

For just as he will say to the impious, “Go into eternal fire” (Matt. 25), so to the righteous: “Come, blessed of my Father, take possession,” etc. (ibid.). And just as they will go into eternal burning, so the righteous into eternal life. But what is eternal life except, as he says, “that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17)? Yet it is already in that glory of which he says to the Father, “Which I had with you before the world was made” (ibid.), that he will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father (1 Cor. 15), so that the good servant may enter into the joy of his Lord (Matt. 25).

## CHAPTER XV. How the righteous will then not suffer with the wicked.

And where is the holiness of the saints if they will not pray for their enemies [Col. 0612C] whom they will then see burning, when they were certainly told: “Pray for your enemies” (Matt. 5; Luke 6)? They pray for their enemies during the time when they can turn their hearts to fruitful repentance and save them by that conversion. For what else ought one pray for enemies except what the Apostle says: “That God may grant them repentance unto the knowledge of the truth, and that they may recover themselves from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive to his will” (2 Tim. 2).

### On the same subject.

Let what you say be accepted. But how will prayer then be made for those who can no longer in any way be changed from wickedness to works of righteousness? The same reason, therefore, why prayer will not then be offered for persons condemned to eternal fire [Col. 0612D] is also now the reason why prayer is not offered for the devil and his angels, assigned to eternal punishment. It is also now the reason why holy people do not pray for unbelieving and impious persons who have died: namely, because they shrink from rendering void the merit of their prayer before the sight of the just Judge for those whom they already know to be assigned to eternal punishment. For even now the righteous who live have no compassion for the dead, condemned, and unjust, when they know that they themselves must still undergo something liable to judgment in their own case. How much more strictly, then, will they despise the torments of the wicked, when, stripped of every blemish of corruption, they themselves will already cling more closely and firmly to righteousness. For their minds, through clinging to the altogether just Judge, are absorbed by the force of strict judgment, so that nothing at all which conflicts with the subtle exactness of that eternal rule will please them.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the vision of God.

If you ask whether God can be seen, I answer: he can. If you ask how I know, I answer: because in the most truthful Scripture we read, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). If you ask how he is called invisible if he can be seen, I answer: he is invisible by nature, but can be seen when he wills and as he wills. For he has been seen by many, not as he is, but in whatever form he was pleased to appear.
