What then is the meaning of the statement of the same authority, “No one has ever seen God” (John 1), and of the Apostle’s clearer explanation: “Whom no human being,” he says, [Col. 0613B] “has seen or can see” (1 Tim. 6)? How, then, did Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Job, Moses, Micaiah, Isaiah, and any others of whom the most truthful Scripture testifies that they saw God, see God, if no one has ever seen God, whom no human being has seen or can see? It is a great question how it is not contradictory that so many ancients saw God, if no one has ever seen God, whom no human being has seen or can see.

Certainly, as Ambrose says, it cannot be denied that the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit has been seen—provided that the vision of the Holy Spirit is to be seen in the form chosen by will, not formed by nature. For we have also received the Spirit as seen in a dove. Thus, “No one has ever seen God,” because no one has beheld the fullness of divinity dwelling in God; no one has comprehended it by mind or eyes. Hence Moses said to God, with whom he spoke face to face as a friend with a friend: “If I have found favor before you, show me yourself” (Exod. 33). What then—was he not himself? If he were not himself, Moses would not say to him, “Show me yourself,” but “Show me God.” Yet if Moses saw his nature and substance, he would much less say, “Show me yourself.” Therefore he himself was present in the form in which he had willed to appear; but he did not appear as himself in his proper nature, which Moses desired to see. That vision is promised to the saints in another life. Hence the answer given to Moses is true: no one can see [Col. 0613D] the face of God and live (ibid.), that is, no one living in this life can see him as he is. For many have seen him, but what will chose, not what nature formed.

If you ask how even the criminal Cain saw him, when he was questioned and judged by him concerning his crime, or how the devil himself saw him when he came with the angels to stand before him (Job 1), if “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,” I answer: it does not follow that those who at some time hear voices made by him also see God. For those who heard him say to the Son, “I have glorified and will glorify again” (John 12), did not see him. Nevertheless, it is not surprising if even those not pure in heart sometimes see God in a form made by his will, while his invisible nature remains hidden and immutable in itself. If you ask whether he can also at some time be seen as he is, I answer that this is promised to the children, of whom it is said: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). The question is not how God is seen in the form in which he willed to appear in this age to certain persons, but how he is seen in that kingdom where his children will see him as he is. For then their desire will be satisfied with good things. For the unworthy will not see God, concerning whom it is said: “Let the impious person be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26), and to whom it will also be said: “Go into eternal fire,” etc. (Matt. 25). But God promised that he would show himself to his lovers, one God with the Father, not in the manner [Col. 0614B] in which he was seen in the body in this age by good and bad alike. For at the future judgment, when he will come in the manner in which he was seen going into heaven—that is, in the same form of the Son of Man—the same form will be seen by those to whom he will say, “I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat” (ibid.). For the Jews also will see him whom they pierced (Zech. 12; John 19; Rev. 20), not that form of God in which he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized (Phil. 2). In that form of God, those who will see God as he is will then see him. Yet they will not see him because in this life they were poor in spirit, meek, mourning, and so forth, but because they are pure in heart; for he who is seen neither in a place nor sought by bodily eyes, who is not circumscribed by sight, grasped by touch, heard in speech, or perceived by movement, will be seen by the pure in heart.

## CHAPTER XVII. The difference between seeing and believing.

We say that seeing differs from believing in this: present things are seen; absent things are believed. Perhaps it is enough, certainly, if by “present things” in this place we understand things available to the senses either of soul or body. Hence they are called *present* from the word’s derivation. For just as I see this light by the bodily sense, so I plainly see my own will, because it is available to the senses of my mind and inwardly present to me. But if someone communicates to me his own will, whose mouth and voice are present to me, nevertheless, because the will itself which he communicates to me is hidden from the sense of my body and mind, I believe it; I do not see it. Or, if I think that he is lying, I do not believe it, even if it happens to be as he says.

Therefore, things absent from our senses are believed if the witness who bears testimony to them is considered trustworthy. Yet what I have said—that those things are believed which are absent from our senses—must not be taken to include things we have at some time seen and remember having seen, of which we are certain, although they are not then present when recalled by us. For they are counted not among things believed but among things seen, and therefore are known, not because we have relied on the testimony of others but because we remember and know without doubt that we ourselves have seen them. Thus our knowledge plainly consists of things seen and things believed; but in matters which we see or have seen, we ourselves are witnesses. In matters which we believe, we are moved to faith by other witnesses, when signs are supplied concerning things which we neither remember having seen [Col. 0615A] nor see—whether in spoken words, writing, or any documents whatever—so that, upon seeing the signs, we believe the unseen things.

Nor do we speak without reason of knowing not only things that we have seen or see, but also things which we believe on trustworthy testimony or witnesses. Moreover, if it is not unfitting to say that we know, this results also in our saying that even what we believe is most certain, so that things rightly believed, although not present to our senses, may rightly be said to be seen by the mind. Therefore, when a person is told, “Believe that Christ rose from the dead,” if he believes, consider what he sees, consider what he believes, and distinguish the two. He sees a person from whose hearing he hears a voice; and the voice itself is counted among bodily things seen, according to what we have said above. These are two things: witness and testimony, one belonging to the eyes, the other to the ears. But perhaps the authority of other testimonies confirms this witness for him—namely, the divine Scriptures or any other sources by which he has been moved to faith. Scriptures belong to bodily things seen: to the eyes, if he reads them, or to the ears, if he hears them.

Therefore, whatever I do not show in such a way that it is apprehended and held as seen by a sense of body or mind, yet concerning which I say something that necessarily is either true or false but is not seen in either of those two ways, remains simply to be believed or not believed. But if it is established by the clear authority of the divine Scriptures—namely, those called canonical in the Church—it must be believed without any doubt.

With respect to other witnesses or testimonies by which one is urged to believe something, you may believe or not believe according to the judgment you make as to whether I, who urge these things upon you, have sufficient credibility to produce or possess faith. For if we believed nothing that we have not seen—that is, nothing which we have not perceived by mind or body in present appearance—and had not learned from the holy Scriptures by reading or hearing, how would we know that there are cities where we have never been, or that Rome was founded by Romulus, or, to speak of matters nearer at hand, Constantinople by Constantine? Finally, how would we know who our parents were that brought us forth, from which fathers, grandfathers, and ancestors we were born? Although we know very many such things, we have not learned them as present to any sense, as we know the sun, [Col. 0615D] our own mind’s will, or the authority of canonical utterances—for example, that Adam was the first human being, or that Christ was born in the flesh, suffered, and rose again—but from the reports of others, whose testimony in this particular class of matters we judged ought not to be doubted.

I think that by this introduction of mine you have sufficiently recognized what it is to see by mind or body, and what believing differs from those forms of seeing. Believing is indeed done by the mind and is seen by the mind, because our faith is plain to our mind.

Yet that which is believed by that same faith is absent both from the sight of our body—as the body in which Christ rose is absent—and from the sight of another’s mind—as your faith is absent from the sight of our mind [Col. 0616A]. I believe that it exists in you, although I do not see it with the body, which you also cannot do, nor with the mind, which you can do, just as I can see my own faith and you cannot.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On bodily and spiritual vision in the future.

It is difficult to say that the saints will then have other bodies such that they cannot close and open their eyes when they wish; but it is more difficult to say that anyone there who closes his eyes will not see God.

For if the prophet Elisha, absent in body, saw his servant Gehazi receiving the gifts which Naaman the Syrian gave him (4 Kings 5)—Naaman whom the prophet had cleansed of the disfigurement of leprosy, though the wicked servant had supposed that he did it secretly without his master’s seeing—how much more will the saints, in that spiritual body [Col. 0616B], see all things, not only if they close their eyes, but even things from which they are bodily absent?

## CHAPTER XIX. Whether our thoughts will be changeable there.

Therefore, the word which sounds outwardly is a sign of the word which shines inwardly, and the latter more properly bears the name “word.” For what is uttered by the mouth of flesh is the voice of the word, and it itself is called “word” because of that from which it was assumed in order to appear outwardly. The same author, shortly afterward, in the same work.

Accordingly, that Word of God is so called that the thought of God is not called such, lest something changeable be believed to exist in God—something which now takes on and now receives a form in order to be a word, or which might lose that form and somehow roll about without form. And shortly afterward: Thoughts of God are indeed spoken of also in the Holy Scriptures, but in the same manner of speaking by which the wrath and forgetfulness of God are spoken of, which plainly have no literal propriety in God. And shortly afterward: And then, indeed, in eternal life, our word will not be false, because we shall neither lie nor deceive. Perhaps even our thoughts will not be changeable, going and returning from one thing to another, but we shall behold all knowledge in a single simultaneous view.

Yet even when this shall be—if it shall be—the creature which was capable of being formed will have been formed, so that nothing will any longer be lacking to the form which it ought to attain; but it will not be made equal to that simplicity in which there is not something formable, formed or re-formed, but where the form itself is neither formless nor formed: there is the eternal and immutable substance [Col. 0616D].

## CHAPTER XX. What and how great future happiness and blessedness will be.

How great will be the happiness where no evil exists and no good is hidden? There will be leisure for the praises of God, who will be all in all. The same author, in the same work: Certainly, wherever the spirit wills, there the body will immediately be. Nor will the spirit desire anything unbecoming to either spirit or body. There will be true glory, where no one is praised through the error or flattery of the one praising. True honor, which will be denied to no one worthy and granted to no one unworthy. Yet no one will seek it ambitiously, where none will be permitted to exist except one who is worthy. True peace, where no one will suffer anything adverse, either from himself or from another. The reward of virtue [Col. 0617A] will be he who gave virtue and promised himself, than whom nothing can be better or greater. For what else is the meaning of what he said through the prophet, “I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Jer. 30, 31), except: I shall be that by which they are satisfied; I shall be whatever is honorably desired by all—life, salvation, sustenance, abundance, glory, honor, peace, and every good? Thus also the Apostle’s saying is rightly understood: “That God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15). For he himself will be the end of our desires: he will be seen without end, loved without weariness, and praised without fatigue. This gift, this affection, this activity will certainly be common to all, like eternal life itself.

But who is capable of conceiving, much less of expressing, the degrees of honor and glory which will also belong, according to their merits, to those who are to receive rewards? Yet it must not be doubted that they will exist. And that blessed city will likewise see in itself this great gift: no inferior will envy any superior, just as the other angels do not envy the archangels.

No one will desire to be what he has not received, although he is bound by the most peaceful bond of concord to the one who has received it, just as the eye does not wish to be the finger in the body, although the peaceful unity of the whole part contains both members. Thus one will possess a lesser gift than another, yet will also possess this gift: not to desire more.

## CHAPTER XXI. That true blessedness consists in three things.

There our being will have no death; there our knowing will have no error; there our loving will have no offense.

## CHAPTER XXII. That, in the future, memory of the past will contribute not to the saints’ pain but to their joy.

[Col. 0618A]

There will therefore be in that city one will, common to all and inseparable in each, free from every evil, set free and fulfilled with every good, ceaselessly enjoying the delight of eternal joys; forgetful of faults, forgetful of punishments. Yet not so forgetful of its own deliverance as to be ungrateful to its Deliverer. So far as rational knowledge is concerned, it will remember its past evils; but so far as the feeling of one who has experienced them is concerned, it will be wholly forgetful. For even the most skilled physician knows, as things are known by art, all bodily diseases; but as they are felt in the body, he does not know very many that he has not himself suffered. Thus there are two kinds of knowledge of evils: one by which they are not hidden from the power [Col. 0618B] of the mind; the other by which they cling to the perceptions of one who experiences them. (For all vices are known in one way through the teaching of wisdom, and in another through the utterly wretched life of a fool.) So too there are two kinds of forgetfulness of evils. The learned and educated person forgets them in one way; the person who has experienced and suffered them, in another. The former, if he neglects his skill; the latter, if he is free from misery.

According to this latter kind of forgetfulness, which I mentioned second, the holy will not be mindful of past evils. For they will be free from all evils, so that these are utterly erased from their perceptions; and yet, through the great power of knowledge that will be in them, neither their own past evils nor the everlasting misery of the damned will be hidden from them. There we shall be at rest and see; we shall see and love; we shall love and praise. Behold what there shall be at an end without end.

[Col. 0617]

# FOUR BOOKS ON THE MORAL MEANING OF NOAH’S ARK

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0617] Once, while I was sitting in an assembly of brothers, with them asking questions and myself answering, many matters had been brought forward. At last our discussion came to this point: all together we began to marvel and sigh especially over the instability and restlessness of the human heart. And since they earnestly desired to have shown to them what cause produces such great fluctuations of thought in the human heart, and then to be taught with all seriousness whether some art or exercise of whatever labor might counter so great an evil, we, wishing as far as God’s inspiration enabled us to satisfy the charity of the brothers in both respects, untied the knot of each question by arguments drawn both from authority and from reason.

In that conference, because I know that certain matters were especially pleasing to the brothers, I wished particularly to commit those matters to writing—not only because I judge them worthy to be written, but because I recognized that certain things there, previously unheard, were for that reason more welcome. First, then, it must be shown whence so great a changeableness arises in the human heart; next it must be indicated how the human mind may be restored to stable peace, and how it may be preserved in that stability.

Although I do not doubt that this is properly the work of divine grace, and that it is possessed not so much through human industry as through the divine gift and the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, nevertheless I know that God wills us to cooperate with him. Thus he bestows the gifts of his mercy freely, yet often withdraws even those which he has bestowed from the ungrateful. Moreover, it is not useless to know both the greatness of our infirmity and the manner of restoration; for one who does not know how great a grace has been granted to him does not understand how great thanks he owes to the Giver.

The first human being was created for this purpose: that, had he not sinned, he might always stand before the face of his Creator through the presence of contemplation; that, always seeing him, he might always love him; always loving him, might always cling to him; and always clinging to him who is immortal, might also possess in him life without end. This, therefore, was the one true good of humanity: namely, full and perfect knowledge of its Creator—full according to that fullness which the creature received when created, not according to that which it was to receive after obedience had been accomplished.

But he was cast from the face of the Lord, because, struck by the blindness of ignorance on account of sin, he came out from the inner light of that contemplation. And the more he began to forget the sweetness of heavenly things, of which he had now lost even the taste, the more deeply he bent his mind toward earthly desires. Thus he became a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth: a wanderer through disordered desire, a fugitive through a guilty conscience. To him too the following words aptly apply: “Whoever finds me will kill me” (Gen. IV). For whatever temptation assails a mind deserted by divine help overthrows it.

The human heart, therefore, which formerly, fastened to divine love, remained stable and, loving the One, remained one, after it began to flow away through earthly desires, was, as it were, divided into as many parts as there are things that it desires. Thus it comes about that the mind which does not know how to love the true good can never be stable. Since it finds no end of its desire in the things it embraces, while it always stretches itself out in desire, pursuing what it cannot attain, it never rests. Hence arises motion without stability, toil without rest, running without arrival; so that our heart is always restless until it begins to cling to him, where it may rejoice that nothing is lacking to its desire and trust that the things it loves will always remain.

Behold, we have shown the disease: a wavering heart, an unstable heart, a restless heart; and the cause of the disease, namely love of the world; and the remedy of the disease, love of God. To these a fourth matter must necessarily be added: the attainment of the remedy—that is, how we may reach the love of God, without which it will profit little or nothing to have recognized the rest.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0619]

These are its chapters:

**CHAPTER I.** What difference there is between the love of God and the love of the world; how we may attain the love of God and become his house and dwelling-place. — **CHAPTER II.** That God dwells in the human heart in two ways; that both the dwelling and God who dwells are called by many names; and that the ark is a model of spiritual building. — **CHAPTER III.** The form and dimensions of the ark according to the literal sense. — **CHAPTER IV.** The ark of the Church, or the Church.

## CHAPTER ONE. What, then, the difference is, etc.

[Col. 0619A] Between the love of this world and the love of God there is this difference: the love of this world seems sweet at its beginning, but has a bitter end; whereas the love of God begins in bitterness, but its last things are full of sweetness. The Gospel narrative shows us this by a most beautiful comparison when, singing of the wedding of our Bridegroom, it says: “Every man first sets out the good wine, and when they have become drunk, then that which is inferior; but you have kept the good wine until now” (John II).

For every man—that is, the carnal person—first sets out good wine, because in his own pleasure he feels a certain false sweetness. But after the frenzy of evil desire has intoxicated the mind, he then serves what is worse, because the thorn of conscience which comes upon it cruelly torments the mind that it had formerly delighted falsely. Our Bridegroom, however, offers the good wine last, when he permits the mind which he intends to fill with the sweetness of his love first to be made bitter by a certain compunction of tribulations, so that, after tasting bitterness, it may drink more eagerly the most sweet cup of charity.

And this is “the first sign which Jesus performed before his disciples, and they believed in him” (ibid.). For the sinner and penitent first begins to have confidence in God’s mercy when, after long weariness of grief, he feels his heart opened by the consolation of the Holy Spirit.

Let us therefore seek how we may attain the love of God, because he himself will gather and make stable our hearts; he will restore peace and grant unceasing joy. No one can love what he does not know. Therefore, if we desire to love God, let us first strive to know him—especially since he is such that he cannot be known without being loved. For such is the beauty of his loveliness that one who can see him cannot fail to love him.

A person who wishes to know the character and secrets of another person makes himself familiar with him, spends much time in his house, and associates with those familiar with him. If he sees that the matters surrounding that person are ordered honorably and wisely, he becomes more certain of that person’s virtue and judges him already worthy of love, since he recognizes that he has found such manifest proofs of uprightness.

Let us likewise inquire where God dwells, where his house is; let us ask those familiar with him about him. Is he prudent? Is he faithful? Is he worthy of praise? Is he gracious? Indeed, if he is humble, he is worthy. If he manages the care of his household well, he is prudent. If he does not know how to defraud those who serve him, he is faithful. If he readily spares sinners, he is gracious. If he has compassion on the afflicted, he is merciful. If he governs those subject to him not by oppressing but by helping, he is humble.

But perhaps you ask where this house of God is to be sought, where it may be found. The whole world is God’s house; the Catholic Church is God’s house; every faithful soul is also God’s house. Yet God dwells in the world in one way, in the Church in another, and in each faithful soul in yet another: in the world, as an emperor in a kingdom; in the Church, as a householder in a home; in the soul, as a bridegroom in a bridal chamber.

Pagans and all unbelievers are in his house—that is, in his kingdom—because by the power of his divinity he holds and governs everything that he has created. False believers are in his house—that is, in the Church—because he entrusts participation in his sacraments to all whom he has called to faith. But the faithful are in his house—that is, in the bridal chamber; and, to speak more truly, they themselves are his house, because he possesses and rules them by dwelling in them through love.

We are all in his house by the creation through which he made us; we are in his house by the faith through which he called us into his house; we are in his house by the love through which he justified us. If you are in God’s house only by creation, the devil is there with you. If you are in God’s house only by faith, the chaff is also with the grain on your threshing floor. But if you are in God’s house through charity, you are blessed, because not only are you in God’s house, but you have begun to be God’s house, so that he who made you may dwell with you in you.

This is the saving dwelling; these are the tabernacles of the righteous, in which the voice of joy and exultation always resounds; there dwell the blessed, whose beauty the prophet desired, in which he desired to dwell, for whose longing he burned. If, therefore, this dwelling has begun to exist in us, let us enter and dwell with him. There we shall find peace and rest, where he deigns to dwell, “whose place has been made in peace.” But if it has not yet begun to exist in us, let us build it; for if we prepare a place for him, he will gladly come to us—Jesus Christ our Lord, who made us for this very purpose, that he might dwell in us.

## CHAPTER II. That God dwells in the human heart in two ways; that the dwelling of God and God who dwells are called by many names; and that the ark is a model of spiritual building.

[Col. 0621D] God dwells in the human heart in two ways: through knowledge and through love. Yet there is one dwelling, because everyone who knows also loves, and no one can love who does not know. Nevertheless, there seems to be this difference: knowledge, through the cognition of faith, raises the structure; love, through virtue, paints the building, as though laying color over it. Each is plainly necessary: for a thing cannot shine if it does not exist, nor can it please if it does not shine.

Enter now into the secret place of your heart, and make a dwelling-place for God: make a temple, make a house, make a tabernacle, make an ark of the covenant, make an ark of the flood. Whatever name you give it, it is one house of God. In the temple let the psalmist worship the Creator; in the house let the son venerate the father; in the tabernacle let the soldier honor the king; in the covenant let the follower listen to the teacher; in the flood let the shipwrecked person implore the helmsman.

God has become everything for you, and God has made everything for you. He made a dwelling-place; he became protection. This one thing is the whole, and this whole is one thing: it is God’s house, the city of the King, the body of Christ, the Bride of the Lamb. It is heaven, sun, moon, morning star, dawn, trumpet, mountain, wilderness, promised land, ship, path in the sea, net, vineyard, field, ark, granary, manger, yoke-animal, horse, storehouse, hall, bridal chamber, tower, camp, battle line, people, kingdom, priesthood, flock, shepherd, sheep, pasture, paradise, garden, palm, rose, lily, fountain, river, portico, dove, garment, pearl, crown, scepter, throne, table, bread, spouse, mother, daughter, sister.

And, to conclude more briefly: all Scripture was made concerning this, for this, and because of this. The world was made for this. For this the Word was made flesh: God humble, humanity exalted. Therefore, if you have this, you have everything; if you have everything, there is nothing further for which to wait, and your heart rests.

I shall give you as a model of this spiritual building Noah’s ark, which your outward eye will see, so that your inward mind may be built according to its likeness. You will see there certain colors, forms, and figures that delight the sight. But you must know that these things are placed there so that in them you may learn wisdom, discipline, and virtue, which adorn your mind.

And because this ark signifies the Church, and the Church is the body of Christ, I have painted the whole person of Christ—that is, the head together with the members—in visible form, so that, when you have seen the whole, you may more easily understand what is afterwards said about the part. I wish to portray this person for you as Isaiah testifies that he saw it; and therefore I shall bring forward his very words and draw from them what I wish to show you, so that the prophet may prove what the letter says.

He says, then: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up” (Isa. VI). “High” is that which is situated on high; “lifted up” is that which has been transferred from lower things to higher. The high throne, therefore, is the angelic spirits; the lifted-up throne is the souls of the saints, transferred from the abyss of this world to the joys of heavenly peace. Since God presides over both, he is said to sit upon a throne high and lifted up.

What follows, “The whole earth is full of his majesty” (ibid.), signifies by “earth” every bodily creature, which is full of God’s majesty. For, just as the divine essence presides over spiritual creation through knowledge, so it fills bodily creation by governing and ordering it. Thus what is said elsewhere—“I fill heaven and earth,” and again, “Heaven is my seat, and earth the footstool of my feet” (Isa. LXVI)—is said here: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up”; then, “The whole earth is full of his majesty”; and “those things that were beneath him filled the temple” (Isa. VI).

The temple is the capacity of angelic or human understanding; and this temple is filled by the things beneath him because the immensity of divine works is so great that no creature’s intelligence is sufficient perfectly to comprehend them. Consideration of them fills our heart; their immensity is not comprehended by our heart. How, then, shall we be able to comprehend the Maker of the work, when we cannot fully grasp the work of the Maker itself?

We may also say that this throne, high and lifted up, upon which God sits, is the eternity of divinity, because of him alone it is said: “Who inhabits eternity” (Isa. LVII). This does not mean that God is one thing and his eternity another, but because the throne belongs to those who reign, he is rightly said to sit upon the throne of eternity: just as neither beginning nor end is found in his essence, so neither is either found in his omnipotence. He has always been; he has always been omnipotent; he has always been full and perfect in himself and from himself, yet not overflowing beyond measure.

Let him therefore say: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up,” because the power of divinity precedes every creature in eternity, surpasses it in dignity, and orders it by power. It follows: “And those things which were beneath him filled the temple.” In this place the temple can be understood as the course of times and the circuit of ages. For times, as they return into themselves in their course, trace out, as it were, a certain circuit of a temple by revolving.

What, then, does he say: “Those things which were beneath him filled the temple”? It is to be understood thus: all the times of the ages are full of God’s works, and every generation tells his wonders. Or it may be read thus: “Those things which filled the temple were beneath him,” because whatever revolves in time is found within and beneath eternity. The immensity of eternity encloses temporal narrownesses within itself, because that which never began is before time; that which knows no end is after time; and that which has not admitted change is above time.

“Seraphim stood above it” (Isa. VI). The two seraphim are the two Testaments. And fittingly, seraphim, which is interpreted “burning,” signifies divine Scripture, which causes those whom it first illumines through knowledge afterwards to burn strongly through love. For while it shows our mind what it ought to desire, it first illumines it and then makes it burn. Thus it burns because it makes others burn, just as elsewhere it is said to shine because it illumines. Of it the apostle Peter says: “We have a more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawn and the morning star arise in your hearts” (II Pet. I).

Perhaps, according to this manner in which the very Scripture is customarily credited with what it accomplishes in the hearts of its hearers, it is said: “The seraphim stood above it.” For it rises when it raises us; it walks when it enables us to advance; it stands when it establishes us in good resolve.

But we must inquire why God is said to sit upon the throne, while the seraphim are reported not to sit upon the throne but to stand. Since above we interpreted this throne in two ways, we must adapt our exposition to each interpretation. If, therefore, we understand the throne of God to mean spiritual creatures, God is rightly described as sitting upon the throne, because the dignity of divinity, being above all things, neither advances in power nor grows in wisdom—since fullness cannot be increased—nor can eternity be changed.

But whenever the human mind, illumined through knowledge of sacred Scripture, is raised up to contemplate heavenly things and has advanced, transcending even the choirs of angels, as far as the presence of its Creator, it indeed ascends above the throne; but it stands and does not sit, because it comes there by advancing through labor, where it had no capacity by nature to remain. Standing belongs to one who labors; sitting, to one who rests. Therefore we stand above the throne; God sits, because we begin by grace to be where he is by nature.

Likewise, if by the throne we understand God’s eternity, we stand above the throne because we can attain his immortality only through the labor of death; and we who by creation are liable to an end are made heirs of eternity by adoption.

“Six wings to one, and six wings to the other” (Isa. VI): that is, each had six wings, which, joined two by two, make three pairs of wings. Each with two wings covers its own body, not the Lord’s: this is the first pair. Each extends two: one to cover the head, not its own but the Lord’s; the other to cover the feet, not its own but the Lord’s: this is the second pair. Each with two flies toward the other: this is the third pair.

If, then, the seraphim signify sacred Scripture, the three pairs of wings are the three senses of the same Scripture: history, allegory, and tropology. Each is twofold because each kindles the souls of readers to love of God and neighbor. The two wings that cover the body of the seraphim are history, which conceals mystical meanings beneath the veil of the letter. The two wings extended to the head and feet of the Lord are allegory, because, when we learn the mystical meanings of divine Scripture, we penetrate by illumination of mind as far as the knowledge of his divinity, which is before all things and after all things.

But one must know that the extended wings reach to the head and feet, yet, touching both, cover them. For whenever we are carried away in ecstasy of mind to contemplate his eternity, we find in him neither beginning nor end. By this same wing we cover his head from ourselves, because we cannot comprehend how there is no beginning in him. We extend a wing to the feet when we consider that he is after all things not in time but in eternity; but we cover the feet because we find no end in him. Thus, by touching his head and feet, we cover them: the more the human mind strives to investigate his eternity, the more it marvels that it is incomprehensible.

But whereas Isaiah does not write, “They covered his head,” but writes, “They covered his face” (ibid.), this must be understood in the sense in which it was said to Moses: “You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII). For that full knowledge of divinity promised to the saints in eternal life—of which the Apostle says, “We shall see him face to face” (I Cor. XIII), and again, “Then I shall know as I also have been known” (ibid.)—is veiled and hidden from those still living in this mortality. But in eternal life it is not veiled, but revealed and manifest, as the Lord testifies in the Gospel concerning the blessed angels: “Their angels always see the face of the Father” (Matt. XVIII).

Therefore, because it was more relevant to the present discussion for the face to remain uncovered, without changing the words of prophecy but passing them over: in order that it may be true that no beginning in God is comprehended, we cover the head above; and in order that what is said may stand—“Their angels always see in heaven the face of the Father”—we leave the face uncovered. The other things also that are said differently here are to be referred not to the prophecy but to the painting.

“With two wings they flew” (Isa. VI). These two wings with which the seraphim flew signify tropology, because, while we are instructed to good works through the reading of divine Scripture, we are raised on high as though by certain wings. With them we also fly one toward another, while through zeal for good works we exhort one another. While flying, moreover, we cry, “Holy, holy, holy,” if by our good works we strive to magnify not our own glory but that of our Father who is in heaven. For what is it to cry, “Holy, holy, holy” (ibid.), except openly to proclaim the glory of the Creator which we have recognized within?

Having briefly explained these matters, let us begin next to treat what follows. For it remains that, after showing what is meant by the reading that the Lord’s head and feet are hidden from us, we should also show what must be thought concerning the rest of the body.

If, therefore, we call the head of God that which existed before the establishment of this world, and his feet that which will be after the consummation of the age, we rightly understand the length of his body to be the intervening span of time between beginning and end. The head and feet, then, are covered because we cannot investigate the first and last things. The body appears because we see the things done in the middle, in this present age.

This body is the Church, which began at the beginning of the world and will endure to the end of the age. This is the ark of which we have proposed to speak, which reaches from head to feet because, from beginning to end, the holy Church extends itself through the succession of generations.

But it must be known that, just as there are things around a human body which are neither in the body nor of the body, so it is also with the body of Christ—that is, the Church—which dwells in the midst of a perverse nation. While it receives the assaults of unbelievers, the ark is battered from without, as though by stormy waves; while it suffers tribulation from false brothers, the body is tortured from within, as though by harmful fluids. Therefore, whatever is contrary to the body, whether inside or outside, is not of the body.

The fact that the Lord’s arms embrace all things on either side signifies that all things are under his power, and no one can escape his hand—his right hand unto reward or his left hand unto punishment. Why, then, should the members be further anxious about the welfare of the body, when they have known such power in the Head? He knows what benefits his body, for through compassion he feels its danger and through power supplies its remedy. He is the one who makes a way in the sea, because, guiding his body—that is, his Church—as an ark amid the storms of this life, he brings it to the harbor of eternal rest.

If, therefore, we wish to be saved, we must enter this ark. And, as I said above, we must make this ark within ourselves, so that we may dwell in it within ourselves. For it is not enough that we are in it outside ourselves unless we have also learned how we ought to make it dwell within us. For this, three things especially must be considered: first, how we ought to build it within ourselves; second, how we ought to enter it within ourselves; third, how we ought to dwell in it within ourselves.

But behold: while we propose to speak of one ark, the sequence of matters so leads our mind that we now see we must speak not only of one but of four. Of these, two were visibly made outwardly, while two are invisibly made within by an invisible structure. The first is that which Noah made with axes and adzes from wooden materials and pitch. The second is that which Christ made through his preachers from the gathering of peoples in one confession of faith. The third is that which Wisdom daily builds in our hearts through continual meditation on God’s law. The fourth is that which mother Grace works in us from the alliance of many virtues in one charity.

The first is in you; the second in faith; the third in knowledge; the fourth in virtue. Let us call the first Noah’s ark; the second, the ark of the Church; the third, the ark of wisdom; the fourth, the ark of mother Grace. Yet in some sense there is one ark everywhere, because there is everywhere one likeness; and what does not differ in property should not differ in name. The form is one, the material diverse: for what exists in wood also exists in the people, and what exists in the mind is the same as what exists in charity.

But we have undertaken to speak particularly about the ark of wisdom. Therefore, we shall run briefly through the exposition of the other three, so that afterwards we may linger more freely in explaining this one.

## CHAPTER III. On the form and dimensions of the ark according to the letter

Those who desire to investigate more diligently the truth of the matters related literally concerning Noah’s ark ought chiefly to inquire into two things: namely, the form and dimensions of the ark.

Concerning the form, Origen says: “I think, so far as appears from the matters described, that it rose from below with four corners and, as these were gradually drawn together toward the top into a narrow space, it was gathered to the dimension of one cubit.”

Many things seem to oppose this opinion. First, this form does not appear suitable for floating. It is clear that a structure of such mass, laden with so many and such great animals and provisions, could by no means float upon the waters coming upon it without being pressed downward for a great part of its height. We may still observe an example of this in ships that carry great burdens. If, therefore, as is said, it began to narrow immediately from the bottom, how could it be that swelling waves would not repel but receive the sides sloping inward from both directions, and that the ark would not so much carry the waters as the waters carry the ark? How could it happen that the whole ark would not immediately sink to the depths?

Again, when it says, “You shall place the door low down in its side” (Gen. VI), “in the side below” seems to signify the lateral wall, in distinction from the side that was above, in the roof, where perhaps a window was placed. And again it says: “Noah opened the roof of the ark” (Gen. VIII). This quite consistently indicates that the ark itself had walls below, upon which was placed a roof adjoining the uppermost storey in which the human being dwelt.

For these and other such reasons, it seems to us that the ark had walls raised on its four sides, with a roof placed above them and narrowed at its summit to the measure of one cubit. What height the walls themselves had, authority does not say; yet, as far as we conjecture, the height of the walls extended to the floor of the fourth storey.

For teachers maintain that the door of the ark was situated between the second and third storeys, so that its lower edge was contiguous with the floor of the third storey, while its entrance was cut higher up in the side of that same storey. Thus two storeys lay below the door and three above it. They say that one storey was arranged to receive the animals’ dung, the second for their food; wild animals were in the third, tame animals in the fourth, and humans and birds in the fifth, which was the uppermost.

It is probable that those two lower storeys, while the ark floated, were pressed down among the waters. The third, however, in which were the animals needing the breath of open air, first rose above the waters, so that, for those coming up to the ark through the water from outside, the door would meet them almost at a level surface. Perhaps “You shall place the door low down” was said in this sense. Or it was called “low down” because, in whatever storey it was placed, it was low down, so that the ark might receive the feet of those entering.

If, however, it is asked whether the height of the individual storeys was equal or not, we cannot prove from authority what should be thought about it. Meanwhile, we ask only that we be permitted what is not contrary to authority. For we wish to distinguish them thus: let us assign four cubits in height to the first storey, five to the second, six to the third, seven to the fourth, and eight to the fifth. Thus the height of the walls will be fifteen cubits, and the height of the roof fifteen cubits.

[Col. 0628A] On the outside walls of this ark there were made nests or small chambers, as though attached to the walls themselves, so that their entrances opened outward while the wall itself remained intact within. These nests, they say, were made for those animals that can live neither always in water nor always on dry land, such as the otter and sea calves. This has been said concerning the form of the ark.

Of its size it is said: “Its length shall be three hundred cubits, its breadth fifty, its height thirty” (Gen. 6). But some say that this size would not suffice to contain so many kinds of animals and the food on which they would live for a full year. The teachers resolve this question as follows. They say that Moses, who, as Scripture testifies concerning him, had been instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians [Col. 0628B], used here, according to the geometrical reckoning in which the Egyptians especially excel, a measure of cubits in which one cubit is reckoned as six cubits. If this reckoning is applied to the dimensions of this ark, spaces of such length, breadth, and height will be found as could truly contain the seeds for restoring the whole world and the divine nurseries of every living thing.

It should also be known that those animals which are not generated by sexual union, but arise from the moisture of the earth, from corpses, or from the corruption of any other substance, as well as those born from the mixture of different kinds, such as mules and hinnies, did not need to be kept in the ark. From this it follows that it was not impossible for a space of such capacity to contain the restorative seed-stock of all the remaining living creatures [Col. 0628C].

But if one wishes to investigate more carefully those matters relating to the theory of geometrical measurements, a great body of instruction is displayed here. For brevity’s sake we shall touch upon only a few points. A finger is the smallest part among common measures that has its own name. For anything smaller than a finger we answer in fractions: a half, a third, or a fourth part. We measure by the finger in this way: joining the thumb transversely to the side of the thumb, we make the roots of the nails correspond in a straight line. By this reckoning four fingers make one palm, and four palms make one foot. A foot and a half make a small cubit; six small cubits make a great cubit; and thus the great cubit contains nine feet. The small cubit is a foot and a half.

Therefore a length of three hundred great cubits contained one thousand eight hundred small cubits; two thousand seven hundred feet; ten thousand eight hundred palms; and forty-three thousand two hundred fingers. Again, five feet make one pace; one hundred and twenty-five paces make one stadium; eight stadia make one mile. Thus it is evident that this ark had, in its length, five hundred and forty paces, four stadia—that is, half a mile—and forty paces. By the same reasoning these figures may be found for its breadth and height.

If you also wish to know what its area was in square feet or cubits—that is, the area of the ark—multiply the greater side by the lesser, and the resulting total is the number of squares in the ark [Col. 0629A]. For example: say that fifty times three hundred makes fifteen thousand: the ark is of so many square cubits. And likewise in other cases.

If you seek the diagonal line of this quadrilateral, let this be your rule. Multiply each side by itself—that is, the greater side by itself and the lesser side by itself—then add the resulting sums together; find the side corresponding to that combined sum, and take it as the diagonal. For example: three hundred times three hundred makes ninety thousand; fifty times fifty makes two thousand five hundred. The side corresponding to their sum is three hundred and four and a half, less one—that is, not a whole number. If you take half of this, you have one hundred and fifty-two and a half, less one. This is the line which extends [Col. 0629B] from the corner to the middle.

If you take this as the base, erect in the middle of the ark a perpendicular of thirty cubits in height, and from that perpendicular, upward from the top of the third storey, take fifteen cubits and use this as the perpendicular; and if you compare this base with it foot by foot according to the geometrical rule, you will see by a remarkable calculation that all the angular hypotenuses come to the measure of one hundred and fifty-two and a half. Likewise, if you compare with the perpendicular the base extending from the front on either side, you will see that the hypotenuses proceeding from the front also extend to one hundred and fifty-two and a half. But the hypotenuses which come from the sides extend to twenty-eight and a half, having bases of twenty-five cubits.

The rule for finding a hypotenuse is this [Col. 0629C]: multiply the perpendicular by itself, likewise the base by itself, add these sums together, and take the side corresponding to the resulting number as the hypotenuse. In this ark the hypotenuses are represented by beams extending obliquely from below to the upper parts.

A *ratetum* is an upright post set up in the middle of the ark as far as the highest cubit. A base is a line lying from the corner of the ark and extending to the perpendicular. A diagonal line is one stretched from one corner to the opposite corner. In these triangles and quadrilaterals you will find many other matters belonging to the subtlety of geometrical science; we omit them all to avoid tedium.

There are others who say that there were only three storeys in the ark: one of them vaulted once, the middle one divided into two chambers, and the upper one into three chambers [Col. 0629D]. They say that Scripture called these divisions of the storeys “upper rooms” (*caenacula*), but called the three storeys themselves *tristega* (“three-storeyed structures”). We have depicted this form rather than the others because we could not easily show the height of the walls in a flat drawing. In this form, the beams rising from either side gradually narrow until they meet at the summit within a measure of one cubit.

## Chapter IV. On the Ark of the Church, or the Church

These things have been said according to the letter concerning Noah’s ark. It remains for us now to see what the ark of the Church is—or, to speak more plainly: the Church itself is the ark, which the supreme Noah, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, governs; and, as governor and harbor amid the storms of this life [Col. 0630A], he guides it through himself to himself.

Its length of three hundred cubits signifies the present age, which runs through three periods: the time of the natural law, the time of the written law, and the time of grace. Through these the holy Church advances from the beginning of the world to its end, and from the present life to future glory.

Its breadth of fifty cubits signifies all the faithful, established under one head, namely Christ. For fifty consists of seven times seven—that is, forty-nine, a number signifying the whole body of the faithful—with one added, signifying Christ, who is the head of his Church (Eph. 5) and the end of our desires. Therefore it is completed in one cubit.

Its height of thirty cubits signifies the thirty books of the divine page: twenty-two of the Old Testament and eight of the New, in which is contained the sum of all that God has done or will do for his Church [Col. 0630B].

The three storeys signify the three orders of faithful people in the holy Church. The first use the world, though lawfully; the second flee and forget the world; the third have now forgotten the world, and these are near to God. The ark narrows in the upper parts and widens in the lower. This signifies that in the holy Church the number of those who live carnally is greater than that of those who live spiritually, so that the more perfect are always the fewer.

At the top the ark narrows to the measure of one cubit, because Christ, the head of his Church, who is the Holy of Holies, is among human beings through a like nature, yet above human beings through singular power.

The hundred years during which the ark was built signify the same as the hundred cubits. For the hundred years signify the time of grace, because the holy Church, which began from the beginning of the world, received redemption in the time of grace through the sacrifice of the spotless Lamb. For then the ark was built, when from the side of Christ hanging on the cross the sacraments of the Church flowed forth in blood and water. When the Lamb was sacrificed, then the bride of the Lamb was born. When Adam was put to sleep, then Eve was fashioned (Gen. 2). Our bridegroom ascended the bed of his marriage chamber; he slept; by dying he showed what had been efficacious from the beginning, and did what had existed from the beginning [Col. 0630C–D].

See whether Scripture intends to say the same thing when it speaks of the construction of this ark, that is, the Church. What do you say? It says: “In the book of life of the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world” (Rev. 13). Who is this? At the end of the age the Son of God came in the flesh; he allowed himself to be crucified for the salvation of humankind, to be killed, to be sacrificed. Therefore the Lamb was slain at the end of the age—for he was slain only once. How then can it stand that he is said to have been slain from the foundation of the world? Could he be slain before he was incarnate? He had not yet assumed anything mortal; how then could he die? But if he was slain from the beginning, he was slain before he was incarnate. If he was slain from the beginning, he was slain not once only, but often—indeed, always. For what was from the beginning always was, and what is from the beginning always is.

But perhaps, if you say, “He was slain from the beginning,” that is, for those who were from the beginning—for their redemption, salvation, and reconciliation—so that by “from the beginning” you define not the time of the slaying but the time of salvation, there will be no inconsistency in saying that he was slain both once and from the beginning. Even before his death occurred, it was efficacious: first there was promise, and then fulfilment. Therefore he was slain from the beginning of the world because from the beginning of the world there were those for whom he was slain at the end of the world.

Yet when he put on beauty—that is, when he assumed immaculate, undefiled, beautiful flesh from virginal members—and girded himself with strength, that is, when through the trophies of the cross he defeated the powers of the air, from that time [Col. 0631B] his throne was made ready; from that time his Church was redeemed; from that time the sheep which had perished was brought back; from that time the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, formerly closed, was opened.

You see, then, how the ark is three hundred cubits long and yet was built not in three hundred but in one hundred years: because the Church, which existed from the beginning of the world, was redeemed at the end of the world. The fact that this ark is six times as long as its breadth and ten times as long as its height displays the likeness of the human body in which Christ appeared; for it too is his body. The length of a human body, from crown to foot, is six times its breadth—from one side to the other—and ten times its height, whose measurement is across the side, from back to belly. Thus, if you measure a human being lying on the back or face down, the length from head to feet is six times the breadth from right to left or left to right, and ten times the height above the ground [Col. 0631C].

The number fifty occurs six times in three hundred, and there are six ages within the three periods of the world. Or three hundred signify faith in the Trinity, or the cross because of Tau, which represents three hundred in numerals and still retains among its people the form of a cross. Fifty signify forgiveness of sins; thirty, the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age.

According to the interpretation in which we distinguish the ark’s internal height into five storeys, the ark is the Church and the five storeys are five states: three of the present life and two of the future. The first state is that of those called carnal, of whom the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal; I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3). The second is that of those called animal or natural persons, of whom he says again: “The natural person does not receive the things of God” (1 Cor. 2). The third is that of spiritual persons, of whom he says: “The spiritual person judges all things, and is judged by no one” (ibid.). The fourth is the state of souls stripped of their bodies; the fifth, that of those rising again in soul and body. This is the highest and is adjacent to the topmost cubit [Col. 0631D].

The fact that the lower storeys rise straight upward according to the height of the walls and do not incline toward the uppermost cubit signifies that, however much progress we make in this life, we are still, as it were, turned away from the face of our Creator. For we rise by merit, but we do not incline toward him through the immediate presence of contemplation. Hence the bride rightly recalls in the Song of Songs that her beloved stands behind the wall (Song 2), because, as long as we are clothed in this covering of corruption, we are kept from his face as though by an intervening wall.

But the fourth and fifth storeys come together in their ascent into one, because the souls of the saints, even now that the burden of flesh has been laid aside, rejoice in contemplating their Creator; and when they receive again their immortal and impassible bodies, then they will cling to him more fully and more closely through the immediate presence of contemplation [Col. 0632A–B]. For what does it signify that the ark gathers upward into one in its roof, except that, when we have been led out of the darkness of this life, we shall refer the end of all our desires to one thing? We shall begin to see God as he is, so that we shall desire nothing except to gaze without interruption upon his face, to be satisfied without weariness by his sweetness, and to enjoy without loss his love. For this is to tend toward him and attain him: always to seek him through desire, find him through knowledge, and touch him through taste.

The storey adjoining the bottom was assigned the animals’ dung, which aptly expresses the life of carnal persons, since those who serve the desires of the flesh become nothing other than rottenness. The second storey above it contains the animals’ fodder. This suitably signifies those who occupy a middle state in the holy Church: they neither wholly yield to the flesh through unlawful desires, nor can they attain the dignity of spiritual persons through contempt for the world. While these, in comparison with spiritual teachers who distribute God’s word, supply their teachers with material support, what else do they become but storehouses for holy animals? [Col. 0632B–C]

The third storey contains animals indeed, but untamed ones. These signify the life of spiritual persons who, while they remain held in this corruption, are subject to God’s law by reason, yet bear in their flesh that by which they still oppose the law. They are animals, therefore, because they live by the reason of the mind; but they are untamed through the unlawful desires of the flesh.

In the fourth storey are tame animals, because, as the Apostle says, “The one who has died has been justified from sin” (Rom. 6). And according to the Prophet’s saying: “On that day all their thoughts shall perish” (Ps. 145). For when they leave the bonds of corruptible flesh, they are thereafter tamed from unlawful desires. The fifth storey contains the human being and birds. In the human being is signified the vitality of reason and understanding; in the bird is expressed the agility of incorruptible nature. Therefore, when “this mortal has put on immortality and this corruptible has put on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15), then, made spiritual alike in mind and body according to our measure, we shall both know all things through the illumination of the mind [Col. 0632D–0633A] and be able to be everywhere through the lightness of the incorruptible body. We shall fly with the mind through contemplation; we shall fly with the body through incorruption. We shall discern with the mind—and, so to speak, discern also with the body—when our bodily senses themselves are transformed into reason, reason into understanding, and understanding passes into God, to whom we shall be joined through the one mediator of God and humankind, the Lord Jesus Christ.

The fact that the ark’s shape does not reach its uppermost point in the likeness of a truncated pyramid can signify that whatever is below God is less perfect. For our Redeemer himself, according to the form of assumed humanity, is less than the Father; and through obedience he subjects to the Father that which he did not receive from the Father through equality of majesty [Col. 0633B].

If anyone wishes to investigate the mysteries of the numbers which we assigned above to the height of each storey, that person will see that four is suitably assigned to the first storey. Since the human body is composed of four elements and framed by a combination of four humors, the life of carnal persons, who serve bodily pleasures, is rightly expressed by the number four. Next, five aptly figures natural persons because of the five senses: although they are not shamefully subject to carnal vices, they do not know what the delight of the spirit is and consequently pursue and love those things outside which pertain to the delight of the senses. Six suits spiritual persons because of the perfection of works [Col. 0633B–C]. Seven, because it signifies rest, belongs to souls resting in hope and awaiting the glory of resurrection. Eight, because it is a sign of blessedness, suits those who, having received their bodies, rejoice in blessed immortality.

There is another thing we may say about the first three storeys. Each of us has three wills within: the first is carnal, the second natural, the third spiritual. The carnal will is to loosen the reins of desire, to obey carnal cravings in every respect without restraint, to be subject to no law, to fear no one, and to do whatever it pleases. Opposed to this, the desire of the spirit seeks to devote itself wholly to spiritual pursuits, even wishing to exclude the necessary uses of the flesh.

Between these two desires, the will of the soul stands in a certain more moderate middle position. It is neither delighted by the shameful acts of vices nor resigned to the pains of virtues. It seeks to moderate carnal passions so as not to consent at all to undergo the necessary pains without which the desires of the spirit cannot be attained: desiring to gain the gift of chastity without chastisement or mortification of the flesh; to acquire purity of heart without the labor of vigils [Col. 0633D–0634A]; to display Christ’s humility without losing worldly honor. Finally, it wishes to attain future goods without losing present ones.

This will would never lead us to true perfection, but would place us in a most miserable condition, unless the wars rising up within broke apart this most lukewarm state. For when, serving this will, we desire to relax ourselves a little, immediately the rising stings of the flesh do not allow us to remain harmlessly in the purity of tepidity in which we delight, but draw us onto the cold path we dread, full of the thorns of vices. Again, when we are inflamed with spiritual fervor and wish to extinguish the works of the flesh without any regard for human weakness, and when, through an exalted heart, we devote ourselves wholly to immoderate pursuits of virtue, the weakness of the flesh intervenes, recalls and delays us from that blameworthy excess of spirit.

Thus the two desires, alternately struggling, oppose one another in such a conflict that the will of the soul—which wishes neither to give itself wholly to carnal desires nor to labor strenuously in virtuous works—is regulated by a certain just moderation. A certain balance of equality is set in the scale of our body. By weighing spirit and flesh, it permits neither the mind, inflamed by spiritual ardor, to outweigh from the right nor the flesh, by the stings of vices, to outweigh from the left. It excludes that lukewarm state of the natural will and beneficially compels us to reach the fourth state which we seek: that we may acquire virtues not through leisure and security but through continual sweat and contrition of spirit [Col. 0634B–C], lest, remaining in that most destructive lukewarmness, God begin to spew us from his mouth.

The Apostle makes this conflict between flesh and spirit and its result clear when he says: “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfil the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. These oppose one another, so that you do not do whatever things you wish” (Gal. 5).

In the moral sense, anyone who strives to separate himself from the delights of this world and devote himself to virtues ought, with God’s grace cooperating, to build within an edifice of virtues. Its length should be three hundred cubits in faith in the Trinity, its breadth fifty in charity, and its height thirty in hope which is in Christ [Col. 0634C–D], so that one may be long in good works, broad in love, and lofty in desire; so that one’s heart may be where Christ is, seated at God’s right hand. Thus the head of the crucified one was set at the height of the cross, while his hands were stretched out across its breadth, so that the affection of our heart might extend even to loving enemies. The body of the crucified one was laid along the length of the cross, so that our activity might not be slack but extended, persevering to the end.

# Book Two

[Col. 0635]

Its chapters are these.

Chapter I. On the ark of wisdom.—Chapter II. On the door and window of the same ark.—Chapter III. On four ways of going out through action.—Chapter IV. On four ways of going out through contemplation.—Chapter V. How an olive branch is brought to the ark of wisdom.—Chapter VI. On the three storeys of the ark of wisdom, or of the intellectual ark.—Chapter VII. That a pillar is erected in the middle of this ark.—Chapter VIII. On the diversity of those ascending the ark.—Chapter IX. On the tree of life and the book of life in the pillar.—Chapter X. On the two things in the tree; and again on the book and tree of life.—Chapter XI. On different books, and which book is called the book of life.—Chapter XII. On three books.—Chapter XIII. On three words.—Chapter XIV. On three trees of life.—Chapter XV. On three books of life.—Chapter XVI. On three words.—Chapter XVII. On three paradises, and a comparison of the three trees which are in them.—Chapter XVIII. On the tree of wisdom and the true tree, its growth and progress.

## Chapter I. On the Ark of Wisdom

[Col. 0635A]

What we intend to say about the ark of wisdom must be distinguished from the things previously assigned allegorically to the Church: what was there shown in reality is here to be sought in thought. Things have a certain mode of being in the human mind, where even those things which in themselves have either already passed or are still future can subsist together. In this respect the rational soul has, in a certain way, a likeness to its Creator. For just as the causes of all things subsisted eternally in the divine mind without change or temporal distinction, so past, present, and future things subsist together in our mind through thought.

Therefore, if by the practice of meditation we begin constantly to dwell in our heart [Col. 0635B], we in some sense cease to be temporal and, as though dead to the world, live inwardly with God. Then we easily despise whatever fortune contrives outside, if our desire is fixed where we are not subject to change. There we neither abandon the past nor await the future; there we neither desire the prosperity of this life nor fear its adversity.

Let us therefore have upright, useful, and chaste thoughts, since it is from such material that we shall build our ark. These are the timbers which float when cast into water and burn when placed in fire, because the flow of carnal delights does not press such thoughts downward, but the flame of charity sets them ablaze. Do not fear this fire in your dwelling. Woe to you if your tent has not burned from it.

Afterward you shall coat your ark with pitch inside and out: outside, so that you may show gentleness; inside, so that you may not lose charity. For you will by no means be able to rest sweetly in the secret place of your conscience unless first you have learned to endure the wicked outside through gentleness and not to hate them within through charity. Pitch is hot by nature and arises from earth struck by lightning; charity is produced in a soul struck by fear of the divine judgment.

Next let us consider the ark’s dimensions. Above we said that three hundred cubits signify the present age. If, then, you lead your thought from the beginning of the world to its end, and in passing consider what and how great are the wonders God has performed, or will yet perform, for his elect, you will measure in your heart a length of three hundred cubits [Col. 0635C–0636A]. If in thought you run through the Church and, having contemplated the life of the faithful, set it before yourself as an example, you extend your heart to the breadth of fifty cubits. But if you have acquired knowledge of the divine page, which is contained in thirty books, you raise your heart to the height of thirty cubits.

This is the ark you must build. These are the boundaries of your fathers which you may not cross, which the Most High established according to the number of the children of Israel when he separated the children of Adam and divided the nations. This is the land you must inhabit and in whose riches you must feed. Rest, therefore, within these walls; remain beneath this roof; dwell in this house. Storm and tempest rage outside; wherever you go out, you will suffer shipwreck.

If in pride you attempt to probe by your own wisdom divine secrets which God did not will to disclose to us through Scripture, you pass beyond the height of thirty cubits. If you do not believe that the Church will endure until the end of the age, but think that it will at some time be deprived of God’s assistance, then you pass beyond the length of one hundred cubits. If you delight in thinking frequently about lovers of this world and their vain way of life, you transgress the measure of fifty cubits [Col. 0636B].

## Chapter II. On the Door and Window of This Ark

The ark of the Flood, as has already been said, is the secret place of our heart, in which we ought to hide from the tumult of this world. But because the weakness of our condition does not allow us to rest long in the silence of inward contemplation, we have a way out through the door and the window. The door signifies departure through action; the window, departure through thought. The door is below, the window above, because actions belong to the body and thoughts to the soul. Hence birds went out through the window, while beasts and human beings went out through the door.

That a bird signifies the soul and a human being the body is shown in the book of Job, where it is said: “A human being is born for labor, a bird for flight” (Job 5). For we are born into this life in such a way that, if we wish to raise the soul through contemplation, it is necessary to wear down the body through labors. The statement that the door was placed in the side [Col. 0636C–0637A] signifies that we should never leave the secret place of our heart through action because of a deliberate purpose, but only because an accidental necessity arises. Perhaps Scripture is not silent about the window without reason: for although it is sometimes permissible to go out through thought voluntarily, we must never go out through action except from necessity. This is also aptly indicated by the fact that the man himself opened the window when he wished, in order to send out the birds. But the door is read to have been both closed from outside by God and opened again by him, so that the man might go out.

## Chapter III. On Four Ways of Going Out through Action

There are four ways in which we go out through action. Some actions are carnal, that is, they belong to the use of the body; others are spiritual, belonging to the instruction of the mind. Both good and evil people go out by both kinds.

Those who serve external earthly activities in order to satisfy pleasure are like the unclean animals which went out of the ark. But those who administer them for the use of necessity are animals indeed, but clean ones. Those, however, who undertake the care of ecclesiastical governance—which is a spiritual action to be performed—and come forth into public from the secret of inner quiet not from ambition but at the command of obedience, are like Noah, who, leaving the ark, offered sacrifice. For such people often kill within themselves all movements of the flesh all the more through abstinence, the more heavily they recognize that they have suffered the losses of inward quiet through occupation.

But those who accept honors in the Church for their own glory, and, seeing themselves placed on high, despise others and refuse to condescend compassionately to the weaker members of the Church, are like Ham, who mocked his naked father’s shame and deserved to receive a sentence of curse for it [Col. 0637B–C].

## Chapter IV. On Four Ways of Going Out through Contemplation

There are likewise four ways in which we go out through contemplation.

The first way is when we consider what every creature is in itself and find all things to be vanity, because every creature, just as it came into being from nothing, so also indicates through daily change that, so far as it is in itself, it tends toward nothingness [Col. 0637C–D].

The second way is when we consider what there is in the same creature by the gift of the Creator and discern in it the likeness of divine reason. Although creatures are subject to change by their own condition, in receiving from the Creator the benefit that they never utterly cease to exist, the temporal work in some way imitates the stability of its eternal Maker.

The third way is when we consider how God uses the ministry of creatures to fulfil his judgments, either by bestowing benefits in his mercy or punishments according to our deserts. In this contemplation we find all things to be instruments of divine providence and evidence of our perversity. In this kind of contemplation we hear every creature speak to us in three voices.

The first voice says, “Receive”; the second says, “Give back”; the third says, “Flee”: “Receive the benefit; render the debt; flee punishment.” The first voice is that of one serving; the second, of one warning; the third, of one threatening.

The voice of one serving is this. Heaven says: “I provide you light by day, that you may keep watch; darkness by night, that you may rest. For your delight I produce the welcome changes of seasons: the spring season, the heat of summer, the fullness of autumn, and the cold of winter. By the alternating increase of days and nights, I extend their spans in a proportionally varied way, so that variety may remove weariness [Col. 0638A–B] and order may produce delight.” Air says: “I offer you life-giving breath, and I send every kind of bird to serve you.” Water says: “I offer you drink; I cleanse filth; I make dry places fertile; and I provide various kinds of fish for your food.” Earth says: “I bear you; I nourish you; I strengthen you with bread; I gladden you with wine; I delight you with all kinds of fruits; I fill your tables with diverse animals.”

The voice of one warning is this. The world says: “See, human being, how the one who made me for you loved you. I serve you because I was made for you, so that you too may serve him who made both me and you: me for your sake, and you for his own sake. If you recognize the benefit, render the debt. You receive kindness: render charity. God gives this, and he requires this.”

The voice of one threatening is this. Fire says: “You shall be burned by me.” Water says: “You shall be drowned in me.” Earth says: “You shall be swallowed by me.” Hell says: “You shall be devoured by me.” For as every creature serves humankind by virtue of its condition, so it threatens sinners according to their consciousness of evil deserts, so that they fear suffering in each creature what they know they have deserved. Hence it is also said that “the wicked flee when no one pursues” (Prov. 28), because the wicked are fearful even in security, just as the righteous are secure even in punishment [Col. 0638B–C].

The fourth way of contemplation is when we look at creatures according to how a person can use them to satisfy the pleasure of carnal desire, and in them think not of aid for natural weakness but of the delight of lust. Eve saw the tree with this eye: how beautiful it was to look upon and sweet for eating; and she took from its fruit and ate (Gen. 3).
