Those who go out in thought in this way are like the raven, which did not return, because, finding outside what wickedly delights them, they no longer wish to return to the ark of conscience.

But the remaining three kinds of contemplation are figured in the departure of the dove. When it had been sent out and found no place where its foot could rest, it returned at evening bearing a green olive branch in its mouth. It went out empty, but it did not return empty, because outside it found what it did not have inside; yet it did not love outside what it brought inward [Col. 0638D].

## Chapter V. How an Olive Branch Is Brought to the Ark of Wisdom

[Col. 0639A]

The green olive branch signifies a good disposition of the mind, because often the more holy men behold divine works outwardly, the more they burn inwardly with love for the Creator. For when they observe the mutability of present things, immediately everything that seems beautiful in this world becomes cheap in their thought; and, as though returning, they carry an olive branch in their mouth, because they desire the beauty of their Creator more ardently the less they have found in created things to delight them. The mind is delightfully fed within because it is not delightfully detained without; and, as though brought back to the haven of its ark, it now dances in security, though formerly it was shipwrecked amid the waves of the world [Col. 0639B].

Likewise, in the second kind of contemplation, whenever we learn to admire in visible things the invisible power and wisdom of God, we bring back, as it were, an olive branch from the waters to the ark, because in mutable things outside ourselves we recognize him whom we love immutably within ourselves. In the third kind of contemplation likewise, while we attend to his judgments outwardly, we are renewed inwardly in his fear and love. Thus, in the first, when the material of vanity is examined, it produces in us contempt for the world; in the second, the image of reason produces praise of God; in the third, the instrument of providential ordering produces fear and love of God; in the fourth, the tinder of covetousness produces an incentive to lust.

Let us therefore beware of this departure, lest we go out rashly. Let no one trust in his own conscience. Dinah was within a virgin, within chaste, within a dove; but because she was a deceived dove, having no heart, when she went outside she changed her color together with her name. For thus it is written: “Dinah went out to see the women of that region. When Shechem, son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of that land, saw her, he loved her, seized her, and lay with her, forcibly violating the virgin” (Gen. 34) [Col. 0639C]. It is clear that she who is violated by force does not go out in order to be corrupted; nevertheless, because she went out rashly, she suffered loss to her chastity even against her will. But what is added—“he joined her to himself”—means this: the raven found a corpse and no longer wished to return to the ark.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Three Chambers of the Ark of Wisdom, or of the Intellect

[Col. 0639D]

There are three chambers in the intellectual ark, signifying three kinds of thoughts: right, useful, and necessary. If I begin to love meditation on the Scriptures and gladly think about the virtues of the saints, the works of God, and whatever else pertains to the correction of morals or the exercise of the mind, I have already begun to be in the first chamber of the ark. But if I still delay and shirk imitating the good that I know, then I may say that my thought is right and useless: right, because what I think about others and recognize in others is good; but useless to me if I do not draw it into my own pattern of life. For another’s virtue does not benefit me if I neglect to imitate it, insofar as I can.

“Hidden treasure and hidden knowledge: what profit is there in either?” (Ecclus. 20) [Col. 0640A]. I hide knowledge if I do not show in action the good that I know; and therefore what I conceal having, though I know it, cannot benefit me. But if I take pains not merely to know but also to do what is good and useful, and if the thought of my heart is diligent in this—so that I make my own, by the exercise of discipline and the pattern of right living, the virtues which I have already learned to love and admire in others—then I may say that the thought of my heart is useful. Then I ascend to the second chamber, and gather my heart more fully into one, so that it may not wander through vain things that do not pertain to usefulness.

The third remains: when I have begun to possess works of virtue, I should also labor to possess the virtues themselves; that is, that what I show outwardly in deed I may possess inwardly in virtue. Otherwise it does not benefit me greatly to possess deeds unless I also possess the virtues of those deeds. Therefore, if I direct the thought of my heart to this end—that I should strive to present inwardly to the divine gaze whatever good appears outwardly in me before human eyes—then I ascend to the third chamber, where the virtues are that are necessary. Yet among all these one is especially necessary: charity, which joins us to God. Therefore, at the summit the ark is gathered into one, so that we may now think one thing, await one thing, desire one thing: our Lord Jesus Christ.

Thus, in the first chamber is knowledge; in the second, work; in the third, virtue; at the summit, the reward of virtue, the Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0640C]. You have these steps in the Psalm where it says, “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge” (Ps. 118); if you reverse the order: “Teach me knowledge, discipline, and goodness” (*ibid.*), O Lord Jesus Christ.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Column Raised in the Middle of This Ark

A column raised in the middle of the ark, thirty cubits high, on which the entire structure rests, its cross-section above being square, one cubit on each side—this is the tree of life planted in the middle of Paradise: that is, the Lord Jesus Christ in the middle of his Church. He is set forth for all the faithful in common as the reward of labor, the payment for work, the goal of the journey, and the crown of the contest [Col. 0640D]. He sprang from the earth and penetrated the heavens; he came down to the lowest things and did not abandon the highest; he himself is above and below: above in majesty, below in compassion.

Above, that he may draw desire; below, that he may provide help. Below, within us; above, over us. Below, in what he took from us; above, in what he set before us. This is “the mountain of the house of the Lord, prepared upon the top of the mountains,” to which all nations flow (Mic. 4), and they ascend to it from the four corners of the ark, as it were from the four regions of the world.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Diversity of Those Ascending the Ark

Some ascend from the heat of the east, others from the heat of the west, others from the cold of the east, others from the cold of the west. The heat of the east is spiritual fervor; the heat of the west is the lust of the flesh. The cold of the east is the swelling of pride; the cold of the west is the blindness of ignorance.

Man was created in the heat of the east; therefore he was placed in the gardens of Eden, in the southern east. But he passed into the cold of the east when he joined himself to him who first said that he would set his throne in the north (Isa. 14) [Col. 0641A]. Then he fell into the heat of the west when, after sin, he found in his members another law resisting the law of his mind (Rom. 7). He then likewise fell into the cold of the west when, struck by the blindness of ignorance, he began to forget the food of that heavenly bread.

In the heat of the east is the beginning of good nature; in the cold of the east, the beginning of guilt. In the heat and cold of the west are the punishments of body and soul. In the heat of the east man was created on high; in the cold of the east man wished proudly to exalt himself; and therefore, in the heat and cold of the west, man fell to the depths.

But through the mediator between God and human beings, the Lord Jesus Christ, behold, these now come from the east and those from the west to recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 8) [Col. 0641B]. They now cry to the north to give, and to the south not to hinder the children of God (Isa. 43). For because Jesus Christ is true God and true man, in his humanity he provides an example, and from his divinity a remedy. By the humiliation of the weakness he assumed, he both restrains our pride and enlightens our blindness; by the power of his majesty he both feeds our souls with invisible food and protects our bodies, through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, from the heat of vices.

Therefore he becomes for us both the tree of life and the book of life: a tree, because he shelters and feeds; a book, because he rebukes and teaches. He rebukes the proud, enlightens the blind, feeds the hungry, and shelters those oppressed by heat. Let the proud hear rebuke and be humbled; let those blind in mind hear instruction and be enlightened. Let those scorched by the heat of vices seek shade, that they may be refreshed. Let those who hunger and thirst for righteousness hasten here, that they may be filled. Let no one make excuses: every person finds a remedy suited to his illness, where even the wicked are given a place to amend themselves, and the good a place to become better.

Let us therefore ascend, setting aside every excuse. Let us ascend eagerly; let us ascend rejoicing, “because we shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. 121) [Col. 0641D]. Let us ascend to the feasts of the heavenly homeland, tribes of Israel, to give thanks to the name of the Lord in the towers of Jerusalem (*ibid.*). Let us lift our eyes upward and see purple paths laid out along the sides of the eternal mountains, and the ways of heaven made straight all the way to the gates of Jerusalem. There the banner of the cross, flashing in lofty light, in rosy light, terrifies enemies and strengthens friends. The gates of the city are open, and in its streets are the voices of those singing “Alleluia.”

You will see many peoples ascending there, girded with psalms, singing from every people, nation, and tongue: some radiant in rose-colored clothing, some shining in white garments, others gleaming in violet-purple attire—every adornment for the solemn festival. Great and innumerable is the people prepared for the day of the Lord [Col. 0642A]. The king is above and invites us; he is below and helps us. The sluggish are stirred, the timid strengthened, the weak made strong, and the valiant made more courageous. Every age, both sexes, every rank run together from all parts of the world and eagerly ascend with gladness and joy to see the king in his beauty. All desire, each one desires, to appear festive on the day of so great a solemnity.

Let us now speak, then, about these steps of ascent by which one climbs to heaven, so that the labor of the journey may frighten no one who delights in the promised reward. There are indeed purple ascents, because one ascends with labor; but charity is spread beneath, by which the labor itself is lightened.

The first ascent is from the cold of the east—that is, from the swelling of pride [Col. 0642B]—because the sinner must first be humbled and rise again through obedience, having fallen into the fault of sin through disobedience. The second ascent is from the heat of the west, because it is then necessary to trample down the vices of the flesh, so that we may not walk according to our desires, and to mortify our members which are upon the earth, so that we may no longer serve sin (Col. 3). The third ascent is from the cold of the west, because when we have already perfectly extinguished fleshly affections in ourselves through abstinence and the exercise of discipline, then we shall be able freely to devote ourselves to meditation upon and instruction from the divine Scriptures, so that through the study of reading and meditation the eye of the mind may again be enlightened, as the Psalmist says: “Depart from me, you evildoers, and I will search the commandments of my God” (Ps. 118). The fourth ascent is from the heat of the east, where we progress from good to better, because we can by no means come to perfection unless we also strive without ceasing to grow in the good things that we do.

But whether we should believe that we raised a column thirty cubits high in the middle of the ark literally in this manner or not makes no difference, provided that we understand that a space of the same dimensions and extent opened upward from the first level. Again, what we said—that the height of thirty cubits signifies divine Scripture, and later our assertion that Christ is figured by the column thirty cubits high—are not contradictory. For all divine Scripture is one book, and that one book is Christ, because all divine Scripture speaks of Christ and all divine Scripture is fulfilled in Christ. In reading Scripture we seek this: that, recognizing his deeds, sayings, and commands, we may deserve to do what he commanded and receive what he promised. Thus, growing both in knowledge of truth and in the merit of virtue, we may attain especially to his likeness and “to the measure of the age of fullness” (Eph. 4) [Col. 0642D].

## CHAPTER IX. On the Tree of Life and the Book of Life in the Column

Therefore, that what we have said may become clearer, we have depicted the aforesaid column in the middle of the ark, inscribing upon it the name *tree of life* on the south side and *book of life* on the north side. Accordingly, on that same side we arranged thirty volumes of the divine page in order upward from the first level—that is, ten in each chamber—because, as we have said, all divine Scripture is that one book, which is the book of life.

And it should be known that, although Christ in his twofold nature consists in one eternal person, according to either nature he may be called both book of life and tree; nevertheless, in a particular sense he became for us the book of life according to the form of assumed humanity, because in his humanity he provided an example. According to the form of divinity he became the tree of life, because through the power of divinity he provides a remedy [Col. 0643A].

## CHAPTER X. On the Two Things in a Tree, and on the Book and Tree of Life

A tree has two things in itself: fruit and leaves. It feeds by its fruit and shelters by its leaves. Thus the power of divinity is refreshment for enlightened minds and shade for those who are weak [Col. 0643B]. The book of life looks to the north, because through the Savior’s humanity light arose for those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death. And the tree of life turns toward the south, so that it may feed and advance the strong by the taste of its sweetness, and hide those who are still weak, lest they fail in the heat of temptations, under the wings of its protection as under a noonday shelter.

Let it not be burdensome if we pursue these things a little further. For now we wish, now in the manner of an expositor to explain the meaning in plain and few words, now in the manner of one meditating, now as though raising doubts, now as though discovering answers, to range here and there with the mind’s keen edge.

## CHAPTER XI. On Different Books, and Which Book Is Called the Book of Life

[Col. 0643C]

There are different books. Some are books written by God; others are written by human beings. Books written by human beings are made from the skins of dead animals or from some other perishable material; and after they have lasted a little while, they too grow old and, in their own manner, dissolve into nothing, leaving thereafter no trace of themselves. And all who read these books eventually die, and no one is found who lives forever. Therefore, since they are made from dead things by mortals destined to die, and cannot give permanent life to their readers or lovers, they are by no means worthy to be called books of life, but rather books of death, or of the dead, or of the dying.

But if I could find such a book as this: one whose origin is eternal, whose essence is incorruptible, whose knowledge is life, whose writing is indelible, whose sight is desirable, whose teaching is easy, whose knowledge is sweet, whose depth is unsearchable, whose words are innumerable and yet are all one Word—this would be the book of life [Col. 0643D]. By distinguishing them in this way, we shall see more deeply.

## CHAPTER XII. On Three Books

There are three books. The first is one made by a human being concerning something; the second, one created by God from nothing; the third, one which God begot: God from himself, God. The first is a perishable work of humanity; the second is a work of God which never ceases to be, in which visible work the invisible wisdom of the Creator is visibly written; the third is not a work of God but the wisdom by which God made all his works, which he begot and did not make, and in which from eternity he had inscribed beforehand all the things that he would make according to the decree of providence and predestination [Col. 0644A]. This is the book of life, in which whatever has once been written shall never be erased, and all who deserve to attain its sight shall live forever.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Three Words

Likewise, there are three words. The first is a human word, which ceases once uttered. The second is the word of God—that is, the work of God—which, having been created, does not subsist unchangeably, yet never ceases. The third is the Word of God, begotten and not created, which knows neither end nor beginning and admits no change; and this is the word of life.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Three Trees of Life

[Col. 0644B]

Likewise, there are three trees of life. The first is that material tree which the Lord God brought forth from the ground in the beginning, when he planted Paradise in its midst. After sin, man was expelled from Paradise lest he touch its fruit. The second is the Lord Jesus Christ, who, according to the form of his assumed humanity, was planted in the midst of his Church as “the tree of life in the midst of Paradise” (Gen. 2); whoever deserves to eat worthily of its fruit shall live forever. The third is the tree of life planted in that invisible Paradise—that is, the wisdom of God—whose fruit is the food of the blessed angels.

The second and third are one tree of life. But man was created for the third; from the first man was expelled [Col. 0644C]; through the second man is recalled. Therefore the tree of life is only in Paradise and cannot be found outside it. There is its place; there it fixes its roots, spreads its branches, and brings forth fruit in its season. And I believe that, because of the flowing of living waters, it is planted beside the fountain which rises in the midst of Paradise and waters the whole Paradise; and therefore neither can its root dry up, nor its branches wither, nor its leaves fall. Rather, it remains green forever.

Thus you have three books, three words, and three trees. If you wish to compare them with one another in each set, you will see how the lowest is as nothing when compared with the middle; yet the middle, compared with the highest, cannot be what the lowest is compared with the middle.

## CHAPTER XV. Again, on Three Books of Life

[Col. 0644D]

For example, we have set before you three books: the first, which is a work of humanity; the second, which is a work of God; the third, which is not a work of God but the wisdom of God through which God makes all his works. Say, then: human work, divine work, and divine wisdom. Let us consider what comparison there is among these.

Certainly, when Solomon looked upon the works of human beings and considered them, he said: “Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. What more does a human being have from all his labor which he labors under the sun?” (Eccl. 1). Therefore it was not enough for him merely to say “vanity,” unless, repeating it twice, he exclaimed: “Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” And rightly so. For if, as the Psalmist testifies, “every living human being is vanity” (Ps. 38), human work is rightly called not merely vanity but vanity of vanities.

But shortly afterward he makes clear what he thinks about the works of God, saying: “I learned that all the works which God has made endure forever. We cannot add anything to them or take anything away; God made them so that he might be feared. What has been made remains” (Eccl. 3) [Col. 0645A]. What, then, shall I say? If I wished to compare human works with the works of God, should I say that a human work is something, or not? Considered in itself, it seems to be something; compared with the other, it seems to be nothing, because it is beyond estimation how greatly it is surpassed.

Yet if, ascending higher, you compare the work to its maker, you find that the entire expanse of time is still less in comparison with the eternity of divinity. So it is also with the word.

## CHAPTER XVI. Again, on Three Words

[Col. 0645B]

One thing is the word of a human being; another is the word of God, the work of God which is not God; and another is the Word of God who is God. But the work of God, because it is visible, is called an external word, like an utterance of the mouth. The wisdom of God, because it is invisible, is called an internal word, like a conception of the mind. And just as an uttered sound immediately perishes while understanding remains, so what God made changes, while what God is does not change. And just as the thought of the heart is known through the utterance of a voice, so in his work the wisdom of the Creator is manifested.

For this work is a beautiful work: a work worthy of God as maker, a work fitting for one who is wise, a work which no one but the omnipotent can make. Therefore by its beauty, as by a certain voice, it proclaims the power of its Creator and speaks his wisdom [Col. 0645C]. This wisdom has made all things so fruitful that it dwells in the things it made, wholly in each and wholly in the whole; neither less in the whole nor less in each. Therefore the whole is not greater and the individual things are not less, because both the whole and each thing speak the whole wisdom.

The word, then, speaks the Word: the word that was made speaks the Word that made it; the word that passes speaks the Word that admits no change; the word perceived by sense speaks the Word seen by the pure heart; the beautiful word speaks the most beautiful Word; the word that delights the eyes of the body speaks the Word that enlightens the eyes of the heart; the created word speaks the Word not created but born; not uttered by the mouth but brought forth from the heart; not a word which, once sent forth, ceases, but one which, being begotten, remains [Col. 0645D].

Therefore, if you compare wisdom with its work, everything that passes is less in relation to that which knows no change than even the instant of a single moment is in comparison with a time of however long duration, which does not exceed the limits of time [Col. 0646A]. So it is with the tree.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Three Paradises and the Comparison of the Three Trees Which Are in Them

There are three paradises. One is earthly, whose inhabitant was the first Adam, earthly. The second is the paradise of the faithful, which is the Church of the saints, founded and inhabited by the second Adam, heavenly—that is, Christ. The third is heavenly, which is the kingdom of God, eternal life, and the land of the living, or rather the living land, in which God dwells.

In the first Paradise the tree of life is a material tree. In the second, the tree of life is the humanity of the Savior. In the third, the tree of life is the wisdom of God, the Word of the Father, the fountain of life, and the source of good; and this is truly eternal life [Col. 0646B].

Now let us come to comparison. Certainly, the tree of life which was in the earthly Paradise could sustain only bodily life without decay. But the tree of life of the paradise of the faithful—that is, Jesus Christ—promises eternal life to those who eat his flesh and drink his blood. Yet he himself, wishing to express how far the sacrament differs from the power, says: “The flesh profits nothing; it is the spirit that gives life” (John 6). It is as though he said: “If you receive me bodily in the sacrament, do not believe that this is sufficient for you unless you also learn to eat me spiritually, insofar as I am the word of life enlightening souls, justifying sinners, and making the dead alive.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Tree of Wisdom and the True Tree of Life, Its Growth and Development

[Col. 0646C]

This, therefore, is truly the tree of life: the Word of the Father, the wisdom of God on high. In the hearts of the saints, as in an invisible Paradise, it is sown through fear, watered through grace, dies through sorrow, takes root through faith, sprouts through devotion, rises through compunction, grows through desire, is strengthened through charity, becomes green through hope, puts forth leaves and spreads branches through circumspection, flowers through discipline, bears fruit through virtue, ripens through patience, is plucked through death, and feeds through contemplation.

But because our discourse has proceeded rather far, let us take a brief breath, praying at the same time to the wisdom of God herself, that she may deign to satisfy us with the taste of her sweetness—she who did not disdain to redeem us through the taste of bitter death [Col. 0646D]. To her be honor and dominion unto the eternal ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0645]

These are its chapters:

CHAPTER I. On the sowing of the tree of wisdom through fear.—CHAPTER II. On the watering of the tree of wisdom through grace.—CHAPTER III. On the decay of the tree of wisdom through sorrow.—CHAPTER IV. On the rooting of the tree of wisdom through faith.—CHAPTER V. On the sprouting of the tree of wisdom through devotion.—CHAPTER VI. On the rising of the tree of wisdom through compunction.—CHAPTER VII. On the growth of the tree of wisdom through desire.—CHAPTER VIII. On its strengthening through charity.—CHAPTER IX. On its greenness through hope.—CHAPTER X. How the tree of wisdom puts forth leaves through circumspection, and what pertains to this.—CHAPTER XI. How it flowers through discipline [Col. 0647].—CHAPTER XII. How it bears fruit through virtues.—CHAPTER XIII. How it ripens through patience and perseverance.—CHAPTER XIV. How it is plucked through death.—CHAPTER XV. How it feeds through contemplation.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0647A]

At the end of the preceding book, by the likeness of a certain tree, we showed how wisdom arises and grows within us. Here we shall explain more fully, treating each point in turn, the stages of that growth which we there touched upon briefly and summarily.

## CHAPTER I. On the Sowing of the Tree of Wisdom Through Fear

First, then, it was said there of wisdom that it is sown through fear. Wisdom is beautifully said to be sown through fear, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1). And just as shoots arise from seeds, so wisdom is born from the fear of the Lord.

For charity itself is wisdom, because through charity we taste God, and by tasting we know him, as the Psalmist says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33) [Col. 0647B]. But the fear of the Lord itself brings charity to us, because, while it teaches us to fear danger, it causes us to love protection. For when the punishments of hell and the torments awaiting the condemned are considered, the mind is suddenly shaken with terror; then, returning to itself and seeking a way of escape, it immediately seeks with desire him through whom it recognizes that it can escape the impending danger. Having found him, it embraces him with the affection of love. Then that horror, intolerable at first, is softened by love. Thus charity is indeed born from fear, but through charity fear is consumed.

Moreover, when the fear of the Lord comes into the heart, it makes one poor in spirit; and poverty of spirit is twofold. For there are bodily riches, in an abundance of temporal possessions; and there are spiritual riches, in the possession of virtues. Therefore each is proved rich before God. Each is excluded from the kingdom of heaven: both the one who desires to abound excessively in temporal and perishing goods, and the one who, considering himself something great, boasts that he stands by his own virtue.

But when the fear of the Lord comes into the mind and sets before our thought the weight of the future judgment and how strict the Judge will be when he comes, it immediately extinguishes every delight of earthly desire; and, usefully recalling our weakness to mind, it shows us how humbly we ought to think of ourselves. Then, once the clamor of earthly desires has been stilled, the mind is immediately composed toward the quiet of inward peace and is prepared, by that very tranquility, to be capable of heavenly wisdom.

For wisdom does not know how to dwell except in a peaceful heart; and therefore those in whom earthly desires still clamor do not know what wisdom is. For, as blessed Job testifies, “The sea says within itself, ‘Wisdom is not in me’” (Job 28), because minds agitated by fleshly cares do not comprehend it. But “the one diminished in activity finds it,” because, when the mind is drawn away from outward things and gathered into itself, it is raised more strongly to contemplate eternal things [Col. 0648A]. Thus the fear of the Lord makes one poor in spirit; poverty of spirit makes the heart tranquil; tranquility of heart is the beginning of heavenly wisdom.

## CHAPTER II. On the Watering of the Tree of Wisdom Through Grace

Second, it was said that it is watered through grace. For as fear is like seed, so grace is like moisture, which waters seed cast into the earth and makes it germinate. Once the human mind has been drawn, by a kind of force, so to speak, away from fleshly delight through fear, it must immediately begin to taste some spiritual joy. Otherwise, if it remains wholly deprived of delight, it cannot grow strong toward the shoot of wisdom, like dry seed without moisture.

Therefore, by the breath of divine grace it comes about that, when the mind has been wholly stripped of bodily passions and earthly desires, it is at once suffused with a certain unfamiliar joy, so that it recognizes the more fully how bitter what it abandoned was, in proportion as it feels what it has found to be sweet. This is the grace that waters continually from above the seed of wisdom cast into the human heart through fear, because the desire for inward sweetness draws those minds which no affection of fleshly desire has bound fast outside.

Let it therefore be said of wisdom: it is sown through fear and watered through grace, because fear first cuts away from the mind the attachment to fleshly delight, and then grace suffuses that same soul—now, as it were, purified and cleansed of impurities—with spiritual delight [Col. 0648C].

## CHAPTER III. On the Decay of the Tree of Wisdom Through Sorrow

Third, it was said that it dies through sorrow. Just as seeds cannot germinate unless they first rot in the earth and in a certain manner die, so we cannot bring forth a good shoot unless we first die to this world through a certain health-giving and life-giving sorrow.

This sorrow concerns exile from the present life. And rightly, after the reception of grace, sorrow is born; for then we truly recognize amid what evils we are, when, enlightened by the infusion of divine grace, we are able in some measure to taste the sweetness of spiritual goods. Hence Solomon says: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1) [Col. 0648D]. For whoever do not know the sweetness of spiritual goods love the passions of fleshly desire even when they afflict them. Therefore grace comes beforehand to the heart in order to awaken it, so that a person may recognize exile and learn to weep over the evils endured.

Thus, after the gift of grace has been received, the mind immediately gives itself to lamentation; it is nourished by sorrow and delights in tears. It now bears present evils with such impatience as it sighs more ardently, having been admonished from nearby, for future goods. It no longer merely leaves the world but flees it; no longer merely puts it second but hates it. And whereas before, compelled by fear, it abandoned the things which it possessed unlawfully, now, pierced by health-giving sorrow, it groans even at having to serve those necessities which the weakness of the human condition requires [Col. 0649A]. And just as before it withdrew itself through fear from unlawful actions of the world, so now it wholly excludes, as far as possible for one still living in this mortality, every appearance of the world from its thought.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Rooting of the Tree of Wisdom Through Faith
Fourth, it was said that it is rooted through faith. There are three kinds of people: unbelievers, those weak in faith, and believers. Unbelievers are the Gentiles, who are ignorant of God [Col. 0649B], who do not believe the Gospel of Christ, and who suppose that, beyond this life which is lived here for a time, there is no other life. These strike their roots into the earth, because they cling the more eagerly to present things the less they know the everlasting goods that follow. They seek earthly things and seek to be happy here, because they judge that after this life they will be nothing. Among their number was that fool whom Eliphaz mocks in the book of Job: “I saw a fool firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty” (Job 5). A fool is one who does not know for what end he was made, who believes that nothing exists beyond what he sees, who does not know how to foresee the evils that remain for him, and who loves these perishable and false goods as though they were to endure forever. Such a man sometimes appears to be firmly rooted [Col. 0649C] while he flourishes for a time; but the wise man immediately curses his beauty, because he recognizes to what evils he will be carried away after these momentary goods.

Of this fool also the Psalmist says: “The fool has said in his heart, There is no God” (Ps. 52); and then, having numbered his accomplices: “There is no fear of God before their eyes” (Ps. 13). For how can those fear God who do not believe that God exists? Hence it is consequently shown that those whom the fear of God does not reach do not attain even to the very beginning of wisdom. Let us now consider those whom we counted second: whether they are rooted, or where they have fixed their roots. They do not seem to have roots. For those weak in faith are persons to whom something concerning the truth has already been persuaded [Col. 0649D], but who still fluctuate in a certain doubtful judgment of mind: they neither wholly contradict nor altogether assent to those things reported in sacred discourse concerning the future rewards of the good or punishments of the wicked. For they see certain things so conducted in this world that one may understand both that God exists and that He cares for human beings, and that all human deeds, whether good or evil, are reserved for judgment.

Considering this, then, they begin to fear what God threatens; struck by that fear, they purpose to do what He commands and to avoid what He forbids. And it sometimes happens that, when they have been trained for a time by this fear, they not only fear what God threatens, but also begin with a certain affection of mind to desire what He promises. But when again they see the wicked flourishing in this world, and many other things in this life so confusedly ordered that the world seems by no means to be governed by God’s providence, but all events to lie subject to chance occurrences, they immediately begin to envy the peace of sinners and themselves desire to flourish in this world. In unspoken thoughts they say to themselves that it is vain to fear judgment; that the punishments of hell and the torments of the wicked are nothing but inventions of foolish people; that this has arisen from fear, not from truth. For surely, if God weighed human deeds so strictly, He would declare it by such manifest indications that thereafter no one could doubt it.

Finally, they say that it is altogether contrary to reason [Col. 0650B] to abandon what is certain for things uncertain, and, in pursuing certain invisible things—whether they truly exist, or whether deceived people have imagined that they exist, no one has ever been granted to know—to despise, with a kind of wicked presumption, the certain and present goods which the common judgment and sense of humankind approves not only as goods but as very necessary to human nature; especially since it is evident that God created all these things only for human benefit. Therefore, they say, no injury is done to God if people use the goods which He created for no other purpose than that human beings might use them.

Such persons, then, who know how to weigh their faith only according to the uncertain course of events, cannot be steadfast. For just as, through a certain levity of mind, they readily believe the word of truth for a time, so also [Col. 0650C] in a time of temptation they readily depart from the faith of truth, because when they are tempted they are easily persuaded that false is that concerning which they had previously doubted even while they seemed to stand firm. The Prophet set forth in himself the type of such people when he said: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps were almost poured out, because I envied the sinners when I saw the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72). And a little later: “‘How does God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?’ For these sinners, abounding in the age, have obtained riches” (ibid.).

For such people question and doubt and are carried about by the heat of their thoughts, not knowing to which side they should rather incline the judgment of their minds. They cannot believe, yet do not dare to deny. Their assertion is doubtful, and their faith suspect [Col. 0650D]. But those who are believers have roots; yet they do not, like unbelievers, strike their roots in this world. Rather, through faith and love they are rooted and founded in God. These are the Lord’s vineyard of Sorec: the faithful vineyard, the righteous vineyard, which He Himself, the good husbandman, planted—indeed transplanted—because “He brought it out of Egypt, cast out the nations, and planted it” (Ps. 79). Of these the Lord says elsewhere through the prophet: “I will plant them upon their own soil, and I will no longer pluck them up” (Amos 9).

For our soil and homeland is God, in whom we are planted when we cling to Him by the devotion of our minds, saying with the Psalmist: “But it is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72). From this soil, indeed, we are no longer plucked up [Col. 0651A] if we remain in His love until the end. Of this rooting also the Holy Spirit says through the prophet: “Whatever remnant remains of the house of Judah shall send roots downward and bear fruit upward” (Ps. 37). In the remnant of the house of Judah, believers are signified: they send their root downward because they fix every thought of their hearts upon inward joys. But they bear fruit upward because, in the heavenly homeland which in this life they always seek through love, they afterward receive the gifts of life as their recompense.

What unbelievers deny, therefore, and those weak in faith doubt, believers both believe and await. And what unbelievers love, and those weak in faith envy, believers flee. Faith, then, is that by which wisdom takes root, because through faith the mind is made firm and the affections are established [Col. 0651B]. But one who wavers in faith can be perfect neither in the fear of God nor in the love of God. For we fear differently what we suspect and what we believe. What we believe, we fear perfectly; but what we suspect, we often neglect to fear precisely because from our very doubt we fall into a ruinous security, so that we come to believe only that to be just which we see does not conflict with our desire. Thus our deceived mind often judges that what it most desires to happen to it is what will rather come to pass. Therefore, lest fear be slack or affection lukewarm, we must have firm and unshaken faith, through which, firmly rooted, we may confirm the goods received in the three preceding stages [Col. 0651C].

## Chapter V. On the Sprouting of the Tree of Wisdom through Devotion

In the fifth place it is added that they sprout through devotion. Devotion is the fervor of a good will which the mind, unable to contain it, reveals by definite signs. It is divided into three: zeal, compassion, and benevolence. Zeal is when the mind, for love of justice, freely offers itself as its defender, unable to endure that truth should suffer calumny. Compassion is when we grieve with the miseries of others. Benevolence is when with ready will we grant requested benefits.

The comparison is apt. We say that seeds sprout when nature, by a certain hidden force [Col. 0651D], breaks open what was whole so that the shoot hidden within may come forth. Likewise, good will, unable to conceal itself, goes out, by a kind of violence, so to speak, into the outward performance of a good work.

## Chapter VI. On the Rising of the Tree of Wisdom through Compunction

In the sixth place it was said of wisdom that it rises through compunction. Here that Gospel parable comes to mind in which the kingdom of heaven is compared to treasure hidden in a field (Matt. 13). The kingdom of heaven is eternal life; eternal life is Christ; Christ is wisdom; and wisdom is treasure. This treasure is hidden in the field of the human heart, where the human being was made in the image and likeness of the Creator. For the human heart was so made that divine wisdom might shine forth in it as in a certain mirror, and that what could not be seen in itself might appear visibly in its image [Col. 0652A].

Truly great is the dignity of the human being: to bear the image of God, continually to behold His countenance within oneself, and always to hold Him present through contemplation. But after that first parent, attaining what was forbidden and touching what was prohibited, scattered his delight upon the earth, the dust of sin cast upon the human heart hid this precious treasure from our eyes, and the darkness of ignorance spread over it cut off the light of wisdom.

This is what was prefigured in Solomon’s temple, where we read that, after Solomon had completed all the work for building the house of the Lord and all things pertaining to the furnishing of the house had been finished, [Col. 0652B] a cloud immediately filled the house, so that the priests could not minister (3 Kings 8). Solomon’s name means “peaceful,” and he signifies Him who is our peace, who reconciled us to God by His blood. And because this same Jesus Christ our Lord is the wisdom of the Father, Solomon builds a temple for God because through the wisdom of God the human heart was made, so that God might dwell in it as in a temple. This is the wisdom that “built herself a house,” because, descending into the world, she says that her delights are with the children of men (Prov. 8).

But this house, once built, is filled with cloud, because the human being, created and then falling through sin from that mirror of inward contemplation, slips into these miserable darknesses of the present life. There one cannot worthily minister to God, because, wrapped in the gloom of ignorance, one now sees only to a very limited extent what ought to be done or avoided [Col. 0652C].

This treasure, therefore, is hidden in the field of our heart; it is found when wisdom rises. Wisdom rises when truth is manifested. Truth is manifested when ignorance is driven away; ignorance is driven away when the mind is enlightened. When ignorance has been expelled, truth is manifested; when truth has been manifested, wisdom rises; when wisdom rises, the treasure is found.

This compunction, like a sharp stake, digs up the soil of our heart; like fire, it burns away rust; and like brightness, it drives away darkness. Through it we ought to dig deep wells in our hearts, casting out from ourselves all earthliness, so that we may find [Col. 0652D] hidden treasures and the concealed vein of living waters. Thus our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob dug wells, seeking the living water of wisdom; and when the Philistines, during their absence, filled those wells with earth, they dug them again and again sought living water, doing this often. So too, if malignant spirits, lying in wait, again fill with earth our hearts, cleansed of all earthliness by the practice of compunction, we must dig them again through compunction and cleanse them again. We must do this until we find living water and discover the precious treasure.

But when we have found it, we must hide it, because what is carelessly revealed is quickly lost. The person who carries the received gift of wisdom in display makes the treasure found manifest [Col. 0653A]. The person who, having received wisdom’s gift, seeks to glory in it not outwardly before human eyes but inwardly before God hides the treasure found. We must also go and sell all that we have and buy this field, because whoever has already had inward joys revealed to him ought gladly, for the sight of them, to despise everything that can delight him in this world.

Yet those who seek wisdom should consider carefully that wisdom must be sought for no other reason than for its own sake. Nothing is better than wisdom; therefore one is unworthy of wisdom who intends through wisdom itself to gain something other than wisdom—who seeks wisdom not to possess it, but to prostitute it for sale. Moreover [Col. 0653B], if Christ is wisdom, one who seeks wisdom for human praise is shown to resemble Judas the traitor, who sold Christ. Let us therefore seek hidden treasures; let us seek wisdom; let us seek Christ—but not as Judas sought Christ, to sell Him rather than to possess Him. Judas sought Christ, found Him, and held Him, but did not retain Him because he sold Him. But the holy women, coming to the tomb with spices, sought Christ and found Him, held Him and retained Him, because they did not seek Him to sell Him but to possess Him (Matt. 28).

Let us say, then, of wisdom: it is sown through fear, watered through grace, dies through sorrow, takes root through faith, and rises through compunction. These stages seem to me to be signified where Abraham is commanded to leave his land, his kindred, and his father’s house, and only then is permitted to be shown the land: “Go forth,” says the Lord, “from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house; and come into the land that I shall show you” (Gen. 12). Therefore, through fear we depart from our land; through grace we depart from our kindred; through sorrow we go forth from our father’s house; through faith and devotion we follow the Lord; and thus, in the sixth stage, the land promised to us is shown through compunction [Col. 0653C].

Through fear we abandon earthly property; through grace and sorrow we change our affections; through faith and devotion we strengthen the mind; through compunction we discover desire. [Col. 0653D] We depart from our land when we abandon the earthly goods possessed outwardly. We depart from our kindred when we renounce the vices that are born in us and from us. We depart from our father’s house when we completely remove from our thoughts the whole world and what is in the world, and fix the entire intention of our mind upon eternal things alone.

Our father, according to that birth by which we were born in sins, is the devil, because according to that birth we belong to the dominion of him who is the author of sin. His house is this world, because by the merit of his perversity he was made prince of this world and of those who love this world. But once we have gone forth from our land, kindred, and father’s house, another land is shown to us by the Lord [Col. 0654A], when, having died perfectly to this world, we are granted already to catch, as it were, from afar some scent of future joys. For, breathed upon by the Holy Spirit, the mind is gladdened with an unfamiliar joy and marvels what that might be like to taste which refreshes so wondrously even by its fragrance.

## Chapter VII. On the Growth of the Tree of Wisdom through Desire

In the seventh place it is added that it grows through desire. For just as compunction is compared to fire, so desire is like the smoke that arises from fire: it ascends straight upward, and the higher it rises, the more it is thinned; finally, lifted aloft, it is wholly withdrawn from the eyes of those who look upon it. For after the rust of sin has been consumed from the mind by the fire of compunction [Col. 0654B], and that inward brightness has begun to gleam in the heart, the mind is immediately raised to a certain watchtower of contemplation. There, in some manner made higher than itself, it sees from afar, so to speak, a luminous region and a new land such as it does not remember ever having seen before or even thought to exist.

The one who sees marvels; in the joy of the present light he reproaches the past darkness of his ignorance. He marvels beneath himself at the depth in which he lay cast down, and marvels above himself at the height toward which he stretches. He rejoices that he has escaped so much of what caused him pain, and grieves that he is still so far from what he loves. Therefore he strives, hastens, rises, and grows through desire. And just as a wisp of smoke is thinned the more it is lifted upward, so, drawing near to heavenly things and evaporating every cloud of earthly desire, he becomes wholly spiritual; at last he withdraws himself from human sight when, refusing any longer to seek these earthly and visible things, he glories inwardly in the hidden place of the Lord’s countenance [Col. 0654C].

## Chapter VIII. On the Strengthening of the Tree of Wisdom through Charity

In the eighth place it is added: it is strengthened through charity. Charity is like wine. Wine makes those whom it intoxicates cheerful, bold, strong, forgetful, and in a certain way insensible. So charity, cleansing the conscience, makes the mind glad; then it makes it bold, when through purity of conscience it gives confidence. Then [Col. 0654D] it increases strength, because, as Scripture testifies, “He who trusts in the Lord is strong as a lion” (Prov. 28). For a clean conscience cannot be overcome by any adversities, because while it always trusts inwardly in God’s help, it easily despises and conquers whatever adversity it endures outwardly.

It also produces forgetfulness, because while it draws the whole attention of the mind toward desires for eternal things, it uproots from the mind all remembrance of things that pass away. It makes one insensible because, filling the mind to its depths with inward sweetness, it despises whatever bitterness is brought from without, as though it were not felt. Charity, therefore, strengthens wisdom by granting the mind confidence, fortitude, and a kind of unconquerable, insensible constancy [Col. 0655A].

If we wish, we can observe in these eight stages the eight Beatitudes set forth in order. What was said, “it is sown through fear,” belongs to what is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). What was said, “it is watered through grace,” belongs to: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (ibid.). What is said, “it dies through sorrow,” belongs to: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (ibid.). What was said, “it takes root through faith,” belongs to: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (ibid.). What was said, “it sprouts through devotion,” belongs to: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” [Col. 0655B] (ibid.). What is said, “it rises through compunction,” belongs to: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (ibid.). What was said, “it grows through desire,” belongs to: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (ibid.). What was said, “it is strengthened through charity,” belongs to: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.).

## Chapter IX. On the Verdure of the Tree of Wisdom through Hope

In the ninth place it is added: through hope it remains green. Hope for future goods is in the mind like a certain spark nourished in tinder. For hope is like a memory of invisible joys, stored up in the human heart [Col. 0655C], which warms it inwardly and does not allow it to wither from the cold of unbelief in the winter of the present life. So long as this hope lives in our mind, the tree of wisdom never withers. Rather, just as a sound tree retains its greenness while it has an even balance of moisture and warmth, so the mind cannot wither when it is nourished both by the heat of the Holy Spirit shining from above and by the practice of good works watering it from below.

## Chapter X. How the Tree of Wisdom Puts Forth Leaves through Circumspection

In the tenth place it is added that through circumspection it puts forth leaves and spreads its branches. There are some in whom wisdom grows upward, and others in whom it spreads itself outward. In contemplatives it rises upward, for through the sharpness of their minds they penetrate as far as the contemplation of heavenly secrets. [Col. 0655D] In those active in life it spreads outward, because they pour out the intention of their minds in many directions toward the administration of earthly matters.

Yet there are some who, through a divinely granted repose, first grow greatly in contemplation; but when they see simpler brethren occupied with earthly tasks, they despise them in comparison with themselves. Although they themselves are barren of good work, they do not hesitate to judge good works in others. Those, therefore, who neglect to stand in humility are shaken by the wind of pride and fall from the height of contemplation. Cast down, they lie exposed to diverse errors and are distracted in many ways from that inward peace [Col. 0656A].

The beginning of these errors is that they are unwilling humbly to acknowledge their weakness, but incautiously exalt themselves because of the gift of God which they have received. For the deeds of others must necessarily seem contemptible to the eyes of those who think so immoderately of their own merits. Nor could they presume to judge another’s life unless they had first become swollen with pride in themselves. Once this error has entered the mind, it spreads its poisons widely; creeping secretly and mingling itself with every movement of the soul, it alters the will, scatters counsels, twists thoughts, corrupts desires, and introduces superfluous cares.

And because the mind, once puffed up, has learned to think great things of itself, it disdains to bring its deeds to the test of reason; and it pursues the lives of others all the more freely as it believes less that there is anything in itself worthy of blame. [Col. 0656B] Yet this pride first disguises itself under the appearance of good zeal, and persuades the deceived mind that no one is a perfect lover of justice who gives assent to another’s fault. Further, it argues that a person who neglects to rebuke a sinner cannot but give complete consent to another’s sin. Thus the mind, deceived by this ill-considered error, gives itself wholly to curiosity; and as the disease gradually grows, while it first becomes accustomed to pursue the errors of others without restraint, it is finally brought to such a state that it attempts either openly to slander or maliciously to interpret whatever it sees.

Thus, if it sees some people taking a little trouble for the common good, it calls them greedy. Those whom it sees to be prudent it calls avaricious. Of those who show themselves agreeable and cheerful to all, it says that they serve the vice of flattery [Col. 0656C]. Those who often display sadness in their faces it believes to be wasting away through envy. And those whom it sees cheerful and devoted in service it declares to be frivolous and restless. Those whom it finds weak or slow it accuses as idle and inert. It considers the abstinent to suffer from the disease of hypocrisy, and those who make greater allowance for necessity to serve luxury.

A manifold confusion follows this error. For evil and pestilent curiosity, which strives wickedly to search out another’s secret, often, even though it finds nothing which it can justly blame, nevertheless does not cease to suspect perversely. But if it finds something worthy of reproof, it immediately draws the swollen mind not toward compassion but toward contempt. Contempt stirs up anger, because a mind swollen with the swelling of pride believes intolerable whatever it suffers from one whom it despises. Then anger grows into indignation; indignation proceeds to insult; insult produces hatred; and inveterate hatred passes into envy. Envy produces weariness in the soul; and when weariness has lodged in the heart, it eats it away like a moth, suffocates inward joy, and wastes away in the conscience itself [Col. 0656D].

The mind becomes burdensome to itself and, remaining motionless like lead, cannot rise upward. It who formerly was accustomed to pierce the heavens on the wings of contemplation now falls beneath himself, weighed down by a heavy burden. [Col. 0657A] He shudders at the darkness which he suffers within and, if it were possible, would wish to flee from himself. Therefore, abandoning conscience, he pours himself wholly outward into earthly activities, so that at least through occupation he may forget his evils. Since he judges every evil lighter than that which he endures within, the wretched man now even loves outwardly the pains of his own occupations. And because through prolonged weariness the palate of his heart has unlearned to taste true sweetness, his soul, thirsting for the vinegar of carnal desire, drinks it with longing.

The devil then corrupts him when he has found him amid outward cares; and, since he no longer resists by any judgment of reason, drags him to whatever precipices of error he pleases. But since we have now said into how many evils pride hurls us, it is fitting also to consider what remedy it is by which divine grace restores us. This antidote is such that it not only restores former health [Col. 0657B], but adds greater strength. It not only repairs what has perished, but also adds what was lacking. Hence God is in every way praiseworthy and glorious, alone merciful and gracious: He freely bestows the gift, freely restores what has been lost, and, although we were unworthy even to receive again what we had lost, restores it in such a way that we seem to have fallen not to destruction but to increase.

Therefore, the one who had grown through wisdom became proud because of his height; and so it is good for him to be cut back and to become accustomed to spreading his branches outward. It is good for him, interrupting for a time his pursuit of contemplation, to be compelled to go out into external matters and undertake their management, so that he may learn by experience how difficult it is to serve outward duties and nevertheless [Col. 0657C] not abandon inward things through desire. When he recognizes himself unequal to the care of the rule entrusted to him, then he may know what he ought to have thought of those whom he had formerly and thoughtlessly despised when they were placed in the same position.

And because greater authority is ordinarily accompanied by greater care, let this very care train him: let him be prudent and circumspect, and not grow dull in idleness; let him strengthen his mind before danger, attending not only to what happens but to what can happen. Let him not place excessive trust in smiling fortune; in adversities, let him not lose confidence; and let him equally despise everything that will have an end, whether it is good or evil. Let him anticipate every outcome by counsel; let him strive to acquire friends before necessity arises; let him not trust in his own judgment more than is fitting [Col. 0657D]; let him love all, but not trust all equally. Let him render due obedience to superiors, love to equals, and fatherly care to subjects.

Thus, through the various pursuits of virtues, let him spread the branches of his wisdom. Then at last that tree of wisdom which formerly, like a flexible reed, had grown badly with a bare trunk, strengthened now by continual practice of the virtues and clothed on every side with the leaves of circumspection, may again raise its summit on high—then better in proportion as it is stronger, more robust, more practiced, and more adorned with circumspection—so that even its very cutting back may seem to have profited it.

But because wisdom itself spreads out its branches through circumspection, let us now define some general modes by which circumspection is exercised. There are four: fear, care, necessity, and desire.

[Col. 0658A]

Fear is anxiety about danger. Care is concern for escaping an evil or obtaining a good. Necessity is an obligation to give, or a need to receive. Desire is the longing to enjoy. Fear presses down; care draws; necessity binds; desire wounds.

Thus farmers, when they wish to spread out the branches of trees, either place weights upon them to press them downward, or hang weights beneath to draw them down; or they set stakes beside them and bind the branches so that they may not rise upward but spread outward; or they graft shoots into the bare trunk itself, so that, growing together with it, they may clothe the tree. Fear, therefore, is like a weight laid upon it; care, like a weight suspended below; necessity is like the stake that binds; desire is like the grafted shoot which wounds.

These four arise from four kinds of evils which a human being endures in this world: the wrath of God, the vanity of the world, the weakness of the human condition, and the envy of the devil. God’s wrath is present when we are crushed by scourges. The vanity of the world is present when, exceeding the measure of necessity, we pass over into pleasure. The weakness of the human condition is that we are easily harmed by adversities and only with difficulty gain strength to do good. Envy is present when, at the devil’s instigation, we are inflamed toward vices. Thus the wrath of God presses down through fear; the vanity of the world draws downward by sending superfluous cares; the weakness of our condition binds us with grievous necessities; the devil’s envy wounds us by inflaming us with unlawful desires.

Yet in all these things the servant of God is trained for a reward; and then even evils made subject to him serve him, when by afflicting him they prove rather than overthrow him.

[Col. 0658C]

For all these passions—namely fear, care, and unlawful desire—are evil; and even the necessity of this present life is called by the Lord a military service. Yet God permits these things to rule for a time in the minds of His elect so that, when through experience they have learned how much misery lies within those false pleasures, they may seek more ardently those eternal and true joys which no sorrow corrupts. And, beneficially, they are sometimes abandoned and permitted for a time to serve the passions of their flesh, so that they may recognize their weakness, presume nothing from themselves, and afterward submit themselves more devoutly to divine grace, in proportion as they have learned more clearly from their preceding fall

[Col. 0658D]

that they do not stand by their own strength.

There is also another reason why it is sometimes useful for God’s servants to be tempted: namely, that the temptations themselves may train them and make them more cautious, because conflicts with vices are exercises in virtues. And just as a person often learns by falling how he ought to set his foot and walk carefully, and one who has often been wounded in battle receives a coming blow more cautiously, so one who is often deceived by the devil afterward detects his tricks more subtly and overturns his schemes.

This explains why we see many people rise to the height of virtue after many crimes, and crush with such strength every assault of the devil raised against them that, in the very matter in which he had often rejoiced to conquer them, he now seems not to have despoiled them but rather to have armed them against himself.

[Col. 0659A]

For this is the deep and hidden counsel of God: that even what the enemy gloried had fallen to him as a victory may benefit His elect for their crown.

Let us therefore now consider how exercises arise from the passions mentioned above, and then how circumspection is increased through those exercises. There are four—fear, care, necessity, and desire—and from three of them, that is, fear, necessity, and desire, the fourth, care, arises. For we strive anxiously to avoid what we fear may happen; we strive anxiously to remove from ourselves what we grieve to have present; and we strive anxiously to obtain what we desire. Thus after the movement of a passion comes the care of solicitude; after the care of solicitude follows effort

[Col. 0659B]

in practical exercise; and through practical exercise the caution of circumspection grows.

Because of the vice of our corruption, we are more anxious to obtain what we perversely desire, or to avoid what we excessively fear. Thus it happens that we easily acquire through evil pursuits the caution of circumspection which we neglected to gain through good pursuits. Often, indeed, one who does not fear the death of the soul is terrified of dying in the body; and one who does not consider the everlasting torments of Gehenna dreads suffering temporal punishments. Often one who has not yet learned to fear the shame which is to come upon sinners before the eyes of God and the holy angels blushes to be held contemptible in human eyes.

[Col. 0659C]

And people labor to avoid things which God’s servants not only need not flee but are even sometimes known to seek fruitfully. Likewise, many do not know the fasting of their own soul, yet sweat intensely to procure food for their belly. And people often willingly endure many heavy and bitter labors to fulfill carnal desires—labors which, for love of eternal life, they refuse to undertake even to a small degree—whereas, on the contrary, the elect labor without ceasing and afflict themselves lest they fulfill the desires of the flesh. They also serve their necessities not without fear, fearing lest what the weakness of their condition requires should overflow into the delight of pleasure.

But all carnal persons who willingly endure labors to fulfill their desires wander not only outwardly in action but also inwardly in mind. And while they learn much through experience of things, they become, as it were, more prudent through their very preoccupation. Of such persons the Lord says in the Gospel: “The children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light” (Luke 16). Yet when such people are otherwise converted from their error through divine compassion, they abandon their wicked pursuits but do not lose the prudence which they learned in them; and they become so much more cautious in doing good as they had formerly been more zealous in committing evil. Hence it is plainly shown that even this profited them: that they seemed for a time to have been abandoned. For this reason it was said above that four things exercise circumspection: fear, care, necessity, and desire.

[Col. 0660A]

There are three worldly or carnal fears: fear of contempt, fear of punishment, and fear of death; and each generates its own cares. Necessity, however, is twofold: one kind is the obligation of giving, the other the need of receiving. For “It is necessary to pay tribute to Caesar” is said in one sense, and “It is necessary to give food to the belly” in another. Indeed, it is necessary that you give tribute to Caesar because you owe it; indeed, it is necessary that you give food to the belly because it needs to receive. Yet both Caesar and the belly are exactors; both food and money are tribute.

But if we consider more closely, Caesar does less harm by taking money than the belly does by receiving food. For Caesar, by taking money once, removes the anxiety; but the belly, by demanding food without interruption,

[Col. 0660B]

never allows us to be free from anxiety. Caesar, in taking money, lightens us more; the belly, in receiving food abundantly, inflames us toward base things. To conclude briefly: in every respect I regard the person who serves the belly as more wretched than the one who serves Caesar.

Necessity, then, is of one kind in the obligation of giving and of another in the need of receiving. That which consists in the obligation of giving is understood in many ways. Superiors owe provision to those subject to them; subjects owe obedience to their superiors; equals owe brotherly love to equals; the wise owe instruction to the unwise; the rich owe sustenance to the poor. But since without prudence and circumspection we can neither render justly what we owe nor obtain by asking what we need,

[Col. 0660C]

what are we taught, while we are subject to these necessities, except prudence and circumspection? And, as was said concerning fears, each necessity likewise generates its own care.

Desire is the longing to enjoy. Some desires are good and others evil. Good desires are spiritual; evil desires are carnal. Spiritual desire, like sweet wine, pleasantly intoxicates; carnal desire, like sour and poisoned wine, either drives those who drink it mad or kills them.

Of that wine it is said: “A cup of unmixed wine, full of mixture, is in the hand of the Lord” (Psalm 74), namely, that which “gladdens the heart of man” (Psalm 103). And elsewhere: “How splendid is the Lord’s intoxicating cup!” (Psalm 22). Much is said in Scripture about that wine.

[Col. 0660D]

But of this wine it is said: “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. 32), a wine pressed from a most bitter cluster, which Babylon offers from the golden cup of her fornications and from which all nations become drunk. Of this wine the Gospel also says: “Every man sets out the good wine first, and when they have become drunk, then that which is inferior” (John 2). But of the former wine it says: “You have kept the good wine until now” (ibid.).

This carnal desire, like a foreign graft inserted into the mind, grievously wounds it. This is the stranger of whom Nathan speaks to David—the stranger who had come to the rich man, and for whose feeding the rich man, leaving his own hundred sheep, took away the poor man’s one little ewe-lamb (2 Kings [= 2 Samuel] 12). For the desire of carnal concupiscence came like a guest and stranger to David when, walking upon the roof of his house, he saw Bathsheba, Uriah’s wife, washing herself and loved her (2 Kings [the citation reads I]). Then, in feeding the stranger, he killed the poor man’s one little ewe, leaving his own hundred sheep, when, leaving his many wives, he took away Uriah’s only wife to fulfill his pleasure.

[Col. 0661A]

Foreign grafts are inserted into the bare trunk in order to clothe it, because almighty God often permits those whom He sees to be lukewarm in their ease and, as it were, naked of good works, to be wounded for a time by unlawful desires, so that they may become fearful and circumspect. But how these desires, though evil, exercise a person is difficult to recognize and more difficult to explain; He who brings it about knows.

## CHAPTER XI. How the tree of wisdom blossoms through discipline.

It blossoms through discipline. In a blossom are three things: hope, beauty, and fragrance; and we find all these, by likeness, in a good work. For as future fruit is promised in a blossom, so in a good work the reward of future recompense is awaited. And we hope that those in whom we discern good works belong to the share of heavenly recompense. Again, as a flower shines by its beauty and delights by its fragrance, so a good work shines by its example when it appears praiseworthy to those present and kindles them to imitation. By its fragrance,

[Col. 0661C]

however, it delights when, through the report of its good reputation, it becomes known to those absent and far away.

## CHAPTER XII. How it bears fruit through virtue.

It bears fruit through virtue. The fruit of a good work is the hidden virtue of a right intention. For beneath the flower of a good work, which shines outwardly through example, there lies hidden within the mind a kind of fruit of virtue. Therefore, whoever displays before human eyes an outward good work empty of virtue is like a tree which blossoms without fruit.

## CHAPTER XIII. How it ripens through patience and perseverance.

It ripens through patience and perseverance. A virtue that has been begun is of no benefit unless it is carried through to the end.

[Col. 0661D]

Accordingly, whoever begins virtue forms within himself, as it were, some fruit of goodness; but if he abandons before the end the virtue that he begins, he falls before the proper time like an unripe fruit unfit for eating. Therefore patience and perseverance are very necessary for us, so that we may persevere steadfastly to the end in the good which we have rightly begun through God’s grace.

## CHAPTER XIV. How it is plucked through death.

It is plucked through death. When the fruit is ripe, it is picked so that it may come to the master’s table. And when we have been brought to the measure of our perfection, we are cut off from this life through death, in order that we may be transferred to the banquet of the eternal King. This is what, in the Song of Love, the bride says to her beloved:

[Col. 0662A]

“Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat the fruit of his apple trees” (Song 5).

And he in turn answers her there:

“Come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk” (ibid.).

Therefore we are plucked through death, so that, like sweet-smelling fruits, we may be presented at the wedding of the eternal King. There we shall be God’s food, because He will take pleasure in us; and He Himself will be our food, because we shall delight in Him, contemplating the face of His glory, so that the prophet’s words may be fulfilled in us: “I shall be satisfied when His glory appears” (Psalm 16).

Let us therefore conclude with the highest degree of perfection and say:

## CHAPTER XV. How it feeds through contemplation.

[Col. 0662B]

It feeds through contemplation. This is the food; this is the refreshment of which the Psalmist says: “You will fill me with joy through your countenance; delights are at your right hand unto the end” (Psalm 15). Amen.

Behold, the tree of our wisdom has reached its highest growth through fifteen degrees; and this number is conscious of a great mystery. First, because it is composed of seven and eight. The number seven signifies the present life, which runs through seven days. The number eight, which comes after seven, signifies eternal life. Seven therefore pertains to the Old Testament, in which temporal goods are promised. Eight, however, accords with the New Testament, in which

[Col. 0662C]

we are commanded to hope for eternal things. Let wisdom therefore grow through seven and eight. Let it begin through seven and reach completion through eight. The first wisdom is to ask God for earthly goods; the second wisdom, and the greatest, is to desire God from God.

Again, fifteen doubled makes thirty; and wisdom, when joined to charity and doubled through the love of God and neighbor, brings us to conformity with the age of Christ’s fullness. Again, in fifteen the middle number is the eighth, having seven on either side. It is sufficiently clear that seven pertains to rest, especially because on the seventh day the Lord rested from every work that He had accomplished (Gen. 2).

Again, through the prophet God promises His lovers “Sabbath for Sabbath, and month for month”

[Col. 0662D]

(Isa. [the citation reads VI]): that is, rest for rest, perfection for perfection; in place of rest of the mind, rest of mind and body; in place of the rest by which they do not consent to evils, rest in which they experience no evils. Likewise, in place of perfection of work, perfection of recompense. For to say “Sabbath for Sabbath” is the same as if He said “rest for rest”; and to say “month for month” is the same as if He said “perfection for perfection.”

The first rest, therefore, the first Sabbath, ought to be for us in the present life a ceasing from evil, so that we may deserve to attain the second Sabbath, in which we shall rest eternally with Christ. But whoever proposes to keep Sabbath from evils in this manner must suffer many adversities in this world before arriving at that future Sabbath. Therefore, in the tree of wisdom, at the eighth

[Col. 0663A]

degree between seven and seven—between Sabbath and Sabbath, as it were—the endurance of labor is set in the center of the middle unity, when it is said, “it is strengthened through charity.” For robust charity is necessary against great tribulations. This is what the Lord did in the Gospel: when He had enumerated seven beatitudes, in the eighth He exhorted His hearers to endure suffering, saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). For what is said there, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake,” is said here as “it is strengthened through charity.”

But now, while we pursue the exposition of the reasons involved, we have strayed too far from our purpose. For this also we ask forgiveness, because, to confess the truth, in this treatise we more often discover matters to be written than we shall write after discovering them. Nor am I ashamed even here to confess my ignorance. Let us now return to our purpose and continue concerning the construction of the ark of wisdom.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0663]

Its chapters are these:

**CHAPTER I.** Where and from what the ark—that is, the house of God—is built.  
**CHAPTER II.** On the order and arrangement of our thoughts, which are not finite, so that the house of God may be constructed from them.  
**CHAPTER III.** On the two works of God, namely creation and restoration, in which the mind must be exercised lest it be distracted by the world.  
**CHAPTER IV.** Why God spoke in secret and obscurely.  
**CHAPTER V.** Why God speaks and has spoken with few people and rarely.  
**CHAPTER VI.** That the elect weigh God’s works differently from the reprobate.  
**CHAPTER VII.** That there are two worlds, visible and invisible.  
**CHAPTER VIII.** On the three kinds of people in relation to the ark.  
**CHAPTER IX.** What are the works of restoration and of human activity.

## CHAPTER I. Where and from what the house of God is built.

[Col. 0663B]
