We wish to speak of the building of the Lord’s house, if indeed we who are unworthy to speak of so great a matter are capable of saying anything worthily. Yet although we are not sufficient of ourselves, He is able to provide us with sufficiency; without Him we are found fit neither, I will not say, to speak worthily about Him, nor even to think anything.

First, the place where the Lord’s house ought to be built must be designated; then the material must be described. The place is the human heart; the material is pure thoughts. Let no one excuse himself. Let no one say, “I cannot build a house for the Lord; my meager poverty is insufficient for such great expenditure—I, an exile and stranger dwelling in a foreign land, who lack even a site. This is a work for kings, a work for many peoples. How then shall I

[Col. 0663C]

build a house for the Lord?”

Why do you think so, O human being? Your God does not require this of you. He does not tell you to buy another’s estate in order to enlarge His courts. He wishes to dwell in your heart: enlarge it; make it spacious. Make it spacious, I say, because the Lord is great and does not know how to dwell in a narrow place. Enlarge your heart so that you may receive Him whom the world cannot contain. Enlarge your heart so that you may deserve to have God as your guest—not, as is customary among people, a guest for one night, but an eternal inhabitant.

Enlarge your heart, then. And if you fail in enlarging it, He Himself will enlarge it—the One to whom a man, once enlarged by Him, said: “I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” (Psalm 117).

And what shall I say about the expense? There is no need to cross seas or search unknown regions in order to acquire precious stones and choice marbles; nor to bring tall cedars, cut down in Lebanon, over the high seas in hired ships; nor to assemble I know not how many thousands of craftsmen, who might exhaust even royal treasuries.

[Col. 0663D]

None of these things is required of you: in yourself and from yourself you will build a house for the Lord your God. You yourself will be the craftsman; your heart, the site; your thoughts, the material. Do not fear your lack of skill: He who requires this of you is a skilled craftsman, and He makes whomever He wishes into craftsmen. From the testimony of the divine Scriptures, we have learned that many have been taught by Him. He taught Noah to build the ark. He showed Moses the pattern according to which he was to make the ark. He instructed Bezalel. He enlightened Solomon with wisdom so that he might build a temple for His name. He also made the Apostle Paul an architect, as well as many others whom it would take long to enumerate.

Finally, no one was ever learned who did not learn from Him, and whoever deserved to learn from Him remained no longer unskilled. But if you delight to hear something of His works: He created from nothing all these things which you see.

[Col. 0664C]

He fashioned the marvelous fabric of this world. He Himself conceived how each thing was to be brought forth into its own forms and kinds, and He created the beauty of the whole universe. Consider, then, how much He can do in invisible things, He who arranged these visible things according to so wondrous a plan.

Invoke Him, therefore; pray to Him; entreat Him, that He may deign to teach you also. Invoke Him; love Him—for to invoke Him is to love Him. Love Him, then, and He will come to you and teach you, as He promised those who love Him: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

He did not say, “Having made a dwelling, we shall come,” but, “We shall come,” He says, “and make our dwelling with him.”

[Col. 0664D]

I understand this to mean that the Lover of a pure heart cannot dwell with us unless He Himself first makes a dwelling for Himself within us. For He Himself is the Wisdom of whom it is said: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9). And elsewhere Wisdom itself declares where and from what material her house is constructed, saying: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel, and am present among prudent thoughts” (Prov. 8). Elsewhere the soul of the righteous is called the seat of wisdom.

It is clear, therefore, that Wisdom has fashioned a house for herself in the human heart from prudent thoughts. There are, then, three things: place, material, and craftsman. As we have said, the place is the human heart, the material is the thoughts of the heart, while the craftsmanship belongs to two, namely God and man; these two work together. For God, who deigns to dwell with human beings, does not disdain to prepare a dwelling for Himself with a human being.

[Col. 0665B]

Accordingly, a person should not despair by considering his own lack of skill or weakness, but should rather attend to Him who deigns to work together with him. For God is power and wisdom; no one can fail with power or be ignorant with wisdom—especially since He is the very One who both cooperates for good with us while we work and grants to us, while we do not work, that we may will and be able to work good.

For God’s work in us is with us—our assistance—and our work in us is from Him and His gift.

Having said these things, let us come to what we proposed: so that after you have recognized where, from what, and with whom you ought to work, you may now recognize how you ought to work. In every building there are three matters chiefly to consider: order, arrangement, and a fixed measure having a determinate beginning and end. It remains, therefore,

[Col. 0665C]

for us to inquire what order and arrangement our thoughts ought to have, so that the house of God may be constructed from them. Then we must also consider carefully how this house, which we build for God to inhabit, can receive a fixed measure, since God Himself, its inhabitant, is infinite and immeasurable. Let us first pursue the matter which we proposed to investigate first.

## CHAPTER II. On the order and arrangement of our thoughts, which are not finite, so that the house of God may be constructed from them.

The number of all things, so far as it concerns the capacity of our understanding, is infinite, because it cannot be comprehended by us. But where there is no definition, there is no certainty; and where there is no certainty,

[Col. 0665D]

there is confusion; and where there is confusion, there can be no order.

From this comes the fact that, when we unrestrainedly open our hearts to the desire for earthly things, a throng of empty thoughts immediately arises, and our mind is carried away in so many directions that even the order of natural discernment is disturbed. For because worldly things, which we desire inordinately, are infinite, the thoughts which we inwardly conceive from the memory of those things cannot be finite either. As, at every moment, different thoughts arise from others and emerge in many ways, we ourselves cannot even comprehend in what order, or how, they come to the heart or depart from it.

Therefore, if we wish to have ordered, stable, and tranquil thoughts, let us strive to restrain our hearts from this immoderate distraction.

[Col. 0666A]

This can be done if we prescribe for ourselves certain fixed and determinate subjects upon which the attention of our heart may continually dwell and our meditation be exercised. There are three possibilities: to be distracted among infinite things, always to remain in the same thing, and to wander moderately. We ought not to have the first; we cannot have the second here; and therefore only this third remains: since we cannot yet truly be stable in heart, let us at least meanwhile gather our hearts back from immoderate distraction, so that, while we continually strive to become less unstable, we may continually begin more and more to imitate true stability.

To make what we say clearer by an example, let us set forth three things: one below, another above, and a third in the middle. Below let us place the world; above, God; and in the middle let us set the human mind.

[Col. 0666B]

Then let us consider below, in this world, a great and dreadful confusion of all things and an infinite distraction of human minds; above, however, with God, perpetual and unshaken stability. After this, let us imagine the human mind ascending from this world upward to God, gathering itself more and more into unity as it ascends. Then we shall be able spiritually to see the form of our ark, which was broad at the bottom and rose upward into a narrow space until it reached the measure of one cubit at its summit.

For in like manner, ascending from this deep place, from this valley of tears, through certain increases of virtues—as though through certain steps arranged in our heart—we are gradually gathered into one, until we attain that simple unity, true simplicity, and eternal stability which are with God.

[Col. 0666C]

No one becomes perfect suddenly; rather, each person tends toward perfection by making progress. So long as one still has something in which to make progress, one has not yet reached the summit of perfection.

Here, if we wish, we may consider the manner of our restoration. Almighty God, to whom nothing is impossible, could indeed, if He wished, immediately and without delay transfer those upon whom He had purposed to have mercy from the labors, miseries, and dangers of this present life, which is full of temptations, to the stability of eternal life. But He wills that His elect pass through various tribulations and many temptations to be purified, so that, when they return to Him through many sorrows, they may learn how far they departed from Him by sinning.

For while they go along, not transported but led back, through repentance by the road by which they had departed through sin, they recognize from the prolonged weariness of the journey itself, so to speak, that they have been brought from far away.

[Col. 0666D]

And all this happens so that the grace of God may be commended to human beings: that they may love God more ardently in proportion as they see that, even when they had been far away, they were less abandoned by Him. Thus He Himself promised through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “I will bring your seed from the east and gather you from the west. I will say to the north, ‘Give’; and to the south, ‘Do not withhold.’ Bring my sons from far away and my daughters from the ends of the earth” (Isa.

[Col. 0667A]

43).

Each of us who remembers where he was and recognizes where he is may perhaps see in himself how a human being is brought from far away through divine mercy and gathered into one from his own dispersion.

It remains now for us to consider what those things are, mentioned above, in which the mind ought to be exercised, so that it may gradually grow accustomed to withdrawing itself from the distraction of this world and rise, strengthened, to that highest stability—that is, the contemplation of God. This can be seen as follows.

## CHAPTER III. On the two works of God, namely creation and restoration, in which the mind must be exercised lest it be distracted by the world.

All God’s works were made for human beings, whether those belonging to humanity’s first creation

[Col. 0667B]

or those made for humanity’s restoration. To humanity’s creation pertains the creation of the world—that is, heaven and earth and all the things which are read to have been made by God in the beginning. To humanity’s restoration pertains the incarnation of the Word, and everything which either preceded that incarnation from the beginning in order to prefigure and foretell it, or has taken place after it until the end of the world in order that it may be preached and believed.

Now, according to those first works which belong to humanity’s creation, God is the God of all, because He created all things and indiscriminately grants these temporal goods to all, good and evil alike. But according to those works which belong to humanity’s restoration, He did not will to be the God of all, but only of those whom He Himself chose before the ages of the world in the purpose of His good will, so that at the appointed time He might call, justify, and glorify them in His beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. 8).

[Col. 0667C]

Hence in Holy Scripture He calls Himself in a special way the God of certain persons, as in the words: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3). For, as has been said, He who created all does not redeem all, but saves some through mercy and condemns others through justice.

Thus the things done for humanity’s restoration do not concern everyone, but only those who are saved. And as they are not for all, so they were not done everywhere, nor did they come to everyone’s knowledge; rather, they were done in certain definite places and times and with certain persons ordered for this purpose according to the depth of the divine counsel.

Although God, according to His omnipotence, could have employed many means for the restoration of humanity, He nevertheless chose especially this one, which was more suited than the others to our weakness, so that He might accomplish the work of His mercy not only powerfully and justly but wisely.

[Col. 0667D]

The first human being abandoned his Creator while he beheld Him present through contemplation; but now the human being seeks through faith the Creator whom he does not see by direct sight. The first human being was able to stand without labor and fell of his own accord; but now, rising voluntarily, the human being returns to God even through torments.

Therefore the counsel of the divine dispensation regarding our restoration is most orderly: the one who fell voluntarily must rise not by compulsion but voluntarily; and the one weakened through free choice does not regain health until he wills through free choice to be healed. Yet it is not from ourselves that we will this; God works it in us. For God’s grace precedes and stirs our free choice so that it can will to be healed, because one who could by himself will to become sick cannot by himself will to be healed.

This, then, is what is now being done in the elect: they are prepared in the present life for future blessedness, so that the human being placed in this misery may deserve to ascend to that blessedness, just as the first human being placed in that blessedness deserved to descend to this misery.

[Col. 0668B]

But the merit by which a human being deserved to be unhappy came wholly from the human being. This merit, however, by which one deserves eternal happiness, does not come from a human being; rather, God’s grace works it in the human being.

It is therefore not without reason that God, recalling humanity after sin from the blindness of ignorance, so moderates His knowledge of Himself that He does indeed become known and yet always remains hidden. For if He revealed Himself to people so openly that no one could doubt concerning Him, then neither faith would have merit nor unbelief a place. He becomes known so that faith may be nourished, and He remains hidden lest unbelief be compelled to yield. He remains hidden so that faith may be tested; He becomes known so that unbelief may be condemned. Because believers have something by which they could doubt, and unbelievers something by which they could believe if they willed rightly, the former receive a reward for faith and the latter punishment for unbelief.

[Col. 0668C]

God was pleased first to make humanity merit the blessedness which He was going to give freely, yet in such a way that both the merit and the reward of merit came from Him. He therefore postpones giving what He will give: full health, full knowledge, and full blessedness. Meanwhile He illumines our blindness through faith, so that by advancing through faith we may deserve to attain His manifest brightness.

## CHAPTER IV. Why God spoke in secret and obscurely.

That is why, from the beginning, God spoke with few people, rarely, obscurely, and in secret. Let us search the Scriptures, and we shall find that God scarcely ever spoke in a crowd [Col. 0668D]; but whenever he wished to make himself known to human beings, he revealed himself not to nations and peoples, but either to individuals or to very few persons, separated from the common throng of humanity—whether in the silence of night, in fields, or in deserts and mountains. Thus he spoke with Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Samuel, David, and all the prophets. Finally, appearing in the flesh, although he spoke openly to the world, he nevertheless led his disciples apart up a mountain in order to reveal his glory to them (Mark 9). Elsewhere he says to them: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Matt. 13); and again: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the rooftops” [Col. 0669A] (Matt. 10).

Nor did he give the law to that ancient people in Egypt, or anywhere else, until he had led them out separately into the wilderness. Nor even there did he do so openly before all: Moses alone ascended the mountain in order to receive the law. What, then, does it mean that God always speaks in secret, except that he calls us to what is secret? And what does it mean that he speaks with few, except that he gathers us together? Consider these two things that I have said: he gathers us and calls us to secrecy.

Before the first human being sinned, there was no need for God to speak to him from without, because he possessed within himself the ear of the heart, by which he could hear the voice of God spiritually. But after he opened the outward ear to the serpent’s persuasion, he closed the inward ear to the voice of God. Therefore, because humanity lost the inward hearing by which it hears God speaking, God, calling us back to himself, cries out from without [Col. 0669B]. Yet whenever he speaks, he always withdraws as though wishing to conceal himself, so that he may both remind the human mind of himself through what he says and draw it to himself by escaping through his concealment.

For he provokes our desire in order to increase it: by speaking, he awakens love of himself within us; by fleeing, he inflames us to follow him. Such indeed is the human heart: if it cannot attain what it loves, it burns more intensely in its desire. Thus in the Song of Songs the Bridegroom comes: “He stands behind the wall, looks through the windows and the lattice” (Song 2), so that he may, as it were, both hide and not hide. “He puts his hand through the opening” (Song 5), touches the Bride, and with a subdued sound, a faint voice, calls her and says: “Come, my friend, my dove. Behold, winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed. Flowers [Col. 0669C] have appeared in our land; the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song 2).

When she hears that the Bridegroom is present, she immediately rises, hastens, opens the bolt of her door (Song 5), and, as though about to receive him as he comes, prepares her arms to embrace him. She can scarcely endure, scarcely bear, scarcely wait. Her soul melts (ibid.), her heart burns, her inmost breast is aflame; she leaps, rejoices, dances, delights, rushes to meet the one who comes. But he, when he seems already to be held, turns aside and suddenly flees, as though slipping out from the midst of her embraces.

What is this? While he is not sought, he seeks; while he is not called, he comes; but when he is sought, he turns aside, and when he is called, he flees. If he does not love, why does he come? Or if he loves, why does he flee? Yet he loves, and therefore he comes; but because he does not love here [Col. 0669D], therefore he flees. What is this that I said, “he does not love here”? In this world, in this age, in this land, in this homeland, in this exile.

But he calls us to his own land, because such love does not befit this country; the security of love would be the prosperity of that land. Delightful love seeks a pleasant place. Therefore he commends his land to us; therefore he praises his homeland; therefore he says: “Flowers have appeared in our land; the flowering vines have given forth their fragrance” (Song 2); “the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” He does this so that we may long for such a region, desire such a homeland, and follow him. There he loves us; there he desires to enjoy our love; there he asks to be embraced by us; there he does not flee those who follow him, but waits for those who come to him.

Therefore he offers himself when he is not sought, in order to kindle us with love of himself [Col. 0670A]. When he is sought, he flees, in order to make us run after him. For unless he first showed himself to us, no one would love him; and unless he fled when he was sought, no one would wish to follow him. “Flowers,” he says, “have appeared in our land”—not “in my land,” but “in our land,” in order to share it with us.

It is as though he said: “I am present to you as a trustworthy messenger; I have seen what I testify, I have heard what I speak. Do not fear, do not distrust, do not hesitate. Follow where I call you, because you are from where I come. You do not have here an abiding city. What you inhabit is foreign territory. You came here from elsewhere; if you remembered your homeland, you surely would not love exile. For this reason I too came here: that I might lead you out from here, not that I might remain here with you. And therefore I cry to you from concealment, because I wish only to make myself known here [Col. 0670B], not to remain. Therefore I call you from afar, because I hasten to return. It is enough that I have come out only so far that I can be heard. I would consider it a loss to myself if I went farther along the remaining road. Every delay is burdensome. Flowers have appeared in our land. Learn how greatly you ought to hasten when you see me fleeing. I would not have come unless I wished to draw you after me.”

This is the reason why God always speaks in secret. Thus in the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel he spoke through parables and riddles. For it is fitting that the secrets of mystical meanings be concealed beneath figures of speech, because they would quickly become cheap if they lay open everywhere to everyone. Thus truth both exercises the faithful through inquiry [Col. 0670C] and remains hidden lest it be found by the unfaithful. The former, because it is difficult to find, it kindles with greater desire; the latter, because they cannot find it at all, it blinds. Thus from the same source the faithful advance and the unfaithful fall: the former, by humbly listening and faithfully investigating the words of God, arrive at knowledge of truth; the latter, through neglect, contempt, or perverse understanding, never attain truth.

We have now said why God speaks obscurely and in secret. It remains to say why he speaks, and has spoken, with few people and rarely.

## Chapter V. Why God speaks, and has spoken, with few people and rarely

The nature of the first human being had been ordered and established by God in such a way that the soul, which ruled the body, would indeed carry out outwardly, through the ministrations of the bodily senses, the things required outside; but inwardly it would always attend through reason to its Creator. That is, by animating the body’s limbs it would move them outwardly to action, but would direct inwardly its intention and desire to the Creator alone; and it would do nothing outwardly that did not proceed from love of him and tend toward love of him. Thus charity would command every action, reason would arrange it, and sense would carry it out and complete it.

As long as it maintained this order of its nature, though it varied outwardly through action, inwardly it remained stable through intention and love. For it aimed at one thing, did all things for the sake of one thing, loved one thing, referred the end of all its wills and actions to one thing, and with the tireless gaze of its mind continually looked to its one Creator [Col. 0671A]. Hence it could not doubt its Creator, who was always present to it inwardly through contemplation. The vision of him both illuminated its heart through knowledge and made it stand firm and rest through love.

But after, by the desert of its transgression, it was cast out from the face of the Lord, it became blind and unstable: blind through the mind’s ignorance, unstable through the flesh’s desire. When these were transmitted from it into all posterity, every evil arose. Through ignorance, human beings finally descended so far that they did not recognize their Creator and either supposed that no God existed at all or attributed divinity to those who were not gods. Through desire, moreover, they were scattered and dispersed among endless errors. For it was inevitable that those pressed down by the darkness of ignorance, who did not know that other, invisible goods existed, would pour themselves out without measure through desire for the earthly things that they saw [Col. 0671B].

Therefore, wishing to gather our hearts from this dispersal and call them back to contemplate inward joys, God speaks outwardly, in order to remind us to return inwardly. But because the mind accustomed to visible things does not know how to rise so quickly to invisible things, he also willed to display certain miracles visibly, in which he might nourish our affection and commend his love to us. These are especially the works which belong to humanity’s restoration. For the things made for humanity’s creation show us more the power of the Maker; but those made for humanity’s redemption chiefly concern love. Therefore God performed these works in order to show what love he bore toward us and call us back from love of this world to love of himself.

He willed, however, to regulate these works so that they should not be infinite, lest they distract our mind—which was to be gathered—in their preoccupation; yet they should be many, in order that they might delight that same mind, still incapable of perfect stability, by the variety of things. Therefore he chose one people and one place in which to initiate mysteries that concerned not merely one people but the salvation of the whole world, so that unity might be commended everywhere and the human mind called back, both inwardly and outwardly, to unity; so that, just as the salvation of all comes from one Savior, so too the beginning of salvation might flow from one place and one people [Col. 0671C].

For he who made all things for us [Col. 0671D] made them, of course, in the way he knew to be most beneficial for us. God performed these things partly through human beings, partly through angels, and partly through himself: very many through human beings, many through angels, few through himself. This was so that, while the human mind advances in meditation upon them from the deeds of human beings to the deeds of angels, and from the deeds of angels to the deeds of God, it may gradually become accustomed to gathering itself into one; and the more it escapes multiplicity, the more it may begin to draw near to true simplicity.

Therefore, while God, by speaking with few and rarely, gathers our minds into one, and by speaking obscurely and in secret draws them upward to himself, what else does he do but, so to speak, fashion in our hearts the shape of a certain invisible ark? Although he made all his works for humanity, he nevertheless willed some of them to be works which would render service to those in health, and others to be works which would bring remedy to the sick. The world could serve a healthy person, but it could not restore a sick one. Therefore, after that first creation of things—whose purpose was to be subject to those who stood—it was necessary that other works be made which would raise up those who had fallen. These are more worthy than the first works in proportion as they are more necessary; and in proportion as they precede in dignity, they extend through a longer time [Col. 0672A]. For those were made in six days; these are accomplished through six ages. The creation of things was made in six days, and humanity’s restoration is completed in six ages.

## Chapter VI. That the chosen and the reprobate assess God’s works differently

[Col. 0672B]

But it must be known that the chosen and the reprobate assess divine works differently. The chosen prefer the works of restoration to the works of the first creation, because the former were made for service, the latter for salvation. But, on the contrary, the reprobate love the works of creation more than the works of restoration, because they seek present pleasure, not future blessedness.

The philosophers of the Gentiles, investigating with a certain superstitious curiosity the natures of things—that is, the works of creation—became vain in their thoughts. Christian philosophers, continually meditating on the works of restoration, drive every vanity from their thoughts [Col. 0672C]. The chosen, considering their own restoration, burn with the fire of divine love. But the reprobate, perversely loving the beauty of created things, grow cold in their love of God. The reprobate, while they immerse their thoughts in transient things, forget their Creator. But the chosen cannot forget their Creator, whose mercy they continually contemplate in connection with their restoration.

The reprobate, while they crave temporal things, lose knowledge of eternal things. But the chosen, while they recall God’s temporal benefits, advance toward knowledge of eternal things. The reprobate fall away from invisible things through visible things; but the chosen ascend to invisible things through visible things. Yet it must be understood that the visible things from which they ascend are different from those through which they ascend. From the works of creation, through the works [Col. 0672D] of restoration, they ascend to the Author of creation and restoration.

These ascents must be understood not outwardly but inwardly, by steps laid out in the heart, from virtue to virtue. Perhaps we shall be able to understand this more easily as follows.

## Chapter VII. That there are two worlds, visible and invisible

Just as we distinguished two kinds of works, namely the works of creation and the works of restoration, so let us understand that there are two worlds: visible and invisible. The visible world is this fabric of the universe which we see with bodily eyes; the invisible world is the human heart, which we cannot see.

And just as, in the days of Noah, the floodwaters covered the whole earth, while the ark alone was borne above the waters and not only could not be submerged, but was lifted higher upward the more the waters swelled, so now we should understand that in the human heart the desire of this world is like certain floodwaters, while the ark borne above them is the faith of Christ, which tramples transient pleasure and longs for the eternal goods that are above [Col. 0673A].

The desire of this world is compared with waters because it is flowing and slippery and, like water running downward, always seeks the lowest places and makes its followers unstable and dissolute. If a person enters into his own heart, he will be able to see how desire always flows downward toward transient things, while faith tends toward the enduring goods above. But since Scripture says that desire [Col. 0673B] dwells in the flesh and faith in the heart, how can we affirm that both are in the heart, unless because we are said to desire according to the flesh when we desire carnally in the heart?

Nevertheless, both desiring and believing belong to the heart. But one has its source in loving earthly things; the other in seeking heavenly things. Therefore desire is below and faith above. Desire is born into the heart from the flesh; faith is inspired into the heart not from the flesh but by God. Therefore, when the Lord praised Peter’s faithful confession, he said: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16). But concerning desire Paul says: “It is no longer I who do it, but sin which dwells in me” (Rom. 7). And in the same place he specifies what “in me” means: “I know,” he says, “that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” [Col. 0673C] (ibid.). Elsewhere he also explains what the sin is that he said dwelt in the flesh: “Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfil the desires of the flesh” (Gal. 5), plainly calling the desires of the flesh “concupiscence.”

Therefore concupiscence dwells in the flesh—that is, below in the heart—while faith dwells not in the flesh but in the spirit. Yet this must be carefully considered: when the Apostle said, “Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfil the desires of the flesh,” he did not say, “You shall not feel them,” but “You shall not fulfil them.” He clearly declared that every human being, as long as he remains in this life, possesses an inescapable tendency to desire owing to the corruption of the first birth; yet, with God’s grace assisting, it is impossible for no one to consent to this concupiscence. Therefore elsewhere he said: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. 6). It is as if he said: “It cannot happen that in your mortal body sin—that is, the tinder of sin, the incentive of vices, the sting of concupiscence—should not exist; but with the assistance of God’s grace it can happen that it does not reign, that it does not rule. It is impossible that you should not feel it; but it is not necessary that you consent to it” [Col. 0673D].

Thus every human being suffers within his heart a certain flood of concupiscence, from which no one is delivered except through the ark of faith. There the evil person, walking on dry ground, is submerged, while the good person, submerged in the depths of the sea, is not harmed. It is indeed a dangerous shipwreck, which is [lacuna]ed. Woe to the person endangered there! No harbor is safe for him, no anchorage secure, no calm tranquil, who is inwardly tossed by the surging tides of his own concupiscence and swallowed up by the insatiable whirlpool of lusts [Col. 0674A].

## Chapter VIII. On the three kinds of human beings in relation to the ark

Here we can consider three kinds of human beings: some who have the flood within and no ark; some who have both flood and ark within, but are not in the ark; and some who have both the flood and the ark and remain in the ark. In the flood without the ark are unbelievers, whom fleshly desires envelop, and who know of no life other than this transient life. In the flood they have an ark but do not remain in it: these are those who have already learned through faith that, after the end of this mutable existence, immortal life is to come, but who nevertheless subject their minds to the pleasure of temporal things, having set that life aside [Col. 0674B].

For Scripture says: “Where your treasure is, there is your heart also” (Matt. 6). Where your pleasure is, there is your thought. But where your thought is, there is the dwelling-place of the inward person. For each person is said, according to the inward person, to dwell where he lives in thought. Therefore those who establish their heart’s pleasure in the vanity of this world, although they possess the ark of faith, are nevertheless inwardly shipwrecked.

But, to pass over the other lovers of the world, how many learned people do we now see who wish to be called Christians, enter the church with the other faithful, and participate in Christ’s sacraments, yet whose hearts more often remember Saturn [Col. 0674C] and Jupiter, Hercules and Mars, or Achilles and Hector, Pollux and Castor, Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle, than Christ and his saints? They love the trifles of poets, and either neglect—or, what is worse, ridicule and despise—the truth of the divine Scriptures.

Let them now see what benefit it is to enter the Church outwardly and inwardly to commit fornication against faith in their hearts. I pronounce to them that at the end they will be joined to those to whom they now join themselves in their thoughts through their heart’s affection; and they will share there in the punishment of those whose life they love here. What does it profit them to have faith and not remain in faith? What does it profit them to have a sound ship, yet in the waves not merely suffer shipwreck, I will not say, but willingly bring it about? What does it profit to know truth and love falsehood?

Those who are truly faithful are not like this. Do you wish to know what they are like? Hear what one of them was like, and understand that all are like him. For those who are one in truth cannot be unlike one another. Hear, therefore, what is said of him: “The law of his God is in his heart” (Ps. 36): this is to have the ark within. And because perhaps this is not sufficient, hear again: “His will is in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 1): this is to dwell in the ark [Col. 0674D]. That person is perfect who loves what he believes, so that he possesses faith working through love, which conquers the world (Gal. 5; 1 John 5).

This is the ark in which we must be saved. It can be borne by the waters, but it cannot be submerged at all, because it makes use of this world for necessity but does not yield to it through covetousness. This is what is said in the Psalm: “This great sea, broad in its expanse; there are creeping things without number; small animals with great; there ships pass through” (Ps. 103) [Col. 0675A].

For within us there is a sea, namely the desire of this world, in which any pleasures that can be found are sprinkled with many bitternesses; these flow downward in our heart according to the fleshly affection. The creeping things are fleshly thoughts, deformed by the foulness of diverse vices. When we admit them disorderly into our heart, we fill our inward parts as though with certain monstrous creeping things. The ship is that spiritual ark, namely our faith, which, suspended inwardly above, tramples the desire of the world.

He said “ships” because of the many [Col. 0675B] souls. For many souls are one soul because of one faith and love; and one faith is many faiths because of many faithful souls. Thus it is said: “Your faith has saved you,” and “my faith,” and “that person’s faith,” although the catholic faith is one. Therefore the ship of faith alone crosses the sea; the ark alone escapes the flood. And if we wish to be saved, it is necessary not merely that it be in us, but that we remain in it.

And let no one, trusting in his own conscience, say: “What have I to do with this ark? The flood of fleshly concupiscence has dried up in me.” Whoever is outside does not know what takes place within. But if a person returns to his heart, he will find there a stormy sea agitated by the savage waves of unclean passions and evil desires, which sink the mind downward as often as they subject it to themselves through consent [Col. 0675C].

For in every human being, as long as one lives in this corruptible life, where the flesh desires against the spirit, there is this flood; or rather, every human being is in this flood. But the good are in it like those who are carried in ships upon the sea; the evil are in it like shipwrecked people tossed about in the waves. In the good, indeed, the waters of this flood begin to lessen in this life and diminish more or less in each person according to the difference of graces. Nevertheless, the earth of the human heart can never be completely dried as long as they live in this life.

And therefore the dove that is sent out finds no place here where its foot may rest, but always returns to the ark. For the pure mind, since in this world it can find nothing upon which to set securely the foot of its affection, fears to remain long outside the protection of inward meditation. But if perhaps it goes out at some time through thought, it returns quickly, like a dove flying away and withdrawing to the solitude of conscience; everywhere it rests from outward noise, as in the ark from the waves [Col. 0675D].

Let us understand, then, that within us is what we flee and within us is that to which we must flee: concupiscence and faith. Concupiscence, which we must flee; faith, which we must grasp. We must ascend from concupiscence, so that by advancing we may leave it behind; we must ascend through faith, so that by holding it we may continually advance to better things. Concupiscence belongs to the works of creation; faith belongs to the works of restoration: through the former we are scattered by loving disorderly through concupiscence, and through the latter we are made firm by believing devoutly.

For this reason divine warnings so often cry out to us and urge us to flee the world—not, of course, that we should go outside heaven and earth, but that we should not remain in the desire of the world. What does “not remain” mean? Who remains in the desire of the world? The person who places the delight of his mind in it and continually directs himself toward fulfilling it; who thinks of it unceasingly and fixes his mind’s purpose in it; who follows it deliberately and delights in it by consent.

Therefore the world is cursed in sacred Scripture and called the enemy of God—not because the substance of the world is evil, but because the beauty of the world seduces souls [Col. 0676A]. The substance of the world would not be something to flee if the desire of the world were not evil. Therefore, when we flee the desire of the world, we flee it because it is evil; but when we flee the substance of the world, we flee it not because it is evil, but because it is an occasion of evil.

For an affection of concupiscence arises from a conceived image of the world. Therefore, if we wish to avoid the desire of the world, we must first exclude from our thought the memory of this world. “In my meditation,” says the Prophet, “fire burns” (Ps. 38). As wood nourishes fire, so thoughts feed desires. If good thoughts are present in meditation, the fire of charity will burn; but if thoughts are evil, the fire of covetousness will burn. For as the eye is fed by an appearance, so the mind is fed by thought; and by a certain shameful commerce the impure mind enjoys its desire when, inwardly through thought, it somehow embraces the thing desired [Col. 0676B].

It also sometimes happens that what we frequently think about idly, we later desire unlawfully; and a person is judged guilty of the deed when he delights through consent in the thought. Therefore, just as the sick abstain from certain foods, not because the foods themselves are evil but because they are not suitable for those persons to consume, so we ought to keep the images of earthly things away from our thoughts, not because the things themselves are evil, but lest our mind, which is weakened of itself, be further corrupted by the recollection of those things.

Moreover, as regards the things themselves, since every creature of God is good, there is no thing that cannot be thought about without sin. And again, if we consider perverse affections, there is no thing concerning which we cannot [Col. 0676D] sin in thinking. For we can think well of evil, ill of good, cleanly of what is unclean, and uncleanly of what is clean. Thoughts must be judged not from the thing from which they arise, but from the affection they produce [Col. 0676C].

We read that holy men not only thought, but also spoke and wrote, about unclean things; they certainly would not have done so if thoughts of unclean things defiled the soul. It makes no difference what the object of thought may be, but what affection follows from the thought itself; for thought does not pollute the mind where delight does not corrupt the conscience.

Nevertheless, as we said, it is beneficial for us to forget this world and erase its memory from our heart, lest perhaps, while we think about it frequently [lacuna], we may bend toward its concupiscence [Col. 0677A].

I think it has now been shown sufficiently clearly from where this boundless dispersal of our thoughts, which we suffer, arises: namely, from the world and its concupiscence, that is, from the works of creation. And likewise, what it is by which our thoughts may be gathered into one: that is, through the works of restoration. And because, as was said above, there cannot be order where there is no end, it remains that, leaving aside the works of creation, we seek the order of our thoughts where things are finite—that is, in the works of restoration.

This is what we proposed above to investigate: namely, what order our thoughts ought to have, so that from them the spiritual house of wisdom may be built within us. And because thoughts arise from things, the order of thoughts must be derived from the order of things. Henceforth, then, leaving aside the works of creation, we shall begin to discuss the works of restoration. We have emerged from the former as from a certain overflowing flood, and now enter the works of restoration as into an ark [Col. 0677B].

## Chapter IX. What are the works of human restoration?

The works of restoration, therefore, are all those things which have been done, or are to be done, from the beginning of the world to the end of the age for the restoration of human beings. In them we must consider both the events themselves and the persons through whom, for whom, and among whom they were done, together with the places and times where and when they were done.

In the works of restoration order is considered in three ways: according to place, according to time, and according to dignity [Col. 0677C]. According to place: what was done near and what far away. According to time: what was done earlier and what later. According to dignity: what is lower and what more excellent. This last is divided into many parts: what is holy and holier; useful and more useful; honorable and more honorable; beautiful and more beautiful; wonderful and more wonderful; rare and rarer; difficult and more difficult; credible and more credible; great and greater; obscure and more obscure; and other such distinctions.

This order according to dignity seems to belong to the height of the ark. Thus, if we say that holy things are counted in the first storey, holier things in the second, and the holiest things in the third, and so with the other things which we have enumerated [Col. 0677D].

But the order of place and the order of time appear in nearly all respects to coincide with the sequence of events. By divine providence it seems to have been arranged that things performed at the beginning of time should be performed in the East, as though at the beginning of the world; then, as time flowed toward its end, the chief course of events should descend as far as the West, so that from this itself we may recognize that the end of the age is approaching, because the course of events has now reached the end of the world.

Indeed, the first human being, already created, is placed in the East, in the gardens of Eden, so that from that beginning the offspring of posterity might spread over the world. Likewise, after the Flood, the beginning of kingdoms and the head of the world were among the Assyrians, Chaldeans, and Medes in the eastern regions [Col. 0678A]. Then supreme power came to the Greeks; finally, near the end of the age, it descended to the Romans in the West, dwelling as it were at the end of the world.

Thus, as the sequence of events runs in a straight line from East to West, those things which were done on the right or the left—that is, toward the north or the south—correspond in such a way through their meanings that whoever considers more carefully cannot doubt that they were so arranged by divine providence. To give a few examples out of many: Egypt lies south of Jerusalem, but Babylon lies north. Egypt means “darkness,” and the south wind is warm. Therefore Egypt signifies this world, placed amid the darkness of ignorance and the heat of fleshly concupiscence. Babylon, however, means “confusion” [Col. 0678B], and signifies hell, where there is no order, but everlasting horror dwells.

We read that the ancient people of the Hebrews first served in Egypt amid mud and brick, and then, after many intervening years, were carried captive into Babylon. What does this event suggest to us except the fall of the whole human race? Because through original sin, being exiled from the heavenly homeland, it is first in this mortal life subjected to vices through ignorance and concupiscence; and then, after this life, it is held captive among the dead in torments—that is, in Babylon, toward the north, where that first apostate angel established his seat.

Therefore, the order of rank pertains to the height of the ark; the order of time, to the length of the ark; and the order of place [Col. 0678C], to both its height and its length. To the length of the ark pertains: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard,” and likewise, having gone out about the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours, and seeing others standing, he sent them into his vineyard (Matt. 20). To the breadth of the ark pertains: “Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their word unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18). To the height of the ark pertains: “For thither the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, a testimony to Israel, to give praise to the name of the Lord” (Ps. 121).

And, lest I create delays by proceeding point by point, I shall tell you briefly what must be said. In these three dimensions all divine Scripture is contained. For history [Col. 0678D] measures the length of the ark, because in the sequence of deeds performed the order of time is found. Allegory measures the breadth of the ark, because the gathering of faithful peoples consists in participation in the sacraments. Tropology measures the height of the ark, because in the advance of virtues the dignity of merits increases.

We may still, if we wish, distinguish the height of the ark differently, so that the teaching may be manifold while the truth remains the same. For we wish the reader to be warned of this: that in this treatise we have often set forth the same matter in different ways, because of the abundant exercise of instruction, so that an intelligent mind may test every path of knowledge—provided only that nothing contrary to truth be either thought or said.

Therefore, just as the ark is divided into three storeys, so too the works of restoration are divided into three orders. In the first order, as in the first storey, is shadow; in the second order, as in the second storey, is body; in the third order, as in the third storey, is spirit—or, if you prefer to say it thus: figure, thing, truth. By this understand that shadow and figure are the same; body and thing are the same; spirit and truth are the same.

Accordingly, those things which, before Christ’s coming, were performed bodily and visibly under the natural law and under the written law, in order to prefigure those things which are now performed bodily and visibly after Christ’s coming in the time of grace, are called shadows, because they were bodily and were figures of bodily things. Our sacraments themselves, which are now visibly performed in this Church, are called body. But spirit [Col. 0679B] is that which the grace of God invisibly accomplishes beneath visible sacraments. For example, to set forward one instance: the Red Sea prefigured baptism, which is now consecrated in the holy Church. Visible baptism itself signifies the cleansing of crimes, which the Holy Spirit invisibly works in souls beneath the sacrament by which bodies are anointed. The Red Sea, therefore, is shadow and figure; the baptism of visible water which we now possess is body and thing; but the cleansing of sins is spirit and truth.

There is also another method, of which we spoke above, by which we can distinguish the height of the ark. For God has wrought the works of restoration partly through human beings, partly through angels, and partly through himself. In the first [Col. 0679C] storey, therefore, we place the works of human beings; in the second storey, the works of angels; in the third storey, the works of God.

Or, in a moral sense: the first storey is faith; the second storey is hope; the third storey is charity.

Or, according to anagogy: the first storey is right thought; the second storey is provident meditation; the third storey is clear contemplation.

Or, according to operation: the first storey is knowledge; the second storey is discipline; the third storey is goodness.

Or, according to the different states: the first storey is nature; the second storey is the written law; the third storey is grace. For if these three are considered according to time, they measure the length of the ark; if they are distinguished according to dignity, they distinguish the height of the ark [Col. 0679D], because, just as they follow one another in time, so they precede one another in dignity.

What then is this ark of which so much is said, and in which such manifold paths of knowledge are contained? Do you think it is a labyrinth? Not a labyrinth, nor toil within, but rest within. Whence do I know this? Because he dwells in it who said: “Come unto me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh [Col. 0680A] you, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 1). For if there is toil where he himself is, how do those who come to him find rest?

But now “his place has been made in peace, and his dwelling is in Zion. There he has broken the powers of bows, shield, sword, and war” (Ps. 75). Therefore every noise and commotion is far away, and there joy, peace, and rest are always present. What kind of ark, then, is this? Do you wish to know what kind? Bear with me while I tell you a little concerning many things.

This ark is like a storehouse filled with every variety of delights. You will seek nothing in it that you will not find; and when you have found one thing, you will see many things disclosed to you. There the whole work of our restoration from the beginning of the world to its end is most fully contained, and the condition of the universal Church [Col. 0680B] is figured. There the history of deeds done is woven; there the mysteries of the sacraments are found; there are arranged the degrees of affections, thoughts, meditations, contemplations, good works, virtues, and rewards. There is shown what we ought to believe, what we ought to do, and what we ought to hope for. There are contained the pattern of human life and the summit of perfection. There hidden things shine forth; laborious things appear easy; and things which in themselves might seem less fitting, when considered in their proper order, are proved suitable.

There a certain body of the universe is fashioned, and the harmony of its individual parts is unfolded. There another world is found, contrary to this passing and transitory one; for the things which pass through diverse times in this world stand together in that world, as it were, in a state [Col. 0680C] of eternity. There present things do not succeed past things, nor do future things come upon present things; but whatever is there is present [lacuna]; for that reason they remain there, endure forever, and rejoice forever: grieving over nothing past, fearing nothing future, possessing what they love, seeing what they desire.

And therefore perhaps the Apostle said: “The form of this world passes away” (1 Cor. 7)—the form of this world, its appearance, its beauty; but that other world, whose form does not pass away, whose appearance does not fade, whose beauty does not fail. That world is in this world, and this world is smaller than that world, because that one contains what this one cannot contain. The eyes of flesh see this world; the eyes of the heart inwardly contemplate that [Col. 0680D] world. In this world people have their pleasures; in that world delights are ineffable. In this world people run and applaud at spectacles of vanity; in that world the pure in heart are exercised in eternal silence and delight in the contemplation of truth. “Which,” etc.

[Col. 0681]

# ON THE MYSTICAL ARK OF NOAH

## CHAPTER HEADINGS

**CHAPTER I.** On the description of the ark by means of the figure of the cross, with the lamb standing at its center and the column raised on high; on the significance, both of the cross and of the spaces left by it, and of all the other colors serving a mystical sense; and on the length, breadth, and depth or height of the ark itself, mystically understood.

**CHAPTER II.** On the mystical significance of the column raised in the middle of the ark; on the raising of the beams over it; on the storeys marked out between the squares by beams fixed in place; on the position of the aforesaid column; and on the mystery of all these things.

**CHAPTER III.** On the band which is extended through the middle of the base along the length of the ark from end to end, and how it figures the Church.

**CHAPTER IV.** On the square at the front of the ark, signifying the four parts of the world through the letters of the name Adam, which begin the names of those parts; on the genealogies of the patriarchs through the setting out of their names from Adam to Christ; and then on the leaders of the New Testament and the saints who followed, according to the arrangement and division of the ark and according to the ages of the world.

**CHAPTER V.** On the threefold division of the ark according to its length, by which are signified the people of the natural law, the written law, and grace.

**CHAPTER VI.** On the threefold division of the ark according to its breadth, by which the aforesaid people are signified, and on the beams placed there.

**CHAPTER VII.** On the inscriptions of the three storeys of the ark, on the distinction of that ark according to its height, and on the twelve steps by which one ascends to them.

**CHAPTER VIII.** A moral recapitulation concerning the aforesaid steps.

**CHAPTER IX.** On ascents to the virtues from the cold of the east.

**CHAPTER X.** On ascents from the heat and cold of the east.

**CHAPTER XI.** On the door of the ark.

**CHAPTER XII.** Four modes of going forth through thought.

**CHAPTER XIII.** On the six little chambers of the ark according to the letter.

**CHAPTER XIV.** On the forty-two storeys.

**CHAPTER XV.** On the character of the four seasons of the year, and the conclusion of the work.

## CHAPTER I. On the description of the ark, therefore, as above

[Col. 0681A]

First, for the mystical description of Noah’s ark, on the plane where I wish to draw the ark I seek the central point; and, having fixed a point there, I draw around it a small equilateral square, after the likeness of that cubit in which the ark is completed. Then I circumscribe around that square another, slightly larger square, so that the space between the outer and inner squares may appear to be, as it were, the border of the cubit.

Having done this, I draw a cross in the inner square, so that each of its arms touches a side of the square, and I overlay it with gold. Then I clothe in color those spaces remaining on the surface of the square between the four angles of the cross and of the square: the two upper spaces with a fiery color and the two lower with sapphire-blue. Thus [Col. 0681B] one half of the cubit, in fiery color, appears to represent fire, and the other half, in sapphire-blue, a cloud.

After this, on the border of the cubit above the cross I write α, which is the beginning. Opposite, below the cross, I write ω, which is the end. At the right arm of the cross I write χ, the first letter in the name Christ, signifying the Decalogue of the law given to the ancient people, first set, as though chosen and righteous, at the right hand. At the left arm I place c, the last letter in this name “Christ,” [Note: [Col. 0681C] An error of the editor.] signifying, in the number one hundred, the perfection of grace given to the Gentiles, who at first, because of unbelief, were rejected and seemed to be placed at the left.

Then I cover the space of the border all around with purple and green: purple on the outside, green on the inside [Col. 0681C]. And in the middle of the golden cross which I had made, I paint a year-old lamb standing. When this is done, the cubit is complete.

If you ask the reason for this, what else does this inscription seem to tell you except that Christ is the beginning and end, the giver of the Old and New Law? And what else does the painting show you than if it said: this cubit signifies that same people whom the pillar of fire and cloud protected—the pillar which went before the people of Israel in the wilderness, illuminating by fire and overshadowing by cloud. He was terrible to the former people through the fire of divine majesty, punishing sins; and to the latter people he appeared gentle through the cloud of humanity, forgiving sins. For human sins he was sacrificed on the cross, like a gentle lamb that did not open its mouth; and for human righteousness, rising again and ascending above the heavens, he was exalted.

To those coming to him from every side, by the purple of blood he offers the example of his Passion, and by the green color the unfading reward of the heavenly recompense. Or, in the purple he sanctifies the blood [Col. 0682B] of Christ’s Passion, and in the green color the water by which he once judged the world. Or, in the purple, the condemnation of the wicked whom he has justly rejected; in the green, the deliverance of the good whom he will save justly and mercifully.

He stands because he invites; he stands because he strengthens; he stands because he helps; he stands because he crowns; he stands because he keeps watch to guard his city.

Thus, when the central cubit has been completed, I draw around the aforesaid center, far outside it, another square, of such size as I wish the ark to be. This square is six times as long as it is wide, because the ark was three hundred cubits long and fifty in width—that is, six times as long as it was wide. Yet, for a more suitable form in the drawing, I have shortened it to nearly four times its width [Col. 0682C].

After this, through the middle of this square—that is, through the middle of the base of the ark—I enclose, by drawing two lines lengthwise, a space of the same width as the inner square of the central cubit. Likewise, across the middle of the breadth, stretching two lines from one wall to the other, I mark a space of the same width. Thus the two bands—one extending through the middle of the length and the other through the middle of the breadth—intersect one another beneath the central cubit in the form of a cross, and correspond to its inner breadth, being exceeded on either side only by its border.

When this has been carried out, I divide each of the spaces lying between the central point—or rather the central cubit—and each corner of the ark into three equal parts by placing points. With a ruler set to each pair of adjoining points, lengthwise and crosswise, I draw a line everywhere from point to point. In this way I form two more squares, each likewise six times as long as its own width [Col. 0683B]. They are separated from one another in such proportion that by as much as the first exceeds the middle square, so much does the middle square exceed the third.

Of these, the third square, which is the smallest and, according to the position of the plane, is enclosed beneath the others, surrounds the central cubit and cuts the two aforesaid bands—the one measuring the length and the other the breadth of the ark—into four parts: one from above and below, the other from left and right. Then the second encloses the third and likewise cuts the aforesaid bands. Then the other, which is outermost on the plane but lowest in height, encloses all the rest and, girding on each side the four outer ends of the two bands, contains them wholly within itself.

When this has been done, if you wish to know how this figure [Col. 0683C] represents the form of the ark, understand that from the band extending through the middle of the breadth of the ark there is made an equilateral square column, raised in the middle of the ark. Its height is less than the breadth of the ark by the amount by which three is less than five, because the height of the ark was thirty cubits and its breadth fifty.

But if you wish to know on what principle the column is to be understood as made from this very band, consider it thus. Let that cubit, which now lies fixed in the middle of the band according to the position of the plane, be raised upward, drawing the band upward with itself as though folding it in the middle. Then let both of its downward-hanging halves be joined, plane to plane, to one another, so that an upright column may appear, at whose summit rises that cubit which, according to the position of the plane, previously lay in its middle.

Let the cubit itself be understood as nothing other than the upper termination of the column; and let the border of the cubit be a kind of rim or projection made at the head of the column to receive the beams rising round about from below. These beams are fixed into the column beneath that same projection, beneath which the summit of the roof is likewise completed, after the likeness of a roof-tile receiving the topmost ridge of roofs.

And although the height of the column does not seem to be greater than half the band, since it is made from the band doubled, it must nevertheless be understood to be greater by as much as thirty is greater than twenty-five; but this could not be represented on the plane. Again, though only one half of the band constitutes the height [Col. 0684A] of the column, the reason both its halves have been drawn is this.

## CHAPTER II. On the mystical significance of the column raised in the middle of the ark; on the raising of the beams over it; on the storeys marked out between the squares by beams fixed in place; on the position of the aforesaid column; and on the mystery of all these things

This column, raised in the middle of the ark, signifies the tree of life planted in the midst of paradise; that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, planted in the midst of the Church according to the form of humanity assumed by him. This Christ is God and man. Therefore the side of the column facing north signifies his humanity, which he assumed for sinners; but the side facing south [Col. 0684B] figures his divinity, by which he nourishes the minds of the faithful. This is why we depicted the height twice on the plane, since it was necessary to represent the surface of each side; and this could not be done without a double figure.

Therefore, once the column has been set in the middle of the ark, beams are raised from each corner up to its summit and fixed into it beneath the projection of the outer rim. Then the two inner squares are raised upward until each, according to its position, is joined at right angles on every side to the same beams, while the outer square remains at the bottom. Then you will see how the space between the first and second squares is reckoned as the first storey; the space between the second and third, as the second; and the space between the third and the uppermost cubit, as the third.

When this is done, you have the completed form of the ark: broad below and narrow above, down to the measure of one cubit. The position of the aforesaid column is such that it rises from the middle of the base of the ark, occupies the middle place in every storey, and bears the entire structure.

Its mystery is this. The column is Christ. Its southern side—which signifies his divinity—is called the tree of life, and therefore has been overlaid with green. But its northern side—which figures his humanity—is called the book of life, and has been overlaid with sapphire-blue. The ark rests upon the column, and his Church rests upon Christ, because it could in no way stand unless he sustained it, according to what is written in the Song of Songs: “Who is this, coming up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” [Col. 0684D] (Song 8).

Again, just as the column measures the height of each storey, so Christ dispenses each person’s virtue and progress. And just as the column distinguishes the levels, so Christ, according to the good pleasure of his will, distributes the gifts of his graces in the holy Church—appointing some prophets, others apostles, others evangelists, and all others whatsoever who share in spiritual gifts.

And just as the column holds the middle place everywhere, so the Lord Jesus Christ says: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. 18). Therefore, if our weakness is so great [Col. 0685A] that we cannot ascend to the third or second storey, let us nevertheless not despair; but let us gather into one through faith in his name and at least be in the first storey. Let us be in the unity of the Church, hold the true and inviolate faith, and he himself will come to us, standing in our midst, rejoicing over our good beginning, ready to help and to raise us to higher things, so that the Lord Jesus Christ may be one in all, one among all, one above all.

## CHAPTER III. On the band which is extended through the middle of the base along the length of the ark from end to end, and how it figures the Church

It remains now to show what is meant by the other band, which extends through the middle of the base along the length of the ark from end to end. For [Col. 0685B] if the ark signifies the Church, it follows that the length of the ark figures the length of the Church. The length of the Church is considered in the duration of times, just as its breadth is considered in the multitude of peoples. For the Church is said to be enlarged when the number of believers is increased and many are gathered to the faith. But its length consists in the extension of times, by which it stretches itself from past things, through present things, toward future things.

The time of its length extends from the beginning of the world to its end, because the holy Church began in its faithful members from the beginning and will endure until the end of the age. For we believe that there is no time from the beginning of the world to the end of the age in which Christ’s faithful are not found.

Therefore this band, extending from one end to the other of the ark, signifies [Col. 0685C] the course of time from the beginning of the world to the end of the age. Its upper half, from the head of the ark to the column, signifies the whole time from the beginning of the world to the Incarnation of the Word; but its other half, from the column downward, signifies the whole time from the Incarnation of the Word to the end of the age.

For this reason, in the upper half, from the head of the ark to the column, is written the line of carnal generation from Adam to Christ. In the other half, from the column downward, are written the names of the apostles, beginning with Peter, and then in succession, in the order in which spiritual sons succeeded their fathers in the governance of the Church. Since from Adam to Christ there was the old generation, which is according to the flesh, the course of times in the earlier part of the age is distinguished by carnal generation. But since in Christ there was a new generation, which is according to the spirit, the course of times in the later part of the age—that is, after Christ’s coming—is determined by spiritual generation.

I arrange these generations in the following manner: I divide the upper half, from the column upward, into three equal parts, and each third is one sixth of the whole length.

## CHAPTER IV. On the square at the front of the ark, signifying the four parts of the world through the letters of the name Adam, which begin the names of those parts; on the genealogies of the patriarchs through the setting out of their names from Adam to Christ; and then on the leaders of the New Testament and the saints who followed, according to the arrangement and division of the ark and according to the ages of the world

[Col. 0686A]

When this division has been made, I begin above at the head and write the first name, Adam, in the following manner. At the very front of the ark I make a small square to figure the four parts of the world. To its upper side, that is, the east, I add A, the first letter of the name Adam. To its lower side, that is, the west, I add D, the second letter. To the right side, that is, the north, I add A, the third letter. To the left side, that is, the south, I add M, the fourth letter.

In Greek, moreover, the individual parts of the world begin with these letters. *Anatolē* (ἀνατολή), that is, “east,” begins with A, and therefore A is placed at the east. *Dysis* (Δύσις), that is, “west,” begins with D, and therefore D is placed at the west [Col. 0686B]. *Arctos* (ἄρκτος), that is, “north,” begins with A, and therefore A is again placed at the north. *Mesēmbria* (μεσημβρία), that is, “midday” or “south wind,” begins with M, and therefore M is placed at the southern side.

Some give the following reason for this: they say that the first parent rightly drew the elements of his name from the four parts of the world, since he was to be spread abroad through all parts of the world in his offspring.

After Adam, according to the line of generation, are written Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah, Shem, Arphaxad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor, Terah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and these are placed in the first division.

In the second division I first write Judah, and around [Col. 0686C] him I arrange the remaining patriarchs, here and there, at right and left, in the following manner. Beginning from the right wall and following the order of generation, I first write Reuben, because he was the firstborn; then Simeon; then Levi. These are placed at Judah’s right; these four were sons of Leah. At Judah’s left, likewise according to the order of generation, Dan is first written, then Naphtali; these were sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant. After Naphtali is placed Gad, then Asher; these were sons of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant. Then Issachar, then Zebulun; these again were sons of Leah. Finally Joseph, and after him Benjamin; these were sons of Rachel.

After this, I place above each name its own half-length image, from the breast upward, such as are sometimes depicted in pictures, which the Greeks more commonly call *eikonas* (εἰκόνας, “images”), so that the twelve patriarchs, arranged transversely across the breadth in their stations, may appear like a senate of the city of God.

Then, returning to the line of generation, after Judah I place Perez, Hezron, Aram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, David, Solomon, Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joram, Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz. These are in the second division.

Then, in the third division, there are placed in order Hezekiah, Manasseh, Amon, Josiah, Eliakim, Jehoiakim, Shealtiel, Zerubbabel, Abiud, Eliakim, Azor, Zadok, Achim, Eliud, Eleazar, Matthan, Jacob, Joseph. Between Joseph and the column [Col. 0687A] I write: “Thus far the first Adam according to the flesh.”

After this I likewise divide the remaining half, from the column downward, into three equal parts. These three upper and three lower divisions are marked by the sides of the storeys where, according to the position of the plane, they intersect the band.

Therefore, once this division has been made, after the column I write Peter first on the line itself; around him, at right and left, the remaining apostles with their images—six at the right and five at the left—so that on one side of the column the twelve patriarchs and on the other side the twelve apostles are set, after the likeness of the twenty-four elders seated around the throne in the Apocalypse.

And just as the twelve patriarchs occupy the breadth of the ark above—because from them the whole ancient people of the written law descended according to the flesh—so the twelve apostles occupy it below, because from them the whole people of the new law, that is, of grace, has been spiritually propagated through faith.

Then after Peter follow: Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus, Alexander, Sixtus, Telesphorus, Hyginus, Pius, Anicetus, Soter, Eleutherius, Victor, Zephyrinus, Callistus, Urban, Pontian, Anterus, Fabian, Cornelius, Lucius, Stephen, Sixtus, Dionysius, Felix, Eutychian, Gaius, Marcellinus, Marcellus, Eusebius, Miltiades, Sylvester, Mark, Julius, Liberius, Felix, Damasus, Siricius, Anastasius, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Sixtus, Leo, Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, Gelasius, Anastasius, Symmachus, Hormisdas, John, Felix, Boniface, [Col. 0687C] John, Agapetus, Silverius, Vigilius, Pelagius, John, Benedict, Pelagius, Gregory, Sabinian, Boniface, Deusdedit, Boniface, Honorius, Severinus, John, Theodore, Martin, Eugenius, Vitalian, Adeodatus, Bonus, Agatho, Leo, Benedict, John, Conon, Sergius, John, John, Sisinnius, Constantine, Gregory, Gregory, Zachary, Stephen, Paul, Stephen, Hadrian, Leo, Stephen, Paschal, Eugenius, Valentine, Gregory, Leo, Sergius, Benedict, Nicholas, Hadrian, John, John, Martin, Hadrian, Stephen, Formosus, Boniface, Stephen, Romanus, Theodore, John, Benedict, Leo, Christopher, Sergius, Anastasius, Lando, John, Leo, Stephen, John, Leo, Stephen, [Col. 0687D] Marinus, Agapetus, John, Benedict, Leo, John, Benedict, Domnus, Boniface, Benedict, John, John, John, Gregory, John, Sylvester, John, John, Sergius, Benedict, John, Benedict, Sylvester, Gregory, Clement, Damasus, Leo, Victor, Stephen, Benedict, Nicholas, Alexandrinus, Gregory, Victor, Urban, Paschal, Gelasius, Callistus, Honorius.

And the space remaining up to the end of the ark will contain those who are to come after us, unto the end of the age.

From Adam to the Flood is the first age of the world, comprising 1,656 years. The second age is from the Flood to Abraham, comprising 292 years. The third, from Abraham to David, has 942 years. The fourth, from David [Col. 0688A] to the deportation, comprises 473 years. The fifth, from the deportation to Christ’s coming, has 585 years. The sixth age, which is now being lived, has no certain series of years, but, like decrepit old age, is to be consumed by the very death of the whole world.

All who have overcome these wretched ages of the world, full of labors, by a blessed death, having already been received into the seventh age of the everlasting Sabbath, await the eighth age of the blessed resurrection, in which they shall reign perpetually with the Lord.

## CHAPTER V. Again, on the threefold division of the ark according to its length, by which are signified the people of the natural law, the written law, and grace
Source/review notes: The draft reverses the referents of natural reason and concupiscence in the distinction between what is natural by original condition and by birth.; Several supplied column references are omitted.

After this I divide the ark into three parts, and take the first part, which extends from the beginning to the twelve patriarchs, [Col. 0688B] as the time of the natural law. The second, which extends from the twelve patriarchs to the column—that is, to the Incarnation of the Word—as the time of the written law.
