The third, which extends downward from the column—that is, from the Incarnation of the Word to the end of the age—as the time of grace. In accordance with these divisions I also distinguish the sides of the ark on either side.

Then, on each side, through each division, I draw three bands of colour, so that they are laterally joined like certain beams extended lengthwise, giving each a suitable width. For the outermost band, appearing as it were on the outside, ought to be broader than the others. The innermost, middle one, as though compressed between the two, will have the least width. Their position varies in this way: the band which is outermost in the first part is [Col. 0688C] middle in the second; that which is middle in the first part is innermost in the second; and that which is innermost in the first part is outermost in the second. Again, that which is outermost in the second part is middle in the third; that which is middle in the second is innermost in the third; and that which is innermost in the second is outermost in the third.

The mystery of this arrangement is as follows. These three colours signify three classes of persons: persons of the natural law, persons of the written law, and persons of grace. For just as there are three periods—the period of the natural law, the period of the written law, and the period of grace—so there are three classes of persons: persons of the natural law, persons of the written law, and persons of grace. Persons of the natural law belong to the time of the natural law; likewise, persons of the written law belong to [Col. 0688D] the time of the written law, and persons of grace to the time of grace.

Yet, if we attend carefully, we find all these classes of persons in each of these periods. For example, during the time of the natural law there were then likewise persons of the written law and persons of grace; but persons of the natural law were then in their own proper place, while persons of the written law and persons of grace were, as it were, in another’s. For the period of the natural law properly belongs to persons of the natural law, because at that time they were more numerous, more conspicuous in their manner of life, and more eminent in status. But persons of the written law and persons of grace still existed, though few in number and hidden in their manner of life. The same must be understood concerning the period of the written law and [Col. 0689A] the period of grace.

Let us now explain who are called persons of the natural law, of the written law, and of grace, so that from the distinction proposed for each we may more easily infer what we say about them. In Sacred Scripture “nature” is customarily taken in three ways: first, for that whole and uncorrupted good in which the first human being was created, according to which sense we say that all things are naturally good. Next, it is taken for that corruption of sin in which we are born, according to which the Apostle says: “By nature we are children of wrath” (Eph. 2), that is, subject to a corruptible birth and to sin. Nature is also taken for those remnants of natural good that remained in humankind after sin.

For natural good could be corrupted in a human being by sin, [Col. 0689B] but it could not be wholly extinguished, because a certain spark of natural reason still lives in the human mind, by which it distinguishes good from evil. According to this the Apostle says: “For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do the things that belong to the law, though they have no law, they are a law to themselves” (Rom. 2).

Therefore, persons of the natural law are those who, having no other law, order their conduct and life by natural reason. Or persons of the natural law are those who, according to the corruption of sin with which they were born, walk in concupiscence after the desires of their flesh. But persons of the written law are those in whom a greater knowledge flourishes, who receive from the traditions of the Scriptures and from precepts that are right and honourable a pattern for living. Persons [Col. 0689C] of grace, however, are those in whose hearts “love has been poured out through the Holy Spirit who has been given to them” (Rom. 5); through him they are enlightened so as to recognize what must be done, and are helped so as to be able to fulfil the good which they have been granted to understand.

From these things we may infer how all three of these classes of persons existed in the time of the natural law. There were then righteous persons, indeed few and still almost unknown to the world, whom God had kindled through the Holy Spirit to love of himself. Often appearing visibly to them and making himself familiar through mutual conversations, he disclosed the way of truth, both by speaking outwardly and by breathing inspiration inwardly. These were persons of grace.

There was again another class of persons who knew these righteous persons [Col. 0689D] more intimately, whether through kinship of family or through closeness of association. Since they had learned from their words and deeds many examples pertaining to righteousness and moral discipline, they imitated them not in virtue but in a certain respectability of this life. Such were all the bad sons or relatives of religious men, and likewise any members of their household who maintained their discipline not through love but through a certain customary way of living. Such persons were, as it were, persons of the written law.

The remaining multitude of humankind was governed neither by divine commands nor by human institutions. Each person’s own will was law; and, while whatever pleased them was permitted with impunity, each especially pursued that toward which a natural impulse drove him—whether the impulse of flesh toward [Col. 0690A] concupiscence or the impulse of reason toward a certain form of justice. Thus these are rightly called persons of the natural law, since they were governed only by a natural movement, whether of concupiscence or of reason.

Concupiscence, as was related above, is called natural because a human being is conceived in it and born with it. Reason, however, is called natural because a human being retains it from the first condition of creation. The latter, therefore, is natural by condition; the former by birth. The latter is natural because we received it when we were first created; the former is natural because, when we were born into this life, we brought it with us and within us.

Such persons belonged to the earliest periods of the age, when there was no law to punish sins. People sinned freely [Col. 0690B] and did not hide their sins: some did not believe that they were sins at all; others acknowledged them to be sins, but regarded them as slight and as capable of being discharged by an easy expiation. But after the law came in and showed people their sins, and at the same time reproved them, forbade them, and imposed punishment, people began to conceal their sins and to display certain works of virtue outwardly—not in order to fulfil righteousness, but in order to avoid punishment. Thus persons of the written law multiplied.

But persons of the natural law became very few; while persons of grace began to become somewhat more conspicuous than before, because the good law, by inviting people to righteousness, made the life of the righteous clearer. But when grace arrived—after the rigour of the law had been transformed into mercy—[Col. 0690C] persons of the natural law again multiplied, as those who had formerly lain hidden through fear of punishment now openly pursued their vices; while persons of the written law diminished.

Nevertheless this period is called the period of grace because now persons of grace, although not more numerous, are more eminent in status. For truth is indeed held by few, but is known by almost everyone and is preferred by the common judgment of all. It is now openly acknowledged that “a human being is justified not by works of the law, as was formerly supposed, but by the grace of God.”

Therefore, in whatever period they occur, persons of the natural law are openly evil; persons of the written law are falsely good; and persons of grace are truly [Col. 0690D] good. Persons of the natural law are partly outside the Church, such as all unbelievers, and partly within the Church, such as those who have faith alone without works; yet they are in no way of the Church, because they are not good. Persons of the written law are only within the Church, because they have faith, but they are not of the Church, because they are not good. Persons of grace alone are both within the Church and of the Church, because they have faith and are good.

The three bands of colour that we arranged on the sides of the ark—green, saffron-yellow, and purple—are intended to signify this. The green colour, which lies on the outside in the period of the natural law, signifies persons of the natural law, who were then more conspicuous. It is in the structure of the ark, yet it is not like the ark; rather, on the outside it resembles the earth. [Col. 0691A] For the ark, whose inner surface is clothed in varied colours according to the diversity of its chambers, ought not to be covered with green in that part where persons of the natural law are placed inwardly, nor with saffron-yellow where persons of the written law are inwardly placed. But where persons of grace are inwardly placed, it ought to have a purple colour, so that only here may the likeness correspond on both sides inwardly, just as the surface of the earth corresponds inwardly with persons of the natural law through the green colour.

The saffron-yellow colour is placed inwardly in the period of the natural law because it signifies persons of the written law, who, according to the prophet’s saying, “were brought up in saffron” (Lam. 4). They were then hidden. This colour is indeed situated in the ark, but is like neither the ark [Col. 0691B] nor the earth, because those who are falsely good resemble neither unbelievers outwardly through works nor believers inwardly through virtue.

Purple, however, lies in the period of the natural law as if compressed in the middle between the other two, because on account of its royal splendour it signifies persons of grace, who were then most hidden. This colour is in the ark both in position and in likeness, because persons of grace are in the Church by possessing faith and are good by possessing virtue. The position of these colours varies in the other periods as their signification requires.

Likewise, persons of the natural law are those who have only dead faith without works. Persons of the written law are those who have faith and works of faith but do not have love. Persons of grace alone have faith working through love.

## CHAPTER VI. On the threefold division of the ark according to width, by which the aforesaid persons are signified, and on the beams placed there

[Col. 0691C]

Next I turn my hand toward the width, and, beginning above at the right corner, extend two beams as far as the line of generation. From there upward—that is, from the line of generation to the left corner—I similarly mark two, the same beams, indeed, but transposed. Then from the right corner to the left I extend two beams there in a continuous line without transposition.

Once the sides have been arranged in this way according to length and width, I distinguish their inscriptions as follows. On the right side, from end to end, I write: “Its length was three hundred cubits.” Opposite, on the left side, in the first section [Col. 0691D] I place “the time of the natural law,” in the second “the time of the written law,” and in the third “the time of grace,” so that the first hundred cubits may be, as it were, the period of the natural law, the second the period of the written law, and the third the period of grace.

In the upper part, from the right side to the left, I write: “Its width was fifty cubits.” Opposite, on the lower side, as an exposition of this title, I write: “The whole body of the faithful under the one head, Christ.” In the upper right corner, above the heads of the two beams which run lengthwise, I place “Mount Zion”; in the left corner, “the sides of the north”; beneath these, opposite the middle, “the city of the great King.”

For the pair of right-hand beams signifies Mount Zion—that is, the Jewish people in both sexes; and the left-hand pair signifies the sides of the north—that is, the people of the Gentiles, likewise [Col. 0692A] in both sexes, hastening to faith. Together they make one city of God, that is, the Church. Therefore, on the upper side there is both a transposition of the beams and a division of the titles; below, however, there is one continuous line and one title, because these two peoples had first been divided in themselves, but afterward became one in the faith of Christ.

Then, in the upper right corner above the heads of the three beams that extend lengthwise, I write across: “Persons.” Afterward, in the left corner, as a specification of this title, I write at the head of the outer beam “of nature”; beneath the inner beam “of law”; and beneath the middle beam “of grace.” By this I intend to signify that these three beams, placed on either side, denote persons of the natural law, of the written law, and of grace, concerning whom [Col. 0692B] we have spoken above.

## CHAPTER VII. On the inscriptions of the three chambers of the ark, its division according to height, and the twelve ladders by which one ascends to them

The inscriptions of the chambers are as follows. On the right side, the first chamber is inscribed “faith,” the second “hope,” and the third “love.” On the left side, the first chamber is inscribed “knowledge,” the second “discipline,” and the third “goodness.” On the upper side, the first chamber is inscribed “nature,” the second “law,” and the third “grace.” On the lower side, the first chamber is inscribed “right,” the second “useful,” and the third “necessary.”

So that this last arrangement may correspond to each of the foregoing, understand it thus: right faith, useful hope, necessary love. Likewise: right knowledge, [Col. 0692C] useful discipline, necessary goodness. Likewise: right nature, useful law, necessary grace.

There are still other distinctions by which the height of the ark is divided. The first chamber is for married persons, the second for the continent, and the third for virgins. Or thus: the first chamber is for those who use the world, the second for those who flee the world, and the third for those who have forgotten the world. Or again: the first chamber is for creeping creatures, the second for walking creatures, and the third for flying creatures.

Likewise, for those ascending through each corner from the rigour of the east—that is, from pride—the first chamber is fear, the second sorrow, and the third love. For those ascending from the colour of the west—that is, from concupiscence of the flesh—the first chamber is patience, the second mercy, and the third compunction. For those ascending from the coldness of the west—that is, from ignorance—the first chamber is knowledge, the second meditation, [Col. 0692D] and the third contemplation. For those ascending from the heat of the east—that is, from spiritual fervour—the first chamber is temperance, the second prudence, and the third fortitude.

Therefore twelve ladders are erected upward through the four corners of the ark: three through each corner; four in each chamber; one in each corner. Each ladder is divided by ten steps, making one hundred and twenty in all—that is, sixty and sixty. By these, sixty men and sixty women ascend to the highest cubit, as it were to God, alternately upon each ladder, like the sixty mighty men who surround Solomon’s bed (Song 3), and the sixty queens (Song 6) who climb to Solomon’s embrace. They ascend by the twelve ladders—that is, by apostolic teaching—through ten paths, [Col. 0693A] that is, through the Ten Commandments of the law, instructed in the faith of the Trinity and in evangelical teaching from the four corners of the world.

From the coldness of the east upward, thirty books of the divine page are written in order: ten in each chamber, that is, one on each step, arranged externally along the sides of the ladders. Each of the books is divided outwardly into three levels, on account of the threefold sense: history, allegory, and tropology.

On the other side of the ladders, from the same corner upward, I write beside the first ladder: “Here ascend those who fear Gehenna, Isaiah calling and saying: ‘Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched’” (Isa. 66). This is said from Isaiah because he is the highest of the books on that ladder, and his book ends in this way. This verse is likewise divided outwardly [Col. 0693B] into three levels at every step, because of the three things spoken of in Ezekiel: lamentation, song, and woe. Lamentation pertains to present misery, song to future glory, and woe to Gehenna. Those who advance through fear ought not merely to fear Gehenna, but also to grieve over present misery and to love future glory. Yet on this ladder fear is primary.

On the second ladder is written: “Here ascend those who mourn the exile of the present life, on account of the vessels of the house of the Lord which are carried captive to Babylon.” This is said because at the end of the book of Chronicles, which is the highest on that ladder, this is narrated. This verse likewise is divided into three levels at every step because of the three things mentioned above; but here sorrow [Col. 0693C] is primary.

On the third ladder is written: “Here ascend those who sigh for their homeland, waiting for the Bridegroom’s return and saying: ‘Come, Lord Jesus Christ’” (Apoc. 20).

Likewise, from the coldness of the west upward, the same thirty books are written—namely, those arranged at the previous corner—ten through each chamber, so that these two corners, distinguished by the order of books, correspond to the northern side of the column, which is called the Book of Life. We shall discuss the mystery of this matter more fully later. And as was done above, so here also we distinguish each book into three levels according to the ascent.

On the other side of the ladders, from the same corner upward, I write beside the first ladder: “Here ascend those who, through ignorance, receive their first knowledge of God in creatures, Scripture teaching [Col. 0693D] and saying: ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth’” (Gen. 1). For Genesis is the first book on this ladder. This verse is divided from bottom to top into three levels, signifying the three admirable things in God’s works: immensity, beauty, and usefulness. Immensity pertains to power, beauty to wisdom, and usefulness to goodness. Whoever wishes to know these more fully should consult the treatise we composed entitled *On the Three Days*.

On the second ladder is written: “Here ascend those who, for instruction in right living, give diligent attention to meditation upon the divine law, hearing Scripture say: ‘I have appointed you to uproot, destroy, ruin, and scatter, and to build and to plant’” (Jer. 1). This [Col. 0694A] is found in Jeremiah, who is first on this ladder. This verse is divided outwardly into two levels because of the two things necessary for right living, which the Psalmist recalls when he says: “Turn away from evil, and do good” (Ps. 36).

On the third ladder is written: “Here ascend those who, with the inward eye cleansed, thirst to contemplate the light of inward vision, as though ascending from Babylon to Jerusalem” (1 Esdr. 4). This, namely, is read in Ezra, who is the first on this ladder. This verse has no division; rather, one line of colour is drawn from bottom to top, because contemplation is uniform and simple.

Likewise, from the heat of the west, from bottom to top, on one side of the three ladders, this verse is written in one continuous line: “Here ascend those who flee from the heat of vices to the tree [Col. 0694B] of life and hide themselves from the burning heat beneath its leaves, as beneath a noonday shelter” (Ecclus. 34). This verse is divided outwardly from bottom to top into seventy-seven levels—that is, twenty-six less one through each ladder. These levels signify what is said in the Gospel concerning forgiveness of sins: “Seventy times seven” (Matt. 18). For seven customarily signifies the universality of that thing to which it is added, while eleven signifies transgression. Seventy-seven, therefore, signifies every transgression remitted to those ascending here.

On the other side of the first ladder is written: “Here ascend those who, through abstinence and affliction, mortify their members which are upon the earth, with their vices and concupiscences” (Col. 3). This verse is divided into [Col. 0694C] forty levels, which number is a sign of abstinence.

On the second ladder is written: “Here ascend those who redeem former sins by alms and other works of mercy” (Dan. 4). This verse is divided into forty-six levels, because almsgiving joined to abstinence, like six joined to forty, makes a perfect work.

On the third ladder is written: “Here ascend those who, contrite in heart and troubled in spirit, offer to God a continual sacrifice of sweet savour” (Ps. 50). This verse is divided into fifty levels, which number is a sign of remission and freedom. For once a person practises these three things—abstinence, almsgiving, and compunction—he will immediately find forgiveness of his sins and the consolation [Col. 0694D] of the Holy Spirit in the beginnings of true freedom.

From the heat of the east, which is the last corner for those returning and the first for those departing, is written from bottom to top in one band: “Here ascend those who no longer pass from evil to good, but advance from good to better, whom the tree of life nourishes and carries forward by its fruit.” This verse is divided on the first ladder into thirty levels, on account of the first order of the faithful in the holy Church, namely married persons, who are signified in the Gospel by thirtyfold fruit. On the second ladder there is a division into sixty levels, which number pertains to the continent. On the third, into one hundred, which number pertains to virgins, than whom there is nothing higher, because they lead a celibate and heavenly life.

On the other side [Col. 0695A] of the first ladder this verse is written: “Here ascend those who lawfully use the world, like creeping creatures in the ark, and like the children of Israel in the plain, eating, drinking, and seeing from afar the glory of God.” This verse is divided into five and a half levels because of good activity that is less perfect. Its perfection is signified in the complete number six, which these persons cannot yet attain.

On the second ladder is written: “Here ascend those who forget and flee the world, like four-footed creatures now walking in the ark, and like Aaron with the elders of the children of Israel upon the ascent of the mountain.” This verse is divided into six levels because of the perfection of work to which these persons have already advanced.

On the third ladder is written: “Here ascend those who have forgotten the world, like birds in the ark, and like Moses alone upon the summit [Col. 0695B] of the mountain in the cloud with the Lord.” This verse is divided into seven levels, because such persons possess rest of mind together with perfection of work.

It should be known, moreover, that these levels must always be inscribed outwardly with verses, so that the verses themselves may extend upward between the levels and the ladders, and they must be differentiated by various colours. To signify history we have used green; for tropology, saffron-yellow; and for allegory, blue.

## CHAPTER VIII. A moral recapitulation concerning the aforesaid ladders

Let us now return to the allegory of the ladders. For those ascending from the coldness of the east, the first ladder is fear, the second sorrow, and the third love. For those ascending from the coldness of the west, the first ladder is knowledge, the second meditation, and the third contemplation. For those ascending from the heat [Col. 0695C] of the west, the first ladder is patience, the second mercy, and the third compunction. These three ladders perfect righteousness. On the fourth ladder follow the remaining three of the four cardinal virtues. For those ascending from the heat of the east, the first ladder is temperance, the second prudence, and the third fortitude. These individual virtues are also depicted in their respective places.

We make the four corners correspond to the four regions of the world, from which those who ascend to the reward of heavenly recompense are gathered: God’s elect, from the heat of the east, from the coldness of the east, from the heat of the west, and from the coldness of the west. The heat of the east is spiritual fervour; the coldness of the east is fear arising from pride. The heat of the west is concupiscence of the flesh; the coldness of the west is the blindness of ignorance.

[Col. 0695D] In the heat of the east the first human being was created; afterward, by becoming proud, he passed into the coldness of the east, as if to the north, into fellowship with the devil. Then through concupiscence of the flesh he fell to the heat of the west, and through ignorance to the coldness of the west. Thus he was scattered and dispersed through the four regions of the world.

But when he is gathered and recalled, he first comes from the four regions of the world to the ark—that is, to the Church—and from there, ascending upward, gradually gathers himself into one until he reaches the summit. Where he first fell, there he first ascends: namely, in the coldness of the east, and there he treads upon the serpent’s head—that is, pride. Then he ascends from the heat of the west, and there he treads upon the serpent’s belly—that is, concupiscence. Then he ascends from the coldness of the west, and there [Col. 0696A] he treads upon the serpent’s breast—that is, ignorance. Then he returns to the heat of the east, where he was created; and, ascending from there, presses down the whole serpent, coiled beneath him, so that on each ladder the last of those ascending appears to tread with his foot upon the serpent as it embraces both side-posts of the ladder.

The two side-posts signify body and soul, which the serpent embraces because it still in some manner holds dominion over both. But those who ascend by the paths—that is, by the divine commandments—everywhere press the serpent down beneath them.

The four Evangelists are also depicted in the four corners of the ark. In the coldness of the east is the lion, to terrify the proud. In the coldness of the west is the eagle, to enlighten the blind. In the heat of the west is the calf, to slay the flesh. In the heat of the east is the human being, to recall humankind to its origin.

[Col. 0696B] By the Book of Life, which faces north, ascend those who come from the coldness of the east and those who come from the coldness of the west. Therefore, on both sides, from the summit of the lower ladder, a hand holding a scroll visibly extends downward on the inside, as though coming from the Book of Life, to reprove on this side and instruct on that. On one is written the reproof: “Woe, woe, woe.” On the other is written the instruction of Judah: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1), as the significance of the ascents of each requires.

By the tree of life ascend those who come from the heat of the east and those who come from the heat of the west. Therefore on both sides a branch extends downward from the summit of the lower ladder, having leaves on this side and fruit on that, so that, as though coming from the tree of life, it may feed these and shade those. [Col. 0696C] The virtues, moreover, are depicted inside along the side opposite each ladder in the following manner.

## CHAPTER IX. Ascents to the virtues from the coldness of the east

First, from the coldness of the east, fear ascends naked opposite the scroll, having cast down below the spoils of pride, because of the fire and worms depicted beneath the foot of the ladder. On the second ladder sorrow is depicted; beside it is the migration to Babylon, beginning from Jehoiakim and thus descending obliquely to the foot of the second ladder, then leaving the ark there for Babylon, whose location is shown there on the map of the world. Beside the third ladder love is painted as one of the virgins, with a burning lamp and a vessel of oil, awaiting the coming of the bridegroom.

Each virtue, with one hand stretched upward, expresses the gesture of one ascending. This distinction must also be observed: people ascend upon the ladders, while virtues are arranged inwardly beside the ladders in the fields.

[Col. 0696D] In the heat of the west, beside the foot of the first ladder, a naked woman to the pubic region emerges from a cave, shaded by the leaves of the aforesaid branch. Opposite her, at the side, the inciter of vices emits fire from mouth and nostrils, to express concupiscence. A little higher upon the same ladder, a naked man is beaten with rods, to express patience. On the second ladder someone gives alms, to signify mercy. On the third ladder someone is portrayed in the likeness of one praying and beating his breast, to denote compunction. All the virtues must look upward, so that nothing may be done for human praise.

From the coldness of the west, beside the foot of the first [Col. 0697A] ladder, someone emerges from a cave with his face wrapped and falls; striking against a stone, he breaks the vessel he carries, to express ignorance, which through various errors dissipates the soul’s integrity. After this, on the same ladder, knowledge is painted standing upright opposite the scroll extended downward by the hand, with the fragments of the vessel beside it. On this scroll, as we have said, is written: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1), because the first knowledge of God is in creatures.

On the second ladder meditation is represented sitting and gathering together the fragments of the broken vessel. On the third ladder contemplation is fashioned in the likeness of a craftsman, melting down the same fragments, so that the molten stream, through the band of colour which we extended upward above beside the verse for this ladder, may appear to run as through a pipe into the middle [Col. 0697B] cubit, as though into coinage. This signifies that the integrity of the soul, which ignorance breaks, knowledge finds, meditation gathers, and contemplation, melting it through the fire of divine love, pours out to be refashioned into the coinage of the divine likeness.

## CHAPTER X. Ascents from the heat and coldness of the east

From the heat of the east, beside the first ladder, temperance is painted in the likeness of a householder seated at a table, eating and distributing alms, as one who lawfully uses the world. On the second ladder prudence is painted in the likeness of a traveller walking, as one who flees the world. On the third ladder fortitude is painted, clothed below in a cloud, as one who has trodden the world beneath her feet and has been raised on high, with hands uplifted [Col. 0697C] above.

This too, as we have said, must be observed: the virtues are to be arranged inwardly beside the ladders, while the people are on the ladders, one on each path, men and women alternately, so that there may be sixty mighty men of Israel and sixty queens.

Let us now briefly repeat the number and order of the aforesaid virtues. For those ascending from pride through the coldness of the east, the first ladder is fear, the second sorrow, and the third love. For those ascending from concupiscence through the heat of the west, the first ladder is patience, the second mercy, and the third compunction. For those ascending from ignorance through the coldness of the west, the first ladder is knowledge or thought, the second meditation, and the third contemplation. For those ascending through the heat of the east, advancing not from vice [Col. 0697D] but through virtue, the first ladder is temperance, the second prudence, and the third fortitude; and there is the consummation of the perfect life.

The first ascent, namely that from the coldness of the east, is in the affections. The second, from the heat of the west, is through works. The third, from the coldness of the west, is in thoughts. The fourth, from the heat of the east, is in the virtues just mentioned. There are many other things that might be said about these matters, which we must necessarily pass over here.

## CHAPTER XI. On the door of the ark

We arrange the door of the ark in this way. Since the column signifies Christ, who says, “I am the door” (John 10), and since, for the aforesaid reasons, the column has been represented in the ark as though twice, that is, on two sides, we therefore paint a door below on either side of the column: [Col. 0698A] in the Book of Life to the north and the Tree of Life to the south. Yet, just as we represent one column on both sides, so we represent one door by both doors.

The door which is to the north signifies through the Book of Life the faith by which we enter the Church from unbelief. This occurs through the humility of Christ, through which we have been recalled. This door must be closed, lest we return again to our former errors. The door which is to the south signifies through the Tree of Life the passage from this life to future glory, that is, to the fruit of the Tree of Life. This door is open, because we ought always to direct the eyes of the mind there, that we may depart from this misery as soon as possible.

We also signify something else through the door. Since the door is below and the window is above [Col. 0698B]—the window which we placed above compunction with the outstretched hand and the dove—the door can fittingly signify departure through action, and the window departure through thought.

There are four ways in which we depart through action. Every action is either earthly or spiritual. To serve earthly actions because of covetousness is one way, like an unclean animal. To arrange them because of necessity is another way, like a clean animal. To undertake spiritual actions because of covetousness is a third way, as an evil person does. To undertake them for the neighbour’s benefit and God’s praise is a fourth way, as a good person does.

Therefore, through the door we have depicted four creatures going out: the unclean animal, an ass; the clean animal, [Col. 0698C] an ox; the good person, Noah; and the evil person, Ham. God opens the door for the good person; the evil person, going out disobediently through the other side, breaks down the doors.

## CHAPTER XII. Four modes of going out through thought
Likewise, we go out by thought in four ways. The first way is when we consider what every creature is in itself. The second way is when we consider what every creature is by the Creator’s beneficence. The third way is when we consider how God employs the service of creatures to fulfil His judgments. The fourth way is when we consider how man employs the benefit of creatures to fulfil his desires. In themselves all things are vain and transitory. By the Creator’s beneficence they are perpetual. While they serve God, they are instruments of righteousness. While they serve man, they become instruments of concupiscence. [Col. 0698D] Thus the raven went out, found a corpse, and settled upon it. I discussed all these matters more fully in the book which I composed on the ark. The first three ways pertain to the dove, that is, to the three kinds of good thoughts: thought, meditation, and contemplation. We think upon vanity; we meditate upon righteousness; we contemplate perpetuity.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the six little chambers of the ark according to the literal sense

Let us now see how the little chambers ought to be arranged. Some say that the little chambers were certain nests—that is, receptacles constructed outside against the wall of the ark—for those animals which can live neither always on dry land nor always in water, but alternately pass now from water to [Col. 0699A] dry land, now from dry land back to water. Since the ark could not be opened for them so often, divine providence arranged that they too should not perish: receptacles were made for them outside against the wall of the ark, their entrance always remaining open externally while the wall of the ark remained unbroken within.

They are believed to have been so arranged that, while the ark floated upon the waters, their entrance would meet level ground for those ascending outside through the water. Scripture does not state the number of these receptacles. Yet, after the likeness of the six cities appointed as refuges for homicides—for they pertain to the same signification—we have arranged six little chambers in the ark in this manner.

First, the River Jordan is drawn through the middle of the ark, that is, from one wall to the other, beside the side of the pillar above, [Col. 0699B] after the likeness of baptism, which in holy Church is, as it were, the end of the Law and the beginning of grace, and whose water of sanctification flowed from Christ’s side. Since three of the six cities are commanded to be established beyond the Jordan and three on this side, we too, following the likeness, place our little chambers: three beyond, that is, above the Jordan, in the upper part of the ark; and three on this side, in its lower part.

The first is placed above at the front of the ark, that is, at the beginning of the natural law. The second and third are in the written Law, that is, on either bank of the Jordan. The fourth, fifth, and sixth are in the time of grace: two beneath the apostles, opposite the two upper ones on either side, and one at the lower end of the ark opposite the first. Thus the natural law has one, the written Law has two, and grace has three. [Col. 0699C]

Their mystery is this. The ark signifies the Church; the flood, the concupiscence of this world. Those animals which frequently go from the ark to the water and again from the water back to the ark signify the weak and fleshly persons within the Church, who through sin often slip into the concupiscence of this world. Yet remedies of penitence have been prepared for them, like certain little chambers in the spiritual ark—that is, in holy Church.

Of these little chambers the natural law had, as it were, one: sacrifice. Two were assigned to the written Law: offering and purification. Grace, however, has three spiritual remedies corresponding to the three fleshly things: confession, prayer, and affliction of the flesh. Confession sacrifices; prayer cleanses; affliction of the flesh slays. [Col. 0699D]

After these, between the natural and written Law, a gate is opened on either side. Through that which is toward the north, the captive people are taken from Jerusalem into Babylon. Through that which is toward the south, the people freed from Egypt enter in, making for the land of promise. How this accords also with the geographical arrangement of places will become clear later in the description of the world-map: Babylon lies north of Jerusalem; Egypt lies south. Therefore, from this gate, by which the people enter below on the inner side of the ark, the forty-two stations are written in sequence as far as the bank of the Jordan: through them the people of God spiritually make their way from Egypt, the natural Law, through the wilderness, the written Law, to the land of promise, grace.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the forty-two stations

[Col. 0700A]

These, then, are the stations: the first, Rameses; the second, Sochot; the third, Etham; the fourth, Siaroch; the fifth, Mara; the sixth, Helim; the seventh, the Red Sea; the eighth, the wilderness of Sin; the ninth, Descath; the tenth, Alis; the eleventh, Raphidim; the twelfth, Sina; the thirteenth, the graves of concupiscence; the fourteenth, Ascereth; the fifteenth, Rethma; the sixteenth, Ramoth; the seventeenth, Lemna; the eighteenth, Redsa; the nineteenth, Caltha; the twentieth, Rapher; the twenty-first, Arada; the twenty-second, Marcloth; the twenty-third, Thaath; the twenty-fourth, Thare; the twenty-fifth, Mercha; the twenty-sixth, Asmona; the twenty-seventh, Maceroth; the twenty-eighth, Maveiachan; the twenty-ninth, Galath; the thirtieth, Gethabatha; the thirty-first, [Col. 0700B] Ebrona; the thirty-second, Asiongaber; the thirty-third, Sin, which is Cades; the thirty-fourth, Mount Hor; the thirty-fifth, Selmona; the thirty-sixth, Finon; the thirty-seventh, Oboth; the thirty-eighth, Gebarin; the thirty-ninth, Dibungath; the fortieth, Solmon deblathain.

And because one of the six little chambers is situated above the bank of the Jordan, at the side of the first station on this side, when it has been reached at the fortieth station, the following two are written above in the second station, likewise as far as the bank of the Jordan. These are: the forty-first, Mount Abarim opposite Nobo; the forty-second, the plains of Moab above the Jordan near Jericho.

Concerning the interpretation and mystery of these stations, perhaps in another work which we intend to make concerning this same [Col. 0700C] ark we shall set forth more fully what must be said; also why the natural Law is compared with Egypt, the written Law with the wilderness, and grace with the land of promise, and what kind of passage there is from the former through the latter to the third. These matters concerning the construction of the ark may suffice for those who either cannot or do not wish to make more.

Yet we have added certain things, which we shall briefly mention. When the ark has been completed in this way, an oblong circle is drawn around it, touching it at each corner; and the space enclosed by its circumference is the world. In this space a map of the world is painted, so that the head of the ark faces east and its end touches west, so that by a wonderful arrangement the geographical disposition of places proceeds from the same beginning [Col. 0700D] as the order of times, and the end of the world is the same as the end of the age.

The pointed projection of the circle which extends eastward at the head of the ark is Paradise, like Abraham’s bosom, as will later appear in the painted Majesty. The other projection, extending westward, contains the judgment of the universal resurrection: the elect on the right, the rejected on the left. At the northern corner of this projection is hell, into which those to be condemned will be thrust together with apostate spirits.

After this, another, slightly wider circle is drawn around the circle mentioned above, so that it appears to form a zone; this space is the air. In this space the four seasons of the year are arranged according to the four regions of the world: spring to the east, summer to the south, autumn to the west, winter to the north. Spring is painted from the waist upward as a boy holding a pipe in his hand and singing. Summer, as a young man, looks at flowers. Autumn, represented at mature age, brings fruits to his nostrils and smells them. Winter, bearing the form of an old man, eats fruits. Each is painted from the waist upward at its own beginning.

## CHAPTER XV. On the qualities of the four seasons of the year, and the conclusion of the work

[Col. 0701A]

Spring possesses the delight of hearing; summer, of sight; autumn, of smell; winter, of taste. For the delight of childhood lies in hearing instruction; the delight of youth in the example of action; the delight of mature age in the desire for uprightness; the delight of old age in the experience of virtue.

Each also occupies one quarter of the year: summer the upper quarter, winter the lower, spring the right, autumn the left. [Col. 0701B] And in each quarter are stretched, as it were, two strings on account of the double quality of each; when these are compared with one another, the musical eight-stringed scale is expressed, from which the harmony of universal concord is tuned. Spring is moist and warm; summer warm and dry; autumn dry and cold; winter cold and moist. Upon all these matters, for the sake of brevity, much discourse will be omitted.

In this same space the twelve winds are arranged, three assigned to each season beneath the ethereal zone, as though plunging downward; and, winged and projecting from the shoulders, one is arranged beneath each month. Of these, four are cardinal winds, each having two subsidiary winds on either side.

From the middle of the east blows Subsolanus, with two winds in agreement with it on either side: Vulturnus on the right, Eurus on the left. From the south blows Auster, or Notus, having on the right Eurus-notus, also called Euroauster, and on the left Libonotus, also called Austro-Africus. From the middle of the west blows Zephyrus, also called Favonius, having on the right Africanus, also called Libs, and on the left Corus, also called Argestes. From the middle of the north blows Aparctias, also called Septentrio, having on the right Circius, also called Thracias, Trasceas, or Thrascias, and on the left Boreas, also called Aquilo. [Col. 0701C] Each principal wind blows with two hearts, and each subsidiary wind with one.

After this, yet another circle is drawn outside the two already mentioned, and the space it encloses is taken for the ethereal zone. In this space the twelve months are arranged according to the order of the seasons, and beneath the twelve months are placed the signs, [Col. 0701D] so that the sign always begins in the middle of the month and, conversely, the month in the middle of the sign. Each of these signs is distinguished above by thirty degrees, the beginning being taken above from the first degree of Aries.

Thus, with all the signs arranged in a circuit contrary to the world, the signs indeed lying back toward the firmament, while the months rise upward from below, the signs, turned upward, appear to stand or walk in the circle called the *aplanes* (“unwandering”); the months, however, appear behind and beneath them, standing in the ether. Thus the signs are shown at the top; beneath the signs, the months; beneath the months, the winds; beneath the winds, the seasons. In this arrangement a great principle and effect of nature is signified, and the whole circuit of heaven is thereby completed.

When the structure of the universe has been constructed in this way, in its upper part the Majesty is depicted, extending upward from the shoulders and downward with the feet, and seated, as it were, upon a throne. [Col. 0702A] His arms are spread on either side, so that He appears to contain all things. With three fingers extended through the middle as far as the globe of the earth, while the others are bent back into the palm, He encloses the heavens.

In His right hand He holds a throne, slanting downward through the space of the air to the place above which, in the lower projection, as we have said, the elect rise on the right; angels stationed there receive them into heaven. Therefore, upon the throne itself is written: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the age” (Matthew 25).

In His left hand He holds a sceptre, directed downward [Col. 0702B] to the place where demons lying in wait seize the wicked who rise on the left. Therefore, upon that sceptre is written: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.).

Then the genealogical line as far as Adam is extended upward, outside the ark, through the middle of the projecting cone to the summit of heaven. On it six roundels are drawn in sequence, so that the last appears to enclose the entrance of the ark itself. These six roundels represent the works of the six days. The first—and highest—must be depicted as the world was on the first day, when light was created. The second, when the firmament was set between the waters and the waters. The third, when the waters were gathered into one place and the earth was clothed with plants. The fourth, when the sun, moon, and stars were made. [Col. 0702C] The fifth, when fish were placed in the water and birds in the air. The sixth, when beasts were made on earth and man.

Thus the Word proceeds from the mouth of Majesty, and the whole order of creatures follows; and the extension of the ark itself reaches from the beginning of the world to the end of the age, having through the middle of the earth, on either side, established places, mountains, rivers, castles, and towns: Egypt to the south and Babylon to the north.

After this, around the throne on both sides, near the middle, two seraphim are painted, who with wings extended upward and downward veil the head and feet of Majesty, while the face remains uncovered. Beneath the wings of the seraphim, above, in the space between the shoulders of Majesty and the wings on either side, the nine orders of angels [Col. 0702D] are arranged, turned toward the contemplation of the face of Majesty.

For the supreme and true Unity itself occupies the middle and highest place. Then the first order of angels has two on either side of the diadem; the second order, three on either side; the third, four; the fourth, five; the fifth, six; the sixth, seven; the seventh, eight; the eighth, nine; the ninth, ten: so that from the first unity arises the origin of all things, and in the second unity the creation of the angels is completed, who together number one hundred and eight. As one falls away from each order, ninety-nine remain; to these man, the hundredth sheep, is added, and the heavenly city is completed.

We say these things concerning the representation of our ark, [Col. 0703A] so that, if anyone desires to behold the beauty of the house of the Lord [Col. 0704A] and His wonders, “of which there is no number,” this model may for the present stimulate his affection. Blessed be God through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0703]

# FOUR BOOKS ON THE VANITY OF THE WORLD AND THE USE OF TRANSITORY THINGS

In two of these I find the speakers designated by the individual letters D and I, by which the teacher and the questioner are sufficiently indicated.

# BOOK I

[Col. 0703B]

**D.** O world, unclean world, why have we loved you so? Is this your fruit? This your promise? This our hope from you? Why did we hope in you? Why did we trust you? Why did we wish to think of you? Behold how we have been deceived. Nothing remains to us; we have been left empty. O world, unclean world, why have we loved you so?

**I.** What do you see, O man?

**D.** Nothing is better than to flee.

**I.** I do not sufficiently understand what you mean. Yet I see, as your bewilderment indicates, that you either suffer something grievous, or have seen something new, or are contemplating evil. Therefore do not conceal whatever it may be; for if there is danger, you will have saved me as well. But if there is no danger and you are disturbed in vain, perhaps I shall console you.

**D.** Rise, ascend, and look with me; and I shall show you [Col. 0703C] great wonders: things old to the ancients, new to those now present, and later wonders for those yet to come.

**I.** When I have seen the thing itself of which you speak, then perhaps I shall understand better what you mean. Show me now, therefore, where I must ascend, so that I too may be able to see these wonders about which you are so disturbed.

**D.** The higher the bodily eye is placed in a loftier position, the more widely it spreads itself through sight. For from above the visual gaze is more easily extended over what lies beneath, when it sees all things as though set before it. Yet precisely because it shines forth through a bodily instrument, it is dimmed within itself in many and various ways, even when no outward obstacle intervenes. Since it is narrow, it is insufficient to comprehend the greatest things; since it is dull, it does not distinguish the smallest; since it is sluggish, when it stretches toward the most remote things, even if nothing intervenes, it is nevertheless dulled by the distance alone; and since it is not penetrating, it does not enter into the innermost things, but wanders only over those placed on the surface of things. Nor can it look back upon what is past or foresee what is to come.

I have said this so that you may know how great are the limitations endured by this bodily sight, which cannot look upon anything unless it is set before it. Among such things, the greatest exceed it in magnitude; the smallest escape it by subtlety; remote things evade it by distance; and inward things withdraw from it in obscurity. [Col. 0704B]

Therefore I do not wish you to think of the sight of this eye when you hear yourself invited to see. You have another eye within, far clearer than this one, which simultaneously beholds past, present, and future; which diffuses the light and sharpness of its sight through all things; which penetrates hidden things and investigates subtle ones; which needs no borrowed light in order to see, but sees by its own proper light.

Since the eye of flesh cannot take in at once the things which I shall show you, you must prepare for this vision not the eye of flesh but the eye of the heart. Place yourself, therefore, as though upon a watchtower of the mind, and direct its gaze to survey on every side the ark of this world, so that the whole world may stand before you as you contemplate it. From there I shall show you all the things which you previously either did not see and therefore did not know, or saw but did not consider as you ought. [Col. 0704C]

**I.** Now I truly confess that, when the eyes of the heart are diligently opened for seeing, nothing in the whole universe is hidden from the observer’s sight. But when I open the bodily eye to see, however widely all things may lie open, what I comprehend is very little in comparison with the whole.

Yet behold: while I try, as far as I can, to raise my heart upward, I discover that hitherto I have been below not only in body but also in heart. For the more I yielded in affection and thought to the contemplation of particular things in the world, the less fit and less free I was for contemplating the totality of things. Now, therefore, I strip my mind of those things to which I formerly clung; and, as though lightened by laying down a burden, I recognize at once that I stand above them all.

For by some wonderful means, I do not know how, this has suddenly happened within me: while I strive to cling through desire to none of them in particular, I begin through contemplation to rise above them all. Begin, therefore; for I now behold the whole world set before me, and whatever you wish to show me from among all things I shall see without delay or difficulty. [Col. 0705A]

**D.** Then do you see this world?

**I.** I see it, and clearly. Never have I seen so well, because never have I considered so carefully.

**D.** What then does it seem to you? What is its appearance?

**I.** Very beautiful. I marvel at such a work of God.

**D.** You find God wonderful in all things; everyone now knows this.

But for the moment let us be silent about God’s works. Seeing these great and such works of men, you began to admire the world. For you must also know that here I take “world” to mean not merely this appearance of the divine work, but the changeability of human affairs in this world. Tell me, then: what are the works of men which you see? What do they seem to you?

**I.** I see great beauty in them too, and when I consider what man is, I marvel how he can accomplish such things.

**D.** If you considered well what man is, you would not marvel that he could accomplish such things, but that he should place confidence in them. But because you have begun to attend to the world, and attend neither to man’s dignity nor to the worthlessness of human work, you admire them so foolishly and disorderly.

**I.** Although you speak very much against my opinion, it may nevertheless be that I too have been deceived and that you have spoken the truth. I would therefore rather listen than dispute, so that, if you can prove your assertion, I may not regret having resisted shamelessly; but if you cannot, I may suffer no harm from having kept silent prudently. Tell me, then, what is the dignity of man and what the worthlessness of human work. For certainly, if one looks only at what appears outwardly, man himself is found to be neither greater in size, nor more handsome in form, nor longer-lasting in time than his own work.

**D.** First I wish to discuss with you the works of men. [Col. 0705C]

You see all the works of men, how great and of what kind they are.

**I.** They seem to me great and quite admirable; but do you judge otherwise?

**D.** I judge entirely otherwise, and I want you to judge otherwise too.

**I.** I am not so obstinate that I should not gladly be overcome by truth. Only proceed wherever you please, and I shall follow.

**D.** Look upon everything, and consider each thing carefully.

**I.** I look and consider, and await what you wish to show me in all these things.

**D.** What do you see?

**I.** I see men sailing upon the sea: great calmness of the sea, great serenity of the air, favourable winds blowing gently, and the ship borne along upon its desired course. I see men reclining in the ship at feasting, singing to lyres, pipes, and citharas, soothing the hearing with every kind [Col. 0705D] of sweet song. I see schools of sea-fish circling about while the waters themselves resound with melody, and, playing as they leap, increasing their joy.

**D.** What does it seem to you?

**I.** What, if not great joy, great delight, and—if it could be lasting—great happiness?

**D.** Is this, then, why the world pleases you?

**I.** And I do not know why it ought to displease me.

**D.** Fix your eye for a little while, and do not turn your gaze away until you see the end.

**I.** I follow those who are going, and wait to see what follows.

**D.** What do you see?

**I.** I fear to say what I nevertheless cannot conceal.

**D.** What then do you see?

**I.** I see the sky blackening on every side; clouds driven and thrown into confusion by a violent clash of winds; the sea swelling with waves and, as though from one deep bottom, being raised all together into a heap. Alas—what did I praise?

**D.** What is it?

**I.** O wretched men, what have you to do with the sea? Why did you trust the deceitful calm? Why were you secure amid uncertainty? Why did you not regard the tranquillity of the sea as suspect? Why did you not fear to entrust your lives to a faithless element? Why did you abandon the firmness of the shore? Why did you not keep to the safe journey on land? What use to you are gains acquired at so great a risk? Behold how slight was the good you pursued, and behold how great a calamity you have incurred. Because you refused to foresee the real evil threatening you, you did not restrain your minds from the desire for the deceptive good that drew you on. O unhappy and wretched men! Behold how swiftly your joy has changed, and into what misery your life has fallen! Formerly, while you rejoiced vainly, the fish of the sea played around you; now the fish of the sea take you, shipwrecked and miserably cast away, as food. [Col. 0706B]

**D.** What does it seem to you? What kind of work of men is this?

**I.** It is vanity, and vanity of vanities.

**D.** Turn now to something else, and see.

**I.** I have turned, and I see.

**D.** What do you see?

**I.** I see men going on their way laden with many great wares; innumerable camels carrying diverse burdens; very many wagons and no few two-horse chariots in the travellers’ company. I see every kind of spice and aromatic; I recognize every kind of precious garment; I behold enormous masses of every metal and every precious stone; horses and mules, slaves, and flocks and herds beyond number.

**D.** From where do you suppose these men come, or where are they going?

**I.** It appears that they come from a distant region and are carrying all these stores of goods to foreign nations to exchange them for profit. The men appear eager and cheerful, and, so far as can be understood from their very joy, to be progressing successfully.

**D.** What does it seem to you?

**I.** I see an undertaking laborious enough, but the novelty of the goods and desire for profit offer sweet consolations to those who labour.

**D.** Wait, and you will see what fruit so great a labour will bring.

**I.** The fruit is present, if only it can endure.

**D.** Wait a little; what is to come will soon arrive.

**I.** They have now gone farther.

**D.** What do you see?

**I.** I see a wedge of armed men emerging from a mountain-pass, and I fear that it is an ambush.

**D.** A tardy fear will not escape pain. [Col. 0706D]

**I.** They descend together in one assault, and like robbers come to plunder the prey. Now I see our travellers anxious and trembling, clustering around their baggage, each taking up arms and awaiting the enemy’s approach before his own load. They look around in every direction; no person is visible to them on either side; all the surrounding places lie deserted far and wide; all human company is far away; no help can even be hoped for. Enemies rush in from every side, make their attack with one purpose—more numerous in multitude, strong in greed, bold because of the solitude.

Why do you struggle in vain, wretched men? Why do you resist? Why, placed in utmost peril, do you wish to lose your lives together with your possessions? Alas for me! Already I behold some killed, some despoiled, some falling dead, and others barely escaping naked. But whether I should call those who fall thus, or those who escape thus, more wretched, I do not know. For the former are freed from misery by dying; the latter, escaping death, are preserved for another misery. Whom should I mourn more? Whom should I rebuke more? I shall mourn those who die and rebuke those who flee. Or rather, are not the former most rightly to be rebuked for such a death and the latter to be mourned for such a flight? For avarice drew the former to a miserable death, while those fleeing death are received by a misery greater than death. [Col. 0707A]

**D.** What does it seem to you? What kind of work of man is this?

**I.** It is vanity, and vanity of vanities.

**D.** Turn again to other things, and see.

**I.** I have turned, and I see.

**D.** What do you see?

**I.** I see the house of a rich man.

**D.** What do you see there?

**I.** An abundance of all things: children thriving, servants lively, fertile flocks, full granaries, overflowing storehouses, health in life, peace in abundance, security in peace, happiness in security.

**D.** What does it seem to you?

**I.** I see here nothing to grieve over or fear. Yet, taught by the earlier examples, I do not presume henceforth rashly to call anyone happy. I would rather hear from you what ought to be thought.

**D.** Do you then consider such a man happy?

**I.** I do not know why I should not.

**D.** What, then, makes a person happier: to possess much, or to need little?

**I.** To need little rather than to possess much.

**D.** Is it therefore happier to need nothing?

**I.** Certainly happier.

**D.** A man, then, should not be judged happy because he possesses much, but because he does not need much.

**I.** Yet people call happy the person who has the means to meet his need, because they have learned by experience how wretched is the one whom lack of goods confines in his necessity. [Col. 0707C]

**D.** If you compare the evils of the poor and of the rich, you will recognize the rich man as more wretched than the poor. For the more the rich man possesses, the greater is his anxiety. While he alone bears the burden of anxiety above all others, the things that he either greedily seeks or miserly preserves profit others more than himself. For the fever of his cares continually torments him. He fears lest his acquisitions fail, because, though his possessions are great, the number of those who would strip him of them is no smaller. He fears the violence of the powerful; he mistrusts the loyalty of his household; he always dreads the snares of outsiders which threaten him. Knowing that he possesses amid the hatred of all, he strives with a kind of wretched and unhappy contention to defend it against all. Thus, while by his pursuit of wickedness he separates himself from the common fellowship of all, he becomes hateful to all and estranged from everyone’s affection.

He is also certain that, if abundance of goods should ever fail him, no compassion from others will receive him. Care for his possessions indeed never leaves him, but meanwhile their use passes to others, so that he must often even give generously to people from whom he can hope for neither honour, gratitude, nor benefit. When he keeps his possessions, he is cursed; when he does not give, he is mocked with empty flatteries. Yet a mind conscious of itself is wounded by mockery no less than by cursing. [Col. 0708A]

Ever bitter, ever sad, ever faint-hearted, always oppressed by care for the present and troubled by fear of the future; never trusting in present goods but always fearing evils about to come: amid such great pains and disturbances of mind, what true health or bodily pleasure, I ask, can exist? What comfort is not made bitter to the body when conscience is torn by such stings? This is the happiness of the rich, which you began to praise when you saw false external goods, because you did not see the true misery within.

**I.** If this is the state of the rich man, he who desires to possess much becomes his own enemy.

**D.** What then does it seem to you? What kind of work of men is this?

**I.** This too is vanity and vanity of vanities.

**D.** Turn now to other things, and see.

**I.** I have turned, and I see.

**D.** [Col. 0708B] What do you see?

**I.** I see a wedding being celebrated.

**D.** What seems to you to be in it?

**I.** There is great joy there, great adornment, and much display; and—to say what seems to me—I judge this work happier than other works of men, because it is especially this which, through the bond of love, gives birth to peace and concord of minds. This commends fellowship, sanctifies love, preserves friendship. From this comes the fruit of offspring; from this our race is extended; from this resistance is made to the grim necessity of death, and the losses of fathers are repaired in children.

Why should I mention that in this one case alone carnal concupiscence—which elsewhere can neither be restrained without great difficulty nor released without shame—is so honestly and modestly received in marital intercourse that scarcely any loss of chastity seems to be felt? For although concupiscence itself seeks to experience its pleasure, no confusion of modesty is produced. Who, then, would judge so many and such great goods contemptible, unless he did not see the evils which follow apart from this?

**D.** You could judge rightly of the goods of marriage if you attended also to its evils. But because you consider only the goods and not the evils of marriage, you do not preserve a correct standard of judgment in considering it. It cannot be denied that marriage possesses certain goods; but if we wish to consider carefully, we shall find that more evils are mixed with them.

For who does not know how rare that concord of minds is? Indeed, when the partnership soon becomes wearisome, the very thing which ought to have produced concord supplies fuel for hatred and discord; and they begin to live together all the more miserably because, being at odds with one another, they are less able to separate. Hence daily quarrels and disputes multiply; after harsh words, cruel blows follow. Neither can escape the other: one house, one table, one bed—where nothing is harsher than to have neither a harmonious companion nor a separated enemy. [Col. 0708D]

For just as nothing hinders those whose minds are one in charity, even if they are separated in body, so it is a great torment for those joined bodily if they cannot agree in mind. Moreover, concerning the propagation of humankind, which you offered as evidence of praise, we grant that it is indeed true—but we maintain that the office of marriage displays not the joy of health but the remedy of weakness. For it would be better that no living person should die than that someone should be born to succeed one who dies.

Now, however, some consolation, whatever its nature, is granted to our unhappiness: those who cannot be retained when dying are restored through those who are born, so that, because we cannot have persons who remain forever, we may at least have persons who constantly succeed them. Let us therefore accept—or rather, endure—this remedy for our pain, whatever it may be; but let us not suppose that it contains the delight of happiness.

We praise a draught which we drink not without bitterness and vomit up not without painful straining, because by that bitterness we expel something greater and more dangerous. If we consider the pleasure of the man who lies with a woman, let us consider also the distress of the woman giving birth. [Col. 0709B] And, to say nothing for the present of the other troubles and disadvantages which follow bodily pleasure—for it itself weakens natural vigour and causes every strength and beauty of the body, both inward and outward, to wither—who can say, except one who has experienced it, how great a labour and trouble it is to receive infants and, besides the other miseries which are better left unspoken, to suckle, rear, nourish, instruct children, form them alike by discipline and learning, and bring them to lawful age?

Who would not say that he has bought the pleasure of one night dearly, when he repays it by the labour and care of so many years? If those marrying wished to attend to this, they would certainly know that they ought to weep rather than laugh at weddings. But now a small bait of concupiscence is placed before them, as it were, on a hook, so that they may be caught for the dreadful necessity of labour and pain. Such is the joy which you see.

**I.** Nothing at all can be contradicted: your arguments are powerful.

**D.** What then does it seem to you? What kind of work of men is this?

**I.** This too is vanity, and vanity of vanities.

D. Turn now to something else and look.

I. I have turned, and I see.

D. What do you see?

I. I see a school of learners. There is a great multitude; I observe people of various ages there: boys, adolescents, young men, old men; and likewise various pursuits. Some are learning to bend their still unformed tongues so as to utter newly fashioned letters and unfamiliar sounds. Others strive first to recognize, by hearing, the inflections, compounds, and derivations of words, then to commit them to memory by comparing them with one another and repeatedly rehearsing them. Others engrave wax tablets with a stylus. Others, guiding a pen with practiced hand, draw figures in various forms and different colours upon parchment. Others, with a keener and more ardent zeal, engage one another in certain disputations about great matters, as it seems, and endeavour in turn to deceive one another by verbal entanglements and riddles. I see some also calculating there. Some, striking a string stretched upon wood, produce melodies of differing sounds. Others expound certain diagrams and forms of measurement. Others clearly set forth, by means of instruments, the courses and positions of the stars and the revolution of the heavens. Others discuss the nature of plants, the constitutions of human beings, and the qualities and powers of all things. Yet although there is not one manner of learning in all these pursuits, there is one will to make progress common to them all. And whether this should be called busy leisure or leisurely business, I judge it, even in your opinion, to be preferable to all human activities, because through it no transient or perishable thing, but the eternal glory of wisdom, is implanted in minds, and its root is planted so as never again to be uprooted.

D. An appearance of truth deceives you. For this too is a habit of this world: whatever is more apt to ensnare human minds it weaves about with a certain likeness of truth, lest it be guarded against or avoided. For the more plainly error is recognized, the more quickly it is rejected. But while hidden error raises outwardly the appearance of truth, inwardly it pours in the poison of falsehood. Such are these pursuits—not of wisdom, but of human folly—by which the imprudent and foolish, with labour as useless as it is obstinate, investigate the natures of things, while they remain ignorant of their own Creator and of the maker of all natures alike; and yet neglect to seek him, as though either truth could be found or happiness possessed without God.

And that you may recognize still more clearly how fruitless—indeed, how harmful—these studies are: they not only fail to enlighten minds for knowing truth, but utterly blind them so that they cannot recognize truth. For they seize the human heart and in some way draw it outside itself, so that, while it is dragged into considering other matters that do not concern it, it does not at all return to the contemplation of itself. Thus birds are customarily caught: in the darkness of the night, on one side a light is shown for them to look at, and on the other a snare is set to catch them.

What advantage, then, is it to a person if he investigates the nature of all things subtly and comprehends it effectively, but does not consider or understand whence he has come or where he will go after this life? For what is this mortal life except a kind of road? We are travellers, and as we pass by we look upon the things of this world as though from the side. What then, if while travelling we see something new and unknown to us—must we stop to investigate it, or turn aside from our journey? This is what those whom you see do: like foolish travellers, forgetting their purpose, they have, as it were, sat down on the road in order to investigate these unfamiliar things which they see. And by the habit and continual practice of this vanity they have become so exiled from themselves that they neither remember that they are on a road nor seek their homeland.

I. If it is as you say, I judge these people more pitiable than all others, since their life is so enveloped in error that not only others, but they themselves, are deceived in their own pursuit.

D. It is altogether so; both their manner of life proves it and their end demonstrates it. Their manner of life is such that nothing could be more shameful; their end such that nothing could be more unhappy: dying, they have no hope of salvation, because while living they refused to walk in the way of virtue.

I. I truly confess that it is entirely absurd to call that person wise who, even though his eye may be open to every other matter, can neither foresee his own destruction nor is willing to avoid it.

[Col. 0712A] And that persons of this kind possess neither prudence concerning what is imminent nor foresight concerning what is to come is sufficiently shown by their slippery life, dissolute conduct, and disgraceful steps.

D. What then do you think: what sort of human undertaking is this?

I. I clearly see that this too is vanity, and vanity of vanities.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0711]

[Col. 0711A] It would take long to demonstrate, point by point, the vanity of this world. Know, however, that of all these things which you see, nothing is permanent (Eccles. II); rather, all things pass away and return to the place from which they arose.

[Col. 0711B] All things, as they have a beginning, so also have an end; but they run differently and do not arrive alike. Some have recently arisen; others have long since set; some pass through the middle interval; others, being born, succeed those that have arisen. Yet all alike flow away and tend toward one place.

O great river, where are you being swept? Your source is small: you flow from a tiny spring and burst forth from a slender vein. You run and grow; you descend and are swallowed up. You run, but downward; you grow, but toward destruction. You come and pass on; you flow out, and you are swallowed up. O stream that does not fail, O course that does not rest, O abyss that is not filled! As much as vanity subjects, as much as mortality draws down, so much does incurable death devour. Neither does the one ever cease to bring forth, nor the other to draw, nor the latter to swallow up.

[Col. 0711C] Things present always pass away; things future always succeed them; and because the succession is continuous, it is thought that there is a permanent condition. For the eyes of mortals are cast downward and do not observe the course of all things; fixed upon minute portions of reality, they do not attend to what is taking place in the whole. Human life upon earth is also short, and its days run their course within an assigned lot. The mind, wrapped in its own darkness, is not very able either to foresee the future or to remember the past. And because it is held occupied only with things set before it, the renewal of present things takes from it the memory of things past.

Hence, when people hear something about the mutability of things, they are immediately astonished and marvel as though something new had happened. For indeed the speech of one speaking presents as new to unreflective minds what in the course of things had long ago become old.

[Col. 0711D] Thus the mutability of present things is always old and always new: old to those who learned it long ago by experience or reason; new to those who now begin for the first time to know it, awakened either by experience or admonished by instruction. Yet this knowledge will be later even for those to come, because those who will exist after us will not possess this knowledge of the world’s mutability as soon as they begin to use the world, but only after long experience.

Look, then, upon this miserable world, and upon those more miserable still who love it. This is the world which we once thought our friend, in which we promised ourselves long times, a quiet life, tranquil peace, and lasting happiness.

[Col. 0712A] This is the world whose beauty we loved, whose appearance we praised, whose pleasantness we desired, whose glory we sought, whose joy we embraced.

[Col. 0712B] Surely you now see how vain all these things are, and that they are never to be sought by the wise or lovers of virtue. For where are our fathers? Where are those rich and powerful men whom we once saw exalted in this world’s glory? Finally, where are all those in whose friendship and familiarity we placed confidence? Behold, they have all passed before us, and we alone have been left behind them.

Let us now think of that age of times past, when we were with them and did not yet know what was to come; when we had with them one purpose, one will, one desire, one dwelling-place, one affection, one love of life, one expectation of death. Now they have been taken from us and, as though running ahead, have departed more swiftly from this place where they were exiles, and arrived more swiftly at that place where they are citizens.
