[Col. 0712C] Therefore, if we truly loved them when they were present, let us now prove our love in their absence. Let us follow in desire to where they are, and desire to arrive with them more quickly and to be together with them. We are shown to be unfaithful and inconstant alike if, because of love for those now present, we forget our former love.

O ancient age, where are you? Long ago, while you existed, I loved you; and now again, when you do not exist, I love you. Your passing has never been able to diminish my love for you. When you existed, I loved you so that you might remain; but now, when you are not, I love you, yet I do not wish you to return here to me. I myself marvel at my desire and consider my affection, yet do not understand it. What, then, do I love in you if I do not wish you to continue, nor desire you to return?

[Col. 0712D] What is this affection, so strange and unheard-of, in which a thing is loved but its presence is not loved? Who will explain to my heart what this love is? I know indeed that I love you, yet I do not wish you to return to me. And perhaps I do not wish you to return again because I desire rather to be with you where you are. Therefore, formerly I loved you perversely, because I wished you to be where I am, so that you might pass through with me; now I love you more thoughtfully, because I wish to be with you where you may remain forever.

I am in exile, while you are in the homeland; and therefore I never tire of thinking of you, because through memory and recollection of you I somehow return in mind to my homeland. O how sweet it is in a foreign land to remember things past!

[Col. 0713A] The mind is not satisfied with desire: it follows the path of what has gone before; inwardly it sees the road by which it may pass, it sees the end toward which it tends, it sees the place to which it may arrive, it sees the harbour where it may rest.

I. Just as formerly, when I thought this world stable, its appearance inflamed me with love for present things, so now, in a wonderful manner, its mutability moves me to desire things to come. I am carried away by affection and drawn by desire to where all things are running. Even now I love in things this very fact that they pass away, because from their very change and from the example of all things I am more ardently kindled to pass from here. All things seem to me to be on campaign; and the clamour of all nature, as all things run together to reach their end, strikes my ears like an exhortation.

D. Then do you acknowledge that all things in this world are perishable and transient?

[Col. 0713B] I. The thing itself proves it, even if I had not recognized it.

D. What then will become of those who put their trust in these things?

I. What except that they will remain empty and void when the very things they love have passed away?

D. It is good, then, to flee from here and seek a more secure dwelling.

I. Nothing is better; but I ask you, teach me where we shall go outside the world, so that, while all things in the world pass away, we may remain stable.

D. For the present, consider this whole world, on account of the mutability of all things, as a kind of flood of running waters.

I. I clearly see that nothing is stable, but that all things rush headlong.

D. Then think of the lovers of this world as shipwrecked persons who, submerged in the depths of this salt sea,

[Col. 0713C] are swept downward.

I. Nothing could be said more fittingly: all who love transient things flow away with those things to which they cling.

D. But I think you do not doubt that nothing passes away with God, but that all things subsist in unchangeable eternity.

I. No one doubts it.

D. Contemplate, then, God as above, in the highest place, and this world as below, in the lowest; God standing always in the same state of his eternity, but this world ever flowing and unstable through the course of its mutability.

I. The matter is clear; continue what you have begun.

D. Then consider the human soul as placed, as it were, in a middle position: by a certain excellence of its condition it rises above this mutability which is below, yet it has not attained to that true immutability which is above with God.

[Col. 0713D] I. This arrangement is beautiful and greatly pleases me.

D. But if the soul immerses itself through desire in things that pass away below, it is immediately swept away through countless distractions and, divided in some sense from itself, is scattered.

I. This distraction is exceedingly dangerous. Yet I should like to know whether anyone so widely scattered can be gathered together again.

D. Certainly, if he raises himself again and, shaking off these lowest things, learns anew to be with himself. For each person is gathered all the more into unity of soul the more, abandoning lower things, he is raised upward in thought and desire, until at last he becomes altogether unchangeable when he reaches that one supreme immutability.

[Col. 0714A] Therefore the soul ascends from this infinite distraction which is below and, as has been said, is gathered all the more into unity the more it is raised upward, until it reaches the true and unique immutability—which is with God—where it may rest forever without any alternation of changeability.

I. Since you had earlier mentioned the flood, it seems to me that now, consequently, you are fashioning some particular form of an ark in the human heart. Indeed, as I consider more carefully, this structure appears wonderful to me; and although I do not yet know why you have turned the discussion toward it, nevertheless I think that what you are trying to show is something great. For you have hitherto proposed to me three things as unknown as they were unheard-of, but now as unusual as they are wonderful.

First is this whole world, with everything in it, flowing past in the manner of running waters; and reality itself is very like it whether we compare its inundations and motions of changeability to a flood overwhelming all things or to a great sea.

[Col. 0714B] Second is the human heart, raising itself from these transient and mutable things and gradually gathering itself into one; so that where it is nearest to mutable things it appears broad below, at its base, like an ark, but is drawn together and in some manner gathered into one where it approaches more closely to eternal and immutable things.

Then, in the highest and third place, you set God, so that he may direct the ark of the human heart, resting below upon this surging salt sea, like a helmsman; hold it like an anchor; and receive it like a harbour. I therefore see these three things: below, this world as a kind of flood; in the middle, the human heart as a kind of ark; above, God as helmsman.

[Col. 0714C] Moreover, this ark amazes me not only by its novelty but also by its magnitude. I see that it is of such immense extent that its base below rests upon the waters of this flood, while its summit above reaches all the way to God. But although I do not suppose that you have recalled these matters without purpose, I desire to know more fully how they bear upon the aim of our discussion.

D. Do you recall what I first began to persuade you of?

I. I do. For you said that this world must be fled and that no hope should be placed in it, because nothing at all that is in it can endure and remain for long. When you had proved this to me by evident and irrefutable truth,

[Col. 0714D] I too began strongly to desire it, yet I could find no way at all by which one ought to flee from here. Then you began to introduce certain matters—I do not know whether to demonstrate this—in which, by a distinction beautiful enough and ingenious, you set this world as a kind of flood below, the human heart as a kind of ark in the middle, and God as helmsman above.

D. Indeed, I introduced these things in order to show you, as you stand in danger, the way of salvation, and to prepare for you, as for one truly shipwrecked, either an ark in a flood or a ship at sea. For since you are tossed in the midst of the deep salt waters of this surging sea, how do you think that you can either escape danger or reach a harbour unless you are carried across by the help of this saving wood—whether you call it an ark or a ship?

[Col. 0715A] I. These new comparisons of yours draw me into a new uncertainty. For if the whole world is sea or flood, to what place outside the world shall we sail, where we may find a tranquil and stable dwelling? Moreover, if the human heart is an ark and ship, how can a person either enter his own heart or cross the world with his heart? Finally, since God, whom you called the harbour, is above, what kind of voyage will this be, in which, in an unusual and unheard-of manner, both the ship’s course is directed upward and the voyager is carried by himself?

D. When we wish to raise the eye of the mind toward invisible things, we ought to look to likenesses of visible things as certain traces of knowledge.

[Col. 0715B] Therefore, when something is called highest in spiritual and invisible matters, it signifies not something situated locally above the summit or vault of heaven, but that which is innermost of all. To ascend to God, then, is to enter into oneself; and not only to enter into oneself, but in some ineffable manner even to pass beyond oneself in one’s inmost being. Thus whoever, so to speak, transcends himself by entering inwardly and penetrating within truly ascends to God.

But when a person, through the senses of the flesh, goes out in desire toward these visible things which are transient and perishable, then surely he descends from the dignity of his condition to certain lowest and abject things. Therefore, what is innermost is nearest, highest, and eternal; and what is outermost is lowest, distant, and transient.

[Col. 0715C] To return from the outermost to the innermost is therefore to ascend from the lowest to the highest, and to be gathered into unity from the dispersion of confusion and mutability. Since we recognize that this world is outside us but God within us, we must pass through ourselves as we return from the world to God, as though ascending from below to above. And in this way we ourselves are, in a sense, carried across the waves when, entering into ourselves from those mutable things that are outside, we find stability.

I. O saving ark, O blessed harbour! Blessed is the person who can escape this stormy salt sea unharmed and arrive at that tranquillity of unique rest. I would wish to enter it; I would wish to be saved in it; I would wish to be carried through in it.

[Col. 0715D] Teach me, then, I beg you, how each person ought to enter the ark of his own heart, and, once within it, by what actions he can escape danger and reach the harbour of desired rest.

D. Since we have once adopted likenesses of things in our speech, it is right that we should continue to maintain them in the course of our discourse as the matter requires. The world is a flood; but the human heart, if it bends itself downward through love of worldly things, suffers shipwreck amid the waves of the age. Mingled with mutable things, it flows amid things slipping away; and it is plunged deeply through its affection for lower things by a twofold danger to salvation, while through its occupation with many things it is widely scattered.

But if it raises itself again from the love of present things by the desire for eternal things, and gathers its thoughts to itself through self-consideration,

[Col. 0716A] it now in some fashion swims above the waves of things, treads underfoot all transient things as they slip beneath it, and, in proportion as it gradually raises itself ever higher and higher through the steps of virtues and gathers itself into unity, displays within itself spiritually the form of an ark.

Some hearts, then, are above; others have submerged themselves below. Below are those hearts which are conformed to this age; above are those whose manner of life is in heaven. Below are those which savour earthly things; above are those which continually meditate upon heavenly things. Therefore the human heart is judged to be above or below according to that with which it is joined through love. And it is rightly said to be outside itself when it falls away toward seeking these external and transient things.

[Col. 0716B] But it returns to itself when it meditates upon those things which concern its salvation. There are, therefore, some things by loving and thinking upon which the human heart is pressed downward and, torn apart, scattered among various things; and there are again some things by loving and meditating upon which it is raised upward and gathered to itself.

For this reason, we must divide the whole realm of things into two, placing in one part the works of creation and in the other the works of restoration. And, to mark their distinction briefly: the works of creation are the elements of this world, made to serve the human being while he stood upright. The works of restoration are the sacraments of the incarnation of the Word, given as a remedy in order to raise the fallen.

[Col. 0716C] These two works were performed at times as different as they are in dignity. The works of creation, as a small indication of divine power, were completed in a short time at the beginning of the world, namely in six days. But the works of restoration, from the beginning of the age to its end, can be completed or brought to fulfilment only over the measured space of six ages, as certain outstanding signs of majesty and divinity.

The works of creation, given for a time, were afterward made subject to servitude. But the works of restoration were given for salvation forever. Therefore the elect love the works of restoration more, whereas the reprobate prefer the works of creation to the works of restoration. The reprobate, cleaving to visible things, flow away with things that pass; but the elect, despising visible and transient things, ascend to eternal things.

[Col. 0716D] The former fall away from invisible things through visible things; the latter ascend from visible things to invisible things. Thus the elect emerge as from a shipwreck from among the works of creation that flow away beneath them; and, borne up through the works of restoration—that is, the sacraments of their salvation—as in a saving ark, they can no longer be submerged at all.

Since, therefore, a person had been scattered by perversely loving the works of creation and had to be gathered together by the works of restoration, the works of restoration themselves were made so that they should indeed be many, yet not infinite: so that the human heart, not yet capable of true stability, might be refreshed by variety and gathered into unity by their limited number. And just as formerly a person had fallen away from the contemplation of God through visible things,

[Col. 0717A] so now, admonished through the visible works of God, he might become accustomed to rise again to contemplate God himself.

Moreover, God wrought some works of restoration through human beings, some through angels, and some through himself. When we pass from contemplating the works of human beings to the works of angels, and again from the works of angels to the works of God, we ascend in the spiritual ark as from the first dwelling to the second, and from the second to the third; and at last we touch the highest cubit, in which the ark is completed, when through the works of God we arrive at the knowledge of him.

The ark is extended to a length of three hundred cubits because, as has been said, “the works of our restoration are extended from the beginning of the world to its end through the three periods of nature, law, and grace, as though through three hundreds.”

[Col. 0717B] Its width, moreover, is set at fifty cubits and its height at thirty, because the whole multitude of the faithful, in whom and for whom these things were done, is expressed by seven times seven—that is, forty-nine—with one head, Christ, added; and the whole sum of the deeds which God has performed from the beginning for humankind is contained in the thirty books of the divine page.

I shall therefore teach you what you must do. Tread underfoot and despise perishable and transient things, and behold, you have emerged from the flood. Continually consider and meditate upon the sacraments of your restoration and the benefits of divine mercy bestowed upon you, and you have entered the ark. But when you lead your thought from the beginning of the world to the end of the age in contemplation of the wonderful works of God, and reflect upon what he has accomplished for our salvation under natural law, under written law, and finally under grace, you measure in your heart, as it were, the length of three hundred cubits.

[Col. 0717C] When, moreover, you consider the whole body of the faithful, you expand your heart, as it were, to the measure of fifty cubits. And when through study and assiduity you comprehend the knowledge of divine Scripture, you raise your heart to the height of thirty cubits.

The length of the ark, then, is in time; its width, in multitude; its height, in the quantity of works. Or again, length may be understood in deeds—that is, history; width in sacraments—that is, allegory; height in virtues—that is, tropology—so that all divine Scripture is enclosed within these boundaries. We have said more concerning these modes of writing in another book which we composed, *On the Ark*; it is unnecessary to repeat all of that here.

[Col. 0717D] One thing alone remains: that we enter this saving dwelling, so that we may both escape these evils which are outside and be able inwardly to find those delights of God’s sweetness which he himself has hidden for those who love him. For this is the house of God and the wine-cellar into which the king brought his bride, that he might order his love within her (Song of Songs I). Once we have entered it, we shall, with God’s help, be able as easily to despise in that joy all the pleasures of this world as, secure there, we shall not fear adversities.

I. How shall we enter into the house of the Lord?  
D. In the multitude of His mercy.  

I. What is meant by “in the multitude of His mercy”?  
D. Because our misery is great, a multitude of mercy is necessary for us. For whenever the mind strives to return to itself and to draw back its affections and thoughts alike into the hidden place of inward contemplation, as many obstacles bar the entrance to it as the desires of the old life, drawing it back to the wanderings of former habit and to errors, do not permit it to remain steadfast. Yet divine mercy must be sought and implored, that it may advance us whenever our misery holds us back from entering into inward rest.

I. Behold, we enter into the house of the Lord: how long shall we remain there?  
D. Until iniquity passes away; until the waters of the flood cease, we must remain in the ark. Afterwards we shall go out safely, because, when this age is ended, there will no longer be anything to fear, when neither the world outside will contain anything perishable nor the human being within anything corrupt.

I. And after we have entered into the house of the Lord, what shall we do there?  
D. We shall be in perpetual peace and gladness. For all who dwell there neither labour nor are anxious, because there is there neither lack of present things nor fear of things to come.

I. What then shall we do there, if we do not labour?  
D. There is one occupation for all there: to contemplate the wonders of God and praise Him in His works. And, if it would not be burdensome to you, I would set forth one example in which I might plainly show how you ought to live in that inward dwelling-place of the heart.

I. Indeed, I earnestly desire this; nor can that in any way be burdensome which brings a desiring mind to the fulfilment of its desire.

D. That inward dwelling-place, which because of various resemblances of things we are accustomed now to call an ark and now a house, is like the house of a wealthy householder; while the soul is like a cherished child, nourished in its father’s house as tenderly as it is dearly loved. Let us therefore consider how a little child lives in its father’s house, because we too ought to live thus in the house of God. For He Himself says: “Unless you become like this little child, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XXVIII).

I. What then does a little child do?  
D. He is not anxious and does not covet. He occupies himself with simple and innocent play; he loves his household so much that, even if transferred to a kingdom, he seeks rather the old familiar things and desires to be present among those to which he is accustomed. He knows his father’s property: now he runs through the field, now in the garden, now in the orchards, now in the meadows, now to the springs, now to the vineyards; in each season of the year he has his own delights. In spring he follows those who plough and sow; in summer he accompanies the reapers, and in autumn the grape-gatherers. Everywhere he finds pasture, everywhere play, everywhere refreshment, everywhere delight. And besides the daily household meals upon which he is fed at home, he is sometimes renewed to his former pleasures when he tastes outside the servants’ provisions as well.

He delights to pluck newly grown fruits; to rub ears of corn, still immature in grain, roasted by the fire; to choose ripening beets; to explore birds’ nests; and to carry home, with great joy and exultation, either eggs or young birds that he has found. As though from his own, however slight, hunting, he seeks refreshment more eagerly than from the resources of others. If perhaps he learns that his father is going somewhere—to an estate, a fortress, a market, or a festival—and will soon return, he wishes to go with him, so that he may see novel and unfamiliar things, and, on his return, tell his companions what he has seen: what manner of dress people wore, what was the situation of places, how great the cities were, how lofty the houses, how abundant the goods for sale; what he found, bought, and brought back.

Therefore he gladly goes out, because he is to return. He sometimes desires to see things outside so that he may return to his own home either richer or more newly refreshed. But he desires to have a permanent dwelling only in his father’s house and with its household, among whom he was born and with whom he was reared: to live with them and grow old among them. He wishes not to be separated from them even in death, lest in dying he leave those whom, while alive, he had as living, familiar, and dear companions. This fellowship, this dwelling, these delights, this gladness—these he always desires to possess. He seeks nothing outside; he covets nothing further.

Let us strive to live thus in the house of the Lord, and we shall find together peace, rest, and gladness. Let us be simple, not coveting what belongs to others; let us love more than the pleasures of this world the delights God has prepared for us, which are found in His house. In these let us continually exercise our heart. Let us gladden our mind and kindle our affection. There we have most lucid springs. We have flowering meadows, level and spacious fields, fruitful vineyards, fertile flocks, an abundant harvest, fruit-bearing orchards, watered gardens, and every kind of delight which the mind may rightly desire or happily possess.

I. Tell me, I pray, more plainly what these delights are which you have enumerated.  
D. Fruit-bearing trees are righteous persons, bringing us the examples of good works for refreshment; springs are the wise; fields are the humble; vineyards are those who cultivate themselves through discipline; gardens and meadows, as it were, flourishing with diverse virtues, are those who refresh others with the harvest of their labour and multiply the flock of the faithful, drawing others to faith by word and example and, as it were, begetting them. These delights we possess outwardly in the house of God, apart from those singular meals by which mother Grace inwardly feeds and refreshes us daily.

Let us therefore now enter; and the Lord will be our guide, that He may direct our steps in the path of His commandments, so that, recalling His mercies which are from everlasting, we may exercise our heart in His love and kindle desire (Ps. CXVIII). When we have entered, I shall lead you, going before you, through everything from the first front of the house to the innermost sanctuary. In length, breadth, and height we shall survey all the upper chambers and the three-storeyed structures; at length we shall ascend, and we shall not cease until we reach the king’s throne.

[Col. 0720A] We shall walk through all the works of our restoration, from the beginning to the consummation of the age, according to the course of times, the events of things, and the deeds of human beings. And when we have contemplated what is within, I shall sometimes open the window of the ark, and, looking alternately upon what is outside, we shall renew the eyes of the mind amid the waters of this flood. For it will be more delightful, by turns, now to behold from a kind of watch-station the evils which we have escaped, and now, with our eyes restored to the inner things, to contemplate the goods which we have found and possess.

I. We shall love those goods themselves more closely if we strive continually, by turns, to remember misery and danger also and to be warned by them.

D. It shall therefore be yours to ask, from all the wonders which you see either within or without, as much as you wish and judge fitting; but it shall be mine to answer your questions as much as I wish. First I shall lead you into the upper part of the house—that is, into the front which faces east—so that our entrance may take place at once from the beginning of the world and from the beginning of the age. For, because the length of the house is three hundred cubits, its upper front touches the east, while its lower end reaches as far as the west. Its left side, however, faces south and its right side north.

By divine providence He ordered the course of events in this way: what was done at the beginning of the age should occur in the east, as though at the beginning of the world; and then, as times ran their course toward the end of the age, the sum of events should descend toward the west—that is, toward the end of the world. Thus the first human being, after he was created, was placed in Paradise, in the eastern region, so that from there, as from the beginning of the world, the entire offspring of the human race might flow out through all lands. Then the first head of kingdoms was in the east among the Assyrians; but in the latest times of the age supreme power descended to the Romans, who were situated in the west.

Therefore, beginning from the origin of all things and proceeding through the works of restoration along the length of the ark toward the end and consummation of all things, a paved path lies through the middle of the age, so that, as we pass along, whatever happens either to the north or to the south—that is, on the right or left, as though outside the ark in the flood—may be open on either side. This walk will indeed be spacious, but not wearisome: within, as we pass, the varied delight of so many things will meet us; and again, to those looking out through the window, the astonishing confusion and fluctuation of worldly mutability outside will lie exposed to their sight far and wide from a lofty watchtower and a most secure station.

I. Behold, we enter upon the beginning of the world; but when I begin to turn my eyes backward, as though outside the world, desiring to know what there was before time, I see nothing.

D. Your questions take their beginning from a lofty source.

## BOOK THREE

Leaving aside transitory matters, the inquiry turns to divine things. The interlocutors are A and R—that is, as I interpret them, Soul and Reason.

[Col. 0721]

[Col. 0721A] A. Whenever I ponder the eternity of God in my mind, I cannot at all comprehend how or where He existed before the beginning of all things. For where could He have been, when there was nothing in which He could have been? This therefore disturbs my reflection: I cannot discover where God was when, apart from God, there was nothing.

R. If you consider all that exists and weigh where this whole is, what place will remain outside it? Let the whole contain everything, since there is nothing which the whole does not contain. If, therefore, you cannot find a place for the universe, how do you confine the Author of the universe in a place? For God did not make the world so that the world might contain God, as though He could not remain fixed without a support; but, just as in eternity He preceded all things, so in immensity He exceeds all things, needing nothing. [Col. 0721B] He was neither completed by the perfection of His work—He to whom, without it and when it did not exist, nothing was lacking—nor did anything accrue to Him from it when it was made.

A. Why then did God make creation, if His goodness was not increased by creation?

R. God made His works out of love, not necessity: not in order to increase His goodness through them, but in order to bestow His goodness upon them. For He made rational creation in order to make it blessed in Himself; He subjected all other things to it for service, setting forth Himself as its reward unto glory. Therefore, in order that the praise of God might be complete, He joined all visible and invisible things in one fellowship. For the rational creation which He had established for His glory, He commanded partly to remain in its purity; partly, joining it to bodily coverings and earthly dwellings, He made it enliven clayey matter with the sense of life.

This dispensation of the Creator was the beginning of a great design, because in their creation He first wished to show what He Himself would afterwards deign to do in them. Therefore, to display eternal love, new exemplars were made and the highest of the lowest things were joined with the lowest; because the lowest of the highest things were to be joined with the Highest of all, so that what the body was to the spirit, the spirit might be to the Creator. For since among created things nothing is more excellent than spirit, and nothing is found weaker or more corruptible than earth, when He gave to the human body, made from earth and possessing corruptible matter, a rational spirit—that is, a rational soul—as its companion, He in some manner joined the lowest things to the highest in one fellowship. He thus set forth an example of the fellowship to come: so that what, then, in creation the body was to the spirit, the spirit taken up to Himself might afterwards become through His gracious condescension.

[Col. 0721D] For as one act of creation had joined the excellence of spirit to the weakness of bodily nature, so one merciful act of gracious condescension ought to join the humility of spiritual creation to the excellence of the Creator.

A. Since it is agreed that the rational spirit given to animate the human body would have been more excellent had it remained in its purity, how did that which brought abasement to the one who endured it pertain to the love of the One who made it?

R. Because the condition of rational creation was humbled in part in order that it might be exalted as a whole, so that it might afterwards be more wonderfully exalted, because it had first been humbled in part without misery. Since all that nature was to be joined in the glory of the Creator’s excellence, it was fitting that it should first learn how far beneath Him it was by nature, though it was to be joined to Him and in some manner made equal through grace; so that it might love the gift of grace in glory more abundantly insofar as it knew more truly the condition of nature in its humiliation.

God therefore demonstrated His power in forming the human being, which He would afterwards display in glorifying the human being, so that humanity might know that, if God could join the so dissimilar natures of body and soul in one covenant and friendship, it would by no means be impossible for Him to raise the humility of rational creation, though far inferior, into participation in His glory. And if the wisdom of the Creator in ordering the fellowship of soul and body was so great that the companionship of the inferior nature is not merely no punishment or misery to the nature so excellent, but that it counts as its greatest punishment when, bound under the law of mortality and subjected to death, it is compelled to suffer separation from that body: how much more ineffable will it be when, joining to Himself in love the same nature which He made, He pours that true and supremely blessed life into the other life made by Him, unto eternal life, and makes the happy and blessed union one that will never suffer division.

A. Yet it seems greatly to conflict with the privilege of love that spiritual nature was joined to a clayey substance. For although the example benefited those who remained in their purity by teaching them to know love, it is clear how much glory it took away from those who were humbled. Therefore, as much as those owe greater gratitude for grace who were taught without abasement, so much those who were humbled for the instruction of others seem to have a just complaint against love.

R. But what was not given in humiliation is repaid in glorification; and they receive so much more in exaltation as they received less in creation. For because through the earthliness of flesh the human being is subjected to the purity of others, afterwards through the glory of that same flesh he is raised to fellowship with angels, so that he may rejoice not only in the glorification of his own spirit, but also so that the glory of that whose lowliness seemed to have harmed him may contribute to the increase of his glorification.

Thus more was given to angels in creation, but more has been bestowed upon human beings in glorification, because they ascend to glory even in that in which, having been somewhat humbled, they seemed inferior to glory; so that they may rejoice alike in one love, having been called to one love and created for one brightness, exulting as they receive one measure of glory, although by a dissimilar distribution.

Therefore God, disposing the rational spirit which He had created for His glory by a differing lot, as has been said, commanded part of it to remain in its purity; while part of it, joined to earthly bodies, was to animate them with life and sense. For those whom He left in their purity He established a dwelling above in heaven; but those whom He joined to earthly bodies He placed below in an earthly habitation. He set before both a rule of obedience, so that the former might not fall from where they were, and the latter might ascend from where they were to where the former were; so that when the latter arrived, the former, without departing above that for which they had been made, might attain to that for which they had been made: that they might be with Him by whom they had been made.

A. Since our purpose has special reference to the creation of the human being, turn your account to what must next be said concerning him.

R. Therefore God placed the human being in Paradise as in a place of instruction and a school of virtues, that there he might be exercised by obedience to the commandment, receiving a reward if he persevered and a punishment if he transgressed. Accordingly, in Paradise only a good was placed, but not the highest good: so that virtue might begin in the good which was only good by purity, while in the good which was not the highest good there might be something by which virtue, having been exercised, could advance.

[Col. 0723C] But because, by transgressing, the human being abandoned obedience, he was struck by the sentence of a curse and received in the nature which he had received incorrupt, the punishment of mortality, to be sown and transmitted to all his posterity. Here all human beings, born mortal from a corrupted root, bear witness to the first transgression. And although indeed through grace we are reborn unto life, nevertheless by nature we are all born unto death and condemnation.

A. What, then, was the subsequent course of the age?

R. The first-formed human being, Adam, expelled from the seat of Paradise so that he might become a father though he was not a son, begot from her whom his side gave forth and his rib produced two sons: a sign and beginning of division. Thus, from that mass of perdition, vessels of wrath and vessels of mercy already then began to be divided. For when the wicked man, envying the righteous, was unwilling to change what he was, he could not endure what he saw. Therefore brother killed brother, forgetting natural affection; and, lest he perish, having received the mark of perdition, he became a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth. For, wishing to flee the witness of his crime but unable to flee his conscience, trembling and stupefied, he began to dwell alone apart; unworthy therefore of human fellowship, because he was the first to break peace, the friend of fellowship and bond of concord.

Adam, when he was one hundred and thirty years old, begot Seth in place of Abel, whom Cain had killed, because the righteous seed could not wholly perish. Seth, when one hundred and five years old, begot Enos, who began to call upon the name of the Lord [Col. 0724A]—not indeed as the first founder of religion, but as an outstanding imitator of his father’s devotion. Enos, when ninety years old, begot Cainan. Cainan, when seventy years old, begot Mahalaleel. Mahalaleel, when sixty-five years old, begot Jared. Jared lived one hundred and sixty-two years and begot Enoch. Enoch lived sixty-five years and begot Methuselah; and Enoch walked with God. After he begot Methuselah, he lived three hundred years and appeared no more, because God took him away to remain outside humankind and to live beyond humankind, so that alive he might await a companion who was yet to be born, and afterwards perish with that companion.

Methuselah, when he had lived one hundred and eighty-seven years, begot Lamech. Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-two years and begot Noah, the boundary of consummation and sign of perfection, under whom iniquity would have its end, mortality its restoration, and justice its consummation (Gen. V).

But Cain, Adam’s son, author of discord and head of division, extending separately the line of his generation, first begot a son whom he called Enoch; and he built a city, which he named Enoch after his son, showing that he sought a dwelling in this life and despaired of being able to attain the inheritance reserved for the saints in the future. Enoch, Cain’s son, begot Irad; Irad begot Mehujael; Mehujael begot Methushael; and Methushael begot Lamech, who killed Cain (Gen. IV), so that he who had dedicated a dwelling in his first son might receive perdition in the seventh.

[Col. 0724C] Conversely, in the line of the righteous Abel is killed first, while Enoch, the seventh—whose name is interpreted “dedication”—is remembered as translated rather than dead. For in this life the wicked indeed first rejoice, while the good endure tribulation; but afterwards, when the wicked perish, the good, then wholly freed from evil, attain eternal life and joy.

Lamech therefore took two wives, one named Adah and the other Zillah (ibid.), thus first setting forth an example of incontinence—first an imitator of his father, afterwards to become a murderer. Adah bore Jabal, who was the father of those dwelling in tents and of shepherds (ibid.), namely the inventor of superstition and avarice; and Tubal [Jubal], who was the father of those playing the lyre and organ (ibid.), following wantonness and the softness of luxury. Zillah also bore Tubal-cain, who was a smith and worker in every work of bronze and iron (ibid.), supplying weapons, namely, to fury. Zillah also bore Naamah, Tubal-cain’s sister, who, in her eleventh generation, signifies the transgression of evil persons and indicates their final purpose. For what does it mean that in the generation of the wicked a woman is placed last, unless it is plainly given to be understood that every aim of the depraved is directed toward carnal pleasure? For whatever they do, they set in this end; and thereby they transgress God’s commandments, because they do not stretch themselves toward His promises.

A. I greatly marvel and am astonished within myself when I consider the divine ordering in past events, because from the very order of passing things I perceive, I know not how, a certain fixed providence.

R. What wonder is there in this? Since God speaks to us through His works, what else do we perceive than the voice of One speaking to us when we open the eyes of our mind to consider His wonders?

A. Continue, then, and let us pursue what remains, so that in the things that have been done we may find Him who made them.

R. What we have said should briefly be recalled to memory. Beginning from the first parent, we have traced two generations separately: one through Seth, which placed the goal of both its number and its progress in ten; the other through Cain—that is, the generation of the wicked—whose extension the number seven contained, while its multitude poured itself out as far as eleven.

God had commanded that the generation of the righteous should not mingle with the offspring of the impious, lest it perhaps draw in the sap of bitterness if it were grafted into a corrupted root. At first God’s command was observed, and the separate religious life of each party remained for a long time. But as the course of time went on, delay nourished negligence, while desire at the same time persuaded presumption; at length the love of flesh overcame reverence for the Creator. And the sons of God saw the daughters of men—that is, believers saw the daughters of the impious—that they were beautiful; and they chose for themselves whomever they wished from among them all. Going in to them, they begot sinful people, an evil seed, who through impious pride would despise God and would not fear to provoke against themselves, by their daily evil works, the wrath and fury of divine vengeance.

[Col. 0725C] “And God repented that He had made humankind upon the earth” (Gen. VI). God repented, not through a change in Himself but because of us. He repented, not because He Himself had done evil, but because that which He Himself had made good had fallen away from the good. Therefore God repented, not by correcting what He had made, because He had made it well, but because He saw corrupted what He had created without corruption for incorruption. Therefore He did not repent of what was His own, but He repented of ours on account of His own: because what was His was good, what was ours was evil, and it was in what was His. For our evil could not have been elsewhere except in what was His but was not itself His; and therefore mercy was moved, lest good, which had not been made for evil, should perish through evil.

Therefore God repented that He had made humankind upon the earth, and He wished to destroy from the earth what was evil upon the earth. And unless a righteous man had stood before Him, the root of the human race would have perished with its vice, and the whole corrupted thing would have undergone judgment together with its corruption, unless truth, with mercy and grace intervening, had delivered the righteous man. For Noah found grace before the Lord, and Noah was a righteous and perfect man in his generation (ibid.). He found grace because, although he was righteous in comparison with the most wicked, such that he ought to please God and not perish, there was nevertheless a reason why he too could not have escaped judgment unless he found grace.

Therefore the righteous man found grace so that he might not perish, because he had also first received this from grace, that he was righteous. And when destruction came upon the world, he was preserved in the world without danger of death, he who had lived in the world without deceit. For he was righteous, but he was not without sin; yet he was not under sin, because he had found grace. Therefore there was shown to him the means by which he could be saved: the wood, and the means by which, when the waters came, he might remain unharmed beneath the roof of the ark which he himself constructed at God’s command, so that seed might be preserved for the age to come.

In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, therefore, the waters of the flood overflowed upon the earth (Gen. VII), and all flesh under heaven upon the earth was destroyed. Noah was in the ark—he himself, his wife, his three sons, and the wives of his sons (ibid.)—eight souls, that they might live and not perish with the world: a sign of the future posterity and a sacrament of resurrection, since they safely escaped the first judgment in water, in order to show forth the figure of the final judgment in fire.

A. Very great and astonishing to all are the works of God, by which He not only executes judgment upon past crimes but also forms examples of things to come. What mind does not collapse in contemplating them—not to say, stand firm—and become wholly dissolved from itself in searching them out? But because we ought willingly to embrace as truth the very things which we fear as miracle and severity, lest we experience them unto condemnation, let us strive always to hear them for instruction.

R. Noah, safe within the enclosure of the ark from the danger of the raging flood, learned from the dove’s indication, in the branch of green olive, that the waters had ceased upon the earth. He went out of the ark when God opened its enclosure and made a way into the beginning of the age to come. All the living creatures which had been preserved there for the propagation of posterity upon the earth were likewise brought out. So also Shem, Ham, and Japheth, his sons, and their wives with him; and the world began again to emerge in another rising, compensating for the losses of the former generation (Gen. VII–X).

The human race, now of a threefold stock, was wholly one in order that it might increase, since it had issued from one root. Shem and Japheth, giving honour to their origin, deserved blessing upon the earth and multiplied in the inheritance of promise. Ham, heir of the curse, possesses in his son the grief which he himself first inflicted upon fatherhood. The human race was then scattered abroad, and evils were multiplied again. People likewise came together, devising evil schemes, so that they might raise themselves up against God and build a structure into heaven while their heart was upon the earth. The children of men did this, provoking wrath from on high; and, remembering no judgment to be feared, they thought that, by ascending, they could sin without punishment, so as to escape water when they were to be judged in fire (Gen. XI).

[Col. 0726D] And behold, that engine of opposition had raised itself to a lofty summit, and the impious rejoiced that their wishes would be fulfilled unto evil, when suddenly the divine regard from above confused all their languages, dispersed their wicked conspiracy, and they were scattered from that place over the whole earth, without their malice departing from them. At this time the great patriarch Eber arose, so that men of virtue should not fail, leaving to posterity a good name beloved by God, so that those who please God might know that they must pass beyond and depart from the most wicked generation.

Then Abram came (Gen. XIII), heir of the name of the fathers; at God’s command he went forth from his own land and passed from Ur of the Chaldeans in order to come into the land of promise, because God had promised it to him. This is the land beloved by God, founded from the beginning and prepared for those who will possess the inheritance: not the land of the nations, which is defiled by the impious, but that land which only the blessed see and find. This land is in heaven, having its figure on earth—not because the good of humanity is on earth, but because that which is possessed in heaven by the spirit is sought through a sign on earth.

Abraham therefore came into the land of Canaan and was a stranger in it all his days, awaiting the promise in hope. Nor was his obedience diminished because of delay, so that he would not have sacrificed his only-begotten son, in whom he had received the promise, had divine providence, by a voice descending from above, not restrained the father’s right hand (Gen. XXII). After him Isaac succeeded, a living sacrifice, standing in joy for his father; and he, when he died, left Jacob as his successor, who was a mighty wrestler, that he might conquer and be blessed.

From him the twelve tribes and the holy people Israel arose. After this Joseph was sold by his brothers (Gen. XXXVII). His father soon followed him, coming with seventy souls into Egypt to dwell there in a time of distress. But after Jacob and his sons died, Israel began to multiply and increase greatly, so that it might become evident that the God of the Hebrews was Lord over all the earth. For now there was a people of God and a holy nation, separated from the nation of the impious, beginning to spring up from the time when Abraham went forth from Ur of the Chaldeans in order to be separated from those among whom he dwelt and not become one with those to whom he was going.

Therefore the people of God, divided from the impious, was at first small within its generation in order that it might grow, so that those who walk the straight way may know that one must begin with small things in order to reach great things. For our God is able to exalt small things and bring down high things, so that no human being may have confidence in his own greatness, because the hope of mortal humanity is like humanity itself.

A. These great men, mighty in virtues in their own ages, with whom God spoke his secrets, saw with their own eyes the ancient things at which our generation marvels as past. But I should like to know what sort of men those were among whom these, approved in conduct, were pleasing; so that, on the one hand, emulation of the good may provoke us, and on the other, contempt for the evil may strengthen an example of patience.  
R. In those times there were evil men, powerful in the world by number, strength, and riches, so greatly superior that the life of the good could exist among them, but could scarcely be recognized by them because of its smallness. For already then the kingdoms of the world, rising in the sons of this age with great pride and pomp, had enclosed the world from the four quarters as though they were to possess it as their own: the Assyrians from the east, where Belus first reigned; the Sicyonians from the west, where Agialeus first reigned; the Scythians from the north, where Thanus first reigned; and the Egyptians from the south, where Mineus first reigned. But the Assyrian kingdom, most famous for power and military strength, was acquired after Belus by his son Ninus [Col. 0728A]. Bereft of his father, and wishing to console his affection for him, Ninus caused carved images to be fashioned in his father’s likeness and thereby laid the foundation of idolatry. For while he wished to make the memory of his parent perpetual among men through sculpted faces, he left to posterity, ignorant of the original cause, an example of error. Seeing the images, men thought that some divinity was present in them; and, rendering worship to the carved image, they made Bel into a notorious evil upon earth. Thereafter, one after another, borrowing [or: imitating] the error together with the name, men in their several languages called different divinities by the same vanity: Bel, Belial, Baalim, Beelzebub, and also Beelphegor. Thus human error adopted the worship of carved images which human folly had first instituted under a vain appearance of piety.

Ninus, moreover [Col. 0728B], enlarged the Assyrian kingdom by courage and industry, and at last subjected almost all Asia to his dominion. Having defeated Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, in war, he killed him and burned the books of his sorcery; so that the justice of God, who orders all things, seems rightly to have granted victory in this case to an impious man, lest impiety should reign. In the forty-third year of this man Abraham the patriarch was born. At that time Abraham lay hidden, obscure among the powerful men of this age, though he was destined to be great and exalted in the kingdom of God.

After Ninus, his wife Semiramis undertook the government of the empire. Assuming male dress and adding cunning to courage, she subdued even the remote peoples of India by war. Extending the empire to the furthest limits of the earth, she built the walls of Babylon on a scale incredible to human minds [Col. 0728C], exalting Confusion, so that she herself might proceed to its work. At last, in the final confusion, known carnally by her son through incest and committing a crime abominable to all, she first defiled her own womb through lust and afterwards stained it with the avenging parricide within it. She was killed by him in a just crime—by him whom she herself had slain [or: defiled] by a greater crime.

After his mother’s death, her son inherited and assumed the mournful empire, becoming a tyrant and the violent successor of his murdered parent. After him the Assyrian empire ran on, transmitting examples of crimes to posterity, so that its people might always occupy themselves with lust and bloodshed, having received from the beginning so cruel and detestable a lesson alike in lust and blood. Nor was it fitting that the kingdom of Babylon should be enlarged by other pursuits [Col. 0728D], except that the sons of Confusion might rage in uncleanness and cruelty. And who could enumerate all the plagues and confusions of those times which the kingdoms of the world, clashing with one another throughout the earth, endured? For in these times the Scythians and Amazons sowed a new and singular evil in the lands; Egypt too, pouring out strength beyond itself and, as though swelling, overstepping its bounds, lost its own possessions while rashly coveting those of others. There are many other things which, if we now attempted to recount them, would not even by themselves suffice for our purpose. But judging the whole from a part, let us see how great is the confusion of this world and how nothing can be secure [Col. 0729A] upon earth, giving thanks that we now despise all these evils with a mind at peace and, as from a safe station, behold without danger the world tossing and boiling within itself.  
A. Let us return again to the domestic narrative [Col. 0730A], for now I prefer to hear what is true; for as greatly as I am disgusted by hearing vain and false things, so greatly am I inflamed toward these.

## BOOK FOURTH

Concerning the inquiry into the mystical ark, and the interweaving of sacred and profane history, through which the instability of kingdoms is also recognized; and it concludes that passing things must be used wisely. In the opening, as I suppose, Reason is denoted by R.

[Col. 0729]

[Col. 0729A] When the time had now come for God to lead his people out of Egypt, he appeared to Moses in the bush through fire [Col. 0729B], showing charity/love (*caritas*) (Exod. III); because it is this which frees from death, and there is no way by which God comes to humanity except through charity. He therefore gave the command that Moses should bring the children of Israel out of Egypt by prodigies, plagues, and signs, so that he might show his wonders and all nations might know that God himself is almighty. Moses came at the command and, dividing the Red Sea with the rod, opened it in order to give a way to the people going toward salvation. Thus the ranks of the children of Israel were led out of Egypt by the path of the deep, while Pharaoh, pursuing them in his strength with chariots and armies, was swallowed up as though he had never existed; and the liberated people sang praise to the Lord (Exod. XIV).

Thereafter, as they advanced by the way of the desert, heavenly service accompanied them [Col. 0729C] in a pillar of cloud and fire going before: showing a road where there was none, furnishing shade in heat and light in darkness (Exod. XIII). The heavens rained manna, and the wind gathered a multitude of birds. The rock poured out drink for the table of God’s children. In such great wonders God made himself known to men, so that on Sinai he might give the law, the commandments, the tabernacle as an image of heavenly things, and the ark of the eternal covenant with its inscribed tablets. After forty years Moses ascended the mountain, saw the land from afar, charged the people concerning the sacred observance of the commandments, and departed in peace (Deut. XXXIV).

Then Joshua his minister arose and brought the children of Israel across into the land of promise. For Jordan could not withstand the sacred wonders; terrified, it fled and opened a way [Col. 0729D] for the ranks of the army that were to cross and fight (Josh. I). Then Joshua destroyed the nations in battles and apportioned the land among the twelve tribes by the measuring-line of distribution (Josh. XV). After him Othniel judged the people, and Shamgar struck down six hundred men with a ploughshare (Judg. III). Ehud exposed himself to danger for the people’s deliverance, and, as a ruthless messenger, destroyed the foreign king. Deborah too, strengthened by the word of prophecy, scattered Sisera and Jabin in the torrent Kishon, and by a glorious victory destroyed the enemies of God (Judg. V). Thereafter Gideon spread out the fleece on the threshing-floor and, after it had received the dew, he too, in a new triumph, carried jars and lamps with three hundred men from the river to battle (Judg. IX). Abimelech, however, with his brain dashed out and the crown of his head crushed, discovered the omen of the bramble [*rhamnus*] trampled by the trees of the forest in the parable [Col. 0730A] (Judg. IX). After these, Tola and Jair were judges in their times [Col. 0730B] (Judg. X). Thereafter Jephthah, bound by a vow for victory in war, sacrificed his daughter, leaving posterity a cruel example of piety (Judg. X). After him came Abessan, judge of the people; Abialon succeeded him, and when Abialon died, Abdon succeeded as judge (Judg. XII).

In their times Troy, famous to all for all its evils, fell, destroyed by the hands of the Myrmidons. I refrain from recounting its sufferings and lamentable disasters, lest I divert you from the subject. After Abdon came Samson, most mighty; he too saved his people in his time by great wonders (Judg. XIII). He struck down a thousand men with the jawbone from an ass’s head, though he had no weapons, when the Spirit rushed upon him (Judg. XV). And [Col. 0730C] he carried off on his shoulders the doors of the gate with their posts, to terrify his enemies (Judg. XVI). One woman conquered the unconquered man, and a woman’s wantonness softened strength terrible to all. Captured, he became a joy to his enemies; condemned to everlasting darkness, he was commanded to turn the millstone’s course, a reproach to the proud. But divine power comes upon him after he has been sufficiently mocked, and, as the hair of his head grows again, his former strength is restored to his wasted limbs. He shakes the columns with arms and hands, and, as the roof falls, takes vengeance upon his enemies through his own death (ibid.). Israel laments him, admiring its savior; him whom it had urged while living toward death, it recognized when dead as redeemer.

Next Eli judged the people for forty years, and, displaying an example of his folly, because he delayed to restrain the intemperance of his sons [Col. 0730D], he fell and paid the penalty together with his perishing sons (1 Sam. I). Then the ark of God was carried away among foreigners because of the people’s sins, but Dagon, falling and mutilated, bore witness to the majesty of the ark (1 Sam. I). Thereafter the hidden shame of rotting bodies compelled the proud to fear fellowship with holiness, and so the ark of the covenant was returned to the worshippers of piety.

The holy prophet Samuel arose (1 Sam. X and following), anointed a king for the people, and Saul, failing to keep the command, was rejected, confirming by the example of his rejection the power of obedience. After this, [someone] is sent to Bethlehem with olive oil in a lentisk [text uncertain], and among his brothers the boy David, who tended sheep in the desert, is sought out to be king in Israel. The Spirit departed from Saul in order to rest upon David; and, when the impious king was tormented by madness, David eased the attack by the mystical melody of his harp [Col. 0731A]. The Philistine fell by his own sword and by the stone of the sling; and the glorious warrior bore away a trophy when Goliath’s head had been cut off. Then, moved by envy, the king persecuted the innocent man. But the hand of the Almighty guided him powerfully, until it set the humble man upon the throne of the kingdom. Saul and Jonathan fell on Gilboa, but David, remembering their love, raised a lament over them. Therefore he was exalted and greatly magnified and became renowned throughout all the earth. He subdued his enemies by might and measured out the land of his foes. In his days the kingdom of Israel was exalted; he magnified its glory and added to and enlarged the worship of holiness (2 Sam. I and following).

After him his son Solomon arose (1 Kgs. I and following), who built the temple for the Lord [Col. 0731B] and displayed his wisdom in his works. For there was no wise man on earth like Solomon, whom God had filled with knowledge and understanding, so that he might investigate all things and be an examiner of marvelous secrets. But the beauty of the flesh deceived his heart, and prudence fell in the sight of foreign beauties. Therefore God divided his kingdom in the hand of his son and gave it to his servant Jeroboam son of Nebat, so that transgression might arise in Israel. Then the ten tribes withdrew, so as not to remain with the house of David. But Judah stood fast in faith, lest the glory of Jerusalem should fall. Jeroboam son of Nebat devised evil in his heart in order to establish his throne by impiety, and set up golden calves to remove glory from Israel. There Israel fell, and [Col. 0731C] Ephraim was cast down; they abandoned the Lord and went away into nothingness, that they might be blotted out from the earth.

Then prophets and men who searched out mysteries arose, and spoke in the Spirit in order to turn away wrath. Elijah the Tishbite came (1 Kgs. XVII), restraining rain from heaven and preventing dew from falling upon the earth. He drew down fire and made flame descend from above in the anger of the Lord’s wrath, in order to show power from on high (2 Kgs. I). The prophets of Baal fell before him, and he alone prevailed in the holy covenant, to give glory to God. At his prayer a dead man arose, as though one asleep had been awakened; and he himself, snatched up in a fiery chariot into the upper air, was seen by men no longer upon the earth (2 Kgs. II and following). Elisha, taking up the mantle, divided the Jordan and crossed over, that he might stand in Elijah’s place with a doubled spirit. He made waters sweet and tempered food of death with seasoning; he too called back souls departing to their dwellings. He led troops sent by another way before the ruler, displaying amid wonders a multitude of fiery chariots. Micaiah saw the Lord upon his throne and, rebuking the king himself steadfastly, was not afraid in his threats [Col. 0731D] (Mic. I). Jonah, swallowed by a whale, was likewise cast out upon dry land, that at the command he might announce overthrow to the Ninevites (Jonah I–II). Isaiah the prophet, also seeing the throne of the Most High, foretold things to come and comforted Jerusalem in time of distress (Isa. I and following).

But in all these things the children of Israel did not turn back from their ways to return to the Lord. Even Hezekiah [Col. 0732A], who seemed to please the Chaldeans, revealed secrets in boastfulness. Therefore God said that he would hand his people over into the hands of the Chaldeans, and sent Jeremiah, sanctified from the womb, to foretell things to come. For Israel, persisting in apostasy, had gone away to the Assyrians, and Judah with Jerusalem did not fear to provoke the Lord to great anger. Therefore he pronounced rejection upon them; and the king of Babylon came and transported Judah into his own land, among the Chaldeans, so that the sanctuary might be desolate. But Ezekiel and Daniel, mighty in wonders, saw visions and kingdoms to come and consoled the exile in a foreign land.

After seventy years the Lord called his people back to Jerusalem, and Ezra, Nehemiah [Col. 0732B], and Zerubbabel built the temple and city. Jesus the high priest governed the people in his time and left behind him, for generations, the dignity of the priestly mitres. But when the fury of indignation came, Mattathias arose with his sons to defend the law of the Lord; men of valor prevailed, so that iniquity might not rule forever. Judas Maccabaeus, a terror to his enemies, girded himself for battle in strength, put armies to flight, and crushed the host of the nations, so that Jerusalem might stand. After him his brother Jonathan arose, exposed himself to danger for his nation, and saved them in his time. After him his brother Simon assumed command in order to establish peace in the land. But, entrapped by the treachery of those near him, he died, leaving an example of courage to posterity [Col. 0732C]. His son John, however, a glorious man, stood in his father’s place as a defense for the people in his time. But the sons of transgression refused to keep the covenant’s pact, and therefore the kingdom was transferred to a foreign seed. For Herod came, who was not of Israel, and seized the scepter of dominion over the people, so that, at the rising of the heavenly kingdom, the carnal kingdom might fail; and that the king of Israel promised from the ages might receive what is eternal when the temporal had passed away and there was no scepter in Judah, thus fulfilling prophecy.

A. At the beginning of great matters we ought rather to fashion the discourse anew from the beginning. Therefore it seems good that the things which must be added from the survey of earlier times should first be explained, so that we may conclude in those matters which must be received for true salvation [Col. 0732D]. Tell me now briefly, therefore, what convulsions and fluctuations the world suffered in its own affairs during the times you have just rapidly passed over. For this is useful, so that we may return again refreshed to our own matters.  
R. After the Assyrian kingdom had long oppressed the world far and wide by much tyranny and shedding of blood, it finally came down to a king who devastated it. By a shameful life he obscured the glory of the preceding kings; like a man turning into a woman, in the perverse order of the first exchange, he became hateful to all through cowardice and disgrace. Arbaces, governor of the Medes, besieged him and compelled him to end his wretched life with a still more wretched death. Suddenly overthrowing that kingdom, famous everywhere for its cruelty, he transferred power to the Medes [Col. 0733A].

Thereafter the Persians under King Cyrus destroyed the kingdom of the Medes. Cyrus himself, having acquired the Chaldean empire, both took and destroyed Babylon, famous from ancient times, lest the world should boast any longer in its exaltation. Cyrus, king of the Persians, magnificent in triumphs, after accomplishing such great deeds thought that nothing further could stand against him. Crossing the Tanais, he invaded the kingdom of the Scythians with a dreadful hand. But, to show that a human being ought not to glory in himself, dead he drank the blood for which alive he had thirsted. Then the Persian kingdom, long boiling over with much pride and cruelty, was finally overthrown by Macedonian hands; crushed and scattered, like a pestilential body dismembered. From this came Egypt with its kings armed in tyranny [Col. 0733B]. Syria, Asia, and Greece tore apart their own vitals by mutual cruelty, until at last, when the time of vengeance had come, Rome, exalting its own power, rivaled the accumulated greatness of all kingdoms. Thus, under alternating upheavals, the world can never be stable: whatever grows for one kingdom, so that it rises, diminishes for another, so that it falls.

A. It is enough for the present to have recalled these things as an example of misery, so that we may return more quickly to those things which we ought always to keep before our eyes and never forget. This, then, I think should now be recalled first in the order of the narrative: how, when the legitimate kings failed in Judaea and a foreigner seized the rule, the heavenly King willed that this should, as it were, furnish a more fitting occasion for his own coming, so that he might claim his own empire [Col. 0733C].  
R. Although the Maker and Lord of the whole world did not descend to earth solely for the kingdom of Judaea—he who purposed by his coming to save the entire world—yet, because prophecies had gone before only in Judaea and he had been announced to those who were chosen as ministers, through whom the dispensation of salvation for all was to be accomplished, it was fitting that the beginning of his coming should be ordered from those among whom he was to be born not for them alone but for all. Nevertheless, if we consider attentively the condition of the whole universe, we find clear reason to understand his coming no less from the kingdom of the Gentiles than from that of the Jews. For since he came both to claim the Jewish kingdom as his own and to conquer and subject to himself the kingdom of the Gentiles as though it were opposed to him [Col. 0733D], he wished to find a foreigner reigning in Judaea and a stable, strong kingdom among the Gentiles, their forces as though gathered into one. It would not have been fitting for him to attack adversaries to be conquered when, their powers having collapsed, they seemed about to fall of themselves, lest victory perhaps be attributed not to the strength of the conqueror but rather to the weakness of those subdued. Therefore he waited until the whole world had fused its forces into a single empire and victorious Rome had proudly raised its head above all kingdoms. Then, when pride ruled, the humble one came, so that in his humility he might cast down the world’s height, openly showing how great he was in his majesty, since, placed in our weakness, he subjected all things.

Therefore, when the Son of God was about to be born in human flesh [Col. 0734A], an angel was sent to the Virgin to announce the coming of majesty, so that the Virgin, who was to give birth under a new law, might conceive in a new manner. Thus the believing Virgin conceived the Word through her ear, so that an incorrupt generation might follow the immaculate conception. The bread of heaven was therefore born in Bethlehem, to refresh the languishing world; and, placed in a manger, he signified that he was food for the holy animals. Angels came to him in the splendor of light and spoke from on high of peace upon earth; and the shepherds, running to the manger, found him wrapped in swaddling cloths according to the sign given them.

A shining star from above stirred the Magi, and by the ray of its splendor led new worshippers of the Godhead to new cradles. The prophets are stirred up and run [Col. 0734B] to meet the one who comes: Simeon and Anna, awaiting the redemption of Israel, take the child into their arms and announce to the world the Savior. Jerusalem, the holy city, having first been dedicated by his coming, he is carried into Egypt so that he may also visit the Gentiles; there, once the time predetermined had been completed, he returns to Judaea, as though after the entrance of the Gentiles, to gather again the remnants of Israel.

Meanwhile, as time ran on, when the Lord of eternity had filled out the age of a man’s body, he came to John at the Jordan, so that by his entry he might sanctify the waters for the washing away of sins. There, with the heavens opened and God’s throne flashing from above, the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove, and a voice likewise came down: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III). When these wonders had been completed [Col. 0734C], the Son of God ascended from the Jordan while the Baptist trembled. Establishing an example for preserving sanctification, he sought the desert, dwelling in the wilderness in fasting for forty days and nights. But, in order to show that human life upon earth is temptation, and that one must conquer everywhere by fighting, the enemy was admitted by the will of the one permitting, not by the power of one raging; and, proposing foolish suggestions, he was refuted by reason, though he was to be punished by power.

Thereafter, victorious and honored by the service of angels, after fasting and hungering for the salvation of humankind, he came forth publicly. With an open exhortation addressed to the world, he announced that the kingdom of heaven had come. To those repenting he promised forgiveness of sins; to those persisting in sin he announced future punishments—the torments of Gehenna prepared in the final judgment [Col. 0734D]. And so that the truth might be manifest everywhere and no one might remain ignorant of the way by which a human being must return to life, he chose twelve disciples to go into the whole world, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom and the word of life to humanity. When he himself had completed the mystery and triumphed over death by his death, and had returned from the lower regions after plundering Tartarus, he ascended before his disciples to the right hand of the eternal Father, there to conquer forever. He sent them into the world to bear witness to the resurrection of life and to baptize, for the remission of sins, those believing in him. While angels testified that he would come for judgment and judge the world according to its works, the disciples, trembling in dreadful fear, immediately set out, proclaiming [Col. 0735A] sacred wonders to all nations.

Filled with the Holy Spirit, they confirmed the word by many miracles and signs. People began to gather from every direction, amazed and astonished at the awe-inspiring things done. Then the world roared. Seeing the rites of its ancient error fall, it refused to abandon what it loved or to accept what it did not know. Thus the heralds of truth were slaughtered lest falsehood be overthrown; but the patience of those dying supplied the living with irrefutable testimony to the truth. When a few grains fell, a multiplied harvest sprang up, because the number of believers increased among the living precisely where it seemed to be diminished among the dying. Marvel, therefore, that the world was subdued by twelve men, and see that those by whom it was done were not such as require much labor to show that the outstanding work was God’s miracle, not the work of men [Col. 0735B]. Few in number and contemptible, they made the world’s wisdom foolish without eloquence; by patience they cast down strength and the onset of ferocity. The number of believers arose throughout the world; faith increased, discipline flourished, and the people of the saints were adorned, their souls rejoicing for the kingdom of heaven and everlasting life and becoming eager amid afflictions.

Then the devil groaned that he was conquered by his own art and that he would be crushed by the very means through which he had thought to crush God’s servants. For the world saw new battles and unexpected victories, and, astonished that it was despised in its bloom, it became barren though formerly loved. But Christ’s soldiers, following their king, could be held neither by threats nor by blandishments: they despised the one promising prosperity and did not fear the one threatening adversity. Therefore heavenly life was cultivated on earth, and flowers of virtues began to spring up in the desert of this age as though from God’s paradise [Col. 0735C]. Some planted roses through martyrdom, others lilies through chastity, others violets through purity; and all the peoples of the saints, flourishing by their presence and virtue, adorned the world. Some shone with miracles; others were radiant with virtues and signs; some deserved to see heaven’s secrets; others foretold future events; others drove demons from possessed bodies. Some appeared marvelous by the grace of healings. Others, presenting examples of virtues among peoples, proved worthy of imitation by those who came after. Others, penetrating the secrets of the wilderness, cultivated with the greatest zeal the habit of the inner human being. These are those whom the world still threatens and hates together: though the proud person despises their humility, the weak person cannot attain their preservation [Col. 0735D].

A. As examples set forth in the ancient fathers taught virtue, so now emulation must be stirred up by the consideration of new examples.  
R. Twelve men, chosen by Christ for the miracle of their contest, first subdued the world, so that he might fulfill old figures with new truth. For the fleece of flesh had now received the dew of deity, and the chosen men, having drunk from the stream with jars and trumpets, went forth to battle. Their weapons for fighting by miracle were not weapons; rather, lamps lay hidden while the earthen vessels were broken. They carried trumpets in their right hands, so that their sound might go out into all the earth and the honor of the Word might use bodily service for its own glorification [Col. 0736A], while, their strength being torn apart in the death of the flesh, the lamps of miracles shone. Therefore the enemies could not stand against God’s warriors when they saw the wonders; and the camp of Midian, prostrated in fear throughout the whole world, paid reverence to the flashing light.

Peter, bearing aloft the standard of the cross, first attacked the enemies; and, in order to defeat the impious priests, he went up to the temple with John, the friend of the Word. At the command of one who willed it, the lame man immediately leapt up; this gathered the crowds of the people together, and Peter, bearing witness before all to resurrection in Christ—the sign of life and death—increased their ranks by thousands. Thereafter in the synagogue of the high priests he humbled their stubbornness by the constancy of reason, because, when the entrance to the prison had been opened and angels served them, they taught in the temple [Col. 0736B]. When five thousand men had believed through the apostles’ teaching, with three thousand added, the number marked out for blessedness was completed. But the enemies, jealous of such glory, could not bear it; and, because they were not found worthy to be received into the calling of possession, they expelled the physicians of salvation.
