Then Philip, lifting high the lamp of signs, sounded the trumpet of preaching and, to bring to completion the ancient contest of the prophets, attacked Samaria, their ancient mother. For already he had preached the sacrificed Lamb to the man raised up in a chariot, receiving the prophets’ untilled fields for cultivation; and therefore, when the foreigner was baptized, he called him back from those alienated. Matthew subdued Ethiopia; Bartholomew and Thomas, India; Andrew, Achaia; John [Col. 0736C], Asia; Simon and Judas Zelotes, Persia; and they attacked and subjected Babylon, that ancient head of pride. Paul, last in time but first in contest, subdued great Greece and the islands of the regions from Jerusalem to many farthest bounds, so that at last, sharing power with Peter the prince, he might triumph at the summit of the world.

Then the deeds accomplished by the soldiers, trained by the skill of their leaders—if all cannot be recounted—must not all be passed over in silence, since they are memorable and worthy of report. Stephen was first: boldly following the king who went before into battle, he challenged the enemies, standing without fear amid the multitude of foes. When they raged in indignation and many could not overcome one, he testified that he saw Jesus at the right hand of God, in order to show the crowd by whose timely help as defender he was invincible [Col. 0736D]. But when torrents of stones flew in the onset of the fierce men, he pitied his assailants, bent his knees in prayer, and there, commending his spotless spirit to God, obtained Saul’s conversion together with the salvation of many.

James, not recoiling from Judaea’s stubbornness, triumphed by the sword, leaving punishment to the tyrant, so that the patience of the saints might be shown, in ordered endurance, to have judgment together with power. Then one after another, acting bravely through varied conflicts of battle, maintained steadfastness, so that the palm of faith might flourish in every nation and those chosen from the beginning might enter into the promise. Peter, having established the throne of truth in Rome, had ascended in triumph through the cross [Col. 0737A], and Clement, successor to the chair, had received the pontifical dignity. He too, challenged, endured his labor bravely; and, lest the enemies’ onset shake the camp of God, voluntarily opposing himself, he repaid the dignity of authority entrusted to him by martyrdom.

Dionysius the Areopagite, having received the command, penetrated Gaul and, fighting in order to conquer, prevailed in establishing the laws of heaven on earth. In order to show the way of life, for the testimony of truth he consecrated the Word by his blood; and, lest death inherit life, making in the dead a sign of life, he carried his head in his hands after being killed.

Lawrence conquered fire on the gridiron and, reproving the flames of the blaze and the astonished Caesar, offered his flesh for eating to one raging in vain against flesh. Vincent, mindful of his name, mocked the tyrant [Col. 0737B] as he threatened cruel things; despising the claws and the rack, he also overcame scourges and fires. Nor would it have been a small matter if women too had not hastened to battle to shame men in the judgment of equity. Agatha came and offered her breasts to be cut off, showing, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, that she did not fear the sword, so that she might minister the milk of faith to believers. Agnes walked fearless amid flames, so that nature might marvel that a sex and age ordinarily accustomed to remain in not yet mature judgment was made strong in martyrdom. Margaret, fighting, conquered with marvelous constancy, so that torments of the flesh might not subject her mind to alienation from righteousness. For she brought the enemy into manifest confusion: defeated, he appeared outside behind her, to be confuted with double disgrace. Cecilia deserved [variant: “purchased”] crowns, proved worthy by chastity; while young men embraced in faith the lilies of incorruption, she also mingled roses with purple, to be adorned in the martyrdom of blood [Col. 0737C]. Lucy, not deigning to bring her betrothed, a robber of chastity, to the sight of immortality [variant: summit], after her mother was healed by prayers, distributed her wealth to the poor, so that, after offering gifts, she might offer herself in addition to God as a sweet-smelling holocaust. The male sex, in boys, matched the victories of women, so that palms of triumph might stand all around in the glory of God.

Vitus came, a boy who, adding virtue to his years, fought manfully and seized the crown through precious wounds: a spectacle never to be regarded without amazement, destined to inspire emulation by his example of glory and courage. Cyricus [Col. 0737D], together with his mother, endured such great and dreadful kinds of torments that you can find nothing further to marvel at, unless perhaps you think that infancy itself should be heaped with glory for the praise of womanly steadfastness. The time had come for the world to be conquered by the patience of Christ’s warriors; and, being about to be pacified, it boiled over a little more than usual in its final apostasy. For it now commands many thousands to be killed at once and rages with cruel slaughter against bands of people, because, defeated, it feared the encounter of single combat.

The glorious ranks of the Thebans armed their legions for the palm of martyrdom, so that it was manifest that to die for Christ was now a matter of desire, not necessity. For Victor too, after the claws and the rack, shattered the millstone together with the laurels, not terrified by the cruel edicts of the raging tyrant [Col. 0738A]; and he shattered the pulleys, because an angel of God, by his presence, gloriously revealed with an open miracle the martyr, invincible in spirit, so that he might conquer. For a voice from above, openly declaring that Victor had conquered, escaped forth; because the palms of triumph—which the eyes of the impious could not see—they had at last to hear, to their perpetual confusion. And many others, again and again, voluntarily offering themselves for martyrdom as though under one leader—and truly under the one Spirit—showed that they could accomplish more by suffering than those maddened men could accomplish by doing harm. Therefore the world could no longer restrain itself without blushing at its own disgrace; but, overcome by patience, it yielded its hands, lest, if it prolonged its cruelty to the end in the limbs that were being cut off, it should kill everyone. For the cause of eternal justice could not perish; and therefore at last the iniquity of the persecutors ceased, while the courage of those who endured, as it does not know how to yield, likewise does not know how to be diminished by threats.

The height of the power of opposition fell, and the ferocity of impious threats was subdued into the humiliation of sinners without resistance, so that the now-placable ruler might be given commands; and the supreme pontiff Sylvester, appeased by the king’s prayers amid great fear, showed forth the living fountain for purification. But when he had learned the power of the Most High in the washing of cleansing, he ordered the altars of demons and the observances of defilement to come to an end in their ruin and confusion, so that he who had formerly been a persecutor might truly become a king in righteousness. The priest of God, strengthened by sacred grace, refuted [Col. 0738C] the rebellious and unbelieving through the power of words and reasoning. In an assembly crowded with people, the king and princes, together with the evidences for the propositions, he expounded the mystical sacraments of the Law; and thereafter, as miracles multiplied, he most truly confirmed openly before all that this was Jesus Christ, who had come into this world by the command of God the Father for the salvation of humankind. The banner of the Cross shines in the holy place; the queen, her vow fulfilled, returned joyfully; and once the sign of glory had been raised up, hostile power could no longer prosper.

After these things, therefore, lilies of peace began to spring up throughout the whole world; and the Church, the mother, already adorned with the purple of martyrs, rejoiced also to be adorned with the whiteness of confessors. For grace did not shine in one place only, but the field, full of blessing, displayed flourishing spectacles even to the ends of the earth [Col. 0738D]. For deserts too, transformed into fertility, flowered in delight as they received an infusion of heavenly richness. Trackless places were full, and dry streams flowed with grace. Paul, Antony, and Hilarion were found to be precious stones where there had been neither value nor adornment; and, set in the foundation, they built upon it a wondrous structure, so that the house of the forest of Lebanon might be built in the desert, and the forest might be reckoned in Carmel as Lebanon. Macarius, Pannucius, Arsenius, and Pastor, joined with Moses in the same Spirit and power, led a great people of God through the desert of the age into the land of promise; and with them all the named men passed over—the holy and chosen men, mighty in wonders [Col. 0739A].

So that the true Solomon might also build a house for the daughter of Pharaoh, Ephrem, Basil, Gregory, Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine, with many others throughout the world, were raised up as columns, fashioned and carved with wondrous wisdom into every form of beauty and grace. For another Gregory, full of the Spirit, also adorned the house with varied beauty, furnishing many lovelinesses and delights of truth. Martin, Nicholas, and Benedict shone forth in wondrous holiness through miracles; and in all these the fullness that hastens toward its end, joining to itself all others who are called, is daily being completed.

Therefore we ought to consider how great will be the glory there, of which all that we see is an image—small indeed in comparison with the excellence of the beauty toward which it tends to be brought to perfection, until it is completed for us [Col. 0739B]. We must raise our minds thither and hasten with our inmost desires, lest perhaps, having already seen an appearance of good in that which is before us, we should look ahead to the reproach of recognition and fail to receive the fruit in the joy of blessedness. For all this is an image on earth of the heavenly Jerusalem, to which those ascend well by the steps of virtues who, through present striving, gather themselves with all their desires toward true peace and eternal stability.

The discourses of human beings are many and various because the human heart is not one. For since the mind within is divided by many desires from the fountain of truth, speech without is consequently carried away into many assertions. Solomon, considering the uncertainty of human life and the way in which the condition of mortality fluctuates through inconstancy—shaken without by the variety of mutable things and dissipated within by the instability of desires—set forth both these matters in himself alike as example and instruction, when he showed himself so often changed by the passage of things and by the weakness of his mind. For we have already heard above how often he transferred his mind to desiring one thing after another; and although, warned by experience, he always despised the vanity of present things when he had encountered it, nevertheless, tossed upon the waves [Col. 0740A] of his desire, he never ceased seeking possessions.

For because he thought that he could find stability in transitory things, in which he might fix his delight in tranquil peace and unshaken constancy, whenever among the things he possessed he either found what he had desired or lost what he had loved, he turned again to seeking other things, striving either to satisfy or to repair his desire. But now at last, having tested all things by experience, he recognizes the mutable condition of things and confesses that nothing among all that passes away can remain forever, saying: “Everything has its time, and all things pass through their allotted spans” (Eccles. III).

Everything has its time, so that nothing may be found everlasting and always abiding; rather, whatever exists either follows something else, so that it does not come from the beginning, or is preceded by something else, so that it does not extend itself to the end [Col. 0740B]. Everything likewise has its time: namely, a fixed and determined time, whether for beginning or for ending, or even for continuing. Thus the prudent mind should not think that in all these things there is anything that can always stand, on which it may place its confidence; but, conforming itself rather to true and abiding goods, it should so despise the vanity of mutable things that, though it uses each thing for its proper time while it is present, it never permits its mind to decline from its own steadfastness as that thing passes away. For the wisest person is one who knows how to turn transient things to use, yet does not know how to let the mind decline from its stability when they fail.

Therefore Solomon acted wrongly when he selected certain things from among all things as though they were more important [Col. 0740C] for his pleasure, and believed that he could be happy in them. For all things are good in their own time to one who uses them well; yet all things subject to mutability, although they offer some consolation in misery, cannot bestow happiness. Therefore nothing is to be rejected in its own time, and nothing chosen outside its proper time; rather, the mind must be so prepared for the use of time that it is not itself changed by the mutability of time.

[Col. 0739]

# Seven Books of Didactic Instruction

## Book One: On the Study of Reading

The chapters of this book are as follows:

Chapter I. That there are two principal means by which everyone is instructed toward knowledge.—Chapter II. On the origin of the arts and the perfection of the soul.—Chapter III. That the study of wisdom is philosophy.—Chapter IV. That the soul has a threefold power, and that the human being alone is endowed with reason.—Chapter V. What matters belong to philosophy.—Chapter VI. On the origin of theoretical, practical, and mechanical philosophy.—Chapter VII. On the three differences among things.—Chapter VIII. On the superlunary and sublunary world.—Chapter IX. In what respect the human being resembles God.—Chapter X. On the three kinds of works.—Chapter XI. What nature is.—Chapter XII. On the origin of logic.—Chapter XIII. A summary of the foregoing.

## Chapter I. That there are two principal means by which everyone is instructed toward knowledge; and what the subject-matter of this work is

[Col. 0741A]

There are chiefly two things by which everyone is instructed toward knowledge: namely, reading and meditation. Of these, reading holds the prior place in instruction; and this book treats of it by giving rules for reading. There are, moreover, three rules especially necessary for reading. First, that each person should know what he ought to read. Second, in what order he ought to read: that is, what first and what afterward. Third, how he ought to read. This book treats each of these three matters separately.

It instructs the reader both of secular writings and of the divine Scriptures. It is therefore divided into two parts, each of which has three divisions [Col. 0741B]. In the first part it instructs the reader in the arts; in the second, the reader of divine writings. It teaches in the following way: first showing what is to be read; then in what order and how it is to be read. So that it may be known what is to be read, in the first part it first enumerates the origin of all the arts; then their description and division—that is, how each contains another or is contained by another—dividing philosophy from its highest point down to its final members. It then enumerates the authors of the arts, and afterward shows which of these arts should especially be read. It further explains the order and manner in which they should be read. Finally, it prescribes a discipline of life for readers; and thus the first part concludes.

In the second part it determines which writings should be called divine Scripture [Col. 0741C]; then the number and order of the divine books, their authors, and the interpretations of their names. Afterward it treats certain properties of divine Scripture which are especially necessary. It then teaches how the person who seeks in sacred Scripture the correction of his character and a pattern of life ought to read it. Finally, it teaches the one who reads it for love of knowledge; and thus the second part also reaches its conclusion.

## Chapter II. On the origin of the arts and the perfection of the soul

Among all things to be sought, wisdom is first, for in it consists the form of the perfect good. Wisdom enlightens a person so that he may know himself; for when he did not understand that he was made above other things, he was like the rest. The immortal mind, illumined by wisdom, looks back to its own beginning and recognizes how unbecoming it is to seek anything outside itself when what it itself is could have been enough for it.

Written on Apollo’s tripod is: **Γνῶθι σεαυτόν**, that is, “Know yourself.” For certainly, if a human being were not forgetful of his origin, he would recognize how nothing is everything subject to mutability. A doctrine accepted among philosophers maintains: “The soul is composed from all the parts of nature.” And the Platonic *Timaeus* says: “From divisible and indivisible substance, and from the mixed substance; likewise from sameness and difference, and from the nature mixed from both, by which the universe is set forth, he formed an **entelechy** (*ἐντελέχειαν*)” [Col. 0742A].

For the soul both embraces and follows first principles: by understanding it comprehends the invisible causes of things, while by the affections of the senses it gathers the visible forms of actual things. Divided into two circles, it gathers motion together: for whether it goes out through the senses toward sensible things or ascends through understanding to invisible things, it draws the likenesses of things back to itself and turns them around again. This is why the same mind that is capable of all things is said to be fitted together from every substance and nature, so that it may represent the form of likeness.

For it was a Pythagorean doctrine that “like things are understood by like”; namely, that unless the rational soul were composed from all things, it could in no way comprehend all things, according to what a certain poet says:

> With earth we comprehend earth; with fire, ether;  
> Moisture with liquid; and what can be breathed, with our breath.

Yet we must not suppose that men most skilled in every part of nature meant this concerning the soul’s simple essence, as though it were extended by any quantity of parts. Rather, to demonstrate more plainly its wondrous power, they said that it consists of all natures—not by composition, but according to the principle of composition. Nor should this likeness of all things be thought to come to the soul from elsewhere or from outside [Col. 0742B]. Rather, by some native power and its own proper strength, the soul itself receives it within itself and from itself.

For, as Varro says in the *Periphyseon*: “Not every variation happens to things from outside, so that whatever varies must necessarily either lose something it had, or receive from outside something other and different which it did not have. We see that a wall receives from outside the likeness of any image when its form is applied to it; but when an engraver impresses a figure upon metal, the metal itself begins to represent something else, not from an inner source, but through its own power and natural capacity.” Thus indeed the mind, marked by the likeness of all things, is said both to be all things and to receive composition from all things—not because it contains them integrally, but because it contains them virtually and potentially.

And this is the dignity of our nature: all possess it equally by nature, but not all know it equally. For the mind, lulled asleep by the passions of the body and drawn outside itself through sensible forms, has forgotten what it was; and because it remembers itself to have been nothing else, it believes that nothing exists except what it sees [Col. 0742D]. But through instruction it is restored, so that we may recognize our nature and learn not to seek outside ourselves what we can find within ourselves. Therefore the highest consolation in life is the pursuit of wisdom: whoever finds it is happy, and whoever possesses it is blessed.

## Chapter III. That the study of wisdom is philosophy

Pythagoras, first of all, called “the pursuit of wisdom” philosophy, and preferred to be called a philosopher rather than a *sophos* [wise man]. For formerly they were called *sophi*, that is, wise persons. He rightly calls seekers of truth not wise but lovers of wisdom, because all truth lies so deeply hidden that, however ardently the mind burns with its love and however earnestly it rises to seek it, it can nevertheless scarcely comprehend truth itself as it is.

He established philosophy as the discipline of those things which truly exist and possess an immutable substance of their own. “Philosophy,” however, “is love, pursuit, and in some sense friendship with wisdom”—not with that wisdom which consists in certain instruments, technical skill, or practical knowledge, but with that wisdom which, needing nothing, is the living mind and the sole primordial reason of things [Col. 0743A]. This love of wisdom is the illumination of an understanding mind by that pure wisdom, and in a sense a drawing-back and recalling of the mind to itself; so that the study of wisdom appears to be friendship with divinity and that pure mind. This wisdom therefore bestows upon the whole race of souls the merit of its divinity and restores them to the proper power and purity of their nature. From it arise the truth of speculations and thoughts, and the holy and pure chastity of actions.

Since this most excellent good of philosophy has been granted to human souls, so that discourse proceeds, as it were, by a thread of a path, we must begin with the capacities of the soul itself.

## Chapter IV. That the soul has a threefold power, and that the human being alone is endowed with reason

A threefold power of the soul is altogether discerned in living bodies [Col. 0743C]. One merely supplies life to the body, enabling it to grow by being born and to subsist by being nourished. Another supplies the faculty of sense-perception. The third rests upon the power of mind and reason.

The function of the first is to be present for the generation, nourishment, and sustenance of bodies, while it exercises no judgment of reason or sense. This is the soul of herbs and trees and of whatever remains fastened to the earth by roots. The second is compound and conjoined; it takes the first into itself and makes it a part of itself, and receives a varied and manifold judgment concerning the things it can perceive. For every animal that possesses sense is also born, nourished, and fed. But the senses are diverse and increase up to the number five. Thus whatever is merely nourished does not also perceive; but whatever can perceive is also nourished, and it is evident that the first power of the soul—namely, that of being born and nourished—is subordinate to it.

Those endowed with sense not only receive the forms of things by which they are struck through the present sensible body; when sense has departed and sensible things have been set aside, they also retain images of forms known through sense and form memory [Col. 0743D]. According to each animal’s capacity, it preserves these images for a longer or shorter time. But they receive those images confusedly and indistinctly, so that they can produce nothing from their conjunction and composition. Therefore they are indeed able to remember, though not all things equally; but they cannot recover and call back what has been lost through forgetfulness. Nor do they have any knowledge of the future.

But the third power of the soul draws with it the two preceding powers of nourishment and sensation and uses them as servants and subordinates. It is wholly established in reason, and is occupied either with the most certain conclusion concerning present things, with the understanding of absent things, or with the investigation of unknown things. This is granted only to the human race. It receives not merely complete and ordered sensations and images, but also, by the full activity of understanding, unfolds and confirms what imagination has suggested. Thus, as has been said, for this divine nature those things which it comprehends through the senses are not sufficient for knowledge; rather, from things conceived by imagination from the senses, it can give names even to absent things and can disclose through the establishment of words what it grasps by the reasoning of understanding [Col. 0744B]. This nature has also the distinctive property of investigating unknown things through those known to it. It must know not only whether each thing exists, but also what it is, what it is like, and why it is.

Human nature alone, as has been said, possesses this threefold power of the soul. Its soul does not lack movements of understanding, because it exercises the power of reason properly in these four matters. For it investigates whether something exists; if its existence has been established, it asks what it is; and if by reason it possesses knowledge of both, it investigates what each thing is like and in that inquiry seeks the further features of its accidents. Once these are known, it asks why it is so and likewise investigates by reason.

Since, therefore, this is the activity of the human mind—to be continually occupied in the comprehension of present things, the understanding of absent things, and the investigation and discovery of unknown things—there are two matters upon which the power of the reasoning soul spends all its effort. The first is to know the natures of things through rational inquiry; the second is first to attain knowledge, which afterward the burden of mortal life may put into practice [Col. 0744C].

## Chapter V. What matters belong to philosophy

But, as I see, by the very order of our discourse we have now entered an inextricable labyrinth, where difficulty arises not from tangled speech but from the obscurity of the matter. Since we undertook to speak of the pursuit of wisdom, and affirmed that it belongs only to human beings by a certain privilege of nature, we seem consequently now to have established wisdom as a kind of governor of all human actions.

For if the nature of brute animals, ruled by no judgment of reason, gives free course to its motions according only to the affections of sense and, in seeking or fleeing anything, makes use not of intelligent discernment but is driven by a blind impulse of fleshly desire, it follows that blind desire does not govern the actions of the rational soul, but wisdom, as governor, always goes before. If this is shown to be true, then we shall say, not inappropriately, that philosophy includes not only those studies concerned with the nature of things or with the discipline of morals, but also the rational principles of all human actions and pursuits [Col. 0745A].

According to this sense, we may define philosophy thus: “Philosophy is the discipline that fully investigates the rational principles of all human and divine things.” Nor should it trouble us that we said above that philosophy is love and pursuit of wisdom—not of the wisdom expressed through instruments, such as architecture, agriculture, and other things of that sort, but of that wisdom which alone is the primordial reason of things. For the same activity can belong to philosophy according to its rational principle and yet be excluded from it according to its administration. For example, to speak of the matter at hand: the theory of agriculture belongs to the philosopher; its practice, to the farmer.

Moreover, the works of artisans, although they are not nature, nevertheless imitate nature and rationally express the form of their model—which is the nature that they imitate. You now see why we are compelled to extend philosophy to all human actions: it follows that philosophy must have as many parts as there are kinds of things to which it is shown to belong [Col. 0745B].

## Chapter VI. On the origin of theoretical, practical, and mechanical philosophy

The end and purpose of all human actions or pursuits governed by wisdom ought to be this: either that the wholeness of our nature may be restored, or that the necessity of the defects to which present life is subject may be moderated. I shall state more plainly what I have said. There are two things in a human being: good and evil; nature and vice. Good, because it is nature, because it has been corrupted, because it is diminished, must be restored by practice. Evil, because it is vice, because it is corruption, because it is not nature, must be excluded. If it cannot be utterly exterminated, it must at least be moderated by applying a remedy. This, in sum, is what must be done: nature must be restored and vice excluded.

The wholeness of human life is achieved by two things: knowledge and virtue. They alone are our likeness to heavenly and divine substances. For since a human being is not a simple nature but is composed of a twofold substance, in one part—the better part, and, to say more plainly what must be said, the part which is the person himself—he is immortal; but in the other part, which is perishable, which alone is known to those who know no way to trust anything except the senses, he is subject to mortality and mutability. In that part one must die as often as one loses what one is. This is the lowest order of things, which has a beginning and an end [Col. 0745D].

## Chapter VII. On the three differences among things

Among things, some have neither beginning nor end, and these are called eternal. Others have a beginning indeed but are bounded by no end, and these are called perpetual. Others have a beginning and an end, and these are temporal.

In the first order we place that for which being and what it is are not different—that is, whose cause and effect are not distinct; which has its subsistence not from elsewhere but from itself: namely, the maker and creator of nature alone.

But that for which being and what it is are different—that is, which comes to being from elsewhere and has flowed into actuality from a preceding cause so as to begin to be—is the nature that contains the entire world [Col. 0746A]. This is divided in two. There is something which, in order to begin to be, comes forth into actuality from its primordial causes without anything moving it, by the decision of the divine will alone; and there it stands immutable, free from every end and change. Such are the substances of things, which the Greeks call **οὐσίαι** (*ousiai*, “essences”); and all the bodies of the superlunary world, which are also called divine because they do not change.

The third class of things has a beginning and an end and does not come into being of itself. These are the works of nature which arise above the earth, beneath the sphere of the moon, with the artisan fire as mover, descending by a certain power to generate sensible things. Of these it was said: “Nothing dies in the world, because no essence perishes.” For the essences of things do not pass away, but their forms do. When a form is said to pass away, this should not be understood as though an existing thing wholly perishes and loses its being; rather, it changes. Or perhaps it should be understood thus: things that had been joined are separated from one another; things that had been separated are joined; things that were here pass there; or things that are now continue then. In all these cases, the being of things suffers no loss [Col. 0746B].

Of these it was said: “All things that arise fall, and things that have grown become old”; because all works of nature, just as they have a beginning, are not exempt from an end. Of those other things it was said:

> From nothing, nothing; and nothing can return to nothing.  
> (Persius, *Satires* III.83.)

This is because every nature has both a primordial cause and perpetual subsistence. Of these temporal things it was said:

> And that which was nothing before returns to nothing;

because every work of nature, just as it flows temporally from a hidden cause into actuality, will likewise, when that actuality has been temporally destroyed, return to that from which it came [Col. 0746C].

## Chapter VIII. On the superlunary and sublunary world

Hence mathematicians divided the world into two parts: the part above the circle of the moon and the part below it. They called the superlunary world “nature,” because there all things endure according to the primordial law; and the sublunary world “the work of nature,” namely, of the higher world, because all kinds of living creatures which are animated there by the infusion of vital spirit receive through invisible channels nourishment poured in from above—not only in order that they may grow by being born, but also that they may endure by being nourished.

They also called this higher world “time,” because of the course and motion of the stars contained in it; and the lower world “temporal,” because it is governed according to the motions above. Likewise, because of its perpetual tranquillity of light and rest, they called the superlunary world Elysium. But this lower world they called the underworld, because of the instability and confusion of fluctuating things [Col. 0746D].

We have treated these matters somewhat more fully in order to show that, in the aspect in which a human being shares in mutability, he is also subject to necessity; but in the aspect in which he is immortal, he is akin to divinity. From this may be inferred what was said above: namely, that the purpose of all human actions converges upon this end, either that the image of divine likeness may be restored in us, or that provision may be made for the neediness of this life, which, the more easily it can be harmed by adverse things, the more it needs to be cherished and preserved.

## Chapter IX. In what respect the human being resembles God

There are two things that restore the divine likeness in a human being: contemplation of truth and the exercise of virtue. For in this a person is like God: that he is wise and just; but the human being is wise and just changeably, while God is wise and just unchangeably [Col. 0747B].

Of those actions that serve the needs of this life, there are three kinds. The first administers the instruments of nature; the second provides defense against troubles that may come from outside; the third provides a remedy against harms already inflicted. Therefore, when we aim at restoring our nature, the action is divine; but when we provide what is necessary for that which is weak in us, it is human. Every action, then, is either divine or human.

We may not inappropriately call the former, because it concerns higher things, *understanding*; and the latter, because it concerns lower things and requires, as it were, a certain deliberation, *knowledge*. If, then, wisdom, as was said above, governs all actions done by reason, it follows that wisdom contains these two parts: understanding and knowledge. Again, because understanding labors both in the investigation of truth and in consideration of morals, we divide it into two kinds: theoretical, that is, speculative; and practical, that is, active, which is also called ethical, that is, moral. But knowledge, because it concerns human works, is appropriately called mechanical, that is, adulterated [Col. 0747C].

## Chapter X. On the three kinds of works

There are three kinds of works: the work of God, the work of nature, and the work of the artisan who imitates nature. The work of God is to create what did not exist; whence: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I). The work of nature is to bring forth into actuality what lay hidden; whence: “Let the earth bring forth green grass” (ibid.), and so forth. The work of the artisan is to join things separated or to separate things joined; whence: “They sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths” (Gen. III).

For neither could the earth create heaven, nor could a human being bring forth grass, because he cannot add even a cubit to his stature. In these three works, human work—which is not nature but imitates nature—is fittingly called mechanical, that is, adulterated, just as an inserted key is called *mechanical*. To explain in detail how the work of the artisan imitates nature would be lengthy and burdensome; nevertheless, we can show it by a few examples [Col. 0748A].

One who cast a statue looked at a human being. One who made a house looked to a mountain. For, as the Prophet says, “You send forth springs in the valleys; waters pass through the midst of the mountains” (Ps. CIII). The heights of mountains do not hold back water; in the same way, a house had to be raised into a certain elevated peak so that it could safely receive the assaults of violent storms. The first inventor of clothing observed that every living creature has certain proper defenses by which it protects its nature from inconveniences. Bark surrounds a tree; feathers cover a bird; scales protect a fish; wool clothes a sheep; hair garments beasts of burden and wild animals; a shell receives the tortoise; ivory makes the elephant unafraid of weapons.

Yet it was not without reason that, while the individual natures of living creatures have their weapons born with them, the human being alone is born unarmed and naked [Col. 0748B]. For nature had to provide for those creatures which do not know how to provide for themselves; but for the human being, an even greater occasion for discovery had to be supplied, so that by his own reason he might find for himself what had been given naturally to other creatures. For human reason shines much more brightly now in discovering these things than it would have shone in merely possessing them. Nor without reason does the proverb declare:

> Ingenious hunger has fashioned all the arts.

For this reason, indeed, those things which you now see as most excellent among human pursuits were discovered. For the same reason arose the innumerable kinds of painting, weaving, carving, and casting, so that together with nature we marvel at the artisan himself [Col. 0748C].

## Chapter XI. What nature is

Since we have now named nature so often, although, as Tully says, “it is difficult to define nature,” the meaning of this term nevertheless does not seem to be wholly passable over in silence. Nor, because we cannot say everything that we wish to say, ought we to be silent about what we can say. The ancients are found to have said many things about nature, yet nothing in such a way that something does not seem to remain. Nevertheless, so far as I can infer from their sayings, they were accustomed principally to use the meaning of this term in three ways, assigning its own definition to each.

In the first way, by this name they intended to signify that archetypal pattern of all things which is in the divine mind and according to whose reason all things have been formed. They said that nature is the primordial cause of each thing, from which it has not only being but also its particular kind of being. To this sense is assigned the following definition: “Nature is that which gives each thing its being” [Col. 0748D].

In the second way, they called nature the proper being of each thing. To this meaning is assigned the definition: “Nature, informing each thing, is called its proper difference.” According to this meaning we commonly say: it is the nature of all heavy things to tend toward the earth, of light things to seek the heights, of fire to burn, and of water to moisten.

The third definition is this: “Nature is an artisan fire, proceeding by a certain way into the generation of sensible things” [Col. 0749A]. For natural philosophers say that all things are generated from heat and moisture. Hence Virgil calls Ocean father; and Valerius Soranus, in a certain verse on Jupiter, speaking of him as ethereal fire, says:

> Jupiter almighty, discoverer of things and kings,  
> Both begetter and begetress, the one and same true God.

## Chapter XII. On the origin of logic

Having therefore shown the origin of theoretical, practical, and mechanical philosophy, it remains to investigate the origin of logic also. I number it last because it was discovered last. The other disciplines had been discovered earlier, but logic too had to be discovered, because no one can discuss matters appropriately unless he has first learned the method of speaking correctly.

For, as Boethius says: When the ancients at first devoted their efforts to investigating the natures of things and the qualities of moral actions, they necessarily often fell into error because they did not possess the distinction between words and concepts. This happened in many respects to Epicurus, who thinks that the world consists of atoms and measures the good by pleasure.

For it is evident that this happened to him and to others for this reason: whatever they had grasped by the reasoning of disputation, they supposed would also come to pass in the things themselves. Yet this is a great error; for things do not stand in the same way in reasonings as they do in numbers. In numbers, whatever result occurs in the fingers of one who calculates correctly must without doubt also occur in the things themselves; thus, if one hundred results from the calculation, then one hundred things must necessarily be subject to that number. [Col. 0749C] But this rule is not equally maintained in disputation. For whatever the course of an argument discovers is not thereby established in nature. Therefore those who inquire into the nature of things while casting aside the science of disputation must necessarily fall into error. Unless one has first attained the science which determines what reasoning keeps to the true path of disputation, what recognizes the plausible, what is trustworthy, and what may be suspect, the uncorrupted truth of things cannot be found through reasoning.

Since, therefore, the ancients, having often fallen into many errors, drew false and mutually contradictory conclusions in disputation, and since it seemed impossible that, when contrary conclusions had been reached concerning the same thing, [Col. 0749D] both conclusions which reasoning had reached in examining the matter should be true—and since it was uncertain which reasoning ought to be believed—it seemed necessary first to consider the true and complete nature of disputation itself. Once that had been known, it could also be understood whether what was discovered through disputation had truly been apprehended. From this arose the discipline of logical skill, which supplies the modes of disputation and methods for distinguishing reasonings, so that one may recognize what reasoning is sometimes true and sometimes false, what is always false, and what can never be false. It is last in time but first in order; for it must be read first by those beginning philosophy. Therefore the nature of words and concepts is taught in it, without which no treatment of philosophy can be rationally explained. [Col. 0750A]

Logic is so called from the Greek word *logos* (λόγος), a term having a double interpretation. For *logos* means “speech” or “reason”; hence logic may be called the science of speech or of reason. Rational logic, which is called discriminative, comprises dialectic and rhetoric. Logic as the science of speech is a genus containing grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric, and it includes eloquence beneath itself. This is the logic of speech which we number fourth, after theoretical, practical, and mechanical philosophy.

Nor should one suppose that logic is called “of speech” because, before its discovery, there were no utterances, as though human beings had not previously possessed mutual speech. [Col. 0750B] Common speech and writing existed before it; but the method of speech and writing had not yet been brought into use, and no precepts for correct speaking or disputing had yet been given. For all sciences existed in practice before they existed as arts. But when people subsequently observed that practice could be converted into art, and that what had formerly been vague and unrestrained could be confined within definite rules and precepts, they began, as has been said, to reduce to art the custom which had arisen partly by chance and partly by nature: correcting what practice had wrongly acquired, supplying what it lacked, cutting away what it had superfluously acquired, and thereafter prescribing definite rules and precepts for each matter.

[Col. 0750C] Such was the origin of all arts; examining them one by one, we find this to be true. Before grammar existed, people wrote and spoke; before dialectic existed, they distinguished truth from falsehood by reasoning; before rhetoric existed, they conducted civil legal affairs; before arithmetic existed, they had the use of counting; before music existed, they sang; before geometry existed, they measured fields; before astronomy existed, they determined the divisions of time by the courses of the stars. But the arts came, which, although they took their beginning from practice, are nevertheless better than practice.

This would be the place to explain who the inventors of the individual arts were, when or where they flourished, and how the disciplines received their beginning from them; but I first wish to distinguish the several arts from one another by a certain division of philosophy. [Col. 0750D]

## CHAPTER XIII. Recapitulation of the foregoing

It is fitting, therefore, briefly to recapitulate what has been said above, so that the transition to what follows may be easier. We have said that there are only four sciences, which contain all the rest: theoretical philosophy, which labors in the contemplation of truth; practical philosophy, which considers the discipline of morals; mechanical philosophy, which orders the activities of this life; and logic, which provides the science of speaking correctly and disputing keenly.

Here, therefore, that quaternity of the soul may not improperly be understood which the ancients, out of reverence for it, invoked in their oath. Hence also this saying:

> By him who gave to it the fourfold number of our soul.

[Col. 0751A]

Having briefly repeated the definition of philosophy, let us show how these are contained under philosophy, and in turn what they contain beneath themselves.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0751]

Its chapters are these:

On the quaternity of the soul.—CHAPTER VI. On the quaternity of the body.—CHAPTER VII. On the quadrivium.—CHAPTER VIII. On arithmetic.—CHAPTER IX. On music.—CHAPTER X. On geometry.—CHAPTER XI. On astronomy.—CHAPTER XII. On arithmetic.—CHAPTER XIII. On the threefold music.—CHAPTER XIV. On geometry.—CHAPTER XV. On astronomy.—CHAPTER XVI. Definition of the quadrivium.—CHAPTER XVII. On physics.—CHAPTER XVIII. What is proper to each art.—CHAPTER XIX. Comparison of the foregoing and division of theoretical philosophy.—CHAPTER XX. Division of practical philosophy.—CHAPTER XXI. Division of mechanical philosophy into seven kinds.—CHAPTER XXII. The first is weaving.—CHAPTER XXIII. The second, armament.—CHAPTER XXIV. The third, navigation.—CHAPTER XXV. The fourth, agriculture.—CHAPTER XXVI. The fifth, hunting.—CHAPTER XXVII. The sixth, medicine.—CHAPTER XXVIII. The seventh, theatrical art.—CHAPTER XXIX. On logic and grammar.—CHAPTER XXX. On the division of grammar.—CHAPTER XXXI. On the method of disputation.

## CHAPTER I. On the distinction of the arts

[Col. 0751B]

“Philosophy is the love of wisdom, which is the self-sufficient living mind and the sole primordial reason of things.” This definition concerns rather the etymology of the name. For *philos* (φίλος) in Greek is called “love” in Latin, and *sophia* (σοφία), “wisdom”; hence it is called philosophy, that is, love of wisdom. But in the addition, “which is the self-sufficient living mind and the sole primordial reason of things,” divine wisdom is signified. It is called self-sufficient because it contains nothing deficient, but beholds past, present, and future things once and simultaneously. It is called a living mind because what occurs once in the divine reason is never erased by any forgetfulness. It is the primordial reason of things because all things were formed after its likeness.

[Col. 0751C] Some say that that with which the arts are concerned always remains. Therefore all arts do this and aim at this: that the divine likeness may be restored in us—a likeness which is form for us but nature for God. The more we are conformed to it, the wiser we become. For then that which has always existed in his reason begins to shine forth in us; because it is transient in us, while it abides immutable in him.

Alternatively: “Philosophy is the art of arts and the discipline of disciplines,” that is, that to which all arts and disciplines look. An art may be called knowledge constituted by the precepts and rules of an art, as in Scripture; a discipline, knowledge said to be complete, as in teaching. Or an art may be called that in which something plausible and probable is treated; a discipline, that in which something is discussed by true arguments concerning matters that cannot be otherwise than they are. Plato and Aristotle wished this to be the distinction between art and discipline. Or art may be called that which is exercised upon subject matter and unfolded through operation, as architecture; whereas discipline is that which consists in contemplation and is unfolded by reasoning alone, as [Col. 0751D] logic.

Alternatively: “Philosophy is meditation upon death.” This is more fitting for Christians, who, having trampled down worldly ambition, live through disciplined conduct in the likeness of their future homeland.

Alternatively: “Philosophy is the discipline which plausibly investigates the reasons of all divine and human things.” Thus the rationale of all studies belongs to philosophy. Not every administration is philosophy; and therefore philosophy seems in some manner to pertain to all things.

## CHAPTER II. Into what parts philosophy is divided

Philosophy is divided into theoretical, practical, mechanical, and logical philosophy. These four contain all knowledge. Theoretical is interpreted “speculative”; practical, “active,” which is also called ethical, that is, [Col. 0752C] moral, because morals consist in good action; mechanical, “adulterine,” because it concerns human works; logical, “of speech,” because it treats of words.

Theoretical philosophy is divided into theology, mathematics, and physics. Boethius makes this division in other words, dividing theoretical philosophy into the intelligible, the intellectual, and the natural: by “intelligible” signifying theology; by “intellectual,” mathematics; and by “natural,” physics. Finally, he defines the intelligible thus:

## CHAPTER III. On theology

“The intelligible is that which, one and the same, subsists of itself always in its own divinity, and is grasped not by any senses but by mind and intellect alone.” This subject belongs to contemplation of God and inquiry into the incorporeality of the soul and the consideration of true philosophy; and this, he says, the Greeks call theology. “Theology” is so called as though it were discourse concerning divine things: *theos* (Θεός) means “God,” and *logos* (λόγος), “speech” or “reason.” Theology, therefore, is when we discourse in some degree upon either the ineffable nature of God or the special [Col. 0753A] creatures by means of their most profound quality.

## CHAPTER IV. On mathematics

Mathematics is called doctrinal science. For *matesis*, when it has an unaspirated *t*, means “vanity” and denotes the superstition of those who place human destinies in constellations; hence people of this kind are called mathematicians. But when the *t* is aspirated, it signifies teaching. Mathematics is that which considers abstract quantity. “Abstract quantity” is called that which, separating by the intellect from matter or from other accidents—such as even, odd, and the like—we treat in reasoning alone; this is what teaching does, not nature.

Boethius calls this the intellectual, which by thought and intelligence comprehends the first intelligible part: namely, the supernal divinity of all heavenly works, whatever possesses a more blessed soul and purer substance beneath the lunar sphere, and finally human souls. Although all these belonged to the substance of that prior intelligible realm, through association with bodies they degenerated from the intelligible to the intellectual, so that they are more understood than understanding, and are blessed with the purity of intelligence whenever they attach themselves to intelligible things. [Col. 0753B]

For the nature of spirits and souls, because it is incorporeal and simple, shares in intelligible substance. But because it descends through the instruments of the senses in a non-uniform manner to comprehend sensible things, and draws their likeness to itself through imagination, it in some sense abandons its own simplicity insofar as it loses the principle of composition. For that which resembles something composite cannot be called altogether simple. Therefore the same thing is, in different respects, both intelligible and intellectual. It is intelligible because its nature is incorporeal and cannot be grasped by any sense. It is intellectual because it is indeed the likeness of sensible things, yet is not itself sensible. For the intelligible is that which is neither sensible nor a sensible likeness. But the intellectual is that which is indeed perceived by intellect alone, yet does not perceive by intellect alone, because it has imagination or sense by which it comprehends things subject to the senses.

Thus, by touching bodies it degenerates; for while it passes through visible bodily forms by the affections of the senses and draws them into itself through imagination, it is divided from its own simplicity as often as it is informed by qualities of some contrary affection. [Col. 0753D] But when, ascending from this distraction to pure intelligence, it gathers itself into one, it becomes more blessed by participation in intelligible substance.

## CHAPTER V. On the quaternity of the soul

Number itself also teaches the principle of this progression and return. Three times one make III; three times three make IX; three times nine make XXVII; three times XXVII make LXXXI. Behold: at the fourth degree the first unity meets you; and you will see the same occur if you carry the multiplication to infinity, so that unity always stands out at the fourth degree.

The simple essence of the soul is most rightly expressed by unity, which is itself incorporeal. The ternary is also suitably referred to the soul because of the indissoluble bond of the middle unity; whereas the quaternary, because it has two middle terms and is therefore dissoluble, properly belongs to the body.

The first progression of the soul, then, is that by which it extends itself from its simple essence, figured by the monad, into a potential ternary, where it now desires one thing through concupiscence, spurns another through anger, and distinguishes between the two through reason. It is rightly said to flow from the monad into the triad, because every essence naturally precedes its power. Again, the fact that the same unity is found three times in the ternary multiplication signifies [Col. 0754B] that the soul exists not in parts but wholly in each of its powers. For we cannot call reason alone, anger alone, or concupiscence alone a third part of the soul, since reason is neither something other than nor less than the soul in substance; anger is neither something other than nor less than the soul; and concupiscence is neither something other than nor less than the soul. Rather, one and the same substance receives different names according to its different powers.

Then, in a second progression, it descends from the potential ternary to govern the harmony of the human body, which is composed by the number nine. For because there are nine openings in the human body, all that by which the body is nourished and governed flows in and out through them, according to natural moderation. Here too there is order, because the soul naturally possesses its powers before it is joined to the body. Thereafter, in the third progression, being now poured forth beyond itself through the senses, it is occupied, by infinite activities, in ordering these visible things, which are figured through XXVII—a solid number extended in three dimensions after the likeness of the body. [Col. 0754C]

But in the fourth progression, released from the body, it returns to the purity of its simplicity. Therefore, in the fourth multiplication, when three times XXVII has grown into LXXXI, the monad appears at the summit, so that it may be clearly evident that after the end of this life, signified by LXXX, the soul returns to the unity of its simplicity, from which it had previously departed when it descended to govern the human body. The prophet declares that the boundary of human life naturally lies in eighty: “If,” he says, “in strength [or powers], eighty years; and what is beyond them is labor and pain” (Psalm LXXXIX).

Some consider this fourfold progression to be that quaternity of the soul of which we spoke above, and call it the quaternity of the soul in distinction from the quaternity of the body. [Col. 0754D]

## CHAPTER VI. On the quaternity of the body

For they assign its own quaternity to the body as well. As the monad corresponds to the soul, so the dyad corresponds to the body. Twice two make IV; twice IV make VIII; twice VIII make XVI; twice XVI make XXXII. Here in the fourth place, likewise, the same number—that is, the binary number—from which the multiplication began meets you. And if you proceed to infinity, it will undoubtedly occur that the binary number always stands out at the fourth degree.

This is the quaternity of the body, in which we are given to understand that everything which receives composition from dissoluble things is itself dissoluble. Do you now see sufficiently clearly, as I think, how souls degenerate from intelligible things to intellectual things: when they descend from the purity of simple intelligence, which is darkened by no image of bodies, to the imagination of visible things; and how they become more blessed again when, gathering themselves from this distraction to the simple fountain of their nature, they are composed as if impressed with the mark of some most excellent form? [Col. 0755A]

To speak more plainly: the intelligible in us is intelligence; the intellectual is imagination. Intelligence is pure and certain knowledge concerning the principles of things alone—that is, God, ideas, and matter (*hyle*)—and concerning incorporeal substances. Imagination is the memory of the senses, adhering to the soul from bodily remnants, and possessing in itself no principle of certain knowledge. Sense is an affection of the soul in the body arising from qualities that occur externally. [Col. 0755B]

## CHAPTER VII. On the quadrivium

Since, therefore, as was said above, it belongs properly to mathematics to consider abstract quantity, its species must be sought in the divisions of quantity. “Abstract quantity is nothing other than a visible form impressed upon the mind according to linear dimension, which exists in imagination.” It has two parts: one continuous, as a tree or a stone, which is called magnitude; the other discrete, as a flock or a people, which is called multitude.

Again, some multitudes exist in themselves, such as three, four, or any other number; others are relative, such as double, half, sesquialter [one and a half times], sesquitertian [one and one-third times], or anything of this kind. Of magnitudes, some are movable, such as the sphere of the world; others immovable, such as the earth. Arithmetic therefore considers magnitude existing in itself; music, that which is relative. Geometry promises knowledge of immovable magnitude; astronomy claims for itself expertise in the science of movable magnitude. Mathematics, therefore, is divided into arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy. [Col. 0755C]

## CHAPTER VIII. On arithmetic

*Arete* (ἀρετή) in Greek is translated “virtue” in Latin; *arithmos* [ἀριθμός], “number.” Hence arithmetic is called the virtue of number. The virtue of number is that all things are formed after its likeness. [Col. 0755D]

## CHAPTER IX. On music

Music derives its name from *moy* [reading uncertain], that is, from water, because no *euphonia*—that is, good resonance—can exist without moisture.

## CHAPTER X. On geometry

Geometry is interpreted “measurement of the earth,” because this discipline was first discovered by the Egyptians. When the Nile, in its inundation, covered their boundaries with mud and confused their limits, they began to measure the earth with rods and ropes. Afterwards it was brought by wise men and extended to the measurement of the spaces of sea, sky, air, and every kind of body. [Col. 0756A]

## CHAPTER XI. On astronomy

Astronomy and astrology seem to differ in this: astronomy takes its name from the law of the stars, while astrology is so called as discourse concerning the stars. For *nomos* (νόμος) means “law,” and *logos* (λόγος), “speech.” Thus astronomy seems to be that which discusses the law of the stars and the revolution of heaven, investigating the regions, circles, courses, risings, and settings of the heavenly bodies, and why each is so called. Astrology, however, is that which considers the stars in relation to observations of birth, death, and any other events; it is partly natural and partly superstitious. It is natural in the conditions of bodies, which vary according to the tempering influence of higher bodies: for example, health, sickness, storm, fair weather, fertility, and barrenness. [Col. 0756B] It is superstitious in contingent matters and in those subject to free choice; this is the branch treated by mathematicians.

## CHAPTER XII. On arithmetic

Arithmetic has as its subject even and odd number. One kind of even number is evenly even; another evenly odd; another oddly even. Odd number also has three species. The first is prime and uncompounded; the second, secondary and compounded; the third, secondary and compounded in itself and, when compared to others, prime and compounded.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the threefold music

There are three kinds of music: cosmic, human, and instrumental. Cosmic music is one thing in the elements, another in the planets, another in times. In the elements, it is one thing in number, another in weight, another in measure. In the planets, it is one thing in position, another in motion, another in nature. In times, it is one thing in days, in the alternation of light and night; another in months, in the waxing and waning of the moon; another in years, in the change of spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

Human music is one thing in the body, another in the soul, another in the union of both. In the body, one kind exists in growth, according to which it increases, and this belongs to all things that are born. Another is in the humors, from whose mixture the human body subsists. Another is common to sentient beings; another is in activities, which belong particularly to rational beings and over which mechanical art presides. If these activities do not exceed their measure, they are good, so that desire is not fed from that from which weakness ought to be nourished, as Lucan relates in praise of Cato:

> For him, feasts meant conquering hunger, and a great household  
> Meant driving winter from a sheltering roof; his costly dress  
> Was to draw a rough toga over his limbs,  
> In the Roman fashion of a Quirite, etc.

Lucan, *Pharsalia*, book II, v. 383 ff. [Col. 0756D]

Music in the soul is one thing in the virtues, such as justice, piety, and temperance; another in the powers, such as reason, anger, and concupiscence. Music between body and soul is the natural friendship by which the soul is joined to the body, not by bodily bonds but by certain affections, in order to move and render the body sentient. According to this friendship, no one has hated his own flesh. This is the music by which the flesh is loved, [Col. 0757A] but the spirit more: so that the body may be sustained and virtue not destroyed.

Instrumental music is one thing in percussion, as in drums and strings; another in wind, as in pipes and organs; another in voice, as in songs and melodies. There are also three kinds of musicians: one composes a song, another performs upon instruments, and the third judges the work of instruments and song.

## CHAPTER XIV. On geometry

Geometry has three species: planimetry, altimetry, and cosmimetry. Planimetry measures a plane, that is, length and breadth, and extends forward and backward, to the right and to the left. Altimetry measures height and extends upward and downward. For the sea is called high, that is, deep; and a tree high, that is, lofty. *Kosmos* (κόσμος) is interpreted “world”; hence cosmimetry is so called, that is, measurement of the world. It measures spherical—that is, globular and round—objects, such as a ball and an egg. It is called cosmimetry after the sphere of the world on account of its excellence, not because it deals only with the measurement of the world, but because the sphere of the world is the worthiest among all spherical things. [Col. 0757B]

## CHAPTER XV. On astronomy

Nor is it contrary that above we assigned immovable magnitude to geometry and movable magnitude to astronomy, because this was said according to their first invention, according to which geometry too is called measurement of the earth. Or we may say that what geometry considers in the sphere of the world—namely, the dimensions of the regions and celestial circles—is immovable insofar as it pertains to geometrical consideration. For geometry considers not motion but space. What astronomy investigates, however, is movable: namely, the courses of the stars and the intervals of time. Thus we shall say universally that immovable magnitude is subject to geometry, movable magnitude to astronomy; for although both deal with the same subject, one contemplates what remains while the other investigates what passes. [Col. 0757C]

## CHAPTER XVI. Definition of the quadrivium

Arithmetic, therefore, is the science of numbers; music is the division of sounds and the variety of voices. Alternatively, music or harmony is the concord of many dissimilar things brought into one. Geometry is the discipline of immovable magnitude and the contemplative description of forms, by which the limits of each thing are customarily made clear. Alternatively, geometry is the fountain of the senses and the origin of utterances. Astronomy is the discipline that investigates the spaces, motions, and returns of heavenly bodies at fixed times. [Col. 0757D]

## CHAPTER XVII. On physics

Physics considers the causes of things in their effects and effects in their causes by investigation:

> Whence comes the trembling of the earth; by what force the deep seas swell,

Virgil, *Georgics*, book II, v. 479.

> The powers of plants, the dispositions and angers of beasts,  
> Every kind of shrub, and likewise stones and creeping things.

[Col. 0758A] *Physis* (φύσις) is interpreted “nature”; hence Boethius also, in the division of theoretical philosophy given above, called physics “natural.” It is also called physiology, that is, discourse distinguishing among natures, which concerns the same subject. Physics is sometimes taken broadly as equivalent to theoretical philosophy. According to this usage, some divide philosophy into three parts: physics, ethics, and logic. Mechanical philosophy is not included in this division; philosophy is restricted to physics, ethics, and logic.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What is proper to each art

Although all arts tend toward the one end of philosophy, they do not all run by one path. Rather, each has certain considerations proper to itself, by which it differs from the others.

Logical consideration concerns things, attending to the concepts of things either by intelligence—when neither the things themselves nor their likenesses are present—or by reason—when the things themselves are not present but their likenesses are. Logic therefore considers the species and genera of things. [Col. 0758B]

What is proper to mathematics is to consider distinctly by reason confused actual things. For example, in the actuality of things a line is not found without surface and solidity—for no body is only long in such a way that it lacks breadth or height; rather, all three are present together in every body. Nevertheless, reason considers a line purely in itself, without surface and thickness. This is mathematical, not because it either is or can be so in the thing itself, but because reason often considers the actual things not as they are, but as they can be; not in themselves, but in relation to reason itself—that is, as reason could allow them to be.

According to this consideration, continuous quantity is said to diminish infinitely and discrete quantity to increase infinitely. Such is the liveliness of reason that it divides every length into lengths, every breadth into breadths, and so forth, and makes even that which lacks interval generate interval for reason itself. [Col. 0758C]

What is proper to physics is to consider the actual things, which are mixed, in an unmixed manner. For the actualities of bodies in the world are not pure, but are composed from the actualities of pure things. Although physics does not find these actualities separately, it nevertheless considers them as pure and in themselves: the pure actuality of fire, earth, air, or water; and, having considered the nature of each separately, it judges concerning the compound and operation of the whole.

It should not be passed over that physics alone properly deals with things; all the other arts deal with concepts of things. Logic treats the concepts themselves according to predicamental constitution; mathematics according to integral composition. Therefore logic sometimes employs pure intelligence, while mathematics is never without imagination, and therefore nothing is truly simple. Since logic and mathematics are earlier in the order of learning than physics and function in some manner as instruments for it—since everyone must first be formed by them before devoting effort to physical speculation—it was necessary that they place their consideration not [Col. 0758D] in the actual things, where experience is deceptive, but in reason alone, where unshaken truth remains; then, with reason leading the way, they descended to the experience of things.

Since, therefore, we have shown how Boethius’s division of theoretical philosophy agrees with the division given above, we shall now briefly repeat both, so that we may compare the individual terms of each division with one another.

## CHAPTER XIX. Comparison of the foregoing and division of theoretical philosophy

Theoretical philosophy is divided into theology, mathematics, and physics; or thus: theoretical philosophy is divided into the intelligible, the intellectual, and the natural; or otherwise: theoretical philosophy is divided into the divine, the doctrinal, and philology. Theology, the intelligible, and the divine are thus the same thing. Mathematics, the intellectual, and the doctrinal are the same thing. Physics, philology, and the natural are likewise the same thing.

Some think that these three parts of theoretical philosophy are mystically signified by a certain name of Pallas, who is imagined to be the goddess of wisdom. For she is called Tritonia, as though from *tritē gnōsis* (τρίτη γνῶσις), that is, “third knowledge”: namely, knowledge of God, which we have called intelligible; of souls, which we have called intellectual; and of bodies, which we call natural. [Col. 0759B]

Yet wisdom takes its name from these three, because, although we may fittingly refer the other three—ethics, mechanics, and logic—to wisdom, we call logic more expressly eloquence because of its fluency of speech, and mechanics and ethics prudence or knowledge because of their circumspection in morals and their practical wisdom in works. Theoretical philosophy alone, however, we call wisdom because it contemplates the truth of things. [Col. 0759C]

## CHAPTER XX. Division of practical philosophy

Practical philosophy is divided into solitary, private, and public. Or otherwise: into ethics, economics, and politics; or otherwise: moral, administrative, and civil philosophy. Solitary, ethical, and moral philosophy are one and the same. Again, private, economic, and administrative philosophy are one and the same. Public, political, and civil philosophy are likewise the same.

*Oeconomus* means “steward”; hence economics is called administrative. *Polis* (πόλις) in Greek means “city” in Latin; hence politics is so called, that is, civil philosophy. When we establish ethics as a part of practical philosophy, ethics must be taken strictly as concerning the morals of each individual person; it is the same as solitary philosophy.

Solitary philosophy is that which, caring for itself, raises, adorns, and increases itself with every virtue, admitting into life nothing over which it does not rejoice and doing nothing that it will regret. Private philosophy is that which distributes the duty of household affairs through a moderate ordering. Public philosophy is that which, taking up the care of the commonwealth, provides for the well-being of all through the ingenuity of its foresight, the balance of justice, the firmness of courage, and the endurance of temperance. [Col. 0759D] Thus solitary philosophy belongs to individuals, private philosophy to fathers of households, and political philosophy to rulers of cities.

Practical philosophy is called active because it carries out its proposed matters by operations. It is called moral because through it an honorable way of life is sought or attained, and institutions tending toward virtue are prepared. It is called administrative when the order of domestic affairs is wisely arranged. It is called civil because through it the welfare of the whole city is administered. [Col. 0760A]

## CHAPTER XXI. Division of mechanical philosophy into seven kinds

Mechanical philosophy contains seven sciences: weaving, armament, navigation, agriculture, hunting, medicine, and theatrical art. Of these, three pertain to the outward clothing of nature, by which nature itself protects itself from inconveniences; four to its inward clothing, by which it nourishes and sustains itself through feeding. This is after the likeness of the trivium and quadrivium: for the trivium treats of words, which are external, and the quadrivium of concepts, which are conceived internally.

These are the seven handmaids whom Mercury received as a dowry from Philology; for all human action serves eloquence when wisdom has been joined to it. Thus Tully says in his book on rhetoric concerning the pursuit of eloquence:

> It makes life safe, honorable, illustrious, and likewise pleasant. For from it very many benefits come to the commonwealth, if wisdom, the guide of all things, is at hand. From it praise, honor, and dignity flow to those who have attained it. From it also comes to their friends a most certain and most secure protection.

[Col. 0760B]

They are called mechanical, that is, adulterine, because they concern the work of the craftsman, which borrows its form from nature. Just as the other seven are called liberal arts, either because they require free—that is, unencumbered and well-trained—minds, since they dispute subtly concerning the causes of things; or because in antiquity only free men, that is, nobles, customarily studied them, whereas commoners and the sons of the ignoble studied the mechanical arts for skill in working.

In this the diligence of the ancients is apparent: they wished to leave nothing unattempted, but to bind everything under definite rules and precepts. Mechanical philosophy is the science to which the manufacture of all things ought to contribute. [Col. 0760C]

## CHAPTER XXII. On weaving
Woolworking includes every kind of weaving, sewing, and twisting done by hand, needle, spindle, awl, reel, comb, card, curling-iron, roller, or any other instruments whatsoever; from whatever material of flax or wool, and every kind of hide, whether shorn or retaining its hair; likewise hemp, cork, rushes, hairs, tufts, or any other such material [Col. 0760D] that can be made into garments, coverings, linen cloths, cloaks, quilts, bed-spreads, curtains, mats, filters, nets, hunting-nets, or ropes. Straw also, from which people are accustomed to weave hats and little baskets: all these crafts belong to woolworking.

### Chapter XXIII. On Armour-making and Craftsmanship

The second is armour-making. “Arms” sometimes means any instruments whatever, as when we say “the arms of war” or “the arms of a ship,” that is, the instruments of war and of a ship. Properly, however, arms are those things with which we are covered, such as a shield, breastplate, or helmet; or with which we strike, such as a sword, battle-axe, or sarissa. Missiles, moreover, are those with which [Col. 0761A] we can cast or shoot, such as a spear or arrow. Arms are said to derive from *armus*, that is, “arm,” because they protect the arm, which we customarily oppose to blows. Missiles (*tela*) are said to derive from the Greek *telon*, that is, “long,” because things of this sort are long; hence *protelare*, “to lengthen,” is also said.

Armour-making, therefore, is called, as it were, the science of making instruments, not so much because it uses instruments in working, as because from the material of some mass lying before it, it produces some instrument, so to speak. Every kind of material—stone, wood, metals, sands, clays—belongs to it. It has two branches: architecture and craftsmanship.

Architecture is divided into masonry, which belongs to stone-cutters and masons; and carpentry, which belongs to carpenters and timber-workers, and to other such craftsmen of both kinds [Col. 0761B] who work with adzes and axes, file and small axe, saw and drill, planes, trowels, levels, polishing, shaping, carving, filing, cutting, joining, coating, in whatever material—mud, brick, stone, wood, bone, sand, lime, gypsum, and any similar substances.

Craftsmanship is divided into hammer-work, which by striking brings a mass into shape; and casting, which by pouring brings a mass into shape. Hence casters are so called because they know how to produce the shape of a vessel from the confused mass.

### Chapter XXIV. On Navigation

Navigation includes all commerce in buying, selling, and exchanging goods, whether domestic or foreign.
