[Col. 0761C] It is most properly a kind of rhetoric peculiar to itself, because eloquence is especially necessary to this profession. Thus Mercury, who is said to preside over eloquence, is called as though he were the merchants’ *κύριος* (*kyrios*), that is, “Lord.”

It penetrates the hidden places of the world, visits shores unseen before, traverses dreadful deserts, and conducts the commerce of human fellowship with barbarous peoples and unknown languages. Its pursuit reconciles nations, calms wars, establishes peace, and changes private goods into the common use of all.

### Chapter XXV. On Agriculture

Agriculture has four kinds: arable land, a field allotted for sowing; cultivated land planted with shrubs and trees, such as vineyards, orchards, and woods; [Col. 0761D] pasture-land, such as meadows, valleys, waste places, and forest-pastures; and flowering land, such as gardens and rose-gardens.

### Chapter XXVI. On Hunting

Hunting is divided into the chase of wild beasts, fowling, and fishing. The chase is pursued in many ways: by nets, traps, snares, precipices, bow, javelins, spear-point, encircling drives, the scent of feathers, dogs, and hawks. Fowling is done with snares, traps, nets, bows, birdlime, and hooks. Fishing is done with seines, nets, fish-traps, hooks, and spears.

The preparation of every kind of food, flavouring, and drink belongs to this discipline. Yet it has taken its name from one part of itself, because in ancient times people were more accustomed to live on game, as still happens in certain regions where bread is extremely scarce: there they have meat for food, and mead or water for drink.

[Col. 0762A] Food is divided into two kinds: bread and *obsonium*, accompaniment to bread. Bread (*panis*) is said either to be, as it were, *ponis*, “that which is placed,” because it is set upon every table; or from the Greek πᾶν, “all,” because no feast is regarded as good without bread; or because it feeds. There are many kinds of bread: unleavened bread, leavened bread, ash-baked bread, reddish bread, sponge bread, cake, oven-baked bread, sweet bread, fine-wheat bread, barley bread, starch bread, fine flour bread, and many others.

*Obsonium* is called, as it were, something added to bread, which we may call “provisions.” There are many kinds of it: meats, dishes, dairy products, vegetables, and fruits. Of meats, some are roasted, some fried, some boiled, some raw, and some salted. Some are called *succidia*, preserved meat; likewise bacon or *taxea*; ham or little ham; lard, animal fat, suet, and fat. There are also kinds of prepared dishes: Lucanian sausages, stuffing, *minutal*, *afrotum*, *mortisia*, *galantiae*, and whatever else the chief of cooks has been able to devise.

[Col. 0762B] Dairy foods include milk, colostrum, *babduta* [reading uncertain], butter, cheese, and whey. Who can enumerate the names of vegetables and fruits? Of flavours, some are hot, others cold; some bitter, others sweet; some dry, others moist. Of drinks, some are only drinks—that is, they moisten but do not nourish, such as water; others are both drink and food—that is, they moisten and nourish, such as wine. Again, among those which are food, some are food naturally, such as wine and every kind of *sicera*; others accidentally, such as beer and meads.

Hunting, therefore, includes all the offices of bakers, butchers, cooks, and tavern-keepers.

### Chapter XXVII. On Medicine

Medicine is divided into two parts: circumstances and operations. [Col. 0762C] There are six circumstances: air; motion and rest; evacuation and repletion; food and drink; sleep and wakefulness; and affections of the soul. These are called circumstances because, if they are moderated, they produce and preserve health; if immoderate, illness.

The affections of the soul are called circumstances of health or illness because they sometimes stir heat violently, as anger does; or gently, as pleasures do; or draw it inward and conceal it, either violently, as terror and fear do, or gently, as distress does. There are also those which stir the natural power inwardly and outwardly, such as sadness.

Every medical operation is performed either internally or externally. Internally are those things introduced through the mouth, nostrils, ears, or anus, such as potions, [Col. 0762D] emetics, powders, clysters, and so forth, which are taken by drinking, chewing, or inhaling. Externally are *epidimata*, poultices, and plasters. Surgery is twofold: upon the flesh, as cutting, stitching, and cauterizing; and upon the bone, as setting it and restoring its joints.

Nor should anyone be troubled that I count food and drink among the properties of medicine, though above I assigned them to hunting; for this has been done according to different respects. Wine too is agriculture when on the vine; the cellarer’s concern when in the store-room; and the physician’s concern when tasted. Likewise, the preparation of foods belongs to the bakery, market, and kitchen; the power of flavour belongs to medicine.

### Chapter XXVIII. On the Theatrical Science

The theatrical science is called the science of games from the theatre, where the people were accustomed to assemble for amusement—not because games were held only [Col. 0763A] in the theatre, but because it was more celebrated than the other places. Some games, however, were held in theatres, others in halls, others in gymnasia, others in amphitheatres, others in arenas, others at banquets, and others in temples.

In the theatre, deeds were recited through songs, masks, dramatic characters, or little suspended figures. In halls they led dances and danced. In gymnasia they wrestled. In amphitheatres they competed in races, on foot, on horseback, or in chariots. In arenas boxers were trained. At banquets they sang to rhythms, musical instruments, and odes, and played at dice. In temples, at solemn times, they sang the praises of the gods.

They counted games among lawful activities because moderate movement nourishes the natural heat in the body and renews its cheerfulness. Or, more probably, because it was necessary for the people sometimes to assemble for amusement, they wished places for gaming to be prescribed, lest, forming little gatherings in inns, they commit shameful or criminal acts.

### Chapter XXIX. On Logic, the Fourth Part of Philosophy; and on Grammar

Logic is divided into grammar and the art of reasoning. Γράμμα (*gramma*) is interpreted in Latin as *littera*, “letter”; hence grammar is so called, that is, the science of letters. A letter properly is a written figure; an element is a sound that is pronounced. Here, however, “letter” must be taken broadly, so that we understand both speech and writing; for both belong to grammar.

Some say that grammar is not a part of philosophy, but a kind of appendage and instrument of philosophy. But Boethius says concerning the art of reasoning: “It can be both a part and an instrument of philosophy, just as the foot, hand, tongue, eyes, and so forth are parts of the body and instruments.”

Grammar deals simply with utterances, treating their invention and formation in themselves, their composition, inflection, pronunciation, and everything else belonging merely to pronunciation. The art of reasoning deals with utterances in relation to concepts.

### Chapter XXX. On the Division of Grammar

Grammar is divided into letter, syllable, word, and sentence; or otherwise, grammar is divided into letters—that is, what is written—and sounds, [Col. 0763D] that is, what is pronounced. Or otherwise: grammar is divided into noun, verb, participle, pronoun, adverb, preposition, conjunction, and interjection; articulated sound, letter, syllable, feet, accents, punctuation marks, critical signs, orthography, analogy, etymology, glosses, distinctions, barbarism, solecism, faults, metaplasms, figures, tropes, prose, metres, fables, and histories.

I pass over the exposition of these matters because it would be longer than the brevity of this little outline requires, and because in this small work I have proposed only to investigate the divisions and names of things, so that merely a certain beginning of instruction might be laid down for the reader. Whoever wishes to know more should read Donatus, Servius, Priscian on accents and on [Col. 0764A] the twelve lines of Virgil, *Barbarism*, and Isidore in the books of *Etymologies*.

### Chapter XXXI. On the Art of Reasoning

The art of reasoning has invention and judgment as its integral parts; demonstration, probability, and sophistry as its divisive parts. Demonstration concerns necessary arguments and belongs to philosophers. Probability belongs to dialecticians and rhetoricians. Sophistry belongs to sophists and quibblers.

The probable is divided into dialectic and rhetoric, each of which has invention and judgment as integral parts. For since these together constitute the genus itself—that is, the art of reasoning—it is necessary that they should be found together in the constitution of all its species. Invention teaches the discovery of arguments and the construction of [Col. 0764B] reasonings. The science of judgment teaches how to judge both.

It may be asked whether invention and judgment are contained under philosophy. For they seem to be contained neither under theoretical, practical, mechanical, nor logical philosophy, though logic would appear the most likely. They are not contained under logic because they are contained neither through grammar nor through the art of reasoning. They are not contained through the art of reasoning, since they constitute it integrally; but no thing can at once be an integral and a divisive part of the same genus. Thus philosophy seems not to contain every science.

But it should be known that “science” is customarily understood in two ways: as one of the disciplines, as when I say that dialectic is a science, that is, an art or discipline; and as any kind of knowledge, as when I say that a person who knows something has science. For example: if I know dialectic, I have science; if I know how to take notes, I have science; and if I know that Socrates is the son of Sophroniscus, I have science. In general, everyone who knows anything can be said to have science.

Yet it is one thing when I say, “Dialectic is a science,” that is, an art or discipline; and another when I say, “Knowing that Socrates is the son of Sophroniscus is science,” that is, knowledge. Of every science that is an art or discipline, it is true to say that it is a divisive part of philosophy; but it cannot universally be said that every science which is knowledge is a divisive part of philosophy. Yet every science whatsoever, whether a discipline or any kind of knowledge, is altogether a part [Col. 0764D] of philosophy, either divisive or integral.

A discipline is a science that has a complete end in which the purpose of the art is perfectly unfolded. This does not apply to the sciences of invention or judgment, because neither is complete in itself; and therefore they cannot be called disciplines, but parts of a discipline, namely, of the art of reasoning.

Again, it is asked whether invention and judgment are the same parts in dialectic and rhetoric. This seems unsuitable, since two opposite genera would be constituted by precisely the same parts. One may therefore say that these two terms are equivocal in relation to the parts of dialectic and rhetoric; or, perhaps better, let us say that invention and judgment are properly parts of the art of reasoning, and are univocal under these names. Yet in the lower divisions of this genus they differ in certain properties, [Col. 0765A] though these differences are not distinguished by these terms; for by them they are signified, not insofar as they compose species, but insofar as they are parts of the genus.

Grammar is the science of speaking [Col. 0766A] without fault. Dialectic is keen disputation, distinguishing truth from falsehood. Rhetoric is the discipline suited to persuading in every matter.

## Book Three

[Col. 0765]

Its chapters are these:

Chapter I. On discipline and its division.—Chapter II. On the authors of the arts.—Chapter III. Which arts ought especially to be read.—Chapter IV. On the two kinds of writings.—Chapter V. On the coherence of the arts.—Chapter VI. That what belongs to each art ought to be assigned to it.—Chapter VII. What is necessary for students.—Chapter VIII. On ability and memory, the two things that belong to nature.—Chapter IX. On the order of reading.—Chapter X. On the manner of reading.—Chapter XI. On meditation.—Chapter XII. On memory.—Chapter XIII. On discipline.—Chapter XIV. On humility.—Chapter XV. On zeal in inquiry.—Chapter XVI. On the four remaining precepts.—Chapter XVII. On quiet.—Chapter XVIII. On examination.—Chapter XIX. On frugality.—Chapter XX. On exile.

### Chapter I. On Discipline and Its Division

[Col. 0765B]

Philosophy is divided into theoretical, practical, mechanical, and logical philosophy. The theoretical is divided into theology, physics, and mathematics. Mathematics into arithmetic, music, and geometry. The practical into solitary, private, and public [philosophy]. The mechanical is divided into woolworking, armour-making, navigation, agriculture, hunting, medicine, and theatrical science. Logic is divided into grammar and the art of discourse. The art of discourse is divided into demonstration, probability, and sophistry. The probable is divided into dialectic and rhetoric.

In this division only the divisive parts of philosophy are contained. There are further subdivisions of these parts, but these may suffice for the present. If in them you consider only the number, [Col. 0765C] you will find twenty-one; if you wish to count the degrees, thirty-eight.

Various authors are recorded for these sciences. Some discovered the arts by beginning them, others by enlarging them, and others by perfecting them; and so several authors are often named for one and the same art. Of these I shall list below the names of a few.

### Chapter II. On the Authors of the Arts

Among the Greeks Linus was a theologian; among the Latins, Varro; and in our own time John Scotus, concerning the ten categories applied to God.

Thales of Miletus, one of the Seven Sages, discovered natural physics among the Greeks; Pliny described it among the Latins. Pythagoras of Samos discovered arithmetic; Nicomachus wrote upon it. Among the Latins Apuleius first, then Boethius, translated it. This same Pythagoras also composed the *Machematetrados*, that is, the book *On the Teaching of the Quadrivium*, and invented five [items; term uncertain] in likeness to human life.

Moses says that Tubal, of the lineage of Cain, was the discoverer of music. The Greeks name Pythagoras; others Mercury, who first established the tetrachord; others Linus, Zethus, or Amphion.

They say geometry was first discovered in Egypt; among the Greeks its foremost author was Euclid. Boethius translated its art. Eratosthenes also was most acute in geometry, and discovered the circumference of the earth.

They say that Ham, [Col. 0766B] Noah’s son, first discovered astronomy. The Chal[lacuna] first taught astrology according to observations of birth. Josephus, however, affirms that Abraham first taught astrology among the Egyptians. Ptolemy, king of Egypt, restored astronomy. He also established the tables by which the courses of the stars are discovered. Some say that the giant Nimrod was the greatest astrologer, and astronomy is also found under his name. The Greeks say that this art was first devised by Atlas, for which reason he too is said to have supported the sky.

Socrates was the inventor of ethics, concerning which he handed down twenty-four books according to positive justice. Then his disciple Plato wrote many books *On the Republic* according to both kinds of justice, namely natural and positive. Then Cicero composed books *On the Republic* in the Latin language. The philosopher Fronto also wrote a book of *Stratagems*, that is, military ingenuity.

The mechanical arts had various authors. Hesiod of Ascra first among the Greeks devoted himself to describing rural matters. Then Democritus; Mago of Carthage also set down the study of agriculture in twenty-seven volumes. Among the Latins Cato first produced a work *On Agriculture*, later polished by Marcus Terentius Varro. Virgil also composed the *Georgics*. Then came Cornelius and Julius Atticus Aemilianus, or the distinguished orator Columella, who embraced the whole body of this discipline. Palladius likewise wrote *On Agriculture*, and Vitruvius *On Architecture*.

They relate that Minerva first showed the Greeks the use of woolworking. They believe that she first arranged the loom, dyed wool, and invented both the olive tree and craftsmanship. Daedalus learned from her, and is believed after her to have made craftsmanship [Col. 0766D] himself. In Egypt, however, Isis, daughter of Inachus, discovered the sowing of flax and showed how garments could be made from it. Likewise she herself discovered there the use of wool. In Libya the use of wool first arose from the temple of Ammon.

Ninus, king of the Assyrians, first waged wars. They believe Vulcan to have been the first smith; divine history, however, maintains that it was Tubal. [Col. 0767A] Prometheus first discovered the use of the ring by impressing a stone with an iron circle. The Pelasgians first discovered the use of ships.

Ceres first discovered the use of grain in Greece at Eleusis; Isis did so in Egypt. Pilumnus discovered in Italy the use of grain and spelt, and the practice of grinding and pounding. Tagus discovered in Spain the practice of sowing. Osiris discovered the cultivation of vineyards among the Egyptians; Liber did so among the Indians. Daedalus first made a table and chair. A certain Roman, Apicius, first devised the arrangements of cookery; having finally consumed his property upon this pursuit, he died by voluntary death.

Apollo was the author of medicine among the Greeks. His son Aesculapius enlarged it in reputation and practice. After he perished by lightning, the practice of healing was neglected for a long time and lay hidden for almost five hundred years, until the time of King Artaxerxes. [Col. 0767B] Then Hippocrates, born to his father Asclepius on the island of Cos, brought it again into the light.

Games are believed to have originated with the Lydians, who came from Asia and settled in Etruria under the leader Tyrrhenus. There, among the other rites of their superstitions, they instituted spectacles. The Romans imitated this custom, summoning performers from there; and thus games were called from the Lydians.

The letters of the Hebrews are believed to have begun with Moses through the Law; those of the Chaldeans and Syrians through Abraham. Isis invented Egyptian letters; the Phoenicians invented Greek letters, which Cadmus the Phoenician brought into Greece. Carmentis, Evander’s mother, whose own name was Nicostrata, discovered Latin letters.

Moses first wrote sacred history. Among the pagans, Dares the Phrygian first published [Col. 0767C] Trojan history, which they say he wrote upon palm leaves. After Dares, Herodotus was regarded as the first historian in Greece. After him Pherecydes flourished in the same period in which Ezra wrote the Law. Alcinon [otherwise Alcman] of Croton is believed to have invented fables first.

Egypt is the mother of the arts: from there they came into Greece, and then into Italy. Grammar was first discovered there in the time of Osiris, husband of Isis. Dialectic too was first invented there by Parmenides, who, fleeing cities and human gatherings, sat upon a rock for a considerable time and thus devised dialectic; hence it was called the Rock of Parmenides.

After the death of his teacher Socrates, [Col. 0767D] Plato migrated to Egypt out of love of wisdom; and there, having acquired the liberal disciplines, he returned to Athens. Gathering disciples at the Academy, his estate, he devoted himself to philosophical studies. He first established rational logic among the Greeks; later his disciple Aristotle enlarged it, perfected it, and reduced it to an art. Marcus Terentius Varro first translated dialectic from Greek into Latin. Cicero afterwards added the *Topics*.

Demosthenes, son of a craftsman, is believed to have been the foremost master of rhetoric among the Greeks; Tisias among the Latins; Corax at Syracuse. This was written in Greek by Aristotle, Gorgias, and Hermagoras, and translated into Latin by Cicero, Quintilian, and Titianus.

### Chapter III. Which Arts Ought Especially to Be Read

[Col. 0768A]

Of all the sciences enumerated above, the ancients specially appointed seven for the training of students, in which they discerned so great a usefulness beyond all the rest that whoever had firmly mastered their discipline would later arrive at knowledge of the others more by inquiry and practice than by instruction. For they are, as it were, certain excellent instruments and rudiments by which a way is prepared for the mind toward the full knowledge of philosophical truth.

Hence they received the names *trivium* and *quadrivium*, because by these, as by certain roads, the active mind enters into the secrets of wisdom. In those times no one appeared worthy of the title of teacher who could not profess knowledge of these seven sciences.

[Col. 0768B] Pythagoras is said to have observed this custom in his teaching: until the seventh year, corresponding to the number of the seven liberal arts, none of his disciples dared demand a reason for the things he said; rather, each gave credence to the master’s words until he had heard everything, and could then discover their rationale for himself.

Some are recorded as having learned these seven with such zeal that they held them all fully in memory. Whatever writings they thereafter took in hand, whatever questions they proposed to resolve or prove, they did not seek in the leaves of books for rules and arguments by which to determine what was doubtful; rather, they had each thing immediately ready in their hearts. Hence, surely, it came about in that age that there were so many wise persons that they themselves wrote more than we can read.

[Col. 0768C] Our scholars, however, either do not wish, or do not know, to preserve the fitting method in learning; and therefore we find many students but few wise persons. It seems to me that no less care should be taken that the reader does not expend labour upon useless studies than that he does not remain lukewarm in a good and useful purpose. It is bad to pursue a good thing negligently; it is worse to expend much labour in vain.

But because not everyone can possess this discernment, so as to understand what is advantageous for himself, I shall briefly point out to the reader which writings seem more useful to me, and afterwards add a few remarks on the method of study.

### Chapter IV. On the Two Kinds of Writings

[Col. 0768D]

There are two kinds of writings. The first kind consists of those called the proper arts. The second consists of those that are appendages of the arts.

The arts are those subordinate to philosophy—that is, those having a definite and determined subject-matter of philosophy, such as grammar, dialectic, and the other arts of this kind. The appendages of the arts are those which merely have a bearing upon philosophy—that is, those occupied with some matter outside philosophy, but which sometimes touch upon certain things taken from the arts in a scattered and confused manner; or, if they are simple narrative, prepare the way toward philosophy.

Of this sort are all poets’ verses: tragedies, comedies, satires, heroic, lyric, iambic, and certain didactic poems; likewise fables and histories; and also the writings of those whom we now habitually call philosophers, [Col. 0769A] who are accustomed both to expand a brief subject through long circumlocutions of words and to obscure an easy meaning by tangled speech, or even to compile diverse matters together and make, as it were, one picture from many colours and forms.

Note the distinction I have made for you: there are two kinds, arts and appendages of the arts. Yet the difference between them seems to me as great as that described in the line:

> As much as the pliant willow yields to the pale olive,
>
> As the lowly *saliunca* yields to crimson roses.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues*)

Thus anyone who desires to attain knowledge, if he abandons the truth of the arts and entangles himself in the remaining writings, will undertake a subject of labour not merely very great but infinite, and gain only a scant reward.

Finally, the parts can make a reader complete without their appendages; but the appendages can confer no perfection without the arts. This is especially so because they possess in themselves nothing that should attract the reader except what is conveyed and adapted from the arts; nor should anyone seek in them anything except what belongs to the arts.

For this reason, it seems to me that one must first devote effort to the arts, where the foundations of all things lie and pure, simple truth is revealed—above all, to those seven already mentioned, which are the instruments of the whole of philosophy. Then, if there is leisure, let the other writings also be read, because things of amusement mixed with serious matters sometimes give greater delight, and rarity makes a good thing precious. Thus, in the middle course of a fable, we sometimes retain more eagerly a maxim that has been found.

Nevertheless, in the seven liberal arts lies the foundation [Col. 0769C] of all learning. They must be kept especially at hand, since without them philosophical discipline ordinarily neither explains nor defines anything, nor can it do so.

### Chapter V. On the Coherence of the Arts

These arts are so joined together and need one another by reciprocal principles that, if one is lacking, the others cannot make a philosopher. Therefore those seem to me to err who, failing to notice such coherence among the arts, choose certain ones for themselves and think that, leaving the rest untouched, they can become perfect through these alone.

### Chapter VI. That What Belongs to Each Art Ought To Be Assigned to It

There is another error, not much smaller than this, which must be avoided with the utmost care. Some people indeed omit nothing from the things that ought to be read, [Col. 0769D] but do not know how to assign to each art what is its own; rather, they read everything in each discipline. In grammar they argue about the theory of syllogisms; in dialectic they investigate case-inflections; and, what is even more worthy of mockery, they read almost the whole book in its title and scarcely finish the beginning by the third lesson. Such people do not teach others; they display their own knowledge. But would that they appeared to all as they appear to me!

Consider how perverse this practice is. Certainly, the more superfluous matter you accumulate, the less able you will be to grasp or retain what is useful. Therefore, in every art two things must chiefly be discerned [Col. 0770A] and distinguished: first, how one ought to proceed within that art itself; second, how one ought to apply the principles of that art to any other matters.

There are two things: treating of an art, and proceeding by means of an art. For example, there is treating grammar, and there is proceeding grammatically. He treats of grammar who handles the rules laid down concerning words and the precepts belonging to that discipline; everyone proceeds grammatically who speaks or writes correctly.

Thus, treating of grammar belongs only to certain persons, such as Priscian, Donatus, Servius, and the like; but proceeding grammatically belongs to everyone. When, therefore, we treat of any art—especially in teaching, where everything must be reduced to brevity and brought back to easy understanding—the matter being treated should suffice, provided it can be explained as [Col. 0770B] briefly and suitably as possible. Otherwise, if we multiply foreign considerations too much, we shall confuse rather than instruct the reader.

Not everything that we can say ought to be said, lest those things which we ought to say be said less usefully. In each art seek only that which is established as belonging specially to it. Then, when you have read the arts and have learned through disputation and comparison what is proper to each, you may at last compare their individual principles with one another, and by reciprocal consideration investigate matters that you previously understood less fully.

Do not multiply side-paths until you have learned the paths: you will run safely when you do not fear going astray.

### Chapter VII. What Is Necessary for Students

[Col. 0770C]

Three things are necessary for students: nature, practice, and discipline. In nature it is required that one readily grasp what has been heard and firmly retain what has been grasped. In practice, that one cultivate natural understanding through labour and diligence. In discipline, that one live honourably and unite good character with knowledge. We shall now touch briefly, by way of introduction, upon each of these three.

### Chapter VIII. On Ability and Memory, the Two Things That Belong to Nature

> [Note: [Col. 0769D] The earlier portion of this chapter, absent from the printed editions, was published by Dom Mabillon in the new edition of the *Veterum* [Col. 0770D] *Analectorum*, p. 132, from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint-Taurin at Évreux.]

Many people have been left by nature so lacking in intellectual ability that they can scarcely grasp even easy matters by understanding. There seem to be two kinds of such persons. Some, though they do not fail to recognize their dullness, nevertheless strive toward knowledge with whatever effort they can; and, [Col. 0770D] sweating unceasingly over study, they seem to attain through the affection of their will what they lack in the result of their work.

But others, because they feel that they cannot comprehend the highest matters at all, neglect even the smallest; and, resting secure in their own torpor, they lose the light of truth in the greatest matters all the more because they avoid learning the smallest matters which they could understand. Hence the Psalmist says: “They refused to understand, that they might do good” (Ps. XXXV [36]). For not knowing is one thing, and refusing to know another. Not knowing is indeed a matter of weakness; but detesting knowledge is a matter of perverse will.

There is another kind of persons whom [Col. 0771A] nature has richly endowed with ability and to whom it has supplied an easy approach to truth. Although their intellectual capacity may be equal, they do not all have equal virtue or willingness to cultivate their natural understanding through practice and instruction. For many, entangled in the business and cares of this age beyond what is necessary, or given over to bodily vices and pleasures, bury God’s talent in the earth and seek from it neither the fruit of wisdom nor the increase of good work. Such persons are surely very blameworthy.

Again, for others poverty of household resources and a slender income diminish the opportunity for learning. Yet we do not believe that they can thereby be wholly excused, since we see very many, suffering hunger, thirst, and nakedness, attaining the fruit of knowledge. And yet it is one thing when you cannot learn—or, more truly, cannot easily learn—and another thing when you can know but do not wish to know. For just as it is more glorious, when no resources are available, to grasp wisdom through virtue alone, so it is surely more shameful to flourish in ability, abound in riches, and grow sluggish through idleness.

Those who devote themselves to learning ought to be strong both in ability and in memory. These two adhere to one another so closely in every study and discipline that, if either is lacking, the other cannot bring anyone to perfection. No profits can be useful where safekeeping is lacking; and he fortifies storehouses in vain who has nothing to store in them. Ability discovers wisdom; memory preserves it.

Ability is a certain power naturally implanted in the mind and effective through itself. Ability comes from nature, is helped by use, is blunted by excessive labour, [Col. 0771C] and sharpened by moderate exercise. Hence someone said quite elegantly: “At last I want you to spare yourself; there is labour in writing—run through the air.”

Two things exercise ability: reading and meditation. Reading occurs when we are formed by rules and precepts from what has been written. There are three kinds of reading: that of the teacher, that of the learner, and private reading. For we say, “I read a book to him,” “I read a book from him,” and “I read a book.” In reading, order and method are especially to be considered.

### Chapter IX. On the Order of Reading
Order is considered in several ways: one in the disciplines, as when I say that grammar is older than dialectic, or arithmetic prior to music; another in books, as when I say [Col. 0771D] that the *Catilinarian* is prior to the *Jugurthine*; another in narration, which proceeds in a continuous sequence; another in arrangement. In the disciplines, order is observed according to nature; in books, according to the person of the author or the subject matter. In narration it is observed according to arrangement, which is twofold: natural, namely when an event is related in the order in which it occurred; and artificial, that is, when what happened later is narrated first, and what happened earlier is told afterwards. In exposition, order is considered according to inquiry. Exposition contains three things: the letter, the sense, and the meaning. The letter is the fitting arrangement of words, which we also call construction. The sense is a certain easy and plain signification which the letter presents at first sight. Meaning is a deeper understanding, [Col. 0772A] which is not discovered except by exposition or interpretation. Here the order is that the letter should first be investigated, then the sense, and then the meaning; when this has been done, the exposition is complete.

## CHAPTER X. On the method of reading.

The method of reading consists in division. Every division begins from finite things and proceeds as far as infinite things. But everything finite is better known and capable of being comprehended by knowledge. Teaching begins from things more known and, through knowledge of them, arrives at knowledge of things which lie hidden. Moreover, we investigate by reason; and division properly belongs to reason, when, by dividing, we descend from universals to particulars and investigate the natures of individual things. For every universal is more determinate [Col. 0772B] than its particulars. Therefore, when we learn, we ought to begin with things which are more known, determinate, and comprehensive; and thus, gradually descending and distinguishing individual things by division, to investigate the nature of the things contained within them.

## CHAPTER XI. On meditation.

Meditation is frequent thought joined with deliberation, prudently investigating the cause and origin, manner and usefulness of each thing.” Meditation takes its beginning from reading; yet it is bound by none of the rules or precepts of reading. For it delights to range through a certain fitting expanse, where it may fix the free gaze of contemplation upon truth; now to touch upon these causes of things, now upon those; now indeed to penetrate every depth, and to leave nothing doubtful and nothing obscure [Col. 0772C]. Therefore the beginning of learning is in reading, its consummation in meditation. Whoever has learned to love it more intimately and wishes to devote himself to it often finds that it makes life most pleasant and affords the greatest consolation in tribulation.

For it especially separates the soul from the tumult of earthly affairs and, even in this life, makes it in some manner taste beforehand the sweetness of eternal rest. And when, through the things that have been made, it has learned to seek and understand Him who made all things, then it both instructs the soul by knowledge and floods it with joy. Hence meditation affords the greatest delight. There are three kinds of meditation. One consists in examining moral conduct, another in searching the commandments, [Col. 0772D] the third in investigating the works of God. Moral conduct concerns vices and virtues. One divine command commands, another promises, another threatens. God’s work is both what his power creates, what his wisdom governs, and what his grace cooperates in accomplishing. How worthy of wonder all these things are, each person knows all the more as he becomes accustomed to meditate more attentively upon God’s wonders.

## CHAPTER XII. On memory.

Concerning memory, I judge that this must especially not be omitted here: just as natural ability investigates and discovers by dividing, so memory preserves by gathering together. Therefore, the things which we have divided in learning we ought to gather together by entrusting them to memory. To gather together is to reduce what has been written or discussed [Col. 0773A] at greater length to a certain brief and concise summary, called by the ancients an *epilogue*, that is, a short recapitulation of what has been said above. For every treatise has some principle upon which the whole truth of the subject and force of its meaning rests, and to which all the other matters are referred. To seek and consider this is to gather together.

There is one spring and many streams: if you follow the winding courses of the rivers, hold fast to the spring and you possess the whole. I say this because human memory is dull and delights in brevity; if it is divided among many things, it becomes weaker in each. Therefore in every course of study we ought to gather some brief and certain point, to be stored in the little chest of memory, from which something may afterwards be drawn when the occasion requires. It is also necessary frequently to repeat this and to bring it back from the belly of memory to the palate, [Col. 0773B] lest it grow obsolete through a long interruption.

Therefore, I ask you, reader, do not rejoice too greatly if you have read much, but if you have understood much; and not merely understood, but have also been able to retain it. Otherwise, neither reading much nor understanding is of profit. Hence I recall that I said above that those who devote themselves to learning need both natural ability and memory.

## CHAPTER XIII. On discipline.

When a certain wise man was asked about the method and form of learning, he replied: “A humble mind, eagerness in inquiry, a quiet life, silent investigation, poverty, a foreign land: these commonly unlock certain obscure matters for the reader.” I think he had heard the saying, “Conduct adorns knowledge,” and therefore joins precepts for living to precepts for reading, so that the reader may recognize both the manner [Col. 0773C] of his life and the method of his study. Knowledge which an unchaste life stains is without praise. Therefore one who seeks knowledge must take the utmost care not to neglect discipline.

## CHAPTER XIV. On humility.

The beginning of discipline is humility. Though its lessons are many, these three especially concern the reader. First, that he should regard no branch of knowledge and no writing as worthless; second, that he should blush to learn from no one; third, that when he has acquired knowledge, he should not despise others.

Many have been deceived by wishing to appear wise before their time. Thus they burst forth into a swelling of pride, so that they begin both to pretend to be what they are not [Col. 0773D] and to be ashamed of what they are; and they recede further from wisdom precisely because they wish not to be wise but to be thought wise. I have known many such persons: though they still need the first elements, they consider themselves worthy to attend only to the highest matters; and they think they become great merely if they have read the writings, or heard the words, of great and wise men.

“We have seen them,” they say; “we have read from them. They often used to speak with us. Those eminent and famous men knew us.” But would that no one knew me, while I knew all things! You boast that you have seen Plato, not understood him; I suppose it is now beneath your dignity to listen to me. I am not Plato, nor have I deserved to see Plato. Plato himself is enough for you: you have drunk from the fountain of philosophy—but would that you still thirsted! A king drinks from an earthen vessel after golden cups. What are you ashamed of? You have heard Plato; you will hear Chrysippus too.

It is said proverbially: “What you do not know, perhaps a little ass knows.” No one has been granted to know everything; nor, conversely, has anyone failed by nature to receive some spiritual capacity. Therefore the prudent reader gladly listens to everyone and reads everything; he despises neither writing, person, nor teaching. He seeks impartially from all people whatever he sees lacking in himself; and he considers not how much he knows, but how much he does not know. Hence they cite this Platonic saying: “I would rather modestly learn what belongs to another than shamelessly put forward what is my own.” Why are you ashamed to learn and not ashamed to be ignorant? That shame is greater than the other. Or why do you aspire to the heights when you lie at the bottom? Consider rather what your strength is able to bear. He proceeds most fittingly [Col. 0774B] who proceeds in due order. Some, while wishing to make a great leap, fall into a precipice. Therefore do not hurry excessively: in this manner you will reach wisdom sooner.

Learn gladly from everyone what you do not know, because humility can make common to you what nature made proper to each person. You will be wiser than all if you are willing to learn from all. Those who receive from everyone are richer than everyone. Finally, regard no branch of knowledge as worthless, for every kind of knowledge is good. If you have leisure, despise no writing—or at least no law—for even if you gain nothing, you will lose nothing, especially since, in my judgment, there is no writing that does not propose something worth seeking, if it is treated in an appropriate place and order; none which does not contain something special, which the diligent investigator of words may gather elsewhere as not found before—something the rarer, the more pleasing [Col. 0774C].

Yet no good thing is good which excludes a better thing. If you cannot read everything, read the more useful things. Even if you can read everything, nevertheless equal labor should not be bestowed on all things. Some writings should be read so that they are not unknown; others, so that they are not unheard of, because we sometimes judge more highly what we have not heard, and a thing whose fruit is known is more easily evaluated. You can now see how necessary this humility is for you: that you despise no knowledge and gladly learn from all.

Likewise, when you begin to have some understanding, it is advantageous for you not to despise others. This vice of pride comes to some people because they inspect their own knowledge too diligently; and, when they seem to themselves to be something, they suppose that others whom they do not know neither are such nor could have become such. Hence too comes the bubbling up of certain trifling talkers, nowadays boasting from I know not where, who accuse the earlier Fathers of simplicity and believe that wisdom was born with them and will die with them. They say that the divine utterances have such a simple manner of speech that it is unnecessary to listen to teachers concerning them; anyone, they say, can sufficiently penetrate the mysteries of truth by his own natural ability. They wrinkle their noses and make grimaces at readers of divinity, and do not understand that they insult God, whose words they proclaim simple indeed in fair-sounding phrase, but tasteless in perverse meaning. It is not my counsel to imitate such people.

For a good reader ought to be humble [Col. 0775A] and gentle, altogether free from empty cares and the enticements of pleasures; diligent and industrious, so that he may gladly learn from everyone; never presumptuous about his own knowledge; fleeing authors of perverse doctrine as though from poisons; learning to examine a matter long before judging it; learning, or seeking, not to appear learned but to be learned; loving the understood sayings of the wise and striving always to hold them before his eyes as a mirror of his own face. If perhaps some more obscure passages do not admit his understanding, he should not at once burst into reproach, believing that nothing is good except what he himself has been able to understand. This is the humility of disciplined readers.

## CHAPTER XV. On eagerness in inquiry.

Eagerness in inquiry pertains to practice, in which [Col. 0775B] the reader needs exhortation more than instruction. For whoever diligently considers what the ancients endured for love of wisdom, what memorable monuments of their virtue they left to posterity, will see that however great his own diligence may be, it is inferior. Some trod honors underfoot; others cast away riches; others rejoiced when wrongs were inflicted upon them; others despised punishments; others, abandoning human society and penetrating the innermost retreats and solitudes of the wilderness, dedicated themselves alone to philosophy, in order that they might be freer for contemplation because they had subjected their minds to none of the desires which commonly impede the path of virtue.

The philosopher Parmenides is said to have sat for fifteen years upon an Egyptian rock. Prometheus, because of his excessive concern for meditation, is remembered as having been exposed to a vulture on Mount Caucasus [Col. 0775C]. Because they knew that the true good lies hidden not in human estimation but in a pure conscience, and that those who cling to perishable things and fail to recognize their good are no longer human beings, they demonstrated by the very distance of their locations how greatly they differed from others in mind and understanding, lest one dwelling contain those whom one purpose did not unite.

Someone said to a philosopher: “Do you not see that people mock you?” And he replied: “They mock me, and asses mock them.” Consider, if you can, how highly he valued being praised by those by whom he did not fear to be blamed. Of another it is likewise recorded that, after all the studies of disciplines and refinements of arts, he went down to the work of a potter; and when they were praising the master of another disciple, they boasted among other things that he was not without skill in shoemaking [Col. 0775D].

I would therefore wish this diligence to be found in our readers, so that wisdom might never grow old in them. Abishag the Shunammite alone warmed the aged David (III Kings 1), because love of wisdom does not abandon its lover even when the body is withering. Almost all bodily powers change in old people, and, while wisdom alone increases, all the rest diminish. For the old age of those who have trained their youth in honorable arts [variant: deeds] becomes more learned with age, more seasoned by experience, wiser with the passage of time, and reaps the sweetest fruits of former studies.

Hence Themistocles, that wise man of Greece, when he saw himself dying at the full age of one hundred and seven years, is reported to have said that “he grieved that he was leaving life when he had begun to be wise.” Plato died writing at eighty-one years of age. Socrates completed ninety-nine years in the labor and pain of teaching and writing. I pass over the other philosophers—Pythagoras, Democritus, Xenocrates, Zeno, and the Eleatic—who flourished in the studies of wisdom even at an advanced age.

I turn to the poets: Homer, Hesiod, Simonides, Tersilochus, who, when old, sang something swan-like and sweeter than usual as death drew near. When Sophocles, after extreme old age and neglect of his household estate, was accused of madness by his own family, he recited to the judge the play of *Oedipus* which he had recently written, and gave such an example of wisdom in an age now broken [Col. 0776B] that he turned the severity of the courts into favor for the theatre. Nor is it remarkable, since even Cato the Censor, the most eloquent man of the Roman people, neither blushed nor despaired of learning Greek letters in old age. Certainly Homer relates that speech flowed more sweetly from the tongue of Nestor, already old and nearly decrepit.

Observe, then, how greatly they loved wisdom, since not even decrepit age recalled them from its pursuit. This great love of wisdom and such abundance in old men is fittingly also inferred from the interpretation of the name mentioned above. For *Abishag* is interpreted “my father is superfluous,” or “the roaring of my father,” by which it is shown that an exceedingly abundant thunderclap, beyond human speech, abides in the meanings of the divine discourse. For “superfluous” in this place signifies fullness, not redundancy. Moreover, *Shunammite* is called “scarlet” in our language, which can quite fittingly signify the fervor of wisdom.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the four remaining precepts.

The four following precepts are arranged alternately, so that one always pertains to discipline and the other to practice.

## CHAPTER XVII. On quiet.

Quietness of life, whether interior—so that the mind does not range abroad through unlawful desires—or exterior—so that leisure and opportunity may be available for honorable and useful studies—belongs in both respects to discipline.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On investigation.

Investigation, that is, meditation, pertains to practice [Col. 0776D]. Investigation appears, however, to be included under eagerness in inquiry. If that is true, it is repeated superfluously, since it was enumerated in the preceding part. But it should be known that there is this difference between the two: eagerness in inquiry signifies the urgency of work, while investigation signifies diligence in meditation. Labor and love accomplish the work; care and wakefulness produce counsel. In labor there is the act of doing; in love, that of completing; in care, that of providing beforehand; in wakefulness, that of attending.

These are the four attendants who carry the litter of philology, because they exercise the mind over which wisdom presides. The chair of philology is indeed the seat of wisdom, which is said to be carried on their support because it advances by exercising itself in these things. Hence it is fittingly said that young men [Col. 0777A] hold the litter at the front because of their strength—namely, *philos kai kopos* (φίλος καὶ κόπος), that is, love and labor—because they accomplish the outward work; at the rear are young women—namely, *epimeleia kai agrypnia* (ἐπιμέλεια καὶ ἀγρυπνία), which are translated care or diligence and wakefulness—because they produce counsel inwardly in secret.

There are some who think that by the chair of philology the human body is signified, over which the rational soul presides, and which four servants carry—that is, the four elements compose it. Of these, the two upper elements, fire and air, are masculine both in activity and in name; the two lower, earth and water, are feminine.

## CHAPTER XIX. On frugality.

They also wish to commend frugality to readers—that is, not pursuing superfluities—which especially pertains to discipline [Col. 0777B]. For, as the saying goes, a fat belly does not produce a keen mind. But what will the scholars of our own time be able to answer to this, who disdain to practice moderation not only in their studies, but even labor to appear richer than they are [Col. 0778A]? No longer does anyone boast of what he has learned, but of what he has spent. Yet perhaps they wish to imitate their teachers, concerning whom I cannot find what I might say worthily.

## CHAPTER XX. On exile.

Lastly, a foreign land is set down, which likewise exercises a person. The whole world is an exile to those who pursue philosophy. Yet, as someone says:

> I know not by what sweetness one’s native soil  
> Draws all, and does not permit them to forget itself.

It is a great beginning of virtue when the mind, trained little by little, learns first to exchange these visible and transitory things, so that afterwards it may be able even to abandon them. He is still delicate whose native land is sweet to him. But he is already strong for whom every soil is a native land [Col. 0778B]; and he is perfect for whom the entire world is exile. The first has fixed his love upon the world; the second has scattered it; the third has extinguished it. I have been an exile from childhood, and I know with what sorrow the mind sometimes leaves the confined ground of a poor cottage, and with what freedom it afterwards despises marble houses and panelled roofs.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0777]

Its chapters are these:

CHAPTER I. On the study of the divine Scriptures.—CHAPTER II. On the order and number of the books.—CHAPTER III. On the authors of the divine books.—CHAPTER IV. On the library.—CHAPTER V. On the translators.—CHAPTER VI. On the authors of the New Testament.—CHAPTER VII. What is apocryphal.—CHAPTER VIII. The rationale of the divine books.—CHAPTER IX. On the New Testament.—CHAPTER X. On the Gospel canons.—CHAPTER XI. On the canons of councils.—CHAPTER XII. That there are four principal synods.—CHAPTER XIII. Who made libraries.—CHAPTER XIV. Which writings are authentic.—CHAPTER XV. Which writings are apocryphal.—CHAPTER XVI. Etymologies of certain terms relevant to reading.

## CHAPTER I. On the study of the divine Scriptures.

[Col. 0777C]

Writings which speak either of God or of invisible goods ought not all, nor they alone, to be called divine. In the books of the Gentiles, indeed, we find many things written with sufficiently plausible reasoning about the eternity of God, the immortality of souls, the everlasting rewards of virtues and the punishments of the wicked; yet no one doubts that such books are unworthy of this designation. Again, when we run through the sequence of the Old and New Testaments, we see a fabric almost wholly woven concerning the condition of the present life and things accomplished in time; and we see only rarely some matters concerning the sweetness of eternal goods and the joys of heavenly life set forth openly. Nevertheless, the Catholic faith customarily calls these writings divine.

The writings of philosophers, like a whitewashed mud wall, shine outwardly with the brilliance of eloquence [Col. 0777D]. Whenever they put forward an appearance of truth, they conceal the mud of error by mixing in falsehood, as though by applying a coat of color over it. Divine utterances, by contrast, are most fittingly compared to a honeycomb: because of the simplicity of their speech they seem dry, yet within they are full of sweetness. It is therefore clear that they have deservedly received such a designation, since they alone are found so free from the contagion of falsehood [Col. 0778C] that they are proved to contain nothing contrary to truth.

“Divine Scriptures are those which the universal authority of the Church has received, as composed by adherents of the Catholic faith, to be counted among the divine books and retained for reading in support of that same faith. There are besides very many other little works written at various times by religious and wise men. Although these have not been approved by the authority of the universal Church, nevertheless, because they do not differ from the Catholic faith and teach certain useful things, they too are counted among divine utterances. Perhaps we shall show them better by enumerating them than by defining them.

## CHAPTER II. On the order and number of the books.

All divine Scripture is contained in two Testaments, namely the Old and the New. Each Testament [Col. 0778D] is distinguished into three orders. The Old Testament contains the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa; the New, the Gospel, the Apostles, and the Fathers.

The first order of the Old Testament, namely the Law, which the Hebrews call *Thorath* [Torah], has the Pentateuch, that is, the five books of Moses. In this order the first is *Bresith* [Bereshit], which is Genesis; the second, *Hellesmoth* [Shemoth], which is Exodus; the third, *Vajetra* [Vayyiqra], which is Leviticus; the fourth, *Vajedaber* [Vaydebar], which is Numbers; the fifth, *Adabarim* [Devarim], which is Deuteronomy.

The second order is that of the Prophets; it contains eight volumes. The first is *Josue bennun*, that is, “Joshua son of Nun,” also called Joshua, Jesus, and Jesus son of Nave; the second, *Sophtim*, which is the Book of Judges; the third, Samuel, which is First and Second Kings; the fourth, *Malachim*, which is Third and Fourth Kings; the fifth, Isaiah; the sixth, Jeremiah; the seventh, Ezekiel; the eighth, *Thareasra*, which is the Twelve Prophets.

Then the third order has eight books [sic; nine are listed]. The first is Job; the second, David; the third, *Masloth* [Col. 0779B], which in Greek means “parables” and in Latin “proverbs,” namely Solomon’s; the fourth, *Coelech*, which is Ecclesiastes; the fifth, *Sira Sirim*, that is, the Song of Songs; the sixth, Daniel; the seventh, *dabra iamin*, which is Chronicles; the eighth, Ezra; the ninth, Esther. Thus they are twenty-two in number altogether.

There are, besides, certain other books, such as the Wisdom of Solomon, the book of Jesus son of Sirach, Judith, Tobit, and the books of Maccabees. They are indeed read, but are not written in the canon.

The first order of the New Testament has four Gospel volumes: those of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The second likewise has four: the fourteen Epistles of Paul, joined together in a single volume, the Catholic Epistles, the Apocalypse, and the Acts of the Apostles. [Col. 0779C] In the third order the first place belongs to the Decretals, which we call *canons*, that is, rules; then come the writings of the holy Fathers and doctors—Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, Ambrose, Isidore, Origen, Bede, and many other orthodox writers—which are so innumerable that they cannot be counted. From this it surely appears how great was their fervor for the Christian faith, for whose defense they left behind so many and such great works for posterity to remember. Hence our own sloth is also rebuked, since we are unable even to read what they were able to dictate.

In these orders the correspondence of the two Testaments appears especially in this: as after the Law came the Prophets, and after the Prophets the Hagiographa, so after the Gospel came the Apostles, and after the Apostles the Doctors in orderly succession. And by a wonderful disposition of divine providence it has been arranged that, although complete and perfect truth is found in every individual part, none is superfluous [Col. 0779D]. We have briefly touched upon the order and number of the divine books, so that the reader may recognize the subject assigned to him.

## CHAPTER III. On the authors of the divine books.

Moses wrote the five books of the Law. Joshua, after whom the Book of Joshua is named, is believed to have been its author. They say that the Book of Judges was published by Samuel. Samuel himself wrote the first part of the Book of Samuel; David wrote the remainder to the end. Jeremiah first collected *Malachim* into one volume, for previously it had been scattered through the histories of the individual kings. Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel each made the books [Col. 0780A] inscribed with their names. The Book of the Twelve Prophets is likewise marked beforehand by the names of its authors: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. They are called the Minor Prophets because their discourses are brief, and so they are included in one volume. Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, the four Major Prophets, are distinguished in their individual volumes.

Some believe that Moses wrote the Book of Job; others, one of the prophets; some, Job himself. David produced the Book of Psalms, but Ezra later arranged it as it now stands and added the titles. Solomon composed Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. Daniel was the author of his own book. The Book of Ezra is designated by its author’s title, and its text contains together the discourses of Ezra himself and Nehemiah. Ezra composed the Book of Esther.

The Book of Wisdom is nowhere found among the Hebrews, and its very style has more the flavor of Greek eloquence. Certain Jews affirm it to be Philo’s. The book *Ecclesiasticus* was certainly composed by Jesus son of Sirach of Jerusalem, grandson of Jesus the high priest (whom Zechariah mentions). It is found among the Hebrews, but is reckoned among the apocrypha. By whom Judith, Tobit, and the books of Maccabees were written is entirely unknown, although, as Jerome testifies, the second book of Maccabees is shown to be more Greek in character.

## CHAPTER IV. On the library.

The name *bibliotheca* comes from Greek, because books are stored there [Col. 0780C]. For *bibliōn* (βιβλίων) means “of books,” and *thēkē* (θήκη) means “repository.” Ezra the scribe repaired the library of the Old Testament after the Law had been burned by the Chaldeans, when the Jews returned to Jerusalem. Inspired by the divine Spirit, he corrected all the volumes of the Law and Prophets that had been corrupted by the Gentiles, and constituted the whole Old Testament in twenty-two books, so that there might be as many books in the Law as there are letters.

Now five letters are doubled among the Hebrews: *caph*, *mem*, *nun*, *phe*, and *sade*. They write the beginnings and middles of words differently with these letters than their endings. Hence five books are considered double by many: Samuel, *Malachim*, *dabre iamin*, Ezra, and Jeremiah with his *cynoth*, that is, Lamentations [Col. 0780D].

## CHAPTER V. On translators.

The translators of the Old Testament are, first, the Seventy, whom Ptolemy, surnamed Philadelphus, king of Egypt and a most discerning patron of every kind of learning, caused to translate the Scriptures of the Old Testament from the Hebrew tongue into Greek. In the pursuit of libraries he emulated Pisistratus, tyrant of the Athenians, who first established a library among the Greeks, and Seleucus, Nicanor, Alexander, and the other predecessors who had devoted themselves to wisdom. He brought into his library not only Gentile writings but divine books as well, so that in his time seventy thousand books were found at Alexandria. He requested the Old Testament Scriptures from Eleazar the high priest and had them translated.

But, though they were each separated into individual cells, they translated all things through the Holy Spirit in such a way that nothing was found in any one of their copies differing from the others even in word order. Therefore their translation is one; but Jerome says that no credence should be given to this account. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion constitute the second, third, and fourth translations. The first of these, Aquila, was a Jew; Symmachus and Theodotion were Ebionite heretics. Nevertheless, after the Seventy Translators, usage prevailed that the Greek Churches received and read their copies. The fifth is the common version, whose author is unknown; consequently it especially claimed for itself the designation “fifth.” The sixth and seventh are Origen’s, whose copies Eusebius and Pamphilus published. The eighth is Jerome’s, deservedly preferred to the others, for it adheres more closely to the words and is clearer in its meaning.

## CHAPTER VI. On the authors of the New Testament.

Many wrote Gospels, but some, without the Holy Spirit, attempted rather to arrange a narrative than to weave the truth of history. Therefore the holy Fathers, taught by the Holy Spirit, accepted only four as authoritative and rejected the rest: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, corresponding to the four rivers of Paradise, the four bars of the Ark, and the four living creatures in Ezekiel.

Matthew first wrote his Gospel in Hebrew; Mark second, in Greek; Luke third, the most learned of all the Evangelists in Greek speech, wrote the Gospel in Greece—as was fitting for a physician—for Bishop Theophilus, to whom he also wrote the Acts of the Apostles; John, fourth and last, wrote his Gospel. Paul wrote fourteen Epistles: ten to churches and four to individuals. Most people, however, say that the last, to the Hebrews, is not Paul’s; some say it was written by Barnabas, while others suppose Clement to be its author. There are seven Catholic Epistles: one of James, two of Peter, three of John, and one of Jude. John the Apostle wrote the Apocalypse when banished in exile to the island of Patmos.

## CHAPTER VII. That the rest are apocryphal, and what apocryphal means.

These are the writers of the sacred books, who, speaking through the Holy Spirit, wrote precepts and a rule of life for our instruction [Col. 0781D]. Apart from these, other volumes are called apocryphal. They are called *apocryphal*, that is, secret, because they are open to doubt. “For their origin is hidden, and it is not clear to the Fathers from whom the authority of true Scriptures has come down to us by a most certain and well-known succession.” Though some truth is found in these apocrypha, yet because of their many falsehoods they have no canonical authority. They are rightly judged not to be writings of those to whom they are ascribed. For many works are put forward by heretics under the names of prophets, and more recent ones under the names of apostles; all of these, under the designation apocrypha, have been removed from canonical authority after careful examination.

## CHAPTER VIII. The rationale of the divine books.

[Col. 0782A]

The Pentateuch is so called from its five books. For πέντε in Greek means “five,” and τεῦχος is called a “volume.” Genesis is so called because it contains the generation of the world. Exodus, from the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt. Leviticus, because it sets forth the ministries of the Levites and the various kinds of sacrifices. The book is called Numbers because it enumerates the tribes which departed from Egypt, and the forty-two encampments through the wilderness. Δεύτερος is a Greek word of three syllables and means “second”; νόμος means “law.” Hence it is called Deuteronomy, as it were a second law, because it repeats matters more fully set forth in the preceding three books.

In the book of Joshua, whom the Hebrews call Joshua ben Nun, the Promised Land is divided among the people. [Col. 0782B] The Book of Judges is named after the leaders who judged the people of Israel before there were kings among that people. Some attach the history of Ruth to this under a single volume. The book of Samuel is so named because it describes his birth, priesthood, and deeds. Although it also contains the history of Saul and David, both are nevertheless referred to Samuel, because he anointed them both. *Malach* in Hebrew is translated “of kings” in Latin; hence it is called *Malachim*, because it sets forth in order the kings of Judah and of the Israelite people, and their deeds.

Isaiah published his book more as an evangelist than as a prophet; its entire composition proceeds in the prose of eloquence. The Song, however, runs in hexameter and pentameter verse. Jeremiah likewise composed his book together with the *Threni*, which we call Lamentations, because they are used in sad and funeral matters. In these he composed a fourfold alphabet in differing metres. The first two are written, as it were, in Sapphic metre, because a heroic clause concludes three verses connected with one another and beginning with one and the same letter. [Col. 0782C] The third alphabet is written in trimeters, and its three verses begin with each set of three letters. The fourth alphabet is like the first and second. Ezekiel has obscure matters at its beginning and end. The Twelve Prophets constitute one volume.

Among the Hebrews, the beginning and end of the book of Job are composed in prose. But its middle, from the place where he says, “May the day perish on which I was born” (Job 3), to the place where he says, “Therefore I reproach myself and repent” (Job 42), [Col. 0782D] all runs in heroic metre. The book of Psalms is called *psalterium* in Greek, *nabla* in Hebrew, and “instrument” in Latin. It is called a psaltery because, when one prophet sang to the psaltery, the choir responded in harmony. They comprise this book in five divisions and one volume of psalms. David composed the psalms, but Ezra later arranged them. Moreover, all the psalms, the Lamentations of Jeremiah, and nearly all the songs of Scripture are metrically composed among the Hebrews, as Jerome, Origen, Josephus, and Eusebius of Caesarea testify. For in the [metres of] Quintus Flaccus among the Latins and Pindar among the Greeks, some poems run in iambics, others resplend in Sapphics, blazing forth in trimeter or tetrameter. [Col. 0783A]

Scripture teaches most plainly that Solomon was called by three names: *Jedidiah*, that is, “beloved of the Lord,” because the Lord loved him; *Qoheleth*, that is, “Ecclesiastes.” Now one who gathers an assembly—that is, a church—is called *Ecclesiastes* in Greek; we may call him a preacher, one who speaks not especially to a single person but to the whole assembly of the people. Moreover, he was called “peaceful,” because there was peace in his reign. Accordingly, in keeping with the number of his names he published three volumes.

The first, called in Hebrew *Massoth*, in Greek *Parables*, and in Latin *Proverbs*, is so called because in it he displayed figures of speech and images of truth under comparative resemblance. These parables, indeed, from the place where he says, “Who shall find a valiant woman?” [Col. 0783B] (Prov. 31), are woven according to the alphabet, like the Lamentations of Jeremiah and certain other songs of Scripture. The second, called *Qoheleth* in Hebrew, *Ecclesiastes* in Greek, and “Preacher” in Latin, is so called because its discourse is directed not particularly to one person, as in Proverbs, but generally to all, as though to the entire congregation and Church. The third is *Shir ha-Shirim*, “Song of Songs,” which is like an epithalamium, that is, a nuptial song of Christ and the Church.

In Proverbs he teaches the little child and, as it were, trains him by maxims in duties; hence his discourse is repeatedly addressed to a son. In Ecclesiastes, however, he instructs the man of mature age not to suppose that anything among worldly things is permanent, but that everything we behold is transitory and brief. Finally, [Col. 0783C] he joins the man now perfected, having trodden down the world and been made ready, to the embraces of the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs. Without doubt philosophers also train their followers in an order not far removed from this course of instruction: first they teach ethics, then expound physics, and bring one whom they see to have advanced in these as far as theology.

Daniel is reckoned among the Hagiographa by the Hebrews, not among the prophets. The Catholic Church does not read him according to the Seventy Interpreters, because that version differs greatly from the truth. Daniel, especially, and the prophet Obadiah, and one part of Jeremiah, are written in Hebrew letters but in the Chaldaean language. Job too has a very close affinity with the Arabic language. Daniel among the Hebrews has neither the history of Susanna, nor [Col. 0783D] the hymn of the three youths, nor the tales of Bel and the dragon.

It is called Paralipomenon in Greek, which we may call “of things omitted” or “of things remaining,” because matters omitted or not fully related in the Law or the books of Kings are repeated in this book summarily and briefly. In Hebrew it is called *Dibre ha-Yamim*, which means “Words of Days”; more significantly, we may call it a Chronicle of the whole sacred history. The fourth book of Ezra is that in which the discourses of Ezra himself and Nehemiah are contained under one volume. The second, third, and fourth are apocryphal.

The book entitled the Wisdom of Solomon is called Wisdom because it clearly expresses the coming and passion of Christ, who is the Wisdom of the Father. The book of Jesus son of Sirach is called Ecclesiasticus because it is devoted, with great care and method, to the discipline of religious conduct for the whole Church. Concerning these two Jerome says as follows:

> There is current the *Paranetos* of Jesus son of Sirach, and another pseudonymous book entitled the Wisdom of Solomon. Of these I found the former in Hebrew, bearing not the title *Ecclesiasticus* among us but *Parables*. Attached to it were Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, so that they might be equal to Solomon’s writings not only in number of books but also in the kind of their subject matter. The second is nowhere among the Hebrews, for its very style has the savor of Greek eloquence. Some of the ancient writers maintain that it is by the Jew Philo.

Thus, just as the Church indeed reads Judith, Tobit, and the books of Maccabees, [Col. 0784B] but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures, so it reads these two volumes for the edification of the people, not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical doctrines. Therefore, just as there are twenty-two letters by which we write in Hebrew all that we speak, and by whose beginnings human speech is comprehended, so twenty-two volumes are counted, by which, as by letters and first elements, the still tender and nursing infancy of the righteous man is instructed in the teaching of God. Some, counting separately among the Hagiographa the history of Ruth and the Lamentations of Jeremiah, and adding these two to the preceding twenty-two, reckon twenty-four books of the Old Law, after the figure and number of the twenty-four elders who worship the Lamb in the Apocalypse.

## CHAPTER IX. On the New Testament

[Col. 0784C]

Just as all the writing of the Old Testament may be called Law, though specifically the five books of Moses are called the Law, so the whole New Testament may generally be called Gospel; yet these four volumes in particular—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—in which the deeds and sayings of the Savior are plainly explained, deserved to be called Gospels. Gospel means “good news,” because it promises eternal goods, not earthly happiness, as does the Old Testament according to the literal understanding.

## CHAPTER X. On the Gospel Canons

Ammonius of Alexandria [Col. 0784D] first devised the Gospel Canons; Eusebius of Caesarea, following him, composed them more fully. They were made so that by them we might find and know which similar or distinctive things the other evangelists said. They are ten in number. The first contains the sections in which all four—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—said the same things. The second, those in which three said the same: Matthew, Mark, and Luke. The third, those in which three said the same: Matthew, Luke, and John. The fourth, those in which three said the same: Matthew, Mark, and John. The fifth, those in which two said the same: Mark and Luke. The sixth, those in which two said the same: Matthew and Mark. The seventh, those in which two said the same: Matthew and John. The eighth, those in which two said the same: Luke and Mark. The ninth, those in which two said the same: Luke and John. [Col. 0785A] The tenth contains those matters peculiar to each of them.

Their explanation is this. Beside each evangelist is placed a number attached to the sections; beneath these numbers is a small table marked below which indicates in which canon the number under which the table stands has been placed. For example, if it is the first table, it is in the first canon; if the second, in the second; if the third, in the third; and so in order you will proceed to the tenth. Therefore, if, on opening any Gospel, you wish to know which of the other evangelists have said similar things, take the adjacent section number and look for the same number in the canon indicated by it. There you will find who said what; and then, in the body of the Gospels, you will find the passages sought, indicated by those numbers, [Col. 0785B] in each Gospel, to have said the same matters.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Canons of Councils

*Canon* is interpreted from Greek into Latin as “rule.” A rule is so called because it guides rightly and never draws one elsewhere. Others have said that it is called a rule either because it governs, because it supplies a norm for right living, or because it corrects what is crooked and perverse. The canons of general councils began in the time of Constantine. For in the preceding years, while persecution raged, there was scarcely any opportunity for instructing the peoples; consequently Christianity was divided into various heresies, because bishops had no means [another reading: permission] of assembling together except in the time of the aforesaid emperor. He himself gave Christians the freedom to assemble openly. Under [Col. 0785C] him also, the holy Fathers, gathered in the Council of Nicaea from the whole world, handed down, according to the evangelical and apostolic faith, the Creed after the apostles.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Four Principal Synods

Among other councils there are four venerable synods which principally embrace the entire faith, like the Gospels or like the four rivers of Paradise. The first, the Synod of Nicaea, of 318 bishops, was held under the Emperor Constantine. In it was condemned the blasphemy of Arian faithlessness, by which Arius himself asserted an inequality within the Holy Trinity; and the same holy synod defined through the Creed that God the Son is consubstantial with God the Father.

The second synod, of 150 Fathers, was assembled at Constantinople under the elder Theodosius. Condemning Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God, it showed that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son, giving the form of the Creed which the whole confession of Greeks and Latins proclaims in the churches.

The third synod, the first at Ephesus, of 200 bishops, was issued under the younger Emperor Theodosius. It condemned Nestorius by a just anathema for asserting two persons in Christ, showing that our Lord Jesus Christ is one person in two natures.

The fourth synod, that of Chalcedon, of 630 [Col. 0786A] priests, was held under the Emperor Marcian. In it, by one judgment of the Fathers, it condemned beforehand Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who declared that the Word of God and flesh have one nature, and his defender Dioscorus, a certain bishop of Alexandria, and also again Nestorius himself together with the remaining heretics. The same synod proclaimed that Christ God was born of the Virgin in such a way that in him they confess the substance both of the divine and of the human nature.

These are the four principal synods, proclaiming most fully the doctrine of the faith.
