Yet any councils which the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, established remain confirmed in all their force after the authority of these four; their acts are set down in this work. *Synod* is interpreted from Greek as “company” or “assembly.” The name *council*, however, is derived from Roman custom. For when cases were being heard, all came together and considered them with a common intention. [Col. 0786B] Hence *concilium* is said to come from common intention, as though *consilium*. For the eyelashes are coverings of the eyes. Hence also *considium* becomes *consilium*, with the letter *d* changing into *l*. An assembly is a meeting or gathering from coming together, that is, from gathering into one. Hence it is also called a convention, just as convention, assembly, and council derive from the association of many into one.

*Epistle* is interpreted in Greek as “a thing sent” in Latin. The canonical epistles—that is, regular ones—are also called catholic, that is, universal, because they were written generally not merely to one people or city but to all nations. The Acts of the Apostles set forth the beginnings of the Christian faith among the nations and the history of the Church at its birth, and are called apostolic. Apocalypse is interpreted from Greek into Latin as “revelation,” [Col. 0786C] in accordance with what John says: “The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave to make manifest to his servant John” (Apoc. 1).

## CHAPTER XIII. Who Made Libraries

Among us, the martyr Pamphilus, whose life Eusebius of Caesarea wrote, strove to equal Pisistratus in zeal for a sacred library. For he had nearly thirty thousand volumes in his library. Jerome also and Gennadius, seeking ecclesiastical writers throughout the world, traced them in order and comprised their studies in a single catalogue-volume.

## CHAPTER XIV. Which Writings Are Authoritative

Among our writers in Greek, Origen surpassed both Greeks and Latins in the number of his works produced through labor on the Scriptures. Indeed, Jerome confesses that he had read six thousand of his books. Yet Augustine surpassed the efforts of all these men by his genius and learning. For he wrote so much that no one could accurately either write out all his books by day and night, or even read them. Others too, Catholic men, wrote many distinguished works: Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria; Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; Basil, bishop of Cappadocia; Gregory the Theologian; Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus; Ambrose, bishop of Milan; Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria; John, bishop of Constantinople; Cyril, bishop of Alexandria; Pope Leo; Proclus; Isidore of Seville; Bede; Cyprian, martyr and [Col. 0787A] bishop of Carthage; Jerome the presbyter; Origen, whose writings the Church neither wholly rejects nor receives in every respect; Orosius, Sedulius, Prudentius, Juvencus, Arator, and Rufinus, who published many books and translated certain Scriptures.

But because blessed Jerome criticized him in some matters concerning freedom of the will, we ought to hold the views held by Jerome. Gelasius likewise made five books against Nestorius and Eutyches, and treatises in the manner of Ambrose. He also made two books against Arius; he likewise composed prefaces to the sacraments, prayers, and epistles on the faith. Dionysius the Areopagite, appointed bishop of the Corinthians, left many volumes produced by his genius. Likewise the Chronicles of Eusebius of Caesarea, and the books of the same author’s Ecclesiastical History: although [Col. 0787B] he was lukewarm in the first book of his narrative, and afterwards wrote one book in praise and defense of the schismatic Origen, nevertheless the Church does not reject him altogether because of the knowledge of individual matters which is useful for instruction. Cassiodorus too wrote a sufficiently useful work in his exposition of the Psalms. There are still many others whose names I omit here.

## CHAPTER XV. Which Writings Are Apocryphal

The itinerary in the name of the apostle Peter, called that of Saint Clement, in eight books: apocryphal.

The Acts of the apostle Andrew: apocryphal.

The Acts in the name of Thomas: apocryphal.

Gospels in the name of the apostle Barnabas: apocryphal.

Gospels in the name of the apostle Thomas: apocryphal.

Gospels in the name of the apostle Andrew: apocryphal.

The Gospels falsified by Lucian: apocryphal.

The Gospels falsified by Titius: apocryphal.

The Book on the Infancy of the Savior: apocryphal.

The Book on the Nativity of the Savior and Saint Mary, or on her midwife: apocryphal.

The book called *The Shepherd*: apocryphal.

All books made by Leutius, disciple of the devil: apocryphal.

The book called *Foundation*: apocryphal.

The book called *Treasure*: apocryphal.

The book on the Daughters of Adam, or Genesis: apocryphal.

The cento concerning Christ, put together in Virgilian verses: apocryphal.

The book called the Acts of Thecla and Paul: apocryphal.

The book called that of Nepos: apocryphal.

The Book of Proverbs written by heretics and marked with the name of Saint Sixtus: apocryphal.

The Revelation called that of Paul: apocryphal.

The Revelation called that of the apostle Thomas: apocryphal.

The Revelation called that of Stephen: apocryphal. [Col. 0787D]

The book called the Passing of Saint Mary: apocryphal.

The book called the Penitence of Adam: apocryphal.

The book in the name of the giant Diogias, who, it is reported by heretics, fought with a dragon after the flood: apocryphal.

The book called the Testament of Job: apocryphal.

The book called the Penitence of Origen: apocryphal.

The book called the Penitence of Cyprian: apocryphal.

The books called Jannes and Mambres: apocryphal.

The book called the Lot of the Apostles: apocryphal.

The Book of Lusan: apocryphal.

The Book of Canons of the Apostles: apocryphal.

The book *Physiologus*, written by heretics and falsely marked with the name of blessed Ambrose: apocryphal.

The History of Eusebius Pamphilus: apocryphal.

The minor works of Tertullian, or Africanus: apocryphal.

The minor works of Posthumianus and Gallus: apocryphal.

The minor works of Montanus and [Col. 0788A] Priscilla and Maximilla: apocryphal.

All minor works of Faustus the Manichaean: apocryphal.

The minor works of another Clement of Alexandria: apocryphal.

The minor works of Cassian, presbyter of Gaul: apocryphal.

The minor works of Victorinus of Poitiers: apocryphal.

The minor works of Faustus of Riez: apocryphal.

The minor works of Frumentius: apocryphal.

The letter of Jesus to Abgar: apocryphal.

The Passion of Cyricus and Julitta: apocryphal.

The Passion of George: apocryphal.

Writings called Solomon’s *Contradiction*: apocryphal.

All phylacteries, written not by an angel, as they falsely allege, but rather by a demon: apocryphal.

These and similar writings, which Simon Magus, Nicolaus, Cerinthus, Marcion, Basilides, Chion, Paul of Samosata also, Photinus and Bonosus, who fell away through a similar error, Montanus too with his most obscene followers, Apollinaris, Valentinus, Manichaeus, [Col. 0788B] Faustus, Sabellius, Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Novatus, Fabatius, Calixtus, Donatus, Eustachius, Nibianus, Pelagius, Julian and Laciensis, Coelestinus, Maximianus, Priscillian from Spain, Lampedius, Dioscorus, Eutyches, Peter and another Peter—one of whom defiled Alexandria and the other Antioch—Acacius of Constantinople with his associates, and likewise all heresies which they, their disciples, or schismatics taught or wrote: we do not retain their names. We confess that they are not only rejected but also removed from every Catholic and Roman Church, and, together with their authors and the followers of their authors, are condemned forever under the indissoluble bond of anathema.

## CHAPTER XVI. Certain Etymologies of Terms Relevant to Reading

[Col. 0788C]

A codex consists of many books; a book, of one volume. *Codex* is said by transference from the trunks of trees or vines, as though *caudex* (“trunk”), because it contains in itself a multitude of books like branches. A volume is so called from rolling. A *liber* is the inner bark of a tree, upon which the ancients were accustomed to write before the use of paper or parchment. Hence they also called copyists *librarii*, and from this comes the name *liber*, “book” or “volume.”

*Scheda*, of which *schedula* is the diminutive, is a Greek name. A sheet is properly something still being corrected and not yet made into books. The use of paper was first discovered at Memphis, a city of Egypt. Paper is so called because the covering of papyrus is stripped off in pieces and glued together, and thus paper is made; of it there are several kinds. Parchment is so called from Pergamum, where it was discovered. It is also called membrane because it is stripped from the limbs of animals. Parchments were at first made yellow in color; later, white parchment was discovered at Rome.

A homily is, as it were, a popular discourse, such as a speech addressed to the people. A treatise is an extensive exposition of one subject. A dialogue is a conversation of two or more persons; the Latins call it a discourse. A discourse is so called because it is sown between the two parties. Commentaries are so named as though “with the mind,” or from *comminiscor*, “to devise.” For there are interpretations or commentaries on law or the Gospel. Some say that the writings of pagans should be called *commenta*, whereas those on divine matters should be called expositions.

Gloss is Greek and means “tongue,” because in some fashion it speaks the meaning of the word placed beneath it. Philosophers call this an *adverb* [another reading: *adverbium*], [Col. 0790A] because it identifies the word whose meaning is sought by one single word; for example, *conticescere* means “to be silent.”

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0789]

Its chapters are these:

CHAPTER I. A preliminary warning concerning certain characteristics of Sacred Scripture.—CHAPTER II. On the threefold understanding.—CHAPTER III. That things too signify in Sacred Scripture.—CHAPTER IV. On the seven rules.—CHAPTER V. What hinders study.—CHAPTER VI. What is the fruit of divine reading.—CHAPTER VII. How divine Scripture ought to be read for the correction of morals.—CHAPTER VIII. That reading belongs to beginners, action to the perfect, and what befits a monk.—CHAPTER IX. On the five stages through which the life of the righteous is exercised.—CHAPTER X. On the three kinds of those who read, or readers.

## CHAPTER I. A Preliminary Warning Concerning Certain Characteristics of Sacred Scripture

[Col. 0789B]

The diligent reader ought not to find it burdensome that we treat so variously and repeatedly of the number, order, and names of the divine books, because it often happens that ignorance of these small matters obscures knowledge of great and useful things. Therefore let the reader settle these matters once for all, so that, when these introductory bolts have, as it were, been opened, he may thereafter run the proposed course with free step, and need not seek new rudiments in each individual book. These matters being disposed of, we shall henceforth treat the remaining subjects which seem relevant to the work proposed.

## CHAPTER II. On the Threefold Understanding

First of all, one must understand that divine [Col. 0789C] Scripture has a threefold mode of understanding: history, allegory, and tropology. Certainly, not everything found in divine utterance is to be forced into this threefold interpretation, so that every individual passage is believed to contain history, allegory, and tropology simultaneously. Although this may suitably be assigned in many cases, it is nevertheless difficult or impossible to observe everywhere.

For as in lyres and similar musical instruments, not everything that is touched produces a musical resonance, but only the strings; yet the other parts throughout the body of the lyre are made in order that there may be places where those things are joined and stretched which the artist, intending to produce the sweetness of song, modulates. So in divine utterances, certain things are placed [Col. 0789D] which wish to be understood only spiritually; some serve moral seriousness; some are said according to the simple sense of history; while others can fittingly be expounded historically, allegorically, and tropologically.

Thus, in a wondrous manner, all divine Scripture has been appropriately fitted and arranged in its parts through the wisdom of God, so that whatever it contains either sounds forth the sweetness of spiritual understanding in the manner of strings, or, through the course of history and the firmness of the letter, holds together and, as it were, joins into one the sayings concerning mysteries scattered throughout it, [Col. 0790B] after the manner of the hollow wood beneath stretched strings. Receiving their sound into itself, it returns it sweeter to the ears—a sound produced not only by the string, but also shaped by the wood through the measure of its body. Thus honey too is more pleasant in the comb. And whatever is sought through greater exertion is found with greater desire.

Therefore divine Scripture must be treated in such a way that we seek neither history everywhere, nor allegory everywhere, nor tropology everywhere; rather, each should be assigned suitably in its proper place, as reason requires. Yet often all are found in one and the same passage: the truth of history suggests something mystical through allegory and at the same time shows, through tropology, what ought to be done.

## CHAPTER III. That Things Too Signify in Sacred Scripture

[Col. 0790C]

It must also be known that in divine utterance not words alone but things too possess signification; this mode is not customarily found to the same degree in other writings. The philosopher recognizes only the signification of words, but the signification of things is greatly superior to that of words, because use instituted the former, whereas nature dictated the latter. This is the voice of human beings; that, the voice of God to human beings. This, once uttered, perishes; that, once created, remains: “A voice is a slight sign of perceptions; a thing is an image of divine reason.”

What the sound of the mouth, which begins and ends its existence at once, is to the reason of the mind, the whole expanse of time is to eternity. The reason of the mind is an inner word, manifested by the sound of the voice, that is, by the outward word; and divine Wisdom, which the Father uttered from his heart, though invisible in itself, is known through creatures and in creatures. From this it is plainly inferred how profound an understanding must be sought in the sacred writings, where one arrives at truth through voice to understanding, through understanding to the thing, through the thing to reason, and through reason to truth.

Since certain less learned persons do not consider this, they think that there is no subtlety in the Scriptures by which minds may be exercised. For this reason they turn to the writings of the apostles, because they conceive nothing else there than the surface of the letter alone, being ignorant of the power of truth. That sacred utterances employ the signification of things we shall show by a brief and clear example. Scripture says: “Be vigilant, because your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion” (1 Pet. 5). If here we say that the lion signifies the devil, we must understand not the word but the thing. For if these two words, “devil” and “lion,” signify one and the same thing, the comparison of the same thing with itself is inappropriate. It remains, therefore, that the word “lion” signifies the animal itself, while the animal signifies the devil. All other such expressions must be understood in this way, so that when we speak of a worm, calf, stone, serpent, and other things of this sort, they signify Christ.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Seven Rules

[Col. 0791B]

This too must be carefully observed: certain wise men have said that, among the other rules governing the expressions of the Holy Scriptures, there are seven. The first rule concerns the Lord and his body. It speaks from one to the other and, in one person, shows now the head and now the body, as Isaiah says: “The Lord clothed me with the garments of salvation and surrounded me with a garment of righteousness, like a bridegroom adorned with a crown and like a bride adorned with her jewels” (Isa. 61). For in one person, named by a double term, he made known both the head—that is, the bridegroom—and the Church—that is, the bride.

Accordingly, one must note in the Scriptures when the head alone is written of, when both head and body are meant, or when the text passes from each to each, or from one to the other, so that the prudent reader may understand what belongs to the head and what to the body. The second rule concerns the one, simple, and mixed body of the Lord. For some things seem to suit one person which nevertheless do not belong to one alone, as in this passage: “You are my child [servant], Israel; behold, I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Return [come back] to me, and I shall redeem you” (Isa. 44). This does not fit one person. For one part is that whose sins he has blotted out and to which he says, “You are mine”; another is that to which he says, “Return to me, and I shall redeem you,” whose sins are blotted out if they return. For through this rule Scripture speaks to all in such a way that the good are rebuked with the evil and the evil praised on account of the good; but the person who reads wisely will learn what applies to whom.

The third rule concerns letter and spirit, that is, law and grace: law, through which commands to be performed are set before us; grace, through which we are helped to act. Or it means that the Law is to be understood not only historically but also spiritually. For it is necessary both to hold the faith historically and to understand the Law spiritually.

The fourth rule concerns species and genus, through which a part is taken for the whole and the whole for a part; for example, if God speaks to one people or city while nevertheless being understood to concern the whole world. For although the Lord threatens one city, Babylon, through the prophet Isaiah, yet, while speaking against it, he passes from the particular to the general and turns his discourse against the whole world. [Col. 0792A] Certainly, if he were not speaking against the entire world, he would not add below in general terms: “To destroy all the earth, and I shall visit the evils of the world” (Isa. 13), together with the other following words concerning the world; hence he adds: “This is the plan which I have devised against the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out over all nations” (Isa. 14).

Again, after rebuking the whole world under the person of Babylon, he returns once more from the general to the particular, as it were, saying what specifically befell that city: “Behold, I shall raise up the Medes against them” (Isa. 13). For Babylon was captured by the Medes in the reign of Belshazzar. In the same way, by speaking in the person of Egypt alone, he intends the whole world to be understood: “And I shall cause Egyptians to clash against Egyptians, kingdom against kingdom” (Isa. 19), whereas Egypt is described as having had not many kingdoms but one kingdom.

The fifth rule concerns times: by it either the greater part of a period is indicated by its lesser part, or the lesser part is understood by its greater part. Thus it is with the three days of the Lord’s burial: although he did not lie in the tomb for three complete days and nights, nevertheless the whole three-day period is understood from a part. Or as when God foretold that the children of Israel would serve in Egypt for four hundred years, and would then depart from it. Yet while Joseph ruled Egypt, they were condemned; nor did they leave immediately after four hundred years, as had been promised, but departed Egypt when four hundred and thirty years had elapsed. There is also another figure concerning times, [Col. 0792C] by which things that are to happen are related as if already done, as in: “They pierced my hands and my feet,” and: “They divided my garments among themselves” (Ps. XXI); and similar passages, in which future things are spoken of as though already accomplished. But why are things still to be done narrated as already done? Because what is future to us is already accomplished in God’s eternity. Accordingly, when something is declared to be yet done, it is spoken according to our perspective; but when future things are called already done, they must be understood according to God’s eternity, with whom all things that are to come are already accomplished.

The sixth rule concerns recapitulation. For recapitulation occurs when Scripture returns to that whose narrative it had already passed over, [Col. 0792D] as when Scripture has mentioned Noah’s descendants (Gen. X), saying that they were according to their languages and nations, and nevertheless afterwards—as though this too had to be placed within this chronological order—it says: “The whole earth,” it says, “was of one lip [of one language, etc.], and one voice was for all” (Gen. XI). How, then, were they according to their nations and according to their languages, if one language belonged to all, unless the narrative had returned by recapitulation to what it had already passed?

The seventh rule concerns the devil and his body. Things are often said of the head himself which more properly suit his body; and things often seem to be said of the members which fit only the head. Thus the head is understood from the name of the body, as in the Gospel concerning tares mixed with wheat, when the Lord says: “An enemy [Col. 0793A] man did this” (Matt. XIII), calling the devil himself “man” and designating the head by the name of the body. Conversely, the body is signified by the name of the head, as the Gospel says: “I have chosen twelve of you, and one of you is a devil” (John VI), plainly indicating Judas, because he was the devil’s body. For the apostate angel is the head of all the wicked, and all the wicked are the body of this head; and he is so one with his members that what is said to his body is often referred rather to him. Again, what is said to him is in turn extended to his members. Thus in Isaiah, when the prophetic utterance has said many things against Babylon—that is, against the devil’s body—it again directs the sentence of its oracle to the head, that is, to the devil, saying: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, you who rose in the morning!” (Isa. XIV).

## CHAPTER V. What hinders study

After prescribing a definite subject matter for the reader and determining, by assigning their names, those writings that especially belong to divine reading, it seems fitting that we should also say something concerning the manner and order of reading. Thus, from what has been said, he may recognize to what he ought to devote his study; and from what remains to be said, he may receive the method and rationale of that study.

But since we understand more easily what ought to be done if we first recognize what ought not to be done, the student must first be instructed concerning what he should avoid, and then informed how he is to accomplish what must be done. We must say what it is that causes so few, so readily countable, persons to be found among the great multitude of students—even though many [Col. 0793C] are strong in natural ability and vigorous through practice—to attain knowledge. And, not to speak of those naturally dull and slow to understand, this especially moves me and seems worthy of inquiry: how it happens that two persons of equal ability and equal zeal devote themselves to one course of reading, yet do not attain its understanding with equal success. One quickly grasps what he seeks; the other labours long and makes little progress.

But it should be known that in every undertaking two things are necessary: work, certainly, and the method of working. These are so interconnected that either without the other is useless or less effective. Nevertheless, “prudence,” as the saying goes, “is better than strength,” because we sometimes lift by skill weights which we cannot move by strength. So it is in every study: whoever works without discernment does indeed labour, but makes no progress; and, as one striking the air, pours his strength out into the wind.

Look at two men passing together through a forest: one toils along byways, while the other follows the shortcuts of the straight road. They hasten onward at the same pace, yet do not arrive equally quickly. What, indeed, should I call Scripture but a forest, whose meanings we pluck in reading like exceedingly sweet fruits and chew over in exposition? Therefore, whoever does not preserve the manner and order of reading amid such a multitude of books is like one wandering amid the density of a wood who has lost the path of the direct road. He belongs among those of whom it is said: “Always learning, and never [Col. 0794A] coming to the knowledge.” For discernment is of such value that without it all leisure is disgraceful and labour useless.

To state the matter generally: three things especially tend to hinder the studies of readers—negligence, imprudence, and fortune. Negligence occurs when we either entirely omit what ought to be learned or learn it with insufficient zeal. Imprudence occurs when we do not preserve a fitting order and method in what we learn. Fortune concerns an outcome that happens by chance or naturally: when we are drawn away from our purpose by poverty, illness, natural slowness, or even scarcity of teachers—because either none are found to teach, or none who teach well. In these matters the reader must be warned concerning the first, negligence; instructed concerning the second, imprudence; and assisted concerning the third, fortune.

## CHAPTER VI. What is the fruit of divine reading

Whoever approaches divine reading in order to be trained should first recognize what its fruit is. Nothing ought to be sought without cause, nor does that attract desire which promises no benefit. Divine reading bears a twofold fruit: it either educates the mind by knowledge or adorns it with morals. It teaches what is delightful to know and what is advantageous for help. Of these, the first—that is, knowledge—has greater reference to history and allegory; the second—that is, moral instruction—has greater reference to tropology. All divine Scripture is directed toward this end.

Certainly, although it is more advantageous to be righteous than wise, I know that more people seek knowledge than virtue in the study of sacred discourse. Yet since I judge neither to be blameworthy, but both necessary and praiseworthy, I shall briefly explain what is appropriate to each intention. First I shall speak of the person who embraces the grace of moral formation. [Col. 0794C]

## CHAPTER VII. How divine Scripture should be read for the correction of morals

Whoever seeks knowledge of the virtues and a pattern for living in sacred discourse ought especially to read those books which commend contempt for this world, kindle the soul with love for its Creator, teach the straight path of life, and show how virtues may be acquired and vices avoided. “Seek first,” he says, “the kingdom of God and his righteousness” (Matt. VI), as though plainly saying: Desire also the joys of the heavenly homeland, and diligently inquire by what merits of righteousness one may come to them. Love and seek both goods; both are necessary. If love is present, it cannot be idle. You desire to arrive: learn how one may arrive where you are tending.

This knowledge is acquired in two ways: by example and by teaching—by example, when we read the deeds of saints; by teaching, when we learn their sayings that concern our instruction. Among these I think the writings of the most blessed Gregory should especially be embraced. Since they seemed to me sweeter than the rest and full of love for eternal life, I do not wish to pass them over in silence.

But one who has entered this path ought, in the books he reads, to learn to be stirred not merely by the elegance of expression but by emulation of the virtues, so that not so much the pomp or polish of words as the beauty of truth delights him. He should also know that it does not further his purpose to be carried away by an empty desire for knowledge and seek writings of obscure and profound understanding, in which the mind is occupied more than edified—lest reading alone so hold him that he is compelled to be free from good works. For the Christian philosopher, reading ought to be an exhortation, not an occupation: it should nourish good desires, not kill them.

I remember that I was once told of a man of commendable life who burned with such love for the holy Scriptures that he devoted unceasing study to them. As his knowledge grew daily, so did his desire. At length, imprudently eager for wisdom, he began—despising the simpler Scriptures—to investigate every profound and obscure matter, and to devote himself intensely to unravelling the riddles of the prophets and the mystical senses of the sacraments. But the human mind, unable to bear so great a burden, soon began to fail through both the magnitude of the subject and the unremitting intensity of attention; and it became so confused by concern over this burdensome occupation that it ceased not only from useful actions but even from necessary ones. Thus the outcome was reversed: he who had begun to read the Scriptures for the edification of his life, because he did not know how to employ the restraint of discernment, now found in those same Scriptures an occasion of error.

But at last, admonished through a revelation by divine mercy, he was told not to apply himself any longer to the study of these writings, but to make a practice of reading the lives of the holy Fathers, the triumphs of martyrs, and other such works written in a simple style. Thus, quickly restored to his former condition, he deserved to receive such a grace of inward rest that one could truly say that the Lord’s saying was fulfilled in him—the saying by which, beholding our labour and pain, he mercifully willed to console us: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you; and henceforth,” he says, “you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI).

I have included this example in order to show those whose calling lies not in literary learning but in the discipline of virtues that reading ought not to be weariness but delight. For the Prophet says: “I did not know learning,” or “commerce”; “I shall enter into the powers of the Lord; O Lord, I shall remember your righteousness alone. O God, you have taught me from my youth,” etc. (Ps. LXX). Whoever reads the Scriptures as an occupation and, so to speak, as an affliction of spirit, is not philosophizing but trading; and such vehement and undiscerning application can scarcely be free from pride.

What shall I say of the simple Paul, who wished to fulfil the law before learning it? His example can surely suffice for us: before God it is not hearers or readers, but rather doers, who are righteous. Moreover, it must be considered that reading commonly produces weariness in the mind and afflicts the spirit in two ways: by its quality, if it is too obscure, and by its quantity, if it is too prolonged. In both matters one must use great moderation, lest what was sought for refreshment be taken to suffocation. Some wish to read everything; do not strive to do so. Let it suffice you: it does not concern you whether you have read every book. The number of books is infinite; do not wish to pursue infinity. Where there is no end, there can be no rest; where there is no rest, there is no peace; where there is no peace, God cannot dwell. “In peace,” says the Prophet, “his place has been made, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. LXXV). In Zion—but in peace: one must be in Zion, but must not lose peace. Contemplate, but do not be over-occupied. Do not be greedy, lest perhaps you always be needy.

Hear Solomon, hear the Wise Man, and learn prudence: “My son, seek no further than these. There is no end to making many books, and frequent meditation is an affliction of the flesh” (Eccles. XII). Where, then, is the end? “Let us all hear together the conclusion of the matter: fear God and keep his commandments; this is the whole man” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER VIII. Reading belongs to beginners, work to the perfect; and what befits a monk

Let no one think, from what I have just said, that I condemn the diligence of readers, when I rather intend to urge diligent readers toward their calling and to show that those who gladly learn are worthy of praise. But there I spoke to the learned; now I speak to those who are being taught and who are beginning the learning which is the first stage of discipline. For the former, the pursuit of virtues is their calling; for the latter, meanwhile, the exercise of reading—yet in such a way [Col. 0796C] that the latter are not without virtue and the former do not wholly omit reading. For work not preceded by reading is often less prudent, and teaching not followed by good action is less useful.

Yet the former must carefully guard against looking back to the things behind; and the latter must be encouraged, if they desire one day to attain the place where the former are. Both, then, ought to exercise themselves and both advance. Let no one go backward: it is permissible to ascend, but not to descend. If you cannot yet ascend, stand in your own place. A person is not free from fault who usurps another’s office.

If you are a monk, what are you doing in the crowd? If you love silence, why do you delight in constantly attending declaimers? You ought always to devote yourself to fasts and tears—and do you seek to philosophize? The monk’s simplicity is his philosophy. “But,” you say, “I wish to teach others.” Your task is not to teach but to mourn. Yet if you desire to be a teacher, hear what you must do: the usefulness of your habit, the simplicity of your countenance, the innocence of your life, and the holiness of your conduct ought to teach people. You teach better by fleeing the world than by following it.

But perhaps you still press the matter, asking: “At least, if I wish to learn, is it not permitted me?” I told you above: read, but do not become over-occupied. Reading may be an exercise for you, but not your calling. Learning is good, but it belongs to beginners. You, however, have promised that you will become perfect; and therefore it is not enough for you to be equal to beginners. You must do something more. Consider, then, where you are, and you will easily recognize what you ought to do.

## CHAPTER IX. On the five steps by which the life of the righteous is exercised

[Col. 0797A]

There are four things in which the life of the righteous is now exercised, and through which it is raised, as by certain steps, toward future perfection: reading or instruction, meditation, prayer, and action. Then follows a fifth, contemplation, in which, as by a certain fruit of the preceding steps, even in this life there is a foretaste of what the future reward of good work will be. Hence, when the Psalmist spoke of God’s judgments, he immediately added in commendation of them: “In keeping them there is great reward” (Ps. XVIII).

Of these five steps, the first—that is, reading—belongs to beginners; the highest—that is, contemplation—to the perfect. Of the intermediate steps, the more a person ascends, the more perfect he will be. For example: the first, reading, gives understanding; the second, meditation, provides counsel; the third, prayer, asks; the fourth, action, seeks; the fifth, contemplation, finds.

If, therefore, you read and have understanding, and already know what ought to be done, this is the beginning of good; but it is not yet enough for you. You are not yet perfect. Ascend, therefore, to the citadel of counsel, and meditate on how you may fulfil what you have learned ought to be done. Many possess knowledge, but few know how one ought to know. Again, since human counsel is weak and ineffective without divine help, raise yourself to prayer and seek his aid, without whom you can do no good: so that his grace, which by preceding you has enlightened you, may also by following direct your feet into the way of peace, and bring to the effect of good action what as yet exists only in will. [Col. 0797C]

Then it remains for you to gird yourself for good work, so that you may deserve to receive by working what you ask in prayer. God wishes to work with you: you are not compelled, but helped. If you work alone, you accomplish nothing; if God works alone, you merit nothing. Therefore let God work, so that you may be able; and work also yourself, so that you may merit something. Good action is the road by which one goes to life. Whoever runs this road seeks life. Be strengthened and act courageously.

This road has its reward whenever, wearied by its labours, we are enlightened by a gracious heavenly visitation, tasting and seeing that the Lord is sweet (Ps. XXXIII). Thus what was said above comes about: what prayer seeks, contemplation finds. You see, then, how perfection meets those ascending by these steps, so that one who remains below cannot be perfect.

Therefore our purpose ought always to be to ascend. But because the changeability of our life is so great that we cannot remain in the same state, we are often compelled to look back upon what has passed; and, lest we lose what we possess, we sometimes repeat what [Col. 0798A] we have passed beyond. For example, one who is vigorous in action prays that he may not fail. One who persists in prayers meditates on what should be prayed, lest he offend in praying. One who sometimes has too little confidence in his own counsel consults reading. Thus, although our will should always be to ascend, necessity sometimes compels us to descend—yet in such a manner that our purpose resides in the will, not in necessity. What we ascend is according to purpose; what we descend is apart from purpose. The latter, then, must not be principal, but the former.

## CHAPTER X. On the three kinds of those who read, or readers

It has, I think, been sufficiently shown that those who have advanced and promise something more of themselves do not have the same calling as beginners. But just as something is permitted to the former which the latter cannot do without fault, so something is required of the latter to which the former are not yet bound.

Now I return to fulfil my promise: to show how divine Scripture should be read by those who as yet seek in it knowledge alone. Some desire knowledge of divine Scripture in order to accumulate wealth, attain honours, or acquire fame. Their intention is as perverse as it is pitiable. There are others who delight in hearing God’s words and learning his works, not because they are saving, but because they are marvellous. They wish to investigate secrets and know unheard-of things: to know much and do nothing. In vain do those marvel at power who do not love mercy. What else can I say such people do but turn divine proclamations into fables? So we are accustomed to attend theatrical entertainments and stage songs: that is, to feed the ear rather than the mind.

Nevertheless, I judge that such persons should not so much be rebuked as helped, since their will is not malicious but unwise. But others read sacred Scripture in order that, according to the Apostle’s precept, they may be ready to give an account to everyone who asks concerning the faith in which they stand (1 Pet. III); in order that they may stoutly overthrow the enemies of truth, teach the less educated, themselves recognize more perfectly the way of truth, and, understanding God’s secrets more deeply, love more closely. Their devotion is surely worthy of praise and imitation.

There are, then, three kinds of people who read sacred Scripture: the first are to be pitied, the second helped, the third praised. But because we intend to provide for all, we desire that what is good in all may increase, and what is perverse be changed. We want all to understand what we say and all to do what we exhort.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0799]

Its chapters are these:

CHAPTER I. How sacred Scripture should be read by those who seek knowledge in it. — CHAPTER II. On the order found in disciplines. — CHAPTER III. On history and the books to be read in it. — CHAPTER IV. On allegory. — CHAPTER V. On tropology and morality. — CHAPTER VI. On the order of books. — CHAPTER VII. On the order of narrative. — CHAPTER VIII. On the order of exposition. — CHAPTER IX. On the letter. — CHAPTER X. On sense. — CHAPTER XI. On meaning. — CHAPTER XII. On the manner of reading. — CHAPTER XIII. Why meditation is now to be omitted. — CHAPTER XIV. Definition of the three remedies concerning philosophy against three corresponding evils, and on another division of philosophy. — CHAPTER XV. On magic and its parts.

## CHAPTER I. How sacred Scripture should be read by those who seek knowledge in it

[Col. 0799A]

I set before you, reader, two things: order and method. If you examine them carefully, the path of reading will easily open before you. Yet in considering them, I shall neither leave everything to your own ability nor promise that my diligence will suffice for you. Rather, I shall run briefly through certain matters by tasting them beforehand, so that you may find some things set down by which you may be instructed, and some omitted by which you may be exercised.

Above, I said that the order of reading is fourfold: one order in disciplines, another in books, another in narrative, and another in exposition. I have not yet shown how these should be assigned in divine Scripture.

## CHAPTER II. On the order found in disciplines

[Col. 0799B]

First, therefore, the reader of divine matters must consider this order which is sought among the disciplines—between history, allegory, and tropology—which of these ought to precede the other in the order of reading. In this matter, it is not useless to recall what may be seen in buildings: first the foundation is laid; then the structure is built upon it; finally, when the work has been completed, the house is clothed with a covering of paint.

## CHAPTER III. On history and the books to be read in it

This, indeed, ought to be done in instruction: first learn history, and, tracing from the beginning the truth of events that have occurred, carefully commit to memory, up to the end, what was done, by whom it was done, and where it was done. For these four things are especially to be sought in history: person, event, time, and place. [Col. 0799C]

Nor do I think that you can become perfectly subtle in allegory unless you have first been grounded in history. Do not despise these small things. Those who despise small things gradually fail. If you had despised learning the alphabet at first, you would now not possess even the name of a grammarian. I know that there are some who want to philosophize at once; they say that fables should be left to pseudo-apostles. Their learning resembles the form of an ass. Do not imitate such people.

> Trained in small things, you will safely attempt great ones.

I dare affirm that I have never despised anything pertaining to education, but have often learned many things that seemed to others like a joke or madness. I remember that when I was still a student I laboured to know the names of all things placed before the eyes or used in ordinary life, judging that no one could freely pursue the nature of things while he still did not know their names. How often I exacted from myself a daily payment from my syllogisms, which, for brevity’s sake, I had marked with one or two words on a page, so that I might hold in memory both the solutions and the number of nearly all the propositions, questions, and objections which I had learned.

I often framed cases and arranged controversies against one another; I carefully distinguished the office of rhetorician, orator, and sophist. I set counting-stones into numerical arrangements and drew a pavement with black charcoal; and, with the example set before the eyes, plainly demonstrated what difference there was between an *ampligonius* [obtuse-angled figure], an *ortogonius* [right-angled figure], and an *oxigonius* [acute-angled figure]. I learned whether a square, with its two sides multiplied into themselves, fills an *embadum* [area], with the *podismus* [linear measure] proceeding on both sides. [Col. 0800B]

I often kept watch over winter nights for the nocturnal horoscope. I often used to play the *Magadan* upon a stretched wooden board, so that I might perceive the distinctions of tones by my ear and delight the mind at the same time with the sweetness of melody. Some regarded these things as childish, yet they were not useless; nor does knowing them now burden my mind.

I do not recount these matters to you in order to boast of my learning, which is either none at all or small, but to show you that one advances most fittingly who advances in order—not like certain people who, wishing to make a great leap, fall into a precipice. Just as there are certain stages in virtues, so there are in the sciences.

“But,” you say, “I find many things in histories which seem to be of no usefulness; why should I occupy myself with things of that kind?” You speak well. There are indeed many things in Scripture which, considered in themselves, appear to contain nothing worth seeking. Yet if you compare them with the other things to which they are connected and begin to weigh them in their entirety, you will see that they are both necessary and fitting. Some things must be known for their own sake; other things, although they do not seem in themselves worthy of our labour, nevertheless must by no means be carelessly passed over, since without them the former cannot be known clearly. Learn everything: later you will see that nothing is superfluous. Knowledge confined within narrow limits is not pleasant. [Col. 0801A]

As to books useful for this reading, if you ask my view, I judge that these should be read most often: Genesis, Exodus, Joshua, the book of Judges, Kings, and Paralipomenon [Chronicles]. Of the New Testament, first the four Gospels, then the Acts of the Apostles. These eleven seem to me to pertain especially to history, apart from those whom we properly call historians.

If, however, we use the meaning of this term more broadly, there is no objection to calling “history” not only the narration of deeds done, but the primary meaning of any narrative, which is expressed according to the proper sense of the words. In that sense, I think that all the books of both Testaments, in the order in which they were enumerated above, pertain to this reading according to the literal sense.

And perhaps, if it did not seem childish, I would insert here some precepts concerning grammatical construction, because I know that divine Scripture is more concise than all other writings in its wording. Yet I prefer to leave these aside, lest too great an interruption extend my undertaking. There are certain passages in the divine page which cannot be read according to the letter. These must be distinguished with great discernment, lest through negligence we pass some things over, or through importunate diligence violently twist them toward something for which they were not written.

Therefore, reader, this is what we set before you: this field of your labour, well furrowed by the plough, will yield you manifold fruit. All things were done in order; proceed in order. Through the shadow one comes to the body. Learn the figure and you will find the truth. Yet I do not now say this in order that you should first labour to unfold the figures of the Old Testament and investigate its mystical sayings before approaching the streams of the Gospel to drink. Rather, as you see that no building lacking a foundation can be stable, so it is also in instruction. History is the foundation and beginning of sacred teaching; from it, like honey from the honeycomb, the truth of allegory is pressed out.

Therefore, if you are going to build, first lay the foundation of history; then, through typological meaning, raise the structure of the mind to the citadel of faith; and finally, through the grace of morality, paint the building as with a most beautiful layer of colour. In history you have that by which to marvel at God’s deeds; in allegory, that by which to believe his mysteries; in morality, that by which to imitate his perfection. [Col. 0801D]

Read, therefore, and learn that “in the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I). Read that in the beginning he planted the paradise of delight, in which he placed the human being whom he had formed (Gen. II); that he expelled the sinner and cast him down into the miseries of this age. Read how the entire offspring of the human race descended from one man; how thereafter the flood overwhelmed sinners; how divine mercy preserved righteous Noah with his sons amid the waters; how Abraham then received the seal of faith; how Israel afterwards descended into Egypt; how God then led the children of Israel out of Egypt by the hand of Moses and Aaron through the Red Sea, fed them in the wilderness, gave them the law, settled them in the promised land, and did many other things.

Finally, when the age was already declining, he sent his Son in the flesh; he promised eternal life to those who repent, after sending apostles into the whole world; and he foretold that at the end of the ages he would come for judgment, to render to each according to his works: eternal fire to sinners, but eternal life and a kingdom without end to the righteous (Luke I). [Col. 0802A] See that from the beginning of the world until the end of the ages, God’s mercies do not fail.

## CHAPTER IV. On allegory

After reading history, it remains to investigate the mysteries of allegories. Here I do not think my exhortation necessary, since the subject itself sufficiently appears worthy in its own right. Yet I want you to know, reader, that this study does not demand slow and dull minds, but mature intellects—minds which maintain subtlety in inquiry without losing prudence in discernment. This is solid food, and unless it is chewed, it cannot be swallowed.

You must therefore employ such moderation that, while subtle in inquiry, you may not be found rash in presumption, remembering what the Psalmist says: “He bent his bow and made it ready; and in it he prepared instruments of death” (Ps. VII). You remember, I suppose, that above I said divine Scripture resembles a building, in that after the foundation has been laid, the structure is raised aloft. It is plainly like a building, for it too has a structure.

Let us not, then, be reluctant to pursue this comparison a little more carefully. Look at the work of a mason. Once the foundation has been placed, he stretches a line straight ahead, drops a plumb line, and then lays carefully dressed stones in order. He next seeks further stones; and if he finds any that do not suit the first arrangement, he takes a file, cuts off the projections, smooths the roughness, and brings the shapeless into form. Then, when the other stones have been arranged in order, he joins them to the rest. But if he finds stones of such a sort that they can neither be reduced nor fitted suitably, he does not take them up, lest, while labouring to break the stone, he break the file.

Attend closely. I have set before you a matter contemptible to those merely looking, but worthy of imitation to those who understand. The foundation is in the earth and does not always have dressed stones. The structure is above the earth and seeks an even construction. So the divine page contains many things according to their natural sense which seem to contradict one another and sometimes introduce something absurd or impossible. [Col. 0802D]

Spiritual understanding, however, admits no contradiction; in it many things may be diverse, but none contrary. This is also signified by the first course of stones to be laid above the foundation, which, as you see, is arranged according to the line stretched out; for upon it the whole remaining work rests and is fitted together. It is, as it were, another foundation and the base of the entire structure. This foundation both bears what is laid upon it and is borne by the prior foundation. All things rest upon the first foundation, but are not in every respect fitted to it. The rest both rests upon and is fitted to this one. [Col. 0803A] The first bears the structure and is beneath it. This bears the structure and is not merely beneath the structure, but within the structure. We said that the foundation beneath the earth figures history, while the superimposed structure suggests allegory. Therefore the base itself of this structure must also belong to allegory. The building rises in many courses, and each has its own base; and the divine page contains many mysteries, each of which has its own beginnings.

Would you know what these courses are? The first course is the mystery of the Trinity, since Scripture contains also this: that before every creature God was three and one. He made every creature from nothing, visible and invisible: behold the second course. He gave free will to rational creatures and prepared grace so that [Col. 0803B] they might merit eternal blessedness; then he punished those who fell voluntarily, and confirmed those who remained steadfast so that they might no longer fall. What is the origin of sin, what sin is, and what the punishment of sin is: behold the third course. What mysteries he first instituted under the natural law for the restoration of the human race: behold the fourth course. What writings were given under the Law: behold the fifth course. The mystery of the incarnation of the Word: behold the sixth course. The mysteries of the New Testament: behold the seventh course. Finally, the mystery of the resurrection itself: behold the eighth course. This is the whole of divinity; this is that spiritual structure which rises upward, constructed in as many, as it were, courses as it contains mysteries.

Would you also recognize the bases themselves? The bases of the courses are the principles of the mysteries. Behold, you have come to reading in order to construct [Col. 0803C] a spiritual building. The foundations of history have already been laid in you; it remains for you now to lay the bases of the structure itself. You stretch the line, set the level, arrange squared stones in order, and, moving about, mark out certain traces of the future walls. The stretched line is the path of right faith; the bases themselves of the spiritual work are certain mysteries of faith by which you are initiated.

For a prudent reader ought to take care that, before pursuing the spacious volumes of books, he is so instructed in each of those matters which more particularly concern his purpose and the profession of the true faith that he may safely build upon whatever he subsequently finds. For amid so great an ocean of books and such manifold windings of opinions, which confuse the reader’s mind both by their number [Col. 0803D] and their obscurity, one will scarcely be able to gather any single thing unless he has first recognized, in summary fashion, some sure principle in each kind, so to speak, firmly supported by faith, to which all things may be referred.

Would you have me teach you how these bases should be made? Look at those things which I enumerated for you a little earlier. There is the mystery of the Trinity. Many books have already been written about it, and many opinions advanced, difficult to understand and perplexing to resolve. It is still too long and burdensome for you to pursue them all, since perhaps you will find many things in which you are more disturbed than edified. Do not press on; thus you will never reach the end. First learn briefly and clearly what must be held concerning faith in the Trinity; what indeed you ought to profess soundly and believe truly.

[Col. 0804A] When afterwards you begin to read books and find many things obscure, many plain, and many written ambiguously, add to your base what you find plain, if perhaps they agree with it. Interpret ambiguous matters in such a way that they do not conflict with it; unlock what is obscure, if you can. But if you cannot penetrate to their understanding, pass on, lest, while you attempt presumptuously what you are unable to accomplish, you incur the danger of error. Do not despise such things; rather, revere them, because you have heard what is written: “He made darkness his hiding-place” (Ps. 17). And if you find anything contrary to what you have already learned must be held with the firmest faith, it is nevertheless not expedient for you to change your opinion daily, unless you have first consulted persons wiser than yourself and especially learned what the universal faith, [Col. 0804B] which can never be false, commands to be believed concerning it.

You must act in this way concerning the mystery of the altar, the mystery of baptism, confirmation, marriage, and all those things enumerated above. You see many people reading the Scriptures who, because they have no foundation of truth, fall into various errors and change their opinions almost as often as they read lessons. Again, you see others who, according to that knowledge of truth by which they are inwardly established, know how to bend whatever Scriptures they encounter toward fitting interpretations and to judge what conflicts with sound faith or agrees with it.

In Ezekiel you read that the wheels follow the living creatures, not the living creatures the wheels: “When the living creatures moved,” he says, “the wheels also moved beside them. And when the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, [Col. 0804C] the wheels were lifted up with them” (Ezek. 1). For as the minds of the saints advance in virtues or knowledge, so they perceive the mysteries of the holy Scriptures to be profound, so that those who seemed to lie low for the simple and those still standing upon the earth appear lofty when raised up. For it follows: “Wherever the spirit went, there the spirit went; and the wheels also were lifted up, following it. For the spirit of life was in the wheels” (ibid.). You see that these wheels follow the living creatures and follow the spirit.

Again, elsewhere it is said: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3), because the reader of divine writings must assuredly be established in the truth of spiritual understanding, lest the points of the letters—which can sometimes be understood perversely—incline him toward any byways. Why was that ancient people, which had received the law of life, [Col. 0804D] rejected, unless because it followed the letter alone, which kills, in such a manner that it did not possess the life-giving Spirit?

I say this not in order to provide people indiscriminately with an occasion to interpret the Scriptures according to their own will, but in order to show that one who follows the letter alone cannot proceed long without error. Therefore we must follow the letter in such a way that we do not prefer our own understanding to the divine authors; and yet not follow it in such a way that we believe the whole judgment of truth depends upon it. “The spiritual person judges all things,” not the merely lettered person (1 Cor. 2). Therefore, in order that you may judge the letter safely, you must not presume upon your own judgment, but must first be taught and formed, and, as it were, lay a base of unshaken truth upon which [Col. 0805A] the whole structure may rest.

Do not presume to be instructed by yourself, lest perhaps, while you suppose that you are leading yourself in, you lead yourself rather astray. This introduction must be sought from teachers and wise persons, who can both establish and disclose it to you, as needed, by the authorities of the holy Fathers and the testimonies of Scripture. And once you have been introduced, confirm by reading the testimonies of Scripture each thing which they have taught. This seems right to me. Whoever is pleased to imitate me in this, I gladly welcome; whoever thinks it ought not to be done in this way, let him do what pleases him—I shall not contend. For I know that many do not observe this method in learning. Yet I am not ignorant how some persons nevertheless make progress.

If you ask which books are especially useful for this reading, I think: the beginning of Genesis, on the works [Col. 0805B] of the six days; the last three books of Moses, on the legal mysteries; Isaiah; the beginning and end of Ezekiel; Job; the Psalter; the Song of Songs; especially the two Gospels, namely Matthew and John; the Epistles of Paul, the Catholic Epistles, and the Apocalypse—yet above all the Epistles of Paul, which by their very number signify that they contain the perfection of both Testaments.

## Chapter V. On tropology and morality

For the present I shall say nothing else about tropology than what was said above, except that the signification of things rather than of words seems to belong more particularly to it. For in it is natural justice, from which the discipline of our morals—that is, positive justice—is born. [Col. 0805C] By contemplating what God has done, we recognize what we ought to do. All nature speaks of God. All nature teaches humanity. All nature produces reason, and nothing in the universe is unfruitful.

## Chapter VI. On the order of books

The same order of books is not to be observed in historical and allegorical reading. History follows the order of time; the order of knowledge belongs more particularly to allegory, because, as was said above, instruction must always begin not from obscure things but from things that are plain and more familiar. It follows, therefore, that the New Testament, in which truth is plainly preached, ought in this reading to be set before the Old, where the same truth is secretly foretold under shadowy figures. The truth is the same in both places, but [Col. 0805D] there hidden, here manifest; there promised, here displayed.

You heard, when the Apocalypse was read, that the book was sealed and that no one could be found to open its seals except the Lion from the tribe of Judah (Rev. 5). The Law was sealed, and the prophecies were sealed, because they foretold secretly the times of the coming redemption. Does not that book seem to you to have been sealed which said: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7)? And another: “But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are small among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth for me one who shall be ruler in Israel; his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5). And the Psalmist: “Shall not Zion say: ‘A man and a man were born in her, and the Most High himself founded her’?” (Ps. 86). And again: “The Lord God,” [Col. 0806A] he says, “has the issues of death” (Ps. 67). And again: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109). And shortly thereafter: “With you is the beginning in the day of your power; in the splendors of the saints, from the womb before the morning star I begot you” (ibid.). And Daniel: “I was looking in the vision of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven one like a Son of Man was coming; and he came to the Ancient of Days, and he gave him power and honor and kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him. His power is an eternal power which shall not be taken away” (Dan. 7).

Who, do you suppose, could have understood these things before they were fulfilled? They were sealed, and no one could open the seals except the Lion from the tribe of Judah. Therefore the Son of God came and put on our nature: he was born of a Virgin, crucified, buried, rose again, ascended into heaven, [Col. 0806B] and by fulfilling what had been promised opened what had lain hidden.

I read in the Gospel that the angel Gabriel is sent to the Virgin Mary and announces that she will give birth (Luke 1). I recall the prophecy which says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive.” I read that, when Joseph was in Bethlehem with Mary his pregnant wife, the time came for her to give birth, and she bore her firstborn son, whom the angel had foretold would reign upon the throne of David his father (ibid.). I recall the prophecy of Bethlehem Ephrathah: “You are small among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth for me one who shall be ruler in Israel.” Again I read: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). I recall the prophecy which says: “His going forth is from the beginning, from the days [Col. 0806C] of eternity.” I read: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). I recall the prophecy which says: “His name shall be called Emmanuel,” that is, “God with us.”

And lest I weary you by pursuing each point, unless you first recognize Christ’s birth, preaching, passion, resurrection, and ascension, and the other things which he performed in the flesh through the flesh, you will not be able to penetrate the mysteries of the ancient figures.

## Chapter VII. On the order of narration

Concerning the order of narration, what must especially be considered here is that the text of the divine page does not always preserve either the natural or the continuous order of speech, because it often places later things before earlier ones; thus, after it has enumerated certain matters, the narrative discourse suddenly returns to earlier matters as though following on from them. [Col. 0806D] It also often connects things separated by a long interval as though they followed immediately upon one another, so that things which it distinguishes by no interval of discourse seem to have been separated by no space of time.

## Chapter VIII. On the order of exposition

Exposition contains three things: the letter, the sense, and the meaning. Every narrative has a letter, for the words themselves are also letters; but sense and meaning are not always found together in every narrative. Some have only letter and sense. Some have only letter and meaning. Some contain all three together. Yet every narrative must have at least two of them.

That narrative has only letter and sense in which something is signified so plainly by the utterance itself [Col. 0807A] that nothing else is left to be understood. That has only letter and meaning in which the hearer can grasp nothing from the utterance alone unless exposition is added. That has sense and meaning where something is plainly signified, and something else is left to be understood which is not disclosed by the exposition.

## Chapter IX. On the letter

Sometimes the letter is complete, when, in order to signify what is said, nothing beyond the words laid down must be added or removed. For example: “All wisdom is from the Lord God” (Sir. 1). Sometimes it is deficient, when something is left to be supplied, as: “The elder to the chosen lady” (2 John 2). Sometimes it is superfluous, when the same thing is repeated for emphasis or after a long interruption, or when something unnecessary is added; as Paul says at the end of the Epistle to the Romans: “But to him,” and then, after many intervening words, adds: “to whom be honor and glory” (Rom. 16). [Col. 0807B] Something here appears superfluous—by “superfluous” I mean not necessary for completing the statement.

Sometimes the letter is such that, unless it is resolved into another form, it appears either to signify nothing or to be incongruous, as in: “The Lord in heaven, his throne” (Ps. 10), that is, “the throne of the Lord is in heaven”; and, “the sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows” (Ps. 56), that is, “the teeth of the sons of men”; and, “Man: his days are like grass,” that is, “the days of man” (Ps. 102). That is, a nominative noun and a genitive pronoun are put in place of a single genitive noun; and many other cases likewise. [Col. 0807C] Construction and continuity belong to the letter.

## Chapter X. On sense

Of senses, one is fitting and another unfitting. Of unfitting senses, one is incredible, another impossible, another absurd, another false. You will find many such things in the Scriptures, as: “They devoured Jacob” (Ps. 78); and: “Under whom are bent those who bear the world” (Job 9); and: “My soul chose hanging” (Job 7); and many others.

There are certain places in divine Scripture where, although the meaning of the words is plain, nevertheless no sense appears, either because of an unusual mode of speaking or because of some circumstance that impedes the reader’s understanding. Such is, for example, what Isaiah says: “Seven women shall seize one man on that day, saying: ‘We shall eat our own bread and clothe ourselves with our own garments; only let your name be called upon us; take away our reproach’” (Isa. 4). [Col. 0807D] The words are clear and plain. You understand well enough, “Seven women shall seize one man”; you understand, “We shall eat our own bread”; you understand, “We shall clothe ourselves with our own garments”; you understand, “Only let your name be called upon us”; you understand, “Take away our reproach.” But perhaps you cannot understand what the whole means together. You do not know what the prophet intended to say—whether he promised a good thing or threatened an evil one. It therefore happens that you believe it is to be understood only spiritually, because you do not see in what way it was said according to the letter.

You will thus say that the seven women are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which seize the one man, that is, Christ, in whom it pleased all fullness of grace to dwell, because he alone received the Holy Spirit without measure. He alone takes away their reproach, so that they may find one in whom to rest, since no other living person possessed what the gifts of the Holy Spirit sought. [Col. 0808A] Behold, you have interpreted it spiritually, and yet do not understand what it says according to the letter.

Nevertheless, the prophet could also have signified something according to the letter by these words. Because he had spoken above of the purpose of the transgressing people, he now adds that such devastation will occur among that same people, and the male sex will be destroyed to such an extent that seven women will scarcely find one man, whereas now one woman is accustomed to have one man. And whereas women are now accustomed to be courted by men, then, with custom reversed, women will court men. And lest one man fear to take seven women at once, since he would have no means of feeding and clothing them, they say to him: “We shall eat our own bread and clothe ourselves with our own garments; you need not be concerned about us. Only let your name be called upon us,” so that you may be called our husband and be so; lest we be called rejected and barren, and die without offspring—which at that time was a great reproach. [Col. 0808B] This is what they mean when they say: “Take away our reproach.”

You will find many things of this kind in Scripture, especially in the Old Testament, expressed according to the idiom of that language; though clear there, they seem to signify nothing among us. [Col. 0808C]

## Chapter XI. On meaning

The divine meaning can never be absurd or false. But although, as was said, many things contrary to one another are found in sense, meaning admits no contradiction: it is always fitting, always true. Sometimes one statement has one meaning; sometimes one statement has several meanings; sometimes several statements have one meaning; sometimes several statements have several meanings.

Therefore, when we read the divine books, amid so great a multitude of ancient interpretations drawn from a few words and fortified by the soundness of the Catholic faith, let us choose above all that interpretation which clearly appears [Col. 0808D] to have been intended by the author whom we read. But if this is hidden, then certainly let us choose what neither the context of Scripture prevents nor sound faith opposes. But if even the context of Scripture cannot be examined and discussed, then at least choose only what sound faith prescribes. For it is one thing not to discern what the writer especially intended, and another to err from the rule of piety. If both are avoided, the reader’s fruit is complete. But if both cannot be avoided, although the writer’s intention is uncertain, it is not useless to have drawn out an interpretation that agrees with sound faith.

Likewise, in obscure matters, most remote from our sight, if we read divine writings about them which, without injury to faith, can give rise to one interpretation or another, let us not cast ourselves with rash affirmation into any one of them, so that, [Col. 0809A] if truth, more carefully investigated, should undermine it, we fall—not fighting for the meaning of the divine Scriptures, but for our own opinion, in such a way that we want our own opinion to be that of the Scriptures, whereas we ought rather to want the Scriptures’ meaning to be our own.

## Chapter XII. On the method of reading

The method of reading consists in dividing. Division occurs both by partition and by investigation. We divide by partition when we distinguish things that are confused. We divide by investigation when we disclose things that are hidden.

## Chapter XIII. Why meditation must now be omitted

Behold, the matters pertaining to reading have now been explained as clearly [Col. 0809B] and concisely as we could. But I omit for the present saying anything about the remaining part of instruction, namely meditation, because so great a matter requires a special treatise; and in matters of this kind it is more fitting to be wholly silent than to say something imperfectly. For it is a very subtle and at the same time delightful matter, which instructs beginners and exercises those who are accomplished, not yet tried by my pen and therefore requiring fuller treatment.

Let us now pray Wisdom to deign to shine into our hearts and to enlighten us in its paths, that it may lead us to a pure banquet, free from animals.

## Chapter XIV. Definition of the three remedies pertaining to philosophy against three corresponding evils, and on another division of philosophy

[Col. 0809C] There are three things: wisdom, virtue, and necessity. Wisdom is comprehension of things as they are. Virtue is a disposition of the mind, in the manner of nature, consonant with reason. Necessity is that without which we cannot live, though we would live more happily without it. These three are remedies against the three evils to which human life is subject: wisdom against ignorance, virtue against vice, necessity against weakness. These three remedies were sought in order to eradicate these three evils; and all art and every discipline was discovered in order to find these three remedies. Theoretical philosophy was discovered for wisdom, practical philosophy for virtue, and mechanical philosophy for necessity. These three came first in use; but afterward logic was discovered for eloquence. Although last in discovery, it nevertheless ought to be first in instruction. There are, therefore, four principal sciences, from which all others descend: theoretical, practical, mechanical, and logical.

[Col. 0809D] Theoretical philosophy is divided into theology, physics, and mathematics. Theology treats of the invisible causes of visible things; mathematics, of the invisible forms of visible things. Mathematics is divided into four sciences. The first is arithmetic, which treats of number, that is, discrete quantity in itself. The second is music, which treats of proportion, that is, discrete quantity in relation to something else. The third is geometry, which treats of space, that is, continuous immovable quantity. The fourth is astronomy, which treats of motion, that is, continuous movable quantity. The element [Col. 0810A] of arithmetic is unity; the element of music, unison; the element of geometry, the point; the element of astronomy, the instant.

Practical philosophy is divided into solitary, private, and public. Solitary philosophy teaches how each person should order his or her own life by honorable morals and adorn it with virtues. Private philosophy teaches how household members and those related by ties of affection should be governed. Public philosophy teaches how an entire people and nation ought to be governed by its rulers. Solitary philosophy concerns individuals; private, heads of households; public, rulers of cities.

Mechanical philosophy treats of human works and is divided into seven branches. The first is cloth-making; the second, armament-making; the third, navigation; the fourth, agriculture; the fifth, hunting; the sixth, medicine; the seventh, theatre.

Logic is divided [Col. 0810B] into grammar and the art of discursive argument. The art of argument is divided into probable, necessary, and sophistical argument. Probable argument is divided into dialectic and rhetoric. Necessary argument belongs to philosophers; sophistical argument, to sophists.

In these four parts of philosophy, the following order must be observed in instruction: logic first, ethics second, theoretical philosophy third, mechanical philosophy fourth. For eloquence must first be acquired; then, as Socrates says in the *Ethics*, the eye of the heart must be cleansed through the study of virtue, so that it may afterward be keen in theoretical philosophy for the investigation of truth. Mechanical philosophy follows last, for by itself it is wholly ineffectual unless supported by the reasoning of the preceding disciplines.

## Chapter XV. On magic and its parts

[Col. 0810C] Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, is believed to have been the first inventor of magic. Some assert that he was Ham, son of Noah, under a changed name. Ninus, king of the Assyrians, later defeated and killed him in war, and caused his books, filled with the arts of evil-doing, to be burned in fire. Aristotle writes concerning this same man that his books handed down to the memory of posterity as many as two hundred and twenty thousand verses dictated by him on the art of magic.

Democritus later enlarged this art, in the time when Hippocrates was renowned in medicine. Magic is not accepted within philosophy; rather, it stands outside it, a false profession, the teacher of every iniquity and wickedness. Lying about truth and truly harming souls, [Col. 0810D] it leads people away from divine religion, urges the worship of demons, introduces moral corruption, and drives the minds of its followers toward every crime and impiety.

Taken generally, it comprises five kinds of evil arts: *mantice*, meaning divination; vain astrology; lot-divination; sorcery; and magical illusions. *Mantice*, however, contains five species. The first is necromancy, interpreted as divination by the dead; for Greek νεκρός (*nekros*) means “dead” (Latin *mortuus*), and Greek νεκρόν (*nekron*) means “corpse” (Latin *cadaver*). Hence divination performed by the sacrifice of human blood, which demons thirst for and delight in when it is shed. The second is geomancy, that is, divination by earth.
