The third is hydromancy, that is, divination by water. The fourth is aeromancy, that is, divination by air. The fifth is divination by [Col. 0811A] fire, called pyromancy. Varro indeed said that there are four elements in which divination consists: earth, water, air, and fire. The first, therefore, necromancy, appears to pertain to the underworld; the second to earth; the third to water; the fourth to air; and the fifth to fire.

Astrology is divided into three species: haruspicy, augury, and horoscopy. Haruspices are so called as though *horuspices*, that is, observers of hours, because they observe times in matters to be undertaken; or *haruspices* as though inspectors of *harae* [entrails], because they consider future events in the entrails and fibres of sacrifices. Augury or auspice sometimes concerns the eye and is called *auspicium* as though *avispicium*, because it is observed in the movement and flight of birds; sometimes it concerns the ears, and is then called *augurium* as though the chattering [Col. 0811B] of birds, because it is perceived by the ear. Horoscopy, also called constellation-reading, is when human affairs are sought in the stars, as genethliacs do, who observe births. [Col. 0812A] These were formerly called magi in a special sense—the magi of whom we read in the Gospel.

Lot-diviners are those who seek divination by lots. Sorcerers are those who, by demonic incantations, bindings, or any other accursed kinds of remedies, accomplish abominable acts through the cooperation and instruction of demons. Magical illusions occur when, through phantasmal deceptions concerning the alteration of things, human senses are deceived by demonic art.

Thus there are eleven in all: five under *mantice*—namely necromancy, geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, and pyromancy; three under astrology—namely haruspicy, auspice, and horoscopy; then three others—namely lot-divination, sorcery, and magical illusion. Mercury is said to have first invented magical illusions. The Phrygians [Col. 0812B] invented auguries. Tages the Etruscan first handed down haruspicy and lot-divination. Hydromancy first came from the Persians.

# Book Seven

[Col. 0811]

I have not found this in the *Didascalicon*, but it is, as it were, an appendix to it; for it treats of meditation, by which from knowledge of visible things we rise also to the knowledge of the invisible divine Trinity. These are the chapters:

Chapter I. On the three invisible attributes of God, from which all things emanate: power, wisdom, and goodness.—Chapter II. On the immensity of divine power, and how we perceive it from the multitude of creatures.—Chapter III. On the magnitude of creatures.—Chapter IV. On their beauty in four respects.—Chapter V. On the position and arrangement of things in place.—Chapter VI. On the arrangement of times.—Chapter VII. On the order considered in each thing from the arrangement of its parts.—Chapter VIII. On the manifold motion of things.—Chapter IX. On the appearance and shapes of things.—Chapter X. On things which are wondrous because they are rare.—Chapter XI. On things which are marvelous because they are beautiful.—Chapter XII. On the various colors of things.—Chapter XIII. On the sensible qualities of things.—Chapter XIV. On the fourfold usefulness of things.—Chapter XV. On three similarities, and on how great is the excellence of divine workmanship above human workmanship.—Chapter XVI. That among God’s three invisible attributes, wisdom must be investigated first.—Chapter XVII. How the Creator of things is shown to be eternal through the rational creature.—Chapter XVIII. That the Creator’s eternity is likewise demonstrated from the fourfold motion of things.—Chapter XIX. That the Creator of things is one and unchangeable.—Chapter XX. That change according to quantity or quality cannot belong to God.—Chapter XXI. That the divine Trinity can be shown from the rational soul.—Chapter XXII. That in divine things the Father loves his own wisdom for its own sake.—Chapter XXIII. That in the Trinity there is mutual love.—Chapter XXIV. The supreme Father’s exhortation to human beings to hear his Son, and through it a proof of the foregoing.—Chapter XXV. That the order of the creation and of the knowledge of things is contrary.—Chapter XXVI. On the three days of invisible light.—Chapter XXVII. That the said mystical days were first fulfilled in the human race and must be fulfilled in us, and how.

## Chapter I. On the three invisible attributes of God, from which all things emanate: power, wisdom, and goodness

[Col. 0811C]

The good Word and wise Life that made the world is perceived by contemplating the world. The Word itself could not be seen; it made what could be seen, and it was seen through what it made. For “his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood and perceived through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1).

There are three invisible attributes of God: power, wisdom, and goodness. From these three all things proceed; in these three all things consist; and through these three all things are governed. Power creates, wisdom governs, goodness preserves. Yet, just as these three are ineffably one in God, so in operation they cannot be separated at all. Power creates wisely through goodness. Wisdom governs kindly through power. Goodness preserves powerfully through wisdom.

The immensity of creatures manifests power; their beauty, wisdom; their [Col. 0811D] usefulness, [Col. 0812C] goodness. The immensity of creatures consists in multitude and magnitude. Multitude exists among similar things, diverse things, and mixed things. Magnitude exists in bulk and space. Bulk exists in mass and weight. Space exists in length, breadth, depth, and height. The beauty of creatures exists in position, motion, appearance, and quality. Position exists in composition and order. Order exists in place, time, and propriety. Motion is fourfold: local, natural, animal, and rational. Local motion is forward and backward, right and left, upward and downward, and around. Natural motion is in growth and decrease. Animal motion is in perceptions and appetites. Rational motion is in actions and deliberations. Appearance is visible form, discerned by the eye, such as colors and bodily shapes. Quality is an inward property, perceived by the other [Col. 0812D] senses: melody in sound by the hearing of the ears; sweetness in taste by the tasting of the throat; fragrance in odor by the smelling of the nostrils; softness in a body by the touch of the hands. [Col. 0813A] The usefulness of creatures consists in what is pleasant, fitting, advantageous, and necessary. Pleasant is what pleases; fitting, what is suitable; advantageous, what benefits; necessary, that without which a thing cannot exist.

Let us now return to the divisions set forth, beginning from the first; and in each kind of division let us inquire how either the Creator’s power is manifested through the immensity of creatures, or wisdom through their beauty, or goodness through their usefulness. And because immensity was first in the division, it ought to be first in the treatment.

## Chapter II. On the immensity of divine power, which we perceive from the multitude of creatures
Listen carefully, therefore, and consider what I am about to say. When there was nothing, what power was it to make something be? [Col. 0813B] What understanding can comprehend what power it is to make even one thing from nothing, however small? If, then, to make one thing, however tiny, from nothing is a power so great that it cannot be comprehended, how great must the power be thought that made so many things? How many? How numerous are they? Count the stars of heaven, the sand of the sea, the dust of the earth, raindrops, birds’ feathers, fishes’ scales, animals’ hairs, the grass of the fields, the leaves or fruits of trees, and count the countless things among all other innumerable things. Countless among things alike, countless among things different, countless among things mixed together.

What things are alike? Those contained under the same genus: for example, one human being and another; one lion and another; one eagle and another; one *honoruscopa* [a bird-name, uncertain] [Col. 0813C] and another. These individual things, and all others of this kind, are alike within their respective genera. What things are different? Those formed by unlike differences: for example, a human being and a lion; a lion and an eagle; an eagle and an *honoruscopa*. These are mutually different. What things are mixed? All things considered together.

How, then, are there infinite things among alike things? How among different things? How among mixed things? Listen. Humanity is one genus, but there is not merely one human being. Who can count them? Lion is one genus, but there is not merely one lion. Who can count them? Eagle is one genus, but there is not merely one eagle. Who can count them? And so in the other innumerable genera of innumerable things: the genera of things are infinite, and within each genus [Col. 0813D] there are infinitely many alike things. Yet all things together are infinite and innumerable.

## CHAPTER III. On the Magnitude of Creatures

But perhaps he who made so many made small things; perhaps he was unable to make many things at once and also make them great. How great, then? Measure the masses of mountains, the courses of rivers, the expanses of plains, the height of heaven, the depth of the abyss. You marvel because you fail; but in failing, you marvel better.

For those reflecting on the immensity of creatures, we have sown a kind of seedbed; let us now pass to contemplate their beauty.

## CHAPTER IV. On Their Beauty under Four Heads

Although the beauty of creatures is perfected in many and varied ways, there are nevertheless four principal respects in which their splendor consists: [Col. 0814A] position, motion, appearance, and quality. Whoever could investigate these sufficiently would discover in them a marvelous light of God’s wisdom. Would that I were as able subtly to discern and suitably to set forth these things as I am able ardently to love them. For it delights me, because it is very sweet and pleasant frequently to treat of these matters, where at once understanding is instructed by reason, the mind is delighted by sweetness, and the affection is stirred by emulation; so that with the Psalmist we are astonished and cry out in wonder: “How greatly magnified are your works, O Lord! You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103); and elsewhere: “You have delighted me in your handiwork, and I shall exult in the works of your hands. How greatly magnified are your works, O Lord! Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep. A senseless man shall not know, [Col. 0814B] nor shall a fool understand these things” (Ps. 91).

For this whole sensible world is like a book written by the finger of God—that is, created by divine power—and individual creatures are like figures, not devised at human pleasure but established by divine decision in order to disclose the wisdom of God’s invisible things. Just as, if an illiterate person sees an open book, he looks at the figures but does not recognize the letters, so the foolish and merely animal person, who does not perceive the things of God (1 Cor. 2), sees outwardly the appearance in these visible creatures, but inwardly does not understand their rationale. But the spiritual person, who can judge all things, while outwardly contemplating the beauty of the work, inwardly conceives how wondrous the wisdom of the Creator is.

Therefore there is no one to whom the works [Col. 0814C] of God are not marvelous: the fool marvels in them only at the outward appearance, but the wise person, through what he sees outwardly, investigates the deep thought of divine wisdom. It is as though, in one and the same Scripture, one person commended the color or shaping of the figures, while another praised their meaning and signification.

It is good, therefore, constantly to contemplate and admire divine works—but for one who knows how to turn the beauty of bodily things to spiritual use. For this is also why Scripture so strongly incites us to desire God’s marvels: that through the things we believe outwardly, we may come inwardly to knowledge of truth. Thus the Psalmist, as though recalling that he had already accomplished something great and promising that he would yet do it, says: “I remembered days of old; I meditated upon all your works, and I shall exercise myself in your inventions” [Col. 0814D] (Ps. 142).

For this reason also, Isaiah says to certain persons who did not know their Creator and offered to idols the worship owed to God: “Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and weighed the heavens with his palm? Who has measured out the mass of the earth with three fingers, and weighed the mountains in a balance and the hills in scales? He sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like locusts. He stretches out the heavens as though they were nothing and spreads them out like a tent” (Isa. 40). And again, when the Psalmist rebuked idol-worshippers in one place, he said: “All the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 95).

What, then, do you think is meant by God’s works being so brought forward in proof of true divinity, and by the saying, “But the Lord made the heavens,” [Col. 0815A] except that creation, rightly considered, shows a person his Creator? Let us also consider how great God’s marvels are, and through the beauty of created things seek that Beautiful One, the most beautiful of all beautiful things—so marvelous and ineffable that no transitory beauty, even if it is true beauty, can be comparable to it.

Since above we said that all the beauty of visible things consists in four respects, let us now proceed in order through each and see how God’s invisible wisdom shines forth from them. I know, indeed, that whatever we say will be inadequate; nevertheless, it is not fitting on that account to be wholly silent, especially where, if it were possible, we ought most fittingly to speak.

[Col. 0815B] We named four: position, motion, appearance, and quality. Let us therefore examine the first first. Position consists in composition and order—that is, in composition and arrangement. Composition ought to have two features: fitness and firmness; that is, the things to be joined ought to come together fittingly and suitably, and, once joined, ought to adhere firmly. Such composition is praiseworthy.

Fitness is considered in quantity and quality: in quantity, lest things too thin and slight be joined in disorder to things gross and bulky; in quality, lest things too moist be joined to dry things, things too hot to cold things, things too light to weighty things, and the like. See whether anything of these is lacking to the beauty of divine works; and if you find that nothing is lacking, you already have something in this respect also at which to marvel.

First, if you look upon the fabric [Col. 0815C] of this universe, you will find with what marvelous reason and wisdom the composition of all things has been perfected—how fitting, harmonious, beautiful, and complete in all its parts. In it, not only do like things preserve harmony, but things which, through creative power, came forth as diverse and opposed, by the direction of wisdom enter in some fashion into one friendship and alliance.

What can be more opposed than water and fire? Yet God’s prudence has so tempered them in the nature of things that they not only do not destroy their mutual bond of common fellowship, but even provide vital nourishment to all things born, so that they may subsist. What shall I say of the structure of the human body, where the joints of all the members preserve such harmony with one another [Col. 0815D] that no member at all can be found whose function does not appear to furnish assistance to another?

Thus all nature loves itself, and, in a marvelous manner, the harmony of many unlike things brought into one produces a single harmony in all things. The composition of all things, therefore, is fitting and harmonious; but how is it firm? Who does not see it? Who does not marvel? Behold how the heavens, which encompass all things by their circuit, are solid and, as though molten from bronze, spread out above on every side. The earth, balanced in the middle by its own weight, remains always immovable, so that the solidity of the heavens on one side and the earth’s stability on the other may compress and bind together the other things fluctuating between them, lest, spread beyond their appointed bounds, [Col. 0816A] they break apart the harmony of the universe.

Behold how streams of waters, scattered inwardly through the bowels of the earth and led outwardly in different directions through their channels, bind together its interior when it tends to split apart, lest it dissolve; and outwardly water it when dry, lest it crack. Behold how, in the construction of the human body, bands of sinews bind the joints of the bones, and how, with marrow distributed within through the hollow channels of the shinbones, the channels of the veins also carry life-giving blood throughout the body; then the covering of skin envelops the tenderness of the flesh, so that the rigidity of the bones may support the body within and the protection of skin may guard it from without.

Who can enumerate the hardness of stones, the solidity of metals, the knotty strength of oaks, the adhesiveness of glues, and countless other things? [Col. 0816B] From this it is clear how firm the bonds of things are: each created thing defends its own nature and being with such effort, while all things together are wholly unable to be dissolved from the harmony of their fellowship.

## CHAPTER V. On the Position and Arrangement of Things in Place

After composition, it follows that we should consider the character of the arrangement of things. No small cause for wonder will arise if someone carefully observes that divine providence has assigned its proper causes to individual places, individual times, and individual things in such a way that in nothing at all is the order of things disturbed.

Behold: heaven is above, and earth below. He placed stars and heavenly lights in heaven, so that they might illuminate all things beneath. In the air he made a path for winds and clouds, so that, scattered according to his purposes, they might pour rain downwards. He commanded masses of water to be received into the bosom [Col. 0816C] of the earth, so that through their channels they might run hither and thither wherever the commanding will directed them. He suspended birds in the air, immersed fish in the waters, and filled the earth with beasts, serpents, and kinds of other creeping creatures and worms.

He enriched certain regions with abundance of grain, some with wealth of vineyards, others with fertility of vegetables, others with fecundity of livestock, others with potent herbs, others with precious gems, others with monstrous animals and beasts, others with varied colors, others with the pursuits of different arts, others with metals, others with different kinds of incense; so that there is no region at all which does not possess something new and distinctive beyond the rest, and likewise none which cannot receive something new and distinctive from others.

Moreover, the very providence of the Creator has established in the common multitude of humankind those things [Col. 0816D] necessary for human use; but those things which nature does not seek for necessity’s sake, but desire seeks for their attractiveness, he has hidden in remote corners of the earth, so that one whom love of virtue does not restrain from excessive desire may at least, overcome by weariness of labor, come to rest.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Arrangement of Times

We have spoken of the arrangement of places. What shall we say of the arrangement of times? Who can sufficiently admire the marvelous reason by which divine providence distinguished the course of times? Behold: day comes after night, so that work may exercise those made sluggish by idleness; night follows day, so that rest may receive the weary for renewal.

[Col. 0817A] There is not always day, not always night, not always equality of day and night, lest either excessive labor break the weakened, or continued rest impair nature, or unvarying sameness generate weariness in the mind. Again, just as the alternation of days and nights renews living creatures, so the four seasons of the year, following one another in order, transform the appearance of the whole world. First, through the warmth of spring, the world is born in a kind of renewal. Then, through summer heat, it is strengthened as though into youth. After this, with autumn’s arrival, it ascends to maturity. Finally, with winter following, it inclines toward decline.

It always declines, however, in order that after decline it may always be renewed; for unless old things first declined from their state, new things could not arise, as though the old occupied their place. [Col. 0817B] This also is sufficiently marvelous in this arrangement: the seasons themselves keep the turns of their changeability by so immutable a law that they neither ever fail in carrying out their office nor, by proceeding otherwise, confuse the order of their first institution.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Order Considered in Each Thing from the Arrangement of Its Parts

Let these examples concerning the arrangement of times suffice. Let us now pursue that order which is considered in each thing according to the fitting arrangement of its parts. This order is internal; the others—namely, those according to place and time—are external. Here too the efficacy of wisdom is no less marvelous: it so fittingly distributes individual things throughout the universe [Col. 0817C] that nowhere does the joining of parts produce opposition among their qualities.

Behold, to give a few examples from many: how much the Creator’s wisdom shines forth in the composition of the human body! Above, a human being is uniform; below, divided in two. For the ruling faculty of the mind—that is, reason, which looks to invisible things—is uniform; and, as the quality of the soul is twofold, so too is desire, which descends below toward earthly things.

Again, the human body’s frame is extended broadly by the arms and fixed below by the legs, because the intention of action extends the mind, while the affection of desires fixes it. Again, in its breadth the extension of the human body ends on either side in the five toes, because, whether the mind is extended broadly through intention of work or fixed below through [Col. 0817D] desire of affection, there are five senses through which it goes outward.

Again, the fingers are distinguished by three intervals of joints, proceeding from one palm in the hands and one sole in the feet, because from one capacity for sensation five senses proceed, in which the first distinction reveals first the sense, then sensing, and afterward the sensible object. Finally, the ends of the outermost joints of each finger, overlaid with nails, appear as though helmeted, so that wherever an obstacle may be encountered, whether by the extended hand or advancing foot, those parts, protected by their own defense, may remain intact.

Similarly, those earthly things adhering outwardly to the senses, like nails, fortify us as things of necessity; but insofar as they do not pertain to necessity [Col. 0818A], they may be cut off, like things outside the flesh and without sensation.

Behold with what rational arrangement the instruments of the senses are placed in the human face. Sight occupies the highest position in the eyes; then hearing in the ears; after it smell in the nostrils; and after that taste in the mouth. We know that all the other senses enter from outside inward, whereas sight alone goes from within outward and perceives things set at a distance with marvelous agility beyond the others. It fittingly occupies the highest place, therefore, as a watchman, so that it may foresee beforehand the danger of things about to come upon the other senses.

After it, hearing is second both in place and nobility; then smell. Taste, however, which can sense nothing except what it touches, fittingly sits lowest, being slower than the other senses. [Col. 0818B] Touch has no special seat; it is universal precisely because it cooperates with every sense. Thus, in the fingers, the thumb, which signifies touch, alone answers to all the fingers gathered together into one, because no sense can exist without touch.

See also how bones are placed within the human body, so that their strength may support the body; then flesh clothes the bones, so that their hardness may receive touch gently; finally skin covers the flesh, so that by its own tenacity it may in some fashion protect the body from harmful things striking it from outside. Observe how that which is soft and weak is placed in the middle as though in a safer position, lest, lacking inward support, it collapse, or, lacking outward defense, it break apart.

What has been illustrated in one example can be found in every [Col. 0818C] kind of thing. Thus bark protects the tree; feathers and beaks protect birds; scales protect fish; and the Creator’s providence has established protections for each thing according to the suitability of its nature.

Thus far we have spoken of position; let us now proceed to motion.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Manifold Motion of Things

Motion is fourfold: local, natural, animal, and rational. Since we cannot say much about each one separately, let us touch on each briefly. See how the Creator’s wisdom appears in local motion. Consider now whence an unfailing spring is always supplied to waters continually flowing away; whence [Col. 0818D] the movement of winds is produced; who governs the tireless course of the stars; who commands the sun to descend through the winter signs; who in turn makes it ascend through the summer signs; who leads it from east to west and brings it back again from west to east. All these things are marvelous and possible to God alone.

What also shall I say of natural motion? Who, do you suppose, grants growth to all things being born, brings forth shoots as though from a hidden bosom of nature into the open, and then makes those same things, withering, return whence they came? To those who look upon these matters attentively enough, they will appear marvelous.

Then follows animal motion, which is in the senses and appetites. Consider, therefore, what kind of being he can be who fashions the senses of all living creatures, creates their appetites, and [Col. 0819A] orders in every individual animal what it ought to desire and how much it ought to desire. Finally, rational motion, which is in deeds and counsels, gives you sufficient cause for wonder if you are willing to attend to how ineffable is the wisdom that bends, commands, and governs all human deeds, all wills, and indeed all thoughts of hearts according to the decision of its own will, so that nothing can occur in the universe which it does not itself will to occur, either by commanding it or by permitting it, for the beauty of its works.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Appearance and Figures of Things

Let what has been said about motion suffice for brevity’s sake. Appearance follows. Appearance is visible form and contains two things: figures and colors. The figures of things appear marvelous in many ways: sometimes through size, sometimes through smallness, sometimes because they are rare, sometimes because they are beautiful, sometimes—if I may speak this way for the moment—because they are in some fashion fittingly ill-fitted; sometimes because one figure exists in many things, sometimes because diverse figures occur in one thing. Let us pursue each in its order.

A figure is considered according to size when some thing exceeds in quantity the measure of its genus; thus we marvel at a giant among human beings, a whale among fish, a griffin among birds, an elephant among four-footed animals, and a dragon among serpents. [Col. 0819B] A figure is considered according to smallness when some thing cannot equal the quantity of its genus: such are the *succerio* in a hair, the moth in a garment, worms and gnats, and similar things. These indeed live among other animals, but differ from them all by the minuteness of their [Col. 0819C] bodies.

Consider, then, at which you marvel more: a boar’s tusks or moths; a griffin’s wings or gnats’ wings; a horse’s head or a locust’s; an elephant’s legs or a gnat’s; a pig’s snout or a *succerio*’s; an eagle or an ant; a lion or a flea; a tiger or a tortoise. There you marvel at greatness; here you marvel at smallness: a small body fashioned with great wisdom—great wisdom into which no negligence creeps. He gave eyes to creatures which the eye can scarcely comprehend; and in bodies so tiny he distributed with complete fullness, in every respect, the features suitable to their nature, so that in the least of them you see nothing lacking of all that nature formed in the great.

## CHAPTER X. On Those Things That Are Marvelous Because They Are Rare

[Col. 0819D] It remains now to speak of those things that are rare and therefore seem more marvelous. Among created things there are some which, when seen, are more marvelous for the very reason that they rarely come to human knowledge: either because they were created pure within their kind, or because they are hidden in remote places and in the concealed recesses of nature.

The Creator’s providence willed to place these apart, so that human society might not be harmed by association with things that are noxious; that human desire might be tested by the attractiveness of precious things; that human sluggishness, stirred by the novelty of rare things, might learn to marvel; and finally, that these good and evil things, placed as though at a distance, might in some way address the human being, so that he may consider with how much zeal he ought to flee eternal evils and seek eternal goods, if he undergoes such great labors to obtain these temporal [Col. 0820A] goods and avoid these temporal evils.

## CHAPTER XI. On Those Things That Are Marvelous Because They Are Beautiful

There follows a discussion of those things that are marvelous because of beauty. We marvel at the form of certain things because they are attractive and suitably fitted together in some special manner, so that the arrangement of the work itself seems in some fashion to indicate that the Creator bestowed special care upon it. Conversely, we marvel at other things because they are monstrous or ridiculous; and the more their construction is removed from human reason, the more easily it can compel the human mind to wonder.

Why, when a crocodile eats, does it not move its lower jaw? How does the salamander remain unharmed in fire? Who gave spines to the hedgehog [Col. 0820B] and taught it to roll itself among apples shaken down by a whirlwind, so that, laden with them, it goes along creaking like a cart? Who endowed the ant, foreknowing the coming winter, to fill its storehouses with grain? Who endowed the spider to weave from its own entrails the snares by which it catches prey? These are witnesses to the wisdom of God.

There is still another true and evident proof of divine wisdom: every genus produces something like itself; and this one likeness, propagated through so many things, does not alter the form of the first origin. A sheep does not produce a calf, a cow a lamb, a hind a hare, a lion a fox; but everything that exists extends its offspring into what is like itself.

Insensible nature likewise maintains this rule. One genus of tree is the linden, another the beech, another the oak. Each has its own appearance, and each preserves the likeness of its own [Col. 0820C] genus. Look at a leaf: how it is divided all around by serrated teeth, how it is interwoven within by veins extending here and there. Count one; count another. Everything belonging to one genus you will find alike both in number and in likeness: as many teeth in one as in another, as many veins in one as in another, such a form in one as in another, such a color in one as in another.

Behold how mulberries and strawberries are marked all around by small grains compacted together; every one is like the other, and all nature is as though it had received the command of someone inwardly dictating to it and nowhere presumes to exceed its bounds. This also is marvelous: that in one body so many members are established, so many forms of members, so many places, so many offices. Behold how many members are in one human body: ear differs from eye, tongue from nose, foot from hand; each has its own form, place, and office; and though they are so different in themselves, all nevertheless cooperate with one another.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Various Colors of Things

Color follows figure. There is no need to discuss the color of things at length, since sight itself proves how much beauty is added to nature when it is adorned, distinguished by so many varied colors. What is more beautiful than light? Though it has no color in itself, it nevertheless in some fashion colors all the colors of things by illuminating them. What is more delightful to see than the heaven when it is clear, shining like sapphire and receiving the eye, soothing its gaze with a most pleasing [Col. 0821A] moderation of its brightness?

The sun glows like gold; the moon is pale like electrum; some stars shine with a fiery appearance; some glitter with rosy light; others in turn display now a rosy, now a green, now a white brilliance. What shall I say of gems and precious stones, whose efficacy is not only useful but whose appearance is also marvelous? Behold the earth crowned with flowers: what a delightful spectacle it provides, how it pleases the sight, how it stirs affection! We see red roses, white lilies, purple violets; in all these not only the beauty but also the origin is marvelous—namely, how God’s wisdom brings such an appearance forth from the dust of earth.

Finally, green—more beautiful than every other beautiful thing—[Col. 0821B] draws the minds of those beholding it, when, in new spring, shoots emerge with a kind of new life and rise upward in their spikes, as though death beneath had been trampled underfoot, breaking forth together into the light as an image of the future resurrection. But why do we speak of God’s works, when we so greatly marvel even at the cosmetic dyes of human artistry, which deceive the eyes with a kind of counterfeit wisdom?

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Sensible Qualities of Things

After appearance, we must discuss the quality of things. The Creator’s providence has bestowed such diverse qualities upon things so that every human sense may find its own delights. Sight perceives one thing, hearing another, smell another, taste another, touch another. The beauty of colors feeds sight; the sweetness of song soothes [Col. 0821C] hearing; fragrance of odor delights smell; sweetness of flavor delights taste; the fitting quality of a body delights touch.

Who can enumerate all the delights of the senses? They are so manifold in each sense that anyone considering any one of them separately would think it enriched in itself alone. For as many delights for the eyes as we have shown in the diversity of colors, so many delights for the ears we find in the variety of sounds. Foremost among these are the sweet exchanges of speech, by which people communicate their wishes to one another: they recount the past, indicate the present, announce the future, and reveal what is hidden. Indeed, if human life lacked these, it would seem comparable to beasts.

What of the songs of birds? What of the pleasing melody of the human voice? What need is there to mention the sweet modes of all sounds? The kinds of harmony [Col. 0821D] are so many that neither thought can run through them nor speech easily explain them. Yet all serve hearing and were created for its delight.

The same is true of smell. Incenses have their own odor; ointments have their own odor; rose gardens have their own odor; bramble thickets, meadows, wastelands, groves, and flowers have their own odor. All things that provide sweet fragrance and breathe pleasant scents serve smell and were created for its delight. In the same way, taste and touch have varied delights, which may sufficiently be understood from the resemblance of those already mentioned.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Fourfold Usefulness of Things

We have spoken, as we could rather than as we ought, concerning the immensity of creatures and [Col. 0822A] their beauty. It remains to pass to consider their usefulness. The usefulness of things includes four kinds: necessary things, conveniences, suitable things, and pleasing things.

Necessary for each thing is that without which it cannot fittingly subsist: for example, bread and water in a person’s food, and woolen or skin garments, or any clothing of that sort, in dress. A convenience is something without which life can nevertheless be lived, though it sometimes gives greater delight: for example, a cup of wine and the eating of meat in a person’s food; fine linen and silk, or any other softer garment, in dress. What is fitting and suitable is that which, though it does not benefit those using it, is nevertheless appropriate for use: such are dyed colors, precious stones, and [Col. 0822B] whatever things of this sort are esteemed. Pleasing things are those not fit for use, but nevertheless delightful to behold: perhaps certain kinds of herbs, beasts, birds, fish, and anything similar.

But it is very worthy of investigation why God willed to create these things which he foresaw would not be necessary for human use—human beings for whose sake he made all things. Yet this will be known more quickly if one considers the cause and manner of the human condition. God made humanity for himself; he created everything else for human beings. He made humanity for himself, not because he himself needed humanity, but so that, since he could give the human being nothing better, he might give himself for humanity’s enjoyment. Every other creature, however, was so made that it was subject to humanity by its condition and served human usefulness.

[Col. 0822C] The human being, placed as though in a middle position, has God above and the world below. By the body, indeed, he is joined downward to the world; but by the spirit he is raised upward to God. It was necessary, moreover, that the condition of visible things should be ordered so that, through them, a human being might recognize outwardly what invisible good he ought to seek inwardly—that is, so that he might see beneath himself what he should desire above himself. The abundance of visible things, therefore, ought not fittingly to suffer any deficiency in any respect, since it was established chiefly in order to proclaim the inestimable abundance of eternal goods.

This is what we said: why God also willed to create things which he foresaw would not be necessary for human uses. For if he gave only necessary things, he would indeed be good, but not rich. [Col. 0822D] But when he joins conveniences to necessities, he displays the riches of his goodness. When conveniences are heaped up by the addition of suitable things, the abundance of his divine goodness is shown. But when, finally, he adds pleasing and delightful things even to suitable things, what else does he make known but the overflowing riches of his goodness?

## CHAPTER XV. On the Three Similar Things, and How Great Is the Superiority of Divine Workmanship over Human Workmanship

Let what has been said briefly concerning the usefulness of things suffice. Yet, to augment divine praise, I would like to attend a little longer to how marvelously God preserved these three things together in his work. How worthy this is of wonder we may perhaps recognize more easily if we first consider how these things cannot coexist [Col. 0823A] together in human work.

Certainly, when a person wishes to make many things, he cannot make great things, because he has proportionally less strength for individual things the more numerous are the things among which the effort of his attention is divided. Conversely, when he strives for greatness, he is hindered from multiplicity, because his strength is insufficient to provide for many things when he expends it especially upon the production of one. Likewise, less care is devoted to the beauty of a work whenever the mind is occupied only with achieving multiplicity or greatness.

We see that a scribe forms small letters more readily, toils more laboriously when forming large ones, and that the more rapidly the pen is drawn, the more misshapen are the letters produced. In making garments likewise, those who love beauty too much often lose usefulness, and those who wish to preserve usefulness cannot have beauty.

But in God’s work, neither does multiplicity diminish greatness, nor does greatness restrict multiplicity; neither multiplicity nor greatness together impairs beauty, nor does beauty remove usefulness. Rather, all things were made as though each had been made singly, so that when you look upon all things together, you marvel at each one.

What has been said about visible things may perhaps seem excessive to someone, considering the brevity required in treating the subject. But such a person ought to consider that a subject so laborious is not easily explained in few words. For since the Apostle says that through the things which are in the world the things invisible in God are made manifest (Rom. 1), anyone wishing to arrive through visible things at knowledge of invisible things [Col. 0823B] must [Col. 0823C] first know those visible things themselves.

For this reason, when I proposed to investigate these matters as far as I could, having enumerated three invisible things at the beginning and likewise set three visible things against them, I judged this to be the most suitable order of exposition: first to set forth some knowledge of visible things themselves, and then, as though the entrance to contemplation had been opened, to proceed through investigation of invisible things. Since, therefore, we have completed what was to be said about visible things, we must now consider how and in what order one ascends through them to invisible things.

## CHAPTER XVI. That among God’s Three Invisible Things, Wisdom Is to Be Investigated First
[Col. 0823D] We have spoken of three invisible realities: power, wisdom, and goodness. We must therefore inquire which of these first presents itself to those who contemplate them in knowledge. And I think that that invisible reality is first apprehended in contemplation which is more expressly and manifestly declared in its visible likeness. Now visible things themselves are called likenesses of invisible things: thus the likeness of invisible power is the immensity of creatures; the likeness of invisible wisdom is the beauty of creatures; the likeness of invisible goodness is the usefulness of creatures. But every creature, the more nearly it approaches the likeness of the Creator, the more clearly it declares its Creator. Therefore that visible likeness ought first to show the invisible [Col. 0824A] exemplar which retains more perfectly expressed within itself the image of the divine likeness.

Now the immensity of creatures pertains more to essence; their beauty, however, more to form. Essence considered without form is formlessness. And what is formless is like God in so far as it exists; but in so far as it lacks form, it differs from God. Therefore what is formed is more like God than that which has no form. Hence it is evident that the beauty of creatures is a more manifest likeness than their immensity, which regards essence alone.

Again, the beauty of creatures, because of their natural form, pertains to condition; usefulness, however, to action, because creatures are useful in that they serve and render obedience to humankind, to whom they are subject. What pertains to condition is more proper and more certain than what pertains to action, because nature imparted condition, whereas institution added action. Therefore the likeness constituted by beauty precedes both immensity and usefulness in knowledge; and it is prior in knowledge because it is more evident in manifestation.

In this likeness, then, we ought first to set the footprint of contemplation, so that, having rightly held the first entrance of inquiry, we may proceed with unerring step to the remaining matters, guided by him whom we seek. It is fitting, moreover, that in the inquiry into wisdom the beginning of investigation should be taken from the very likeness of wisdom, because the Father is manifested through his wisdom—not only when he sent his wisdom into flesh, but also when through his wisdom [Col. 0824C] he created the world.

The beauty of creatures, which we have said is the likeness of God’s wisdom, comprises four things: position, motion, appearance, and quality. But among these four there can be no doubt that motion holds the higher place, because things capable of motion are nearer to life than things which cannot be moved. Motion, moreover, is fourfold: local, natural, animal, and rational. But natural motion surpasses local motion, because in natural motion not only is an image of life expressed, but life itself is in some manner begun. Again, animal motion excels natural motion by as much as that which senses excels the merely sensible. Finally, rational motion is set above all, because in it not only sense is moved toward animation, but reason also toward understanding [Col. 0824D]. Among creatures there can be no likeness more evident than this, because what possesses understanding most manifestly shows invisible wisdom.

## CHAPTER XVII. How the Creator of things is shown, through the rational creature, to be eternal.

The first and chief mystery of wisdom, then, is created wisdom—that is, the rational creature. Since it is visible in one respect and invisible in another, it has become both the door and the way of contemplation. In so far as it is visible, it is the door; in so far as it is invisible, it is the way. It is a door because it first opens to the mind an entrance into contemplation. It is a way because it leads the soul running in contemplation to its end. It is a door because in some measure it visibly displays invisible things. It is a way because it leads those proceeding from visible things through invisible things [Col. 0825A] to behold the Creator alike of visible and invisible things.

A human being can recognize this in himself. For no one who is soundly wise fails to see that he exists. Yet if a person begins truly to attend to what he himself is, he understands that of all the things in him which are seen or can be seen, none is himself. For that in us which is capable of reason, although, so to speak, poured into and mingled with the flesh, nevertheless distinguishes itself from the substance of flesh by its own reason and understands itself to be foreign to it. Why, then, should a human being doubt that invisible things exist, when that very thing which is truly the human being, and whose existence he does not at all doubt, appears to be invisible? Thus the door of contemplation is opened to a person when, led by his own reason, he enters upon knowing himself.

[Col. 0825B] But once he has entered, there remains a path to be run to its end: namely, that each person may arrive, from consideration of himself, at knowledge of his Creator. For that in us which does not possess a fleshly essence cannot have its matter from flesh; but, as it differs from flesh, so it recognizes itself as alien to the origin of flesh. Yet it most truly recognizes that it has a beginning in this: although it understands that it exists, it does not remember always having existed—although intellect cannot exist without understanding [variant: “understanding”]. Therefore, if intellect cannot exist unless it understands, it follows that we must believe that what we know has not always understood has not always existed, and thus began at some time.

But, as has already been said, what has a spiritual essence cannot have a bodily origin, because whatever is derived from pre-existing matter [Col. 0825C] is proved to be bodily. If, therefore, our invisible part has had a beginning, it remains that it was made not from pre-existing matter but from nothing. But what is nothing cannot give existence to itself; and therefore, whatever has had a beginning has undoubtedly received existence from another. And what is not from itself cannot give existence to others. Therefore, whoever it is that granted existence to things did not receive existence from another.

This is also clearly proved from the fact that, if we believe that everything which exists is a creature, we find no end in the series of things. Our nature, therefore, teaches us that we have an eternal Creator, whose own and proper attribute is self-subsistence; for if he had received existence from another, he could not truly be called the first origin of things. For if at some time he was not from himself [Col. 0825D], he has no beginning from himself; nor can he be called first if he received existence from another. Therefore, if he is Creator, he has always existed.

Likewise, what is from itself cannot cease to be. For whatever is from itself has being and that which it is as the same thing; and it is evident that no thing can be divided or separated from itself. Therefore, that for which being and what it is are the same necessarily always exists, because nothing can be separated from itself. If, then, whatever is from itself has being and what it is as the same thing, and has not received existence from elsewhere, it necessarily follows that it always exists and cannot have taken away from it from elsewhere what was not given from elsewhere. We must therefore confess that the one whom we believe to be Creator can have neither beginning [Col. 0826A] nor end. For that which has always existed has no beginning; and that which never ceases has no end. Therefore nothing but the Creator is eternal, nor can the Creator be anything but eternal.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That the Creator’s eternity is also proved from the fourfold motion of things.

In rational motion we find this knowledge: namely, that we have an eternal Creator, who lacks a beginning because he has always existed, and suffers no end because he will always exist. The other motions also attest this knowledge—namely, animal, natural, and local motion.

For animal motion includes sensation and appetite. Every natural appetite finds fulfillment in things, and there is no ordered desire that cannot attain its own effect. [Col. 0826B] For example: living creatures are hungry and find something to eat; they thirst and find something to drink; they are cold and find something by which to warm themselves. It is evident, therefore, that providence went beforehand, by whose counsel this provision was made then, lest the aid now necessary for the needs of things should be lacking. For he who established appetites himself prepared sustenance for those appetites. Nor could it in any way come about, if events were fortuitous, that in every case the appropriate effect should so correspond to every desire.

Natural motion proves the same. For just as it is impossible for something to come from nothing by itself, so it is altogether impossible for something to receive growth by itself. That is: what cannot give itself a beginning cannot give itself increase. Whatever comes to a growing thing as an increase [Col. 0826C] is proved to be other than what previously existed by itself alone without increase. Therefore, if nothing can grow unless something is added to it which it did not previously have, it is evident that no growing thing receives increase by itself. He, therefore, who gives growth to growing things gave a beginning to things that did not exist.

Local motion proves the same. For we see some creatures moved by perpetual motion, others moving according to time, and still others in one way or another. Although things move so differently, the order of things is nowhere confused. Hence there can be no doubt that there is within them the ordering governance of one who rules all things by a fixed law. On what grounds, then, do we deny providence, if every rational appetite naturally finds sustenance prepared for it, and if it never happens at all that what nature desires in one thing nature does not possess in another? Likewise, since motions and growths, so various and diverse in their outward course, nevertheless never confuse their order, how can we deny that there is an inward ordering? [Col. 0826D] Therefore there can be no doubt that an invisible ruler presides within, who both anticipates by his providence the events of all things and orders them by his wisdom.

## CHAPTER XIX. That the Creator of things is one and unchangeable.

One, I say. For nature itself teaches this also: that there is one maker of all things and one ruler. For if different counsels of rulers presided within, the courses of things themselves would sometimes diverge outwardly from one another. But now, since all things run together so harmoniously toward one end, they surely indicate that there is one fountain and origin from which they proceed.

But because “one” is understood in various ways, we must consider in what manner the Creator of things is called one. There is oneness by collection, oneness by composition, oneness by likeness, oneness by essence, and oneness by identity. There is oneness by collection, as when we call a flock one, though it contains many animals. Oneness by composition, as when we call a body one, though it contains many members. Oneness by likeness, as when we call a voice one though many have uttered it. But none of these is truly one. They are called one only in some respect because they approach unity in a certain manner.

[Col. 0827B] Therefore we must not suppose that the Creator of things is one by a collection of diverse things, by a composition of parts, or by a likeness of many, since even that rational element in us can find none of these things in itself. For what we see composed of a multitude of parts is proved by our very reason not to be rational, but to be joined to the rational. If, therefore, our rational element is truly one, how much more should its Creator be believed to be truly one?

Now that is truly one which is one essentially, for which to be is wholly to be one, and whose being is simple. Whatever, therefore, is truly one is simple and cannot at all be divided into any parts; and thus it admits no division of parts because it admits no composition of parts. Therefore, for the Creator of things, being and what he is are one, because the being which he is is wholly one and simple.

But we must further consider that certain things are truly one and yet are not supremely one, such as souls, which are one essentially but are not one unchangeably. What is both truly and supremely one is one essentially and unchangeably. It remains, therefore, if we believe God to be truly one, to inquire whether he can also be called supremely one. This we establish truly if we prove him altogether unchangeable. But because we cannot know how God is unchangeable unless we first recognize in how many ways any thing can be changed, we must first describe all the modes of changeability and then [Col. 0827D] show individually how they are excluded from God.

All changeability occurs in three ways: by place, form, and time. A thing changes locally when it passes from place to place; that is, it ceases to be where it was and begins to be where it was not. This change is external and changes nothing of the thing’s own essence, because, if it ceases to be where it was, it does not cease to be what it was; and if it begins to be where it was not, it does not begin to be what it was not.

A thing changes formally when, while persisting in the same place according to its essence, it either receives by increase something it did not previously have, loses by diminution something it previously had, or begins by alteration to possess something it had before in a manner [Col. 0828A] different from that in which it previously possessed it. Change according to time arises from the two preceding kinds, because nothing can change temporally unless it changes either formally or locally. Hence it plainly follows that whatever can be changed neither in form nor in place is altogether unchangeable.

Therefore, if it is established that God cannot be changed either in form or in place, there will be no doubt that he is altogether unchangeable. We easily exclude local change from him if we show that he is everywhere. For what is everywhere is in every place, and what is in every place cannot pass from place to place.

There are many indications that God is everywhere. First, our own soul: reason does not doubt that it is a simple essence, and sense proves that it is diffused through the whole body which it animates. For whatever part of an animate body is injured, there is one to whom the sensation of every pain is referred; and this would not happen at all if the one and same soul were not diffused everywhere. If, therefore, the rational spirit of a human being, although simple, is diffused throughout the body it governs, it is unfitting to believe that the Creator, who rules and possesses all things, is confined in some one place rather than fills all things.

[Col. 0828B] Indeed, the very motions of things, which proceed everywhere under such certain and rational governance, show that there is a life moving inwardly. Yet we must by no means believe that, just as human sensation is personally joined to the body which it endows with sensation, so that Creator-Spirit is personally joined to the body of this sensible world. For God fills the world in one way, and the soul fills the body in another. The soul fills and contains the body, because it is circumscribable; God fills the world, but is not enclosed by the world, because, present everywhere, he can be comprehended nowhere.

Furthermore, since we see that the effects of divine power are nowhere absent, why should we doubt that this same power of God is present in all things? But if God’s power is everywhere, and God’s power is not other than God, it is evident that God is absent nowhere. God does not, like a human being, require another’s power in order to act; for a person often accomplishes by another’s help what he cannot do by his own power. Hence, according to a customary manner of speaking, a person is sometimes said to act where he is undoubtedly absent in person [Col. 0828D], as when a king residing in his own city is said to fight with enemies far away, to conquer, or to be defeated, because his soldiers, at his will and command, fight, conquer, or are overcome by force.

The same is true when someone stretches out a rod or throws a stone toward something far away and is said to touch whatever the stone or rod touches. There are many such cases, but none of them is properly so described, because what one does is attributed to another. But God, who himself performs all things by his own power, must be present in deity wherever he is present in operation.

If anyone perhaps asks how the divine essence, which is simple, can be everywhere, let him know that “simple” is said differently of a spirit and of a body. A body is called simple because of smallness; [Col. 0829A] but when a spirit is called simple, not smallness but unity is signified. Therefore the Creator is simple because he is one, and he is everywhere because he is God. Existing in every place, he is comprehended nowhere, because, filling all things, he contains and is not contained. Since, therefore, he is in every place, he cannot be changed locally; and since he is comprehended by nothing, he is not local.

## CHAPTER XX. That change according to quantity or quality cannot belong to God.

But neither can the changeability which is according to form occur in him. For whatever changes according to form changes either by increase, diminution, or alteration; but the divine nature receives none of these, as can easily be seen one by one.

It does not increase. For whatever grows by increase receives something beyond itself. But whatever receives something beyond what it has in itself must receive it from elsewhere, because no thing can give itself what it does not have. Yet from whom could the Creator of things receive something which he does not have, when everything that exists proceeds from him? Therefore he cannot grow, because he can receive nothing greater than himself; nor can he be diminished. For whatever can become less than itself is not truly one, because what divides itself in separation was not the same in union. Therefore God, for whom being and what he is are wholly one, can in no way become less than himself.

[Col. 0829C] Therefore perfection cannot be increased, unity cannot be diminished, immensity cannot be comprehended, and he who is everywhere present cannot be changed locally. It remains to show how alteration alone cannot befit the divine nature. And because alteration of bodies is different from alteration of spirits, and because from what has been said above it is established that God is not a body but a spirit, when we speak of God we need not discuss at length alteration in bodies. We shall nevertheless touch on it briefly, in order to come more suitably to alteration in spirits.

Alteration of bodies occurs through transposition of parts and change of qualities. Alteration of spirits occurs through knowledge and affection. Spirits change in affection, being now sad and now cheerful; in knowledge, being now less wise and now more wise. But there are two principal things which are accustomed to change the affection of one who acts: either that he has done something in the past of which he ought to repent, or that he proposes something disordered for the future.

But that God does not repent of what he has done is shown clearly enough by this unchangeable course of all things, which so does not abandon the pattern of the first institution under the perpetual law. And that he proposes nothing disordered is proved by the rational outcome, which nowhere contradicts itself in the vast body of nature. Therefore God’s will is always unchangeable: he neither changes his counsel concerning the past nor his purpose concerning the future.

Likewise he must be believed unchangeable in knowledge. For human knowledge is subject to changeability in three ways: through increase, diminution, and succession. Through increase, as when we say that we do not know; through diminution, when we forget what we know. [Col. 0830A] Succession, moreover, is fourfold: in essence, form, place, and time.

Human knowledge undergoes succession in essence when we think now of this, now of that, because we cannot comprehend all things simultaneously by our perception. In form, when we attend to the very same thing now as one sort of thing, now as another, because we cannot do both at once. In place, when we direct our thought now here, now there, because we cannot be everywhere at once in thought. In time, when we consider now past things, now present things, now future things. Knowledge also changes in time when we now interrupt knowledge once possessed and now resume knowledge once interrupted, because we cannot retain it without interruption.

But divine knowledge admits none of these changes. It does not increase, because it is full. For he who creates, governs, penetrates, and sustains all things cannot fail to know all things. And he who is present to all things in deity cannot be absent in vision. It cannot be diminished, because whatever he is is not from elsewhere; rather, whatever he is is himself, from himself—from the one, and one whole being that he is.

[Col. 0830B] What shall I say of succession? How can wisdom admit succession when it comprehends all things simultaneously and at once beneath one ray of vision? Simultaneously, because it comprehends every essence, every form, all places, and all times. At once, because it neither experiences interrupted vision nor interrupts vision once possessed; but what exists once always exists, and what always exists is whole. It sees all things; it sees all things concerning all things; it always sees; and it sees everywhere. For nothing new comes to it, nothing foreign, nothing its own [as an addition].

When something is future, it foresees it; when present, it sees it; when past, it retains it. Nor does it foresee, see, or retain anything other than what is in itself; but what comes in time was in its vision, and what passes away in time remains in its vision.

Suppose your entire body were an eye, and that for you being and seeing were not different things. Wherever a thing turned itself, it could not fail to be present to you, and, remaining unmoved beneath a single gaze, you would comprehend whatever lay before your sight in every direction. Indeed, you would see before you only whatever stood around you on every side, facing you. The thing would pass, but the vision would remain; and wherever it turned by its own movement, it would be present only to that which remained still. [Col. 0830D] But now, because you see only in part, you do not see unchangeably; and when the thing passes from the one seeing, either it ceases to be seen or it draws vision along with itself in changeable fashion. But if you were wholly an eye, you would not see so changeably.

Whatever is partial is changeable, and whatever is not partial is not changeable. But God, for whom being, living, and understanding are the same, since he is not partial in essence, cannot be partial in wisdom either. As his essence is unchangeable, so also is his wisdom unchangeable. Let this suffice concerning divine knowledge. But it should be known that this knowledge is also called vision, wisdom, foreknowledge, and providence: vision because it beholds; wisdom because it understands; foreknowledge because it anticipates; providence [Col. 0831A] because it orders. Many difficult and perplexing questions arise concerning these matters, which we are reluctant to insert into this concise treatment. Let us therefore proceed to what remains.

## CHAPTER XXI. That the divine Trinity can be shown from the rational soul.

Since some time ago we entered, with the eye of contemplation, from visible things into invisible things, the path of inquiry has penetrated thus far: we no longer doubt that the Creator of all things is without beginning, without end, and without changeability. And we have found this not outside ourselves but within ourselves. Let us consider, then, whether this same nature of ours teaches us anything further about our Creator—whether perhaps it shows not only one, but also three.

Certainly the rational mind is one, and it generates understanding from itself: one generates one. When it contemplates this understanding—how subtle, true, fitting, and delightful it is—it immediately loves it and takes delight in itself in it. It sees and marvels at once, and wonders that it could have found something of this sort in itself. It greatly desires always to behold it, always to possess it, always to enjoy it, always to delight in it. It pleases in itself; it pleases for its own sake; nor is anything sought outside it, because in it everything is loved. In it the contemplation of truth is delightful to see, pleasant to possess, and sweet to enjoy. With it the mind rests within itself, nor is it ever wearied by the solitude of its own inner recess; for it rejoices in one companion, though not a solitary companion.

[Col. 0831C] Consider, then, these three: mind, understanding, love. Understanding is born from mind; love arises from mind and understanding together. Understanding comes from mind alone, because the mind begets understanding from itself. Love, however, comes neither from mind alone nor from understanding alone, because it proceeds from both. First mind; then mind and understanding; afterward mind and understanding and love. And this is so in us.

But reason teaches that it is very different in the Creator. Since we believe that he has always existed, we must also confess that he has always possessed wisdom. For if he is said ever to have been without wisdom, it cannot in any way be found who afterward made him wise or from whom he received wisdom; and it is both utterly absurd and contrary to all reason to believe that he who is the fountain and origin [Col. 0831D] of wisdom ever existed without wisdom.

Therefore wisdom has always been in him, from him, and with him. Wisdom has always been in him because he has always possessed wisdom and has always been wise. Wisdom has always been from him because he himself begot the wisdom which he possesses. Wisdom has always been with him because what is begotten does not divide itself from the begetter. It has always been begotten and is always begotten: when begotten, it does not begin; when begotten, it does not cease. It is always begotten because it is eternal; it has always been begotten because it is perfect.

Therefore there is he who begot, and there is he who was begotten. He who begot is Father; he who was begotten is Son. And because he who begot has always begotten, he is eternal Father. And because he who was begotten has always been begotten, the Son is coeternal with the eternal [Col. 0832A] Father. Likewise, he who has always possessed wisdom has always loved wisdom; and he who has always loved has always possessed love. Thus love is coeternal with the eternal Father and Son.

Yet the Father is from no one; the Son is from the Father alone; and love is from Father and Son together. But since above we have maintained that the Creator of all things is supremely and truly one, we must confess that these three are substantially one in God. Since, likewise, he who is begotten cannot be he from whom he is begotten, nor can he who proceeds from the begetter and the begotten be he who begets or is begotten, the invincible reasoning of truth compels us to recognize in the Godhead a Trinity of persons and a unity of substance.

Therefore in the Godhead the three share one common and equal eternity, and eternal equality, because that which the one Godhead makes common to all cannot be dissimilar in the individual persons. Therefore the three are one, because there is one substance in three persons; but the three are not one person, because, just as the distinction of persons does not divide the unity of the Godhead, so the unity of the Godhead does not confuse the distinction of persons.

## CHAPTER XXII. That in divine things the Father loves his wisdom for wisdom’s own sake.

But it is pleasing to consider a little more attentively how it has been said that the Father loves his wisdom. For human beings often love their knowledge for the sake of a work, rather than the work for the sake of knowledge. Such are the knowledge of farming, weaving, painting, and other arts of this kind, where skill is judged wholly useless [Col. 0832C] unless the fruit of usefulness follows in the work. But if this is said of God’s wisdom, then plainly the work is preferred to its maker. Therefore it must be said that wisdom is always more precious than its work and must always be loved for its own sake. If at times a work of wisdom is preferred to wisdom itself, this is not from a judgment of truth but from human error.

For wisdom is life, and the love of wisdom is the happiness of life. Therefore, when it is said that the Father takes delight in himself in wisdom, far be it from our understanding to believe that God loves his wisdom because of the works which he performs through it. Rather, he loves all his works only because of it. For this reason he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3); not in [Col. 0832D] earth or heaven; not in the sun or moon and stars; not even in angels or in those things which are most excellent among creatures. For although these too are pleasing in their own way, they cannot please except in him and through him. Indeed, they are worthy of his love in proportion as they approach more nearly his likeness.

Therefore God loves not wisdom because of works, but his works because of wisdom. For in it is everything beautiful and true; and it is wholly desire: invisible light and immortal life, whose sight is so desirable that it can delight the eyes of God; simple and perfect, not superabundant yet full; alone, yet not solitary; one, and containing all things.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That in the supreme Trinity there is mutual love.

[Col. 0833A]

But since we believe there are three persons in the one Godhead, it remains to inquire whether what is said of any one of them can also be said of the others. It has been said that the Father loves the Son. It remains, therefore, to consider whether it may likewise be said that the love of Father and Son loves the Son, and that the Son loves himself; likewise, that the Father loves himself, that the Son loves the Father, and that the love of Father and Son loves the Father; likewise, that the love of Father and Son loves itself, that the Father loves his own love and the Son’s, and that the Son loves his own love and the Father’s. Finally, whether the love by which each loves himself is one and the same love by which each loves the other mutually. But we shall find these matters more readily [Col. 0833B] if we recall what has already been said.

For in the foregoing arguments we maintained that God is the first cause and origin of all good things. But no good can be more excellent than that which is the fountain and principle of all things. Therefore God is the supreme good. Happiness, moreover, is nowhere more rightly placed than in the supreme good. Therefore God alone is properly and principally blessed. But how can one be blessed if that very thing which one is does not please one? Whoever, therefore, is blessed loves both himself and what he himself is.

If, then, Father and Son and the love of Father and Son are one and are one God, and if true blessedness exists in God alone, it is necessary both that each loves himself and that each loves the other mutually. Blessedness could not truly be so called—indeed, it would rather be supreme unhappiness—if they were divided by contrary will and could not be separated from one another by the same nature.

Therefore, just as Father and Son and the love of Father and Son are one in nature, so they cannot fail to be one in will and love. They love themselves with one love because they are one; nor is what each loves in the other anything other than what each loves in himself, because what each is does not differ from what the other is. What the Father loves in the Son, the Son likewise loves in himself; and what the love of Father and Son loves in the Son, the Son likewise loves in himself. Likewise, what the Son loves in the Father, the Father loves in himself; and [Col. 0833D] what the love of Father and Son loves in the Father, the Father loves in himself. Likewise, what Father and Son love in their love, the love of Father and Son loves in itself. Likewise, what the Father loves in himself, he loves in the Son and in his love. And what the Son loves in himself, he loves in the Father and in his love. And what the love of Father and Son loves in itself, it loves in the Son and in the Father.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The supreme Father’s exhortation to humankind to hear his Son, and through it the proof of the matters stated above.

Hear whether the voice of the Father agrees with what we are saying. “This,” he says, “is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). He did not say separately, “I am well pleased in myself”; nor did he say separately, “He [Col. 0834A] pleased me”; nor indeed did he say together, “I am well pleased in myself, and he pleased me.” Rather, he said: “I am well pleased in him”; that is, what pleases me concerning myself is in him. It is not outside him, because what I am, he is. For since I am nothing other than he, I cannot please myself outside him. “This, therefore, is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Whatever pleases me pleases in him and through him. For he is the Wisdom through whom I made all things; in him I eternally disposed whatever I made in time. And I love each of my works more greatly in proportion as I see it agree more perfectly with that first disposition. Do not suppose that he alone is mediator in the reconciliation of human beings, since through him the condition of all creatures also becomes commendable and pleasing to my sight [Col. 0834B]. In him I examine all the works that I make; and I cannot fail to love what I behold as like him whom I love. He alone offends me who departs from his likeness. Therefore, if you wish to please me, be like him; listen to him. And if perhaps by acting wickedly you have departed from his likeness, return to him by imitating him. In him a command is given; in him counsel is given: the command, that you may persevere; the counsel, that you may return. Would that you had kept the command! But because you have transgressed the command, at least listen to the counsel: listen to him!

The Angel of Great Counsel is sent to us; and he who was given to created beings for glory, may the same one come to those who are lost for healing. Listen to him. He is Creator, and he is also Redeemer; he who, as God with me, created you, comes alone to you as man with you [Col. 0834C]. Listen to him. He is form; he is medicine; he is example; he is also remedy. Listen to him. It would have been happier always to have retained his likeness; but now it will be no less glorious to return to imitation of him. Listen to him.

O human being, why do you plead your ignorance? Behold, your very nature accuses you; it itself convicts you. You know what you are, whence you come, what maker you have, what mediator you need—and still, shamelessly defending yourself, you cry out against God. You know that you are evil, and that you were not made evil by a good maker; yet you remain silent and do not cry out to him who made you, that he may come and restore you, who created you in order to redeem you. Do not doubt his power: see how great his works are [Col. 0834D]. Do not doubt his wisdom: see how beautiful his works are. Do not doubt his benevolence: see how they serve your benefit. Thus by his work he shows you how much he can accomplish in your redemption. He likewise shows you what a judge you may dread to await, if you refuse to have him as Redeemer. No one can resist him, because he is almighty; no one can deceive him, because he is most wise; no one can corrupt him, because he is supremely good; no one can evade him, because he is everywhere; no one can endure him, because he is eternal; no one can bend him, because he is unchangeable. Therefore, if we do not wish to experience such a judge, let us seek him as Redeemer.

## Chapter XXV. That the order of creation and the order of knowledge are opposed to one another

[Col. 0835A]
