When long ago we began to proceed from visible things toward investigating invisible things, we first passed from bodily creation to incorporeal—that is, rational—creation; then from rational creation we arrived at the Wisdom of God. Now, however, returning, we shall proceed first from the Wisdom of God to rational creation, and then, after considering rational creation, to bodily creation. That is the order of knowledge; this, the order of creation. For in knowledge bodily creation, which is visible, first presents itself; then knowledge passes from bodily creation to incorporeal creation; finally, when the path of investigation has been opened, it reaches the Creator of both.

But in creation, rational creation was first made in the image of God; then bodily creation, so that rational creation might recognize externally in it what it had received inwardly from the Creator [Col. 0835B]. In the Wisdom of God is truth; in rational creation, the image of truth; in bodily creation, the shadow of the image. Rational creation was made for the Wisdom of God. Bodily creation was made for rational creation. Therefore every movement and turning of bodily creation is toward rational creation, and every movement and turning of rational creation ought to be toward the Wisdom of God, so that, while each thing always clings by conversion to that which is above it, it may disturb in itself neither the order of its first creation nor the likeness of its first exemplar.

Whoever, therefore, by the path of investigation passes from visible things to invisible things, ought first to lead the gaze of the mind from bodily creation to rational creation, and then from rational creation to contemplation of its Creator [Col. 0835C]. But in returning from invisible things to visible things, one descends first from the Creator to rational creation, and then from rational creation to bodily creation. The order of knowledge in the human mind, however, always precedes the order of creation, because we who are outside cannot return from the inner things unless we first penetrate the inner things with the eye of the mind. Yet the order of creation always follows the order of knowledge, because even if human weakness is at times admitted, however faintly, to contemplate inner things, the flux of its mutability does not permit it to remain there long [Col. 0835D].

## Chapter XXVI. On the three days of invisible light

After we have arrived, insofar as God has deigned to grant it, from visible things to knowledge of invisible things, let our mind now return to itself and consider what benefit it may derive from this knowledge. For what profit is it to us if we recognize in God the loftiness of majesty and gather no benefit from it for ourselves? Yet behold: as we return from that inward secret place of divine contemplation, what shall we be able to bring back with us? What except light, as those coming from the region of light? For it is fitting and necessary that, if we come from the region of light, we should bring light with us to drive away our darkness.

[Col. 0836A] And who will be able to know that we have been there, unless we return enlightened? Let it therefore appear that we have been there; let it appear what we saw there. If we saw power there, let us bring the light of divine fear. If we saw wisdom there, let us bring the light of truth. If we saw kindness there, let us bring the light of love. Let power awaken those sluggish toward love; let wisdom enlighten those blinded by the darkness of ignorance; let kindness inflame the cold with the warmth of charity. Consider, I ask you, what light is but day, and what darkness but night. And just as the bodily eye has its day and its night, so also the eye of the heart has its day and its night.

There are, therefore, three days of invisible light, by which the inward course of spiritual life is distinguished. The first day is fear; the second is truth; the third is charity. The first day has its sun, power; the second day has its sun, wisdom; the third day has its sun, kindness [Col. 0836B]. Power belongs to the Father, wisdom to the Son, kindness to the Holy Spirit. One kind of days is ours outwardly; another kind we have inwardly. Our outward days pass even when we do not wish them to; but our inward days, if we wish, can remain forever. For of the fear of the Lord it is said that it “endures for ever and ever” (Ps. 18 [19]). Nor is there any doubt that truth remains forever, because although it begins in this life, it will then be full and perfect in us, when he who is truth itself appears openly after the end of this life. Likewise it has been said that “charity never fails” [Col. 0836C] (1 Cor. 13).

These are good days, which never pass away. For those days are evil which not only do not remain forever but cannot remain even briefly. Of those days the Prophet says: “Man is like grass; his days have declined like a shadow” (Ps. 102 [103]). Those are the days deserved by sin; these are the days bestowed by grace. Of those days the Prophet said: “In my days I will call” (Ps. 114 [116]), he who elsewhere said: “At midnight I arose to confess to you” (Ps. 118 [119]). But he calls those days his own because he does not love the other days. As Jeremiah says: “Lord, I have not desired the day of man; you know” (Jer. 17). These are the days with which Job was filled, of whom it is written that “he died old and full of days” (Job 42). For he could not have been full of the other days, since those that had passed no longer were [Col. 0836D].

The evil know only those days which are outside; but the good, who have deserved already to see the inward days, not only do not love those outside but even curse them. “Let the day perish,” says blessed Job, “on which I was born, and the night in which it was said: ‘A man has been conceived.’ Let that day be turned into darkness; let God not seek it from above, nor illuminate it with light” (Job 3). Therefore we ought rather to love those days which are within, where darkness does not follow light, where the inner eyes of the pure heart are illuminated by the splendor of the eternal Sun.

Of these days the Psalmist sang: “Declare from day to day his salvation” (Ps. 90 [96]). What is “his salvation” except his Jesus? For Jesus is interpreted “Saviour” or “saving one” [Col. 0837A]. He is called saving because through him humanity is restored to salvation. John, speaking of him, says: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). Likewise the Apostle Paul calls Christ Jesus “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 2 [cf. 1 Cor. 1:24]). Therefore, if Jesus Christ is the Wisdom of God, and truth came through Christ Jesus, it is evident that truth came through the Wisdom of God. Thus the day of wisdom is truth.

Wisdom itself speaks to the Jews concerning this its day, saying: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8). For the truth of God is the redemption of the human race. He had promised this beforehand; and when he afterward fulfilled it, what else did he show but that he himself was true? Rightly, moreover, was this truth fulfilled through Wisdom, from whom all truth comes. Nor could anyone other than he in whom the fullness of all truth abides have been sent to fulfill the truth [Col. 0837B]. Abraham, therefore, rightly rejoices in the day of truth, because he desires truth to be fulfilled. And he surely saw that day in the Spirit when he recognized that the Son of God would come in the flesh for the redemption of the human race.

Therefore let it be said: “Declare from day to day his salvation”: the second day from the first into the third—the day of truth from the day of fear into the day of charity. At first there was one day, the day of fear; another day came, the day of truth. It was added, not substituted, because the earlier day did not depart. Behold two days. Again there is passage into the third day, into the day of charity; but when that too came, it did not expel the earlier days [Col. 0837C]. Blessed are these days! Human beings can be filled with these days, since those present do not pass away when future ones arrive. Where the number increases, brightness is multiplied.

## Chapter XXVII. That these mystical days were first fulfilled in the human race and ought to be fulfilled in us, and how

At first human beings, placed under sin, were set apart by the law and began to fear God as judge, because they recognized iniquity. To fear him, then, already meant to know him; for surely they could not have feared him at all unless they recognized him in some way. That recognition was already some light; it was already day, but not yet bright, because it was still darkened by the shadows of sin. Therefore the day of truth came, the day of salvation, to destroy sin, illumine the brightness of the earlier day, and not remove fear but transform it for the better.

Yet the brightness was not full until charity was joined to truth. For Truth itself says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 14 [16]) [Col. 0837D]. Thus all truth both removes evils and restores goods. Behold the three days: the day of fear, which reveals evil; the day of truth, which removes evil; the day of charity, which restores good. The day of truth makes bright the day of fear; the day of charity makes bright both the day of fear and the day of truth, until charity is perfected, all truth is perfectly revealed, and the fear of punishment passes into reverential fear.

“Declare from day to day his salvation” (Ps. 95 [96]). The prophet Hosea spoke of these days, saying: “After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. 6). We have heard, and rejoiced, how our Lord Jesus Christ, rising on the third day, revived and raised us from the dead in himself [Col. 0838A]. But it is altogether fitting that we should repay him his benefit; and that, just as we rose in him when he rose on the third day, so we also, rising on the third day for him and through him, should cause him to rise in us. Nor should we believe that he does not wish to have repaid to himself by us what he first chose to bestow upon us.

Therefore, just as he chose to have three days in order to accomplish our salvation in himself and through himself, so he gave us three days in order that we might accomplish our salvation in ourselves through him. But because what was enacted in him was not only a remedy but also an example and sacrament, it had to take place visibly outwardly, so that it might signify what ought to take place invisibly in us. Therefore his days were outward; our days must be sought inwardly. We have, therefore, three inward days by which our soul is illuminated. Death belongs to the first day, burial to the second, resurrection to the third.

The first day is fear; the second is truth; the third is charity. The day of fear is the day of power, the day of the Father; the day of truth is the day of wisdom, the day of the Son; the day of charity is the day of kindness, the day of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0838B]. Certainly the day of the Father, the day of the Son, and the day of the Holy Spirit are one day in the brightness of divinity; but in the illumination of our mind the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have, as it were, different days. This is not because it should in any way be believed that the Trinity, inseparable in nature, can be separated in operation, but so that the distinction of persons may be understood in the distinction of works.

Therefore, when reflection upon God’s omnipotence stirs our heart to wonder, it is the day of the Father. When the wisdom of God, considered, illuminates our heart through recognition of truth, it is the day of the Son. When the kindness of God, attended to, inflames our heart toward love, it is the day of the Holy Spirit. Power terrifies; wisdom illuminates; kindness gladdens. On the day of power we die through fear. On the day of wisdom we are buried through contemplation of truth, away from the tumult of this world [Col. 0838C]. On the day of kindness we rise through love and desire for eternal goods.

For this reason Christ died on the sixth day, lay in the tomb on the seventh day, and rose on the eighth day: so that, in like manner, power on its day may first kill us outwardly through fear, away from carnal desires; then wisdom on its day may bury us inwardly in the hidden place of contemplation; and finally kindness on its day may cause us, made alive by desire for divine love, to rise. For the sixth day belongs to labor, the seventh to rest, and the eighth to resurrection [Col. 0838D].

[Col. 0839]

# A Short Treatise on the Power and Will of God: Which Is Greater?

[Col. 0839A]

A question is raised concerning God’s power: whether it is greater than his will. For if God can do more than he wills, his power would seem greater than his will. But if his power is greater than his will, something unequal would seem to exist in him, and God would not be wholly harmonious with himself. How, then, is the whole that he is one, if greater and lesser are found there? But if for him to be able and to will are the same thing, his power and his will are the same. And if for him to be able and to will are the same thing, whatever he wills he can do, and whatever he can do he wills.

Now he wills everything that he does, because one who voluntarily does whatever he does does nothing against his will. Conversely, he does everything that he wills, because power to do everything is present when will is not absent. If, therefore, God cannot do more than he wills, nor wills to do more than he does [Col. 0839B], it follows beyond doubt that he cannot do more than he does.

Further: if God can do more than he wills, he can act against his own will and do what he does not have in his will; and his power is contrary to his will. Hence it seems to follow that he does everything that he can and wills, just as everything that he does he can and wills. Thus he wills everything that he can, just as he can do everything that he wills. But if one accepts that God can do nothing other or otherwise than he does, he works all things by necessity and is bound and constrained by the law of his works, so that the condition of his work rules over him. But it is impious to confess this.

“How then,” they ask, “are willing and being able the same for God, if his power is greater than his will?” Consider what they say. “God’s power,” they say, “is greater than his will according to you.” Why? “Because you say that God can do more than he wills.” Attend carefully. If God’s power must for this reason be called greater than his will—because he can do many things that he does not will to do—then let his will also be called greater than his power, because he does not do many things that he can do, because he does not will to do them [Col. 0839C]. For if power is called greater because it surpasses will, let will also be called greater because it restrains power. Yet just as power is not constricted in that it does nothing without will, so will is not overcome in that it is not extended to everything within the scope of power.

There are three things: inclination, effect, and relation. God’s will and power are one in inclination and in effect, but not one in relation to an object. How are these two one in God in inclination? Because in him neither is will without power, nor power without will. Power would be without will if he ever possessed a power that he did not will to possess. Conversely, will would be without power if he ever willed something not from strength but from weakness. Therefore, because his power is always voluntary and his will powerful—for he wills all the power that he can have, and wills from power everything that he wills—therefore in him neither is power without will, nor will without power [Col. 0840A].

Likewise, in effect, will can in no way be separated from power, nor power from will. For whatever God does by will, he also does by power; and again, whatever he does by power, he also does by will, because he does all that he does both by will and by power. Therefore God exercises both will and power in every work of his; nor are they divided in the work, since they cannot be divided in the worker. Thus God’s power and will remain undivided both in inclination within himself and in effect through himself, yet show themselves differently in relation to what is outside himself.

For God is truly said not to will everything that he can do, since he can do many things that he does not will to do, while he wills to do nothing that he cannot do. Therefore his power has regard to certain things to which his will does not have regard. But his power has regard to everything to which his will has regard. Thus divine power is sometimes related to objects differently from will, but in itself it has nothing other than will, because it has nothing contrary to will [Col. 0840B].

[Col. 0840C]

But they say: “If God can do something that he does not will, he can do something against his will. But if he can do something against his will, he is not almighty, since he can be compelled and led to what he does not will.” But observe how their claim hangs together: that if God can do something that he does not will to do, therefore he can do something against his will. He would indeed act against his will if he did what he did not will to do. Yet it does not follow, because he can do something that he does not will to do, that he can act against his will. For if he did what he can do but does not will, he would then will to do what he did; just as now, because he does not will to do it, he does not do what nevertheless he could do if he willed.

Thus foreknowledge and predestination in God, if they are considered in relation to their objects, are different, although they are one in God. For [Col. 0840D] foreknowledge extends both to evil and to good; predestination [Col. 0841A] only to good. He foreknew all future things, but predestined only the elect. Likewise predestination, when it is understood as disposition, cannot nevertheless be made equal in scope to foreknowledge, because God’s foreknowledge relates both to what he will do and to what he will permit. Predestination [Col. 0842A], however, relates only to what he will do. For Ambrose says: “God predestined the hell of the ungodly, but he did not predestine the guilt of the ungodly.” For he predestined what he was going to do; but what he was not going to do, though he was going to permit it, he did not predestine but foreknew.

[Col. 0841]

# A Short Treatise on the Four Wills in Christ

[Col. 0841B]

You inquire concerning the will of God, and likewise concerning the will of man. Christ was God, and therefore divine will was in him. And because he was also man, human will likewise was in him. I do not mean the human will produced by human guilt and vice, but that which human nature requires. Therefore divine will was in Christ insofar as Christ was God; and likewise human will was in him insofar as he was man.

Human will, however, is considered in three ways: according to reason, according to compassion, and according to the flesh. Therefore in Christ there was the will of divinity, the will of reason, the will of compassion, and the will of flesh. The will of divinity pronounced its judgment through justice; the will of reason approved truth through obedience; the will of compassion sighed at another’s evil through fellow-feeling [Col. 0841C]; the will of flesh murmured at its own evil through suffering.

See whether all these are not in Christ. That leper, who prayed for healing and confessed majesty, confessed the power of the divine will, saying: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me” (Luke 5). And the Lord, in order to show both the judgment and the power of that divine will, said with regard to the judgment, “I will”; and added with regard to the power, “be cleansed” (ibid.). This is an example of divine will in Christ.

With regard to the will of reason, which was subject to divine will through obedience, he said: “The spirit indeed is willing” (Matt. 26). With regard to the will of flesh, which, through the weakness of suffering, resisted the passion by shrinking in horror from punishment, he said: “But the flesh is weak” (ibid.) [Col. 0841D]. The spirit was willing by the will of reason, following the disposition of the divine will in the suffering of his flesh. But the flesh was weak, resisting suffering by the natural providence through which it had received the capacity to hate its own evil.

Accordingly, Christ willed to suffer according to the preceding will of his divinity in its disposition, and according to the will of reason, approving and following the divine disposition. But according to the will of flesh, by which, naturally, insofar as he was man, he did not hate that same flesh of his, he did not will to suffer. Yet even in this he was not contrary to the divine will, because his very not willing was willed by the divine will.

[Col. 0842B]

There was still another will in Christ: the will of compassion, or humanity. For compassion itself is called humanity; and those who are compassionate and readily sympathize with others’ miseries are called humane. For it is proper to humanity to sympathize and be moved by compassion at another’s misery. A beast can suffer, but to suffer-with is proper to humanity. Therefore the will of compassion is called the will of humanity, because it belongs to a human being to be moved by compassion. This likewise is found in Christ according to the nature of his humanity.

“When he drew near Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it” (Luke 19). Why did he weep if he did not grieve? Therefore he did not will what he grieved over. What did he grieve over? Destruction. If he grieved over their destruction, he did not will their destruction. In what way did he not will it? According to the divine will, certainly, he willed what was to be just [Col. 0842C]. According to the will of reason, he assented to justice and approved justice. But according to the will of compassion, without hatred of justice, he grieved for misery; just as according to the will of flesh he did not accuse justice but rejected punishment.

Each will performed what was its own and pursued what belonged to it: the divine will, justice; the rational will, obedience; the will of humanity, mercy; the will of flesh, nature. Nor was one contrary to another; rather, each sought what belonged to itself, so that although it was directed toward something different, it was not contrary to another. That is, although each had a will directed to a different object, it did not have a refusal opposed to another will. For just as it belonged to divinity by nature not to abandon justice, so it was right for flesh to preserve nature, and for compassion not to love another’s misery.

Thus in Christ there was the will of divinity, dictating justice; the will of reason, approving justice; the will of humanity, through which he willed evil for no one; and the will of flesh, through which he did not will punishment for himself [Col. 0842D]. It was therefore right for the flesh not to will its suffering, because this was according to nature; and it was right for God to will that suffering, because this was according to justice. For the flesh did not therefore refuse it because God willed it, just as God did not therefore refuse it because the flesh refused it.

Likewise, what compassion mercifully did not will, according to the feeling of sympathy, in the punishment or destruction of the wretched, it by no means did not will against God, who justly willed it. Rather, it loved what belonged to it—mercy—and yet did not disapprove what did not belong to it—justice.

It must certainly be understood that the flesh’s being consumed with fear of suffering, and compassion’s being passibly moved by love of fellow-feeling, belong only to the present life. In this life compassion is owed even to the wicked as long as they can be corrected; and suffering is not removed from the good as long as they can become better. But when “this mortal has put on immortality and this corruptible incorruption” (1 Cor. 15), then just as neither suffering nor fear of any suffering will afflict the flesh, so the mind will undergo no pain arising from sympathy with another’s grief [Col. 0843A]. There flesh will have security against suffering, and the soul will have purity in compassion. The security of flesh will arise from impassibility; the purity of mind from truth.

Understand what I say. To suffer and to suffer-with are both punishments. Suffering was given to humanity for iniquity; but suffering-with was commanded for goodness. For it is just and right before God that one who suffers should suffer-with, so that iniquity may be removed through suffering and goodness exercised through compassion. Indeed, it belongs to the goodness of mortal life to adapt oneself to one’s condition in others and become a participant, through compassion, in another’s suffering—so that, just as what one suffers belongs to necessity, what one suffers-with may be a work of goodness.

But where suffering will not exist, suffering-with will not exist. This is not because there will be cruelty toward another’s punishment, but because no torment will arise from another’s misery. Here to suffer-with is a virtue; there, not to suffer-with is blessedness [Col. 0843B]. Here you suffer-with by will, are moved by compassion, and grieve-with through goodness. There you do not suffer-with through blessedness, are not moved through eternity, and do not grieve-with through impassibility. Thus suffering-with cannot exist except where suffering can exist, because suffering-with itself is suffering.

Certainly, those who do not put off suffering there do not lay aside suffering-with; for just as they suffer corruptibly for their own iniquity, so they suffer carnally with others’ unhappiness, according to the disposition of mortal life. Hence that rich man, placed in torments, is concerned for his brothers, so that this might be added to the fullness of his misery: that another’s misery might torment him even in his own punishment. But Abraham saw even the torment and nevertheless, remaining in the certainty of blessedness without the pain of compassion, rejected him according to justice, saying: “Son, you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke 16) [Col. 0843C].

Hence also the Psalmist, foreseeing how, in that joy of eternity, the hearts of the righteous, clinging immovably to divine justice through love of truth, will be able to desire or approve nothing other than what they know accords with it, said: “I will enter into the power of the Lord; O Lord, I will remember your justice alone” (Ps. 70 [71]). But in this life, where we can neither perfectly know nor foresee the judgment of that same divine justice, we may without injustice will certain things which are not just according to it; because it belongs to us only that, where we do not know what rather pleases God, we should choose above all what accords with compassion [pietas].

But where the judgment of divine justice is shown to be immutably fixed, there is thereafter no place for compassion contrary to it. For if anything should move us there through fellow-feeling, it would arise either from a vice ruling the affections or from weakness unable to resist the suffering of corruptible nature [Col. 0844A].

For there are three modes of compassion. One compassion arises from vice, another from nature, another from virtue. Compassion from vice occurs when the affections are touched by blameworthy grief where they were formerly held by unlawful love. Compassion from nature occurs when the mind, through its inborn inclination to compassion, grieves over others’ afflictions whenever it sees nature oppressed or afflicted contrary to the measure of compassion or humanity. Compassion from virtue occurs when we suffer with another’s pain for God’s sake—namely, when we see justice oppressed or innocence afflicted.

Is compassion from vice blameworthy? Compassion from nature is irreproachable; compassion from virtue praiseworthy. The first is reproved; the third is praised. The second has neither guilt, because it is from nature, nor reward, because it is not from virtue. Therefore, in this life, as long as mortal flesh can be injured by suffering, the changeable mind can also be touched by compassion. But where both will truly be impassible, then certainly no suffering can exist in the flesh and no compassion in the mind [Col. 0844B].

Now, therefore, each rightly uses its mutability if the flesh does not abandon patience in suffering and the mind does not exceed the measure of justice in compassion. If, then, you ask for the time of compassion: as long as we can suffer, we ought to suffer-with. If you ask for its place: the misery of compassion must be shown there where the mercy of suffering is not yet to be despaired of [Col. 0844C].

David, while his son was sick, shed tears; when he had died, he washed his face (2 Kings 12), in order to show that the wretchedness of compassion must be borne only so long as the mercy of suffering is not beyond hope. Yet there is a certain impulse of compassion that pursues even ruined nature with pity: according to it, in the likeness of our race, just as we are angry at guilt that ought not to be left uncorrected, so we pity nature that ought not to be extinguished. But mortal life, subject to change, for the present bears its share of misery; afterward, when translated into incorruption, it will lay it aside. Now [Col. 0844D], weak in both respects—namely, in suffering in the flesh and compassion in the mind—it will then be healed in both, so that through the immortality of the flesh it may be strengthened against suffering, and through the immutability of the mind against compassion. For just as to suffer is a sickness of the flesh, so to suffer-with is a sickness of the mind. Therefore God-made-man, who came to remove both, endured both. He assumed suffering in the flesh; he assumed compassion in the mind. He willed to be infirm in both for our sake, in order to heal us, who were infirm in both. He was made weak through suffering in his own punishment; he was made weak through compassion in another’s misery. He endured suffering so far as to die for those who were to die; he received compassion so far as to weep for those who were perishing. On account of misery he gave up his flesh to suffering; [Col. 0845A] on account of mercy he troubled his soul to compassion. In his flesh he suffered pain for us by suffering; in his mind he suffered-with us by compassion. And just as the weakness of the flesh in him, according to the inclination of nature, did not will his own punishment, so the piety of his mind, according to the inclination of mercy, did not will another’s misery.

For just as, according to the will of the flesh, he asked that the cup of suffering be taken away from him—though he foreknew that it would not be taken away—so, according to piety, he prayed that the sentence of condemnation might be mitigated for others, though he foresaw unchangeably that it would stand. For piety did what belonged to it by showing mercy, and reason followed what belonged to it by obeying the divine dispensation. Therefore there was no contradiction. If Christ as man, according to the impulse of piety which [Col. 0845B] he had assumed in his humanity, willed something which nevertheless, according to the divine will by which he disposed all things with the Father, he foreknew would not come to pass: this belonged to true humanity, that he should be moved by piety; and this belonged to true divinity, that he should not be moved away from his own ordinance. Thus in each respect he did what he ought. Nor was he therefore contrary to himself if, according to piety fitting to humanity, he willed what, according to justice due to divinity, he did not will; for he willed both this willing and that not-willing.

It is written: “Jesus groaned in spirit and troubled himself” (John 11). Observe here: “He troubled himself” (ibid.). How did he trouble himself? What was this disturbance by which Jesus [Col. 0845C] troubled himself? It was piety itself; it was compassion itself that was the disturbance. A good disturbance: rightly was he troubled who was moved by piety. He troubled himself. Compassion troubled him, and he troubled himself, he who voluntarily received compassion. [Col. 0846A] Just as he gave himself up when Judas gave him up, so he troubled himself when compassion troubled him. This is well known and established by common usage. One says to a person when he suffers something: “You have troubled yourself; you have brought this evil upon yourself.” Thus Jesus troubled himself when compassion troubled him, which he had voluntarily assumed; and he gave himself up when the one to whom he had granted power to give him up gave him up. Thus Jesus, in the humanity he assumed, so long as he willed to bear it as passible, bore, according to the property of humanity, both suffering in the flesh and compassion in the mind. Yet now, [Col. 0846C] translated into immutability, it can neither suffer unto corruption nor suffer-with unto disturbance. For we know Christ according to [Col. 0846B] the human being; we know him both as suffering and as compassionate (2 Cor. 5).

“My days have failed like smoke, and my bones have dried up like a firebrand” (Psalm 101 [MT 102]). The days failed because of suffering; the bones dried up because of compassion. Because of suffering the flesh died; because of compassion the soul was dried up. The pain of compassion was, as it were, a certain frying of the soul: by it he burned with pity, was pressed down by fellow-feeling, and was dried up by despair—despair, I say, not on his own account, but on account of those who were neither to be corrected in evil nor delivered from evil. In all these things we know Christ according to the flesh, when we acknowledge that he bore true mortality in true humanity (2 Cor. 5). But now we do not know him according to the flesh, since, having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him. And the life that he lives, he lives to God (Rom. 6).

[Col. 0845]

# ON THE WISDOM OF CHRIST’S SOUL: WHETHER IT WAS EQUAL TO THE DIVINE WISDOM

## PREFACE

[Col. 0845D]

To G., Hugh, a sinner: prudent and devout investigator of the divine word among others and above others.

I have learned that it has happened more than once that, in the treatment of difficult matters, either the folly of the reporter corrupted the hearer, or the rashness of the hearer brought disrepute upon the reporter. Therefore it seems to me that equal caution is required, especially where one cannot think otherwise without danger: we should neither rashly assert our own views nor hastily judge those of others. For I know “how great,” as blessed Augustine says, “are the dreams produced by the human heart”; and by that judgment through which it is deceived in knowing itself, it does not rightly discern the other things that lie outside itself.

For what do you suppose is the reason that people usually hold such diverse opinions about the truth of things? Is truth a matter of names? Behold—for the moment let us say nothing [Col. 0846C] about [Col. 0846D] God—why is it that dialectic has so many diverse and so contrary, not to say perverse, opinions? Do all know the one reality that is, but invent different things from a love of deception? I do not think so. Rather, they recount their five dreams; and the dreams by which they themselves were first deceived inwardly through opinion, they afterward unknowingly use to mislead others. And, as blessed Job says to his arrogant friends, who presumed of themselves more than they ought (Job 12), they suppose that wisdom is no longer merely dying with them, but has actually arisen from them.

It is fitting, therefore, that the very fact which makes us timid in our own assertion should do so: namely, that in asserting the one truth we already see so many persons disagreeing. For because truth is seen from afar, it produces divergent judgments; and each person can grasp only as much of it as [Col. 0847A] he himself is. Indeed, what we apprehend concerning the knowledge of things is in us; and the intellect of the heart judges the things outside it as true in the manner in which the mind inwardly forms itself in representation. Hence, while the mind is inwardly corrupted and wrongly disposed, the intellect also is deceived in its judgment about outward things.

This is the very cause which sometimes even among persons united in their sentiments tends to produce controversy over words; yet this becomes more pardonable when it is not obstinate. Therefore, if we who appear to be interpreters of the word of God and investigators of truth should perhaps find this among ourselves at some time, as often happens, let us return quickly to agreement, lest, if we begin stubbornly to defend our own utterances, we seem to have understood something else.

I have learned that the question which your charity [Col. 0847B] has deigned to ask me concerning Christ’s soul was long ago debated among certain wise men; and I have learned, both from others reporting about them and from themselves reporting about themselves, what those whom we judge more worthy of belief thought. But since I am often pressed on this question, I profess myself to be one who would not wish anything on this subject to be either so curiously and superstitiously investigated by everyone, or so confidently asserted. Hence I am now constrained by a twofold consideration in this matter, since I see that I owe silence to your prudence and an answer to your kindness. Besides all this, the difficulty of the subject presents itself; perhaps I shall not be able to discuss it as briefly as is fitting, since, if I exceed due measure in speaking, I fear that I shall appear superstitious. Yet I wish—and very much wish—to be accused in some [Col. 0847C] respect of ignorance rather than to appear a despiser of charity, and to have unpolished words rather than a perverse heart.

## THERE FOLLOWS A DECISION OF THE QUESTION CONCERNING CHRIST’S SOUL: WHETHER IT POSSESSED KNOWLEDGE EQUAL TO THE DIVINITY

You ask concerning Christ’s soul—that is, concerning that rational spirit which animated the human flesh in Christ the man, and which the Word united to himself, with the flesh and in that very flesh, into unity of person—so that Christ might be one in one person, with two natures and three essences: one person, namely, because the same one is man, on account of what he assumed, and God, on account of what he was; two natures, divine and human, in one God and man, not in one nature; three essences, divinity, [Col. 0847D] flesh, and soul, distinct without separation and united without confusion. Concerning that soul, I say, through which the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1), you ask whether it possessed knowledge equal to the divinity.

You add also that, if that soul—which, although ineffably united to the creative nature, was nevertheless undoubtedly a creature—possessed knowledge equal to the divinity, then surely a creature was equal to the Creator. Yet his work cannot be made comparable with the Creator in equality, though it can be assumed into the fellowship of unity. It is very different to be united by condescension and to be compared in majesty. You could perhaps have shown many other things absurd in this fashion. But I desire to refute falsehood together with you just as I desire to profess truth.

For how could God be immeasurable if some creature, however excellent or singular, attained equality with him? [Col. 0848A] “Great,” says the Psalmist, “is the Lord, and great is his power; and of his wisdom there is no number” (Psalm 146 [MT 147]). And Solomon says: “There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against God” (Prov. 21). Where there is no measure, how much can be said to exist? A portion is sought where no number is found. “Of his wisdom there is no number.” What, then, am I to say? Christ’s soul either was not a creature, or it could not be made equal to the Creator. Indeed, because it is a creature, I say not merely that it cannot be made equal to the Creator, but, more boldly, that it cannot even be compared with him.

“You say, then, that it possessed wisdom less than the Word?” [Col. 0848B] But I ask: what do we mean when we call a soul wise? Do we not call it wise by wisdom? For who is wise if he is not wise by wisdom? Yet one in whom wisdom is, is wise in one way; he who is wisdom is wise in another. A creature is wise because it is in wisdom. The Creator is wise because he himself is wisdom. Yet no one can be wise without wisdom, whether by that wisdom which he has or by that wisdom which he himself is. Therefore, if Christ’s soul is wise—indeed, since it is wise—is it wise beyond doubt by that wisdom which it has, or by that wisdom which it itself is? A creature, though wise by participation in wisdom, cannot itself be wisdom. What, then, is that wisdom by which Christ’s soul is wise?

What does John say concerning the Word? “He was,” he says, “the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” [Col. 0848C] (John 1). What is the Word but wisdom? For he whom John calls the Word of God, Paul calls the wisdom of God: “Christ,” says the apostle Paul, “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1). Therefore Christ himself is both Word and wisdom. The Word is wisdom, and wisdom is the Word. The Word is wisdom because “My heart has uttered a good word” (Psalm 44 [MT 45]). Wisdom is the Word because “I, Wisdom, came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature” (Ecclus. 24). Therefore wisdom is the word of the heart, and the Word is the wisdom of the mouth; for when the word is said to proceed from the heart and wisdom from the mouth, it is shown that wisdom and Word are the same.

[Col. 0848D] Therefore, if the Word enlightens, wisdom enlightens, because the Word could not enlighten if it were not wisdom. For what does a word do without wisdom? A word makes a sound; wisdom enlightens. Wisdom itself is light, and God is light, because God is wisdom. And when God enlightens, wisdom enlightens, and enlightens by light; nor does he enlighten by another light, but by that light which he himself is. For he is light, and the Word is light, and wisdom is light, because the Word is wisdom and wisdom is God. “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world.” What then? Does this light enlighten the wicked, and does God enlighten the wicked? How, then, are they blind? Hear what follows: “And the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1). What does it mean, “The light shines in darkness”? And what do darkness do if the light is there? “And [Col. 0849A] the darkness did not comprehend it.”

Yet the light itself shines and enlightens; but not all who see by it see it. The light shines; let us know that it shines through itself and enlightens from itself. It shines: it shines through itself and enlightens from itself. For he “was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world.” John was light, for “you are the light of the world” (Matt. 5), but he was not the true light, because he was “a burning and shining lamp” (John 5); nor did he shine through himself and enlighten from himself, as does the light which enlightens every human being coming into this world. Whom did he say? He did not say the good, nor the spiritual, but every human being coming into this world.

For there is one sun, and every eye is illuminated by it, but not all who see by it recognize it. [Col. 0849B] Similarly, the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world, is poured out upon all, shines upon all, illumines all; but one person sees by it, another sees it. The wicked are enlightened so that they may see other things, but do not see him through whom they see, because the light shines in darkness and the darkness did not comprehend it. The good, however, are enlightened so that they may see him from whom and through whom they see, so that they may refer to him and love in him all that they see, and love him above all that they see. Therefore all who see are enlightened through him, but more excellently those who see him. Those who see are enlightened through him and from him, because he is the light from whom they are enlightened. How could light enlighten unless it enlightened from itself [Col. 0849C]? How could it enlighten unless it offered for participation that which it itself is?

But perhaps one fears that it may be polluted by the unclean, darkened by the dark; and that it is unworthy for the holy, undefiled thing to be said communicable to profane, defiled persons, and the true thing communicable to those in error. Such thoughts are superfluous, because the light which shines in darkness, just as it is not darkened by the dark, so is not corrupted by the contaminated, remaining bright in darkness and undefiled amid filth. For although all things are in it and it is in all things, nevertheless neither is the ugliness of the whole creation ugly to it, nor does wickedness harm it, nor does error cause it to err. Therefore it shines and enlightens, neither through another nor from another; but it offers to all who are to be enlightened for communication that which it itself is and by which it itself shines, and it possesses the whole of it.

[Col. 0849D] Hear again: “The Lord,” Scripture says, “gives wisdom” (Dan. 2). Perhaps he gives some accident by which we are affected, so that we become wise.

For what is wisdom? Is it not an accident? Therefore the Lord gives wisdom. What wisdom? “All wisdom is from the Lord God” (Ecclus. 1). Very well: because all accidents are from the Lord God, from whom are all things that are. Or perhaps some accident is not from God, because sin is not from him? Yet all wisdom is from God. How is it from him? Perhaps because his gift is from him; because his creation is from him; and because every substance is from him? What is great, new, or wonderful in the statement, “All wisdom is from the Lord [Col. 0850A] God,” if it is some accident from him from whom every substance is? How, then, is all wisdom from the Lord God? Is it because it is his work, or because it is his gift?

If wisdom is a creature, what is folly? Did God create wisdom but not create folly? Then some accidents God created, while others have being but do not have it from him. Who would dare either say this or approve it once said: that something has being and does not have it from God? What are we to say? God, then, did not create accidents, and some other is the creator of wisdom while God is its giver? Therefore God could give wisdom but could not create it? Therefore he received from elsewhere what he gave; he gave what was not his; and he could receive what he had not possessed. Who would say this? Who of sound mind would admit it even into [Col. 0850B] his thought?

How, then, is all wisdom from the Lord God—whether because it is his gift or because it is his work? For if it is a work, it does not always exist, because what began at some time did not possess perpetual existence. What, then, does he say? “All wisdom,” he says, “is from the Lord God; and [Col. 0850C] it was always with him and is before the age” (ibid.). This is remarkable: then accidents were always with God; and if accidents were always with God, substances were not. Or is all wisdom from God, but not all wisdom with God? Far be it. Rather, all wisdom is from him, all wisdom is in him, all wisdom is with him, and it always is.

And what shall we do with wisdom that is an accident? Is it not itself always with God? How, then, is it said, “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and it was always with him and is before the age”? What, then, shall we do with it? Let us exclude from the sanctuary of wisdom the fictions and phantasms of folly—those I-know-not-what things and empty dreams—which are truly accidents for us, because they were not created with us. Let us recognize the true wisdom by which we are wise, whoever we are that are wise, whatever we know wisely, even if we do not know wisdom itself. Let us attend to the light shining in darkness, lest we be darkness; for “the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” “And the darkness,” he says, “did not comprehend it”—or rather, did not apprehend it. For how could they comprehend what is incomprehensible? “And the darkness did not comprehend it.”

What, then, did the light do? Light comprehended light. [Col. 0850D] And what is this light? Certainly, if light comprehended light, those who were made light by the light comprehended the light. Those illuminated by the light comprehended the light. Those who received that light above themselves into themselves comprehended the light. They comprehended it by likeness, not by equality.

This, then, is the one and true light of all rational spirits, especially of the saints: that which enlightens every human being coming into this world. It is participated in by all without diminution of itself; and, although it is the same in all, it is not perceived by all in the same way. For whatever it is, it is wholly what it is and wholly everywhere; there is neither more nor less in it. Yet according to the difference of participation, all who, according to [Col. 0851A] their condition or the gift of the grace-bestower, are more or less capable of this same communication and participation receive more or less from it. Participation, therefore, is sometimes greater and sometimes less; but that which is participated is not sometimes greater or less. Rather, it is itself everywhere the same, whole, full, and perfect.

Therefore, when we call souls wise and call them wise by wisdom, let us think of this wisdom, and believe that it alone is that by which all rational minds possessing the power of understanding and discernment are wise. “This,” he says, “is eternal life: that they may know you, the only God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17). The knowledge of God, therefore, is eternal life. And what is the knowledge of God? Is it an accident? Then love of God is an accident, and blessedness is an accident, and [Col. 0851B] our blessedness consists in accidents. Why should God himself not rather be our blessedness? He is the wisdom by which we know, the love by which we love, the joy by which we exult.

Therefore there is one wisdom by which all are wise; yet they are not wise in one manner, because they are wise by participation. And if all who are wise are wise by this wisdom, much more is that soul wise by this wisdom which was united to Wisdom itself. It did not flourish through a chance share in it by participation, but possessed fullness through the privilege of unity. For what could it have had less of wisdom when the fullness of wisdom itself was incorporated into it? “In him,” he says, “dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2). Of whom did he say this, if not of Christ? How, then, does all the fullness of divinity dwell in Christ?

There are three essences in [Col. 0851C] Christ: flesh, soul, and divinity. What, then, dwells in what? Does divinity dwell in divinity, or divinity in the soul, or divinity in the flesh? But what does it mean to say that divinity dwells in divinity? Was that either fitting to say or necessary to hear? Therefore the fullness of Christ’s divinity dwells in Christ’s humanity. And if the fullness of Christ’s divinity, then also the fullness of God’s wisdom. For what is Christ’s divinity but God’s wisdom? Therefore the fullness of God’s wisdom dwells in Christ’s humanity. Where? In the flesh, or in the soul, or at once in flesh and soul? Or in the flesh through the flesh? Then wisdom would dwell in the flesh and not dwell in the soul. Far be it! The seat of wisdom is the soul of the righteous, and the house of wisdom is Christ’s soul.

[Col. 0851D] And what did I say: “Christ’s soul is the house of wisdom”? I ought to have said more, if I could have said more. I called it a house because wisdom dwells in it; but because it dwells bodily, I ought to have said more. What does “dwells bodily” mean? It was made one with that in which it dwells, and through it one also with him in whom that thing dwells. In what way one? Not by changeability of nature, but by unity of person: one person, not one essence. Therefore divinity was incorporated with its dwelling-place; to the dwelling-place into which it pours fullness, it united truth.

“Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven pillars” (Prov. 9). What kind? “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and [Col. 0852A] piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11). Behold the seven pillars in the house of wisdom. “She has hewn out seven pillars.” From where did she hew them? She hewed them from a mountain. From what mountain? From a shadowy and dense mountain. From what mountain? From the mountain of divine majesty she hewed the seven pillars. She hewed them, but did not cut them off. She received them, but did not take them away. She placed in the construction of the house pillars hewn from the mountain and yet not separated from the mountain; nor did she diminish the mountain.

And what wonder is it if Wisdom, in building her house, raised pillars hewn from the mountain and not separated from it—Wisdom who came to dwell in the house and nevertheless remained where she had come from? Wisdom, therefore, built herself a house. What kind of house? That of which it was said: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily.” And again: [Col. 0852B] “In Christ it pleased all the fullness of divinity to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven” (Col. 1).

See what we are doing. The Apostle testifies that fullness is there; yet we say that whole Wisdom is not in her house. Thus one half dwells within, and the other half outside. And where will she be sought if she is not found at home? “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily.” Where fullness is, nothing is lacking; where nothing is lacking, everything is present. But perhaps the fullness of divinity is there and the fullness of wisdom is not.

Truth says: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2). But you say quite well: all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are there, but [Col. 0852C] they are hidden. He bears them yet does not see them. But may this thought be far from our understanding. They are hidden, not so as to be hidden from him, but so that the ungodly may not see them in him. They are hidden so that they may be brought forth at the appropriate time. They are hidden and stored away. Hidden, lest through him they be opened to the unworthy; stored away, that they may be worthily kept in him. They are stored away lest they be tarnished by some rust of sins, polluted by some filth of crimes or contagion of vices. They are stored away as in a pure vessel, as in a clean dwelling, lest someone perhaps be able to cast a stain upon them and they then begin to bear reproach.

“On that day seven women shall seize one man, saying: ‘We shall eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be invoked over us; remove our reproach’” (Isa. 4). Therefore they are stored in him, but they are not hidden from him.

[Col. 0852D] “No one,” he says, “has ever seen God. The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him” (1 John 4; John 1). If he has declared him, he has seen him. From where do we prove this? “He who is from the earth speaks of the earth; he who comes from heaven is above all; and what he has seen and heard, this he testifies” (John 3). Therefore he saw. In what did he see? In divinity or in humanity? Perhaps he saw in divinity and declared in humanity. Then those who heard, in what did they see? Or, if they did not see, why did they hear? Therefore he saw in divinity and he saw also in humanity; yet these things are from divinity [reading uncertain], and those who heard them could see them only through the illumination of the divine light [Col. 0853A].

Thus there was fullness of divinity in Christ’s soul, and fullness of wisdom in Christ’s soul; and through the fullness of wisdom Christ’s soul was fully wise. “Therefore,” they say, “Christ’s soul has as much wisdom as God has.” What does comparison accomplish where there is one alone? There is one wisdom of God by which Christ’s soul is wise. It is not wise by participation, so that it may know this or that thing in it and through it; rather, it is wise by possessing fullness, so that it possesses the whole. Therefore let us not say “so much” or “as much”; rather, let us say that the whole wisdom of God is in Christ’s soul, and Christ’s soul is wise from the whole wisdom of God. Yet Christ’s soul is not equal to God, because it is not God’s wisdom.

For to be wise by wisdom [Col. 0853B] is very different from being wisdom, since one who is wise by wisdom has received from elsewhere what he has; while one who is wisdom has from himself what he knows wisely. There, grace; here, nature. And what is grace there is nature here; yet grace there does not transform nature into immensity, nor does nature here confine grace to measure. Whoever dares to say that the fullness of wisdom was not in Christ’s soul must say that Christ’s soul was not fully wise. Therefore the whole wisdom of God was in Christ’s soul, because the whole wisdom of God was united and embodied with Christ’s soul; yet Christ’s soul was not equal to God. For it could not be compared with the divine nature, although it had received grace without measure, because its nature was passible while its grace was immeasurable.

As for the argument you offered—that if it possessed knowledge [Col. 0853C] equal to God’s, it would also possess blessedness equal to God’s—there is no need at present to say how it fails to cohere, because we remove equality of comparison where we demonstrate singularity of unity. And it is very different to have the same thing and to be the same thing: having pertains to grace; being pertains to nature. But let us grant that a plurality of wisdoms or knowledges permits comparison. Does equal wisdom make equal blessedness? Then greater wisdom makes greater blessedness and lesser wisdom lesser blessedness; and demons are so much more blessed than human beings as they surpass them in knowledge. And what shall I say of charity? “Knowledge puffs up; charity builds up” (1 Cor. 8). Therefore those who know more cannot immediately presume that they possess greater love, because seeing and loving are very different things. “Now,” he says, “they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (John 15).

[Col. 0853D] Yet it makes no difference here whether equal knowledge of any thing is accompanied by equal love, because where there is one wisdom, just as there cannot be comparison, so there cannot be equality among different things. You afterward added and said: Since wisdom is a great and spiritual good, if Christ’s soul has wisdom equal to God’s, then it will be false that God has a greater sufficiency in every good than his creature. And further: just as a creature cannot be equal to the Creator, so the good of one cannot be equal to the good of the other. But this is rightly and truly said where the creature’s good is found to be other and different from the Creator’s good. [Col. 0854A] But where it is one and the same thing, what room can there be for greater or less?

For what is the true good of a creature, especially a rational creature, other than God? Or what is God’s good other than himself? If, therefore, God is the true and only good of the creature, and God’s good cannot be other than himself, is God thereby less or greater than himself because he himself is both his own good and, at once, the good of his creature? Let, then, this excessively frequent repetition of comparison finally cease where there is a singularity of unity.

Next, in order to prove the assertion you proposed, you brought forward the Apostle’s words, by which you think to establish that Christ’s soul possessed wisdom inferior to God’s. For he says: “Who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one [Col. 0854B] has known the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2). Therefore, it seems, Christ’s soul did not know them, if no one has known them except the Spirit of God—unless perhaps someone wishes to reply that Christ’s soul was the Spirit of God.

But what are these things of God which no one has known except the Spirit of God? Surely those of which it is said in the same place: “Eye has not seen, apart from you, the good things which you have prepared for those who love you” (Isa. 64). For “eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2), and so forth. Therefore no one knows these things except the Spirit of God. And what follows? “But God has revealed them to us through the Holy Spirit.” Which Spirit? He adds: “We have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit of Christ, that we may know the things given to us by God” (ibid.). Therefore, just as the Spirit of God is the Spirit [Col. 0854C] of Christ, so those to whom these things have been revealed through the Spirit also know them. Christ’s soul, therefore, knows these things much more, and knows them fully and perfectly, because it received the fullness of the Spirit himself.

“For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3). “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1). We too, whoever merit to know these things, and however much we merit to know them, receive from his fullness not fullness itself but a portion of grace. “Father,” he says, “I have made known, or revealed, your name to the human beings whom you gave me” (John 17). What is a revelation to a human being but an inspiration of knowledge? Did he, then, reveal the name to others when he himself lacked its knowledge? Far be it!

[Col. 0854D] Again: “But when that Spirit of truth comes, whom I shall send to you, he will teach you all truth” (John 16). Why had the teacher himself not first learned all truth from that Spirit of truth, whom he sent to his disciples in order to teach them all truth? But he sent the Spirit and did not lose the Spirit. He distributed its gifts to faithful human beings as he willed, while retaining the fullness himself. He pours it into others but does not pour it out from himself; filling others without emptying himself, enriching others without diminishing himself. Therefore what the Spirit of God knows, Christ’s soul also knows through the Spirit of God—and knows fully—because it possessed the fullness of the Spirit of God.

Finally, you bring forward certain words of blessed Ambrose, and you show how they are to be understood or qualified, lest they seem to conflict with your assertion [Col. 0855A]. For he says that “the soul of Christ has by grace all that God has by nature.” To these words you think it should almost be added that, lest perhaps without this qualification we should say that it possesses absolutely all that belongs to the Godhead, we might seem to attribute eternity to a creature that had a beginning, immensity to that which has a limit, and immutability and the other things known to belong to the divine nature alone to that which was mutable and could be subject to suffering. But this qualification, although it does not seem altogether to be rejected, has a far more fitting and convenient explanation to which this statement may be accommodated.

For the soul of Christ [Col. 0855B] is said to have by grace all that God has by nature because the fullness of the Godhead is united to it in the Word: in time by grace, whereas it has been in God from eternity by nature. The former has in time, because it received, what the latter had from eternity, because it was. It received, not so as to pass, changed, into the nature of that which it received, but so as to ascend, exalted into fellowship with it. The former received what it did not have; the latter could neither receive what it did not have nor cease to be what it was. What, then, did the soul of Christ receive? The fullness of Godhead, the fullness of wisdom, the fullness of power. It received all that God is. How did it receive it? Not through changeability of nature, but through firmness of person. It received it not because it was essentially changed into that, but because it was ineffably united [Col. 0855C] to it. It received it not so as essentially to become that, but so as personally to be one with it. Nevertheless, it received and possesses all that he did not receive and possesses.

Therefore, does the soul of Christ possess eternity, if it possesses all that God possesses? Why should it not? Let it be said. Although it is not necessary in every respect to admit such a use of words, it possesses immensity; it possesses eternity; it possesses by grace all that God possesses by nature. How does it possess these? Must we perhaps suppose, because we say that it has eternity and immensity, that what began to exist lacks a beginning, or that what has received circumscription is without end? Does it also possess God so as itself to be God? Or, because it is not God, does it therefore not possess him? Yet how does it possess him? It possesses him as personally united, not as naturally inherent [Col. 0855D]; it possesses the whole, not because a creature can be eternal or immense, but because it is united with the Eternal and the Immense. For what are eternity and immensity? Are they accidents? Are eternity and immensity, then, accidents of God? Far from it! Therefore, when it is said that God has this by nature, it is understood that God is this. But when it is said that the soul of Christ has this by grace, it is understood that it is united to him. Therefore the soul of Christ has by grace all [Col. 0856A] that God is by nature.

Yet it does not follow from this that the Creator’s work is equal to him; for, when it received the immensity of grace, it did not lose the condition of its nature. It received what it did not have, but did not cease to be what it was. It received the fullness of wisdom, in which and through which it was fully and perfectly wise; nevertheless, it did not receive wisdom so as itself to be Wisdom.

And what need is there to pursue each point? I shall briefly show you what seems to me to be held in this matter. We believe that the full, perfect, and whole wisdom of God was in the soul of Christ; and that from this Wisdom that same soul was fully and perfectly wise, not by partaking of it, but by possessing it whole—the Wisdom which it uniquely conceived and ineffably comprehended. Why did it comprehend it ineffably? Because it received according to fullness.

John was “a burning and shining lamp” (John 5); he had comprehended the light, because he was not darkness. But because John had comprehended only in part, he could not comprehend that ineffable comprehension in Christ; instead he said: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (John 1). Therefore John could not loosen Christ’s sandal-strap. In him it was to receive from the fullness; above him, to comprehend the fullness. Thus, what he knew he was able to say; what he had not conceived, he chose to believe; he did not presume to investigate. Therefore he was unwilling to loosen the union, lest we should presume to compare ourselves with unity. What do you think? Do not those wish to loosen the strap of the incarnate Word [Col. 0856B] who divide the unity of the ineffable mystery by a distinction based on comparison?

Therefore the soul of John received from the fullness; the soul of Christ comprehended the fullness. I say “comprehended,” not in equality of nature, but in fullness of grace and the proper character of union. Behold, I have said, for one who asked—and for one who commanded—that which I judged more worthy of approval in this assertion. But in doubtful matters, if I cannot prevail by manifest authority, I wish others to receive me in such a way that they assist me while I am seeking, and do not refute me when I have found.

But whoever persists in contending that the wisdom by which the soul of Christ was wise was one thing, and that which was united to the soul of Christ another: I wish to prejudge no one. Let them see in what sense they assert this, lest perhaps it be a carnal sense, pronouncing their own view rather than the true one. This one thing [Col. 0856C] I affirm without hesitation: either there was no wisdom in the soul of Christ other than the divine Wisdom, or, if there was another, it was not like that Wisdom. One who does not believe this is not believing well. As for the rest, I do not compel, but advise. He who believes me in these matters believes with me; he who does not believe me, let him believe himself, until he comes to believe with me. Yet let each in the meantime strive humbly to abound in his own understanding, not to presume arrogantly. Farewell.

[Col. 0857]

## Epistolary Treatise on the Virginity of Blessed Mary

### Prologue

[Col. 0857A]

To the holy bishop G., Hugh, servant of your blessedness.

You told me that a certain person had raised with your Paternity a question concerning the virginity of blessed Mary. His irreverence in it greatly displeased you, because he had spoken, not as he ought, with modesty concerning a most sacred matter. Therefore, as had been agreed, I send in writing, for reading, those things which seemed to require saying on this subject. Farewell.

## Chapter I. That Mary did not alter her purpose of virginity in her marital consent

Concerning the uncorrupted virginity of the Lord’s mother, faith devoutly and devotion faithfully confess this: her perfection was in no way diminished by marital consent, just as her chastity was not violated by conception [Col. 0857B], nor her integrity taken away by childbirth. For this same woman remained a perpetual virgin: when she was betrothed to a man, she nevertheless did not abandon or alter her purpose of continence; when she was made fruitful—not by a man—she conceived without lust; and when she bore a son, she gave birth without pain.

What do you say now, contentious inquirer and impious hearer? Are you amazed, or do you doubt? If you marvel at what ought to be marveled at, you are not astonishing; if you do not believe what ought to be believed, you are not to be tolerated; if you strive to assert falsehoods, you are not to be heard; if you labor to attack truths, you are to be refuted; finally, if you deny what is manifest, you are to be confuted. I confess that I cannot bear with equanimity your rash presumption: with such shameless and frivolous talk you attempt to profane what is pure and stain what is untouched. Foolishly, with these your darknesses, you have struck against the mother of light.

[Col. 0857C] What, indeed, was the purpose of those arguments of yours, fit to be hissed away? You had woven them by long and protracted rumination, as though you were about to bring forth some new and great discovery; then—as is your habit—you began seeking ears that itch to hear them. You showed yourself more foolish to the learned than learned to the foolish. What was it? Did you wish to be a teacher—an announcer of novelty, or a defender of truth? But let it be so: you had discovered something to teach. Why did it seem good to you to defame chastity and attack truth?

But perhaps—as I rather suspect—you were plotting nothing against truth. Rather, in the habitual frivolity that has become ingrained in you, seeking the breezes of popular fame, you thought you would demonstrate the sharpness of your intellect if you first wrapped the matter, as it were, in the obscurity of a question [Col. 0857D] before others, so that afterward, in solving it, you might appear as a teacher. But now the matter has turned against you. In your question you have been shown rash, but in the solution you have not been found learned.

Let us nevertheless see what this great and grave question is, insoluble, as you suppose, only to you. [Col. 0858A] Indeed, even if it were grave, it would be far more truly so for many others than for you, in proportion as you foolishly presume it for yourself alone. Let us nevertheless see what it is.

First, you ask whether marriage can exist without consent to marital intercourse—that is, whether those who do not consent to one another in rendering the debt of the flesh can mutually contract marriage. Perhaps, then, you were moved by what you had heard said: “Marriage is made not by intercourse but by consent.” And rightly would it have moved you, if you had not heard the statement but had supposed that it was to be understood as though “consent to intercourse” had been added. Therefore you ask whether marriage can exist without consent to intercourse.

After this, to those who answer you that without such consent there is no true marriage, you seem, as I hear, to add your own opinion; perhaps because someone who answered your question otherwise would impose upon you thereafter the necessity [Col. 0858B] of silence. Then, this having been granted and established—namely, that marriage cannot stand without the agreement of such consent—you go on and ask whether there was a true marriage between Mary, the mother of the Lord, and Joseph, whom Scripture is found repeatedly to call Mary’s husband, while it also unquestionably names Mary herself the wife or spouse of that same Joseph.

Once this is granted—for it is absurd to deny it, since it is proved by the manifest authority of Holy Scripture and confirmed by the testimony of the Catholic religion—you infer and say: “If it was a true marriage, then there was consent to carnal union there, and Mary is found to have given her assent to intercourse of the flesh with her husband. If this is true—or rather, since, if it is not true, it cannot be called a true marriage—why is Mary said to have remained always a true virgin, when it is not denied that she was at some time a true wife? For either she did not consent, and was not a true wife; or she consented, and did not remain a true virgin. For in the very act [Col. 0858C] she abandoned her purpose of virginity, when by consent she voluntarily subjected herself, in the sacrament of marriage, to the obligation of carnal intercourse. And thereby, because she abandoned her purpose of virginity in consenting to carnal union, she ceased already to be a virgin in mind, even if she remained a virgin in body.

“What, then, is this Virgin of virgins, singular in integrity, unique in chastity, surpassing in dignity? What are these praises and unceasing commendations—indeed, rather, what are these daily flatteries—by which we proclaim Mary’s virginity singularly praiseworthy and excellently glorious above all others? She ought not merely not to be preferred to all virgins, but even to be placed below many who have been proved virgins in body and have kept the purpose of virginity inviolate in a chaste and devoted mind [Col. 0859A] unto the end. Let the virginity of Agnes and Mary now be compared, and let whichever has been proved higher in merit rightly be held higher also in praise. Agnes showed herself so unconquerable in keeping virginity that not even death itself, when inflicted, could cast her down from her purpose. Mary showed herself so changeable that the affection of one man, and a poor man, inclined her to consent. Agnes so loved virginity that she judged whatever precious thing was promised in comparison with it to be despised, and whatever hardship was imposed for its defense not to be feared. Mary so easily despised virginity that she abandoned it even with no reward promised, and renounced it with no punishment imposed.

“What therefore remains but for us to say that she who voluntarily fell from her purpose of preserving virginity holds an inferior rank in the merit and praise of virginity, even if she remained a virgin in body; while she who, together with bodily integrity, preserved the purpose of virginity inviolate unto the end holds the superior rank?”

This, then, is what you glory in having discovered through great and laborious investigation. Though you have both a corrupted mind and flesh, you do not fear falsely to accuse the mind of the immaculate woman—whose flesh you cannot accuse. It would have been far better either to have spoken the truth at first, if you did not ignore it, or, if you could not do that, at least to have kept silent about the perversity by which you have violated the hearing of the simple with your words. But what will you do if the manifest truth so frees those whom you have corrupted by false opinion from the danger of error, that it nevertheless does not cleanse you from the guilt of rashness?

Let us now see, then, whether the mother of the Lord could both be a true [Col. 0859C] wife and remain a true virgin. Let us examine, as you demand, what marriage is; and from the definition proposed, let us consider whether marital consent and the purpose of virginity could coexist in the virgin mother.

For what is marriage but a lawful partnership between a man and a woman, in which partnership each, by equal consent, owes himself or herself to the other? This obligation, however, must be considered in two ways: namely, that each preserves himself or herself for the other, and does not deny himself or herself to the other. Each preserves himself or herself, of course, so as not, after such consent, to enter into partnership with another. Each does not deny himself or herself, so as not to withdraw from the mutual and common partnership.

Therefore voluntary consent lawfully made between man and woman, by which each promises himself or herself as owing to the other—this is what makes marriage. And marriage is the partnership itself, bound by such consent, which, while one spouse lives, does not release the other from the obligation. There is also another consent: namely, to mutually demand and render carnal intercourse. This establishes a similar agreement between man and woman. It is the companion, not the maker, of marriage; an office, not a bond. Yet it too is undertaken by an equal vow on both sides, and must likewise be held by an equal obligation. This obligation also, as I mentioned concerning the former consent, must be rendered in two ways: each must preserve himself or herself for the other, and neither must deny himself or herself to the other. That is, neither may give the power over his or her body for this act to another, nor oppose the other in it.

Of that obligation by which both man owes himself to the woman and woman to the man [Col. 0860A] in preserving themselves for one another, the Apostle says: “The woman who is under a husband, while her husband lives, is bound by the law.
