But if her husband has died, she is released from the law of her husband” (1 Cor. 7). “Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man.” Of the obligation by which man owes himself to woman and woman to man in not denying themselves, the same Apostle says: “The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife” (ibid.).

But the necessity of this obligation does not subject married persons mutually to one another where, when their marriage was contracted or confirmed, consent to this act did not precede it. Yet, though this office ceases, one should not believe that the truth or force of marriage ceases; rather, marriage is all the more truly and holily marriage when it is bound in the bond of charity alone and not in the concupiscence of flesh and the ardor of lust. What? Would marriage be holy in concupiscence of the flesh and not in charity? Far from it! It is called holy and true much more truly and rightly where chastity has nothing of which to be ashamed, but charity has something in which to glory.

“But how, then, do spouses become mutually obligated to each other? For what must they henceforth preserve themselves for one another, or in what must they not deny themselves, if this cause is removed? Apart from this, there seems no reason why a man should be joined to a woman or a woman to a man; or why they should be said to be bound in a partnership with the mutual obligation known to belong to marriage.”

Perhaps this will seem so to you, who regard flesh and flesh alone. Could you find nothing else in marriage by which to confirm that marital partnership is sanctioned and holy solely for that purpose? Is it not far greater for two to become one in mind than for them to become one in flesh? If each makes the other a sharer in his or her flesh, and this can be holy, does each make the other a sharer in his or her soul, and is that not holy? Far from it!

“They shall be two in one flesh: this is a great sacrament in Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5). “They shall be two in one heart: this is a greater sacrament in God and the soul.” Behold how they bind themselves by voluntary pledge: that henceforward and always, in every sincerity of love, every care of solicitude, every affection of devotion, every practice of compassion, every power of consolation, and faith of dedication [Col. 0860D], each may be to the other what each is to himself or herself; that each may regard the other as made one with himself or herself, and in all prosperity and adversity may show the other an undivided partner and sharer, not only of consolation but also of tribulation and endurance.

Finally, insofar as concerns outward bodily need, let each care for the other as for his or her own flesh; but insofar as concerns the inward love of the heart, let each keep the other’s spirit, as far as lies within him or her, in peace and tranquillity, free from disturbance. Thus, resting in the peace and fellowship of holy partnership, while neither lives for self but for the other, each lives more happily and blessedly for self. These are the goods of marriage and the happiness of the chaste fellowship of those who love—goods which those cannot see who seek in marriage [Col. 0861A] nothing but the ill-sweet pleasure of the flesh. You see, then, what and how great goods remain to marriage even apart from intercourse of the flesh; indeed, rather, what and how great evils—that is, what bondage and what pain—are excluded from marriage apart from intercourse of the flesh.

But you say to me again: “The first and principal cause of marriage was the propagation of children. That this was not to occur without mingling of the flesh is plainly shown by the fact that in the beginning, after God had formed man from the clay of the earth, he is said afterward to have made woman as a helper for him. Certainly, she was made for no other help than that, for the propagation of future offspring, the woman might become for the man a collaborator in sowing, a receiver of seed, a place for its formation, and a mother who gives birth. Therefore woman was joined to man for no other purpose than that through her and with her, by carnal intercourse, the man might pour forth his seed into the origin of posterity and furnish the substance of flesh to those who would be born from flesh.

“For this is also confirmed by the fact that, after God had joined woman to man, wishing to declare the cause of that partnership, he first, as it were, made both fruitful by the grace of his blessing for the power of generation: ‘Increase,’ he said, ‘and multiply and fill the earth’ (Gen. 1). Thus he gave both command, that they might know why they had been joined, and grace, that they might fulfill what they had been commanded. Therefore, from the office which is enjoined by the command of their Creator upon both who have been joined and united, the cause of the partnership itself is clearly and indubitably demonstrated [Col. 0861C]. For it would be wholly absurd that, when he prescribed the form of life and the ministry of action for their partnership, he should not command to be carried out above all the purpose for which he had wished them to be joined.

“Hence Adam himself, recognizing the purpose for which woman had been made, says: ‘This is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’ (Gen. 2). Behold: the mingling of flesh in the marriage of the first parents is so plainly prescribed for their performance and prophesied as to be future that one who calls marriage true without it cannot be doubted to be opposed both to God commanding and to man consenting with God.” You perhaps thought that this was how our above-mentioned assertion should be opposed.

All, then, that you bring forward—that God is read to have made woman as a helper for the first man; that, after woman had been joined with man, he is remembered to have commanded them both to increase, multiply, and fill the earth; and finally that the future mingling of flesh between man and woman is prophesied by the man—you hold to prove that true marriage can in no way exist where there has been no consent to carnal union. So it seems to you.

First, then, let us agree that you will answer me whether two were joined in one flesh because they were made from one flesh, or made from one flesh because they were to be joined in one flesh. For the text says: “This is now bone from my bones and flesh [Col. 0862A] from my flesh; therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” What is “therefore”? Is it that they are one flesh because they are from one flesh? But it does not say: “The two shall be one flesh; therefore this is now bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh.” Rather it says: “This,” he says, “is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh; therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.”

He said three things: “A man shall leave his father and mother”; “he shall cleave to his wife”; and “the two shall be one flesh.” What is “therefore”? Therefore he shall leave his father and mother; therefore he shall cleave to his wife; therefore the two shall be one flesh. “Therefore”—on account of what? On account of this: “This is now bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh.” Therefore they are one flesh because they are from one flesh, not from one flesh because they are one flesh.

“Therefore the two shall be one flesh. This is now bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” Let us consider each of these statements, lest you may perhaps have said against yourself what you thought should be said for you.

“A man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” Perhaps he intended “he shall cleave to his wife” and “the two shall be one flesh” to say the same thing, so that cleaving to one’s wife means nothing but two becoming one flesh—as though the statement were merely: “A man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife,” and that cleaving itself should be understood as nothing other than mingling of flesh. Let us examine whether this can stand.

“A man,” he says, “shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife.” He shall leave them and cleave to her. Therefore he departs from them and comes to her. What he withdraws from them, he gives to her. What is this? “A man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife.” Therefore he leaves father and mother in that respect in which he cleaves to his wife; in that respect in which he cannot cleave to his wife unless he leaves father and mother.

“A man shall leave his father and mother.” In what respect shall he leave them? Shall he leave them in cohabitation or in love? And, if it must be said, shall he leave them in sexual union? If a man leaves father and mother in cohabitation and cleaves to his wife, then can he not have a wife in his father’s house? Or can he not love his wife unless he has hated his father and mother? For the third matter proposed need neither be repeated nor ought to be named.

Yet in these ways a man cleaves to his wife: in cohabitation, in love, and in carnal union. But a man can live together with his father and mother and his wife; he can love his father and mother and his wife at the same time. Therefore a man does not leave father and mother and cleave to his wife either in cohabitation or in love—much less, in that which neither existed nor could exist, does he leave father and mother and cleave to his wife in carnal union [Col. 0863A].

In what respect, then, does a man leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, unless in that unique partnership in which each owes himself or herself to the other? In it, a man does not put aside affection for father and mother so as to choose affection for his wife alone; rather, he puts affection for father and mother after that for his wife, in order to prefer the latter to the former, so that he may have that affection not merely, but uniquely. Therefore “he shall cleave to his wife” is spoken not of mingling of flesh but of affection of heart and the bond of social love. Thus, by the words “he shall cleave to his wife,” understand the sacrament of marriage, which is in the spirit; but by the addition, “the two shall be one flesh,” recognize the office of marriage, which is in the flesh, not the covenant of marital union.

Therefore, “a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” Here is marriage: “he shall cleave to his wife”; and here is the office of marriage: “the two shall be one flesh.” Why, then, shall a man leave father and mother and cleave to his wife? It is a great matter: he prefers the end to the beginning. Father and mother are the beginning, whence he comes; wife is the end, where love rests. There, condition alone has produced love; here, love alone makes an election apart from condition. A man therefore loves his father and mother, and once received life from them; but he loves his wife more, because he chose to live always with her [Col. 0863C]—a wholly divine sacrament and profound mystery, and a beautiful and wondrous example of the human condition.

We have our beginning, from which we received existence; and we have our end, without which we cannot be blessed. From the former, by the condition of nature, we come to existence; in the latter, by the election of grace, we receive blessedness. All things that are have existence from the former; but not all receive blessedness in the latter. Therefore it is a lesser thing, and less to be loved, to exist from the former. But it is much greater, and more to be loved, to be blessed in the latter. Yet both are great and worthy of love: to exist from the former, and to be blessed in the latter.

God, therefore, is one thing to those who have received from him only that they may exist [Col. 0863D], and another thing to those who have received him as their reward so that they may not merely exist from him but be blessed in him. The former have received from him what they themselves are; the latter receive from him, in order that what they are may be blessed, what he himself is. Therefore what we are is less to be loved, and what we are in blessedness more to be loved, because in the former there is only that which we are; but in the latter, together with what we are, there is also that which he is, from whom we received what we are.

“A man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife,” so that, setting aside old things when new things have come, he may come away from the beginning through love and rest in the end through love. You now see what and how great a sacrament marital love sets forth: through it the rational soul learns to choose without end fellowship with its own end, and to cleave by that indivisible bond of love and equality of unique affection [Col. 0864A].

This was the principal cause of marriage, for which God instituted it: that, having left his father and mother, a man might choose to be joined to his wife uniquely and singularly in an ever-indivisible love. Upon this partnership, however, for the benefit of multiplying the future race, and for the sake of a definite and rational sacrament, he afterward imposed the office of generation—not in order that marriage might consist in it, but in order that marriage might grow in merit through the obedience of this ministry, and appear more fruitful through the fecundity of offspring.

Therefore it is rightly said: “A man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” In that he cleaves to his wife is the sacrament of the invisible partnership which must be made in spirit between God and the soul; while in that the two are one flesh is the sacrament of the invisible participation made in flesh between Christ and the Church [Col. 0864B]. Great, then, is the sacrament, “The two shall be one flesh,” in Christ and the Church; but greater is the sacrament, “The two shall be one in heart,” in one love, in God and the soul.

Perhaps it has not yet been sufficiently shown that marriage is not a union of flesh but of heart, lest you think the ministry of the office surpasses the holiness of the sacrament. You insist that consent to the flesh is the holiness of marriage, and you do not concede that the marriage bond is valid apart from the agreement to intercourse, because it plainly says: “The two shall be one flesh,” and does not plainly say: “The two shall be one spirit.”

What was plainly said first, “one flesh,” was afterward plainly said, “one spirit,” because “what is carnal is first; then what is spiritual” (1 Cor. 15). Through the carnal father it was first said, “one flesh”; through the spiritual teacher it was afterward said, “one spirit.” God speaks through the prophet, saying: “I will not accept anything propitiatory from your hand. And you said, ‘For what reason?’ Because the Lord has borne witness between you and the wife of your youth, whom you have despised. Yet she is your companion and the wife of your covenant. Did not one make [them], and is there a remnant of his spirit? And what does the one seek except the seed of God? Therefore guard your spirit, and do not despise the wife of your youth. When you have hated her, dismiss her, says the Lord God of Israel” (Mal. 2).

There, then, it was said: “This is now bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh”; here it is said: “She is your companion and the wife of your covenant. Did not one make [them], and is there a remnant of his spirit?” There she is called a part of flesh; here she is named a portion of spirit. There it was said: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth”; here it was said: “What does the one seek except the seed of God?” Therefore he seeks here in the spirit the seed of God, who there commanded the seed of flesh to be multiplied in the flesh. There it was said: “The two shall be one flesh.” Here it is said: “When you have hated her, dismiss her,” in order to show that the same mingling of flesh, which there is foretold as to occur between man and woman, profits nothing here without the covenant of love which is in the spirit.

For this is what “When you have hated her, dismiss her” means: not that God commands separation, but that he teaches that, without the covenant of love, even if bodily partnership remains, it is empty and without force [Col. 0865A]. Therefore the force of the sacrament of marriage is not in flesh but in mind; nor is the consent required for completing its holiness which was prescribed to married persons before sin for the sake of an office. After sin, however, it descended so far that it is now permitted as a remedy.

Therefore the sacrament of marriage must by no means be measured by that in which, then, marital chastity was exercised rather than sanctified, and in which, now, marriage is sanctified but the weakness of married people is indulged. Hence, in former times, when faith was in one people and the time required the number of believers to be multiplied, carnal intercourse was practiced by one man with many women, yet the unique sacrament of exclusive love was not injured. But now, when the people of God must rather be multiplied by spiritual generation, in order to commend the unity of the unique sacrament which is in the spirit, only one woman is joined to one man in one flesh.

Then, because of necessity, liberty of the flesh was relaxed outwardly in practice, while holiness was nevertheless kept whole inwardly in the power of the sacrament. Now, because of perfection, even the works of the flesh are outwardly confined to unity; yet the unity of the unique sacrament is not thereby effected, but commended. These things have been said for the purpose proposed: to show that marriage can be holy and true without consent to carnal intercourse, and that the holiness of the sacrament of marriage does not consist in assent to intercourse of the flesh.

[Col. 0865C] After this, it remains for us to bring forward a discussion concerning the Virgin Mother and to inquire by what reasoning or authority it may be proved that she was both truly a wife and yet, in consenting to marriage, did not alter her purpose of virginal chastity: “The angel Gabriel was sent by God into the city of Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary” (Luke 1). Therefore Mary was already betrothed when the angel Gabriel was sent to her by God. Let us see what follows: “And the angel, entering in to her, said: Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee; blessed art thou among women. And when she had heard this, she was troubled at his saying, and considered what manner of salutation this might be. And the angel said to her: Fear not, Mary, for thou hast found grace with [Col. 0865D] God. Behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb and shalt bear a son,” etc. And Mary said: “How shall this be, since I know not a man?” (ibid.).

This is the utterance of the Virgin that we were seeking, in which she herself refutes the enemies of her virginity. Let us therefore take testimony concerning her from herself. “How, then, shall this be?” That is: How shall it happen that I bear a son, since I know not a man? She did not say, “I have not known a man.” For this would have posed no obstacle to a betrothed virgin who was going to know a man and bear a son, but was not going to remain a virgin. She did not, then, say, “I have not known a man,” since this would have been neither a miracle of past virginity nor an impediment to future childbirth, if she had not yet known a man and had formed no purpose thereafter [Col. 0866A] of not knowing a man.

She certainly did not say, “I have not known a man,” but “I know not a man.” “How,” she says, “shall this be? I know not a man, and I am said to be about to bear a son. How, then, shall this happen: that I should bear a son and not know a man? Because I know not a man.” What does “I know not a man” mean? I have a purpose not to know a man; I have a purpose to preserve inviolate unto the end the honor of virginity.

It is as if someone were to say: “I do not drink wine; I cannot taste this cup.” That is, because I have made a vow not to drink wine, I cannot taste this cup. And just as it is said: “The Nazirites do not cut their hair” (Deut. 33; Judith 13, 16), that is, they have a vow not to cut their hair, so it is said: “I know not a man.” How, therefore, shall this be, [Col. 0866B] since I know not a man?

And the angel said to her: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee” (Luke 1). Do not, he says, because of your purpose of virginity, distrust the promise of offspring. The Holy Spirit shall come upon you. You shall conceive a son, not from a man but from the Holy Spirit. My promise will indeed be fulfilled, but your purpose will not be violated. You have vowed that you will not know a man, and I foretell that you shall bear a son; and therefore you wonder whether perhaps the promise may prove void while the purpose remains, or whether the purpose may be violated if the promise is fulfilled.

For here the possibility of nature does not suffice, nor does human reasoning grasp how a virgin may give birth, how one untouched may generate a son, and how flesh may proceed from flesh without the act of the flesh. Therefore you wonder [Col. 0866C] how this shall be, because you know not a man. For meanwhile, so far as you are concerned, you can find no reason why you should doubt your perseverance; and for this reason you ask how you may trust my promise. “How shall this be, since I know not a man?” “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee.”

Do not distrust the promise because of your purpose, since the Holy Spirit shall come upon you. Do not fear for your purpose because of the promise, since the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, lest your integrity be corrupted through intercourse. The power of the Most High shall overshadow you, lest your chastity be defiled through lust. The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High [Col. 0866D] shall overshadow you. You shall supply the substance, and you shall not experience desire. You shall not receive seed from a man, and yet, being fruitful, you shall bring forth in a son the fruit of your womb.

Do not, then, say: “How shall this be, since I know not a man?” For this shall not happen through a man but through the Holy Spirit; for the Holy Spirit shall come upon you and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. Behold, we now have Mary: a betrothed virgin, yet still persevering in her purpose of virginity. She was truly a betrothed virgin, and no less truly persevered in her purpose of virginity. What more do you seek? Does the name of betrothal still leave some ambiguity for you?

For you had heard that the angel was sent to a betrothed virgin, but had not heard that he was sent to a married woman. Perhaps, [Col. 0867A] then, you say: Mary was already betrothed to Joseph, but she was not yet his wife, because he had not yet taken her as his own. For if he had taken her as his own from that time, why was he later told: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary thy wife” (Matt. 1)? Therefore she was not yet a wife when the angel was sent to her, but only betrothed; and hence it could happen that she did not alter her purpose of virginity when she was betrothed, but altered it when she became a wife. Perhaps this is still the objection you will raise on your side.

But far be it from us to believe that, after she had heard that she was to be made fruitful by a heavenly birth, she in any way gave consent to carnal intercourse—she who, even before she had learned the secret of the divine sacrament that was to be fulfilled in her, kept her vow [Col. 0867B] to preserve virginity so inviolate that, though she pledged herself to become a wife, she nevertheless proposed to guard it until the end with the same devotion with which she had begun, and with the same perseverance.

Therefore she was betrothed, she was a wife, she was a true virgin, and she had not abandoned her purpose of virginity. Thus we confess a betrothed virgin; we confess a virgin made a wife; and thereafter a mother too—and a virgin who always maintained inviolate her purpose of virginity, while the enduring glory of chastity reigned together with the modesty of a wife and the honor of a mother.

Look now, and consider carefully this virgin, our maiden: singularly chaste, supremely beautiful, uniquely pure. But I know your eye: it is bleary, and the more intently it is directed, the more perversely it looks. “The Law,” you say, “declared: ‘Cursed be the barren woman who does not bear and who leaves no seed in Israel’” (Deut. 7:14; Exod. 23:26). But she gave birth and was not barren; she left in Israel the seed of blessing, [Col. 0867C] in whom, according to the promise, all nations are blessed with Israel—all who shall be blessed in the Lord God of Israel.

Nevertheless, in Wisdom we have heard that blessed is the barren and undefiled woman who has not known a bed in transgression, for she shall have fruit at the visitation of holy souls (Wisdom 3). Again, in the prophet the Lord shows how great a reward for continence he has stored up with himself, saying: “Let not the eunuch say: Behold, I am a dry tree. For thus saith the Lord to the eunuchs: Those who keep my sabbaths, and choose the things that I have willed, [Col. 0867D] and hold fast my covenant, to them I will give in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters: an everlasting name which shall not perish” (Isa. 56).

Who, then, is this man who curses barrenness in continence, who does not see the purity of continence and does not understand its fruit? Yet let us hear what he produces.

“Mary,” he says, “did not escape the curse, since through her purpose of virginity she incurred barrenness.” But further: Why did she wish to marry after having vowed continence? There are two alternatives. Either, because of the curse of barrenness, she ought not to have purposed virginity; or, because of her vow of chastity, she ought not to have married if she was to remain a virgin. But now, if it is rightly called wicked to choose a curse [Col. 0868A] rather than a blessing, what is to be said of her making a vow of integrity and marrying?

I gladly accept the fact that, through your obstinacy, the Virgin’s praise is increased. Thus truth desires to be made manifest; thus injustice desires to be refuted. Let us see, therefore, what that thing is for which you think the Virgin should be censured. Namely, you say, that by her purpose of virginity she incurred the curse of barrenness. How great, then, is the curse of barrenness? Surely as great as the blessing of fruitfulness. And how great, then, is that blessing of fruitfulness?

When God blessed those first parents of our race, he said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.” Therefore he gave them the blessing of fruitfulness. He gave them much, then, when he gave them the blessing of fruitfulness, when he said: “Increase [Col. 0868B] and multiply, and fill the earth.” Did he not say this also to the birds of heaven, and to the beasts and cattle of the earth: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth”?

For when the fifth day of the nascent world had been completed, after God had brought forth from the waters the kinds of fish and birds, Scripture added and said: “God, seeing that it was good, said: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let birds multiply upon the earth’” (Gen. 1). Again, when he brought Noah out of the ark with all the living creatures of the earth according to their kinds, spreading the gift of his blessing over all, he again said: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 8), “and fill the earth.”

According to that mercy by which he saves human beings and beasts (Ps. 35), he opens his hand [Col. 0868C] and fills every living thing with blessing (Ps. 144). Therefore the blessing of fruitfulness was given not only to human beings but also to cattle. What evil, then, did Mary do? “She chose,” he says, “the curse of barrenness rather than the blessing of fruitfulness.” Observe the fairness of this. Our judge condemns the Virgin because she despised the blessing of cattle and, choosing virginity, received the blessing of angels.

The Psalmist says: “My heart was inflamed, and my reins were changed; and I was reduced to nothing and knew not.” I became as a beast before thee, and I am ever with thee. Thou hast held my right hand; thou hast guided me in thy will; and thou hast received me with glory. For what have I in heaven? And apart from thee, what have I desired upon earth?” (Ps. 72).

Therefore the Prophet, having found what is stored up for him in heaven, gladly despises, by comparison with it, whatever he had hitherto loved on earth; and, now pursuing heavenly things with spiritual love, he is ashamed that for so long he had been a beast through carnal delight. “For my heart was inflamed,” he says, “and my reins were changed.” That is: Why should I desire to multiply on earth through the seed of the flesh, when I know that an inheritance is preserved for me in heaven? “God of my heart, and God is my portion forever” (ibid.). This is that best part which Mary chose, and which shall not be taken away from her (Luke 10). And because she understood herself to be in honor, she was not compared with senseless mute beasts, nor made like them (Ps. 48). Therefore she wished to seek something above the condition of cattle; and so she judged it a small thing—or rather thought it unworthy—to set the blessing of cattle before her honor. [Col. 0869A]

You ask: If virginity was better than fruitfulness, why did God first bless fruitfulness and later the Law curse barrenness? Hear why. First, when the world was made by the Creator, fruitfulness was blessed so that human beings might multiply. Later, when God was acknowledged by one people only, barrenness was cursed through the Law so that believers might multiply. Finally, when the time was approaching in which God would now be worshipped by all nations, virginity was blessed so that all might be called away from works of the flesh to a celibate life. Hear something further.

If that first blessing of fruitfulness was unto salvation, and that second curse of barrenness unto damnation, then fruitfulness of the flesh is merit and barrenness is fault. Thus those women who bore many children were better than those who are recorded to have had none or few. Keturah was better than Sarah. Peninnah was better than Hannah, and likewise many others whom Scripture records as pleasing God, not in a multitude of children but through the merits of virtues.

But far be it from us to say either that fruitfulness of the flesh is a merit or that barrenness is a fault. Far be it from us to believe that the Law cursed barrenness of the flesh in order to show it damnable before God, rather than in order to show it, in that time when continuance of the race was sought in a multitude of children, unfruitful among human beings [Col. 0869C] and, for that reason, in a sense dishonorable.

Therefore the Virgin Mary is not to be blamed or accused of contempt for the Law in which barrenness is cursed. Rather, she alone is to be praised in a singular manner: considering that the first words of the Law were not to be understood carnally, she chose to become on earth an outcast of the people and a reproach among human beings, so that through the purity of integrity she might become in heaven a companion of angels.

And fittingly the Virgin Mary, first among women, by accepting in her flesh for our sake the curse of the Law out of love for chastity, freed us from the curse of the Law. Hence she alone was deservedly granted to bear a son and remain a virgin, so that, because she was the first freely to prefer virginity to fruitfulness of the flesh, she might now be both fruitful in the flesh and whole in virginity. Do you now see what your accusation amounts to? [Col. 0869D]

There remains, then, the task of giving the reason why Mary consented to have a husband after her vow of virginity. Perhaps this holy woman consented to have a husband in order that her purpose might be concealed, Joseph himself approving this and proposing the same thing. Or perhaps Joseph himself was not aware of this purpose—which could have occurred—and, when her parents commanded marriage, she feared to be disobedient; and therefore she consented to marry a particular man, strengthened by a special confidence through the Holy Spirit, who had kindled her from the beginning with love of chastity, and by an unwavering hope in God: that divine mercy would so preserve her that she could both render obedience to her parents’ will in contracting marriage and nevertheless find in that marriage nothing by which she would be compelled to break her vow of virginity, which she had undertaken out of love for chastity. [Col. 0870A]

She accepted marriage, therefore, but did not change her purpose of virginity. Because she loved chastity and maintained obedience, there was found in her both marital holiness without loss of virginity, and fruitful virginity without the reproach of barrenness.

Thus the blessed patriarch Abraham, a model of faith and example of obedience, had received the promise that in Isaac his seed would be blessed. Yet afterwards, when commanded by God to sacrifice Isaac, the son whom he had as his only son by Sarah his wife, he obeyed without delay or hesitation, knowing with certainty that, although the command seemed contrary to the promise according to human reasoning, the promise could nevertheless, by that power through which all things are possible to God, be fulfilled together with obedience to the command.

And thus it happened that the devotion of obedience, by which he did not delay to obey God’s command, found its reward; and the faith by which he believed God’s promise obtained the effect of that faithful promise. So also here it could have happened that this blessed Virgin, entrusting every desire of hers to God, held such confidence in him that she believed without doubt both that she could render to her parents the obedience owed to them and that, by his protection, she could preserve inviolate, in whatever way he willed, her vow of chastity, of which he alone was aware. [Col. 0870B]

But whether this occurred in this way or otherwise, we must in no way doubt that blessed Mary, after the vow and purpose of preserving virginity and continence, accepted the sacrament of marriage for a definite and rational reason; that she nevertheless did not alter her purpose of virginity; that she truly took the name of wife; and that she steadfastly maintained her vow of integrity. [Col. 0870C]

## Chapter II. That the most holy and perpetual Virgin Mary conceived not by a man but by the Holy Spirit, and bore the only-begotten Son of the Most High Father, Christ God and man

Having proved, then, the first part of the proposition—that Mary, in her marital consent, did not alter her purpose of virginity—we must now proceed in order to the exposition of the second part: that she conceived without lust, not by a man but by the Holy Spirit. The position of the first part required a more extended discussion because it was more disputed. But this matter, since there is less doubt concerning it, requires not so much proof as exposition.

We must first ask how the statement that blessed Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit ought to be understood. For we know—and all have now learned through the very frequent experience of nature—that when a woman is said to have conceived by a man, nothing other than this is meant: she received, through intercourse of the flesh, the substance of flesh for the generation of flesh. This substance of flesh, transferred from the man’s flesh through that very intercourse, becomes one flesh with the woman’s flesh, so that what is to be born, truly taking its origin from the substance of both, may be generated from him through her, and also from her. Thus a woman conceives by a man when, through intercourse of the flesh, she receives from the man’s flesh seed for the generation of flesh. [Col. 0871A]

Nor does she conceive anything other than what he is from whom she conceives, or than what she herself is who conceives; and what she conceives, that she bears. What, then, shall we say? Did the Holy Spirit pour into the Virgin’s womb seed for birth from his own substance? But how could a spiritual substance supply seed of flesh? Or perhaps what was conceived was not seed of flesh, yet what was born was flesh? What are we to say? How did Mary conceive by the Holy Spirit? And if she conceived by the Holy Spirit, how was the Holy Spirit not the Father of Christ?

All these matters require great consideration, lest human understanding, in a difficult and very obscure matter, presume something beyond its capacity. We ought not to doubt them because they are obscure, nor ought we rashly define anything because they are to be believed. Let us ask, then, what Mary conceived. Either she did not conceive flesh and did not generate flesh; or, if she generated flesh, she conceived flesh. For what she conceived, that she generated. But how could that which is not flesh supply flesh, or flesh generate that which is not flesh? Let us consider how this intricate inquiry, or method of questioning, may be soundly and suitably understood. [Col. 0871B]

First, then, let us examine how the work of nature is completed in conception according to nature’s ordinary and customary operation. In parents who generate carnally and, through intercourse of the flesh, fashion flesh that is to be born from flesh, nature on both sides supplies substance for creating the offspring, so that flesh may proceed from the flesh of both, though the flesh is to be formed only in the flesh of one.

Yet this contribution—which nature pays as a certain due, by the ordinance of the Creator, for the completion of the structure of the human body—is required of nature entirely without necessity or compulsion, so that it is inclined to render it only by love alone and, if one may say so, by spontaneous affection. For there is nothing besides love alone that can exact this due from nature; but when nature has been persuaded by voluntary affection, then indeed it willingly and gladly comes to the assistance of itself from each side in completing the work. Certainly, whatever is violently seized from one unwilling is shown utterly unsuitable and ineffective for accomplishing such an end. [Col. 0871C]

Love alone, therefore, can persuade nature and in a manner compel it, while willing, to sow offspring. In a woman, love for the man, and in a man, love for the woman, ordinarily brings this about: because nature in either one alone is not sufficient to itself, each comes to the aid of the other through love, so that what neither could accomplish alone, each can accomplish together with the other.

Thus the seed of human offspring, which is to be formed by the woman alone, is conceived after being sown jointly by man and woman. As has already been said, nature accomplishes this in the woman through love for the man, and in the man through love for the woman. For this reason a woman is said to conceive only by a man, although she receives from both herself and the man that by which she is made fruitful. And she rightly conceives by the man alone, [Col. 0872A] because what is conceived is received in one respect from the man’s flesh, but in another respect is manifested through the man’s love.

She therefore conceives by the man not only what she receives from the man, but also what she receives from herself through love for the man. We wished to set this out beforehand because of the statement that Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit. Mary therefore conceived by the Holy Spirit, not because she received from the substance of the Holy Spirit seed for birth, but because, through the love and operation of the Holy Spirit, nature supplied from the Virgin’s flesh the substance for a divine birth.

For because the love of the Holy Spirit burned singularly in her heart, the power of the Holy Spirit worked wonders in her flesh. And the operation in her flesh of him whose love admitted no companion in her heart had no precedent. Therefore the Virgin conceived only that which she received from her own flesh through the love and operation of the Holy Spirit; and from that alone, without admixture of male seed, she bore a son. [Col. 0872B]

Therefore the lust of the flesh did not bring about conception in the Virgin, who neither received seed from a man’s flesh nor conceived from her own flesh through love for a man, but through the love and operation of the Holy Spirit. Nor is the Holy Spirit therefore to be called Christ’s Father because his love brought about the Virgin’s conception; for he did not give the Virgin seed for birth from his own essence, but through his love and power supplied to the Virgin herself, from her own flesh, the substance required.

Thus Christ was born from the Virgin because he received the substance of flesh from the Virgin’s flesh. [Col. 0872C] And he was conceived by the Holy Spirit because she, being a virgin, conceived from her own flesh alone, without admixture of male seed, through the operation and love of the Holy Spirit.

Hence the angel says to the Virgin who is to give birth: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee” (Luke 1). For the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin so that, by his operation, Christ’s flesh might be formed from the Virgin’s flesh. And the power of the Most High overshadowed her, so that, while supplying the substance of flesh, she might not burn with carnal desire. Such, then, is how we think the statement that the Virgin conceived by the Holy Spirit should be understood. In this way it may also be maintained that she is said to have felt no lust in conceiving.

## Chapter III. That Mary bore Christ without pain and without loss of virginity

[Col. 0872D]

There remains now the last of the three points proposed: to demonstrate that she also gave birth without pain and suffered no loss of virginity in giving birth. I have sometimes heard of a virgin conceiving, but not of a virgin giving birth, because she conceived from a man what she bore. Rightly, indeed, integrity was impaired in childbirth because virginity was defiled in conception; and it was just that what was not conceived without lust should not be born without pain. Childbirth would in no way bring pain if conception had not experienced lust. For if the fault of unlawful pleasure did not defile the woman conceiving, the penalty of pain would never torment the woman giving birth.

For that first mother of our race and of pain, after she had conceived evil pleasure, then at last heard that she would bear children in pain, in order to show openly that she gives birth with pain not because she conceives by a man, but because she conceives with lust. For who can say whether, if humankind had not sinned, human childbirth, even when conceived by a man, would either corrupt integrity or violate chastity? And indeed, if chastity were not violated, why would integrity be corrupted? Let whoever can say so. [Col. 0873A]

But in order that the second restoration might be above the first condition, and the grace of the Savior might surpass the nature of the race, blessed Virgin Mary not only conceived without lust, but also did not receive her offspring from a man’s seed. Therefore she brought forth her son without pain and remained after childbirth a virgin, adorned with the beauty of integrity. [Col. 0873B]

## Chapter IV. The question whether it is plausible that marriage can be contracted without consent to intercourse
Since the questions have not yet come to an end, I am compelled daily to add exposition upon exposition and to coat an old wall with fresh plaster. For minds still unformed, ever weakened by a new error, nothing can be explained sufficiently; while wrapped in their own darkness and unable to see another’s light, they complain that whatever they cannot understand is obscurely said, and so transfer the deficiency of their own minds into an accusation against the words.

In the treatise which I composed on the virginity of the blessed Mary, a question was considered, the chief issue being whether it could in any way be shown [Col. 0873C] that marriage might be ratified without consent to intercourse. When we set forth what was necessary for determining this proposition, the reasoning made clear that the sanctity of the sacrament of marriage does not at all rest upon consent to the flesh. Accordingly, in defining what the sanction of marriage requires, we stated that marriage is a lawful partnership between a man and a woman in which, even with bodily intercourse excepted, each, by equal consent, owes himself to the other: namely, that he keep himself for her, lest he pass into union with another, and that he not deny himself to her, lest he sever himself from the mutual fellowship.

This might have sufficed for those to whom manifest reasoning suffices. Yet again, those who refuse to acknowledge in the Mother of the Lord both the true sacrament of marriage [Col. 0873D] and a true purpose of virginity, because they maintain that marriage is not valid without assent to bodily intercourse, endeavor on this ground to overthrow our definition—which excludes the necessity of flesh from marriage. “If,” they say, “marriage is nothing other than such a partnership, in which, bodily intercourse also being excepted, each by equal consent owes himself to the other, under an obligation to preserve and not deny himself for that inseparable union and fidelity which exists in common fellowship, why may marriage not be celebrated most rightly and most sacredly also between persons of the same sex, and an indivisible partnership be sanctioned by praiseworthy charity? For what prevents a man from binding himself to a man, or a woman to a woman, by such a covenantal bond and affection of fellowship?”

But if it is altogether absurd and wholly excluded from human reason that the sacrament of marriage should be celebrated between persons of the same sex, where nevertheless such a covenantal fellowship is not prohibited, it follows that in the marriage covenant we must acknowledge as necessary, so far as consent is concerned, the union of the flesh itself—which does not exist unless constituted in both sexes. They therefore compel us, if we wish to maintain that assent to intercourse is in no way necessary in the marriage covenant, to show how this partnership marked out in our definition cannot be sanctioned between persons of the same sex.

For this purpose, the one point might have sufficed: divine institution ordained this bond for joining the two sexes; therefore, a bond in the same sex, even if it were made, would be as alien from the sacrament of marriage [Col. 0874B] as it would, for that very reason, be unlawful. Likewise, even between different sexes, it would be impermissible between mother and son, and would for that reason lack the holiness of the sacrament of marriage. For he who said, “A man shall leave his father and mother and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2), plainly taught that this union between mother and son is disordered and therefore unchaste, since, in establishing marriage, he showed that one must not seek one’s mother but leave her.

This reasoning alone would suffice to prove that the sacrament of marriage cannot exist between persons of the same sex, however bound by chaste and indissoluble charity. Yet, as is right in every divine assertion, we must attend not only to the defence of ourselves who speak, but also to the edification [Col. 0874C] of those to whom we speak. We must therefore explain why the sacrament of marriage—which in different sexes requires for its sanctification nothing beyond the voluntary charity of a perpetual and undivided fellowship—cannot nevertheless be sanctioned in the same sex by a similar and identical bond.

We do so as follows. In marriage there are two things: the sacrament of marriage and the sacrament of the marital office. That is, marriage and the office of marriage are both sacraments. Marriage consists in the covenant of love; the office of marriage consists in the begetting of offspring. Thus conjugal love is a sacrament, and in spouses the mingling of flesh is a sacrament. But conjugal love is the sacrament of that love which exists in the spirit [Col. 0874D] between God and the soul. The mingling of flesh in spouses is the sacrament of that participation which exists in the flesh between Christ and the Church.

Therefore conjugal love ought not to be between equals, because that of which it was the sacrament was not between equals. Thus male and female are joined in the love of one fellowship, just as God and the soul were joined in the love of one fellowship. Do you not now see where the whole argument of our discussion tends? Look upon these two fellowships of charity: on earth, male and female; in heaven, God and the soul. Consider with what reasonable providence all things have been arranged.

God created male and female, and created the female from the male; and because she was made from him, she was placed under him. To him it was given to excel both in keenness [Col. 0875A] of reason and in bodily strength; to her it was ordained that she should be subject not only by obedience but also by nature. God therefore willed that she should rest in his strength and foresight, as in support for her frailty; and that her weakness should awaken compassion in him, so that the man might in some fashion love the woman out of compassion, while the woman might love the man more from necessity.

Thus, the man’s love for the woman is in some measure a benefit, because he is overcome by pity so that he does not abandon weakness. But the woman’s love for the man is more a duty, because natural necessity compels her to seek protection. Thus the whole advantage of love is in some measure referred to the woman, because in her lies the cause for which she both loves the man and is loved by him.

The sacrament of love has therefore been made clear: love is a sacrament, and love is the sacrament of love. No lengthy exposition is now needed to show how, in the figure of this sacrament, the man is the image of God and the woman presents in herself the type and form of the rational soul. It is evident that, just as a man’s love for a woman is inclined toward her by a kind of pity and natural compassion, while a man is loved by a woman more through the necessity of her condition, so God first loves the rational soul by gratuitous mercy, and afterwards turns it—yet voluntarily and willingly—toward love of himself by a certain reasonable necessity.

He first loves us freely, so that afterwards, loving, we may turn to him who loves us; and thus there may be one fellowship of love, for our sake, because it is necessary to us, [Col. 0875C] and for his sake, because in him it is blessed. In this delightful intercourse of love, the love of God is in some fashion the head, because love first springs from him toward us and, turned back from us, is referred to him. By similar reasoning, in conjugal charity, which is the sacrament of this love, the man’s love is the head, because the man first joins himself to the woman in love through compassionate mercy, so that the woman’s love, turned toward the man through instruction and received through voluntary kindness, may become one in the fellowship of charity.

Therefore the Apostle says: “The head of the woman is the man; the head of the man is Christ; and the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11).

[Col. 0876A] For what in the sacrament of marriage is the chaste, holy love of a man for a woman, that in the sacrament of faith is Christ’s love for the Church; that, in the incarnation of the Word, is God’s love for human nature. For this reason, in the song of love, when that eternal charity and ineffable love—whether God’s love for the soul or Christ’s for the Church—had to be expressed in words, not as it was, but as it could be, nothing among visible things or human affections could be found more similar than the love of bridegroom and bride. Nor could that invisible and spiritual love be made known otherwise than through its own sacrament: so that, while hearing through the Word what human affection knew, the heart might inwardly taste through love what it did not know.

For in the same place he wished the bride to signify the mutual interchange of charity, by which she, joined to one alone, admits neither division within her own bond nor partnership with another, when she says: “My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies” (Song 2), “until the day breathes and the shadows decline” (Song 7). And again: “I am my beloved’s, and his turning is toward me” (Song 6).

The bridegroom himself also commends the privilege of united and exclusive love: “There are sixty queens,” he says, “and eighty concubines, and maidens without number. One is my dove, my perfect one; one to her mother, chosen by her who bore her” (Song 6).

Therefore, because of the sacrament of eternal love, God willed to sanctify marriage; because of the usefulness of human propagation, he created sex. Yet conjugal love is a sacrament not because of unlike sex, [Col. 0876C] but because of differing nature. For it attributes reciprocal charity to love not merely toward a different sex, but toward a nature unlike its own; and yet inequality of sex distinguishes the inequality of nature. Chaste love is not differently affected merely by such sex; rather, in such sex it is affected in this way because of such a nature. Hence it cannot be affected in this way outside such sex, because outside such sex such a nature is not found.

Let this suffice for those who ask how conjugal love—while bodily intercourse is excepted from it—cannot be sanctioned with equal truth on both sides in the same sex.

[Col. 0875]

# A SHORT TREATISE ON THE MANNER OF SPEAKING AND MEDITATING

(Edited from the Rouen manuscript of Saint-Ouen by Dom Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, col. 883.) (G)

## NOTICE

This little treatise was supplied to us by a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint-Ouen at Rouen, written four hundred years ago, and bearing the title: “Hugh of Paris, On the Manner of Speaking and Meditating.” Its style wholly represents Hugh of Saint-Victor. Although he is thought to have been a native of Ypres, we believe that he was called Parisian because he lived, wrote, and died as a regular canon in the Parisian monastery of Saint-Victor.

But it will not be out of place to preface this treatise with Otbert’s distinguished letter to John concerning the death of this same Hugh, which we have drawn from the manuscript of Prully. (It appears among the Prolegomena to Hugh, above, in vol. I of his Works.) —Editor.

# HUGH OF PARIS ON THE MANNER OF SPEAKING AND MEDITATING

[Col. 0877]

[Col. 0877A] **1. Humility necessary for one wishing to learn.**—Humility is the beginning of learning. Though its lessons are many, these three especially concern the reader. First, he should regard no branch of knowledge and no writing as worthless. Second, he should not be ashamed to learn from anyone. Third, when he has acquired knowledge, he should not despise others.

Many are deceived because they wish to seem wise before their time, and therefore are ashamed to learn from others what they do not know. But you, my son, gladly learn from everyone what you do not know. You will be wiser than all if you are willing to learn from all. Those who receive from all are richer than all. Finally, regard no branch of knowledge as worthless, for every kind of knowledge is good. Despise no Scripture—or at least no law—if you have leisure. If you gain nothing, neither do you lose anything. For the Apostle says: “Read everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thess. 5).

A good reader ought to be humble and gentle, wholly removed from worldly cares and the enticements of pleasures, and diligent, so that he may gladly learn from everyone. Let him never presume upon his own knowledge; let him seek not to appear learned, but to be learned. Let him seek the sayings of the wise and earnestly strive always to keep them before the eyes of his mind as though they were a mirror of his own face.

**2. Three things necessary for study.**—Three things are necessary for students: natural ability, practice, and discipline. In natural ability it is considered whether one readily grasps what is heard and firmly retains what has been grasped. In practice, whether one cultivates natural understanding by labor and diligence. In discipline, whether one lives commendably and joins good conduct to knowledge.

[Col. 0877C] **3. Let him be strong in intelligence and memory.**—Those who devote themselves to learning should possess both intelligence and memory. These two cleave together in every study so closely that, if either is lacking, the other cannot bring anyone to perfection; just as no gains can be useful where safekeeping is lacking, and in vain does one fortify storehouses who has nothing to put away.

**4.** Intelligence is a certain power naturally implanted in the mind and capable of acting by itself. Memory is the mind’s or soul’s most firm retention of things, words, propositions, and meanings. Intelligence discovers; memory keeps guard. Intelligence proceeds from nature, is aided by use, is blunted by excessive labor, and sharpened by moderate exercise. Memory is especially aided and strengthened by the practice of retaining and constant meditation.

There are two things that exercise intelligence: reading and meditation. Reading is the process by which we are formed by rules and precepts from what has been written. Likewise, reading is an investigation of meaning by means of what is set before it [Note: [Col. 0877D] A word is missing here.]. There are three kinds of reading: that of one teaching, one learning, or one examining for himself. For we say: “I read a book to him,” “I read a book from him,” and “I read a book.”

[Col. 0878A] **5. On meditation.**—Meditation is frequent thought accompanied by deliberation, prudently investigating the cause and origin, manner and usefulness of every thing. Meditation takes its beginning from reading, yet is built up by no rules or precepts of reading. For it delights in ranging across a kind of open field, where it may fix the free gaze of contemplation upon truth: now touching upon these causes of things, now upon those, now penetrating all that is deep, leaving nothing doubtful and nothing obscure.

The beginning of instruction, then, lies in reading; its completion lies in meditation. Whoever has learned to love meditation more intimately and to devote himself to it more frequently will find that it makes life very pleasant and brings the greatest consolation in tribulation. For it is chiefly meditation that withdraws the soul from the tumult of earthly activities and, even in this life, makes it somehow taste beforehand the sweetness of eternal rest. And once the soul has learned through things made to seek and understand him who made them, meditation both instructs it with knowledge and fills it with joy; hence meditation affords the greatest delight.

[Col. 0878B] **6. Three kinds of meditation.**—There are three kinds of meditation. One consists in examining conduct, another in searching the commandments, and a third in investigating the works of God. Conduct concerns vices and virtues. One divine command enjoins, another promises, another threatens. God’s work is both what his power creates, what his wisdom governs, and what his grace cooperates in bringing about. The more attentively a person has grown accustomed to meditate upon God’s marvels, the more he knows how worthy all these things are of wonder.

[Col. 0878C] **7. What we are taught must be entrusted to memory.**—Memory gathers and keeps what intelligence investigates and discovers. What we have separated in learning, we must gather together and entrust to memory. To gather is to reduce to a brief and concise summary things written or disputed at length; the ancients called this an *epilogus*, that is, a brief recapitulation of what has been said above. Human memory delights in brevity; if it is divided among many things, it becomes smaller in respect to each.

Therefore, in every study or discipline we ought to collect some brief and definite point and store it in the little chest of memory, from which something may later be drawn when the need arises. We must also repeat these things often and bring them back from the belly of memory to the palate, lest they grow stale through prolonged interruption.

[Col. 0879A] **8. The three visions of the rational soul. The distinction between meditation and contemplation.**—The rational soul has three visions: thought, meditation, and contemplation. Thought occurs when the mind is transiently touched by awareness of things, when the thing itself is suddenly presented to the mind through its image, whether entering through sense or rising from memory. Meditation is the persistent and penetrating reconsideration of a thought, striving to explain something obscure or searching to penetrate what is hidden. Contemplation is the clear and free gaze of the soul, extended in every direction over things to be seen.

The distinction between meditation and contemplation seems to be this: meditation always concerns things hidden from our understanding, whereas contemplation concerns things manifest either according to their own nature or according to our capacity. Meditation is always occupied with investigating one thing; contemplation extends to grasp many things, or even all things. Meditation, therefore, is a certain inquisitive and penetrating power of the mind for investigating obscurities and disentangling complexities. Contemplation is that liveliness of understanding which, having all things open before it, grasps them by clear vision; and thus, in some manner, contemplation possesses what meditation seeks.

[Col. 0879B] **9. Two kinds of contemplation.**—There are two kinds of contemplation: one, the first and belonging to beginners, is the consideration of creatures; the other, the last and belonging to the perfect, is contemplation of the Creator. In Proverbs Solomon proceeds as though meditating; in Ecclesiastes he ascends to the first degree of contemplation; in the Song of Songs he carries himself to the highest.

Therefore, to distinguish the three by their proper names: the first is meditation, the second is speculation, the third is contemplation. In meditation, the mind, kindled by devout affection, is clouded by the untimely rising of disturbance from carnal passions. In speculation, the novelty of an unfamiliar vision raises the mind in wonder. In contemplation, the taste of marvelous sweetness transforms the whole soul into joy and delight. Thus meditation contains concern, speculation wonder, and contemplation sweetness.

[Col. 0879C] **10. Three elements in exposition.**—Exposition contains three things: the letter, the sense, and the meaning. The letter is the fitting arrangement of words, which we also call construction. Sense is the easy and suitable signification which the letter presents at first sight. Meaning is a deeper understanding, which cannot be found except through exposition or interpretation. Their order is that first the letter, then the sense, and afterward the meaning should be sought; when this is done, exposition is complete.

[Col. 0880A] **11. Three kinds of vanity.**—There are three kinds of vanity. The first is the vanity of mutability, which belongs by condition to all perishable things. The second is the vanity of curiosity or covetousness, which belongs to human minds through their disordered love of transient and vain things. The third is the vanity of mortality, which belongs to human bodies through their liability to punishment.

**12. The functions of eloquence.**—A certain eloquent man said—and said truly—that the eloquent speaker ought to speak so as to teach, delight, and move (St Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book IV, ch. 14). He then added: “To teach belongs to necessity, to delight to sweetness, to move to victory.” Of these three, what is placed first—namely, the necessity of teaching—lies in the matters we speak; the other two lie in the manner in which we speak.

Therefore, one who by speaking endeavors to persuade others of what is good, despising none of these functions, so that he may teach, delight, and move, should pray and act that he may be heard intelligently, willingly, and obediently. When this is done fittingly and appropriately, he may deservedly be called eloquent, even if the hearer’s assent does not follow.

To these three—teaching, delighting, and moving—that same author of Roman eloquence appears to have intended to refer when he likewise says: “He, therefore, will be eloquent who can speak of small matters in a subdued style, of moderate matters in a moderate style, and of great matters in a grand style.” Let one who wishes both to know and to teach learn everything that must be taught, and acquire the faculty of speaking as befits an ecclesiastical man.

But when a person speaks intending to teach, so long as he is not understood, he should not suppose that he has yet said what he wishes to say to the person he wishes to teach. For even if he has said what he himself understands, he must not be considered to have spoken it to the one by whom he has not been understood. But if he has been understood, he has spoken, however he has spoken.

Therefore the teacher of the divine Scriptures, defender of the right faith, and assailant of error ought both to teach good things and, in this work of speech, to reconcile the hostile, raise up the negligent, and inform the ignorant what is being done and what they ought to expect. But wherever he finds—or himself makes—his hearers well-disposed, attentive, and teachable, the remaining tasks must be carried out as the case requires. If those who hear must be instructed, this should be done through narration, if indeed it is necessary for the matter in question to be made known. But in order that doubtful matters may become certain, reasoning supported by proofs must be employed.

## ALCUIN

[Col. 0880D] Marcus Tullius also says: “Memory is the treasury of all things. Unless it is employed as guardian over matters and words conceived and discovered, we understand that everything in the orator, however excellent, will perish.” We have no other precepts from him except practice in learning, the habit of writing, diligence in thinking, and caution against drunkenness, which harms every good study and deprives the mind of its soundness.

# PART THREE OF THE WORKS OF HUGH OF SAINT-VICTOR: MYSTICAL OPUSCULES

[Col. 0881]

# EXPOSITION OF THE RULE OF BLESSED AUGUSTINE

## CHAPTER ONE. ON LOVE OF GOD AND NEIGHBOUR; ON UNITY OF HEARTS AND COMMUNITY OF GOODS

[Col. 0881A]

These precepts set down below are called a rule because in them a norm for living rightly is expressed for us. A rule is so called because it rules rightly or teaches rightly. What we call a *regula*, the Greeks call a *kanōn* (κανών, “rule”). Hence those established in monasteries, who live canonically and apostolically according to the regular precepts of the holy Fathers, are also called *canons*, that is, regulars. To them it is said:

> These are the things which we command you to observe, you who are established in the monastery.

The divine precepts are read to us so that, once read, they may be understood and fulfilled. We must fear the judgment in which it is said: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12). Hence Paul says: “For not the hearers of the law, but the doers, shall be justified” (Rom. 2). Let us therefore hear the sacred commands of the gracious Lord, and let us remember his commandments in order to do them. For, as blessed James says: “If anyone has looked into the perfect law of liberty and has continued in it, becoming not a forgetful hearer but a doer of work, this one shall be blessed in his deed” (Jas. 1). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke 11). Therefore let us humbly attend to the commands given to us who are established in the monastery.

> First, the reason for which you have been gathered into one is that [Col. 0881C] you may dwell in the house with one mind, and that you may have one soul and one heart in God.

First we are admonished concerning unity and concord—such concord as is in God. For concord in committing sin is evil; but concord in doing good, pursuing justice, and serving God is good. This is the reason for which we have been gathered into one: namely, that in divine service all of us may have one spirit and one soul in this house, and that we may have one soul and one heart in God.

For if we have been gathered into one bodily, we ought also to dwell together spiritually. It does no good that one house contains us while differing wills divide us. God regards unity of mind more than unity of place. Behold: in one house we are many people—different characters, different hearts, different souls. One intention and one love for God ought to join all these into one.

[Col. 0882B] We must therefore be of one mind and one will in this: that we serve God, love God with all our heart and all our soul, and love our neighbor as ourselves. The virtue of concord is therefore necessary to us. It can be possessed if, when a brother comes to the monastery, he begins to strip himself of his own will and to imitate him who says: “I came not to do my own will” (John 6); and again: “Father, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. 26).

For what most produces concord is that each person strive in what is good to do not his own will but that of another. This is a mark of great humility. From it obedience is born; charity, peace, justice, and the virtues of the Church grow. But if I wish to do my own will and another his, divisions arise, along with quarrels, anger, and strife, which are works of the flesh. As the Apostle says: “Those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5).

There are some in the community [Col. 0883A] [the transmitted word “beamus” is uncertain]. And therefore he commands us to dwell with one mind; [some are] obstinate in their own judgment and wise in their own eyes. What they have conceived in their minds they defend as though by reason; they seek not to conform themselves to others, but others to themselves. If they see that others do not obey them, they are immediately stirred and disturbed. Such people are accustomed to rebel against the commands of their elders; the passion of disobedience and impatience reigns greatly in them. Such persons are unfit for concord. For, in the Apostle’s words, “they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened; professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1).

Pride is indeed great darkness of heart, and it is a very foolish wisdom to wish to set oneself above others. Against this the same Apostle says: “If anyone among you seems to be wise, let him become a fool, that he may be wise” (1 Cor. 3). For the wise fool is wise, and according to God it is great wisdom to judge oneself inferior to everyone. Hence it is written: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3). Thus the Lord, when his disciples were disputing which of them seemed to be greater, immediately recalls them to the concord of humility, saying: “Whoever is greater among you shall be your servant. And the Son of Man himself came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matt. 20).

Therefore let us dwell in the house with one mind. For it is good and pleasing to God for brothers to dwell together as one (Ps. 132). Our fasts and prayers do not please him so much as concord. Thus he says in the Gospel: “Go first and be reconciled to your brother, and then, when you come, you shall offer your gift” (Matt. 5). These words make clear that one who lacks concord cannot offer sacrifice to almighty God.

We must therefore consider how great is the power of concord before God, without which even the sacrifices that blot out sins are not pleasing. And we should know that when we come to conversion, we undertake combat against the devil. Nothing does he fear as much as the unity of charity. If we distribute all that we have for God’s sake, the devil does not fear this, because he himself possesses nothing. If we fast, he does not dread it, because he takes no food. If we keep vigils, he is not terrified, because he does not sleep. But if we are joined by charity, he is exceedingly afraid, because on earth we retain what he scorned to preserve in heaven.

Thus the holy Church is described as “terrible as an army drawn up in battle array,” because, just as enemies are afraid when they see an army well marshalled and united for battle, so the devil is terrified when he sees spiritual persons, girded with the arms of virtues, living in the unity of concord. He grieves bitterly when, defeated, he cannot divide and penetrate them through discord. Hence it is written of the Lord: “His place was made in peace” (Ps. 75). “There he broke the powers, the bow, the shield, the sword, and war.” These words show that concord breaks all the devil’s weapons.

[Col. 0884A]

> And may you have one soul and one heart in God.

These are the firstfruits of the Spirit which, from the beginning of our conversion, we ought to offer to almighty God, as Wisdom itself commanded: “My son, give me your heart” (Prov. 23). For we are first drawn to God by heart and will. Therefore, if we are separated bodily from the world, let us be joined to God in heart and soul, so that we may truly say: “But it is good for me to cling to God.” For “he who clings to God is one spirit with him” (Ps. 72; 1 Cor. 6).

Let us therefore cling to him, so that through him we may be strong, so that we may be one in him, and so that, blessed with him, we may say to him: “My soul has clung after you” (Ps. 62). Charity separates us from the world and joins us to God. Thus we shall have one soul and one heart in God if we love God with all [Col. 0884B] our heart and with all our soul. “God is charity, and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4). And because charity does not seek its own interests, it rightly follows:

> And do not call anything your own, but let all things be common to you.

For we ought not to possess anything as our own or call anything “mine,” but “ours”: “our cloak,” “our tunic,” “our house,” and similarly in all other things. We ought to hold all things in common and call everything by a common name.

But here we should consider how great is the difference between carnal and spiritual brothers. The former divide what is common to them; the latter place in common what had been divided. There, each seeks what is his own; here, they seek not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ. This kinship therefore is greater than that one, because the latter fails while this one grows. The one contains division; the other unity. The one passes away with the world; the other remains in the world to come.

For this reason we now live together in this house, that afterward we may remain in the heavenly kingdom. “We are children of God,” says the Apostle, “but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. Yet we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). And Paul says: “We have here no abiding city, but seek the one to come” (Heb. 13). Therefore we ought not to have private possessions, but all things should be common to us.

[Col. 0884D] People make portions for themselves in this world: one chooses silver and gold; others, houses and households; another, a great name, power, and glory; this person one thing, that person another, each in a different way. But the portion of the godly is God himself. If we wish to have such a portion, such an inheritance as the Lord is, we must make ourselves such that we are worthy to possess him and to be possessed by him.

Therefore, if we wish to possess God as our inheritance, we must possess nothing outside God. For one to whom God is not sufficient is excessively greedy. If, for example, we seek anything at all—gold, silver, possessions—the Lord disdains to become a portion together with such portions. These are Jeremiah’s words: “I do not receive an inheritance among the other tribes; rather, like a priest and Levite, live on tithes, and, serving the altar, I am supported by the offering of the altar. Having food and clothing, I shall be content with these.”

[Col. 0885A] “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). And because, while we live here, we require bodily necessities, it rightly follows:

> And let food and clothing be distributed to each of you by your superior.

The Lord willed his churches to be ordered in this way: some should devote themselves to spiritual matters, while others should provide them with temporal things. Therefore he willed some to be superiors and others subjects. The office of superiors is to provide bodily necessities for their subjects; the ministry of subjects is to devote themselves to spiritual pursuits: to be free for reading, prayer, and contemplation, and to serve the heavenly Lord in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.

Therefore they ought to live the more carefully with regard to themselves because another’s care does not entangle them. The Lord ordained that those who serve at the altar should live from the altar. “The laborer is worthy,” as he himself says, “of his wage” (Luke 10). Therefore, if we live on Christ’s provision, it is right that we labor in Christ’s service. We then receive our wage worthily if we have first been good laborers.

For the Apostle Paul says: “If anyone is unwilling to work, let him not eat” (2 Thess. 3). If we do not labor and yet eat, we become guilty of so much the greater a sin because we receive God’s benefits unworthily. We must therefore serve him by whom we are fed if we wish without danger to the soul to receive what is distributed. We ought to be so much the more diligent [Col. 0885C] in good work as we receive these things without great labor.

For what wonder if those occupied with temporal affairs live less diligently and religiously, and frequently offend in their thoughts, words, and actions? The use of the world sometimes draws a person into sin even unwillingly.
