But those who lack both care of the world and occasion for sin, the less religiously they live, the more they offend the heavenly Judge; and even in the smallest negligences they offend at grave danger to the soul.

Let us therefore consider why food and covering are granted to us: so that our entire desire may be first to seek the kingdom of God and his justice, for the sake of which all these things are added to us (Matt. 6). How they should be distributed is shown when the text adds:

> Let not all things be distributed equally to all, because you are not all equally able; but rather to each according to what each has need of.

And he confirms this by apostolic authority, saying:

Thus indeed you read in the Acts of the Apostles that all things were common among them, and distribution was made to each according as each had need (Acts 4).

This is not to be understood as meaning that what each needed was distributed to each so abundantly that they had no want. For although it is written that there was no needy person among them (Acts 4), we also read of the Apostles themselves that they served God in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness (2 Cor. 11). [Col. 0886A] From these words it is to be inferred that many are needy in body, but not in spirit. Those, however, who deny themselves for Christ’s sake overcome nature itself by the strength of their spirit. For the love of God, which is strong as death, extinguishes not only unlawful desires but even bodily and natural affections themselves. In the primitive Church there was such an abundance of spiritual grace that they were not merely content with little, but counted even the very fact of possessing nothing among the highest delights. Hence the Apostle says, “Having nothing, and possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6). Thus too a certain holy man says: “Our poverty sufficed us, so that it was counted as riches” (Tob. 5). Again the Apostle says: “Godliness with contentment is great gain”; and, “Having food and clothing, let us [Col. 0886B] be content with these” (1 Tim. 6). In such matters, therefore, we ought not to heed the will of the flesh, but the health of nature. For carnal desire seeks more than necessity requires. Therefore, in the statement that what each needs should be given to each, this measure must be observed: the flesh is to be nourished so that it may serve, and again restrained so that it may not grow proud; the necessity of nature is to be preserved, while the excess of concupiscence is cut away.

But those who possessed anything in the world, when they enter the monastery, should willingly wish it to be held in common.

This is what the brethren of the primitive Church did. For it seemed fitting to them that those who had grace in common should also have possessions in common; and [Col. 0886C] that those who had one spirit should also have one expenditure. The word “willingly” is well added, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9). We ought to give earthly things willingly, that we may be able to purchase heavenly things. For the kingdom of heaven is worth as much as you possess. Nothing is cheaper when it is bought; nothing more precious when it is possessed. There are two things which must be relinquished for God’s sake: namely, the capacity to possess and the will to have. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). And again: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9). The former concerns possessions; the latter, the will. For it is not enough to abandon outward possessions unless we cut off inward concupiscence. [Col. 0886D] Hence it follows:

But those who had nothing should not seek in the monastery things which they could not have possessed outside it.

Even those who had nothing outside possess within themselves something that they can relinquish for God’s sake: namely, the will to possess. Hence it is written: “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20). For God regards disposition more than wealth. Thus it is said through the Wise Man: “My son, give me your heart” (Prov. 23). This cannot happen unless carnal appetite is first cut away. Therefore we are first commanded to abandon what we have; then not to seek earthly things, so that afterward we may more freely long for heavenly things. And lest it should appear that worldly poor people who convert ought not to be supplied with necessities [Col. 0887A] because they are commanded to seek nothing in the monastery, it is added:

Nevertheless, let what they need be given to their weakness, even if their poverty, when they were outside, could not itself obtain even necessities.

For whether they are rich or poor, noble or low-born, whoever come to the service of Christ, it is right that they should live from Christ’s provision. For “the labourer is worthy of his wages” (1 Tim. 5).

Yet they should not think themselves happy because they have found food and clothing such as they could not find outside.

For many come to conversion not so much for the salvation of the soul as for bodily necessity; [Col. 0887B] they worship not God but their belly, of whom the Apostle says: “Whose god is their belly” (Phil. 3). To such people the Lord says in the Gospel: “Truly I say to you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of my loaves” (John 6). The entire purpose and happiness of such persons is that they may be well fed, well clothed, and temporally comfortable. Because they desire earthly things, they are deprived of heavenly ones. For they have received, as the Lord says, their reward (Matt. 6). We must therefore take the greatest care not to cling to temporal goods. Accordingly the Psalmist warns us: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61). Earthly things ought indeed to be for our use, but heavenly things for our desire. For there is a certain wonderful and great abundance [Col. 0887C] of God’s sweetness which he possesses in himself, concerning which it is said: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2). Hence it is written: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16). That satisfaction, therefore, ought to be our happiness.

## CHAPTER II. ON HUMILITY

Let them not hold their heads high because they are joined to persons whom outside they would not have dared to approach; but let them set their hearts on things above and not seek vain earthly things, lest monasteries begin to be useful to the rich rather than the poor, if the rich are humbled there and the poor puffed up.

To hold one’s head high is a sign of pride. If heaven was of no benefit to proud angels, it is clear that a monastery will be of no benefit to proud human beings. Even if the place is holy, the manner of life holy, and the works seem holy, everything will be rendered useless by the vice of pride. For pride brings a fall. Therefore holy David prays to the Lord that the foot of pride may not come upon him, because there those who work iniquity fell; they were cast out and could not stand (Ps. 35). By contrast, monasteries are beneficial to the humble. For they are teachable by God, as it is written: “He will teach the meek his ways” (Ps. 24). And again: “He sends forth springs in the valleys” (Ps. 103); that is, he bestows his grace upon the humble. They do not lose the good works they perform, because they do not abandon humility, the guardian of virtues. And because, according to the Gospel’s command, [Col. 0888A] they take the lowest place at table, and according to the prophet choose to be lowly in the house of the Lord, they deserve to be heard by him, as it is written: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 18). And again: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5).

Likewise, those who seemed to be something in the world should not disdain their brothers who came to that holy fellowship out of poverty. Rather, they should strive to glory not in the rank of wealthy parents, but in the fellowship of poor brothers.

Brothers who have come to a holy fellowship and common life must take the greatest care that one should not disdain another, though he may be richer, [Col. 0888B] nobler, or wiser. For, as the Apostle says: “God has chosen the weak things of the world, and the lowly and despised things, so that no flesh may glory in his presence” (1 Cor. 1)—that is, neither the powerful in their power, nor the wise in their wisdom, nor the rich in their riches. For with God there is no respect of persons (Col. 3). The same Lord is rich toward all who call upon him. We are rightly commanded to glory not in the rank of rich parents but in the fellowship of poor brothers, because he who is rich in his glory became poor for our sake. He deigned to associate not with the rich but with the poor, so that we too might be poor for his sake, because the kingdom of heaven is promised to the poor. To glory in riches belongs to the vanity [Col. 0888C] of the world; to glory in poverty belongs to blessedness.

Let them not be puffed up if they have contributed something from their own resources to the common life; nor should they be more proud of distributing their riches to the monastery than if they were enjoying them in the world.

From the preceding statement and what follows, two kinds of pride are indicated to us: one carnal, the other spiritual. For to disdain the poor and glory in nobility belongs to the pride commonly found among worldly people. To exalt oneself over works of mercy is spiritual pride, which is accustomed even to corrupt spiritual persons. Spiritual pride is more to be feared than carnal pride, [Col. 0888D] because to exalt oneself on account of a good work or virtue is to fall from a height. The higher the ascent, the more perilous the fall. The Lord says in the Gospel: “When you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your alms may be in secret; and he who sees in secret will repay you” (Matt. 6). By the right hand is signified upright action; by the left, worldly favour and self-exaltation. By these words we are warned to strive to conceal the good actions we perform from self-exaltation; otherwise we shall have no reward from our Father. Then he shows how great the vice of pride is when he adds:

For every other iniquity is carried out in evil deeds, so that they may be done; but pride lies in wait even for good deeds, so that they may perish.

[Col. 0889A] From this it is clear that pride is greater than the other vices. Through vices it destroys the human mind, and through virtues as well. Pride is hateful to God and to human beings; concerning it it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10). It is first in committing sin and last to remain in the conflict. For when a servant of God has overcome the other vices and has already ascended to the heights of virtues, he still has a battle against pride; unless he conquers it, he has laboured in vain in all the rest. Therefore, when we do good outwardly, let us guard the heart inwardly against self-exaltation, for no action accompanied by pride pleases God. Hence Scripture warns us: “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for death and life proceed from it” (Prov. 4).

And what benefit is there in scattering one’s possessions to give to the poor and [Col. 0889B] becoming poor, when the wretched soul becomes prouder by despising riches than it had been by possessing them?

It does us no good to abandon our possessions unless we abandon ourselves as well. For the Lord does not say, “Blessed are those poor in possessions,” but “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). In contempt for possessions one ought to become humbler, not prouder; and it would be better to retain them in the world than to abandon them in such a way as to become proud of it in the monastery. Thus, just as that soul is blessed which distributes its possessions to the poor for the Lord’s sake in order to be humbled, so that soul is wretched which is thereby exalted. Certainly unhappy is one who travels by the way of virtues toward vices, and incurs punishment from the very source from which he ought to have received reward. Every proud person is so much the lower [Col. 0889C] as he raises himself higher, and falls more deeply as he is raised more loftily. Having cut away certain vices, he returns to the unanimity which he first commended, saying:

Therefore live all of you with one mind and in harmony, and honour God in one another, whose temples you have become.

We live with one mind if we have one mind in God, like the primitive Church, which had one heart and one soul. “With one mind” concerns the will; “in harmony,” which follows, concerns good conduct. This is the right order of life: first, that the will be one; then, that life be harmonious. A brother who wishes to live harmoniously must first put away corrupt habits, lest he be perverse, disorderly, [Col. 0889D] undisciplined, and oppress the others by his anxiety; then he must regulate his actions and his entire life so that he may be able to live in harmony according to God with those among whom he lives. There are some who, after leaving the world, still wish to follow their own wills. Again, many seek in their conduct to appear worldly. Therefore it is said: “Therefore live all of you with one mind and in harmony.” We honour God in one another if we love one another for his sake, carefully keep his commands, and become his holy temple through the indwelling of his Spirit in us. It is ours to honour God; it is God’s to dwell in us and enlighten us by grace.

[Col. 0890A] “Let them not be puffed up if they have contributed something from their own resources to the common life,” etc., as far as “were enjoying them.”

It is better to retain one’s possessions in the world than to distribute them in the monastery in such a manner as to wish to exalt oneself because of them. For if people exalt themselves, they are cast down. Whoever swells with pride over what he does well falls by the very path on which he makes progress. A good action with self-exaltation does not raise one up but weighs one down. Blessed, therefore, is the soul that can say with the Prophet: “O Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up; neither have I walked in great matters nor in things too wonderful for me” (Ps. 130). Truly happy is the person who has no hidden pride in the heart, nor open pride in the body, countenance, clothing, speech, actions, or any other movements. And if he does not [Col. 0890B] walk in great matters—that is, if he does not count himself among the great because he was noble or powerful, because he contributed his riches to the common life, or because he is useful in some office. And if he does not walk in things too wonderful for him, so as to wish to appear admirable and praiseworthy on account of religion and holiness bestowed upon him from above by God. Yet someone who has no stirring of pride from such things is rarely found. In order that God’s servant may overcome all these kinds of pride, he must always think humbly of himself and not exalt his soul, but restrain it in humility, according to what is written: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3). For the words that follow are greatly to be feared: “Every other [Col. 0890C] iniquity,” etc. For greed is not practised except in evil deeds; lust is not practised except in evil deeds; and the other vices likewise. Pride alone lies in wait even for good deeds so that they may perish. Therefore the Pharisee lost his good deeds because he boasted that he had performed them. Augustine: “There are some who glory more vainly in contempt for vain glory.” Likewise, many exalt themselves more vainly in contempt for riches; concerning them it follows:

And what benefit is there in scattering one’s possessions to give to the poor and becoming poor, when the wretched soul becomes prouder by despising riches than it had been by possessing them?

As though he said openly: What benefit is poverty with pride? A humble rich person is better than a proud poor person. A humble sinner is better than an exalted righteous person. [Col. 0890D] Therefore God’s servant ought in all things to be prudent and watchful: first, not to do evil; then, not to neglect good; afterward, not to swell with pride over what he does; for the things we do are truly good when we always preserve them in humility. And we are truly Christ’s poor when we are humble for Christ’s love. Thus: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). Hence it follows plainly:

Therefore live all of you with one mind and in harmony, and honour God in one another, whose temples you have become.

Poverty and humility generate charity. Charity nourishes unity; unity and [Col. 0891A] harmony make us the temple of God. Then we truly honour God when we live with one mind and in harmony. For we show that we are Christ’s disciples if we keep the unity of Christ’s charity. Hence the Lord says: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13).

## CHAPTER III. ON PRAYER AND FASTING

Be diligent in prayers at the appointed hours and times.

To pray before the time is foresight. To pray at the appointed time is obedience. To let the time for prayer pass is negligence. Prayer ought to be more frequent in proportion as it is more beneficial. We ought to pray earnestly and fervently. For the goods [Col. 0891B] which God promises us are great. “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2). He does not wish his goods to become cheap through the ease of seeking and finding them. A precious and desirable reward calls for an eager trader. Therefore the Lord exhorts us in the Gospel, saying: “Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7). For the kingdom of God is not promised to the idle, lukewarm, and negligent, but, as Scripture says: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11). God loves persistence and importunity in prayer. If the goods are great, the desires ought not to be small. The greatness of our desires should correspond to the greatness of the rewards. [Col. 0891C] If the Lord does not hear us at the first tears, we must not on that account cease from seeking and knocking; rather, we must persevere with such persistence and repeatedly call upon the Saviour with such insistent cries until he fulfils the desire of the one praying. If any of us feels his conscience, thoughts, or actions stained by the filth of vices, he ought continually to implore the Redeemer’s mercy with lamentation and seek the intercessions and help of the saints. If, following the example of the Canaanite woman, we persist and remain steadfast in prayer, the grace of our Redeemer will be present, to correct every fault in us, sanctify what is unclean, and calm what is troubled. For he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity, if we cry to him diligently with the voice of the mind. And so that the brothers may be able to pray secretly and quietly, [Col. 0891D] it follows:

In the oratory let no one do anything except that for which it was made and from which it takes its name, so that if perhaps some persons, outside the appointed hours, wish to pray when they have leisure, they may not be hindered by those who think that something must be done there.

Our Lord drove sellers and buyers from the Temple, saying: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. 21), in order to teach that nothing other than prayer should be done in the Lord’s house. Every church is established for this purpose: that prayer may be made there. It is the house of God and the gate of heaven. There sinners are reconciled and the righteous sanctified; there divine mysteries are accomplished and heavenly sacraments are celebrated. [Col. 0892A] Hence Solomon says: “Lord, if your people turn and pray toward your sanctuary, you will hear them and forgive their sins” (3 Kgs. 8). Therefore the greatest care must be taken that nothing be done in the sanctuary which either offends the eyes of the divine Majesty or hinders those who wish to pray there. How we ought to pray is shown when it follows:

When you pray to God with psalms and hymns, let that be active in your heart which your voice utters.

The mind of those chanting in church ought to agree with their voice, so that the saying of the Apostle may be fulfilled: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14). Perseverance in prayer deserves to be fruitful only if we meditate in the mind upon what we ask with the mouth. For we often pray while directing the heart elsewhere, and do not even recall what [Col. 0892B] we say. But God does not hear the prayer to which the one praying does not attend; this often happens through the prompting of the devil. Knowing the usefulness of prayer and begrudging us the grace of obtaining what we ask, he sends a tumult of thoughts upon those who pray, in order to divide the mind from prayer and take away prayer’s fruit. Against his malice we ought to have firmness of mind, so that the more the crowd of thoughts assails us, the more firmly our mind may remain fixed in the uprightness of its position. It helps greatly toward purity of prayer if at every place and time we restrain ourselves from unlawful actions; if we always discipline both our hearing and our tongue against idle talk; and if we accustom ourselves to walk in God’s law and search his testimonies with the whole heart. Whatever we are accustomed often to do, [Col. 0892C] say, or hear must necessarily return to the mind as though to its familiar and proper dwelling-place.

And do not sing except what you read has been appointed for singing. But what is written so as not to be sung must not be sung.

For it is not fitting that ecclesiastical chant should be performed according to the discretion of different persons; it must be firmly observed according to the writings and institutions of the elders. Likewise, the other customs of the monastery should be ordered with authority and discernment. If anything ought to be changed or instituted, this should not be done quickly or lightly, nor at the discretion of only two or three persons; but, with the brothers assembled, it should be ordered as the sounder part of the canonical community determines. And it should be known that ecclesiastical authority is to be followed in all things more than reason, because authority always belongs to obedience and humility, whereas reason sometimes belongs to presumption. In ordering these matters, maturity and gravity must always be maintained. “Did I use fickleness,” says the Apostle, “so that with me there should be yes and no?” (2 Cor. 1). For it is honourable and devout not to alter anything readily or lightly.

Tame your flesh by fasts and abstinence from food and drink, as health permits.

The flesh indeed desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; but lest the flesh prevail, spiritual persons must restrain that same concupiscence through the power of the spirit. [Col. 0893A] When the flesh is tamed, the spirit is strengthened. But when the phrase “as health permits” is added, the virtue of discernment is commended. For even good things perish unless they are done with discernment. Each person ought therefore to tame the flesh through abstinence only as far as the health of nature permits. Whoever afflicts his flesh beyond measure kills his fellow citizen; whoever restores it with more food than is proper nourishes an enemy. Thus it must be nourished so that it may serve; tamed so that it may not grow proud. In every abstinence this must always be kept in view: that vices may be extinguished, not the flesh.

But whenever anyone cannot fast, he should nevertheless take no food outside the hour of the meal, unless he is ill.

The first vice among the seven principal vices is [Col. 0893B] gluttony. The temptation of this vice sometimes arises from small and cheap things. For the first human being was tempted not by pork but by an apple; Esau not by chicken but by lentils; our Saviour himself not by meat but by bread. There are three kinds of this vice. One is when someone uses food or drink without moderation. Another is when someone desires excessively delicate food or drink. The third is when someone wishes to take food or drink outside the proper hour. We understand “outside the hour” to mean before the third hour. For until that hour it is not fitting that a brother should eat or drink unless he is ill. An ill person is permitted at every hour, for no law is imposed upon the sick. For those who are not fasting but are not ill, we understand the proper time for refreshment to be from the third hour to the sixth; for those fasting, from the ninth hour until evening. [Col. 0893C] Since the Apostle commands that all things be done decently and in order (1 Cor. 14), we ought not only to use food and drink temperately but also to observe the appointed hours, lest we give anyone offence from our manner of life. It is very unbecoming for us to live blamefully when we ought to show others a pattern of right living.

## CHAPTER IV. ON THE REFRESHMENT OF THE TWOFOLD HUMAN BEING

When you come to table, until you rise from it, listen without noise and disputes to what is read to you according to custom, so that not only your throats may receive food, but your ears may hunger for the word of God.

[Col. 0893D] Those hunger for the word of God who desire to hear it. Many hear sacred reading, yet depart empty from the reading itself; they have no affection for it and feel no savour in it, and whatever they hear they readily lose. Hearing what they hear becomes judgment for them. By contrast, it is written: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5). They shall be filled because they first hungered. By hungering, a person becomes worthy afterward to be satisfied. Therefore we must first prepare our heart to hunger for and desire the word of God; divine grace will be present to pour itself within us and refresh us with spiritual sweetness and savour, and to make us delight in singing: “How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord, sweeter than honey to my mouth,” [Col. 0894A] and, “The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces” (Ps. 118). We ought to be participants not only in the bodily table but also in the spiritual one; to receive not merely food for the body but food for the soul. And the better the soul is than the body, the more the food of the soul ought to delight us beyond that of the body. Whenever divine Scripture is read or explained to us, we ought to consider it spiritual food, sent to us by God to refresh our hearts so that we may not fail on the way and to strengthen us against the devil’s temptations and the dangers of this world. We ought unceasingly to hunger for such food and retain it continually in the mind, so that we may say with the Prophet: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (ibid.). Whoever hides sacred [Col. 0894B] speech in his heart has in it life-giving food for the soul, which defends him from death—that is, from sin—and moreover brings him to eternal life. Now let us hear what it adds concerning the sick.

If those who are sick are treated differently in food because of their former custom, this ought not to be troublesome to others, nor should it seem unjust to those whom some custom has made stronger.

As though it said openly: those who are stronger should not be distressed if they see the sick treated more mercifully. Rather, because they are stronger, they ought to maintain in themselves the strictness of abstinence and bear the weakness of others patiently through compassion.

Nor should they think those persons richer because they receive what [Col. 0894C] they themselves do not receive; rather, they should rejoice for themselves because they are capable of what the others are not capable of.

For it is better to abstain than to receive more. The former belongs to strength; the latter, to weakness. Each person ought to rejoice for himself who, by the gift of divine grace, is so sound and strong that the common food and drink of the others can suffice for him, and who seeks nothing delicate, [lacuna; surviving Latin “it” uncertain] anything superfluous. For the less one desires and the more strictly one lives, the happier one is. For narrow and confined is the way that leads to life. Therefore let him rejoice who can live sparingly for Christ’s sake. A sparing life kills vices, extinguishes lust, nourishes virtues, strengthens the spirit, and raises the mind to heavenly things.

And if to those who have come to the monastery from more luxurious habits [Col. 0894D] some food, clothing, or coverings are given which are not given to others who are stronger and therefore happier, those to whom they are not given ought to consider how far these persons have come down from their worldly life to this life, although they have not been able to attain the frugality of others who are stronger in body.

Why ought they to consider these things? Namely, so that they may recognize by reason that it is just for those who have descended farther to receive more. And once they know this to be just, they should not wish all to receive what they see only a few receive. For those who are less capable must be borne with. This is what follows:

Nor should all desire to receive what they see a few receive in addition, [Col. 0895A] not because they are honoured, but because they are endured; lest the detestable perversity occur that, in monasteries where industrious rich persons become poor as far as they can, poor persons become luxurious.

It is indeed most detestable for a poor person to become luxurious where a rich person desires to become industrious—that is, abstinent. Yet we often see this occur, or happen, in many cases. For the more noble and luxurious persons were in the world, the more abjectly and strictly they afterward live in the monastery. And many, the more abject and poor they were, the more afterward they seek self-exaltation and luxury in the monastery. But, as we have said, it is very detestable and perverse for a poor person to seek luxuries where a rich person strives through abstinence to [Col. 0895B] labour for God’s love. The one serves the belly; the other, the spirit. The one proceeds by the broad and spacious way toward punishment; the other by the narrow and confined way toward glory.

## CHAPTER V. ON THE CARE OF THE SICK

Certainly, just as the sick need to receive less lest they be burdened, so after illness they should be treated in such a way that they may recover more quickly, even if they have come from the lowliest poverty of the world, as though their recent illness had conferred upon them what former habit had conferred upon the rich.

There are certain illnesses in which, if food is taken, it does not help but burdens; then the sick must [Col. 0895C] receive less lest they be burdened. But when the illness has passed, they should be treated so that they may recover more quickly. In this restoration of the brothers there should be no respect of persons; the lowliest poverty should not be despised in matters demanded by human need, when recent illness grants them what former habit grants to the rich. For whoever is merciful to another finds God merciful to him. Hence he himself says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5). Blessed John also says: “Whoever sees his brother in need and closes his heart against him, how does the charity of God remain in him?” (1 John 3). Therefore, if we wish to possess God’s charity, we ought to perform works of mercy for our brothers. When we do this, without doubt [Col. 0895D] we serve him who will say to his elect at judgment: “I was sick and you visited me; I was hungry and you gave me food” (Matt. 25), and other similar words. Their reward is then bestowed in the saying: “Receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid.). Therefore, when we serve our brothers for God’s sake, we seek the kingdom of heaven itself; and though the works are transitory, the reward remains eternal.

But when they have regained their former strength, let them return to their happier custom.

It is a happy custom to cut away fleshly desires which wage war against the soul; it is a happy custom to abstain; it is a happy custom to chastise one’s body and reduce it to servitude.

[Col. 0896A] This is all the more fitting for servants of God, the less they are in need, lest the pleasure of food hold those already strong whom necessity had relieved when sick.

To relieve sickness it is necessary to care for the flesh; but once that flesh has become strong, the same care for the flesh must be cut back, lest the pleasure of food hold servants of God, lest those who ought to serve the soul become slaves to gluttony. Therefore, the less they are in need, the more fitting it is that the pleasure of food should not hold them, lest the vice of gluttony take away the virtues of the soul. No one obtains the palm of spiritual contest unless he has first conquered within himself the incitements of the flesh through afflicting the appetite of the belly. For one does not rise to the conflict of spiritual combat unless the enemy placed within us—namely, the appetite of gluttony—has first been tamed. If we do not first [Col. 0896B] overthrow what is nearer to us, we pass in vain to attack what is far away. Many, ignorant of the order of combat, neglect to tame gluttony and rise to spiritual battles; sometimes they indeed perform many acts of great strength. But while the vice of gluttony rules, they lose through fleshly allurement all they have done bravely; and when the belly is not restrained, all the virtues are together overwhelmed through fleshly concupiscence. This is signified by the fact that the chief of the cooks destroyed the walls of Jerusalem: he destroys the virtues of the soul when the belly is not restrained. The people led out of Egypt perished in the wilderness because, despising manna, they sought flesh foods. Esau lost the [Col. 0896C] glory of the firstborn because, through the great cunning of desire, he coveted cheap food—that is, lentils. For it is not food but appetite that is at fault. Thus we often take richer foods without guilt and taste more humble ones not without a burdened conscience. We should therefore take those things which the necessity of nature seeks, not those suggested by the lust of eating.

Let them consider richer those who have been stronger in enduring frugality.

From strength in frugality the vices of the flesh are subdued; from the mortification of vices springs the growth of virtues. These are the true divine riches by which the souls of the continent are enriched. Hence it follows:

It is better to need less than to have more.

It is better to endure some want for the Lord’s sake [Col. 0896D] than to abound. For want endured for the Lord’s sake generates humility, which is the beginning of all honours; abundance, however, produces pride, which is the beginning of all evils. Therefore, in order to restrain the will and appetite of the flesh, God’s servant should always incline toward having less, so as to wish to possess less even of food and clothing than is necessary. For we have as a helper of the inward intention this human being whom we carry outwardly; and although the impulses of wantonness are in him, in him also are available the dispositions for good action. It is therefore necessary that our inward person should preside as an equitable judge between himself and the outward person whom he bears, so that his outward person may always be sufficient to serve the due [Col. 0897A] ministry and may never proudly resist with an unyoked neck.

## CHAPTER VI. ON OUTWARD AND INWARD DRESS

Let your dress not be conspicuous, and do not seek to please by clothing but by character.

This holy man did what he taught; for it is written that his garments and footwear were neither excessively elegant nor excessively mean, but were of moderate and suitable appearance. He is also read to have said of himself: “I confess that I am ashamed of costly clothing. It does not suit this profession; it does not suit this admonition; it does not suit these limbs; it does not suit these grey hairs.” Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, those who wear soft [Col. 0897B] garments are in the houses of kings” (Matt. 11). Garments are called soft because they make the mind soft. A royal household delights in soft garments; the Church of Christ delights in rough and humble ones. Such ought to be the garments of clerics: nothing in them should be noticeable as novelty, nothing belonging to pride and vain glory. It is not delicate clothing that adorns a priest, but purity of mind that adorns a cleric. Let us therefore adorn ourselves with spiritual ornaments: namely chastity, humility, gentleness, obedience, patience, and charity. These are the garments by which the soul can please the heavenly Emperor; for the invisible Bridegroom seeks not outward but inward beauty. As it is written: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44). Therefore our riches, [Col. 0897C] our beauty, are good morals. Blessed is that soul to which it is said in the Song of Songs: “How beautiful you are, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you!” (Cant. 4). Let us therefore strive to please the invisible Lord, not by clothes but by character, so that there may be fulfilled in us what is commanded through the Apostle: “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the newness of your mind” (Rom. 12). For though our outward person is decaying, yet the inward is renewed day by day (2 Cor. 4).

He then adds concerning walking, standing, and other movements, saying:

> When you go out, walk together; when you arrive where you are going, stand together. In your walking, standing, and all your movements, let nothing be done which offends anyone’s sight, but only what befits your holiness.

[Col. 0897D] Thus the holy Church of the perfect not only flourishes in the honor of religion, but also possesses the beauty of integrity, as it is written: “My flowers are the fruits of honor and integrity” (Ecclus. 24). For it is religious and fitting that, just as brothers dwell together, so too they should walk together and stand together. The Apostle also commanded that all things be done with propriety and according to order (1 Cor. 14). Something spiritual may also be understood in this bodily union. The society of the saints is described as terrible, like an army drawn up in ordered ranks. For when an army prepares itself for battle, it hastens first to unite and arrange itself, lest it be broken through or penetrated by enemies. So indeed our spiritual battle-line, [Col. 0898A] which is commanded to stand well joined and ordered together and to walk together, is daily fortified for battle against the devil, so that by its very unity it may terrify the ancient enemy, who fears nothing so much in the servants of God as the unity of concord.

But we must carefully observe what is said:

> In all your movements let nothing be done which offends anyone’s sight, but only what befits your holiness.

Canons ought to live in such a way that no one can justly reprove them. It is indeed utterly unsuitable for those to live blameably whose order requires them to set before others an example of holiness. For to them belongs the saying: “Be holy, because I too am holy, says the Lord” (Lev. 19). [Col. 0898B] Truly we ought to be holy, since we have undertaken the name and habit of religion and holiness, have been devoted to divine worship, consecrated to Christ’s sacred altars, and ordained for the divine mysteries. “Thus let a man regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the ministries of God” (1 Cor. 4). Yet the Apostle does not command that we should be such, but says: “Thus let a man regard us.” For a holy life alone does not suffice for us unless there is also a good reputation. A good life is necessary for our own sake, but a good reputation for the sake of others. Hence the Apostle again says: “We must have a good testimony from those who are outside” (1 Tim. 3). Therefore we ought to live so that life may accord with the name and profession may be maintained in deed; so that, if the order is holy, the manner of life may be holy, and what is well said [Col. 0898C] about us may be proved by the testimony of good conduct.

For then we live religiously if we restrain unlawful impulses under discipline; if we strive to curb our limbs and senses, so that they cannot serve wantonness and frivolity; if our look is simple and humble, lest the eye gaze fixedly at what the mind unlawfully desires; if our hearing is pure and discerning, rejecting superfluous and vain things and gladly receiving the things of God; if our speech is seasoned with salt, detesting idle and harmful things and commending good and lowly things; if there is purity in the heart, modesty in the face, gravity in walking, reverence in standing, sobriety in movement, and religion in dress—so that holiness may shine everywhere, integrity may prevail, humility may be preserved, and in [Col. 0898D] all your movements nothing may be done which offends anyone’s sight, but only what befits your holiness.

> Though your eyes may fall upon some woman, let them be fixed upon none. For when you go out, you are not forbidden to see women; but to desire them, or to wish to be desired by them, is sinful.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks upon a woman so as to desire her has already committed adultery in his heart” (Matt. 5). And because desire arises through an unlawful look, by which the integrity of the mind is violated, it is necessary that the servant of God always restrain his sight, lest through desire and impurity of heart he offend God. Holy David, [Col. 0899A] because he cast his eyes upon a woman and fixed them upon her, being overcome by unlawful desire committed adultery and murder. Therefore, if so great a man fell through carelessness of the eyes, we, who are far removed from his holiness, ought especially to fear so deadly a precipice. Let us therefore hold fast the saying of blessed Job: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not think upon a virgin” (Job 31). For because the holy man perceived that the inward mind is corrupted through outward sight, he made a covenant with his eyes, lest they carelessly look upon what it would unlawfully desire. Certainly, vice is not overcome unless its cause and opportunity are diligently avoided.

Hence Lot, fleeing from Sodom, is commanded not to look back, nor to remain anywhere in all the surrounding region, but to save [Col. 0899B] himself in the mountain. Whoever desires perfectly to flee the inducements of vices ought to remove himself from their sight and vicinity and ascend to the heights of virtues, so that he may remain as far removed from vices as he is separated from them by virtue and in body. And that sight is a cause of desire is shown when it is added:

> Desire for women both desires and is desired, not only by a silent inclination but also by inclination and sight.

As though he openly said: Desire does not arise inwardly only by silent will, but is also generated through outward sight. For unless holy David had gazed fixedly upon the woman, he would by no means have fallen into so great a temptation of the flesh. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Death has ascended through our windows” (Jer. 9). The death of the soul is desire; our inward mind is the house; the windows of this house are the five bodily senses. Death therefore ascends through the window and enters the house when the vice of desire bursts through the senses into the inward places of the mind. [Col. 0899C] Therefore, lest the living sense perish within through outward desire, we must guard the windows of our house with such diligence that we may all the more easily restrain desire itself, the less we permit any entrance to lie open to vices.

For the following saying must be greatly feared:

> Do not say that you have chaste minds if you have unchaste eyes, because an unchaste eye is the messenger of an unchaste [Col. 0899D] heart.

For outward members often disclose what lies hidden within, and the disposition of the mind is frequently recognized by the bearing of the body. The fault is less while it lies concealed; but it becomes greater when it begins to appear publicly.

And it must be known that one kind of unchastity is carnal, another spiritual. Spiritual unchastity is that which occurs only inwardly through the delight of thoughts. Carnal unchastity is that which is consummated bodily. It occurs in many ways. For lust is nourished and practiced by such incitements—now through sight, now through hearing, now through touch, now through thought, now through speech, now through action—and the soul is separated from [Col. 0900A] God, chastity flees from one’s conduct, and lust is exercised in the mind. Hence it is added:

> And when, even though the tongue is silent, they disclose their unchaste hearts to one another by mutual gaze, and delight in one another’s ardor according to the desire of the flesh, then chastity itself flees from their conduct, even though their bodies remain untouched by unclean violation.

Chastity indeed flees from one’s conduct when a lustful will is inflamed more and more by mutual glances. Even if the body is not touched by unclean violation, nevertheless that unclean violation is committed by sight, desire, thought, and delight; and by these very incitements, as by certain steps, sin increases. A small thought produces delight; delight, consent; consent, action; action, habit; [Col. 0900B] habit, necessity. For the Apostle says that there is a law of sin in the members (Rom. 7); this law is habit, which we conceive by sinning, and from which, even when we wish, we do not depart, because we are held by the bond of necessity through habit. It is therefore good to correct a fault when it begins to appear, because, if it begins to remain, it makes the crime monstrous. And what does the Psalmist say of such persons? “They have prolonged their iniquity; the just Lord will cut the necks of sinners” (Ps. 128).

> Nor should he who fixes his eye upon a woman, and loves her fixed gaze upon himself, suppose that he is not seen by others when he does this. He is certainly seen, even by those by whom he does not think himself seen.

This we often see in those who wish to conceal their faults: while they suppose that they practice vices cautiously and secretly, they unwittingly reveal themselves, and the fault thought to be hidden is openly recognized by others.

> But behold, suppose it is concealed and seen by no human being: what will he do about that Watcher from above, from whom nothing can be hidden? Or should He be thought not to see because He sees all the more patiently in proportion as He sees more wisely?

Therefore, in all things in which we sin by deed, speech, or thought, we ought greatly to fear the gaze of the heavenly Judge. For even if our vices sometimes do not appear to human beings, all things are naked and open to His eyes. And this ought to restrain us from sin, because in His judgment nothing can remain unpunished. Against the inducements of vices we ought to set the torments of hell; against passing delight, the pain of everlasting fire. He is very foolish who, because he serves lust for a brief time and feeds his miserable desire with small pleasures, loses heavenly delight and incurs eternal damnation.

> Therefore let that holy man fear to displease Him, lest he wish to please an evil woman. Let him think upon Him as seeing all things, lest he wish to appear evil in a woman’s eyes. For fear of Him is commended even in this matter, where it is written: “He who fixes his eye is an abomination to the Lord.”

From these words it is clear that, if we fix our eye upon a woman, we are abominable to our God, whom we ought to please. And from Him from whom we ought to receive glory, [Col. 0901A] we shall receive punishment. Therefore it is necessary that, if divine love does not separate us from our vices, fear at least restrain us; and, if heavenly joys do not delight us, eternal punishments at least terrify us. A person begins to withdraw from sin when he fears to displease his Creator.

If someone says, “How shall I fear God?”—if you wish to fear God, think upon Him as seeing all things. Does an evil conscience entice you? Think that God sees you. Whatever evil there may be in you, consider that God sees it all. Whatever we have done, said, or pondered in our mind, let us always attend to God’s eyes over us; let us always fear to displease Him. This is the way of righteousness; these are the beginnings of wisdom, as it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1). [Col. 0901B]

It follows:

> Therefore, whenever you are together in church or anywhere that women are present, guard one another’s chastity.

Great is the virtue of chastity, and it is much commended in the divine Scriptures. This virtue is heavenly and spiritual. For it lifts a person from earth, joins him to angels, unites him to God, and makes the earthly heavenly and the carnal spiritual. This virtue even transcends human nature. For a person’s being modest and chaste is brought about not so much by human as by divine power. Through it the invisible Bridegroom loves us. For a soul does not please God unless it is chaste and modest. If it serves impurity and lust, it is abominable and rejected by Him. The virtue of chastity is acceptable to God and to human beings. The ancient enemy of humankind envies us this virtue [Col. 0901C] and does not cease to assail it. He himself is the persuader of impurity and lust; he corrupts many, spares no clerics, indulges no monks, and, what is more lamentable, even casts down the religious themselves.

It is therefore necessary that we guard one another’s chastity with the utmost vigilance. For if we lose it, we lose everything, even ourselves. Whoever loses chastity loses his soul, loses God, and loses himself. But we live together for this purpose: that we may guard one another, correct one another, and instruct one another, so that what each cannot do by himself he may be able to do through another. And because our protection comes not from ourselves but from God, it is rightly added:

> [Col. 0901D] For God, who dwells in you, will guard you in this way also through yourselves.

Our own protection is not sufficient unless the divine protection is also present. Hence it is written: “Unless the Lord guards” (Ps. 126), etc. No one can guard chastity, either in himself or in another, except through God. But if He dwells in us, through Him we shall be able to do what we cannot do through ourselves. Let us therefore strive to live in such a way that He may deign to dwell in us and us in Him, so that through Him we may be righteous and chaste—He who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER VII. ON THE CORRECTION OF BROTHERS

> If you notice in any one [Col. 0902A] of yourselves that immodesty of the eyes of which I speak, admonish him at once, lest what has begun should proceed, but let it be corrected promptly. But if, even after admonition, you see him doing the same thing again, whether then or on any other day, whoever is able to discover it should report him as one wounded who needs healing. Yet it must first be shown to a second or third person, so that he may be convicted by the testimony of two or three, and restrained with suitable severity.

This statement accords with apostolic and Gospel words. For blessed Paul says: “If a person is overtaken in any fault, you who are spiritual instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. 6). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, correct him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take with you two or three, that every word may stand by the mouth of two or three” (Matt. 18). [Col. 0902B] Fault must indeed be investigated and corrected with the utmost diligence. For if we do not amend it in this age, we shall be condemned in the age to come. Hence the Apostle says: “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10). It is better, therefore, to amend one’s life here than then to perish. Whoever loves correction is wise. Hence it is written: “Correct a wise man, and he will love you.” But when a fool is corrected, he grows angry. Yet what does the Apostle say to his disciple? “Be urgent,” he says, “in season and out of season” (2 Tim. 4). “In season” he said for the sake of those who willingly heard the word of preaching; “out of season” for the sake of those who heard unwillingly. Likewise those who reprove faults sometimes must be importunate, but this importunity [Col. 0902C] is not from anger but from charity. Often, when the person disturbed because he is corrected begins to reflect upon the love with which his brother reproved him, he rejoices in the rebuke and strives to amend what he did wrongly.

> Nor should you judge yourselves ill-disposed when you report this. For you are not the more innocent if, by keeping silent, you allow your brothers to perish whom you could correct by reporting them. If your brother had a wound in his body which he wished to conceal because he feared being cut, would it not be cruel for you to keep silent, and merciful to report it? How much more, then, ought you to reveal it, lest it rot more grievously in the heart.

If he who conceals a wound in his brother’s body is cruel, much more cruel is he who does not report the wound of sin in his brother’s soul, and he is guilty of the death of the person whom he permits to perish by silence. For as the former is condemned through an act, so the latter is condemned through silence. Since he who does not expose a fault is cruel, conversely he who does not conceal it is merciful. Nor can anyone show greater mercy toward a miserable person than to grant life to one who is perishing. Great reward is also owed him by the Almighty, who said: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5). And James says: “Whoever causes a sinner to turn from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (Jas. 5). The order in which a fault ought to be reported is shown when he adds:

> But before it is shown to others, by whom he is to be convicted [Col. 0903A] if he denies it, it must first be shown to the superior, if, after admonition, he neglects to be corrected, lest perhaps, being corrected more secretly, he need not become known to the others.

When a fault is committed secretly, the brother who has sinned ought to be corrected in private by the other brothers who know of that fault. If he neglects to listen to them, it ought to be reported to the father of the monastery, so that he too may correct the brother in private; thus, if the fault still hidden can perhaps be corrected more secretly, it need not become known to all. But if he denies it, witnesses should then be brought forward so that, once convicted, he may be judged more strictly. This is what follows:

> But if he denies it, then others are to be brought against the one denying it, even before everyone, so that he may be accused not by one witness but convicted by two or three. Once convicted, [Col. 0903B] according to the judgment of the superior, or even of the presbyter to whose administration that judgment belongs, he must undergo corrective punishment.

He who is not corrected by gentle chastisement must necessarily be corrected more sharply. Those things which cannot be healed mildly must be cut away with pain. But one who, privately admonished concerning sin, neglects to be corrected must be publicly reproved, so that the wound which does not know how to be healed secretly may be amended openly. Public sins are not to be purged by a secret method. Those who sin openly must be reproved openly, so that, as they are healed by open rebuke, those who sinned by imitating them may be corrected. Therefore, the one who refused private correction, once publicly convicted, must undergo corrective punishment.

> [Col. 0903C] If he refuses to endure it, even if he does not leave, let him be expelled from your community. For this too is done not cruelly but mercifully, lest he destroy many by a pestilential contagion.

For it is better that one be condemned for the salvation of many than that many be endangered by the example of one. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you. For it is expedient for you that one of your members perish, rather than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna. And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you” (Matt. 5). By the right eye or right hand we may understand some necessary friend of ours. He who provides [Col. 0903D] in matters is our eye; he who ministers in necessities is our hand; and if he provides in spiritual matters, he is our right eye or right hand. If such a necessary person causes others to stumble in God’s service, he must be cut off from the body—that is, from the community. For it is better to lose the comfort of one than for the whole body to perish through one.

> And what I have said concerning not fixing the eye must also be carefully and faithfully observed, with love for persons and hatred of vices, in discovering, forbidding, reporting, proving, and judging all other sins.

Hence the same blessed doctor says elsewhere: “People are to be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved.” For it is one thing to love what they have become, another to [Col. 0904A] hate what they do. There are some who reprove the faults of others not so much from charity as from the bitterness of hatred, not so much because they wish them to be corrected as because they wish to exercise the hatred which they carry in their heart. And this is not according to God. It belongs more to vengeance than to discipline. Let them beware, therefore, lest they reprove anyone with anger and indignation, but rather with gentleness and charity. And if at times, because the fault demands it, harshness sounds in the voice, let gentleness nevertheless always remain in the mind. As the Apostle commands, saying: “You who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. 6). He rightly adds: “Considering yourself, lest you too be tempted” (ibid.). For attend to yourself, you who reprove another, because you are a sinner and frail, lest you be grievously [Col. 0904B] tempted if you attempt to reprove someone in indignation rather than compassion. Therefore let this be done with love for persons and hatred of vices: let love be preserved in the heart toward the person, and hatred toward the vice, because severity is owed to vices but compassion to nature.

It follows:

> But whoever has progressed so far in evil as secretly to receive letters from someone, or any gift whatsoever, if he confesses it freely, let him be spared and prayer be offered for him.

He calls the brother who secretly receives something one who has progressed far in evil, because to conceal something is to break the order. He incurs a great evil who proves to be a transgressor of his order. Unless the holy [Col. 0904C] prophet had known that it was a great evil for his disciple Gehazi to receive a secret gift from Naaman the Syrian (4 Kgs. 5), he would never have struck him so terribly with the affliction of leprosy. Thus by his example he taught us that anyone committing a similar sin deserves severe correction. Yet, if he confesses it freely, he is to be spared and prayer offered for him. For a fault becomes lighter when it is humbly disclosed by voluntary confession. Hence David says: “I said, ‘I will confess,’ and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Ps. 31).

> But if he is discovered and convicted, let him be corrected more severely according to the judgment of the presbyter or superior.

Because the graver the fault, the graver the discipline appropriate to it. For he grievously and mortally offends who also conceals the evil he does. Blessed Jerome writes thus concerning secret letters and little gifts: “Holy love,” he says, “does not have secret letters, little cloths, and frequent small presents. Whoever delights in such things is deceived by great vanity. And the more he delights in the lowest things, the more he is cast out from the things above.” Grave evils are accustomed to arise from such matters. But one who desires perfectly to avoid vices strives not only to avoid things evil in themselves, but also shuns those things from which either a wrongful act or an evil reputation may arise. We, however, who ought to live well and offer a good example to others, ought not to do such things as may give anyone even evil suspicion.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON THE SAFEGUARDING OF COMMON PROPERTY

[Col. 0905A]

> Keep your garments together under one keeper, or two, or as many as may be sufficient to shake them out lest they be harmed by moths. And just as you are fed from one pantry, so let yourselves be clothed from one wardrobe.

Because he commands garments to be kept under one keeper or several, there seem to be two reasons. First, lest through careless neglect they be damaged by moths. Second, lest a brother think that the garment he has is his own property if he were permitted to store it for himself in a private place. The words that follow seem to agree with this statement; for he says:

> And, if possible, let it not concern you which garment suitable to the season is brought out for you; [Col. 0905B] whether each receives what he had deposited or another garment which someone else had had, provided only that what each needs is not denied to anyone.

He says “if possible” because, if this seems difficult to someone, he may be permitted to receive the garment which he himself had deposited. For it would belong to greater perfection if someone had come to such contempt of self that he was content solely with what the body needs, as the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, we ought to be content with these” (1 Tim. 6). He does not specify how much or what kind, but notes only those things sufficient for nature. For in imperfect persons pleasure always desires more than necessity. As blessed Augustine says: “Human nature is content with little, but custom has added much; will and [Col. 0905C] pleasure have joined still more.” If anyone loved God perfectly and utterly renounced carnal desires, he would cut away many superfluities which he now holds as though necessary. Let us therefore learn to love God with the whole heart, so that through love for Him we may strive both to be content with necessities and to cut away superfluities; so that, while what each needs is not denied, no one may demand beyond what is needed. Charity does not seek its own things; charity puts common things before private things; charity makes one lowly in the house of God. Whoever has possessed it perfectly will cut back even from what he himself needs.

> But if disputes and murmurings arise among you from this, when someone complains that he has received something worse than he had before, and considers himself unworthy because he is not [Col. 0905D] clothed as another brother of his was clothed, then prove by this how much you lack that inward holy garment of the heart, since you quarrel over the garment of the body.

The garment of your heart is sanctified through the grace of God, through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, when peace, charity, goodness, humility, patience, concord, gentleness, and other such things are present. These are our inward riches: namely, good character and virtues. But if we begin to contend, murmur, and quarrel among ourselves, we immediately remain empty of these spiritual goods. For virtues cannot remain with vices. “A little leaven corrupts the whole mass” (1 Cor. 5). Hence each ought to examine himself and carefully weigh how much he lacks inwardly [Col. 0906A] and how great a loss he incurs when, for passing things, he loses that by which he ought to be blessed. Therefore disputes and contentions must be greatly avoided, because these are works of the flesh; and, as the Apostle says, “those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5). Therefore he admonishes us elsewhere, saying: “Do nothing through contention or vain glory; each judging the others superior to himself, not each considering what is his own, but what belongs to another” (Phil. 2). For these two things are very powerful in removing disputes and producing concord: when someone judges himself inferior to all and considers what belongs to another more than his own. In these two, humility and charity are commended; they not only do not tend to discord, but also restore those in discord to concord. And because these things which have been said concern the more perfect, he moderates the precept for the less perfect when he adds:

> Nevertheless, if your weakness is tolerated so that you receive what you have deposited, still keep in one place, under common keepers, what you put away.

That is, when the very thing received for private use is kept in a common place, we may regard it not as private but as common.

> Certainly, however, let no one make anything for himself; but let all your work be done in common, with greater diligence and more frequent readiness than if each of you were making private things for yourselves.

He then adduces and explains the apostolic statement, saying:

> For charity, of which it is written that it “does not [Col. 0906C] seek its own things,” is understood thus: it puts common things before private things, not private things before common things.

This is the reason why no one should work for himself, but things should be done in common with greater diligence and more frequent readiness than if they were private. This is the reason, I say, because charity does not seek its own things, but puts common things before private things. If Christ’s charity does not seek its own things, none of us ought to work for himself. And if Christ’s charity puts common things before private things, then we ought to carry out common things with greater diligence and more frequent readiness than if they were private. For the fruit of charity is greater than that of private possession. “For what eye has not seen nor ear heard, God has prepared this for those who love Him” (1 Cor. 2).

> Therefore, the more you care for the common good rather than your own [Col. 0906D] private things, the more you should know that you are making progress; so that in all things used by passing necessity, charity, which remains, may prevail.

Passing necessity indeed uses temporal things and temporal pursuits, in which charity ought always to prevail, because no one can please God without charity. Therefore charity must always stand foremost in all that we do, because it is the mother of virtues and the root of all goods. This is the higher way by which one tends toward heaven, of which the Apostle Paul says: “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12). He makes great progress in this charity who, for the love of God, despises all the things of this world, desires to retain nothing for himself, [Col. 0907A] and shares in common whatever he has. Truly he walks by the exalted way who, having trampled earthly things underfoot, is raised in mind and desire to heavenly things.

Charity consists in love of God and neighbor. Love of God is expressed in three ways, so that nothing may remain in a person which is not subjected to divine love. For we are commanded to love God with all the heart—that is, to refer all our thoughts to God; with all the mind (Deut. 6), so that we direct to Him all the reason by which we understand and discern; with all the soul (ibid.), so that we direct all the affections of the soul to God. In love of neighbor two things must be kept: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to others” (Tob. 4); and “What you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. 7). From this twofold virtue of love for [Col. 0907B] neighbor arise all the virtues by which we usefully desire things that ought to be desired and avoid things that ought to be avoided. By these two principles the neighbor is rightly loved, when he is both cherished with benefits and harmed by no malice. Therefore charity must always prevail in all things which passing necessity uses. For whatever we do or say ought to look to the charity of God or of neighbor, so that in all our conduct the highest aim of our intention may always consist in charity. “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (Matt. 22).

> It follows, therefore, that if anyone gives some garment or any other item to be counted among necessities to his children or to persons connected with him by some necessity who are established in the monastery, it should not be received secretly, [Col. 0907C] but should be in the power of the superior, so that, having been brought into the common stock, it may be given to whoever needs it.

For in the whole manner of life, it is not permitted to receive anything secretly, or to have anything received secretly, nor to retain anything as private property. But if anything is given to someone, it must be handed over to the superior, so that it may be given to whoever needs it. Thus avarice is extinguished; thus superfluity is cut away. Thus charity is nourished and holy poverty preserved, because when it is not permitted to retain earthly things, the mind is compelled to think of heavenly things.

But there are some who are seriously troubled when what they receive from others is not permitted to be retained by them. They love little gifts; they delight in private possessions. Often they are inflamed with such desire even for small and worthless things that, on their account, they are accustomed to disturb the concord of the brothers. That this occurs by the devil’s persuasion is beyond doubt. For the crafty enemy knows everyone’s dispositions and qualities, discerns their inclinations, and tempts each person precisely where he knows he has greater power. He does not care whether he deceives through something great or small, provided only that he can corrupt a brother’s charity. We must be cautious and vigilant against the crafty enemy, guard against his snares in every sort of material thing, and trample underfoot with strength of mind every earthly thing through which he can deceive us, so that we may be able to sing with the Prophet: “The snare has been broken, and we have been delivered” (Ps. 123). But because some are caught in this matter, it is added:

> If anyone conceals something given to him, let him be condemned by the judgment for theft.

[Col. 0908A] The Apostle says: “Thieves and robbers shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6). For theft is a criminal sin, as it is written: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness,” etc. (Exod. 20). Therefore, since it is reckoned among criminal evils according to the judgment of the canons, each person ought to judge theft as he judges adultery, homicide, and false witness. A brother who conceals an article entrusted to him occupies in the holy Church the place of Judas the traitor, who was a thief and robber and, having the money-box, carried away and hid what was put in for the Lord. He burned with such a vice of greed and avarice that he sold and betrayed his Lord, as the devil had put it into his heart. But in seeking gain he found death, as it is written: “While [Col. 0908B] he thirsts for gain, he comes to the snare.” Such are the fruits of avarice. Let the brothers therefore beware of desiring profits or concealing any object, lest, while at the devil’s persuasion they commit so detestable a fault, they incur, by the righteous judgment of almighty God, the punishment of death and everlasting condemnation.

## CHAPTER IX. ON CLEANLINESS OF CLOTHING AND BODIES

Let your garments be washed, whether by yourselves or by fullers, according to the judgment of the superior, lest an excessive desire for clean clothing contract inward stains upon the soul.

He himself explains why he commanded garments to be washed according to the superior’s judgment: namely, lest [Col. 0908C] a brother contract stains in his soul if he desires to have clean clothes beyond measure. For the more anyone is outwardly made clean for vain glory, the more he is inwardly defiled. Superiors, therefore, should take care lest those subject to them sin through the finery of their clothing. For it is not the brightness of clothing but uprightness of character that adorns a cleric. Hence the Apostle warns us, saying: “Do not be conformed to this world, but be reformed in the newness of your mind” (Rom. 12). For those who seek the form of this world do not seek the form of the inward person. And the more outward beauty is loved, the less inward beauty is cared for.

This is the true and spiritual cleanliness which God requires of us, saying: “Wash yourselves; be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes” (Isa. 1). For he does not say, “Blessed are those clean in [Col. 0908D] body,” but, “Blessed are the clean in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). And lest anyone suppose that care of the flesh is likewise to be cut off, he adds:

Even the bathing of the body, when the necessity of illness compels it, is by no means to be denied. But let it be done without murmuring, on medical advice; thus, even if he does not wish it, at the superior’s command he is to do what must be done for his health. But if he wishes it and it is perhaps not expedient, his desire is not to be obeyed.

This judgment seems to agree with the Apostle’s words, which forbid care of the flesh in its desires, not in its necessity. For there is a great difference between necessity and desire. What arises from necessity is useful; what arises from desire is a vice. [Col. 0909A] Yet there are some who say that bodily medicine does not befit religious life. But if they considered carefully, they themselves would recognize that what we eat and drink, the clothing with which we cover ourselves, and the earthly things which we use for necessity, are medicine for the body.

Let it therefore be done without murmuring, on medical advice.

And well he says: “Let one unwilling in necessity be compelled; let one willing from desire be restrained,” because necessity, not desire, must be obeyed. For sometimes, even when it harms, that which delights is thought beneficial. Behold why a person ought not obey his own desire: he is often so deceived by it that he believes what harms him benefits him. Thus evil desire deceives people; thus it pretends that what is evil and [Col. 0909B] destructive is good. Behold why Holy Scripture so strongly condemns desire and carnal pleasure: because they draw people toward death while people themselves do not know it.

Sometimes, even when it harms, that which delights is believed beneficial.

But, according to the Apostle’s saying, we must abstain from fleshly desires which wage war against the soul, because the flesh indeed desires against the spirit. Yet the desire of the flesh must be restrained through the discipline of the spirit. Some, however, pursue the rigor of the spirit beyond measure; others, the softness of the flesh. The former, while desiring to live spiritually, sometimes destroy the flesh along with its vices. But [Col. 0909C] it must be understood that virtue, if it lacks measure, is turned into vice. The latter, who wish to live carnally, are intent upon care of the flesh and nourishing their own desires. Therefore a measure must be established for both: the former must be compelled to do what must be done for health; the latter must be restrained from doing what they carnally desire. The body’s health is to be preserved for serving God; the flesh’s desire is to be extinguished. And because he spoke of manifest illness, he adds concerning hidden pain:

Finally, if the pain is hidden, when a servant of God says what pains him, he is to be believed without doubt.

For one whom good conduct and holy manner of life commend as a servant of God is rightly to be believed. [Col. 0909D] Truth or falsehood is not known from the mouths of those speaking; rather, “By their fruits you shall know them,” says the Lord. They are not deceitful; they are not double-minded; they are not among those who have spoken false things in heart and mouth. As servants of God are in heart, so are they in speech. A good life gives credibility to words. An evil life makes even truth itself doubtful. Therefore those who are unquestionably good are to be believed without doubt.

In another sense: if the pain is hidden, he is to be believed without doubt. For the servant of God fears to offend God not only in deed but also in word. We ought to present ourselves as such that whatever we say may be believed without doubt. Life ought to commend speech, and good deeds bear witness to truth, [Col. 0910A] as our Savior says of himself: “If you do not believe me, at least believe the works. The works which I do, they bear witness to me” (John 10). For many are not believed even when they tell the truth, because they are evil or are suspected of being evil. But if our life begins to be good beyond suspicion, our words will at once be believed true without doubt. The less good anyone is, the less he is believed; the more religious he begins to be, the greater the faith accorded to his words. But because the necessity of illness sometimes seeks things contrary to itself, he therefore adds:

Yet if it is not certain whether what delights is expedient for healing that pain, let a physician be consulted.

[Col. 0910B] Their words are to be believed, but their desires are not immediately to be indulged; for unlawful desires tempt even servants of God. Therefore, if it is not certain, let a physician be consulted. Let one be sought who can make the uncertain certain. Nor is it surprising that we seek physicians’ advice, since we read that the Apostle Paul used medical counsel. For he instructs his disciple Timothy in his Epistle, saying: “Use a little wine because of your stomach and your frequent infirmities” (1 Tim. 5). Thus the discerning teacher moderates his disciple from the rigor of abstinence, lest, broken by frequent sufferings, he grow weak in the good work of preaching. It was indeed good for the disciple to render the fruit of patience in illness; but the Apostle foresaw that it would be more useful if, recovering somewhat through medical treatment, [Col. 0910C] he might win souls for God. From among different goods, the more useful must be chosen. Strengthened by this authority, we ought to seek bodily medicine for this purpose: that thereby we may render a greater fruit to the Lord.
