Let them not go to the baths, or wherever it may be necessary to go, in fewer than two or three persons.

The Apostle says: “We provide what is good not only before God but also before all people” (2 Cor. 8). For ourselves, a good conscience suffices; for others, our reputation ought not to be stained but to have strength among us. One who, trusting in his conscience, neglects his reputation is cruel, especially when placed in the position concerning which the Apostle says, writing to his disciple: “In all things show yourself an example of good works” [Col. 0910D] (Titus 2). Again, elsewhere he says: “We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to people.” Those who love us seek what they may praise in us; those who hate us speak evil of us. But we, placed between the two, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, ought so to guard both our life and our reputation that we need not be ashamed to be praised by detractors. Thus two or three ought to go together, both for companionship and for the testimony of a good reputation. Hence Solomon says: “Woe to one alone, if he falls and has no one to raise him; if there are two, they will warm one another” (Eccl. 4). And he rightly says that one must go with those whom the superior has commanded: namely, so that the superior may provide for personal safety and the subject may preserve the virtue of obedience.

[Col. 0911A] The care of the sick, whether those to be restored after illness, those suffering from some weakness, or even from fevers, ought to be assigned to someone, so that he himself may request from the storeroom what he foresees each person needs.

A brother who fears God should be chosen to exercise the greatest care for the sick, to endeavor to minister whatever they need, and to serve them with such diligence and affection as though he were serving the Lord Jesus Christ himself. For he will say at judgment: “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matt. 25). And again: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” (ibid.). The stronger, therefore, ought to bear the weakness of the infirm. For thus divine love is fulfilled, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you shall fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6). The law of Christ is love. [Col. 0911B] The office of love is to bear one another’s burdens. Different times and different illnesses cause us to bear one another’s burdens. Nothing proves a friend so much as bearing a friend’s burden. But the sick person himself, whom one serves for love of God, ought to consider and take the utmost care not to grieve the one serving him by excessiveness or impatience. Let him endeavor to give thanks to God, lest the illness given him for the cleansing of his soul be turned into an increase of guilt.

But whether those set over clothing or those set over books, let them serve their brothers without murmuring.

Let them conduct themselves in such a way, and serve their brothers with such love, that they themselves do not sin by murmuring concerning the ministry entrusted to them, nor cause others to murmur through their negligence. [Col. 0911C] Murmuring is a grave sin, as Gregory testifies when he says: “No one who murmurs receives the kingdom of heaven; no one who receives it will be able to murmur.” And Solomon says: “The heart of a fool is like the wheel of a cart” (Ecclus. 33): it carries hay and murmurs. Such, therefore, are those in the community who, subject to the flesh, do not cease from murmuring. The Apostle says: “Neither murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by serpents” (1 Cor. 10). Why by serpents, unless because the serpent is venomous, and everyone who murmurs has the devil’s poison on his tongue? James says: “The tongue is a restless evil, full of deadly poison” (Jas. 3). Therefore we must beware of murmuring, lest we perish through deadly and diabolical [Col. 0911D] poison.

Let books be requested at a fixed hour; whoever asks outside that hour is not to receive one.

Above, he commands diligence in prayers at appointed times. Therefore the times at which we ought to pray and those at which we ought to read must be distinguished. Elsewhere he also admonishes concerning work, that no one should do anything for himself, but that all your works should be done together. The Rule commends to us these three things, which are very necessary for our soul: prayer, reading, and work. For by prayer we are cleansed, by reading instructed, and by work made blessed, as the Holy Spirit says in the Psalm: “Because you shall eat the labors of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127). And since it says that books are to be requested each day, [Col. 0912A] it commends frequent reading. A servant of God ought to read frequently. Divine reading is exceedingly useful. For through reading we learn what to avoid, what to do, and toward what we should strive. Hence the Psalmist says: “Your word is a lamp to my feet” (Ps. 118). Perfection of sense and understanding are increased. Reading instructs us toward prayer and work, and forms us for the contemplative and active life. Therefore it is written in the Psalm: “Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. 1). These are the weapons—prayer, reading, and work—by which the devil is overcome. These are the instruments by which eternal blessedness is gained. By these weapons vices are restrained; by these nourishments virtues are fed. But even if reading ceases, the work of the hands ought to follow, because [Col. 0912B] idleness is the enemy of the soul; and the ancient enemy, when he finds someone free from reading or prayer, easily drags him into vices. For by the practice of reading you will learn how both to live yourselves and to teach others; through work of the hands and mortification of the body, you will deny nourishment to vices, provide for your own needs, and have something from which to give to those suffering want.

But when clothing and footwear are necessary for those in need, those under whose charge the requested articles are placed should not delay giving them.

This is what was said above: that they should serve their brothers without murmuring. Lest, when they delay giving necessary things, they cause the brothers to murmur and become an occasion of sin, let them endeavor to serve their brothers [Col. 0912C] for God’s sake and to supply necessities at suitable times. And let them do this without murmuring, without sadness, without delay, with joy and cheerfulness, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9), so that all may have what they need according to the resources of the community and the means of the place; and those who serve may thereby have a greater reward from the Lord.

In the clothing and footwear of clerics, however, a suitable measure must be observed: they must not be precious or excessively bright, nor too shabby and cheap; neither more elaborate than is fitting nor more disordered than is proper. They ought therefore to be such as to commend both religious life and decency. Let the brothers to whom necessities are supplied beware of demanding anything importunately [Col. 0912D] or anything unbefitting their religious profession. For whatever superfluity they possess is deadly to them. Let them consider, therefore, that what they spend consists of the offerings of the faithful for the redemption of sins. And hence let them not glory in using such things, but rather fear what was said in the Old Testament concerning priests: that they ought to bear the iniquity of the people. Therefore let them be anxiously concerned, with great fear, for those in whose gifts they share, because there is great danger. It is healthier for Christ’s poor, as has already been said, always to need less rather than to possess more. For how shall we be poor unless we bear want for God with equanimity? Therefore, in proportion as we remember having committed unlawful acts, we ought to abstain from lawful things. For through the narrow [Col. 0913A] gate we must enter, so that we may be able to reach the breadth of heavenly joys. For the more constricted a life we lead here, the greater glory we shall possess in heaven.

Have no disputes, or end them as quickly as possible, lest anger grow into hatred, make a beam out of a speck, and make the soul a murderer. For thus you read: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3).

Thus vices often grow little by little. Certainly, when we are unwilling to restrain the tongue from idle speech, we descend into harmful speech; from there we sometimes fall into murmuring and detractions; very often even into quarrels and strife; then into anger and hatred. And, according to Solomon’s saying, while we neglect to correct small things, we fall into greater ones (Ecclus. 19). [Col. 0913B] Therefore, while vice is born from vice, iniquity is prolonged. Hence the prophet says: “Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of vanity!” (Isa. 5). And the Psalmist: “They have prolonged their iniquity; the righteous Lord will cut down the necks of sinners” (Ps. 128). Therefore sin must above all be avoided at its beginning. It is better to prevent than to correct. For if it happens that one sins through frailty, the fault which is quickly recognized is easily corrected. Hence the Lord says to the serpent concerning the woman: “She shall crush your head” (Gen. 3): the serpent’s head is crushed when sin is corrected where it is born. Each person should therefore be watchful, so that he may promptly strive to amend himself where he knows that he has sinned. As great as the difference between a speck [Col. 0913C] and a beam, so great is the difference between anger and hatred. For hatred is long-standing anger, which has received so much from age that it is rightly called old. It can happen that, if you are angry with a person, you may still wish him to be corrected; but if you hate him, you cannot wish him to be corrected. By anger the eye of the mind is troubled; by hatred it is even extinguished. Hence the Apostle says: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness” (1 John 2). No angry person finds his own anger unjust. Therefore from every indignation one must swiftly return to the gentleness of meekness. For a persistent emotion easily passes into hatred of the person who is not quickly forgiven. Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER X. ON SEEKING FORGIVENESS AND REMITTING OFFENCE

[Col. 0913D] Whoever injures another by insult, curse, or even an accusation of wrongdoing should remember to make satisfaction as soon as possible for what he has done; and the injured person should forgive without dispute.

He grievously offends who injures another by insult or curse. The Apostle says: “The revilers shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘You fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 5). Therefore, as he has grievously sinned, he ought to repent grievously, and with his whole heart and in all humility seek pardon from the person whom he injured; and the injured person should forgive without dispute. Isidore says: “Whoever is slower to be reconciled with his brother is slower to make God favorable to himself.” [Col. 0914A] For in vain does one seek to have God reconciled and made propitious to oneself while neglecting promptly to appease one’s neighbor. Yet there are some who, confident in their own merits, reluctantly grant pardon to those who sin against them. But it profits nothing to have remained uninjured if one is not ready to forgive, since it is rather a great fault when a brother’s offenses are remitted too slowly.

Truth itself testifies that the servant who owed ten thousand talents, when he repented, received release of the debt from his lord; but because he did not remit the debt of one hundred denarii which his fellow servant owed him, he too was ordered to pay what had already been forgiven him (Matt. 18). From these words it is evident that if we do not forgive from the heart what has been done against us, that too is again demanded which we rejoiced had already been forgiven us through repentance.

[Col. 0914B] But if they have injured one another, they ought mutually to forgive one another their debts, because of your prayers, which, indeed, the more frequent they are, the sounder they ought to be.

Every day we say to God: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6). If we do not forgive our debtors—that is, those who sin against us—when we say to God, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive,” we indict ourselves by our very prayer, provoke God to anger against us, and bring upon ourselves a curse rather than a blessing. Thus prayer, which ought to be salutary for us, becomes harmful, and, by praying, we increase the sins which we ought to diminish.

[Col. 0914C] For the daily, light, and brief sins without which this life cannot be lived, the daily prayer of the faithful will make satisfaction. For it belongs to those who have already been regenerated by water and the Holy Spirit to such a Father to say: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (ibid.). This prayer entirely removes these small, daily sins. It also removes those from which even a life of the faithful, lived wickedly, departs when, through repentance, it is changed for the better. But just as “Forgive us our debts” is truthfully said, because there are no lack of debts to be forgiven, so also “as we forgive our debtors” must be truthfully said. What is said must be done, because it is itself an almsgiving to forgive a person seeking pardon.

There are indeed many kinds of almsgiving, through which, when we perform them, we are helped so that our sins may be forgiven. But none is greater than that by which we forgive from the heart whatever anyone has sinned against us. To be kindly disposed or even beneficent toward one who has done you no evil is a lesser good; but it is far greater, and an act of most magnificent goodness, that you should also love your enemy, always wish good to one who wishes you evil, and do what you can, so that you may hear Jesus saying: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you; and pray for those who persecute you” (Matt. 5).

But since these are the marks of the perfect children of God, toward which every believer ought to strive and bring the human mind through prayer to God and through struggle and wrestling with oneself; nevertheless, because this great good is not possessed by so great a multitude as is required for us to be heard when it is said in prayer, [Col. 0915A] “Forgive us our debts as we also forgive our debtors,” beyond doubt the words of this pledge are fulfilled if a person who has not yet progressed so far as to love even an enemy nevertheless, when asked by the person who has sinned against him to forgive, forgives from the heart. For when he prays and says, “Forgive us as we also forgive our debtors,” he surely wishes himself to be forgiven when he asks: that is, “Forgive our debts when we ask, just as we forgive our debtors when they ask.”

Now, if a person asks the person against whom he sinned, and is moved by his sin to ask, he ought not to be counted so much an enemy that it is difficult to love him as it was difficult while he was acting in hostility. [Col. 0915B] But whoever does not forgive from the heart one who asks and repents of his sins must by no means suppose that his own sins are forgiven by the Lord. For Truth cannot lie, when it says: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your offenses” (Matt. 6).

One who, though often tempted by anger, nevertheless hastens to obtain forgiveness from the person whom he recognizes that he has wronged is better than one who is slower to anger and slower to bend toward seeking forgiveness.

In some, anger rises more quickly and leaves more readily; others are moved slowly but hold it longer. Another person—which is worse—both receives the flames of anger more quickly and lays them aside more slowly. Yet some receive them more slowly and lose them more quickly. [Col. 0915C] In these cases the reader plainly recognizes that the last comes nearer than the first to the good of tranquillity, while, in evil, the third surpasses the second.

Let us consider how great is the fault of anger: through it, when meekness is lost, the likeness of the heavenly image is marred. Through anger justice is abandoned, as it is written: “The anger of man does not work the justice of God” (Jas. 1). Through anger the grace of social life is lost, as it is written: “Do not be closely associated with an angry man, lest perhaps you learn his paths and take a snare for your soul” (Prov. 22). For one who does not restrain himself by human reason must live alone like a beast. Sometimes anger does not put forth the hand but turns the tongue toward the missiles of curses. At other times, [Col. 0915D] while the inflamed mind is withheld from customary speech, it is, as time passes, utterly separated from love of neighbor; sharper goads enter the mind, and causes arise that provoke more severely. Thus the speck becomes a beam in the angry person’s eye, while anger is transformed into hatred.

We fear being despised by our neighbors; we disdain to endure the injury of words. If perhaps a quarrel arises with a neighbor, we are ashamed to make satisfaction first. The carnal heart, while seeking the glory of this life, rejects humility. Often the very person who is angry wishes to be reconciled with the one disagreeing with him, but is ashamed to go first to make satisfaction. Let us therefore consider the deeds of our Head, that we may see where the errors of our perversity lie. Behold: by sinning we made discord between ourselves and God; [Col. 0916A] yet God first sent his envoys to us who had denied him, so that we ourselves, who sinned, might be recalled to God’s peace. Therefore let human pride be ashamed, and let each person be confounded if he does not make satisfaction to his neighbor; because after our fault, God himself, the offended party, entreats us through intervening messengers so that we may be reconciled to him.

But whoever does not wish to ask forgiveness, or does not ask from the heart, is in the monastery without cause, even if he is not expelled from it.

Since the Lord is so concerned for our reconciliation that he allows his gifts to be left before the altar and to remain incomplete, and allows his ministries to be interrupted until you go, resolve your anger, and break off your enmity with your brother, are we not ashamed, but [Col. 0916B] allow enmities to remain for many days and draw out long discord like a rope? God punishes not only the angry and those mindful of malice, but also those who offend persons in anger, or neglect and scorn to appease them. Those who suffer, and appear to suffer, injuries necessarily grieve and become angry; but those who inflict them bear neither grief nor anger. For this reason he brings the person who is free from anger to the one who is in grief and not free, showing that the harm of this offense lies rather with the person who gave the cause of sin. Yet even so we are not corrected. For we persist in grieving our brothers over trifles, and, as though we had done no evil, neglect to make satisfaction, consign the fault to forgetfulness, and allow it to be prolonged [Col. 0916C] for a long time, not knowing that the more prolonged the discord, the more abundant will be our punishment.

For where friendship remains, nothing is readily accepted or readily believed that could produce dissension. But if hostilities have once taken possession, everything done, said, or heard is received and understood in such a way as to advance greater and longer enmities. If there is anything evil, that alone is believed and confirmed. Therefore the Lord commands the gift to be left before the altar and one first to be reconciled with one’s brother, so that we may learn from this that, if God does not permit reconciliation to be neglected or postponed even at the time when we are commanded to approach the service of God, how much more this matter ought to be attended to at other times.

[Col. 0916D] If it happens that we become angry, we are commanded to end our anger or enmities within the day. We are bound by the precept which says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4). But we, on the contrary, are not content merely to prolong anger beyond the setting of the sun; we also lay snares for one another, desiring to overthrow our neighbors by deeds or words, biting and devouring one another—which is plainly madness. For what else do the insane and those filled with a demon do except tear their own limbs apart with bites? Therefore one who is at discord with his brother is in the monastery in vain, because he neither appeases God by sacrifices nor can make progress by good works.

Therefore spare one another from harsh words.

Solomon says: “A gentle answer breaks anger; a harsh word stirs up fury” [Col. 0917A] (Prov. 15). And again: “A sweet word softens enemies and multiplies friends” (Ecclus. 6). And Paul: “You who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. 6). Therefore holy persons should beware of harsh words.

If such words have been uttered from your mouth, do not be reluctant to bring forth from your mouth the remedies by which the wounds were made.

First, we should take the greatest care not to disturb anyone with harsh words. But if we sometimes sin through frailty, we ought immediately to make satisfaction and, in place of a harsh saying, bring forth a sweet and conciliatory one, so that the medicine of humble confession may heal the wound of disturbance. But, as we said above, it is better first to avoid a vice than afterward to correct what has been committed. Therefore the servant of God ought [Col. 0917B] always to set a guard upon his mouth, so that he may not sin with his tongue—especially when a sinner stands against him, namely, someone slanderous and abusive—as it is written: “There are many proud and envious persons who do not cease to provoke the servants of God” (Ecclus. 5). Therefore, if you have understanding, answer your neighbor; but if not, let your hand be upon your mouth, lest you be caught by an undisciplined word and put to shame (Ecclus. 5).

But when the necessity of discipline, for restraining conduct, compels you to speak harsh words, if you yourselves perceive that you have exceeded the measure, you are not required to seek pardon from those subject to you, lest, among those who ought to be subject, governing authority be weakened while humility is observed too greatly.

This often happens to great teachers: [Col. 0917C] when they burn with compelled correction, they exaggerate the measure of correction, and the tongue says something it ought not because love does not inflame the mind as much as it ought. Hence the Lord rightly commanded through Moses, saying: “If anyone goes simply with his friend into the forest to cut wood, and in cutting the wood the axe slips from his hand, and the iron, falling from the handle, strikes and kills his friend, he shall flee to one of the aforesaid cities and live, lest perhaps the neighbor whose blood has been shed pursue him under the goad of grief, seize him, and strike his life” (Deut. 9).

For we go into the forest with a friend whenever we turn with any neighbor to consider our faults; and we cut wood simply when we cut away the vices of sinners with pious intention. But the axe slips from the hand when reproof extends itself into harshness further than necessary; and the iron springs from the handle when a word goes too far in severity of correction and, striking a friend, kills him, because the uttered insult slays its hearer’s spirit of love. For the corrected person’s mind rushes into hatred if an immoderate reproof instructs him more harshly than it ought. But the one who incautiously strikes the wood and destroys his neighbor must flee to three cities, in order that he may live defended in one of them. For if, turned to the tears of repentance, he is hidden in the unity of the sacrament under hope, faith, and love, he is not held guilty of the homicide he has committed, and when the kinsman of the slain finds him, he does not kill him. Because [Col. 0918A] that righteous Judge, who joined himself to us through participation in our nature, undoubtedly does not exact vengeance for the liability of fault from one whom faith, hope, and love hide beneath his pardon. Therefore it is added:

Yet pardon must be sought from the Lord of all, who knows with how great a goodwill you love those whom you perhaps correct more severely than is just.

The measure is sometimes exceeded through zeal for wickedness, sometimes through zeal for justice; often deliberately through studied speech, often through an excess of speech. But the Lord attends not so much to the speech as to the intention. Thus a fault is more quickly forgiven when it is not at all committed through a purpose of malice.

[Col. 0918B] But the love among you ought not to be carnal but spiritual.

There are some who love their neighbors through the affection of kinship and flesh; nevertheless, sacred writings do not oppose them in this love. But one thing is what is bestowed voluntarily upon nature, another what is owed through obedience to the Lord’s commands out of love. Such persons indeed love their neighbor, yet do not attain those lofty rewards of love because they bestow their love not spiritually but carnally. The sole proof of being disciples of almighty God is the keeping of love. Hence he himself says: “By this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13). If this love truly fills our heart, it is usually shown in two ways: if we love friends in God and enemies for [Col. 0918C] God’s sake.

Often the mind is deceived by the appearance of love toward an enemy and falsely thinks that it loves him. But love of an enemy is truly kept when we are neither saddened by his prosperity nor gladdened by his ruin. Love begins indeed from two commandments, but extends itself to innumerable things. Its beginning is love of God and neighbor; but love of God is distinguished in three respects, because we are commanded to love the Creator with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all the strength.

In this matter it should be noted that when the divine word commands us to love God, it not only tells us this, but also instructs us as to the extent of that love when it adds: “With all your strength,” so that whoever desires perfectly to please God may leave nothing of himself for himself. Love of neighbour, however, [Col. 0918D] is reduced to two commandments. Thus it is said: “See that you do not do to another what you do not wish done to yourself” (Tob. 4). And Truth itself says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. 7). By these two commandments, namely of the two Testaments, malice is restrained by the one and kindness is commended by the other: so that, since each person does not wish to suffer evil, he refrains from harming; and again, by rendering to his neighbour the good which he desires to be done to himself, he exercises kindness for that neighbour’s benefit. But when these two principles are considered with careful attention, the heart is directed toward innumerable services of virtue: lest the restless mind burn with desires to inflict what it ought not, or, slackened by idleness, grow torpid in rendering what it ought.

[Col. 0919A] For when a person takes care not to do to another what he would in no way wish to endure from another, he watches himself with diligent attention: lest pride lift him up and, casting down his mind to contempt for his neighbour, exalt him; lest ambition tear apart his thoughts and, while extending them toward the desire for another’s possessions, constrict them; lest lust defile him and, subjecting him to desires, corrupt him through unlawful things; lest anger embitter him and inflame him even to uttering insults; lest envy gnaw at him and, rival of others’ prosperity, consume itself with its own torch; lest excessive talkativeness carry off his tongue and extend it to the wantonness of detraction; lest malice arouse hatred and provoke his mouth even to the missile of cursing.

And again, when he considers that he should do for another what he expects another to do for him: namely, that he should return good for evil, and better things for good; [Col. 0919B] that he should show the gentleness of long-suffering toward the insolent; that he should render the grace of kindness to those sick with the plague of malice; that he should fortify the discordant with peace; that he should inflame the concordant with desire for true peace; that he should give necessities to those in need; that he should show the way of uprightness to those who err; that he should soothe the afflicted by word and compassion; that he should restrain by rebuke those inflamed with desires of this kind; that he should moderate the threats of the powerful by reasoned argument; that he should relieve, with whatever assistance he can, the straits of the oppressed; and that he should oppose patience to those resisting from without, while offering discipline together with patience to those who are proud within; that gentleness toward subjects should so temper zeal that, if zeal burns for vengeance, it does not depart from the pursuit of justice, yet does not in burning transgress [Col. 0919C] the boundary of mercy; that he should draw ungrateful people into love by acts of service; that, when he cannot correct his neighbours’ evils, he should keep silence; that he should dread lest silence amount to consent in things which can be corrected; that he should so endure what he keeps silent about as not to conceal in his heart the poison of grief; that he should so offer the gift of kindness to the ill-disposed as not to fall away from the rule of uprightness through favour; that he should give his neighbours all that he can, but not become inflated by giving; that he should so avoid the precipice of pride in the good things he offers as not to become sluggish in the exercise of good; that he should so distribute what he possesses as to consider how great is the generosity of the One who rewards, and, when he gives earthly things, not think excessively of his own want, nor let sadness darken the bright light of his offering.

Therefore the law of God is rightly called manifold [Col. 0919D], because one and the same charity, if it has fully taken hold of the mind, kindles it in many ways to innumerable works. This law of God is manifold, because it is suitably applied, without alteration, to each particular circumstance of affairs, and, though situations vary, it joins them without itself varying. Paul aptly shows the manifold character of this law when he says: “Charity is patient, is kind,” and so forth (1 Cor. 13).

## CHAPTER XI. ON OBEDIENCE

Let the superior be obeyed as a father, and still more the presbyter who bears the care of you all.

Obedience alone is the virtue which implants the other virtues in the mind and preserves them once implanted. Samuel says: “Obedience is better [Col. 0920A] than sacrifice” (1 Sam. 15), because by sacrifices another’s flesh is bound, but by obedience one’s own will is bound. Solomon says: “The obedient man speaks victories” (Prov. 21), because, when we humbly submit to another’s voice, we conquer ourselves in our heart. Obedience, indeed, is commanded to be kept by us even unto death. By obedience evil must never be done; yet sometimes, by obedience, even a good work being done ought to be set aside.

But because adverse things are sometimes not commanded, it should be understood most carefully that obedience is sometimes nonexistent if it has anything from itself, whereas at other times, if it has nothing from itself, it is very slight. For when worldly success is commanded, when a higher position is imposed, one who pants after receiving these things through his own desire empties obedience [Col. 0920B] of its virtue for himself. Again, when contempt of the world is commanded, when one is ordered to undergo reproaches and insults, unless the mind desires these things of itself, it diminishes the merit of obedience for itself, because it descends unwillingly and reluctantly to those things which are despised in this life. Therefore obedience ought, in adversities, to have something of its own; and again, in prosperities, to have nothing whatever of its own: so that in adversities it may be the more glorious insofar as it is joined even by desire to the divine order; and in prosperities it may be the more lowly insofar as the very glory which it receives by divine appointment is utterly removed from the mind.

The adornment of obedience is always joined to innocent minds, as the Lord testifies when he says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10). [Col. 0920C] Certainly the innocent person obeys the Redeemer; and one who disdains to obey cannot be innocent.

Therefore, in order that all these things may be kept, and that anything kept less than perfectly may not be negligently passed over but carefully amended and corrected, it will chiefly belong to the superior to refer to the presbyter—whose authority among you is greater—whatever exceeds his measure or capacity.

These rules have indeed been given so that all things may be observed, and, if anything has been observed less perfectly, it ought quickly to be amended. For we cannot negligently pass over anything without peril to our souls. We have, moreover, vowed specifically to observe these things and sworn to live according to them. And the Psalmist says: “You have commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly” (Ps. 118). And the apostle James says: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2). [Col. 0920D] It will therefore belong to the superior and to him who is guardian of the order to refer to the presbyter who has greater authority—that is, to the abbot—whatever he cannot himself decide according to the canonical rule. But if, in a community where there is a canonical order, there is no abbot but a bishop, the bishop himself is designated by the name “presbyter.”

For this reason prelates have been established in the Church: that they may preserve what is well ordered, correct what has gone wrong, and shape the life and conduct of their subjects by word and example, following the model of the Apostle, who says: “Reprove, exhort, rebuke” (1 Tim. 4). They should vary their seasons, blending encouragements with terrors: [Col. 0921A] they ought to rebuke more harshly the undisciplined and restless; to exhort the obedient, gentle, and patient that they may advance toward what is better; and to rebuke or punish the negligent, contemptuous, and proud. Nor should they overlook the sins of offenders; but, as soon as they begin to arise, they should cut them off at the root as far as they are able, remembering the peril of Eli the priest on account of his sons. The more honourable and intelligent should be corrected by a first and second admonition; the wicked and hard-hearted, proud and disobedient, should be restrained by the rod and chastisement, recalling: “A fool is not corrected by words; strike your son with a rod, and you will deliver his soul from death” (Prov. 23).

But he who presides over you should not consider himself fortunate through the power of domination, but through the service of charity.

[Col. 0921B] For those who preside in such a way that they rejoice in the power of lordship are not true shepherds but hirelings. They desire rather to rule than to benefit; they seek not the fruit of souls but temporal gain, not heavenly glory but earthly honour. Of such persons the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6). But those who preside in such a way that they rejoice in the service of charity hold the example of the true Shepherd, who came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a redemption for many. Those are truly prelates and administer the charge of government according to God who labour only in order to draw more people with themselves to God; who take delight in burden rather than honour, charity rather than power, service rendered to others rather than service received from others. [Col. 0921C] As the Apostle says: “Though I was free in all things, I made myself the servant of all, that I might gain all” (1 Cor. 9). Yet, on account of the authority of governance, he ought to be honoured by his subjects. Hence it is added:

Let the superior be set before you in honour.

That is, he ought to be honoured because he holds Christ’s voice in the monastery. Therefore the Lord himself says to the shepherds: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10). God’s servants should therefore honour their master, whose authority they have accepted over themselves for the love of God. Yet, the more he is honoured outwardly, the more he ought to fear, and, despising himself, to place in his thoughts above himself those from whom honour is offered to him. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0921D] In fear before God, let him be laid beneath your feet.

Thus it is written: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Sir. 3). And again: “My son, they have made you their leader; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Sir. 32). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18). For each person is the greater before God the humbler he is in his own estimation. But let us hear what he ought to be in conduct.

Let him present himself to all as an example of good works.

For just as he surpasses them in honour, dignity, and rank, so he ought to go before them in holiness, so that his subjects may learn from his example how they ought to live.

[Col. 0922A] Rebuke the restless, comfort the faint-hearted, receive the weak, be patient toward all.

He who holds a place of governance ought not to inflict evils but to endure them, so that by his gentleness he may be able to soothe the angry. For the physician of souls ought to oppose the medicines of virtues to the passions of vices, first carefully investigating everyone’s conduct, so that he may know what he ought to apply to each person.

Let him gladly accept discipline, and impose it so as to be feared. And although both are necessary, let him desire rather to be loved by you than feared, always considering that he must render an account to God for you.

A teacher of the Church ought to be wise and disciplined, because he rightly imposes discipline on others only when he himself lives in a disciplined manner, when he draws from himself [Col. 0922B] the teaching which he exercises in another. These are the words of the Apostle speaking to the Hebrews: “Persevere in discipline: God offers himself to you as to sons. And what son is there whom his father does not correct?” (Heb. 12). These two things, however, are necessary for a ruler to show his subjects: fear, namely, to those who are proud, rebellious, and hard-minded; love, however, to those who gladly, humbly, and devoutly serve the Lord God.

And although both are necessary, let him desire rather to be loved by you than feared.

For the more a prelate is loved, the more he is heeded. And that service which is done from willingness and love is more pleasing to God than that which is done from fear. Therefore the gentle Master says to his disciples: “I shall [Col. 0922C] no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15). For the Lord does not wish us to fear him as a master, but wishes us to love him as children love a father, and to keep his commandments not from fear of punishment but from love of justice. He who is judge of souls must always consider this: that he has God as judge above himself, so that he may carry out the care of governance with as much solicitude as he reflects that he must render a stricter account for those entrusted to him before the severe Judge. Everyone ought to be very solicitous in good work, so that in all that he does he may always consider the final end. Hence it is written: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Sir. 7).

Therefore, by obeying all the more, have mercy not only on yourselves but also [Col. 0922D] on him, who, the higher the place in which he stands among you, is involved in the greater danger.

Whoever is raised to a place of governance is involved in great danger. For the higher the rank, the more dangerous the fall; and from him to whom more is entrusted, more is required. It is a great danger to live both for oneself and for others, and to provide at once for temporal and spiritual matters. He must care for himself in such a way as not to neglect others; think of others in such a way as not to abandon himself by forgetting himself; administer temporal things in such a way as not to grow cold toward spiritual things; and burn zealously for spiritual things in such a way as to remain solicitous about temporal matters. Therefore subjects ought to obey their prelate all the more because they see him labouring all the more for them. When they do this, they have mercy not only on themselves but also, by their greater obedience, [Col. 0923A] on him. They have mercy on themselves, of course, because they save their own souls. For it is written: “Have mercy on your soul by pleasing God” (Sir. 30). They also have mercy on him who presides, because they lighten his burden by obeying. For since it is written: “A wise son makes his father glad” (Prov. 10), spiritual fathers rejoice more and labour more freely for their children insofar as they see them obeying spiritual disciplines more faithfully.

May the Lord grant that you observe all these things as lovers of spiritual beauty, fragrant with the good odour of Christ through good conduct, established not as servants under the law but as children under grace.

Prayer is fittingly added after reading. For reading and preaching are like sowing a field; [Col. 0923B] praying is like covering the seed. Just as, if those who sow in a field neglect to cover it, birds come and carry off all that appeared to have been sown, so too those who scatter in the field of their heart the seeds of God’s word by psalmody, reading, and preaching: unless afterward, through prayer, they enclose and in a sense bury these seeds in the heart, birds come—that is, the fleeting, empty, and vain thoughts of this world—and snatch away what had been sown in the heart. Therefore, after reading and preaching, one must always pray, so that the power of God’s word may remain in the heart and spiritual fruit may grow in action. He says well:

As lovers of spiritual beauty.

For no one can fulfil all these rules except through love of justice, which is the spiritual beauty [Col. 0923C] of the soul. No one acts well unwillingly, even if what he does is good. What follows:

And fragrant with the good odour of Christ through good conduct,

belongs to both good life and good reputation. Hence the Apostle says: “We are the good odour of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2). Those are servants under the law who serve the Lord from fear; those free under grace fulfil the divine commandments from love. “The grace of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5): it fulfils the law. “The law is not laid down for the just person” (1 Tim. 1); “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3). We shall run freely in the way of God’s commandments if our heart is enlarged in the charity [Col. 0923D] of God.

## CHAPTER XII. ON CONSTANT MEDITATION UPON THE RULE

But so that you may be able [Col. 0924A] to examine yourselves in this little book as in a mirror, lest through forgetfulness you neglect anything, let it be read to you once each week.

It is commanded to be read so that it may be retained frequently in memory. For blessed James says: “Whoever looks into the law of perfect freedom and remains in it, not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work—this person shall be blessed in his deed” (Jas. 1). He rightly calls this little book a mirror, because in it we can examine, as in a mirror, what we are like: whether beautiful or ugly, just or unjust; whether any one of us lives according to the rule; whether he advances or declines; whether he pleases or displeases God. Sacred Scripture indeed presents to us our inward image: it shows what is beautiful and what is deformed in the soul; how the beauty of justice ought to be preserved; how [Col. 0924B] the adornment of virtues ought to be ordered; and how the stain of vices ought to be wiped away.

It is the habit of the wicked always to conceal evils and never to reconsider what they have done. Whatever they do, they pass over with a blind mind. On the contrary, holy men do not cease daily to examine their life in the sacred Scriptures and vigilantly to weigh their conduct. If they find anything deformed, disordered, or unarranged, they immediately endeavour to reform and arrange themselves according to what they see written, so that they may be found holy and without blemish before God both in body and soul. Therefore the Psalmist says: “Then I shall not be ashamed when I look upon all your commandments” (Ps. 118). And the Apostle exhorts, saying: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. 4). And again: “Our inward person is renewed from day to [Col. 0924C] day” (2 Cor. 4). Hence it is plainly added:

And when you find yourselves doing what is written, give thanks to God, the giver of all good things.

Thanksgiving is always owed by us to the Father of lights, from whom, as Scripture testifies, “every good gift and every perfect gift” descends (Jas. 1). No one is blessed through God’s gifts who is ungrateful to the Giver. And the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4). We are therefore rightly admonished to give thanks to the Lord our God, so that a person may recognize, if he lives well, that he has this by God’s grace, and that he will attain progress in the love of justice from no other source. This reflection makes one devout. For this is the wisdom called piety, by which the Father of lights is worshipped. He is worshipped by the sacrifice of praise and by thanksgivings, so that [Col. 0924D] his worshipper may glory not in himself but in the Lord.

But when any one of you sees that he lacks something, let him grieve over the past, take care for the future, praying that his debt may be forgiven and that he may not be led into temptation.

[Col. 0925]

## THESE ARE ITS CHAPTERS:

CHAPTER I. By what means knowledge of right living is found.—CHAPTER II. What ought to be done in every action.—CHAPTER III. What ought to be done in each place.—CHAPTER IV. What ought to be done at each time.—CHAPTER V. What ought to be done with regard to each person.—CHAPTER VI. How those who wish to advance through instruction ought to conduct themselves.—CHAPTER VII. On imitating the examples of the saints.—CHAPTER VIII. On the things to be observed in the sacred Scriptures.—CHAPTER IX. How a person ought to be circumspect in all his works.—CHAPTER X. What discipline is and how much it avails.—CHAPTER XI. On discipline to be observed in dress.—CHAPTER XII. On discipline to be observed in bearing.—CHAPTER XIII. On discipline to be observed in speech, and first, what ought to be said.—CHAPTER XIV. To whom one ought to speak.—CHAPTER XV. Where one ought to speak.—CHAPTER XVI. When one ought to be silent and when to speak.—CHAPTER XVII. How one ought to speak.—CHAPTER XVIII. On discipline at table, and first in dress and bearing.—CHAPTER XIX. On the threefold observance of discipline in food: and first, what ought to be eaten.—CHAPTER XX. Second, how much ought to be eaten.—CHAPTER XXI. Third, how one ought to eat.

## PROLOGUE. On the three things that lead to blessedness: knowledge, discipline, and goodness

[Col. 0925A]

Because, brothers, by the Lord’s generosity you have turned from the vain manner of life of this age through holy desire, and purpose to return with all the intention and desire of your mind to him who made you, you must now learn the very way by which you may reach him whom you seek. For he is the true and everlasting life: just as no one can live apart from him, so everyone who lives in him and with him is blessed. If, therefore, you seek God—or rather, because you seek him—you certainly desire to possess true and perpetual blessedness. But no one can come to blessedness except through virtue, and virtue is not [Col. 0925B] truly acquired in any other way unless the discipline of virtue is diligently maintained. For the practice of discipline directs the mind toward virtue, and virtue leads to blessedness. Accordingly, the exercise of discipline ought to be your beginning; virtue, your perfection; and the reward of virtue, eternal blessedness. This, brothers, is the way, and that is the homeland: the way along which we run and the homeland which we desire to reach.

The Psalmist had seen this way and this homeland when he said: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118). He had seen this way and this homeland when he said: “Your discipline corrected me unto the end” (Ps. 17). For God’s discipline corrects unto the end, because, fully and perfectly reforming the human being, it leads him through virtue to blessedness. [Col. 0925C] He had also then seen this way and this homeland when he said: “Teach me goodness and discipline and knowledge” (Ps. 118). For he considered that one comes to blessedness through goodness, and therefore asks to be taught goodness because he desired through it to attain that blessedness. But because he again saw that discipline was necessary in order to attain goodness, he added and said: “Teach me discipline.” For he was prepared to keep discipline, and he not only willingly offered himself for [Col. 0926A] keeping it, but also prayed that he might be worthy to receive it. Finally, because he saw that no one can observe the discipline of good work who does not possess the knowledge of true discernment, he also asked that this be given him as a kind of foundation and beginning of holy conduct: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge.”

And, to show himself fit to learn these things, he finally added: “Because I have believed your commandments” (ibid.), as though saying to God: “You ought to teach me how I should serve you, because I no longer resist your commands through obstinacy. I believe that what you command is good; I believe that what you promise is true. For your sake I have now consented to leave my own things; and therefore I ask that through you I may be worthy to obtain your good things, ‘because I have believed your commandments.’” So also you, brothers, have now believed his commandments through God’s grace; you have left your own things for his sake. Now seek his things from him, so that through his things you may be worthy to come to him.

[Col. 0926B] You have believed his commandment which says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19). You have done what he commanded; you hope for what he promised. Now ask from him what is needed to obtain it. No carnal affection now hinders you from receiving his grace: you have left father and mother, brothers and sisters, relatives and connections, and have girded yourselves to run his way. You place nothing before his love; you seek him alone, for the gaining of whom you regard all the blandishments of this world as bitter wormwood and all [Col. 0926C] glory and beauty as dung. Enter his way and run toward him: the sooner you reach him, the sooner you will have rest. The way to him is knowledge, discipline, and goodness: through knowledge one goes to discipline; through discipline one goes to goodness; through goodness one goes to blessedness. This is why we have begun to speak with you: that, insofar as the Lord grants, we may instruct you concerning this way by which one goes to him.

## CHAPTER I. By What Means Knowledge of Right Living Is Found

[Col. 0927A]

First, therefore, you ought to know that this knowledge—which pertains to the formation of right and honourable living—a person must gather and acquire for himself in many ways: partly by reason, partly by instruction, partly by example, partly by meditation on the sacred Scriptures, and partly by continual examination of his own works and conduct.

By reason, in this way: one ought carefully to consider and, insofar as one can, discern for oneself what is permitted and what is not permitted, what is fitting and what is not fitting, in every action, every place, every time, and with regard to every person.

## CHAPTER II. What Ought to Be Done in Every Action

In every action: that is, how sacred and divine [Col. 0927B] mysteries ought to be performed; how human duties and things pertaining to bodily use ought suitably to be carried out; how reverent, how careful, how devout and religious a person ought to show himself in God’s service; how willing, cheerful, and ready he ought to present himself in relieving his neighbours’ necessities; how sparing, honourable, and troublesome to no one he ought to be in seeking and accomplishing what pertains to himself—so that he may always be sparing toward himself, ready toward his neighbour, and devout toward God. One should learn to break one’s own will in all things and, in all things, to bend oneself to the wills of others, insofar as this is established to be lawful and fitting. What one ought to be like while sitting, lying down, walking, speaking, being silent, eating, fasting, finally, when doing something and when at leisure.

## CHAPTER III. What Ought to Be Done in Each Place

[Col. 0927C]

One must consider not only what one should do, but also what one should do in each place. There is one manner of conduct in the place where God is worshipped, another where the body is refreshed; one in a place appointed for speech, another where silence is observed; finally, one indoors, another outdoors; one in private, another in public. Although a person ought to abandon discipline in no place, yet it must be preserved more diligently and carefully where neglect produces scandal among more people, or observance provides an example for good imitation. One must therefore discern [Col. 0927D] which things are such that they can never be omitted in keeping discipline, and which, in turn, are such that they may at one time be omitted and at another exercised according to place and time. Yet things necessary in public often first require some practice in private, because, if we entirely neglect them in secret, we are afterward unable to use them in public when needed. Then we either fail altogether in discipline and give scandal to onlookers, or, trying ineptly to feign what is not in us, provoke ridicule.

## CHAPTER IV. What Ought to Be Done at Each Time

Likewise, the times for acting must be distinguished. One manner of life belongs to night, another to day. Night is the time of silence and rest; day the time of labour, [Col. 0928A] movement, and work. At night people ought to be by themselves, either refreshing their weary limbs with sleep or exercising their minds in silence through prayers or holy meditations. During the day, however, they come together from their private places, making themselves available to be seen and imitated by one another. Then it is permitted for each to give and receive from another examples of good works and exhortations of words. Then one who pries into another’s actions is rightly called shameless; then one who neglects to imitate another’s actions, insofar as is fitting, is deservedly called sluggish and useless.

Nor ought our appearance after we have eaten to be the same as it was before we took food. Before taking food, it is fitting that we be more cheerful, lest our very abstinence seem burdensome and unpleasant; afterward, however, more modest [Col. 0928B] and quiet, lest it be thought that through the vice of gluttony we have been inflamed with drunken excess. Before taking food is a time for instruction and prayer; afterward, for work: because the mind ought to be exercised while it is still light for spiritual study, and the flesh ought to be restrained when the heat of its incitement has been more strongly aroused by food.

Likewise, feast-days require one kind of study and manner of life, while other days on which work is permitted require another. On feast-days we ought to gather more eagerly and readily at church, attend more devoutly to the celebration of the divine mysteries, persevere longer in prayer, show greater devotion toward divine worship in dress, walk, and action; do nothing that is not holy, nothing that is not divine, nothing that is not orderly; restrain the tongue from idle speech, keep the feet from running about and wandering, lower the eyes, incline the face, raise the mind, devote every action and every movement alike of heart and body to the divine service, and, so to speak, honour feast-days by a certain renewal of conduct.

[Col. 0928C] On other days, however, when work is permitted, let no one at all appear idle; but each person ought to exercise himself in the work assigned to him—not that which he himself has chosen—according to the capacity of his knowledge and strength. For as much beauty as the repose of leisure adds to feast-days, so much ornament does the labour of work confer upon other days: so that whoever refuses to be at rest on feast-days is judge of his own vanity, while one who is not diligent on working days is a witness to his own sloth. For vanity agitates carnal minds lest they rest even on the former days, and sloth binds them lest they exercise themselves in good work on the latter. Therefore careful discernment of times must be maintained in good work, because, just as an evil work is praiseworthy at no time, so a good work is in a sense judged worthy of blame if it is not done at an opportune time.

## CHAPTER V. What Ought to Be Done with Regard to Each Person

The distinction among persons, insofar as it concerns love, must be made according to merit; but insofar as it concerns veneration, according to age and office. We ought to love the better and honour our superiors, because it is insolence both in one who despises virtue in a person because of an inferior rank, [Col. 0929A] and in one who despises a superior rank because of an inferior life. Therefore honour should be offered to the latter and love to the former, yet in such a way that honour for the latter is voluntary and love for the former reverent. For reverence without love is more servile, while love without reverence ought to be judged childish. We must thus render the benefit of love to better persons with such humility and reverence that we seem to be subject to them as though by necessity; and we must pay the service of submission to superiors with such affection and cheerfulness that we appear bound to them rather by the debt of love alone. To the latter let us render what is theirs as though we were bestowing our own; to the former let us offer what is ours as though rendering back what is theirs.

[Col. 0929B] Finally, we infer that the distinction among persons ought to be observed in six ways from these considerations: three according to rank and three according to manner of life. Some are superior in rank, others equal, others inferior. To superiors we ought to show obedience, fear, service, and veneration; with equals, preserve peace and harmony, outdo one another in service, kindness, and honour, and assign them a higher place in every deed and word. If perhaps we are compelled in some matter to go before them, we should, with all humility and reverence, not command what is to be done but indicate it; and if it happens that they go before us, we should obey with cheerfulness and devotion, as subjects by necessity.

[Col. 0929C] To inferiors we should always render kindness and assistance; never reproach them; correct without insult; govern without pride; punish without cruelty; cherish with mercy. We should not demand veneration, but love fellowship and equality; submit to those greater than ourselves through fear; serve equals through charity; become equal to those lesser than ourselves through humility; be ready toward those who command, modest toward those who obey, silent toward those who curse, and restrained toward those who praise.

Likewise, in respect of manner of life, we ought to regard some as though superior to us, others as though our equals, and others as though inferior to us. The manner of life of those whose deeds, although we do not presume to condemn them, we nevertheless ought not to imitate, is inferior to ours. The manner of life of those is equal to ours which is so adapted to our weakness that it both offers an example of virtue and, through the practicability of working together, admits us into fellowship in its exercise [Col. 0929D]. The manner of life of those is above us which we can indeed reverence and admire, but cannot imitate. The manner of life of those is superior to ours who, through a long exercise of discipline, have made such progress that, although our weakness begins to seek their virtue through love, it is nevertheless unable to equal it through imitation. The manner of life of those is, as it were, equal to ours whose works are so accommodated to our powers that in them there is nothing exceeding our capacity, and yet our devotion finds in them enough that it can imitate. The manner of life of those is, as it were, inferior to ours who either cannot do as much as we are able to do, or do such things as we ought not to imitate [Col. 0930A].

Accordingly, in these matters such discernment must be maintained that, toward those who are superior, we should endeavor to show reverence in every place and in every work or word, and whatever they do or wherever they may be, we should not presumptuously thrust ourselves upon them as though making ourselves their equals. For we ought in some manner silently and from afar to contemplate such an example of virtue for our imitation, yet never presume to seek partnership in working with them, so that, while everywhere yielding place to them, it may readily be clear from our modesty how humbly we think of ourselves and how highly of them.

But from the negligent, and especially from those whose deeds or pursuits appear worthy of reproof, we must withdraw with such caution that we flee what they do and yet do not presume to judge what they are [Col. 0930B]. Let us reflect, in the case of such persons, that neither an example is given to us nor judgment permitted us, because perhaps ignorance or weakness excuses in them what, if done by us, would have no excuse. Therefore, just as we do not presume, out of reverence, to seek the company of the perfect, so also we ought, out of caution, to avoid the company of these: honoring the former, because we are not worthy to be joined to such persons; avoiding the latter, because if joined to such persons we can easily be corrupted.

Moreover, just as one who always desires to associate with superiors shows himself to be proud, so one who constantly desires to live with worse persons shows himself to be depraved. Therefore, when we refuse to seek the company of the wicked, a double fruit of benefit comes to us [Col. 0930C]: we both flee guilt and bear witness to our innocence.

Our daily and frequent association, therefore, ought to be with those who are intermediate and our equals; and among them, whenever we see persons more fervent in good work, we should seek their company and familiarity more eagerly. With these we must take such care to preserve peace and concord that, in no matter whatsoever, so far as lies within us, brotherly love may be disturbed. Let us strive never to inflict injury or annoyance upon them, but to endure with an even mind, for love of brotherly charity, any injury inflicted upon us; to do nothing contentious or arrogant toward them; but always to be ready to yield, even to those who persist obstinately [Col. 0930D], in every work, and gladly to assist those who labor.

And because among equals there is sometimes a perverse kind of rivalry in virtue—namely, that they envy one another the success of their virtues and, therefore, in performing good work strive to outstrip one another merely lest they seem inferior—we must restrain ourselves with such moderation of discernment that, as has been said, we neither impose our help upon unwilling persons nor withhold it from those who ask it; for suspicion of envy may arise in either case. But if at any time we wish to bring assistance to persons laboring in some undertaking, this must be done with such humility and gentleness that they themselves may clearly see that we seek not superiority in the work, but partnership in the labor.

As for ourselves, however, we must strive most earnestly [Col. 0931A] never to be found less patient in toil, less eager in obedience to commands, or less fervent in carrying out works of charity, so that our good manner of life may offer an incentive to virtue to those from whom it has taken the pattern and example of good work. Brothers, if you are willing constantly to ponder these matters, you will quickly know and understand what is the way of discipline which leads you, through the exercise of good work, to the perfection of goodness. But even if you are perhaps not sufficiently able by yourselves to investigate and discern these matters as fully as is fitting, with the Lord’s help you will have instruction and examples of the good, where you will hear what ought to be done and see deeds that have been done. And lest the service of our exhortation be lacking to you in this matter also [Col. 0931B], I shall now briefly show what manner of persons you ought to present yourselves as, both for receiving instruction and for imitating the examples of the good.

## CHAPTER VI. What manner of persons those who wish to advance through instruction ought to be.

Since, therefore, you come to be trained in the school of virtues, you ought to know that disputes of words no longer concern you in any way, because the pursuit of spiritual instruction requires not disputants but listeners. Thus Moses says to the people being instructed in the law of God: “Hear, O Israel, and observe, that you may do” (Deut. VI); he did not say, “And speak,” but rather, “Be silent.” And as the apostle James warns: “Let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak and slow to anger” (Jas. I).

And observe how aptly, after forbidding excessive speech, he also added a command concerning the avoidance of anger, saying, “slow to speak and slow to anger,” so as clearly to show that one who will not restrain his tongue from excessive speech cannot long keep his mind unharmed from the fury of anger [Col. 0931C]. For excessive speech produces disputes; disputes incite the tongue to quarrels and revilings; revilings inflame the mind to anger and, what is still more serious, to brotherly hatred. Therefore Scripture says: “In excessive speech sin will not be lacking,” and, “In excessive speech you will not escape sin” (Prov. X). And the apostle James affirms that every kind of beast can be tamed, but that the tongue is an untamable pest, which sets ablaze the whole course of our nature; and that, for this reason, the man who does not offend in his speech is perfect (Jas. III).

For there is no doubt that strife and disputes always arise from a pestilential root: unless the heart first swelled inwardly through pride, the tongue would never outwardly relax itself from the restraint of humility into insulting speech. But while we proudly wish to seem wiser than others, we are ashamed either for our ignorance to be exposed by others or for another’s wisdom to be acknowledged as though to our own humiliation. Thus we sometimes, against our conscience, either shamelessly defend our own error or maliciously attack another’s truth. This is [Col. 0932A] the wisdom of this world, which the same apostle James calls carnal and demonic—cunning and malicious (ibid.)—seeking only those paths of craftiness by which it may conceal its own error and corrupt another’s truth, however manifest it may be, in the opinion of foolish and senseless people.

But such is not the wisdom which comes from above. It does not know how to love even itself against the truth; it is always ready either gladly to seek from those who possess it the good which it does not possess, or truthfully to accuse, with others and before others, the evil which it endures. Therefore the same apostle James says of it: “But the wisdom which is from above is first indeed chaste, then peaceable, modest, open to persuasion, consenting to good things, full of mercy and good fruits, judging without pretense” (ibid.). Therefore, dearest brothers, restrain your tongues not merely from a superfluity of empty words, but maintain measure and moderation even in things that are right; and in the conference of holy persons choose rather to be hearers than teachers. Keep your mouths closed and your ears open; and the more modest you are in speaking, the more discerning be in understanding.

Let it suffice you, if perhaps circumstances so require, humbly to communicate what you know to those who ask; but against those who resist, never presume obstinately to defend your words. For, as we have already told you, quarrels furnish causes of many troubles; and as soon as the tongue is indiscreetly loosened into excessive speech, a door is opened, as it were, to the enemy for disturbing the peace of your heart [Col. 0932C]. It remains, therefore, brothers, that if you truly desire to be disciples of truth, you should strive to show yourselves such persons as may readily be persuaded by truth. For the teaching of truth itself loves hearers who humbly receive it when it is presented by the wise and do not arrogantly despise it when administered even by simpler persons; who in the knowledge of God—that is, in the skill of acting well—consider all others more prudent and wiser than themselves; who are not ashamed to have as teachers all from whom they can learn what they do not know; who gladly approve the good sayings of everyone; and who, when they recognize that the errors of others concern them, endeavor according to circumstances either to correct them modestly or to overlook them prudently. Finally, such hearers adorn the pursuit of knowledge with discipline of character and demonstrate the gentleness and modesty of their minds not only by guarding their mouths, but also in the bearing and movement of their bodies [Col. 0932D].

And now I shall briefly, if I can, set forth a few words concerning the examples of the good which I judge ought presently to be spoken to you.

## CHAPTER VII. On imitating the examples of the saints.

Why do you think, brothers, that we are commanded to imitate the life and manner of life of the good, unless it is that through their imitation we may be reshaped into the likeness of the new life? For in them the form of the likeness of God is expressed; and therefore, when we are stamped with them through imitation, we too are fashioned into the image of that same likeness.

But it must be known that unless wax has first been softened, it does not receive an impression; so too a person is not bent to the form of virtue by the hand of another’s action unless first, through humility, he is softened from every rigidity of pride and contradiction [Col. 0933A]. Nor can one ever be reformed for the better through another’s example while, through the vice of pride, he attacks the good of others and defends his own evils. Therefore, if we truly wish to imitate the good, we must first dispose our hearts through true humility toward obedience, so that our life may return the more swiftly to newness the more readily it inclines itself, through voluntary obedience, toward every form of virtue that it sees; and so that the imprint of another’s goodness may begin to adhere to it the more deeply the more earnestly it endeavors to imitate the good of others rather than criticize it.

The form of a seal offers us still another consideration, not to be despised, for the present matter [Col. 0933B]. For the figure which projects outwardly upon the seal appears marked inwardly by the impression in the wax; and that which is shown carved inwardly on the seal is displayed as a figure outwardly in the wax. What else, then, is suggested to us by this, except that we who desire to be reshaped through the example of the good, as through a most finely carved seal, find in them certain lofty and, as it were, projecting traces of works, and certain lowly and, as it were, depressed traces?

Indeed, the works of saints which, in human estimation, pertain not to dignity but to usefulness lie, as it were, pressed downward in their manner of life. But when they perform such deeds as draw human minds to admiration of them, they display in themselves, as it were, certain projecting carvings [Col. 0933C]. Therefore what projects in them ought to be stored inwardly in us, and what is depressed in them ought to be raised up in us. For when we take their deeds for imitation, we ought to perform the lofty things in secret and the lowly things openly, lest the former, if displayed, begin through love of popular favor to serve empty glory, or the latter, if concealed through fear of lowliness, lose the reward of recompense.

I do not know what excuse of ignorance a person can henceforth have, when so many ways are already shown to him by which he may attain knowledge of the truth. Behold: after the discernment of his own reason, by which he is directed; after the teaching of the wise, by which he is instructed; after the examples of the good [Col. 0933D], by which he is trained; the commandments of the Scriptures are added, by which he is formed for every manner of life. Finally, temptations are added, through which, trained by daily experience, he is made more certain of the truth of the commandments.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the matters to be attended to in the sacred Scriptures.

But you, brothers, who have now entered the school of discipline, ought first in divine reading to seek what forms character toward virtue rather than what sharpens the intellect toward subtlety; and you should prefer to be formed by the commandments of Scripture rather than to be hindered by questions. When, therefore, you read the divine Scriptures, carefully weigh what is said there to kindle in you love of God [Col. 0934A], what is effective for contempt of the world, for avoiding the snares of the enemy, for nourishing good affections and extinguishing petty desires, and what most quickly kindles the heart through the ardor of compunction. Consider what teaches discipline in action, humility in thought, and patience in adversity; what, finally, teaches a person to be confident in doing good and watchful in avoiding evil. Scripture read in this way imparts saving understanding; and this wisdom itself—which you willingly despise for the sake of virtue—you afterwards find more fully through virtue.

## CHAPTER IX. How a person ought to be watchful in all his works.

There remains this final point, and perhaps the most necessary of all [Col. 0934B]: namely, that a person should be watchful and provident in all his works, examining within himself by daily scrutiny his thoughts, words, and deeds alike. For the wise always learn by acting, and through the exercise of good works grow by daily advances into a greater knowledge of virtue. Through experience of what they do, they become more cautious concerning what must afterwards be done.

For a person sees that a work which is believed to have begun with a good intention often casts him all the more swiftly into the snare of deception because, secure concerning the beginning of his intention, he pays less heed to the end of the action; and, imprudently, he runs as if along a level path into a pit, because he sees what he is doing but does not attend to what ought to follow from what he has done [Col. 0934C]. Likewise, he does not consider that it sometimes happens that the affection of the mind is so ambiguous that a person cannot discern the quality of his intention except from the end of the work. But if he carefully considers toward what end the inclination of his mind tends, then he plainly recognizes as a vice that in which his mind had previously flattered itself falsely as virtue.

Again, there is another reason why watchfulness is necessary for a person everywhere: namely, because a person becomes more skillful even in doing what is good the more diligently, surveying his own deeds, he strives daily to surpass himself in progress. He carefully considers what he does, what he ought to do, whether he does what must be done; whether he does it to the required extent and in the required way [Col. 0934D]; whether he mixes some evil with a good work; whether he carries out the good he does with the devotion it requires; whether he loves another’s good as his own; and whether he rebukes his own evil as another’s.

Each day he calls his life to judgment. In the morning, when he ought to rise, he considers what he did during the night; in the evening, when he goes to bed, he considers what he did during the day: how much more eager than usual he has been in doing good, and how much more steadfast than usual in overcoming evil. If he has presumed to do any of those things which ought not to have been done, or if he has been tripped up by the snares of the enemy in any work of his, he considers how, through recognition of the deception that has passed, he may avoid that enemy’s future fraud; so that neither a temptation that comes upon him may cast him down unprepared into an evil deed [Col. 0935A], nor present negligence deceive him, lacking discernment, in a good work.

Whoever exercises his heart in such a pursuit, I think, will quickly attain that good and saving knowledge which, as we said above, the psalmist asked might be given him for preserving discipline and goodness. It remains, therefore, that we should also set forth the matters concerning discipline which must be shown to us. We shall teach you first what discipline is; then what it accomplishes; and finally how it ought to be observed.

## CHAPTER X. What discipline is, and how great its power is.

Discipline is a good and honorable manner of life, for which it is too little merely not to do evil; it also strives to appear blameless in every respect even in those things which it does well. Again, discipline is the ordered movement of all the members and a fitting arrangement in every bearing and action [Col. 0935B].

You have heard what discipline is; now consider how useful and how necessary it is. Discipline is the restraint of desire, the prison of evil longings, the bridle of wantonness, the yoke of pride, the bond of anger. It tames intemperance, binds fickleness, and stifles all disordered movements of the mind and unlawful appetites.
