For just as disordered bodily motion is born from instability of mind, so, too, when the body is held in restraint through discipline, the mind is strengthened toward constancy. And little by little the mind is inwardly composed toward quiet, when, through the observance of discipline, its evil movements are not allowed to flow outward.

Therefore integrity of virtue exists when, through the inward guarding of the mind, the limbs of the body are governed in an ordered manner [Col. 0935C]. For it is the inner guard that keeps the bodily limbs outwardly ordered. But one who loses the stability of mind subsequently flows outward into instability of movement and, by outward mobility, shows that he stands upon no inward root. Hence Solomon says: “A faithless man, a useless man, walks with a perverse mouth; he winks with his eyes, scrapes with his foot, speaks with his finger, devises evil with a perverse heart, and at every time sows quarrels” (Prov. VI).

For this reason he first called such a one—whom he wished to characterize both by lack of discipline and by discord—“faithless” or “apostate,” because unless he had first fallen inwardly from the sight of his Creator through a turning away of mind, he would not afterwards have come outwardly to instability and the sowing of quarrels. Therefore the bodily members must be bound outwardly by discipline, so that the state of the mind may be made firm inwardly; thus, while outward restraint is set on every side against inner mobility that must be checked, the mind may at last be gathered into peace within itself [Col. 0935D].

For discipline restrains the movements of all vices; and in proportion as it suppresses evil desires by restraining them outwardly, good desire is strengthened inwardly through it. And little by little the same form of virtue is impressed upon the mind through habit which is preserved outwardly in the bearing of the body through discipline. Behold, we have seen how great the power of discipline is; let us now consider how it ought to be preserved. Discipline is especially to be observed in four things: in clothing, in gesture, in speech, and at table—that is, in eating.

## CHAPTER XI. On preserving discipline in clothing.

[Col. 0936A]

In clothing, discipline is preserved in five ways: in kind, quality, color, cut, and arrangement of garments. In kind: namely, that our garments should not be excessively costly. In quality: that they should not be excessively fine or soft. In color: that they should not be excessively bright, or darkened beyond what the purpose of a religious manner of life requires in any other way. In cut: that they should be composed decently and religiously and bear the mark of humility; that is, neither excessively large, hanging down, or flowing, nor excessively tight, nor distorted in any other manner according to worldly vanity. Arrangement concerns the manner of wearing them. For there are certain foolish persons who, desiring to please fools, arrange their garments about themselves with a kind of artifice [Col. 0936B]. Others, with greater buffoonery, absurdly turn them about; others spread them out and extend them as broadly as possible in order to make a display of themselves. Some rashly gather their crumpled garments into one mass; others twist and fold them about themselves. Others, straining and splitting them with all their effort, expose to the gaze of onlookers, to be counted, every contour of their bodies in a most shameless kind of indecency. Others, tossing and fluttering their rags, reveal the frivolity of their minds through the very mobility of their clothing. Others, walking in trailing robes, sweep the ground; and with hanging borders—or rather tails trailing behind them like foxes—they cover up their own footprints.

Quite rightly, indeed: so that after they have passed, their memory may perish and they may no longer remain in remembrance in the land of the living [Col. 0936C]. In order to show themselves to belong to the number of those of whom the Psalmist says, “Not so the wicked, not so; but like dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth” (Ps. I), wherever they go they stir up dust like a tempestuous whirlwind. And they themselves, children of darkness, take away from the eyes of human beings that light outwardly which they have lost inwardly through a blinded mind.

Yet there is one respect in which we take vengeance upon them even in the present life: with the same rags by which they cast a cloud of dust before our eyes, they wipe the mud of the streets in order to level the road for our feet. What more shall I say? I am weary of enumerating all the displays of vanity in which fools and senseless persons take their fashions from women—indeed, from prostitutes—and, with as much disgrace as superstition, have almost changed their sex by their clothing [Col. 0936D]. There are a thousand other ways by which utterly vain and superstitious people desire to offer themselves as a spectacle to those who look on.

But the servant of God ought to despise all these things with great constancy, since he sees that none but fools and persons worthy of ridicule devote themselves to such pursuits. For all these things are contrary to true religion, and plainly show how alien from religion are all who devote attention and care to them. But, by God’s grace, all who are now established in religion and pursue such things, wishing through them to please people, become more contemptible and despicable to all people. Conversely, those who despise these things for God’s sake are considered not only dearer and more honorable before God, but also before people [Col. 0937A].

Let miserable and foolish persons, then, ignorant of every kind of honor, go and groom their rags—those who do not understand how justly the ornamentation of costly garments is censured in men professing a religious life, when it is forbidden even to women through the apostle Paul: “not in costly apparel” (1 Tim. II). Let them see, therefore, how great—not merely a censure, but a shame; indeed, rather, how great a condemnation—they deserve who, in a religious profession, devote themselves to the adornment of costly clothing. For that rich man who in the Gospel is clothed in purple and fine linen is afterwards buried, to be eternally tormented in the torments of hell (Luke XVI).

But what is censured in purple except color and price, and what in fine linen except softness? Therefore, when he is said to have given his flesh both adornment in purple and softness in fine linen, he is proved beyond doubt to have been at once proud and luxurious [Col. 0937B]. Thus he who first unlawfully supplied his body with incentives to vices rightly afterwards received it for torment by the flame of punishment. Yet this rich man had not as yet renounced his own possessions; but because he would not preserve moderation in what he possessed, after his unlawful use of temporal things he came to everlasting punishment. If, therefore, he merited so great a condemnation because he abused what was his own, what do we think those persons will do who, possessing nothing of their own, do not fear to expend another’s alms upon the adornment of their own pride?

“Woe to them, because they,” as the prophet says, “eat the sins of the people” (Hos. IV), “and turn sacrifices aside into the deep” (Hos. V): because what others offer for the redemption of their souls, these persons receive and, through unlawful use, turn to the condemnation of their own souls. “Woe to the crown of Ephraim’s pride and to the falling flower” (Isa. XXVIII), because “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass has dried up and the flower has fallen, because the spirit of the Lord’s wrath has blown upon it. The grass has dried up and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord remains for ever” (Isa. XL).

Why, then, does ash and dust take pride (Ecclus. X), fleeting smoke and vapor appearing for a little while? (Jas. IV). What is a human being but decay, and the son of man but a worm? A worm himself, and worms his inheritance [Col. 0937C–D], for a human being will inherit worms, beasts, and serpents (Ecclus. X). However much it may be adorned and embellished, what else is flesh but flesh? What profit, then, is there in seeking glory in clothing that clings outwardly for a time, while failing to consider the rottenness of corruption which is within us and remains always?

Therefore lovers of religion ought to demonstrate by their works how greatly they despise earthly things. They should not embellish dying flesh with superstitious adornment, but prefer the ornaments of character to the pomp of garments. They should love garments more cheap than costly, more coarse than fine, more rough than soft, more dark than bright, and more negligently than carefully arranged or fitted; so that, if they cannot cut off every comfort in their clothing [Col. 0938A], they may nevertheless never presume to use it for display.

Perhaps these matters might have sufficed to teach modesty and humility to persons of good will; but I know that hard and rebellious minds do not easily turn aside from the way of their former error unless they are checked in these matters by sharper bits. Such persons must be tightly constrained in every observance, even to the smallest detail; and, lest evasion be left any occasion for deviation, they must be bound at every step by definite commands.

## CHAPTER XII. On preserving discipline in gesture.

Gesture is the movement and disposition of the bodily members in every manner of acting and bearing oneself. It is found blameworthy in six ways: namely, if it is soft, lax, slow, hasty, insolent, or disturbed [Col. 0938B]. Softness signifies wantonness; laxness, negligence; slowness, idleness; haste, instability; insolence, pride; disturbance, anger.

For it has already been shown above that disordered bodily movements indicate corruption and dissolution of the mind, where, on Solomon’s testimony, we showed the faithless or apostate man outwardly expressing the turning away of his soul through external signs. For he says: “A faithless man, a useless man, walks with a perverse mouth; he winks with his eyes, scrapes with his foot, speaks with his finger” (Prov. VI). That is, when the mind is inwardly released from self-guarding, the limbs are outwardly stirred in a disorderly fashion to every act. And just as the body of a paralytic retains its shape but cannot preserve the functions of its limbs in their actions [Col. 0938C], so such a person is driven headlong by impatience and fluctuation of mind toward any object whatever, but in all that he does is governed by no moderation of reason.

But it must be known that among these faulty gestures some seem in a certain way similar to one another; and just as the vices from which they arise do not differ greatly among themselves, so these outward motions likewise maintain a certain mutual affinity of perversity. Thus the soft and the insolent gesture are alike; so are the lax and the slow, and the hasty and the disturbed. For the vices themselves are alike: wantonness and boastfulness, negligence and idleness, restlessness and impatience. Therefore all these disordered gestures, because they proceed from the inner corruptions of the soul, are found severely attacked and censured in many passages of Scripture [Col. 0938D]. Although we cannot enumerate them one by one, nevertheless, lest we appear to exaggerate such a matter for no reason, we shall review a few of them by way of example.

Concerning soft and insolent gesture, the Lord rebukes wantonness and an arrogant soul through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “Come down; sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit upon the ground: there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans, because you shall no longer be called soft and tender. Take the millstone, grind meal; uncover your shame, bare the shoulder, uncover the legs, cross the rivers” (Isa. XLVII). And shortly afterwards: “Sit silent; enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans, because you shall no longer be called lady of kingdoms” (ibid.).

Therefore she who is commanded to come down is rebuked for insolent gesture and the mark of arrogance. Hence it is aptly added [Col. 0939A], “there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans,” because a person is often held in greater contempt by others in proportion as he exalts himself more through the swelling of arrogance, so that the saying of Truth may be fulfilled: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke XIV). This is further stated when it says: “Sit silent; enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans, because you shall no longer be called lady of kingdoms” (Isa. XLVII). For great shame then follows a person when he sees himself despised by others precisely in the matter in which he himself boasts.

But because wantonness and softness are companions of insolent and proud persons, after rebuking arrogance he also attacks wantonness when he adds: “Take the millstone, grind meal; uncover your shame, bare the shoulder, uncover the legs, cross the rivers [Col. 0939B], because you shall no longer be called soft and tender” (ibid.). How hateful, therefore, wantonness and insolence are to God is plainly shown by the fact that Scripture threatens, with so severe a judgment, humiliation to the arrogant and harshness to the soft.

Again, through the same Isaiah it is said against the wanton and insolent: “Thus says the Lord: Because the daughters of Zion have been lifted up, and have walked with outstretched necks, and went with gestures of their eyes and clapped as they went, walking and advancing with a studied step of their feet, the Lord will make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion” (Isa. III). “They walked with outstretched necks and gestures of their eyes”: here arrogance is marked. “They went and clapped as they went, walking and advancing with a studied step of their feet”: here wantonness is marked. It follows [Col. 0939C]: “The Lord will make bald the daughters of Zion”: this is the punishment of the arrogant. “And the Lord will uncover their hair”: this is the punishment of the wanton.

And because the luxury of costly garments usually follows these vices, its punishment is also added when it says: “On that day the Lord will take away the ornament of their footwear, and the crescents, necklaces, chains, bracelets, turbans, hair-bands, anklets, little necklaces, perfume-vessels, earrings, rings, gems hanging upon the forehead, changes of clothing, cloaks, linen garments, pins, mirrors, fine linen, headbands, and thin garments; and instead of sweet fragrance there shall be stench; instead of a belt, a rope; instead of curled hair, baldness; instead of a breast-band, sackcloth” (ibid.). Behold how carefully he enumerates every insignia of vanity, in order to show how strictly these things, in which people think there is no fault or only a very slight one, are weighed by God [Col. 0939D].

Solomon rebukes the lax and the slow, saying: “I passed by the field of a lazy man and by the vineyard of a foolish man; and behold, nettles had filled it all, thorns had covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed. When I saw this, I laid it up in my heart, and by the example I learned discipline” (Prov. XXIV). “How long will you sleep, O lazy one? How long will you not rise from sleep?” (Prov. VI). “You will sleep a little, doze a little, fold your hands a little to rest, and your poverty will come like a runner, and your need like an armed man” (Prov. XXIV).

And again: “Go to the ant, O lazy one, and consider her ways and learn prudence; for though she has neither guide, instructor, nor ruler [Col. 0940A], she prepares her food for herself in summer and gathers what she may eat in winter” (Prov. VI). Again, concerning the lazy person: “As vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the lazy person to those who sent him” (Prov. X). And concerning the lax person: “The hand of the strong shall rule, but that which is slack shall serve under tribute” (Prov. XII). And again concerning the lazy person: “The lazy person both wishes and does not wish, but the soul of workers shall grow fat” (Prov. XIII). Again, concerning the lax person: “He who is soft and lax in his work is the brother of one who destroys his own works” (Prov. XVIII). Again, concerning the lazy person: “The lazy person hides his hand beneath his armpit, and is weary if he must bring it to his mouth” (Prov. XIX). Again: “Desires kill the lazy person, for his hands refused to do anything” (Prov. XXI). And again: “The lazy person says: ‘There is a lion in the road; I shall be killed in the midst of the streets’” (Prov. XXII). Again: “As a door turns on its hinge, so the lazy person turns in bed” (Prov. XXVI).

And in the book of Ecclesiasticus it is said concerning the lazy, slow, and lax person: “The lazy person shall be stoned with a muddy stone, and all shall speak of his contempt. The lazy person shall be stoned with the dung of oxen, and everyone who touches him shall shake off his hands” (Ecclus. XXII) [Col. 0940B]. There are many other things, if I wished to enumerate them, which are said in the Scriptures for the rebuke or mockery of such persons; but for the present exhortation these things that have been said to you may suffice.

A hurried, restless, and turbulent manner is again rebuked by Solomon, where, as we have already shown in the preceding example, it is said of the apostate man: “A faithless man, a worthless man, walks [Col. 0940C] with a perverse mouth; he signals with his eyes, scuffs with his foot, speaks with his finger, devises evil with a wicked heart, and at all times sows quarrels” (Prov. 6). His destruction will come upon him suddenly, and he will have no remedy thereafter. How near he is to destruction he sufficiently shows by his own conduct: through the vice of restlessness he loses peace within himself even before he finds anything resisting him from without. And how headlong he will be precipitated, should he find an occasion for anger, is plain, since his own inward frivolity and impatience sweep him precipitately into rage when nothing external disturbs him.

Thus, fittingly, after Solomon had enumerated the signs of inconstancy and frivolity, saying, “He signals with his eyes, speaks with his finger, scuffs with his foot,” he finally expressed the mark of rage, saying, “At all times he sows quarrels” [Col. 0940D]. For, as has been said, first peace and inward tranquillity are broken up by the vice of frivolity and restlessness; then the agitated mind is cast down into the pit of rage. Although the very words, “He walks with a perverse mouth, signals with his eyes, scuffs with his foot, speaks with his finger,” are signs both of rage and of restlessness, nevertheless this is usually the order of destruction: first, through restlessness, a person abandons the steadiness of seriousness; and so at last breaks forth into the impatience of rage.

This manner—namely, hurried or restless—also has an affinity with the soft and brazen manner, because frivolity sometimes denotes wantonness and sometimes impatience. The restless manner agrees with the wanton and brazen, as Solomon says:

“From the window of my house I looked through the lattice, and I see the simple youths; I observe a foolish young man, who passes through the streets near a corner and walks close to the way of a strange woman’s house, in the dark, as evening approaches, amid the darkness and gloom of night. And behold, a woman meets him in the dress of a harlot, prepared to ensnare souls; talkative and wandering, impatient of quiet, unable to keep her feet at home. Now outside, now in the streets, now lying in wait near the corners; and, having seized the young man, she kisses him and flatters him with a brazen countenance” (Prov. 7) [Col. 0941A].

“At once he follows her, like an ox led to sacrifice, and like a wanton lamb, unknowing; nor does he know that the fool is being dragged to bonds, until an arrow pierces his liver; like a bird hurrying into a snare, not knowing that its life is in danger. Her house is the way to hell, penetrating the inner chambers of death” (ibid.).

Therefore let no one henceforth [Col. 0941B] think that those who, contrary to discipline, bend their limbs into shameful motions and disorderly gesticulations depart only slightly from it. Scripture would never rebuke these outward movements of the body in us so severely unless every dishonourable posture and indecent movement of the outward person flowed from the inward corruption of the mind. Discipline is therefore of great value for restraining the evil motions of the soul, so that evil desires, when they are held fast by the guard of discipline and prevented from flowing outward, may eventually become altogether unaccustomed even to arise and move inwardly.

Since, then, we have described the vices of gesticulation, order requires that we now define what measure of discipline should govern every gesture. Even if perhaps we cannot do so in every particular [Col. 0941C], it is still more expedient to say something for instruction than to remain wholly silent.

First, then, it must be carefully observed that each member keep its own function and not usurp another’s; next, that each one perform its own work so becomingly and modestly that, through lack of discipline, it does not offend the eyes of those who look on. For in either case there is fault worthy of rebuke: whether the members confuse their actions with one another, or whether they do not properly carry out what they ought rightly to do.

A distinction of actions must be preserved among the members: each member should perform the act for which it was made, so that the hand does not speak, the mouth does not hear, and the eye does not assume the office of the tongue. For there are some who do not know how to listen unless their cheeks stand open; as though sensation ought to flow through the mouth into the heart, they open their palate to the speaker’s words. Others—what is worse still—when acting or listening, thrust out their tongues like thirsty dogs, and at every action twist and roll their lips as though they were a millstone. Others, while speaking, extend a finger, raise their eyebrows, and roll their eyes in a circle, or fix them as if in some profound contemplation, displaying pretensions to some inward magnificence. Others toss their heads, shake out their hair, arrange and adjust their clothes, lean upon their sides with their elbows, and stretch out their feet, forming a quite ridiculous display [Col. 0941D]. Others, as if both ears had not been made for hearing, turn their necks and oppose only one ear to the approaching voice. Others, fashioning some sort of pose, close one eye while looking and open the other. Others, more ridiculously still, speak with half their mouths.

Moreover there are a thousand grimaces, a thousand sneers and wrinklings of the nose, a thousand distortions and contortions of the lips, which deform both the beauty of the face and the comeliness of discipline. For the face is the mirror of discipline; it requires the greater watchfulness because a fault in it can be concealed the less. The face must therefore be regulated and mortified in its gestures, so that it is neither insolently harsh nor softly relaxed, but always possesses a stern sweetness and a sweet severity.

Others walk by rowing with their arms and, by a double monstrosity, at one and the same time walk downward upon the earth with their feet and fly upward through the air with their arms [Col. 0942B]. What sort of monster, I ask, is this, which fashions in itself at once a human gait, the rowing of a ship, and the flight of a bird? One is tempted to cry out here in the words of that poetic satire:

> If a painter chose to join a horse’s neck  
> to a human head, and to spread diverse feathers  
> over limbs assembled from every quarter, so that a woman,  
> beautiful above, ended foully in a black fish.  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry*, vv. 1–5)

Certainly this pattern of monstrous figuration seems to me like this:

> ... such vain shapes as a sick man’s dreams  
> will fashion, so that neither foot nor head  
> can be restored to a single form.  
> (ibid., vv. 7–10) [Col. 0942C]

But lest we seem to be producing satire rather than instruction—since much still remains to be enumerated—we must not forget modesty here either. Perhaps even by silence we shall better show the negligent and undisciplined how greatly they ought themselves to blush for such things.

Yet they should know that there is one vice which first inwardly destroys the stability of the mind and afterward outwardly disturbs the order of action in the members. This is proved by the testimony of Solomon already so often mentioned, where in the apostate man a turning-away and dissipation of mind is said first to have preceded, and thereafter confusion and disturbance of action to have followed. For in the words, “A faithless man, a worthless man” (Prov. 6), dissipation of mind is denoted; but in the words, “He walks with a perverse mouth, scuffs with his foot, signals with his eyes, speaks with his finger” (ibid.) [Col. 0942D], confusion of action is shown.

Hence also comes what is said in the book of Ecclesiasticus: “A man is known by his appearance, and a prudent man is known by the meeting of his face. A person’s clothing, the laughter of his teeth, and his manner of walking tell of him” (Ecclus. 19). For by that which is done outwardly, whether well or ill, the inward quality of the soul is plainly shown to the eyes of observers.

And therefore, to calm this disturbance, the guard of discipline must be applied, restraining each member to its own office, so that while one member acts, another either remains altogether still or, if its service is found necessary to the former, moves in its own proper motion to cooperate decently and orderly [Col. 0943A]. Thus nothing is done confusedly or perversely among the bodily members; rather, each should know in what it ought to assist another and in what it ought to preserve itself at rest while another moves.

For the human body is like a kind of commonwealth, in which particular offices are allotted to the several members. When one member disorderly claims the office of another, what does it do but disturb the harmony of the whole? And when one impedes another’s movement by its own movement, it certainly resists that arrangement which nature governs.

The first safeguard of discipline in gesture, therefore, is that every member confine itself to the office for which it was created and not confuse another member’s service through its own interference [Col. 0943B]: that the eyes see, the ears hear, the nostrils smell, the mouth speak, the hands work, and the feet walk; so that the offices of the members are neither exchanged nor disorderly mixed.

The second safeguard of discipline in gesture is that each member do what it does in the manner and measure in which it ought to be done: neither more nor less, nor otherwise than is proper. Thus in its action it should be directed and moved so as never in any respect to exceed the boundary of moderation or the form of propriety. That is: to laugh without opening the teeth; to look without fixing the eyes; to speak without extending the hands and pointing with the fingers, without twisting the lips, tossing the head, or raising the eyebrows; to walk without affectation in one’s steps or gesticulation of the shoulders; to sit without spreading the legs apart, crossing one foot over the other, stretching or shaking the shins, or alternately leaning on either side; to lie down without flinging the limbs apart [Col. 0943C].

And, to bring our discussion of this matter to an end: a person’s manner in every action ought to be graceful without softness, composed without slackness, serious without slowness, lively without restlessness, mature without insolence, and severe without turbulence. A turbulent manner corrects a soft one, and a soft one a turbulent; a brazen manner corrects a slack one, and a slack manner a brazen; a hurried manner a slow one, and a slow manner a hurried one. For between contrary vices, virtue is the middle boundary.

Let what has been said concerning gesture suffice for the present instruction. But if any are so hard of heart that they cannot be formed by these admonitions [Col. 0943D], they ought to be urged by sharper goads, so that they may do unwillingly what they refuse to do willingly. For I know how difficult it is to bend a heart hardened by malice into the form of discipline and the appearance of propriety; but when hard material is not easily bent into shape, it is necessary to apply both the burning of a fiercer flame and the blows of a heavier hammer.

## Chapter XIII. On maintaining discipline in speech; and first, what ought to be said

In speech five things must be observed: what is said, to whom it is said, where it is said, when it is said, and how it is said. What ought to be said is first distinguished by this general rule: idle words must never be used in disciplined speech [Col. 0944A]. Idle words are all those which are harmful, dishonourable, or useless.

Useless words are those which benefit neither speaker nor hearer. Dishonourable words are those unfitting for the dignity either of the speaker, the hearer, or the person spoken about. Harmful words are those which by their persuasions lead their hearers either into error or into wickedness.

These three kinds—harmful, dishonourable, and useless—may be distinguished in two ways: according to the nature of the matters about which speech is made, and according to the qualities of the persons through whom, to whom, or about whom speech is made. The qualities of persons are considered in four ways: according to age, knowledge, office, and condition.

According to age, because one kind of speech suits old people and another young people. According to knowledge, because one kind suits the wise and another the simple. According to office, because one kind suits those who transact external affairs and another those who devote themselves to the repose of a more secluded life and to the study of contemplation. According to condition and rank, because one kind suits prelates and another subjects [Col. 0944B].

Old people ought to speak about the discernment required for giving sound counsel; young people, about diligence in doing good; wise people, about the mysteries of Scripture; simple people, about examples of good works. Those who manage outward affairs, about the skill of acquiring; those who lead a quiet life, about the discipline of living. Prelates, about the provision of necessities; subjects, about obedience to commands. And everyone who speaks should, according to the quality of his own person, seek a fitting subject about which to speak.

## Chapter XIV. To whom one ought to speak

It follows that, after a person has chosen what to say, he must also carefully consider to whom he should say it. For, as a certain wise man says: “He who tells a word to one who does not listen is like one who rouses a sleeper from heavy sleep” (Ecclus. 22). And again: “Do not speak much with a fool, and do not go with an insensible person” (ibid.).

And Solomon says: “He who rebukes the wicked begets a stain for himself. Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you. Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you. Give an opportunity to a wise man, and wisdom will be added to him. Teach a just man, and he will hasten to receive it” (Prov. 9) [Col. 0944D].

But again, in the book of Ecclesiasticus, concerning discernment in speaking, it is said: “Speak of holiness with an irreligious man, and of justice with an unjust man; with a woman, of the things she envies; with a coward, of war; with a merchant, of a voyage; with a buyer, of selling; with an envious man, of giving thanks; with an ungodly man, of piety; with a dishonourable man, of honour; with a farm worker, of every kind of work; with an annual hireling, of finishing the year; with a lazy servant, of much labour” (Ecclus. 37).

This makes it clear that the good ought sometimes to seek and sometimes to avoid conversation with the wicked. The good should seek such conversation when they hope to correct the wicked by their exhortation and trust sufficiently in their own steadfastness not to fear being corrupted by the wicked person’s evil suggestion [Col. 0945A]. But when they consider both the other’s hardness and their own weakness, it is expedient for them to flee, lest, while unable to correct the other by their admonitions, they themselves begin gradually to incline toward that person’s wickedness.

Therefore, when we speak for our own edification, let us speak with those whose teaching can instruct us in virtue. But when we speak for the edification of our neighbour, let us speak with those whom we hope to amend from their wickedness through our exhortation. Otherwise, to wish to teach the wise is pride, and to rebuke the obstinate is folly. For one who does not show reverence to a better person wrongs his neighbour; and one who does not reform a fool’s madness but provokes it against himself wrongs himself.

Therefore, whoever speaks with another should first consider whether he speaks for his own sake or for the other’s. If he speaks for his own benefit, he should see that the other is such a person that benefit may come to him from conversation with that person. If he speaks for the other’s sake, he should take care that the other is not someone who either has no need of his exhortation or is so obstinate in evil that he will not allow himself to be corrected by another’s exhortation [Col. 0945B].

If this is so, we ought never to speak except for our own instruction or that of others; and in speech itself we must preserve such discernment that we always strive to learn from the wiser and to instruct the less learned—provided, of course, that they permit themselves to be taught.

And as in asking questions we speak especially of what presses us most, so in teaching we must bring forward what best suits the person of the hearer, so that we may apply the appropriate remedy of our speech against the vice which we wish to heal in that person. Thus, as was said above, one ought to speak with the irreligious about holiness, with the unjust about justice, and with the lazy about much labour.

We easily recognize, then, to whom one should speak if we carefully consider the nature of what is said. For that which most suitably offers a remedy to cure the evil in which each person labours most ought especially to be said to that person [Col. 0945C].

For example, when we wish to praise steadfastness, we ought to direct our speech to the fainthearted, not to the proud. Since the vice of pride sometimes conceals itself under the pretext of steadfastness, if we begin to praise steadfastness to the proud, we confirm them more deeply in their vice while believing that we exhort them to virtue.

Let us therefore exhort the timid to steadfastness; the proud to fear; the prodigal to frugality; the avaricious to liberality; the stingy to humanity; the gluttonous to thrift; the rash to counsel; the lukewarm to fervour of zeal; the talkative to silence; those too silent to exhorting speech; the sluggish to eagerness; the impatient to gentleness; the negligent to justice; the cruel to indulgence; the brazen to modest shame; the hasty to calm; the incautious to prudence; the forgetful to attentiveness; and the shameless to modesty. In short, whatever we wish to say, let us first infer from the nature of our speech itself to whom it ought to be said [Col. 0945D].

## Chapter XV. Where one ought to speak

[Col. 0946A]

The third discernment in speaking follows: when we wish to say something, we should first consider where it is appropriate to say it. For there are certain places in which perpetual silence must be kept. There are others in which human speech—that is, conversation with one another—is not permitted, except for words by which a person speaks with God and to God, when through prayers, readings, hymns, and canticles, uttered openly or silently, he serves God.

Thus blessed Augustine says that nothing should be done in an oratory except that for which it was made. There are likewise other places in which words ought to be spoken for discipline and moral instruction; and still others in which discussions concerning the understanding and exposition of Scripture may take place—with discipline and reverence, however, that is, without contention, shouting, or any disgraceful manner of speech [Col. 0946B]. Finally, there are other places in which greater liberty of speech is permitted, so that conversation is allowed not only about spiritual matters but also about the management and provision of outward affairs.

I cannot find places in which vain and superfluous words ought to be spoken. Therefore we ought neither to introduce idle conversation into holy and sacred places; nor, in places where discipline is to be treated, to ventilate questions or verbal disputes; nor, in places where the meaning of divine Scripture is to be discussed, to mingle external business; nor to disclose publicly things which ought to be revealed only to a few.

## Chapter XVI. When one ought to be silent and when one ought to speak

[Col. 0946C]

The fourth discernment in speaking is to consider when something ought to be said. There is a time when nothing should be said, and a time when something should be said; but there is never a time when everything should be said. There is a time when nothing should be said, because there is “a time for silence”; and a time when something should be said, because there is “a time for speaking.” But there is never a time when everything should be said, because, as the same Solomon says: “Golden apples in silver settings is one who speaks a word in its proper time” (Prov. 25).

Every word, then, has its own time when it ought to be uttered and a time when it ought to be silent. When one ought to speak will be shown better if we first show when one ought to be silent. The time of silence ought to precede the time of speaking, because one first learns through silence, at the time for silence, what one afterward utters by word at the time for speaking. Therefore Solomon does not say, “A time for speaking and a time for silence,” but “A time for silence and a time for speaking” (Eccles. 3), because, as was said, one first receives in silence the form of speaking that one afterward maintains in speech at the time for speaking [Col. 0946D].

Sometimes we ought to be silent because another has begun to speak first, lest perhaps, if we interrupt that person’s discourse by bringing forth our own words, we offend both the speaker and the hearers together. Sometimes we ought to be silent because we perceive that the minds of our hearers are not yet prepared for what we wish to say. Sometimes we ought to be silent to avoid wordiness, or because we ourselves, who are about to speak, have not yet found within ourselves a fitting form of speech. For the minds of hearers are certainly more offended if a discourse that ought to edify is delivered confusedly and without order.

Sometimes we ought to be silent because those present are not at all the kind of people to whom we ought to address the word. This may happen in two ways: either reverence is owed to the dignity of the person, or the person’s malice is judged incorrigible and therefore unworthy of admonition [Col. 0947A].

We can prove each of these points by examples from Scripture, since we find each confirmed by not one but many scriptural testimonies. That we ought not interrupt the discourse of those who began speaking before us, but should always reverently endure and wait for [Col. 0947B] others speaking—especially those who speak useful and right things—for the preservation of discipline, is shown by holy Job. Speaking of his own discipline and of others’ reverence toward him, he says among other things: “Those who heard me waited for my judgment; and they listened in silence for my counsel. They dared add nothing to my words, and my speech fell upon them like dew” (Job 29).

Again, the Lord teaches by his example that we must often keep silence because of the weakness of hearers. When he saw the apostles still weak and unequal to instruction in higher teaching, he said: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16).

Again, Solomon shows in Proverbs that we must sometimes be silent in order to avoid hasty speech: “In much speaking sin will not be lacking, but he who moderates his lips is most prudent” (Prov. 10) [Col. 0947C]. Again: “The lips of the just consider what is pleasing, but the mouth of the wicked speaks perverse things” (ibid.). Again: “He who answers before hearing shows himself to be foolish and most worthy of confusion” (Prov. 18).

Again, in Ecclesiasticus: “Do not carry yourself into every wind, and do not go in every way; for thus a sinner is proved to have a double tongue. Be gentle in hearing the word of God, that you may understand; and with all wisdom give a true answer. If you have understanding, answer your neighbour; but if not, let your hand be over your mouth, lest you be caught in an undisciplined word” (Ecclus. 5).

Again, the same book shows that one must often keep silence out of reverence for a person: “Before you inquire, do not blame anyone; and when you have inquired, rebuke justly. Before you hear, do not answer a word; and in the midst of elders do not add speech” (Ecclus. 11) [Col. 0947D].

Again, Solomon teaches that we must often keep silence because of the malice of hearers: “Do not speak in the ears of fools, for they will despise the instruction of your speech” (Prov. 23). Again: “Do not contend with the wicked, and do not envy the ungodly” (Prov. 24). Again: “If a wise man contends with a fool, whether he grows angry or laughs, he will find no rest” (Prov. 29).

Whoever wishes to avoid these impediments to speech will perhaps easily and without difficulty recognize when to speak, if only he attends to this: one time is when permission is granted to someone who wishes to speak; another is when failure to speak is counted against someone who does not wish to speak [Col. 0948A]. The wise person guards equally against both: against being silent through negligence when one ought to speak, and against falling through permitted license into wordiness whenever one is allowed to speak.

The time for speaking is therefore rightly discerned if a person neither remains silent when he ought to speak nor speaks at all times when he may. It remains now, after we have shown what, to whom, where, and when one ought to speak, to show also how one ought to speak.

## Chapter XVII. How one ought to speak

The quality—that is, the manner—of speech consists in three things: with what gesture, in what tone, and with what meaning something is said. Discipline commands that the speaker’s manner be modest and humble, the tone subdued and pleasant, and the meaning true and agreeable [Col. 0948B].

The speaker’s manner should be modest, so that while speaking he does not move his limbs disorderly, shamelessly, or turbulently, nor diminish the attractiveness of his speech by signals of the eyes or by an indecent shaping or alteration of the face. The speaker’s manner should be humble, so that his speech may find favour with his hearers.

The speaker’s tone should be subdued, lest by noise and immoderate shouting he unjustly frighten or justly offend his hearers. It should be pleasant, lest by the harshness of its utterance it become more burdensome to the minds of its hearers in proportion as it reaches the ears more harshly and disagreeably.

The meaning—that is, the sense—of speech ought to be true, because a deceptive word, even if spoken eloquently or elaborately [Col. 0948C], is nevertheless judged by the hearer, if understood, either harmful or idle. Yet speech must have sweetness along with truth, because truth itself often becomes bitter to the hearer if it is uttered against him either without reason or without love—that is, untimely or impiously.

Let us prove each of these points by testimonies of sacred Scripture. Solomon shows that an undisciplined manner makes speech contemptible: “Well-ordered words do not become a fool” (Prov. 16). Again: “A parable is not beautiful in the mouth of a fool” (Prov. 17). Again: “Instruction is a fountain of life to its possessor; the teaching of fools is folly” (Prov. 26). Again: “A man is known by his teaching, but one who is vain and without understanding will be exposed to contempt” (Prov. 12). Again: “As a lame man has beautiful legs in vain, so a parable is unbecoming in the mouth of fools” (Prov. 26) [Col. 0948D].

Solomon likewise testifies that an air of haughtiness makes a person’s speech unwelcome to hearers: “Wisdom is too high for a fool; at the gate he will not open his mouth” (Prov. 24). Again he says: “The poor person will speak with entreaties, but the rich will speak harshly” (Prov. 18).

How much clamorous speech ought to be avoided by the disciplined is shown by the very author of discipline, of whom it is written through Isaiah: “He will not cry out, nor show partiality, nor will his voice be heard outside” (Isa. 42). That harsh and quarrelsome speech must be wholly excluded from disciplined discourse is proved by the same authority: “The lips of a fool involve themselves in quarrels, and his mouth provokes disputes” (Prov. 18) [Col. 0949A].

The same writer also indicates how much a lying word is to be avoided: “A false witness will not go unpunished, and one who speaks lies will not escape” (Prov. 19). But Ecclesiasticus plainly shows how much a sweet word avails in speech: “A sweet word multiplies friends and softens enemies, and a gracious tongue abounds in a good person” (Ecclus. 6).

## Chapter XVIII. On discipline to be maintained at table; first, in bearing and gesture

At table there is a twofold safeguard of discipline. A person ought there to preserve discipline in bearing and discipline in food. Discipline in bearing has three forms: discipline of silence, discipline of sight, and discipline in holding oneself in check [Col. 0949B].

Silence during meals is necessary because the tongue, which at every time is prone to slip into sin, is more dangerously loosened to speech when inflamed by excess in eating and drinking. For this reason the rich man who had served talkativeness amid feasting, once placed in hell, burned more intensely in his tongue (Luke 16).

Guarding the eyes during meals is necessary because it is especially unbecoming there for a person to have wandering eyes, looking about inquisitively and—to say something stronger—shamelessly observing what others are doing. Rather, with eyes modestly lowered, one should attend only to what is set and placed before oneself.

The restraint of oneself likewise must not be neglected there, so that nothing indecent or dishonourable is done either in bearing or in gesture [Col. 0949C]. Nothing should be done with noise or commotion, but all the limbs should be held in discipline with modesty and tranquillity.

Not as some do: when they have sat down to eat, by restless agitation and confused movements of their limbs they reveal the intemperance of their minds. They toss their heads, stretch out their arms, spread their hands aloft, and, with no small indecency, as though they were about to swallow the entire meal at once, display enormous exertions and most unbecoming gestures. They pant and sigh because of the constriction, so that you would suppose that they seek a wider entrance for their roaring belly, as if the narrowness of the throat could not provide sufficient abundance to the hungry stomach [Col. 0949D].

Sitting in one place, then, their eyes and hands run about to everything near and far. At once they break up bread, pour wine into cups and bowls, turn platters in a circle, and, like a king about to attack a besieged city, hesitate where first to begin the assault, since they desire to make an incursion at once on every side.

Perhaps, in saying these things too freely, we have forgotten modesty; but shamelessness sometimes does not know how to blush unless it is openly put to shame. Therefore everyone should preserve discipline within himself during meals in these three ways: restrain the tongue from talkativeness, hold back the eyes from roving observation, and keep all other members with modesty and quiet.

## Chapter XIX. On the threefold observance of discipline in food; first, what ought to be eaten

[Col. 0950A]

There follows also a threefold observance of discipline in food: observance of what one takes, of how much one takes, and of how one takes it. The observance of what one takes means that one should neither seek food that is too costly and delicate, nor require food that is too rare and unusual, nor desire it too sumptuously and elaborately prepared. In the first case luxury is rebuked; in the second, curiosity; in the third, superstition.

There are some whose throats suffer from a rather ridiculous infirmity: they cannot swallow unless the food is rich and delicate. If frugal or simple food is offered them, they immediately allege indigestion of the stomach, dryness of the chest, shivering of the head [Col. 0950B], or other such things as frivolous excuses.

Others scorn the delicacies and luxury of food with great firmness, but then, with no less—or more tolerable—fastidiousness, utterly despise the use of ordinary foods. They seek out novel and unusual kinds of food, so that a troop of servants often runs through all the surrounding villages for the sake of one person’s stomach; and scarcely at last, by uprooting unknown roots from distant desert mountains, drawing a few little fish from the depths by deep searching, or gathering unseasonable arbutus fruits (strawberry-tree fruit) from dry brambles, can they restrain the insolent appetite of one person.

And indeed I cannot fully see what vice agitates such persons, unless perhaps it is that, through a certain arrogance of spirit, they delight in keeping many people occupied in their service; or that, through the swelling of pride, they wish to seem as superior to everyone else in merit as they are different from them in food [Col. 0950C].

Others apply an excessively superstitious care to preparing foods, devising countless kinds of boiling, frying, and seasoning: now soft, now hard; now cold, now hot; now boiled, now roasted; now seasoned with pepper, now with garlic, now with cumin, now with salt—desiring according to the habit of pregnant women. Such people certainly ought not only to be rebuked but even ridiculed: like tavern-keepers, they stretch out their palate at every water-clock for the sake of eliciting flavours.

Therefore, to heal these vices, the rigor of discipline is necessary, that it may restrain these insolences of gluttony within a fixed limit, so that it does not spread itself out toward immoderate delicacies, novelties, or superstitious preparations of food [Col. 0950D].

## Chapter XX. Secondly, how much ought to be eaten

Next follows the safeguard of discipline concerning how much one ought to take. Its measure seems to me to be this: neither contrary to propriety nor beyond necessity. Not every stomach holds the same amount: one is content with this much, another with that. The person for whom less suffices falls into excess before reaching the shamefulness of gluttony; the one who needs much often injures the propriety of eating even before reaching excess.

Therefore, one for whom little is enough should guard more carefully against excess; but one who needs much should attend more carefully to propriety [Col. 0951A]. For the former will not reach shamefulness unless he has passed the bounds of moderation; nor will the latter fall into excess unless he has first forgotten propriety.

## Chapter XXI. Thirdly, how one ought to eat
Finally, there is the observance concerning food: how one ought to take food. That is, how cleanly and how temperately. To offer a few examples of uncleanliness in eating will suffice, so that, when it is seen in certain of its aspects, it may readily be avoided everywhere by analogy. Some people, while eating, when they wish to empty their bowls, wrap or cast upon the dishes square pieces from the serving-platters, dripping with fat or poured-over gravy, until, after the insides have again been scooped out, they replace what remains in its former place. Others, while drinking, plunge their fingers halfway into their cups. Others wipe their greasy hands on their clothes and then return to handling food. Others, using their bare joints as spoons, fish for their vegetables [Col. 0952A], so that in the same broth both hand-washing and stomach-filling seem to be sought. Others repeatedly thrust half-chewed crusts and pre-bitten little rolls into the food, and dip in their cups the food-remnants from their teeth, making mouthfuls of them. These things, as we said above, ought to have been shameful for those who describe them, had they not first been presumed by those who do them. But now let him endure the shame of hearing who was unwilling to possess discipline in doing. Yet let these remarks, offered by way of example concerning the uncleanliness of undisciplined eaters, suffice.

We understand temperance in eating to consist in a person’s eating slowly and not with excessive haste. Here we indeed advise everyone, so far as possible, to keep due proportion and measure; yet we presume to lay down no law, because, [Col. 0952B] as we said above, one person is thus and another otherwise. For the present, brothers, we have spoken these things to you concerning knowledge and discipline. But pray that God may give you goodness. Amen.

[Col. 0951]

# SOLILOQUY ON THE EARNEST OF THE SOUL

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0951] To the beloved brother G., and to the other servants of Christ dwelling at Hameris Leva, H., your servant—such as he is—in your holiness: may you walk in one peace and attain one rest.

I send this Soliloquy of Love, entitled *On the Earnest of the Soul*, to your charity, that you may learn where you ought to seek true love and how you should stir your hearts, through the zealous study of spiritual meditations, toward the joys above. Therefore, dearest brother, I ask that you receive it with the others in remembrance of me; let not what is sent especially to you exclude the rest, nor let what is given to all in common diminish the prerogative of the gift. I do not wish here to provoke you by the polish of composition, but because I could not conceal the devotion of my affection toward you. Greet brother B., brother A., and all the others whose names, although I cannot now enumerate them individually, I nevertheless desire may all be inscribed in the book of life. Farewell.

# SOLILOQUY ON THE EARNEST OF THE SOUL

*The interlocutors are the Man and the Soul.*

[Col. 0951]

[Col. 0951C] **MAN.** I shall speak privately with my soul, and in friendly conversation I shall require of her what I desire to know. No outsider shall be admitted; rather, with consciences laid open, we alone shall exchange words. Thus I shall have no fear in seeking hidden things, nor will she have shame in giving true answers.

Tell me, I pray, my soul: what is it that you love above all things? I know that love is your life, and I know that you cannot exist without love. But I wish you to confess to me without embarrassment what, among all things to be loved, you have chosen. I shall say more, so that you may understand more clearly what I am asking you. Look upon the world and all that is in it. There you will find many beautiful and enticing forms, which draw human affections and, according to the diverse pleasures of those who use them, kindle desires to enjoy them. Gold has its gleam; precious stones have theirs; bodily beauty has its appearance; painted hangings and dyed garments have their colour. Such things are countless. But why should I enumerate them for you? Behold, you too know them all; you have seen nearly every kind and experienced very many. You recall that you have already seen much, and you still see much in which you can test and verify what I say. Tell me therefore, I beseech you: which one thing, out of all these, have you made your own, so that you wish to embrace it especially and enjoy it always? [Col. 0953A] For I am certain that either you love something among these visible things, or, if you have now put all these aside, you have something else that you love above them all.

**SOUL.** Just as I cannot love what I have never seen, so among all these visible things I have not yet been able to love nothing; nevertheless, among them all I have not yet found what ought to be loved above everything. For I have already learned through many experiences that the love of this age is deceptive and fleeting; I am always compelled to exchange it, either when what I had chosen for myself comes to perish, or when something else, more pleasing, comes along. Thus I still toss uncertainly upon the waves of desire: I can neither exist without love nor find true love.

**MAN.** I rejoice that you have at least not fixed yourself in the love of temporal things; but I grieve that you do not yet rest in the love of eternal things. You would be more unhappy if you made your homeland out of exile; but now, because you wander in exile, you must be recalled to the way. You would make your homeland out of exile if you wished to have eternal love in this passing life. But now you wander in exile because, while you are drawn about through desire for temporal things, you do not find the love of eternal things. Yet it can be a great beginning of salvation for you that you have learned to change your love for the better. Thus you will be able to be torn away from every love of temporal things if a greater beauty is shown you, one that you may embrace more gladly.

**SOUL.** How can that be shown which cannot be seen? And how can what cannot be seen be loved? Certainly, if among temporal things and things that can be seen there is no true and enduring love, while what cannot be seen cannot be loved, everlasting misery attends one who lives forever if enduring love is never found. For no one can be blessed without love, since one is plainly miserable even in this alone: that one does not love what is. Indeed, who would call blessed—not to say human—a person who, forgetting humanity and rejecting the peace of society, loved only himself with a certain solitary and wretched love? It is necessary, therefore, either that you approve love for visible things, or, if you remove this love, that you show other things which may be loved more healthfully and pleasantly.

**MAN.** If you think that these temporal and visible things ought to be loved because you discern in them a beauty proper to their kind, why do you not rather love yourself, who in your own form altogether surpass the grace and beauty of visible things? Oh, if you looked upon yourself! Oh, if you saw your own face, you would surely recognize how worthy of blame you were when you thought that something outside yourself was worthy of your love!

**SOUL.** The eye sees all things, but does not see itself; and with that light by which we behold everything else, we do not see our own face, in which the light itself is situated. Human beings learn their faces from others’ reports, and know the appearance of their countenance more often by hearing of it than by seeing it—unless perhaps you bring forward some mirror of another kind, in which I may know and love the face of my heart. Yet anyone would rightly call foolish the person who continually contemplated the likeness of his own countenance in a mirror in order to feed his love. Therefore, because I cannot contemplate what my own face and the appearance of my countenance are like, I more readily extend the affection of my love to things that seem admirable outside myself. Especially since love never allows itself to be solitary, and it is already, in a certain way, not love if it does not pour out the force of its affection upon another as a companion of equal fellowship.

**MAN.** One with whom God is present is not solitary; nor is the power of love extinguished if its desire is restrained from low and worthless things. Rather, the person who admits into the fellowship of love either dishonourable things or at least things not worthy of love does himself a greater injury. First, therefore, each person must [Col. 0954B] consider himself; and, once he has known his dignity, he must not love what is lower than himself, lest he injure his love. For even things that are beautiful considered in themselves become cheap when compared with more beautiful things. And just as it is unfitting to join ugly things to beautiful, so it is altogether indecent to equate with beauty things that possess only a certain lowest and imaginary beauty.

You do not wish, soul, to have a solitary love; yet do not have a prostituted one. You seek one alone; seek one chosen uniquely. You know that love is fire, and fire seeks fuel in order to burn. But take care not to cast into it what supplies smoke or stench instead. Such is the force of love that one necessarily becomes like that which one loves; and, joined through affection, one is in some manner transformed into its likeness by the very fellowship of love. Therefore, soul, attend to your own beauty, and you will understand what kind of beauty you ought to love.

Your own face is not invisible to you. Your eye sees nothing well if it does not see itself. For when it is rightly clear-sighted for contemplating itself, no foreign likeness outside it, nor shadowy image of truth, can deceive it. But if perhaps that inward vision of yours has been darkened through neglect, and you are unable to contemplate yourself as is fitting and beneficial, why do you not at least weigh from another’s judgment what you ought to think of yourself? You have a bridegroom, but do not know it. He is the fairest of all, but you have not seen his face. He saw you, for unless he had seen you, he would not have loved you. He has not yet wished to present himself to you, but he has sent gifts: he has given an earnest, a pledge of love, a token of affection. If you could know him, if you saw his appearance, you would no longer doubt your own beauty. For you would know that one so beautiful, so comely, so elegant, so incomparable, would not have been captivated by your appearance unless singular beauty, admirable beyond others, drew him.

What then will you do? Now you cannot see him, because he is absent. Therefore you neither fear nor blush to wrong him: you despise his singular love and shamefully, shamelessly prostitute yourself to another’s lust. Do not act thus. If you cannot yet know what he is like who loves you, at least consider the earnest that he has given. [Col. 0955A] Perhaps in his very gift, which you possess, you may recognize with what affection you ought to love him and with what zeal and care you ought to preserve yourself for him. His earnest consists in signs; his gift is noble. For it was not fitting that one so great should give little things, nor would a wise man have given great things for a small matter. Great, then, is what he has given you; but greater is what he loves in you.

Great, then, is what he has given. What has your bridegroom given you, soul? Perhaps you wait, and do not know what I am about to say. You reflect from whom you have received some great thing, yet find that you have nothing of such a kind, or have received nothing, of which you can boast. I shall tell you, then, so that you may know what your bridegroom has given you. Look back upon this whole world and consider whether there is anything in it that does not serve you. All nature directs its course to this end: that it may wait upon your service, attend to your benefit, and provide alike for your pleasures and your necessities with unfailing abundance. This heaven, this earth, this air, these seas, with all things that are in them, do not cease to fulfil this purpose. In this purpose the cycle of seasons, by yearly renewals and recurring births, renews what is old, restores what has fallen away, repairs what has been consumed, and supplies perpetual nourishment.

Who, then, do you think established this? Who commanded nature thus to serve you with one consent? You receive the benefit and do not acknowledge its author. The gift is manifest; the giver is hidden. Yet reason itself does not permit you to doubt that this is not your due, but another’s benefit. Whoever he is, therefore, he has bestowed much upon you who has given you all this and so great a gift. He who could give so much and who willed to give so much must be greatly loved; he loved greatly. Thus the one who loves so greatly and is so greatly to be loved is revealed by his gift. As it is foolish not voluntarily to desire the love of one so powerful, so it is impious and perverse not to return the love of one so loving.

See, then, foolish and rash soul, see what you are doing when you desire to be loved and to love in this world. The whole world is subject to you; yet you do not disdain to admit into the fellowship of your love—not the whole world, I say, but I know not what, scarcely some tiny portion of the world, which is distinguished neither by beautiful form, necessary usefulness, great size, nor highest goodness. Certainly, if you love these things, love them as subjects; love them as servants; love them as gifts; [Col. 0955D] as your bridegroom’s earnest, as a friend’s presents, as the Lord’s benefits. Yet do so in such a way that you always remember what you owe him, and love neither these things instead of him nor along with him, but these things for his sake, and him through these things and above these things.

Take care, soul, lest—God forbid!—you be called not a bride but a prostitute, if you love the gifts of the giver more than the affection of the lover. You commit a greater wrong against his love if you accept his gifts and nevertheless do not render love in return. Either reject his gifts, if you can; or, if you cannot reject them, render the return of love. Love him; love yourself for his sake; love his gifts for his sake. Love him in order that you may enjoy him; love yourself because you are loved by him. In his gifts, love the fact that [Col. 0956A] they have been given by him. Love him for yourself and yourself for him; love his gifts as given by him to you, for your sake. This is pure and chaste love: it has nothing filthy, nothing bitter, nothing transitory; it is beautiful in chastity, pleasant in sweetness, stable in eternity.

**SOUL.** Your words have set me aflame: I have conceived ardour and burn inwardly. Although I have not yet seen him whom you declare to be so lovable, yet the sweetness of your discourse and the pleasantness of your exhortation themselves—so I confess—kindle me to love him. Indeed, I am compelled by your arguments to love above all things him from whom I see that I have received all things as a pledge of love. Nevertheless, one thing still remains which greatly diminishes for me the happiness of this love, unless the hand of your consolation wipes that away also, as it has the rest.

**MAN.** I confidently promise you that in this love there is nothing that ought rightly to displease; yet, lest I seem rather to mislead your credulity than to bear witness to truth, I want you to disclose to me what moves you, so that, strengthened again by my arguments, you may grow still firmer in longing for him.

**SOUL.** I wish you to remember—though I do not suppose you have forgotten—that a little while ago, when you commended a worthy and honourable love, you said that love ought to be not only one, but also uniquely chosen: that is, established in the beloved alone and in him alone who is to be loved, because love is not perfectly praiseworthy if either another is loved with the one beloved, or one who is not supremely to be loved is loved alone.

Behold, then, I love one uniquely chosen and uniquely beloved. But I suffer this injury in my love: though loving one alone, I am not loved alone. For you yourself recognize how many there are—or at least what kinds of beings there are—with whom this pledge of my love, which you set before me, is shared in common. How, then, shall I be able to boast of the privilege of singular love, when I have received what you declare so great not merely in common with brutish creatures, but even with the beasts themselves? What more does sunlight give to me than to reptiles and worms of the earth? All alike live; all alike breathe; the food and drink of all are the same. What is so great in this? What is so singular? You surely see what it is like. Therefore you do not sufficiently establish that he ought to be loved singularly unless you also show that he has loved singularly, at least in some respect. I admit that these things would indeed be great and worthy of singular love if they had been given singularly.

**MAN.** This carefulness of yours cannot displease me, because it shows that you desire to love perfectly, since you so carefully investigate the ground of perfect love. I gladly undertake, therefore, to discuss this matter with you: both to defend the love of one so excellent from the wrong of which you complain, and at the same time to restore you wholly, lest you waver from his love through any suspicion.

There are three kinds of things in which you may find what troubles you. Distinguish the gifts you have received from your bridegroom. Some are given commonly, some specially, some singularly. Commonly given are those which serve all together with you for your sake. Specially given are those granted, together with you and for your sake, to many but not to all. Singularly given are those given to you alone.

What then? Does he love you less because he has granted some of his gifts to everyone together with you? Would he have made you happier if he had given the world to you alone? Behold: no human beings have been created upon earth; no beasts exist; you alone possess the world’s riches. Where, then, is the welcome and useful fellowship of human life? Where are the comforts and pleasures you now enjoy? See, then, that even in this he has bestowed much upon you: he created these things together with you for your consolation. If this world and all these things serve you, how are they not all made for your service?

Does the master of a household eat his bread alone? Does he drink his beverage alone? Does he alone clothe himself in his garments? Does he alone warm himself by his fire? Does he alone dwell in his house? Yet whatever those possess who serve him, whether through love or subjection, is not without reason called wholly his. Therefore, whether those things that serve you or those things necessary to those who serve you, all have been given to you, all render you service.

**SOUL.** You have cut off, rather than uprooted, what troubled me. For I complained that, though I love uniquely, I am not uniquely loved, because I see the pledge of my love granted equally to others. Your arguments, however, have persuaded me to believe that even those things have been given to me singularly which I see given in common for the use of those serving me. In this respect, I confess that you have spoken suitably enough, but not sufficiently, concerning what troubled me. For from this I learn that all things by which the life of irrational creatures is sustained ought rather to be assigned to my dominion, because even the things by which they are nourished are allotted for my use. Yet the privilege of singular love is not thereby established, since these things are known to be subject not to me alone but equally to all human beings—and indeed to many besides.

In all the things granted in common for human use, therefore, those err who ascribe anything singularly to their own dominion, unless they unjustly claim something more for themselves. There is, then, a certain special love of the Creator toward human beings, in which human beings have grounds for boasting above other creatures, but not above one another. For when, in support of singular love, you say that fellowship with human beings also has been given to me among other gifts, I can find nothing singular in this, since I have been granted to them as much as they have been granted to me. In this fellowship, not only am I harmed by the loss of the glory of singularity, but also by the baseness of sharing it. For how many unbelievers, how many wicked persons, how many impure persons are there who can boast equally in this fellowship?

**MAN.** You ought not to be disturbed that good and evil persons share alike in the use of temporal things, nor should you suppose that they are equally loved by God because you see them sharing all these things with you alike. For just as beasts were created not for themselves but for human beings, so wicked people live not for themselves but for the good. And just as their lives serve the advantage of the good, so there is no doubt that everything by which their life is sustained must be referred to the increase of the good.

Wicked people are allowed to live among the good so that their society may train the life of the good: by their prosperity they warn the good to seek higher goods which the wicked cannot share; by their wickedness they compel them to love virtue more closely. Finally, when the good see them deprived of divine grace and rushing through every precipice of vice, they learn how great thanks they ought to return to the Creator for their salvation.

Indeed, the design of divine providence required this for the increase of our salvation and as instruction toward glorification: just as in the life of beasts we say that the highest happiness does not consist in using them, so also in the life of wicked people we learn that the highest happiness does not consist in ruling them. Therefore these things had to be granted alike to good and evil persons, because otherwise the good would not believe that higher things were reserved for them unless they saw that these things were common to both good and evil.

Do not therefore complain further about the fellowship or happiness of wicked persons; nor think that they are to be counted with you in the privilege of singular love because you have them as companions in the use and dominion of passing things. For even in this, as we have already said, they advance your salvation: they are able not only to use these things with you, but also to rule them.

But what shall I say concerning the fellowship of the good? For this alone now remains: you must consider whether you cannot boast of the singular love of your bridegroom because you are loved by him not without the fellowship of the good. Therefore I wish you to remember that statement which I brought forward above in support of my case, though then you judged it perhaps less suitable to prove the point at issue. I now repeat it, so that I may examine it more carefully before you: whether its truth may support what we strive to establish.

For I said that fellowship with human beings was also granted to you as a gift of your Creator, so that you might draw from it consolation in living and not pine away, deprived in a certain solitary and inactive life. Therefore, just as the life of the wicked is an exercise for you, so the life of the good is a consolation. Surely these are people whom you ought not to reject as companions either in your happiness or in your love. For if you truly love the good, whatever benefit is bestowed upon them, the charity within you rejoices in it not as in another’s possession but as in your own.

Although it would be blessed to enjoy this love even alone, it is nevertheless far more blessed to delight in it amid the shared rejoicing of many good people. For when the affection of love is extended also to those who share in it, the joy and sweetness of charity are enlarged. Spiritual love becomes singular for each person most perfectly when it is common to all. It is not diminished by the participation of many, for its one and identical fruit is found whole in each person.

Thus fellowship with the good does nothing to bar the privilege of your singular love, because your bridegroom loves you in all whom he loves for your sake; and consequently he loves you also singularly, because he loves nothing apart from you. Nor should you fear that his mind is drawn apart, as it were, in affection for many and thus is less toward each individually because it seems somehow distributed and divided among all. He is present to each as though to all, because he would not bestow upon individuals a different or greater affection of love if he loved them individually without the participation of all.

Therefore let all uniquely love the One, so that all may be uniquely loved by the One. For there is no other besides the One who ought to be uniquely loved by all, nor can any other besides the One uniquely love all. Let all, moreover, love themselves in the One as though one, so that through love of the One they may become one. This love is unique, yet not private; alone, yet not solitary; shared, yet not divided; common and singular; belonging individually to all and wholly to each; neither decreasing by participation, nor failing through use, nor growing old with time; ancient and new; desirable in affection, sweet in experience, eternal in fruit, full of delight, refreshing and satisfying, and never producing disgust.

**SOUL.** Your arguments are very pleasing to me, and I confess that I now begin to desire this love more ardently for the very reason that I had previously begun to reject it more strongly. Yet one thing remains for my desire; if I can attain it through you, I shall not doubt that I have been fully satisfied in every respect. That is, if it can somehow be shown how this bridegroom of chastity is present to each whom he loves as though to all, both in affection and in effect. And I shall not be able to doubt concerning his affection if I know this to be true in effect.

**MAN.** O my soul, if you persist so earnestly in what you have begun, and do not consider yourself satisfied unless you recognize a benefit of your bridegroom that is wholly singularly bestowed, I gladly assent to your request even in this. For I know that this insistence of yours arises from devotion rather than importunity. For your best lover has provided even in this, lest there be nothing in which you can glory singularly in him. As he has given common and special gifts, so he has bestowed singular gifts.

Common gifts are those which come into the use of all, such as sunlight and the breath of air. [Col. 0959D] Special gifts are those granted not to all but, as it were, to a certain fellowship, such as faith, wisdom, and discipline. Singular gifts are those bestowed personally upon each individual: for example, Peter’s primacy among the apostles, Paul’s apostleship among the Gentiles, and John’s privilege of love.

Consider, therefore, my soul, what common gifts you have received with all, what special gifts with some, and what singular gifts alone.
