In all those things he has loved you which he has bestowed either commonly upon all together with you, specially upon certain persons, or singularly upon you alone. Again, he has loved you together with all those whom he joined to you through participation in his gift. He has loved you above all those whom he preferred you to by the gift of singular grace. You are loved in every creature; you are loved with all good people; you are loved above all evil people. And lest it seem a small thing to you that you are loved above all evil people, how many good people are there who have received less than you?

But because, in your desire for singular love, I see you striving rather for what has been singularly given, although much could still be said about the things in which and the people with whom you are loved, I wish what has already been said to suffice. Yet I do not wish you to consider it a small thing to be loved in such great gifts and with such companions: in them you have all good people as companions, while evil people, like all things that have been created, are subject to you.

You have seen, therefore, my soul, how many things there are in which you are loved; you have seen what kind of persons they are with whom you are loved. Now consider, so far as you can, above whom you are loved. I speak to you, my soul: you know what you have received, and you need to know it still better, lest you begin either to presume upon things you have not received or to fail to return thanks for those you have.

Would that I could call them to mind as is beneficial for you and pleasing to him who gave them to you! For he himself gave you these things so that you might always keep them in memory and never grow cold toward his love through forgetfulness. First, consider, my soul, that once you did not exist, and that you received from his gift the ability to begin to exist. Therefore, that you came to be was his gift.

But had you given him anything before you came to be, for which he might render this to you—that you came to be? Absolutely nothing. You had given nothing, and could have given nothing before you came to be; rather, you freely received from him the gift of coming to be. Above whom, then, were you preferred in being made? Who could receive less than the one who received the gift of coming to be? Yet, unless this were to receive something, that which did not exist could not begin; and unless being were better than not being, the one who exists would have received nothing more than the one who does not.

Why, then, my God, did you make me, unless because you willed me to be rather than not to be? You loved me more than all those who did not merit to receive this from you. Therefore, my God, when you gave me being—a good and great good—you gave me your good, good and beautiful; and, in giving this to me, you preferred me above all those to whom you did not will to give this great good of yours.

O my soul, do we say something when we say this to our God? To our God, by whom we were made—made though we did not exist—and who has made us receive more than all those who were not made? Yes, indeed, we say something; we say much when we say this; and we ought always to say it, lest we ever forget him from whom we have received so great a good. Even if he had given nothing further, he would still always deserve to be praised and loved by us for this alone.

But now he has given more, because he gave not only being, but beautiful being, comely being. As existence surpasses nothingness, so form surpasses mere existence: in the latter, what exists pleases greatly; in the former, what exists in such a fashion pleases still more. In this, my soul, see yourself preferred above all those whom you see have not received so excellent and surpassing a good of existence.

Nor could the generosity of the best giver stop here. He gave something more, and drew us more closely to his own likeness; he wished to draw to himself through likeness those whom he drew to himself through love. He gave us, therefore, being and beautiful being; he also gave us life, so that we surpass both things that lack being in essence, by our existence; things that are disordered or unformed, by our form; and things without life, by our life.

You are bound by a great debt, my soul. You have received much, and had nothing from yourself. And for all these things you have nothing to render except love. For what is given through love can be repaid neither better nor more fittingly than through love. You received all this through love. God could also have given life to his other creatures, but in this gift he loved you more. Nor did he love you more because he found more in you deserving of love; but because he freely loved you more, he made you such that now he loves you more deservedly.

**SOUL.** The more I hear, the more I desire to hear. Continue, I pray, and recount what follows.

**MAN.** After being, after beautiful being, after living, the power of sensation was given; the power of discernment was also given. And it was given through that same love which, unless it had preceded, nothing would have been given by the giver and nothing received by the needy.

How lofty and how beautiful you were made, my soul! What did this great and splendid adornment intend, except that he who clothed you prepared his bride for his bridal chamber? He knew for what work he created you; he knew what kind of adornment befitted that work. Therefore he gave what was fitting, and what was so fitting that he himself who gave it loved it.

He adorned you outwardly with senses and illumined you inwardly with wisdom: giving the senses as an outward garment, wisdom as an inward one; hanging the senses outside like shining gems, and adorning within the face of your countenance with wisdom as with natural beauty. Behold, your adornment surpasses the beauty of every gem; behold, your face exceeds the grace of every form. Such indeed it was fitting that she should be who was to be brought into the bridal chamber of the heavenly king.

How greatly you were loved, and above how many you were loved, when you were made such! What a singular gift—one not granted to all, to be granted only to the loved and to those worthy of love! You could have gloried greatly, and you ought greatly to have guarded yourself: lest you lose so great a gift, defile so great an adornment, corrupt so great a beauty; [Col. 0961D] lest, having lost or diminished it, you become more miserable than you would have been had you not received it or had it not been perfected; lest, together with the loss of beauty, the shame of ugliness torment you, and, rejected, you become more worthless than if you had not been received.

Therefore this had to be preserved and that avoided: the former, so that what was preserved might endure; the latter, so that what was guarded against might not happen. But see what you have done, my soul. You abandoned your bridegroom and prostituted your love to strangers. You corrupted your integrity, defiled your beauty, scattered your adornment. You became so worthless, so ugly, and so unclean that you seemed no longer worthy of the embraces of such a bridegroom. Thus you forgot your bridegroom and, for such great benefits, did not give fitting thanks. You became a prostitute, and through your excessive fornications your breasts became slack. Your brow became wrinkled; your cheeks withered; your eyes languished and grew dull; your lips were covered with pallor; your skin dried up; your strength was broken; you became hateful even to your lovers.

**SOUL.** I had hoped that that great praise would tend toward another end; but, as I see, you have said these things for my greater shame, to show me more worthy of hatred because, having received such great benefits and failed to preserve them, I have been proved more ungrateful. I would therefore rather either that what has been said had not happened, or at least that what happened had not been said, so that forgetfulness might cover shame, if presumption had not avoided guilt.

**HUMAN BEING.** These things were said not to put you to shame, but to instruct you, so that you may become more indebted to him who both made you when you did not exist and redeemed you when you had perished. I also recalled that fact as confirmation of his love, so that, taking occasion from it, I may now begin to tell you how greatly this your bridegroom—who appeared so exalted when he created you—deigned to humble himself when he restored you. There he was so sublime; here so humble; yet here no less lovable than there, because here no less wonderful than there. There he powerfully bestowed great things upon you; here he mercifully endured dreadful things for you. For, in order to raise you again to that place from which you had fallen, he deigned to descend to this place where you lay; and, in order that what you had lost might justly be restored to you, he deigned in compassion to suffer what you were enduring. Therefore he descended, assumed, endured, conquered, restored: he descended to one subject to death, assumed mortality, endured the Passion, [Col. 0962C] conquered death, restored humanity. Behold, my soul: stand amazed at such great wonders, such great benefits displayed for your sake. Consider how greatly he loves you, who deigned to do such things for you. You had been made beautiful by his gift; by your iniquity you became foul. Yet by his mercy you were cleansed again and made beautiful—though love was at work in both cases. Long ago, when you did not exist, he loved you in order to create you. Afterwards, when you were foul, he loved you in order to make you beautiful; and, to show you how greatly he loved you, he chose to free you from death only by dying, so that he might not merely bestow the benefit of mercy, but also display the affection of love. Now, moreover, he loves you with such pure love as though you had always remained with him; he neither reproaches you with your guilt nor casts his benefit in your teeth. And if henceforth you wish to persevere faithfully with him, to love him as is fitting, and to preserve your love for him undefiled, he promises that he will give you things greater than the former ones.

**SOUL.** In a certain way I now begin to love my fault, because, as I see, it has benefited me greatly to have done such harm: through it, what I desired above all things to know is made known to me more clearly than daylight. O my happy fault! While he is drawn to cleanse it away by love, his very love is opened to me as I desire it and long for it with all my heart. I should never have known his love so well if I had not experienced it amid such great dangers. O how happily I fell, since after my fall I rose again more happily! [Col. 0963A] No love is greater, no affection more sincere, no charity holier, no feeling more ardent: he died innocent for me, finding in me nothing that he might love. What, then, Lord, did you love in me? And what did you love so greatly that you died for me? What such thing did you find in me, for which you were willing to endure things so great and so harsh?

**HUMAN BEING.** O my soul, accuse yourself before the Lord, because until now you have been ungrateful for such great benefits of his and have refused to recognize his many mercies. But, that you may understand still better how much you owe him, while I continue to recount his remaining benefits in the order begun, I want you to attend carefully.

**SOUL.** I always desire to hear what is so sweet to me that I would wish you endlessly to repeat the same thing, rather than hasten on to hear the other things that remain.

**HUMAN BEING.** You had therefore gone away and perished; and because you had been sold into slavery under your sins, he came after you to redeem you. He loved you so greatly that he paid the price of his own blood for you, and by such a bargain both brought you back from exile and redeemed you from servitude.

**SOUL.** I did not know that God loved me so greatly. I ought no longer to be worthless in my own eyes, since I pleased God so much that he chose even to die for me rather than lose me.

**HUMAN BEING.** And what if you begin to consider how many, and of what kind, have been cast aside in comparison with you—those who could not attain the grace granted to you? Surely [Col. 0963C] you have heard how many generations of human beings have passed away from the beginning until this day, all of whom, without knowledge of God and without the price of their redemption, slipped away into everlasting destruction. Your redeemer and lover preferred you to all of them when he bestowed upon you this grace which none of those deserved to receive. And what will you say? Why do you think that you were preferred to all of them? Were you stronger, wiser, nobler, or richer than all of them, that you deserved to obtain this special grace before them all? How many strong, how many wise, how many noble, how many rich persons were there among them! Yet all alike were left behind, cast aside, and perished. You alone were chosen above all of them; and you can find no reason why this was done for you except the freely bestowed love of your Saviour. Therefore your bridegroom, your lover, your Redeemer, your God, chose you and chose you beforehand. He chose you among all, took you from among all, and loved you above all. He called you by his own name, so that his memorial might always remain with you. He wished you to share in the name and in the truth of the name, because he anointed you with that oil of gladness with which he himself had been anointed, so that the one called a Christian, from Christ, may be anointed from the Anointed One.

**SOUL.** Much, I confess, has been bestowed on me; but I ask you: if, as you maintain, I have already been chosen, why am I still delayed, since I cannot yet come to the embraces of the bridegroom?

**HUMAN BEING.** Do you not know, then, my soul—do you not know how foul you formerly were, how polluted, misshapen, and squalid, torn apart and scattered, full of every horror and deformity? And how do you seek to be introduced so quickly into that chamber of modesty and chastity unless you are first, at least through some care and effort, cultivated and restored to your former beauty? This is what you are now awaiting; this is why your bridegroom still withholds his presence from you and does not yet admit you to mutual embraces and sweet kisses: for what is polluted ought not to touch what is clean, nor is it fitting for the ugly to behold the beautiful. But when you have been prepared and suitably adorned, then at last you will enter without shame into that chamber of the heavenly bridegroom, to remain there. Nor will you then be ashamed of your former ugliness, when you will have nothing ugly or worthy of shame. [Col. 0964B] Therefore first strive to cultivate your form, adorn your face, arrange your attire, wipe away your stains, restore purity, correct your conduct, preserve discipline, and, once all things have been changed for the better, make yourself a bride worthy of a worthy bridegroom.

I wish to say something that will make you more cautious, lest, because you hear that you are chosen, either pride make you swollen or negligence make you lax. Have you never heard what King Ahasuerus did when he repudiated Queen Vashti because of her insolence? It was a notable event, a useful example, a grave danger. She was cast aside because of her pride; and the king’s decree was issued that beautiful virgin maidens should be gathered from his whole kingdom, brought to the city of Susa, and placed in the women’s house under the authority of [Col. 0964C] Hegai the eunuch, superintendent and guardian of the royal women; there they were to receive women’s cosmetics and all else necessary for use. Thus they were lavishly supplied, groomed, and adorned in accordance with royal magnificence. For six months they were anointed with myrtle oil; for another six they used certain perfumes. Thus prepared and adorned, they passed from the women’s quarters to the king’s bedchamber, so that she who pleased the king more than all the others might sit in the royal throne in Vashti’s place (Esther 2).

See how many were selected so that one might be chosen—namely, she who appeared more beautiful and more adorned than the rest in the king’s eyes. The king’s attendants select many for preparation; the king himself chooses one for the marriage chamber. The first selection, of many, was made according to the king’s command; the second selection, of one, was made according to the king’s will. Let us consider, then, whether this example may perhaps be applied to the matter now under discussion. The King, Son of the highest King, came into this world, which he himself had created, to betroth to himself a chosen wife, a unique wife, a wife worthy of royal marriage. But because Judaea despised receiving him in the form of humility in which he appeared, she was cast aside. The king’s servants—namely, the apostles—were sent throughout the whole world to gather souls and bring them to the city of the King, that is, to the holy Church. In it is the house and dwelling-place of the royal women—that is, of holy souls—which conceive and bear children not for slavery but for a kingdom. Because they serve God not from fear but from love, they bring forth, as it were, offspring of good works into freedom. [Col. 0965A] Many who are called enter the Church through faith, and there receive the sacraments of Christ, like certain ointments and remedies prepared for the restoration and adornment of souls. But because the mouth of Truth says, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20), not all who have been admitted to this preparation are to be chosen for the kingdom, but only those who strive to cleanse and cultivate themselves by these means, so that, when they are brought before the king’s presence, they may be found such as he would rather choose than reject.

See, therefore, where you have been placed, and you will understand what you must do. Your bridegroom has placed you in the dining hall where women are adorned; he has given you varied perfumes and diverse kinds of cosmetics, and ordered royal food from his own table to be served to you. He has bestowed whatever can avail for health, refreshment, restoration of beauty, and increase of adornment. Take care, then, that you are not negligent in cultivating yourself, lest in the end, when you are presented before this bridegroom, you be found unworthy—may it not be so!—of his company. Prepare yourself as becomes the bride of a King: the bride of the heavenly King, the bride of the immortal Bridegroom.

**SOUL.** You have again made me bitter and struck me with no slight fear. For, so far as can be understood from your words, I have changed my purpose but have not escaped danger. I have changed my purpose because I have turned away from him who formerly led me astray with wandering and unstable love, and have turned to a single love. I have not escaped danger because, [Col. 0965C] as you maintain, unless I strive in every way to make myself worthy, I shall not attain the fruit of this love. It remains, therefore, that you explain to me more carefully this dining hall in which the royal women are nourished; the royal food given to them; the ointments with which they are anointed; and all the other things provided for cultivation or adornment. For, stirred by love of him, I am henceforth moved to devote effort to those things without which I see that I cannot attain the affection of love. And would that I might deserve to be that one whose beauty and adornment the king will praise! How happy she is, and how more chosen than the chosen, who brings her effort to this end! I should now count every labour insignificant if I could bring my effort to this end. I ask, therefore, that you not be reluctant to teach me each of the remedies by which I ought to refashion my face into this beauty, because I ardently desire to please him whose love toward me I know to be so gracious and whose affection so delightful.

**HUMAN BEING.** This is indeed what you must do. And I pray that he who has now granted you the will to do it may also grant you strength to accomplish it. You ask what the dining hall is; ask also what the king’s bedchamber is. Set these two dwellings before yourself, because you need to consider them. There is, then, a dining hall and there is the king’s bedchamber. In the dining hall brides are prepared for marriage; in the bedchamber the marriage is celebrated. The present Church is like the dining hall, in which the brides of God are now prepared for the marriage to come. The heavenly Jerusalem is like the King’s bedchamber, in which the marriage itself is celebrated. After the time of adornment, they pass from the dining hall to the King’s bedchamber, because after the time of doing good works they come to receive the fruit of their good work. The present Church is called a dining hall because of the three orders of believers: married persons, the continent, and rulers or virgins.

Let us now see what are the ointments, kinds of perfumes, foods, and garments prepared for the adornment of the brides. Nor should this be omitted: just as the bridegroom first loves them freely when they are in a sense foul and ugly, so he freely provides them with every assistance for adornment. They have nothing from themselves except what they receive from him, by which they may please him; so you should know that even this belongs to love: that you have means to adorn yourself, though indeed you have nothing from yourself unless you receive it from him.

First there is the font of baptism, and the washing of regeneration, in which you wash away the filth of former sins. Then comes chrism and oil, by whose anointing you are marked with the Holy Spirit. After this, anointed and made radiant by the anointing of gladness, you come to the table and receive there the nourishment of Christ’s body and blood. Inwardly nourished and refreshed by it, you drive away the harmful emaciation caused by your former fastings; restored to your former fullness and strength, you become young again, as it were. Then you put on garments of good works and are adorned, as though with varied ornament, by the fruit of almsgiving, with fasts and prayers, holy vigils, and other works [Col. 0966C] of mercy. Finally come the fragrant virtues, whose sweetly breathing scent drives away all the stench of former defilements, so that you seem in some way wholly changed and transformed into another person, becoming happier, more vigorous, and healthier.

Holy Scripture is also given to you as a mirror, so that you may see your face in it and ensure that the arrangement of your adornment lacks nothing or contains nothing other than what is fitting. What then do you say, my soul? Do you know whether you have yet received any of these things? Surely you have been washed in the font; surely you have eaten the same food and drunk the same drink from the King’s table. But perhaps you have again become polluted: you have tears by which you may wash yourself again. The anointing has again faded in you: anoint yourself again through good and devout devotion. You have again been worn out by prolonged fasting: washed again with tears and renewed by the anointing of devout devotion, return to your refreshment.

See with what merciful ordering help comes to meet you everywhere. You did not have, and it was given to you; you lost it, and it is restored to you. You are nowhere abandoned, so that you may know how greatly he who loves you loves you. He does not wish you to perish; and therefore he waits with such patience and mercifully permits you, if you wish, to restore again and again what you have so often lost through negligence. O how many have already perished who received these things with you, but did not deserve to receive them again with you after losing them. You are therefore loved more than all of them, because what is lost is restored to you so graciously, whereas it was so strictly denied to them when lost.

Has no grace for good works been given you? Yet, by his gift, a good will has not been denied you. If you perform great works, you are mercifully raised up; if you do not perform great works, perhaps you are beneficially humbled. He knows better than you what is expedient for you; and therefore, if you wish to think rightly of him, understand that all he does to you is done well. Perhaps you do not have the grace of virtues; but while you are shaken by the impulse of vices, you are more firmly established in humility. Humility in weakness gives God a sweeter fragrance than prideful virtue. Therefore do not dare to prejudge his ordering; but always pray to him with fear and reverence, that he may help you as he himself knows best. If any evils still remain in you, may he mercifully wash them away; if any good things have begun, may he graciously bring them to completion; and may he lead you to himself by whatever path he wills. [Col. 0967B]

What more shall I say to you? Is there anything still that we can say to show love? I speak to you, my soul: is there anything? What do you say? If you speak of what is yours, you will not be able to speak of what is another’s; if of what is another’s and yours, still not of everything. For who can say everything? And yet we know that love is the source of all things. Behold, two people are born: both have the same nobility of birth and the same hour of birth. One is left in poverty; the other is raised up in riches; and love works in both cases, because it humbles one by poverty and consoles the other by abundance. One is weak and the other strong. The latter is restrained lest he accomplish evil; the former is strengthened so that he may become capable of a good work. Love approves both; it does not reject them. One is enlightened through wisdom; the other is left in the simplicity of his own understanding. [Col. 0967C] Love wills to be present to both: to the one, that he may despise himself; to the other, that he may strive to know his Creator. Such is God’s love toward us; and human weakness endures nothing whatsoever that he, insofar as his goodness is concerned, does not order for our good.

## CONFESSION

I confess your mercies to you, Lord my God: how you have not abandoned me, sweetness of my life and light of my eyes. What shall I repay you for all that you have given me? (Ps. 115.) You wish me to love you; and how shall I love you? How greatly shall I love you? Who am I, that I should love you? Yet I shall love you, O Lord, my strength, my firm foundation, my refuge, [Col. 0967D] my deliverer, my God, my helper, my protector, the horn of my salvation, and my upholder—and how much more shall I say? You are the Lord my God (Ps. 17).

O my soul, what shall we do for the Lord our God, from whom we have received so many and such great goods? For he was not content to bestow upon us the same benefits as upon others: even in our evils we recognize him as a singular lover, so that we may love him singularly for all our goods as well as all our evils. You gave me, Lord, to know you and, above many others, to understand mysteries of yours revealed to me. You left other people of my own age in the darkness of ignorance and poured into me, above them, the light of your wisdom. You granted me to know you more truly, love you more purely, believe in you more sincerely, and follow you more ardently. You gave me a receptive mind, ready understanding, tenacious memory, eloquent tongue, pleasing speech, persuasive teaching, effectiveness in action, grace in conduct, progress in study, success in undertakings, consolation in adversity, caution in prosperity; and wherever I turned, your grace and mercy went before me everywhere.

You have done everything for me: often, when I seemed spent, you suddenly delivered me; when I wandered, you led me back; when I was ignorant, you taught me; when I sinned, you corrected me; when I was sad, you consoled me; when I despaired, you strengthened me; when I fell, you raised me; when I stood, you held me; when I went, you guided me; when I came, you received me. You have done all these things for me, Lord my God, and many others [Col. 0968B] of which it will always be sweet for me to think, always to speak, always to give thanks, so that I may praise and love you for all your benefits, Lord my God.

Behold, my soul, you have your pledge; and in your pledge you recognize your bridegroom. Keep yourself untouched for him; keep yourself unpolluted, whole, undefiled. If you were once a prostitute, you have now become a virgin, as his love is accustomed to restore integrity to those who have been corrupted and preserve chastity in those who are whole. Always consider how great a mercy he has shown you, and from this judge how greatly you are loved by him: you know that his benefit has never failed you.

**SOUL.** I truly confess that this love is rightly called singular: though it pours itself out upon many, it nevertheless embraces each person uniquely. Truly it is a beautiful and wondrous good, common to all and yet wholly possessed by each individual; presiding over all, filling individuals, present everywhere, caring for all, and nevertheless providing for each as though for all. When I consider his mercies toward me, it certainly seems to me that—if it is permissible to say so—God somehow does nothing except provide for my salvation. I see him so wholly occupied with guarding me as though he had forgotten everyone else and wished to attend to me alone. He always presents himself as present; he always offers himself as ready. Wherever I turn, he does not leave me; wherever I am, he does not withdraw; whatever I do, he stands beside me. Finally, that he is the continual observer of all my actions and thoughts, and, as far as his goodness is concerned, an inseparable co-worker, he plainly demonstrates by the very effect of his work. [Col. 0968D] Hence it is clear that, although his face cannot yet be seen by us, his presence can never be escaped.

I confess, however, that when I consider this more carefully, I am overwhelmed alike with fear and profound shame: I behold him whom I so ardently desire to please as present everywhere to me and seeing all my secrets. O how many things are in me for which I blush before his eyes, and because of which I now fear more that I may displease him than I trust that I can please him by those things in me that are praiseworthy—if there are any! Would that I might be hidden from his eyes for a little while, until I had wiped away all these stains, and then at last appear unspotted and without stain before his gaze! For how shall I be able to please him in this deformity, when I myself too am vehemently displeased by it? O ancient stains, O foul and ugly stains, why do you cling so long? Go away, depart, and presume no longer to offend the eyes of my beloved. Do not deceive yourselves: you will not remain with me forever, with his help, although you have not yet been expelled because of my sluggishness. I have sworn concerning you that I shall neither retain nor love you any longer, because I utterly detest and wholly abhor your ugliness. Henceforth, even if I could remain unseen by my Bridegroom, I would nevertheless not wish to be stained by you. How much less do I wish it now, since I lie open before him and since his offence grieves me more, certainly, than even my own ugliness. [Col. 0969B]

Depart, then. You cling to me henceforth in vain, because, even while remaining with me, you are not mine. I judge you alien to my allotted portion and wish henceforth to have no fellowship with you. I have another model to which I desire to conform, and I look continually to another; and, so far as I can, I increasingly draw likeness from it. From it, too, I have learned that I must expel you, and I now know how I shall do so.

**HUMAN BEING.** A remarkable thing is taking place between us—perhaps you do not marvel at it because you do not yet understand what I mean to say. I consider how, from the beginning of our conversation, you have brought forward many things that seemed contrary to love, and how through them the power of love has always been not weakened but more fully proved. You said that love could not be at once singular and common; but precisely from this it was proved still more wondrous, because it was shown to be both common and singular. Again, you said that you were not perfectly loved, because you had heard that you were chosen for preparation but had not yet seen yourself taken into the marriage chamber. Yet again, love toward you is shown to be so much greater inasmuch as, by its patience, your perfection awaits a greater fulfillment. Finally, you have now begun to doubt whether, in this deformity which you endure, though unwillingly, you can be loved by him. But when you doubted this, did you not remember that long ago you had been wholly foul and yet loved? If, therefore, he deigned to love you when you were wholly ugly and had no beauty at all, how much more will he love you now, when you have already begun to be adorned and to lay aside your former ugliness? For this also belongs to the praise of his love: that he deigns to love what is imperfect. Although he still sees certain things in you that do not please him, he nevertheless loves this very thing: that you too have already begun to hate in yourself what displeases him. [Col. 0970A] For he looks not so much at what you are as at what you intend; he considers not what you are, but what you wish to be—provided that you strive, as much as you can, to deserve to become what you have not yet begun to be.

**SOUL.** I ask you kindly to receive this final question of mine. What is that sweet thing which sometimes touches me in remembrance of him and affects me so powerfully and sweetly that I begin somehow to be taken wholly out of myself and drawn away I know not where? Suddenly I am renewed and wholly changed, and I begin to feel well beyond my power to describe. The conscience is made joyful; all the misery of former sorrows is forgotten; [Col. 0970B] the mind exults; the understanding becomes clear; the heart is enlightened; desires are delighted. And I see myself already elsewhere—I know not where—and as though I held something inwardly in the embraces of love. I do not know what it is, yet I strive with all my effort always to retain it and never to lose it. The mind struggles delightfully, as it were, lest it depart from that which it always desires to embrace; and, as though it had found in it the end of all desires, it exults supremely and beyond expression, seeking nothing further, desiring nothing more, wishing always to remain thus. Is that my beloved? I ask you, tell me, so that I may know whether it is he; and, if he comes to me again, I may beseech him not to depart but to remain always.

**HUMAN BEING.** He who visits you is indeed your beloved; but he comes invisibly, secretly, incomprehensibly. He comes to touch you, not to be seen by you; to remind you, not to be grasped by you; not to pour his whole self into you, but to offer himself to be tasted; not to satisfy desire, but to draw the affections. He presents certain first-fruits of his love, not the fullness of perfect satisfaction. And this above all pertains to the pledge of your betrothal: he who will give himself to be seen by you and possessed by you forever in the future now sometimes offers himself to you for tasting, so that you may know how sweet he is. At the same time, meanwhile, you may be consoled for his absence when you are continually refreshed by his visitation, lest you fail. I ask you, my soul: we have already said much. After all these things, know one, love one, follow one, lay hold of one, possess one.

**SOUL.** This I seek, this I desire, this I long for with all my heart.

[Col. 0969]

## ON THE PRAISE OF CHARITY

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 0969D]

To Peter, servant of Christ, from H.: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33).

[Col. 0970D] As I considered, dearest brother, how I might call your love to remembrance of me, it first occurred to me to write to you concerning love itself, [Col. 0971A] asking from you nothing other than the gift of that very love. Therefore I have done what I could: I have commended charity in such words as I was able, so that, while you read its praise, you may know how ardently I both love it in you and ask it from you. Nor ought your charity itself to be angry with me if, to its flame already burning strongly, I myself, though lukewarm, apply the small breath of my words—not so much that it may burn more fiercely as that it may recognize the endeavor of my desire toward it. Read, therefore, and love; and read what you read for love’s sake so that you may love. Everything is done from love: love sends, love receives, love is what is given, and love is what is repaid.

## ON THE PRAISE OF CHARITY
Charity is known to have had so many advocates already [Col. 0971B] that, if I should begin to say anything in its praise, it might perhaps seem presumption rather than devotion. For who among the saints has existed from the beginning of the world who did not commend charity to us either by word or by deed? Charity made Abel a martyr (Gen. IV); charity led Abraham out from his own land (Gen. XII): for the former, through charity, innocently endured death, and the latter, through charity, willingly abandoned his native soil; through charity each exchanged earth for heaven.

Charity alone, from the beginning, persuades the servants of God to flee the enticements of this world, to trample pleasures underfoot, to restrain the desire of the flesh, to break appetites, to despise honours, and finally to reject every allurement of this present life; indeed, for the sake of eternal life, it persuades them not [Col. 0971C] to fear even death itself. Paul had experienced this power of love when he said: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword? But I am persuaded that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, nor strength, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. VIII).

Accordingly, in the Song of Songs the bridegroom instructs the bride concerning the power of love, saying: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, set me as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell” (Cant. VIII). Death indeed destroys the living, while hell spares not even the dead [Col. 0971D]. Love, however, is strong as death, because, as death kills the sensation of the flesh, so love kills the inclination of fleshly desire. Jealousy is hard as hell, because it compels those whom desire for eternal things draws inwardly not only to reject outward blandishments, but also to endure every adversity and hardship in order to attain that which they love.

Let us consider how many martyrs have already passed through torments into the kingdom of heaven. What power of love, then, do we believe burned in those whom we see not sparing even themselves for God's sake? Let us consider what they left behind, what they followed, and by what way they passed. We see what they left; we do not see, but believe, what they followed; we have heard by what way they passed. They left temporal goods behind; they followed eternal goods [Col. 0972A]; they passed through torments. Let us now gather our heart together and see whether it is willing for us to leave all things of this world, neither to love nor to smile upon glory, honour, and riches; neither to delight in flattering prosperity nor to rejoice in happy circumstances. “Your eyes have seen my imperfection” (Ps. CXXXVIII). How far I see myself to be from this—not merely from perfection, but even from the beginning of perfection!

Yet certainly it was too little for the friends of God merely to despise and trample these things for love of eternal goods. Having cast all these aside, they ran eagerly toward their desire; they could be restrained neither by threats nor by torments. Charity drew them, and therefore greed did not draw them back, nor adversity frighten them. Thus they ran: they had left the world behind them and had God before them. But torments were interposed, so that it might be asked either with what desire they sought Him or with what constancy they had despised the world [Col. 0972B]. Truth was questioned, charity was tested, iniquity was confounded.

They approached punishment without fear; and as deeply as love had wounded the mind within, so greatly did the flesh outwardly despise its wounds. They came forward and passed through; and in dying they confessed that for which, while living, they had run in desire. O charity, how sweetly you tasted to them, how sweet you were to those whom you compelled to endure such things for your sake! With what bonds did you draw them to yourself—those whom the world, both drawing them back through blandishments and repelling them through torments, nevertheless could not destroy? They ran because you drew them; they passed through because you helped them; they arrived because you received them. How unquenchably you burned in their hearts [Col. 0972C], since neither insults nor rewards nor punishments could overwhelm you! These things overflowed like certain rivers, yet “many rivers and many waters could not extinguish charity.”

O charity, what shall I say of you? How shall I praise you? If I tasted you, I would value you; if I knew how great your worth is, I would weigh out a price for you. But perhaps you exceed my narrow limits, and I shall not be able to find your price within myself. Nevertheless, I shall give what I have; I shall give all that I have; I shall exchange for you the whole substance of my house. Everything in the dwelling-place of my body, everything in the dwelling-place of my heart, I shall give for you; when I have given everything, I shall account everything as nothing. All the pleasures of my flesh, all the delights of my heart, I shall gladly spend for you, so that I may be able to have you alone [Col. 0972D], to possess you alone.

You alone are dearer to me than all that is mine; you alone are more useful to me, you alone sweeter, you alone more delightful, giving greater delight, satisfying more abundantly, saving more safely, preserving more happily. I shall also proclaim you to others. Tell me, O human heart: which do you choose more—to rejoice always with this world, or to be always with God? What you love more, that you choose rather. Hear therefore, so that you may either correct your love or not delay your choice. If this world is beautiful, what do you think is the beauty where the Creator of the world is? Love, then, so that you may choose; love better, so that you may choose more healthfully. Love God, so that you may choose to be with God; therefore through love you choose.

But the more you love, the more swiftly you desire to arrive, and you hasten to grasp; therefore [Col. 0973A] through love you run and through love you grasp. Likewise, the more you love, the more eagerly you embrace; therefore through love you enjoy. See how love is everything to you: it is itself choice, it is itself running, it is itself arrival, it is itself abiding, it is itself blessedness. Therefore love God; choose God; run, grasp, possess, enjoy.

“But,” you say, “I have already chosen. By what way shall I run, so that I may arrive?” One runs to God by the way of God. “I cannot,” you say, “run an unfamiliar way alone; give me companions, lest I go astray.” Run along the way of God with those who run in it. You cannot have better companions on the way than those who long ago ran upon it, and who, through long experience of running and practice in labour, fear neither error nor failure.

“What then,” you ask, “is the way of God, and who are those running [Col. 0973B] upon it?” “The ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous shall walk in them.” Therefore justice is the way, and the righteous are those who run in the way. And lest it trouble you that I call them walkers and again call them runners: to walk swiftly is itself to run. So did he who said, “I ran in the way of your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII). And elsewhere: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (ibid.). Thus understand walking and running to be the same, lest he should call himself more blessed than the blessed if, while they walked, he himself ran.

You therefore have the way; you have companions on the way; you have an inheritance in your homeland; you have that by which you may go, those with whom you may go, and the place where you may rest. The way by which you go is justice. Those with whom you go are those who love and pursue justice. The place to which you arrive and in which you rest is both the author of justice and the fountain [Col. 0973C] of life. No way is straighter than justice; no fellowship better than the fellowship of the righteous; no rest more tranquil than God. Go on securely; go on swiftly, so that you may arrive quickly and rest happily. To go on quickly is to love ardently.

See, then, how your entire good depends upon charity. Through charity you choose the way; through charity you run the way; through charity you arrive at your homeland. Do you wish to know that you choose the way of justice only through charity? “If anyone loves me,” says the Lord, “he will keep my words” (John XIV). But elsewhere it is said of that word: “Your word is truth” (John XVII); and again the Psalmist says of it: “I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments” (Ps. CXVIII). If, therefore, the Lord’s word is truth [Col. 0973D], the way of truth is certainly chosen through that charity by which the Lord’s word is fulfilled. Therefore charity chooses the way of justice.

But is the way of justice not chosen without charity, and run without charity? Hear the same testimony of the Psalmist, which I mentioned above: “I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” (ibid.). For what is an enlarged heart except a heart burning with love, a heart filled with charity? The heart, therefore, is enlarged through charity; and with the heart enlarged, the way of justice is run. Thus through charity you choose; through charity you run; through charity you grasp and enjoy.

“God,” says the Apostle John, “is charity; and he who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him.” Whoever therefore has charity has God, possesses God, and abides in God [Col. 0974A] (I John IV). O good charity, through which we love God, choose God, run to God, arrive at God, and possess God! What more shall I say of you, charity? I have called you guide upon the way of God. And what if I were to call you the very way of God? Certainly, charity, you are the way.

Yet you are not a way as other ways are. “I will show you,” says the Apostle Paul, “a still more excellent way” (I Cor. XII). He spoke of you, O charity. For you are the surpassingly excellent way, the pre-eminent way, making crooked ways straight and showing straight ways. You are the head of straight ways: all straight ways go forth from you and return to you. For God’s commandments are His ways; they all depend upon you and subsist in you. You are the fullness of justice, the perfection of the law, the completion of virtue, the knowledge of truth.

Therefore you are a way, O charity. What kind of way? A surpassingly excellent way: receiving, directing, and leading onward. Whose way? The way of man to God, and the way of God to human beings [Col. 0974B]. O blessed way, which alone knows the exchange involved in our salvation! You bring God down to humanity; you direct humanity to God. He descends when He comes to us; we ascend when we go to Him. Yet neither He nor we can pass to the other except through you. You are mediator, reconciling opponents, joining those separated, and in some manner making equals of those so unequal. You humble God; you exalt us; you draw Him down to the lowest things and raise us to the highest.

Yet His descent is not abject but merciful, and our exaltation is not proud but glorious. Great, therefore, is your power, charity: you alone were able to draw God from heaven [Col. 0974C] to earth. O how strong is your bond, by which God could be bound and a bound human being broke the bonds of iniquity! I do not know whether I can say anything greater in your praise than that you drew God from heaven and raised humanity from earth to heaven. Great is your power: through you God was humbled to this extent, and humanity exalted to this extent.

I behold God born of a woman: an infant, wrapped in swaddling clothes, crying in a cradle, sucking at breasts. Then I see Him seized, bound, beaten with scourges, crowned with thorns, smeared with spittle, pierced by a lance, fastened with nails, given gall and vinegar to drink—there suffering indignities, here dreadful pains. Yet if we seek why He deigned to undergo the former or endured the latter, we find no cause other than charity alone [Col. 0974D].

O charity, how great is your power! If you have prevailed so greatly over God, how much more over human beings! If God endured such things for humanity, what will a human being refuse to endure for God? Yet perhaps you conquer God more easily than humanity; perhaps you have greater power over God than over humanity, because the more blessed one is, the more it owes to God to be conquered by you. You knew this very well: in order to conquer more easily, you first overcame Him. While we were still rebellious against you, you compelled Him, obedient to you, to descend from the throne of paternal majesty to assume the weakness of our mortality.

You brought Him bound by your bonds; you brought Him wounded by your arrows. This was further so that humanity might be ashamed to resist you when it saw that you had triumphed even over God. You wounded the impassible [Col. 0975A], bound the unconquerable, drew the immutable, and made the eternal mortal. You did all these things to soften our hard hearts and to pierce our insensible affections, so that they might free themselves from their torpor and your arrows might penetrate them more easily.

Nor did you do this in vain, for many have thus been conquered by you; many have now surrendered to you. Many now bear your arrows fixed in their hearts and desire that they be driven in yet deeper. For they have been wounded delightfully and sweetly; they neither grieve nor are ashamed that they have received your wounds. O charity, how great is your victory! You first wounded one, and through him afterward conquered all. O charity, I have praised you as much as I could; yet I consider deeply whether there may still be something more excellent that can be said in your praise [Col. 0975B]. For I do not know whether it is perhaps greater to call you God, or to say that you conquered God.

If the former is greater, I will gladly and confidently say even this of you: “God is charity, and he who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him” (I John IV). Hear, O human being, and do not any longer regard it as a small thing if you have charity: hear that God is charity. Is it a small thing to have God abiding within oneself? To possess charity is so great a thing, for God is charity. Charity alone has this privilege, that it is called and is God, so that this can belong to no other thing. For it is not said, “God is humility,” or “God is patience,” as it is said, “God is charity.” For although every virtue is God’s gift, none except charity has this, that it can be called not only God’s gift but also God.

Charity [Col. 0975C] is God’s gift because the Holy Spirit is given by God to the faithful; but it is God because that same Spirit is consubstantial in the same Godhead, and coeternal, with Him by whom He is given. God therefore bestows the remaining gifts of grace even on those whom He rejects, but charity—like His very self—He keeps as a reward only for those whom He loves. Charity, then, is a proper fountain from which an outsider does not share. For, as has been said, even those alienated from God by a reprobate life sometimes receive the other gifts of grace. But an evil person cannot have charity; whoever has it is no longer alienated from God, but himself abides in God, and God in him. Charity is so intimate with God that He Himself is unwilling to make His dwelling where charity is absent [Col. 0975D].

“If anyone loves me,” He says, “he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV). Therefore, if charity is with you, God comes to you and abides with you. If you withdraw from charity, He too withdraws from you and does not remain with you. If you have never had charity, God has never come to you nor dwelt with you. If you have abandoned charity once begun, God has departed from you. If you have persisted in charity once begun, God is with you and remains with you.

Charity heals every sickness of the soul; charity uproots the roots of every vice; charity is the origin of every virtue [Col. 0976A]. Charity enlightens the mind, cleanses the conscience, gladdens the soul, and reveals God. The soul in which charity dwells is not puffed up by pride, ravaged by envy, scattered by anger, troubled by evil sadness, blinded by avarice, inflamed by gluttony, or defiled by lust. It is always clean, always chaste, always tranquil, always joyful, always peaceful, always kindly, always modest; secure in adversities, restrained in prosperity; despising the world, loving God; making the goods of all its own through love, gladly sharing its own goods with all; not fearing poverty and not eagerly craving abundance.

The person in whom God’s charity is always thinks [Col. 0976B] of when he will arrive at God, when he will leave the world, when he will escape scandals, and when he will find true peace. His heart is always above, and his desire raised toward things above. Whether he walks, sits, works, or rests, whatever he does, his heart does not depart from God. When silent, he thinks of God; when speaking, he desires to speak of nothing except God and what pertains to love of God. By exhorting others to charity, he inflames himself and commends charity to all. By word and deed alike he shows everyone how sweet is the love of God, and how bitter and impure is love of this age.

He mocks the glory of this world, rebukes its anxiety, and shows how foolish it is to place confidence in things that pass away. He marvels at the blindness of people who love these things [Col. 0976C]; he wonders how everyone has not long since despised all these transient and perishable things. He thinks that what tastes sweet to him is sweet to all, that what he loves pleases all, and that what he knows is evident to all. By these signs charity reveals itself and distinguishes those in whom it dwells not only inwardly by their will but also outwardly by their manner of life.

So much has now been said about charity; and yet still more can be said about charity, and as much ought to be said as cannot be said. What, then, O good charity, O dear charity, can I say worthy of your praises? Surely, after the great praises of those before me, my littleness would presume to say nothing of you, if it were ever possible to say enough about you. Flow into us, therefore, O sweet and pleasant charity; enlarge our heart, expand our desire [Col. 0976D], stretch wide the bosom of our mind, and enlarge the dwelling-place of our heart, so that it may receive God as guest and abiding resident.

May our only Redeemer and Saviour, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, pour and spread you in our hearts through His Holy Spirit, so that He Himself with the Father may deign to come to us and make His dwelling in us—He who, with the same Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0977]

# ON THE MANNER OF PRAYING

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0977A]

To the lord and most beloved father H.: I pray that you receive this small gift of my affection with that kindness with which I know that I have offered it in devotion. I have sent to your charity a short discourse on the power of prayer, composed in an unpolished style. In it you have set out distinctly the ways in which the mind of one praying is kindled to compunction amid the words of prayers; and it is also shown why, when we are praying for our own salvation or that of others, we recite Scriptures which have no form of petition. Therefore I have written about prayer in order to ask for prayer. Since, through a long devotion to piety, you have now tasted its sweetness more perfectly, you ought all the more gladly both to receive the gift and [Col. 0977B] to bestow the gift. Farewell.

## CHAPTER I. That, from considering our own misery and God’s mercy, we ought to be stirred to pray to God

From our misery together with His mercy we can discern with what zeal and disposition God ought to be prayed to by us. For what could more effectively stir a person to eagerness in prayer than the misery and calamity of the many evils by which he is afflicted? And what could more pleasantly draw him toward the fulfilment of prayer than the mercy of his Creator, which he experiences so often amid his evils? Therefore, lest the human mind be sluggish in praying, it is compelled by its need; but lest it pray trembling and distrustfully, it is summoned by God’s loving-kindness.

Prayer is raised on these two wings: namely, human misery and the mercy [Col. 0977C] of the Redeemer. For while the mind continually stirs itself to devotion by alternating consideration of these, it flies upward, lifted by a certain impetus of spiritual desire. Holy meditation is thus necessary to prayer, so that prayer cannot be wholly perfect unless meditation accompanies or precedes it. For those who neglect to consider their evils are easily deceived through ignorance, either by asking for nothing or by asking for something other than what is fitting; or else, through sloth, they grow lukewarm by asking less worthily than they should.

First, then, it is necessary that, if we wish to pray to the Lord wisely and profitably, we exercise our mind by constant meditation and learn, in considering our misery, what it is necessary for us [Col. 0977D] to ask; and, in considering the mercy of our God, with what desire we ought to ask. Let us consider how brief our life is, how slippery its path, how uncertain death. Let us consider that we entered this life grieving, pass through it in pain, and shall leave it in mourning. Let us consider with how many bitter things even whatever sweet or pleasant thing presents itself to us upon the path of this life is mingled; [Col. 0978A] how deceptive, suspect, unstable, and transitory is everything brought forth by love of this world, everything promised by temporal appearance and beauty.

Some evils are those with which we are born and from which, as time progresses, we are delivered either by God’s hidden grace or by manifest effort. Others, however, come with us into this life and do not depart from us before death. Still other evils grow upon us over time and again pass away as time runs its course. Others we contract after birth and do not shed before death. And who could enumerate all the evils of this life? For, to pass over the evils that oppress all people alike, what are we to think of the secret dangers of individuals, of which each is conscious within himself? If anyone [Col. 0978B] wishes to consider what evils he has done and endured from his earliest age, and sets before his eyes the past seasons and days of his life, and carefully considers how many vain labours he has borne, how often he has toiled in vain for the love of this life, how often he has found deceptive outcomes in laborious undertakings, and how, after long courses, he has not yet obtained any rest, he will know what judgment he can make concerning this life.

But when he considers the wretchedness of this life, let him also attend to the sweetness and delight of the heavenly homeland, and weigh what he has found and what he has lost, where he lies and from where he has fallen, so that from both he may understand how greatly he ought to mourn in this exile. Hence Solomon says: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. I), because the more a person understands his evils, the more deeply [Col. 0978C] he sighs and groans.

Finally, it remains that, amid the remembrance of our evils, we also recall God’s mercy, because we seek His future compassion more confidently if we consider how He has had mercy on us in the past. Let us call to mind the goods He has granted, and how He has often mercifully delivered us when we stood in dangers; how He was never overcome by our sins so as to cease showing mercy; how He reminded those forgetful of Him about Himself, called back those turned away from Him, kindly received those coming to Him, pardoned penitents, guarded those who persevered, sustained those standing, raised those who had fallen, changed evil pleasures into bitterness, and yet afterward bestowed His consolations upon those beneficially made bitter.

Finally, He restored perfect rest and peace to those cleansed by tribulation: He who was never absent even from sinners, in order to correct them, nor from the righteous, in order to guard them [Col. 0978D]. Whoever has exercised his mind with meditations of this sort before the time of prayer comes to prayer perhaps neither unprepared nor lukewarm. For constant meditation produces knowledge; knowledge once acquired drives out ignorance and produces compunction; compunction once acquired puts sloth to flight and produces devotion; and devotion perfects prayer.

Knowledge is when a person is enlightened to self-knowledge. Compunction is when, from consideration of his evils, the heart is touched by inward sorrow. Devotion is a pious and humble disposition toward God, generated from compunction [Col. 0979A]. For the mind, terrified by the greatness of its evils and despairing of its own powers, turns itself to God. And it seeks His protection all the more ardently as it more plainly sees that nothing outside God remains to it in which it can trust.

Devotion, therefore, is a turning toward God in a pious and humble disposition. It is humble because of awareness of one’s own weakness; it is pious because of consideration of divine mercy. It contains within itself the three principal virtues: faith, hope, and charity. For a person would not turn himself to God through devotion unless he believed that he could be saved by Him and hoped that He wished to show mercy. Finally, unless he loved Him more than his evils, he would never flee from them and choose refuge for himself in Him. He therefore believes, hopes, and loves. He believes in power, hopes for mercy, and loves protection.

Prayer, then, is nothing other than devotion of mind: that is, a turning toward God through a pious and humble disposition, supported by faith, hope, and charity. But since the mind is kindled to devotion in many ways, and devotion itself of mind is expressed in speech in various ways, we ought to distinguish separately certain kinds of prayer, so that we may more clearly indicate its power.

## CHAPTER II. On the three kinds of prayer and the classes of supplication

[Col. 0979C]

There are three kinds of prayer: supplication, petition, and insinuation. Supplication is a humble and devout entreaty without a specified request. Petition is a stated request accompanied by an indeterminate narration. Insinuation is the making known of one’s wish, without a request, through narration alone.

There are three classes of supplication: winning favor (*captatio*), insistence (*exactio*), and pure prayer. Winning favor (*captatio*) is what is done before petition in order to prepare and incline the hearer’s mind; and we do this in three ways. First, when we say something that commends our person or cause, whether by enumerating our merit, our weakness, or something else that can commend our cause or person to the one before whom we lay our petition. The second mode of *captatio* is when we set forth something in praise of the one to whom we pray, thereby signifying that he is dear and pleasing to our mind, so that through our charity we may in turn deserve his love. The third mode of *captatio* is when we say something that lowers the cause or person of our adversary in the hearer’s mind, so that it may appear worthy of hatred rather than love. *Captatio* is effected in these three ways.

Holy Scripture most frequently uses this class of supplication. For this is what we do wherever we sing God’s praises, wherever we recite our weakness, or wherever we recount the wickedness of our adversaries; indeed, whenever, before stating a petition [Col. 0980A], we utter whatever is worthy of God’s ears and suited to our need.

Insistence (*exactio*) is what is usually done after a petition has been made, when, lest our petition fall into the hearer’s forgetfulness, we make him remember it frequently with a kind of—so to speak—importunity and insistence. This remembrance seems to be renewed in three ways: namely, when we repeatedly say something either about his person, our own person, or our cause, by which we renew in his mind either ourselves, our cause, or our petition. This class of supplication is as importunate in the sight of human beings as it is pleasing and praiseworthy before God.

Pure prayer is when, from an abundance of devotion, the mind is kindled so greatly that, after turning to God in order to make a request, it forgets even its own petition through the greatness of its love; and while it vehemently longs to enjoy the One whom it sees through love, and now desires to attend wholly to Him, it gladly postpones concern even for the matter for which it came [Col. 0980B]. This kind of praying is the ideal; and as it is unique above all the others, so it is more precious with God than all the rest.

Among these three classes of supplication, *captatio* holds the lowest place, *exactio* the middle, and pure prayer the highest and most excellent. For *captatio* contains fear, *exactio* confidence, and pure prayer perfect love.

It should also be known that supplication is sometimes made through names alone, as in: “My mercy, my refuge, my protector, my deliverer, my God, my helper” (Ps. CXLIII). Sometimes it is made through verbs alone, as in: “Look,” “have mercy,” “be appeased,” “give heed,” and “act.” Sometimes it is made through names and verbs together, as in: “Give ear to my words, O Lord; understand my cry. Attend to the voice of my prayer, my King and my God” (Ps. V).

But that class of supplication which is made through names alone is, the more imperfect it is in outward expression, the more full it is inwardly of an abundance of love [Col. 0980C]. For this is characteristic of affection: the greater and more fervent it is inwardly, the less it can be expressed outwardly by speech. The class of supplication expressed by verbs alone indicates less devotion than this one, but more than the kind pronounced by names and verbs together, with full expression of meaning. Therefore, what is done by names alone seems to belong to pure prayer; what is done by verbs alone, to *exactio*; and what is done by names and verbs together, to *captatio*. Thus pure prayer is more transformed into jubilation, draws near to God, arrives more swiftly, and obtains more effectively.

[Col. 0980D]

## CHAPTER III. What petition and insinuation are

Petition is a stated request accompanied by an indeterminate narration, as in: “Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit in my inward parts” (Ps. L). It is made in three ways: by entreating, by asking, and by simply requesting. Entreaty is when a more pressing necessity compels one to persist more devoutly in prayers. In moderate matters we ask; in very small matters we simply request. These three, therefore, have their distinctions: adjuring is the highest, asking the middle, and simply requesting the lowest.

Insinuation is the making known of one’s wish without a request, through narration alone [Col. 0981A]. This too is made in three ways: through fear, confidence, and contempt. It is made through fear when either the cause that we pursue is great or the person whom we ask is great, as in: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (John XI). For she wished to ask that the Lord raise her dead brother; but because she was afraid on account of the greatness of the matter and reverence for the person, she chose rather to insinuate than to petition. “Lord,” she says, “if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” She said that from which her wish might be understood, but presumption not censured, so that, if she were not heard, she might not suffer the disgrace of refusal, while, if she were heard, she might obtain the fulfilment of her wish.

Insinuation is made through confidence when we trust either in the ease [Col. 0981B] of the matter or in the goodwill of the person, and therefore neglect to express our desire openly because we hope that by insinuation alone we can obtain it. Such is the saying which the Lord’s mother makes at the wedding when the wine fails: “They have no wine” (John II). She did not say: “I ask you to supply the deficiency of the cup by creating or changing wine”; rather, she judged that the privilege due to maternal reverence was such that whatever she indicated she wished, even by hinting, ought not to be refused by her Son.

This indeed would have been just had she asked of Him something that He could do according to the nature which He bore as received from her. But now she is in some manner rightly rebuked, because she was demanding miraculous obedience from the nature that she had not given. And He says to her: “What have I to do with you, woman?” (ibid.) [Col. 0981C]. For to work a miracle is the power of God, not of a human being. Therefore, when Christ as man is asked by His mother for a miracle, the same Christ—as God rather than as man—accuses the woman, not the mother, of presumption. Mary, therefore, ought not to demand a miracle of Christ as a mother from a son, but—as a woman, if need required—to ask it humbly from God.

Insinuation is made through contempt when either the matter is trivial or the person asked is humble. This is wholly excluded from divine prayer, but among human beings is practised with great eagerness especially by the proud and powerful. And, as we have shown in the cases above, so also in these three we find a distinction. Insinuation through confidence is fitting for the perfect, through fear for beginners, and through contempt for the wicked [Col. 0981D]. The remaining matters which we proposed to discuss concerning prayer must next be added.

## CHAPTER IV. Why, when praying, we sometimes read matters in which no words of petition are expressed.

Some people are indeed troubled by the fact that, in our prayers, when we wish to ask God for either our own salvation or that of others, we are accustomed at times to chant even psalms which either contain no words of petition or do not pertain to the petition we are making. They raise a similar objection concerning other Scriptures which we frequently use in prayer, when such passages either do not have the form of prayer or do not accord with the matter we are pursuing. “For what good,” they say, “does it do in prayer [Col. 0982A] to utter words in which we are found either to ask nothing from God or to ask something other than what is necessary? He does not pray, but rather mocks and provokes God to anger, who, having come before His presence as though to make a request, suddenly turns aside to repeat other matters which seem irrelevant.”

“See,” they say, “we wish to entreat God for forgiveness of our sins. What good does it do us for this purpose if we chant either ‘Why did the nations rage?’ (Psalm II), or ‘Give ear, O my people’ (Psalm LXXVII), or another psalm of this kind? Is it not ridiculous to suppose that we are praying while singing such things?”

Some perhaps say and think that there is no usefulness whenever we mingle such matters with our prayers. But whoever carefully considers the aforesaid kinds of prayer will readily discern how such words too can be effective when spoken in prayers. For this manner of praying is often found more efficacious for obtaining what is sought than even that in which those who pray explicitly express the form of their request. And although, as we have said, this may be understood clearly enough from what has been mentioned above, yet if it is specially demonstrated here, what follows except that the truth becomes still more evident?

There is this difference between praying to a human being and praying to God: a human being cannot know our need unless informed by another, whereas God knows, even before He is asked, what we need. Therefore, the human being who is asked is instructed by our account, so that he may know what we want; he is moved by our supplication, so that he may grant what we ask. But in prayer made to God [Col. 0982C], an account is not necessary—unless perhaps a person recounts matters in order better to understand his own petition, so that, reminded by his own narration, he may consider what he asks, and, stirred by consideration of his petition, pray more devoutly.

Certainly, so far as God is concerned, supplication alone is sufficient; for, as we have said, God need not be instructed in order to know, but He must be entreated in order to grant. Yet in no other way is God more quickly bent toward granting than when the mind of the one praying turns wholly toward Him with the full affection of devotion. Therefore, whatever the words of one who prays may be, they are not inappropriate if they can suitably be uttered for this purpose alone: either to stir the affection of the one praying to the love of God, or—what is greater—to show that, already aflame with His love, the affection has been stirred.

They show this [Col. 0982D] not in order to instruct God, as though He did not know our hidden things, but so that, while we express outwardly our inward desire, we ourselves may be inflamed the more to love by our very words. Devotion of heart alone, then, could suffice as far as God is concerned, were prayer not also formed in speech in order to kindle the mind of the one praying to greater devotion. For, as we have said, if narration is inserted into a petition, God is not instructed, but the one praying is reminded to consider what he asks, in order to pray more devoutly. If, however, there is supplication alone, because it signifies that devotion is within the heart, it inflames the mind to greater devotion.

But because human affection is aroused to the love of God in diverse ways, it is now pleasing to distinguish those modes one by one [Col. 0983A], and, once distinguished, to demonstrate them by examples.

## CHAPTER V. By what three principal ways the affection of those who pray is stirred toward God

First, however, it must be understood that nearly all this kind of praying—which seems to some to be wholly excluded from the practice of prayer—belongs to captatio, the winning of favour. Although above we reckoned this captatio as a kind of supplication, yet in a broader customary sense we seek to win favour not only by supplicating but also by requesting and by insinuating.

In captatio the goodwill of the hearer is obtained. This occurs in three ways: either when we say something in praise of him, or when we recall something concerning our own misery, or when [Col. 0983B] we bring forward something that pertains to the humiliation of our adversaries.

Let us say, therefore, that all those Scriptures which some consider should not be employed in prayer ought usefully to be recited by those who pray, and may fittingly be recited among the vows of our prayers, because they stir within us the affection of devout piety. By recounting the praise of God, they provoke our heart to His love; by recalling our misery, they humble us before His presence; by heightening the wickedness of our adversaries, they give us a salutary concern and greater confidence before Him.

We know the praise of God in His power and goodness; our misery in the fact that we are frail and sinful; and the wickedness of our adversaries in that they are cunning to plunder and impious to oppress. Therefore, whether we who pray recall the praise of God in His goodness and power, our own misery in our weakness and guilt, or the wickedness of our adversaries in their tyranny and cunning, for the exercise of the mind and the increase of good devotion, we do nothing unsuitable. Through the devout affection which these very words stir in us, we are praying everywhere.

For, to embrace everything briefly: whenever we recount the praise of God, whatever the words may be and however lengthy, what does our heart inwardly say through them all except this one thing: that, admiring Him, it loves Him, and loving Him, it admires Him? Likewise, when in prayer we speak before Him concerning our misery [Col. 0983D], whatever the words may be and however lengthy, what does our heart say in them except this one thing: that we confess that we seek His mercy and place all our confidence in Him? The nearer this devotion is to humility, the more acceptable it is to God.

Again, when in our prayers we accuse before God the wickedness of our adversaries, whatever the words may be and however lengthy, what else do we ask through all these things except the just judgment of God for our deliverance: that He may rescue us from those by whose tyranny we are unjustly oppressed and whose wickedness we justly abhor? And because we willingly leave vengeance upon our enemies and judgment in our cause to God’s decision, what is there that we ought not justly to obtain from God because of this [Col. 0984A] humility and devotion?

Therefore, whenever anyone chants psalms or any other Scriptures in prayer, let him carefully consider which affection they serve, and with all his strength stir his heart toward that affection to which he sees what he says to pertain most. For if he possesses the affection of the words he utters, through that very affection he will better know the force of the words and receive understanding; and through understanding the words he will kindle his affection to greater devotion.

## CHAPTER VI. How pleasing to God is the fervent affection of one who prays

How greatly a good affection of heart pleases God is shown even by human custom, although it is corrupt, through a certain imitation of virtue. We certainly see how flatterers pretend devotion toward those from whom they seek something. Often they go to meet them as they approach; they honour them, when standing amid a crowd, with pompous greetings; they prepare the way for them when they wish to pass; they tell others to make room; they cry out that their masters are coming; they set chairs in the midst, spread cushions, and fall at their feet.

They recount the great deeds of ancient forefathers; even if they find nothing in them to praise, they turn the deeds of predecessors to the praise of those persons.
