They not only say but swear that they are devoted and faithful; and what they do not wish to be, they labour by every effort to appear to be. Do you suppose that they could rightly be censured if they were what they are not, but pretend to be? If it were evil to be such as they are, why do they strive so zealously to appear such? Indeed, if they were what they pretend to be and are not, they would truly be praiseworthy. And for no other reason is their petition often rejected by human beings than because they are known not to be what they pretend to be.

If, therefore, they are rightly rejected in their petitions because they are known not to be what they pretend to be, then, in order that we may deserve to receive from God what we ask, let us strive truly to present ourselves to God as they pretend to be. Let us show outwardly in words that inwardly we have toward God an affection of devotion. And let us not only show it, but possess what we show. Otherwise, if we only show it, we shall be not true lovers but flatterers; and because we cannot deceive God by display [Col. 0984D], we deceive ourselves instead.

Moreover, just as flatterers first offer simulated devotion and by it seek to gain the favour of those whom they entreat, so let us anticipate the face of the Lord with our prayers; and, that we may deserve to obtain what we ask, let us offer not simulated devotion but true charity. Let us call blessed the friends of our Lord; let us be indignant at His enemies; let us praise His power, magnify His mercy, admire His wisdom, exalt His nobility, approve His justice.

Likewise, let us recount to Him our misery, make known to Him our need, make known and reveal to Him our weakness, confess our guilt to Him, say and believe that there is no other through whom [Col. 0985A] we can be rescued or through whom we hope to be delivered. Likewise, let us show Him the wickedness, cruelty, injustice, and tyranny of our adversaries—the demons and perverse human beings: that those who persecute us oppose Him; that those who contradict Him are hostile to us; that we hate what He hates and love what He loves; that we would rather suffer for His sake the hatred of His enemies than have peace with them against Him.

Therefore, all Scriptures of this kind which are suitable for winning favour—whether that captatio is effected by supplication, request, or insinuation—must not be considered alien to the practice of prayer. For although some of their narratives contain no petition, all nevertheless contain affections [Col. 0985B] of virtue which they kindle in us, and through which those who pray obtain more swiftly than through a vocal petition.

## CHAPTER VII. On the various modes of affection, and the psalms suited to each

Since, therefore, all the power of prayer lies in affections of piety, let us enumerate a few of them and demonstrate them by examples. For although we cannot enumerate them all—for affections are infinite—we may nevertheless infer from some of them what is praiseworthy and acceptable to God in all.

There is an affection of love, when the mind, perhaps seeing or remembering what it loves, is suddenly seized by the fire of love. There is an affection of admiration, when, contemplating something new and wonderful, it is stirred to astonishment. There is an affection of congratulatory joy, when, seeing something welcome and pleasing, it is suffused with a certain gladness. There is an affection of humility, when, from consideration of its own weakness, it voluntarily restrains itself from self-exaltation. There is an affection of sorrow, when, from consideration of its evils, it somehow wastes away and grows weak. There is an affection of fear, when it is shaken by consideration of impending punishments. There is an affection of indignation, when it is inflamed into hatred of adversaries by the very magnitude of their injustice. There is an affection of zeal, when, from love of justice, it is kindled to desire vengeance. There is an affection of good confidence, when, from some new and singular confidence, it is encouraged more than usual to avenge something.

Of these affections, the first three belong especially [Col. 0985D] to that kind of Scripture in which praise is offered. For from recalling goodness arises an affection of love; from recalling power and strength arises an affection of admiration; and from recalling some prosperous event or happy deed arises an affection of rejoicing. The following three belong to the kind in which misfortune and misery are recalled. The affection of humility arises from recalling one’s own weakness; the affection of grief arises from recalling present evils or remembering past ones; the affection of fear, from foreseeing future ones.

The last three affections suit more closely that kind of Scripture in which invective and accusation against adversaries are made: indignation, namely, against their wickedness [Col. 0986A]; zeal against their injury; and greater confidence in God’s mercy because of their malice.

These are examples of each. From an affection of love is sung the psalm: “I will love you, O Lord” (Psalm XVII). From an affection of admiration is sung the psalm: “O Lord, our Lord” (Psalm VIII). From an affection of rejoicing is sung the psalm: “All nations” (Psalm XLVI). In all these there is praise.

From an affection of humility is sung the psalm: “In you, O Lord, I have hoped” (Psalm XXX). From an affection of grief is sung the psalm: “How long, O Lord, will you forget?” (Psalm XII). From an affection of fear is sung the psalm: “O Lord, not in your fury” (Psalm VI). In all these there is supplication mingled with complaint.

From an affection of indignation is sung the psalm: “Why do you boast in wickedness?” (Psalm LI). From an affection of zeal is sung the psalm: “God, Lord of vengeances” (Psalm XCIII). From an affection of good confidence is sung the psalm: “Judge me, O Lord, because…” (Psalm XXV), etc.

## CHAPTER VIII. That in the same psalm there is often a transition from one affection to another

Yet it must be understood that this is not characteristic of all psalms, namely that a single affection runs through their whole course. Often there is a transition from one affection to another, according as the minds of those who pray are customarily affected in diverse ways. To explain how this may be recognized in each individual psalm would require the treatment of a longer work. Nevertheless, we wish to demonstrate it in a few cases by way of example.

Perhaps I begin to consider how great is the happiness of being with God, how great likewise is the misery of living in this world, and finally how great the calamity of being perpetually tormented in hell. From this meditation, suddenly drawn by love of the heavenly homeland, and led by that very affection, I run into these words: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the wicked” (Psalm I). If we inquire into the whole sequence of this psalm according to the inward sense of compunction, what do we find it saying everywhere except this: Happy are those who have never withdrawn from God; happy are those who have always remained with Him; happy are those who have persevered faithful and devoted in His service.

For unhappy and miserable are those who have removed themselves from Him and have not wished to persevere with Him, or who afterward have not returned to Him. Thanks be to Him for however long I have remained; shame to me for however long I have departed [Col. 0986D]. Now, however near I am, I do not wish to withdraw; however far away I am, I desire to return. Would that I might reach Him; would that I might never depart from Him: “Help me, my God” (Psalm CVIII). This, then, is an affection of love arising from praise.

Again, an example of another affection. I considered within myself how great God’s power is, and then I began to marvel at the madness of human beings, who are mortal and yet do not at all fear to oppose His will. Compelled by this admiration, I cried out and said: “Why did the nations rage?” (Psalm II). This is admiration mingled with indignation: we marvel at their madness and are indignant at their presumption.

Or, certainly, when we see within ourselves the frequent and importunate assaults of vices from without, yet inwardly place confidence in God’s help, we rebuke the very distress of our temptations with a certain indignation, saying: “Why did the nations rage?” And the whole point of the psalm tends to this: strengthened through God’s power, we may despise insolent adversities and may confidently reckon ourselves stronger than our adversaries in proportion as we are nearer to God. Let us attend to their swift destruction. Let us set God’s magnificence against their pride, which must be broken. With all reverence let us always subject our mind to His service, admiring His power above us and despising their insolence below us. This is an affection of admiration mingled with indignation, arising from praise.

The course of the following psalm is not woven according to one affection, but often passes from affection to affection [Col. 0988A]. For example: placed in straits (Psalm III), I begin to consider how greatly I have always trusted in God’s mercy; yet, because I see myself in some manner abandoned by Him, I burst forth from an affection of grief into these words: “O Lord, how many are they who trouble me! Many rise up against me” (ibid.). Then, returning from an affection of grief to an affection of good confidence, I say: “But you, O Lord, are my protector” (ibid.), so that I may relieve sorrow through confidence and restrain confidence through sorrow.

And who can, by speaking, enumerate all the powers of the psalms, all those fiery compunctions of holy affections, by which the mind is kindled in prayer and a sacrifice most pleasing to God is offered upon the altar of the heart?

[Col. 0987]

## ON THE BRIDEGROOM’S LOVE FOR THE BRIDE

[Col. 0987B] “I will go by myself to the mountain of myrrh and to the hills of Lebanon, and I will speak to my bride” (Song of Songs IV).

A certain bridegroom speaks here, who has a bride and promises that he will visit her. Observe, therefore, that this bridegroom is not always at home. For he perhaps guards against his love becoming cheap, and because it would sooner become wearisome if he were always present, he sometimes withdraws himself and sometimes departs for a time, so that, while he is sought in absence, he may be held more closely in presence. Perhaps he was absent when he said these things. But lest a longer delay should somehow produce forgetfulness, he planned to return and said: “I will go for myself.”

He speaks with himself about what he will do, because it is sweet to speak of what is sweet to do, and, I know not how, we are never weary of speaking of what we greatly desire. “I will go,” he says, “by myself” [Col. 0987C]. He goes by himself because singular love admits no partner to its secret. He goes by himself because he does not wish for a companion on the journey—he who allows no companion in love.

But you ask: who is this bridegroom, and who is his bride? The bridegroom is God; the bride is the soul. The bridegroom is at home when he fills the mind through inward joy; he departs when he withdraws the sweetness of contemplation.

But in what sense is the soul called God’s bride? A bride, because she has been given the earnest of gifts of grace; a bride, because she is joined to Him by chaste love; a bride, because through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit she is to be made fruitful with offspring of virtues. There is no soul that has not received an earnest from this bridegroom. But one earnest is common, another special.

The common earnest is that we are born, that we perceive, that we understand, that we discern. The special earnest is that we have been regenerated, that we have obtained remission of sins, that we have received the charisms of virtues. Whatever each person has is an earnest given to that person. Wealth is an earnest to the rich person, by which he is sustained lest the hardship of poverty break him. [Col. 0988B] Poverty is an earnest to the poor person, by which he is disciplined lest, in abundance, he overflow into incontinence. Strength is an earnest to the strong person, by which he is fortified so as to prevail for a good work. Weakness is an earnest to the weak person, by which he is restrained lest he accomplish evil. Simplicity is an earnest to the foolish person, by which he is humbled lest he grow proud.

Indeed, whatever human frailty endures in this life, the merciful Creator, insofar as His goodness is concerned, dispenses it either for the correction of perversity or for the advancement of virtue. Therefore we ought to give thanks in all things, so that, recognizing His mercy everywhere, we may always advance in His love.

“I will go by myself to the mountain of myrrh,” he says, etc. Myrrh, which is bitter to taste and preserves dead bodies from decay, signifies the mortification of the flesh. Lebanon, whose name means “whitening,” signifies purity of the flesh. This, then, is the way by which the Bridegroom comes to the bride: the mountain of myrrh and the hills of Lebanon. First, by abstinence, He kills the desire of the flesh; then, by purity of heart, He wipes away the mind’s ignorance. Finally, as though on the third day, the Bridegroom comes to converse and kindles the soul with desire for Himself.

Therefore he fittingly said “mountain of myrrh,” not “hill of myrrh,” and “hills,” not “mountain of Lebanon”: because in affliction we ought to be steadfast, and in the success of virtues humble. For the height of a mountain signifies the eminence of magnanimity, while the moderate elevation of a hill signifies the restraint of humility. Again, his use of “mountain” in the singular and “hills” in the plural signifies that in mortifying outward pleasure, little is what we lose, while in the inward illumination of the mind, manifold is the good that we find.

On the mountain of myrrh we receive strength against the flesh’s desire. On the hills of Lebanon we receive illumination of mind against ignorance. In the Bridegroom’s conversation [Col. 0989A] we receive charity against ill will and hardness of heart. Power is appropriated to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and charity to the Holy Spirit. For when we sin through frailty, we sin against the Father, as though against power. When we sin through ignorance, we sin against the Son, as though against wisdom. But when we sin through ill will, we sin against the Holy Spirit, as though against love.

Therefore, sinning against the Father and the Son is forgiven either here or in the future. For one who sins through frailty or ignorance has some excuse in guilt and should accordingly have some remission in punishment: either in this age, if he repents, so that he may obtain pardon more easily; or in the future age, if he persists in evil, so that he may experience a more tolerable punishment.

But the sin of those who sin from malice has no excuse. Therefore their punishment ought not to have remission: whether they repent in this age, they must be punished by full satisfaction; or, if they do not repent, they must be punished by full condemnation in the future age. Thus such persons receive remission neither here nor in the future age—not because pardon is denied to those who repent, but because full retribution is due to complete sin.

“I will speak,” he says, “to my bride.” God speaks to the soul in two ways: one way to the harlot, another to the bride; one way to the ugly, another to the beautiful; one way to the sinful woman, another to the justified. He rebukes the ugliness of the former; he praises the beauty of the latter [Col. 0989C]. By rebuking, he shakes the former with fear; by praising, he kindles the latter to love. He speaks to the former when he shows her her stains; to the latter when he recalls to her memory the gifts he has bestowed upon her. He enlightens the former’s darkness, so that she may recognize what she is and mourn what she has done; he touches the latter with the affection of inward sweetness, so that she may recall what she has received and not forget him who gave it.

“I will speak,” he says, “to my bride.” If I am the Bridegroom, if I have spoken to the bride, know that I can speak of nothing except love. Therefore, after the bridegroom had said these things within himself, he immediately set out; and, coming and seeing the bride, he was at once, as it were, drawn into admiration by her appearance and burst forth in these words: “You are wholly beautiful, my nearest one” (ibid.) [“You are wholly fair, [Col. 0989D] my friend,” etc.], etc. Or this may be joined to what precedes: “I will speak to my bride,” namely thus: “You are wholly beautiful, my nearest one,” etc. But the following is more pleasingly understood: “You are wholly beautiful, my nearest one”; therefore wholly beautiful because nearest. If you were not nearest, you would not be wholly beautiful.

See what he said: “You are wholly beautiful, my nearest one.” Every soul is either turned away from God or turned toward God. Of those turned away, one is distant and another most distant. Of those turned toward him, one is near and another nearest. She who is distant is indeed ugly, but not wholly so. She who is most distant is wholly ugly. Likewise, she who is near is beautiful, but not yet wholly so; she who is nearest is wholly beautiful. “You are wholly beautiful, my nearest one, and there is no stain in you” (ibid.). He is wholly beautiful in whom nothing of beauty is lacking. He is wholly beautiful in whom nothing ugly is present. I am wholly beautiful, because everything beautiful is in me. You are wholly beautiful because nothing ugly is in you. “There is no stain in you.”

“Come to Lebanon [from Lebanon], beautiful one.” He invites and calls her because he came to her not to remain with her, but to draw her to himself. “Come to Lebanon, come to Lebanon; you shall come [come], you shall be crowned” (ibid.). By inviting twice he says, “Come”; the third time, affirming, he adds, “You shall come.” But what is this affirmation except rejoicing, by which he rejoices in our good purpose? As though he said: I praise obedience; I do not fail to recognize the devotion you have purposed for God. I call and you answer; I invite and you are ready. Therefore you shall come.

But why does he say twice, “Come”? So that one who is outside himself [Col. 0990B] may first return to himself, and one who is within himself may ascend above himself. First, it is within us and warns transgressors to return to their heart; then it is above us, inviting the justified to himself. “Come,” he says, “come. Come from outside into yourself. Come from within, more inwardly, and indeed most inwardly, above yourself to me. Come to Lebanon, bride; come to Lebanon. Come from Lebanon; come to Lebanon. Come from Lebanon made white, to Lebanon not made white but white. Come from a cleansed heart to the cleanser of hearts, not cleansed but clean. You will not reach me if you remain in yourself: ascend above yourself and you will find me. You shall come, and you shall pass to Mount Seir, or Savir” (ibid.).

Seir is interpreted “bristly” or “hairy.” Savir, however, means “night-bird” or “stench”; and Seir is the same as Edom, that is, Esau. Esau and Jacob were two brothers [Col. 0990C]: Esau was born first, but was afterward supplanted by Jacob, who was born later. Esau was a hunter and devoted to rural pursuits; Jacob, a simple man, lived at home. What, then, do these two brothers signify except the two impulses in a human being, namely the desire of the flesh and of the spirit? For we know what the Apostle says: “Not first that which is spiritual, but that which is fleshly is first.” This is Esau being born first. But when the desire of the spirit is strengthened, then the desire of the flesh withers. This is Esau being supplanted by Jacob, born later. Likewise, the desire of the flesh, like Esau the hunter, feeds outside; but the desire of the spirit, like Jacob the simple man, delights within.

Thus Seir, “hairy,” is the shameful and unbecoming impulse of the flesh. And it is rightly called hairy, because, just as a hair fixes its root in the flesh but, by growing out, extends beyond the flesh, so the impulse of the flesh arises from necessity but, by growing beyond measure, flows forth into pleasure. And just as a hair may be cut without pain but cannot be pulled out without pain, so the appetite of the flesh, insofar as it concerns superfluity and is, as it were, outside the sensation of the flesh, is cut away without injury; but insofar as it concerns necessity and is, as it were, within the flesh, it cannot be uprooted without injury.

We have said what Seir is; now let us see what Mount Seir is. This Seir has a mountain, and it has a valley; indeed, to say more, it has a mountain, a plain, and a valley. But in the valley it is weak; on the plain it is strong; on the mountain it is unconquerable. Seir on the mountain is the appetite of the flesh in necessity; Seir on the plain is [Col. 0991A] the appetite of the flesh in satiety; Seir in the valley is the appetite of the flesh in pleasure. When the flesh receives sustenance only in order to live, Seir is on the mountain. But when it seeks nourishment for strength, Seir is on the plain. When, however, it demands luxuries for wantonness, Seir is in the valley.

Why, then, is it unconquerable on the mountain? Because the sustenance of the flesh is necessary to those still living in this mortality. Why is it strong on the plain? Because bodily strength is sometimes useful to the soul’s progress. Why is it weak in the valley? Because bodily pleasure is always superfluous. In the valley it is forbidden; on the plain it is permitted; on the mountain it is rewarded. In the valley it serves; on the plain it fights; on the mountain it reigns. In the valley there is luxury; on the plain, temperance; on the mountain, frugality. In the valley, with grace assisting, it is easily trampled; on the plain it is conquered with difficulty; on the mountain, so that it cannot be overcome, our daily weakness itself continually supplies it with strength.

He who cuts away superfluities tramples Seir in the valley. But he who diminishes something from necessities conquers Seir on the plain. He, however, who grants nature only what is necessary for sustenance, as it were renders to Seir on the mountain a more exact service. Yet it must be known that this Seir is easily conquered where it rules most dangerously; but where it is wholly unconquerable, there it may be tolerated without danger.

If, however, Seir is read as meaning “night-bird” or “stench,” it can suitably be referred to the same carnal impulse. It is called a night-bird either because the enticement of pleasure comes secretly, creeping in under the appearance of necessity [Col. 0991C], or because blindness of mind is born through bodily delight. Therefore, the night-bird is the hidden and unforeseen impulse of the flesh. Why the desire of the flesh should be called a stench needs no explanation now.

“And Hermon.” Hermon is interpreted “his anathema.” Whose “his”? The anathema’s own. Thus it would be as though one said “the anathema of an anathema.” First, therefore, we must ask what an anathema is; then we must add what the anathema of an anathema is. Anathema is separation; the anathema of an anathema is separation from separation. And perhaps, if it is evil to be separated, then it is good to be separated from one who is separated.

Who can better be called an anathema than the apostate angel, who first separated himself through pride from the fellowship of that heavenly city [Col. 0991D]? Through the demerit of his transgression, when he refused to be a member of the Head, he was cut off from the unity of that body and became the head of all the wicked. It is clear, moreover, that every human being, according to the first generation in which he is conceived in sin and born in sin, is a member of this head and belongs to his fellowship. But whoever, regenerated through the sacraments of faith, becomes a member of Christ, is separated from the unity of this body.

Who, then, is the anathema but the devil and his members? And who are the anathema of the anathema but those who, separated from the body of the devil, have become members of Christ? We have already said what Hermon signifies; now let us see what Mount Hermon signifies. For, as was said above concerning Seir [Col. 0992A], so it may also be said now concerning Hermon: some are Mount Hermon, others the plain of Hermon, others the valley of Hermon.

The valley of Hermon may be said to be those who, indeed, are already separated from the devil through faith, but still lie cast down in the lowest desires through a carnal life. The plain of Hermon consists of those faithful persons who, holding a certain middle state, are neither cast down to the bottom through bodily pleasure nor able to be raised to the heights through spiritual conduct. Mount Hermon, however, consists of those who are separated from the devil not only through faith but also stand raised against the devil through excellence of virtue and steadfastness of mind. And these are precisely the people whom the ancient enemy envies more: he sees them not only divided from himself, but also raised against himself. These, therefore, are those whom he strives continually to oppress by persecution—those whom he sees have withdrawn from himself and stand against himself. Such people often endure tribulations all the heavier because they have the common enemy of all singularly hostile to themselves.

Therefore, nothing is better understood by Mount Seir than frugality, and nothing better by Mount Hermon than the patience of the saints. There follows: “From the dens of lions” (Song of Songs IV). What is meant by the dens of lions except, so to speak, sleeping cruelty? And what is sleeping cruelty except the pleasure of the flesh, which unwittingly delights those whom it now later torments—first through conscience and then through punishment? Observe how, amid the delight of carnal pleasure, the punishment of future condemnation now sleeps.

Solomon says: “The lips of the harlot drip a honeycomb, and her throat is more polished than oil; but her latter end is bitter as wormwood, and her tongue sharp as a two-edged sword” (Prov. V) [Col. 0992C]. And again: “Whoever is little, let him turn aside to me”; and she spoke to the senseless: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread more pleasant.” And he did not know that giants are there, and that her guests are in the depths of hell (Prov. IX).

And the Lord, speaking to blessed Job about the ancient enemy, says: “He sleeps under the shadow, in the hiding-place of the reed, in moist places” (Job XL). For the devil rests in those minds which, cold within from the heat of divine love, float without amid the flow of carnal pleasures. These delights now seem soft in experience, but later will be felt as cruel in punishment. For now the lion lies down and sleeps, because the devil, pretending to be gentle to the minds of carnal people through the delight of sin, has not yet shown what he will be. But then he will begin to awaken, when those whom he now keeps voluntarily in guilt by seducing them with unlawful delights, he will afterward, openly raging, drag unwillingly to torments.

There follows: “From the mountains of leopards” (Song of Songs IV) [“from the impulses of leopards”]. A leopard is produced from a lion and a panther. The lion is cruel, and the panther spotted. Thus the lion suitably signifies demons on account of cruelty, and the panther heretics on account of variety: because they divide the unity of faith by diverse and perverse doctrines, they bear a body infected, as it were, with certain spots. Who, then, are [Col. 0993A] leopards except proud lovers of this world, whom the devil first begets into unbelief through the teaching of heretics and then inflames to vices through love of this world?

The mountains of leopards are the riches and pomp of this age, in which the wicked exalt themselves and more fiercely persecute the life of the elect when they see the elect cast down in this world and themselves exalted. Therefore it is rightly said to the bride: “You shall come, and pass to Mount Seir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.” But what is it to go from the dens of lions to Mount Seir except to go from incontinence [Col. 0994A] to chastity, from pleasure to frugality? And what is it to go from the mountains of leopards to Mount Hermon except to go from pride to humility and from cruelty to patience?

And note that he said “from dens,” not “from a den”; “from mountains,” not “from a mountain”; and “to a mountain,” not “to mountains.” From dens to a mountain, from mountains to a mountain: that is, we advance from many things to one, because the more we begin to approach God by fleeing the world, the more we are gathered into one. Which may he grant to us, etc. Amen.

[Col. 0993]

# A Golden Little Work on Meditation, or the Art of Meditating

[Col. 0993B]

Meditation is frequent thought investigating the manner, cause, and reason of each thing: the manner—what it is; the cause—why it is; the reason—how it is. There are three kinds of meditation: one concerning creatures, one concerning the Scriptures, and one concerning morals. The first arises from wonder, the second from reading, the third from self-examination.

In the first, wonder produces questioning, questioning investigation, and investigation discovery. Wonder concerns arrangement; questioning, cause; investigation, reason. The arrangement is that in heaven all things are equal, while on earth some are high and some low: this gives rise to wonder. The cause is that earth is for earthly life and heaven for heavenly life: this gives rise to questioning. The reason is that such as the earth is, such is earthly life; such as heaven is, such is heavenly life: this gives rise to investigation.

In reading [Col. 0993C], however, one must consider as follows. First, reading supplies the material for knowing truth; meditation arranges it; prayer lifts it up; action orders it; contemplation rejoices in it itself. Meditation in Scripture concerns how one ought to know. An example is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI). Meditation is added to the reading: why did he say first, “Turn away from evil,” and afterward, “Do good”? The cause is that unless evils first depart, good things do not arrive. The reason is that, just as evil shoots are first uprooted, good ones are afterward planted.

Likewise, why did he say, “Turn away from evil”? Because evils meet us on the road. Likewise, turn away because, where we cannot resist by strength, we escape by turning aside through counsel and reason. Likewise, we turn away from evils by avoiding the material of sin: for pride, riches; for incontinence [Col. 0993D], abundance; for concupiscence, physical beauty; for envy and contention, the love of possessions. This is to turn aside.

Likewise, if one is commanded to turn away from every evil, so one is commanded to do every good. And just as the person who does not turn away from every evil is guilty, so also the person who does not do every good is guilty. But if this is so, who is not guilty? Therefore we are commanded to turn away from every evil. But some goods are of necessity, others of free choice. Those of necessity are those contained in commandment and vow [Col. 0994B]; regarding the rest, if anything is performed beyond what is required, it is rewarded; if nothing is done, it is not imputed.

Likewise, meditation in reading concerns how the things known to exist are, and how those things which must be done are to be done. For meditation is the devising of counsel as to how the things which are known are to be fulfilled, because they are known to no purpose unless they are fulfilled.

Likewise, meditation in reading is of threefold consideration: according to history, allegory, and tropology. According to history, it is when we either seek or wonder at the reason for things done, completed in their proper times, places, and manner. In this, consideration exercises the meditator upon divine judgments, which in no times lacked rectitude and justice, by which what ought to have been done was done and what was just was rendered.

According to allegory, meditation works upon the arrangement of preceding events, observing the signification of future things, wonderfully fitted by reason and providence as was appropriate for the construction of understanding and the form of faith. In tropology, meditation works by seeking what fruit the sayings bring forth: what they intimate ought to be done, or teach ought to be avoided; what the reading of Scripture sets forth for instruction, exhortation, consolation, or fear; what it illuminates for the understanding of virtue, nourishes in affection, and teaches as a manner of life for the path of virtue.

Meditation in morals concerns affections, thoughts, and actions. With regard to affections, it must be considered that they are right and sincere: that is, directed to what they ought to be directed, and existing as they ought to exist [Col. 0994D]. For it is evil to love what one ought not to love; and similarly, it is evil to love in a way one ought not what one ought to love. Therefore an affection is good when it is directed to what it ought to be and exists as it ought to exist.

Amnon loved his sister, and his affection was directed toward what it ought to have been; but because he loved wrongly, it did not exist as it ought to have existed (II Kings XIII). Therefore affection can be directed to what it ought to be directed toward, without existing as it ought. Yet it can never exist as it ought unless it is directed to what it ought to be directed toward. In relation to what it ought to be directed toward, it is right; in the manner in which it ought to exist, sincere.

With regard to thoughts, it must be considered that they are pure and ordered. They are pure when they are neither produced by evil affections nor produce evil affections. They are ordered when they arise reasonably, that is, in their proper time. For even to think good things at an improper time is not without fault: for example, to think of prayer during reading, and of reading during prayer.

With regard to actions, it must first be considered that they are done with a good intention. A good intention is simple and right: simple without malice; right without ignorance. For one that is without malice has zeal; but one that is ignorant does not have zeal according to knowledge. Therefore intention must be both right through discernment and simple through kindness [Col. 0995B]. Secondly, with regard to actions, it must be considered that things begun from a right intention are brought to their end with persevering fervour, so that neither perseverance grows sluggish nor love grows cold.

Likewise, meditation in morals ranges over a twofold consideration: inwardly and outwardly. Outwardly, it concerns reputation; inwardly, conscience. Outwardly, it considers what is fitting and what is advantageous: fitting for example, advantageous for merit; advantageous to us for merit and to our neighbours for example. Inwardly, it concerns conscience, so that conscience may be clean and suffer no accusation either for sluggishness in good or for presumption in evil. A clean conscience is one that is neither justly accused concerning the past nor unjustly delighted concerning the present.

Likewise, meditation in morals exercises its consideration [Col. 0995C] so as to apprehend every impulse arising in the heart—whence it comes and whither it tends: whence it comes according to origin, whither it tends according to end. Every impulse is from something and toward something. Thus impulses of the heart sometimes have a manifest origin and sometimes a hidden one; and a manifest origin is sometimes manifestly good, sometimes manifestly evil. What is manifestly good is from God; what is manifestly evil is either from the devil or from the flesh. For these three are the authors of all suggestions, and all inspirations that come invisibly to the heart proceed from them.

Likewise, hidden impulses are sometimes good and hidden, sometimes evil and doubtful. Those that are good are from God; those that are evil [Col. 0995D] are either from the devil or from the flesh. Therefore, impulses that are manifest, whether good or evil, are judged from their first origin. But those doubtful in origin are tested by their end. For the outcome makes manifest what was hidden from the beginning; and therefore one who cannot judge his impulses from the beginning should investigate their end and completion.

For things that are doubtful or uncertain are hidden goods or evils. And the evils, as has been said, are either from the devil or from the flesh. Both are evil, and they do not differ in being evil; but they differ because those from the flesh arise more frequently from necessity, whereas those from the devil arise more often contrary to reason. For what is suggested by the devil, just as it is alien to a human being, is also frequently alien to human reason: for example, a person who has just eaten his fill suffers hunger; one who shortly before was drunk burns with thirst; one rising after a long sleep is heavily oppressed by sleep. Thus the works of the devil are discerned in this: they are foreign to humanity and alien to human reason.

The works of the flesh and its suggestions, however, more often have necessity as their preceding cause. But because they exceed measure and limit, they grow into superfluity. For example, when food is immoderately desired after hunger, or when moderation is not observed in eating after abstinence.

Likewise, meditation upon morals is exercised through a threefold judgment. First, it judges between day and night. Second, it judges between day and day. Third, it judges every day. To judge between night and day is to divide evils from goods. To judge between day and day [Col. 0996B] is to possess discernment between good and better. To judge every day is to estimate individual goods according to their merit.

Likewise, meditation upon morals considers end and direction in every manner of life. The end is that toward which one tends; direction is that by which one arrives more easily. For everyone who tends toward something directs his course according to something; and whoever goes more directly arrives sooner. There are certain goods in which even much movement is little progress. Others bring forth great fruit through brief labour. Therefore these too must be discerned, and those that benefit more must be chosen more readily. For whatever benefits more is better, and every work ought to be judged according to its fruit.

Many who lack this discernment have laboured greatly [Col. 0996C] and progressed little, because they kept their eye outwardly only on the appearance of the work, not inwardly upon the fruit of virtue. For they rejoiced more that they did great things than that they performed useful things; and they preferred those things in which they could be seen to those by which they could be improved.

Likewise, meditation in morals first considers the duties owed, whether by commandment or by vow, and judges that those things must first be done which, when done, possess merit, but when not done incur guilt. Therefore those things must first be done which cannot be omitted without fault. After these, if anything is added by voluntary discipline, it must be so done that what is owed is not hindered. Some desire what they ought not, who are unable to do what they ought. Others, even if able to do what they ought, introduce voluntary hindrances by desiring what they ought not.

Likewise, meditation upon morals considers two evils especially to be avoided in good action: affliction and preoccupation [Col. 0996D]. Affliction leads to bitterness; preoccupation to dissipation. Through affliction, the sweetness of the mind is made bitter; through preoccupation, tranquillity is scattered. Affliction occurs when a person is consumed through impatience by things which he is unable to do. Preoccupation occurs when he is agitated through impatience in doing things which he is able to do. Therefore, lest the mind be bitterly embittered, let it patiently bear its own incapacity; and lest it be wrongly preoccupied, let it not extend its ability beyond its measure.

Likewise, meditation upon morals judges the manner of life by another consideration, proving that it is neither good impatiently to desire things that are not done [Col. 0997A], nor good foolishly to disdain things that are done. For the person who always desires what he does not do and disdains what he does does not enjoy present things or find satisfaction in future ones. For he abandons things begun before completion and seizes upon things to be begun before their time. Therefore it is good to be content with one’s own good and to increase present goods by goods that come afterward, not to cast them aside for future goods.

For change of good things is fickleness [Col. 0998A], whereas the practice of virtue is something else altogether. They travel very different paths who cast aside old things for new and who ascend from lower things to higher. For the person who seeks change is fastidious; the person who desires progress is diligent. Therefore he proceeds most rightly who is so fervent for what is better that he is not fastidious in what is good, but first endures until he attains what comes later in its proper time.

[Col. 0997]

# On the Fruits of the Flesh and the Spirit (G)*

## Chapter I. On the three theological virtues and the four cardinal virtues born from humility.—Chapter II. On comparison of like things with one another and with unlike things: virtues with virtues, vices with vices, and virtues with vices.—Chapter III. On pride and its companions.—Chapter IV. On vainglory and its companions.—Chapter V. On envy and its companions.—Chapter VI. On anger and its company.—Chapter VII. On sorrow, or acedia, and its company.—Chapter VIII. On avarice and its company.—Chapter IX. On gluttony, or greed of the belly, and its company.—Chapter X. On lust and its company.—Chapter XI. On humility and its companions.—Chapter XII. On prudence and its company.—Chapter XIII. On justice and its company.—Chapter XIV. On fortitude and its companions.—Chapter XV. On temperance and its companions.—Chapter XVI. On faith and its companions.—Chapter XVII. On hope and its companions.—Chapter XVIII. On charity and its company.—Chapter XIX. On love and its twofold rationale.

## Prologue

[Col. 0997B]

Since every utterance of the divine page aims to persuade humanity of the good of humility and to urge with greater care the avoidance of the evil of pride—especially since in the one lies the beginning of salvation and life, and in the other the beginning of ruin—it seems necessary to set before the cultivator of virtues, as it were visibly and in outward form, the fruit and efficacy of humility itself and of pride. Thus an imitator of either kind, pride or humility, may recognize from the quality of their fruits what reward he obtains from the practice of either.

Accordingly, we set forth two little trees, unlike in fruit and ascent, for every rough and newly converted person, adding a few definitions of vices and virtues; from their roots the growth of fruits may become evident, and, attracted by its fruit, he may discern which of the two trees ought to be chosen. Pride, indeed, is the root of the fruits of the flesh; humility, of the fruits of the spirit. When this difference in the roots is observed, it reveals the desire of one who seeks their fruits in moderation.

Finally, the old Adam places himself upon the height of the vicious tree; the new Adam holds the primacy of spiritual increase. If, then, you set what is superior beside what is inferior—that is, good beside evil—you will understand clearly what stands out and what weighs more heavily in them. For when the qualities of opposites are compared, the estimate of better things is quickly apparent. Therefore, having examined the roots, branches, and fruits, it is for your judgment to choose what you will.

## Chapter I. On the three theological virtues and the four cardinal virtues born from humility

[Col. 0997D]

For, as has been said, humility is the foundation of all virtues, because “everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” [Col. 0998B] (Luke XIV). And the kingdom of heaven is opened to the poor in spirit (Matt. V). But faith first joins humility among the virtues, because “without faith it is impossible to please God,” and “the righteous lives by faith” (Heb. XI). But what do you gain by faith if you do not seek by hope what you embrace by faith? For “we hope for what we do not yet see,” and “hope does not disappoint” (Rom. V). But because in hoping we love what we already possess by faith, charity succeeds hope; and thus faith, which works through love, rightly proceeds.

Prudence teaches and forms how these three virtues—hope, faith, and charity—are to be distinguished and held. Justice adorns and perfects them. Fortitude preserves and strengthens them; and lest they run into excess or be improperly confined within their own limits, temperance moderates and discerns.

If, then, you add these four virtues to the three above, this sevenfold number of virtues brings to its practitioners the fullness of sevenfold grace, through which the structure of vices is dissolved, the body of the devil is overcome, and, by the path of justice, the fountain and source of all virtues is approached.

## Chapter II. On comparing equals with one another and with unequals: virtues with virtues, vices with vices, and virtues with vices

If you join like things to like, the equality of the parts testifies to the excellence of each part. But if you compare unlike things, the difference of one from the other is more apparent. Thus the conjunction of equals conceals the difference of the individual parts; but the differing quality of each seems to grow through comparison with the other [Col. 0998D]. Compare white with black, the wise with the foolish, the proud with the humble, evil with good; and from these opposite and distant things an argument for their proper nature seems to accrue to each kind.

So consider the fruits of the trees previously set forth. For the great bitterness of the root of pride with its shoot is easily perceived from the abundant sweetness of holy humility. Therefore, one who has resolved to overcome the furies of vices by the opposition of virtues should know that it is useful to consider with subtle examination their natures and qualities; once these are examined, all their force will be considered in humility’s triumphs.

Therefore humility, which holds the highest place in the primacy of virtues, is encircled by the sevenfold crown of theological and cardinal virtues. From these, other virtues, as though derived from a fountain, bring a certain perfection through their practices and show the prize that is promised to those who contend but bestowed upon those who conquer [Col. 0999B]. Pride, the highest of vices, confronting humility, shows in its battle-line the material of death and certain ruin to its followers. Let it not, therefore, be burdensome to consider the retinues of both, differing in nature and effect, so that, having rejected vices through reason, one may triumph through virtue.

## Chapter III. On pride and its companions

Pride is a certain desire for glory and superiority, for singular excellence and for elevation of a swelling mind above every assembly. Its principal companions are these:

Lust, greed of the belly, avarice, sorrow, anger, envy, vainglory.

These seven principal vices—if we may say something in the language of secular learning—may in a certain respect be called subordinate genera: that is, species in relation to the higher thing, namely pride, from which they proceed; but genera in relation to lower things, namely the vices arising from them. For example, we say that the evil of pride is a certain substantial genus, and that vices flowing from pride are certain substantial species, such as animal, human being, horse, etc.—but only in a certain respect. So we say that night multiplies darkness and silence conceals wickedness, although in the former case light and in the latter voice have merely ceased, and there are many similar expressions.

Let no one be offended here by the artificial and external colouring, which I have used in order to show more clearly the fountain and stream—that is, pride with its appendages. Therefore now, with definitions appended, let us examine the array and retinue of pride’s malice.

## Chapter IV. On vainglory and its companions

Vainglory is an improper agitation of the inner and outer person, moved by the desire to please. Its companions are hypocrisy, disobedience, boasting, presumption of novelties, arrogance, talkativeness, and obstinacy.

Hypocrisy is to cloak, by artifice, a concealed vice with the simulation of virtues.

Disobedience is, through the hardness of an obstinate mind, unwillingness to comply with one to whom one ought to submit when he commands what is just.

Boasting is vainly to proclaim and promise greater things about oneself than are true, driven by the arrogance of the mind.

[Col. 1000A] Presumption of novelties is, contrary to the character of one’s rank or powers, to attempt some novelty with singular swelling pride.

Arrogance is to parade what one does not possess and to boast of what one has not received, from the desire to please people.

Talkativeness is that through which inward frivolity is displayed by a foolish outpouring of words.

Obstinacy is, from an irrational and inflexible stubbornness of mind, unwillingness to yield to what is better.

## Chapter V. On envy and its companions

Envy makes the mind burn with grief at another’s good and honour, unwilling to see them. Its companions are hatred, affliction, exultation, malice, detraction, bitterness, and whispering.

[Col. 1000B] Hatred conceals more persistently and tenaciously the impulse of an angry mind, with the hope of vengeance, and persecutes with malevolence the person himself, not merely his vices.

Affliction amid prosperity is the torment of a hateful mind arising from the advancement of one less pleasing to it.

Exultation amid adversity is the excessive display of joy at another’s downfall because of hatred once conceived.

Malice is the desire for another’s harm without hope of obtaining any good from it.

Detraction is the biting and envious diminishment of another’s glory and reputation by words or signs.

Bitterness is a certain solitude of a mind deprived of spiritual joy [Col. 1000C] and distracted, and a sickness caused by another’s good.

Whispering is that through which one person is stirred to hatred of another by a kind of hissing, whether of hateful flattery or disparagement.

## Chapter VI. On anger and its company

Anger is the constrained fury of an excited mind, burning with the desire for vengeance. Its companions are clamour, blasphemy, insult, lamentation, rashness, fury, and indignation.

Clamour is the loud and shameless reproach of a deed committed.

Blasphemy is a curse hurled against another with a certain shameful irreverence of abusive speech; or it is the diminution of the divine or human name, effected by swearing or reproaching.

[Col. 1000D] Insult is the publication of another’s dishonour under the impulse of resentment and bitterness.

Lamentation is what, when the mind is embittered, satisfies in tears the vengeance it can exercise no more fully against a superior.

Rashness is the undisciplined outburst of an insolent mind devoid of reason.

Fury is the unbridled madness of an impatient and powerless mind, arising from adversities conceived within.

Indignation is a certain troubled contempt for an inferior arising from arrogant malevolence.

## Chapter VII. On sorrow, or acedia, and its company
Sorrow is the anxiety of a troubled mind arising from a frustrated wish amid adverse circumstances, and weariness in rightly carrying out a good undertaking. [Col. 1001A] Its companions are despair, rancour, torpor, fear, acedia, complaint, and faint-heartedness.

Despair is the shattered governance of hope with respect to one’s condition of life or return to the virtues; or it is the casting away of hope of obtaining salvation or pardon.

Rancour is the weakening and corruption of soul and body arising from black bile or excessive sluggishness of the powers.

Torpor is the sloth of a languishing mind, slackened movement, and dullness of the whole body.

Fear is that through which a fluctuating distress is generated in the mind by expectation of adverse things.

Acedia is sorrow or weariness born of excessive confusion of mind; or excessive bitterness of mind, [Col. 1001B] by which spiritual joy is extinguished and the mind, through a kind of beginning of despair, is overthrown within itself.

Complaint is to disclose the hidden distress of the heart in impatient words, and to make oneself appear less capable than one is.

Faint-heartedness is the inert and unconsidered dejection of a broken mind arising from weariness amid adverse circumstances.

CHAPTER VIII. On avarice and its company.

Avarice is an insatiable and dishonourable desire for glory, riches, or any other things whatever. Its companions are love of money, perjury, violence, usury, fraud, robbery, and deceit.

Love of money (*philargyria*) is that through which, by a singular appetite for [Col. 1001C] scraping together money, the reins of self-restraint are loosened; for it is interpreted as “love of silver.”

Perjury is the denial, made by false swearing, of acknowledged truth for the fraudulent purpose of gaining an advantage or avoiding a loss.

Violence is that through which wickedness or injury, for the sake of advantage, is powerfully and forcibly inflicted upon an inferior.

Usury is the receipt of interest upon money or another thing lent.

Fraud is that through which provision is secretly made for one’s household, poverty, or malice by clandestine appropriation.

Robbery is the violent plundering of another’s goods by an onslaught proceeding from an avaricious mind.

Deceit is that through which the truth of a matter is veiled by deceptive manoeuvres, [Col. 1001D] or hatred of another, or one’s own advantage, is pursued.

CHAPTER IX. On greed of the belly, or gluttony, and its company.

Greed of the belly is the immoderate satisfying of a gaping desire for foods or drinks of whatever kind. Its companions are drunkenness, surfeit, dullness of mind, languor, luxuriousness, and forgetfulness.

Drunkenness is that through which a certain forgetfulness of itself is produced in the mind by indulgence in excessive drink.

Surfeit is the enticing and greedy desire for food for the body’s sake alone.

Dullness of mind is the blunting of keen reason, brought on by the gross perceptions of fleshly intemperance.

[Col. 1002A] Languor is the idleness of a sickly mind contracted through the vice of voracity.

Luxuriousness is the desire, beyond one’s station and need, for splendid, delicious, and costly food or drink.

Forgetfulness is that through which, when the mind has been buried under vices because of gluttony, negligence of honour and salvation is induced.

CHAPTER X. On lust and its company.

Lust is the slippery and unrestrained prostitution of mind or body descending from unclean desires. Its companions are pleasure, wantonness, idleness, petulance, unsteadiness, blandishments, and delights.

Pleasure is the inclination of a foul mind towards unlawful things with a certain slippery sweetness.

Wantonness is an indecent movement of the unrestrained body, appearing in a shameful place through fleshly intemperance.

[Col. 1002B] Idleness is the languid dejection of both the inner and outer person from the praiseworthy exercise of the virtues.

Petulance is the wanton impulse of the whole body toward a beloved object, arising from the conception of carnal thoughts.

Unsteadiness is a fault of a broken mind, arising outwardly from the pressure of slippery carnality; or it is the wavering of the limbs through immoderate sexual indulgence.

Blandishments are an outward display, made to the senses, of vicious pleasures with a certain sweetness.

Delights are the indulgence of bodily enticement with a certain superfluity.

CHAPTER XI. On humility and its companions.

[Col. 1002C]

Now that you have recognized the dreadful array of pride, which draws to the left, attend to the army of humility, which leads to the right. And, having recognized the citizens of Babylon, attend to the citizens of Jerusalem.

Humility is the voluntary inclination of the mind arising from consideration of one’s own condition or of one’s Creator. Its principal companions are prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance, faith, hope, and charity.

CHAPTER XII. On prudence and its company.

Prudence is a provident and discerning judgment of good and evil in the safeguarding of oneself. Its companions are fear of the Lord, cheerfulness, counsel, memory, understanding, foresight, and deliberation.

Fear of the Lord is the vigilant keeping, in faith and good conduct, of the divine [Col. 1002D] commandments. For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.

Cheerfulness is the joyful and circumspect readiness of the mind to accomplish a good work.

Counsel is the subtle insight of the mind for examining and directing matters.

Memory is a kind of imaginative representation of things past for the view of the mind.

Understanding is to weigh and discern the state of present things with rational keenness.

Foresight is that through which future events are inferred by shrewd subtlety.

Deliberation is the full consideration of maturity and prudence before any undertaking.

CHAPTER XIII. On justice and its company.

[Col. 1003A]

Justice is that through which the good of the community is maintained and each person is not denied his due dignity. Its companions are law, severity, equity, correction, observance of an oath, judgment, and truth.

Law is that through which things to be done are commanded and things not to be done are forbidden.

Severity is that through which judicial punishment, following the strictness of truth, is more rigorously imposed upon the sinner.

Equity is the most fitting recompense of merits, weighed impartially on the scales of justice.

Correction is the restraint by the bridle of reason of an error inborn or introduced by habit.

Observance of an oath is that which, after a decree has been promulgated to the citizens, [Col. 1003B] prevents its rash transgression through an oath pledging its perpetual preservation.

Judgment is that through which, after the merits have been heard, either punishment or reward is deservedly rendered.

Truth is that through which a statement or deed is presented unchanged by convincing reason.

CHAPTER XIV. On fortitude and its companions.

Fortitude is the steadfast endurance by the mind, amid adversities, of labours and dangers undertaken. Its companions are magnanimity, confidence, endurance, repose, stability, constancy, and perseverance.

Magnanimity is a certain noble excellence of mind that manages difficult and arduous matters finely and courageously.

[Col. 1003C] Confidence is, from consciousness of the virtues, to establish an unmoved mind amid adversities and to trust in a good outcome.

Endurance, or patience, is the long-suffering bearing of another’s wickedness or annoyance.

Repose is that through which a certain security is brought to the mind by contempt for transitory variety.

Stability is the retention of a mind, fixed and not altered by any variety of places or times, though tossed about amid diverse things.

Constancy is a perpetual and unmoved tenor of life, like to itself and worthy of its own condition.

Perseverance is that which, through a certain perfection of the virtues—long-suffering bringing it to completion—strengthens the mind lest it abandon what it has begun before attaining its end.

CHAPTER XV. On temperance and its companions.

[Col. 1003D] Temperance is the firm and discriminating dominion of reason over unlawful impulses of the mind. Its companions are discernment, accommodation, silence, fasting, sobriety, affliction of the flesh, and contempt for the world.

Discernment is the provident reason that regulates human movements by judging the causes of things.

Accommodation is, while preserving one’s own virtue, to adapt oneself justly and piously to the manners of those living with one.

Silence is the restraint of one’s tongue even from useful words, with a certain fruitful quiet of mind.

Fasting is the vigilant inward keeping of measured abstinence.

[Col. 1004A] Sobriety is temperance of both the inner and outer person, pure from enticements; it is so called because it is set apart and separated from drunkenness.

Affliction of the flesh is that through which the seeds of a wanton mind are restrained by discriminating chastisement.

Contempt for the world is love of eternal things, induced by reason through consideration of transient things.

CHAPTER XVI. On faith and its companions.

Faith is that which, in holy striving, causes the mind to depend, from the truth of things set forth beforehand, upon invisible things to come. For it is the proof of things not seen. Its companions are religion, purity, obedience, chastity, reverence, continence, and affection.

Religion is that through which the rites of divine worship are performed in reverent service.

[Col. 1004B] Purity is the consummate integrity of both the inner and outer person, through regard either for divine love or fear.

Obedience is the voluntary renunciation of one’s own will, resting upon devout zeal.

Chastity is the clean and honourable disposition of the whole body through the taming of the furies of vices.

Reverence is the chaste worship offered to God because of the faith which we have concerning Him.

Continence is that through which the impulses of carnal affections are restrained by the governance of counsel.

Affection is the outpouring toward one’s neighbour of devout love, conceived in holy joy through faith.

CHAPTER XVII. On hope and its companions.

Hope is a movement of the mind steadfastly suspended toward receiving those things which it seeks with assured reason. Its [Col. 1004C] companions are contemplation of things above, joy, modesty, confession, patience, compunction, and long-suffering.

Contemplation of things above is the death of carnal affections through the exultation of a mind raised aloft.

Joy is the spiritual delight of a mind hastening onward, arising from contempt for present things.

Modesty is the shamefacedness of a chaste and honourable disposition concerning praiseworthy progress.

Confession is that through which the hidden sickness of the soul is disclosed in praise of God, in hope of obtaining pardon.

Patience is the voluntary and unconquerable endurance of adversities in view of eternal glory.

Compunction is a kind of burning of the sighing soul, born either from fear of punishment or love of [Col. 1004D] reward.

Long-suffering is the tireless endurance of labours for the fulfilment of just desires.

CHAPTER XVIII. On charity and its company.

Charity is an affection of the mind and a devout love, fervently and rightly directed toward God and neighbour. Its companions are grace, peace, piety, gentleness, liberality, mercy, indulgence, compassion, kindness, and concord.

Grace is that in which the affectionate observance of mutual goodwill is shown from one person to another.

Peace is the ordered tranquillity of minds agreeing in the good.

[Col. 1005A] Piety is an affection, helpful to all by grace, arising from the sweetness of a kindly mind.

Gentleness is that through which the tranquillity of the gentle or moderate person exceeds the bounds of its own repose because of no one’s wickedness.

Liberality is that through which a free mind is constrained by no stinginess in giving away its possessions.

Mercy is a gentle and impartial condescension toward all, and a compassionate inclination of mind toward the afflicted.

Indulgence is the remission of another’s guilt, arising from consideration of one’s own.

Compassion is that through which a certain affliction is generated in the sympathetic mind from a neighbour’s pain.

Kindness is the fervent manifestation of a loving mind, with a certain splendid sweetness of conduct.

Concord is an unbroken and united embracing of minds in agreement upon what is right.

CHAPTER XIX. On love and its twofold character.

We continually sow discourse concerning love, if perhaps in our hearts a spark may flash forth and blaze into fire, either consuming all or purifying all. For from it comes everything that is good, and from it comes everything that is evil. One fountain of love springing within pours forth two streams. One is love of the world, namely covetousness; the other is love of God, namely charity. For the human heart is the middle place from which the fountain of love bursts forth. When it runs outward through appetite, it is called covetousness; but when it directs its desire inward, it is called charity. [Col. 1005C] Therefore there are two streams flowing from the fountain of love: covetousness and charity. Covetousness is the root of all evils, and charity the root of all goods. Yet we find that nothing other than love divides our desires in so many ways and leads one heart in different directions. Though in accordance with nature it is a single and unique movement of the heart, in action it is divided: when it moves itself disorderly—that is, toward things to which it ought not to move—it is called covetousness; but when it is ordered, it is called charity. [Col. 1006A] We wish to commend a great matter, if indeed we can accomplish what we wish.

Almighty God, who needs nothing because He Himself is the highest and true good, who is He who neither can receive from another so as to grow—for all things are from Him—nor lose from what is His so as to decline—for all things remain unchangeably in Him—created the rational spirit solely out of charity, from no necessity, in order to make it a participant in His blessedness. Moreover, so that it might be fit to enjoy so great a blessedness, He placed love within it, as it were making the spiritual palate sensitive through this [Col. 1006B] to the taste of inward sweetness, so that through love itself it might savour the delight of His happiness and cling to Him with tireless desire.

Therefore, through love God joined the rational creature to Himself, so that, always cleaving to Him, it might in some way draw by affection from Him the good by which it was to be made blessed, drink of Him by desire, and possess Him by joy. Thus the rational creature alone was joined in fellowship to its Creator through love, which is the bond of affection binding both to Him—the more happily, the more strongly. For this reason too, so that undivided fellowship and perfect concord might be maintained on both sides, the bond was doubled in the charity of God and neighbour: so that through charity toward God all might cleave to the One, and through charity toward neighbour all might become one with one another; so that what each could not contain within himself from that One to whom all adhered, he might possess more fully and perfectly in another through charity toward neighbour; and the good of all might become the entire good of each.

[Col. 1009]

PART FOUR OF THE WORKS OF HUGH OF ST VICTOR.

[Col. 1011]

LETTERS.

FIRST LETTER. TO RANULPH OF MAURIAC. That charity never fails.

[Col. 1011A]

To his beloved brother R., Hugh, a sinner.

“Charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13). I had heard this and knew that it was true. But now, dearest brother, experience has come, and I know plainly that charity never fails. I had set out abroad and came to you in a foreign land; and it was as though it were not foreign, because I found friends there. Yet I do not know whether I first made them friends or was made their friend. Nevertheless, I found charity there and loved it; nor could I grow weary of it, because it was sweet to me. I filled the pouch of my heart, and grieved that it proved narrow and could not hold it all; nevertheless, I filled it as much as [Col. 1011B] I could. I filled all that I had, but could not contain all that I found. Therefore I took as much as I could contain; and, burdened by a precious price, I did not feel the weight, because my burden lifted me up.

Now, after completing a long journey, I still find my pouch full, and nothing has fallen from it, because charity never fails. There, therefore, dearest brother, among other things your memory was first found, and from it I sealed this letter, wishing that you may be sound and safe in the Lord. Therefore return love for love, and pray for me. May the Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.

LETTER II. TO THE SAME. On the solution of four questions proposed by Ranulph of Mauriac.

[Col. 1011C]

HUGH TO RANULPH OF MAURIAC.

The fervour of your charity has brought us the weight of questions. First, you request that an exposition be made for you of that work called *The Supper of Cyprian*. Since it was not then at hand, we have received a fitting excuse from you.

QUESTION 1. Next you ask what is meant by that dispute of Michael with the devil over the body of Moses, mentioned in the Epistle of the Apostle Jude. Here we think it sufficient to say that our fathers, who before us ministered the word of God, understood the body of Moses to mean the Jewish people, of whom Moses himself had been the head. By Michael, however, they understood the divine [Col. 1011D] power as it were contending with the devil—that is, with the hostile power—for that same people, that it might be saved; nor was the hostile power repelled by any other curse than that the Lord, who chose Jerusalem, drove back the enemy’s power from those whom He chose from that people for salvation through grace alone.

QUESTION 2. You ask again which books are to be understood, and whether they still survive, of which mention is made in the Book of Numbers and Joshua, and likewise in Kings and Chronicles, when it is said: “Is not this written in the Book of the Just and the Book of the Wars of the Lord?” And likewise: “in the book of Gad the seer, and of Addo, or Shemaiah, or Ahijah the Shilonite.” We therefore, following the interpretation of the teachers also in this matter, understand the Book of the Just and the Book of the Wars of the Lord to be no other books than these very books in which these things are written, [Col. 1012B] in the manner of the Scriptures commending their own narrative, when, for its confirmation, authority seems to be doubled by the introduction of its own testimony as though it were another’s.

But we judge that the books of Gad, Addo, Shemaiah, and Ahijah were separate books composed by the authors named above, but have by no chain of transmission come down to us. Whether they are still possessed by the Hebrews is uncertain; although, after the Law was burned by the Chaldeans, it is considered more probable that these too were removed from among them and do not now survive.

Concerning the statement in Kings and Chronicles, “Are not these things written in the book of the Sayings, or Chronicles, of the kings of Judah or Israel?” (3 Kings 15), although this has not been proposed in your question, if I add something beyond what is due, when you return, even if you do not choose to repay it, do not nevertheless be angry. For it may be that there are some who do not know this either; and if they consult you together with me, it should not displease you.

Accordingly, we judge the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah and likewise the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel to be separate books in which the deeds of the kings—of Judah and Israel, that is—were recorded, not by a single author but at different times and by different authors, as events happened. From these, the matters judged more worthy of remembrance were excerpted by later authors, composed in a more polished style, and set forth in these books, namely Kings and Chronicles, in a concise narrative. Those, therefore, are the books to which Kings and Chronicles refer those wishing to know further matters. [Col. 1012D] We believe that these have neither come down to us through translation nor now exist among the Hebrews.

QUESTION 3. You ask likewise how the Saviour’s saying is to be understood: “Everyone who has left a wife, etc., for my sake, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19), when He Himself says elsewhere (Matt. 5) that a wife cannot rightly be dismissed, except for the cause of fornication, nor ought she to depart from her husband. Here it is rightly understood that what a person cannot fittingly do for his own sake, he can sometimes rightly do for God’s sake. But he does it rightly for God’s sake when he does it according to God.

Therefore, to leave a wife for God’s sake is either to abstain through continence for God’s sake, so as not to take one; or, when her guilt requires it or her consent permits it, not to be held by concupiscence so as not to depart. Therefore, the person who can leave according to God rightly leaves for God’s sake. But as long as he cannot leave according to God, he cannot leave for God’s sake. When, however, the cause of God requires it, she may not only be left but even rightly hated, so that in her, for God’s sake, what is contrary to God may not be loved.

QUESTION 4. You ask also what is meant by the Apostle’s saying in the Epistle written to the Hebrews: “It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, have also tasted the heavenly gift, have been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have fallen away, to be renewed again unto repentance” (Heb. 6). This is more difficult to hear because it seems to remove the remedy of repentance and induce despair in sinners. Therefore, the word of God should not be interpreted in such a way that we understand something in it contrary to truth.

Thus, when it says that those once enlightened and made partakers of the heavenly gift cannot, after a fall, be renewed unto repentance, we understand it in either of two ways. First, a person can indeed sin by himself, but cannot by himself, without the assistance of divine grace, be corrected, as it is written: “A spirit passing and not returning” (Ps. 77). Or secondly: after a fall, a person cannot be renewed so as to be what he would have been had he not sinned. For example, if a virgin is defiled, she can repent, but cannot again be a virgin. Even if by repenting she perhaps becomes better than she was when she fell, nevertheless she cannot make herself such as she would have been had she not [Col. 1013D] sinned and had she nevertheless performed the good deeds she now performs.

Accordingly, in some manner the loss arising from past guilt is plainly irrecoverable: even amid the present gains of righteousness, that which was lost through past guilt is always seen to be lacking; and, if it were present, there would be more. This impossibility can also be understood fittingly in another way. A sinner once redeemed by Christ’s death and freed from the oldness of sin, if he falls again, cannot in that respect be renewed again, because he cannot have another death of Christ for renewal; although he can seek it again [the text may read *poscit*, “seek/request”] and can be renewed again by the same death.

The sinner is therefore fittingly frightened, so that, since Christ—by whose death he was redeemed—cannot die again, he may take care not to repeat sin just as he sees it impossible that Christ’s death should be repeated for sin. As it is written (Heb. 10), for those sinning willingly after receiving pardon, no sacrifice for sin remains—that is, neither this sacrifice as an excuse nor another as a remission. For “willingly sinning” should not be understood of those of whom it is said: “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8). For even for those who sin willingly while established in Christ, this sacrifice is not left as an excuse from condemnation, just as it is granted to penitents, even for voluntary sins, for remission. Thus those who have fallen after receiving grace cannot again be renewed and yet can be renewed, because that by which they are renewed cannot be repeated so as to be something else; but it can be recovered anew by those [Col. 1014B] who are to be renewed, so that, once it has been recovered, having lost it may not be damnable.

LETTER III. TO JOHN, ARCHBISHOP OF SEVILLE. That Christian faith must be held not only in the heart but also confessed with the mouth.

To John, Archbishop of the people of Seville, Hugh, servant of the cross of Christ.

What, dearest brother, what shall I say to you? If we begin to speak to you, perhaps you will take it ill. That man was strong and great, and a despiser of all torments; and no one spoke a word to him, because they saw that his grief was severe (Job 2). How, then, shall we be able to speak to you amid the severity of so great a grief? Yet if you grieve as much as you ought to grieve [Col. 1014C; variant: “as much as you are to be grieved for”], what shall we do for you? Shall we hold back the speech conceived within us, which our heart and soul have already begun to bring forth, not—as in their case—from impatience to speak, but from the violence of grief?

Can charity, then, remain silent, so as not to burst forth and cry out in its pains and the distress of its tribulation? For already the sword has reached the soul, and deceitful death comes sparing the flesh in order to extinguish the spirit. You know, brother, what I mean. Your soul is at stake. See what you do. Christ sets His death before you; the Christian, his redemption. The one seeks what He bought; the other, what he redeemed. The former complains that He gave Himself as your price in vain; the latter laments that one redeemed by a price has been lost.

But you say: “I know my conscience. Let no one frighten me. It is not the tongue but the conscience that makes a Christian. I love Christ; that is enough for me. He seeks no more. I gave Him what is chiefly mine. He has my heart; let Him possess it. I may say whatever I please to a human being. The Lord Himself knows that I deny unwillingly. The tongue says this, not the conscience. I deny with my mouth, but confess with my heart.”

Listen, brother. Scripture says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 16 [recte 10]). How then do you think you can have salvation if you do not have confession? You deny Christ and say that you have the Holy Spirit? What, then, is the meaning of the Apostle’s saying: “No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Jesus be accursed’” (1 Cor. 12)? If you say, “Jesus be accursed,” how do you have the Spirit of Christ? But if [Col. 1015A] you do not have the Spirit of Christ, you are not Christ’s. Scripture says: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Him” (Rom. 8).
