Listen again: “Whoever,” He says, “is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when He comes in His majesty” (Luke 9). But you say, rightly enough: “The person who denies Christ from shame is justly condemned, justly unacknowledged by Christ. For it is no small thing to prefer shame to Christ. I have more to offer in my defence. I am not ashamed, but afraid. What frightens me is greater. He Himself knows that I cannot endure suffering. Therefore He spares weakness and accommodates devotion. He does not attend to the voice but looks to charity. ‘No one has hated his own flesh’” (Eph. 5). “I fear for my flesh, which I cannot hate.”

O deceptive delusion! Then will you love the flesh and blaspheme the Creator? What, then, is the meaning of His saying: “Whoever loves his soul more than me is not worthy of me” (Luke 14)? If you cannot rightly love your soul more, can you love your flesh more? But you say: “I do not love my flesh more; for I love our God more than my flesh.” Let us see. What you love more, that you choose in preference. Your God says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but can do nothing to the soul” (Matt. 10). Thus God says this, and the flesh contradicts it. See now: what you love more, that you choose in preference.

What a shepherd! How would you lay down your soul for your sheep (John 10), when you do not lay down your soul even for your own soul? You are unwilling to give your flesh for your soul, yet would you give your soul for your sheep? What a shepherd! That good Shepherd did not act so: He laid down His soul for His sheep and deigned to die for His flock. What do you think? If He had feared death as you do, what sheep, do you suppose, would still have been freed from death? He considered that He was choosing a good shepherd for His sheep, one who, when the wolf came, would not flee or hide himself under a cover of fear, abandoning the sheep to danger. The wolf came; he could not seize the sheep; but he seized, indeed dragged away, the shepherd. A wondrous thing! The sheep is bold, and the shepherd trembles. What a shepherd! If you were going to be such, why did you take charge of sheep? If you accepted the dignity, why do you not render the goodness? “The good shepherd lays down his soul for his sheep” (ibid.).

But you say: “Peter denied with his mouth; yet, because he did not deny in his heart, the Lord looked upon him, and he was called by name to the joy of resurrection with the other apostles.” This, as I hear, is the chief thing you advance in your defence. Then the Lord looked upon Peter denying Him. Why? That He might make him confess: first weeping, afterwards confessing. He looked toward compunction; He called to confession. Therefore, if you have Christ’s regard, where are the tears? But if you weep, why do you not confess? If you follow Peter in denying, why do you not imitate him in confessing?

Finally, brother, if you are a Christian, where is the sign of your King? I see an alien mark upon your forehead. Do you know what will happen to those who bear the mark of the beast? The servants of our God are sealed upon their foreheads, and none can escape the sentence of [Col. 1016A] destruction except those alone who are fortified by the seal of the sign of Tau, the cross of Christ. The cross on the breast, faith in the heart; the cross on the forehead, confession in the mouth: both are owed, both are required. Christ claims the whole for Himself: the heart for faith in Him, the mouth for confession of Him.

But the torturer stands by; the drawn sword threatens. Listen: “Whoever loves his soul will lose it; and whoever loses his soul in this world for my sake will keep it unto eternal life” (Mark 8). Whoever loses for my sake will receive from me. I shall keep what has been entrusted to me, so that I may restore it better. Do not be afraid at all. “Not a hair of your head shall perish” (Luke 21). Why are you anxious about your soul, when you have received even assurance concerning a hair?

But perhaps you will tell me that many today live within the bosom of the Church in faith and confession of Christ who, if questioned in this way, would by no means confess Christ. To this I answer you in the prophetic voice that “the judgments of the Lord are a great deep” (Ps. 35). We cannot search out the depth of God’s judgments or penetrate His unsearchable ways. “I will have mercy,” He says, “on whom I will have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I will show mercy” (Rom. 9; Exod. 33; Rom. 9).

If, therefore, it is pleasing in His sight to spare some of His little ones, whom mother Church either bears while conceived or nourishes once born, and not permit them to come to these more grievous interrogations of temptation, who are you to say to Him: “Why do You act thus?” (Job 9). It does not befit your excellence to understand yourself to be counted among such persons. Among the great servants you had received a place not as a little child, but as guardian and provider for little children. Therefore Jesus said to you, as to one great and strong and fit for the first or nearest following: “Follow me” (John 11). Thus, having obtained the place nearest after Him, He exhorted you to follow Him, so that afterwards you might confidently say to your followers, whom you ought to have guided toward life: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11).

If, therefore, the Lord wished to call you, as a great and faithful servant, to the glory of imitating Him, consider what it means for you, looking to His little ones who are meanwhile to be cherished, not pressed, to say: “But what of these, Lord?” (John 21). The one whom you think you imitate said this, though you ought not to imitate him in all things, not understanding the dignity of that calling or rightly discerning the mercy of the divine dispensation. For this reason he heard the sentence of a just rebuke, that he might learn to obey rather than judge: “Thus I will that he remain until I come. What is that to you? Follow me” (ibid.).

This, therefore, brother, is the word that you must hear most attentively and diligently: follow your King and attain Him. Follow Him unto punishment; attain Him unto glory. If suffering for Christ is required, you have no excuse. “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8). But if you deny Him even without suffering, I say not merely that you are without excuse, but more: you stand accused.

Wretch, where is your soul, that you do not consider [Col. 1017A] what you have become, what glory you have lost, and into what misery and confusion you have fallen? Look upon yourself: what are you? Where are your crown and glory? You have forsaken your King. “Every nation follows its gods, and certainly they are not gods” (Jer. 2). You have forsaken your Lord and God and have become vile, the reproach of the worst. What a shepherd [Col. 1018A] of Christians! How will you feed Christ’s sheep, when you have lost yourself? The sheep were given to be fed by one who would become a wolf. What a shepherd! Blush, wretch, and be confounded! The eyes of Christians are upon you. You are seen from afar. You cannot hide. Your error has made you known. You cannot escape shame unless you show confession.

A DOUBLE APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF HUGH. I. TO THE DOGMATIC WORKS.

[Col. 1017]

HUGH OF FOLIETO, AS IT APPEARS: FOUR BOOKS ON THE CLOISTER OF THE SOUL.

BOOK ONE.

PROLOGUE.

[Col. 1017B]

You asked us, most beloved brother, to seek out and offer to the brothers dwelling with you certain remedies for temptations—namely, dishes of spiritual delight. I sought, brother, and I found. In the wilderness of the Old Testament I discovered a few health-giving roots. From the well-cultivated soil of the Gospel I brought back certain fruits of good flavor. From the books of commentators and certain other wise men, as though from gardeners’ plots, I gathered certain flowers, so that, heaped together in one place, they might yield a sweet fragrance. Thus from the roots—that is, from the sayings of the Old Testament—the sick, by chewing them over, may receive some remedy for health. [Col. 1018B] Let the stronger, however, be refreshed from the fruits of the Gospel as from a good work. Let the delicate be delighted by meditating upon the varied flowers of expositions.

Thus the apostle Paul, having come ashore from the sea at the island of Malta, gathered a quantity of brushwood, in order to light a fire against the cold for the companions who had escaped with him from the peril of the sea (Acts 28). Hence Bede, On the Acts of the Apostles: “By ‘brushwood,’” he says, “are meant all manner of exhortations which avail to kindle charity; plucked from the wholeness of the Scriptures, as it were from leafy branches, they are cut off.”

Morally understood, therefore, the sea signifies the world; the ship, the life of this age; shipwreck, the peril of life; coming forth from the sea, renunciation of the world; and the island rising above the sea [Col. 1019A] signifies the harbor of right conduct. Paul stirs up to love of Christ those brothers chilled and sluggish through the word of preaching, and drawn out from the waves of the worldly storm. The brushwood of exhortation is words; the fire signifies charity. By the viper which came out when driven by the heat of the fire are signified unclean spirits or detractors from the truth. It attacks Paul’s hand—that is, it tries to impede the work of spiritual teaching—by inflicting the bite of detraction and pouring in the poison of envy.

Brother, I shudder at this viper; and lest it introduce the poison of detraction, it is fitting that we avoid it. Therefore disclose our name to none, brother, lest through the author’s lack of learning and the lowliness of his person the labor of our work be cheapened, and lest the viper recognize whose hand it ought to attack. It also seems good that the extent of this little work be divided into four books, for the relief of the mind, because, as blessed Augustine says: “The reader’s attention is refreshed by the end of a book just as the traveler’s labor is refreshed by lodging.”

The first book contains what harms those living in a cloister or wishing to renounce the world. The second teaches the ordering of the material cloister, in which the outward person is held. The third orders the cloister of the soul. The fourth commends the pursuit of the dwelling of the unmade cloister, which is in heaven. It also urges that here among the brothers there be shown the peace which the supreme abbot, namely Christ, has there with those subject to him.

## Chapter I. That those beginning to build must seek a place for the foundation

[Col. 1019C] Those beginning to build must seek a place for the foundation, lest the mass of the wall built upon it lean toward collapse. Accordingly, those who wish to build firmly reasonably make their foundation, after overturning and casting out the earth, upon solid rock—though found with great labor. Yet the reasoning differs according to the differing kinds of buildings.

“For kings build themselves spacious palaces, but their houses are their tombs forever” (Ps. 48). They place strong towers upon lofty mountains, surround them with ramparts and enclose them with walls; they move mountains, not with their own hands but with those of the poor; by diverting rivers through mere command, they ward off the strength of enemies. Yet none of these things can oppose death.

Bishops construct houses not unequal to churches in size; they delight in having painted chambers, and images there are clothed in precious garments of colors. Meanwhile the poor person walks without clothing and cries at the door with an empty belly. O astonishing yet perverse delight! A painted wall bears Trojans dressed in purple and gold, while old garments are denied to Christians. Arms are supplied to the Greek army, a shield gleaming with gold is given to Hector, but bread is not offered to the poor man crying at the door. And, to confess the truth, the poor are often stripped while stones and timber are clothed. They adorn palaces with columns and set doors before houses—would that these enclosed the poor rather than shut them out.

“The citizens of their cities diligently arrange their fortifications, so as to repel the attacks of enemies; they set watches, insert [Col. 1020A] iron bars into the gates, and strengthen their gates with guards. But do you, O Lord, set a guard over my mouth, that I may not sin with my tongue” (Ps. 140).

Monks make themselves cloisters in which the outward person may be restrained; but would that they made cloisters in which the inward person might be kept in order! Thus, brothers, some build towers so that they may plunder more safely; others delight merely in luxury and excess. Others, out of necessity and fear, lest they be oppressed by the powerful—as we have said—do not cease from labor. But some establish cloisters for the Lord as camps of the Lord; and as the servants of kings, by restoring a tower’s fortification, more securely exclude the deceits of enemies, so the inward and outward person, placed within the defenses of cloisters, escape the snares of the ancient enemy and the fragile accidents of temporal things.

We therefore believe it useful to introduce two persons, so that what lies hidden and obscure in more subtle matters may become clear through matters set before the eyes. For just as it might happen if two companions entered a certain fortress when it was about to be besieged by enemies—one prudent or discerning, the other undiscerning or imprudent; one sluggish, the other alert—so it is with the inward and the outward person. The discerning man prepares defenses by day, raises bulwarks, assigns to each his post of defense, entrusts offices of command to certain companions, teaches concord, appoints a time for fasting, lest hunger, which enters through closed gates, gain mastery of the armed men instead of victory; he condemns treachery, lest the enemy enter through someone; but above all he proclaims and urges the need for enduring steadfastness in patience. [Col. 1020C]

At night he sets watches, goes about among the sentries, rebukes the sleepy, and most often of all rouses his companion, because he is sluggish, and teaches him because he is undiscerning. If the enemies draw nearer, he prepares engines of war; the battering ram strikes the gate. Then he goes out armed, withstands the enemy, repels the enemy’s assault by strength because he is alert, and destroys their engines by foresight because he is discerning. The discerning man acts thus not for a time but continually, lest the fortress be handed over to adversaries, and lest he himself be captured, handed over to the officer exacting payment, thrown into prison, and dragged to tortures.

The life of such a man instructs the conduct of those who hear him, and even gives weak minds a desire to speak of him. For to hear good attentively and to wish to become good is a great part of goodness. This, brothers, is the office of the discerning and alert person. But the office of the undiscerning and sluggish person is to obstruct the discerning and delay the alert. The labor of the alert man and the learned foresight of the discerning make this man, while he acts in such ways, a participant in praise and glory. When the fortress is freed from enemies, he receives the favor of his Lord along with his companion and is rewarded with him.

So it sometimes happens, brothers, that the sluggish person is drawn to the reward; but we have more often found the contrary in this partnership. A remarkable thing! This man, who had formerly been such a one—whose uprightness, though it had proved burdensome to them, nevertheless deserved praise even from enemies, and whose foresight had been a wall to his companions—this very man, I say, overcome by a kind of continual pressure from his companion, consents to the sluggish one, tolerates the undiscerning one, and follows the wanderer. Behold, brothers: the sluggish person throws down the alert in wrestling; the undiscerning deceives the discerning. Thus, wandering outside the fortress, they are captured by enemies; they receive punishment as a gift and torment as the reward for labor.

Let, then, a corresponding comparison be applied: let what could occur in the two persons mentioned be shown in the inward and outward person. No one doubts that the outward person—namely, our flesh—is undiscerning and sluggish; but the Creator’s goodness fashioned the soul, that is, the inward person, by its nature discerning and alert. Behold: both have entered the cloister, that is, God’s fortress. Behold: troops of enemies cry out on every side. Some threaten in order to terrify; many flatter in order to deceive; some also promise in order to pervert; nearly all lie in wait in order to seize. “They have all become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13). [Col. 1021B]

Outside, the whole world clamors against those going forth; inside, the upright in heart are shot at in secret. Fiery darts fly; enemies fight from afar; many die. No one can escape the danger of a single day without a wound. As we have said, through some of his army the devil threatens those in the cloister so as to terrify them; through others he flatters them so as to deceive; through others he promises so as to pervert; through the rest he lies in wait so as to seize.

But who are those who threaten the inward and outward person, now placed within the defenses of the cloister, or even others who are thinking of renouncing the world? First, let your goodness hear. When someone, dearest brothers, has entered the cloister, or while still placed in this world has begun, at the admonition of the grace of the Holy Spirit, to consider with bitterness of mind something concerning renunciation of this world, then the prince of this world instills threats through the delight of temporal things and heaps up terrors through the varieties of pleasures. It will perhaps not be useless to make known how the ancient enemy does not cease to threaten through the delight of temporal things.

## Chapter II. How the devil does not cease to threaten through the delight of temporal things

First, the devil attacks the outward person—that is, our flesh, which above we compared to a sluggish and undiscerning companion—by means of delight. [Col. 1021D] He sets before it the form of religious life and its customs, hostile to the flesh; he shows it the difficulty of its purpose. Having done this, he displays how ready the fragility of human nature is to fall: the roughness of the garment, the hardness of the bed, the constant use of coarse foods, the intolerability of labor, the cruelty of superiors, the discord of brothers—all these he sets before the mind’s eyes. He adds the long stretches of nightly vigils, the weariness of the cloister, appointed hours of silence, the length of fasting, and even the withdrawal of coarse foods. And, in order to terrify more severely and, if possible, draw a person into despair, he carefully investigates and announces what evil may arise from these things.

He declares all these things hostile to the weakness of the flesh; and he speaks the truth, but we endure them willingly because from them we await the reward of eternal blessedness. He asserts that incurable diseases will arise from them. It is not good, he says, to disturb the body’s constitutions, since the removal of food changes the constitutions; from changed constitutions comes disturbance of nature; from disturbed nature, infirmity; and from infirmity, death. Behold, brothers, the devil teaches medicine; behold, he has become a physician and speaks of bodily constitutions. He proclaims that various diseases will arise if religious observance is maintained. But why does he do this? Not because he wishes to heal, but because he may kill; not because he may cure diseases, but because he may inflict death more securely.

He sees that the strength of lust can be reduced by the withdrawal of food, and therefore he does not delay in threatening illness. He fears that idleness will perish and drowsiness be destroyed; therefore he displays the intolerability of labor and the prolonged intervals of vigils. He believes that humility is nourished by poverty, and therefore seeks occasions by which he may hinder humility’s coming. “For poverty,” as blessed Gregory says, “is usually the guardian of humility in good minds.” He does not cease to repeat these things constantly to those in cloisters; he sets them before the thoughts of many who are considering renunciation of the world.

O cunning of the ancient enemy! O intelligence without wisdom, yet not without malice! He condemns abstinence, fasting, and the other things mentioned above, and asserts that through them the nature of the flesh fails; yet he is silent about the vice of excess, through which nature is choked or exceeds its bounds. Thus, brothers, the prince of this world threatens the outward person—that is, the flesh—through the delight of temporal things, in order to terrify it; thus he attacks the place of defense where he knows it is weaker.

But the discerning and alert inward person, namely the soul, roused by the tumult of threats, joins its companion without delay in defense, fulfilling what blessed Ambrose says of Noah’s ark: “The presence of a good guard is more frequent,” he says, “where the walls are more fragile.” It exhorts its sluggish companion not to fail; it uses Solomon’s counsel: “My son, when you come to the service of God, prepare your soul for temptations” (Ecclus. 2). It reasonably teaches the undiscerning one how he ought to endure the threats of enemies; it commends the good of religious life and condemns the vice of most evil delight. It warns him not to dread the tossing of this life, because it is for a time; rather, let him cast the anchor of hope and say: “I shall wait for him who saved me from faintheartedness and the storm; for he will not give the righteous person over to tossing forever” (Ps. 54). [Col. 1022D]

Again it urges him not to be saddened in his struggle, nor disturbed by the voice of the enemy and the oppression of the sinner, but to say: “I am ready and am not troubled, that I may keep your commandments” (Ps. 118). With these and many other encouragements the inward person consoles the outward, although it is attacked with it and troubled in its own discipline. For when the flesh is afflicted in itself or endures the insults of secular people, then “the inward person,” as blessed Augustine says, “wearied in affection and surrounded by the barking rage of many, struggles against hatred in order to bring love to perfection, and is saddened in the very struggle.” Therefore let it say with the Prophet: “Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise my supplication; attend to me and hear me” (Ps. 54).

Peter was troubled in his struggle when he walked among the waves. He saw a strong wind coming, and when he began to sink he cried, saying: “Lord, I perish; save me” (Matt. 14). “By what strong wind was Peter troubled?” asks blessed Augustine while expounding that passage. “He was troubled,” he says, “by the voice of the enemy and the oppression of the sinner.” Thus the devil tries through temptations of this kind to remove anyone from charity; and we resist him with the Apostle, saying: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress [Col. 1023B] (Rom. 8), or any of the things which follow?” Therefore let no one separate us from charity. Whoever possesses charity cannot fear the threats of the ancient enemy, because “charity casts out fear” (1 John 4); nor will one who uses the shield of charity yield to assaults of delight, because “charity bears all things patiently” (1 Cor. 13).

Let the inward and outward person, therefore, use this shield for defense, lest they either be terrified by threats or yield to assaults. And let this suffice concerning the first proposition.

## Chapter III. How the devil flatters in order to deceive

First the ancient enemy presents threats through the delight of temporal things; now, however, he flatters the person through the beauty of temporal things in order to deceive. For delight is joined to beauty, so that beauty itself is the cause of delight.

We believe that this concerns what we read written in the Old Testament concerning the patriarch Abram. When Lot wished to separate from him and was granted by his uncle freedom to choose a possession, he lifted up his eyes and looked upon the whole region of the Jordan, which was watered, before the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, like the paradise of the Lord. He chose this; but afterward war arose among various kings, and the history relates that Lot was captured by four kings. When Abram learned this, he counted his household servants and, with three hundred and eighteen men, gained victory and freed his nephew (Gen. 13–14).

Notice, brothers, that when Lot wished to separate from Abram, he looked upon the region of the Jordan, watered like the paradise of the Lord, and set the beauty of the place before usefulness. “For the weaker person,” as blessed Ambrose says, “chooses pleasant things and despises useful things.” Thus, not only did he descend to the pleasant region of the Jordan, captivated by the beauty of the place, but there he is also known to have been captured by enemies.

Perhaps someone would like us to speak more carefully about the example brought forward. Let the diligent reader, therefore—who cannot possess books of expositions whenever or whichever he wishes—listen, not to me but to blessed Ambrose, whose authority we wish here to follow, giving either his meaning in other words or his very words. And that we may speak for fuller instruction, it will not be difficult to note the interpretations of the names. Abram means “father,” Lot “declension,” and Jordan “descent.” [Col. 1024A]

All these can be applied to a human being, because the mind of a righteous person is called a father. For just as a father presides over his children, so the mind presides over righteous thoughts and governs the wandering motions of the senses with a certain sweet fatherly affection. Lot, however, is called “declension.” Therefore Lot is separated from Abram when someone declines from the righteousness of his mind.

There are two ways in which one is said to decline. Blessed Ambrose says: “When Lot declined from evil—that is, error, disgrace, crime—then he was joined to his uncle; but when he declined from good—that is, from what is just, innocent, holy—he became associated with disgrace.” Lot is said to be separated from Abram because the land could not receive them. For, as blessed Ambrose says, one soul does not naturally receive differing motions that are opposed to each other. Thus the land signifies the soul; Lot, certain movements of vices declining from the righteousness of the mind; Abram, the perfection of the mind. The same soul cannot simultaneously contain both perfection of mind and a multitude of vices without separation taking place there.

In the separation, Lot himself is given the choice; but, as it is said, boasting is dear to those who turn aside from truth. Hence, when the devil in his first creation departed from truth—that is, from God—he is read to have first incurred the guilt of pride. So too Lot lifted up his eyes, which is a sign of arrogance. Scripture shows lofty eyes to be the mark of pride (Prov. 6). Departing from truth, the devil descended from heaven; departing from Abram, Lot descended to the towns of the Jordan. For he descends to the towns of the Jordan because, as Ambrose says, “he abandons the fellowship of virtue who chooses appearance rather than truth.”

The text goes on to say that Lot was captured and that five kings were overcome by four. But who are those four kings who triumphed over the five, led away all the cavalry of the Sodomites, and also captured Lot, the son of Abram’s brother? “The five kings,” says blessed Ambrose, “are the five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch.” The four kings are bodily and worldly allurements, since both human flesh and the world consist of four elements. They are rightly called kings because sin has its dominion and a great kingdom. Hence the Apostle: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey its desires” (Rom. 6). [Col. 1024D]

Our senses therefore easily yield to bodily pleasures and worldly things, and are captured by a certain power of these things. But bodily pleasures and the enticements of this world are conquered only by a mind that has become spiritual, clings to God, and wholly separates itself from earthly things. Every declension is captured by these. Hence John’s saying: “Woe to those dwelling on the earth!” (Rev. 8) does not encompass all people—for some are situated on earth whose citizenship is in heaven—but those whom the affection of earthly conduct and the charm of this age conquer.

Therefore, brothers, let us be sojourners rather than inhabitants of this earth. “A sojourner,” as blessed Ambrose says, “bears the appearance of a temporary lodging-place; but an inhabitant places all the hope and use of his substance there where he thinks he will dwell.” Thus the one who is a sojourner on earth is an inhabitant of heaven; but the one who is an inhabitant of earth is a possessor of death. So Lot—that is, declension—is captured while he dwells in Sodom. Let the outward person, therefore, brothers, keep Lot and Abram before his eyes and use this example, lest, drawn by the beauty of passing things, he separate himself from his companion, that is, the inward person.

## Chapter IV. On the four causes of temptation, which every person must avoid and which especially those renouncing this world must hold in contempt

[Col. 1025B]

There are four kinds of things pertaining to beauty which we call causes of temptation. They must be avoided by everyone, and especially held in contempt by those renouncing this world. But let us set forth by examples, according to our capacity, what these causes of temptation are and why and how they must be avoided.

The first of these four is the pleasantness of a place, as with cities and towns, which receive attractiveness not only from their situation but also from the charm of their inhabitants. The second cause is a place of riches: where riches are, there is danger. The third cause is costly adornment, such as the care of fat horses and the elaborate variety of clothing. The fourth is the beauty of women, whose voice, as is said, flatters the ears and whose face flatters the eyes.

We have heard what these four causes of temptations are; now it remains to say why they must be avoided. These things must be avoided because from women’s beauty is born the pleasure of the flesh; from variety in clothing is supplied the desire to please; a place—that is, cities and towns—provides the opportunity to obtain what pleases; and by an abundance of riches, what pleases is generally obtained. Thus, brothers, all these things come together so that temptation may be completed; and therefore they are called causes of temptations. Beauty supplies delight, adornment desire, place opportunity, and riches the effect.

These are the four: the first is that with which temptation occurs; the second, that for which it occurs; the third, that in which it occurs; and the fourth, that through which it is brought to action. For with a beautiful woman carnal pleasure is accomplished, which would not occur with an ugly one. She pleases on account of bodily adornment, though without adornment she would displease those who see her. In a suitable place, the matter is brought to completion, whereas unsuitability would prevent it. But even if those three things converge—even if you are handsome and go about in very ornate garments—yet if money is lacking, she will find a suitable reason for delay. It remains, then, that through money the begun temptation receives its end.

Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, while washing herself on the roof of her house, pleased David because of her beauty; she pleased him and drew him to crime (2 Sam. 11). Bathsheba, therefore, was the cause with which temptation occurred. When Judah went to Timnah to shear sheep, he found Tamar, his daughter-in-law, seated at a crossroads in the clothing of a prostitute; having found her, he had intercourse with her (Gen. 38). What then, brothers? Did Tamar please Judah because of her beauty, when he did not even know who she was? It follows, therefore, that the adornment of her prostitute’s clothing was in some way the cause for which Judah completed carnal pleasure.

Amnon, son of King David, loved his sister Tamar vehemently. He sought and found the opportunity of a place; pretending illness, he obtained from his father his sister’s coming; alone, he approached her when she was alone; he demanded intercourse; she refused; he overpowered her refusal, inflicting violence upon her once overpowered (2 Sam. 13). Let Tamar therefore teach us [Col. 1026B] to flee the opportunity of a place, lest premeditated temptation be enacted in it.

Similarly, Judas Iscariot sought an opportunity to hand Jesus over to the Jews (Luke 22). We know also that Jesus was handed over to the Jews through money. For we know that Judas was a thief and kept the money-box (John 12), as is shown even more clearly by the report that he brought thirty pieces of silver back to the temple and cast them down there. Let each one of us therefore fear being deceived through money, since one of the Twelve sold for so small a price him who ought to be loved above gold and topaz, and who had exchanged even the price of the world for so small a price.

Let those, then, who carry money-boxes, preserve funds, frequent markets and fairs for the needs of the brothers, or visit the houses and courts of secular people, hear these things so that they may take care for themselves. Let such brothers therefore avoid Bathsheba’s roof, Tamar’s crossroads, and the chamber of Amnon, son of King David. Let them also avoid persons of ill repute, suspect lodgings, giving and receiving little gifts, and gathering a great deal of money, lest a snare lie hidden in that by which they perish along with another.

We have set out what those four causes of temptations are and why they must be avoided. Now let us indicate, according to the measure of our weakness, how they may be avoided. We can avoid women’s beauty and the carnal delight arising from it, lest it harm us, through chastity of the eyes and heart. This relates to what is read as written by blessed Augustine in the Rule for Clerics: “An unchaste eye,” he says, “is the messenger of an unchaste heart.” He who condemns unchastity praises chastity. For these are immediate opposites, and one of them must necessarily be present in its proper subject. A chaste eye is the gatekeeper of the heart: it sits at the door and does not permit what harms to enter; it reports nothing but what is fitting; whatever it knows to be indecent it excludes and drives away. But an unchaste eye, seeking what pleases, ranges everywhere; it allows willing things to enter, but warns and urges unwilling ones.

Hence Scripture says: “The eyes are the first darts of an adulteress” (Ecclus. 26). People ordinarily use three kinds of weapons for defense: darts, spear, and sword. Those at a distance are wounded by darts, directed at people whom the spearpoint cannot touch; the spear is brandished in hand-to-hand battle; the sword performs its office. Unchastity uses similar arms to assault the outward person, as the history of the Old Testament relates to have happened in the patriarch Joseph. For Scripture says: “His master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph” (Gen. 39). These are the darts of unchastity, by which many are wounded even from a distance. [Col. 1027A]

Joseph opposed to these darts the chastity of his eyes. For it is written (Prov. 5): “Do not give heed to a deceitful woman, lest you be caught by her eyes or seized by her eyelids; for lust is wanton.” Of this wantonness of the eyes blessed Augustine says in the Rule for Clerics: “If you notice this wantonness in any one of you, admonish him at once, lest what has begun go forward, but let it be corrected immediately.” Lust is not only wanton but also brazen. For Joseph’s master’s wife said to Joseph himself: “Sleep with me” (Gen. 39). This is the thrust of the spear: the speech of the flattering adulteress. Against it is set purity of heart. For the purity of a clean heart does not admit poisonous speech, but hears Scripture saying: “Let not a harlot deceive you with much flattering speech, nor bind you with the snares of her lips” (Prov. 5).

Lust is not only wanton and brazen but also importunate. For Joseph’s master’s wife seized his garment; and Ambrose says: “He could be held by the garment who could not be held in mind.” This is the sword by which one is pierced at close range: namely, the soft touch of the adulteress. Joseph resists it through purity of heart and body. He rejects the adulteress’s touch and tears away the fringe lest contagion creep in; and therefore it is written: “Do not be moved toward another woman, nor embrace one who is not yours” (ibid.). By these means Joseph teaches us not to be drawn through women’s beauty into delight.

Love of coarse clothing destroys the adornment of garments and the desire supplied by it. For no one who truly despises his own attire delights in another’s ornament. Constant residence in the cloister excludes the opportunity of a place, lest it be suitable for temptation. For those who roam through other people’s houses, who delight in continual association with secular people, who pursue spectacles abroad, who make themselves ready not for common necessity but for their own will, and who have no reasons for their journeys but invent them—such people, I say, as they are quick to roam about, are perhaps likewise inclined toward what opportunity of place supplies. [Col. 1027D]

Constant residence in the cloister is therefore secure: concern for household affairs does not disturb it, nor do people’s visits trouble it. There among the brothers is maintained a careful mutual watch; there the discerning diligence of superiors provides for those subject to them; there silence removes the occasion for conversations; continual reading already extinguishes [object uncertain in the source]. For it is written: “Anger expressed increases; anger deferred diminishes” (Prov. 30). There discipline compels the other motions of the heart to serve chastity, and every opportunity for evil is excluded by constant residence in the cloister.

Through voluntary poverty, moreover, the desire for money—of which we have spoken above—is rooted out. It remains, therefore, that through chastity of heart and eyes carnal delight be excluded; through love of coarse clothing the variety of costly garments be removed; through constant residence in the cloister the opportunity for evil be deprived; and through voluntary poverty the desire for money be annihilated. Let the inward and outward person use these things for defense, lest he be deceived by the beauty of temporal things, which flatters him through those four causes.

Let him set heavenly things before earthly, eternal things before transitory, things more beautiful before beauty, and better things before good things. Earthly things decay, await an end, lose the flower of beauty, and are deprived of the fruit of goodness. Heavenly things have no end: they do not decay through weakness, are not broken by old age, and are not annihilated by antiquity. Happy is the eternity which lacks corruption; unhappy is that eternity [Col. 1028B] which is eternally accompanied by the failure of corruption, which endures in order to be tormented, and is tormented eternally because people would sin without end if they could.

Therefore the one who follows the flattering beauty of temporal things is deceived. Let him instead set spiritual beauty before it, that he may see the King in his beauty.

## Chapter V. How the devil promises in order to pervert
At times it happens that those who cannot be sufficiently frightened, and do not yield to blandishments, are more readily bent by promises of gifts. Therefore, in the third place, let us more fittingly consider who they are that promise such things to the inner person in order to pervert him. It is worldly prudence itself that promises in order to pervert. For it promises two things, namely precious things and lofty things: that is, riches and honors—the one belonging to covetousness, the other to pride. [Col. 1028C] These are the sides of the ladder by which the devil descends from heaven to hell.

Worldly prudence promises us things, but gives nothing; and if people sometimes receive what it promises, it is not given but bought. The world gives wealth, but not freely. For one who makes himself the slave of sin for its sake does not receive it freely. It gives honors, but not without a price. To whom does the world promise riches, and whose are the riches it promises? How does it give, and where does it give, what it promises? To robbers it promises the farmer’s substance, the widow’s sheep, the orphan’s fields; to the usurer, his neighbor’s house, an extensive estate, an abundance of wealth. Behold those to whom it promises, and whose are the things it promises. Foolish is this providence which heaps up treasure [Col. 1028D] and does not know for whom it gathers it (Ps. 31).

To soldiers it promises gain amid swords, amid a hail of missiles, under fear of imprisonment, under danger of death; to merchants it promises profit beyond the sea, through the jaws of death. There is the fear of shipwreck; there wealth and lives are entrusted to the winds. Behold how and where it gives what it promises. In both cases there is danger; in both, the means of acquiring are difficult. There it promises profit where it may provide a grave.

To those in the cloister it promises again the license of wandering which the strictness of the cloister had taken away; idle people’s fabulous confessions, the applause of the streets, spectacles of the marketplace, abundance of food, softness of clothing, and, to include everything, freedom to do whatever pleases—it heaps up all these things for them. Behold a difficult battle. Behold Jabin, king of Hazor, fighting against the children of [Col. 1029A] Israel. Behold, he sends to the Canaanites dwelling by the sea, through the mountains and through the plains; to King Simeon [Semeron], and to Fennendor [Ceneroth]; and he gathers many others whom it is difficult to enumerate (Josh. 11).

But what does the Lord say to Joshua son of Nun, who assumed leadership after Moses? “Do not fear them,” says the Lord, “for tomorrow at this hour I will deliver them wounded before Israel; you shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire” (ibid.). Let him hear this who belongs to the army of Jesus—not the son of Nun, but the Son of God. For this battle may also be found in a single person.

Jabin, king of Hazor, gathers an army. Jabin means “perception without prudence”; Hazor, however, means “court,” that is, the world. He sends, [Col. 1029B] therefore, to the Canaanites who dwell in coastal places, near the waves—those who, amid mountains and waves, set everything in motion; who are of the race of Canaan, son of Ham, son of Noah. Ham means “heat,” but Canaan “commotion.” Whoever is heated is quickly moved.

He sends also to the mountains: that is, to those who glory in lofty things and walk amid things great and wonderful beyond themselves. He sends also to the plains: that is, to those who relish earthly things, delight in the flat expanse of pleasures, and are like the cattle of the field, bent toward vices. He sends also to King Simeon, whose name means “hearing.” At times “hearing” is understood in a good sense, as when it is said, “The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping” (Ps. 6), according to which Simeon, one of the patriarchs, received his name (Gen. 29). For the Lord had heard [Col. 1029C] his mother’s prayer.

Conversely, “hearing” is spoken of when someone hears the command of the devil. For he is accustomed to say, “If you fall down and worship me, I will give you all these things” (Matt. 4). And he is recorded as having said to Eve: “You shall be as gods” (Gen. 3). He promised that they would be gods in order to make them guilty. Thus Simeon is named from this, because those who so hear the devil encounter the Israelites along with the king of Hazor.

He sends also into Fennendor, which means “turning.” “Turning” is said in two senses. There is the turning by which one turns to God. There is also that other turning of which the Apostle says to the Galatians: “You were running well; who hindered you?” (Gal. 5)—that is, who turned you aside from the good course and upright work? These are those who follow Jabin king of Hazor, that is, worldly [Col. 1029D] prudence. Therefore let the inner and outer person take care that, after overcoming enemies of this kind, they do not delay to hamstring their horses and also burn their chariots with fire.

In this army there is a chariot of pride, in which, by analogy, we may identify the wheels by which it is borne, the horses that draw it, the charioteer who directs it, and the person who rides in the chariot.

## Chapter VI. On the Chariot of Pride

There are four things that draw the chariot of pride: love of ruling, love of one’s own praise, contempt, and disobedience. Its wheels are boastfulness of mind and arrogance, verbosity and frivolity. The charioteer in this chariot may be the spirit of pride. Lovers of the world are those borne in this chariot. The horses are unbridled, the wheels unstable, the charioteer perverse, [Col. 1030A] and the passenger weak. In each there is danger, because pride always threatens a fall and ruin.

The wheels follow the horses. For love of ruling precedes boastfulness; love of one’s own praise, arrogance; contempt, frivolity; and disobedience, verbosity. For the disobedient commonly burst out into words of self-defense. The front wheels of this chariot are higher than the rear ones; consequently, it knows how to descend, not to ascend. It knows the road to hell, not to the mountain of the Lord.

Likewise, let us not delay to hamstring the chariot of pleasure and the horses of lust, and whatever vices draw people, as though with horses, into sin. Such horses can indeed be hamstrung by vigils and prayers, fasting and continual labor. But chariots can be burned by the fire [Col. 1030B] of the Holy Spirit. This is the fire; these are the weapons of those in the cloister. These are they who kill Jabin; who do not fear the agitation of the Canaanites dwelling near the sea; who do not yield to the proud dwelling in the mountains; nor mingle with those given to pleasure, delighting in the plain of the fields. They do not heed the aforesaid Simeon, nor turn aside with those of Fennendor; but they kill the king with his army, hamstring the horses, and burn the chariots.

Let us therefore mount the chariot of the highest King and pursue the enemies. For Christ has his own horses, of whom the prophet says: “You mounted your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3). “Their,” as Blessed Ambrose says on *Blessed Are the Undefiled*, [Col. 1030C] “bridles are peace; their reins are love, bound together by the bonds of concord and subjected to the yoke of faith; bearing the good charioteer, the Word of God, upon the four wheels of the Gospel. By his whip worldly allurements are put to flight, and the prince of this world is driven out.”

A wondrous thing: wheel ran within wheel, and the swiftness of the chariot was not impeded; that is, the New Testament ran within the Old Testament, by which it was proclaimed.

## Chapter VII. How the Devil Lays Snares in Order to Seize

Now, finally, we must speak of pride, which lays snares in order to seize. Although it was the beginning of sin, “yet,” as Blessed Augustine says, “it was first, and will be the last destroyed. It is that which possesses and holds the worldly; vexes and [Col. 1030D] calls back the newly converted; but tempts and mocks the righteous.” It appears in worldly people, is recognizable in the newly converted, and sometimes lies hidden among religious persons. It dwells in the minds of worldly people through their will; in the newly converted it gives off the odor of former practice; into religious minds it insinuates itself by suggestion. It lies in wait for worldly people in order to ensnare them in wicked action, but for religious persons it lays snares through the glory of human praise.

As truthful history relates, Eleazar killed an elephant and is said to have been killed by the elephant. For the elephant fell upon Eleazar and crushed him beneath the mass of its body (1 Macc. 6). Eleazar signifies those who reject the world’s pomp through humility. The elephant signifies the pride of the world. For while we gladly endure rough clothing, while [Col. 1031A] we love thin garments, while we use cheap food, while the hand grows rough with labor, the skin stiffens with cold, and darkens in the sun, then Eleazar kills the elephant. But when in such things we seek popular favor or praise, the falling elephant crushes Eleazar.

Pride is fittingly figured by the elephant, for the nature of each has a similar constitution. The elephant’s nature is said to be such that the bones of its legs lack joints; hence it cannot bend itself, but always stands. If at any time it wishes to give its body rest, it leans its side against a tree while standing, and thus sleeps and rests. But the inhabitants of the region in which such beasts live commonly cut down a tree during the day, so that when night comes both may fall and the elephant may be killed. Both things occur: [Col. 1031B] the tree is cut down and the beast is killed.

All these things suit pride, and such is its constitution. The limbs of pride are inflexible. When a proud person speaks, if you impose silence on him, he does not comply, but, as Solomon says, “the fool utters all his spirit” (Prov. 29). If, while he gives ear to conversations, you rebuke him, he disregards it; if he does something and you oppose him, he does not stop. Thus his legs cannot bend. The action of pride always stands, as we said of the elephant; but one who stands thus stands badly.

The proud person leans his side upon his own will, as upon a tree, in order to find rest. For whatever we do by the disposition of our own will, we undertake with a tranquil mind; but if it is ordered otherwise, it is reckoned labor. Let the tree of self-will therefore be cut down, [Col. 1031C] so that the beast of pride may fall and be killed. But, as we have said, we must beware lest, in falling, it crush someone.

Thus pride lies in wait for the newly converted. But it lays snares for religious persons in three ways: namely, when someone considers himself alone to be righteous; when he places excessive confidence in his righteousness; or when he ceases from good work. Elijah, considering himself the only righteous person, burst out in these words: “Lord, they have overthrown your altars, killed your prophets, and I alone remain among them” (3 Kings 19). To him the Lord is recorded as replying: “There still remain seven thousand who have not bent their knees before Baal” (ibid.).

But Peter, speaking with excessive confidence, said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. 26). Yet he denied him, and therefore he had spoken too confidently. Tobit signifies those who cease from good work. For it is written concerning Tobit: “Wearied from burial, Tobit came into his house; and when he had thrown himself down beside the wall and fallen asleep, hot droppings from a swallow’s nest fell into his eyes, and he became blind” (Tob. 2). When someone ceases from good work, then Tobit, wearied from burial, comes into his house.

Tobit’s house morally signifies our flesh. The swallow’s nest, made of mud and lined within with light feathers, fittingly represents delight in earthly things. “Swallows,” as Bede says on Tobit, “because of their light flight, figure pride of heart and frivolity; their filth immediately blinds those over whom it has dominion. [Col. 1032A] For he sleeps as though beneath a swallow’s nest who heedlessly subjects his mind to frivolity and pride.” Therefore pride mocks religious persons in these ways—pride “which,” as Blessed Augustine says, “also lies in wait for good people, that they may perish.”

Just as, brothers, we showed far above that something may happen concerning the two companions, the discreet and the indiscreet, so the inner person, resisting the snares of pride, rejecting the gifts of worldly prudence, refusing the blandishments of temporal beauty, and spurning the threats of carnal pleasure, moves his companion—the outer person—exhorts him to battle, and draws him toward the reward. Hence Eusebius of Caesarea says: “Receive, Lord, the twofold service of soul and flesh; for at your command and with your help we have overcome the common enemy by a common purpose.”

Thus the frailty of my body has its own special fruits. I stood spiritually against adversaries by understanding, discernment, and counsel; this flesh fought bodily by the sweat of labor, sobriety, and fasts. “Therefore,” as the same Eusebius of Caesarea says, [Col. 1032B] “both persons must labor and wrestle with all their strength, so that the nobler part may rather lift the lower with itself to the heights of heaven than the lower drag the higher down into the depths of hell.”

Therefore after victory a reward is given; an inheritance of the kingdom is given to each; the reward of eternal blessedness is bestowed. Thus the outer person rejoices with the inner—that is, the glorified flesh rejoices with the spirit—because it awaits no further loss through corruption.

## Chapter VIII. How the Mind Becomes a Den of Robbers, a House of Trade, and a Brothel of a Harlot

[Col. 1032C]

But sometimes, brothers, as we said above, the contrary occurs, and we wonder how it can occur. For who would not wonder that the discerning can be deceived by the undiscerning, or that the strong can be overcome by the sluggish? We wonder at this order of nature, and at its manner as well: reason succumbs, animality rules, the weakness of the flesh deprives the mind of virtue, and thus the Lord is cast out so that the enemy may be received.

Alas! Christ threatens and is not feared; he promises, and is not believed; he entreats, and we become worse. What does Christ promise? Eternal life. What does he threaten? Eternal fire. How does he entreat? By waiting in mercy. He does not permit in order to pervert, but in order to convert. Yet he is cast out, and that which is written in the Gospel happens: [Col. 1032D] “My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers” (Matt. 21).

Thus the human mind sometimes becomes a den of robbers, becomes a house of trade, becomes a harlot’s brothel. It becomes a den of robbers when someone, envying his brother, lies in wait to slander him and strips him of the garments of virtues. It becomes a house of trade when, for the things we do, we frequent the marketplace of human favor and there, buying and selling, receive praise for good work like foolish merchants. It becomes a harlot’s brothel when, in the chamber of a chaste mind, a brothel of lustful delight is set up.

Let secular people fear this, and let them hold before themselves the analogy which we gave concerning the two companions, lest, when [Col. 1033A] they have entered the cloister of religious life, they again become subject to the power of the old enemy when he attacks. But now, brothers, let us who have entered the cloister say something, according to the measure of our weakness, in exhortation of secular people against those things which the devil above threatened through the delight of temporal things.

Let secular people whom temporal delight holds captive, who shrink from the habit of religious life, hear how sweet is the fellowship of true religion. Let the poor hear and rejoice; those of moderate means hear and exhort others; the rich hear and be strengthened. For religion is abundant for the poor, sufficient for those of moderate means, tolerable for the rich, generous to the infirm, compassionate toward the delicate; moderate toward the stronger, merciful toward penitents, severe toward the perverse, excellent toward the good. These are the nine benefits of religion. Let us therefore dwell more carefully [Col. 1033B] upon each, so that the goodness of religion may be known from its benefits.

## Chapter IX. That Religion Is Abundant for the Poor

Religion, I say, is abundant for the poor. Let the poor therefore hear and rejoice; let them hear and obey. There are three kinds of poverty. Some lack temporal goods unwillingly, and this is commonly called want. For they lack goods and lack good will, than which nothing can be richer. For nothing is richer than good will.

There are others who abound in goods and yet are poor in spirit; and this is golden poverty, because, though riches flow in, their hearts refuse to set themselves upon them. Both this poverty and the former have danger, but the wise person avoids danger. Solomon was wise, and he desired another poverty. Which? [Col. 1033C] That which would provide what is necessary for sustenance. What is it? Moderation (Prov. 30). This is the third kind; philosophers call it frugality. Hence Seneca, in his letter to Lucilius, when praising voluntary poverty, says: “Frugality is voluntary poverty.”

There are some who come from this world into religious life or the Church “whose poverty,” according to the testimony of Blessed Augustine, “was such when they were outside that they could not even find necessities for themselves. Their pantry was supplied not by inheritance or patrimony, but by the labor of their hands; and if the hand ceased, bread failed.” Want, which provides almost nothing, supplied such people with whatever clothing it could. Such people sometimes enter churches that abound in ample possessions, so that in the Church they may be honored, though in their own house they could only have been contemptible.

If perhaps they enter a church in which poverty is loved, they immediately consider departing; they invent reasons; they call that place’s observance intolerable; they allege the excessive severity of the superiors; they bring forward against themselves certain things about the brothers which, because they do not wish to endure them, they say they cannot endure. They contrive all this cunningly, so that they may more suitably transfer to a richer church. They seem humbly to request release from the bond of their profession, mixing harsh words with soft. For they threaten scandal if they depart badly, and swear that they can have a tranquil mind in another church, but never in their own.

But if at last what they request is denied, then you would hear how they raise their necks [Col. 1034A] against those whom they had not dared to approach outside. Then you would see how the rich are humbled there and the poor puffed up. Answering their abbot with unrestrained boldness, they accuse certain brothers, call them criminal, call certain people “righteous” ironically; and those whom they cannot deny to be righteous, they call, in envy of their goodness, excessively righteous. What more? At last, having broken the vow of their purpose, they depart. They rejoice to be honored, forget their former lowliness, are ashamed of their lineage, refuse to be called by their own name, and love titles of dignity. If they are called abbots, provosts, or priors, the eye smiles, the face brightens, signs of conscience appear on the countenance, and thus the mind announces what it desires. To poor people of this kind Christ promises not the kingdom but hell.

There are, however, others who came to the Church from poverty. If necessities are given them, their humility regards them as superfluities. They think one day of idleness sacrilege; they judge it a fault to be filled with cheap food; they consider themselves equal to no one and bound to serve all; they are ashamed to have even somewhat good clothing; and unless discernment tempered their humility, they would doubt whether it is lawful to use lawful things. Such people follow the poor Christ along the straight way, because the poor follow the poor and the humble follow the humble. Temporal things are given to these for necessity, and heavenly things are promised them for eternity. This is the first benefit of religion: that it provides necessities to those in need and is unwelcome to no one.

## Chapter X. That Religion Is Sufficient for Those of Moderate Means

Religion is sufficient for the person of moderate means. It ought to suffice [Col. 1034C] because it supplies necessities. It gives enough; it gives freely. But perhaps someone may say: “It neither gives enough nor gives freely.” “It does not,” he says, “give freely, because, while it bestows and furnishes necessities, it demands labor.” God did not will that necessities should be given in return for labor; rather, for temporal labor eternal rest is promised and given.

It gives enough, as we have said. For human condition is needy in two ways: one, in which nature fails; the other, which afflicts nature. Hunger makes nature fail; cold afflicts nature. But moderation restores both. For it gives that by which nature may be warmed and by which it may recover strength, and this is sufficient for nature. For to satisfy human nature, not color but warmth is sought; not pleasure but nature’s sustenance.

Therefore moderation gives enough, [Col. 1034D] and gives freely. Moderation is like a level road, on which neither the height of riches threatens a fall to those ascending, nor the depth of want denies hope of rising to those falling. This is the royal road of which the Lord speaks to Moses: that he should proceed by the royal road and turn neither right nor left (Deut. 5).

There are three roads and three persons who walk upon them: want, moderation, and riches; the poor person, the person of moderate means, and the rich person. Moderation is the middle road which must be kept, which leads to the city of the highest King; while on the right and left are want and riches. Moderation is like a certain measure by which the extent of all goodness is bounded. For example, when someone departs from justice, as is recorded of the priest Eli, then, so to speak, he falls short of the measure of goodness in a kind of definiteness. But [Col. 1035A] when justice is extended through intemperance even to cruelty, he exceeds the measure of goodness in a kind of length. This is the measure sufficient for the person of moderate means, because it neither withdraws necessities nor supplies superfluities. The first benefit, then, was to give necessities to those in need; the second is not to withhold necessities from the person of moderate means.

## Chapter XI. That Religion Is Tolerable for the Rich

Religion is tolerable for the rich; it can be borne. The yoke of oxen humbles their necks; the burden drawn tames the pride of the flesh—which proceeds, as it were, from fatness. So Christ’s yoke bends our stiffness of neck, lest we be like a horn-goring ox that sheds blood. His burden mortifies our flesh, lest, becoming wanton, it dissolve into lust or, wandering, pursue idleness.

Our burden is the life of Christ; his teaching is imposed upon us as a yoke. The one is light; the other sweet. But perhaps someone will say: Christ’s burden is not light but heavy; his yoke is not sweet but harsh. For Christ’s life is to suffer reproaches, possess nothing, afflict the body, and die for one’s neighbor. But for whom is this burden light? Hear for whom: Paul says, “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1); and elsewhere, “I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9).

A wondrous thing: secular people shrink from these things every day, and suffer these things every day. They fear suffering reproaches for Christ, but for the world they suffer everlasting reproaches. They greatly fear dying for Christ, and yet daily die for temporal gain. Is it not light to die for one’s neighbor and be with Christ? Hope of reward lessens labor. Truly the life of Christ is a light burden, because it carries neither much nor for long. The boundary of death is near, and religion is free from the weight of riches: it does not acquire with covetousness, does not possess with love, and does not grieve if it loses.

Christ’s yoke is sweet (Matt. 11). For his teaching is like a yoke because it is accustomed to subjugate proud necks; but love is the bond. Hear how sweet a yoke is placed upon our necks: “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22); and elsewhere: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5). Behold, brothers, the yoke with its bond: that is, the teaching concerning love. Love fastens the yoke upon the neck, because we are subjected to the yoke of teaching when teaching is received with love.

But the devil’s yoke burdens and crushes. His yoke is sin; its bond is the habit of sinning; the burden borne is the punishment of sin. Two are held beneath this yoke, namely flesh and spirit. The rich are pressed beneath this yoke: for the pride of the rich suffers much—chains, prisons, cold, and sometimes hunger. We know, brothers, the tables of the rich, and some of you know them too. Insolence finds a place there for itself, not simplicity; to some food is given without drink, and conversely. Many rise hungry from the table and nevertheless, with a certain urbanity, console their hunger. Already the dinners of the rich have ceased to precede supper: [Col. 1036A] for the supper of the rich is either meager or nonexistent.

But the table of religion is ordered, sufficient, and not excessive. No one loses his place there in shame, because humility orders everything. Soldiers also fast in order to plunder others’ goods; likewise scholars fast in order to become more subtle; yet they do not wish to fast so as to hear: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). Christ says, “I will refresh”; man says, “I shall fail.” Whom should I believe? I believe that he who could make a human being can also refresh him.

“Come,” he says, “you who labor”—who labor, I say, in mud and brick (Exod. 1). The mud of Egypt is sticky, foul-smelling, mixed with blood; its bricks are indissoluble, baked by the fire of covetousness and the flame of lust. The rich labor in these things. Great is the labor of the rich: they keep watch while plotting against the poor. Hence cold, [Col. 1036B] hence thin garments. One bears the weight of armor; another walks unarmed among missiles. The labor of the cloister is lighter, yet it is feared. The weight of a tunic is lighter than that of armor. The cloister is safer than a fortress. Obedience to an abbot is safer than the command of a king. The latter sends men among swords; the former avoids danger.

Many labor, but it does not profit them. Saul and Agag, king of Amalek, labored, but their labor was vain. David and Solomon labored—one by fighting, the other by building—and the labor of both was useful (1 Kings 15). David fought in order to conquer; Solomon built in order to rest. Let us fight with David, not against David in Judaea, so that we may dwell with him in Jerusalem.

David suffered much. While he was still in his father’s house, he defeated the lion and the bear. In the army of Israel he killed Goliath [Col. 1036C] (1 Kings 17). But while he served Saul and obeyed him, going out at the king’s command, Saul nevertheless planned to kill him. David had gained the favor of Jonathan, who informed him of the king’s intention (1 Kings 18). When Saul had died and David received the kingdom, he was attacked by his son Absalom. With the elders of the people he escaped danger by fleeing; he did not desire his son’s death, but mourned both son and king when dead (2 Kings 15, 18).

The moral sense is clear. When David, while still a boy in his father’s house, defeated the lion and bear, this occurs when someone still living in the world destroys pride and lust within himself. After this, entering the army of Israel, he killed Goliath: that is, joined to the congregation of faithful brothers, he overcomes the devil. He becomes obedient to superiors even when they are perverse; and this is to go in and out at Saul’s command.

David is troubled by Saul, but gains the favor of Jonathan, who consoles him, because he possesses the gift of the Holy Spirit by which he is consoled. For Jonathan is interpreted as “of the dove,” that is, the Spirit’s gift. When Saul has died, David, whom the Lord chose, is raised by the people to the kingdom, because one who has learned humbly to be subject is elevated to the honor of leadership. Absalom persecutes his father, for superiors suffer much from spiritual children. David mourns his persecuting son because every spiritual father grieves at the perversity of his children, which is the death of the soul.

David mourned three: son, friend, and enemy—that is, Absalom, Jonathan, and Saul. [Col. 1037A] David fulfills the whole law: natural, written, and evangelical. The natural law, when he mourns his son; the written law, when he grieves for his friend, Jonathan; the evangelical law, when he mourns his enemy, Saul. Such a person does not shrink from the labor of the cloister, but dances with David naked before the ark (2 Kings 6).

The labor of the cloister is tolerable because moderation tempers labor and takes from the rich only what is superfluous. Religion removes what harms and supplies what is necessary; therefore it is tolerable for the rich.

## Chapter XII. That Religion Is Generous to the Infirm

Religion is generous to the infirm. There are four kinds of infirmity. Some are infirm through old age; others through injury to their limbs; others through an illness which departs after a time; others are held continually by sickness. There are some whose old age is talkative, irascible, full of proverbs, and occupied with idle tales. Though their dimming eye grows dark, though the trembling hand ceases from work, though the foot no longer knows its office, though they walk bent over in body and mind alike, nevertheless, as Blessed Augustine says in the book *On the Twelve Abuses of the Age*, speaking of the irreligious old man, [Col. 1037B] “his heart and tongue do not grow old. These are those who glory when they have done evil, who boast that they were rich, who recount the wars of secular rulers rather than the peace of the saints, and wish to be called to lawsuits because they know past events.”

Such persons would accuse Susanna if you wished to praise her, and would praise the adulterous woman Jezebel; therefore their judgment shall return upon their own head, and the angel of the Lord shall come down to cut them in two (Dan. 13).

There are others who, though they do not see the earth with their eyes, contemplate heaven with their mind. Though they stumble with their feet and their whole body sways, they do not stumble with their tongue and do not waver in mind. They are silent about harmful things; they recount what gives instruction; they subject the inner person to labor when they cannot subject the outer person. They persist in prayer; they reconsider all their years in the bitterness of their soul; and therefore their youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s (Ps. 102).

Of those who suffer injury to the limbs, bodily distress, or sickness, there are indeed some who bear bodily affliction impatiently. They consult a physician, and if they do not recover at once, they become angry at their illness and despair of health. But what shall I say, brothers, about such people? They do not bear a headache graciously; how, then, would they endure torments of the head for Christ? They fear the lash; how would they suffer beheading for Christ?

There are others who do not serve the flesh, but desire the flesh to serve the spirit; who seek no physician except Christ and cry with the prophet: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed” (Jer. 15). They bear their infirmity alone, because they do not trouble anyone with complaints. They are not complainers like those of whom we have spoken.

There are four things concerning which the infirm complain: infirmity, medicine, food, and observance. Some complain of infirmity because they bear its burden unwillingly. Others complain because they cannot take part in the labor [Col. 1038A] of the brothers. Some complain concerning medicine because, as they say, they are not helped by brotherly love. Others are saddened because the Church suffers loss on account of their infirmity. Some complain about food because it is not supplied sufficiently, or in the manner or at the time they wish. Others grieve because they eat delicate food while doing no work, and because someone serves them while they serve no one.

Some complain about the observance, attributing the cause of their infirmity to the severity of the order; and thus they ruin by evil what they had done well. But there are others who complain about the observance because, separated from the community of brothers, they are treated more delicately. Yet if, from their bed, they hear the voices of the brothers chanting psalms in choir, then they meditate upon the psalms, praying in the chamber of the heart with the doors shut. And though they have spent the entire night awake, distressed by their pains, they nevertheless judge blessed those who labored while serving God through part of the night.

They do not leave the side of their bed; yet they regard as happy those who bear the weariness of the cloister graciously. They confess that they fulfill nothing of the observance; but, unless I am mistaken, they fulfill the whole of it. They are confined in the cloister of infirmity; they are disciplined by the rods of anxieties and the thorns of pains; they fast, keep watch, and labor, because infirmity denies them food, sleep, and rest. Yet if a softer bed is prepared for them, or if they are compelled to sleep without stockings, as though they had done something criminal, they fear to end their life in such a condition.

Such people need consolation, lest they fail through bodily distress or the affliction of the inner person. Let them hear what the angel says to Peter: “Gird yourself, and put on your sandals” (Acts 12). Hence Bede, commenting on the Acts of the Apostles: [Col. 1038C] “Peter had for a while loosened the fastenings of his tunic because of the harshness of the prison, so that, with the tunic hanging down around his feet, he might somehow temper the cold of the night,” providing an example to the infirm that, when we are tested by bodily distress or human injury, it is lawful for us to relax somewhat the strictness of our rule.

Let them therefore use the counsel of the wise, lest they fail; for these things were written for our instruction. These are the matters we have said, in some fashion, concerning the varieties of infirmity. Now let us briefly show how religion is generous toward the infirm. Blessed Benedict says: “Above all and before all, care for the infirm must be undertaken.” Behold how generous religion is toward the infirm. “Before [Col. 1038D] all,” he says: that is, what the sick brother asks for ought to be prepared more quickly than for any of all the brothers. “Above all”: that is, more abundantly than for the rest, so that, if necessities are given to others, more and more delicate things are sought for the infirm: more things, so that something from among many may please them; more delicate things, so that, when they taste them, they may be refreshed by something.

## Chapter XIII. That Religion Is Compassionate toward the Delicate
Religion is compassionate toward the delicate.

There are four kinds of delicate persons: those delicate by will, by habit, by birth, and by nature. Delicate by will are those who, although they can use coarser foods, do not wish to do so; instead, seeking varied and refined dishes, they answer the belly and obey its demands. But I answer the belly too, my brothers: [Col. 1039A] when it cries out, I restrain it not with bread but with the rod—that is, not by satiety but by abstinence. For as a father corrects his pampered son’s bad habits with a rod, so through abstinence the pleasure-seeking impulse of belly and throat is restrained.

Concern for the belly makes me anxious, now desiring these foods, now those. But I say to it: “What are you asking for, belly? Shall several dishes sometimes be prepared for me alone, while one dish is given to many brothers? One for many, and many for one? Far be it!” What then? “It is necessary, therefore, as blessed Gregory says, that we should use food not for stuffing the belly, but should learn,” with blessed Paul, to be satisfied and to be hungry, to abound and to suffer want (Phil. IV), “lest we grant more to the flesh than necessity requires, and thus refined pleasure be excluded.”

Many are delicate by habit, although they are [Col. 1039B] from the common people. While they were in the world, they served their bellies; once placed in the Church, they refuse to change their customary food, lest illness result. They fear illness and bring death upon their own souls. They claim that the habit of their former life is the cause of their incapacity; but, as the saying goes, a bad habit must be abolished.

Delicate by birth are the children of noble families. Just as in the world they were nobler in dignity of lineage, so among the assembly of brothers they wish to be considered nobler through luxurious food. Yet those noble by birth are often made nobler by the progress of good works. They boast that they are not delicate: humble in speech, dress, and conduct; pleasant in company; receptive when corrected; sound in counsel; consolers of the brothers. Such people do not put forward the authority of their lineage in order to be honored in the Church, [Col. 1039C] nor do they glory in the rank of their parents; rather, they conceal occasions of pride, lest their foot slip into sin.

Delicate by nature are those whose constitution is such that they cannot bear the burden of labor, fasting, and vigils. They also dislike refined foods; they are a burden to themselves; weakened by the sun’s heat, they are quickly tired, and at once grow numb with cold. Nature has likewise formed some among the common people in this way. Religion is compassionate toward all these.

There is both true and false compassion; yet each is commonly expressed in three ways: by mouth, heart, and deed. Feigned compassion by mouth occurs when someone consoles another’s loss with tearful words. Compassion by heart occurs when someone who abounds in riches encounters a person oppressed by illness or poverty and, moved by pity, bends the inclination of the mind in compassion; [Col. 1039D] yet, passing on, does not help the needy person. This compassion has conceived but is barren: it has not given birth. For almsgiving ordinarily springs from the conception of true compassion; but avarice, like a poisoner, strangles the offspring lest it come forth into the light.
