It obstructs the fruit of almsgiving and casts out from the human heart, as from a woman’s womb, dead, the conception of compassion that arose from the seed of pity. That compassion which exists only in speech is flattering; this other is called barren.

There follows another kind: it gives much, but does so in order to be praised or to receive more. It does not bear the weight of true compassion, but is lifted up by the lightness of empty glory; it does not sympathize, but glories, and may therefore be called pride. Thus one of these says, by flattery, that she is [Col. 1040A] a friend; another, by feigning tears, deceives even the wise; while a third, by giving much, receives greater things.

These same three kinds of compassion may also be understood favorably: when someone kindly consoles his brother; when someone is truly contrite in heart; or when he pities and lends to a poor person, seeking no repayment but being drawn to the gift solely by the impulse of pity. One is consoling compassion; another is compassion of pity; the third, compassion of refreshment.

Some have compassion on themselves, some on a brother, and some on a superior. The first belongs to moderation, the second to love, the third to prudence. Some are restrained by shame or by a desire to afflict the flesh, lest they be willing to have compassion on the flesh’s need and necessity. If they were moderate, they would have compassion on themselves, lest they [Col. 1040B] kill a fellow citizen. Others are compelled by love to have compassion on their brother; but because they do not have the means to complete works of compassion, they carefully make known to the superiors—whose duty it is to provide and bestow necessities—what that brother is like and what he is able to bear.

They also have compassion on their superior, lest the one who ought to lead the way fail upon the road. Hence a certain practice has become established in the community of some brothers: they appoint one of the brothers over their abbot, to whom the abbot is obedient in arranging his own care. Thus, whenever it seems suitable to that brother, he causes his abbot to make allowance for himself in eating meat or in something similar, lest the rigor of office break human frailty. This is compassion of prudence.

There are three things by which true compassion is tested: hidden benefits, poverty, and death. If a benefit is [Col. 1040C] bestowed secretly, it extinguishes the desire for human praise. When someone has mercy upon a poor person, he removes the expectation of temporal repayment. When he does not refuse to suffer death for his neighbor, he does not put love of the world first. For these are the three things that ordinarily weaken the limbs of compassion: human favor, temporal reward, and love of the world. Whoever suffers death for his neighbor truly has compassion. Thus Christ suffered for us because he truly had compassion.

## CHAPTER XIV. That religion is moderate toward the stronger.

Religion is moderate toward the stronger. Measure must be maintained in all things, for whatever exceeds measure exceeds strength as well. Measure preserves a thing unharmed; immoderation destroys it. Measure weighs with an even balance the burdens [Col. 1040D] of the stronger as of the weaker, lest the stronger be weighed down or the weaker crushed beneath the burden.

There are three kinds of strong persons: some are strong in mind, others in body, others in knowledge. Some are strong in knowledge. Although they may lack a loving disposition of mind, and although bodily strength may not be available to them, yet through a certain rational knowledge—by which they recognize both their Creator’s kindness and their own negligence—they bend the rigor of their minds and compel their bodies to serve their Creator. They bear their brothers’ burdens by consoling them; they lift up the fallen by teaching; and, should they themselves fall, they rise quickly lest they give scandal, because they are wise. They bear two heavy burdens: a failing mind and infirm flesh. They cover the hidden things of heart and mind, and govern the works of the flesh by discernment alone; thus [Col. 1041A] they learn to love well because they know how to act well.

Strong in body are those whom nature has made robust for enduring labors. Some of them can do what is useful but will not; others can and will; others again are willing to do more than they can endure. Goliath, though strong in body, could have acted well but would not. David could and did wish to serve his Creator. The righteous themselves sometimes wish to do more than they are able to endure: they so tame the pride of the flesh that their strength fails when they wish to work. If they fast, their stomach weakens; if they read, they suffer dizziness; if they perform any labor, they suffer headache. This happens because they have zeal, but not according to knowledge.

There are certain matters in which knowledge is especially necessary: fasting, vigils, and labor. Unless rest and refreshment follow [Col. 1041B] labor, human nature cannot endure labor. But measured work, abstinence from luxurious food, and the vigils established by the holy Fathers bring the healing of health to body and soul. Those who live in this way possess strength of both soul and body according to knowledge.

There are others, strong in body but weak in mind, who spare themselves, love themselves, pursue idleness, and devote themselves to tales. Such people are accused of theft, robbery, and lying. They are thieves because they withhold from the common need what they had made common when, denying themselves, they renounced the world. They are robbers before God because, in the sight of him who knows the hidden things of hearts, they violently take away from the common life what they know or are able to do. They lie before God and men [Col. 1041C] because they can render what they vowed, but will not. Thus they are thieves before their brothers, robbers before God, and liars before men and God. They deceive brothers who do not know what they can do; they offend God, before whose eyes all things are naked and open (Heb. IV); and they do not render to God what they vowed in the presence of their brothers. For this is characteristic of theft, robbery, and lying: the first occurs secretly, the second openly, and the third otherwise than promised.

It remains for us now to say something concerning those who are strong in mind. Some are strong, others stronger, others strongest. Tobias was strong (Tob. I), Job stronger (Job I), Abram strongest (Gen. XII). Strength of mind is tested in two ways: by covetousness and by carnality.

[Col. 1041D] Tobias did not yield to covetousness when he entrusted a weight of silver to his needy kinsman Gabael; he did not love money more than his neighbor. Job lost his property, but what did he say? “The Lord gave; the Lord took away. As it pleased the Lord, so it has been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord.” Abram left what he possessed and obeyed the Lord’s voice, not under compulsion but willingly.

Tobias entrusted; Job lost; Abram left behind: the one money, the other property, the third land, house, and kindred. One acted in hope, another patiently, the other willingly: the first by compassion for the needy, the second by patient endurance, the third by obedience to him who commanded. Thus they do not yield to covetousness, which consists in three things: love of possessing, grief at losing, and compulsion in leaving behind. Likewise, the three each repel their own three [Col. 1042A] forms of carnality and do not yield to it.

Tobias did not love his son more than he ought, nor did he place carnality above spirituality, but beneath it. He taught good things to his son when present and prayed for him when absent (Tob. IV). Job did not grieve for the death of his children more than was necessary. He shed tears for their death, rendering to his neighbor the debt of compassion. While they lived, however, Job rose early and offered burnt offerings for each one; and Job did this every day (Job I). Abram, however, not only sent Ishmael away, but also Isaac, whom he had begotten in old age by a barren wife—he who was the father’s love, for he is the one whom he loved, Isaac; the mother’s consolation; the joy of both (Gen. XXI–XXII). This son, I say, such as he was, Abram offered to God for sacrifice.

Thus, brothers, we ought to be strong in mind, [Col. 1042B] like Tobias. If one of us speaks with his friend, let him teach him good things; if he is absent, let him pray for the absent person. But if he wishes to be stronger, when his possessions are taken away, let him not pursue his enemies. Job did not pursue the Chaldean enemies when they took away his possessions.

We pursue enemies in three ways: by hand, tongue, and mind. We pursue them by hand when we recover by force what robbers had taken by force, contrary to the Apostle, who says: “Do not demand back what is yours.” For one who claims back with litigation claims back wrongly (I Cor. VI). We pursue them by tongue when, by complaint or accusation before those in authority in order to receive back our goods, we leave our neighbors—even though they are wicked—bound under sentence of death; not giving place to wrath, as the Apostle says, but avenging ourselves (Rom. XII). We pursue them in mind [Col. 1042C] when we do not cease to pursue in hatred and the insolence of a wretched mind what we cannot obtain by force or trickery. The Apostle forbids this, saying: “Be at peace with all” (ibid.).

What then, brothers, shall I say of those who pursue a neighbor over an ox or an ass? What would they do if you announced the death of a son? What if you said that the death of seven sons, as was announced to Job, had happened? Blessed Job therefore instructs those in the cloister concerning patience: how they ought to bear losses of temporal goods, and how it is fitting to grieve over the death of carnal friends. He bore both kindly: neither did he pursue an enemy because of the loss of possessions, nor did he turn his heart toward hatred—which is the death of the soul—because of the death of his children.

But whoever wishes to be strongest, like [Col. 1042D] Abram, who did not lose his possessions but left them; who did not love his son so as to offend God’s Son—such a person, I say, should renounce all that he possesses and sacrifice with the sword of God’s word those whom he loved carnally or with carnal affection.

Abram was strongest, but blessed Lawrence was stronger than the strongest. Let us hear how Abram left his own things behind, while Lawrence scattered his own things and gave them to the poor (Ps. XI). Abram offered his son to God; Lawrence offered himself for the Son of God. The former prepares fire, binds his son, draws the sword, but hears the angel forbidding him to carry it out. The latter, placed upon the fire, preaches Christ; he does not exasperate the executioners who press him or the coals that serve him with words. He becomes a burnt offering to the Lord—that is, wholly consumed: [Col. 1043A] inwardly by the fire of love, outwardly by the flame of tribulation. Because the former became obedient, he receives his son unharmed; because the latter perseveres in torments, he is received by the Son of God unto salvation. This is the strength of love. Of it it is written: “Love is strong as death” (Song VIII); and, to confess the truth, love is stronger. For nothing separates us from the love of Christ.

There are, therefore, as we said above, three kinds of strong persons: strong in body, mind, and knowledge. In these consists the strength of all religion. For one who knows, wills, and is able to act well, if he keeps measure, is perfect.

## CHAPTER XV. That religion is merciful toward penitents.

Religion is merciful toward penitents. A human being repents in three ways: by mouth only, by heart only, or by mouth and heart together. [Col. 1043B] Saul repented by mouth, Peter by heart, David by mouth and heart together.

David committed three offenses against Uriah his servant: treachery, murder, and adultery with his wife. Yet, when the prophet Nathan accused him, he judged himself in heart and said aloud: “I have sinned against the Lord.” Because he repented in heart, he heard from the same prophet: “Your sin has been forgiven” (II Kings XII).

Peter denied three times; yet the Lord looked upon him, because he wept bitterly (Luke XXII). He washed with tears the foul contagion of his tongue.

Saul sinned in three ways: by pride, disobedience, and excuse for sin. He sinned by disobedience when he did not kill the Amalekite sinners, as the Lord had commanded, but, turning toward plunder, did evil in the sight of the Lord (I Kings XV). He sinned by [Col. 1043C] excusing sin when Samuel said: “What is this sound of flocks that rings in my ears, or of herds that I hear?” (ibid.), and Saul replied: “They brought them from Amalek; for the people spared the better sheep and herds in order to sacrifice them to the Lord your God, but we killed the rest” (ibid.). Saul excuses himself but accuses the people. “The people,” he says, “spared what the Lord had not commanded us to spare; but we killed the rest, as the Lord commanded.”

Hence Bede, On Samuel: “Saul declares that he killed with the people those things which were killed at the Lord’s command; but that he did not spare, rather the people spared, those things that were kept contrary to the Lord’s prohibition.”

He sinned through pride when at last he said to Samuel: “I have sinned; but now honor me before the elders of my people and before Israel” (I Kings XV). [Col. 1043D] Saul’s pride was immoderate, but Samuel’s humility measured. The reprobate seeks honor, and the prophet honors the reprobate.

So also in our times many are found who, reproved by spiritual masters, repent only with their mouths and fear being deprived of honor. Indeed, if we see such people among us, we either refuse to tolerate them or accuse them because they are incorrigible. Samuel, however, not only tolerates but honors them. Hence Bede, On Samuel: “We too ought, after the example of blessed Samuel, to deal modestly with such persons.” We ought not to expose those whom we do not doubt are incorrigible and condemned by divine judgment—especially those whom we know to be distinguished by some ecclesiastical rank, which the binding of Saul [Col. 1044A] suitably represents.

For many disparage prelates, though, while disparaging them, they would nevertheless wish to be what those prelates are. But if what they had judged should happen to them, they are no better than those whom they had judged.

Therefore, as we said above, Saul sinned through pride, disobedience, and excuse for sin, and so became a participant in the pride of the devil, the transgression of Adam, and the excuse of Eve. Adam sinned against the Father, Eve against the Son, and the devil against the Holy Spirit. Adam accused the Father’s goodness; Eve, the Son’s wisdom; the devil, the Holy Spirit’s kindness. Adam accused the Father’s goodness when he said: “The woman whom you gave me deceived me” (Gen. III). Eve rebuked the Son’s wisdom, implying that he had not acted wisely because he placed [Col. 1044B] in paradise the serpent by which she was deceived. The devil, however, fails to recognize the kindness of the Holy Spirit when, despairing of forgiveness, he persists in the greatest sin, that is, pride. Hence the Psalmist says: “And I shall be cleansed from the greatest sin” (Ps. XVIII). Here blessed Augustine says: “The greatest sin is pride.”

These three—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—give testimony in heaven against Saul: the Father, who is truth, concerning his deceitful excuse; the Son, who was obedient to the Father unto death (Phil. II), concerning his disobedience; and the Holy Spirit, concerning his persistence in sin. We who excuse our sins, who are disobedient and proud, must beware lest these three give testimony against us in heaven.

[Col. 1044C] Saul did not obey his superior, nor did he spare his inferior; rather, he spared himself while accusing the people subject to him, excusing himself, and rejecting Samuel’s command. Whoever dishonors a priest, though a layman, sins against a superior, namely Samuel. For priesthood is worthier than kingship. We know this to have been prefigured in the Lord’s Passion by the servant of the high priest whose ear Peter cut off; his name was Malchus (John XVIII), which is interpreted “king.” Malchus served the high priest because priesthood is worthier than kingship.

Some may wonder—perhaps doubting Saul’s damnation—at what we have said. Let them read Jerome, Against Jovinian, and there they will find three ranks of men: rams, sheep, and goats. David is numbered among the rams, Jonathan among the sheep, Saul among the goats. Saul is therefore on the left, because goats are on the left; Jonathan is on the right, because he is found among the sheep. Jerome says there that Jonathan was worthy of a prophet’s love.

[Col. 1044D] Let us now return to our subject and see how religion is merciful toward penitents. A person repents in three ways, and God has mercy in three ways. He waits for the sinner, consoles the despairing, and rejoices together with the penitent. He calls the sinner back by the gift of grace, consoles the despairing through hope of forgiveness, and strengthens the penitent through promises of glory.

A human being also has mercy upon another in three ways. A superior has mercy on a disciple, a disciple on a superior, and sometimes a disciple on a disciple. A superior has mercy on a disciple when [Col. 1045A] he gently corrects the sinner with words, raises the despairing to hope by examples of mercy, and loves the corrected person after his offenses. I say this because some, when a person close to them sins, despise him and, what is worse, admit that they do not love him as before. Peter sinned, but Christ did not despise him; he looked upon him and loved him.

A disciple has mercy upon a superior in three ways: when he does not resist an angry master, does not disparage a sinful one, or endures a perverse one. David fled Saul when he was angry; when Saul was relieving himself in the cave, David did not kill him though he could have; and he endured Saul’s perversity as long as he lived (I Kings XXIV).

Likewise a disciple has mercy upon a disciple when he sympathizes with the sinner in prayer, corrects him privately between himself and that person, or [Col. 1045B] kindly forgives a person who sins against him.

## CHAPTER XVI. That religion is severe toward the perverse.

Religion is severe toward the perverse. Severity preserves propriety, chastises frivolity, and is feared by the unlearned. It is the adornment of the old, the rod of the young; it ornaments the persons of prelates and gives color to the appearance of virtues. For as redness mixed with whiteness, when suitably arranged, makes a face pleasing to those who look upon it, so severity mixed with rectitude, if seasoned with sweetness, adorns the countenance of religion.

The sweetness of a superior draws to repentance; severity corrects the sinful disciple; rectitude gives a law to the delinquent. Thus severity permits neither frivolity, nor sweetness laxity, [Col. 1045C] nor rectitude any transgression of the line of justice. Hence the Psalmist: “The Lord is sweet and upright” (Ps. XXIV).

Some wish to be severe but do not know how; while wishing to be severe, they become cruel. They display anger in place of severity, bitterness in place of sweetness, and cruelty in place of rectitude. Thus the countenance of religion is disfigured where eyes blaze from the flame of cruelty and pallor is mixed with lividness, because these proceed from anger and bitterness. A superior’s anger disturbs the sinner; bitterness persecutes him; cruelty afflicts him. A superior’s anger causes the perverse to fall and provokes the righteous to anger.

There are two kinds of perversity: open and hidden. Some are so perverse that they openly defend their own evil actions, while detesting and attacking the good actions of others. [Col. 1045D] They are incorrigible: they believe good to be only what they themselves will; they never fulfill obedience, or fulfill it carelessly; they provoke humble brothers and disturb silence. That Philistine who came forth from the camp of the Philistines and challenged the children of Israel bore the figure of such people (I Kings XVII).

His size and the variety of his armor morally signify the condition of the perverse—who are great in their own eyes—and the qualities of their morals. David is read to have come to conquer this Philistine. But this battle takes place in three ways: historically, mystically, and morally—that is, between Goliath and David, between Christ and the devil, and between any righteous person and some member of the devil.

It happened first in fact, occurred in mystery, and now exists also in morals. [Col. 1046A] Therefore, when David was sent by his father Jesse to visit his brothers, who were in the army of Israel—his father had sent him, as the history relates, saying: “You shall visit your brothers to see whether they are doing rightly, and learn with whom they are stationed”—he came to the battle-line and to the army, which had gone forth and raised a cry for battle. Israel had drawn up its line, and the Philistines had also prepared themselves opposite; and David ran to the place of battle, asking whether all was going well with his brothers. While David was still speaking, that bastard man appeared, coming up—Goliath by name, a Philistine of Gath, from the camps of the Philistines (ibid.).

The history says, “You shall visit your brothers to see whether they are doing rightly, and learn with whom they are stationed.” And the Lord, coming in the flesh, visited us, teaching carefully what things we should rightly do and with whom we ought to live in due order. We also see this happen morally each day when prelates teach their subjects the rectitude of good action [Col. 1046B] and instruct them with whom they ought to maintain the order of a good life, lest one newly converted be joined either with a perverse person who makes him perverse, or with a lukewarm brother.

David came to the army of Israel and found them shouting for battle, with the Philistines prepared opposite. Prelates too sometimes come and find discord among brothers. David ran to the place of battle and asked whether everything was going well with his brothers. Prelates run both in the inclination of mind and with the steps of their feet, anxious for the salvation of their own people, investigating whether their works are right or still seem to need correction. They inquire into their habits and learn by sight and hearing what is the cause of discord. [Col. 1046C]

Hence Bede, On Samuel: “Even now the Lord does not cease to perform this very thing through his members, when, distinguishing good persons from evil, he distributes his gifts to the former and leaves the latter empty.”

While David was still speaking, that bastard man appeared, coming up—Goliath by name, a Philistine from Gath and from the camps of the Philistines. When a righteous person speaks and teaches what is right, and inquires what is harmful, that bastard appears—that is, the devil descending into someone’s heart. From where? From an evil thought to insulting words; from insulting words to perverse deeds. “Goliath” means “revealed.” To whom? To those who can say: “For we are not ignorant of his devices.” “A Philistine from Gath.” “Philistine” is interpreted “falling through [Col. 1046D] drink”:” falling from the height of pride, soaked with the drink of despair, and forgetful of mercy.

Gath, interpreted “winepress,” as Bede attests, most fittingly signifies the multitude of the wicked—the city, that is, of the devil, ever exercised in tormenting the good in the world. For as the grape is pressed and squeezed in the winepress, and the wine is separated from the grapes, the wine passes to the Lord’s banquet while the grapes are assigned a place in the dungheap; so the righteous are trampled by the multitude of the wicked. And as wine is separated from grapes in the winepress, so the righteous are tested in tribulation, while the unjust withdraw in time of temptation. Thus the Philistine was from Gath, one from the multitude of the wicked.

“And a bronze helmet was upon his head, and he was clothed in a coat of mail; and he had bronze greaves [Col. 1047A] upon his legs,” and his bronze shield covered his shoulders.” Helmet, coat of mail, greaves, and shield are different kinds of defense by which the devil tries to defend his own folly—he who is the head of all the ungodly.

Morally, the perverse cover their head with a helmet when they praise the intention of a perverse action. They shade their left side with a shield when they excuse the evil aspect of a wicked action. They have greaves on their legs, which are as it were the extremity of the body, because they persevere in obstinacy to the end. They put on a coat of mail, which covers the whole body, when they defend the whole action.

These forms of armor are said to be made of bronze, a metal more resonant than the rest. For whatever the perverse person does, he does not acknowledge it in humble confession, nor defend it by the reasoning of truth, but with the clamorous noise of worldly eloquence, confirming it by examples of the reprobate. [Col. 1047B] Hence it follows: “And his armor-bearer went before him.” Goliath’s armor-bearer may be any reprobate person whose examples go before and assist in confirming the malignity of the perverse. From these examples authority is drawn; from them weapons of defense are taken. This is open perversity.

Hence it follows: “Standing, he cried out against the battle-lines of Israel.” He stands and cries out because, set upon the mountain of pride, the perverse person does not cease, with the voice of detraction, blasphemy, and scandal, to provoke humble brothers who contemplate God in mind.

Thus the head of perversity is the intention of a wicked action; [Col. 1047C] the left side, its evil aspect; the legs, the end of the action; the body, the whole action; the helmet, praise of the intention; the shield, excuse of the evil aspect; the two greaves, perseverance and obstinacy; and the coat of mail, the open defense of the whole action. By these weapons the Philistine is known when he advances to battle.

But there are others whose perversity is hidden: by their counsel they spur brothers to anger and stir them to quarrels; by their counsel they cause Absalom to rise against David—that is, they incite spiritual sons against their fathers to discord; they scheme for David to die in the camp, as is read of Ahithophel (II Kings XVII). Religion ought to be severe toward both kinds: openly resisting the openly perverse to their face, and changing the counsels of those who are secretly perverse.

Thus David crushed the Philistine’s forehead with a stone; [Col. 1047D] thus Hushai destroyed Ahithophel’s counsel. The Philistine’s forehead is knowledge of perversity. The Philistine is struck in the forehead, therefore, when the perversity of a fool, once recognized, is beaten back by a wise person. Hushai is interpreted “silence”; Ahithophel, “ruin of a brother.” Thus Hushai’s counsel destroyed Ahithophel’s counsel, because through silence the counsel of those who are like the ruin of brothers is brought to nothing. Hushai ensures that the army of Israel is not disturbed, because through silence the assaults and incursions of speech are reasonably kept away from the assembly of brothers who desire to see God.

These two things belong to severity: sparing speech and rigor of speech. Sparing speech preserves concord; rigor of speech corrects what needs correction. Severity is affable, not garrulous; it displays [Col. 1048A] sternness, but is not quarrelsome. Severity differs from cruelty: the former corrects, the latter torments; the former befits the righteous, the latter accompanies the perverse. Severity threatens, but does not curse.

The Philistine cursed David, but David did not curse the Philistine. “You come to me,” he says, “with sword and spear and shield, but I come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts” (I Kings XVII). Many curse the Philistine but do not come against him in the name of the Lord. He curses the Philistine who, when he hastens to correct someone falling through the devil’s drink, brings forth not words of humility but of pride, not of exhortation but of anger, not gentleness but reproaches.

Nor does one come to the Philistine in the Lord’s name who attributes the correction of the perverse person to his own religious standing, nobility, or literary learning in which he excels, rather than to [Col. 1048B] divine grace. Many come in this way, and therefore God does not hand the Philistine over into their hands.

David’s not cursing the Philistine belongs to kindness; his ascribing the effectiveness of his coming to God belongs to humility; and his threatening belongs to severity. But what does he threaten? “I shall take your head from you,” he says, “and shall give the corpses of the Philistine camps to the birds of heaven and the beasts of earth” (ibid.).

The head of the Philistine signifies the devil; the corpses of the Philistine camps morally signify the carnal affections of the reprobate, who are the devil’s camp. A corpse is, as it were, flesh given to worms. As rotten flesh provides nourishment to worms, so carnal affections nourish perverse thoughts.

The birds of heaven signify those who are raised up on the wings of contemplation to think [Col. 1048C] heavenly things. The beasts of earth correspond to those who know how to cultivate their own ground, who supply earthly necessities to the brothers while caring for household affairs; elsewhere Rachel and Leah (Gen. XXIX), Martha and Mary (Luke X), signify them. To these birds of heaven and beasts of earth are given, for correction, the corpses of the Philistine camps—that is, the carnal affections of the reprobate.

Thus religion openly corrects the perverse and thus secretly provides against the counsel of the perverse.

## CHAPTER XVII. That religion is best for the good.

Religion is best for the good. The distribution of possessions makes people good; renunciation of the world makes them better; but life together in religion makes them best. The world is worst for the good; [Col. 1048D] religion, however, is best for both good and bad. For it sometimes makes a good person out of a bad one, a better person out of a good one, and the best out of a better one; and this happens when God visits the ungodly. Hence the Psalmist: “You visited the earth and made it drunk” (Ps. LXIV).

God visits both good and bad earth: better earth and best earth. By fear he visits bad earth; by incipient charity, good earth; by abundant charity, better earth; by perfect charity, best earth. God visits bad earth when someone is pierced by fear of judgment and refrains from unlawful acts. But he visits good earth through incipient charity when someone distributes what is his, renounces the world, changes his clothing, keeps peace with his brothers unless he is slandered by someone; but, if slandered, does not bear the slander, and is still slightly [Col. 1049A] disturbed, angry, and hateful. He does not bear patiently the weariness of the cloister; he abhors the lowliness and sameness of the food. The food of the soul, however—that is, the word of God—seems bitter to him if he is at times corrected rather sharply.

Thus, when the sons of the prophets came to Elisha’s house, Elisha ordered his cook to prepare them a meal. But when they tasted the pottage cooked with herbs and found it exceedingly bitter, they began to cry out: “There is death in the pot, man of God! There is death in the pot, man of God!” (4 Kings IV). Elisha’s pot differs from the Egyptian pots. Those are pots of meat; this is a pot of herb pottage. Those are seasoned with the fat of the rich, from which iniquity proceeds; this one is sweetened with Elisha’s flour, which is charity. Bitterness follows their sweetness; but sweetness follows the bitterness [Col. 1049B] of this one.

Elisha arose, took the flour that he had, and put it into the pot; and thus what had previously been bitter became sweet. Elisha, whose name is interpreted “solar,” signifies Christ; the cook, teachers; the pottage, the word of God; the flour, charity. Elisha therefore puts flour into the pottage when someone is visited by the Lord through abundant charity, so that one for whom coarser food had previously been distasteful, or who was accustomed to become lightly angry or to resist obedience, may now obey, embrace frugality, and love his enemy. Charity abounds when an enemy is loved; but it is not perfect unless it is ready to die for one’s neighbor. “No one has greater charity than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV).

But perfect charity [Col. 1049C] loves its enemy and does not fear to die for its neighbor. It casts out fear; it loves and awaits the Lord. Hence the Psalmist: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened; and endure the Lord” (Ps. XXVI). Wait through hope, lest you despair through fear; act manfully through incipient charity; let your heart be strengthened through abundant charity, so that through the patience of perfect charity you may await the Lord. Thus religion is best for the good because it leads them to perfection.

Let what has now been said concerning the nine benefits of religion suffice, so that we may briefly touch, as it were in passing, upon something further concerning life together in the same religion.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Four things are to be carefully noted in religion.

Four things are to be noted in religion. For it is pleasant [Col. 1049D] and gentle, quiet and secure. It is pleasant in living together, gentle in speech, quiet in mind, secure in action. Yet it is not so pleasant as to be undiscriminating; nor so gentle as to endure injustice; nor so quiet in mind as not to think upon the good; nor so secure as not to fear the Lord. Rather, it is so secure that it does not abandon a good work because of human fear.

Religion is likened to a chaste woman whom someone loves in order to take her as his wife: namely because she is beautiful, because she abounds in riches, because she is of noble birth, and because she is wise—so that he may delight in her beauty, glory in the nobility of his children, have his own estate increased by hers, and preserved by her prudence. Religion may be compared to this woman: it is beautiful in contemplation, [Col. 1050A] wise in circumspection, noble because free from the servitude of sin, and rich in inheritance, whose inheritance is the eternity of the heavenly kingdom.

The lustful man loves a beautiful woman but does not love a chaste one, if at some time a carnal-minded person, touched by the beauty of religion, assumes its habit. But when he finds the purity of chastity, what had pleased him displeases him. Thus the wife of Abraham, whom the king of Egypt had seized because of her beauty, he returned untouched to her husband, saying: “Behold, your wife is before you; take her and depart from here” (Gen. XII).

On this passage blessed Ambrose says in the second book which he wrote on Abraham:

> “Let us consider in our mind an intemperate man, who, unwillingly captured by a certain beauty of chastity, thinks that its grace ought to be pursued; then, unaware of the handmaids with which it proceeds attended—namely sobriety, modesty and reserve, sparingness in food, flight from wantonness, serious caution, watchful guardianship—suddenly inflamed by the heat of drunkenness, or by the heat of his own flesh, or by encountering a more attractive form, he is unable to contain himself or to resist the law of the flesh. Does he not say: ‘I thought it easier to pursue chastity. It is above my shoulders, beyond my strength; rare is the person to whom this is joined.’ Let her depart, then; let her depart from the bounds of my thoughts.”

And turning to someone who admonishes him, who has endeavored to introduce into his mind the habit of chastity by saying that it will not be arduous or impossible, but has many companions, is akin to the diligent, and suited to the willing, he says: “What is this that you have done to me? Why did you not tell me [Col. 1050C] that she is your wife?” That is, that she is held not by a casual connection but by lawful marriage. “But you said that she was your sister.”

Who, brothers, is ignorant that this has happened in churches in our own times? There are some who believe religion to be delicate and pleasurable, free from labor, and given to leisure. They indiscriminately take up the religious habit, make a vow, and bind themselves by the bond of profession. But when they learn the rule of religion and its customs, which oppose the flesh, they burst out with these words: “We thought,” they say, “the burden of religion lighter.” For who can bear the weariness of the cloister, prolonged silence, the burden of labor, and sparingness in food? Thus they return Abraham’s wife, expelling her in order to remain free in Egypt. They cast off the religious habit and persist in [Col. 1050D] the desires of their flesh.

But Abraham went up from Egypt to Bethel—that is, leaving behind the fellowship of carnal pleasures, he remains in the house of God. For Bethel is interpreted “house of God.” Abraham is a figure of religion, an example to those living together.

There are three things which ordinarily disturb the peace of those living together: when someone is moved to anger for his own sake, for a friend’s sake, or for advantage’s sake. Abraham removed these three things while he was living with his nephew. He removed the first by saying, “Let there be no quarrel between me and you”; the second, when he said, “nor between my shepherds and your shepherds” (Gen. XIII). He addressed the third: “Behold,” he says, “the whole land is before you.” That is: if the disagreement concerns me, a friend, or a possession, I yield everything; but if our dispositions do not agree, depart from me.

Oh, how much Abraham promised his nephew, so that he would not be compelled to depart from his nephew! But this is also a matter of virtue and discipline. For a certain philosopher said before our time that these four things belong to a good man. First, that he make all people his friends. Second, that if he cannot make friends, he make no enemies. Third, that if this is not possible, he withdraw by common agreement. Fourth, that if anyone pursues one who yields, he defend himself as he can.

We recognize the first three in Abraham’s deeds; but the fourth is not found in the same way, since even toward one who had withdrawn he preserved a father’s affection, so that he not only did not pursue him, but also freed and rescued him when taken captive. Finally, although the Apostle teaches those first three things, by his precepts he removes this fourth addition of philosophy. For, wishing to instruct a disciple or a peaceable people, he says: “If it be possible, live peaceably with all people” (Rom. XII). Then, if this cannot be done, at least there must be neither discord nor enmity. Therefore he adds: “Not avenging yourselves, beloved” (ibid.). In this the third point is included: we should in no way wish to avenge ourselves; rather, “give place,” he says, “to wrath” (ibid.). You also have the fourth: withdraw instead, and entrust vengeance to God rather than exact it yourself.

But now, brothers, because we have extended the space of the first little book, let us, living together in peace, bearing one another through patience, and entrusting vengeance to God, bring it to an end.

# SECOND BOOK

[Col. 1051]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1051B]

Dearest brother, as I am about to speak of matters pertaining to the building up of the material cloister, I may perhaps seem to some rather harsher than usual. Yet I condemn no one: I praise those who are more removed from the world; I admonish those who possess many and dangerous things; and I instruct those who rejoice in poverty and humility.

Still, I know that there are many in the greater churches who, although they possess much, nevertheless in other respects love poverty; who possess as though not possessing, use what they possess as though not using it, love examples of poverty, and, as they read diligently what has been written about poverty, behold themselves and groan beneath the burden of riches. These are poor in spirit, not in outward habit. But we are poor only to the eye: [Col. 1051C] we have changed place, not disposition; clothing, not mind.

There are also some in the greater churches who are lofty of eye, swollen with the spirit of pride. When poor brothers come to them, they look at them sidelong, mock them, speak against them; idle themselves, they levy a contribution, like dogs with envious teeth gnawing the bones of poor brothers. They hate Jerome’s sackcloth, Benedict’s tunic, Eulalius’s water-pot, Arsenius’s tears, Paul’s nakedness, and Elisha’s pot. From these, therefore, dearest brother, as I prayed above, keep your name far away.

## CHAPTER I. On the building of the material cloister.

Since, brother, we are going to say something, following moderation, about the ordering of the material cloister, four matters suitably present themselves for your consideration: who they are, who are to hold the order; what they are to hold; where they are to remain; and from what they are to live. Thus they should be numerous and of good purpose; buildings should be available for their life together; and they should have necessities for sustenance.

Yet let there be circumspection in number, devotion in purpose, moderation in buildings, and frugality in possessions: lest, if the crowd grows, disorder arise; or despair creep in because the purpose is difficult; lest pride enter through the magnitude of the buildings, [Col. 1052B] or temptation insinuate itself through abundance of possessions. “For those who wish to become rich fall into temptations and into the snare of the devil” (1 Tim. VI).

## CHAPTER II. On the number of brothers to be received.

As we have said, circumspection must first be maintained in the number of brothers, so that only as many may live together as can live in order; lest, using poverty as an excuse, they live irregularly, or, because of the multitude living together, seek unlawful things for their necessities. For those who gather many people must necessarily seek much for their food. But while they seek more, concern for outward things increases; ecclesiastical benefices are dispersed among different regions, and the brothers also are scattered. They live alone among secular people, unwilling to endure fraud and ready to contend in court.

But those who live together in cells, two or three, or even four or five, are not restricted by cloistered rule. They speak when, to whom, and how they wish. Yet I do not condemn either their life or that of the former group; I merely point out what danger lies hidden in each. Among these, however, certain monks whom we know to be heirs of blessed Benedict preserve discretion: if the number of brothers becomes excessive and a more remote site of property is given to them, they send no fewer than twelve brothers, lest the work of religion be corrupted through the negligence caused by too few persons.

## CHAPTER III. On the temperance and compassion to be exercised toward the brothers.

[Col. 1052D]

Next, the rule of our purpose must be moderated, lest we either live loosely in pleasures or, because of the severity of the purpose, abandon what we have begun. Blessed Ambrose says on the Psalm *Blessed are the undefiled*:

> “What shall I say of these people? There are among us those who have fear of God, but not according to knowledge, laying down harsher precepts than human nature can endure. There is fear in them, because they seem to themselves to be taking care; but there is ignorance in them, because they do not have compassion on [Col. 1053A] nature or estimate its capacity.”

Let us therefore have compassion on nature. For compassion is not outside the order of nature; yet neither should compassion be directed to excessive delight of the flesh, but to its support.

There is also compassion in regard to our purpose. Blessed Augustine says in the rule which he set before us to be observed:

> “If to those who have come to the monastery from more delicate habits something is given in food, clothing, or covering which is not given to others who are stronger and therefore happier, those to whom it is not given should consider how far the former have come down from their secular life to this one, although they have not been able to attain the frugality of others who are stronger in body.”

Let moderation, then, order the rule of our purpose: moderation knows how to distribute its own things equally to all.

## CHAPTER IV. That the brothers’ buildings should be outside the dwelling-place of secular people, and should be modest.

It seems fitting to us that the brothers’ buildings should be established outside the dwelling-place of secular people, lest the silence of the cloister or the repose of the dormitory be disturbed by the noise of a turbulent crowd; lest, while the tongue is silent, the heart answer back, or while the body receives rest, the mind remain restless.

The brothers’ buildings should not be superfluous, but humble; not luxurious, but decent. Stone is useful in construction; but what profit is carving in stone? This was useful in the building of the Temple, for it was a figure of signification and example. Let Genesis be read in a book, not on a wall. Eve is clothed on the wall, while a poor man lies naked beside the wall. [Col. 1053C] Adam is given a tunic of skins, while a multitude of brothers is cramped by winter hardship.

Let this be permitted—if it ought to be permitted to anyone—to those who live in cities or villages, to whom a crowd of people comes together, so that their simplicity may be held by the pleasure of painting, since they are not delighted by the subtlety of Scripture. But for us, who delight in solitude, a horse or an ox in the field is more useful than one on a wall. Here they satisfy the eyes by being seen; there they labor to provide for necessity.

We wish there to be two guest-houses: one assigned to brothers who wear the religious habit, and also to certain secular persons whom the foresight of the abbot or brothers has determined should be received there; the other, more remote house, we wish to be assigned for receiving those who may disturb the cloister’s peace by speech or dress.

Thus three things must be maintained in buildings: position, arrangement, and construction. By their position they should be removed from secular people; by their arrangement they should remove secular people; by their construction they should be not superfluous but useful.

## CHAPTER V. What brothers may be permitted to possess.

We permit brothers to have fields, vineyards, flocks of livestock, gardens, meadows, and pools suitable for raising fish, for these supply necessities for food. But they should not receive tithes, except from the fields which they cultivate; nor estates, nor the revenues of estates, nor market rights, nor toll-money, nor—so to speak—the hard-earned pennies of passing merchants. For what justice is there in compelling a widow, if she sells a sheep, to pay a coin in market dues? Let them not hold the office of judge, nor lord it over soldiers in the manner of princes; rather, let them aid the oppressed and render services to poor brothers.

There are four things to be observed by us in possessions: that we do not acquire lawful things unjustly; that we do not use what has been justly acquired unlawfully; that we do not possess many things, even lawful ones; and that we do not defend unlawful things by lawful means. For acquiring badly, or using acquired goods badly, makes unlawful what was lawful. But possessing many things is close to covetousness; and so what is loved too much is sometimes wont to be defended badly.

Two things commonly acquire unlawfully: covetousness and pride. Two things make bad use of acquired goods: gluttony and lust. Two persons wish to possess badly: the prodigal and the miser, one in order to gather, the other in order to squander. And two things defend possessions: intemperance and worldly prudence. Pride shut heaven against the devil; gluttony took Paradise from the first parent; avarice opened hell to the rich man; and intemperance still corrupts the world. All these things, brother, follow riches. For riches are a place for vices, while humility is the seat of virtues, and poverty is the place of humility. Of it blessed Gregory says: “Poverty is accustomed to be the guardian of humility for good minds.”

## CHAPTER VI. That three things are to be considered in food.

Since the fault of the first parent began through eating, we must take care that, just as he deserved expulsion through the food of Paradise, so we too may not be barred from entry. Three things, therefore, are to be considered in food: [Col. 1054C] what, when, and how much we eat—that is, the kind of food, the time, and the measure—lest we take something unlawful, outside the proper time, or beyond measure.

Adam ate what was unlawful in Paradise and was expelled (Gen. III); Jonathan ate outside the proper time and was cursed by his father (1 Kings XIV); but the people of Israel ate beyond measure at the graves of lust and were slain (Num. XI). Adam transgressed the Lord’s command; Jonathan broke what the multitude of the people observed; Israel was deceived by fullness of food. Thus transgression deserved expulsion; neglect of the common vow, a curse; and satiety, death.

In these things, brothers, we are daily deceived: murmuring in the desert with Israel, longing for Egyptian meats and pots (ibid.), transgressing the commands of prelates, [Col. 1054D] and negligently observing what is held in common by the brothers.

Let us now pass to those things which moderation permits to be possessed for the brothers’ necessity. Let them use fruits of trees and things growing from the earth; let their pottage be seasoned with butter, oil, or milk, not with animal fat. Let them abstain from meat, unless necessity or a dispensation permits it somewhere outside the convent. Brothers may use wine in the community; nevertheless, we believe that we should take the greatest care—though we say this with embarrassment—that what is mercifully granted should not, as some are accustomed to do, be demanded as though it were owed. For we do not promise; we grant. But if locality or poverty denies what we grant, let them use without murmuring what the region or the property provides.

Let no one of our purpose recoil from an abstinence which excludes from all kinds of food only the sight of meat, while allowing and kindly supplying everything else. In those kinds of food which we have said are lawful for the brothers’ necessity, three things are to be observed: manner, measure, and number. Manner: that they use what is set before them moderately. Measure: that what is set before them suffice for support, not for pleasure. Number: that they be refreshed from some of what is set before them, lest the flesh, afflicted by excessive abstinence, fail, or become wanton through satiety.

There should be equality in measure—not equality of quantity, but of sufficiency. Hence blessed Augustine: “Not equally to all, because not all of you are equally strong.” This is equality not of quantity [Col. 1055B] but of sufficiency. For a thing is distributed equally when the distributor apportions to each person according to what each needs.

Many are often deceived in this matter when they see a more refined kind of food allowed to someone more delicate. “This,” they say, “is not an equal religion, which receives persons and honors the rich.” Thus there comes about, as blessed Augustine says, “a detestable perversity: that in the monastery, where the wealthy become industrious as far as they can, the poor become delicate.” Such people seek the measure of pleasure, not of necessity.

Four measures are said by analogy to exist: the measure of avarice and of pleasure; the measure of dispensation and of necessity. The law observed among buyers and sellers can be applied to them by analogy. The measure of avarice is excessive stinginess; that of pleasure, excess; that of dispensation, generosity; and that of necessity, sufficient equality. Avarice withholds from necessity; pleasure exceeds necessity; dispensation mercifully adds to necessity; necessity demands what is due to need.

Merchants sometimes use two measures: one, smaller, by which they distribute their own goods when selling; and another, larger, by which they receive the goods of others when buying. It is larger for themselves, smaller for their neighbor. If certain prelates use the measures of avarice and pleasure, they supply their subjects with the small vessel of excessive stinginess, while themselves using the full bushel-measure of excess. They preach frugality to their subjects, but themselves pursue pleasure.

There are also other merchants who use correct measures and mercifully bestow a gift upon the buyer out of generosity alone. To these may be compared the generosity of certain prelates who, while providing necessities for their subjects, sometimes add certain pleasurable things for the less perfect, lest they fail. Let us therefore use the measure of discretion in the house of religion, for this is the measure sufficient for each person.

## CHAPTER VII. On the number of dishes.

Careful consideration must be given to the number of dishes, lest, if you offer one dish to many, it prove unacceptable to someone; or, if you allow a multiplicity of dishes, you incur the vice of excess. “Therefore, on fasting days two cooked dishes should suffice, so that,” as blessed Benedict says, “those who cannot be refreshed by one may be refreshed by the other.” Let there be a third dish from things growing from the earth, or from some other thing which can be eaten raw.

On other days, for the reason stated above, let it be permitted to have two cooked dishes at the hour of dinner, and at supper one raw or cooked dish, according to the will of the one arranging it. Besides these, there are other dishes of mercy which pertain to the dispensation of prelates. Prelates may, beyond the things granted, send from their own table something to the brothers generally or to an individual brother, out of the generosity of accommodation. Nor should those whom some custom has made stronger think it unjust if the master’s mercy sometimes provides for those less able to endure, or for those who bear excessive labor.

## CHAPTER VIII. On clothing and the number of garments.

To you, brothers, it is said: “Let your clothing not be conspicuous, and do not seek to please by clothing, but by conduct.” Four things are conspicuous in religious clothing: meanness, excess, scantiness, and costliness. In meanness are marked vainglory and pretence; in costliness, pride or pleasure; in scantiness, intolerance or despair; but in excess are marked love of the world rather than love of God, love of the palace rather than love of Paradise.

Let us therefore use the measure of moderation, and hear the Apostle saying: “Not in costly clothing” (1 Tim. II). And Jerome, against the monk Jovinian:

> “It is a great exultation of the soul, when you are content with little, to have the world beneath your feet, and to exchange all its power, feasts, and lusts—for which riches are acquired—for cheap foods and a coarser tunic.”

Different people say different things about diversity of dress. Some maintain that between purple and sackcloth, between silk and haircloth, linen is the middle. But we, who are not of the royal household but of the Church, place wool in the middle. It neither oppresses anyone with excessive roughness nor departs far from the softness of linen clothing. “Those who are clothed in soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. I); but in the desert it is not softness of clothing but roughness that ought to be sought.

Hence blessed Augustine says: “I confess that I blush for costly clothing.” And blessed Jerome says: “Sackcloth and fasting are the arms of penitence and remedies for sins, because an empty belly and a mournful garment implore God more earnestly.”

Let two tunics, therefore, suffice for each of our brothers: one pellicea (fur garment) over a pellitium (fur-lined garment); pelles (skins or furs), without a pallium (cloak) [the wording is uncertain]; a cowl; breeches; stockings; foot-coverings; and, for work, a scapular. Their bedding shall be as follows: a linen mattress filled with flock, a linen head-cloth, a pillow, a belt, a knife, a comb, needles.

## CHAPTER IX. On those who, wandering and idle, speak against brothers who labor.

“Because you shall eat the labors of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. XXVII). But what shall befall those who are not in the labor of human beings? (Ps. LXXII). They shall not be scourged with light penalties, but tortured with more grievous torments.

And what shall I say of those wandering and idle persons who, free for tales and overflowing the soul with words, mock and malign brothers intent upon manual work at the appointed [Col. 1057A] hours? “Shall not the labor of their lips cover them?” (Ps. CXXIX). Concerning these persons, who walk disorderly and not according to the apostolic pattern, the Apostle writes to the Thessalonians:

> “We declare to you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you withdraw from every brother walking disorderly and not according to the tradition which they received from us. For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us: for we were not disorderly among you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread for nothing; but in labor and toil, working day and night, lest we burden any of you. Not as though we did not have the right, but in order to give ourselves as a pattern to you for imitating us. For when we were with you, we declared this to you: if anyone is unwilling to work, neither should he eat. For we have heard that some among you walk disorderly, doing nothing but meddling. To such persons we declare and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ that, working in silence, they should eat their own bread.”

## CHAPTER X. That the prelate should be wise, not negligent.

All these things which we have said above can be ordered and, once ordered, preserved, unless they are hindered by the negligence of prelates. For if the head is sickly, the other members also will be weak. The members follow the head, and disciples follow the teacher.

There are three heads: the head of the body, the head of the congregation, and the head of the mind. In each of these heads there are ears and eyes. For the prelate has eyes: namely, discreet brothers who report what they see in [Col. 1057C] the subjects. The reason of the mind also has eyes: those of actions and contemplations. Therefore the prelate ought to be wise, not negligent. “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccl. II), that is, in Christ: so that he may show himself to his subjects such as Christ showed himself to his disciples for imitation, and may be able to say with the Apostle, “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. IV).

Prelates ought chiefly to imitate Christ in three things, because they are in Christ’s place: dignity, power, and office. Christ was priest, king, and servant: priest, when he offered himself as a victim on the altar of the cross; king, when he reigned from the wood; servant, when he provided water for Peter’s feet. Dignity therefore belongs to the priest, power to the king, [Col. 1057D] office to the servant; reverence is due to dignity, obedience to power, and care to office.

Two of these things, therefore, are due to prelates; the third to subjects. Subjects must offer reverence and obedience to prelates, while prelates must expend care upon subjects. What, then? Should subjects not imitate prelates in these matters? No. But when they see prelates humble in dignity, gentle in power, and serving in administration with household care, they themselves should be humble and gentle, and graciously undertake the duties assigned to them.

There are some who blame the occupations of prelates and condemn their comings and goings. They do not know their reasons; and even if they learn them, they are troubled. They intrude upon deliberations and ask why, how, and by whom something was done. Thus Mary, who ought to remain silent, maligns Martha; and she who was accustomed to hear the Lord’s words becomes a servant of talkativeness. This is false Mary.

For there is a true Mary and a false Mary; a true Martha and a false Martha. True Mary is silent, listens, and weeps. False Mary complains that she does not go out, that she does not arrange external matters, that she does not mix with secular people. True Mary buys ointment and frequents the tomb in order to anoint the dead. She buys by the price of a good work, frequents by the desire of devotion, and anoints with the word of consolation. False Mary sells and frequents not the tomb but the marketplace. Yet I fear that when she returns, she will find the door shut with the foolish virgins (Matt. XXV).

True Martha complains that she serves alone, that she is troubled by the solitary management of the household, and that she does not hear the Lord’s words with her sister. But what does the Lord say to her? “Martha, Martha, [Col. 1058B] you are anxious and troubled about many things. Yet one thing is necessary” (Luke X). Christ teaches what is necessary: “One thing,” he says—that is, that the mind always remain the same, neither broken by adversity nor lifted up by prosperity. Hence it is said of Hannah: “And her countenance was no longer changed in diverse ways” (1 Kings I). Countenances are not changed in diverse ways when the mind does not incline from virtues to vices.

Thus also, after the water was stirred, many went down into the pool, and one was healed (John V). And the Psalmist asks one thing from the Lord (Ps. XXVI). Unity of life, therefore, is health of soul. But false Martha does not complain that she serves alone; rather, she delights in outward things alone. Yet because like seeks like, she wishes to have false Mary as her companion. Although one thing was necessary for them, one thing is nevertheless contrary to them, because, when they ought to preserve unity, they devote themselves to slander. Such persons do not revere the dignity of prelates or fear their authority; rather, they abuse cloistered rule and disturb the statutes of the cloister.

## CHAPTER XI. That there are twelve abuses of the cloister.

There are twelve abuses of the cloister, by which the whole sum of religion is disturbed: a negligent prelate, a disobedient disciple, an idle young man, an obstinate old man, a courtly monk, a litigious monk, costly clothing, exquisite food, gossip in the cloister, strife in chapter, disorder in choir, and irreverence near the altar. Let us dwell upon each, saying a few things about each individual matter.

## CHAPTER XII. On negligent prelates. The first abuse.

[Col. 1058D] There are some who know, are able, and wish to govern; some who know and are able, but do not wish to do so; some who neither know nor are able, but wish to do so; and some who neither know nor are able nor wish to do so. To know, to be able, and to will may belong either to charity or to pride; to know and be able but not to will, either to humility or to indolence; neither to know nor be able, but to will, to covetousness and folly; neither to know nor be able nor to will, to discretion and prudence.

For those who know, are able, and wish to govern: if they wish to be useful, this belongs to charity; otherwise, to pride. But those who know and are able, yet do not wish to govern: their refusal belongs to humility; but if, though they know, they withdraw entirely, it belongs to indolence. Those, however, who neither know nor are able but wish to govern, [Col. 1059A] seem ambitious in wishing; and foolish if they desire what they neither know nor are able to do. Certainly those who neither know nor are able nor wish to govern act prudently. For it is the height of discretion to refuse what you cannot do, and of prudence to foresee what you do not know.

Four of the things mentioned above—folly and indolence, ambition and pride—produce negligence. The other four—prudence and discretion, humility and charity—remove negligence itself, even if it has been fostered. Counsel belongs to prudence; judgment, to discretion; watchfulness, to humility; diligence, to charity. The counsel of prudence separates evils from goods; the judgment of discretion chooses the better things; the watchfulness of humility avoids harm to the virtues; diligence avoids danger. Negligence has no place among these.

But those whose eyes of prudence are covered by the darkness of folly, [Col. 1059B] who lie numbly inactive, away from the exercise of good work; who through covetousness are drawn aside to pleasures; and who through pride do not condescend to the humble—these, I say, negligence possesses and dissolves their works. Through folly negligence enters; through indolence it remains; it feeds upon the desire of ambition; through pride it reigns.

Let the negligent shepherd therefore hear what is said both to him and to the diligent shepherd: “The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep, but the hireling flees” (John 10). He gives his life for his sheep who, ascending the dangerous place of rule, closes the door of silence and keeps the flock of those in the cloister in peace. He lays down his life who goes out alone to endure disputes concerning household affairs; who walks amid the tongues of flatterers and detractors; who labours for the weak and feeds those who labour; [Col. 1059C] who consoles the faint-hearted and contends in rebuke with the proud.

Such a shepherd may say: “I know my sheep, and mine know me” (John 10). The sheep know the shepherd whom they often see present, whom familiarity makes known and beneficence makes a friend. The shepherd, moreover, knows his sheep when he diligently observes the character and deeds of those subject to him. Hence it is written: “Consider diligently the countenance of your flock” (Prov. 27). He considers the countenance of the flock who does not fail to know what each of his subjects can do: reason reveals this to him through confession as to their hearts, through circumspection as to their works, through experience as to what they can do, and through results as to what they will.

“And,” he says, “they hear my voice” (John 10). [Col. 1059D] There are three voices of the shepherd: the gentle, the sweet, and the loud. The gentle voice belongs to the sick, the sweet to the dying, the loud to the deaf. He is sick who is tempted; he dies who despairs; he is deaf who does not hear; but those hear who obey. Thus at times the sick man hears the gentle voice of consolation, the despairing man the sweetness of entreaty, and the deaf man the severity of rebuke.

“And mine follow me” (ibid.). The sheep follow the shepherd. Which shepherd? The one who goes before them. Where? To life, if the one going before is diligent; to death, if he is negligent. “For if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit” (Matt. 15). How do they go before? By life and teaching.

Thus there will be “one fold and one shepherd” (John 10). The shepherd ought to be one within himself, and one with his flock: one within himself, so that he fulfils in deed what he teaches in words; so that [Col. 1060A] he is not changed from gentleness by anger, not raised up by prosperity, not broken by adversity, but remains the same through persevering patience. The shepherd maintains unity with the flock when he is not divided from those subject to him by more costly clothing or more delicate food; when, through compassion, he becomes one with the weak, and through dispensation one with those requiring delicacy, so that with the Apostle he may say: “I became all things to all, that I might gain all” (1 Cor. 9).

But the negligent shepherd flees. There are certain prelates who flee from what they command. When they impose burdens heavy and impossible to bear, yet refuse to move them with a finger, they flee from what they command. They flee when they withdraw themselves; they flee when they wander about, roaming through other people’s houses; they flee when they seek their own interests. [Col. 1060B] Though present, they flee when, seeing negligences, they hide themselves in silence. They flee who, far from the community, live in idleness; who withdraw from the common counsel of the brethren; who do evil and refuse rebuke.

Hence blessed Gregory says: “It pleases them that, while they freely do even unlawful things, no subject should contradict them.” And elsewhere: “The prelate thinks himself wiser than all those over whom he sees himself to have greater power.” This is what they love: to seem wise and to be powerful. This was the cause of the ruin of angels and men. The angel says: “I will set my throne in the north” (Isa. 14). And he said to man: “You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 1). Let the prelate therefore fear what man and angel incurred. For the angel fell when he wished to be more powerful; [Col. 1060C] man became foolish when he wished to appear wiser.

There are also three kinds of negligent prelates: those who live well but permit their subjects to live badly; some who live badly but compel their subjects to live well; and some who live badly and wish their subjects to live badly. Those who live well, therefore, but permit their subjects to live badly, do indeed go before by example; yet, because they do not rebuke those who stray by correcting them, they sin. For although they themselves live well, they must nevertheless render an account to the Lord of the flock concerning the flock committed to them. Why do they take up the care of the flock and flee the burden of labour? If they do not know, why do they undertake it? If they know and permit sin—when they could live well alone—why do they [Col. 1060D] incur death?

Such prelates nurture the sons of Eli, who sleep with the women who keep watch at the entrance of the tabernacle; who do not permit those coming to Shiloh to sacrifice, but before the fat is burned seize the raw flesh (1 Sam. 2). Like Eli’s sons are those who live badly under prelates living well. They sleep with women either when they do this in fact, or when they join themselves to desires of the flesh. They hinder those who come to Shiloh from sacrificing when, by words and examples, they turn newly converted persons away from the exercise of good action. They do not permit the fat to be burned, because, having extinguished the fire of charity, they do not impart to good action the heart’s sweetness. They seek raw, not cooked, flesh because, fleeing the fire of tribulation, they withdraw themselves from poverty and labour.

For the vices of the flesh are usually cooked away in the furnace of poverty. [Col. 1061A] They desire raw flesh so that they may cook it for themselves when, how, and as much as they wish. Such are certain persons who remain in the cloister as though in Shiloh, and do nothing except what, how, and as much as they themselves wish.

But those who live badly and compel their subjects to live well call back the erring, but kill the strong. They call back by their words and kill by their examples. They strive to appear religious because they have religious persons beneath them. They boast of those persons’ patience, not of their own. What they refuse to do, they command; they themselves do what they think others ought not to be permitted to do; they compel their subjects and wish to be compelled by no one.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the disobedient disciple. The second abuse.

[Col. 1061B] The disease of disobedience proceeds from the swelling of pride, just as pus flows from a wound, so contempt flows from an ulcer. The disease of disobedience is a languor of the soul. For one who is able but unwilling to act lives, but languishes. He lives in capacity, but languishes in will. The first man languished with this disease: while he lived in capacity and was sound in will, he was set over the beasts of the earth; but through the fault of disobedience he was made subject to them, and even now, through his descendants, serves flies and gnats.

When bodily infirmity gathers into a swelling, it sometimes produces illness. Thus the carnal mind, through the swelling of pride, very often incurs the illness of disobedience. There are two kinds of swelling: the hard and the soft. Hardness of swelling in the flesh is the obstinacy of carnal persons in their manner of life. [Col. 1061C] It is usually treated in three ways: by plaster, ointment, and iron—that is, by the example of a good work, the word of admonition, and the discipline of correction. For when the mind does not discharge its pus through confession, or does not promise amendment in response to admonition, it remains for it to receive the incision of iron—that is, the correction of discipline.

But the swelling is soft when the inflated mind delights in pleasures, pursues idleness, and lies numb in drowsiness. From these, then, the soul’s languor is born: when a proud mind, constrained by the hardness of obstinacy or dissolved by softness, does nothing. At times disobedience assumes for itself the name of obedience, so that it may glory in the name alone. But because obedience is spoken of in many senses, it is useful to return to the discussion of it more deeply.

[Col. 1061D] The name “obedience” is applied to a command, an act, and a place: it indicates what is commanded, shows what is done, and names the place in which someone resides. It is said of a command, “He enjoins obedience upon him”; of an act, “He fulfilled it”; of a place, “He resides at that obedience,” when he maintains some remote estate or farm. The first is easy; the second difficult; the third partakes of both. For it is easy to command, but hard to fulfil. A place, moreover, is at times pleasing and at times displeasing. It pleases some not because it abounds in brethren, but in fish; it pleases because it abounds in servants and stories; it pleases because one person possesses everything alone. Thus it comes about that it is called an obedience when it is not one.

Many desire this “obedience” in order that they may be [Col. 1062A] outside obedience. It is commonly sought in many ways: by assistance, counsel, and ingenuity—by the aid, namely, of relatives, by the assembly of brethren, and by the contrivance of pretence—so that what cannot be obtained through relatives or the exhortations of brethren may at least be attained through the ingenuity of pretence. This obedience, therefore, which is granted to someone by the demand of relatives, the deceptive exhortation of brethren, or even the pretended display of good work, has the name of obedience but lacks the reality.

This obedience is also attained in other ways, when what cannot be achieved by those three preceding means is obtained by the promise of a gift. Thus Simon Magus still remains in the Church with Peter, and Sapphira with Ananias (Acts 5, 8): Peter signifies good prelates; Simon, Ananias, and Sapphira, bad subjects.

[Col. 1062B] Simon wished to buy grace; these people wish to buy obedience. Ananias and Sapphira concealed part of their property; these people devote themselves to the business of acquiring money. This is obedience with simony.

There is another kind of disobedience which nevertheless is called obedience, concerning which it is said: “Because you obeyed the voice of your wife more than mine, cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. 3). There are four voices: the voice of wife, world, devil, and God. “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84), not what the devil speaks, not what flesh or world speaks. The voice of the wife is the voice of the flesh; the voice of flesh is pleasure; the voice of the world, vanity; the voice of the devil, wickedness; the voice of God, goodness.

They obey the voice of the wife who [Col. 1062C] do not resist the suggestions of the flesh, and they obey the voice of the wife more than the voice of the Creator. But the Creator’s voice says of prelates to subjects: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23). He indicates that you should obey even perverse prelates, since he commanded obedience even to those who act badly; thus you may go in and go out with David under Saul (1 Sam. 18), and honour that same man, though rejected, with Samuel (1 Sam. 15). Therefore those who do not obey or venerate prelates, even though perverse, testify that they themselves are disobedient and proud. Yet do not obey even good men in evil, nor contradict perverse men in good.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the idle young man. The third abuse.

[Col. 1062D] Idleness produces folly; labour, knowledge. There is labour and idleness of the inner person, and labour and idleness of the outer person. The labour of the inner person is the labour of knowledge; that of the outer person is the exercise of action. The labour of knowledge is divided into three: the labour of discipline, of exercise, and of teaching. In childhood comes the labour of discipline; in youth, that of exercise; in old age, that of teaching: so that one who does not know may learn in childhood; may put into use in youth what he has learned; and may teach in old age what he has put into use.

There is another inner labour: that of thought and meditation, so as to attain the rest of contemplation; so that, if anything is hidden obscurely through forgetfulness under the cloud of doubt, it may become clear by thought, clearer by meditation, and clearest by contemplation. For when memory presents something heavenly to the mind, [Col. 1063A] it is first seen in thought as if confused; then it is distinguished by meditation; finally it is perceived by contemplation. Thus thought is kindled by consideration, meditation is inflamed by discernment, and contemplation is illumined by thought. For thought is in the mind as smoke in fire; meditation as a flame with smoke; contemplation as fire with flame but without smoke.

But when the mind labours in considering heavenly things, thought is impeded by involvement in temporal matters, meditation is disturbed by idleness, and contemplation is recalled by curiosity. Thus it sometimes happens that the idle mind lies numb in pleasure. When, therefore, the inner person lies in the bed of pleasure, numbed in the sleep of indolence and deluded by dreams of curiosity, he summons and exhorts [Col. 1063B] the outer person to incline his ear to gossip, speak vain things, clothe himself in soft garments, eat in the morning, let the cock mark the end of reading for supper, and have brethren rising for vigils encounter him as he is going to sleep; while they keep watch, let him sleep; when they return, let him rise.

But perhaps it would be better if they said nothing than if, swallowing syllables or words, they chanted the psalms while yawning.
