This is the slowness of idle people, who do nothing at the appointed hour but always keep company with delay. These are they who wait with the ass and do not ascend the mountain with Isaac, carrying straw and a goad—things belonging to the ass, not the fire and sword that belong to sacrifice. For Abraham said to his servants: “Wait here with the ass; I and the boy, when we have worshipped, will return to you” (Gen. 22).

[Col. 1063C] The servants are the childish movements of the mind, who wait with the ass because they always love slowness. The two servants are said to be the idle and the lukewarm, carrying the goad of the flesh and the straw of frivolity. But Abraham, whose name is interpreted “father of many nations,” that is, the mind begetting many thoughts, ascends with the boy—that is, with a pure heart—carrying fire and sword in his hands. By fire we understand charity; by sword, the word of preaching. Thus he carries fire and sword in his hands who fulfils in works what he loves and what he preaches.

“I and the boy,” he says, “will return to you.” Both must return: that is, the power of reason and purity of mind must return to the care of the flesh, not in its desires but in its necessities. For the flesh always seeks [Col. 1063D] abundance of food and freedom for idleness. Necessities, however, should be supplied, not withheld. But lest it be idle while food is supplied, let those things appropriate to the ass follow: namely, the rod and burden—the rod of correction and the burden of labour.

For between rod and burden there is no place for idleness (Ecclus. 33). Let the inner and outer person therefore labour, lest it be said to them: “Why do you stand here idle all day?” (Matt. 20). They stand idle all day who, throughout the whole time of their life, cease from good work and persist, numbed in the marketplace of vain glory.

Yet let prelates hear the cause of idleness. “No one,” they say, “has hired us” (ibid.): neither bishops the people, nor priests, nor abbots, nor priors the community. For to what would they hire them? Perhaps to seek [Col. 1064A] honour rather than labour, to the court rather than the vineyard. There the issue is the weight of money, not its amount; guilt concerns the testing of silver, not the cleansing of sin.

There are, nevertheless, good prelates who hire workers for labour: they teach by word and go before by example. Persons of different ages come to this labour—boys, young men, and old men—and at different times: evening, morning, and midday. Boys in the morning, young men at midday, old men in the evening; Maurus in the morning, Paul at midday, Gentianus in the evening. Here we understand youth broadly, so as to include not only adolescence but mature age as well. This is the age suited to labour. At this age Paul, wishing to redeem the time, devoted himself not only to contemplation but [Col. 1064B] also to labour (1 Cor. 4). Thus Jacob returns to his homeland with Leah and Rachel (Gen. 31); thus Lazarus is aided toward life by the prayers of Mary and Martha (John 11).

Jacob returns with Rachel and Leah when someone advances in the desire to work well and joins active with contemplative life. Lazarus, moreover, is interpreted “helped.” He is raised when someone is freed here from the death of sin through good works and tears. Therefore no one is excused from labour—not boys, not young men, not old men—yet youth alone bears the burden and heat of the day. It bears materially the burden of labour and the heat of the sun; morally, it bears the burden of carnal frailty and endures the heat of lust. By the labour of the hands the burden of temptations is destroyed; in idleness temptation is multiplied. By labour the flesh is [Col. 1064C] afflicted; by idleness it is nourished.

But a young man in idleness is like a young ox without a yoke: because he is not held by the bond of obedience within the equality of fraternal fellowship, he runs about, like a wanton ox, through the desires of his own will.

## CHAPTER XV. On the obstinate old man. The fourth abuse.

Among the abuses of this age, only one is greater than the obstinacy of an old man: though near death, he does not dread death’s coming; though, as it were, placed at the doorway of this world, he looks outside, yet does not attend to his departure from the present life or consider his entrance into the future one. He hears death’s messengers but will not believe them.

There are three messengers of death: accident, illness, and old age. Accident announces doubtful death; illness, grievous death; old age, certain death. Accident announces death hidden; illness, [Col. 1064D] death appearing; old age, death present. From the uncertainty of death should follow fear; from the severity of illness, pain; from the certainty of old age, not obstinacy but humility. Yet perhaps the threefold cord by which the old man is bound is not easily broken.

The threefold cord is the practice of evil habit. It is made from three things, when, in idle persons, thought is joined to speech and speech to action. For when, from childhood onward, pleasure has made a path in an old man’s mind by thought, vanity in speech, and perversity in action, what happens except that these three are twisted together into a habit as into a rope? The noose in the rope is temporal sweetness in habit; the rope wound around him is [Col. 1065A] the impediments of the flesh. Thus we are deceived by sweetness and bound by habit.

But he had escaped the noose and broken the cord who said: “My soul has been delivered from the snare of hunters; the snare is broken, and we have been delivered” (Ps. 123). But Absalom, hanging by his hair from the oak (2 Sam. 18), signifies the hardness of every obstinate person. While fleeing his father’s army, he happened to catch his hair in a dense oak. Absalom is interpreted “the father’s peace,” because his father endured him even while he persecuted him; he was not the son’s peace, for the son was unwilling to endure his father.

The oak is shown to be harder within, but more fragile without. Absalom hangs from it because inward obstinacy of mind and outward frailty of flesh accompany him. He hangs by his hair because he is held by love of superfluity. [Col. 1065B]

The mule on which he rode passed on, but he himself remained hanging from the oak: because the lust and deceit to which he had always devoted himself perished, but the punishment of sin remained. His heart is pierced by three spears: avarice, pride, and lust. Hence even to this day a great heap of stones is cast upon him, because he is weighed down by a multitude of sins or punishments. Nor is it surprising that a great heap of stones should be upon him who, through obstinacy, bore an unrepentant heart to the end.

There are also three kinds of obstinate persons. The first are those who are not wholly obstinate and improve through correction. The second are those who become worse through admonition. The third are those who promise amendment [Col. 1065C] but do not do it. Manasseh became better through correction (2 Chron. 33); Nabal worse through admonition (1 Sam. 25); Pharaoh harder through affliction (Exod. 8).

Manasseh, placed in prison and bound with chains and fetters, came to know God, whom formerly, while free, he had refused to know. Such are certain cloistered persons who, as long as they are their own masters, live perversely; but when they are held in the cloister as if in prison, bound by the chains of obedience and fear, and even fetters are added because they are not permitted to wander or go outside, it sometimes happens that, corrected, they love the God whom they had formerly despised. Those who had made freedom into servitude make necessity into virtue. Thus an authority not their own, through correction, makes devoted those whom their own will had made perverse. [Col. 1065D]

Nabal, however, signifies certain teachers who become worse through the admonition of their subjects. They deny food to David’s servants; they do not offer God’s word to those wishing to live purely. But they prepare a feast for their shearers because, given to idleness, they love the conversations of flatterers. Nabal accuses David and says: “Today servants have increased who flee their masters” (1 Sam. 25).

Perverse prelates indeed grieve when they see the number of religious persons increase. They fear when they see David—that is, good subjects—anointed king, and Saul cast down—that is, perverse prelates deprived of the honour of prelacy. But why do they fear? Lest they themselves also be deprived of honours; lest someone better be set in their place.

[Col. 1066A] “And Abigail told Nabal all the words which she had heard from David, and his heart died within him, and he became as a stone” (ibid.). Good subjects admonish their perverse masters concerning negligence, but through admonition they sometimes become worse. Nabal’s heart dies and he becomes as a stone when someone is hardened in sins unto eternal death. After Nabal’s death, Abigail is made queen, because one who has lived well under a perverse master deserves sooner to be raised to the governance of souls, so that he may obtain the kingdom with David and reign eternally with Christ.

For David sent messengers to Abigail, and she followed them. Abigail follows David’s messengers when any faithful person imitates in life and conduct the teachers of the Church. And [Col. 1066B] five maidservants went with her (ibid.). Her five maidservants are the five bodily senses, which go with Abigail like attending girls when, through the purity of continence, they perform service in obedience to every righteous person.

But Pharaoh, who promised Moses that he would release the people of God, yet did not release them (Exod. 1), signifies those who promise amendment toward a better life but do not forsake sin. They seek not contrition in the spirit of the dove but delay in the voice of the raven. Their land is afflicted with various plagues and is not softened, but through the habit of sinning is hardened more and more.

Then the Lord turns waters into blood when someone understands the causes of things carnally. The earth produces frogs when vain chatter rules in a talkative person. [Col. 1066C] The dog-fly plague (*cynomia*) and gnats (*cyniphes*) are importunate impulses of the mind and dog-like habits. The death of cattle signifies the death of thoughts, which are commonly likened to cattle when they lack rational understanding. For “man, being compared with senseless beasts, became like them” (Ps. 41 [Vulgate numbering]).

The sixth plague occurs when blisters swell and the inner organs are corrupted; this happens when the mind’s inward parts swell with hatred and boil over in anger. The plague of hail upon the crops signifies manifest wickedness in deeds. The plague of locusts is instability of soul: it harms by mouth when it detracts, and leaps when it extends itself toward carnal affections. The plague of darkness signifies the blindness of souls, which is shown to be tangible when the perverse things [Col. 1066D] the mind thinks are carried out in deed; for what can be touched by hand is tangible.

Observe that between the plague of hail and that of darkness the plague of locusts is placed in the middle. For from wickedness, signified by hail, there comes, as it were, a leap of locusts into the blindness of eternal damnation. The final plague is the death of the firstborn. Morally understood, the firstborn of the mind are the will and intention of every action; when will and intention are corrupted, they are struck dead like the firstborn of the Egyptians.

By these plagues is afflicted the obstinacy of the old man: he delights in carnal things, rejoices in talkativeness, is importunate and burdensome to all, is inclined to vices after the manner of beasts, swells with anger, is [Col. 1067A] openly injurious, is unstable in everything, lacks the light of truth, and therefore gropes himself.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the courtly monk. The fifth abuse.

Since we are about to say a few things concerning the courtly monk, I acknowledge that the same judgment should be made concerning a courtly canon or lay brother. For although their dress differs, their religious disposition ought to be the same: they should seek to please not by clothes but by character.

When, therefore, a monk is called courtly, the accompanying term denotes something frivolous. Those who love the company of secular persons, willingly insert themselves into the counsels of princes, and are privy to secrets and act as intermediaries, may be called courtiers. If you know the perverse counsels of princes and become their intermediary, I fear that you may consent to them.

The order of the cloister and that of the court are [Col. 1067B] very different. There “you sit in ambush with the rich in secret places, that you may kill the innocent” (Ps. 8 [Vulgate numbering]); here you hear: “I have not sat with the council of vanity, nor will I sit with the wicked” (Ps. 25). There “your right hand is full of gifts” (ibid.); here you wash your hands among the innocent. There the goods of the poor are violently taken away; here they are voluntarily offered by the poor. There “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed” (Ps. 10); here, however, the righteous man is blessed.

If, therefore, you wish to be a courtly monk, you praise what you ought not, defend what is not expedient, do what is not permitted, and say what is not fitting. Yet there are two courts of secular princes: those of some who build churches and those of some who destroy them. Access by religious persons is necessary to both; [Col. 1067C] but the access of courtly monks is useless and dangerous. This is David’s court; that is Absalom’s. In both, the counsel of Hushai is necessary.

I read that Ahithophel had at one time been David’s counsellor, but that he nevertheless withdrew from him and remained with Absalom (2 Sam. 15). Perhaps there is occasion to speak more closely about the testimony cited. For there are two courts: David’s and Absalom’s. In both the counsel of Hushai prevailed, not the counsel of Ahithophel. Hushai is interpreted “silence”; Ahithophel, “the ruin of a brother.” “A man of tongue shall not be established on the earth; evil shall hunt the unjust man to destruction” (Ps. 139). But “if you love to see good days, keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit” (Ps. 33). This is Hushai’s counsel; that is Ahithophel’s.

[Col. 1067D] For the tongue rests in moisture and easily slips. In the latter is the ruin of brethren; in silence peace is nourished, and David is preserved from death. Hushai, moreover, as Scripture says, was David’s friend (2 Sam. 15). But how did he love him? David says: “I became mute and was humbled, and I kept silence even from good things” (Ps. 33). Thus the righteous man loves the fruit of silence so much that he is silent even about certain good things. Thus he loves Hushai’s counsel: he sets silence as a guard upon his mouth, speaking only by permission.

David sings a psalm “for the words of Hushai”: the words of Hushai are words of silence, a veil of mystery (Ps. 38). Yet there are three silences: silence of mouth, tranquillity of mind, and the veil of mystery. The words of the first silence are discreet; those of the second, secret; those of the third, the disclosure of [Col. 1068A] mystery.

You know the history; observe the mystery; set forth the moral meaning. Absalom persecuted David; Judas, Christ; the appetite of the flesh, the soul. Absalom burned with desire to reign. This is “the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 9): covetousness. It is the head from which the tresses of vices hang.

This is the hair that Absalom nourished, that weighed him down, and that was cut only once a year; then he weighed his hair at two hundred shekels by the public weight. Absalom is interpreted “the father’s peace.” He is also Judas. Hear the father’s peace: “He who dips his hand with me in the dish, he will betray me” (Matt. 26). Hear the son’s peace: “Whomever I shall kiss, he is the one; seize him” (ibid.). By a kiss he promises peace, yet afflicts.

He nourished his hair—but how? “He was a thief, and [Col. 1068B] had the money-box” (John 12). And he was shorn once a year, when he once brought back thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the Temple. He weighed his tresses at two hundred shekels—a number belonging to the unclean—because, moved by repentance, he said: “I have sinned, betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27). Had he known the justice of the weight—that is, the price of the blood—he would not have run to the noose but hastened humbly to the Lord’s cross.

But he weighed by the public weight, not by the weight of the sanctuary (Zech. 5). For he set the talent of lead, upon which the devil sits, not the light weight of mercy, beneath which the Lord places his hand. He set the weight of despair, not of mercy. He possessed that weight and lacked the other; and perhaps, because he was unwilling to show mercy, he hesitated to seek the pardon of mercy.

[Col. 1068C] Hear the weight of the sanctuary: “I have sinned; I made my offence known to you and did not conceal my injustices. I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31). The just weight, abounding in mercy, makes known its offence and confesses its injustice; and the more sin is disclosed by the person, the more it is governed by God.

Hear the public weight, the weight of Cain. He says: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon” (Gen. 4). He weighed his own wickedness more heavily than God’s mercy. The appetite of the flesh also nourishes hair, because it produces a superfluity of thoughts. This hair weighs down the mind, “while the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9).

He who, shorn once a year, weighs his hair at two hundred shekels does so [Col. 1068D] when, only once in the entire span of his life, he renounces worldly desires—and that at the end. For then alone he is stripped of what he possesses, when he is separated from earthly things by the final cutting-off of death. He weighs earth more than heaven: he loves more to be in the house of clay than in the house not made by hands, which is in heaven; more in the transitory than in the eternal. And this is by the public weight, not the sanctuary’s weight.

Hear the sanctuary’s weight, Paul’s weight: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1). Hear the public weight: “Woe to those dwelling on earth” (Rev. 8)—not those who dwell there in body, but those who love it in heart. Let the monk therefore love Hushai’s counsel, that is, the silence of the cloister. But let him reject Ahithophel’s counsel, [Col. 1069A] so that he may not love the business of princes nor, wandering about, seek access to secular people.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the litigious monk. The sixth abuse.

It sometimes happens that monks who frequent law courts hear cases, investigate lawsuits, and, if the necessities of their own case ever arise, return to court with greater confidence. Nor do they defend only their own cases, but those of others as well: this they love, this they pursue. They love the decrees of councils, not the secrets of mysteries. They chew over decrees, not psalms; they become advocates in cases and employ rhetorical flourishes. They crave praise because they speak on behalf of many. Yet a monk who speaks much displeases many.

They contract unlawful marriages and sometimes dissolve lawful ones. They name fathers and forefathers whom they do not know, recount degrees of kinship, [Col. 1069B] affirm that this man descends from that one, judge matters uncertain, and very often testify to what they do not know. If, moreover, they unite some unlawful marriages, they allege the common good, promise peace for the churches, peace for the people, and safety for the country. But if the matter cannot be brought to its intended result in this way, the litigious monk then arranges for what could not be done elsewhere to be done at Rome. Thus, on behalf of a secular prince, he willingly endures the cold of the Alps and the heat of Italy—though perhaps he would unwillingly endure far lighter things for his spiritual master. Laden with documents, he returns supported by authorities; he sets a day for the case and produces persons ready, if you wish, to swear that a thing is so, and, if you wish, to swear again that it is not so. These are the affairs of princes.

Hear the judgment [Col. 1069C] of John the Baptist in a similar case: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6). What then shall I say? Does not the monk prefer to be a lawyer among those reclining at table with Herod, rather than to be kept in chains and prison with John? At that banquet, even if he does not see John’s head upon the dish, he nevertheless sees what is acquired by shed blood: the widow’s cow and the poor man’s pig. In the prince’s prison a poor man dies, and yet the monk, eating from the poor man’s substance, flatters the prince.

But I myself also, dearest friend, sometimes morally recline at banquet with Herod: I behold the dancing girl, I see John’s severed head on the dish. For Herod is interpreted as “the glory of skin.” “All [Col. 1069D] the glory of the daughters of Zion is within” (Ps. 44); but the glory of the daughters of the world is outward. Therefore I sit at banquet with Herod when, amid the pleasure of vices, I seek the favor of empty glory; I behold Herod’s daughter dancing when the vanity of curiosity pleases me. These are the two things that take away John’s head: vanity and curiosity. John is interpreted as “the grace of God.” God is the head of this grace. The head is therefore separated from the body when someone attributes to himself, rather than to God, the good which he performs. Such persons do not find grace with God, because they do not seek it. For the proud seek favor among men; the humble seek grace with God. Hence Paul says: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not empty” (1 Cor. 15).

The litigious monk hears the Apostle [Col. 1070A] saying, “Do not demand back” (Luke 6). He hears it and determines: “Do not demand back,” he says, “by litigation; pursue it without causing trouble.” Yet, if anything is taken from him, he does not refuse to undergo judgment; nor does he avoid the danger of perjury when either he himself or someone else swears for him. Therefore the Apostle complains that we are unwilling to suffer wrong, that we contend in courts, and that, inflamed with anger, we avenge ourselves, saying: “Beloved, do not defend yourselves, but give place to wrath!” (Rom. 12).

Alas! Where is true religion? Where is the wholeness of perfection? Where is the foundation of charity to be found? Perhaps among cloistered religious, who judge themselves, accuse themselves daily, and dread the sentence of the supreme Judge, saying: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, because no living person shall be justified in your sight [Col. 1070B]” (Ps. 142 [143]). For cloistered religious examine the true judgments of the Lord, not secular judgments; they keep the law of the Lord by living, meditating, and loving. By living, purity of conscience is usually attained; by loving, the perfection of charity.

For the law of the cloistered has its judges, witnesses, and counsellors. In the law of the Lord there are two witnesses: life and conscience; two judges: meditation and knowledge; two counsellors: love of neighbor and love of God. A good life is a good witness. Before God, conscience is witness; before human beings, life. Knowledge and meditation agree in judgment when what is done or said is provided for through careful consideration. But the whole justice of the law just mentioned depends on those two preceding counsellors: “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” [Col. 1070C] (Matt. 22). If, then, anything of perfection exists in this world, it can be found among cloistered religious. Yet integrity cannot be preserved unless poverty is loved. For those who abound in riches, if they set their hearts upon them, are weighed down by cares and entangled in business.

## Chapter XVIII. On Costly Clothing. The Seventh Abuse.

In living, the Apostle teaches what the habit of religion ought to be, for he says: “Not in costly clothing” (1 Tim. 2). If he denies costly dress to women of luxury, do you suppose that he grants a more costly habit to a monk? The bridegroom loves the bride’s chastity more than costly clothing, and simplicity more than braided hair. Thus the immortal Bridegroom loves the inward habit more than the outward. The soft seek soft things, [Col. 1070D] the proud costly things, the luxurious beautiful things. Outward excess, therefore, announces the vanity of the mind.

According to the Rule: “I think that what is cheaper when available, not what is more expensive, ought to be bought, so that there may be a difference between the clothing of a palace and that of a monk.” “Those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. 11). I, an insignificant canon, speak of monks. But what ought to be said of certain canons of our own order? Both mind and face blush deeply. Their beds are supported by feather mattresses; they are carefully furnished with linen sheets and blankets, covered with *cothurni* and coverlets—so that, if perhaps you saw them, you might suppose them to be the bed of a bride desiring her bridegroom. The canon’s cappa and the monk’s cowl differ in no respect from a soldier’s cloak; indeed, as a certain wise man says, soldier and monk [Col. 1071A] divide between them, from the same cloth, the cowl and the military cloak.

There is not much difference between the dress of a regular and of a secular canon; but if you should happen to see a regular canon, you would insist that you had seen an archdeacon or a bishop. But perhaps you will say that luxurious things suit the luxurious, adducing a testimony from the Rule. Blessed Augustine says:

> “If, to those who have come to the monastery from luxurious habits, something in food, clothing, or bedding is given which is not given to others who are stronger and therefore happier, those to whom it is not given ought to consider how far the former have descended from their secular life to this life.”

We agree with the authority: let enough be given to the delicate person lest he fail, but not enough for him to grow proud. Hear also, dearest friend, blessed Augustine:

> “Let it not happen [Col. 1071B]—that detestable perversity—that in a monastery, where, insofar as they can, the industrious become rich, the poor should become luxurious.”

I lie if I have not seen some whose poverty, when they were outside, was such that they could not find even necessities themselves. Because they found food and covering such as they could not find outside, they raised their necks and wished to associate with persons whom they had not dared to approach outside. Leaving the poor church, they went about among richer communities in order to be received there; and those who had always been accustomed to have old or cheap garments now strive always to have new or costly ones; those who before conversion had nowhere possessed a bed of their own now, if they happen to wish to go somewhere, carry the ornaments of their bed with them.

But I fear that [Col. 1071C] dreams of vanity are seen in such beds, and that in them the soul suffers the illusion of the flesh. Just as the body rolls softly about upon an outward bed, so the soul, stripped of virtues, languidly delights in the bed of pleasure. Therefore, while the Beloved is sought upon the bed of a loose mind, he is not found. Upon this bed lies the paralytic, loosened in every joint of his limbs—that is, the soul dissipated in every action.

On Jacob’s bed a stone, not the feather of lightness, was put beneath the head; that feather is carried by the wind of pride toward the north, when it says: “I will set my throne in the north; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). Jacob, on his journey, placed a stone beneath his head and slept; he saw a ladder, angels ascending and descending, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder (Gen. 28). He sleeps on the journey who, in the passage [Col. 1071D] of the present life, closes from the desire for worldly things those eyes which he had opened to concupiscence. He sees the angels: how greatly, in desire, they cleave to God above them; how greatly, in the affection of charity, they condescend to us who are weak. He also sees the Lord leaning upon the ladder, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God (Ps. 13 [14]). Nor is it surprising that he sees this, who has placed his head upon the stone—that is, his mind in Christ.

You have heard about the bed; hear about clothing: “And his mother clothed him with the very good garments of Esau, which she had with her” (Gen. 27). Perhaps, when you hear that his mother clothed him in very good garments, you likewise seek to be dressed in costly clothing; when you read that Joseph’s tunic was long to the ankles, you try also to possess a longer one. [Col. 1072A] Do you not know that, as the Apostle says, “all these things happened to them figuratively” (1 Cor. 10)? Do you not know that in Jacob the fragrance of the garments signifies the renown of virtues, and in Joseph the long tunic the perseverance of long-suffering? These, then, are the garments which Rebecca had with her and with which she clothed Jacob when he was blessed by his father: for persevering patience is the guardian of virtues, so that each person may enjoy blessing at the end.

Among those too who wear tunics, pleasure has set foot—not because they use shirts, but because of a certain delicate cloth, popularly called *saia*. Thus, by displaying a woolen garment they exhibit the harshness of their manner of life, but in delighting in delicate cloth they seek the softness of pleasantness. I myself, unless I am mistaken, saw a monk clothed in a shirt, speaking [Col. 1072B] and saying: “The yarn costs more than the shirt; but to be clothed in a tunic is a great difficulty.” But perhaps you will say that such a man was sick. On the contrary: he was healthy and wanton, riding a fat horse, abounding in possessions, and frequenting courts. Yet before he assumed the habit of conversion, he had been accustomed to go on foot and was not always clothed in linen. And therefore this abuse can be called not only an abuse of the cloister but also an abuse of the world.

## Chapter XIX. On Exquisite Food. The Eighth Abuse.

Religion does not deny what the necessity of nature requires, but it forbids what the excess of gluttony desires. Some secular persons are accustomed to excuse themselves because they consume such varied and delicate foods, because food is prepared with such great labor and swallowed so quickly. Yet perhaps certain religious [Col. 1072C] ought no less to excuse themselves—those who may be called more luxurious. For those who seek more delicate things may be called more luxurious.

When you read that Jonathan sinned by tasting honey (1 Sam. 14), Esau by a dish of lentils (Gen. 25), and the Sodomites through fullness of bread (Gen. 13 [Ezek. 16:49]), do you suppose that it is without danger to delight in so many dishes of meat, so many kinds of fish, and so many varieties of fried food? Does not the palace differ from the refectory as Egypt differs from the desert? If, then, we are in the desert, is it surprising if we long for the pots of meat? The person whom desire for flesh tempts longs for the pots of meat. But why do these sigh for them, who always have pots of meat? “Their food,” he says, “was still in their mouths, and the wrath of God rose against them” (Ps. 77 [78]). “Food is for the belly and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them [Col. 1072D]” (1 Cor. 6). “He slew their fat ones and brought down the chosen men of Israel” (ibid.); and there are those “whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame” (Phil. 3).

Scripture often speaks through likeness, so that what cannot be distinguished in one matter may be discerned in something similar. The belly is likened to God when it says: “Whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in shame.” Temples are ordinarily built for gods, altars erected, ministers appointed to serve, cattle sacrificed, and incense burned. For the god Belly, the kitchen is a temple, the table an altar, cooks are ministers, cattle are sacrificed, meats are cooked, and the smoke of seasonings is the fragrance of savors. These things are not built in Jerusalem but in Babylon, because their god is the belly and their glory is in shame.

He is indeed chief of the cooks [Col. 1073A] who destroyed the walls of Jerusalem, carried the vessels of the Lord into the house of the king of Babylon, and made the vessels of the temple into vessels of the palace; or, to speak more truly, made the vessels of the divine table into vessels of the kitchen (4 Kings 25 [2 Kings 25]). For the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3). In this temple the vessels are hearts. They are vessels of the Lord’s temple when, full of virtues, they please the divine will; they become vessels of the palace when they desire to please some human power. They also become vessels of the kitchen when the heart which had formerly served sobriety afterward serves gluttony.

Hence Jeremiah says: “Those who were nourished in saffron embraced dung” (Lam. 4). Saffron grows in the East; it gives color and flavor. [Col. 1073B] Therefore those are nourished in saffron who, at the beginning of their conversion, are inwardly refreshed by the savor of virtues and outwardly colored by the example of good works. But those thus nourished in saffron embrace dung when, after a life of sobriety and continence, concern for the belly calls them back. It sometimes happens that one who lived soberly in his own house before conversion afterward becomes gluttonous in the monastery.

The god Belly is appeased by the offerings of varied dishes, bends his ear to gossip, is aroused by varieties of flavors, is soothed by conversation rather than prayer, rejoices in idleness, and delights in drowsiness. The belly is therefore likened to God because it is served in every respect with such great devotion. Thus the monk has canons and lay brothers who serve it more zealously—namely, those who live slackly in the Church of God under the guise of leisure, who seek not secret prayers [Col. 1073C] but the fabulous talk of idlers. Among them are heard not the sobs and sighs of a contrite mind, but laughter, guffaws, and the belches of a stuffed belly.

This abuse is more pitiable than the other abuses: that you should be shown to have lived more luxuriously in the church than in your own house, and it should be said of you: “He feeds the barren woman who does not bear, and does no good to the widow” (Job 24). The barren woman who does not bear is the flesh, which, according to the word of the Lord, “profits nothing” (John 6). The widow is the soul bereaved of her heavenly Bridegroom. He does her no good who serves the desires of useless flesh and gives no attention to the soul’s care in cultivating virtues.

## Chapter XX. On Gossip in the Cloister. The Ninth Abuse.

[Col. 1073D]

Some know that an abundance of food is usually accompanied by a flood of words. Many also know that fullness of the belly is followed by frivolity in action and vanity in mind. For it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32). It says “to play,” not “to read.” For there are some who, after the varied dishes of a delicate meal, when they sit in the cloister, devote themselves not to reading and silence but to gossip and curiosity. They never and nowhere preserve the proper place and time for speaking and keeping silence; rather, unstable and idle, they now summon these persons and now those to conversation.

“Set a guard over my mouth,” says the Psalmist, “and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. 140 [141]). He said “a door,” not “a wall.” For if a wall were set up, permission to speak would seem to be wholly denied. [Col. 1074A] But a door is set up, which is closed and opened according to time and place. There is a time and place for speaking and for silence. Thus the door is opened in the cloister at the hour appointed for reading, in chapter for confession, and in church for prayer. It is closed again in the cloister against conversation, in chapter against self-excuse, and in church against empty chanting.

This door is more often closed to brothers newly converted, lukewarm, and perverse. Yet it is opened to the same persons on account of the necessity of work, instruction in the order, or edification of the mind. This door may be called permission to speak, which is opened or closed when it is granted or denied. Through this door those often enter [Col. 1074B] who break down the door of the mind, for the fascination of trifling talk deceives the heart.

Yet care must be taken that this door not stand open to the wind coming from the region of the desert, lest the house, shaken at its four corners, be overthrown and Job’s children be crushed and die (Job 1). The region of the desert is the multitude of demons or of perverse brothers abandoned by God. From them comes the wind—that is, a grievous temptation rushes in, which overthrows conscience from its tranquility. The house of the mind, established upon four corners—that is, prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice—is sometimes troubled when shaken by the wind of temptation or the storm of words.

For prudence is often broken through sloth, temperance through pleasure, fortitude through fear, and justice through love [wrongly directed]. When these are shaken, the virtues of the mind—wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear—die when struck by their opposites. [Col. 1074C] Wisdom is overwhelmed by folly, understanding by dullness, counsel by rashness, fortitude by fear, knowledge by ignorance, piety by hardness, and fear by pride. But the boy escapes this ruin who brings word to blessed Job—that is, discernment of mind, which deals with the soul so that repentance may preserve what it had begun to lose.

These are the reports proper to cloistered religious: not the wars of secular princes, but the conflicts of temptations. Therefore, dearest friend, delight in these reports, not in external ones. “Another messenger came to blessed Job and said: ‘The Chaldeans formed three bands, invaded the camels, and took them away; they also killed the servants with the sword, and I alone escaped to tell you [Col. 1074D]’” (Job 1). The fierce Chaldeans are demons; the camels are good administrations of earthly matters; the servants are watchful circumspections; and the messenger who escapes signifies discernment of soul.

The camel, partly a clean animal because it chews the cud and partly unclean because it does not divide the hoof, signifies good administrations of earthly things. The devil strikes these now through sluggish action, now through hasty action; now he confounds them through lazy or immoderate speech; and almost always he crushes them beneath excessive loads of thought. Thus the Chaldeans seize the camels in three bands when unlawful thought, superfluous activity, and disordered speech confound the cares of stewards.

Often a man considers what he owes to himself and what to his neighbors; he neither neglects himself through excessive concern for others nor postpones others through care for himself. But while he diligently performs both, some sudden occasion arises that overwhelms all his circumspections. [Col. 1075A] Thus discernment alone reports the losses to the soul and, as it were, calls the Lord to lamentation. Hear, then, dearest friend, what the boy who escaped reports to you—that is, what the purity of discernment reports to the mind. Hear of the loss of the camels and the fall of the servants. The former are carried off; the latter die. The concerns of administration are taken away when, through negligence, the purity of circumspection perishes.

Many cloistered persons delight in talking about kings, recounting the fortunes of soldiers, speaking for persons by whom they are not known, defending the sides of many, becoming angry for many, and litigating for many—though they do not know what they deny or affirm. But if there is talk of kings, the cloister’s reading teaches the contests [Col. 1075B] of kings, the disasters and outcomes of wars: how Saul dies, and who reported his death to David.

“When David had returned from the slaughter of Amalek and had remained at Ziklag, a man came from Saul’s camp to David. David said to him: ‘Where do you come from?’ He answered: ‘I have fled from the camp of Israel.’ ‘What is the matter?’ he said. He answered: ‘Saul and Jonathan his son have perished.’ ‘How do you know,’ he said, ‘that they are dead?’ The young man answered: ‘By chance I came upon Mount Gilboa, and Saul was leaning upon his spear. Looking back behind him and seeing me, he called me. When I answered, “Here I am,” he said: “Who are you?” I said to him: “I am an Amalekite.” “Stand over me,” he said, “and kill me”; and I killed him’” (2 Kings 1 [2 Sam. 1]).

These are the reports that cloistered persons ought to chew over. For when David returned from the slaughter of Amalek, a man came to him from Saul’s camp [Col. 1075C]: that is, after the mortification of vices, the desire of the flesh returns and reports not only its own falls but also tells of the failings of others. Thus it comes about that, through the examples of great persons, it inclines other minds toward fleshly pleasure.

For whom does Saul signify except proud prelates in the Church, who seem to themselves to stand out above all the people from the shoulder upward? He falls struck by the Amalekite on Mount Gilboa when the unstable mind, set upon the mountain of pride, runs through diverse desires of the flesh. The Amalekite stood over Saul in order to kill him, because a soul ruled by fleshly pleasure quickly perishes. But you, dearest friend, command one of your servants—that is, the spirit of pure discernment [Col. 1075D]—to kill in you this Amalekite who has dared even now, daily, to stretch out his hand against the Lord’s Christ. For these things greatly harm prelates: the love of one’s own preeminence and the pleasure of the flesh.

Perhaps, dearest friend, you would prefer to hear reports of peace rather than war, of concord rather than discord. The queen of Sheba knew reports of this sort. Having heard Solomon’s renown, she entered Jerusalem and spoke to him all that she had in her heart. He taught her everything that she had proposed; and, seeing the city which he had built, the foods of his table, the dwellings of his servants, the order of his ministers and their garments, the cupbearers, and the burnt offerings which he offered in the house of the Lord, she said: “True is the report which I heard in my own land about your words and your wisdom. I did not believe those who told me until I myself came, saw with my own eyes, and discovered that not even half had been reported to me. Your wisdom [Col. 1076A] and works are greater than the report which I heard” (3 Kings 10 [1 Kings 10]).

Sheba is interpreted as “captive,” or, as some wish, “conversion” or “burning.” For when someone is still held in the world under the law of sin, having heard the renown of Solomon through the word of preaching, he is converted to the Lord; once converted, he is set ablaze with the fire of charity. Entering Jerusalem, when she begins to love peace, she speaks to him through confession all that she had in her heart; and he teaches all the words which she had proposed: if she repents, she has forgiveness.

The queen of Sheba sees the wisdom of the true Solomon, which he showed us through the humility of the Son. She sees the house of the Church, which he builds daily through the grace of the Holy Spirit. She sees the food of the table and the dwellings of the servants [Col. 1076B]—that is, the various senses of Scripture and the congregations of religious persons. She sees the order of ministers—that is, the statutes of those living rightly. She also considers the garments: the bodies of martyrs and confessors, the former purple with the redness of their own blood, the latter black through the exertion of labor or pale through mortification of the flesh. She sees the cupbearers, who, along with the food of preaching, pour out the wine of compunction. She also kindles the burnt offerings offered on the altar of the contrite heart.

But when the newly converted soul sees these things, what follows is said of it: “And she had no more spirit.” It had spirit, and it did not have spirit. For it had a humbled, not exalted, spirit; the spirit of grace, not [Col. 1076C] of wickedness; the Spirit of God, not the spirit of the world. “True,” she says, “is the report which I heard in my land; and I did not believe those who told me until I myself came, saw with my own eyes, and discovered that half had not been reported to me.”

Therefore, for one captive, liberated, converted, and enkindled, it seems too little merely to hear preaching unless one comes through affection, sees through knowledge, and proves through effect. For when one sees in the house of conversion the goods of contemplation, and reflects within oneself upon what, while still in the world, one had heard concerning the goods of the active life—namely, works of mercy, kindness, and concord; the weight of labor, affliction of the flesh, plainness of food, and quiet of silence—and again considers through contemplation the rewards of the future life, where for the just there will be eternal goodness, blessed eternity, joy without pain, and rest without labor [Col. 1076D]: when, I say, one sees these things, one says: “Half had not been reported to me.”

Do you not know that Mary chose the better part, which shall not be taken away from her? (Luke 10). The better and longer it is, the greater it is. For in the active life the end lies in labor; but in the contemplative life there is neither failure in good things nor limit in delight.

## Chapter XXI. On Litigation in Chapter. The Tenth Abuse.

The all-powerful God, in kindly providing for the frailty of mortals, established in the Churches three things: physicians, places, and remedies. These three are signified by the Samaritan, the inn, and the wine and oil. The physicians are the prelates; the places, the chapters; the remedies, the modes of penance. Therefore discern in the Samaritan the prelate; in the inn [Col. 1077A] the chapter; and in the pouring in of wine and oil, the soothing of consolation and the harshness of correction. In this chapter there is also the pool of compunction, in which the infirm man was healed after the stirring of true confession. Yet only one is healed. For unless unity is present, health is absent. Those, therefore, who love contention destroy unity. This abuse is thus intolerable: that you should quarrel where you ought to accuse yourself; that guilt should be increased where it can be erased; that, where you despise Christ’s vicar, you should despise Christ.

For he himself says of prelates: “He who despises you despises me” (Luke 10). But perhaps someone will say: “I can endure a religious superior; but when I consider the negligence of prelates, I refuse obedience; when I see brothers worse than myself, I do not wish to endure their accusations.” When you say [Col. 1077B] that the brothers are worse than yourself, you have become worse. Why do you despise your master? Do you not know that Christ was judged before Pilate? Do you not know that the King of heaven was scourged on earth by soldiers? (Matt. 27.) Christ bore the cross for your sins, not for his own, and do you reject the rod? He was not ashamed to be scourged before the people, and do you disdain to be stripped before your master? Christ is accused and is silent before the soldiers, in order to give us an example of patience; you are accused and quarrel, in order to be an example to the brothers of perversity and malice.

Why, then, do you resist the Holy Spirit? They resist the Holy Spirit who, with hardened minds, refuse to repent; who contradict truth and despise the humility of confession. If you persist in this, you sin against the Holy Spirit. But he who sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven [Col. 1077C] either in this age or in the age to come (Luke 12). Why, then, do you introduce the strife of contradiction into the place of forgiveness? This place is more hateful to the devil than all others: here he loses those whom he acquired elsewhere. For this is a place consecrated to the Holy Spirit.

The Father is everywhere, the Son everywhere, the Holy Spirit everywhere; yet, as we have said, this place is said to be assigned to the Holy Spirit. For certain things can be said of the person of the Son which ought not to be said of the person of the Holy Spirit. The Incarnation belongs to the Son, and we do not read that the Holy Spirit became incarnate. So also forgiveness of sins belongs properly to the Holy Spirit. The persons are distinct, but God is the same, with one essence; and therefore, according to the distinction of persons, diverse offices are assigned to each. [Col. 1077D] In the Father is considered the mercy of compassion; in the Son, the affection of redemption; in the Holy Spirit, the kindness of forgiveness. Moved by compassion, the Father sent the Son to redeem; he also promised the Holy Spirit, in whom he would forgive sins. Do you see how the authority of the sender belongs to the Father, the humility of the obedient one to the Son, and the forgiveness of the penitent to the Holy Spirit? The chapter is therefore the workshop of the Holy Spirit, in which the children of God gather so that they may be reconciled to him.

Do not be, brother, like Satan among the children of God (Job 1). He is called Satan among God’s children who disturbs his brothers, slanders them, and maliciously lies in wait for them. “Satan” means “adversary.” And he is Satan who contradicts his master and opposes the brothers. To him God says: “Whence do you come?” (ibid.). [Col. 1078A] The one who is never stable but always loves instability is asked whence he comes. Hence it is added: “I have gone around the earth and walked through it” (ibid.). For this is what perverse brothers are accustomed to do: wandering about, they make rounds of workshops, their parents’ homes, and neighboring churches.

But when Satan went out from the presence of the Lord, he afflicted blessed Job and his possessions. Likewise, certain perverse brothers, both when they remain in cloisters and when they go out, trouble those who live well, within and without. Yet I know that whatever wrongdoing is committed within or without is released in chapter through confession. This is the house neighboring paradise. [Col. 1078B] For from the house of confession a passage is made to the blessedness of eternal peace.

There are, then, three houses in which we lodge after leaving the prison of the ancient enemy: the house of mercy, the house of obedience, and the house of pardon. In the house of mercy we are received by the Father, visited through compassion; in the house of obedience we are redeemed by the Son through his Passion; in the house of pardon we are freed by the Holy Spirit through grace from the yoke of sin. The first house, for those renouncing sin, borders on Egypt. The second house, for those advancing in good, is near the desert. The third, for those delighting in the Lord, is joined to paradise. Be humble, therefore, so that you may be exalted in paradise.

I beg you, do not be in chapter as Satan was in heaven or as Adam was in paradise. One despairs; the other makes excuses. Satan, however, is worse insofar as he is more despairing. Do you not know that Satan was expelled from the chapter of heaven, Adam from the chapter of paradise, Judas from the chapter of Christ? The first chapter was [Col. 1078C] in heaven, the second in paradise, the third in the garden. Yet God presided in each. In the first, the primary sin was pride; in the second, disobedience; in the third, avarice and unbelief. Of the first it is said: “I shall set my throne in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). Of the second: “Do not eat of the tree of good and evil” (Gen. 2). Of the third: “And he returned the thirty pieces of silver and threw them in the temple” (Matt. 27).

The punishment of the first sin was a fall; of the second, toil; of the third, a noose. Of the first it is said: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). Of the second: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3). Of the third: “He hanged himself with a noose and burst open in the middle” (Matt. 27). To these three are assigned three orders of cloistered persons: [Col. 1078D] those, namely, who seek the seat of prelacy; those who can neither preside nor are willing to obey; and others who, being familiar attendants upon their masters, carry money-bags and secretly torment their masters by slander.

What then? Do rank, power, and familiarity harm? An angel was created in such great rank that he was called Lucifer; yet, failing to consider the rank of his Creator, he sought an exalted seat and fell. So some among cloistered persons, while they excel through nobility of birth, flourish in learning, please by musical voice, or surpass the other brothers in any art, seek the seat of self-exaltation; and those who ought to be humbler because of such a great gift swell with proud contempt against the weaker and unlettered.

You know also the power of the first parent, who, “though he was in honor, did not understand” (Ps. 43); but when he disdained obedience to his Creator, he became subject to the creature [Col. 1079A] over which he had been placed. So some sometimes grow proud because of authority granted them; and although others obey them, they themselves will not obey their prelates. From what, therefore, came downfall in rank, subjection in power, and disturbance in familiarity? Again, whence came evil in the angel, when no evil had preceded it or was then present? Whence came sin in the first human being, who ought rather to have believed the command of his Creator than the suggestions of the ancient enemy? How did Judas, who had been so intimate with Christ, come to agree in evil with the Jews? Again, why did Christ make so intimate with himself one whom he knew to be worse among the disciples? Where am I wandering? To what heights am I climbing? This belongs to a work more exalted and more subtle.

Yet I know that, if [Col. 1079B] Satan came to the chapter of confession, he could obtain the pardon of forgiveness. But lest a human being should despair on hearing that an angel of such rank had despaired, a human being of such power had sinned, and a disciple of such intimacy had apostatized, God shows us examples of certain people who sinned, did not despair, and became friends of God. Do you not know Peter’s denial? (Matt. 26.) Do you not know Thomas’s doubt? (John 20.) Did he not love Mary after her sin? (Luke 7.) Christ loves the humility of those confessing, not the obstinacy of the proud, who “incline their heart to words of malice, to make excuses for excuses in sins.”

But you, most gracious Lord, incline my heart to perform your ordinances at all times, lest you incline my heart to words [Col. 1079C] of malice (Ps. 140), but rather to righteousness. “For the righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18). Why do you wish to conceal yourself from him to whom nothing is hidden, to whom every heart lies open, who sees in secret, who knows human thoughts? Adam hid himself in paradise after his sin, but he who was naked could not be hidden (Gen. 3). For before the eyes of almighty God all things are naked and exposed (Heb. 4).

Also, through the excessive simplicity of prelates or the perversity of subjects, quarrels are often multiplied in chapter; for where the severity of discipline is lacking, disputes arise and brawls increase. They speak of outward business in the house of confession; they bring sheep and oxen into chapter, so that where speech ought to be had concerning souls, concern is instead given to oxen. Among such words the simpler [Col. 1079D] brothers are stirred up, the discerning are troubled, the wrathful find an opening, and the perverse find a time for speaking. Martha complains; Mary answers, because there is no one to answer on her behalf. For where the excessive simplicity of prelates does not preserve the peace of those in the cloister or rebuke the faults of those serving, there neither is Martha restrained nor Mary’s silence kept.

I read Martha’s complaint, but I do not read Mary’s answer; yet I read that Christ answered the one on behalf of the other. Prelates can be instructed in Christ’s answer. For he exhorts Martha and praises Mary: the former, lest she cease from good work; the latter, that she may persevere in contemplation. Such is the beautiful order of those who live rightly: in a troubled chapter, no one should answer a brother except [Col. 1080A] one who knows both what is owed and what is fitting. In these three persons can be signified the pattern of perfect religious life: Martha represents those who serve, Mary those in the cloister, Christ the prelates.

Therefore, in chapter, where the authority of a discerning prelate prevails, let no one speak unless commanded, except to bring a charge against someone, to ask about the rule, or humbly to confess his own fault. In observing these matters there are a supreme physician and perfect medicine: a severe but not cruel master, and reasonable discipline. But if anyone refuses to undergo corrective punishment and, being clamorous and shameless, despises not only the brothers but also the master, then, even if he has not departed, let him be cast out from your fellowship. “For,” as blessed Augustine says, “this is done not cruelly but mercifully, lest through pestilential contagion he destroy very many.” [Col. 1080B]

## CHAPTER XXII. On Disorder in Choir. The Eleventh Abuse.

Since not only in the other places of the workshops, but even in every movement, nothing should be done that offends anyone’s sight, it seems fitting to me that, above all in church when one comes to the work of God, the propriety of humility should be observed more carefully, so that we who gather in church before the presence of God may not there become worse.

For there are some who, wandering in mind, staring with their eyes, and disordered in bearing, look about and survey the flat surfaces of the walls; they sing one thing and think another. In choir they are present in body, but in the marketplace in mind; now they are within, now they go outside. Nor are they merely disordered within; [Col. 1080C] once they go outside, they are curious as well. They utter the words of psalmody but do not attend to the meaning of the psalmody. Hence blessed Gregory says: “When the voice of psalmody is performed with the intention of the heart, through it a path is prepared in the heart for almighty God, so that either the mysteries of prophecy or the grace of compunction may be poured into the attentive mind.” The same author, in the same work: “When compunction is poured out through psalmody, a way is made for us in the heart, through which we arrive at Jesus in the end.”

There are also others disordered in voice, who pride themselves upon the modulation of their voices. They not only delight in the gift of grace, but, swelling with self-exaltation, despise others. They sing something other than what the books contain, and perhaps will say something else again if they are to sing that same thing again. So great is the fickleness of their voice—perhaps also of their mind. They sing, perhaps, [Col. 1080D] in order to please people rather than God. Those who sing thus do not sing with Mary, Moses’ sister, but in the palace with Herodias, in order to please those reclining at table or Herod. I fear that, just as they delight in the height of their voice, they also delight in exaltation of mind.

Yet no one sings more loftily than he whom the Lord is accustomed to hear from his holy mountain; no one more sweetly than he to whom the Lord inclines his ear. David says: “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain” (Ps. 3). Be therefore in the valley of humility, that you may deserve to be heard on the holy mountain. If you sing in such a way as to seek praise from others, you sell your voice and make it not yours but the buyer’s. Beware lest you turn the monastery into a theater.

[Col. 1081A] You have your voice in your power; possess your mind as well. You break your voice; break your will also. You preserve harmony of voices; preserve harmony of conduct also, so that through example you may be in harmony with your neighbor, through will with God, and through obedience with your master. This is harmony of conduct.

There are also three kinds of sounds, produced by striking, blowing, and singing. Striking belongs to the cithara; blowing, to the organ; singing, to the voice. This harmony of sounds can be assigned to harmony of conduct: to the striking of the cithara, the work of the hands; to the blowing of the organ, the devotion of the mind; to the singing of the voice, the exhortation of speech. Strike, therefore, the strings of the cithara with the hand of good work, that by the example of mortified flesh you may be in harmony with your neighbor. Fill the organ of your heart with breath—that is, with the Spirit of holy [Col. 1081B] inspiration—so that you may render to God the sweet sound of devout devotion. Again, that you may be in harmony with your master, sing a new song, the song of obedience, not the song of contradiction and disobedience.

What use is sweetness of voice without sweetness of heart? As through the rising notes of music you lower and raise your voice, so through the ascents and descents of virtues lower and raise your mind. Lower it by descending to compassion for your neighbor; raise it by ascending to contemplation of God. Do not sing with Lucifer in heaven or with the first human being in paradise; rather, sing in the temple with Christ, casting out from it those who sell and buy (Matt. 21): casting out those who sell grace given to them and those who buy vain glory. The devil’s song is covetousness; the first human being’s song, pleasure; the second’s, charity.

In the devil’s song [Col. 1081C] there are three false notes, and in the first human being’s song three discordant and dissonant ones. In the devil’s song the first note is self-exaltation, the second suggestion, the third despair. Likewise, in the first human being’s song the first note is delight, the second consent, the third excuse. From these six notes the song of discord is composed.

The devil’s music began to sing from a higher note: for in heaven it began the antiphon of self-exaltation, saying, “I shall set my throne in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). Thus it began more loftily than it ought. For if it had not exceeded the rule of subjection, it would have sung with the other angels the song of everlasting happiness. But descending from heaven, it began the antiphon of suggestion in paradise, and that of despair in hell.

[Col. 1081D] Christ’s music, therefore, differs from the devil’s music: the latter begins from a higher note; the former from a lower. Hear, then, the teacher giving us instruction about spiritual music: “Learn from me,” he says, “for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11). Do you see how spiritual music begins from the note of humility? In Christ’s music there are six notes mutually harmonious and concordant. The first note of concord is humility of heart; the second, mortification of the flesh; the third, compassion; the fourth, consolation; the fifth, prayer; the sixth, devotion.

Observe, therefore, how in harmony of conduct there are descents and ascents of virtues. Observe how humility accords with mortification, mortification with compassion, compassion with consolation, [Col. 1082A] consolation with prayer, and prayer with devotion. Observe again, in the descents, how devotion relates to prayer, prayer to consolation, consolation to compassion, compassion to mortification, and mortification to humility. In these six notes is sung the new song, the song of charity. In them is heard the jubilation of unity, the harmonious melody of devotion, the sweetness of contemplation.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Irreverence near the Altar. The Twelfth Abuse.

Holding in my hands the last of the twelve abuses of the cloister, I approach its examination, intending to say a few words, since I find myself alone among the rest more negligent in this respect. Although I come to [Col. 1082B] the altar with hands washed, face cleansed, and clothed in white garments, yet perverse in deed, polluted in speech, and unclean in heart, I do not fear to handle Christ’s body with my hands. I come proud to the humble one, angry to the gentle, cruel to the merciful; and yet the humble one endures the proud, the gentle the angry, the merciful the cruel.

I come as a servant to the Lord, not from love but from fear; not from devotion but from habit. I come to the Lord whose servant I have struck; I come to the Father whose Son I have killed. I struck him by word; I killed him by example; yet I do not fear the Lord or reverence the Father. Remaining amid the crowd of brothers, disturbing some and disturbed by another, I sometimes come to the peacemaker. In such a state I also approach the kiss of peace, though I ought first to have been reconciled before approaching the kiss of my disturbed brother.

Upon the altar I behold the same one [Col. 1082C] whom Simeon, receiving him in his hands, blessed with thanksgiving in the temple (Luke 2). It is good to carry the Savior as a child in one’s hands and to have the fruit of salvation in one’s works. For whoever carries the child in his hands—that is, purity in his works—is heard when he prays, so that he may be dismissed in peace. When children were presented in the temple, a lamb, turtledoves, and doves used to be offered at this purification. But what am I to offer, when I can possess none of these?

Shall I offer a pig from among those I have fed for so long? Shall I offer blessed Benedict’s blackbird, which so often and so importunately comes fluttering before me? Shall I offer the ostrich that I have nourished since my conversion? Perhaps I shall offer the pig of uncleanness in place of the lamb of innocence; the blackbird of pleasure in place of the turtledove of chastity; the ostrich of hypocrisy in place of the dove [Col. 1082D] of simplicity.

For what, in a moral sense, is a pig rolling in a muddy wallow but a sinner returning to the uncleanness of sin? What is a fluttering blackbird but pleasure tempting through suggestion? Or what is an ostrich in the desert but hypocrisy in one who has converted? I still have with me husks as food, namely the food of pigs, because worldly tales still resound in my mouth; they are, as it were, food for unclean spirits. A husk, as I find it written, is a kind of legume, largest and loudest in its pods, but barren and nearly empty because of the scarcity of grains. Therefore worldly tales, resounding with barren sweetness, are signified by husks. When, then, I tell worldly stories, I gather fools; and, as pigs follow husks, the unclean follow trifles.

[Col. 1083A] Alas, how often the blackbird of temptation comes before me, and how slowly I run to the brambles and nettles of correction. “When, however, as blessed Gregory says, blessed Benedict was pressed by a temptation of the flesh, he saw dense thickets of nettles and brambles growing nearby; he cast himself naked amid those thorn-pricks and nettle-burnings, and by wounds of the skin drew out the wound of the mind, because he turned pleasure into pain.” Such a person may approach the altar: when the blackbird of pleasure comes before him, he humbly runs to the severity of correction.

But how shall I approach, who bear the feather of the ostrich in the habit of religion, so as to please not by my conduct but by my garments? Like an ostrich, I feign flight, yet touch the earth with my feet: I flutter in habit, but touch the earth in affection. For the feather of contemplation does not lift one [Col. 1083B] from earthly things when it is weighed down by the mass of fleshly frailty. Hence blessed Job says: “The feather of the ostrich is like the feathers of the heron and the hawk” (Job 39). The ostrich’s feather is said to resemble the heron’s and the hawk’s feather when someone feigns in outward habit that he has the life of some ancient father. They are alike, then, in feathers but differ in body, because the ostrich is larger in body and therefore cannot be lifted from the earth. Those who savor earthly things and thirst after them are accustomed to be weighed down by fleshly desire.

Hence Truth says: “These are they who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7). Outwardly I am covered with sheep’s fleece, but inwardly I rage with greed. Before the Lord I stand at the altar with hands stretched out, as though crucified, [Col. 1083C] imitating the cross but not bearing it. Whose cross? Perhaps that of the thief—but would that it were the one to whom it was said: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23).

For there are three crosses: first, that of the thief who despaired; second, that of the thief who prayed and said, “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (ibid.); third, that of Christ. The first deserved the cross, but it did not benefit him for salvation. The second indeed deserved it, yet it benefited him for salvation. The third did not deserve it, yet bore it, and it benefited us. Three kinds of people can be likened to these three. The first are those who bear the cross by mortifying the flesh, yet it does not benefit them because they do not repent. There are others who mortify the flesh, and it benefits them [Col. 1083D] for salvation: they pray and are heard; they also hear the saying, “Today you shall be with me in paradise.” When do they hear this? When, reading the Gospel, they say: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

There are others who are free from the penalty of sin, entangled in no crimes, who refrain from perverse action, idle speech, and unclean thought. In their hands is constant labor, on their tongue prayer, in their mind purity; they bear the sins of others as though they were their own. These are they who bear the cross not for their own sins but for the sins of others. Thus the first cross is the devil’s, the second that of any righteous person, the third Christ’s. The first is of malice; the second, of penance; the third, of righteousness.

Each has four dimensions. In the devil’s cross there is height, by which [Col. 1084A] he exalts himself above everything that is worshiped. Its depth is despair, of which it is said: “When a sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18). Its breadth belongs to the carnal, who follow the broad and spacious road. Its length is obstinacy. In the righteous person’s cross, depth is humility; length, constancy in labor; height, contemplation; breadth, prayer, which in its breadth embraces not only a friend but also an enemy. Christ’s cross has the depth of fear, the height of hope, the breadth of charity, and the length of perseverance.

I am tormented on the first cross; I strive toward the second; I long for the third. I fear the first, seek the second, desire the third. In the first is punishment alone; in the second, punishment with pardon; in the third, glory. Punishment belongs to the cross of malice; pardon to the cross of [Col. 1084B] penance; glory to the cross of righteousness. Therefore I fear punishment, seek pardon, and desire glory.

But perhaps you ask whether you can find the measurements of both crosses. Blessed Job possesses the depth of the Lord’s cross, David its height, Peter its breadth, Naboth its length. Of the depth of fear it is said: “There was a man upright and fearing God” (Job 1). Of the height of hope David says: “In you, Lord, I have hoped; let me not be confounded forever” (Ps. 30). Peter shows us the breadth of charity, saying: “Before all things, maintaining constant mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4). You hear breadth when he says, “covers a multitude of sins.” This too is the broad commandment: that he who loves God should love [Col. 1084C] his brother also (Prov. 10).

Of length it is written: when Ahab, king of Israel, wished to turn Naboth’s vineyard into a garden (3 Kings 21), Naboth, understanding this morally, preferred to die rather than consent that the labor of cultivating the flesh should be turned into a garden of pleasure. He wished that the measure of length in the good of perseverance should have death as its limit. Therefore above the depth of fear is placed the height of hope, lest the mind be led through fear into despair. After hope is set charity, and after charity perseverance, so that the one who hopes may love and persevere in that which he loves. A diligent reader may assign the dimensions of the first and second crosses whenever he wishes. But let us return to what we began, so that we may be able to offer a sacrifice worthy of God.

There are three kinds of sacrifice: one, [Col. 1084D] of the Lord’s body; another, of a contrite heart; the third, of mortified flesh. Therefore sacrifice of humility in the mind and of affliction in the flesh must precede, so that there may be devotion in the consecration of the Lord’s body. After Abraham had offered sacrifice to the Lord following his victory over the five kings—a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, a three-year-old ram, and also a dove and a turtledove—he divided the bodies of the animals but left the birds undivided. Birds came down upon the divided bodies, but Abraham drove them away (Gen. 15).

Birds are spiritual persons; animals, carnal hearts. Animals are divided against one another when perverse desires are torn apart. But birds remain undivided because spiritual persons always preserve the bond [Col. 1085A] of unity. Birds descend upon the divided bodies because, amid the division of carnal persons, demons seek the fodder of their desire. There are also other birds—namely, importunate thoughts—which sometimes intrude during the very sacrifice of our prayer and wish to snatch away or defile what we offer in ourselves to God. But when Abraham drives them away, the birds flee; for the hand of holy discernment drives out unclean spirits and perverse thoughts within.

By the heifer, as some maintain, which is a heavy animal, is signified sensuality; by the she-goat, which seeks high places and has sharp sight, intellect; by the ram, which is a stiff-necked animal, carnal imagination, which resists the spirit with the horns of pride. These are said to be three years old, so that they may be imbued with love for the undivided [Col. 1085B] Trinity.

But I am not only burdened by the approach of birds; I am also troubled by the importunity of flies, which, coming from Egypt, still follow those sacrificing in the desert. In the former I fear theft; in the latter, stain. There are three flies of Egypt: vanity, curiosity, and pleasure. The fly of vanity troubles and stains the sacrifice of the humbled heart; the fly of curiosity, the sacrifice of prayer; the fly of pleasure, the sacrifice of mortified flesh. Therefore I approach the altar vain, curious, and subject to pleasure.

There are many others in the world who are not merely vain, curious, and pleasure-loving, but approach Christ’s table with ambition rather than devotion; they would not approach unless they hoped to receive [Col. 1085C] something for themselves. Peter came to Jesus; Judas also came; the crucifying soldiers came as well (Matt. 27). Religious persons come daily to Christ’s body, but so too do perverse priests, who offer at the devil’s table the things offered at Christ’s table. It is the same gaming table: at one they invoke God, at the other they swear falsely. For they do not devote themselves to prayer but delight in games. They neither know nor learn God’s law; given over to idleness, they apply themselves to feasting and drunkenness; they thirst after earthly things and savor earthly things. They are constantly in the streets, seldom in church; slow to investigate the fault of a sinner, ready to track a hare’s footprints; swifter to gather dogs than to summon the poor; more willing to offer bread to a dog than to a poor person. Many serve them at table; no one serves at Mass. They wish to have female [Col. 1085D] servants or male servants with them, but they cannot have clerics because they do not wish to.

These are those whose bedchamber is more richly furnished than their church; whose horse is dearer than their missal; whose cape is more handsome than their chasuble; whose shirt is more luxurious [Col. 1086A] than their alb. Behold how the gold has grown dark, the finest color has changed, and the stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street (Lam. 4). The gold has grown dark with the soot of sins; the color of beauty and holiness has been changed into the foulness of vices.

Who are these stones of the sanctuary scattered at the head of every street, if not—as a certain wise man says—the priests of Christ and ministers of the holy altar, the holy society of canons consecrated to God, and likewise the multitude of virgins and nuns? These ought always to appear in the hidden presence of God; they should never need to be seen outside, never be occupied with alien or worldly business. But, what is more grievous, they are lamented as scattered like stones of the sanctuary at the head of every street because, though [Col. 1086B] by life and prayer they ought always to be within, in contemplation of God, through a reprobate life they are everywhere occupied outside.

Behold, now there is scarcely any activity of secular life which priests of Christ do not administer; no worldly business in which ministers of the altar do not involve themselves; no wickedness in affairs in which the monastic order does not entangle itself; scarcely any seductive pleasure of life by which the chastity of nuns does not defile itself. The stones of the sanctuary are therefore scattered in the streets when religious persons of every kind follow the broad paths of the world. And they are scattered not only in the streets but at the head of every street, when through desire of this world they perform worldly works yet seek from their religious habit the summit of honor or praise.

[Col. 1086C] Thus they are scattered at the head of the streets, because they lie low through the service of worldly work while wishing to be honored for the appearance of holiness. What then is it when such people approach the altar, seeking nothing but temporal things?
