And what abuse in cloister or in the world can be greater or more grievous than approaching the sacrifice of the Lord’s body without reverence and without devotion?

The matters we have stated can instruct the reader’s mind, if harmful things are avoided and useful things retained: let prelates diligently guard their subjects; let subjects kindly obey their prelates; let the old be devout and the young industrious; let there be propriety in dress and moderation in food; let them be constant in the cloister and seldom at court; let them be not courtiers but cloister-dwellers; attentive to psalms, not lawsuits. Let there be in the cloister not [Col. 1086D] noise but reading; in chapter not quarrels but confession; in choir a severe simplicity; around the altar, the propriety of reverence. Upon these ordinances of observance depends the whole sum of religious life.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1085]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1085D]

You know, dearest friend, that the matters we have set forth concerning the ordering of the material cloister have not merely been written down, but have also been arranged according to place, time, and persons, [Col. 1086D] and put into practice among us. But perhaps you wonder whether all agreed, or whether some who did not agree withdrew. None withdrew; all agreed, except certain lay brothers who still bear the yoke [Col. 1087A] and murmur—such people as had lived more poorly in the world than they now live, and who now seek in the monastery things that they could not have possessed even outside it.

Thus, when David set out to defeat the Amalekites, some went while others remained with the baggage (1 Sam. 30). The idle and weak remain with the baggage of clothing and food; the ready and strong do not fear to go to battle. Therefore those who love clothes, food, and the repose of the flesh do not go forth to defeat the Amalekites—that is, to destroy fleshly pleasures. For this is the meaning of *Amalek*: “a lapping people.”

Thus the sons of Gad, the sons of Reuben, and the half-tribe of Manasseh refuse to cross the Jordan and go to war with their brothers; instead, they prefer to obtain the land of Jazer, suitable for feeding animals (Num. [Col. 1087B] 30). Those who seek the land of Jazer for animals are those who feed the irrational motions of the mind in fleshly desires.

None of the clerics, dearest friend, is now in discord; but each kindly bears the burden of religious life, and what was formerly more burdensome to them is now more pleasing. For this reason I labor: that I may always live quietly with them, die with them in peace, and be with them and under them as brother and fellow servant. But now let us pass to the matters to be said concerning the cloister of the soul.

## CHAPTER I. That Contemplation Is Called the Cloister of the Soul.

Contemplation is called the cloister of the soul. When the mind withdraws into its enclosure, it meditates upon heavenly things alone; it is separated from earthly things, set far from the crowd of carnal thoughts; it shuns the sweet affections of the flesh, restrains the wandering motions of the senses, delights in the Lord, enjoys angelic sweetness, reads in the book of life, keeps peace through silence, preserves harmony of conduct in the choir of virtues, and contemplates the goodness of the supreme Father and the blessedness of the angelic creation. It considers a goodness lacking nothing and a blessedness needing nothing. It considers the Father’s power, the Son’s wisdom, and the Holy Spirit’s kindness. While it contemplates these three, it is consoled in three ways.

For we have sinned against the Father, sinned against the Son, and sinned against the Holy Spirit. Through weakness we have sinned against the Father, as though against power; through ignorance against the Son, as though against wisdom; through malice against the Holy Spirit, as though against kindness. Therefore the Father’s power consoles us, by which sins are punished, so that we may gain strength against the frailty of the flesh; the Son’s wisdom consoles us, restoring what fails through ignorance; and the Holy Spirit’s kindness consoles us, lest despair enter in.

The circuit of this cloister is adorned with the columns of virtues, supported by the foundations of patience, squared by the rule of justice, and fortified by the adjacent workshops of virtues. The boundaries of the cloister are outwardly enclosed by a wall of good work; with the gate of silence shut, they prevent the wandering mind’s steps. Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, went out from this cloister to see the women of a foreign land. When Shechem, son of Hamor, saw her, he loved her, seized her, and lay with her; his soul clung to her, and he soothed the sorrowful girl with flattery (Gen. 34).

Hear blessed Gregory:

> “Dinah goes out to see the women of a foreign land when every mind, neglecting its own pursuits and concerning itself with the actions of others, wanders outside its proper habit and order. Shechem, prince of the land, oppresses her, because the devil corrupts her when he finds her occupied with outward concerns. And his soul clung to her, because he receives her into union with himself through iniquity.”

But when the mind comes to its senses after sin and tries to lament what it has committed, the corrupter brings before its eyes both hope and security, in order to take away the benefit of sorrow. Thus it is rightly added there: “And he soothed the sorrowful girl with flattery.” At one time he speaks of others’ deeds as more grievous; at another, says that what has been done is nothing; at another, speaks of the Lord’s mercies; at another, promises that time still remains for repentance. Thus, while the deceived mind is led on by these things, it is held back from the resolve to repent.

Thus, dearest brother, the mind sometimes goes out; and, having gone out, it is ensnared when entangled in worldly cares. But Dinah’s brothers do not permit their sister to remain long in a foreign house. After killing Shechem together with the other males and plundering the city, they take away their sister, while carrying off the women as captives (ibid.). Jacob’s sons bring back their sister after killing Shechem with the remaining males when the manly motions of the soul struggle against vices, the devil having been expelled; and, after the greater vices have been rooted out, they compel the mind violated by carnal desire to remain with them, as though forcibly rescued from enemies. The captive women are carried away when the soul’s pleasures, exiled beyond the land of the flesh, are deprived of carnal desires.

Thus Jacob’s sons, gathered together, depart from that region with their sister: when the mind comes to its senses after a fall, it withdraws farther away, its companies of virtues assembled, lest it again be captured by carnal desires. Nor does it merely withdraw farther away; it also ascends higher. For it goes up to Bethel (Gen. 35). This happens when the mind establishes within itself the ascent of virtues. Thus Bethel is reached when the heart of each person becomes the house of God—for Bethel is so interpreted. In this house an altar is raised to the Lord; in this house the order of the spiritual cloister is established.

## Chapter II. On the Four Sides of the Cloister

[Col. 1088D] Just as the structure of a material cloister is customarily made from four sides, so by analogy the square form of the spiritual cloister may be assigned to four virtues of the soul: contempt of self, contempt of the world, love of God, and love of neighbour. Of these four sides, one faces west, another north, a third east, and a fourth south.

When we see the continual failings of the flesh, when we observe the soul’s daily settings, then we sit, as it were, on the side of the cloister that looks toward the west. For what else do we see but sunset when, the rays of the heavenly sun withdrawn from us, we feel the day of divine knowledge fail? When the sun withdraws, darkness increases and brightness diminishes; so, when the sun of righteousness withdraws, blindness comes upon the wretched mind.

But one who considers the darkness of deep night—that is, the hard sins of worldly people—and their cold hearts frozen in the frost of despair, sits, as it were, on the side of the cloister that looks northward. After the darkness of deep night—that is, after the blindness of greed and hatred—the dawn of righteousness spreads the rays of the heavenly sun: it illuminates the mind’s inner chamber, puts the clouds of temptations to flight, drives out the numbness of cold, nourishes the warmth of love, and invites one to the love of neighbour. As the morning star precedes the sun, so love of neighbour precedes love of God. This side of the spiritual cloister, therefore, looks toward the east of charity. For God begins to be loved when one’s neighbour begins to be loved. And just as the rising sun ascends to the southern region, so through love of neighbour one ascends to the charity of God.

[Col. 1089B] We are on the side of the cloister which faces south when, with the sun of charity burning, we see the light of the divine majesty but faintly because of its excessive brightness. Although the ray of contemplation illuminates the land of the heart in a straight course, and although the mind has either the smallest shadows of temptation or none at all, yet when we wish to see the fullness of the Godhead, reason is hindered so that we cannot. Thus the mind, established within these four fortifications of virtues, has nowhere to turn: neither to the pleasure of the flesh, nor to the vanity of the world, nor to hatred of neighbour, nor to contempt of God.

## Chapter III. On the Four Orders of Columns, and How an Order of Twelve Columns Proceeds from Contempt of Self

[Col. 1089C] Upon these four sides of the cloister, as it were, four orders of columns are arranged. From contempt of self proceeds an order of twelve columns: humility of heart; affliction of the flesh; humble speech; lowliness of dress; scanty food; the burden of labour; love of subjection; contempt for honour; fleeing praise; preferring another’s counsel to one’s own; obedience to subjects; and distrust of oneself.

These columns are cut, carved, and polished. They are cut when, by the discernment of virtue, they are separated from vices. They are carved when the hand puts into action what the mind thinks. Thus Solomon is said to have made projecting carvings in the Temple (1 Kings 6). The carvings project when the thoughts of the mind appear outwardly in example and action. But how are they polished? When they are struck by the adversity of tribulation. What is polished becomes even: even, not raised up; smooth, not rough.

Therefore the first column, humility of heart, is polished when it preserves evenness, when it is not embittered through anger and does not admit the inequality of pride, which thinks that no one is its equal. Rather, it becomes a heart subject to God, friendly toward its neighbour, and moderate toward itself. The evenness of the mind preserves the line of religious observance.

For there are some who now waste themselves by affliction of the flesh, now return to the pleasure of the flesh; who often keep vigil while others sleep, but more often sleep while others keep vigil. Now they speak humbly, now loftily; now mildly, now harshly. Now they boast of brothers, now of parents. Now they make a clamour about nothing but the statutes of the order; now they want to hear nothing but tales. Now they delight in having white, now black, now middle-coloured cowls; now a cheap habit pleases them, now a moderate one, now an excessive one. Now they give themselves vegetables for food and water for drink; now they use refined dishes and various cups. Now they labour; now labour displeases them. They love to be subject in order that they may be able to rule; they flee honours in order that honours may come to meet them. This is the unevenness of the columns; this is their roughness.

The apostle Paul teaches evenness and smoothness [Latin *laevitatem*; alternatively *lenitatem*, “gentleness”]—smoothness [Latin *Laevitatem*; alternatively *Laenitatem*, “gentleness”] when he says: “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. 12). And in the same place: “Beloved, do not defend yourselves, but give place to wrath” (ibid.). He teaches evenness where he says: “I know how to be humbled, and I know also how to abound; everywhere and in all things I have been instructed, both to be full and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want. I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4).

Hence blessed Gregory says:

> “He who is not puffed up by the things he receives, who does not twist them to the use of vainglory, who does not possess for himself alone what he has received, but mercifully shares it with the needy—he knows how to abound.”

He who uses food received not for gluttony but for the restoration of strength, and gives the flesh no more than necessity requires, knows how to be full. He who endures lack of food without grumbling, and does nothing on account of the need for sustenance by which the soul incurs the snare of sin, knows how to hunger. Therefore, one whom pride does not raise up in abundance and greed does not provoke in necessity knows how to abound and knows how to suffer want.

But when Paul said, “I can do all things,” lest he exceed the balance of evenness through the swelling of self-exaltation, he immediately added, “in him who strengthens me.” For those who attribute to God what they do, and, thinking humbly, distrust themselves—such persons do not see the fruit of their labour vanish away, because it is neither lifted into the air of vainglory nor carried off by the wind of self-exaltation.

## Chapter IV. On the Foundations of the Columns: Three Kinds of Foundations Found in Scripture

Just as foundations placed beneath material columns bear the weight of their building, so the virtue of patience sustains the burden of the spiritual building. In Scripture three kinds of foundations are found: bronze, silver, and gold. Bronze possesses strength; silver, brightness together with strength; gold, splendour together with strength and brightness. Strength belongs to work, brightness to speech, splendour to the mind. One who keeps patience well in these three things firmly bears the structure of virtues, as though he were a golden foundation.

Moses used these three in constructing the tabernacle—bronze, silver, and gold (Exod. 36). Moses built the tabernacle, which morally signifies the cloister of the soul. We may assign three tabernacles: the material, mystical, and moral—that is, the tabernacle of Moses, the tabernacle of Christ, and the tabernacle of every righteous person. Moses’ tabernacle was a harmonious construction made from various kinds of ornaments. Christ’s tabernacle is the Church. The tabernacle of the righteous person is every faithful soul. One is made of incorruptible setim wood; another of tireless saints; the third of virtues.

[Col. 1091A] Moses raised his in the wilderness, Christ in the world, and the righteous person in the soul; yet all built in the desert. Wilderness is called desert because it is not inhabited by human beings; the world too is called a desert because it had deserted Christ. Similarly, the soul is called a desert when it is not made fruitful by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Moses placed the ark in his tabernacle; Christ, his own flesh in his; the righteous person, conscience in his. Moses’ ark is adorned inside and out with purest gold. Christ’s flesh is gilded inwardly by divinity and outwardly by the brightness of miracles. The conscience of the righteous shines inwardly with the splendour of purity and outwardly with works of brightness.

Moses placed boards around the tabernacle; each board had two mortices, so that one might be joined to another. Two foundations were placed under each board, on either side of the corners, where the mortices of the sides end at the corners. The boards arranged around the circumference morally signify the order of virtues. The two mortices in each board are the mind’s affection and the performance of the deed. When the mind agrees with the work, the firmness of the mortice preserves the connection, lest one board exceed another. The two foundations under each are perseverance and long-suffering in prosperity and adversity.

There are also other kinds of foundations, now found in our buildings: wooden, stone, and painted. But these are more fragile than the foregoing, for they can be destroyed more quickly. Fire burns the wooden foundation; frost breaks the stone one; the painted foundation bears nothing, but is supported by another. These may sometimes be discerned in the building of our mind by the eye of understanding. When we are inflamed by the torches of anger or the flames of lust, what else is destroyed in us but the foundation of patience or the strength of abstinence? When charity grows cold within us and the mind is divided among diverse desires, is not the stone foundation split into pieces by the frost of temptation? A painted foundation is truly feigned patience: it has likeness but not reality, colour but not strength. The patience of pretence exists in display, not in action.

Therefore let us raise in the building of our mind foundations of enduring patience—foundations that cannot be broken by frost or burned by fire, that bear the boards of virtues and sustain the weight of the columns, that is, obedience to superiors.

## Chapter V. On the House of Guests: The Mind of the Wise Must Be Hospitable

Among the adjoining workshops of the spiritual building, the house of guests appears first. It stands open, with the doors of mercy opened, to those who have wandered into a far country when they return to the cloister of the soul. The house of guests may indeed be called the compassionate mind. Hence Ambrose says:

> “The mind of the wise ought to be hospitable. For the mind performs the office of hospitality when it compassionately bears with the faults of offending brothers.”

This house has its servants to minister to guests. Charity opens the door to the pilgrim who knocks; cheerfulness receives the one entering; affability keeps the one received; sharing feeds the hungry; humility serves the weary. These are what are owed to the guest, what the householder provided for the returning son who, by living dissolutely, had squandered his share of the estate (Luke 15). Seeing him coming from afar, he ran to him, embraced him, killed the fatted calf, arranged the choir, and set the music playing.

So too the mercy of spiritual fathers, which presides over subjects with a fatherly affection, sees the offending disciple returning through repentance as coming from afar, by compassion; it runs to him by pardoning; embraces him by making itself familiar to him; kills the calf by preaching mortification of the flesh; arranges the choir and plays the music by teaching harmony and unity of conduct. Thus compassion invites the despairing person; charity draws the unwilling; mercy pacifies the angry; cheerfulness restores confidence; affability makes one familiar; familiarity opens the secret; the disclosure of secrets preserves friendship; preaching instructs; harmony of conduct makes one a friend to one’s neighbour; humility makes one a friend to God.

But while these things occur, I fear that the brother who was outside may arrive and say: “Father, behold, for so many years I have served you; I have never transgressed your commandment; and you never gave me even a kid so that I might feast with my friends. But after this son of yours, who devoured his property with prostitutes, came, you killed the fatted calf for him” (ibid.). Truly, he is said to be outside the house of compassion who does not know the benefit of consolation, who knows only how to rebuke and not how to entreat.

Yet the mercy of a ruler must be so tempered that the offender’s fault does not remain unpunished. Thus spiritual fathers sometimes receive certain offenders whom their brothers despise, because those brothers scorn to enter the house of compassion; so they remain outside, and those who ought to have compassion on their brothers become more cruel than their superiors.

Christ did not bring the lost sheep back to the folds by violent hand, but bore it home upon his own shoulders. The angels too rejoice over one sinner doing penance (ibid.). What then, dearest brothers? Angel and Creator agree when a sinner is converted, while brother disdains to have compassion on brother when the spiritual father mercifully forgives his offending son.

Samuel came down from the height into the town in order to anoint Saul king (1 Kings 3). Samuel’s descent signifies an example of condescension; the anointing shows that he who descends should show mercy, and that he who offers the effect of compassion should anoint with the soothing oil of consolation. The superior comes down to the inferior in order to raise him to honour: so that the one who followed asses may rule souls—that is, so that one who pursued the irrational affections of the flesh may be chosen to rule and possess those same affections spiritually.

One who lies down is not raised unless the person who raises the fallen bends down. Hence blessed Gregory says:

> “No one raises the fallen unless he bends the uprightness of his own position through compassion.”

Such persons are sometimes raised by love, sometimes by fear. But one raised by the fear of discipline is compelled, as it were, to rise by himself; one drawn by the sweetness of love is helped, as it were, by the compassion of one who gently encourages him. Love raises, draws, and sustains; fear compels and raises, but torments.

To this belongs what blessed Augustine says to superiors concerning subjects:

> “Let them desire more to be loved by you than feared. Yet love should not spare too much, nor should fear terrify too much; but fear should so accompany love that fear produces neither hatred nor love permits negligence.”

Hence blessed Job says: “When I sat as a king with an army around me, I was nevertheless a comforter of those who mourned” (Job 29). Behold fear arising from the authority of government, but love from the sweetness of consolation. Thus the Samaritan poured wine and oil into the wounds of the man who fell among robbers (Luke 10): by the wine signifying the severity of strictness, by the oil the gentleness of mercy. Hence blessed Gregory says:

> “A certain blending of the two must be made, so that subjects are neither wounded by excessive harshness nor loosened by excessive kindness.”

In the ark of the tabernacle, too, there were together the rod and the manna (Heb. 9): the rod of strictness and the manna of sweetness. Thus the Psalmist says: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22). We are struck with the rod; we are supported with the staff. This is the rod of guidance through correction; this is the staff of support through consolation. But, as was said above, superiors should desire to be loved by their subjects more than feared, lest the face of excessive severity drive away those whom the kindness of compassion ought to cherish through consolation.

## Chapter VI. On the Chapter-House of the Soul: As Brothers Assemble in Chapter to Correct Faults, So Reason Summons Thoughts

[Col. 1093C]

Just as a multitude of brothers gathers in chapter at appointed hours to correct faults, so the mind’s reason sometimes summons diverse thoughts into the secret chamber of the heart: to cast out the incorrigible, rebuke the restless, correct the negligent, instruct the simpler, calm the angry, restrain the pleasure-seeking, rouse the sluggish, console the faint-hearted, and teach the undiscerning.

In this spiritual chapter-house reason occupies the abbot’s place; conscience accuses faults; perversity makes excuses; pride defends guilt; innocence confesses; humility judges itself; arrogance judges others. After the manner of perverse brothers, vices oppose commands; after the manner of simple brothers, virtues obey. Yet virtues sometimes accuse one another. Mercy accuses justice; justice mercy; decorum humility; humility decorum.

Mercy accuses justice because it has stretched out its hand even to cruelty, uttered words of anger, and changed the face of gentleness. Justice, in turn, accuses mercy because it has not put on the countenance of severity, has left sin unpunished, and has not rebuked the offender even with words. Humility accuses decorum because it exceeds moderation, follows excess, and employs not merely what is fitting but what is pleasurable. Decorum, in turn, accuses humility because it loves excessive poverty, does not provide the body with what is necessary, and loves nakedness, raggedness, and want.

For mercy sometimes speaks too leniently, justice too cruelly, humility too sparingly, decorum too abundantly; yet they do not cease to be virtues, though they are imperfect. While they are accused, they are, as it were, stripped for receiving discipline. But how are they stripped? When what is hidden is disclosed through confession of faults.

There are two kinds of discipline: inward and outward. Inward discipline is correction of conduct through the strictness of the heart; outward discipline is correction of actions through affliction of the flesh. Outward discipline sometimes produces inward discipline, because when the mind is not scattered among outward things, it returns to the love of rest. To this belongs the statement that Lamech begot Noah (Gen. 5): that is, discipline begets rest. For *Lamech* is interpreted “striking,” which belongs properly to discipline; *Noah* is interpreted “rest,” which is born when the mind is restrained from outward things by discipline.

This is Noah, who builds the ark (Gen. 6): that is, he builds the soul, which orders irrational animals in the lower part and places human beings and birds in the upper part—that is, he subjects carnal motions and sets spiritual ones above them. But if the flood of the flesh should overflow, then he enters the ark of the mind. Though torrents of anger, streams of lust, and whirlpools of gluttony flow around it; though the fountains of pleasures, the abyss of desires, and the seas of disturbances boil up—Noah nevertheless enters the ark safely: that is, the tranquil mind, with the door of silence shut outside, possesses the soul.

Lamech is also said to have killed Cain (Gen. 4). *Cain* is interpreted “possession.” Whose possession? The devil’s, not God’s; one’s own, not the master’s; private, not common. Cain is killed while lying among the leaves, because the perverse person wallows in lightness of heart and multiplicity of words. Thus Cain is killed by Lamech, and Noah is begotten from another Lamech, because the perverse person is sometimes cast out through discipline and, nurtured through discipline, becomes a person of tranquil mind.

Cain is accused of the death of his brother. Those who obey no one, possess themselves, and show their brothers the example of perverse conduct—what else do they do but kill the soul of their brother with their own hands, that is, with their own acts? What, then, is more useful than discipline, which begets rest and kills the perverse?

## Chapter VII. On Spiritual Work: After Chapter, Brothers Go Out to Labour; So the Mind Goes Out from Contemplation of Heavenly Things to Meditation on Scripture

[Col. 1094D]

After chapter the brothers customarily go out to the labour of their hands. So, after the rest of contemplation, the mind goes out to attend to the labour required by bodily necessity. It goes out from contemplation, having enjoyed heavenly delight. It goes out—and descends. Where, and how? It goes out from contemplation of heavenly things to meditation on the Scriptures. There, remaining for a while, it hears of the misery of this present life and the blessedness of the life to come; it considers the rewards of the righteous and attends also to the punishment of the condemned. Then, drawn by love of the rewards and touched by fear of punishments, it descends to the remembrance of its own sins.

When it recognizes its own fault, it more readily forgives another’s; and therefore, after remembering sins, it descends to compassion for its neighbours, and from there proceeds to care for them. This may also be shown by an analogy: someone goes out from a bedroom into a house, from the house into a portico, from the portico into a street, and from the street into a field. The mind goes out from contemplation of heavenly things to meditation on Scripture, as from a bedroom into a house; from meditation on Scripture to remembrance of sins, as from a house into a portico; from remembrance of sins to compassion for neighbours, as from a portico into a street; and from compassion for neighbours to caring for them, as from a street into a field.

Therefore in contemplation there is rest; in the other things, labour. In meditation on Scripture we labour, fearing that we may lose the rewards of the righteous. In remembrance of sins we labour and groan, lest we be among the condemned. In compassion for neighbours there is the labour of action. In the first we are warned; in the second instructed; in the third moved; in the fourth made worthy. Scripture warns us what we ought to do; remembrance of sin teaches us to repent; compassion moves us to love; and good work makes us worthy that help may be given to us who help others.

The mind also goes out into the garden to see the gardener, namely Christ, who plants the shoots of virtues. It goes out also to water the vegetables—that is, to bewail the frailty of the flesh with tears. But as the sun shines more brightly after rain, so Christ appears more kindly after the watering of tears, extending the rays of his knowledge and illuminating hearts with a word of consolation.

Mary Magdalene went out to the tomb as though into a garden, to plant and water. She found him who gives increase and heard: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom do you seek?” (John 20). Behold: after the rain of compunction, the brightness of consolation shines forth. But she, on hearing him ask whom she was seeking, supposing him to be the gardener, said: “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I will take him away” (ibid.). Mary despaired of the fruit of her labour because she doubted the truth of the resurrection. Hence it is said that she turned backward (ibid.). She turns backward who, through doubt, had cast down her gaze from the Lord’s face. Mary had planted through love, but doubted the fruit of the resurrection because its fulfilment was delayed. But when she recognizes Christ, she gathers the fruit. For what good would the seed of corruption, the flower of birth, or the maturity of the Passion have been, unless the fruit of the hoped-for resurrection followed?

The mind goes out again to dig around the fig tree, so that what was barren may bear fruit (Luke 13); it casts in a basket of dung—that is, it renders the memory of sin foul-smelling. It also enters the vineyard to dig around it and cut off its shoots—that is, the growths of excess—so that what luxuriates in branches may abound in fruits. Hence in the Song of Songs: “Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field, let us remain in the villages; let us rise early for the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the flowers bear fruit” (Song 7).

“Let us go out into the field,” it says. The mind goes out from contemplation to examining itself; it goes out from care of itself to care for its neighbour, so that it may console the faint-hearted, rebuke the restless, and become a field of virtues when it had formerly been a place of briars and thorns. “Let us remain in the villages,” that is, among those who are *villani*, rustic and slow to receive the teaching of Christ’s court. For some cloister-dwellers are like courtiers, while others are *villani*, disordered people who seek not the edification of the mind but the filling of the belly; they gape after earthly things and savour earthly things. Among these we must remain for a time by teaching and discipline.

“Let us rise early for the vineyards.” Those who wish to cut off the vineyard-shoots—that is, the excesses of souls—must rise early: they must not be sluggish, but take the lead in example and action. “Let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the flowers have borne fruit”: that is, let us make it visible whether the mind flowers in good thoughts and bears the fruit of good work.

What then? Must one not rest amid one’s works? Let the mind therefore say: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat beneath the shadow of him whom I desired” (Song 2). Three things are to be considered in the apple tree: pleasant shade, good fruit, and sweet fragrance. Christ gives the shade of commandments, which protects from the heat of vices, so that the sun may not burn by day nor the moon by night (Ps. 120). He has fruit among the leaves—that is, good work among words. For it is written of him: “He did what he taught” (Acts 21). The fragrance of his fruit is sweet—that is, the good reputation of good work.

Therefore the mind that wishes to be at rest sits under the shadow which it desires. But sometimes it sits on grass, sometimes on a footstool, sometimes on a bench, and sometimes on a chair. It sits on grass when it subjects the flesh; on a footstool when it subjects the world. Hence blessed Jerome says: “It is a great exultation of the soul to have the world beneath its feet.” When it sits on a bench, let it choose the lowest place, so that it may hear: “Friend, come up higher” (Luke 14), lest it go down in shame and hear: “Give this man your place” (ibid.). One who follows humility is called to higher things; one who chooses pride descends to lower things. They sit upon the chair not of justice but of pestilence; of them it is said: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 27).

After the repose of rest, the mind rises again to work, to gather clusters from the vineyards of Engaddi (Song 1), not from the vineyard of the Sodomites; from the vineyard of Sorec, not from the suburbs of Gomorrah; to carry bundles of myrrh between its breasts; and to gather in the field of Boaz the ears of grain which had escaped the reapers’ hands (Ruth 2).

The mind gathers clusters from the vineyards of Engaddi and the vineyard of Sorec when it seeks the fruits of penitents or the rewards of the elect. *Engaddi* means “fountain of the kid”; *Sorec*, “chosen.” Into this fountain kids descend; newborn lambs ascend from it. For in the fountain of compunction the stains of the flesh are washed away: the stench of the kid, that is, the pleasure of sin, is washed away; the kid’s wantonness, that is, the lust of the flesh. From the vineyards of Engaddi comes good wine; from the vineyards of Soreth comes excellent wine. The beloved are made drunk with the former, the most beloved with the latter. The former is mixed with water; the latter is pure. The former is still troubled by its natural sediment—that is, by carnal pleasure; the latter is not troubled even by any temporal tribulation. The former retains the taste of old vessels—that is, memory of sin; the latter breathes forth purity—that is, the sweetness of a purified heart.

Therefore wine from the vineyards of Engaddi and the vineyard of Soreth is seasoned with spices and honey; wine from the vineyard of the Sodomites and the suburbs of Gomorrah is seasoned with poisons and gall. “For their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable poison of asps” (Deut. 32). *Gomorrah* means “dryness”; *Sodom*, “barrenness.” For those who are far from the fountain of compunction, who are not moistened by the rain of preaching, who are not sprinkled with the heavenly dew—that is, the subtlety of contemplation—it is no wonder if they are dry or barren. Moisture produces fruitfulness; dryness, barrenness.

One carries bundles of myrrh between one’s breasts who, with a compassionate heart and the labour of hands, supports the needs of neighbours. One carries bundles of myrrh who tames the pleasure of the flesh through affliction—by fasting, keeping vigil, and labouring. One carries bundles of myrrh between one’s breasts who places within the heart, which is between the breasts, the stoning of Stephen, the fire of Lawrence, the cross of Peter, and the death of Christ through compassion. Hence in the Song of Songs: “My beloved shall remain to me like a bundle of myrrh between my breasts” (Song 1). The Beloved remains as a bundle of myrrh between the breasts of the bride when Christ’s Passion is renewed with bitterness in the heart of each person through remembrance.

One gathers ears that have escaped the reapers’ hands in the field of Boaz (Ruth 2) who diligently seeks out sayings left untouched by great teachers. Thus Ruth the Moabitess—that is, the sinful soul—followed her daughter-in-law and came into Judaea, the land of confession. There, in the field of Boaz, following behind the reapers so as not to depart from their teaching, she gathers their ears, that is, their sayings, which the Law commanded to be left as food for the widow, orphan, and stranger. Then, threshing her harvest with a rod—that is, with subtle discernment—she finds three measures, which are the threefold senses according to the measure of Christ’s gift. From these, therefore, we are sustained in time of famine, so that our soul may live.

## Chapter VIII. On the Refectory of the Soul: Three Tables Are Set in the Spiritual Refectory, at Which Christ Ministers
Just as the outward person is refreshed at a material refectory for a time with food and drink, so the inward person, in the refectory of holy meditation, is given the wine of compunction to drink and is nourished with diverse dishes of examples. In this refectory three tables are set out: that is, the threefold sense of Holy Scripture—the historical, the mystical, and the moral. The first table is for the simple, the second for teachers, and the third is common to both. At the first the food is coarser, at the second subtler, at the third sweeter. The first contains the flavour of examples, the second the force of mysteries, the third the sweetness of morals. At one Christ serves wine, at the second he breaks bread, at the third he teaches. The first nourishes by miracles, the second by figures, the third by words. The reality of miracles strengthens faith; the fulfilment of figures, hope; and moral teaching, charity.

For when water is changed into wine, when Lazarus is raised, the leper cleansed, and the blind man enlightened, then the simpler crowd marvels; but faith thereby grows, because God is believed to have done this. But when bread is broken for the disciples and declared to be Christ’s body, when the temple is promised to be destroyed and, after three days, rebuilt as a figure of the resurrection—when this is seen to have occurred, is not hope kindled concerning the glory of the resurrection to come? For he spoke of the temple of his body. When Christ speaks in parables, when it is assigned to which soils the seed of the sower is suited, what else is ordered in human minds but love for the word of God? [Col. 1098A]

Therefore tables are set out, and breads are set out as well. Moses brings kneaded bread; the Apostle, barley bread; Elijah, bread baked under ashes. Barley is covered with a most tenacious husk, in which the Old Testament is figured, overshadowed as it is by legal observances. By unleavened bread is signified the bread of tears granted to God’s people as food when they leave Egypt. But by bread baked under ashes is denoted the life of sinners, who carry ashes above themselves so long as they burn with desire for carnal pleasures. Hence it is written: “Ephraim has become a cake baked under ashes, which is not turned” (Hos. VII). A cake under ashes has its lower part cleaner, and that which is uppermost dirtier. [Col. 1098B]

Thus the mind that thinks earthly thoughts carries ashes upon itself. But if the cake is turned, when the ashes have been shaken off, it appears wholly clean. Elijah had been fed by this ash-baked bread, not yet well shaken free of ashes, when, fleeing from the face of the harlot woman, he came to Beersheba of Judah; there, leaving his servant, he went one day’s journey into the wilderness and, sitting beneath a single juniper tree, cast himself down and slept; and behold, at his head was a cake baked under ashes and a vessel of water (III Kings XIX).

Thus he flees who renounces the world; he flees the harlot woman who flees lust. He comes to Beersheba of Judah, the land of confession, and leaves his servant there: that is, abandoning childish acts, he rises to manly ones. He proceeds a day’s journey into the wilderness who, preserving the unity [Col. 1098C] of common life, renounces worldly things and seeks spiritual ones. He sits under a single juniper tree who, though unwilling, endures the thorns of sin. Hence the Apostle says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward person; but I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind” (Rom. VII).

And he cast himself down and slept when, failing in his love for the heavenly person, he rests in the tinder of sin as though in the shade of the juniper tree. He is awakened by an angel when he is aroused by the word of God, which comes at midnight from the royal dwelling. And behold, at his head is ash-baked bread. The head of the mind is reason. There ash-baked bread is found, because the mind is not yet wholly cleansed from the memory of sin. He rose and ate, and slept again: not, as before, in the shade of the juniper, but in love of the mystery; not now eating ash-baked bread, but strong and solid food. That it was strong is clear, for “he went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights, unto the mount of God, Horeb.” Strong food is charity. For “charity bears all things, endures all things” (I Cor. XIII); it advances and raises the mind even to the height of divine contemplation. [Col. 1098D]

The ministers who rise up also set before them various kinds of wine: Stephen, namely, raisin wine; Isaiah, wine mixed with water. Two persons are made drunk. Noah is interpreted “rest,” Lot “declining.” There is rest of mind and rest of flesh. Those who seek the rest of the flesh are made drunk with wine mixed with water; but those who seek rest of mind, with raisin wine. Paul sets out vegetables (Rom. XIV); the three boys serve pulses [Col. 1099A] (Dan. I). By vegetables Paul gives the weak, and by pulses the three boys give the refined an example of preserving sobriety.

There follow three general dishes: lamb, ram, and cow. Abel sets forth the lamb, Abraham the ram, Joshua the cow. The lamb dumb before its shearer is Christ humble in his Passion, and ourselves patient in tribulation. The ram caught by its horns among the thorns is Christ on the cross by his hands, and ourselves by works of obedience. The ram preceding the flock is Christ leading the people by his life, and prelates leading the community by example. The cow slaughtered outside the camp signifies Christ put to death outside Jerusalem, and ourselves being mortified outside worldly vanity. In the lamb is simplicity of heart; in the ram, strength in work; in the cow, the milk of preaching. [Col. 1099B]

But let there not be in us simplicity without discernment, nor discernment without the milk of teaching; rather, let us be like those who “fly as clouds,” “prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X): lest there be a cloud without rain, a serpent without prudence, or a dove without simplicity. Rather, let the dove lack gall, the serpent venom, and the cloud dryness, so that the simplicity of the righteous may be without bitterness, prudence without malice, and teaching without vanity.

After dishes of flesh, three kinds of fish are offered: fish from the sea, from the river, and from the pond. Fish from the sea are secular persons; fish from the river, teachers; fish from the pond, cloistered persons. Yet let such fish be offered as have scales and fins: that is, the roughness of right conduct and the wings of contemplation. A fish from the sea is Cornelius; from the river, Paul; from the pond, Maurus. [Col. 1099C] Thus Peter sets Cornelius at table (Acts X), Ananias Paul, and Benedict Maurus. For when the deeds of Cornelius, Paul’s conversion, and the life of Maurus are read, what occurs except that the mind is nourished by their examples? Such fish, therefore, are to be eaten—that is, their lives and morals are to be imitated. Cornelius is to be imitated by secular persons in faith and works; Paul by teachers in life and teaching; Maurus by cloistered persons in humility and obedience.

That the water offered itself to Maurus to be trodden upon was due to the virtue of obedience and the merit of his master. That he ascribed the power of the miracle to his master taught the office of humility. Others bring other fish also. James and Andrew bring fish from the sea; Tobias, from the river; Honoratus, from the mountain. James is interpreted “supplanter,” [Col. 1099D] Andrew “manly.” Those who overthrow vices—that is, who act manfully—draw fish from the sea, that is, secular persons, to the shore of conversion by the example of good works.

But Tobias, who goes down to the river, is Christ descending to the world, and the righteous person descending to tears. Tobias goes down to wash feet; Christ, to wash away sins; the righteous person, to cleanse carnal affections. Tobias finds a fish; Christ, the devil; the righteous person, any member of the devil. Tobias draws out the fish; Christ cast out the devil; the righteous person converts the impious. Tobias disembowels the fish by throwing away its entrails; Christ disembowels the devil by exposing his malice; the righteous person does so by casting out through confession the secrets of the breast. [Col. 1100A]

These do not lack salt with which to season their fish: Tobias has material salt, Christ mystical salt, the righteous person moral salt. Thus Tobias does not lack material salt with which the fish is seasoned; Christ, the salt of wisdom by which the devil is warded off; the righteous person, the salt of teaching by which the newly converted person is instructed. Honoratus also brings a fish from the mountain: namely, an example of sobriety and abstinence.

Moses likewise brings various kinds of dishes: “honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone; butter from the herd, and milk from the sheep, with fat of lambs and rams, the children of Bashan, and goats, with the marrow of wheat, and the purest blood of the grape” (Deut. XXXII). You hear “rock” and “hardest stone.” The rock was Christ before the Passion; the hardest stone, after the resurrection. First, a rock because of the firmness of his patience; afterward, the hardest stone because of the eternity of his immortality. He was a rock, for he could be broken because he was still mortal; but now he is the hardest stone, because, having become immortal, he can die no more. [Col. 1100B]

By honey from the rock, therefore, is signified the honey-sweet teaching of preaching; by oil from the hardest stone, the Spirit of consolation proceeding from the same source. For this outpouring of oil is the remission of sins through the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, if you have, dearest one, a clean vessel with you—or rather, since you have one—receive honey from the rock. For he says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI). Behold honey of humility with the sweetness of meekness. As honey harmonizes in medicinal preparations with every variety [Col. 1100C] of ingredients, so every kind of virtue is seasoned with the sweetness of humility.

But by butter from the herd is signified, in the patriarchs and prophets, the richness of spiritual teaching. For as the richness of milk is known to rise above in vessels, so in prophetic words there is found an abundance of spiritual understanding concerning divinity and humanity. Yet this richness does not assume the form of butter unless it first hardens when agitated by pounding. So too God would not be known in a human being unless God, having become man, were first scourged, fastened to the cross, and raised from the dead by the power of divinity. We are therefore fed by this butter when, in prophetic words, we delight in the contemplation of divinity.

By milk from the sheep is signified innocence of heart among the simple. [Col. 1100D] Hence the Prophet says: “He fed them in the innocence of his heart, and guided them by the understandings of his hands” (Ps. LXXVII). Innocence pertains to the heart; cleanness of works to the body: so that the intention of the heart may be innocent and the works of the flesh clean. These are milk and wool: we ought to be fed by this milk and clothed in this wool. These things, therefore, pertain to the simplicity of cloistered persons, who are clothed in purity of flesh and harm no one.

But in the fat of lambs and rams is signified the love of brothers in prelates. These are called “children of Bashan” (Deut. XXXII), that is, of fatness, in which is shown the sweetness of charity. By goats, indeed, is figured the life of penitents, who are imitators of Christ’s sufferings. This is what is meant by “goats with the marrow of wheat”: namely, penitents [Col. 1101A] mortifying their flesh and imitating the sufferings of Christ. But the utterly pure blood of the grape is the blood of Christ, troubled by no dregs of sins. Therefore those who resist perversity even to the shedding of blood return, by drinking a cup for the cup which the Saviour drank for us. Hence also the Prophet says: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXV).

There are also other foods of Egypt, to be especially avoided, because they very often produce illness and sometimes death. If you ask what they are, so that they may be avoided: these are harmful foods—garlic, onion, and leeks—which the children of Israel longed for in the wilderness along with the pots of meat. Yet when eaten they cause severe swelling and flatulence; they disturb the brain, burden the eyes, and provoke tears. [Col. 1101B] Egyptian meats are worldly pleasures, in which the illnesses of the soul lie hidden and later appear outwardly in their effects and actions. Pride causes swelling; a flood of words produces windiness; anger troubles the brain; sloth burdens the eyes of the heart. These, therefore, provoke tears of penitence, if you set them before the eyes of the mind in the hand of discernment.

Therefore, that you may live soundly in fitting moderation,

Avoid harmful foods and take wholesome ones.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Dormitory of the Soul

The tranquillity of the mind may by analogy be called the soul’s dormitory. In it the bed of conscience is placed, the hay of the flesh is spread beneath, and the sleep of peace is gathered. In these the soul sleeps, sleeps and rests. Guard yourself, therefore, dearest one, lest the roof of the dormitory be uncovered by the storm of temptations. Arrange the bed of conscience, lest the disordered mind cease from rest. Spread beneath it the hay of the flesh, so that animality may lie subject to the reason of the mind. Restrain the crowd of vices, lest they hinder the sleep of one at rest.

For the arrangement of a dormitory ought to be such that none of the cloistered keeps any private thing stored beside his bed. So too let the bed of conscience be such, if it is searched, that nothing of one’s own will may be found in it. Care must also be taken that something hidden beneath the hay of the flesh does not offend the eyes of the abbot who sees all things. But in order that you may sleep and rest “in peace and in the same place” (Ps. IV), seek peace and pursue it (Ps. [Col. 1101C] XXXIII). For it vanishes from the sight of the mind just as sleep vanishes from the eyes.

There are, therefore, four things to be considered which are accustomed to disturb the sleep of peace: an enemy, a servant, a wife, and a neighbour. The enemy is the devil; the servant, the world; the wife, the flesh; the neighbour, any fellow human being.

Therefore, when the devil is cast out, the world is subjected, the flesh is afflicted, and one’s neighbour is loved, what else occurs but that peace is established on every side? Among these things the mind has nowhere to turn aside: not to hatred of a brother, not to love of the flesh, not to the pride of the world, nor to the malice of the devil. Behold how Solomon has peace on every side around him (III Kings IV). He has peace around him who is not disturbed by the memory of past sins, troubled by desire for future things, broken by adversities, or raised up by prosperity. This is true peace.

There is true peace and false peace. Of false peace it is said: “Peace, peace—and there was no peace” (Jer. VI). Of true peace Abishai says to David: “Peace, peace be to you, and peace to your helpers” (I Chron. XII). There are three kinds of false peace: imagined peace, pretended peace, and commanded peace. When we seek peace among secular people, when we recall those at discord to concord, secular people suppose that we have peace among ourselves. When outwardly we walk in sheep’s clothing, while inwardly, like ravening wolves, we rend and scatter the flock of simple brothers (Matt. VII), we pretend peace but do not possess it. But when prelates command peace to subjects and do not restrain them under the laws of discipline, they teach peace only, but do not maintain it. “For,” as blessed Gregory says, “it is not enough that you teach peace by words alone, unless you also apply your hand to correction.” [Col. 1101D]

Do you see how, when it is not in us, secular people suppose peace; perverse cloistered persons pretend it; and lukewarm teachers command it without maintaining it? Thus it is supposed by those who do not know, pretended by those who do not have it, and commanded by those who do not maintain it.

Three kinds of true peace are said to exist: tested peace, confirmed peace, and certain peace. The peace of God is sometimes given to human beings; once given, it is tested; once tested, confirmed; once confirmed, made certain. It is tested by temptation, confirmed by tribulation, and made certain by living together. For by living together one recognizes true peace, though tongue and habit may outwardly speak it hypocritically. Tongue and habit sometimes say, “Peace, peace”; but if the mind is questioned, it answers that there is no peace. Whether peace of mind is genuine is demonstrated by the duration of continual cohabitation, so that peace may be in deed, not in speech. The tongue sometimes preaches peace, but more often disturbs it. But when habit, heart, and tongue agree, they preserve peace. Where the unrestrained tongue runs about, it dissolves peace. [Col. 1102A]

This seems morally pertinent to the story that, when the tribe of Dan sought a possession in which to dwell—for until that day it had received no lot among the other tribes—the sons of Dan came to the house of Micah and found there an ephod, a carved image, and a molten image (Judg. XVIII). Dan is interpreted “judgment.” For “the righteous person is at the beginning his own accuser” (Prov. XVIII). The sons of Dan seeking for themselves a lot of inheritance signify certain people from the world who provide for themselves a house of conversion in which to dwell.

At times they find there an ephod, that is, the religious habit, and with it a carved image of perverse action and a molten image of talk. You know, brothers, that when a molten object is to be made, a kind of metal is set in the fire with bellows placed round about it. There is a tumult of bellows drawing in and sending out air; ashes are stirred, the flame grows, and sparks fly. So it is accustomed to happen in certain churches when idle brothers gather together in one place. They set in the midst metal—that is, matter for rumours. The bellows draw in and send out air when brothers hear and repeat rumours. There is heard there the tumult of bellows, that is, the dissension of the impatient; ashes are stirred because the more volatile are quickly agitated; the flame grows when anger is kindled; sparks fly, that is, words of discord. [Col. 1102B]

Thus Aaron, to make a molten calf, requested earrings from the children of Israel (Exod. XXXII). Earrings are rumours; for as gold is put upon the ear, so rumour is put upon hearing. From these, then, proceeds the calf of wantonness, which, if it goes before us, takes away the straightness of our path. For it does not walk gravely, but runs about in play. Therefore, when some come from the world to the house of religion and find these things, they believe that they have discovered the house of Micah. Micah is interpreted, “Who is here?” But when they find an ephod—that is, the religious habit—and a molten image—that is, words of detraction—they sometimes go out and depart; marvelling at such a conversion, they say, “Who is here?” Many indeed become worse through their company; but many, departing from them, pass on to better things. [Col. 1102C]

These, dearest one, are the things that trouble the peace of the spiritual dormitory, because they disturb the tranquillity of a quiet mind. Rumour agitates one beginning to sleep; curiosity wakes him; and so, sleeping, he turns from one side to the other while distracted and troubled by curiosities. But when he renounces the curiosities of the world, he sleeps peacefully. Of these things, therefore, the prophet Ezekiel says: “And he shall sleep upon his left side” (Ezek. IV). When the prophet says this, he morally presents the person of every newly converted individual. For he sleeps upon his left side who calmly presses beneath himself whatever opposes him. But when he bears upon himself the iniquities of the house of Israel, attributing to his own deserts the sins he had committed, he presses down the pride arising from contempt for vices. And when he bears the years of iniquity under a fixed number of days, although he may have served sin long, he nevertheless hopes for pardon after the labour of penitence.

Hear, therefore, what follows: “And when you have completed these things, you shall sleep upon your right side.” For when vices fall, while virtues obey, then he turns himself from the left side to the right; and the virtues render services to the one who loves rest, whereas vices previously resisted him. Blessed is the soul to which vices are servants and virtues obedient, which in the dormitory of tranquillity has arranged the bed of the mind so as to enjoy the sleep of peace; which does not go out under the darkness of night—that is, does not withdraw in the time of temptation; which does not run through the streets of the city or enter the brothel of luxurious pleasure; which, when captured, is not dragged into the darkness of prison, that is, the mind’s forgetfulness; and which does not lie in the bed of dissolution, namely in the pleasure of unrestrained flesh. [Col. 1102D]

For the inward person goes out clothed in garments when he delights in meditating through the streets of the city of secular people. Perhaps to this pertains the fact that Holy Scripture says that some sleep in dust, some in a woman’s lap, some in a bed, and some in prison: Job in dust (Job VII), Samson in a woman’s lap (Judg. XVI), Peter in the depths of prison (Acts XII), while the paralytic is reported to have lain in a bed (Matt. XXIX [sic]).

For blessed Job says: “Behold, now I shall sleep in the dust” (Job VII). He sleeps in dust who delights in frivolity. Of Samson it is said that, sleeping in a woman’s lap, he lost the affection of strength. For nothing debilitates the mind more quickly than when someone bends the affection of the heart toward lust. But Peter sleeps in prison: that is, in forgetfulness of himself and the blindness of ignorance. He sleeps between two soldiers, namely between the vices of the flesh and the vices of the mind, which fight against the soul, because vices always fight against virtues. The paralytic lies in the bed, loosened from every joining of his limbs: that is, scattered in every action and thought. [Col. 1103A]

Do you see, dearest brother, how all these things were written for our instruction? Do you see that by dust is signified frivolity, by a woman’s lap pleasure, by the depth of prison the blindness of ignorance, and by the paralytic’s bed the disturbance of the dissolute brother? Shake yourself free, therefore, from the dust; rise from the woman’s lap; loose the bonds of your neck; take up your bed and walk. But if you ask where you ought to go, follow Rebecca’s counsel: depart from Esau, go with Jacob, turn aside to the house of Laban, so that there you may make use of marriage with Leah and Rachel, and return enriched with children and flocks of sheep to your homeland (Gen. XXXVII [sic]).

But if, as you return, Esau should meet you, embrace you, clasp your neck, kiss you, and weep, beware lest you be deceived (Gen. XXXIII). If he says to you, “Let us go together,” do not consent [Col. 1103B] (ibid.); for he proceeds with force, while your little ones and flocks of sheep must move gently. Rebecca is interpreted “much patience.” Rebecca’s counsel is therefore an exhortation to patience: withdraw and turn aside from those things in which you fear danger to the soul.

Rebecca commanded Jacob two things: to withdraw from Esau and to serve Laban. David commands the same thing: “Turn aside,” he says, “from evil, and do good” (Ps. XXXIII). By hairy Esau is signified carnal affection. Therefore he departs from Esau who does not consent to carnal desires. He goes with Jacob who, struggling against vices, walks in the undefiled way and meditates day and night on the law of the Lord. Those who serve Laban serve God. “For Jacob did these three things,” says blessed Ambrose: “he obeyed his mother, yielded to his brother, and served his uncle.” [Col. 1103C]

How sweet it is, even while labouring, to dwell in Laban’s house! Nothing is difficult to one who loves; nothing is burdensome to one who desires to come into Rachel’s embrace. For the days of labour seem few in comparison with the greatness of love. Jacob therefore received Leah also (Gen. XXIX): that is, the active and the contemplative life. He is enriched with children and flocks of sheep when he abounds in good works and in a multitude of simple thoughts. But when he returns to his homeland, the brother whom he had formerly fled meets him. A remarkable thing: even the perfect are sometimes flattered by carnal affection. Behold how Jacob walks with Esau, embraces, clasps, kisses, and weeps (Gen. XXXIII)!

Jacob’s walking is the soul’s spiritual will; Esau is its carnal will. The embrace is pleasure; the clasp, covetousness; the kiss, flattery; the weeping, carnal affection. Thus he walks with his feet, embraces with his arms, clasps with his hands, kisses with his lips, and weeps with his eyes. The two feet with which Esau walks—that is, carnal affection with the spiritual mind—are frivolity and vanity of will. The two arms are the delights and riches of pleasure. The two hands with which he clasps are the rapacity and tenacity of covetousness. The two lips are the winning of favour and the display of carnal friendship, which pertain to flattery. The two eyes are social connection and kinship, which look toward affection of the flesh. [Col. 1103D]

These are the things that flatter us as we walk in the way of the Lord. Therefore, dearest one, if Esau meets you, ask him to depart; flee your perverse brother so that you may have peace; go with Jacob, for little ones walk with him. Those who overthrow vices always love the fellowship of humility. Seek, therefore, Jacob’s bed; for he placed his bed in the spiritual dormitory. There Samuel sleeps; there Joseph sleeps. Joseph sleeps in a house (Matt. II); Samuel in the temple (I Kings III); Jacob on the journey (Gen. XXVIII).

Joseph sees an angel appearing to him in sleep; Samuel hears the Lord speaking with him; Jacob not only sees angels ascending and descending, but also sees and hears the Lord looking upon him and speaking to him. Joseph hears an angel warning him; Samuel, the Lord reproving him; Jacob, the Lord promising him. Joseph hears: “Take the child and flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you; [Col. 1104A] for Herod will seek the child to destroy him.” Samuel hears: “I foretold to Eli that I would judge his house for ever because of its iniquity, since he knew that his sons acted unworthily and did not correct them.” Jacob hears: “The land in which you sleep I will give to you.”

By these three men three kinds of people may morally be signified: beginners in Joseph, those making progress in Samuel, and the perfect in Jacob. The beginner is warned to flee; the person making progress is taught to correct; the perfect person is invited to receive. Joseph is called “increasing,” that is, a beginner. For the beginner grows when, at the beginning of conversion, the newly converted advances from virtue to virtue. He takes the child when he holds to the rule of new life. For in a child there is hope of growth, and in one newly converted hope of progress. Nor is he commanded only to take the child, but also the mother—that is, good will. Good will may be called the mother of a good purpose. [Col. 1104B]

“Flee,” he says, “into Egypt”: that is, attend to the world, consider yourself, call back to mind the darkness of former sins, so that, if you are stirred by the goads of vainglory, you may humbly meditate on what you were in the world. “And remain there until I tell you”: that is, do not turn the eyes of your mind away from the sight of worldly downfall and from awareness of your own frailty, until you are called back from Egypt to Jerusalem—that is, from considering former sins to contemplating the blessedness of heavenly peace. “For Herod will seek the child to destroy him.” Vainglory, signified by Herod, sometimes attacks the minds of the newly converted in order to destroy good beginnings. For Herod means “skin of glory.” All the glory of the daughters of God is within (Ps. XLIV); all the glory of the daughters of the world appears outwardly.

For just as the flesh of animals is covered outwardly with skin, so the animal spirit, spreading itself outward through the desire of vainglory, delights in outward things. This is Herod, who secretly calls the Magi in order carefully to ask them the time of the star (Matt. II). He calls secretly because vainglory afflicts the mind in secret. Vainglory tempts the minds of those seeking the Lord in order to learn from them more subtly the manner and intention of their conversion: namely, what intention the mind possessed when the hope of a religious life to be sought appeared to it; whether someone converted in wisdom trusts in his own understanding; whether a rich person glories in the understanding granted him; whether a stronger person glories in labour, or a nobler person in lineage; whether the spirit attends to temporal or spiritual things; whether it looks, in the prospect of a religious life, to the advantage of temporal benefit. [Col. 1104C]

In these matters counsel is daily given us by Herod—that is, by vainglory—that each may pass through him and return through him. When Herod has died, Joseph is warned to bring back the child with its mother. The child with the mother is purity in the will; it returns when Herod dies. For when the world is despised, when the flesh is afflicted, and the mind is not puffed up by the glory of praise in any of these things, know that empty glory is altogether annihilated. Therefore, in order that the humility of beginners may be preserved, let us flee into Egypt.

[Col. 1104D] But if we wish to follow the height of those making progress, let us go up to the high place; let us go up to Shiloh, for Samuel dwells there in the temple. People make progress in four ways: in themselves, beside themselves, above themselves, and beneath themselves. In you is the mind; beside you, your neighbour; above you, your superior; beneath you, your disciple. Thus you make progress in yourself through a good life; in your neighbour through teaching; in your master through admonition; in those subject to you through correction. Behold how Samuel dwells in the temple; behold how he speaks to Eli the words of the Lord; how afterward he is set over the multitude of the children of Israel (I Kings III). You dwell in the temple when you exercise your heart in holy meditations. You open the doors of the temple when you teach your neighbour. You speak the words of the Lord to Eli when you admonish your master concerning the amendment of the brothers. You rule the multitude of the children of Israel when you restrain those subject to you under the law of discipline. [Col. 1105A] This is the life of those making progress.

But in Jacob, as we have said, is figured the life of the perfect. Observe the life of blessed Jacob: he was the son of Isaac and Rebecca—that is, of laughter and patience, namely of spiritual joy and temporal patience—so that there may be joy in contemplation and the virtue of patience in tribulation. Hence it is said: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. XII). This is the sacrifice with a tail. For the tail of the sacrifice is the completion of perseverance in good acts. This is the bronze base; this is the long robe; this is the length of the Lord’s cross, upon which Christ, ascending, ended the course of his temporal life. In this, possession of the soul is promised to us when it is said: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke XXI).

Stretch out, therefore, dearest one, your limbs along the length of the cross—that is, in perseverance in good action—so that, sleeping in peace with Christ, you may die. At the bottom—that is, in humility—the place of the spiritual building is sought; in breadth—that is, in charity—the foundation is laid; the wall of good works is raised on high; beneath hope of divine protection the roof is placed above; but it must be brought to completion in the length of patience. Therefore the person who perseveres in peace places his bed in the spiritual dormitory, that is, in tranquillity of mind. This is sweet to the spiritual mind—indeed, nothing would be sweeter to it than to remain in the dormitory of a tranquil mind, delighting in the bed of a clean conscience as in white linen—were it not necessary for us to rise and pray. [Col. 1105B]

## CHAPTER X. On the Oratory of the Soul
It seems fitting, dearest friend, that we pass from the bedchamber of a tranquil mind to the oratory of devout devotion. “I will arise, and go forth, and prostrate myself.” I will arise from the bed of a clean conscience, that I may prostrate myself in prayer; I will go out from Solomon’s house, that I may enter the Savior’s temple. For one who dwells in the house of peace will deserve to pass into the blessedness of eternal salvation.

Let us therefore attend to human frailty; let us also attend to divine mercy. By these two feet one proceeds to the temple; with these two feet the head and tail of the ancient serpent are trodden down. The head of the ancient serpent [Col. 1107D] is pride; its tail is despair. Therefore, by remembering our own frailty we tread upon the head of pride; but by hope in divine compassion we tread upon the tail of despair. With these feet we walk upon the sea. Now the sea is a swollen heart, a fleshly heart. In this sea waves arise: namely, the surge of anger, the assaults of lust, the whirlpool of gluttony, the storm-wind—that is, the disturbance of an agitated mind. The depth of this sea is the will of every sinner. The end of this depth can scarcely be found, because a human being would always sin if permitted. Therefore we walk upon the sea when we subject the flesh. But whoever prays, let him pray in hope.

When, therefore, we pray while standing before the majesty of the highest Judge, three things must be considered: presentation, winning of favor, [Col. 1108A] and petition—so that we present our misery, win good will, and ask forgiveness. This is the order for suppliants: mercy looks upon misery, diligence upon good will, grace upon forgiveness. There are certain matters which should be recalled in prayer: oppression, deliverance, and justification. To the presentation of misery belongs the remembrance of oppression; to the winning of favor belongs the remembrance of deliverance; to the petition for forgiveness belongs the remembrance of justification.

Let us therefore humbly lay before the merciful Judge the various oppressions by which we are burdened. For “He looked upon the prayer of the humble, and did not despise their petition” (Ps. 101). There are three things by which we are oppressed: prison, captivity, [Col. 1108B] and sickness. The sick person is weighed down by weakness and pain; the prisoner by chains and fetters; the captive by servitude and labor. These things too must be laid before the compassionate Judge, because “He looked down from heaven to earth, to hear the groaning of those in fetters, to release the children of the slain” (ibid.).

There are four matters to note in captivity, four in prison, and four in sickness. In captivity, namely, there are place and time, the weight of labor, and the cruelty of the taskmaster. Place: when we are in Egypt; time: for as long as we have lived wickedly; the weight of labor: the extent of the work; the cruelty of exaction: Pharaoh’s obstinacy. Thus under Pharaoh—that is, under the devil—we are held in the world, making bricks while we remain under sin.

But concerning matters belonging to prison, the prophet says: “Those sitting in darkness and [Col. 1108C] the shadow of death, bound in poverty and iron” (Ps. 106). They sit in darkness who remain in ignorance of their own frailty. The shadow of death is the image of future condemnation itself. A shadow follows a body, and eternal death accompanies the image of a vicious life. Those may be called beggars who run through other people’s houses, seeking from door to door what is necessary for sustenance. So too we are beggars, because we covet with the desire and affection of the mind our neighbors’ possessions, which we cannot possess. In this beggary we are bound with iron, because we are weighed down by harsh and oppressive sins. For heavy and inseparable sins are iron and indissoluble chains.

Four matters belong to sickness, of which [Col. 1108D] the prophet says: “Hungry and thirsty, their soul failed within them” (ibid.). And again: “Their soul abhorred all food” (ibid.). You hear that they hunger and thirst, abhor and loathe. They hunger and thirst for things contrary to health; they abhor and loathe things suited to health. For they hunger for curiosity and thirst for pleasure; they abhor and loathe the word of God, which is the strength of the soul and spiritual nourishment. Thus in hunger and thirst the torment of desire is produced; in loathing we recognize deficiency. They fail, therefore, in themselves and through themselves, because they do not suffice for themselves through themselves. Therefore, lest by remaining wholly in themselves they utterly fail, let them advance into God. Of such persons the prophet says: “They cried to the Lord when they were troubled, and He delivered [Col. 1109A] them from their necessities” (Ps. 106).

We have therefore, dearest friend, set forth those things which concern misery; let us now win favor. For He is the one of whom it is said: “The Lord led them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke their chains. He satisfied the empty soul, and filled the hungry soul with good things” (ibid.). “He sent His Word and healed them”: He sent the Word in order to heal the sick person, that is, the command of which it is said, “Speak the word, and my servant shall be healed” (Matt. 8). Therefore the power must be praised and the benefits of deliverance proclaimed, so that the favor of the Deliverer may be won.

For He led us out, brought us back, guided us, and brought us in—from prison to our homeland, by the straight way, into the city of habitation. Having brought us out of prison, He redeemed us at the price of His blood; that they might go by the straight way, He went before [Col. 1109B] them by the example of good works; He accompanied them as they went, becoming a sharer in their tribulations; and He healed those remaining in their own house by the medicine of virtues.

“I will cry to God Most High, to God who has done good to me” (Ps. 56). For “He delivered me from my strongest enemies, and from those who hated me” (Ps. 17). There are strong enemies, stronger enemies, and strongest enemies. The strong enemies are the vices of the flesh; the stronger, the vices of the mind; the strongest are devils. Those who hate me are false brethren, or any neighbors who speak ill of me.

But perhaps someone will say: “The Lord has not delivered you from these.” The Lord has indeed delivered me in will, although at times I still lie subject to them through my former habit and persistence in sinning; although at times I am held by the vanity of the mind; although at times I succumb through [Col. 1109C] weakness of the flesh; although at times I am deceived by the devil’s cunning.

But he will again say: “He has not delivered you from those who hate you, for they have prevailed over you.” He has indeed delivered me through patience, by overcoming malice. For when through patience I bear perverse persons, although grievously afflicted, nevertheless I conquer by prevailing. For it is written of this: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21). Therefore, the one who endures possesses.

You have heard then, dearest friend, how great are the things God has done for my soul. For “He has not removed my prayer and His mercy from me,” but “the Lord has become my protector” (Ps. 65). Therefore, once our misery has been presented through the enumeration of tribulations, and favor has been won by remembering benefits, forgiveness must be sought for the commission of sins.

Thus, clasping the footprints of the merciful Judge’s feet, [Col. 1109D] I will cry out and say: “Stretch forth Your right hand to the work of Your hands” (Job 14). For “the right hand of the Lord will exalt me; I shall not die, but live, and recount the works of the Lord” (Ps. 117). Therefore I shall kiss the Lord’s feet, lest I die through guilt; I shall rise to kiss His hands, that I may live through good works; resting upon the extremities of His feet and crawling with my hands, I shall stretch myself out, that I may receive the kiss of His mouth.

The kiss of the mouth is the reconciliation of the human race effected through the incarnation of the Mediator. At the feet, therefore, misery is recognized; at the hand, forgiveness is given; at the mouth, grace. Thus in the one He is found compassionate, in another generous, in the third gracious. You now have where the servant may cast himself down for guilt, where the poor person may receive a gift from the rich, where friend may be honored by friend.
