[Col. 1110A] Around the feet there is dust; approach the hand: it will shake you free, support you, and draw you to the kiss of the mouth. In the first is the sigh of sorrow; in the second, the exercise of labor; in the third, the sign of love. This is Mary’s sigh; this is Martha’s labor; that is John’s love. Here Mary weeps; there Martha complains; there John rests.

In these three may be marked three affections of the soul: the affection of those confessing their own misery, the affection of those doing penance, and the affection of those seeking grace. You will recognize the affections through their effects. Mary washes the Lord’s feet with her tears, dries them with her hair, and kisses them with her lips (Luke 7). Do you see in the affection of confession the effect of compunction? Do you see how she spreads out for drying the hair which she formerly used to arrange for pleasing others? She pours out water not from a vessel but from her eye; she dries not with a cloth but with her hair. In those things by which she pleased the world, she serves God.

[Col. 1110B] We may similarly identify three things in Martha: concern, agitation, and complaint. She is concerned lest what she does be done sluggishly; she is agitated lest it be done half-heartedly; she complains in order to receive help, lest it be done late (Luke 10). Such indeed ought to be the dispositions of those doing penance: if anything is prescribed for them, it should be performed diligently. They are also troubled if matters arise in which, through chance or weakness, they may sometimes offend by sinning. They complain in order to be helped, because they earnestly entreat that the prayers and intercessions of religious persons may gain them favor.

Observe again in John the disposition of those seeking grace; consider again the effect so that you may recognize the disposition. He forsook, as they say, carnal marriages; [Col. 1110C] at supper he reclined upon the Lord’s breast (John 13); when the Lord hung on the cross, he was present with Mary His mother (John 19). He therefore seeks the gift of grace by the effect of purity, by the showing of presence, and by constancy of attendance. Purity sees God; presence touches Him; frequent attendance knows Him. Thus vision obtains blessedness, touch health, and knowledge consolation.

Of the first it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). Of the second: “She touched the hem, and the flow of blood ceased” (Matt. 9). Of the third: “Mary frequented the tomb, and knew the Lord who consoled her and said to her: ‘Woman, why do you weep? Whom do you seek?’” (John 20). John therefore displays purity and frequents the presence, in order that he may receive [Col. 1110D] grace.

Let those who have escaped the pleasures of the flesh, who rest in the bosom of the Church, and who devoutly stand daily by the Lord’s Passion, have confidence in these things. Let the pure company of young men especially, before all others, have confidence in them: those who, with John, have renounced the blandishments of miserable flesh; who, with righteous Lot, turning away from the impious, escaped the sulphurous and therefore foul-smelling flames of the Sodomites (Gen. 19); who sleep in Jesus’ breast; who apply their minds to imitating the ministry of Holy Scripture; who hold in their mind the memory of the Lord’s Passion and bear in their flesh the cross of mortification; who in every respect please the world, yet, fleeing the world, serve God.

For at this age the hair turns golden, [Col. 1111A] the flesh shines like ivory, the rosy face is adorned with the jewels of the eyes, bodily health supplies strength, and youthful age promises the prospect of a longer life. Then reason flourishes, and the bodily senses flourish as well. Then sight is sharper, hearing readier, gait straighter, countenance more pleasing. Therefore those who tame themselves at this age and join themselves to God await John’s reward. To disciples of this kind the Lord grants the affection of His sweetness; to those thus disposed He shows Himself more intimate than to others; and just as He entrusted the Virgin to the virgin John, so He joins pure flesh to their pure heart.

Such persons offer a living sacrifice, pleasing to God, unblemished—not lacking ear, eye, foot, or tail. Let the late conversion of old men hear this: through the debility of old age [Col. 1111B] their ears are stopped, their eyes troubled, and, to sum up all things briefly, they fail in themselves and through themselves. They offer not an unblemished Lamb but, so to speak, a docked pig. For as a pig lay in filth, so the old man lay in vices; and as a pig feeds on husks, so the old man takes delight in tales and rumors. Sometimes, moreover, he is converted and dies at the same time; and therefore this sacrifice lacks the tail’s function in this period of life—unless perhaps you say that it had its tail in its head, that is, the beginning of conversion at the end.

Old men of this sort love the heirs whom they formerly left behind in a carnal manner; they love foolishly, they love feebly. They love too carnally those whom they are still unwilling to have converted with them spiritually. They love foolishly when they leave to wicked people what they have acquired wickedly. Again, they love others feebly, [Col. 1111C] when they do not bear their losses and tribulations with equanimity.

John loved sweetly, but not foolishly. John loved sweetly because, just as a nail is driven out by a nail, so he drove out carnal sweetness by spiritual sweetness. He loved wisely. For no one loves more prudently than the one who entrusts himself to the counsel of wisdom and truth. Nor did he merely love wisely; he also loved courageously, because, when the Lord hung upon the cross, the beloved did not hesitate to remain with the Beloved (John 19).

Thus purity has the affection of sweetness, presence the discernment of wisdom, and frequent attendance the compassion of patience. Take care, therefore, not to consent to flesh that flatters; do not trust the deceiving world; do not trust the persecuting devil. Rather, set Christ’s life against pleasures, because you have put on Christ; hold forth Christ’s life against the world’s false promises, because you have not entrusted yourself to the world; set Christ’s strength before persecutions, because you have not been ashamed of Christ’s cross.

[Col. 1111D] Delight, therefore, in the beauty of purity, the uprightness of justice, and the strength of patience. This is the little bed of contemplatives; here you will rest, here you will sleep, here you will seek grace and find it. Here, in the white linens of purity, as though upon the soft mattress of patience and in the bed of a conscience of true peace, you will take sleep.

There are three things which disturb the peace of this rest: the uncleanness of the bedclothes, dreams, and the hardness of the bed. The uncleanness of the bedclothes [Col. 1112A] is the foulness of the flesh; dreams are worldly joys; the hardness of the bed is impatience. In these clothes are the worms of one’s own flesh: the affections of unclean flesh and the thoughts of a corrupt mind. Lust’s sting pricks like a gnat; the appetite of gluttony bites; the adornment of pride troubles. One is deceived by dreams while rejoicing in favors, exalted by honors, and glorying in familiarity with eminent persons. All these things pass away like dreams, like a passing breeze, like a guest of one night departing early in the morning.

For you lie upon a hard bed when you cannot patiently endure the harshness of tribulation. Therefore, to wash the bedclothes of this bed Mary Magdalene supplied water; Martha wrung them with her hands that they might dry; [Col. 1112B] John kindled the fire. She supplied the water of sorrow; Martha, the wringing of labor; John, the fire of love. These three therefore concur in producing cleanliness: water, hands, and fire—that is, sorrow, labor, and love. Water washes away stains; the hand wrings; fire dries. Sorrow washes away foulness; labor draws out moisture; warmth supplies whiteness.

The first water is dirty, the second muddy, the third clear: dirty because of committing sin, muddy because of remembrance, clear because of putting it away. For guilt has filth, punishment has disturbance, forgiveness has joyfulness. The first washes the feet, the second the hands, the third the face. The feet are the affections of the soul; the hands are works of penance; the face is pure intention. The feet—that is, the affections defiled by the filth of sin—are washed. The hands—that is, works of penance—which are sometimes rough with dust, that is, vanity, are washed. But the face, although clean, is washed when the pure intention, inflamed by longing to come to God, weeps.

[Col. 1112C] These are the feet, hands, and face of every faithful soul. These are Jacob’s feet, by which he went out from Mesopotamia of Syria (Gen. 31), that is, from the height of pride. With these hands he wrestled; with this face he looked toward the face of the Lord (Gen. 32). With these feet Jacob refused to go with Esau (Gen. 33), that is, with carnal affection. These are the hands with which he held the rod and staff: the rod of direction through correction, and the staff of support through consolation. This face he turned away from Esau’s face. Jacob turns his face away from Esau when any righteous person does not consent to fleshly desires.

Concerning these feet too the Prophet says: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps were almost poured out. Yet You held the hand of my right hand, and guided me in Your will, and received me with glory” (Ps. 72). What greater glory can there be for a human being than for humanity itself to be united with the Word? What greater glory for a servant than that the servant and the Son be clothed from the same cloth? Behold, we see the Son seated at the Father’s right hand, clothed in the mantle of our flesh. Behold, we see our nature exalted above the angelic nature. This is my glorying; this is the exaltation of my head. “What then have I in heaven, and what have I desired from You upon earth? Nothing else than to cleave to God [Col. 1113A] and place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72).

Attend to this, dearest friend, daily and in person, in the oratory of pure devotion: with the knee of obedience bent, the hands of good works raised, and the head of the mind humbled. Do not delay, but hasten; run through the altars of the temple; enter the Holy of Holies. For there is the bronze altar, there the golden altar, there the Holy of Holies. On the bronze altar flesh is sacrificed; on the golden altar incense; in the Holy of Holies are the tablets of the Law. Sacrifice, then, flesh, if you still have any with you; kindle incense; attend to God’s Law. In the sacrifice of flesh is understood the mortification of fleshly desires; in the fragrance of incense, prayer; in the tablets of the Law, contemplation of divine wisdom.

Here indeed you have whom to pray to, where, and for what: namely, for the sins of miserable [Col. 1113B] flesh, at the altar of the heart, for the mercy of divine majesty. But since we have mentioned the temple, and we ourselves, as the Apostle says, are the temple of God (2 Cor. 6), perhaps it would please you, dearest friend, if we said something by way of expounding that material temple itself, so that we might assign a mystical or moral sense to the things done in the material temple.

## CHAPTER XI. On Solomon’s Temple

It should therefore be noted by whom, with what assistance, where, when, how large, and of what sort this temple was made, so that we may explain it briefly. It was founded by Solomon, with Hiram king of Tyre assisting, on Mount Moriah, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, in the 480th year after the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt; it was exceedingly beautiful [Col. 1113C], made of marble and adorned with cedar paneling and the purest gold (3 Kings [1 Kings] 6).

This temple may therefore be referred to Christ Himself, the mediator of God and human beings, who said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”; for He spoke of the temple of His body (John 2). It also pertains to the Church itself, or, morally, to every faithful soul. Hence the Apostle says: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?” (2 Cor. 8 [citation as printed]). Behold how, through assumed flesh, He became a temple for us; behold how we became one for Him through the indwelling Spirit. Each of us, then, is a spiritual temple.

Solomon built this temple; his name is interpreted “peaceful.” That is, it is the mind at leisure with itself, free from public care, possessing itself, tranquil and at rest. History relates that Solomon, intending to build a temple for the Lord, sought assistance from Hiram, king of Tyre, who had been David’s friend at all times, and that Hiram sent him workmen, timber, and gold (3 Kings [1 Kings] 5). Hiram is interpreted “living on high.” Those live on high who, removed from the plain of pleasures, ascend by the narrow and steep way which leads to life unto the height of virtues. These are those who dwell on the mountains of Israel, whence help will come to us (Ps. 120). Those who thus live send cedar timbers from Lebanon, cut down by the word of preaching.

The timbers from Lebanon are those who were lofty and glorious in the world. For when we see those who had been rich in the world becoming poor in a monastery, nobles serving and becoming humble, powerful persons becoming subject, wise persons made despised in face and dress, are not such people, by the example of good action, placed in the building of the spiritual temple? They are transferred from the mountain of pride to the mountain of justice, from the forest of crooked worldliness to uprightness of life and the dwelling-place of holiness.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Craftsmen of the Temple

Hiram also sent craftsmen, because religious brethren are sometimes sent from the cloisters of those who live on high to other cloisters. Building the house of the Lord through the skill of governance and the discipline of discernment, they introduce there the form of true religion. They render equal and polished, through the craft of true wisdom, stones cut from the mountain but still uneven and rough; that is, through the art of discipline they make angry and incorrigible brethren [Col. 1114B] gentle and meek.

They lay cedar planks over marble, joining them beneath the line of equality, when they restrain brethren beneath the equality of fraternal fellowship. They carve them by discipline and paint them by teaching. He also sent gold, so that from the brightness and purity of the metal we may be taught to possess charity, which surpasses the other virtues.

For these things Solomon provided Hiram every year with many cors of wheat and oil as food for his household (3 Kings [1 Kings] 5). Let them receive whence they may live and whence they may see. For they receive wheat: namely, a share in the fruits of good action, which they had sown there through the exercise of discipline and through the word of preaching. They receive oil also; for those who desire to preside over others acquire from it the light of foresight and discernment.

Nor should it be passed over that Solomon says to Hiram: “Command,” he says, “that cedars be cut down for me from Lebanon, and let my servants be with your servants” (ibid.). Hiram’s servants cut the timber; Solomon’s servants set the measure. To cut timber is to cut away vices in human beings. To set measures is to preserve moderation in correction. This too is what we said above: those who wish to construct a spiritual temple for themselves should wish to have with them, at least by example, some of those who live on high.

“There is not,” he says, “among my people a man who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians” (ibid.). The Sidonians are interpreted “hunters.” These are those who pursue not only in themselves but also in others the animal impulses; who know how to track the footprints of beasts—that is, who prudently learn hidden human actions from conjectures and signs of conscience—and strike the beasts they find with arrows, because they condemn the deeds of fleshly persons by the authorities and sayings of the ancient Fathers. Such persons, I say, kill daily and eat those whom they have killed, because by preaching they convert to the body of the Church all fleshly persons who have died to the world. Hence Peter too was told: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10).

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Temple Laborers

Solomon chose laborers from all Israel; the levy amounted to thirty thousand men, and he sent them to Lebanon ten thousand in each month (3 Kings [1 Kings] 5), so that for two months they were in their own homes. The number thirty contains three and ten within itself; for thirty is three times ten. Three signifies knowledge of the Holy Trinity in the confession of true faith; ten, the reward of the Gospel denarius.

The division into three months assigned to each cutting of timber mystically represents the three evangelical virtues: almsgiving, fasting, and prayer. The one month in which we go out to cut the temple’s timber is almsgiving, in which we labor for our neighbor through works of mercy. The other two months, in which the laborers remain in their homes, are fasting and prayer, in which each person, chastising the flesh spiritually, turns inward to the Lord and devotes himself to himself.

These three months may also morally signify three virtues: reading, meditation, and preaching. The month in which we cut timber [Col. 1115B] is preaching; the second and third are meditation and reading. In one, therefore, we labor outside; in the other two we are at home, resting, refreshed, and preparing tools. At the table of Scripture we are refreshed in reading; we sharpen tools in meditation; while laboring in preaching, we hold the axe. Here we cut timber—that is, vices; there we sharpen tools—that is, abilities; in the other place we take food, tasting moral teaching by example.

These are the moral months; they properly pertain to those in cloisters. These are the temple laborers of whom it is said: “Adoniram was over such a levy” (ibid.). By Adoniram, whose name is interpreted “my Lord is high,” is truly signified that high Lord who regards the lowly. He is placed over such laborers when through Him it is ordered which persons should devote themselves to oral reading, and which ought to apply themselves to meditation and preaching. For from the gift of His grace alone is our disposition given, and its effect follows.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Those Who Carry Loads

Solomon also had seventy thousand who carried loads, and eighty thousand stonecutters in the mountain, apart from the overseers who presided over every work, three thousand three hundred in number, giving orders to the people and to those doing the work (3 Kings [1 Kings] 5). Above you had cutters of timber; now you also have cutters of stones. For stonecutters are usually called *latomi*. There are also others who carry loads, because they support others.

Humility carries timber; patience, [Col. 1115D] stones; stability, gravel or sand; gentleness, lime; continence, water. For they carry from the mountain of pride to the spiritual building the proud through humility, the hard through patience, those given to instability through steadiness, those melted by the fire of anger through gentleness, and those poised to fall through continence. You hear of the height of timbers, the hardness of stones, the lightness of gravel, the heat of lime, and the flowing of water.

When water is mixed with lime and gravel, it becomes something other than it had been before: it becomes mortar, by which stones are joined in a building. Things which had previously been light and loose are now made somewhat firm in that very union. When mortar is placed between stones, it grows harder and harder; and sometimes stones can be broken more quickly than the mortar itself can be crushed. The same thing is commonly done daily in the Church: those who had been unstable and dissolute in the world are found stable and firm in a congregation even among perfect brethren. Mortar may also morally be understood as harmony of conduct. Those who do the work place stones in mortar. And just as a stone cannot be raised high without mortar, so a wall of virtues cannot be raised without the mortar of concord.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Overseers of Works

The overseers of works are teachers of Scripture, who teach how we ought to bear burdens—our own or others’—and how to instruct the ignorant and correct the contemptuous. Of them the Apostle says: “Reprove the disorderly, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient toward all” (1 Thess. 5).

[Col. 1116B] The king commanded that great, precious stones be brought out for the foundation of the temple and squared (3 Kings [1 Kings] 5). In building the Lord’s house, the foundation is laid first; it is not found firm unless the earth has been overturned and cast out, so that we may not build upon earth but upon rock. “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10). In this foundation precious and great stones are brought out: that is, persons great in life and reputation are set in place, cleaving to their Creator.

Yet stones must first be squared and then laid in the foundation. The squaring of stones may be compared to the steadfastness of the elect. The elect are squared when they are established among the four virtues—prudence, temperance, courage, and justice. For then, wherever the elect person is turned, he remains firm, lest prudence incline toward cowardice, temperance toward pleasure, courage toward fear, or justice toward love.

Squared stones also have six surfaces: below and above, before and behind, right and left—that is, prelacy and subjection, hidden and open things, prosperity and adversity. Therefore, if you are a squared stone, you will stand firmly on whichever side you lie.

“The masons of Hiram and the masons of Solomon cut them.” Precious stones are dressed by Solomon’s masons and Hiram’s masons. For the life of the elect is squared only by those who keep peace and mortify the flesh. For if you live strictly and do not keep peace, or if you keep peace and live dissolutely, you do not dress the stone well. Thus sing on the timbrel, that you may sing in the choir (Ps. 150). Those sing on the timbrel who mortify the flesh; those sing in the choir who preserve harmony of conduct.

Moreover, the Byblians prepared the timber and stones. Byblos is a city of Phoenicia; in Hebrew it is rendered Gobel or Gebal, which is interpreted “defining” or “determining.” Those who wish to instruct the minds of faithful persons for spiritual building ought to be such that they know how to define what should be done and what rejected; to draw away from the world those clinging to earthly things, and to instruct those whom they have drawn away. For those who prepare the work of the spiritual temple must take care which virtues they first place in the foundation of humility.

## CHAPTER XVI. When the Temple Was Made

It was made, therefore, in the four hundred and eightieth [Col. 1117A] year after the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt. In the fourth year, in the month Zio—this is the second month of King Solomon over Israel—he began to build the house of the Lord (3 Kings [1 Kings] 6).

You hear that Solomon laid the temple’s foundation long after the children of Israel’s departure from Egypt. For you do not lay the foundations of the spiritual temple’s building as soon as you renounce the world. The crossing of the Red Sea still remains, containing in itself the color of blood and the agitation of disturbance. You are still disturbed, and still glory. But you must be in peace and humility.

In the desert you first find water, but very bitter water (Exod. 15). For when you forsake sins, you still groan; but the water becomes drinkable when the wood of the cross is laid upon it. When Christ’s Passion is recalled, the mind becomes sweetened, because remission of sin is promised to it through the death of the Lord and Savior.

You still endure wars and contradictions, lest you cross over; you still long for the pots of flesh (Exod. 16). But when you draw near to the promised land, you drink the river’s water, the water of the Jordan: sweet water, yet not flowing silently (Exod. 17). But when, from the waters of Siloam, which flow silently (John 9), you raise your eyes in order to see, then you approach the mountain of vision, upon which you lay your building’s foundations.

Therefore you do not do this under Moses, but under Solomon; not even in the first year of his reign, but in the fourth. Years, months, days, and nights are distinctions of human life. Every faithful soul has, morally speaking, years, months, days, and nights, by which it signifies its actions.

[Col. 1117C] The first year of King Solomon over Israel is self-abasement; the second, subjection of the world; the third, expulsion of the devil; the fourth, love of neighbor. In the first, one is humbled, when one chooses and desires rather to be abased in the house of the Lord than to dwell in the tents of sinners (Ps. 83). In the second, one subjects the kingdom to oneself—that is, this world. In the third, one casts out the enemy—that is, the devil. In the fourth, one gains peace by loving one’s neighbor. In the first three one prepares material; in the fourth one builds.

Nor is this in the first month of the year, but in the second. Among the Hebrews the first month of the months of the year was April, the second May. In April the earth is renewed; in the same month Passover was observed, that is, *phase*, which is interpreted “passage.” When you have recently passed from vices to virtues, when you are still new in love, you cannot yet lay the temple’s foundations. But when you love your enemy, then, as it were in the second month, you lay the foundation.

For the first month in the year of love is to love a friend; even the Gentiles do this. The second is to love an enemy. The third is to love God. Therefore, when you love an enemy, you set out the temple’s foundation in breadth. When you love God, you raise the walls of the spiritual building on high (Matt. 5).

Days and nights may likewise be assigned within these months and years. For the soul has day, the light of contemplation, and night, the darkness of temptations. The one is illuminated by the unfailing sun, the other by the waning moon. Here you see God; there you offend your neighbor. By day you laugh; [Col. 1118A] by night you weep. Hence Jeremiah: “Weeping, she wept in the night” (Lam. 1). A mind shaken at times by the storm of temptations grieves, but afterward rejoices when gladdened by the ray of contemplation.

You now have, dearest friend, the time of the foundation. It remains that the place of this same temple be determined, concerning which the book of Paralipomenon speaks plainly.

## CHAPTER XVII. Where the Temple Was Founded
Solomon began to build the temple in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, which had been shown to David his father, in the place which David had prepared on the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite (2 Chron. 3). Therefore the house of the Lord must be built in Jerusalem upon a mountain—that is, in a peaceful mind, namely in the higher part of the human being. This mountain is called Moriah, or “vision,” because the Lord dwells in the peaceful mind and desires to be seen there by the eye of contemplation [Col. 1118B]. It had been shown to David and prepared by him. For it is shown by the strong hand—that is, by one who works well through the Spirit—and prepared by that same hand through desire. It is on the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite, which must be cleansed by the winnowing-fan of discernment from the chaff of vain thought. Ornan means “enlightened”; Jebusite, “trodden underfoot.” For the mind sometimes possesses the light of discernment and the illumination of knowledge, yet is still trodden down by unclean spirits and entangled in worldly cares. But when the Jebusite sells David the king the site of his threshing-floor, on which Solomon would build the Lord’s temple, it is no longer called Jebus but Jerusalem. For the mind which renounces all that it possesses, having overcome the devil who trampled it down, sees in peace [Col. 1118C] the God whom it had desired. It therefore receives, in exchange for the site of its threshing-floor, the kingdom of eternal blessedness.

Since the size of a building is customarily measured according to the layout of its site, it seems fitting to add here something concerning the temple’s three dimensions. For it was sixty cubits long, twenty wide, and one hundred and twenty cubits high (ibid.). The length of the house is the long-suffering endurance of good work during the exile of this pilgrimage. Its breadth is charity, which not only rejoices in a friend’s prosperity but also sympathizes with an enemy’s loss. The loftiness of its height is hope for the reward of eternal recompense. Thus, morally speaking, you are long in good action, broad in mercy, and high in desire: that is, perseverance may endure to life’s final end; mercy may stretch out [Col. 1118D] its hands to the poor; and the height of desire may taste the sweetness of eternity.

In this length, breadth, and height of the walls are arranged different orders of stones. Mystically, human beings are arranged; morally, virtues. For we distinguish three temples: the material, the mystical, and the moral. The first is on a mountain; the second in the mind; the third in the congregation. One is made of timber and stones, another of virtues, the third of righteous people. You now have the site and material, builder and measure of each temple. But since we have undertaken to speak of the moral and spiritual temple, we shall insert something about the mystical temple for the building up of those in cloisters, and shall run through what remains with a somewhat fuller moral exposition [Col. 1119A].

Let us therefore build the spiritual temple: that is, our heart turned toward God. For, as we said above, we have the mountain in Jerusalem—the site of the building, namely a peaceful mind. We have the material, timber and stones, that is, diverse virtues. We have also the builder: the understanding which rationally discerns every particular. We likewise have the measures of length, breadth, and height: perseverance in good work during this pilgrimage of exile; the generosity or breadth of beneficence; and the hope of desire. The order of the stones is the progression of virtues directed upward, while the mind is lifted from virtue to virtue to the summit of perfection. From these are raised the walls of the temple, namely upright actions.

In the structure of the mystical temple, Abel is placed as the first [Col. 1119B] stone in the order, from whom the line of righteousness extends to the last righteous person. Abel is interpreted as “mourning,” “vanity,” “vapour,” or “wretched.” Let us therefore consider what the interpretation of this name signifies, so that the variety of its moral meaning may urge the mind to good action. “Vanity” looks to the world; “mourning,” to sin; “vapour,” to yourself; “wretched,” to God. Therefore flee, mourn, consider, and entreat. Flee the world, because it is vanity; mourn sin, because it is iniquity; consider your flesh, because it is frail and, like vapour, appears for a little while (James 4); entreat God, because you are wretched, while he is merciful and gracious (Jonah 4).

This stone is placed first [Col. 1119C] in the temple porch, for Abel was the first among the fathers of the Old Testament. This stone is placed in the moral porch, for the porch of the temple morally signifies renunciation of the world. Therefore, if you build this porch, it is fitting that you adopt the meaning of the name mentioned above: first, let it please you to flee the vanity of the world, bewail the iniquity of sin, and consider the frailty of miserable flesh; and, because you are thus wretched, direct your complaint to God himself, who is merciful. These things must be placed upon the foundation of humility and arranged in the breadth of charity, so that all may be done in charity.

You now have the porch morally—that is, the renunciation of the world, which is before the temple—and mystically, the fathers of the Old Testament. The heart turned toward God [Col. 1119D] is the moral temple; the Church is the mystical one. In this temple blessed Stephen is, as it were, placed first, so that the rule of righteousness may be set out from him. Stephen is interpreted as “our norm”; but our norm is the rule of righteousness, by which the equality of the stones—that is, the order of virtues—is directed. Arrange the virtues in the building of your heart according to the straightness of this rule. You do this when you willingly endure tribulations, love your enemy, and pour out prayers for persecutors. Thus, with Stephen, you are now near the oracle through the eye of contemplation: you see the Son of the Father standing at the right hand (Acts 7). You see him standing, not as seated, but as one wishing to offer assistance to a builder. For if you enter the oracle, you will see him at rest.

Morally, the oracle is the secret place of contemplation [Col. 1120A]; mystically, it signifies the heavenly kingdom. In it seraphim is placed as the first stone, because it clings near, through love, to the foundation of the divine majesty. Seraphim are called “burning” or “kindled,” kindled by that fire of which it is said: “Those who draw near to me draw near to fire” (Lev. 10). This fire is kindled in water, burns in the whirlwind, and shines in secret. This fire is the ardour of love: it is kindled in the water of compunction, burns amid the storms of tribulation, and shines in the secret place of contemplation.

Do you see how this stone in its order accords with the second stone and the first? Abel morally signifies the grief of repentance; Stephen, endurance of tribulations; seraphim, the flame of love. This is the sorrow of beginners, the labour of those making progress [Col. 1120B], and the love of the perfect.

For Solomon made a door in the porch, in the temple, and in the oracle (2 Chron. 3). Mystically, as Bede says, the door of the porch is prophetic discourse; the door of the temple is Christ; the door of the oracle is entrance into the heavenly homeland. But morally, in the porch of renunciation, the door is knowledge of the world; in the temple of conversion, knowledge of oneself; and in the oracle of contemplation, knowledge of God. For when you consider within yourself the instability of the world—namely, that you are placed amid the uncertainty of riches, the slipping of pleasures, and the danger of dignities—you approach the door of the porch. But when you consider the failing of your own flesh, the beginning of childhood, the brief moment of youth, and the evening of old age, you hasten to pass through the door of the temple. When, however, you consider God’s goodness [Col. 1120C], a goodness lacking nothing; blessedness needing nothing; and draw near “to see the good things of his chosen ones, to rejoice in the gladness of his nation” (Ps. 105), then you prepare to enter through the door of the spiritual oracle.

## Chapter XVIII. On the equinox, under which the sun shone three times upon the ark of the covenant in the temple

Note also, as we read, that at the equinox the sun, by the straight lines of its rays through the three doors—the porch, temple, and oracle—was accustomed to illuminate the ark of the covenant. For the straight ray of consideration from the sun of understanding penetrates the clouds of thoughts, which move about through the air of meditation, and through the three doors mentioned above [Col. 1120D] illuminates the ark—that is, the conscience. This occurs whenever an equinox takes place.

An equinox occurs when days become equal to nights and nights to days. The soul has moral nights and days: prosperity and adversity, losses and gains, sadness and joy, purity and disturbance of mind, the light of contemplation and the darkness of temptation. When the soul weighs these matters, it balances days and nights as though under an equal measure. There are two equinoxes, the vernal and the autumnal. There are also four seasons of the year: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Spring signifies temperance of mind; summer, the fervour of charity; autumn, lukewarmness; winter, numbness—lukewarmness in the mind, numbness in action. From the autumnal equinox the nights begin to increase [Col. 1121A], and from the vernal, the days.

In the winter of numbness, the darknesses of temptations increase; in the summer of fervour, the illuminations of contemplation are multiplied. In some minds, however, the autumnal equinox occurs. For there are many who, though lukewarm, consider the misery of the world, the failing of the flesh, and the blessedness of eternity; and so the sun of righteousness and understanding, sending rays of consideration through the doors mentioned above, illuminates the ark of conscience. From this equinox days diminish and nights increase, because although the lukewarm consider all these things, they nevertheless withdraw in the time of temptation. The cold of winter also accompanies the long nights: that is, the sloth of mind and body. Nights increase while temptations multiply. The moon of negligence traverses these nights, covered by the cloud of forgetfulness [Col. 1121B] and darkened by the mist of ignorance.

But others have emerged from winter’s cold and stand, as it were, at the vernal equinox: spring rises in them, summer follows them, and of them it is said: “You formed summer and spring” (Ps. 74). In spring all things are renewed; in summer they ripen. In spring the earth is adorned with flowers, and the life of the newly converted person with good habits. From the vernal equinox, therefore, days increase until the perfect day of eternal blessedness; from the autumnal equinox, however, nights increase until the unbroken night of eternal damnation. No night interrupts that day; no brightness of light illumines that night.

## Chapter XIX. On the windows of the temple

[Col. 1121C] Solomon also made slanting windows in the temple (1 Kings 6). The slanting windows are the teachers of the Church who, while instructing the faithful in the Church by the word of preaching, receive, as it were, the sun’s light and fill the inner spaces of the temple with brightness. They are called slanting windows because they widen the bosom of the mind in love, widen it for compassion toward one’s neighbour, and extend it in contemplation of God.

There are also seven other windows in the temple of every faithful soul: namely, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit—“the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord.” Through the window of fear enters the light of confession; through the window of piety, the light of condescension; through the window [Col. 1121D] of knowledge, the light of circumspection; through the window of fortitude, the example of good action; through the window of counsel, the ray of deliberation; through the window of understanding, the light of discernment; through the window of wisdom, the light of edification. Wisdom builds and illuminates; through it Christ our God, the sun of righteousness, rises in the mind. By teaching and by the example of one’s conduct, Christ fills the secret place of our heart with the light of wisdom. Hear the slanting character of the windows; hear the diffused brightness of their light. For nothing lies hidden in the secrecy of the mind which does not appear in the light of true confession.

## Chapter XX. On the walls of the temple

Solomon built the inner walls of the temple with cedar boards [Col. 1122A], from the floor of the house to the top of the walls, and over the cedar boards he laid gold (1 Kings 6). The walls of the mystical temple are the faithful peoples, who, succeeding one another through the course of time after the manner of walls, are raised upward like rows of stones. They are made of marble, adorned with cedar boards, and covered with gold. In the strength of marble, faith may be understood; in the height of cedar, hope; and in the preciousness of gold, charity, which surpasses all other virtues. Thus the firmness of faith is laid beneath, that it may be clothed with the loftiness of hope and adorned with the preciousness of gold—that is, charity.

The temple’s walls are covered with cedar from the floor to the top of the walls because perseverance in hope [Col. 1122B] ought to have no end in this life. From the first righteous person to the last, the Church ought, under hope’s protection, to labour in good works and the pursuit of virtues.

Morally, however, in the spiritual temple the structure of the walls is the progression of virtues. Thus it is made of Parian marble, clothed with cedar, and adorned with gold. Parian marble is known to be white; cedar drives serpents away by its scent; gold surpasses all kinds of metal by its purity. In marble, then, we find purity’s whiteness; in cedar, fragrance; in gold, brightness: namely, the whiteness of cleanness, the fragrance of a good reputation, and the brightness of a good conscience. Thus the whiteness in marble is like purity in the mind; the fragrance in cedar, the sweetness of reputation arising from the example of good action; and brightness in gold [Col. 1122C] is like purity of conscience in the soul.

## Chapter XXI. On diverse carvings and the lathe

Moreover, he carved all the walls of the temple round about with diverse carvings and with the lathe (1 Kings 6). Mystically, the walls of the temple are carved with diverse carvings when diverse gifts are assigned through the Spirit to different faithful persons: so that to one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another gifts of healing, to another interpretation of words (1 Cor. 12). The walls are also carved with the lathe when no faithful person opposes any command of divine Scripture, but from the heart cries with the Psalmist: “I am ready and am not troubled, that I may keep your commandments” (Ps. 119); and with another prophet: “Here am I; send me” (Isa. 6). [Col. 1122D] Those who obey divine commands are upon the lathe.

Morally, however, the walls of the temple are carved with diverse carvings when images of diverse things are impressed in different places, so that each virtue may possess a form suited to it according to moral understanding. Therefore, in every place of the intelligible temple, consider and imprint the image of an ox—that is, gentleness. Elsewhere imprint the figure of a lion, namely the strict rigour of severe discipline. Imprint the dove, the form of simplicity. Add also the turtledove, that is, chastity. Join to these the ram, the leader of the sheep: that is, a teacher leading the crowd of disciples by word and example. Set among them the purity of the lily or the rose of martyrdom. Thus you have diverse carvings in the spiritual temple when you place within the soul the varieties of virtues.

They are also carved by the moral lathe [Col. 1123A] when the virtues of the soul are arranged in the revolving movement of obedience beneath the chisel of preaching. The teaching of words may be called the lathe-worker’s chisel. The lathe-worker is the vigour of discernment in the mind, who is said to have before him the lathe—that is, rational understanding. Four things are considered in a lathe: the chisel, the rod, the strap, and the wood under the foot by which the instrument is moved. In the chisel, therefore, teaching is understood; in the rod, discipline; in the strap, made from a dead animal, the mortification of the flesh in which the spiritual soul is held bound; and in the wood moved under the foot, the swiftness of obedience may be signified. For obedience ought to be swift and, as it were, placed beneath the feet, so that it may be performed with humility and without delay. Hence in the Song of Songs: “His hands are rounded, golden, full of hyacinths” [Col. 1123B] (Song 5).

Hands become rounded when the affections of the mind are readily turned to whatever actions are required. They are golden when the affections of the mind are made pure from every appetite of fleshly desire. They are full of hyacinths when they burn with love and desire for the heavenly homeland. The two points of the chisel between which whatever is turned on the lathe is set are fear and love: fear of punishment and love of eternal blessedness. Between these we have the soul fixed, yet not in such a way that it ceases to maintain its revolving course.

Note also that, by the word of teaching as by the lathe-worker’s chisel, superfluous things are cut away through instruction. The rod, leaning down and rising up from above, threatens discipline after the manner of one striking. The strap is fastened to the top [Col. 1123C] of the rod and to the wood held beneath the foot. These mortify the flesh and tame the mind: namely, the labour of obedience and the correction of discipline. The wood beneath the foot is pressed, the rod threatens from above, because we are compelled toward obedience when restrained by the laws of discipline. The soul is pricked by the two points of the chisel, between which it is placed: the one, lest you return to the world; the other, that you may pass into the kingdom. Fear compels, but love draws. Thus the person placed on the spiritual lathe turns between them and says: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready” (Ps. 108). He says “ready” twice: inwardly in the mind and outwardly in action—within, to think what is right; without, to do what is beneficial.

## Chapter XXII. On the cherubim, palms, and diverse pictures on the walls of the temple

“And he made in them cherubim, and palms, and diverse pictures, as though projecting from the wall and advancing” (1 Kings 6). Solomon makes cherubim on the walls of the mystical temple when Scripture’s commands, in which is a multitude of knowledge, teach the faithful to imitate them. He makes cherubim when he teaches that what angels possess in heaven should be achieved on earth; when he teaches human creatures to possess an angelic life; and when those who love God above others also surpass others in the world by a multitude of knowledge.

Do you not now see some persons withdrawn far from the world and endowed with such knowledge that secular learning is subject to them? They are not merely called to the counsels of princes but also take part in the affairs of kings; having begun to rule their own [Col. 1124A] conduct, they rule even that of others and are honoured by persons of higher rank. These are they who speak wisdom among philosophers, whose eloquence rhetoricians marvel at. For those whom they saw in the world trained in no arts, or in few, they now hear speaking about every subject; and they recognize that these have attained such a multitude of knowledge that they unfold in words for the wise of this world the depth of divine Scripture and the secrets of heaven.

He makes palms when he promises, without doubt, that those who lawfully contend after the contest will possess hope and remembrance of eternal recompense. He makes pictures projecting from and emerging from the wall when the elect attain through good habit the ability to seek what should be said and done by bringing it forth from themselves rather than from others.

Morally [Col. 1124B], he makes cherubim on the wall when, through the spirit of knowledge which knows how prudently to arrange all things, he orders virtues in the mind; when with two wings he lifts himself from earthly things, and with two wings covers his body lest it be seen by the eye of vainglory. Let him also possess zeal according to knowledge and preserve moderation, so that he knows how to endure want and abundance, to be filled and to hunger (Phil. 4). Thus may there be in him the manifold knowledge of the angel mentioned above: inwardly, in ordering and arranging virtues; outwardly, in multiplying good works.

He makes palms when, triumphing over the devil in the conflict of vices, he emerges victorious. For the palm signifies victory: after victory’s end we adorn the victorious hand with a palm. We fight daily and conquer daily, because daily we wrestle [Col. 1124C] with the devil and daily overcome him. Therefore daily we hold the palm in our hand—that is, victory in the conflict. We also have a difficult battle against flesh and blood, so that we sometimes do the very things we do not wish. But when, God granting it, we conquer, we hold the palm in hand and attain victory through patience. For it is written: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21).

He also made diverse pictures projecting from and emerging from the wall. Diverse pictures project from the wall and emerge when the things thought in the soul are carried out in deed, “that your light may shine before people” (Matt. 5). This happens when mercy appears in action, kindness in [Col. 1124D] the countenance, humility in dress, modesty in living with others, and patience in tribulation. If you wish to know the effect of mercy, it is that which sympathizes with the miserable and aids the needy. From the sweetness of kindness comes a gentle and mild expression. But if the soul is humble, its outward appearance likewise comes to resemble it: threadbare, lowly, and plain. The gestures of modesty are shown from the bearing of the conscience, so that a person appears outwardly as he is inwardly. The effect of true patience, however, projects and emerges when you endure prosperity and adversity with cheerfulness.

## Chapter XXIII. On the pavement of the temple

Moreover, he covered the pavement of the house with gold, inside and outside, in the oracle and in the temple (1 Kings 6): that is [Col. 1125A], in contemplation before God and in action before one’s neighbour. The mystical pavement is the humble harmony of brothers, who in spiritual fraternity humbly cast themselves down under the rule of a master, to be trodden upon even by persecutors, in concordant fellowship. Thus knowledge, which puffs up, may not in the arrangement of the pavement place among the brothers an obstacle of inequality; noble birth may not create in anyone a stumbling-block of pride; and one who has brought something of his own from the world into the monastery may not desire to be more lax in labour, more prepared in dress, more refined in food, or more honoured than the others. Rather, when the brothers have been arranged upon the pavement of willing submission, let each receive according to the work that each has, in accordance with the ordinance of apostolic direction.

He therefore covered the pavement with gold, first laying marble stones upon the ground, and then placing fir boards over the marble (2 Chron. 3) [Col. 1125B]. In the marble he signifies the strength of faith; in the fir, the height of hope; and in the gold, the value of charity. These are the things upon which one who desires to reach the heavenly kingdom must walk.

Morally also, the pavement of the house is covered with gold within and without, in such a way that marble is first laid down and then fir boards are placed over it. In the marble, therefore, is understood the weakness of purpose; in the fir, the loftiness of desire; in the gold, purity of intention. You now have the fir in the middle with marble and gold, so that whatever you desire, you may steadfastly preserve in purity of life. The moral pavement, then, is the humble harmony of dispositions: covered with gold within and without—within by purity of intention, without by the most brilliant radiance of good examples. This gold shines in the pavement of the temple of contemplation and in the oracle of devout conduct. You tread upon this pavement when you walk steadfastly in purpose and in the purity of heavenly desire.

This, dearest one, is the soul’s oratory. If you pray bowed low in this oratory, you see gold, not earth. For where purity of mind is, the dust of earthly desire does not appear. There was nothing in the interior of the temple that was not covered, as Scripture says, with the purity of gold. If you look upward, you see gold, because when you contemplate heavenly things, you love God purely. When you look at the walls, you see gold, because when you love your neighbour, you love that neighbour for God’s sake, so that you may love purely. There was nothing [Col. 1125D] in the temple that was not covered with gold (1 Kings 6), because in the mind of the perfect there is nothing not clothed with the purity of surpassing love.

But because no one quickly becomes supreme, and “the righteous person at the beginning is his own accuser” (Prov. 18), and because one must again ascend by steps to the building which is on the mountain: if you hasten to rise to the beauty of such exaltation, you must ascend little by little through the steps of virtues. Therefore consider the arrangement of the material building, so that you may arrange within yourself the material and order of the spiritual one.

For in the material structure of the temple there was an outer court, which in the book of Chronicles is called the great basilica, into which the common people gathered (2 Chron. 4). Animals were brought into it, so that the priests might receive them from the people’s hands. There was also another court, called the priests’ court, in which the bronze sea was placed for washing the priests’ hands and feet (ibid.). There were basins there for washing the victims, and there a bronze altar for sacrificing them. It follows: and the porch of the temple, in which Solomon set two bronze columns; then the temple, in which were golden tables and golden lampstands, and also the golden altar set before the door of the oracle (1 Kings 7). In the inner house there was also the oracle, containing the ark of the covenant, in which were the tablets of the Law. Let us dwell upon these matters which we have briefly touched, so that we may be able to draw from them something for the edification of those in cloisters.

## Chapter XXIV. On the outer court

[Col. 1126B] Solomon made the great basilica (2 Chron. 4), that is, the outer court, in which are signified the hearts of carnal persons. Because they remain in common and simple faith, they belong to the building of the temple. Yet they are not such as to sacrifice victims themselves; rather, they offer them into the hands of priests, that the priests may pray for them. They also offer victims when, from the abundance of the possessions they own, they support by offerings needy persons or ministers of the Church. They cry to the Lord concerning the sick when, from the depth of their earthly dwelling, they earnestly desire with the whole longing of their mind to be delivered. They are far removed from the temple, yet direct their gaze toward it. They admire the gold’s brilliance and the beauty of the work when they reverence with devout affection the life of exalted persons, which they cannot attain in practice [Col. 1126C].

But morally, the outer court signifies the remembrance of sins. Animals are brought there to be offered to the priests when animal impulses are recalled to memory. This occurs when the mind recalls the calf of wantonness, the goat of lust, and the bull of pride. For the soul very often rejoices in vanity, delights in fleshly desire, is inflated by knowledge, and desires to be exalted by honours. The soul offers all these things to the high priest by the hand of mercy, that they may be placed as a burnt offering upon the altar of contrition. It also beholds, though standing far off, with the eye of discernment—when the temple is opened—the beauty of that temple, when in any converted persons it observes the comeliness of character appearing outwardly through the example of good work [Col. 1126D]. It cries to the Lord when, concerning the things in which it lies, it pants and sighs to the Lord.

## Chapter XXV. On the inner court

Solomon also built the inner court with three rows of polished stones and one row of cedar timbers (1 Kings 6). The inner court signifies the life of those who not only offer victims but also sacrifice and slay them. For they afflict their flesh in labours and fasts and burn it with the fire of tribulation. The three rows of polished stones are three kinds of people: believers, those who hope, and those who love. The single row of cedar timbers can by analogy be assigned to those who work well. For faith without works is dead [Col. 1127A] (James 2). And it fittingly says “polished,” so that each person may know what he ought to believe, hope, and love; lest there be found in faith the roughness of error, in hope the deficiency of fear, and in charity the obstacle of resentment. Rather, let faith be polished by the exercise of good work, hope by desire for eternity, and charity by the practice of service. Therefore join timber to stone, cedar to marble, faith to work, lest faith be feigned, hope empty, and charity fruitless. When you consider these things, you polish the stone and join cedar to marble.

Solomon also morally built the inner court with three rows of polished stones and one row of cedar timbers. Morally, the inner court is confession of sins. The one row of cedar is long-suffering perseverance in repentance. For cedar is joined [Col. 1127B] to marble when perseverance in repentance is continued in true confession. The three rows of polished stones in the court of confession are three qualities in the building of the mind: fear, grief, and shame. These stones are frequently roughened by their inequality, and therefore must be carefully and skilfully polished. Fear is made rough by the greatness of sin, grief by its multitude, and shame by its foulness.

For when the soul considers the shameful things it has done and shudders, though no one sees, to recall them in the secret of conscience, it is no wonder if it is ashamed to confess these same things to another. When it considers that, shameful though they were, it nevertheless committed many such things, it is no wonder if a soul entangled in the many bonds of vices grieves deeply. Again, when it considers not only the multitude of its shameful offences but places even their greatness before the eyes of the mind, it is not surprising if it fears and recoils; but it must above all beware lest it despair [Col. 1127C].

The stones, therefore, must be polished, lest the minds of the faithful be made rough by despair. Fear must be polished by the kindness of mercy, grief by the constancy of repentance, and shame by purity of conscience. In polishing stones three things must be identified: oil, stone, and hand. Oil is poured from above; a harder stone is rubbed upon the surface; and the hand presses the stone and, by pressing, draws it. Thus the kindness of mercy, like oil, softens the roughness of stones; constancy of repentance, like a stone, wears away the roughnesses of sins; and purity of conscience, like a hand, finally wipes away sin’s stains. This is the oil of the Spirit; this is the cornerstone; this is the right hand of God the Father. The first softens, the second presses, the third draws.

I pray you, most gracious Father, soften my grief, press down my soul’s fear, extend your right hand to the work of your hands, raise me as I lie fallen, and draw me once raised. For when you pour in the oil of the Holy Spirit, you dissolve the heart’s hardness by softening it. But when you set forth the humility and patience of the Son, you press down within us the swelling of pride by his example (Job 14). And thus we come to the right hand which you have long extended in expectation, so that with the elect we may be at the Father’s right hand. These things, therefore, must be considered in the court of confession [Col. 1128A], arranged under the rule of righteousness and the line of preaching. This court is also called the inner court and the priests’ court. It is rightly called inner, because whatever is revealed through confession ought to remain concealed, as it was before. It is also called the priests’ court because priests are especially permitted to minister in the court of confession.

## Chapter XXVI. On the molten sea in the temple
He also made the molten sea, ten cubits from rim to rim, round all about (3 Kings 7). As, above, confession is morally signified by the court of the priests, so compunction of heart may be signified by the bronze sea. For just as the priests were accustomed to wash in the bronze sea, so the minds of the faithful are daily washed in the bitterness of compunction. This vessel deserved to be called by the name of sea because, on account of the bitterness of sins, it is compared to the sea. It is also called bronze. For bronze, above the other kinds of metal, is very resonant. Indeed, when bronze is touched by someone, it creaks and, as though in the manner of one grieving, makes complaint. Thus, when the vessel of compunction is touched by the hand of self-reproach, it gives forth a ringing as it emits a lament.

That vessel was molten: this occurs when the material of metal, placed in the fire, flows through the channel of a conduit into the completed form. The fire is the burning heat of tribulation; the material of metal is the kind of sin. Through the course of remembrance, as through the passage of a channel, it is carried into the shape of a vessel when the mind, softened by the burning heat of the Holy Spirit, is refined so as to make a vessel of compunction. It was also ten cubits from rim to rim. For in the number ten hope is understood, which is promised to those who labour. Therefore, from the rim—that is, from the beginning of the first conversion—up to the rim of perfect separation through death, whoever forms the vessel of compunction within the compass of his mind hopes for forgiveness. For tears wash away the filth of sin—I mean, if they are placed within the court of true confession. And it was round all about, because not only past and future things, but also prosperity and adversity, ought to be watered with weeping. For the roundness of the sea signifies the scope of discerning compunction: when it regards what is before and behind, at the right hand and at the left, and permits nothing to pass without the bitterness of compunction, what else is being done except that the roundness of circumspection is imposed upon the bronze sea? [Col. 1128B–D]

And its height was five cubits. This is the elevation of the five bodily senses. But because the diversity of the senses flows away through the varied pleasures of the world, the author fittingly adds: “And a cord of thirty cubits encircled it round about” (ibid.). The cord is the discipline of commandments, by which we restrain things that flow away whenever we bind back our deeds and thoughts from our pleasures. This cord is said to be thirty cubits because, when you have reached the boundary of thirty years, you who were formerly more lax in your youthful years should at least, when you have reached mature age, restrain the looseness of pleasure.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the ten basins of the Temple

[Col. 1129A]

Solomon also made in the inner court ten basins for washing the flesh of the sacrifices (3 Kings 7). For just as the priests washed in the bronze sea, so in the basins the flesh of the sacrifices was washed, in order that both what was offered and those who offered it might be clean. In the bronze sea the hands and feet of the priests were cleansed of dust; but in the basins the flesh of the sacrifices was pressed free of blood—from the dust of vanity and the blood of pleasure. Therefore, in the bronze sea and in the basins we ought to understand two kinds of compunction: namely, that of fear and that of love. In the one, the works of the hands are washed; in the other, the pleasures of the flesh. Thus sacrifices washed in the basin of compunction and pressed by the hand of right action are borne by the priest to be kindled upon the altar of contrition. [Col. 1129A–B]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the bronze altar in the Temple

And the bronze altar is fittingly said to resemble contrition of heart, because in contrition of heart the desires of the flesh are kindled by the flame of tribulation. This bronze altar signifies something by its size, by the kind of metal, and by the position of its place. It was broad, because more people lament the lusts of the flesh than rejoice in the purity of heavenly desire. It was also bronze, because many say: “With the mind we serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7). It stood before the doors of the Temple porch, because few are those who renounce all that they possess in order to draw near to the door of the porch. For the porch of the Temple is, as we said above, renunciation of the world. In this porch two columns are raised, one of chastity and the other of sobriety, so that those who renounce the world may live soberly and chastely for God. [Col. 1129B–C]

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the golden altar, the golden table, and the Temple lampstands

After the porch of renunciation follows the Temple of right conduct. In this Temple there is a golden altar, a golden table of presentation, and lampstands made of the purest gold. Incense was burned upon the altar, loaves were set upon the table, and lamps upon the lampstands. The golden altar is the hearts of the elect; the incense, good works; the arrangement of the incense, the example of good work. The smoke that rises upward is the intention of prayer, which tends from the affection of the heart toward the heavenly things to be desired.

The golden table is divine Scripture; the loaves are the apostles or their successors, from whose actions the minds of the faithful are refreshed as from loaves. These loaves may suitably be called “loaves of presentation,” because they are set forth before the whole world for imitation. The ten lampstands are the ten commandments of the Law; the lamps are the light of teaching.

These may also be expressed otherwise. Let the altar, then, be love; the table, reading; and the lampstands, meditation. The purity of the gold in the altar is a mind perfected in love. The purity of the gold in the table is sound understanding in reading. The purity of the gold in the lampstands is pure affection in meditation: so that love may seek nothing carnal, reading may teach nothing heretical, and meditation may desire nothing earthly. Incense is kindled on the altar, loaves are placed on the table, lamps on the lampstands: incense of prayer, loaves of refreshment, lamps of knowledge. For through prayer God is sought; through refreshment he is tasted; in the light of knowledge he is seen. In seeking, he is desired; when tasted, he becomes sweet; when known, he is loved. Incense has fragrance, loaves flavour, knowledge love. Prayer indeed breathes forth God; loaves have savour; knowledge loves. God pours pleasantness into the fragrance, sweetness into the flavour, and love into love, so that the fragrance may be pleasant, the taste sweet, and love delightful. [Col. 1129C–1130B]

All these things ought to be present in conversion. They are ministered by priests and Levites in the temple of conversion. But if you desire to enter the oracle, enter into the sanctuary of God, that you may understand their latter end (Ps. 72): namely, that of those who perished because of their iniquity, and that of those whose death is precious in the sight of the Lord (Ps. 115). For there you will understand both the rewards of the righteous and the punishments of the condemned.

In this oracle Solomon placed the ark of the covenant, and in it the tablets of the Law. The oracle is the secret of divine revelation. There Solomon placed the ark; and there also one who desires peace places his mind. Within it are the tablets of the Law, namely, knowledge of divine strictness. Here the high priest alone enters. For few are those to whom the secret of the divine counsel is revealed. Here pray alone, if you desire to be solitary, if you love the sweetness of quiet. Take care, therefore, that your prayer may be discerning and secret, sweet and humble: discerning because of the unlearned, secret because of hypocrites, sweet and humble in its desire, so that it may love what it desires and, “not thinking high things,” may desire humble things. Let it be pure and tranquil; let prayer ask for no temporal advantage, nor let curiosity disturb the tranquillity of prayer. If, therefore, you desire to be such, you hasten to reach that cloister not made with hands, which is in heaven. [Col. 1130B–D]

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1129]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1129D]

You ask, dearest one, you ask and most earnestly entreat that I should carry out more swiftly than usual what I promised. For you request the final—that is, the fourth—part of the little book which you call *The Cloister of the Soul*, so that you may receive, as it were, a whole loaf from my hand. Yet it is strange that you ask for bread from the hand of a poor man, unless perhaps because coarser bread is sometimes more wholesome for some people.

For I have no other bread except that begged at doorways—that is, formerly preached to us through the mouths of teachers—or gathered from ears of grain in another’s field, namely, collected from sayings in the field of divine Scripture. Thus one lives, and in such things is the life of my spirit. “I remembered these things, and poured out my soul within me” (Ps. 41). I do not possess bread sifted from the fine flour of subtle intellect, but bread shaken through the sieve of a coarser understanding by the simplicity of speech. For I have not inserted Greek, barbarous, or unusual words that confuse the simple; rather, I have endeavoured to make clearer, in a simpler style and plainer words, even those things which I found obscurely expressed by others. Therefore I desire to please the simple, and so I seek words by which I may be able to please them.

Thus Christ, placed between two animals, was wrapped in cheap swaddling-cloths (Luke 2). The wisdom of God is placed between ox and ass, that it might instruct the untaught and admonish the slow: it might instruct one crude in understanding, one slow in intelligence; it might instruct simplicity through humility. He, therefore, who allowed himself to be wrapped in cheap cloths will perhaps allow me to speak of him in simple words. Likewise, he who is shown to the magi by a star is announced to shepherds by an angel, so that he who spoke to the wise through a sign might become known to the simpler through a simple word (Matt. 2).

Now I shall no longer delay saying something, according to the measure of my weakness, concerning those things which belong to the cloister not made with hands, which is in heaven, so that from the very order and love of that supreme abbot and of the heavenly spirits themselves the diligence of prelates and the humility of subjects may be taught and instructed. I shall therefore follow behind the reapers, lest I seem to stray from the teaching of those who went before.

## CHAPTER I. On the great city Jerusalem

A certain part of the great city Jerusalem is still led as a pilgrim upon the earth; another part is established securely in heaven. This Jerusalem will one day pass over to that heavenly Jerusalem, in which no one will die, but all will live without end in eternal blessedness. For no one will deserve to pass over to that eternity of blessedness unless, by living well in this world, he conforms himself in character to the citizens of that country.

But those who desire to lead a celibate life in this present world will be conformed in the future life to the heavenly citizens. For four cities are said to exist in divine Scripture, each of which is called Jerusalem: the material, the mystical, the moral, and the anagogical. Material Jerusalem is a city situated in Judaea; mystical Jerusalem is the Church; moral Jerusalem is any faithful soul; anagogical Jerusalem is the heavenly country. The first consists of stones and wood; the second, of the righteous and those being made righteous; the third, of virtues; the fourth, of angels and human beings. The material Jerusalem will at some time be destroyed; the mystical will be transferred; the moral will be built up; but the anagogical will never be shaken for eternity. The first contains historical events, the second figures of mysteries, the third examples of moral conduct, the fourth the diverse heavenly dwelling places. It remains, therefore, that we should discuss something concerning the matters we have set forth, for the edification of cloister-dwellers. [Col. 1131C–1132A]

## CHAPTER II. That Jerusalem is historically in Judaea

As divine Scripture testifies, Jerusalem is remembered to have been founded in the region of Judaea (1 Chron. 36). They relate that this city had walls and gates, bars and locks, lanes and streets. *Judaea* is interpreted “confession,” and *Jerusalem*, “vision of peace.” Jerusalem, therefore, is placed in Judaea because the peace of the Church is established firmly in the confession of the true faith. Whoever confesses Christ to be God proclaims the peace of the Church and labours mystically in building Jerusalem. But whoever, in the confession of the true faith, acknowledges the glory of the eternal Trinity and worships unity in the power of majesty, fortifies the Church against every adversity by the firmness of this same faith.

It is a beautiful order: first to acknowledge, then to worship, and finally to hasten to fortify oneself with the sign of the cross. For though one acknowledges the Trinity and worships unity, unless one believes that Christ is God and man and that after death he rose from the dead, one destroys rather than fortifies the Church. The Jew does not acknowledge the Trinity, nor the Gentile unity; yet Abraham saw three and worshipped one (Gen. 18). “We will confess to you, O God; we will confess and call upon your name” (Ps. 74). We shall confess the person of the Father; we shall confess the person of the Holy Spirit; but by invoking more familiarly we shall confess the person of the Son, namely Jesus Christ. For Jesus, as is said, is interpreted “Saviour.” Under this name we believe that Christians are to be saved. If, therefore, a human being at any time sins, it is not surprising that a sinful human being should confidently have recourse to the human God. For “there is one mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2). Christians therefore have recourse to him because they believe that through him they can be reconciled to God. [Col. 1132A–C]

## CHAPTER III. Again, on the same matter morally

Morally, Judaea signifies confession of sins, in which the faithful soul, judging itself, humbly accuses itself. In this Judaea Jerusalem is said to have been founded, because in confession of sin the repentant sinner is reconciled to God. “We will confess to you, O God; we will confess and call upon your name” (Ps. 74). By saying “we will confess,” Scripture declares confession to be necessary. Yet by repeating “we will confess,” it displays the mercy of divine compassion and intimates that you should not despair: if the one who sins again repents, God does not reject him.

“Let us go again into Judaea,” says the Lord (John 11). The Lord urges his disciples to go again into Judaea, so that, if anyone has sinned, he may repent and again humbly confess his sin. In whatever hour a sinner groans while confessing his sin, Scripture testifies that he will undoubtedly be saved (Ezek. 18). Observe how he loves, who receives the sinner so often and so graciously. If you consider this, you know the Lord’s mercy. “God is known in Judaea,” he says (Ps. 75). God is known in Judaea because in the confession of sin the mercy of God is openly manifested. Through compassion he calls back the sinner; through patience he waits and endures.

Christ is born in Bethlehem of Judaea but is brought up in Nazareth; nevertheless, he is called not a Bethlehemite but a Nazarene. Scripture recalls that Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judaea because, through confession, God spiritually descends to the human being. Nazareth is interpreted “flower” or “purity.” Therefore, he is nourished and dwells in Nazareth who delights in the flower of purity and always loves it. [Col. 1132C–1133A]

## CHAPTER IV. That there are many who destroy Judaea and Jerusalem

Many things hinder confession. For many enemies invade Judaea and do not allow Jerusalem to remain at peace. In the book of Maccabees I find it written that King Demetrius sent Nicanor, commander of the elephants, into Judaea, commanding him to capture Judas Maccabaeus himself and scatter those who were with him. Yet when Nicanor heard of the valour of Judas’s companions, he feared to settle the matter by bloodshed. Therefore he sent messengers that they might give and receive right hands. When counsel concerning this had long been held and the commander himself had referred the matter to the multitude, all were of one mind in consenting to friendship, and they formed a suitable plan.

Nicanor stayed in Jerusalem and did nothing unjust, and he dismissed the crowds of people who had assembled. Demetrius, angered by this, wrote to Nicanor, saying that he took the agreement of friendship very badly, but ordering him to send Maccabaeus bound to Antioch without delay. Nicanor therefore came to the most holy Temple and commanded the priests to hand Judas over to him. Stretching out his hand against the Temple, he swore: “Unless you hand Judas over to me bound, I shall level this sanctuary to the ground and dig up the altar” (2 Macc. 14).

Nicanor learned that Judas was in the regions of Samaria and considered joining battle with all his force on the Sabbath day; yet he did not succeed in carrying out his plan. Raised up in the utmost pride, he had thought to set up a common trophy over Judas. But Maccabaeus trusted with all hope that help would come to him from God, and urged his men not to be afraid. He armed each of them, not with the protection of shield and spear, but with words and exhortations. Nicanor and those with him advanced with trumpets and songs. Judas and those with him, having called upon God in prayers, joined battle: fighting with their hands, indeed, but praying to God with their hearts. They struck down thirty-five thousand, greatly gladdened by the manifest presence of God; and they learned that Nicanor had fallen with his weapons.

Judas commanded Nicanor’s head and his severed hand with its shoulder to be carried to Jerusalem. He also ordered the tongue of the impious Nicanor, cut off, to be given piecemeal to the birds (2 Macc. 15).

The moral meaning is plain. *Demetrius* is interpreted “excessively pursuing”; *Nicanor*, “standing lamp”; *Judaea*, “confession”; and *Judas*, “confessing.” Whom, then, can we understand by Demetrius, who pursues excessively, except the devil? And whom by Nicanor, the standing lamp, except the exaltation of the mind? Nicanor is set over the troops of elephants whenever pride rules over the minds of the incorrigible.
