For the bones of elephants’ legs have no joints; hence they are likened to the proud, who are in no way able to bend from their purpose. Nicanor, that is, the spirit of arrogance, is therefore sent by Demetrius, that is, by the devil. He is sent into Judaea in order to destroy the land of confession, capture Judas, and scatter those with him: that is, to hold fast through curiosity those who confess their sins, bind them by perverse habit, and hinder those who comfort confessing persons, troubling prayer and thought. [Col. 1133B–1134A]

But when Nicanor hears of the strength and greatness of soul of Judas’s companions, he fears to settle the matter by bloodshed. Judas has companions, namely the diverse virtues of body and soul. He has as a companion the groaning and contrition of the heart. He also has labour and fasting as associates. And he has innumerable other companions: the works of repentance and the thoughts of a humbled mind. Nicanor therefore fears to settle matters by bloodshed against Judas’s companions, because the spirit of pride does not withstand such forces. For these are the things that resist flesh and blood.

Therefore Nicanor sent three messengers to give and receive right hands. He sends three messengers whenever, in some good of thought, speech, and action, a sinner consents to confession. They give and receive right hands when they promise one another that they will consent in good works. And when counsel about these things had long been taken, and the commander himself had referred it to the multitude, all were of one opinion: to consent to friendship. Long counsel is taken so that Nicanor may be reconciled to Judas. For it scarcely, if ever, happens that a proud person can be humbly joined to confession.

But when the matter is brought to the point of consenting to friendship, they appointed a day on which they might confer privately with one another. A day is appointed between Judas and Nicanor whenever the mind of any person is inflamed with desire to confess sins; a day is appointed when the sinner is invited to the light of confession. And then the matter is transacted privately when a penitent humbly confesses sin. Judas and Nicanor make a fitting conversation when a sinner reveals what he has done badly and the one to whom he confesses imposes various forms of penance; when the former humbly judges himself and the latter strengthens him lest he despair; when one renounces the evils he has committed and the other instructs the penitent in the good things he ought to do. [Col. 1134B–D]

Nicanor stayed in Jerusalem and did nothing unjust, and dismissed the crowds of people who had assembled. Nicanor remains in Jerusalem when, after repentance, a sinner preserves peace and does nothing unjust, because in peace he rests from those things which he had been accustomed to do wickedly. He dismisses the crowds of people who had assembled because he cannot be disturbed by past things; rather, after confession he bears with equanimity those matters which he previously endured with difficulty.

He always held Judas dear and was inclined toward the man from his heart. Nicanor loves Judas when a sinner diligently considers those things which he recalls having done badly. And he was inclined to the man from his heart: for concerning what he remembers that he did formerly with neck held high, he afterwards prostrates himself in confession with the head of his mind humbled.

“King Demetrius, angered, wrote to Nicanor, saying that he took the agreement of friendship very badly, but ordering him to send Maccabaeus bound to Antioch without delay.” When Nicanor is led with Judas into the good of peace, then King Demetrius is angered, because when a sinner returns to the peace of confession, the devil rises up fiercely. He orders Judas to be sent bound to Antioch without delay, so that in this way the good of confession may be hindered without delay. He demands that Judas be bound so that he may weaken the work of repentance which follows confession. For those who hold others captive have the practice of binding their hands crossed behind their backs. By hands we customarily understand good works. Hence it is written: “Clap your hands” (Ps. 46), that is, with works. Therefore, the one who bears his hands bound behind his back commits to oblivion the good work which he had been accustomed to hold before his eyes. Demetrius does not cease to do this: if he can, he seeks to render Judas—that is, someone confessing his sins—bound with the cords of sins and deprived of good works. [Col. 1135A–B]

Nicanor comes to the most holy Temple in Jerusalem, not to preserve but to destroy peace; and he commands that the man be handed over to him by the priests, so that he may weaken the powers of confession among those to whom confession belongs. Angry, he stretches out his hand against the Temple because the proud man does not refrain from doing things contrary to religion. “Unless,” he says, “you hand Judas over to me bound, I shall level this sanctuary of God to the ground.” Indeed, if they handed Judas over to Nicanor, no stone would remain upon another in the building of the Temple. “The Temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3). For if the power of confession were destroyed, every faithful soul would be destroyed. No stone would remain upon another because the spirit of pride would overthrow the humility of confession. “And I shall dig up the altar,” he says: that is, I shall utterly overthrow devotion of heart, upon which the incense of prayers is burned.

Nicanor learned that Judas was in the regions of Samaria and planned to join battle with all force on the Sabbath day. *Sabbath* is interpreted “rest,” and *Samaria*, “guarding.” Therefore, the regions of Samaria are places of guarding; the Sabbath is a quiet heart. When someone rests in good work and guards himself with diligent circumspection, then Nicanor—that is, the spirit of pride—does not succeed in carrying out his plan and joining battle with Judas on the Sabbath day in the regions of Samaria.

Nicanor, raised up in the utmost pride, had thought to establish a public trophy over Judas. Nicanor establishes a common trophy over Judas whenever a proud person seeks not private glory but common glory from the overthrow of confession; for when a sinner defends and excuses his fault, Nicanor utterly triumphs over Judas. But when he judges and afflicts himself, then Judas triumphs over Nicanor and humbly conquers. Maccabaeus, however, trusted with all hope that help would come to him from God. Judas not only places hope in present things, but also trusts, with God’s help, concerning future things; and he more confidently calls upon him whom he patiently awaits to be favourable to him after death. [Col. 1135B–1136A]

Nor does he arm his companions only with the protection of shield and spear, but he forms their minds with excellent words and exhortations. Nicanor and those with him advanced with trumpets and songs. A trumpet is hollow within and is made of bronze, a metal that is very resonant; it signifies the vanity of the world. But for the trumpet to make a sound, someone must place it to his mouth, draw in breath, and emit it. One puts the trumpet to his mouth so that it may sound when, through the sweetness of worldly eloquence, he seeks the approval of others. He draws in breath when he is puffed up with pride by the desire for vain glory. He emits breath so that the trumpet may sound whenever, by words of boasting, a proud person puffs up the ears of his hearers. Nicanor, therefore, and those with him advance with trumpets and songs when they soothe the minds of hearers with the pleasure of vain glory or boasting.

But Judas and those with him, having called upon God, joined battle through prayers: fighting with their hands, indeed, but praying to the Lord with their hearts. These three things are necessary for one who confesses: namely, tongue, heart, and hand, so that contrition may be in the heart, prayer upon the tongue, and action in the hand. In contrition of heart, the sinner should blot out guilt; in prayer he should seek pardon; in action he should perform penance. And they learned that Nicanor had fallen with his weapons. In this battle Nicanor dies when guilt is recognised in the heart, when pardon is sought with the tongue, and when the hand humbly performs what is imposed through penance. When this is done, Nicanor dies, because then the proud person is recalled to humility. [Col. 1136A–C]

Judas commanded Nicanor’s head and the severed hand with its shoulder to be carried to Jerusalem; he also ordered Nicanor’s cut-off tongue to be given piecemeal to the birds. Nicanor’s head is the intention of perverse action; his hand, perverse work; his tongue, words of detraction. One cuts off Nicanor’s head who condemns the intention of perverse action. One cuts off his hand who judges and reproves perverse work. The tongue is cut off when idle speech is removed through silence. Nicanor’s tongue is ordered to be given piecemeal to birds when a penitent seeks the intercessions of the saints for the evils he has done.

The birds also are any spiritual persons. They are birds because, removed from earthly things, they live on high. One divides the tongue among birds of this sort when he pours out diverse prayers for diverse sins. Judas commanded these things to be carried to Jerusalem. For it will profit nothing to cut off sins unless one keeps peace. [Col. 1136C–D]

## CHAPTER V. On those who defend Judaea and Jerusalem
Far afield, brother, have we wandered in order to say something about confession for the edification of those in the cloister; yet I shall delay no longer in saying something briefly about confession. For it is the beginning and the end of human conduct, and no one can attain the mystical, moral, or even heavenly Jerusalem [Col. 1137A] who, while living or at the point of death, lacks confession of faith or confession of sin. Those who depart from the world and leave the body must go forth with Judah as their leader—that is, with confession going before.

Judah Maccabee first held command among his brethren (1 Macc. 3). The tribe of Judah first pitched its tents, by the divisions of its army, east of the tabernacle of the covenant (Num. 2). By the Lord’s command, Judah was the first, with his divisions, to move the camp. On the first day Nahshon son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah, presented his offering (Num. 7). Judah Maccabee first held command among his brethren because confession holds first place among the other virtues and leads to salvation.

“Judah and his brethren went out,” it says, “and they fought against the sons of Esau in the land which is toward the south” (1 Macc. 5). Judah goes out when what lies hidden in the heart proceeds through the mouth in confession. And he fights against the sons of Esau when, by the hand of good action, he uproots carnal affections. Above all he destroyed those who were in the land toward the south, because he more swiftly extinguishes those who burn with the desire of the flesh. His brethren too go out and fight with him whenever virtues akin to confession assist the work of confession.

“But Maccabee,” it says, “having assembled a multitude, became intolerable to the nations; and coming unexpectedly upon fortresses and cities, he burned them, occupied advantageous places, and inflicted no small slaughter upon the enemy” (2 Macc. 8). Judah assembles a multitude because confession associates many virtues with itself. And he becomes intolerable to the nations—that is, to the [Col. 1137C] vices of the soul and the affections of the flesh. Coming unexpectedly upon fortresses and cities, he burns them. Fortresses are hearts full of rebellion; cities are worldly pleasures full of vices, because they abound in riches. Judah enters these unexpectedly when, through the preceding grace of the Holy Spirit, confession bends toward humility hearts devoted to lofty pleasures. He enters and burns them because those whom the grace of the Holy Spirit fills, it makes ardent. He occupies advantageous places, so that by the advantage of their position he may overcome the enemy without danger. Judah occupies advantageous places when he assigns penitents places suited to religious life. He inflicts no small slaughter upon the enemy when a multitude of vices is overcome in confession.

He first goes out and is the last [Col. 1137D] to return from battle, because he waits not only for the willing but also for those slow to confession, and joins them at the end. As the history relates, Judah gathered up those at the rear and encouraged the people along the entire way, until they came into the land of Judah. When Judah was returning from the battle which he had fought against Timothy, he did not cease to gather up those at the rear (1 Macc. 5).

Timothy is interpreted “beneficent.” For the devil has certain ministers whom people call beneficent: they nourish those subject to themselves in idleness and pleasure, allow them to live perversely, and are called beneficent by some because this is done. But when Timothy had pitched his camp beyond the stream and Judah, coming to the watercourse, drew near, Timothy said [Col. 1138A] to the commanders of his army: “If Judah crosses over to us first, we shall not be able to withstand him; but if he fears to cross over, we shall cross to them and shall be able to prevail against him.” And Judah crossed to them first, and the nations were crushed (ibid.).

Judah was not afraid to cross the watercourse first when someone confessing his sins approaches confession with tears. But would that Timothy crossed the watercourse to Judah, so that one accustomed to live voluptuously might repent with tears. Thus Judah is not afraid to cross the river first, and when he returns, he follows the army from the rear. He gathers the scattered because he calls the diverse motions of the mind back into unity of mind; he raises up the weary when he consoles those broken by the labor of a prolonged journey. [Col. 1138B] He rebukes the slow and reproves their laziness lest they be captured by enemies; he instructs the wounded not to despair, but calls and kindles them again toward hope of salvation; he lifts up the burdened and helps them by words and examples lest they collapse beneath their load.

Those who live dissolutely are scattered; the weary are those for whom the life of Christ has become burdensome; the slow are those whom no one can induce to act well. We call wounded those whom we see struck by the devil’s darts. The burdened are those who groan sorrowfully beneath the burden of a long religious life. It follows: “He encouraged the people along the entire way, until they came into the land of Judah.” Judah does not cease to encourage the people along the entire way, because the penitent sinner relies throughout the whole journey upon the aid of prayers, until he reaches the land of Judah—that is, until through confession he becomes steadfast in the firmness of good work. [Col. 1138C]

Among the first tribes Judah, as we said above, when going out from Egypt, pitched its tents by the divisions of its army east of the tabernacle of the covenant. It moved camp first. On the first day Nahshon son of Amminadab, prince of the tribe of Judah, presented offerings. The tribe of Judah pitches its tents first because one who confesses his sins places hope in God’s mercy. “For here we have no abiding city, but seek one to come” (Heb. 13). It is said to pitch its tents toward the east because at the beginning of confession it is enlightened by the ray of knowledge. It recognizes and judges what it has done badly; it foresees and discerns what may in future be done without fault. It hastens [Col. 1138D] to move camp first so that it may reach the land of promise by the steps of the virtues.

On the first day Nahshon son of Amminadab, prince of the tribe of Judah, offered his offering, because one who desires voluntarily to offer himself approaches more swiftly to make the offering. Nahshon is interpreted “serpentine”; Amminadab, “my father is willing.” The serpent, it is said, strives to pass through a narrow opening in order to cast off its old skin. So the sinner goes out through the narrow opening of confession in order to put off the old man and put on the new, who is renewed day by day through confession. In this opening of exacting confession, indeed, the skin is said to remain—that is, the glory of worldly conduct. For the serpent’s skin remains where pride lies cast aside through the humility of confession; and the skin [Col. 1139A] is left where the sinner is separated from perverse custom by the strictness of discipline.

Do you see how those who belong to Judah hold first place in every matter? Do you hear how, in the book of Judges, after Joshua’s death Judah obtained the leadership? For Scripture says: “After the death of Joshua, the children of Israel consulted the Lord, saying: ‘Who shall go up before us against the Canaanite and be leader in the war?’ And the Lord said: ‘Judah shall go up; behold, I have delivered the land into his hands’” (Judg. 1).

Joshua is interpreted “savior.” The death of Joshua is the deprivation of spiritual life. The children of Israel consult the Lord when those who desire to see God seek a leader for reaching the land of promise. “Who shall go up before us,” they say, “against the Canaanite, and [Col. 1139B] be leader in the war?” He goes up who advances from virtue to virtue. He strives to go up against the Canaanite who fights with all his strength against worldly affairs. For warfare is waged daily in worldly affairs, because the mind often glories in what it thinks or the hand performs. But Judah is chosen to conquer these, so that what is sinned in worldly affairs may be blotted out by the virtue of confession. “Judah,” says the Lord, “shall go up,” because one who humbly confesses his sins will lead the people of virtues to the land of promise. And behold, the land is delivered into his hand when the virtue of confession rules over earthly desires.

“Canaanite” is interpreted “merchant” or “humble,” because the mind often glories even in humility and becomes humble for a long time in order afterward to become exalted, borrowing humility for the sake of exaltation. And Judah says to Simeon his brother: “Come up with me into my allotted portion” (ibid.). Judah is interpreted “confession,” Simeon “hearing.” For one who confesses sins must deserve to be heard by the Lord, so that the devotion of brotherly prayer may follow the contrition of true confession; and one who humbles himself before God in confession should seek without ceasing the suffrages of the saints and the prayers of brethren. Behold how Judah with Simeon—that is, confession with brotherly prayer—fight against the Canaanite, that they may destroy him and obtain the land of promise.

“Then the children of Judah besieged Jerusalem, took it, struck it with the edge of the sword, and gave the entire [Col. 1139D] city to the fire.” Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace.” There is true peace and false peace. The children of Judah therefore besiege Jerusalem when those who confess their sins accuse themselves of having maintained false peace with their brethren. They besiege and take it when those who had held false peace do not resist true peace. They strike it with the edge of the sword when they cut down vices with the sword of the teaching of God’s word. “Giving,” it says, “the entire city to the fire.” Jerusalem is given to the fire by the children of Judah when, after confession, the heart of every convert is set aflame by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Thus the children of Judah possess Jerusalem: they build up the peaceful mind by their conduct, strengthen it by good works, and maintain the concord of true peace; and those accustomed to have a feigned peace with their brethren [Col. 1140A] truly love their brethren with all the depths of their soul.

From what we have said, we infer quite clearly that, when the children of Israel went out from Egypt, Judah became His sanctification. “When Israel went out of Egypt, Judah became His sanctification, Israel His dominion” (Ps. 113). The prophet recounts to us the departure of the Israelite people from Egypt, so that through the historical sense we may understand the mystical and moral senses. The mystical departure of the Israelite people is the departure of the whole Church from the devil’s power. The moral departure occurs whenever, through repentance, any faithful soul is stripped of sins.

You hear that Jacob and Israel depart from Egypt. For there are some who do not yet cease to struggle against vices; and there are others who, having subdued vices, strive to see God. “The house of Jacob [went] from a barbarous people” (ibid.). *Barbarus* (“barbarian”) is said to derive from *barba* (“beard”) and *rus* (“countryside”). Hence Cassiodorus, setting out the meaning of this word, says: “A barbarian is so called from beard and countryside: one who has never lived in a city, but is known always to have lived in the fields like a wild beast.” Therefore the house of Jacob strives to depart from a barbarous people when the mind is separated from uncultivated manners and from the savagery of the heart.

“Judah became His sanctification.” Let one who struggles against vices not fear when he goes out from Egypt, because Judah—that is, confession—sanctifies one who overthrows vices by fighting. In Israel’s departure from Egypt, confession makes a righteous person out of an ungodly one. When he has departed from Egypt, it protects him as he travels through the desert from the assault of enemies. And when he has reached the land of promise, it keeps him unharmed. [Col. 1140C]

I would gladly say still more about confession, if I did not fear to cause weariness to the fastidious reader. Yet, God granting it, so long as I live I shall remain in Judaea, an inseparable companion of Judah.

## CHAPTER VI. On Jerusalem in the mystical and allegorical sense

Mystically, Jerusalem is the Church spread everywhere throughout the world. For Jerusalem signifies the peace of the Church. Under the interpretation of this name we customarily understand “vision of peace.” This city has many enemies—namely, many heretics of different kinds—who not only disturb the Church’s peace by their attacks, but also strive with all their might to overthrow it from the position of its rectitude. This city also has citizens [Col. 1140D] and friends: all Catholic men, who not only oppose heretics in word but also, fighting even to the shedding of blood, do not cease to resist them.

Arius, Ebion, Cerinthus, and other heretics have attempted in many ways to overthrow the peace of the Church by their assertions. But blessed Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, and the other Catholic men, strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, confronted them openly in order to defend the Church’s peace. Stephen, whose name is interpreted “our rule,” is recorded to have fought even to blood. For Stephen set before us the rule of righteousness: he was the first not to hesitate to die for the Lord. The death which the Savior deigned to suffer for all, Stephen was the first to render back to the Savior. [Col. 1141A] Stephen is stoned; Peter is crucified; and what is said is fulfilled: “Follow me” (John 21). Peter imitates Christ by a like death—that is, by the passion of the cross.

Simon is called not only Peter but also Cephas. Cephas, according to some, is interpreted “head”; hence those without a head are commonly called *acephali*. Simon, however, is interpreted “obedient.” For just as members are subject to the head, so subjects ought to obey their prelates. Peter, moreover, is interpreted “acknowledging.” We recognize Peter’s falling away if we attend more carefully to his threefold denial. But if we attend to Peter’s remembrance, we shall be able to know his acknowledgment of the denial. “For Peter remembered the word which the Lord had said: ‘Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times’; and he went [Col. 1141B] outside and wept bitterly” (Luke 22).

Peter is said to have denied Christ three times; and, lest he despair, Christ asks Peter three times whether he loves Christ. “Do you love? Do you love? Do you love?” “I love. I love. I love.” “Feed. Feed. Feed.” Do you love the Father? Do you love the Son? Do you love the Holy Spirit? “I love, I love, I love”—with heart, mouth, and work. “Feed, feed, feed”—by life, teaching, and example (John 16). Behold how Peter is examined so that the Lord’s flock may be entrusted to him to feed. Behold: he who had previously denied Christ at a maidservant’s voice now strengthens his brethren; and he who could not endure a woman’s words does not refuse to bear the cross for the Lord.

Therefore the citizens of Jerusalem are those who defend the Church’s peace. David is recorded to have been king in this city, which at that time was held loftier than the other [Col. 1141C] cities (2 Sam. 5). David is interpreted “strong of hand.” In this city, therefore, he who was strong of hand held the primacy, he who by dying laid death low.

## CHAPTER VII. On Jerusalem in the tropological sense

Every faithful soul is called Jerusalem when, despising secular cares, it contemplates heavenly things by meditation. This city abounds in a multitude of citizens—that is, in an abundance of simple thoughts and virtues. There are also in this city very strong men, namely manly affections of the mind. David, “strong of hand,” is said to have obtained the primacy of this city.

For abundance of true peace is often accustomed to follow the virtue of good work. Hence, after David, Solomon obtains the kingdom in Jerusalem [Col. 1141D] (1 Kings 2), because a mind that abounds in good works is accustomed to remain in peace. While David was alive, however, Solomon is anointed king, because while the affection for good work flourishes, the mind rules over its quiet state. “Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet,” it says, “anointed Solomon king at Gihon” (1 Kings 1). Zadok is interpreted “righteous”; Nathan, “giving”; Solomon, “peaceful”; Gihon, “struggle.”

Solomon is anointed king at Gihon because it is achieved with great difficulty that the mind should rule even over itself in peace, so that it may govern in peace the people subject to it—that is, the diverse movements of the flesh and the crowds of manifold thoughts. Solomon is not anointed unless he is raised to the summit of prelacy. “Honors change character.” For then Solomon—that is, the peaceful mind—[Col. 1142A] needs anointing, because a position of leadership scarcely, if ever, lacks the swelling of pride. Thus Solomon must be anointed lest the dry skin break—that is, lest the people be separated from their ruler—but that the ruler’s mind may be softened with the oil of humility.

Solomon is anointed king when the peaceful mind is made fruitful by the grace of the Holy Spirit. A humble and quiet mind is the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit. A well-oiled skin can often be stretched lengthwise or upward without injury. So the peaceful mind is drawn toward every work of mercy if it is repeatedly anointed with the oil of true humility. “Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet,” it says, “anointed Solomon.” Zadok and Nathan anoint Solomon king when justice and mercy make the mind of anyone in power moderate, [Col. 1142B] so that it may be extended through dispensation, lest it either break through anger or separate others from itself by the excessive oppression of cruelty.

“And they set him upon the king’s mule.” A mule is born of a mare and an ass. Hence this animal is naturally tempered from the horse’s swiftness and the ass’s slowness; and by this animal we understand temperance. Solomon, seated on a mule, is led to Gihon because one drawn into the struggle of governing must be moderated by temperance.

Would that those who hold primacy in the Church were such: that, struggling at Gihon against vices, they might labor; that, anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit, they might be able to extend themselves in compassion toward their brethren; that they might walk midway between Zadok and Nathan; and thus have justice on one side and mercy on the other, and sit upon the king’s mule, maintaining the measure of temperance and discernment in all things. Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, would not have divided the people after his father’s death if he had humbly sat upon the mule which David left to Solomon. For if he had kept measure, he would not have divided the kingdom.

Rehoboam came to Shechem, for all Israel had assembled there to make him king. Then the whole multitude of Israel came and spoke to Rehoboam, saying: “Your father imposed a very harsh yoke upon us. Therefore now lessen somewhat your father’s very harsh rule and the very heavy yoke which he imposed upon us; relieve us, and we will serve you.” He said to them: “Go away until the third day, and return to me.” [Col. 1142D] Therefore he took counsel with the elders. They said to him: “If today you obey this people and speak gentle words to them, they will be your servants all their days.” But he abandoned the counsel of the elders and consulted the young men who had been brought up with him; and the young men said to him: “Thus shall you speak to this people: ‘My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke.’” When the people saw that the king would not hear them, they answered him: “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse? Return to your tents, Israel” (1 Kings 12).

When Solomon dies, Rehoboam his son is advanced to the kingdom. All Israel is also assembled at Shechem to make him king. Solomon is interpreted “peaceful”; Rehoboam, “breadth of the people” or “impulse of the people.” Then [Col. 1143A] Solomon—that is, peace—dies in the mind of any person when the impulse of anger is rooted in that mind so as to reign. All Israel is also gathered at Shechem, “shoulder,” in order to bend the shoulder to labor. It complains that a most grievous yoke is imposed upon it. But Rehoboam requests a delay of three days so that meanwhile he may take counsel concerning what has been said. Yet the impulse of anger, which never knows how to consent to mature counsel, follows youthful counsel, because youthful impulse is accompanied in every respect by frivolity.

On the third day the people returned to Rehoboam, but Rehoboam answered the people harshly. “My father,” he says, “struck you with whips; I shall strike you with scorpions” (ibid.). The people hear what they had feared; but lest the impulse of anger proceed even to cruelty, the simplicity of those who see God withdraws from Rehoboam—that is, from the impulse of anger—fleeing what it fears. [Col. 1143B] You hear that after Solomon’s death Rehoboam reigned in Jerusalem, because the impulse of anger inhabits the mind that had long maintained peace.

In the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign, Shishak king of Egypt went up to Jerusalem and took the treasures of the house of the Lord, the royal treasures, plundered everything, and took away the golden shields which Solomon had made; in their place King Rehoboam made bronze shields (1 Kings 14). Shishak is interpreted “fine linen of haircloth.” Haircloth is the garment of penitents, for those who know how to mourn their sins clothe themselves in this garment. Fine linen, however, is a kind of cloth delicate in fineness and softness. “Those who are in kings’ houses are clothed in soft garments” and seek pleasure (Matt. 11). [Col. 1143C] Therefore those who make fine linen out of haircloth turn the harshness of life into pleasure.

Shishak took the treasures from the house of the Lord—that is, the secrets of divine counsel. He also took away the royal treasures because pleasure dissolves wise dispensations. The treasures which Solomon—that is, the peaceful mind—had perhaps gathered, Shishak king of Egypt—that is, worldly pleasure—does not cease to scatter while Rehoboam reigns. The golden shields are the words of Holy Scripture. They are shields because they defend the firmness of true faith; golden because they proceed from purity. Solomon made these shields because the quiet mind prepares words of defense against heretics in peace. “In their place King Rehoboam made bronze shields.” Bronze shields are worldly words. They are shields because they often resist truth; they are made of bronze—that is, of the resounding material of secular eloquence. For when bronze is struck, it is heard far away, because an impetuous mind, when struck by the hand of rebuke, is provoked to lawsuits and quarrels. But when gold is struck, it does not screech with a clamorous ringing voice; even when struck hard, it remains silent. Likewise, a peaceful mind, even when touched by insult, endures the insult silently. [Col. 1143D]

“And he plundered everything” (1 Kings 14). Shishak king of Egypt plunders everything because the pleasure of the flesh consumes for its own uses whatever others have gathered.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the wall of Jerusalem, mystically and morally

Mystical Jerusalem—that is, the Church—is said to possess [Col. 1144A] the wall of divine Scripture, by which it repels the subtle snares and open assaults of heretics. “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; they shall not cease day or night to praise the Lord’s name” (Isa. 62). The watchmen of the walls are teachers of the Scriptures. They guard the walls because they give vigilant attention to the divine law. They do not cease to praise the Lord’s name day and night because in prosperity and adversity they cry to God. This name which they invoke is called Jesus; Jesus is interpreted “Savior.” Those who invoke the Savior’s name are those who desire that all people be saved.

Morally, the wall of the faithful soul is the structure of good action; the watchmen of the walls are the diligent guarding of circumspections. These keep watch in the night of negligence through foresight and prepare defenses in the day of discernment. [Col. 1144B] They do not cease to praise the Lord’s name because they cry to God with continual desires for the soul’s salvation.

Citizens cry out, and enemies cry out too. Yet the cry of enemies is very different from that of citizens. Catholics cry out, and heretics cry out as well. “Their heart,” Jeremiah says, “cried to the Lord concerning the walls of the daughter of Zion. Their heart cried” (Lam. 2). Whose? The heart of heretics. The wall of the daughter of Zion, however, consists of those who defend the truth of faith. Heretics cry out over the walls when they glory that they say things more weighty than those said by teachers of the Catholic faith. They cry out over the walls because they consider themselves superior to the Church’s teachers in the conflict of disputations. They cry to the Lord, not in contrition of heart but in the cruelty of wickedness. Heretics are over the walls while they prevail and destroy. Their heart cries to the Lord when, through the pride of heart, it detracts from divine power.

Morally, by enemies we may understand the carnal affections of the soul; by the heart of enemies, carnal delight; by the wall, the order of virtues. Therefore the heart cries to the Lord because the delight of the flesh labors to interrupt the order of virtues. The Lord permits this wall to be destroyed because of the fault of the citizens when either the Church does not resist heretics or any faithful soul does not resist vices. Hence Jeremiah says: “The Lord has planned to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion” (ibid.). The Lord plans to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion so long as He bears the faults [Col. 1144D] of sinners in patience. He plans and destroys when He leaves to enemies for punishment those whom He had patiently awaited. Nor does He destroy only the city’s walls; He also gives the walls of its towers into the hands of the enemy. Hence the aforesaid prophet says: “The Lord has given into the hand of the enemy the walls of her towers” (ibid.).

The walls of the towers are those who surpass others in the elevation of their life. The walls of the towers are also the discriminating circumspections of virtues, which rise above other virtues. Therefore the walls of the towers are given into the hand of the enemy when either the Church’s teachers are subjected to heretics or the soul’s highest virtues to vices. When this occurs, Jerusalem is inhabited without a wall. Hence it is said: “Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall” (Zech. 2). The wall of Jerusalem is said to stand unharmed when the Church is fortified by the words of divine Scripture, with no one opposing it. The tower-walls also stand when the teaching of prelates is commended by their life and conduct. [Col. 1145A]

## CHAPTER IX. On the gates of Jerusalem, morally

Jerusalem also has gates: namely, the discerning exhortations of the holy Fathers, through which we enter the Church and go forth to eternal life. “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23). Princes are good or evil teachers. The gates of evil teachers are perverse suggestions, but those of good teachers are holy exhortations. Through the latter one goes to heaven; through the former one descends to hell. The former are weighed down; the latter are raised up. The latter are eternal because [Col. 1145B] they lead to the eternity of perpetual blessedness; the former are the gates of death because they lead to the abyss of perpetual damnation. Through the latter the King of glory enters; through the former the devil, king of pride.

“Her gates are fixed in the earth,” Jeremiah says (Lam. 2). The gates of Jerusalem are said to be fixed in the earth whenever the Church’s prelates delight in the love of earthly things. They are raised up whenever they seek heavenly things. Hence it is said through the prophet Ezekiel: “The gate looked toward the way of the north” (Ezek. 9). The way of the north is the life of the sinner. The gate looks toward the way of the north when any spiritual teacher considers and rebukes the sinner’s life. For a teacher is called a gate because through him one reaches eternal life by the straight path.

By gates of the soul, moreover, we may understand the various bodily senses. They are gates because through them those who overthrow the city enter and depart; and those who sometimes fortify and preserve the citizens of the same city also depart and enter. These gates lie fixed in the earth when the bodily senses wholly cling to earthly desires. But they hang raised upon their bars whenever the bodily senses are open to divine contemplation. [Col. 1145C]

## CHAPTER X. On the gates of Jerusalem from the words of Nehemiah

In the words of Nehemiah son of Hilkiah I remember having read concerning the gates of Jerusalem something which I wish to insert into this work for the edification of those in the cloister:

“I went out by night through the Valley Gate, and before the Dragon Spring and the Dung Gate; and I inspected the ruined wall and its gates burned by fire. And I passed to [Col. 1145D] the Bridge Gate and the king’s aqueduct, and there was no place for the beast on which I rode to pass. And I went up by the torrent of Kidron, inspected the wall, returned, came to the Valley Gate, and went back” (2 Esdr. 2).

The Valley Gate is the virtue of humility. Jerusalem enters through the Valley Gate when someone humble in heart returns to peace and is reconciled to God in mind. He goes out through the Valley Gate to see the destruction of the city when he hastens humbly to repair the ruins of the Church or the falls of the soul.

“And before the Dragon Spring.” A spring is the source of a stream, and the devil is the beginning of angelic and human falling-away. By the spring the devil is understood. Hence “devil” is interpreted “flowing downward.” He flows downward who withdraws from God in heart and deed. The devil [Col. 1146A] is the Dragon Spring—that is, the beginning of pride. For from the devil the sin of pride took its origin. Hence, after the flood of pride, he deserved the fall of ruin. The dragon is said to be greater than the other serpents because the head of pride is remembered to have touched even heaven. Therefore he passes before the Dragon Spring because he calls to mind the ruin of the angel and the fall of humankind.

“And [I went] to the Dung Gate.” The Dung Gate is the virtue of confession. For just as dung is carried outside the city through the gate, so through confession the stench of sin must be cast out of the mind. “And I inspected the ruined wall of Jerusalem and its gates burned by fire.” He inspects and surveys Jerusalem’s ruined wall who carefully attends to the falls of the flesh and the breaches of the mind. He inspects the gates burned by fire—that is, the bodily senses consumed by the fire of lust and the flames of anger. [Col. 1146B]

“And I passed to the Bridge Gate.” A bridge is built where passage is made from one place to another. We make a bridge when we do penance. We put timbers on the bridge when we subject the flesh to the soul that is crossing. We cross the bridge when we migrate from vices to virtues. But if “Spring Gate” is read, as I find written in some manuscripts, it is no wonder that the Spring Gate follows the Dung Gate, so that the stench of sin may be cleansed by tears.

“And [I passed] to the king’s aqueduct.” The aqueduct is the desire to contemplate God. Water is grace. The aqueduct is said to belong to the king—that is, to reason, which governs all things by its judgment. “And there was no place,” it says, “for the beast on which I rode to pass.” When he came to the king’s aqueduct, there was no place for the beast to cross. The beast is dullness of mind or sensuality of flesh. Therefore, if the king’s aqueduct is love of contemplation, if the aqueduct is the grace of the Holy Spirit, and if the beast is dullness of mind or sensuality of flesh, it is no wonder that sensuality of flesh cannot so swiftly pass over to the grace of contemplation. [Col. 1146C]

“And I went up by the torrent of Kidron.” Kidron is interpreted “sad” or “sorrow.” The soul brought back from captivity—that is, newly converted to God—at the beginning of conversion, sorrowing and sad, goes up through the torrent of compunction. For this is the fitting order: first it should weep for what it has done badly, and afterwards rise to the joy of divine contemplation. “And I inspected the wall.” Again he inspects [Col. 1146D] the wall. He who repeatedly reviews in recollection the falls of the body and the ruins of the soul again inspects the destroyed wall. “And I returned, came to the Valley Gate, and went back.” He returns to the Valley Gate through which he had gone out. By this it is indicated that whatever is done should be seasoned by the benefit of humility.

## CHAPTER XI. On the bars of the gates of Jerusalem, mystically and morally

Jerusalem has bars in its gates: namely, firm authorities of Scripture, which firmly assert what they say. “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion, because He has strengthened the bars of your gates” (Ps. 147). He strengthens the bars of the gates who confirms by authority what he teaches. Therefore let Jerusalem praise the Lord; let Zion praise its God, because He has strengthened [Col. 1147A] the bars of the gates of each. For whatever prophecy had foretold concerning Christ, the authority of the Gospel demonstrates to have happened.

The bars of the gates have a key and a bolt. Those who keep the key are those who exercise care for the Church. The key is the ruler’s power. By the bolt we may understand the command of obedience. The key drives and draws back the bolt because the authority of prelates excludes some, forbidding them entrance, and compels others to remain within. Indeed, it forbids those who have entered to go out, and powerfully prevents the excluded from entering. Morally, the soul has bars in its gates because it keeps the bodily senses closed, lest they stand open to enemies—that is, vices. It opens them whenever it discloses the heart’s secret to the beloved. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “I opened the bolt of [Col. 1147B] my door to my beloved. This door has a key and a bolt” (Song 5).

It has the key, namely discernment; the bolt, the measure of discernment. Reason bears the key in order to bar from entrance into the mind what is harmful, while allowing through the key of discernment what is fitting to enter. But sometimes the bars are found bolted, so that even if the beloved comes, he cannot enter; and even if reason, which carries the key, approaches, it cannot enter. This happens whenever the mind exceeds the measure of discernment. But reason waits outside until, if possible, it draws back the bolt by trying. It applies the key of discernment and turns it by warning, yet does not turn the mind.

But when the bearer of the key cannot enter, the axe of discipline must break the bolt of obstinacy, so that what could not be achieved by admonitions may afterwards be accomplished by the strength of discipline. It also sometimes happens that one who ought to carry the key is accustomed to lose the key repeatedly. Therefore it is necessary that someone discerning provide for those who frequently lose the key of discernment—because they do not know how to take care of themselves—and, when the time comes, take care concerning their secrets.

## Chapter XII. On the Bars of the Gates of Jerusalem

As we said above, the gates are the discerning exhortations of the holy Fathers. The bars of the gates are their ordinances. They are called bars because they bear the gates. The gates hang upon the bars, yet not so that they cannot be moved: they remain attached to the bars. Upon the bars the gates move, so that they may be kept shut or opened. [Col. 1147D] Likewise, the ordinances of the Fathers are at times observed strictly and at times moderately relaxed by dispensation. Note also that the bolts always remain attached to the gates, whereas the gates retain mobility around the bars. Thus the authorities of the holy Fathers ought to be immovable; but ordinances are customarily altered at times according to time, place, and person.

By the bars of the gates we may also understand the counsels of the Jews, concerning whom it is said through the prophet: “He has destroyed and broken her bars” (Lam. 2). He destroyed and broke their bars when he did not permit their plans to reach their effect. Their plan was to kill Christ. He destroyed and broke their plan because he reduced to nothing what they had intended to do. He reduced it to nothing because Christ rose from death. He destroyed their plan [Col. 1148A] when he cast them far from their land. He broke their plan when he scattered them, subjected to different nations, through various regions.

Morally: “And he broke her bars.” The bars are certain virtues of the soul which support the gates, lest the bodily senses waver from their stability. He destroyed and broke the bars when, by God’s permission, he subjected the virtues to vices after the strength of the mind had been taken away. Elsewhere too it is said of bars: “For he broke the gates of bronze and shattered the bars of iron” (Ps. 106 [107]). Hence Cassiodorus, on the Psalter: “The bronze gates,” he says, “are men’s vicious habits. The iron bars, moreover, do not improperly seem to us to be the unclean spirits.” For these two metals appear to have been used because of the strength of sins. But divine power broke these things, despaired of by human strength, [Col. 1148B] when, in mercy, it looked upon those in danger by the light of its coming.

Bars in divine Scripture may also be understood as those by which the ark was customarily carried through the wilderness by the children of Israel. “You shall make,” he says, “bars of shittim wood, and cover them with gold; and you shall pass them through the rings which are on the sides of the ark, so that it may be carried by them. They shall always remain in the rings and shall never be removed from them” (Exod. 25). The ark is the Church; the bars are the teachers of the Church. The bars are made of shittim wood, a kind of wood said to resemble the white thorn. Thus the bars are made of incorruptible wood—that is, of men who do not succumb to corruption. He covers the bars with gold who shows his neighbours, more surely by example, the power of good work. He passes the bars through the rings who applies his mind more attentively to the words of the four Gospels. Nor is he ever withdrawn from them, [Col. 1148C] but meditates day and night on the law of the Lord (Ps. 1).

## Chapter XIII. On the Streets of Jerusalem

The aforesaid city is said to have streets and broad ways. The streets in the Church are the continent and the married. For just as in a material street there are two rows of houses, so in the street of the Church there are two orders: namely, the continent and the married. In the book of Ezra I find it written that Malchijah son of Herem built half the street in Jerusalem (2 Esdr. 3). He builds half the street in Jerusalem who preserves the lawful rights of married persons. The other half of the same street is said to be built by him through whom the purity of the continent is wholly guarded. Between these orders [Col. 1148D] of houses there is, as it were, a middle way: the active life. Those who hasten to arrive at the heavenly Jerusalem therefore walk by this way.

There are, moreover, greater and lesser streets in Jerusalem. The greater streets are the active and the contemplative lives. The lesser belong to those who derive from them or adhere to them. There are also certain moral streets in the soul: namely, the various kinds of virtues. For just as in a material street there are different ranks of people, so in the streets of the soul there are different dispositions. The soul has a street of fear and a street of love. The street of fear descends to the Valley Gate—that is, to humility. The street of love leads to the Bridge Gate—that is, to contemplation of the future recompense.

Servants and hired labourers dwell in the street of fear. In the street of love dwell those who await the inheritances of the Fathers. [Col. 1149A] Servants serve through fear of punishment; hired labourers seek a reward for their labour; sons labour for love alone, not so that they alone may possess the inheritance, but so that they may live without end with their Father.

Other streets may also be identified in moral Jerusalem: the street of priests and the street of those who sell shields. The street of priests is the street of holy exhortation, leading to the Dung Gate—that is, to the gate of confession. For as dung is cast out through the Dung Gate, so through the gate of confession the stench of sin is cast out. There is also a street of those who sell shields. Some buy shields and bear shields because they defend their brethren in need. Others make shields and sell shields because, although they have the ability and power to help others, they nevertheless do not help brethren in need without payment.

Shields are words of defence. He holds a shield in his hand who fulfils by deeds what he says with his mouth. He raises a shield against enemies who provides help according to his ability in defence of the poor. The martyrs bought shields because, in defence of the divine law, they gave their bodies over to torments. Judas Maccabaeus and his brothers bought shields when, in defence of their brethren, they left their possessions to be ravaged by enemies. The Maccabees, however, bought golden shields. For history records that the Maccabees possessed golden bucklers: “The sun,” it says, “shone upon the golden bucklers, and the mountains shone from them” (1 Macc. 6). Golden bucklers are aids of defence free from [Col. 1149B] admixture of temporal profit. In these bucklers, therefore, the sun shines, because in purity of heart justice appears more brightly through the example of good action. “And the mountains shone from them.” Mountains are persons exalted in life and morals. Mountains, therefore, receive brightness from golden bucklers because, when one righteous person acts well, the other eminent men become brighter through the renown of good opinion.

Yet in the army of King Antiochus there were many who bore golden bucklers with them. As we said above, golden bucklers are words uttered in defence of one’s neighbour without admixture of temporal profit. But these men’s bucklers are golden because, when they utter words of defence for their neighbours, they say that they speak not for payment but for justice. Yet when the sun of justice [Col. 1149C] shines upon these bucklers, then the truth appears. Thus the mountains receive brightness from them, because against their falsehood the mountains—that is, the righteous—become brighter by the light of truth.

Note also that in Jerusalem there is said to be a house of shield-sellers, lest what we have said seem strange to anyone. For Scripture says: “Malchijah son of the goldsmith built as far as the house of the Nethinim and of the shield-sellers, opposite the Judgment Gate” (2 Esdr. 3). They sell shields who readily accept gifts for justice. But Scripture says that the house of shield-sellers is opposite the Judgment Gate. For conscience reproves those who sell justice; and the houses of those whose mind and conscience oppose truth are placed opposite the Judgment Gate. This happens mystically or morally whenever an ecclesiastical man is overcome by greed, or whenever a mind is rewarded by the praise of flattery. [Col. 1149D]

Nor is it surprising if this happens in Jerusalem—that is, in the Church or in the soul—when, conversely, in Damascus—that is, in the world or in the worldly mind—a street called Straight and a house of Judas are found. For the Lord said to Ananias in a vision: “Rise and go to the street which is called Straight, and seek in the house of Judas one named Saul of Tarsus; for behold, he is praying” (Acts 9). Ananias means “the grace of the Lord”; Judas, “confession”; Saul, “one looking upon temptation”; Tarsus, “the exploration of joy.” Ananias is sent to Saul when the grace of repentance is granted to one who considers sin. He considers and looks upon temptation who attends to the time and place, the pleasure and the consent, of temptation. Such a person is sought and found in the house of Judas: he remains in the house of confession while still dwelling in the world. This house is placed in the street called Straight. For one who remains in the house of confession undoubtedly keeps to the goal of right living. But one who is a Tarsian endures the heavenly man upon earth, that afterwards he may become an explorer of heavenly joy. [Col. 1150B]

## Chapter XIV. On the Broad Ways of Jerusalem

There are said to be broad ways in Jerusalem. Thus Jeremiah says, when in his Lamentations he spoke of the citizens of Jerusalem: “When they failed, as though wounded, in the broad ways of the city” (Lam. 2). Jerusalem therefore has good and bad citizens; it has chaff and threshing-floors. In its granaries it has grain together with [Col. 1150C] chaff. In the broad ways of Jerusalem are the good, but they do not fail, because they do not succumb, being devoted to the vanities of the world. But the evil are in the broad ways of the city and fail, because, being wandering and unstable, they do not resist the pleasures of the flesh.

The broad ways are wide paths which lead those walking upon them to death. “When they failed,” he says, “as though wounded, in the broad ways of the city.” Sins are like wounds. They fail as wounded men in the broad ways who, failing in goodness, do not recover themselves from delight in sin. This too seems relevant to what is written in the same place: “When the little one and the suckling failed,” he says, “in the broad ways of the town” (ibid.). The little one is the simple and untrained people. The suckling is a teacher who preaches carnal things. The broad ways of the town are the pleasures [Col. 1150D] of this world. Thus the little one and the suckling fail in the broad ways of the town when prelates, together with their subjects, abandoning good works, seek carnal things everywhere.

Such broad ways sometimes have mud and sometimes abound in dust and dryness. Hence the Psalmist says: “I will grind them,” he says, “like dust before the face of the wind; I will wipe them away like the mud of the streets” (Ps. 17 [18]). Dust is the dissolution of human frailty; wind is the spirit of pride. The wind lifts dust by its force whenever someone praises the life of any dissolute person with flattering words. It produces a whirlwind in the dust when the impulse of exaltation disturbs dissolute actions. Thus David, the strong-handed one, grinds his enemies like dust when he permits the dissolute actions of the wicked to remain in dissolution. “I will wipe them away like the mud of the streets.” Mud in the streets is the uncleanness of the flesh. David therefore has enemies—that is, the lustful and slippery. “And I will wipe them away,” he says. From where? Perhaps from the book of life. [Col. 1151A]

## Chapter XV. On the Four Broad Ways of Jerusalem, Morally Understood

There are said to be four broad ways in the city of Jerusalem: the broader street, the street of the house of God, the street before the Water Gate, and another street before the Ephraim Gate. Of the broader street it is said: “And they left Jerusalem as far as the wall of the broader street” (2 Esdr. 3). Of the street of the house of God it is said: “All the people sat in the street of the house of God, trembling because of the sin and the rains. And Ezra the priest arose and said to them: You have transgressed and have taken foreign wives” (1 Esdr. 10). Of the street before [Col. 1151B] the Water Gate it is said: “All the people assembled as one man in the street which is before the Water Gate, and they told Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses, which the Lord had commanded Israel” (2 Esdr. 8). Of the street by the Ephraim Gate it is said: “The people went out and brought branches from the trees, and each made himself booths upon his roof, and in his courts, and in the courts of the house of God, and in the street of the Water Gate, and in the street of the Ephraim Gate” (2 Esdr. 3).

The building of Jerusalem’s walls is abandoned by the children of Israel when they approach the wall of the broader street. The broader street is secular life; the wall of the street is the adversity of life. Hence the disciples who were at Damascus lowered Paul in a basket through the wall (Acts 9). Accordingly Bede, on the Acts of the Apostles: “The wall of Damascus,” he says, “which is interpreted ‘drinking blood,’ is the adversity of the world.” King Aretas, whose name means “defence,” is understood as the devil. The basket, customarily made of reeds and palms, signifies the union of faith and hope. For the reed signifies the greenness of faith; the palm, hope of eternal life. If, therefore, anyone sees himself surrounded by the wall of adversity, let him hasten to climb into the basket of virtue, that he may escape. [Col. 1151C]

“All the people sat in the street of the house of God, grieving for the sin and for the rains.” The house of God is the house of conversion (1 Esdr. 10). It is said to have a street whenever it is outwardly entangled in secular affairs. But those who have long been accustomed to run joyfully through the street sometimes sit in the same street mourning for sin, because those who had pursued worldliness in the house of God afterwards return to themselves and desire to possess a tranquil mind. Nor can they remain outside merely because of sin, but also because of the rains; with all the desires of their soul they seek to be within. “It is the time of rain,” they say, “and we cannot endure to stand outside.” Rain is catholic teaching; the person pressed by the rain of spiritual teaching cannot endure to stand outside.

Ezra the priest also arose and said to them: “You have transgressed and have taken foreign wives, so as to add to the sin of Israel; and now make confession to the Lord God of your fathers, and do his pleasure, and separate yourselves from the peoples of the land and from foreign wives” (ibid.). Behold the rain—that is, the teaching of rebukes. [Col. 1152A] Foreign wives are secular concerns. Confession is made concerning these when guilt is recognized. He separates himself from the people of the land and from foreign wives who neglects earthly things and hates secular concerns.

Next comes the street before the Water Gate, in which the people assemble as one man, asking Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses. The Water Gate is the admonition of the Scriptures; the street is the memory of sins. Thus a street is said to be before the Water Gate because sin is recalled to memory through the admonition of the Scriptures. In it the people are gathered as one man when, persevering in unity, they are united in love with teachers and brethren. In this way they ask for the book of the law of Moses to be brought, so that by the law they may correct what they have done contrary to the law’s commands.

The street before the Ephraim Gate is placed last. For nothing benefits one who labours unless the fruit of the work is gathered at the end. Ephraim means “fruitful.” The beginning of good work, therefore, is the gate of the penitent. We may call and designate this street repentance. It is a street when we still mourn in it for what we have sinned, but wipe away its mud while we labour in repentance. At times we go out from the street and at times return to it: we go out from the street when we withdraw from secular life; we return to the street when we call our mind back to the things we have done wrongly.

“Go out,” he says, “to the mountain, and bring branches of olive, branches of myrtle, and branches of palms, that booths may be made” (Num. 8). We go out to the mountain [Col. 1152C] when prayer lifts us to the mountain of mercy. Perhaps this is the Mount of Olives. “Bring,” he says, “branches of olive”—that is, works of mercy. For Greek *eleos* [printed *oleos*] is called “mercy” in Latin. Myrtle is said to signify the virtue of temperance; the palm grows upward. Thus by the olive is meant a work of mercy, by the myrtle the virtue of temperance, and by the palm hope of pardon. With these branches and boughs booths are made in the street of the Ephraim Gate when the aforesaid virtues defend us on every side from the frost of torpor and the heat of pleasure. Therefore we set up booths in the street before the Ephraim Gate when, wiping out what we have done badly through works of mercy, we desire to arrive at the hope of victory. [Col. 1152D]

## Chapter XVI. Again, a Moral Interpretation of the Four Broad Ways of Jerusalem

Morally, by the broader street we may understand the wandering of the mind. The streets of the city are the wandering pleasures of the mind. *Plateia* in Greek is called *latitudo*, “breadth,” in Latin. It is broad in deed, broader in speech, broadest in thought. When we defend with words what we have done badly, we approach the broader street. It is grievous to sin; more grievous to defend sin; most grievous to consent to sin through delight. Therefore, when guilt is defended, the street is widened. But while Jerusalem is being built and the broader street is approached, the building of the city is abandoned. This happens when guilt is excused in words. [Col. 1153A] No one can build up a person defending the guilt of his own offence; but when guilt is recognized, then the city wall—that is, good work—is allowed to be built.

In the broader street, as we have said, guilt is defended; but in the street of the house of God it is accused and corrected. The house of God is the mind in which the grace of the Holy Spirit dwells. The street of the house of God is the recollection of sin. Those who had been accustomed to run through this street now sit there, trembling for sin; and those who had long cultivated foolish joy mourn their sin. In this street Ezra the priest, who sacrifices flesh—that is, the mind which slays within itself the desires of the flesh—rebukes the people because they had transgressed the Lord’s command. “Separate yourselves,” he says, “from the people of the land and from foreign wives” (1 Esdr. 10). The people [Col. 1153B] of the land are desires for earthly things; foreign wives are the blandishments of the flesh. Those separate their mind from these things who disregard the desires of the world and mentally oppose the enticements of wretched flesh.

Next comes the street before the Water Gate. The Water Gate is the grace of tears. The street before the Water Gate is contrition of soul over pleasure in sin. In this street the people gather as one man: the people of thoughts, scattered in various directions, when gathered into one by contrition, enters the inner chamber of the mind and desires to hear the book of the law, so that it may correct the guilt of transgression and become attentive in meditation upon the divine law. The soul is led to the street before the Ephraim Gate when, through the fruit of good work, it is recalled to hope of pardon.

Thus in the broader street we do nothing; indeed, we abandon the building of Jerusalem. In the street of the house of God we turn over the earth and sow. In the street before the Ephraim Gate we gather fruit. There we pitch booths in which, through hope of mercy, we store grain. In these streets also the sick were placed upon beds, so that, when Peter came, at least his shadow might overshadow one of them, and all might be freed from their infirmities. The sick are those who labour under the disease of sin. They are placed in the streets when they recall the pleasure of their sins, so that, when Peter comes—that is, when sin is recognized through recollection, for Peter means “recognizing”—at least [Col. 1153D] his shadow may overshadow one of them, so that his intercession may cool each person’s soul from the heat of vices. This is the shadow which refreshes the sick person, so that it may restore him, freed from infirmities, to health.

## Chapter XVII. On Those Who Destroy the Temple, and Those Who Cleanse and Renew It

In the preceding book we said much concerning the building of the temple; now let us briefly hear what the history says concerning its destruction. As truthful history relates:

“Antiochus the Illustrious, son of King Antiochus, who had been a hostage at Rome, went up to Jerusalem with a heavy multitude. He entered the sanctuary proudly, took the golden altar, the lampstand of light, and all its vessels; he took the hidden treasures which he found, and, having taken everything away, departed into his own land. But after two years the king sent the chief collector of tribute into the cities of Judah. He came to Jerusalem with a great crowd, suddenly attacked the city, destroyed many people of Israel, took the spoils of the city, burned it with fire, destroyed its houses and its surrounding walls, led women and children captive, and took possession of the cattle. They built the city of David with a great strong wall and strong towers, and it became their citadel. There they placed a nation of sinners and lawless men; and there they placed weapons and provisions” (1 Macc. 1).

King Antiochus goes up to Jerusalem when the devil rules in the Church, or when carnal appetite rules in the soul. He goes up with a heavy multitude—that is, with an abundance of offences and with the weight of every criminal [Col. 1154B] sin. He enters the sanctuary proudly when the spirit of pride opens to itself hearts sanctified through confession. He took the golden altar and the lampstand of light: that is, purity of prayer and the light of divine contemplation. He took all the vessels of the sanctuary: namely, the various kinds of virtues. He crushed everything when he reduced the various forms of virtue to nothing. “And he took the hidden treasures which he found, and, having taken everything away, departed into his own land.” The treasure is understanding of wisdom, hidden from the devil but known to God. The devil finds it when, through the vice of vainglory, he makes it visible to others. Antiochus departs into his own land after removing everything whenever the devil, having taken away virtues, leads the minds of the faithful back to earthly desires.

“After two years he sent the chief collector of tribute into the cities of Judah.” Greed receives tribute because it exacts many demands both in the Church and in every soul. It comes to Jerusalem with a great crowd in order to disturb the peace of the simple. It attacks the city and destroys from Israel the people of simple thoughts. It takes the city’s spoils when it strips the mind of the garments of virtues. It burns the city with fire when it consumes the soul with the flames of desire. It destroys the houses within and its walls round about: that is, consciences within and perfect actions round about. It leads captive the women—that is, the imperfect affections of the mind—and their children, namely their imperfect acts. It possesses their cattle when the devil or carnal appetite holds irrational motions of the soul in its power. [Col. 1154D] What the children of Israel had been accustomed to guard, the Antiochenes slaughter and eat.

They build the city of David when they turn the mind of any strong-handed person—that is, of one acting well—to the opposite side. They fortify it with a great wall and strong towers when they set perverse works and defences of those works round about it. “And it became their citadel”: that is, the pride of a perverse mind. “There they placed a nation of sinners and lawless men”: in the soul, a nation of vices; in the Church, grievous enemies of the Christian faith, namely heretics. “And there they placed weapons and provisions.” Weapons are words of defence; provisions are earthly pleasures. Those who feed the mind upon earthly pleasures fortify the citadel with such foods.

“But King Antiochus, intending to go into Persia, left Lysias, a noble man of royal lineage, over the royal affairs; and he commanded him concerning all that he wished, and concerning the inhabitants of Judaea and Jerusalem, that he should send an army against them to crush the strength of Israel and the remnant of Jerusalem” (1 Macc. 3). “Lysias gathered sixty thousand chosen men and five thousand horsemen; they came into Judaea and pitched camp at Beth-horon. Judas met them with ten thousand men; they joined battle, and five thousand men of Lysias’s army fell. But Lysias, seeing the flight of his own men and the boldness of the Jews, went to Antioch” (1 Macc. 4).

Lysias is sent by Antiochus to destroy Judaea and Jerusalem when the spirit of luxury is dispatched by the devil to overthrow the peace [Col. 1155B] of confession. Lysias means “begetting.” For luxury begets many children because each day it produces from itself diverse motions of the flesh. They come into Judaea and pitch camp at Beth-horon: they enter the land of confession and camp in Beth-horon because they invade the land of confession through anger. Beth-horon means “house of anger.” There is an upper Beth-horon, the anger of prelates, and a lower Beth-horon, the anger of subjects. Whichever of these the foreigners occupy, they disturb the land of confession.

“Judas met them with ten thousand men.” Judas meets Lysias’s army with ten thousand men when confession, supported by the Ten Commandments of the law, manfully resists the various motions of luxury. “They joined battle, and five thousand men of Lysias’s army fell.” Judas joins battle with Lysias’s army when the mind opposes luxury with all its strength. Thus five thousand fall from Lysias’s army when the five bodily senses succumb to confession’s sword-edge. Lysias sees the flight of his own men and the boldness of the Jews, and goes to Antioch. Lysias goes to Antioch because luxury seeks an abundance of riches. Antioch means “the silence of poverty.” Poverty is said to be silent where riches rule.

After Judas had put Lysias, sent by Antiochus, to flight, and he had departed defeated to Antioch, Judas said to his brethren: “Behold, our enemies are crushed; let us now go up to cleanse and renew the sanctuary. And they went up to Mount Zion, [Col. 1155D] and saw the sanctuary deserted, the altar profaned, the gates burned, shrubs grown in the courts as in a forest or upon mountains, and the chambers destroyed; and they tore their garments and mourned with great mourning” (ibid.).

When Lysias has been put to flight—that is, luxury destroyed—and the enemies have been crushed, namely the works of luxury, Judas ascends Mount Zion when true confession seeks lofty things through the steps of the virtues. He ascends to cleanse and renew the sanctuary. “Create in me a clean heart, O God,” he says, “and renew a right spirit in my inward parts” (Ps. 50 [51]). Cleanse from vices; renew with virtues. He sees the sanctuary deserted who recognizes that the holiness of the mind has been abandoned by God.

For, as is said in the same book, “the temple was full of luxury and revelry among the Gentiles; and men who committed fornication with harlots lived there, and women freely thrust themselves into the sacred precincts” (2 Macc. 6). The temple is said to be full of luxury when the soul takes pleasure in voluptuous thoughts of luxury. Revelries take place there when the vices of the flesh nourish the mind mutually with various dishes of pleasures. Fornicators dwell there with harlots when vices of the flesh agree with the thoughts of the mind. Women freely thrust themselves into the sacred precincts when the softness and blandishments of the flesh freely hide themselves in the inner recess of the mind. The altar is read to be profaned and full of unlawful things when the mind desires and longs for what is forbidden in the divine law. The gates lie burned when the entrances of the senses, set ablaze by burning desire, stand wholly open to incoming vices. [Col. 1156B] The shrubs born in the courts are unlawful desires, which, just as shrubs grow without cultivation, do not cease to rise spontaneously in the soul. The destroyed *pastophoria* are the hidden chambers of the mind, destroyed by foreigners—that is, by unclean spirits. For *pastophoria* are little cells made in the innermost parts of treasuries, or chambers in which the governors of temples dwell. Judas cleanses these things from the aforesaid impurities and does not cease to renew them daily.

## Chapter XVIII. How Judas Appointed Men to Fight Those Who Were in the Citadel Until the Sanctuary Was Cleansed

“Judas appointed men to fight those who were in the citadel until the sanctuary should be cleansed” (1 Macc. 4). By the citadel we may understand the reason of the mind, [Col. 1156C] which foreigners possess as often as vices rule the mind, in order to estrange it from virtues. Yet it is remarkable that the children of Israel occupy Jerusalem, while foreigners rule in the citadel and have power in it. If the Apostle had not untied the knot of this question, someone might perhaps wonder how this could be so. The Apostle says: “I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin” (Rom. 7). Behold, one law is in the members and another law is in the mind. “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5). Thus foreigners sometimes rule in the citadel; and many of the people who oppose Judas remain in the city. For many things harmful to the mind remain together with confession itself, and yet cannot be expelled. Many things also arise from evil habit which do not obey reason but conquer reason by a kind of persistence.

Likewise, Ephraim did not expel the Canaanite who dwelt in Gezer, until Pharaoh king of Egypt took Gezer and gave it as a dowry to his daughter (3 Kings 9; Josh. 16). Ephraim means “fruit-bearing”; Pharaoh, “scattering”; Canaanite, “motion”; Gezer, “building.” Therefore, with those who gather the fruit of good work, motions of the flesh do not cease to dwell, but serve them under tribute as long as the children of Ephraim rule and preside over the city. But when Pharaoh king of Egypt takes and scatters Gezer—that is, the soul built up with virtues—he does not cease to slaughter all who dwell in it: that is, the virtues [Col. 1157A] of the soul. “And he gave it as a dowry to his daughter” (2 Macc. 4). The daughter of Pharaoh king of Egypt is the law of sin. Thus the king of Egypt gives Gezer as a dowry to his daughter when the law of sin registers as her dowry the carnally living soul; and Gezer is given as a dowry to Pharaoh’s daughter when the building-up of body and soul is subjected to the law of sin.

Jason, the brother of Onias, also built a gymnasium and an ephebia beneath the citadel in Jerusalem. “When Antiochus, who was called the Noble, had assumed the kingdom, Jason, the brother of Onias, sought the high priesthood. Having approached King Antiochus, he promised him three hundred and sixty talents of silver; moreover, he promised another hundred and fifty if he were granted authority to build a gymnasium and an ephebia for himself, and to enrol as Antiochenes those who were in Jerusalem. When the king had consented, and Jason had obtained the office, he immediately began to transfer his fellow-countrymen to Gentile customs; and he dared to establish a gymnasium beneath the very citadel and to place the finest youths in brothels” (ibid.).

“Jason, the brother of Onias, sought the high priesthood.” From that time, O Lord, from that time there was a priesthood for sale—and still is. Jason is still in the Church with Onias; the election of some is still conducted by prayers and by payment. Those who become teachers in the Church by this method sometimes build a gymnasium and an ephebia in Jerusalem—that is, in the Church. A gymnasium is a house in which the games of the Gentiles used to take place. Prelates build a gymnasium in Israel when they tell secular stories among the brethren: when they ought by their exhortations to move their hearers to weeping, they move them to laughter. They establish an ephebia in Israel when they are not ashamed to keep with them persons who are suspect and notorious. They want those who are in Jerusalem to be enrolled as Antiochenes because they desire to be rich and to seem rich. Those who before their conversion had been accustomed to go about in the world with few companions now frequent courts with a great crowd and lavish display; by this the simple are given to understand that poverty does not suit prelacy. [Col. 1157C]

Morally, however, Jason means “desiring.” A gymnasium is a place where the games of the Gentiles were anciently held. An ephebia is a brothel in which *ephebi*, youths, were customarily placed. The *ephebi* are the manly affections of the soul. Jason intends, with the consent of King Antiochus, to place them in brothels because carnal desire, at the devil’s prompting, sometimes subjects those same affections to lust. Those build a gymnasium in Jerusalem who, light and unstable in mind, exult in the games of curiosity. Those desire to be enrolled as Antiochenes who abound in heaps of riches.

Behold, both in the citadel and beneath the citadel are those who oppose Judas—that is, confession.
