Judas, as we said above, appointed men to fight those who were in the citadel until he should cleanse the sanctuary (1 Macc. 4). The men are the manly affections of the soul; they fight those who are in the citadel when virtues manfully resist vices. Judas, therefore, appoints men for battle when true confession places the virtues in order in their own positions. Thus he places fear of punishment in the first place, sorrow for guilt in the second, the labour of repentance in the third, and the fruit of almsgiving in the fourth. But lest he despair, he joins hope of pardon to fear, consolation to sorrow, recompense to labour, and to the fruit of almsgiving the visitation of the poor. [Col. 1158A] He also joins fasting to compunction, vigils to prayer, and reading to meditation. Thus Judas besieges the citadel all around until confession cleanses the mind of impurities.

## Chapter XIX. On Judas and His Brothers Simon, Jonathan, Joanna, and Eleazar
After Judas had put to flight Lysias, whom Antiochus had sent, Judas said to his brothers: “Behold, our enemies have been crushed. Let us now go up to cleanse and renew the holy places” (1 Macc. 4). Judas is said to have four brothers [Col. 1158B], namely Simon and Jonathan, Joanna and Eleazar. These five are sons of Mattathias. Mattathias means “gift of God”; Judas, “confessing”; Simon, “obedient”; Jonathan, “giving column”; Joanna, “the grace of God”; and Eleazar, “God’s help.” These, then, are sons of Mattathias, because all these things proceed from the gift of God.

Thus Judas cleanses; Simon builds; Jonathan renews; Joanna adorns; Eleazar protects and preserves. Judas cleanses the temple, because confession purges the mind of vices. Simon builds, because obedience labours so that the structure of good work may rise on high. Jonathan does not cease to renew the holy places, because dove-like simplicity builds what the craftiness of the ancient enemy—that is, the devil—daily [Col. 1158C] destroys, and destroyed in the first man. Joanna adorns the front of the temple with golden crowns, because the grace of God commends the recognition of a victorious mind through its conduct. But all these things achieve nothing unless they are done through Eleazar—that is, with God helping and directing. For if you attribute what you do not to God but to yourself, you do not build, but overthrow.

“And Judas chose priests without blemish, having a will toward the law of God; and they cleansed the holy places, and built the house within; and they sanctified the sanctuary and the courts, and made new holy vessels; and they brought the lampstand, the altar of incense, and the table into the temple. And they offered a new sacrifice upon the altar of burnt offerings” (ibid.). Judas chooses priests without blemish when he renders spotless the virtues that minister upon the altar of the heart. They have a will toward the law [Col. 1158D] of God, because otherwise they would not offer a sacrifice rich in marrow; and they cleansed the holy places—that is, the devotion of the mind—from every stain of wickedness. They built the house within, namely conscience itself, with the various qualities of good habits. And they sanctified the sanctuary and the courts: the mind within and works without. And they made new holy vessels. They make new holy vessels who, in the newness of conversion, fashion their hearts according to the commandment of the new man—that is, Christ.

“And they brought the lampstand, the altar of incense, and the table into the temple.” By the lampstand we may understand the word of God; by the light of the lampstand, the teaching of the word; by the altar of incense, devotion in prayer, not the sweet smoke of flattery; by the table, remembrance of Holy Scripture. [Col. 1159A] For just as someone is refreshed by what is set upon a table, so the mind is, as it were, nourished by various dishes through the things it recalls. “And they offered a new sacrifice upon the altar of burnt offerings.” They sacrifice upon the new altar of burnt offerings when, in contrition of heart, they slay the desires of the flesh. These things, then, renew the mind and cleanse it when polluted by uncleannesses.

Therefore, those who remain in this city Jerusalem—that is, in peace; who have Judas—that is, confession—as their leader above all others; who cleanse the temple—that is, the mind—of vices and daily restore what has been destroyed: I believe that, if they do not fail, they will pass without delay from this Jerusalem to the heavenly one.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Heavenly Jerusalem

[Col. 1159B] That heavenly city which is called Jerusalem is fortified on every side by the impregnable wall of perfect security. In this city are twelve gates, through which the souls of the blessed hasten to enter that cloister not made by hands which is in heaven. Each gate is made from a single pearl, because the righteous who attain the heavenly homeland will enter through unity of faith and purity of mind. Its streets are paved with pure gold and precious stones, because nothing but purity is found there. Alleluia is sung through all its streets, because throughout it the glory of divine praise is proclaimed everywhere (Rev. 11).

In this city, Jerusalem—which is interpreted “vision of peace”—is founded the cloister of perfect blessedness. This cloister [Col. 1159C] is said to have the square form of steadfast stability, sides of equity, foundations of perseverance, columns of virtues, and capitals of divine protection. In this cloister the assembly of angels sits and maintains there the order of perfect charity. There diverse offices are entrusted to diverse angelic spirits, one to each. For there are angels, archangels, thrones and dominions, principalities and powers, virtues, cherubim, and seraphim.

Over this assembly of angels God the almighty Father is set in the manner of an abbot. This assembly is governed in the manner of a prior through the wisdom of the Son (who is less than the Father according to his humanity), and is guided by the grace of the Holy Spirit. To this cloister the righteous hasten to come, leaving all that they possess, so that therein they may receive the habit [Col. 1159D] of perfect religion—that is, the garment of immortality and innocence. Yet they still await in places assigned for this purpose, until they may reach that chapter of the great judgment, so that, when they are to receive the garment of perfect religion, they may hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Peace That Is in the Heavenly Jerusalem

As we have often said above, Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace.” Yet many see peace who are unable to attain it. “Seek peace,” he says, “and pursue it” (Ps. 33). Seek it when lost; follow it when fleeing. Seek it in this world; pursue it in the world to come. Unless you seek it in the present, you will without doubt not possess it in the future.

If you ask how [Col. 1160A] you ought now to pursue peace, listen to Jesus, who, ascending into heaven, left peace to his disciples, as the Evangelist John testifies concerning him, saying: “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave to you. I do not give to you as the world gives” (John 14). If you attend, you hear that there are two kinds of peace: one which Christ gives, another which the world gives. The peace of the world is that you depart from God and consent to the devil. But the peace of Christ is that you cast out the devil and love God.

The peace of the world is that the world may please you and you the world, so that, sated with earthly pleasures, you may eternally succumb to the torments of hell. The peace of Christ is that you patiently endure the adversities of the world even unto death, so that after death you may await more securely the happiness of the life to come. “In peace, in the selfsame, you shall sleep and rest” [Col. 1160B] (Ps. 4). He sleeps and rests “in peace, in the selfsame” who never departs from tranquility of mind. But because this cannot be accomplished in this world, it may therefore be assigned to those who dwell in the heavenly Jerusalem.

For there is eternal peace from the eternal Father. This is Jerusalem, which is interpreted “vision of peace,” “the city whose participation is in the selfsame” (Ps. 121). We should know that this Jerusalem which is now in action contains indiscriminate peoples; that other one undoubtedly receives the perfect. This one rejoices amid oppositions; that one in unceasing security. This one is full of the tears of penitents; that one knows no tears. Its participation is said to be “in the selfsame” because those who share in that perfect blessedness never change the state [Col. 1160C] of their uprightness, but always remain in unchangeable stability with God, who is himself the Same, and whose years shall not fail (Ps. 110).

There the spirit will not consent to the flesh in evil, nor will the flesh oppose the spirit in good. There will be neither decrease nor increase of the body, nor any end of age. A child will not grow into a young man there, nor will any young man grow old. There will be no old age there, nor the decline of old age. Fear will not give anyone pallor there, nor anger redness, nor labour sweat, nor sickness pain. Nor is it surprising that those who abide with the unchangeable Creator always possess the form of incorruptible perfection.

## CHAPTER XXII. That the Heavenly Jerusalem Is Said to Be in Judaea, Both Mystically and Morally

This heavenly Jerusalem is said, both mystically and morally, to be in Judaea [Col. 1160D], because Judaea is interpreted not only “confession” but also “praising.” “Praising, I shall call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies” (Ps. 17). He calls upon the Lord in praise who humbly entreats him for his transgressions, who attributes praise to God in all things and credits nothing to his own merits; for humility willingly ascends to the place from which pride unwillingly fell.

“Therefore I shall praise the name of God with song, and magnify him with praise. And it shall please God more than a young calf bringing forth horns and hoofs” (Ps. 68). “I shall praise the name of God with song,” that is, with the melody of love; “and magnify him with praise.” He magnifies God in praise who loves in his mind the works of God’s power and mercy, and recounts them to others for the praise of the Creator.

A young calf [Col. 1161A] is any person newly converted, who sacrifices himself to God when he slays the wantonness of his flesh by fasts and prayers. He brings forth horns when he takes up the strength of defence against vices. He brings forth hoofs when he adds discerning caution to the advances of good works. The calf is a clean animal: it chews the cud and divides the hoof. So the newly converted person first considers and reconsiders in the mind, and then discerns what ought or ought not to be done.

Above the sacrifice of the young calf, bringing forth horns and hoofs, the sacrifice of praise pleases the Lord. “The sacrifice,” he says, “of praise shall honour me; and there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God” (Ps. 49). There is a sacrifice of an animal, and there is a sacrifice of praise. The sacrifice of an animal is the affliction of mortified flesh. The sacrifice [Col. 1161B] of praise is the disposition of a humbled heart. For one who praises the Lord humbles himself and honours God. And there is the way to God, because through humility one goes to the heavenly Jerusalem. “By which I shall show him the salvation of God”: in the heavenly Jerusalem the salvation of God will indeed be shown to one who praises. For by the path of humility we return to the heavenly homeland.

Jacob walked this path when he returned from Syrian Mesopotamia to the land of Canaan; fleeing Laban his uncle and fearing Esau his brother, he crossed Jacob’s ford. And when all that belonged to him had been brought across, he remained alone. And behold, a man wrestled with him until morning. When he saw that he could not overcome him, he said to him: “Let me go, for dawn has now risen.” He answered: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” He said therefore: [Col. 1161C] “What is your name?” He answered: “Jacob.” He said: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel.” And he blessed him in that same place. And Jacob called the name of that place Phanuel, saying: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved” (Gen. 32).

Jacob means “wrestler”; Israel, “seeing God”; Mesopotamia, “exalted calling”; Laban, “white”; Esau, “red” or “vain”; Canaan, “humbling” or “merchant.” Jacob returns from Syrian Mesopotamia when the mind of any person struggling against vices withdraws from self-exaltation. He hastens to the land of Canaan when he hastens to undertake the work of true humility. He flees Laban, his uncle, when he does not consent to the whitening of vain glory. He fears encountering [Col. 1161D] Esau, his brother, lest carnal inclination overthrow the state of the mind through vain delights. He crosses the ford when he despises every pleasure. When all that belongs to him has been brought across, he remains alone, so that, gathering his mental strength to himself and withdrawn from the world, he may pray to the Lord more securely.

This pertains to what follows: “And behold, a man wrestled with him until morning.” Jacob wrestles with the man when the mind of any righteous person entreats the Lord more earnestly than usual. And he said to him: “Let me go, for dawn has now risen”—that is, cease now from prayer and supplications, because the light of freedom shines in your mind. For as long as he bowed himself to the Lord with the greatest tears, he could not depart from him.

“And he blessed him in that same place.” He is blessed in the same place because he is never changed from the constancy [Col. 1162A] of his good purpose. “And he called the name of that place Phanuel, saying: ‘I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved.’” Phanuel means “face of God.” Jacob, therefore, is blessed when the Lord is seen by him, because the vision of God is the highest blessing. Jacob then becomes Israel, because after the labours of good action one reaches the light of contemplation. “There Jacob shall exult, and Israel shall rejoice” (Ps. 13). “There my soul shall exult in the Lord, and shall delight in his salvation” (Ps. 34). Then the heavenly Jerusalem will be situated in Judaea, because angelic and human creation will then praise the Lord in peace.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That the Wall of the Heavenly Jerusalem Is of Jasper

[Col. 1162B] “The structure of the wall of the aforesaid city was of jasper stone” (Rev. 21). The structure of the city’s wall consists in the diverse works of every person who does good. Good works are walls, indeed, because they resist not only the devil but also vices. They are made of jasper stone—that is, of every person who perseveres in a good purpose. For a stone lies firmly in the wall of good work when someone maintains the line of upright conduct.

Jasper has a green colour, like the firmness of our purpose. For just as a tree, while it is green, retains the vigour of natural growth, so the greenness of jasper signifies the firmness of every person persevering in a good purpose. Green colour is sometimes found in painting, sometimes in dyeing. It grows in herbs and is created in gems. In painting, stone or wood is covered with green colour, but colour [Col. 1162C] in a painting is soon erased. In dyeing, cloth is steeped in green colour, but it is often discoloured by rain or excessive heat. Greenness grows with herbs, but withers in winter frost or is dried by summer heat. In certain gems green colour is created; yet it is not changed by the length of time, nor darkened by any cloud of obscurity.

By these four different effects of colour, four kinds of people may be identified. Just as what is painted is easily erased, so there are many who quickly abandon what they have resolved. There are others who persevere for a while in the dye of greenness, but when some occasion arises, as though they had lost their colour, they alter their reputation for good opinion. We also know others whom we compare by likeness to the greenness of herbs: although they live religiously in childhood and [Col. 1162D] youth, when they approach old age they scatter their minds in the frost of temptation; and, inflamed by the excessive heat of lust, they burn in old age. Thus, at the point of death, having lost the greenness of their purpose, they die with the herbs.

But the righteous person is said to possess the greenness of gems, which is created in the gems themselves and remains, when he maintains the firmness of his purpose without failure. Those, therefore, who remain in the greenness of a good purpose ought to be placed like jasper in the structure of the wall of the aforesaid city.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Gates of the Heavenly Jerusalem

The aforesaid city has twelve gates in its wall. The gates of the city are made from twelve pearls, such that each gate is made only from one pearl (Rev. 21). This kind of stone is found [Col. 1163A] in certain sea-fish. For it is written concerning sea-shells that a little white stone, as it were, grows in their flesh. The little stone is produced from heavenly dew, which at certain times of the year the shells draw in. They say, moreover, that white pearls are better than those which turn yellow. The conception of morning dew makes the former white; old age or evening air produces the latter dark.

Mystically, however, the pearl signifies evangelical teaching or the sweetness of heavenly life. Hence we read in the Gospel parable concerning the man seeking fine pearls that, having found one precious pearl, he went away, sold all that he had, and bought it (Matt. 18). Hence Gregory says: “Whoever has perfectly known, insofar as possibility permits, the sweetness of heavenly life, gladly leaves behind all that he had loved on earth.” In comparison with it all things become worthless; he abandons his possessions and disperses what he has gathered. The mind burns with desire for heavenly things; nothing on earth pleases it. Whatever had seemed pleasing in earthly appearance is seen as ugly, because the brightness of the precious pearl alone shines in the mind.

You now have, through the pearl, the sweetness of heavenly life and evangelical teaching. These are the pearls from which the twelve gates are made. As we have said above, pearls are made from dew, which the shells draw in at certain times of the year, because the righteous who live in the sea of this world sometimes taste, however slightly, the sweetness of divine contemplation. Hence blessed Gregory says: “Dew falls gently from above.” And as often as we receive the dew of heaven, so often [Col. 1163C] do we see something of things above, however slightly, through the infusion of inward contemplation. Therefore, one who is nourished in the sweetness of divine contemplation is said to be created from dew.

Observe that the structure of the aforesaid city has the colour of perpetual greenness. Observe also that pearls are said to be white. Attend, therefore, to whiteness and to greenness. Whiteness in the gates is the purity of chastity; greenness in the wall is perseverance in purpose.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Bars of the Gates of the Heavenly Jerusalem

Divine Scripture speaks concerning the bars of the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem, recalling that the Prophet said to that same Jerusalem: “He has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you” (Ps. 147). He strengthens the bars who makes them firm so that they may no longer [Col. 1163D] be opened. When he says that the bars have been strengthened, he shows that the doors of the blessed city are closed. A bar is placed upon a gate in order that permission to enter may be denied. This happened at the time when the Bridegroom entered, as is said in the Gospel concerning the virgins: “And those who were ready entered with him to the wedding, and the door was shut” (Matt. 25).

As a certain wise man says, the door was shut “not as a penalty of confinement, but for everlasting blessedness, because thereafter none of the saints will go out, nor will any stranger enter.” Then the blessedness of the righteous will be secure, since it is received under such a law that it can never be lost, because that city will have the God who can be contemplated within it. And therefore no one desires to depart from it, because nothing comparable to him can be seen apart from him.

“He has blessed your children within you.” Jerusalem is told: “He has blessed your children within you,” that is, in peace. For he has made peace its borders, because in the Jerusalem to come no disturbance of discord will exist anywhere. This peace will have no end. “And he satisfies you with the fat of wheat” (ibid.). Hear what follows: because the righteous are satisfied in that city from the fat of wheat. The fat of wheat is the present contemplation of God’s face. By it the perception of the righteous is refreshed in such a way that it seems to surpass every satisfaction. If here he refreshes us by participation in his body, how will he satisfy there those whom he has filled with the whole light of divinity? This is a wonderful taste, proceeding from perfect knowledge of divinity.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Streets of the Heavenly Jerusalem

Just as there are many dwelling places in the house of God the Father (John 14), so those who understand the divine Scriptures spiritually [Col. 1164B] may, in an anagogical sense, assign diverse streets in the heavenly Jerusalem. The diversity of streets is distinguished by diversity of merits. Different merits indeed receive different gifts of reward.

In a material street some kill others; in a mystical street heretics seduce Christians; in a mortal street vices drive out virtues. But in the heavenly streets neither does one kill another, nor does a heretic seduce a Christian, nor does vice drive out virtues. And where none of these things occurs, the tranquility of peace is preserved on every side. Here, like resident tenants, we pay rent and render tribute; there we are granted freedom and are not burdened by enforced service or any exaction from anyone. Here thieves break in and steal; there neither do thieves break in nor does moth destroy (Matt. 6).

In the heavenly streets dwell the angels, citizens of heaven, who lack nothing but abound in unfailing riches. The souls of the righteous pass to those streets when, after death, they depart from this valley of tears. There are nine distinct kinds of streets there, because there are nine orders of angels: angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominions, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim.

But “why,” as blessed Gregory says, “have we set forth these choirs of angels by enumeration, unless we carefully explain their respective mysteries? Those who announce lesser things are called angels; those who announce the highest things, archangels.” When angels come to minister something to us, they also derive their names among us from their ministries. Michael means “Who is like God?”; Gabriel [Col. 1164D], “strength of God”; Raphael, “medicine of God.”

Whenever something of miraculous power is done, Michael is said to be sent, so that from the deed itself and the name it may be understood that no one can do what God is able to do. Hence silence occurred in heaven when the dragon made war with Michael the archangel (Rev. 12), so that he who had proudly exalted himself to God’s likeness, slain by Michael, might learn that no one rises to God’s likeness through pride. Gabriel also is sent to Mary (Luke 1), and his name is “strength of God.” For he came to announce him who appeared in humility in order to defeat the powers of the air. Raphael, as we have said, means “medicine of God.” When he touched Tobit’s eyes, as though in the office of healing, he wiped away [Col. 1165A] the darkness of his blindness (Tob. 11). Therefore, since he was sent to heal, it was fitting that he should be called God’s medicine.

But “because,” as blessed Gregory says, “that heavenly city consists of angels and human beings, we too ought to draw something from those distinctions among the heavenly citizens for the practice of our own way of life, and to kindle ourselves with good pursuits toward the growth of virtues.” Since it is believed that as great a multitude of human beings will ascend there as the multitude of angels that remained, it remains that the human beings who return to the heavenly homeland should imitate, on their return there, something from these companies.

For there are many who understand small things, yet do not cease to announce even those small things devoutly to their brothers. These, therefore, run in the number of angels. There are some who, filled by the gift of divine generosity, are able both to grasp and to announce the highest secrets of heaven. To what order, then, are these assigned if not to the number of archangels? There are others who perform wonders and secretly work signs. To what do these belong, if not to the lot and number of the heavenly virtues? There are some who even drive evil spirits from possessed bodies, casting them out by the power of prayer and the force of authority received. To what order do these assign their merit, if not among the number of heavenly powers?

There are some who, having received virtues, even surpass the merits of the elect; being better than the good, they rule also over their elect brothers. To what order, then, have these received their lot if not among the ranks of principalities? There are some [Col. 1165C] who so rule over every vice and desire within themselves that, by the very right of their purity, they are called gods among men. To what order do these run if not to the number of dominions?

There are some who rule themselves. As they examine themselves with watchful attention, always cleaving to divine fear, they receive this gift of virtue: that they can rightly judge others also. Since divine contemplation is present to their minds, the Lord, sitting in them as upon his throne, examines the deeds of others and wonderfully dispenses all things from his seat. What, then, are these but thrones of their Creator? Or to what order are they enrolled if not among the ranks of the heavenly seats? Through them holy Church is governed, and even the elect are often judged concerning certain of their weak actions.

There are some who are so full of love for God and neighbour that they are rightly called cherubim. For, as we have said, *cherubim* means “fullness of knowledge”; and, as Paul says, we have learned that “the fullness of the law is charity” (Rom. 13). Therefore all who are fuller than others in love for God and neighbour have received the lot of their merits among the ranks of cherubim.

There are some who, kindled by the flames of heavenly contemplation, pant only for desire of their Creator. They desire nothing now in this world; they are nourished by love of eternity alone; they reject all earthly things and mentally transcend everything temporal. They love and burn, and rest in their very burning. Burning through love, they also kindle others by speaking. [Col. 1166A] Those whom they touch by speaking, they immediately cause to burn in God’s love. What, then, should I call these but seraphim? Their heart, transformed into fire, both shines and burns: for they enlighten the eyes of minds toward things above and, by piercing them into tears, cleanse away the rust of vices. Therefore those who are so inflamed with love for their Creator—where do they receive the lot of their calling but among the number of seraphim? Those who maintain, to the extent of their ability in this world, the manner we have described will come to those streets to remain there without end.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Streets of the Heavenly Jerusalem

“The streets of Jerusalem shall be paved with pure gold and precious stones” (Rev. 21). The street of the heavenly city is the breadth of perfect charity. Precious stones [Col. 1166B] are the righteous bought with the precious blood of Christ. That city is paved with gold because it is clothed on every side with the purity of love.

“And not merely with gold,” as blessed John says in the Apocalypse, “but with pure gold like clear glass.” Hence blessed Gregory says in the *Morals*: “By the designation of gold in sacred speech, the splendour of the heavenly city is sometimes understood.” The gold of which that city consists is said to be like glass, so that by gold it may be signified as bright, and by glass as transparent. We know that gold shines with a brightness greater than all metals. The nature of glass, however, is that it shines outwardly by visible purity and inwardly by transparency. In another metal, whatever is contained inside is hidden; in glass, whatever liquid is contained within is shown outwardly as it is.

“What else, then, in gold and glass,” as blessed Gregory says, “do we understand but that heavenly homeland, that fellowship of blessed citizens? Their hearts shine toward one another with brightness and are transparent with purity.” Since all saints will shine with the highest brightness in eternal blessedness, the city is said to be built of gold. But because their very brightness is open to one another in the hearts of others, and, when one looks upon the face of each person, one simultaneously penetrates that person’s conscience, this gold is said to be like clear glass.

For there the physical bulk of the limbs will not conceal the mind of one person from the eyes of another; the soul will be manifest, and even the harmony of the body will be manifest to bodily eyes. Thus each person will then be visible to another just as he can now be visible [Col. 1166D] to himself. For our hearts, so long as we are in this life, cannot be seen from one person by another, and are enclosed not in glass vessels but in vessels of clay.

Therefore that city, in which all saints shine with such brightness and are transparent with such clarity that they disclose their hearts individually, is said to consist of gold like clear glass: gold, to signify brightness; glass, transparency. It remains, then, that in that heavenly Jerusalem one person’s conscience will be open to another, and nothing hidden will remain hidden in secret. Therefore in the streets of the heavenly Jerusalem there will be no mud of earthly pleasure or dust of worldly vanity, but they will be paved with gold of perfect brightness, like glass of undisturbed purity.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Length, Breadth, and Height of the Heavenly Jerusalem

[Col. 1167A]

We know, as Scripture relates, that the length, breadth, and height of the aforesaid city are of equal measure. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “The length, breadth, and height of the city are equal” (Rev. 21). Hence blessed Gregory, commenting on Ezekiel: “Because the holy city Jerusalem which God inhabits is formed from angelic and human nature together,” angelic creation being above and human creation below, these two creatures may be signified by the height and breadth of the city, since the latter still dwells in the depths while the former remains in the heights.

But breadth and height are equal, because the humility of human beings will at some time be brought [Col. 1167B] to equality with angels. Hence it is written: “They will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22). John also says: “The measure of a human being, which is that of an angel” (Rev. 21), because a human being is brought up to that height of glory in which the angels rejoice to be established. Therefore the breadth of the city is as great as its height, because all the elect who now labour in the depths will at some time not be unequal to those highest spirits.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Cloister of the Heavenly Jerusalem

In the heavenly Jerusalem there is set a cloister of perfect blessedness, fortified on every side by four principal rooms. On one side is placed the oratory, on another the cellar, on the third the refectory, and on the [Col. 1167C] fourth the dormitory: that you may pray, have abundance, be refreshed, and be able to rest.

Eternal peace is called, by analogy, an oratory, because those who have escaped the chains or prison of this world flee to it that they may be saved. To the oratory of perfect peace is joined the cellar of the abundance of divine sweetness. The cellar of the abundance of divine divinity is followed by the refectory of eternal satiety. Yet even if you are in peace, even if you abound in riches, even if you enjoy your possessions at will, none of this profits unless you rest in the dormitory of a tranquil mind.

Observe that such rooms are not stripped open by the whirlwind of winds or destroyed by age, but remain sound and whole [Col. 1167D] without end: peace without disturbance, abundance without diminution, satiety without disgust, rest without weariness. Do you see how peace pertains to the oratory, abundance to the cellar, satiety to the refectory, and rest to the dormitory?

Observe also that security, as it were a side of the cloister, adjoins the oratory—that is, eternal peace. To the cellar of abundance, as it were a side of the cloister, adjoins the virtue of sufficiency. Delight adjoins the refectory of satiety. The virtue of gratitude adjoins the dormitory of rest. Thus peace is secure, abundance sufficient, satiety delightful, and rest welcome. Therefore rest excludes labour, satiety hunger, abundance poverty, and peace rapacity.

Whoever desires to attain that cloister of perfect blessedness must, while still remaining in the house of probation, diligently learn the order of the aforesaid cloister. The house of probation is the regular life. In this house we learn what we ought to do in the future. Here we are tested, that there we may be refreshed. In this house Christ is our master of novices; for he teaches us the order of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Therefore one who loves peace, for whom what he has is sufficient, who strives to be satisfied with heavenly desire and delights in it with all the inmost marrow of his heart, and who endures even adversities with thanksgiving—such a person, I say, while still placed in the house of probation, possesses in part the order of perfect blessedness. But when he reaches that cloister, he will possess the rule of perfection not in part but in its entirety.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Columns of the Cloister of the Heavenly Jerusalem

[Col. 1168B]

In the cloister of perfect blessedness there are four orders of columns, distinguished by four different properties of colour. The first order is saffron-coloured, the second red, the third snow-white, the fourth azure. The first resembles saffron, the second the rose, the third the lily, the fourth the violet. These four varieties of colour signify four orders of the elect. For saffron resembles ripe fruit. Likewise the ancient fathers, living to maturity, when they pass from this world to the heavenly Jerusalem, become, as it were, saffron-coloured columns in the cloister of perfect blessedness, made from living stones. And those who had long been accustomed to bear the fabric of the Church suitably adorn the cloister of perfect blessedness by their splendour, like saffron-coloured columns.

The second [Col. 1168C] order of columns is painted with a rosy colour, by which the blood of the martyrs is fittingly signified. The angels marvel at the colour of these columns, and they marvel also at their strength. They marvel at Stephen’s red colour; they marvel at Lawrence’s flaming colour; they marvel at the strength which could not be broken by stones; they marvel at the strength which remained unharmed amid fire. The third order of columns is snow-white, and signifies the purity of confession. For the life of confessors is polished on every side by fasts, vigils, and continual prayers; and those accustomed to preserve purity of mind and body keep without end the brightness of purity in the cloister of future blessedness. The fourth order of columns [Col. 1168D] is said to possess the colour of the sky when it is serene, because the colour of the violet, when it blooms, imitates the appearance of the air. Nor is it surprising if the integrity of virgins bears in heaven the likeness of heaven, since on earth it remains whole and free from the corruption of fleshly frailty. John, cast into a vat of boiling oil, came out unharmed; and he who had the integrity of virginity as his companion was immune from the corruption of the flesh. Nor did the heat of torture harm that flesh which the heat of lust had never at any time inflamed. Therefore in the first order are the ancient fathers, in the second the martyrs, in the third the confessors, in the fourth the virgins.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Squareness of the Cloister

The cloister of perfect blessedness is set in a square, so that on every side the firmness of equality may be maintained in it: [Col. 1169A] that it may not be exalted by prosperity, broken by adversity, grieved over the past, or fear that any misfortune can happen in the future. The measure of a square does not stand rightly if one side is made shorter and another longer. Therefore the measure of each side must conform to the line of perfect prosperity. Let this line have, as the length of perfect happiness, eternity. Thus in that length there will be a measure of length without end.

In Ezekiel’s book it is written concerning the building which the prophet is said to have seen on a mountain: that building had a court which was laid out everywhere with equal sides. The squareness of the aforesaid cloister is likened to the arrangement of that court. “This court,” says blessed Gregory, “is the multitude of the faithful, who, while they possess prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance, have the measure of the spiritual building in a square.” The length and equality of the four sides is, in every righteous person, perseverance unto death in the four virtues mentioned before.

But perhaps someone doubts whether any perfect person exists among the faithful, since blessed Gregory, in his book on Ezekiel, asks whether there were any “who might be found to live perfectly in the commandments of God.” He answers: “There certainly are.” Hence Ezekiel says: “And he measured the court, one hundred cubits in length, square” (Ezek. 40). The number of a hundred, assigned to the court as a square, is the measure of perfection in every righteous person. Therefore those are perfect who remain in the squareness of this court, because [Col. 1169C] when they depart from this world they will reach that cloister of perfect blessedness, in which they will endure without any deficiency. There prudence cannot be deceived, fortitude cannot be broken, justice cannot be overthrown, and temperance cannot be diminished or increased; and in that perfection there will be an end without end.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Order of the Heavenly Cloister

In the cloister of perfect blessedness angels dwell, in order that they may preserve there the order of eternal happiness. They lack nothing, and therefore need not labour. They neither hunger nor thirst, because they are satisfied with heavenly bread and drink from the torrent of delight. They always behold the face of the Father, because among rational creatures they possess the most perfect knowledge of him. [Col. 1169D] They love God and desire him; yet they are neither tormented by desire nor wearied by satiety.

Likewise, in the material cloister there are many who love the order of future happiness. They need little, because they have nothing for their own use beyond food and clothing. They even withhold from the flesh those things conceded to its necessity. They overcome nature, because they lead a heavenly life on earth; they devote themselves to contemplation and desire to see God. Whatever may happen in the meantime, they patiently await the coming of the Judge. In this life they endure every adversity, that after the resurrection they may become equal to the angels. Hence blessed Gregory says: “He who for our sake became less than the angels made us equal to the angels through the power of his abasement.”

Thus by dying he taught us not to fear death; by rising, [Col. 1170A] to trust in life; by ascending, to glory in the inheritance of the heavenly homeland, so that the members may rejoice to follow where their head is seen to have gone before. All of us who have been born in his faith are without doubt his body. Therefore human frailty must not despair of itself. Let it consider the blood of the Only-Begotten, and in its price see how great that which is worth so much truly is. Let it consider attentively where the head has gone before; and let what is bound by commandments for living be strengthened by example for hoping. Let it trust in the heavens and hope for the heavenly homeland; let it know itself to be the companion of angels, and rejoice that in its head it has been set above angels. Therefore those who in this world endure for a time the weariness or labours of the cloister shall live without end in quiet with angels in the cloister not made by hands—which is in heaven.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Book of Life

[Col. 1170B]

Those who dwell in the cloister of perfect blessedness undoubtedly study the reading of divine wisdom. No bodily necessity draws them away, nor does any impediment of labour hinder them. For those who remain in the cloister of perfect blessedness lack nothing; setting aside all cares, they attentively read the book of life.

There are four books of life: the first was written in paradise, the second in the desert, the third in the temple, and the fourth was written from eternity and is still held in the heavenly cloister. The first was written by God in the human heart; the second by Moses on tablets of stone; the third by Christ on the ground; the fourth in divine foreknowledge. The first is the book of generation, the second of correction, the third of grace, the fourth of divine wisdom.

[Col. 1170C] The book written in paradise was corrupted there and not amended. The book written by Moses in the desert was corrupted many times and amended many times. The book written in the temple was accused by the Jews, yet it was not rejected by God. But the book of divine wisdom, written by God from eternity, has never been corrupted: it remains ever the same and bears no stain of falsehood.

When someone considers what he ought to do and arranges it rationally, he reads, as it were, in the book of reason. But when he sins and, being reproved, repents, he studies by reading in the book of correction. And if, accused by someone, he hears from the Master, “Where are those who accused you? Go, and sin no more” (John 8), he reads in [Col. 1170D] the book of grace: “But Jesus, bending down, wrote with his finger on the ground” (ibid.).

You now have the writer of the book and its title; you have the pen and stylus; you also have the parchment. The bending down is the condescension of the merciful God. The writer is Jesus, that is, Saviour. All these things concur so that he who bends down may save, and he who condescends may grant salvation. The title begins in this work: *The Book of Grace*. For merits had not gone before so that sins might be forgiven; rather, they are forgiven through grace going before.

The pen or stylus is the finger of God, that is, the graciousness of the Holy Spirit. With this stylus the tablets of Moses were written. Of the same finger the magicians said in Egypt: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8). The parchment is the earth—that is, hearts full of earthly desires, dried of blood and hairs, that is, of superfluity [Col. 1171A] and fleshly desires. The material of the book is repentance; its purport concerns mercy. Its purpose concerns the case: for it intends to show mercy to the sinner.

If one asks under which part of philosophy it is placed, it is placed under ethics. Ethics is moral knowledge. For this book treats of the destruction of evil habits and the building up of good ones. It renders the reader well-disposed, teachable, and attentive. It makes him well-disposed by forgiving sin. It makes him attentive by promising the reward of future recompense. It makes him teachable by instructing the reader’s mind with heavenly doctrines.

“Where are those who accused you? Go, and sin no more.” Perhaps those who accused you sin in the same way as you sinned. “For all have sinned and need the glory of God” (Rom. 3). “And they went out one by one” (John 8), that they might follow the devil who had gone before. For of him it is said: “Satan went forth from the presence of the Lord” (Job 2). He went forth not to heal blessed Job, but to afflict him. Likewise, these men had not come to free the woman caught in adultery, but to stone her. It is not the justice of the law for a person to judge another when he is reproached by the consciousness of his own sin.

“Go,” he says, “and sin no more.” Go after Christ, not after the devil; go in the way of God’s commandments; go by the path of justice. Do not sin. And if at any time the frailty of the flesh compels the mind, let the will resist.

These three books—the book of reason, correction, and grace—are written in one codex. This codex is divine Scripture, concerning which John says in [Col. 1171C] the Apocalypse: “And I saw an angel descending from heaven, and he had in his hand an open book. And I took the book from the hand of the angel and devoured it; and it was sweet in my mouth like honey. And when I had devoured the book, my belly was made bitter” (Apoc. 10).

Hence blessed Gregory says: “We devour the book when we receive with eagerness the words of life.” In this expression, “devouring,” what else is rebuked but the torpor of our sloth? For we do not seek out the Lord’s words and mysteries for ourselves, and we unwillingly hear sayings from others. Therefore we devour and eat the book when we read the words of God. Many indeed read and yet are fasting from the reading itself. Many hear the voice of preaching, yet after the voice depart empty and fasting. For even if they receive in their minds an understanding of sacred speech, by forgetting and not observing what they heard they do not store these things in the inner parts of the heart.

But those read and are not fasting from reading who understand and preserve those matters in which they labour. These devour and eat the holy book and are not fasting, because memory has not lost the commandments of life which the understanding was able to grasp. Sometimes such persons, by the gift of heavenly grace, also receive the word of teaching and, from the food of truth which they themselves inwardly chew over with delight, sweetly feed their neighbours as well. “And I devoured it, and it was sweet in my mouth like honey.” The book which is devoured and eaten becomes sweet in the mouth like honey. Sacred Scripture is said to be sweet in the mouth of the person whose inward life is filled with [Col. 1172A] its commandments, because it is pleasant to him to speak when it has been inwardly impressed so as to be found there. For one whose evil life and accusing conscience rebuke him does not possess the word of God.

“And when I had devoured the book, my belly was made bitter.” Hence blessed Gregory says in his commentary on Ezekiel: “In sacred speech, the belly is sometimes customarily put for the mind.” Thus Jeremiah says, “My belly aches” (Jer. 4). He ached in his belly who felt affliction of mind. But it must be known that, when the word of God begins to be sweet in the mouth of the heart, that person’s mind undoubtedly grows bitter against itself.

There are also other books, concerning which John says in the Apocalypse: “And the books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged from those things which were written in the books, according to their works” (Apoc. 20). The books which are opened refer to those in which the heavenly commandments are seen expressed in the deeds of their possessors. “And the dead were judged from those things which were written in the books,” because in the displayed life of the righteous, as in the unfolding of books, the unrighteous read the good which they refused to do and are condemned by comparison with those who did it.

“And another book was opened, which is the book of life” (ibid.). Hence blessed Gregory says: “The book of life is the very vision of the coming Judge.” In it every commandment is written, as it were, because whoever sees him immediately understands, with conscience as witness, whatever he did not do. It is called a book because the righteous person, studying in the book of divine wisdom, is freed from vices. It is also called the book of life because it frees the righteous from eternal death and will reward him in the future with perpetual [Col. 1172C] freedom. Those whom it frees in the present from guilt, it will make immune from punishment in the future.

Hence blessed James says: “The wisdom which is from above is first pure, then peaceable” (Jas. 3). It is pure, as is read in the *Pastoral Rule*, because it understands chastely; and peaceable because it does not through pride separate itself at all from fellowship with its neighbour. Therefore one who loves the wisdom coming down from above reads, as it were, in the book of life. When he reaches the cloister of perfect blessedness, reading continually in that book, he will be perfect in the knowledge of the divine law.

Concerning this book a certain wise man said that “its origin is eternal; its essence incorruptible; its knowledge life; its writing indelible; its inspection desirable; its teaching easy; its knowledge sweet; its depth capable of instruction; [Col. 1172D] its words innumerable—and yet one word is all things.” The letters of this book are written in the cloisters of Christ’s humanity, but illuminated by the gold of divinity. Whoever reaches the contemplation of that book, instructed in the knowledge of the divine law, shall live for eternity.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Little Meadow in the Midst of the Heavenly Cloister

The greenness of the little meadow in the middle of a material cloister refreshes the eyes of those in the cloister and makes them more eager for reading. For green has the natural property of soothing the eyes by the sight it affords. Likewise, the greenness of the little meadow in the midst of the heavenly cloister refreshes the eyes of the heavenly citizens and continually strengthens them by its newness. For the pleasantness of the future life, like the greenness of a little meadow, refreshes the minds of the heavenly [Col. 1173A] citizens by its newness. Nothing there will be old or passing away; rather, it will undoubtedly remain always in the newness of its greenness. It will neither grow in spring nor fail in autumn; it will not be dried by summer heat nor wither in winter cold. For there will be no variation of time where there is always the unchangeableness of eternity.

Hence blessed John says in the Apocalypse that “time shall be no more” (Apoc. 10). Yet what we have said is remarkable: after the resurrection there shall be no time; and unless authority said this, it might perhaps perplex the minds of the simple. “And,” John says, “the angel lifted his hand to heaven and swore by him who lives for ages that time shall be no more” (ibid.). Hence blessed Gregory says (*Morals*, book 4): “The time of our mortality will at some point pass away so completely that it will no longer be, as the angel testifies in sacred speech, saying: ‘By him who lives for ages, time shall be no more.’ For even if the prophet says, ‘Their time shall be for ages’ [Ps. 80], because time fails moment by moment, he called their failure by the name of time, showing that those who are separated from the consolation of the inward vision fail by a failure utterly without end.”

Thus “time” signifies the varied failing of human mutability. The aforesaid greenness will not be watered by an abundance of rain, but by the infusion of dew, because it does not need preaching but the dew of divine contemplation. For where each person will know the One who knows all things, no one will need the instruction of preaching.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Tree of Life in the Midst of the Heavenly Meadow

[Col. 1173C]

In the midst of the heavenly meadow—which we have compared to future pleasantness—the tree of life is placed, so that life may exist in pleasantness. For pleasantness is not happy when life is confined within the bounds of death. But when life is without death, then the pleasantness of life will be happy with life, so that man may hear what the Lord says through the prophet: “I will fill him with length of days, and I will show him my salvation” (Ps. 90). Length of time is the expanse of eternity; the showing of salvation is the vision of the Saviour. This salvation is the tree of life.

There are different trees of life. The tree of life is, first, a material tree which was from the beginning in the midst of paradise. There is also the tree of life, like a certain tree [Col. 1173D] of justice, in the midst of the moral cloister. There is also Christ, the tree of life, in the midst of the Church. But in the midst of the cloister of future blessedness the Wisdom of God the Father is, as it were, the tree of life.

Lest man should touch the fruit of the first tree after sin, before he was cast out of paradise he heard the Lord say: “See lest perhaps he take from the tree of life” (Gen. 3). But the tree of justice, which is the tree of life, is placed in the cloister of the soul so that the virtues of the mind may delight in it. The cloister of the soul is the secret place of contemplation. The tree of justice is planted in the ground of good will, rooted in the depth of humility, grows through desire, spreads its branches, produces through example the fruit of good work, and feeds the hungry person with the sweetness of contemplation.

Of this tree blessed Job says: “A tree has [Col. 1174A] hope: if it is cut down, it grows green again, and its branches bud” (Job 14). Hence blessed Gregory says in the *Morals*: “By the name of tree, at one time the cross, at another a righteous person, and at another the incarnate Wisdom of God are signified.” In the tree of the cross we have hope of salvation. What is said here of the tree is applied to the justice of every human being. For the tree has hope because the righteous person awaits the recompense of future blessedness. “If it is cut down, it grows green again.” Hence blessed Gregory says: “When the righteous person is afflicted in the death of suffering for truth, he is restored in the greenness of eternal life.” And he who here was green through faith, there grows green through hope. “And its branches bud,” because often from the suffering of a righteous person the faithful are multiplied in love for the heavenly homeland and receive the greenness of spiritual life [Col. 1174B] as they rejoice that he acted bravely for God.

Therefore the soul, with its virtues, is satisfied from the fruit of the tree of justice placed in the midst of the moral cloister. There is also the tree of life in the form of Christ’s humanity in the midst of the Church. This tree has hope. For, as was said above, the incarnate Wisdom of God is signified by it. This tree, therefore, has hope because, if it is cut down, it grows green again: since, although Christ could be killed through suffering, by the glory of the resurrection he returned again to the greenness of life. Its branches bud, so that through his resurrection the faithful, multiplied, may grow far and wide. The fruit of this tree is Christ’s flesh and blood. Those who feed themselves on this fruit await without any scruple of doubt the salvation of eternal life.

[Col. 1174C] But the tree of life in the midst of the cloister of future blessedness—that is, the Wisdom of God the Father—was from the beginning of creation the food of angels; whereas the incarnate Wisdom of God became redemption for sinners and salvation for the righteous. Beneath the branches of this tree, that is, beneath the shelter of divine protection, the righteous dwell. They delight in its sight and rejoice in its pleasantness; they are satisfied by the sweetness of its fruit, that is, by contemplation. Its fruit preserves salvation and grants life. Therefore this is the tree of life, because it keeps life unharmed without end.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Silence of the Heavenly Cloister

Some ask whether silence is kept in the heavenly cloister for an hour or continuously. But nothing prevents us from first setting forth something concerning silence which authority teaches and explains to the ignorant. For John says in the Apocalypse: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Apoc. 8). Hence blessed Gregory says: “Bodily solitude does no good if solitude of heart is absent.” For one who lives removed in body but has inserted or entangled himself in the tumults of human intercourse and earthly desires is not in solitude. But if someone is bodily pressed by crowds of people and yet suffers no tumult of worldly cares in his heart, he is not in a city.

Of this inward secrecy it was said: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour.” Heaven, indeed, is the soul of the righteous. For when the soul of the righteous directs itself to eternal and lofty things through the elevation of contemplation, [Col. 1175A] it suppresses the tumults of thoughts rising from low things, and makes within itself a certain silence for God. But because this silence of contemplation and this rest of mind cannot be perfect in this life, silence in heaven is not said to have occurred for a full hour, but “as it were for half an hour,” so that not even the half may be felt completely when “as it were” is added. For as soon as the mind begins to raise itself and be flooded with the light of inward rest, at the return of the movement of thoughts it is confounded by its own dullness and, being confounded, is blinded. This silence, therefore, is properly described as occurring not for a whole but for half an hour, because this contemplation is not brought to completion, however ardently it may be begun.

This authority may also be interpreted otherwise, so that silence of obedience may be attributed to the angels in heaven before the devil’s fall. For the multitude of angels remained silent before [Col. 1175B] the fall as long as it humbly obeyed the will of its Creator. But the devil broke silence, spoke pride, and burst forth into these words: “I will place my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). This silence is said to have remained in heaven for about half an hour because the devil is reported not to have kept it long after his creation.

Likewise, just as Lucifer acted in heaven, so certain brothers behave in the material cloister. They keep the silence of obedience; but, like Lucifer, they shine in nobility of birth and brilliance of learning. Those who ought to have surpassed the other brothers in humility offer the simpler brothers an example of perversity. They wish to appear equal to their masters and draw the simpler brothers to themselves by seductive words. And just as Lucifer fell from heaven like lightning, so each person falls proudly from the height of his order. Inflamed with anger, thundering in words, sending forth threats of lightning-flashes, they depart from the cloister as from heaven and drag others with them. They live among secular people and excuse themselves; they even labour, just as the devil deceives human beings, to render perverse by their persuasion those among whom they live.

They keep the obedience which the devil enjoined upon the first man; they are disobedient to the praise of God and his commandments. Thus beneath the silence of disobedience they live quietly, because they rebuke no one and do not wish to be rebuked by anyone. Of this quiet silence the book of Wisdom says: “When all things kept quiet silence and the night in its course had reached the middle of its way, your almighty Word, leaping from heaven from the royal thrones, [Col. 1175D] sprang as a stern warrior into the midst of the land of destruction” (Wis. 18).

There are three silences. The first silence belonged to the angels in heaven before the devil’s fall; the second belonged to human beings on earth after the fall of the first parent; the third will be in heaven after the resurrection, and will never have an end. The first was for angels alone, the second for human beings alone, the third will be for angels and human beings. The second silence lasted from Adam until Christ. Yet in the meantime the law entered, promised certain things, but at last failed in its promise. Therefore, seeing that no one could be justified through the law, man was silent.

Thus, when all things kept quiet silence—truly all things, because both those before the law and those under the law did so. For the former despaired in petition, while the latter had failed in the promise. Yet it is remarkable that this silence is called quiet when it was held under the devil’s dominion, unless perhaps someone says that he who holds a thing without opposition possesses it quietly. For quiet silence is said to be that which is possessed with no one preventing it.

“And the night in its course had reached the middle of its way.” Night, that is, sin, began from the devil, descended to the first man, and ran actually through each person. “Had reached the middle of its way.” There is a way upward and a way downward: upward to heaven, downward to hell. The middle way is the span of the present life. At that time night held the middle way in its course because it was its own, and no one could ascend to heaven; rather, death drew all alike, righteous and unrighteous, down to hell.

[Col. 1176B] Therefore, when death was dragging everyone down to the lower regions and sin, with every hope removed, had reached its height, the almighty Word, leaping from heaven from the royal thrones, came, broke silence, and showed the way of return by which he had himself come—namely, obedience to the Father. Thus the one who through disobedience had wandered from the way of truth might seek salvation by following Christ in the way of obedience. He did what he taught, because “a stern warrior sprang into the midst of the land of destruction.”

Stern, I say, because: “For the words of your lips I have kept hard ways” (Ps. 16). By the affliction of the flesh and the shedding of blood he conquered the devil and rescued the human race, and this in the midst of the land of destruction. It is called a land of destruction because, through Christ’s passion, the devil is cast out and destroyed from the hearts of the faithful. “For our King has worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73). He was king and had come from royal thrones; when he returned to heaven, he caused those whom he had freed from the devil’s slavery to sit with him in the heavenly places, to reign with him.

Therefore, when humanity reaches that blessed silence of future blessedness, it will have nothing further to ask. Then iniquity will be silent and charity will abound; nothing whatever will be lacking there, where each person will possess within himself the One who possesses all things. Then God will be all in all (1 Cor. 13).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That Angels and the Souls of the Saints Speak to God

[Col. 1176D] Whether anyone may speak in the cloister of future blessedness. Perhaps, brother, you would be pleased to hear what authority says about this. Hence blessed Gregory says (*Morals*, book 2): “It must be known that, when incorporeal nature is said to speak, its speech is by no means formed in one and the same manner.”

For God speaks to angels in one way, angels to God in another, God to the souls of the saints in another, and the souls of the saints to God in another. Since no opposition from bodily nature hinders spiritual nature, God speaks to the holy angels by revealing to their hearts his hidden and invisible things, so that in the contemplation of truth itself they may read whatever they ought to do; and the very joys of contemplation are, as it were, commands of a voice. What is inspired to those who see is spoken, as it were, to those who hear.

Thus, when God infused into their hearts the retributive punishment to be inflicted against human pride, he said: “Come, let us descend and confound their languages” (Gen. 11). To those who cling to him he says, “Come,” because never to diminish from divine contemplation but always to increase in divine contemplation, and never to depart in heart, is to be always coming, as it were, by a stable movement. To them he also says: “Let us descend and confound their languages.” Angels ascend insofar as they behold the Creator; angels descend insofar as they oppress by strict judgment the creature raising itself unlawfully. Therefore God’s saying, “Let us descend and confound their languages,” is to show them in himself what is rightly done and, through the power of inward vision, to inspire their minds by hidden movements with the judgments to be carried out.

But angels also speak to God, as John says in the Apocalypse: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity” (Apoc. 5). For the voice of angels in praise of the Creator is the very admiration of inward contemplation. To be struck with wonder at the miracles of divine power is to have spoken, because the movement of the heart aroused with reverence is a great cry of voice in the ears of the uncircumscribed Spirit. This voice unfolds itself, as it were, through distinct words while it takes shape through innumerable modes of admiration. Therefore God speaks to angels when his inward will is made manifest to them in vision; angels speak to the Lord when, by looking above themselves, they rise into a movement of wonder.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That God Speaks to the Souls of the Saints

[Col. 1177C]

God speaks to the souls of the saints, and the souls of the saints speak to God. Hence it is said in John’s Apocalypse: “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those slain for the word of God; and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?’” (Apoc. 6).

Hence blessed Gregory says: “What is it for souls to utter a petition for vengeance except to desire the day of the final judgment and the resurrection of their dead bodies? Their great cry is indeed their great desire. For each cries the less insofar as he desires the less; and he gives forth the greater voice in [Col. 1177D] the ears of the uncircumscribed Spirit insofar as he pours himself more fully into desire for him.” Therefore the words of souls are their very desires. For if desire were not speech, the prophet would not say: “Your ear has heard the desire of their heart” (Ps. 9).

But how are they said to ask when it is certain that they do not fail to know either God’s will or the things which are to come? They drink from him, therefore, what they thirst for from him. They would disagree with the will of the Creator if they did not ask for what they see him willing; and they would cleave to him less if they called upon one willing to give with a more sluggish desire.

God also speaks to the souls of the saints, as, when they desire the resurrection of their bodies, they are told by the divine answer: “Rest yet a little while, until the number of your fellow servants and your brethren is completed” (Apoc. 6). To say to desiring souls, “Rest yet a little while,” is to breathe into them, amid the burning of desire, the comfort of consolation from foreknowledge itself—so that the voice of souls is what they desire in love, while the speech of the answering God is what confirms them, amid their desires, in the certainty of recompense. Thus his answer that they must wait for the gathering of their brethren is to infuse into their minds a willing patience for delay, so that, while they desire the resurrection of the flesh, they may rejoice in the increase of brethren yet to be gathered.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. That God Will Speak to Human Beings after the Resurrection

On the testimony of authority, I have learned how God is accustomed to speak to angels and to the souls of the saints. [Col. 1178B] Yet I still desire to know how he ought to speak to human beings after the resurrection, so that what I have undertaken to write may not contradict authority.

Hence blessed Gregory says: “When, after the resurrection, the Lord is shown to us in vision, he will then make known to us how he presides over all creatures. Then, the darkness of our mind having been wiped away, he will manifest himself in clear vision, and then will be fulfilled what Truth says in the Gospel: ‘The hour is coming when I shall no longer speak to you in parables, but shall openly announce to you concerning the Father’” (John 16).

For the Son openly announces the Father because, by that which he is—the Word—he enlightens us from the nature of divinity. Thus he declares that he will openly announce the Father when, through the then-revealed vision of his majesty, he shows both how he, who arises from the begetting One, is not unequal to the One who begets him, [Col. 1178C] and how the Spirit, proceeding from them both, is coeternal with both. For then we shall see openly how that which exists by arising from another is not subsequent to the one from whom it arises; how the one who is brought forth by procession is not preceded by those from whom he proceeds. Then we shall see openly how the one is, divisibly, three, and the three are, indivisibly, one.

Therefore, when the Rewarder of works appears in judgment, the words of exhortation will cease; and we, having escaped the straits of the present life and been received also into that contemplation of joys, will no longer have any need to hear the words of teachers.

## CHAPTER XL. What Human Bodies Will Be Like after the Resurrection
[Col. 1178D] When the question is asked what kind of bodies human bodies will have through the resurrection, let not me but blessed Gregory be heard. “Our Redeemer,” he says, “promised us the resurrection which he displayed in himself; and, because the members follow the glory of their head, he will bring it about in us at the end of the world.” But behold, I hear of the resurrection, yet I inquire into the result of that resurrection. For I believe that I shall rise again, but I wish to know in what manner. I must indeed know whether I shall rise in some other body, perhaps subtle or aerial, or in the body in which I die. But if I rise in an aerial body, then I shall no longer be the one who rises. For how can the resurrection be true if the flesh cannot be true? Plain reason therefore suggests that, if there is no true flesh, the resurrection will undoubtedly not be true either. For that cannot rightly be called a resurrection in which that which fell does not rise again. We must therefore believe that our body, in the glory of that resurrection, will by no means be untouchable, subtler than winds or air. It will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but touchable through the truth of its nature. Therefore, in the glory of the heavenly kingdom, the flesh will exist according to nature, but it will not exist according to the desires of suffering; for, with death’s sting overcome, it will reign in eternal incorruption. We therefore believe and confess that after the resurrection our flesh will be both the same and different: the same in nature, different in glory; the same in truth, different in power. It will thus be subtle because incorruptible; it will be touchable because it will not lose the substance [Col. 1179A] of its true nature.

## CHAPTER XLI. In what places the souls of the righteous are before the resurrection.

Since simpler brethren are uncertain in what places souls are before the resurrection, we wish them to be made more certain concerning these matters by the words of divine Scripture. For blessed Gregory says (*Morals*, book VIII): “When, at the death of someone, either a holy or an evil spirit has received the soul departing from the enclosure of the flesh, it will retain it with itself eternally and without any change: so that the soul, once exalted, may not fall into punishment, nor, once sunk in eternal punishments, rise again to the remedy of deliverance. For the mercy of the Redeemer does not after death set free one whom grace before [Col. 1179C] death did not restore to pardon.”

Likewise (book IV): “God’s elect and perfect men, after they depart from their bodies, are not, as the ancient fathers were, delayed by periods of waiting from receiving their heavenly homeland. For as soon as they depart from the bond of flesh, they rest in a heavenly abode.”

But what is said in the fourth book of the *Dialogues*, namely that the souls of the righteous are received into heaven before the restoration of their bodies, we can neither affirm of all the righteous nor deny of all. For there are souls of certain righteous persons which are still delayed from the heavenly kingdom in certain dwelling-places. And what else is indicated by the loss involved in this delay except that they possessed something less than perfect righteousness? Yet it is clearer than light that the souls of the perfectly righteous, as soon as they leave the enclosure of this flesh, are received into heavenly seats. This, moreover, will increase for the righteous themselves on the day of judgment as the recompense of their righteousness: now they will enjoy the blessedness of their souls alone, but afterward also that of their bodies, so that they may rejoice also in that flesh in which they suffered pains and torments for the Lord.

Furthermore, it must be known that, although all baptized infants who die in that infancy must be believed to enter the heavenly kingdom, it must not be believed that all little children—namely, those already able to speak—will enter the heavenly kingdoms; for the entrance to that heavenly kingdom is closed to some by their parents, if they are badly brought up.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the supreme abbot, that is, God Almighty.

[Col. 1180A]

God, Creator of all things, almighty Father, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII), who works all things while at rest and yet is not constrained while intent: he so encompasses outward things that he fills inward things; he so fills inward things that he encompasses outward things; he so governs the heights that he does not forsake the depths; he is so present to the lowly that he does not depart from those above; he so lies hidden in his own form that he is nevertheless known in his operation; he is so known in his work that he cannot be comprehended by the estimation of one who knows him; he is so present that he cannot be seen; he is so incapable of being seen that his very judgments nevertheless bear witness to his presence; he so offers himself to be understood that he nevertheless clouds for us the very ray of understanding himself; and again, he so restrains us in the darkness of ignorance that he nevertheless mingles rays of his brightness with our minds, so that, raised up, the mind may see something, and, struck back, may tremble; and because it cannot see him as he is, it may at some time know him by living.

There are, moreover, certain prelates in the Churches who, though intent upon diverse works, nevertheless work in repose. They fill the inner parts of their house with teaching, but encompass its outer parts with providential care; yet they do not devote themselves to teaching so as to cease from care, nor do they so pursue outward concerns as to grow cold toward spiritual teaching. They govern the heights and yet do not forsake the depths: the former with authority, the latter with humility. For they do not depart from the wise, yet they condescend to simpler brethren. Thus they lie hidden from the brethren in their intention, yet are sometimes known in their activity; thus they are known in their work that they can scarcely be criticized by the judgment of one who knows them. Thus they are sometimes present without being seen, since, though absent in body, they are nevertheless present by watchful oversight. Thus they offer themselves to be understood by others that they can scarcely be understood even by the discerning. Yet they do not so obscure the secret of their mind that they fail, at the time and place they judge appropriate, to disclose it. And because with their whole heart’s affection they cling to the supreme Abbot, while still placed on earth they bear the form of that supreme Abbot. They cannot be turned aside from their purpose, and they compel those beneath them to keep their own purposes. They rebuke others and wish to be rebuked by them. For they desire to have nothing in themselves which they do not display to the eyes of men and to the eyes of the divine majesty.

And because they find written, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V), in order to see God in the future they cleanse the eye of their heart from the dust of earthly vanity. For in the future life God will be seen by those whose mental eyes are purified from vices. Hence blessed Gregory says: “We shall see God himself, who will be the reward of our labor, so that after the darkness of this mortality we may rejoice in the light of divine contemplation. This vision is indeed now begun by faith, but will then be completed in direct sight, when we shall drink at its very source the coeternal Wisdom of God, which we now receive through the mouths of preachers as though through flowing streams.”

I also find written in the book of the *Dialogues* that, just as evil persons will know evil persons in punishment, so good persons will know good persons in the kingdom. In this knowledge, indeed, the fullness of recompense for each party increases: the good rejoice more abundantly when they see those whom they loved rejoicing with them; and the evil, when they are tormented with those whom they loved in this world while despising God, are consumed not only by their own punishment but also by theirs. Yet something more wonderful takes place in the elect: they not only recognize those whom they knew in this world, but recognize as though seen and known good persons whom they had never seen. For since all there behold God in a common brightness, there is nothing they do not know there, where they know him who knows all things. For then, in the enclosure of perfect blessedness, God will preside over angels and human beings, who can lack nothing, because, in the manner of an abbot, the wisdom of God will provide all things for all. There no one will fail in his proper rank, because each will read in the book of divine wisdom, in which the order of nature is written.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the prior, who went before us to labors and leads us to rest.

Just as a wise person is made known by few words, and again, as little said is enough for a wise person when someone reports to him a few things out of many, so, when someone speaks to simple people, he must speak to them more fully and in plainer words.
