For this reason I have extended the treatise at greater length, because I intended to speak to simpler brethren. Yet before I set an end to this work, I shall say in passing something about the founder of our order for simpler brethren.

The founder of our order was sent from the enclosure of the supreme Abbot, namely, from the bosom of God the Father. He came into this world; he put on the habit of humility; he put on the garment of flesh; he called sinners to the enclosure of perfect religious life. He sent grace beforehand, offered mercy, and promised forgiveness. He gathered a community and established its number: namely, the twelve apostles, and many disciples, as it were converts. He built the Church, spread throughout the whole world, and instituted the common life according to the rule established under the holy apostles. As a prior goes before the others to labor and, after labor, brings them back to the rest of the cloister, so Christ, after the labor of this world, will lead his own [Col. 1181D] to rest—after the labor, that is, of worldly tribulation, to the rest of divine contemplation.

The twelve apostles, whom I shall enumerate so that we may at least in some measure follow them, are Peter, Andrew, James, John, Thomas, James, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon, Judas, and Judas Iscariot (Matt. X). Peter is interpreted “acknowledging”; Andrew, “manly”; James, “wrestler”; John, “grace”; Thomas, “twin”; James, “supplanter”; Philip, “mouth of a lamp”; Bartholomew, “son of him who suspends the waters”; Matthew, “given”; Simon, “obedient”; Judas, “praising” or “confessing.”

Those, therefore, who acknowledge God’s goodness like Peter; act manfully like Andrew; wrestle against vices like James, aided by John’s grace; who, like Thomas, even if they sometimes doubt, afterward turn so as to believe; who supplant vices like James; proclaim God with open mouth like Philip; suspend waters like Bartholomew, because they raise from earthly things peoples placed amid the world’s fall; who renounce all they possess and give themselves as Matthew did; obey God as Simon did; and, like Judas, confess their sins and devote themselves to divine praises—such persons do not depart from God. Nor do they, like Judas Iscariot, carry money-bags, change their place, and betray their masters with a kiss while they slander them by plotting against them. Those who are such depart from God.

But those who remain with Christ in tribulations will in the future share in heavenly glory. Those who followed him to labor will follow him [Col. 1182B] to rest. They will be with him in the enclosure of perfect blessedness and will enjoy the sweetness of divine contemplation. Delighting in the flowers of perpetual loveliness, they will read in the book of life. Under the shadow of the tree of life, as under the shadow of divine protection, they will rest: “This is my rest for ever and ever; here will I dwell, for I have chosen it” (Ps. CXXXI).

There I shall see God, my Savior. “For I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God my Savior” (Job VIII). He did not say “Creator,” but “Redeemer.” For he who created all things redeemed us from our captivity by his passion. And he who fell beneath the hands of the ungodly lives in heaven. Therefore on the last day I shall rise, so that in my flesh I, a true human being, may see the true human being, God. “This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom” (ibid.). Hence blessed Gregory says: “We believe that we have nothing more certain than what we hold in our bosom.” Therefore, one held hope laid up in his bosom who confidently relied, with true certainty, upon the hope of resurrection.

“I will praise God in my life” (Ps. CLXV), so that I may be able to praise him in the future life. I shall praise God for the work of human creation; and after the fall of the human race, I shall praise him for the mercy of restoration; I shall praise him also for the good of the future resurrection. But I shall add something further to all this praise. For after the first creation a human being could both sin and die; after restoration, he did not cease to sin and die; but after the resurrection he will cease both to die and to sin. And this praise is above every praise [Col. 1182D], because it will not be impeded by any mischance and will have no end. Therefore God is wonderful in his saints; the God of Israel himself will give strength and power to his people. Blessed be God (Ps. LXVII). In the present he is wonderful in his saints in the working of miracles; in the future, admirable in rewarding the good. In the present he gives his people, still in faith, steadfast strength and the power of patience; but in the future he will give the strength of incorruption and the power of immortality. May God, blessed through all ages, grant this to us. Amen.

[Col. 1181] These are the matters that we have found printed concerning *The Cloister of the Soul* under the name of Master Hugh of Saint Victor, regular canon of Saint Victor at Paris. Yet because they differ somewhat from his style and profession, I would rather agree with the person who judged it to be by Hugh of Folieto. For he passed from the canonical Rule of Saint Augustine to the stricter Rule of Saint Benedict, and thus frequently mentions the institutions of both. In an old copy, however, I read that it was ascribed to Hugh, prior of the canons of Saint Lawrence in the district of Amiens; accordingly, in my judgment, the matter remains undecided.

[Col. 1183]

# ON THE MEDICINE OF THE SOUL, BY HUGH OF FOLIETO, AS IT SEEMS. (G)*

## PROLOGUE. On the twofold healing or medicine, namely that of the soul and that of the body, of which the following little work will treat.

[Col. 1183A]

You ask me, dearest brother, not to omit sending you the things that I had begun to write to John the physician concerning the medicine of the soul. As you say, you believe that they will be useful to many. If carefully considered, they not only preserve souls unharmed but also bestow health upon human bodies. For in brief discourse they teach what benefits or harms body and soul. But I wish your discernment to know that, through negligence, I lost what I had begun to write about the medicine of the soul before it had been copied elsewhere. Yet, dearest friend, I shall take care to send you without delay whatever I can bring back [Col. 1183B] to memory. Do not wonder if I compose, less systematically and as though they were certain excerpts gathered into one, things which I had laboriously sought out and arranged in their proper places.

But perhaps someone will say: “What you are seeking is new; these things are found written in the divine page.” Indeed, precisely because some of these things are found written in the divine page, I left them committed to memory for the edification of cloistered people. For in the Gospel we read of the leper, the paralytic, the fever-stricken person, and many others who are said to have been wonderfully healed by the Lord. Nor do I think that this was done merely for the restoration of bodies, but also for the edification of conduct and the healing of souls. And in certain other books I found some things written about oil, ointment, and eye-salve, which I learned had been understood spiritually by the holy Fathers. Nor was I ashamed to insert the sayings of others into this reading. It remains, therefore, for me to satisfy your request and to render to the petitioner the debt which I have long delayed.

## CHAPTER I. On the human being, who is called a microcosm—that is, a lesser world.

A human being is customarily called by the ancients a *microcosm*, that is, a lesser world, because by likeness he bears the form of the greater world. A great correspondence may be observed between the composition of the human body and the constitution of the world. Thus heaven is compared with the head, air with the breast, sea with the belly, and earth with the lowest part of the body. In heaven God resides, and in the human head the mind holds primacy. In God are three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and in the human head three powers: understanding, reason, and memory. There are also two great lights in heaven, sun and moon; and in the head two eyes, which illuminate the firmament of the face. The sun and moon illuminate day and night and, by their brightness, grant people the light of knowledge concerning things. The eyes, however, receive within themselves images of things by their subtle faculty, and thus, reporting through understanding to reason concerning the things we see, make us certain.

Likewise, in the breast, as in the air, thoughts fly like clouds. At one time there is the brightness of joy, at another the darkness of sadness. There arise there the winds of temptations, which disturb the mind. When the air is divided, there are flashes of anger; the fire of hatred follows, that is, a burning of the mind, which, as often as it descends from on high—namely, from a prelate—harms those subject to it. These storms are at times restrained by rains, at times by snows, at times by hail. For holy exhortation calms some; the gentle soothing of consolation calms others; and the severity of rebuke calms still others.

Moreover, just as waters gather in the sea, so a collection of humors tends to gather in the belly. There the liver produces a flooding of blood; there is an outpouring of bile; and there is also, after the manner of Charybdis, an emission and drawing-in of phlegm in the lung. There is, as it were, the hardening of the spleen like Circe’s. Therefore, in such a disturbance of the sea, that is, a boiling of the belly, there occur certain agitations and expulsions, sometimes through the upper region and sometimes through the lower: the latter by evacuation, the former by vomiting. [Col. 1184C] For just as the sea does not long tolerate within itself anything foul-smelling, so the belly, needing food daily, cleanses itself through the secret passage of nature lest it long retain matter that has putrefied.

Likewise, the extremities of a human being, that is, the feet, are compared with the earth, because they are, like it, of a cold and dry nature. For when the extremities of a sick person grow cold, they announce death, because they approach the earth, whose nature they assume.

## CHAPTER II. On the four elements of the world; the four humors of the human body; and the four seasons of the year as applied to the mind or soul.

There are four elements of the world: fire, air, earth, and water. There are four humors of the human body: blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm. There are, moreover, four seasons of the year: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Fire is hot and dry in nature; air, hot and moist; earth, cold and dry; water, cold and moist. Likewise, blood is hot and moist in nature; yellow bile, hot and dry; black bile, cold and dry; phlegm, cold and moist. So too spring is hot and moist in nature; summer, hot and dry; autumn, cold and dry; winter, cold and moist. Therefore the elements correspond to the humors, and the humors to the seasons.

But the soul too is said, by analogy, to possess its own elements. In place of fire it employs the subtlety of understanding; in place of air, purity of mind; in place of earth, the stability of reason; in place of water, mobility of intellect. In order that the mind may rightly understand faith by means of understanding, discern purely, believe firmly, obey without delay the precepts of faith, and thus, by acting well, live soundly—for “faith without works is dead” (Jas. II)—it is necessary that subtlety be tempered by purity, purity by subtlety, stability by mobility, and mobility by stability.

For as fire seeks the heights and air occupies the middle region, so care must be taken that understanding does not entertain thoughts too lofty, lest it depart from truth through the lightness of subtlety; rather, let it be restrained by purity, which calls it back and says: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think soberly” (Rom. XII). Care must also be taken lest stability be dissolved through mobility, or mobility through stability; rather, “be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (Jas. I).

Likewise, the mind employs four humors: in place of blood, sweetness; in place of yellow bile, bitterness; in place of black bile, sadness; [Col. 1185C] in place of phlegm, composure of mind. For physicians say that sanguine persons are sweet, choleric persons bitter, melancholic persons sad, and phlegmatic persons physically composed. Let there be sweetness in contemplation, bitterness at the remembrance of sin, sadness at its commission, and composure at amendment. It must also be considered lest spiritual sweetness be disturbed by temporal bitterness, or bitterness felt over sin be corrupted by carnal sweetness; lest useful sadness be disturbed by idleness or sloth, or the composed mind be dissolved through unlawful things.

The soul too is said to have its own seasons: in place of summer’s heat it employs charity; in place of winter’s cold, the torpor of temptation; and in place of autumn and spring, temperance and moderation. Therefore be temperate in heart and moderate in action; for the soul that keeps balance lives healthfully.

## CHAPTER III. On phlegm and phlegmatic persons.

I wish, as far as I can, to discuss carefully a few points concerning the four humors of the human body for the edification of the soul, so that differences of character may more easily be recognized from the dispositions of the humors. First, therefore, I shall begin to speak about phlegm, so that I may take the beginning of my discussion from things cold and moist.

Phlegm has its seat in the lung, whose nature is cold and moist. Hence people become slow, forgetful, and sleepy. It imitates the nature of winter, the nature of water, and the nature of decrepit old age. It is purged through the mouth and increases in winter. At this season choleric persons fare better and phlegmatic persons worse; young people better and decrepit people worse. The illness arising from phlegm is most severe, such as a daily fever; the illness arising from bile is less bad, such as a tertian fever. At the same time, it is beneficial to use hot and dry things.

The nature of phlegm can therefore be compared with composure of mind. Phlegm has its seat in the lung, as composure has its seat in discernment. For the composure of mind is assisted by the benefit of discernment. Just as the lung draws in and emits air, so discernment retains what is good and expels what is evil. Phlegm is said to be cold and moist in nature. There is a coldness by which we are refreshed from the heat of vices, and a moisture of compunction by which we are cleansed from the filth of sins. Of the first it is said: “Relieve me, that I may be refreshed before I depart and am no more” (Ps. XXXVIII). [Col. 1186B] Of the second: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch” (Ps. VI).

Hence people become slow, forgetful, and sleepy: slow to do evil; forgetful, so that they forget their people and their father’s house (Ps. XLIV); sleepy, so that in peace they sleep and rest together (Ps. IV). But coldness and moisture are understood in another sense: by coldness, torpor in charity; by moisture, torpor in action. For “because iniquity shall abound, the charity of many shall grow cold” (Matt. XXIV). Thus from corrupted phlegm—that is, from the composure of a corrupted mind—people become slow to do good, forgetful so as to forget the Lord their Creator, and sleepy, so that, if the enemy prevails, they sleep in death.

There is also a condition of mind like water, because it is dangerous through flooding, troubled through waves, and unstable through its motions. It imitates winter storms, for it is assailed by the tempests of temptations. It bears the likeness of decrepit age because the defects and disobedience of the old man, that is, Adam, scarcely depart from the mind. It breathes through the mouth: for the excesses of the mind are purged through the mouth of inward confession. It also increases in winter, when tribulation from temptations multiplies. At this season choleric persons fare better and phlegmatic persons worse; young people better and decrepit people worse. Young and choleric persons are hot and dry; phlegmatic and decrepit persons are cold and moist. Therefore, those who weep for their sins but do not yet burn with the kindled love of heavenly things are not surprisingly called phlegmatic. Their condition of mind is more quickly subject to temptation and corruption.

The most severe illness is that which arises from phlegm, that is, from the mind’s own corruption. For from the mind’s own corruption arises a daily fever, namely the continual burning of the flesh. Again, at this season—that is, in winter—hot and dry things must be used: without doubt, the examples of the elect. For the works of the elect are kindled by the burning of the Holy Spirit. It should be noted that the coldness of this season usually comes from the sun’s excessive remoteness. For then the sun enters Capricorn, which is said to be the lowest sign. Observe the nature of the animal from which the sign takes its name, so that you may derive from it something of moral significance. For the goat bears the likeness of sinners, because, just as a goat stinks from corrupted humor through a continual fever, so the sinner stinks from the habit of sinning. Yet it grazes on high rocks, when the sinner delights in the words and examples of exalted men. Therefore at this season the sun enters Capricorn when the Sun of righteousness illuminates the sinner with the rays of the Holy Spirit. After Capricorn it enters Aquarius, so that it may wash away the stench of the flesh with tears. It ascends also as far as Pisces, the third sign, and reaches the end of winter, so that, as a fish lives beneath waters, the sinner may live in tears.

## CHAPTER IV. On blood and sanguine persons.

After winter’s cold and rains—after, that is, the refreshment and tears of a contrite heart—one comes to the mildness of spring and the serenity of the air, that is, to purity of mind in the newness of conversion. Therefore, after what we have said concerning phlegm, let us turn to what must be said concerning the nature of blood.

Blood has its seat in the liver and is moist and hot in nature; it increases in spring. At this season the illness arising from a quartan fever is bad, while that arising from blood, such as synocha, is most severe. At this season old people fare better and young people worse; the decrepit better and children worse. At this season too cold and dry things should be used.

As we said above, blood is the sweetness of contemplation. It has its seat in the liver as in its source, for in the liver’s heat is the place of fervent digestion; from there blood is sent through the limbs, that it may undergo a third digestion by their heat. The first digestion occurs in the stomach, the second in the liver, the third in all the limbs. Therefore, from the ardor of love as though from the heat of the liver, the sweetness of one contemplating spiritual things flows forth after the manner of blood. It is hot and moist in nature: heat from love, moisture from fear. By this heat and moisture children—that is, those newly converted—grow, and they are compared with spring and air, that is, with newness of life.

It increases in spring. For when someone is newly converted, he is more abundantly delighted by spiritual sweetness. At this season the illness arising from melancholy, such as quartan fever, is bad; that arising from blood, such as synocha, is most severe. For at the beginning of conversion, while the mind of the contemplative delights, if from the abundance of good works—like an inundation of blood—there arises the swelling of pride, then a synocha fever arises, as it were, from corruption of the blood. It may then happen that blood, which is nature’s friend, becomes life’s enemy. For physicians say that synocha fevers are friends of death.

At this season old people fare better and young people worse; the decrepit better and children worse. For from the nature of a similar season the material of illness is increased. But when, in an opposite season, an illness contrary to the season arises, the pain of the contrary illness is mitigated, because opposites are cured by opposites. Therefore in spring cold and dry things should be used. Thus, lest the heat of blood boil up through desire for vainglory, the mind must recall the coldness of temptations and the barrenness of dryness, and avail itself of the benefit of this regimen, so that it may be healthier in spring and the love of praise may not be sought at the beginning of conversion.

Notice also that in spring, through the season’s heat and moisture, the pores of the earth open. Flowers of grasses of diverse colors are produced—that is, virtues of diverse kinds—and it becomes, as it were, our spring in our mind. Hence it is said: “Summer and spring, you formed them” (Ps. LXXIII). By spring understand the newly converted, tempered by gentleness; by summer, those more advanced, burning with the fire of charity. At this season the ascending sun is said to occupy three signs: Aries at the beginning, Taurus in the middle, Gemini at the end. Observe, therefore, in Aries leadership; in Taurus, the yoke; in Gemini, fellowship: the leadership of prelation, the yoke of subjection, the fellowship of cohabitation. Thus you may know how to preside, to be subject, and to live together. Learn also to be simultaneously in fear and labor with love. This, therefore, is spring’s temperance: namely, the gentleness of a newly converted mind.

This season is usually unstable: now rainy because of winter’s proximity, now dry because of summer’s proximity; now cold for the same reason, now hot. Hence people more readily fall ill in March, because human bodies, recently opened by the new heat, are immediately harmed when their former cold suddenly returns. Likewise, the newly converted are usually agitated by the movement of instability; and although their hearts have been opened by the new heat of love, they are nevertheless sometimes corrupted by the sudden cold of an unforeseen suggestion. At one time they are moistened by the flooding of their previous sins, like rain; at another they are dried by desire for heavenly things, like the sun’s ray. Care must be taken lest the illness which had arisen in winter’s cold return in March—that is, at the beginning of conversion—and kill the sick person.

## CHAPTER V. On yellow bile and choleric persons.

It seems fitting to us, dearest friend, after the humor of blood, to discuss yellow bile. Yellow bile has its seat in χολῆ (*cholē*), that is, in the gall. Its nature is hot and dry. Hence people become irascible, ingenious, keen, and volatile. It resembles fire, summer, and hot youth. It is purged through the ears and increases in summer. At this season phlegmatic persons fare better and choleric persons worse; decrepit people better and young people worse. The illness arising from bile is most severe; that arising from phlegm is less bad. At this season, therefore, it is useful to use cold and moist things.

But, as we said above, bitterness must be assigned as the virtue corresponding to yellow bile. For as sweetness is signified in blood, so bitterness is signified in yellow bile, so that you may not only be sweet in spiritual things but may also grow sternly bitter against vices. It is hot and dry: hot with the fervor of good will, dry from the moisture of unstable thought. It makes people irascible against vices, ingenious in destroying the devil’s contrivances, keen so as to think subtly concerning things, and quick so as swiftly to grasp what they hear. It resembles fire, summer, and hot youth, for these are hot and dry in nature. Thus from yellow bile you may have bitterness against sin; from youth, strength against the devil; from fire, the brightness of understanding by which to know God; from summer, the ardor to love one’s neighbor.

It is purged through the ears. For when you gladly hear what you ought to do, you purge through the ears of the heart the excesses of yellow bile. It increases in summer. For the more charity abounds, the more iniquity is held in hatred, because human beings must be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved. At this season phlegmatic persons and old people fare better, while choleric persons and young people fare worse. Old people are phlegmatic; young people are choleric. The former are cold and moist in nature; the latter hot and dry. Therefore old and phlegmatic persons fare better if they fall ill in summer, that is, in the opposite season. For they can be cured more quickly, because opposites suit opposites.

But young and choleric persons fare worse in a similar season if they think thoughts too lofty, if they burn with excessive desire for prelation. Hence at this season the illness arising from bile is most severe, while that arising from phlegm is less bad, because the material of illness is increased by the season’s similar nature. At this season it is useful to use cold and moist things. For amid so great an ardor of charity, one must attend to the coldness of the preceding winter—that is, the falls of sinners—in order to strengthen the good. “If you stand, take heed lest you fall” (I Cor. X). For the higher the step, the more grievous the fall. Therefore temper heat with cold and dryness with moisture; and lest you ever grow too hot, consider Peter’s fall, and consider also his tears.

[Col. 1189C] Peter fell; after his fall, he wept bitterly.

Our fall, like Peter’s, and our tears have been of benefit to us. Use this ointment, therefore; for you are not yet better than Peter. Peter burned with excessive heat when he said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Mark 14). The immensity of that heat was excessive self-confidence born of excessive loving affection. And therefore, because he blazed more fiercely than he ought, he dried up, saying: “I do not know the man” (Matt. 26). It was necessary, therefore, both to temper his dryness and to extinguish the flame of excessive confidence. “Having gone out, he wept bitterly” (ibid.). Peter is interpreted as “acknowledging.” And the response worthy of Delphic Apollo is: Γνῶθι σεαυτόν, “Know yourself.” For if you consider what you were like before conversion, you will at once pour the dew of tears upon your dryness [Col. 1189D] and temper excessive heat by recognizing your fragility.

But in the aforesaid season, that is, in summer, the sun rises as far as Cancer, and there the summer solstice takes place. This is the most excellent way shown to us by the Apostle, of which it is elsewhere said: “Faith, hope, and charity remain; but the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. 13). Therefore, in the perfection of charity there is a solstice, so that we love nothing more than God. Cancer is called a tropical—that is, turning—sign, so that from the love of God you may turn to love of your neighbour. For this is the return from Cancer to Virgo: from fervent love of God as far as chaste love of one’s neighbour.

In the same summer the sun is said to occupy three signs: Cancer at the beginning, Leo in the middle, [Col. 1190A] and Virgo at the end, so that charity may have in Cancer a compassionate turning toward one’s neighbour; in Leo, watchful circumspection; and in Virgo, purity of love. Cancer moves backward. A lion, even while asleep, has open eyes. A virgin is one who still does not know carnal intercourse. Therefore, let the one who turns to love of his neighbour keep watch in this respect: that the neighbour be loved for no other reason than God. It is characteristic of this season to dry up the roots of herbs and trees, when the minds of the faithful are nourished by no moisture of earthly delight.

## CHAPTER VI. On black choler, black bile, and melancholics

It remains now to say something briefly about the nature of black choler. It rules on the [Col. 1190B] left side. It has its seat in the spleen; it is cold and dry; it makes people irascible, fearful, sleepy, and at times wakeful. Its evacuation is through the eyes. It increases in autumn. At this time the sanguine are better off and melancholics worse off; old people are worse off and children better off. The illness that arises from melancholy is the worst; that which arises from blood is less bad. At this time also one must use warm and moist things.

In black choler, as we have said elsewhere, sorrow may be understood: that we should be sorry for the evil things we have done. Yet another kind of sorrow is also said to exist, when the mind is tormented by longing to pass over to God. It rules on the left side because it is subject to vices, which belong to the left side. It has its seat in the spleen because, although it is saddened by the delay of the heavenly homeland, nevertheless it rejoices in the spleen as though in hope. For, as I recall having read, physicians testify that laughter is generated in the spleen. From this proximity, therefore, I think it quite fitting that melancholics sometimes laugh and sometimes weep.

It is cold and dry. Coldness and dryness are sometimes taken in a good sense and sometimes in a bad. Coldness is taken in a bad sense when it is said: “Now winter has passed and gone away” (Song 2), so that in winter’s cold one may understand the torpor of devotion. It is used in a good sense where it is said: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Ps. 65). Thus, after heat and dissolution, we may pass into rest. Fire indeed burns; water dissolves. The adversity of tribulation burns, while the prosperity of a flattering world dissolves. But a vessel hardened by fire does not fear water. After passing through temptation, the Lord will lead us into refreshment of mind.

Likewise, “dry” is understood in two ways. Hence the Psalmist says: “And his hands formed the dry land” (Ps. 164). He calls the land of our heart dry when it has been dried of evil humours. Yet dry may also be understood otherwise: when the aridity of the mind lacks the heavenly dew, that is, the dew of the Holy Spirit. It makes people irascible, according to: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4); fearful, because “Blessed is the man who is always afraid” (Prov. 28); sometimes sleepy and sometimes wakeful—that is, at times burdened with cares, at times watchfully intent upon heavenly [Col. 1191A] desires.

It resembles autumn, the earth, and old age, so that in earth it may imitate the earth’s stability; in old age, follow the gravity of elders; and in autumn, the ripeness of fruits. Its evacuation is through the eyes. For when those vices for which we become sorrowful have been cast out through confession, we are purified through tears. It increases in autumn—that is, in mature understanding. For the more you attend to the maturity of understanding and age, the more the immensity of sorrow over committing sin ought to grow.

At this time sanguine persons are better off and melancholics worse off; old people worse off and children better off. Through blood you had the sweetness of charity; now through black choler, or melancholy, you have sorrow for sins. In spring, the newness of life; in autumn, maturity—so that maturity may be tempered by life’s newness, and life’s newness by the maturity of counsel. Thus may the newly converted person desire to attain the maturity of perfection, and may the old person recall how fervent he was at the beginning of his conversion. If, therefore, in this way you consider ages and humours alternately in spring and autumn, you preserve the natures of both sound in contrary seasons.

At this time one must also use warm and moist things. For it is not enough, for preserving the soul’s health, to be dried of the moisture of pleasures and cooled from the heat of vices, unless you are also bedewed with the dew of heavenly contemplation and at the same time kindled by the love of the Holy Spirit.

In autumn the sun customarily occupies three signs: Libra at the beginning, Scorpio in the middle, and Sagittarius at the end. You know, dearest one, that [Col. 1191C] autumn gathers ripe fruits at its end. You also know that at this time the equinox occurs. Therefore, if you have attained maturity; if you do not refuse of your own accord to be pressed like a cluster of grapes; if you are wine and of good flavour; if you desire to reach the cellar of the highest King, so as to say, “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1), consider the sign of Libra; consider the solstice. For Libra weighs nights and days in an equal balance—that is, good and evil deeds. Scorpio threatens with its tail and stings with its barb. For the sting in the tail is pain at the end. And when you have reached old age, fear, because the danger of death will hang over you.

After the sign of Scorpio, the sun enters Sagittarius. Sagittarius consists of two natures, namely beastly and human. Its upper [Col. 1191D] part resembles a human being, its lower part a wild animal. Those who live rationally are worthy of heaven; those who live bestially are worthy of hell. It holds a bow and shoots an arrow. Now there is a double bow: the bow of the Lord and the bow of the devil. Spiritual people rely upon the former; animal people upon the latter. “For sinners have bent their bow, that they may shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” [in secret places at the blameless] (Ps. 10). For the place and habit of religion conceal some as blameless, and the devil does not cease to harass them with hidden snares. Sinners also have the bow of hidden malice and the string of wickedness. They also have a quiver—that is, a case—in which they carry arrows, namely perverse thoughts, since “sinners have bent their bow; they have prepared [Col. 1192A] their arrows in the quiver” (ibid.). They prepare arrows because the perverse strive for this purpose: to overthrow others. But “the Lord will break the bow and shatter the arrows” (Ps. 45).

The bow of the righteous is spiritual understanding; its string is doctrine; its arrows are words of teaching; its quiver is memory. The Lord has bent this bow and prepared it. The Lord prepares the bow when he explains to us the understanding of sacred Scripture. From this bow are sent “the sharp arrows of the mighty” (Ps. 119); for they wound in such a way that they pierce hearts. “For the Lord knows,” as Augustine says, “how to shoot toward love.” No one shoots more beautifully toward love than one who shoots with the word. For he shoots in order to make one a lover. With this arrow the Bride is wounded: “I am wounded by charity [I languish with love]” (Song 2). [Col. 1192B] Would that I too, struck by this dart, might die to this world.

## CHAPTER VII. On the mixture of the elements

We know that among the four elements of which every body is composed, two are light and two heavy; each has two extremities and one middle. Thus fire has one upper extremity, which is more active, subtler, and lighter; another lower extremity, joined to air, which is less active, less light, and less subtle; and between the two is a mean or tempering. The same is true of air. Likewise, the upper extremity of water, joined to air, is less heavy, less mixed, and less dull; the lower is more so; between the two is a mean or tempering. Likewise with earth.

As in the elements, so also in their qualities one must observe heat, coldness, moisture, and dryness. For mixtures in bodies are made from these. Therefore, when heavy things are mixed with light, hot with cold, moist with dry, all that must come to be comes to be according to the requirements of their diversity. In some light elements predominate; in others, heavy ones. Yet some things are wholly of a fiery nature, such as the stars. In others the upper extremities of the light elements predominate; these are more active and lighter, and thus are borne through the air, as birds are. Among these, those having the upper extremities of the upper extremity of the light elements are more active and lighter, such as the eagle; those having the middle are less so, such as cranes; those having the lower portions are heavier, such as geese and ostriches.

Among those in which the mean of the light elements predominates are creatures not so light, but moderately light, such as the larger quadrupeds. Those having the upper parts of that middle extremity are lighter; those having the middle are less so; those having the lowest parts are slower. In some, however, the lower extremity of the light elements predominates, and they are heavier, such as reptiles. Of these, those that possess the upper parts of that lower extremity of the light elements are more active, such as serpents; those possessing the middle are less so, such as toads; those possessing the lower parts are slower, such as the tortoise.

Among those in which the heavier elements predominate, they are more weighty than those just mentioned. Where the first extremities of the heavy elements predominate, they are less heavy, as fish are. Among these, those possessing the first extremity [Col. 1193A] of the upper extremity of the heavy elements are more active; those possessing the middle of that upper extremity are less so; those possessing its lowest part are slower. Where the middle of the heavy elements predominates, they always adhere to the earth and grow, as trees and herbs do. Of these, those possessing the upper parts of that middle of the heavy elements grow higher, such as pine and fir; those possessing the middle of that middle grow less, such as hazels; those possessing the lower parts grow little, such as shrubs. Where the lower extremity of the heavy elements predominates, they are heaviest, such as stones and metals.

You now see, dearest one, that the diversity of things arises from the mixture of the elements. You also see that stars are wholly of a fiery nature. These should indeed be compared to prelates, because their minds burn with spiritual love and shine with good examples. Of these it is said: “Those who instruct many unto righteousness shall shine like stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. 12). They not only illumine our darkness by the word of preaching, but also keep a higher place before others. For they excel in life and, by acting well, maintain the boundary of uprightness.

There are, however, some prelates of lesser merit who, by the merit of their life, are likened to the eagle. The eagle flies higher than other birds. It urges its young to fly and compels them to look upon the brightness of the sun with unblinking eyes. It nourishes those willing to do this and casts the unwilling from the nest. The eagle flies higher than other birds when the prelate removes himself from earthly desires. It urges its young to fly when it invites those subject to it, by words and examples, to act well. It compels these young to behold the brightness of the sun with unblinking eyes when it draws the minds of disciples to contemplate the brightness of the divine substance. It nourishes those willing to do this because it feeds with the word of teaching those who desire to see God. It casts out the unwilling, for it declares that those who turn their eyes from knowledge of God must be expelled from the kingdom.

Cranes and geese are different orders of subjects, which keep formation in flight and fly in flocks. They signify those who both maintain the uprightness of justice and love assemblies. Cranes have long legs and a long neck: they rise above earthly things and keep silence of mouth. Geese also, which are talkative birds, may be compared to those who, although they live orderly in some respects, nevertheless neglect the virtue of silence. They tear one another with their beaks and cry out together, because by backbiting they wound one another with reproaches and sometimes, from inward feeling, contend in curses.

Between birds and reptiles are the larger quadrupeds, which raise themselves somewhat upward but do not go far from the earth. They serve human uses. They may therefore be assigned to simpler people who, although they long for earthly things, nevertheless render service to those living spiritually.

Where the lower extremity of the light elements prevails, creatures are heavier and reptilian; they crawl on breast and belly because they join themselves, by the will of the heart and the pleasure of the flesh, to inward desires. Those having the upper parts of that extremity of the light elements are more active, such as serpents; those having the middle are less so, such as toads; those having the lower parts are slower, [Col. 1194A] such as the tortoise. These reptiles have light, poison, and a sting. For serpent, toad, and tortoise signify certain varieties of people contained in the world: the serpent, the cunning; the toad, the proud; the tortoise, the slothful. The slothful have the mud of earthly delight; the proud, the poison of envious detraction; the cunning, the sting of piercing invective.

Where the heavier elements predominate, creatures are more weighty than those above mentioned. Yet some are heavy, some heavier, and some heaviest. Fish are heavy; herbs and trees heavier; metals and stones heaviest. Fish lie constantly in water and mud. Herbs and trees cling to the earth by roots. Unless removed from it, stones and metals lie hidden beneath the earth. Like fish in waters are those agitated by the cares of the fluctuating age. Others are like herbs and trees, clinging with all their desires to earthly cupidity as to roots. Stones and metals are the hard and incorrigible hearts of carnal people.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the four faculties serving the human constitution

Natural philosophy teaches that four faculties serve the human constitution: the appetitive, retentive, digestive, and expulsive. For they serve the nutritive faculty, and the nutritive faculty serves generation. For when a child is first born, it must be nourished with milk until, through the growth of time, it can be fed with stronger foods.

Thus a child is nourished with milk whenever one newly converted is instructed concerning Christ’s humility. From that breast, drawn from the bosom of divine mercy, the milk of true humility is given to our tenderness, until we can enjoy that bread of charity; if you strive to eat of it continually, no one will be able to overcome you. For “charity bears all things, endures all things” (1 Cor. 13), so that it preserves the constitution of the mind strong and sound.

There is, however, a difference between the delights of the body and the delights of the heart. When bodily food is not presently available, the body is tormented by a grievous desire and by fleshly appetite. But when it is available and eaten, eating leads through fullness to disgust. Spiritual food is the opposite: when it is not possessed, it becomes cheap; but when it is received by the eater, it is hungered after with a greater desire as it is tasted. Thus, in bodily food appetite produces fullness, and fullness [Col. 1194D] disgust; in spiritual food appetite produces fullness, and fullness produces desire. In bodily food fullness harms and disgust displeases; in spiritual food neither fullness burdens nor desire torments.

Therefore the food of life is the word of teaching. When the aforesaid faculties serve in their proper order, they preserve the condition of the human constitution sound. The mind desires the food of doctrine when it gladly hears the word of preaching; it retains it when what it receives through the ear of the heart lies kept in the belly of memory. It desires, retains, and digests when what had been received and retained it changes into diverse humours—that is, into good morals. Yet it does not merely desire, retain, and digest: it also expels, if it knows how to reject things that do not suit its morals. But if what ought to have been expelled remains within, it brings corruption even to good deeds.

Conversely, there are some who desire no food but disdain them all. Others desire every kind of food, but quickly vomit up what they receive. Others again desire and retain, but have no digestion through the limbs. Still others desire, retain, and digest, but do not expel through nature’s secret passage what ought to have been expelled. Those who do not desire the food of doctrine but disdain it cannot live long. Of them it is said: “Their soul abhorred all food, and they drew near even to the gates of death” (Ps. 106). For those who refuse to hear the word of preaching already hasten toward the entrance [Col. 1195B] of eternal damnation. Those who desire food but do not retain it, casting it from the belly of memory because the stomach of the mind is disturbed, languish long. There are others who desire and retain but do not digest through the limbs, because they do not turn into good actions what the belly of memory retains. Those who do not expel what should have been expelled are those who incorporate into themselves what does not suit their morals. Therefore, when the aforesaid faculties do not serve in their proper order, they alter nature from its state of soundness.

It should also be noted that the four aforesaid faculties draw their powers from the four elements. When the elements are joined in a body that has suitable members, since fire is hot and dry and belongs to the appetitive faculty; earth, cold and dry, to the retentive; air, hot and moist, to the digestive; and water, moist and cold, to the expulsive—it necessarily follows from their nature that fire draws; earth naturally retains what fire draws; air naturally dissolves what earth retains; and water softens what air dissolves.

It must also be considered, as we said above, that by fire is signified the brightness of understanding; by earth, firmness of mind; by air, purity of life; and by water, the mobility of discernment. When understanding, kindled with spiritual ardour, thinks heavenly things, it creates a spiritual appetite in the mind, and desire arises in the human heart so that it eagerly seeks the food of holy exhortation. What appetite draws through understanding, stability of soul keeps firmly. What the soul keeps firmly, purity of mind faithfully orders through good morals. What does not suit its morals, discernment separates, removes, and expels. Thus the mind does not depart from due balance, and by preserving that balance it does not succumb to the sickness of sin.

## CHAPTER IX. On the physician and the nine kinds of signs foretelling good or evil

A physician ought to be like a prophet, so that he may judge not only concerning present things but also concerning past and future things: that he may know the present illness and the occasion of the illness; that he may know what is the matter of the disease or its cause; and finally, from present signs, may know the end of the disease—namely death or health.

There are [Col. 1196A] nine kinds of signs signifying good or evil, which Hippocrates mentions in the *Prognostics* and treats fully in that same book. The first kind is the strength of a patient who easily endures his disease; its opposite is the weakness of a patient unable to bear his disease. The second is the lightness of a patient who moves easily; its opposite is the heaviness of a patient whose motion is sluggish and indolent. The third is an appearance of the limbs like that which he had when healthy—that is, while he was well; its opposite is a distribution of the limbs unlike the appearance he had when healthy. The fourth is soundness of mind and easy appetite; its opposite, disturbance of mind and difficult appetite. The fifth is the goodness of sleep, occurring at a suitable time and helping the patient; its opposite is the badness of sleep, occurring at an unsuitable time and harming the patient. The sixth is ease of breathing; its opposite, constriction of breathing. The seventh is equality of pulse resembling the natural pulse; its opposite, inequality—now large, now small, now strong, now weak. The eighth is strength of faculty at the place of digestion; its opposite, weakness of faculty at the place of digestion. The ninth is praiseworthy evacuation, cleansing through sweat or urine; its opposite, blameworthy evacuation.

As we said above, then, a physician ought to be like a prophet, so that he may judge not only present things but also past and future. Morally understood, the physician is any prelate who, just as a bodily physician cures the sick physically, ought likewise to cure subjects spiritually. For as disease is in the flesh, so sin is in the mind. Therefore the spiritual physician must attend to the matter of sin and to its cause—the occasion from which it proceeds and the end toward which it tends—so that he may destroy the cause, gradually remove the matter, and see whether the sin arose from the person himself or from another. For “evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15). In order to remove the occasion for sinning, he should expel from the fellowship of the good a perverse brother, lest “the contagion spread” and, as blessed Augustine says, “lest he destroy very many by deadly contagion.”

Likewise, the physician must weigh from the sick person’s face the signs of conscience. Hence Hippocrates in the *Prognostics*: “First,” he says, “you shall carefully observe the patient’s face.” According to the significance of his name, Hippocrates is interpreted “ruler of a horse.” *Prognostics* are properly called judgments of future signification, but improperly judgments of the present and future. Hippocrates, therefore, is called ruler of a horse. Physicians believe the horse to be of a balanced nature. Hence it is quiet in peace and prepared for wars, because horses are armed for war (*Aeneid* 3). Yet a horse must be governed by reins. Likewise, the spiritual physician—namely every prelate—must govern the mind of the inner person with the reins of discernment, lest, if it exceeds the measure of equity, it incur the disease of dissipation.

Hence it is said of that highest Physician: “His countenance beheld equity” (Ps. 10). He beholds equity because he loves a balanced mind. He beholds equity because he loves one who remains steadfast in the purpose of good work. For the way of the Lord is equitable. The equity of the way is balance in life. Hence David says: “Give me life in your equity” (Ps. 118). Equity of life is the enlivening of the soul.

## CHAPTER X. On the first kind in particular

The first kind of signs signifying good or evil is the strength of a patient who easily bears his illness, or the weakness of a patient unable to bear it. One becomes ill when tempted; one dies when one despairs. Therefore, although someone may sometimes sin, if he nevertheless remains so strong that he does not cease from good work, this strength of the patient is a sign of good. But if the sick person’s mind is so weak that it ceases from the inclination toward good work, it is a sign of death and future damnation.

## CHAPTER XI. On the second kind

[Col. 1197B]

The second kind is the lightness of a patient who moves easily, or the heaviness of a patient whose movement is sluggish. When the inner person slips after being affected by some temptation, if he is so light that he easily turns back to virtue, hope of recovered health is granted. But if the patient’s heaviness is so great that, being obstinate, he cannot turn from sin, it is a sign of an evil outcome—namely everlasting destruction.

## CHAPTER XII. On the third kind

The third kind is the appearance and disposition of members resembling that of oneself when healthy, or a distribution of members unlike the appearance of oneself when healthy. In the inner person, the appearance of members is the arrangement of morals; in external members, the distribution of actions. A person is then like himself when healthy so long as actions follow the balanced condition of a religious mind. But he is not like himself when healthy when he is altered by works of perversity.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the fourth kind

The fourth kind is soundness of mind and easy appetite, or disturbance of mind and difficult appetite. He is said to be of sound mind who is not alienated from right counsel. He readily desires food who gladly hears the word of life, which is the food of the soul. But one whose mind is troubled and whose appetite is difficult, if he does not desire the word of life, must incur the death of perpetual damnation.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the fifth kind

[Col. 1197D] The fifth kind is the goodness of sleep occurring at a suitable time and helping the patient, or the badness of sleep occurring at an unsuitable time and harming the patient. He sleeps at a suitable time who sleeps at night—that is, who has a tranquil mind in adversity. In this repose he dreams of God, and sleep of this kind helps the patient. But he sleeps at an unsuitable time who sleeps by day—that is, who delights in worldly prosperity. For the more this sleep pleases, the more it harms the patient.

## CHAPTER XV. On the sixth kind

The sixth kind is ease of breathing or constriction of breathing. Ease of breathing—that is, of the inner person—is consoling speech, as when one reproves and corrects a sinner with gentleness. But constriction of breathing is harsh speech, of which it is said: “You shall rule them with severity and with power” (Ezek. 34).

## CHAPTER XVI. On the seventh kind

The seventh kind is equality of pulse resembling the natural pulse, or inequality of pulse—now large, now small, now strong, now weak. The arteries proceed from the heart; equality of pulse in the arteries is uniformity of life proceeding from the affection of the heart. But when the mind is turned in the contrary direction, inequality of mind through diverse movements indicates the danger of death.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the eighth kind

The eighth kind is strength of faculty at the place of digestion, [Col. 1198B] or weakness of faculty at the place of digestion. The first place of digestion is the stomach, the liver the second, and the remaining members the third. When the food of the soul is digested in the stomach of memory through recollection, in the heat of the liver through love, and in the other members through action, then strength of faculty exists at the place of digestion. But if weakness of faculty follows, it is a sign of death.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the ninth kind

The ninth kind is praiseworthy or blameworthy purification through sweat. For just as the pores of flesh are opened in any sick person, so that purification from illness may occur through sweat, so praiseworthy purification of the mind occurs through confession of sin. Moderate sweat is also commended if it is present in all the members. But when [Col. 1198C] sweat flows from the whole body, it indicates the strength of all the members, which is a sign of good. Likewise, the sweat of confession ought to arise from the sin of every action.

But when sweat occurs only in a certain part of the body, for example in the head, this happens because of weakness of the members. Morally, by the sick person we understand the mind; by the head, intention; by the rest of the body, the distribution of ensuing actions; and by sweat, confession. Therefore, when someone praises his own intention and knowingly excuses the evil he has done, the purification of his sweat is considered blameworthy, because the sweat of confession does not open pores that excuse, by obstinacy, holds tightly closed.

## CHAPTER XIX. On headache

[Col. 1198D] “My head hurts,” the child said to his father (4 Kings 4). Since the head is the principal member of a human being, it signifies the principal work of the mind; headache is the desire for worldly happiness. It is called pain because it is sought with labour, possessed with fear, and lost with sorrow. By the child we understand the purity of the soul of every penitent. Thus the child’s head hurts when the purity of the soul repents of the mind’s transgression. But the aforesaid child’s head hurt twice, when purity of soul wept over the pleasure and consent of sin.

“My pain,” David says, “shall return upon my head” (Ps. 7). Headache is likewise the sickness of excessive cupidity. This pain returns to the head [Col. 1199A] when the mind is anxiously tormented by desire for temporal things. “Behold,” he says, “he is in labour with injustice; he conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity” (ibid.). He conceived the pain of evil desire in thought; he labours with injustice by defrauding his brother in speech; by possessing wrongly, he gave birth to iniquity in action.

This pain sometimes arises from heat, sometimes from swelling. Heat is the ardour of excessive cupidity. Therefore, if you are to become healthy, do not fail to remove the matter of the disease. “He has scattered; he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains for age upon age,” and so forth (Ps. 111). One who gives to the poor seeks no repayment of any temporal advantage. Therefore, if by generously giving what you possess you despise the world, you will diminish the appetite of anxious cupidity.

You will not only remove the matter of the disease, but also anoint the head with rose oil; such oil is said to be of a cold nature. Rose oil is the blood of martyrs. When you read the sufferings of the saints, you anoint the head with rose oil. But before pouring in the oil, you must shave the head—that is, cut away superfluities. Thus you both destroy the matter of the disease and check the heat of fevers with the fomentation of cold oil. Flee, therefore, the heat of the flesh; seek the shadow of divine protection. Ask the highest Physician, and say: “Lord, Lord, strength of my salvation, you have overshadowed my head in the day of battle. Do not deliver me over to the sinner according to my desire,” and so forth (Ps. 139).

The repetition of the name arouses the affection of mercy. “Strength of my salvation,” he says. For he gives every person the strength to be saved. For he himself is “a refuge and strength, a helper in tribulations which have found us exceedingly” (Ps. 45). “You have overshadowed my head in the day of battle.” The day of battle is worldly prosperity. It is called a day of battle because in it the flesh fights daily against the spirit, and often one is overcome by the other. The heat of day is the heat of evil desire. Therefore the highest Physician places over the head—that is, the mind—a shadow, namely the enduring endurance of patience, lest excessive heat of evil desire weigh down the mind, lest it make the righteous person conform to the sinner according to his own desire.

Headache also arises from swelling whenever the mind glories in an abundance of good work. Swelling of the head is exaltation of mind. “Those who hate you have lifted up their head” (Ps. 82). The lifting up of the head [Col. 1199D] is pride of mind. “Those who hate you,” he says: those who hate do not obey; but one who loves obeys gladly. Hence the Lord says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14). The performance of a work is an indication of love.

But one must anoint the head with violet oil, so that one may mitigate the heat of swelling. The violet is a lowly herb which, although it springs from the earth, does not rise far above the earth in height. Thus the oil of humility will calm the pride of mind. Take care, however, lest “the oil of the sinner make your head fat” (Ps. 140). The oil of the sinner is the flattery of adulation. This does not destroy the swelling of the head, but increases and nourishes it.

But in order to heal fully the disease of swelling, keep Solomon’s oil with you. For he says: “Let not oil fail from your head” (Ecclus. 9). Hence Gregory says: “Let not oil fail from the head,” that is, let charity not fail from the mind.

## CHAPTER XX. On pain of the crown of the head
His pain shall return upon his own head, and his iniquity shall descend upon his crown (Ps. VII). Above we said that the head of the inner person is the mind; now we may call the crown of the head the mind’s reason. For as the crown of the head divides the hair toward the right and left sides, so the mind’s reason distinguishes good and evil thoughts. Iniquity descends upon a person’s crown when the malice of sin oppresses the reason subject to it. But this weakness of the crown—that is, dizziness of the head—usually occurs in such a way that the head seems to be split into two parts [Col. 1200B]. The head is split into two parts when the mind’s reason is divided among different things. If this weakness befalls anyone, we ought to order the sufferer’s head to be bound with a band or a fillet, that is, with a linen cloth. The head is bound with a band or linen cloth when the mind is bound with a band, that is, with corrective teaching. By this remedy the mind’s reason is brought together into unity. Hence the Psalmist also says: Yet God shall crush the heads of his enemies, the hairy crown of those who walk on in their transgressions (Ps. LXVII). The heads of enemies are the minds of the proud. The hairy crown is the subtle ingenuity of questions in subtle disputation. It is called a hairy crown because, by a certain resemblance, it is morally compared with the fineness of hairs. But when the mind is scattered among diverse questions [Col. 1200C], disputes arise. Yet, as is said, a dispute is badly settled by another dispute. Care must be taken that the help of medicine not be absent from this weakness, for a disease of this kind creeps like a cancer. Hence the Apostle says to Timothy: Avoid profane and vain babblings, for they make much progress toward ungodliness, and their speech creeps like a cancer (II Tim. II). And shortly afterward: Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they generate disputes. But the servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel, but to be gentle toward all (ibid.). Excessive talk commonly harms those suffering pain in the crown. But if you would provide the sick person with a complete remedy, place silence upon his mouth as the best electuary and medicine.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Falling Hair

[Col. 1200D]

Hair arises from a thick and hot vapor, produced from fiery and inflamed humors. As this vapor increases, the hairs also grow, being nourished by it. Whoever loses this vapor loses the hairs as well. Therefore the hair corresponds to the character of the vapor, just as we see herbs becoming sparse or increasing according to the dryness or moisture of the earth. If the vapor is entirely lacking, people lose their hair and become bald. No medicines help them so that their hair may grow again. But if the vapor is not wholly lost, but merely corrupted by some humor, a certain illness arises, called *alopicia* or *alopecia*. This disease is called *alopicia* because foxes—called in Greek ἀλώπεκες, *alopecae*—often suffer from it [Col. 1201A].

As we said above, the mind is the head of the inner person, while the hairs of the head are the mind’s discriminating thoughts. Morally understood, the aforesaid vapor is prudence exercised concerning future matters. For from vapor the hairs that cover the head grow daily; and from prudence proceed discriminating thoughts, which conceal the mind’s secret place. Whoever lacks this vapor will become bald. Likewise, a spirit that has no prudence in its actions appears bald. Discriminating thoughts do not cover its mind; instead, they make what lies hidden within open to those looking from without. No medicines, however, will avail where discriminating thoughts are lacking.

But if the vapor is not wholly lost, but [Col. 1201B] merely corrupted by some humor, and the illness called alopecia arises, the heat of the skin at that spot may reveal from which humor this illness originates. For if it is active, hot, and dry, we do not doubt that it has arisen from red choler. As is read in the *Passionary*, it must be treated with myrobalan—that is, the ointment-bearing nut—violet, wormwood, and similar things. Myrobalan benefits the sight of the eyes. The violet is a lowly herb. Wormwood is exceedingly bitter. These three, together with things like them, assist the prudence of the mind, so that the hairs—that is, discriminating thoughts—may grow and not fall out. For you must diligently examine the disease of sin with the eyes of the heart; confess humbly; repent bitterly. By this medicine you will cause the hairs—that is, provident thoughts—to adhere to the head [Col. 1201C].

For hairs sometimes fall from the head and drop to the earth; and this happens whenever the mind’s thoughts desire earthly things and long for what is earthly. But they adhere to the head whenever they adhere to contemplation of the divine majesty. [Col. 1202A] Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: Your hairs are like flocks of goats that have climbed Mount Gilead (Song IV). By the hairs is understood the subtlety of thought, compared with goats because, like goats, it seeks lofty places; and if it is at any time constrained by temporal necessity, nevertheless it does not fall away in intention from the eternal good.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Pain of the Forehead

“You have acquired the forehead of a harlot; you refused to be ashamed” (Jer. III). The prophet speaks of an adulterous woman, seeming, as it were, to lament and complain concerning her. By her the divine word understands the soul which, desiring to see God, has been accustomed to cover the forehead of chastity with the veil of simplicity. But if the disease of sin comes upon it, it bears an uncovered forehead through shamelessness; and, having formerly lived rightly, once it has cast aside the veil of simplicity, it does not cease to proclaim sin. If a graver fault happens to someone in religious life, that person furnishes an incentive to the worldly. For the higher the rank, the more grievous the fall.

Hence Isaiah says: Be ashamed, O Sidon, says the sea (Isa. XXIII). Thus Gregory: “Often the conduct of religious persons is put to shame by the conduct of worldly persons, when the latter assume deeds beyond their customary condition, while the former do not stir their hearts in accordance with their own rule.” For in Sidon is figured the steadfastness of religious persons, while in the sea is figured the life of worldly people. Thus Sidon is, as it were, brought to shame by the voice of the sea when, by comparison with the life of worldly people, the life of religious persons—who appear fortified and, as it were, steadfast—is condemned [Col. 1202C].

“You refused,” he says, “to be ashamed.” One who refused shame refused repentance. Therefore the blush of the forehead is the shame of the penitent. If anyone desires to be cured of this weakness, it is necessary to apply the plaster of modest shame to the forehead.

[Col. 1201] Here ends the little book *On the Medicine of the Soul*, so far as it has been discovered to survive; for, as is evident from the prologue, its author had intended to treat the spiritual healing of many more diseases and ailments.

[Col. 1201]

# TWO BOOKS ON MARRIAGE

The first concerns avoiding carnal marriages; the second, embracing spiritual marriages. (G)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1201] When I see you, dearest friend, tossed upon the waves of this world, I fear that, either weighed down by the burden of riches or driven by the force of youth, you may encounter the danger of Scylla’s whirlpool. For the love of a woman is a kind of whirlpool of death, like a wave that submerges. A woman’s love binds; but it binds more heavily when it is tightened by the indissoluble knot of marriage. Therefore we cast you the end of a spiritual rope, that you may be drawn out and not held fast by the bond of marriage. The end of the spiritual rope is the word of holy exhortation. By this rope Jeremiah, sunk in the mud of the old cistern, was drawn out and breathed again (Jer. XXXVIII). Jeremiah is drawn out of the cistern and cleansed from the contamination of mud when the sinner, leaving the world through repentance, is absolved from the stain of sin. Jeremiah was drawn by a rope wrapped in old rags; we, however, are drawn by the examples of the ancient Fathers. Hear therefore, my beloved, what are the disadvantages of marriage; and yield assent not only to the warnings of philosophers but also to those of divine teaching, for we shall set forth examples from both.

# BOOK I

[Col. 1203]

## CHAPTER I. An Exhortation to Avoid Carnal Marriage, Based on Theophrastus and Other Philosophers and Orators, Both Latin and Greek

[Col. 1203A]

There is said to be a golden little book of Theophrastus, *On Marriage*, in which he asks whether a wise man should take a wife. Having determined that a wise man should sometimes enter marriage if she is beautiful, well mannered, of honorable parents, and if he himself is healthy and rich, he immediately adds: “But all these qualities rarely concur together in marriages. Therefore a wife should not be taken by a wise man.”

First, philosophical pursuits are impeded; nor can anyone serve books and a wife equally. Many things are necessary for married women’s use: costly garments, gold, jewels, expenditures, maidservants, various furnishings [Col. 1203B], litters; then, through whole nights, complaining laments: “She goes out in public more finely dressed; everyone honors her; but I, poor wretch, am despised in the gathering of women. Why were you looking at the neighbor woman? Why were you speaking with the maidservant? Coming from the forum [printed *de toto*, sic], what did you bring?” We cannot have a friend or companion; a wife suspects that affection for another is hatred of herself. If a most learned teacher is in some city, we can neither leave our wife nor travel there with such a burden. It is difficult to support a poor wife; it is a torment to endure a rich one. Add that there is no choosing a wife: whatever kind comes along, such must be accepted. Whether she is irascible, foolish, ugly, proud, or foul-smelling—whatever her fault—we learn it after marriage.

A horse, an ass, an ox, a dog, and all the cheapest slaves [Col. 1203C], garments and cauldrons, a wooden chair, a cup and an earthenware pitcher, are first inspected and then bought. A wife alone is not displayed, lest she displease before she is taken. Therefore one must always attend to her appearance and praise her beauty, lest, if you look at another woman, she think herself displeasing. She must be called “mistress”; her birthday must be celebrated; one must swear by her health and pray that she may survive; she must be honored, along with her nurse and bearer, her father’s servant and foster-brother, her curled procurator, and the eunuch castrated for long and secure lust—under which names adulteries lie concealed. Whomever she loves, they too must be loved without payment. If you entrust the entire management of the household to her, you must be her servant; but if you reserve anything for your own judgment, she will think that she is not trusted, and she turns to hatred and quarrels [Col. 1203D]. Unless you quickly take precautions, an old woman will prepare poisons.

If you admit goldsmiths, gold dealers [sic], merchants in gems and silken garments, chastity is endangered. If you forbid them, you inflict the wrong of suspicion. But what does vigilant guarding avail, when an unchaste wife cannot be kept, while a chaste one ought not to be? Necessity is indeed an unreliable guardian of chastity; and she alone is truly to be called chaste who had the opportunity to sin but did not wish to do so. Whether a wife is beautiful or ugly, the man who takes her is pressed by disadvantage on either side. For the beautiful woman is quickly loved by others; [Col. 1204A] the ugly quickly becomes desirous. It is hard to guard what many love; it is burdensome to possess what no one thinks worthy of possessing. Yet it is a lesser misery to have an ugly wife than to guard a beautiful one. Nothing is safe when the desires of an entire people sigh after it. One man solicits by beauty, another by talent, another by wit, another by generosity; and so at last that which is attacked from every side is conquered in some way.

But if a wife is taken for management of the household, relief in illness, and escape from solitude, a faithful servant manages things far better—obedient to the master’s authority and complying with his administration—than a wife who thinks herself mistress precisely when she acts against her husband’s will, that is, when she does what pleases her rather than what is commanded. Friends, and household-born servants bound by benefits, can attend a sick man more readily [Col. 1204B] than she who charges us with her tears and sells them in expectation of an inheritance, and who, boasting of anxiety and care, troubles the sick man’s mind with despair. If she herself becomes ill, one must be ill with her and never leave her bed. Or if she is a good and pleasant wife—which nevertheless is rare or nonexistent—when she is giving birth, we are tormented doubly together with one who is in danger.

But a wise person can never be alone. He has with him all good persons who now are and, still more, who once were; and he transfers his free mind wherever he wishes. What he cannot encompass in body, he encompasses in thought. And if he lacks a multitude of people, he speaks with God. He is never less alone than when he is alone. Moreover, to take a wife for the sake of children—lest our name perish, or that we may have supports in old age and use certain heirs—is utterly foolish. For what does it matter to us, as we depart from the world, if another is not called by our name, when even a son does not immediately bear his father’s name, and countless people are called by the same name? And what help for old age is it to nourish in one’s house someone who may perhaps die before you, or be of utterly perverse character, or at least, when you have reached mature old age, think you too slow to die? Setting forth these and similar considerations, what reader does Theophrastus not move toward the tranquil life of continence? For tranquil is the life of continence: it is not disturbed by suspicion of a wife, not troubled by the expenses of maidservants, nor thrown into confusion by the perversity of children. It produces the flower of cleanliness, bears the fruit of purity, and gives forth the fragrance of a good conscience [Col. 1204D]. It wipes away the stains of the flesh, makes the soul pure, and restrains the flow of thoughts.

But if anyone has not experienced the disadvantages of a wife, let him believe one who has. For when Hirtius asked Cicero to marry Terentia’s sister after his divorce, he refused, saying that he could not devote himself equally to a wife and to philosophy. Socrates too is said to have had two wives, Xanthippe and Miron, the niece of Aristides. When they frequently assailed him with abuse, they finally turned their attack against him and, after treating him badly [Col. 1205A], pursued him for a long time as he fled.

But perhaps someone thinks he has provided for harmony if he takes a poor wife. Marcus Cato the Censor had a wife named Paula, low-born, given to wine, unruly, and—what no one could easily believe—proud toward Cato. The Macedonian king Philip, against whom Demosthenes’ *Philippics* were written, was customarily shut out of his bedroom by his angry wife when he entered. What then, my beloved? Are you more learned than Cato? More powerful than King Philip? A proud woman does not submit to a wise man, nor does an angry woman fear a powerful one. Euripides’ tragedies are wholly directed toward reproaches against women; hence Hermione says: “The counsels of wicked women deceived me.”

Herodotus writes [Col. 1205B] that “a woman puts off modesty together with her garment. What she does without a witness, she forgets as though she had not done it. But if a witness is present, by the artifice of her tongue she compels him to confess that he did not see what he saw. What she cannot excuse with words, she excuses with tears.” She flatters with her eyes, seduces with kisses, presses with embraces, and conquers. In a woman, beauty is loved, not soul. Love of beauty enervates manly spirits; since it does not consider to what it has attached itself, it is recognized as devoid of reason.

As I recall having read, Aristotle and Seneca wrote books on marriage in which each condemns love of beauty. “Love of beauty,” they say, “is forgetfulness of reason, a charm very near madness, foul and wholly unfitting for the minds of the wise. It confounds deliberations, breaks lofty and generous spirits [Col. 1205C], drags them from great thoughts down to the lowest, and makes them complaining, irascible, reckless, harshly domineering, slavishly flattering, useless for everything—even, at last, for love itself.” For when it burns insatiably with desire for enjoyment, it wastes much time on suspicions, tears, and complaints; it makes itself hated, and at last becomes hatred itself.

Plato has set forth the whole indictment of love, and Lysias explained all its inconveniences: how one led not by judgment but by frenzy becomes a most burdensome guard over the beauty of wives. Seneca further relates that he knew a well-dressed man who, when going out in public, bound his wife’s breast with a band; he could not do without her presence even for a moment [Col. 1205D]; and husband and wife drank no potion unless it had been drawn through alternating lips. They did other things afterward no less foolish, into which the unthinking force of burning passion burst forth. Jerome says of this same example in *Against Jovinianus*: “The origin indeed of the love was honorable, but its magnitude was shameful.” Yet it makes no difference from what honorable cause anyone goes mad. Hence Sextus says in his *Sentences*: “A husband who loves his own wife too passionately is an adulterer toward her.” For all love of another man’s wife is base; excessive love of one’s own is likewise base. A wise man ought to love his wife with judgment, not passion, so as to govern the impulses of pleasure and not be carried headlong into intercourse. Nothing is more shameful than to love one’s wife as though she were an adulteress.

Certainly those who say that they unite themselves with wives for the sake of household property and the human race, and rear children, [Col. 1206A] should at least imitate cattle: once their wives’ wombs have swollen, they should not destroy their children, nor present themselves to their wives as lovers but as husbands. Wives are commonly taken not to avoid fornication but to fulfill luxury; not for offspring but for money. Thus when Martia, daughter of the younger Cato, was asked why, after losing her husband, she did not marry again, she replied that she could not find a man who wanted her more than he wanted what was hers. By this saying she elegantly showed that wealth is more commonly chosen in wives than chastity, and that many men take wives not with their eyes but with their fingers. The best wife is one whom neither avarice secures nor luxury joins.

Xenophon’s most beautiful book, the *Oeconomicus*, reports, in speaking of civic marriage, that “husband and wife should sweat equally in labor.
