The man should seek outside food and the other necessities of human life; the woman should manage the home and guard the offspring and produce of sheep and other livestock” [Col. 1206B]. But women’s labor afterward changed: those accustomed to work began to rule, and idleness sometimes accompanies domination. Hence Columella, speaking of women’s luxury, says: “They dissolve into luxury and idleness,” so that they do not even deign to undertake the care of wool-working. Garments finished at home are distasteful to them; in perverse desire, those things please them most which are purchased at great cost and with nearly entire estates. They are burdened by the care of farming implements, and say that it is the most degrading occupation to remain a few days at a country estate. For they love the crowds of cities, the applause of streets, the spectacles of the forum, and the conversations of idlers [Col. 1206C]; they delight in attending dances and judge seeing and being seen to be the highest good.

Which, then, dearest friend, pleases you: the woman who pursues idleness, the one who delights in domination, or the one worn out by labor? For luxury follows idleness, pride follows domination, and quarrels follow labor. Therefore whoever loves the companionship of a destructive wife labors and is afflicted by these and similar cares. It remains now, dearest brother, that, having presented the examples of philosophers in explaining a woman’s conduct, we should pass to the testimonies of Holy Scripture.

## CHAPTER II. A Condemnation of Dealings with Women and of Carnal Marriage, with Testimonies from Holy Scripture

Woman is the cause of evil, the beginning of fault, the tinder of sin. For it is written: From woman sin had its beginning [Col. 1206D], and through her we all die (Ecclus. XXV). She is the one who overthrows the righteous, deceives the wise, and defeats the strong. Did not the sight of a woman draw David, a holy man—who did not yield to lion and bear, who crushed the Philistine’s forehead with a stone—into sin? What strength so great profited Samson, or what wisdom so celebrated profited Solomon? For a woman conquered them both.

For just as fire is not satisfied by combustible materials, and avarice is never satisfied with money, so a woman’s ardor never says, “Enough.” A man’s own wife is usually wearisome to him, but another’s is not loved without danger. His own wife overcomes him with words; another softens her speech and seduces the lover’s heart with much flattery of her lips. Thus Solomon says [Col. 1207A]: “That you may be delivered from the strange woman, and from the foreign woman who softens her words. Her house bends toward death, and her paths toward hell. All who enter to her do not return, nor do they attain the paths of life” (Prov. II).

And in the same book it is written: “The lips of a harlot drip honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil. But her end is bitter as wormwood, and her tongue sharp as a two-edged sword. Her feet go down to death, and her steps penetrate to hell. They do not walk upon the path of life; her steps are wandering and untraceable. Therefore now, my son, hear me, and do not depart from the words of my mouth. Keep your way far from her, and do not approach the doors of her house, lest you give your honor to strangers and your years to the cruel, lest strangers be filled with your strength [Col. 1207B], and your labors be in another’s house, and you groan at the last when you have consumed your flesh and your body, and say: ‘Why did I hate discipline, and why did my heart not yield to reproofs? Why did I not hear the voice of those teaching me, nor incline my ear to my instructors?’”

There are two things in a honeycomb: honey and wax. Likewise, in the face of a harlot there are two things: attractiveness and charm—that is, beauty of face and sweetness of speech. Wax kindles fire; honey gives sweetness. Thus a harlot’s beauty inflames the flesh with the fire of lust, while the enticement of her flattering speech overthrows the mind. Honey drips from wax when the harlot softens and sweetens her words. But the bitterness of eternal death accompanies this sweetness. [Col. 1207C] Hence it follows: “Her end is bitter as wormwood, and her tongue sharp as a two-edged sword.” The sword signifies the death of eternal condemnation; wormwood signifies the bitterness of despair.

Guard your soul, therefore, from an evil woman and from the flattering tongue of a foreign woman. Let not your heart desire her beauty; do not be carried away by her gestures, for the price of a prostitute is scarcely one loaf of bread (Prov. VI). A woman loves in order to deceive; she deceives in order to seize. She loves what you have, not what you are. This is she who, as Solomon says, meets the foolish young man in harlot’s attire, prepared to capture souls: talkative and wandering, impatient of rest, unable to keep her feet at home; now outside, now in the streets, now lying in wait by the corners. Having seized the young man, she kisses him and flatters him with a brazen face [Col. 1207D], saying: “I have vowed sacrifices for your welfare; today I have paid my vows. Therefore I came out to meet you, desiring to see you, and I found you. I have woven my bed with cords; I have spread it with embroidered coverings from Egypt. I have sprinkled my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon. Come, let us be intoxicated with breasts and enjoy the embraces we desire until daylight dawns. For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a very long journey. He has taken a bag of money with him. He will return home on the day of the full moon.”

She entangled him with many words and drew him along with the flatteries of her lips. Immediately he follows her like an ox led to slaughter, and like a frolicking, ignorant lamb; he does not know that, foolishly, he is being led into bonds, until an arrow pierces his liver; like a bird hurrying to a snare, unaware that its life is at stake [Col. 1208A]. “Therefore now, my son, hear me and attend to the words of my mouth. Let not your mind be drawn away in her paths, nor be deceived by her ways. For she has brought down many wounded; and all the strongest have been slain by her. Her house is the ways of hell, penetrating the lower regions of death” (Prov. VII).

What is loved in a woman? Perhaps what is customarily loved in any flower. In a flower there is color; in a woman, beauty. But both are short-lived. The rose reddens, lilies are white, the violet imitates dusky purple; yet in winter the rose does not bloom, the lily does not give fragrance, nor does the violet grow. But just as springtime alone clothes itself in the outstanding beauty of flowers, so a woman’s youth alone is colored by the grace of beauty. And as a flower is sometimes burned by frost or withers under hoarfrost, so a woman’s beauty languishes through illness or vanishes in old age [Col. 1208B]. Every woman either will die in youth or become old. If she dies, grief follows if you love her; if you await her old age, no one finds an old woman pleasing. Therefore one should not love what so quickly displeases or is so lightly abandoned.

She who parts the hair of her crown with a golden needle, paints her forehead, colors her face, and adorns her fingers with gems, will become food for worms, food for the serpent. A serpent will coil about her neck; a snake will constrict her breasts. And the more beautiful and tender her flesh has been, the more swiftly it will rot into putrefaction. This she will suffer in the earth. But what will be in hell? Hear Isaiah speaking of the daughters of Zion, who walked with outstretched necks, lifted up by the glances of their eyes, and with measured step: “The Lord,” he says, “will make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion and uncover their hair. The Lord will take away the adornment of footwear, crescents, necklaces, chains, bracelets, mitres, hairbands, anklets, little chains, perfume vessels, cloaks, pins, mirrors, earrings, rings, jewels hanging on the forehead, changes of garments, fine linen, headbands, and veils” (Isa. III) [Col. 1208C]. “And instead of a sweet odor there shall be stench; instead of a belt, a rope; instead of curled hair, baldness; and instead of a breast-band, sackcloth.” Here the worm; there fire. Here decay; there torment without end. Yet there will be the worm of conscience, nourished here by the pleasures of the flesh, which will there stir up the pain of despair. Behold, human being, what you love; behold what you are and what you love. You are ash and dust, yet you are lifted up by the wind of pride.

The nearness of women harms; living with them has drawn many into sin—“their voice,” as blessed Gregory says, “flatters the ears, and their face the eyes.” Woman harmed in paradise; she still harms on earth and draws people down to hell. Therefore it is the wise person’s task to make provision lest she close heaven. Thus it is read in Ecclesiasticus: “Do not dwell among women, for from garments comes the moth, and from woman the iniquity of man” (Ecclus. XLII). Hence Solomon says in Proverbs: “Can a man hide fire in his bosom so that his garments are not burned? Or walk upon coals and his soles not be scorched?” (Prov. VI). Thus one who goes in to his neighbor’s wife shall not be clean when he has touched her.

When Job was sick, suffering the loss of his possessions, grieving anxiously in his heart over the death of his children, [Col. 1209A] afflicted by bodily distress, and scraping his discharge with a potsherd, amid all these things nothing remained that could afflict him more grievously than his mad and perverse wife. For she said to her sick husband: “Do you still remain in your simplicity? Bless God and die” (Job II). As we said, woman harmed in paradise; but, as you hear, she does not cease even upon the dung heap. She was present with Peter in the praetorium, and she spoke with Herod in the palace. In the praetorium she gave Peter occasion for denial; in the palace she dared say to Herod: “Give me on a dish the head of John the Baptist” (Mark VI).

Therefore let dwelling with lion and dragon be more pleasing than living with a wicked woman. For a woman’s wickedness changes her face, blinds her countenance like a bear, and makes her appear as a sack among her neighbors [Col. 1209B]. Her husband groaned, and on hearing of it sighed a little. Turn your face, therefore, away from a woman, especially from an adorned woman; do not look upon another’s beauty. For because of beauty a woman alters her face, and many have perished. This desire burns like fire. Amnon, son of David, burned with love for Tamar his sister and perished (II Kings XIII). Shechem, son of Hamor, burned and perished through love for Dinah, daughter of Jacob (Gen. XXXIV). Thus many who admired another woman’s beauty became reprobate.

Is it not written of her in Proverbs: “A harlot is a deep pit, and a foreign woman a narrow well” (Prov. XXIII)? “She lies in wait on the road like a robber, and she will kill those whom she sees unwary.” Is not the price of a prostitute or harlot [Col. 1209C] scarcely a single loaf of bread? Does not one who supports prostitutes lose his substance? (Prov. VI). Behold two opposites, if you are lustful and avaricious. For lust seeks a lavish giver; avarice, a sparing one (Prov. XXIX). These are the two contrary mistresses of whom Augustine says that they command contrary things. Avarice says, “Keep”; luxury says, “Spend.” You lose if you spend badly; but if you do not spend, you do not obtain what you love.

Cohabitation supplies the nourishment of luxury, provides it strength, and puts fuel beneath the fire. Unless you remove the straw lying beside the fire, the fire does not cease; so lust is not extinguished so long as it is fed by carnal desires. Fire is extinguished in two ways: either by removing the wood or by sprinkling water upon it. Thus the flame of lust, when the incentives of the flesh are removed [Col. 1209D], or when the mind is irrigated by an abundance of tears, is smothered so that it may not harm.

## CHAPTER III. A Friend Is Invited to Compunction of Heart and to the Fountain of Tears, That He May Avoid the Allurements of the Flesh
Come then, dearest friend, to the fountain of compunction, which rises in the valley of humility and flows down through the slopes of the valleys—that is, through the hearts of the humble. Its water extinguishes the flame of lust, tempers the heat of vices, washes away the filth of minds, and quenches the thirst of carnal desires. From this fountain the garden of chastity is watered; by it likewise the nurseries of virtues are moistened. Its moisture nourishes the olive-groves of mercy, produces the rose-beds of martyrdom, the lilies of chastity, and the violets of inviolate virginity, and sends forth the varied flowers of well-ordered youth. Just as this earth, made more fertile by the moisture of waters and the heat of the sun, [Col. 1210A] yields more abundant fruit to its cultivator, so the garden of our soul, when it is suffused with an abundance of tears, when it is warmed by heavenly dew and by the heat of the Holy Spirit, gives increase to the crop of virtues, causes the shoots of righteousness to spring up, multiplies the clusters of grace in the vineyards of charity, and also multiplies the abundance of wine—that is, understanding of the divine word.

For minds situated in the valleys of humility, illuminated by the ray of contemplation, are protected by the heat of the Holy Spirit from the frost of temptation and, by the moisture of inward compunction, are filled with divine understanding. Just as a gently sounding stream, when it strikes against stones, makes little leaps and with a kind of delightful murmur charms the ears of its hearers, so the stream of compunction, when the memory of sins [Col. 1210B] occurs, produces sobs and sounds the sweet murmur of psalms in the ears of the heart. For when the memory of sins occurs, the mind draws sighs from each of them. Thus the leaps of the stream are the sobs of the soul; and the meditation upon psalms is the murmuring water of the flowing stream.

It is sweet to remain beside the banks of this fountain and to behold, as in a mirror, the face of one’s birth (James 1), so that, if any stain is recognized on the face, it may be cleansed with water. It sometimes happens that the fountain of compunction is filled with earth and has no outlets, but, with the channels of its veins blocked, overflows full of pitch and mud. Then the fountain is filled with earth when the mind thinks of nothing but earthly things, as is said in Ezekiel concerning the building seen on the mountain: “And the earth,” he says, “was up to the windows, and the windows [Col. 1210C] were closed above the doors” (Ezek. 41).

By the building the Church is signified; by the windows of the building, the prelates of the Church. The windows are closed because the earth was up to the windows. For Church prelates, intent upon earthly desires, withdraw from those subject to them the light of the word; and this is for the windows to be closed. Thus the fountain of compunction, while it is filled with earth, dries up unless the earth is cast out. But the earth is cast out when, through confession, the mind is absolved from guilt.

Yet when it has newly been cleansed, it is still darkened in three ways. It is darkened by depth, muddied by silt, and stirred by wind. The depth of the fountain is the mind’s habitual persistence in sins through long custom. The silt is carnal delight, because—even though the soul renounces sin—a certain sweetness of pleasure sometimes remains in the flesh through its former habit. [Col. 1210D] It is stirred by wind when the newly converted mind is somewhat moved by the wind of received suggestions. But when the wind ceases, when the silt sinks to the bottom, and when the depth of the fountain is illuminated by the ray of contemplation, then the mind receives tranquility, and what was dark becomes bright.

Therefore the fountain becomes pure, purer, and most pure. It becomes pure through knowledge of oneself; purer through knowledge of the world; most pure through knowledge of God. Knowledge of oneself generates humility; knowledge of the world generates contempt for the world itself; knowledge of God generates the ardor of charity. Knowledge of oneself illuminates the depth; contempt for the world drives away delight; and the ardor of charity calms the movements of the winds—that is, of temptations. Thus, [Col. 1211A] those three things are gathered together: clarity, purity, and tranquility. Clarity is in understanding, purity in conscience, tranquility in conduct.

Let those, then, who sit beside the rivers of Babylon come to the fountain of compunction. But how will they come? By remembering Zion. Hence the Psalmist: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, O Zion” (Ps. 136 [137]). Those who examine the waves of worldly confusion—which is to be upon the rivers of Babylon—if they contemplate heavenly things, are stirred to tears by the desire for them alone. For, in the manner of a river, all worldly things pass away. Riches are lost; honors change; buildings collapse; costly garments are worn out or consumed; friends die—these by the sword, those by old age; these by accident, those by sickness. Beauty vanishes; [Col. 1211B] age slips away; a boy quickly becomes a youth, a youth an old man, an old man decrepit.

Thus worldly things pass away, yet many pursue them. Some sit upon the currents of lust; others are swept away by the torrent of anger; one is drowned by the whirlpool of gluttony; another is swallowed up by the abyss of greed. One is overthrown by the onrush of talkativeness; another delights in the pools of idleness. Idleness is compared to a pool, because, just as a pool nourishes an abundance of fish, so idleness nourishes a multitude of cognitions. These are rivers of death, filled with the clinging mud of vices.

Cry out, then, dearest friend, that you may be drawn from the pit of misery and from the mud of dregs (Ps. 39 [40]); that you may come, drink from the fountains of Israel, and draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Savior (Isa. 12). The fountain of compunction is one of the fountains of the Savior. In this [Col. 1211C] fountain are salvation and healing. Peter drank from this fountain and received salvation. Mary Magdalene came to this fountain and was healed from the sickness of many sins.

The fountains of Israel flow into this fountain. For there are seven fountains of Israel by which the minds of those who see God are watered: that is, there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit—the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord. From the fountain of wisdom proceeds the water of teaching. The Spirit of understanding sends forth the stream of foresight. From the fountain of counsel proceeds the vein of consolation; from the fountain of fortitude, strength for good work. The fountain of knowledge sends forth the groan of sorrow: “For he who adds knowledge adds labor.” The fountain of piety [Col. 1211D] gives forth the flow of compassion; while the stream of fear produces the fruit of confession.

Thus the soul thirsting for God is pierced by fear and is pierced also by love. For when it thinks upon the exile of the present life, or recalls the punishment of hell, it is afflicted with tears and tormented by sighs. But when, consumed by a long anxiety of grief, assurance of pardon arises, or when the mind is delighted by contemplation of heavenly things, then delay in passing to the kingdom is a burden, and the mind is tortured by desire. From these four affections of the soul, as from four streams—two descending from the upper watering-place and two rising from the lower—the fountain of compunction is increased and grows.

This is the land that Caleb gave to his daughter Achsah, sitting on an ass and sighing and saying: “Give [Col. 1212A] me, father, a blessing. You have given me a southern and dry land; join to it a watered land.” And her father gave her the upper watering-place and the lower watering-place (Josh. 15). Achsah represents every faithful soul; the ass, the flesh subject to that soul; the southern land, the ardor of a good mind. The upper and lower watering-places are the two kinds of compunction, fear and love. The groaning of one who sighs signifies the sorrow of repentance.

Therefore, by the upper and lower watering-place are understood fear and love. When we pour forth tears from consideration of present misery or remembrance of the punishment of Gehenna, we direct, as it were, twin aqueducts from the lower watering-place—that is, from fear—to the fountain of compunction. But when the soul casts fear outward and the mind [Col. 1212B] is softened by love; when delay torments the mind and the soul ascends in desire, then, as it were, two streams descend to the fountain of compunction from the upper watering-place—that is, from love.

This is the inheritance of Achsah, daughter of Caleb, son of Jephunneh. Whoever takes her as wife will be enriched with such an inheritance. Caleb is interpreted “heart,” Jephunneh “conversion”; for those who turn toward the heart possess the watering-places of compunction and delight in the southern land—that is, they rule over a good mind burning fervently with the heat of the Holy Spirit.

In these streams the stains of the soul are washed away and the pollutions of the flesh are cleansed. In the lower watering-place the garments of the soul are cleaned of grosser stains; in the upper they become cleaner; but in the southern land they are dried. Fear washes, love cleanses, heat dries. In the lower watering-place is fear; [Col. 1212C] in the upper, love; in the southern land, heat. Fear comes from punishment, love from desire, heat from fire. Sensuality fears; reason delights; the soul is illuminated by the ray of contemplation. In the one, stains are laid aside; in the other, cleanliness is received; in the third, brightness. Fear expels the sins of actions; love eliminates the faults of thoughts. But the fire of meditations dries up the moisture of carnal pleasures. Hence the Psalmist: “And in my meditation fire is kindled” (Ps. 38 [39]).

Something else may also be said by analogy concerning this flooding and cleansing by spiritual waters. Material cloths are customarily washed first in cold water and afterward in warm water, and then laid in the rays of the sun to dry. Water is mixed with ashes and strained, so to speak, [Col. 1212D] through the cloth, lest the ashes pass through; and thus what is washed is more quickly cleaned. When tears of compunction are stirred by love for heavenly desires, the water is, as it were, set near the fire. When carnal frailty is considered, the water is, as it were, mixed with ashes. It is strained through the cloth and the ashes are stirred when, through remembrance of death, the soul considers the disturbance of carnal frailty.

By this lye of compunction the stains of the soul are washed away: namely, the blood of homicide, the poison of envy, the stench of lust, the dust of levity, the smoke of greed, the cloth of a menstruating woman, the filth of pleasure. We have strayed far, dearest friend, and left the road we began, like a traveler who, finding a fountain beside the road, rests his side upon the bank, delights in the flowery grass, marvels at the clear waters, [Col. 1213A] relieves his thirst, cools the heat of the journey, and, having washed his face, washes his hands and feet.

So too, one who finds the fountain of compunction washes the face of the soul, because he adorns the appearance of the mind. He washes also the works of the hands, and the affections of thoughts, [Col. 1214A] by which the mind advances, as with feet, toward the things it desires. It would please us to linger longer beside the streams of this fountain, at least in speech, unless the end of our undertaking pressed upon us.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1213]

### CHAPTER I. On the two wives and the two lives.

[Col. 1213A]

Let us rise, then, and return to our subject. We have shortly before disclosed the disadvantages of carnal marriage; now let us invite our companion to the sweet embraces of spiritual marriage. First, however, I warn him to beware of enjoying an unlawful marriage or taking such a wife as offends the mind of either mother or father.

Isaac had two sons, and each had two wives. [Col. 1213B] Esau took Judith, daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, daughter of Elon of the same people; both offended the mind of Isaac and Rebekah (Gen. 26). But Jacob joined to himself in marriage Laban’s daughters Leah and Rachel (Gen. XXIV). What do these two brothers signify except the two movements in a human being, namely the concupiscence of flesh and spirit? What do Esau’s wives signify except love of one’s own praise and worldly wisdom? What do Jacob’s wives signify except the active and contemplative life?

To this belongs what is said: “Esau became a skillful hunter, but Jacob was a simple man, dwelling at home,” or “in tents” (Gen. 25). The hunter follows the flesh and feeds upon flesh, because carnal desire, pursuing carnal things, is nourished by carnal desires. But the spiritual soul, like Jacob the simple man, dwells in tents because inwardly it delights in meditating on spiritual things.

Esau pursues wild beasts; [Col. 1213C] Jacob, sheep. The one sheds blood; the other gives milk. The one has wool; the other useless hair. The one bears a bow to wound and sets snares to deceive; the other holds a staff of support through consolation and a rod of guidance through correction. Moreover, when Esau perceived that his father would not gladly receive the daughters of Canaan, besides the wives he had previously had he took Mahalath, daughter of Ishmael, son of Abraham, as wife (Gen. 28). Ishmael was the son of the slave-woman Hagar. Hagar signifies the flesh, Ishmael the appetite of the flesh, and Ishmael’s daughter the care of the flesh. Therefore he takes Ishmael’s daughter who makes provision for the flesh in its desires.

Jacob’s wives alone are praised: in one, fruitfulness is commended; in the other, beauty. [Col. 1213D] Yet some are pleased only by Rachel, others only by Leah. For some love the beauty of contemplation, the quiet of silence, the mirror of reading, purity of conscience, and the consolation of devout meditation. They cling to divine charity as if to Rachel’s face; they are bound by the inward vision of the soul as by her delightful embraces. But others are pleased with Leah’s fruitfulness alone. By the word of preaching they beget children; some of these they nourish with the milk of consolation, while others with the food of stronger fare. They necessarily serve in labor, administer household affairs, provide necessities to their brothers, and are like sails or haircloth coverings by which the whole beauty of the tent is protected from wind and rain.

Among us, however, [Col. 1214A] both are taken—that is, Rachel and Leah—lest Leah’s labor become intolerable or Rachel’s repose be held in weariness; rather, at appointed times, they succeed one another. Let labor follow prayer, prayer labor, reading meditation, meditation preaching. Thus Jacob at times went in to Rachel, but was accustomed to go in to Leah more often. [Col. 1214B]

Therefore one must take a wife who does not offend the mind of the supreme Father, who does not disturb the joy of eternal blessedness. For Isaac means “joy” or “laughter.” Again, care must be taken not to take a wife forbidden by the law. For when the people of Israel were going forth from Egypt and conquering the seven nations—that is, the Canaanites and Perizzites with the other five nations—the Lord said: “You shall not make a covenant with them, nor join in marriages; you shall not give your daughter to his son, nor take his son for your son, because she will lead your son astray” (Exod. XXXII).

The moral sense is clear. [Col. 1214C] Those go out from Egypt who renounce the world; those conquer the seven nations and possess their land who free the land of their heart from the dominion of the seven principal vices. Not to make a covenant with them is not to give consent to delight. Not to join in marriages is not to carry out the works of delights. The sons and daughters of the Canaanites are their perverse works and evil suggestions or thoughts. The sons and daughters of the Hebrews are good works and devout thoughts. These two mutually contrary peoples are joined together when a good work consents to a suggestion, or a good thought to a wicked deed.

But a Hebrew son is led astray by a Canaanite daughter when the counsel of a good work is overthrown by a perverse suggestion. Thus Eve’s suggestion changed the counsel of the first parent, offered the apple of pleasure, and led him into the transgression of disobedience. If this is understood spiritually, Eve daily offers the apple to the first parent, because the flesh suggests to the spirit an inclination of the will. For carnal pleasure is compared by analogy to an apple. In an apple are three things: scent, color, and taste; and in pleasure, likewise, three things: favor, honor, and love. The favor of the world is like the scent of the apple; [Col. 1214D] honor is its color; love, its taste.

For just as a sweet scent is drawn in through the nostrils, so the favor of worldly reputation is sought with every desire of the soul. Yet the apple lacks beauty of color if pleasure is deprived of the honor of worldly power. Taste follows scent when the desire for pleasure is fulfilled in deed. The devil shows Eve the color of the apple by suggestion; Eve smells it by delight; Adam consents through love of delight. These things occur daily within us: the devil suggests, the flesh delights, [Col. 1215A] the spirit consents. Therefore a guard must be set, lest sensuality rule rather than submit, and lest the folly of the flesh deprive the soul of the strength of reason.

### CHAPTER II. How a wife already taken is to be kept, or, if she is displeasing, repudiated.

Perhaps, dearest friend, I exhort you in vain not to take a wife, since perhaps you have already taken one. But if you have, see whether she pleases you; take care that she is neither a slave-girl, nor adulteress, nor ugly. For it is written through Moses:

> “If a man takes a wife and has her, and she does not find favor in his eyes because of some ugliness, he shall write her a bill of divorce, give it into her hand, and send her from his house. And when she has gone out and married another husband, and he too hates her, gives her a bill of divorce, and sends her from his house—or if he has died—[Col. 1215B]the former husband will not be able to take her again as wife, because she is defiled and has become abominable before the Lord” (Deut. 24).

Hear, dearest friend, what blessed Gregory says about this example:

> “A man takes a wife when he undertakes the care of an earthly activity. When he has recognized her ugliness, he gives her a bill of divorce and sends her from his house, because often that same earthly activity, which before it was possessed was loved passionately, when it has been possessed reveals its ugliness—namely, when it is seen to be polluted through sin. Therefore the man sends her from his house, so that he may cast her love from his mind. When she has gone out, she takes another husband, because another desires the earthly activity that you abandon; but perhaps it will one day become hateful even to him, [Col. 1215C] so that he may profitably dismiss it.”

It is well said, moreover, “he sends her away, or has certainly died,” because every person will either dismiss earthly care or die: that is, either he will not succumb to it in his soul, or because of it he will utterly perish in the life of the soul. Therefore, whether the husband who follows her sends her away or dies, the former husband cannot take her again as wife, because she is defiled. That is, the one who has once abandoned earthly care and concern for the present life must never return to it; for by his own judgment he has already defiled himself, since he abandoned it in the first place because he recognized it as defiled.

You now have, dearest friend, a suitable ground for separation. For the ground of separation is an occasion of ugliness, of stench. But perhaps the constant presence of stench does not permit one to discern what it is, and especially how much it harms anyone. [Col. 1215D] Nor do noses discern the stench of worldly care unless they have become accustomed to the fragrance of a good odor. But one who is removed from stench, who dwells among the fragrant flowers of virtues and is refreshed by the scent of good works as by spices, who delights in bodily purity and guards purity of heart—such a one perceives the foul cloud of sin and avoids the contaminating stain of superfluity.

Cast out the wife, therefore, and with the wife you will cast out the stench: that is, expel worldly care from the house of the mind. For the spiritual soul and worldly care will not dwell together soundly. Rather, the soul is separated from earthly things when it clings to heavenly things, when inwardly it is suffused with the dew of divine contemplation and enjoys the sweetness of spiritual grace; [Col. 1216A] then it swiftly and easily discerns the most evil odor of sin.

Come then, dearest friend, that you may run as a young man with the maidens and say: “We run after the fragrance of your ointments; the maidens loved you exceedingly” (Song 1). Let us run, then, that we may be anointed. For there are some who do not run because, steeped in the constant presence of excessive stench, they do not perceive the fragrance of virtues. There are others who walk with slow step and thus either scarcely or never arrive. They proceed slowly because they rely upon the steps of lesser virtues.

There are also others who run, [Col. 1216B] of whom there are two kinds: those who run and arrive, and those who, while running, encounter certain persons and converse with them; but while they linger, they forget where they were going. Cornelius ran; Zacchaeus ran; each ran in faith and works. Ananias and Sapphira run, but do not arrive. Those in the world sometimes run in vain, and those in cloisters run as well. The former are sometimes detained by the delights of the world so that they do not leave the world; the latter are recalled by the pleasures of the flesh so that they return to the world. Thus the obstacles of miserable flesh impede the course of good work. Of this course the Apostle says: “You were running well; who hindered you?” (Gal. 5).

The weak run that they may become healthy; for those who delight in the fragrance of ointments are healed by their touch. The fragrance of ointments is the sweetness of virtues; their anointing is the performance of good works. Three kinds of spiritual ointment are said to exist: the first, by which swellings are reduced; the second, by which fractures are made firm; the third, by which pains are drawn out. The ointment of humility cures the swelling of pride. The ointment of consolation restores the injury of a broken mind. By the ointment of confession, the force of inveterate pain is drawn from the innermost parts. [Col. 1216C] But it works more quickly when it is rubbed in by the hand of continual exhortation.

Confession also sometimes bears the likeness of a medicinal drink; for just as the inward parts of the belly are healed by a drink, so the infirm vices of the mind are fought by confession. Contraries, therefore, are healed by contraries, for virtues enter as vices withdraw. This is the running of the maidens, namely the progress of virtues. Therefore let young men and virgins run, old men with the younger (Ps. 148). But whoever loves more runs more swiftly. The bride runs ahead—that is, the perfect soul; [Col. 1216D] the maidens follow—that is, the less perfect.

### CHAPTER III. On spiritual nuptials, their dishes, ornaments, ministers, and consummation.

Whence do they come, and whither do they run? From Egypt to a wedding. To whose wedding? To that of the son of the supreme King. Who are those who come to it? Poor people and prostitutes, fools and the ignoble; yet the Lord of the wedding distributes his gifts among them, dividing to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12). Nor does only the fragrance of ointments draw them: the savor of the dishes does as well. For those dishes taste of God.

There they will hear new songs of love. For the bride sings: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1). There they will see the King in his beauty [Col. 1217A] (Isa. 33), “fairer in form than the sons of men” (Ps. 44 [45]). There they will touch the hem of his garment so that the flow of blood may cease (Matt. 9)—that is, the inconstant pleasure of the flesh. Thus all the senses of the soul perceive something good concerning him. Smell has perceived the fragrance of scent; taste, the sweetness of flavor; sight, the beauty of things; hearing, delightful sounds; touch, pleasant things. But these are sometimes found spiritually in the soul. For the soul smells when it thinks spiritual things, hears when it attends, sees when it understands, tastes when it delights, and touches when it acts.

Thus souls come from Egypt to the wedding when, renouncing the world, [Col. 1217B] they are spiritually joined to God in order to beget the offspring of virtues through the increase of time. They had been poor because they had long lacked heavenly riches; prostitutes because in the house of their mind they had raised a brothel of lustful pleasure; foolish because they had followed worldly wisdom; ignoble because they had served sin. But Christ enriches the poor, exalts the ignoble, makes the prostitute a wife, and makes the foolish wise.

Come then, dearest friend, to see the ministers of the wedding clothed in purple and fine linen, holding flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys, wearing ankle-length tunics, girded with belts, and carrying various dishes. Those clothed in fine linen and holding lilies are the righteous, who have sought bodily purity through great labor. Fine linen grows from the earth and is made of flax. When flax is uprooted, it is thrown into water; when taken out, it is dried in the sun’s rays; once dried, it is beaten with hammers; once broken, it is rubbed by hands; it suffers the divisions of iron so that it may be separated from the awns and tow; [Col. 1217C] it is drawn into thread, made into cloth, and turned to the use of garments. But it is not called fine linen unless fineness and slenderness of thread are joined with whiteness.

The soul of the righteous is clothed in fine linen and works flax when the mind, separated from earthly desires, works good. It is long held under waters and afterward dried by the sun, because after sin it is watered by tears and illuminated by the ray of contemplation. But such a person undergoes the hammer, is rubbed by hands, and is separated from the tow, because he does not fear the tribulation of persecutors but is purified by the constancy of tribulation. When flax is drawn into thread, it is transferred and turned from the left hand to the right, and moistened with saliva. So too the mind, when it is drawn from vices to virtues, is turned toward good by hand and saliva—that is, by the example of good work and the word of exhortation.

Some are clothed in linen but not in fine linen. [Col. 1218A] Those who abandon not only sins of the flesh, which are like coarser threads, but also carefully examine the faults of thoughts, are clothed in fine linen. From these threads the fabric of religious life is woven. They are clothed in an ankle-length tunic and girded with belts. The ankle-length tunic is the perseverance of long-suffering in good works. The belt that girds the loins is chastity, by which the flux of lust is restrained. This is Joseph’s tunic; this is Jonathan’s belt.

Others are clothed in purple, which imitates the color of blood. Christ was the first to dye this purple; Stephen, clothed in it, was the first to minister to Christ. In spiritual nuptials different persons perform different services. Confessors provide water for the washing of hands and kindle lamps. [Col. 1218B] For it is written concerning them: “Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12). For inwardly they burn with the affection of charity, but outwardly they shine through the example of good work. They give water to the hands, for they do not merely weep for their own sins, but also for those of others: this is to give water to the hands, to come to the aid of the liabilities of sins with tears.

The martyrs, however, serve different kinds of flesh: Stephen, flesh stoned; John, flesh fried in oil; Lawrence, flesh roasted by fire; Vincent, flesh sprinkled with salt; Hippolytus, flesh torn apart. John gives a head upon a platter; James presents his own [head] to those who strike him; Dionysius carries his own [head] in his hands; Sabinus, severed hands. [Col. 1218C] Virgins likewise serve tender flesh: Agatha, breasts; Agnes, sides burned; Margaret, flesh cut by rods; Thecla, flesh rescued from flames.

There is heard Mary’s drum, and David strikes the lyre with the singers. After the various dishes of divine Scripture, after the drum of mortified flesh, after the sweet music of the lyre, which signifies harmony of conduct, the soul that seeks to marry Christ enters its chamber—that is, the secrecy of the mind—prepares the bed of conscience, scatters flowers of virtues, and says: “Behold, you are fair, my beloved, and beautiful; our bed is flowering; the beams of our houses are cedar, our ceilings cypress.” If it is ours, then it is common. To whom? To bridegroom and bride: that is, to Christ and to every faithful soul.

But you, dearest friend, cast off worldly anxiety; adorn the chamber of your mind with the flowers of virtues; and make your soul such that the Son of the supreme King may adopt it. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for everlasting ages. Amen.
